## Volume front matter

### Series title page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be surveyed at a glance; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers, and in what places of their works, commented upon the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and one easily preferred to all others if the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, and the low price are taken into account—and especially if one considers this collection, unique, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

### First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Augustine of Hippo

[Column 0009]

## Preface to Volume Seven

After publishing the dogmatic works by which Augustine forms the Church and instructs her in piety, we must next publish his polemical writings, composed with his pen turned against the Church’s enemies in her defense. First among the polemical works there presents itself the great work against the Pagans, the earliest adversaries of the Christian name and, above all others, the most hostile to it. These men always persecuted the worshipers of the one true God, either by open war, by force and cruelty, or at least by hateful accusations.

Everyone understands from reading the ancients—Tertullian, Arnobius, and Cyprian, each of whom in his own time strove through apologetic writings to repel the reproaches of the impious—that this was always the custom of idolaters: whenever some disaster befell the world, they attributed it to the Christian religion. Later, under the Emperor Honorius, when the army of the Goths inflicted the greatest calamity upon Rome, the complaints of the unbelievers revived, and they began to revile the true God with their customary bitterness and insult, attributing the destruction of the City in the most hateful manner to the Christian religion.

Since the laws of the emperors now permitted no one to worship the gods, they loudly proclaimed that Rome, deprived of the tutelary gods to whom its founders had entrusted its protection, had fallen into unavoidable ruin, and that the whole evil had arisen from those Christians themselves who, during the sack of the City, had not escaped the common danger and the injuries of captivity.

Then Augustine, burning with zeal for the house of God, resolved to compose a work against the blasphemers, entitled *The City of God*. In the *Retractations*, which is customarily placed before the work, he himself briefly explains how, through immense labor, he vindicates the Christian religion; more fully, the subject matter of the individual books, which in this edition we present for the first time at the beginning of the volume, makes this clear.

He divides the work chiefly into two parts. The first, comprising the first ten books, answers the Pagans and removes from their minds their ancient opinions about the worship of the gods—worship which some argued to be useful for this life, and others for the life to come. The second explains the origin, course, and final end or appointed destinies of both Cities, the earthly and the divine, in which all of us—angels and human beings—are included in one way or the other.

He composed this work of the greatest importance with the greatest care, in proportion to the excellence and dignity of its subject, and as was fitting for a man endowed with supreme genius and adorned with knowledge of every kind. For it is astonishing to say how great is the variety of subjects here, how abundant the learning, how skillful and refined the method of argument. It is as though the energetic defender of the City of God wished nothing to be lacking in these books—neither art and industry, nor sacred or secular learning. Indeed, all learned disputants who thereafter undertook the defense of divine religion against the impious considered that they should seek assistance and resources from these books, as from a most richly stocked treasury.

Macedonius, the vicar of Africa, had seen no more than the first three books of this work when, amazed with admiration, he wrote back to Augustine:

“I am affected in an extraordinary way by your wisdom, and so forth. For those works of yours which you have published possess such acuteness, knowledge, and holiness that nothing could surpass them.”

A little later, concerning the same books, he says:

“I have unfolded your books; for they were not so languid or inert as to allow me to care about anything other than themselves. They laid hold of me, seized me away from other causes of anxiety, and bound me in their chains. So may God be favorable to me: I am uncertain what I should admire more in them—the perfection of priesthood, the doctrines of philosophy, the full knowledge of history, or the charm of their eloquence, which can entice even the unlearned, so that they do not stop until they have unfolded them, and, once they have unfolded them, still seek further. For the shamelessly obstinate have been refuted,” and so forth. (*Letter* 154, §§1–2.)

Paulus Orosius, in the preface to the books of his *Histories*, which he completed at Augustine’s urging, praises Augustine for persisting in completing the eleventh book against the Pagans:

“Of these,” he says, “ten rays, as soon as they rose aloft from the watchtower of ecclesiastical clarity, shone throughout the whole world.”

Cassiodorus Senator, in the sixteenth chapter of his *Institutions*, orders that we “read through the books *On the City of God* with tireless devotion.”

Nor should the Frankish kings be passed over here: Charlemagne, who, according to Einhard, “took delight in the books of Saint Augustine, and especially in those entitled *The City of God*.” Concerning him the Saxon poet says in the fifth book of his *Annals*:

> Those which Augustine wrote concerning the blessed citizens of heaven,  
> He had often heard with loving attention.

Likewise Charles V, surnamed the Wise, who, because these same books had been translated into French and dedicated to him, raised and honored the author of the translation with the highest dignity.

We owe this outstanding work to the efforts of Marcellinus. Although Augustine was sufficiently moved to write by his love for the heavenly City, he was also prompted by Marcellinus, whose request on this matter appears in a letter to Augustine:

“I beg you to compose books concerning all these matters … which at this particular time will be of incredible benefit to the Church.” (*Letter* 136, §3.)

In his reply Augustine initially indicates that he would prefer to discuss these matters “not in the form of a book, but in an exchange of letters, if that can be sufficient.” [Column 0011] Later, however, after resolving the Pagans’ questions there, he promises to answer everything that might be brought against them, “either in letters or in books.” (*Letter* 137, §§1, 20.)

He wrote this letter to Marcellinus, in which he leaves open the question whether he should publish “either letters or books” against the Pagans, in the year of Christ 412. We must therefore depart from Baronius’s opinion, according to which these books were begun in 411 because they arose on the occasion of the Roman disaster that occurred in 410.

We consequently do not think they were begun until shortly before the murder of Marcellinus, which we observe to have taken place in September of 413, according to the letter to Caecilianus (*Letter* 151, §6, note a). For from the beginning of the second book onward, the discourse is never again addressed to Marcellinus himself, although all the books are dedicated to him.

In a letter to Evodius written toward the end of 415, the holy Doctor mentions that he had added the fourth and fifth books to three others (*Letter* 169, §1); these two were begun and completed in that same year, 415. He was writing the eleventh book, after the previous ten had already been published, around the year 416, as Orosius testifies in the preface to his *History*, begun at approximately that time.

Augustine himself mentions the fourteenth book in the first book of *Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, which he published around the year 420. Finally, the *Retractations* prove that this immense work, which Augustine says occupied him for several years, was completed not long after the end of 426. In the second book, chapter forty-one, which was certainly completed in 426 or 427, the final book of *The City of God* is cited.

Nor should one here refer to what we note on this matter at chapter eight of the twenty-second book, or at the end of the eighteenth book, where the opinion of Baronius and Coquaeus is examined—namely, that the later books of *The City of God* were not written before the year 429.

There is no need to say anything about our own labor. Certainly we do not regret having examined and read through so many copies, whose list is given below. For we learned, not only from the admonition of scholars but also from our own use and experience, that these books, because of their more recondite learning and the Greek and Roman antiquities scattered throughout them, require comparison with ancient codices more than most works do.

The division of the chapters together with their summaries, which some wished to reject, is found in codices written nine hundred years ago. It is in fact worthy of belief that this division was added to Augustine’s works, either by his order or for the assistance of readers, but after the work had been completed, as had formerly been done in the Sacred Books.

Finally, concerning the commentaries on this work—which, persuaded by the advice and authority of prudent and learned men, we have passed over—we examined them carefully and took care to transfer here the more illuminating observations excerpted from them for difficult passages.

[Column 0011]

## List of the codices according to which Augustine’s work *The City of God* was newly reviewed

[Note: In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1, and also several manuscript codices, among which the following deserve particular notice:

The Corbie codex, numbered among the German codices as 766 in the Royal Library at Paris, written in uncial letters that display marks of great antiquity and apparently belonging to the seventh century. It contains only nine books, but includes the summaries of ten books.

The parchment codices numbered 2050, 2051, and 2052 are assigned to the tenth century and comprise all twenty-two books. Codex 2050 is by far the worst of them, and 2051 the best.

Another parchment codex of the same century, numbered 2053, is of good quality but contains only ten books.

Another Corbie parchment codex, in the German Library where it is preserved, is designated as number 258. It also belongs to the tenth century and contains all twenty-two books, written out with the greatest accuracy. It must be numbered among the most approved.

The former Corbie codex, now German, a parchment manuscript numbered 253, contains twelve books, from the eleventh through the twenty-second. It is assigned to the eleventh century and is not to be despised. M.]

### Manuscript codices used by the Benedictine Fathers

Five codices from the Roman Library of the Vatican; two from the Royal Library at Paris; three from the Colbert Library; one from the Navarre College; one from the Gervasian College; one belonging to Anthony Faure, doctor of theology of the University of Paris; two from the German Abbey; one from the Church of Reims; one from the Church of Beauvais; one from the Church of Senlis; one from the Abbey of Blessed Mary at Soissons; one from the Abbey of Saint Vincent at Laon; one from the Abbey of Saint Ouen at Rouen; one belonging to Emeric Bigot; one from the monastery of Jumièges; one from the monastery of Bec; one from the monastery of Lérins; [Column 0012] one from Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea; two from the Cistercian Abbey; one from the Abbey of Cygirannus; two from the Abbey of Corbie; one from the Abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims; one from the Abbey of Saint-Aubin at Angers; one from the Abbey of Vendôme; and, finally, seven Belgian codices, or rather variant readings collected from them through the work of the Louvain theologians.

### Published codices

**Vind.** That is, the codex printed by Vindelinus at Venice in 1470.

**Am.** The book printed through the efforts of Johann Amerbach at Basel in 1490.

**Er.** Produced from the Frobenian press at Basel in 1529 under the direction of Desiderius Erasmus.

**Lov.** The volume printed by Christopher Plantin at Antwerp in 1576 according to the recension of the Louvain theologians.

# Twenty-two books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, to Marcellinus, on *The City of God against the Pagans*

[Note: Begun around the year 413 and not completed before the year 426.]

[Note: See *The City of God*, book 2, chapter 43 of the *Retractations*, column 647, from the words “Meanwhile Rome” through column 648, ending with the words “the most glorious City of God.” M.] (C, S)

## Book One

He rebukes the Pagans who attributed the calamities of the world, and especially the recent devastation of the city of Rome by the Goths, to the Christian religion, which prohibits the worship of the gods. He discusses the advantages and disadvantages that, as usual, were then shared by the good and the wicked. Finally, he checks the insolence of those who alleged that Christian women’s chastity had been violated by soldiers.

## Preface: On the purpose and subject of the work undertaken

I have undertaken, dearest son Marcellinus, to defend the most glorious City of God—whether in this present course of time, while it lives by faith as a pilgrim among the ungodly (Habakkuk 2:4), or in that stability of its eternal seat which it now awaits in patience (Romans 8:25), until justice is turned into judgment (Psalm 93:15), and which it will thereafter obtain through an incomparable final victory and perfect peace—in this work which you have undertaken and which I owe to my promise, against those who prefer their own gods to its Founder.

[Note: The editions Vind., Er., and Lov. read “the work undertaken for you.” Amerbach’s edition, however—that is, the Amerbach edition—and several manuscripts of good quality read “the work undertaken by you.” For the work had been proposed by Marcellinus in *Letter* 136 among Augustine’s letters, §3, and promised to him by Augustine in *Letter* 138, §20, as we have just noted in the preface to this volume. Some of the aforementioned codices continue: “and which I owe to my promise to you.”]

It is a great and difficult work; but God is our helper (Psalm 61:9). For I know what strength is needed to persuade the proud how great is the power of humility, by which all earthly heights—wavering with temporal change, not seized through human arrogance but bestowed by divine grace—are surpassed.

For the King and Founder of this City, of which we have begun to speak, disclosed to his peoples in Scripture the judgment of the divine law, in which it is said: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5).

Yet the inflated spirit of the proud soul also desires what belongs to God, and loves to have this said of itself in praise:

> To spare the conquered and subdue the proud.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.854.)

Therefore, concerning the earthly city also—which, when it seeks to rule, is itself ruled by the desire to rule, even though peoples serve it—we must not pass over in silence whatever the plan and ability of this undertaking require us to say.

## Chapter One: On the adversaries of the name of Christ, whom the Barbarians spared during the devastation of the City because of Christ

[Note: The printed editions add “after they had been defeated.” This word is absent from the manuscripts.]

For from this group come the enemies against whom the City of God must be defended. Yet many of them, having corrected the error of their impiety, become quite suitable citizens of that City. Many others, however, blaze against it with such fires of hatred and are so ungrateful for the evident benefits of its Redeemer that they would not now move their tongues against it if, while fleeing the hostile sword, they had not found in its sacred places the life of which they are proud.

Are not those Romans themselves hostile to the name of Christ whom the Barbarians spared because of Christ? The places of the martyrs and the basilicas of the Apostles bear witness to this: during that devastation of the City they received within themselves those who fled to them, both their own people and strangers.

[Note: Orosius, book 7, chapter 39, writes that after capturing the City Alaric gave his men this order: “If anyone should have fled to the holy places, and especially to the basilicas of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, they were to allow such persons above all to remain unharmed and secure.”]

Up to that point the bloodthirsty enemy raged; there the fury of the slaughterer reached its limit. To that place were led by merciful enemies those whom they had spared even outside those very places, lest they fall into the hands of men who possessed no such mercy.

[Note: Marcella and her daughter Principia experienced this humanity of the Barbarians. They were found in their own house and led to the basilica of Saint Paul, as Jerome testifies in his *Letter* 154 to Principia. Sozomen likewise tells of another woman who was led by a soldier to the basilica of Saint Peter, so that her chastity might be spared, in book 9, chapter 10.]

Yet the same men, elsewhere savage and raging in the manner of enemies, once they came to those places where what would elsewhere have been permitted by the law of war had been forbidden, restrained all their ferocity in striking and broke the desire to take captives.

Thus many escaped who now disparage Christian times and attribute to Christ the evils that city suffered. But the benefits bestowed upon them, so that they might live, for the honor of Christ, they do not attribute to our Christ but to their own fortune. Rather, if they possessed any sound judgment, they ought to attribute to that divine providence which customarily corrects and crushes the corrupt morals of human beings through wars the harsh and severe things they suffered from their enemies.

That same providence also trains a just and praiseworthy mortal life through such afflictions and, once it has been tested, either transfers it to better things or keeps it still in these lands for other purposes. But the fact that the savage Barbarians spared them—either wherever they were, because of the name of Christ, or in places most devoted and most extensively dedicated to Christ’s name, chosen in their greater mercy to accommodate the multitude—contrary to the customs of war, this they ought to attribute to Christian times.

From this they ought to give thanks to God; from this they ought truthfully to hasten to his name, so that they may escape the punishments of eternal fire. Many of them falsely invoked that name in order to escape the punishments of present destruction.

For among those whom you see insolently and arrogantly mocking Christ’s servants, there are many who would not have escaped that death and disaster unless they had pretended to be Christ’s servants. Even now, with ungrateful pride and most impious madness, they resist his name with a perverse heart, so that they may be punished in everlasting darkness—the name to which they fled with their mouths, even deceitfully, in order to enjoy temporal light.

## Chapter Two: That no wars were ever conducted in such a way that the victors spared the conquered because of the gods whom the conquered worshiped

So many wars have been waged and recorded, either before Rome was founded or from its origin and imperial rule onward. Let them read and produce some instance in which a city was captured by foreigners in such a way that the enemies who captured it spared those whom they discovered to have fled to the temples of their gods. Or let them produce a barbarian commander who ordered that, once a town had been broken into, no one should be struck who had been found in this or that temple.

Did Aeneas not see Priam

> staining with blood before the altars  
> The fires which he himself had consecrated?  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.501–502.)

Did Diomedes and Ulysses not,

> Having slain the guards of the citadel’s summit,  
> Seize the sacred image, and with bloodstained hands  
> Dare to touch the virgin fillets of the goddess?

Yet what follows is not true:

> From that moment the hope of the Greeks began to flow away  
> And, slipping backward, to retreat.  
> (Ibid. 2.166–170.)

For afterward they conquered; afterward they destroyed Troy with sword and fire; afterward they slaughtered Priam, who had fled to the altars.

Nor did Troy perish because it lost Minerva. What, then, had Minerva herself lost earlier, so that Troy should perish? Perhaps her guardians? This much is certainly true: once they had been killed, she could be carried away. For it was not human beings who were protected by the image, but the image that was protected by human beings.

How, then, could an image be worshiped as the guardian of the homeland and its citizens when it could not protect its own guardians?

## Chapter Three: How imprudently the Romans trusted that the household gods who had been unable to protect Troy would be of benefit to them

Look at the sort of gods to whom the Romans rejoiced that they had entrusted the City for protection.

O most pitiable error! They are angry with us when we say such things about their gods, yet they are not angry with their own authors, whom they paid to study them, and whom they additionally considered worthy of public salaries and honors as teachers.

Indeed, in Virgil—whom little children read so that the great, most illustrious, and best of poets, once absorbed by their tender minds, may not easily be erased by forgetfulness—according to Horace:

> The fresh jar will long preserve the scent  
> With which it was once steeped.  
> (*Epistles* 1.2.69–70.)

In this Virgil, then, Juno is introduced as hostile to the Trojans, provoking Aeolus, king of the winds, against them, and saying:

> A race hostile to me sails across the Tyrrhenian sea,  
> Carrying Ilium into Italy and its conquered household gods.  
> (*Aeneid* 1.71–72.)

Were prudent men, then, to entrust Rome to these conquered household gods so that it might not be conquered? But Juno spoke thus like an angry woman who did not know what she was saying.

What of Aeneas himself, so often called pious? Does he not tell the story in this way?

> Panthus, son of Othryas, priest of Phoebus and of the citadel,  
> Himself drags the sacred objects, the conquered gods, and his little grandson,  
> And, crazed with fear, hastens toward the threshold.  
> (*Aeneid* 2.319–321.)

Does he not say that the gods themselves, whom he does not hesitate to call conquered, were entrusted to him rather than that he was entrusted to them, when he is told:

> Troy entrusts to you her sacred objects and her household gods.  
> (Ibid. 2.293.)

If Virgil therefore says that such gods were both conquered and entrusted to a human being so that they might somehow escape even in defeat, what madness is it to think that Rome had wisely been entrusted to these guardians and could not have been devastated unless it had lost them?

Indeed, to worship conquered gods as guardians and defenders—what is this other than to hold not good divinities but evil omens?

[Note: The printed editions read “but evil demons.” The manuscripts of better quality read “but evil omens,” that is, signs of the destruction and disaster to come. Codex 766 reads “evil names.”]

For it is far more reasonable to believe not that Rome would never have come to this disaster had those gods not previously perished, but rather that those gods would have perished long ago had Rome not preserved them as far as it could.

Who, when he considers the matter, does not see how vain it was to assume that a city could not be conquered under the protection of conquered guardians, and that it perished because it lost its divine guardians, when the very fact that it wished to have guardians who were destined to perish could by itself have been a cause of its destruction?

Therefore, when poets wrote and sang these things about conquered gods, it did not please them to lie; rather, truth compelled sensible men to confess them.

[Note: Lov. reads “to the poets.” The other books read “the poets,” in the accusative, a case that Augustine often joins to the verb “it pleases.” Thus in book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 25: “saying in me rather whatever pleased him.”]

But these matters must be treated more suitably, carefully, and fully elsewhere. For now, let me explain as best I can what I had begun to say about ungrateful people: they blasphemously attribute to Christ the evils that they deservedly suffer because of the perversity of their morals. Yet they do not even deign to consider that, although they are such people, they are spared because of Christ. In the madness of sacrilegious insolence, they exercise against his name the very tongues with which they falsely invoked that name in order to live, or which they restrained in fear at places consecrated to him, so that, having been kept safe and protected there, where they were unharmed by the enemy because of him, they might from that place leap forth against him with hostile curses.

[Note: Vind., Am., and most manuscripts read “of perversity.” Codex 766 has the same reading.]

## Chapter Four: Concerning Juno’s asylum in Troy, which saved no one from the Greeks, and the basilicas of the Apostles, which defended all who fled to them from the Barbarians

Troy itself, as I said, the mother of the Roman people,

[Note: Sallust, chapter 6 of *The Conspiracy of Catiline*: “The city of Rome, as I have learned, was founded and first inhabited by Trojans who, under the leadership of Aeneas, refugees wandering in uncertain settlements …”]

could not, by fortifying its citizens in the sacred places of its gods, protect them from the fire and sword of the Greeks, who worshiped those very same gods. Indeed:

> In Juno’s asylum,  
> Phoenix and savage Ulysses, chosen as guards,  
> Were preserving the plunder; here the treasure of Troy,  
> Snatched from the burning shrines, tables of the gods,  
> Solid-gold mixing bowls, and captive garments  
> Were heaped together. Boys and frightened mothers  
> Stood around in a long line.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.761–767.)

The place sacred to so great a goddess had evidently been chosen not as a place from which captives could not be led out, but as a place in which captives could be shut up.

Now compare that asylum—not of some common god or one of the crowd of the plebs, but of Jove’s own sister, wife, and queen of all the gods—with the memorial shrines of our Apostles.

To Juno’s asylum were carried the spoils snatched from burning temples and from the gods, not to be returned to the conquered but to be divided among the victors. To the Apostles’ shrines, however, whatever was discovered elsewhere to belong to those places was brought back with honor and the most reverent respect.

[Note: Orosius, book 7, chapter 39, writes that when a soldier discovered precious vessels entrusted for safekeeping to a virgin consecrated to God, Alaric, as soon as he learned that they belonged to the basilica of the Apostle Peter, ordered them to be returned there.]

There, liberty was lost; here, it was preserved. There, captivity was enclosed; here, it was forbidden. There, the conquered were oppressed by their dominant enemies for the sake of possession; here, they were led by merciful men so that they might be freed.

[Note: Codex B reads “here they were led by merciful enemies.” On the authority of our manuscripts, we have removed the word “enemies.”]

Finally, the temple of Juno had been chosen by the greed and pride of the frivolous Greeks.

[Note: Cicero speaks of the frivolity of the Greeks in his speech *For Flaccus*, chapters 3 and 7, and elsewhere. This was their reputation among the Romans, who therefore called them “little Greeks.”]

But the basilicas of Christ were chosen by the mercy and humility even of savage Barbarians.

[Note: Here chapter 5 begins in the manuscripts.]

Unless, perhaps, the Greeks in that victory of theirs did spare the temples of the gods whom Greeks and Trojans had in common,

[Note: The Greeks and Trojans worshiped the same gods.]

and did not dare to strike or enslave the wretched and conquered Trojans who fled there, while Virgil, in the manner of poets, invented these things. No: he described the customary conduct of enemies who overthrow cities.

## Chapter Five: On the general custom of enemies who overthrow conquered cities, and what Caesar thought about it

Caesar also does not fail to mention this custom in his own judgment, as Sallust, the historian renowned for the truth of his account, records it when he reports Caesar’s opinion in the Senate concerning the conspirators:

> To seize virgins and boys; to tear children from their parents’ embrace; to subject married women to whatever the victors might desire; to plunder shrines and houses; to carry out slaughter and fires; finally, to fill everything with weapons, corpses, blood, and mourning.  
> (Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 51.)

[Note: Vind., Er., and the Gallican and Roman manuscripts read “Cato.” But since the words now quoted by Augustine are Caesar’s in Sallust, not Cato’s, the Amerbach edition—which the Louvain theologians followed—thought it appropriate, with the editors Valois and Trivet, to correct the reading to “Caesar,” although, as they themselves observe, the books commonly read “Cato.” What if Augustine, as sometimes happens even to learned men, suffered a lapse of memory, or used Sallust from a divergent or corrupt text? Codex 766 reads “Cato.”]

If he had omitted shrines, we would suppose that enemies customarily spared the dwellings of the gods. Yet these threats were not made by foreign enemies, but by Catiline and his associates, the most distinguished senators and Roman citizens, and it was Roman temples that they feared.

But these men were, evidently, ruined men and traitors to their country.

## Chapter Six: That even the Romans did not capture cities in such a way as to spare the conquered in their temples

Why, then, should our discourse roam through the many nations that waged wars against one another and nowhere spared the conquered in the shrines of their gods? Let us look at the Romans themselves. Let us, I say, recall and examine the Romans themselves, of whose pre-eminent glory it was said—
“to spare the conquered and subdue the proud,” and that they preferred to forgive an injury received rather than pursue it (Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 9, at the end): when they had stormed and captured so many great cities in order to rule far and wide, let it be shown to us which temples they customarily received, so that whoever took refuge in them might be set free. Did they do this, while the writers of those same historical events kept silent about it? Is it really so that those who most eagerly sought out whatever they could praise would pass over these, in their own view, most illustrious proofs of piety? Marcus Marcellus, an outstanding figure of the Roman name, who captured Syracuse,

[Note: [Col. 0019] Syracuse is a city in Sicily. While besieging it, Marcellus was often repulsed by the devices of Archimedes of Syracuse; only in the third year did he finally capture it. What Augustine says here about Marcellus is read in Livy, book 25, chapter 24.]

a most splendid city, is said first to have wept over its impending destruction and to have shed his own tears before shedding its blood.

[Note: [Col. 0019] Livy relates this in book 25, chapter 24.]

He also took care that chastity should be preserved even among the enemy. For before the victorious commander ordered the town to be stormed, he decreed by proclamation that no one should violate the body of a free person.

[Note: [Col. 0019] The same author, in the same work, chapter 25.]

Yet the city was overthrown according to the customs of war, and nowhere is it recorded that so chaste and merciful a commander ordered that whoever fled to this or that temple should depart unharmed.

[Note: [Col. 0019] Our manuscripts read *haberetur* (“should be regarded/held”). M.]

Surely this could not have been passed over, since neither his tears nor his proclamation for the protection of chastity could be kept silent. Fabius, the destroyer of the city of Tarentum, is praised for abstaining from the plundering of statues. When his secretary asked him what orders he would give concerning the statues of the gods, of which many had been captured, he sweetened his self-restraint with a joke. He asked what sort they were; and when he was told that there were not only many large ones but also armed ones, he replied, “Let us leave the Tarentines their angry gods.”

[Note: [Col. 0019] Tarentum, a city of Calabria that had defected from the Romans to Hannibal, was recovered by Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, who handed it over to the soldiers for plundering. This is the Fabius of whom Ennius wrote:

“One man, by delaying, restored the state to us.”

Livy reports his reply concerning the statues of the Tarentines in book 27, chapter 16.]

Since, then, the historians of Roman events could not keep silent either about the tears of the former, or the laughter of the latter, or the chaste compassion of the former, or the witty restraint of the latter, when would they have passed over the matter if they had spared certain people out of honor for some one of their gods, so that they forbade killing or captivity in any temple?

## CHAPTER VII — That during the destruction of the City the harsh actions occurred according to the custom of war, whereas the merciful actions proceeded from the power of Christ’s name

Whatever devastation, slaughter, plunder, burning, and suffering was inflicted in that most recent Roman disaster was the work of the customary practices of war. But what was done in a new manner—what caused barbarian savagery, with its unprecedented appearance, to seem so gentle that the largest basilicas were selected and assigned for filling with people who were to be spared, where no one would be struck down, from which no one would be dragged away, and to which many were led by merciful enemies for liberation, from which no persons whatsoever were carried away to be made captive, even by cruel enemies—this must be attributed to the name of Christ and to the Christian age. Whoever does not see this is blind; whoever sees it and does not praise it is ungrateful; whoever resists one who praises it is insane.

Far be it from any prudent person to attribute this to the barbarians’ savagery. He terrified, restrained, and wonderfully tempered the most brutal and savage minds—the one who, through the prophet, foretold so long beforehand:

“I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not withdraw my mercy from them” (Psalm 88:33–34).

## CHAPTER VIII — Concerning the advantages and disadvantages that are generally shared by the good and the wicked

### 1

Someone may say: Why, then, does this divine mercy reach even the impious and ungrateful? Why should we suppose, except because it was granted by the one who daily causes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45)?

Although some of them, reflecting on these things, correct themselves from impiety through repentance, while others, as the Apostle says, despise the riches of God’s goodness and forbearance and, in accordance with the hardness of their heart and their unrepentant heart, store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works (Romans 2:4, 6), nevertheless God’s patience invites the wicked to repentance, just as God’s scourge trains the good in patience. Likewise, God’s mercy embraces the good in order to nourish them, just as God’s severity corrects the wicked in order to punish them.

For divine providence has chosen to prepare for the future good things for the just, which the unjust will not enjoy, and evils for the impious, by which the good will not be tormented. But he has willed these temporal goods and evils to be shared by both, so that goods would not be sought with excessive eagerness when the wicked are also seen to possess them, nor evils shamefully avoided when the good too are often afflicted by them.

### 2

It makes a very great difference what use is made either of the things called prosperous or of those called adverse. The good person is neither lifted up by temporal goods nor crushed by evils; the wicked person, however, is punished by this kind of misfortune because prosperity corrupts him.

Yet God often displays his action more clearly even in distributing these things. For if he now punished every sin with manifest punishment, it would be thought that nothing had been reserved for the final judgment; and again, if God openly punished no sin now, divine providence would be believed not to exist. Similarly, in matters of prosperity, if God did not grant them with unmistakable generosity to certain people who ask, we would not say that such things belonged to him; but if he gave them to everyone who asked, we would conclude that he should be served only for the sake of such rewards. Such service would not make us devout but rather greedy and avaricious.

Since these things are so, whenever the good and the wicked are afflicted alike, they are not for that reason themselves undifferentiated, simply because what both endure is not differentiated. The dissimilarity of those who suffer remains even amid the similarity of their sufferings; and although they are under the same torment, virtue and vice are not the same.

For just as gold glows beneath the same fire while straw smokes, and beneath the same threshing-sledge the chaff is crushed while the grain is cleansed; and just as oil is not confused with dregs because they are pressed out by the same weight of the press, so one and the same force rushing upon them tests, purifies, and refines the good, but condemns, devastates, and destroys the wicked.

Thus, in the same affliction, the wicked curse and blaspheme God, while the good pray and praise him. The important difference lies not in what each suffers, but in the character of the one who suffers it. For when shaken by an equal motion, mud exhales a horrible stench, while perfume gives off a pleasant fragrance.

## CHAPTER IX — Concerning the causes of correction, on account of which both the good and the wicked are scourged alike

### 1

What, then, did the Christians suffer amid that devastation of things,

[Note: [Col. 0021] Several manuscripts read *vastatione* (“devastation”) instead of *vastitate* (“desolation”). The Corbie manuscript 766, together with other more authoritative manuscripts, supports *vastitate*. M.]

that would not benefit them if they considered these events more faithfully? First, as they humbly reflect on the very sins with which God, in his indignation, filled the world with such calamities, although they are far removed from criminals, profligates, and the impious, they nevertheless do not consider themselves so entirely free of offenses that they judge themselves unworthy of suffering temporal evils on their account.

[Note: [Col. 0021] Lov. reads *indignos* (“unworthy”), contrary to the sense and to the other books, which read *dignos* (“worthy”).]

For, apart from the fact that everyone, however commendably he may live, yields in some matters to carnal desire—even if not to the monstrosity of crimes, the whirlpool of profligacy, or the abomination of impiety, nevertheless to some sins, whether rare or all the more frequent because they are lesser—apart from this, who is easily found who treats those very people, on account of whose dreadful pride, lust, avarice, and detestable iniquities and impieties God, as he foretold by threatening, crushes the earth (Isaiah 24 and elsewhere), as they ought to be treated? Who lives with them as one ought to live with such people?

For most often people culpably refrain from teaching, warning, and sometimes even rebuking and correcting them, either because they are reluctant to undertake the effort, or because they are ashamed to offend them openly,

[Note: [Col. 0021] Some manuscripts omit *coram* (“openly/before them”).]

or because they avoid hostility, lest it hinder and harm them in these temporal matters—whether those which our desire still longs to obtain or those which our weakness fears to lose.

Thus, although the life of the wicked is displeasing to the good, and for that reason the good do not fall with them into the condemnation prepared after this life for such people, nevertheless, because they spare their damnable sins while fearing them in their own, even though minor and pardonable, matters, they are rightly scourged with them temporally, although they are by no means punished eternally. Rightly do they experience this life as bitter when they are divinely afflicted together with the wicked—the life whose sweetness they loved, yet did not wish to be bitter to those who were sinning.

### 2

If, however, someone refrains from rebuking and correcting those who act wrongly because he is looking for a more suitable time, or fears that they may become worse as a result, or fears that they may obstruct weaker people who need to be trained in a good and devout life, crush them, or turn them away from the faith, this does not seem to arise from an opportunity for greed but from a plan of charity.

What is blameworthy is that those who live differently and recoil from the deeds of the wicked nevertheless spare the sins of others—sins which they ought to discourage or rebuke—while avoiding their offense lest it harm them in matters that the good and innocent may legitimately use, but which they love more eagerly than is proper, as people who are pilgrims in this world and profess hope for their heavenly homeland.

For not only weaker people who lead married lives, have children or seek to have them, and possess houses and households—the people whom the Apostle addresses in the churches, teaching and exhorting them how they ought to live, wives with husbands, husbands with wives, children with parents, parents with children, slaves with masters, and masters with slaves (Colossians 3:18–22)—eagerly acquire many temporal and earthly things and are distressed to lose them, and therefore do not dare offend people whose utterly polluted and criminal life displeases them; even those who occupy a higher station in life, who are not entangled in marital bonds and use little food and clothing,

[Note: [Col. 0022] The very old Corbie manuscript reads *ac tegimento utuntur* (“and use clothing”).]

often consult their own reputation and safety

[Note: [Col. 0022] The word *consulentes* (“consulting”) is absent from Am. Er. and the manuscripts. It can be deleted without damage to the sense, so that the words immediately following—“while they fear the plots and attacks of the wicked”—refer to the preceding words, namely “their reputation and safety.”]

and, while fearing the plots and attacks of the wicked, refrain from rebuking them.

Although they do not fear them so much that they yield to any of their terrors and wickedness by committing similar deeds, they nevertheless generally do not wish to rebuke the very actions which they do not commit, even though they might perhaps correct some people by rebuking them, lest, if they were unable to do so, their own safety and reputation should fall into danger and ruin.

They do this not from the consideration by which they see their reputation and safety to be necessary for the benefit of people needing instruction, but rather from that weakness which takes pleasure in a flattering tongue and human praise (1 Corinthians 4:3), and which fears the judgment of the crowd and the torment or destruction of the flesh. That is, they act because of certain bonds of desire, not because of the duties of charity.

### 3

It does not therefore seem to me a small reason why the good are scourged together with the wicked when God is pleased to punish corrupt morals also by the affliction of temporal penalties. They are scourged together, not because they lead the same evil life, but because they love temporal life together—not equally, certainly, but together. The good ought to despise it so that, when corrected and reformed, the wicked might attain eternal life; and if they refused to become companions in attaining it, they would be endured and loved as enemies, because, as long as they live, it is always uncertain whether they will change their will for the better.

In this matter those to whom the prophet says, “He indeed will die in his sin, but I will require his blood from the hand of the watchman” (Ezekiel 33:6), have not an equal but a far graver responsibility.

For this purpose watchmen—that is, overseers of the peoples—have been appointed in the churches, so that they do not spare sins when rebuking them.

[Note: [Col. 0023] The word *speculator* (“watchman”) exactly translates the Greek *episkopos* (ἐπίσκοπος, “overseer”), as L. Vives demonstrates in greater detail.]

Yet a person who is not an overseer is not entirely free from this kind of fault if, among those with whom the necessities of this life associate him, he knows of many things that ought to be admonished or reproved and neglects them, avoiding their offense because of those things which he uses in this life legitimately but enjoys more than he ought.

Furthermore, the good have another reason why they are afflicted by temporal evils, as Job was: so that the human spirit itself may be tested and known, and it may be shown with what strength of devotion it loves God freely.

[Note: [Col. 0023] St. Chrysostom, in *Homily 1 to the People of Antioch*, enumerates eight causes of the varied and manifold affliction of the saints in this world and confirms each individually from Scripture. COQUAEUS.]

## CHAPTER X — That the saints lose nothing in the loss of temporal possessions

### 1

When these things have been rightly considered and examined, observe whether anything evil happened to the faithful and devout that was not turned to their good—unless, perhaps, the apostolic statement is to be regarded as empty, where he says, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28).

## [CHAPTER X]

They lost everything they possessed. Did they lose their faith? Their devotion? The goods of the inner person, who is rich before God (1 Peter 3:4)?

These are the riches of Christians, with which the Apostle said that one is wealthy: “Devotion with contentment is indeed great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and ruin. For the love of money is the root of all evils,”

[Note: [Col. 0023] In Paul, *philargyria* (φιλαργυρία, “love of money”). The Vulgate has *cupiditas* (“desire/greed”).]

“and by desiring it some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains” (1 Timothy 6:6–10).

### 2

If, then, those whose earthly riches perished in that devastation possessed them in the manner they had heard from this man who was poor outwardly but rich inwardly—that is, if they used the world as though they were not using it (1 Corinthians 7:31)—they were able to say what that man said when severely tested but by no means overcome:

“Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return to the earth. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Thus, as a good servant, he possessed great resources in the very will of his Lord; by that will he grew rich in mind and was not distressed by the things left to him while alive,

[Note: [Col. 0023] The manuscripts read *relictus* (“left behind”). The printed editions have *relictis* (“with the things left behind”), which weakens the complete antithesis Augustine intended between *vivens relictus* (“left behind while alive”) and *moriens relicturus* (“about to leave behind when dying”). Codices 766 and 2051 read *relictus*, while the inferior manuscripts 2052 and 2053 have *relictis*. M.]

things he would soon leave behind when dying.

But those weaker people who, although they did not place these earthly goods before Christ, nevertheless clung to them with some degree of desire, learned by losing them how greatly they had sinned through loving them. They grieved in proportion to the extent to which they had involved themselves in grief, as I recalled above that the Apostle said.

For it was necessary that the discipline of experience be added to them, since they had for so long neglected the discipline of words. When the Apostle said, “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation,” and so forth, he certainly condemned desire in riches, not possessions. For elsewhere he commands, saying:

“Command those who are rich in this world not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches,

[Note: [Col. 0024] The printed editions add *suarum* (“their”), which is absent from the manuscripts.]

but in the living God, who supplies us abundantly with all things for enjoyment. Let them do good, be rich in good works, give readily, share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Timothy 6:17–19).

Those who acted thus with their riches consoled themselves for light losses with great gains. They rejoiced more over what they had safely preserved by giving readily than they grieved over what they had more easily lost by holding on to it fearfully. For what could perish on earth was what they had been reluctant to transfer from there.

Those who accepted the counsel of their Lord, who said, “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and dig through and steal; but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where the thief does not approach and moth does not corrupt. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matthew 6:19–21), proved in the time of tribulation how rightly they had understood this, since they had not despised the truest teacher and most faithful and unconquerable guardian of their treasure.

For if many rejoiced that they had their riches in a place to which the enemy did not happen to gain access, how much more certainly and securely could those rejoice who, at the command of their God, had transferred them to a place to which the enemy could not approach at all?

Thus our Paulinus, bishop of Nola, who from being extremely wealthy became voluntarily poor and abundantly holy, when the barbarians devastated Nola itself,

[Note: [Col. 0024] The Goths, under Alaric, after sacking the City, spread through Latium, the Volscians, Campania, and other provinces of Italy, and destroyed Nola itself, a city of Campania.]

prayed in his heart, as we later learned from him, while he was being held by them:

“Lord, do not let me be tormented because of gold and silver; for where all my possessions are, you know.”

For he had all his possessions where the one who had shown him to store and treasure them had directed him.

[Note: [Col. 0024] Lov. and our manuscripts, except 766, read *monuerat* (“had admonished/instructed”). Manuscript 766 and most printed editions read *monstraverat* (“had shown”). M.]

He had also foretold that these evils would come upon the world. Therefore, those who had obeyed their Lord’s instruction about where and how they should store their treasures did not lose even their earthly riches when the barbarians invaded. Those who regretted not having obeyed learned what should be done with such things—if not through wisdom beforehand, at least through experience afterward.

### 3

But some good Christians were tortured in order to make them reveal their possessions to the enemy. Yet they could neither betray nor lose the good by which they themselves were good. If they preferred to be tortured rather than betray the mammon of iniquity, they were not good.

They should have been reminded that, for the sake of gold, they were suffering as much as should be endured for Christ, so that they might learn to love him instead—the one who would enrich those who suffered for him with eternal happiness—not gold and silver, for which it was most wretched to suffer, whether it was concealed by lying or betrayed by telling the truth.

For amid the tortures no one lost Christ by confessing him; no one preserved gold except by denying him. Consequently, perhaps the tortures that taught them to love an incorruptible good were more useful than those goods which, without yielding any useful fruit, tormented their owners because of their love for them.

But some who had nothing to betray were tortured because they were not believed. Perhaps these people desired to possess something and were not poor in holy intention. They had to be shown that not possessions but their very desires deserved such tortures.

If, however, because of a resolve to live a better life they did not possess hidden gold or silver, I do not know whether it happened to any such person that he was tortured because he was believed to possess it. Nevertheless, even if it did happen, surely the person who amid those tortures confessed holy poverty was confessing Christ. Therefore, even if he did not deserve to be believed by the enemy, a confessor of holy poverty could not be tortured without heavenly reward.

### 4. [XI.]

“They say that prolonged hunger also devastated many Christians.” The faithful and good turned this, too, to their advantage by enduring it devoutly. Those whom hunger killed, it freed from the evils of this life, as bodily illness does; those whom it did not kill, it taught to live more sparingly and to fast for longer periods.

## CHAPTER XI — Concerning the end of temporal life, whether longer or shorter

But many Christians too were killed, and many were destroyed by a foul variety of deaths. If this is something to be endured with grief, it is certainly common to all who have been born into this life. This much I know: no one has died who was not at some time going to die.

The end of life makes a long life and a short life the same in this respect. For one is not better and the other worse, or one greater and the other shorter, when neither exists any longer.

What difference does it make by what kind of death this life ends, when the person whose life ends is not compelled to die again? Since innumerable deaths, so to speak, threaten each mortal person amid the daily hazards of this life, as long as it remains uncertain which of them will come, I ask whether it is better to undergo one death by dying or to fear them all while living.

I do not fail to recognize how much more sluggishly one chooses to live for a long time in fear of so many deaths than to die once and thereafter fear none. But one thing is what the weak and fearful sense of the flesh recoils from, and another is what carefully examined reason demonstrates.

A death preceded by a good life should not be considered evil; for nothing makes death evil except what follows death. Therefore those who must necessarily die should not be greatly concerned with what happens to make them die, but with where they are compelled to go by dying.

Since Christians know that the death of the devout poor man among the tongues of licking dogs was far better than that of the impious rich man in purple and fine linen (Luke 16:19–31), what harm did those horrible forms of death do to the dead who had lived well?

## CHAPTER XII — Concerning the burial of human bodies, which, even if denied to Christians, deprives them of nothing

### 1

“But in such a great slaughter of corpses they could not even be buried.” Pious faith, holding to the prophecy that beasts consuming them will not harm bodies destined for resurrection, whose head will not lose a hair (Luke 21:18), does not greatly fear this either.

Truth would never have said, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28), if anything that enemies might wish to do to the bodies of the slain could harm the life to come.

Unless perhaps someone is so absurd as to argue that those who kill the body should not be feared before death, lest they kill the body, but should be feared after death, lest they prevent the slain body from being buried.

What Christ said would therefore be false: “Those who kill the body, and afterward have nothing more that they can do” (Luke 12:4), if they have so much that they can do to corpses. Far be it that what Truth said should be false.

He said that they do something when they kill because, while the body is being killed, sensation is present in it; afterward they have nothing more that they can do because there is no sensation in the dead body.

Many bodies of Christians therefore were not covered by earth, but no one separated any of them from heaven and earth, which are wholly filled by the presence of the one who knows from where to resurrect what he created.

It is indeed said in the Psalm:

“They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Psalm 78:2–3).

But this is said more to heighten the cruelty of those who did these things than the misery of those who endured them.

Although these things seem harsh and dreadful in human eyes, “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:15).

Accordingly, all these things—that is, care for the corpse, the provision of burial, and the pomp of the funeral rites—

[Note: [Col. 0026] Only the Lov. edition reads *pompae exsequiarum* (“of the pomp of the funeral rites”).]

are comforts for the living rather than aids for the dead.

If a costly burial benefits the impious, a cheap or nonexistent one will harm the devout. A crowd of attendants provided splendid funeral rites in human eyes for that rich man dressed in purple; but in the sight of the Lord, the ministry of angels provided far more glorious rites for that poor man covered with sores. They did not carry him out to a marble tomb but bore him into Abraham’s bosom.

### 2

Those against whom we have undertaken to defend the City of God laugh at these things. Yet even their philosophers have scorned concern for burial,

[Note: [Col. 0027] Such as Diogenes the Cynic, Anaxagoras, Theodorus of Cyrene, and others. See Seneca, *On Tranquility of Mind*, chapter 14, and Letter 92; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book 1, chapter 42 and following.]

and often entire armies, while dying for an earthly homeland, did not care where they would later lie or to what beasts they would become food. Poets were even allowed to say plausibly of this matter:

“Heaven covers the one who has no urn.”

[Note: [Col. 0027] Lucan, book 7, verse 819, speaking of those killed in the battle of Pharsalus, whom Caesar forbade to be burned or buried.]

How much less ought they to insult Christians over unburied bodies, when they are promised that the restoration of the flesh itself and of all its members will be returned and reconstituted in an instant—not only from the earth but also from the most hidden recesses of the other elements into which their dissolved corpses have withdrawn (1 Corinthians 15:52)?

## CHAPTER XIII — What is the proper reason for burying the bodies of the saints

Yet this does not mean that the bodies of the dead, especially of the just and faithful, should be despised and cast aside. The Holy Spirit used them as instruments and vessels for every good work.

[Note: [Col. 0027] Most manuscripts, and those of better quality, read *sancte usus est spiritus* (“the Spirit used [them] in a holy manner”): that is, the mind of the just, through the holy use of the body, produced good works.]

For if a father’s garment and ring, or anything of that kind, is dearer to descendants in proportion to their greater affection for their parents, the bodies themselves should certainly not be despised, since we wear them much more familiarly and closely than any garments.

For these belong not to an adornment or aid applied externally but to the very nature of the human being.

Hence the funerals of the ancient righteous were attended with dutiful piety, funeral rites were celebrated, and burial was provided (Genesis 25:9; 35:29; 50:2–13, and elsewhere). While they were still alive, they themselves instructed their sons concerning the burial or even the transfer of their bodies (Genesis 47:29–30; 50:24). Tobias is also commended, on the testimony of the angel, for having gained favor with God by burying the dead (Tobit 2:9; 12:12).

The Lord himself, who was to rise on the third day, praises and commends for proclamation the good work of the devout woman who poured precious ointment over his body and did this for his burial (Matthew 26:10–13). The Gospel also commendably remembers those who took his body down from the cross and carefully and honorably cared for its covering and burial (John 19:38–42).

These authorities, however, do not teach that corpses possess any sensation; rather, they indicate that the bodies of the dead also belong to God’s providence, which is pleased by such acts of piety, because of the affirmation of the resurrection.

Here too we learn profitably how great a reward can result from alms which we provide to the living and sentient, if before God even what is performed through dutiful care and attention for the lifeless limbs of human beings is not lost.

There are indeed other matters which the holy patriarchs intended to be understood as spoken in the prophetic spirit concerning the burial or transfer of their bodies. But this is not the place to discuss them, since what we have said is sufficient.

If the things necessary to sustain the living, such as food and clothing, do not break the strength of the good in enduring and tolerating hardship, even when they are lacking amid severe affliction, nor eradicate piety from the heart but instead make it, through exercise, more fruitful, how much more will the absence of the things customarily used in caring for funerals and burying the bodies of the dead fail to make miserable those who are already at rest in the hidden dwelling places of the devout?

Accordingly, when these things were unavailable for the corpses of Christians during the devastation of that great city, or even of other towns, it was neither the fault of the living, who could not provide them, nor the punishment of the dead, who cannot perceive them.

## CHAPTER XIV — Concerning the captivity of the saints, who were never without divine consolation

“But many Christians were also led into captivity.” This would indeed be most miserable if they could have been led somewhere where they did not find their God.

The Holy Scriptures contain great consolations even for this calamity. Three youths were in captivity; Daniel was in captivity; other prophets were in captivity—and God, their comforter, was not absent.

Thus he did not abandon his faithful under the rule of a people, though barbarian, yet human, who did not abandon the prophet even in the belly of a beast (Jonah 2).

Those with whom we are dealing prefer to mock this as well rather than believe it. Yet in their own writings they believe that Arion of Methymna, a most famous lyre player, when thrown from a ship, was received on the back of a dolphin and carried to land.

[Note: [Col. 0028] Herodotus wrote the story of Arion of Methymna, a town on the island of Lesbos, in book 1 of the *Muses*, chapters 23–24. Ovid follows it in the *Fasti*, book 2, verses 80 and following, as does Aulus Gellius, book 16, chapter 19.]

But our account of the prophet Jonah is more incredible. Certainly it is more incredible because it is more marvelous, and more marvelous because it is more powerful.

## CHAPTER XV — Concerning Regulus, in whom there is an example of captivity voluntarily endured even for the sake of religion, although it could not benefit him as a worshiper of the gods
1. Yet these people have, concerning captivity voluntarily endured for the sake of religion, a very distinguished example among their own illustrious men. Marcus Attilius Regulus, commander of the Roman people, was a captive among the Carthaginians.

[Note: [Column 0028] The surname *Attilius* is absent from the Viadutine edition and the manuscripts. Aulus Gellius, book 6, chapter 4; Appian, *Punic Wars*, chapter 4; Polybius, book 1, chapter 29; and many others relate the history of Marcus Regulus, who, having been elected consul with Lucius Manlius Vulso in the First Punic War, was the first Roman to lead an army into Africa and was captured by the enemy.]

Since the Carthaginians preferred that their own men be returned to them by the Romans rather than retain Roman captives, they sent this Regulus in particular, together with their envoys, to Rome in order to obtain this, having first bound him by an oath that, if he failed to accomplish what they wanted, he would return to Carthage. He went, and in the senate argued the opposite, because he did not consider it advantageous to the Roman republic to exchange the prisoners. Nor, after making this recommendation, was he compelled by his countrymen to return from them to the enemy; rather, what he had sworn, he fulfilled voluntarily.

[Note: [Column 0029] The manuscripts of Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and all our copies read *sed quia juraverat* (“but because he had sworn”).]

But they killed him with contrived and dreadful tortures. For they shut him inside a narrow wooden container in which he was forced to stand, and pierced it on every side with extremely sharp nails, so that he could not incline any part of himself without the most atrocious pain; they killed him even by keeping him awake.

[Note: [Column 0029] Some books read “they killed him even by strangling him,” but incorrectly. Cicero’s statement in the speech *Against Piso*, chapter 19, is relevant here: “The Carthaginians killed Marcus Attilius Regulus by keeping him awake, after cutting off his eyelids and fastening him in a machine.” Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 2, excerpt 1, gives a substantially similar account.]

With good reason, certainly, they praise a courage greater than so great a misfortune. And he had sworn by the gods whose worship, being forbidden, these people suppose to have brought such disasters upon the human race.

[Note: [Column 0029] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Lovaniensis read *quorum pro cultu prohibito* (“whose worship was forbidden”). *Pro* is absent from Erasmus and most manuscripts.]

Therefore, if the gods were worshiped in order to make this life prosperous, and if they either wished or permitted these punishments to be inflicted upon one who had sworn truthfully, what could they do in their anger that would be more severe against a perjurer? But why should I not bring my reasoning to a conclusion concerning both matters? Regulus certainly worshiped the gods in such a way that, for the sake of keeping faith with his oath, he did not remain in his homeland, nor go elsewhere from it, but did not hesitate to return to his most bitter enemies. If he thought this useful for the present life—which he deserved to end in so dreadful a way—he was undoubtedly deceived. For by his own example he taught that the gods are of no benefit to their worshipers for temporal happiness, since he, devoted to their worship, was defeated, led away captive, and, because he refused to act otherwise than he had sworn by them, was tortured and killed by a new, previously unheard-of, and excessively horrible kind of punishment.

But if the worship of the gods returns happiness after this life as its reward, why do they slander Christian times, saying that this calamity befell the City because it ceased to worship its gods, when even someone worshiping them with the greatest devotion could become as unhappy as Regulus? Unless, perhaps, in opposition to the clearest truth, someone is driven by such great folly and extraordinary blindness that he dares to argue that an entire city worshiping the gods cannot be unhappy, while one man can be—namely, that the power of their gods is more capable of preserving many than individuals, although a multitude is composed of individuals.

2. But if they say that Marcus Regulus could have been blessed even in that captivity and under those bodily tortures by virtue of his spirit, then let us seek the true virtue by which a city too can be blessed. For a city is not blessed in one way and a human being in another, since a city is nothing other than a harmonious multitude of human beings.

[Note: [Column 0029] Some copies read *consors* (“sharing the same lot”) instead of *concors* (“harmonious”).]

For the moment, therefore, I do not discuss what sort of virtue Regulus possessed. For now it is enough that, by this most distinguished example, they are compelled to admit that the gods are not to be worshiped for the sake of bodily goods or of those things that happen to a person externally, since Regulus preferred to be without all these things rather than offend the gods by whom he had sworn.

But what are we to do with people who boast that they had such a citizen, while fearing to have such a city? If they do not fear it, then let them admit that something like what happened to Regulus could also happen to a city worshiping the gods as devotedly as he did, and let them not slander Christian times.

But since the question arose concerning those Christians who were also led away captive—

[Note: [Column 0030] Several manuscripts read “who were also taken captive.” Thus do our manuscripts of the M family.]

—let those who insolently and recklessly mock the most salutary religion on this account look at this and be silent. For if it was not a reproach to their gods that their most devoted worshiper, while keeping faith with his oath to them, left his homeland, having no other homeland, and was killed among his enemies by the punishment of a long and novel cruelty—

[Note: [Column 0030] Lovaniensis reads “by a long death and punishment,” while other printed editions and the manuscripts disagree.]

—then the Christian name is much less deserving of blame in the case of those consecrated to their Lord who are held captive. Awaiting their heavenly homeland in true faith, they nevertheless know themselves to be strangers even in their own dwellings (1 Peter 2:11).

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Whether the virtue of the spirit could have been defiled, without the consent of the will, by sexual violations suffered by captivity, perhaps even by holy virgins

They think they bring a serious charge against Christians when, exaggerating their captivity, they add that sexual violations were committed—not only against other men’s wives and virgins betrothed to be married, but even against certain consecrated women. Here, however, it is not faith, piety, or the virtue itself called chastity that is confined by certain difficulties, but rather our argument, caught between modesty and reason.

[Note: [Column 0030] Modesty forbids calling even the violation of the body not evil; reason requires this conclusion.]

We are concerned here not so much to answer outsiders as to offer consolation to our own people. Let this, then, first be established and firmly maintained: the virtue by which one lives rightly commands the bodily members from the seat of the spirit, and the holy body becomes holy through the use made of it by a holy will. While that will remains unshaken and steadfast, whatever another person does to or in the body—something that cannot be avoided without personal sin—is beyond the guilt of the person who suffers it.

But since what is done to another’s body may pertain not only to pain but also to lust, whatever such an act may have been, even if it does not dislodge chastity retained with the utmost steadfastness of spirit, nevertheless imposes shame. It must not, however, be thought to have been done with the consent of the mind merely because it perhaps could not be done without some bodily pleasure.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Concerning voluntary death out of fear of punishment or dishonor

Accordingly, who would not wish to pardon those women who killed themselves so as not to suffer anything of this kind? And whoever charges those who refused to kill themselves with a crime, lest they avoid another’s disgrace by committing a crime of their own, will himself not be free from the crime of folly.

[Note: [Column 0030] Most manuscripts read “he himself will not avoid the crime,” and a very few of them, instead of *carebit* (“will be free”), have *cavebit* (“will beware”). The Corbie manuscript reads: “he himself will not avoid the crime of folly,” which is correct.]

[XVII.] For certainly, if private authority does not permit anyone to kill another human being, even a guilty one, when no law grants permission to kill him—

[Note: [Column 0030] Lovaniensis reads “if private authority does not permit anyone,” while the other editions and manuscripts omit *alicui* (“anyone”).]

[Column 0031] —then plainly even one who kills himself is a murderer. And he becomes more guilty by killing himself in proportion as he was more innocent in the matter for which he thought he ought to be killed.

For if we rightly detest Judas’s deed, and truth judges that, when he hanged himself, he increased rather than expiated the crime of that wicked betrayal—because, despairing of God’s mercy and repenting destructively, he left himself no place for saving repentance (Matthew 27:3)—how much more ought a person to abstain from killing himself when he has no such punishment within himself to punish?

For when Judas killed himself, he killed a wicked man; and yet he ended this life guilty not only of Christ’s death but also of his own, since, although he was killed because of his crime, he was killed by another crime of his own.

[XVIII.] But why should a person who has done no evil do evil to himself, and by killing himself kill an innocent human being, so as not to suffer another who is guilty; and commit a personal sin against himself so that another’s sin may not be committed against him?

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Concerning another person’s lustful violence, which the unwilling mind suffers through an assaulted body

1. But it is feared lest another person’s lust defile one. It will not defile her if it belongs to another; but if it defiles her, it will not belong to another. Since chastity is a virtue of the spirit and is accompanied by courage, by which it resolves to endure any evil rather than consent to evil, while no courageous and chaste person has control over what is done to the flesh but only over what the mind accepts or rejects, who, in sound mind, would think that she loses her chastity if another person’s lust is exercised and gratified against her will upon her seized and violated body?

[Note: [Column 0031] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts read “who, in sound mind.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “who, then, in sound mind.”]

For if chastity perishes in this way, then chastity will certainly not be a virtue of the spirit, nor will it belong among those goods by which one lives well; rather, it will be numbered among bodily goods, such as strength, beauty, sound and unimpaired health—

[Note: [Column 0031] Several manuscripts omit “and unimpaired,” and some read *sanitas* (“health”) instead of *sana* (“sound”). Manuscript 766 likewise has this reading.]

—and whatever else is of this kind. Even if these goods are diminished, they do not diminish a good and just life at all. But if chastity is something of this kind, why is the body endangered for its sake, lest it be lost? If it is a good of the spirit, it is not lost even when the body is violated.

Indeed, when the good of holy continence does not yield to the uncleanness of carnal desires, the body itself is also sanctified. Therefore, when the will persists with unshaken resolve in not yielding to them, holiness does not perish from the body itself—

[Note: [Column 0031] Vindobonensis and the manuscripts read “holiness does not perish.” Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read “chastity does not perish.”]

—for the will to use the body in a holy manner perseveres, and, insofar as it depends upon that will, so does the capacity to do so.

2. The body is not holy merely because its members are intact, or because they have not been touched at all. For they can suffer violence after being wounded by various accidents, and physicians sometimes, while assisting health, do things to them that horrify the observer.

A midwife, examining a certain virgin’s integrity with her hand, destroyed it—whether through malice, ignorance, or accident—while making her inspection.
