I do not think anyone could be so foolish as to suppose that something of the holiness of the body itself was lost in this case, although the integrity of that bodily member had already been destroyed.

Accordingly, when the disposition of the spirit remains—the disposition through which the body too deserved to be sanctified—the violence of another’s lust does not take holiness away from the body itself, since the steadfastness of her continence preserves it.

But if a woman, corrupted in mind and having violated the resolution she had vowed to God, proceeds to her seducer so that he may defile her, do we still call her holy in body as she proceeds, after the holiness of spirit by which the body was sanctified has been lost and destroyed? Far be such an error from us. Rather, let us learn from this that the holiness of the body is not lost when the holiness of the spirit remains, even when the body is violated, just as the holiness of the body is lost when the holiness of the spirit is violated, even though the body remains untouched.

Therefore a woman who has been violently assaulted without any consent of her own and oppressed by another’s sin has no reason to punish herself by voluntary death—how much less before this occurs, lest a certain murder be committed while the very violation, although another’s, remains uncertain?

[Note: [Column 0032] Lovaniensis reads “Therefore, since she has no reason…” The word “since” is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XIX  
### Concerning Lucretia, who killed herself because of the sexual violation inflicted upon her

1. Will those against whom we defend the holy minds and bodies of Christian women assaulted in captivity perhaps dare to contradict this evident reasoning—that, when the body has been violated, with no change for the worse in the resolution of chastity through consent, the disgrace belongs solely to the one who violated and had intercourse with her, not to the woman who, having been violated, gave no consent to her violator?

[XIX.] They certainly praise Lucretia, a noble and ancient Roman matron, with lavish encomiums on her chastity. After the son of King Tarquin had violently assaulted her body and lustfully possessed her, she revealed the crime of the most wicked young man to her husband Collatinus—

[Note: [Column 0032] Some old books read *Conlatino*. In Livy, however, he is called *Collatinus*.]

—and to her kinsman Brutus, men of the highest distinction and courage, and bound them to avenge it. Then, distressed and unable to endure the shame of what had been done against her, she killed herself.

[Note: [Column 0032] Livy narrates this in book 1, chapters 57–58.]

What are we to say? Is she to be judged an adulteress or chaste? Who would think there is any difficulty in this dispute? Someone, declaiming on this matter with truth and distinction, said: “Strange to say: there were two, but one committed adultery.” Splendidly and most truthfully said. For he observed, in the mingling of two bodies, the utterly polluted desire of one and the most chaste will of the other; and, attending not to what was done by the joining of the limbs but to what was done by the difference between their minds, he said: “There were two, but one committed adultery.”

2. But what is this? The woman who did not commit adultery is punished more severely. He was expelled from his homeland together with his father—

[Note: [Column 0033] This is discussed below, book 3, chapter 25.]

—while she was killed with the supreme punishment. If the violation imposed upon her against her will is not unchastity, then the punishment of a chaste woman is not justice.

I appeal to you, Roman laws and judges. Certainly, after crimes had been committed, you did not wish any criminal to be killed with impunity without being condemned. If, then, someone brought this case before your judgment and proved to you that a woman had been killed who was not only uncondemned but also chaste and innocent, would you not punish the perpetrator with appropriate severity?

That is what Lucretia did. That celebrated Lucretia killed, in addition, the innocent, chaste Lucretia who had suffered violence.

[Note: [Column 0033] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads “Lucretia killed the violated Lucretia in addition.”]

Deliver your verdict. But if you cannot do so because the person whom you could punish is not present, why do you praise the killer of an innocent and chaste woman with such extravagant acclaim? Certainly, before the judges of the underworld—even such judges as are celebrated in the poems of your poets—you cannot defend her in any way, since she is placed among those

> who by their own hand brought death  
> upon themselves, though innocent, and, hating the light,  
> cast away their lives. For one who longs to return above,  
> the Fates stand in the way, and the unfordable marsh  
> binds him with its gloomy waters.

[Note: [Column 0033] Nearly all written copies read *Fas obstat* (“divine law stands in the way”) instead of *Fata obstant* (“the Fates stand in the way”), and *inamabilis* (“unlovable”) instead of *innabilis* (“unfordable”). Some also read *tristisque* (“and gloomy”) instead of *tristique* (“with gloomy”), and *undae* (“of the waters”) instead of *unda*. There are no fewer discrepancies in the old Virgilian books. Our manuscripts all read *fas* instead of *fata*, and *inamabilis* instead of *innabilis*. Manuscript 766 alone has *tristis* instead of *tristi*.]

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 6, lines 434–439.)

Or is she absent from that place because she did not kill herself innocent, but conscious of wrongdoing? For what if—something only she herself could have known—although the young man violently attacked her, she was also enticed by her own desire and consented, and, punishing herself for this, grieved so deeply that she thought it had to be expiated by death?

Even so, she ought not to have killed herself, if she could have practiced fruitful repentance before the false gods. Nevertheless, if this is indeed the case, and the saying “There were two, but one committed adultery” is false, but rather both committed adultery—one through open assault, the other through hidden consent—then she did not kill herself innocent, and thus her learned defenders can say that she is not among those in the underworld “who by their own hand brought death upon themselves, though innocent.”

But the case is so hemmed in on both sides that, if the murder is diminished, the adultery is confirmed; and if the adultery is cleared, the murder is increased. There is no way out when the question is put: If she was violated, why was she praised? If chaste, why was she killed?

[Note: The printed editions read *adultera* (“an adulteress”); the manuscripts read *adulterata* (“violated” or “sexually defiled”).]

3. Yet, for our purpose in this most distinguished example of this woman, to refute those who insult Christian women assaulted in captivity while wholly lacking any thought of holiness, it is enough that her admirers said in her eminent praise: “There were two, but one committed adultery.” For they considered Lucretia to have been such a woman that she could not have been defiled by any adulterous—

[Column 0034]—consent.

Therefore, the fact that she killed herself because she endured an adulterer—

[Note: [Column 0034] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *adulterium* (“adultery”).]

—even though she was not herself adulterous, was not love of chastity but weakness of shame. She was ashamed of the disgrace committed against her, even though it was not committed with her; and, as a Roman woman eager for praise, she feared excessively that people might think that what she had suffered violently while alive she would have suffered willingly had she remained alive.

Thus she thought that she had to present that punishment before the eyes of men as a witness to her mind, since she could not demonstrate her conscience to them. She was ashamed that she might be thought an accomplice in the deed if she patiently endured what another had wickedly done to her.

This is not what the Christian women who suffered similar things and continue to live did. Yet neither did they avenge another’s crime upon themselves, lest they add their own crimes to the crimes of others: if their enemies had committed sexual violations against them through lust, they did not, through shame, commit murders against themselves.

Within them they have the glory of chastity and the testimony of conscience; they have these before the eyes of their God and do not seek anything further where they have no further means of acting rightly. They must not depart from the authority of divine law while wrongly avoiding the offense of human suspicion.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That there is no authority granting Christians the right to voluntary death in any circumstance

For it is not without reason that nowhere in the holy canonical Books can we find a divine command or permission that we inflict death upon ourselves either to attain immortality itself or to escape or avoid any evil.

[Note: [Column 0034] The printed editions read *canonicisque* (“and canonical”). The particle *-que* is absent from the manuscripts.]

We must understand that we are forbidden to do so where the Law says, “You shall not kill,” especially because it did not add, “your neighbor.” When it prohibited false testimony, it said: “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:13, 16). Yet no one who bears false witness against himself should therefore think himself free from that crime.

For the rule of loving one’s neighbor was received by the person who loves from the love of himself, since it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:39). Moreover, if one who falsely testifies about himself is no less guilty of false testimony than if he did this against his neighbor—although in the commandment forbidding false testimony the prohibition is expressed as being against one’s neighbor, and those who do not understand correctly might think that it is not forbidden for anyone to be a false witness against himself—how much more must it be understood that a person is not permitted to kill himself, since in the statement “You shall not kill,” with no qualification added afterward, no one, certainly not even the person to whom the command is given, is understood to be excepted?

For this reason some people even try to extend this commandment to beasts and livestock, so that from it they conclude that it is not permissible to kill any of them.

[Note: [Column 0034] Such were the Marcionites, according to Epiphanius, *Heresy* 42, and the Manichaeans, according to Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 6, chapters 6 and 8. (Coquaeus.)]

Why, then, not extend it also to herbs and to everything that is nourished and fixed in the earth by its roots? For this class of things, although it does not feel, is said to live; and consequently it can also die, and therefore, when force is applied to it, can be killed. Hence the Apostle, speaking of seeds of this kind, says: “What you sow is not made alive unless it dies”—

[Note: [Column 0035] The printed editions read “unless it first dies.” *First* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of Paul.]

(1 Corinthians 15:36). And it is written in the Psalm: “He killed their vines with hail” (Psalm 77:47).

Does this mean that, when we hear “You shall not kill,” we consider it wicked to pull up a shrub and insanely assent to the error of the Manichaeans?

When these ravings have been dismissed, then, and when we read “You shall not kill,” if we do not understand the words to have been spoken about plants because they have no sensation, nor about irrational animals—flying, swimming, walking, crawling—

[Note: [Column 0035] The manuscripts read “irrational.”]

—because they are not joined to us by any rational bond, which was not granted to them in common with us, and therefore, by the most just ordering of the Creator, both their life and death are subordinated to our uses, it remains that we understand the words “You shall not kill” to refer to a human being. Therefore, neither another person nor yourself.

[Note: [Column 0035] Thus the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads “therefore, not another person, and consequently not yourself.”]

For whoever kills himself kills nothing other than a human being.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Concerning the killings of human beings that are exempted from the crime of murder

The same divine authority itself has made certain exceptions to the prohibition against killing a human being. But with the exception of those whom God commands to be killed, whether by a law promulgated or by an explicit command addressed to a particular person for a particular time, the person who performs the service is not himself the killer, just as a sword is an instrument for the person who uses it.

[Note: [Column 0035] The printed editions read “just as a sword is an instrument for the user.” The manuscripts do not have *est* (“is”), in whose place *debet* (“must be”) is properly understood.]

Therefore those who, with God as their authority, have waged wars, or who, exercising public authority according to his laws—that is, by the command of the most just reason—have punished criminals with death, have in no way acted against the commandment that says, “You shall not kill.”

Abraham was not only not charged with the crime of cruelty but was even praised under the name of piety because he wished to kill his son, not wickedly but obediently (Genesis 22). And it is rightly asked whether what Jephthah did should be regarded as commanded by God, when he killed his daughter, who came out to meet her father, after vowing to God that he would sacrifice whatever first came out to meet him when he returned victorious from battle (Judges 11).

Samson likewise cannot be excused for bringing down the house upon himself together with his enemies except on the ground that the Spirit, who worked miracles through him, had secretly commanded this (Judges 16:30).

With these exceptions, then—those whom either the just law generally or God, the very source of justice, specifically commands to be killed—whoever kills a human being, whether himself or anyone else, is entangled in the crime of murder.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### That voluntary death can never belong to greatness of spirit

1. Those who have perpetrated this deed against themselves may perhaps be admired for greatness of spirit, but they are not to be praised for sound wisdom. Indeed, if one consults reason more carefully, even greatness of spirit is not properly named where a person, unable to endure either hardships or another’s sins, kills himself.

A weak mind is revealed instead: one unable to bear either the harsh servitude of its own body or the foolish opinion of the crowd. The greater spirit is rightly said to be the one that can endure a troubled life rather than flee from it, and that can despise human judgment—especially popular judgment, which is usually enveloped in the darkness of error—in comparison with the light and purity of conscience.

Accordingly, if it is thought that a person acts with great spirit when he brings death upon himself, then Cleombrotus—

[Note: [Column 0036] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and nearly all the manuscripts read *Theobrotus*. Cicero calls him “Cleombrotus of Ambracia.”]

—is the one found in this greatness of spirit. They say that, after reading Plato’s book in which he discussed the immortality of the soul, he threw himself from a wall and thus departed from this life for the one he believed to be better.

No calamity or crime—whether real or imagined—was forcing him to remove himself because he could not bear it. Rather, the only thing present was greatness of spirit for seizing death and breaking the agreeable bonds of this life.

Yet Plato himself, whom he had read, could have testified that this was done with greatness rather than rightly. Plato would certainly have done this above all and most emphatically, or even commanded it, if, with the mind by which he perceived the soul’s immortality, he had not judged that such a deed should not only not be done but even be prohibited.

2. [XXIII.] But, they say, many killed themselves so as not to fall into the hands of their enemies. We are not merely asking whether this was done, but whether it ought to have been done.

Sound reason must be placed even above examples. Examples do indeed agree with it, but those examples that are more worthy of imitation in proportion as they are more excellent in piety. The Patriarchs did not do this; nor the Prophets; nor the Apostles.

For Christ the Lord himself, when he advised those who suffered persecution to flee from one city to another (Matthew 10:23), could have advised them to lay hands upon themselves so as not to fall into the hands of their persecutors.

Moreover, if he neither commanded nor advised those whose departure from this life he promised to receive into eternal dwellings to leave it in that way (John 14:2), then, whatever examples the nations ignorant of God may bring forward, it is clear that this is not permitted to those who worship the one true God.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### What sort of example Cato provides, who killed himself because he could not endure Caesar’s victory

Yet, apart from Lucretia, about whom we have said above as much as seemed sufficient, these people do not readily find anyone whose authority they can invoke except Cato, who killed himself at Utica—

[Note: [Column 0036] This was Cato the Younger, great-grandson of Cato the Elder. He was called Uticensis because he killed himself at Utica, a city in Africa. Livy, book 114; Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, chapter 31, and *Tusculan Disputations*, book 1, chapter 30, discuss him.]

—not because he alone did this, but because he was regarded as an educated and upright man—

[Note: [Column 0036] The innocence and wisdom of both Catos became proverbial. Hence Juvenal’s statement, book 1, satire 2, line 40: “A third Cato fell from heaven.” Velleius Paterculus, book 2, chapter 45; Seneca, *On Tranquility of Mind*, chapter 15; Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 54; and others praise his uprightness at length.]

—so that people may rightly think that what he did could also have been rightly done or may rightly be done.

What, then, shall I say about his deed, except that some of his friends, educated men who more prudently dissuaded him from doing it, judged it the act of a weaker rather than a stronger spirit? It demonstrated not honorable character avoiding disgrace, but weakness unable to endure adversity.

Cato himself indicated this in the case of his beloved son. For if it was disgraceful to live under Caesar’s victory, why did the father, the author of this disgrace—

[Note: [Column 0037] The word *pater* (“father”) is absent from the manuscripts.]

—urge his son to hope for everything from Caesar’s clemency? Why did he not force him to die with him?

For if Torquatus laudably killed his son, who had fought against the enemy in defiance of orders, even though he had been victorious—

[Note: [Column 0037] Livy, book 8, chapter 7; Aulus Gellius, book 9, chapter 13; and Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 7, mention the consul Manlius Torquatus, who ordered his son Manlius to be struck down with an axe because he had fought contrary to orders, although successfully.]

—why did Cato, who did not spare himself, spare his defeated son after he had been defeated? Was it more disgraceful to be victorious against orders than to endure a victor against honor?

In no way, then, did Cato judge it disgraceful to live under the victorious Caesar. Otherwise he would have freed his son from this disgrace by the father’s sword—

[Note: [Column 0037] Some books read “by paternal madness.”]

What is the explanation, then, except that, to the extent that he loved his son, for whom he both hoped and wished that Caesar would spare him, he begrudged the glory of Caesar himself, lest Caesar should also spare Cato—as Caesar is said to have stated—

[Note: [Column 0037] After learning of Cato’s death, Caesar is said to have said: “O Cato, I begrudge you your death, for you have begrudged me the opportunity to save you.” Plutarch, *Cato*, chapter 72; Appian, *Civil Wars*, book 2, chapter 99.]

—or, to express it more mildly, was ashamed of it?

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### That Christians stand out much more in the virtue by which Regulus surpassed Cato

Those against whom we are arguing do not want us to prefer to Cato the holy man Job, who preferred to endure such dreadful evils in his flesh rather than escape all his torments by killing himself, or other saints of the highest authority and most trustworthy faith in our Scriptures, who preferred to endure captivity and the domination of enemies rather than inflict death upon themselves.

But from their own writings let us prefer Marcus Regulus to that same Marcus Cato. Cato had never defeated Caesar, to whom he scorned to submit after being defeated, and, so as not to submit, chose to be killed by his own hand.

Regulus, however, had already defeated the Carthaginians, and, as a Roman commander under Roman authority, had brought back a victory to the Roman people—a victory to be lamented if won from fellow citizens, but praised because it was won from enemies. Yet, after being defeated by them, he preferred to endure serving them rather than remove himself from them by dying.

Thus he maintained both patience under the domination of the Carthaginians and constancy in his love for the Romans, neither taking his defeated body away from his enemies nor his unconquered spirit away from his fellow citizens.

He did not refuse to kill himself because he loved this life. He proved this when, because of the obligation of his promise and oath, he returned without hesitation to the same enemies whom he had offended more severely by his words in the senate than by his weapons in war.

Thus, though he despised this life so greatly that, when enemies raged, he preferred to end it through whatever punishments rather than kill himself, he undoubtedly judged that it was a great crime for a person to kill himself.

Among all their praiseworthy men, distinguished by their notable virtues, they cannot produce a better Roman: neither prosperity corrupted him, for amid such great victory he remained extremely poor—

[Note: [Column 0038] See Livy, book 18 of the epitome, and Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 4.]

—nor misfortune broke him, for he returned fearlessly to such terrible punishments.

Moreover, if the bravest and most distinguished men, defenders of their earthly homeland and, though worshipers of false gods, not deceitful but exceedingly truthful swearers, men who could have killed their conquered enemies according to the custom and law of war, refused to kill themselves after being defeated by their enemies; and, although they were not at all afraid of death, preferred to endure victorious masters rather than inflict death upon themselves, how much more will Christians, worshiping the true God and longing for their heavenly homeland, refrain from this crime if divine providence temporarily subjects them to enemies, either to test or to correct them?

For the Most High, who came so humbly for their sake, does not abandon them in that humiliation—especially since they are bound by no military authority or laws of such military service to strike down the enemy after he has been conquered.

[Note: [Column 0038] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “to endure the conquered enemy,” which is less suitable.]

[XXV.] What sort of evil error, then, creeps over a person so that he kills himself either because he has sinned against an enemy or so that the enemy may not sin against him, when he does not dare to kill the enemy himself, whether he has sinned or is about to sin?

## CHAPTER XXV  
### That sin must not be avoided through sin

But it is to be feared and guarded against lest a body subjected to the lust of an enemy entice the mind, through a highly seductive pleasure, to consent to sin. Therefore, they say, a person ought to kill himself before committing this—not now because of another’s sin, but because of his own.

By no means will a mind do this—if it is subject to God and to his wisdom rather than to the concupiscence of the body—that is, consent to the lust of its flesh aroused by another’s lust.

[Note: [Column 0038] Some manuscripts read “arousing.” A little later, most have “than one who is subject to the body and to concupiscence.” Manuscript 766 reads “than one who is subject to the body and to pleasure.”]

Nevertheless, if it is a detestable and condemnable crime even to kill oneself, as the manifest truth proclaims, who could be so foolish as to say: “Let us sin now, lest perhaps we sin later; let us now commit murder, lest perhaps afterward we fall into adultery”?

If iniquity so dominates that sins are chosen rather than innocence, is an uncertain future adultery not preferable to a certain present murder? Is it not better to commit a disgraceful act that can be healed by repentance than such a crime that leaves no place for saving repentance?

I have said this for the sake of those men or women who think they ought to inflict violence upon themselves so that they may die, in order to avoid not another’s sin but their own—lest, under another’s lust, their own lust perhaps also be aroused and they consent.

But far be it from the Christian mind, which trusts in its God—

[Note: [Column 0038] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads “which trusts in its God.”]

—and rests its hope upon him, relying on his help; far be it, I say, from such a mind to yield to any bodily pleasures in consent to disgrace.

[Note: [Column 0038] Thus Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “to any pleasures.” Manuscript 766 likewise has this reading.]

And if that disobedience of desire which still dwells in mortal limbs moves, as though by its own law, contrary to the law of our will, how much more is there no guilt in the body of one who does not consent, if there is no guilt in the body of one who is asleep?

## CHAPTER XXVI — How deeds known to have been performed by holy women, although they are not permitted, should be understood

“But,” they say, “certain holy women, during the persecution, threw themselves into a river that would carry them away and kill them, in order to escape those who were attacking their chastity. In this way they died, and their martyrdoms are celebrated throughout the Catholic Church with the greatest veneration.” [Note: In ancient times this kind of martyrdom became famous in the Church. Ambrose praised Pelagia, her sisters, and their mother in *On Virgins*, book 3, and in Letter 7 to Simplicianus. They may perhaps not have been other women, as Baronius suspects under the year 303, but those mentioned by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 8, chapter 24.]

I dare not pass judgment rashly concerning these women. For I do not know whether divine authority persuaded the Church, through testimonies worthy of belief, to honor their memory in this way; and it may indeed have been so. For what if they did this not because they had been deceived humanly, but because they had been commanded divinely—not while they were in error, but while they were obeying? So it is with Samson: we are not permitted to believe anything else concerning him. [Note: See above, chapter 21.]

But when God commands, and makes it known without any ambiguity that he commands, who could call obedience a crime? Who could accuse an act of dutiful submission? Yet it does not follow that anyone who resolves to sacrifice his son to God acts without sin, simply because Abraham also did this commendably. For a soldier, too, when he kills a man in obedience to the authority under which he has been lawfully placed, is not guilty of homicide under any law of his state; indeed, if he failed to do so, he would be guilty of deserting and despising his military command. [Note: Most manuscripts read, “under which he has been constituted by the laws.” Manuscript 766 reads “lawfully” for “by the laws.” M.] [Note: If *soldier* here is understood as the executioner and interrogator who kills a condemned man, there is no need, with Leonardo Coquaeus, to distinguish the matter according to a just war or one whose injustice is uncertain to the soldier. That an interrogator was also called a soldier is clear from other passages of Augustine. In Sermon 302, section 13, he says: “Consider, among the ranks of the authorities, one appointed to punishment and condemned … he may not be struck except by one who serves as a soldier for this purpose. The interrogator serves as a soldier; the condemned man is struck by him.” This should apparently be explained by another passage of Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, book 1, sections 11–12: “For a soldier too is commanded by law to kill the enemy; if he refrains from that killing, he suffers punishment from the commander.”]

But if he had done this on his own initiative and authority, he would have fallen into the crime of shedding human blood. Therefore, by the very authority by which he is punished if he acts without an order, he will be punished if he fails to act when ordered. If this is so when the commander orders it, how much more when the Creator orders it?

Therefore, whoever hears that he may not kill himself should do so if the one whose commands may not be despised has ordered it—provided only that he carefully consider whether the divine command is truly certain and unmistakable. We knock at the door of conscience through the ear; we do not usurp judgment over hidden things. “No one knows what is in a person except the person’s own spirit, which is within him” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

This is what we say, affirm, and establish by every possible argument: no one ought to inflict voluntary death upon himself as though by fleeing temporal troubles he might avoid eternal ones; no one ought to do so because of the sins of others, lest he himself begin to possess as a most grievous personal sin what had not polluted him when it belonged to another; no one ought to do so because of his own past sins, since those sins are precisely why this life is more necessary, so that they may be healed through repentance; and no one ought to do so as though out of desire for the better life hoped for after death, because the better life after death does not receive those who are guilty of their own death.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Whether voluntary death should be desired in order to avoid sin

There remains one reason, which I had begun to discuss, for which it is thought useful for a person to kill himself: namely, lest he fall into sin, whether seduced by pleasure or overcome by raging pain.

If we admit this reason, it will advance so far that people ought to be urged to kill themselves precisely when, washed in the bath of holy regeneration, they have received remission of all their sins. For that is the time to guard against all future sins, when all past sins have been erased. But if voluntary death is rightly chosen, why is it not chosen above all at that moment? Why does each baptized person spare himself? Why does he thrust his liberated head once more into so many dangers of this life, when by the simplest act of killing himself he could avoid them all, and when it is written: “Whoever loves danger will fall into it” (Ecclesiasticus 3:27)?

Why, then, are so many and such great dangers loved—or at least, even if they are not loved, undertaken—when a person remains in this life although he is permitted to depart from it? Has such foolish perversity truly overturned the heart and turned it away from consideration of the truth, so that if a person ought to kill himself lest he fall into sin under the domination of one captor, he should nevertheless think himself obliged to live in order to endure the world itself, full of temptations at every hour, temptations of the kind feared under a single master, and countless others without which this life cannot be lived? [Note: Some manuscripts have *of the kind feared under a single master*. Others read *such as are feared under a single master*. Several, together with the printed editions of Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and Louvain, have *of such a kind as is feared under a single master*.]

Why, then, do we spend time in those exhortations by which we strive, in addressing the baptized, to kindle them toward virginal integrity, widowly continence, or even fidelity to the marriage bed, when we have better shortcuts removed from every danger of sin? By these shortcuts, if we could persuade people to seize death and inflict it upon themselves immediately after the recent remission of their sins, we would send them to the Lord healthier and purer.

Moreover, if anyone thinks that this should be undertaken and recommended, I will not say that he is foolish, but that he is insane. With what face, then, could he say to someone, “Kill yourself, lest, while you live under a master barbarous and unchaste, you add a greater sin to your small sins”? For he could not say anything more criminally than this: “Kill yourself, once all your sins have been absolved, lest you commit such sins again, or even worse ones, while you live in a world alluring through so many impure pleasures, frenzied with so many unspeakable cruelties, and hostile through so many errors and terrors.”

Since it is wicked to say this, it is certainly wicked to kill oneself. For if any just reason for doing this voluntarily could exist, there would plainly be no more just reason than this one. But since even this is not just, there is no such reason at all.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — By what judgment of God hostile lust was permitted to sin against the bodies of continent women

### 1

Therefore, faithful women of Christ, do not let your life be burdensome to you because your chastity was made a spectacle for your enemies. You possess a great and genuine consolation if you retain a clear conscience: you did not consent to the sins of those who were permitted to sin against you. [XXVIII.]

But if you perhaps ask why they were permitted to do so, the providence of the Creator and Ruler of the world is indeed profound, “his judgments are inscrutable, and his ways untraceable” (Romans 11:33). Nevertheless, examine your souls faithfully, lest perhaps you lifted yourselves too proudly on account of this good of integrity, continence, or chastity, and, taking pleasure in human praise, even envied some others because of it.

I do not accuse what I do not know, nor do I hear what your questioned hearts answer you. Yet if they answer that this was so, do not be surprised that you have lost the thing by which you eagerly sought to please human beings, while what cannot be displayed to human beings has remained with you.

If you did not consent to those who sinned, divine assistance was added to divine grace so that it might not be lost; human disgrace followed upon human glory so that it might not be loved. Take consolation in both, you who are fainthearted: on one side you were tested, on the other chastened; on one side justified, on the other corrected.

But those whose hearts, when questioned, answer that they never took pride in the good of virginity, widowhood, or married chastity, but rejoiced with trembling in God’s gift, agreeing with the humble (Romans 12:16), and never envied anyone else’s excellence in holiness and chastity—those who, setting human praise aside, preferred that the number of such women should be greater rather than that they themselves should stand out more prominently in a small group, since praise is usually offered in greater measure to the rarer good that demands it—such women should not complain that this was permitted, even if barbarous lust violated some of them. Nor should they therefore believe that God neglects these events because he permits what no one commits with impunity.

For certain burdens, as it were, of evil desires are released through God’s present but hidden judgment, and reserved for the manifest final judgment. [Note: In the Louvain edition, *certain things* is repeated in this manner: “and certain things are reserved for the manifest final judgment,” which conflicts with the sense and with the other books.]

Perhaps, however, these women, who rightly know that their hearts were not inflated and exalted by the good of chastity, nevertheless endured hostile violence in the flesh because they possessed some hidden weakness that might have been raised into the arrogance of pride had they escaped that devastation in humility.

Therefore, just as some were taken away by death “lest wickedness change their understanding” (Wisdom 4:11), so something was taken away from these women by force, lest prosperity change their modesty.

In the case of both groups—those who had already grown proud because they had endured no shameful contact from anyone, [Note: This is the reading of manuscripts of good authority. The printed editions read “had endured”; and below, “had been touched.”] and those who might perhaps have grown proud had they not been touched by the violence of the enemy—chastity was not taken away, but humility was taught. The tumor of pride that was already swelling in the first group was remedied; in the second, the pride that was threatening was forestalled. [Note: The printed editions read *was encountered*, but the reading in the fewer manuscripts is *was remedied*.]

### 2

Nor should we pass over the fact that some women who endured these things may have thought that the good of continence belonged among bodily goods, remaining intact only if no one’s lust touched the body. They may not have understood that it rests solely upon the strength of the will, aided by God, so that both body and spirit may be holy; nor that it is a good which cannot be taken away from an unwilling mind. Perhaps this error was removed from them.

For when they consider with what conscience they served God, and, with unshaken faith, do not believe that he could in any way abandon those who served and invoked him in this manner, [Note: Manuscript 766 reads “in no way.” M.] they cannot doubt how greatly chastity pleases him. They see that it necessarily follows that he would never have permitted such things to happen to his holy ones if the holiness he bestowed upon them and loves in them could perish in this way.

## CHAPTER XXIX — What the household of Christ should answer unbelievers when they reproach Christ for not freeing it from the fury of its enemies

The whole household of the supreme and true God possesses its consolation—not a deceptive one, nor one founded upon the hope of unstable or passing things. It does not regret even this temporal life, in which it is trained for eternal life; it uses earthly goods as a foreigner, without being captured by them, and through evils it is either tested or corrected.

But those who mock its testing and say to it, when it has perhaps fallen into some temporal misfortune, “Where is your God?” (Psalm 41:4), should themselves say where their gods are when they suffer the things they seek to avoid by worshiping those gods, or by insisting that they ought to be worshiped. [Note: It is sufficiently well known that this was customary in the days of the republic. But when Alaric was pressing Rome under siege, and plague and famine were afflicting the city, the senators decided that sacrifices should be offered in the Capitol and in the other temples to the divinities. So report Sozomen, book 9, chapter 6; Nicephorus Callistus, book 13, chapter 35; and Zosimus, book 5, chapter 41. Coquaeus.]

For the household of God answers:

“My God is present everywhere, wholly present everywhere, confined nowhere. He can be secretly present and absent without moving. When he harasses me with adverse circumstances, he either examines my merits or chastises my sins, and reserves eternal reward for me in return for the temporal evils I endure piously. But who are you, that it should be worthwhile to speak with you even about your gods, much less about my God, who is terrible above all gods? For ‘the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens’” (Psalm 95:4–5).

## CHAPTER XXX — The shameful prosperity in which those who complain about Christian times would wish to abound

If that Scipio Nasica of yours, once your pontiff, were alive—the man whom the entire senate selected as the best man when, amid the terror of the Punic War, the Phrygian rites were being introduced and an excellent man was being sought—you perhaps would not dare to look upon his face—he himself would restrain you from this shamelessness. [Note: When Italy had been exhausted by the Second Punic War and harassed by Hannibal, an image of the mother of the gods was brought from the Phrygian city of Pessinus. The Romans had understood from the Sibylline verses that it should be installed at Rome so that the enemies might be driven away. When an excellent man was being sought, on the order of the Delphic oracle, to receive it properly, Scipio Nasica was chosen. From Cicero, *Speech on the Responses of the Haruspices*, chapter 13; Livy, book 29, chapter 14; and others.]

For why do you complain about Christian times when you are afflicted by misfortunes, unless you want your luxury to be secure and, with every restraint of hardship removed, to revel in utterly depraved ways? You do not desire peace and abundance of every kind of resource so that you may use these goods honorably—that is, moderately, soberly, temperately, and piously—but so that an infinite variety of pleasures may be sought through insane extravagance, and so that prosperity may produce moral evils worse than raging enemies.

But that Scipio, your chief pontiff, chosen by the judgment of the entire senate of that age—as must often be emphasized—as the best of men, fearing this calamity for you, did not want Carthage, then Rome’s rival in imperial power, to be destroyed. When Cato proposed that it be destroyed, Scipio opposed him, fearing that security would become an enemy to weak minds, and seeing that terror was necessary to citizens who were, as it were, orphans in need of a suitable guardian. [Note: Plutarch, *Cato the Elder*; Livy, book 49, epitome, and elsewhere.]

His judgment did not deceive him. The truth of what he said was proved by events themselves. For once Carthage had been destroyed—once the great terror of the Roman state had been removed and extinguished—such great evils immediately followed upon prosperity that, after concord had been corrupted and broken, first through savage and bloody seditions, [Note: Those of Tiberius Gracchus and then of his brother Gaius, in which civil bloodshed first occurred. The former took place ten years after the destruction of Carthage. Ludovicus Vives.] and then through the linking of evil causes, such slaughter was produced by civil wars and such blood was shed, while the frenzy of proscriptions and plunder burned with such ferocity, that those Romans who, when their lives were more upright, feared evils from their enemies suffered, after losing their integrity of life, even more cruel things at the hands of their fellow citizens. [Note: From the sedition of Gaius Gracchus arose the tribunate of Livius Drusus, whom the senators set against the equestrians who judged according to the Gracchan law. From this came the Social War, because the citizenship promised by Livius Drusus was not granted. From this came the Mithridatic War, when Mithridates, king of Pontus, relying on Italy’s discord, ordered many thousands of citizens conducting business in his kingdom to be killed. From this came the civil wars of Marius, when Marius wished to take the province and the Mithridatic War away from Lucius Sulla. From these seeds came the wars of Sertorius and Lepidus, Catiline’s conspiracy, and finally the war against Pompey. Then came Caesar’s rule; after Caesar was killed, the civil wars followed: the Antonian War, the Philippian War of Brutus and Cassius, the Sicilian War of Sextus Pompey, and the Actium War. At last the republic was transformed into monarchy and tyranny. Ludovicus Vives. See also Sallust, *War with Jugurtha*, chapter 41 and following; Velleius Paterculus, beginning of book 2.]

That very lust for domination, which was more unmixed than the other vices of the human race and had existed throughout the Roman people, after it had prevailed among a few who were more powerful, also crushed and exhausted the rest beneath the yoke of slavery.

## CHAPTER XXXI — Through what stages of vice the Roman desire to rule grew

For when would that desire have ceased in those most arrogant minds, until, through a continuous succession of offices, it reached royal power? The opportunity for continuing offices would not have existed unless ambition had prevailed. Ambition would not have prevailed at all unless the people had been corrupted by greed and luxury.

A greedy and luxurious people became so through prosperity—the very prosperity that Scipio Nasica, with the greatest foresight, judged must be feared. He did not want the greatest, strongest, and wealthiest enemy city to be removed, so that fear might restrain desire, desire so restrained might not run riot, [Note: Some manuscripts read “with desire restrained.” This is also the reading of Codex 766. M.] and luxury, once checked, might not allow greed to rage. When these vices were barred, virtue useful to the state would flourish and grow, and a freedom suited to that virtue would remain with it.

This too arose from, and proceeded from, that same most provident love of country: your chief pontiff, chosen by the senate of that age—as must often be said—as the best man, without any disagreement in the voting, restrained the senate when it was attempting to build a theater auditorium. [Note: The theater was called a *cavea* because, being suitably furnished with benches for the spectators’ seating, it resembled a kind of cave. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, book 1, section 51, says: “The theaters fall—the caves of depravity and the public professions of shameful acts.”]

By a most serious speech he persuaded them not to allow Greek luxury to insinuate itself into the manly customs of their country, nor to join foreign depravity in weakening and enervating Roman virtue. His authority carried such weight that, moved by his words, the senate’s prudence thereafter forbade the benches that the people had already begun to use, once they had been hastily set up for the duration of the games, from being placed there again. [Note: This is reported by Livy, book 48, epitome; Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 4, section 2; and Appian, book 1, *On the Civil Wars*, chapter 28.]

With how much greater determination would he have removed the theatrical games themselves from Rome if he had dared to resist the authority of those whom he believed to be gods—those whom he did not understand to be harmful demons, or whom, if he did understand this, he nevertheless thought should be appeased rather than despised!

For the heavenly teaching that was to be proclaimed among the nations had not yet been revealed: the teaching that, by cleansing the heart through faith, changes the human disposition through humble devotion so that it may pursue heavenly or superheavenly things, and frees it from the domination of proud demons.

## CHAPTER XXXII — The institution of theatrical games

Nevertheless, know these things, you who do not know them; and you who pretend not to know them, pay attention—you who murmur against the liberator from such masters. [Note: Erasmus alone has “you who murmur, having been liberated from such masters,” which is less satisfactory.]

Theatrical games, spectacles of depravity, and license for frivolity were instituted at Rome not because of human vices but at the command of your gods.

You would confer divine honors more tolerably upon that Scipio than worship such gods; for those gods were no better than their own pontiff.

Observe, if your mind, drunk for so long on the wine of error, permits you to consider anything sound. The gods ordered theatrical performances to be exhibited to them in order to calm the pestilence of bodies. [Note: Livy, book 7, chapter 2; Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 4, section 4.] But the pontiff, to guard against the pestilence of souls, prohibited the theater itself from being built.

If, in any light of understanding, you place the soul above the body, choose which one you will worship.

Nor did the bodily pestilence subside because a delicate madness of theatrical games entered among a warlike people previously accustomed only to circus games. Rather, the cunning of wicked spirits foresaw that the pestilence would soon cease at its proper end and used this opportunity to introduce another pestilence, far more serious and one in which they greatly rejoice—not into bodies, but into morals.

That pestilence so blinded the minds of the wretched with darkness and so disfigured them with deformity that even now—something that may perhaps seem incredible if our descendants hear it from us—after the city of Rome had been devastated, those whom this pestilence had possessed, and who were able to flee from there and reach Carthage, went mad every day in the theaters, competing to support the actors.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — The vices of the Romans, whom the destruction of their country did not correct

O deranged minds! What is this immense thing—not error, but madness—that, while the peoples of the East were mourning your destruction, as we have heard, and while the greatest cities in the most distant lands were observing public mourning and grief, you sought out theaters, entered them, filled them, and behaved even more insanely than before?

That stain upon your souls, that overthrow of probity and decency, was what Scipio feared for you when he prohibited the construction of theaters; when he saw that prosperity could easily corrupt and ruin you; and when he did not want you to be secure from the terror of the enemy.

For he did not consider a state happy when its walls stood but its morals collapsed. Yet in you what the impious demons led you astray into has had greater power than what prudent human beings sought to prevent.

This is why you do not want the evils you commit to be charged to you, but charge the evils you suffer to Christian times. For in your security you do not seek a peaceful state, but luxury without punishment—you who, corrupted by prosperity, could not be corrected even by adversity.

That Scipio wanted you to be frightened by the enemy, lest you should flow into luxury. You, even when crushed by the enemy, did not restrain your luxury. You lost the benefit of calamity: you became most miserable and remained most depraved.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — The mercy of God, by which he tempered the destruction of the city

And yet that you are alive is God’s doing. By sparing you, he warns you to correct yourselves through repentance. Even to you, though ungrateful, he granted the means of escaping hostile hands either under the name of his servants or in the places belonging to his martyrs.

Romulus and Remus are said to have established an asylum where anyone who took refuge would be free from every charge, seeking in this way to increase the population of the city they were founding.

A remarkable precedent was offered beforehand in honor of Christ. [Note: Most manuscripts, together with Vindobonensis, have *was advanced* rather than *preceded*. This is also the reading in our manuscripts.]

The destroyers of the city established what its founders had established earlier. But what great thing is it if the founders did this so that the number of their citizens might be increased, while the destroyers did it so that the multitude of their enemies might be preserved?

## CHAPTER XXXV — The sons of the Church hidden among the impious, and false Christians within the Church

Let the redeemed household of the Lord Christ and the pilgrim city of Christ the King answer these and similar objections, if it can do so more fully and suitably. [XXXV.]

Let it certainly remember that among its very enemies there lie hidden future citizens, lest it think fruitless, even among them, that it bears them as enemies until it reaches their confession. [Note: *Those who confess* does not mean the final declaration, when consciences will be exposed in the future life, as Ludovicus Vives interprets it, but the profession of the Christian faith that they must make in the present life in order to be admitted into Christ’s household.]

For from their number the city of God also has with it, so long as it journeys in this world, people joined to it by communion in the sacraments who will not be with it in the eternal lot of the saints. Some of these are hidden, others are open. Even among the enemies themselves, they do not hesitate to murmur against God, whose sacrament they bear—at one time filling the theaters with them, at another filling the churches with us.

There is even less reason to despair of correcting some of these people, since among the most open adversaries there lie hidden friends predestined to become such, though they are still unknown even to themselves.

For these two cities are entangled and intermingled in this age until they are separated by the final judgment. Concerning their origin, progress, and appointed ends, I shall explain what I think should be said, insofar as I am divinely assisted, for the glory of the city of God, which will shine more clearly when compared with those who are alien to it. [Note: Many manuscripts read *alternately* or *by contrast*.]

## CHAPTER XXXVI — The subjects to be discussed in the following argument

But I still have certain things to say against those who attribute the disasters of the Roman state to our religion, by which they are prohibited from sacrificing to their gods.

We must recall whatever evils, and however great, may come to mind—or may seem sufficient—that the city endured, or that the provinces subject to its rule endured, before their sacrifices had been prohibited. They would undoubtedly attribute all these things to us if our religion had already been clear to them, or if it had in this way prohibited them from their sacrilegious rites.

Next, we must show what kind of morals they possessed, and for what reason the true God—whose power governs all kingdoms—deigned to assist them in enlarging their empire. We must show how little those whom they regard as gods helped them, and indeed how much harm those gods caused by deceiving and misleading them.

Finally, we shall address those who, although refuted and convicted by the clearest evidence, try to assert that the gods should be worshiped not for the usefulness of the present life, but for the sake of the life that is to come after death.

If I am not mistaken, this question will demand much more labor and deserve a more elevated discussion. It will require us to argue against philosophers—not against just any philosophers, but against those who enjoy the highest glory among them and who agree with us on many points: concerning the immortality of the soul, the fact that the true God created the world, and his providence by which he governs the whole universe that he created. [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts agree almost unanimously on *more subtle*. Erasmus has *subtle*. According to our codices, *more subtle* should be read.]

But since even in those matters in which they disagree with us they must be refuted, we ought not to fail in this task. Once their impious objections have been refuted to the extent of the strength God grants us, we must assert the city of God, true piety, and the worship of God, in which alone eternal blessedness is truly promised.

Let this, then, be the limit of this volume, so that from here onward we may take up our beginning from another point.

# BOOK TWO

In this book, an argument is undertaken concerning the evils that Rome suffered before Christ, while the worship of false gods was flourishing. It is first demonstrated that the Romans were not liberated from the evils of morals and the vices of the soul—evils that ought to be regarded either as the only evils or as the greatest evils—but were instead burdened with them through the agency of false gods.

## CHAPTER I — The manner required by the necessity of the argument

If the human understanding, weakened by habit, did not dare to resist the clear reason of truth, but submitted its sickness to salutary teaching as to medicine until it was healed through the divine assistance obtained by faithful devotion, there would be no need for a lengthy discourse to refute any error of vain opinion for those who think rightly and explain their thoughts in adequate words.

But now the greater and more terrible sickness of foolish minds is this: even after a full explanation has been given, with all that one person owes another, they defend their irrational impulses as though they were reason and truth. [Note: Some manuscripts read “worse” instead of “more terrible.”] This happens either through excessive blindness, by which they do not see what is plain, or through the most stubborn perversity, by which they cannot tolerate even what they do see.

Consequently, we are often compelled to speak at length about matters that are clear, as though we were offering them for inspection to people who do not look at them, but who, in a manner of speaking, grope at them as though they had to touch them, while keeping their eyes closed.

Yet what end will there be to disputing and what limit to speaking if we always think that we must answer those who answer us? Those who cannot understand what is said, or who are so hard through the perversity of their minds that, even when they understand, they do not obey, answer and “speak iniquity” (Psalm 93:4), and are vain without tiring.

If we wanted to refute their contrary statements every time they resolved, with an unyielding front, not to care what they say, [Note: The older books read “not to think.” This is also the reading of manuscript 766. M.] provided only that they contradicted our arguments in some way, you can see how endless, wearisome, and fruitless that would be.

Therefore, my son Marcellinus, I do not want you—or others whom this labor of mine serves usefully and generously in the love of Christ—to judge my writings by expecting an answer every time you hear something contradicted in what you read. Otherwise you may become like those little women whom the Apostle mentions: “always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 3:7).

## CHAPTER II — What was dealt with in the first book

In the preceding book, when I had undertaken to speak about the city of God—the subject from which, with God’s assistance, this entire work was begun—I saw that I first had to answer those who attribute the wars by which this world is crushed, and especially the recent devastation of the city of Rome by the barbarians, to the Christian religion, by which they are forbidden to serve demons through wicked sacrifices. [Note: Most manuscripts have *resist* rather than *answer*. This is also the reading of manuscript 766.]

Rather, they ought to attribute to Christ the fact that, because of his name and contrary to the established custom and practice of warfare, the barbarians provided them with religious and very spacious places, left inviolate, to which they might flee. In many cases they honored service devoted to Christ—whether genuine or merely feigned through fear—in such a way that they judged unlawful for themselves what the law of war would have permitted them to do against those people. [Note: The better manuscripts read *service devoted*; the printed editions read *service owed*.]

From this arose the question why these divine benefits reached even the impious and ungrateful, and why those harsh acts likewise, acts committed with hostility, afflicted the pious together with the impious.

I lingered for some time over this question, which extends over many matters; for it often troubles many people in connection with all daily gifts of God and human calamities, both of which frequently befall good and evil alike, mingled and without distinction, in order to resolve it as the task I had undertaken required. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain have *they are accustomed*; Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and several manuscripts more suitably have *it is accustomed*: understand “that question,” which he says is extended over many matters. Our manuscripts have *they are accustomed*.]

I did so especially to console holy and pious women whose chastity had been violated by the enemy in a way that inflicted the pain of shame but did not remove the steadfastness of their purity, lest they regret their lives when they have no reason to regret their wickedness. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain have *among whom*. It is unnecessary to add *among*, which is absent from the other books.]

Next, I said a few things against those who, with the most shameless insolence, harass Christians afflicted by those misfortunes, and especially the modesty of humiliated women, even though they are utterly depraved and irreverent, degenerate far from those very Romans whose many noble qualities are praised and celebrated in literary memory—indeed, violently opposed to their glory.

They had made the Rome acquired and enlarged through the labors of the ancients more shameful when standing than when falling. For in its ruin, stones and timbers fell, but in their lives every defense and adornment—not of walls, but of morals—collapsed; their hearts burned with more disastrous desires than the buildings of that city burned with fire. [Note: Louvain has *the Rome acquired with care*. Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmus have *the Rome built with care*. But the manuscripts consistently have *acquired* and lack the word *with care*.]

With these words I brought the first book to an end.

From that point, therefore, I began to discuss the evils that this city endured from its origin, whether within its own boundaries or in the provinces already subject to it—evils that they would attribute entirely to the Christian religion if, even then, the evangelical teaching had resounded with complete freedom against their false and deceitful gods.

## CHAPTER III — The history to be taken up in order to show what evils befell the Romans while they worshiped the gods, before the Christian religion began to spread extensively
Remember, however, that in recalling these matters I am still arguing against the uninstructed, from whose ignorance this common proverb also arose: “The rain is lacking because of Christians.”

[Note: [Col. 0049] The printed editions read *defecit* (“has failed”); three of them—Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus—continue, “because of the Christian name.” But the old books do not add “name,” and all read *defit* (“is lacking”) instead of *defecit*. Several manuscripts of the best quality, omitting some intervening particles, punctuate the following words thus: “because they are Christians.” For those educated in their liberal studies who love history know these matters very easily. So too our manuscripts.]

There are indeed people educated in liberal studies who love history and therefore know these matters very easily; but, in order to make the crowds of the uneducated intensely hostile to us, they pretend not to know them and strive to confirm among the common people that the disasters by which the human race must be afflicted at fixed intervals of place and time occur because of the Christian name, which is spread throughout the world with immense renown and the most illustrious fame, in opposition to their gods.

[Note: The proverb directed against Christians is recorded in slightly different words in *Expositions on the Psalms* 80.1.]

[Note: Among those learned dissemblers must be counted Aurelius Symmachus, prefect of the City, who wrote such things in the *Report* submitted to Valentinian in the year 384, which Saint Ambrose refuted. See section 14 in the Ambrosian edition. In order to refute that calumny, Paul Orosius, at Augustine’s request, undertook to write his *History*. See his preface addressed to Augustine.]

Let them therefore recall with us that, before Christ had come in the flesh, before his name had become known among the peoples with that glory which they vainly envy, the Roman state had been crushed by calamities of many kinds and in many ways. In these matters let them defend their gods, if they can—if those gods are worshiped for the purpose of preventing their worshipers from suffering such evils, which, if their worshipers now suffer any of them, they insist must be charged to us. Why, then, did those gods permit the evils I am about to mention to befall their worshipers before the name of Christ, once proclaimed, had offended them and forbidden their sacrifices?

## Chapter IV — How the Worshipers of the Gods Never Received from Their Gods Any Precepts of Moral Conduct, and How Every Kind of Shameful Practice Was Celebrated in Their Sacred Rites

First, why did their gods not take care that their worshipers should not have the worst possible morals? The true God deservedly neglected those who did not worship him; but those gods, whose worship human beings—most ungratefully, they complain—are prevented from practicing, why did they not assist their worshipers in living well by any laws at all? Surely it would have been appropriate that, just as these people cared for the sacred rites of those gods, so those gods should care for the deeds of these people.

But the answer is given that each person is wicked by his own choice. Who could deny this? Nevertheless, it was the responsibility of the gods who were consulted not to conceal from the peoples who worshiped them the precepts of a good life, but to provide them through clear proclamation; to address and rebuke sinners through prophets; openly to threaten punishments for those who acted wickedly and promise rewards to those who lived rightly. What such thing ever rang out in a clear and commanding voice in the temples of those gods?

In our youth, we too sometimes went to spectacles and mockeries of sacrilege.

[Note: [Col. 0050] He reverses the false designation by which pagans called sacred games, or rites of games, sacred.]

We watched the possessed and listened to the performers of musical instruments; we took pleasure in the most shameful games presented to gods and goddesses, to the virgin Caelestis and to the mother of all, Berecynthia. Before her litter, on the solemn day of her ritual washing, the most wicked actors publicly sang such things as would be unworthy to hear not only for the mother of the gods, but for the mother of any senators or respectable men whatsoever—indeed, such things as even the actors’ own mothers ought not to hear.

[Note: Caelestis received a particularly prominent worship in Africa, as Tertullian testifies in *Apology* 24. He also speaks of her in chapter 23 of the same work, and Augustine mentions her in many places, including *Expositions on the Psalms* 62.7 and 98.14, and Sermon 105.12. Ludovicus Vives, compelled by no authority or argument, here confuses her with the mother of the gods, Berecynthia. Augustine, however, clearly distinguishes them, inserting the connecting particle and then adding “and to Berecynthia, mother of all”—that is, of gods and goddesses. The manuscripts left this to be supplied; the printed editions add “of gods.”]

For human modesty has toward parents a certain regard that even depravity itself cannot remove. The actors themselves would have been ashamed to perform at home, before their mothers, for the sake of rehearsal, the obscenity of words and deeds that they performed publicly before the mother of the gods, while an enormous crowd of both sexes watched and listened. If curiosity enticed that crowd to be present, at least offended chastity ought to have driven it away in shame.

[Note: On the day before the Ides of April, the Great Mother of the Gods was led by her priests in a magnificent procession to the Almo River, which flows into the Tiber not far from Rome. There, at the confluence of the two rivers, she was washed according to an ancient custom. On the first day when she had been brought there from Asia, she had been washed by a priest, and this rite thereafter became sacred and was repeated every year. Ovid discusses the custom in *Fasti* 4.337 ff.; Lucan in book 1, line 600; and Prudentius in *The Martyrdom of Romanus*.]

What kind of sacrilege is this, if those practices are sacred? What kind of pollution, if that is a washing? They called these performances *Fercula*, as though a banquet were being celebrated, by which the unclean demons might be fed, as it were, with their own feasts. Who could fail to perceive what sort of spirits delight in such obscenities—unless he is ignorant whether there are any unclean spirits deceiving people under the name of gods, or unless he is living in such a way that he wishes these spirits, rather than the true God, to be favorably disposed toward him and fears them when they are angry?

## Chapter V — The Obscenities by Which the Mother of the Gods Was Honored by Her Worshipers

I would not wish the judges of this matter to be those people who strive to take pleasure in the vices of a most disgraceful custom rather than to resist them, but that very Scipio Nasica, who was chosen by the senate as an excellent man and into whose hands the image of that same demon was received and carried into Rome. He could tell us whether he would have wished his mother to deserve so well of the state that divine honors should be decreed to her, just as it is agreed that the Greeks, Romans, and other peoples decreed such honors to certain mortals whose benefits toward them they had valued highly, believing that those persons had been made immortal and received among the number of the gods.

[Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* 2.24: “Human life and common custom have adopted the practice of raising to heaven, through popular report and public consent, men outstanding for their benefits.”]

Surely, if it had been possible, he would have wished such great happiness for his mother. But if we then asked him whether he would have wished those shameful practices to be celebrated among her divine honors, would he not have loudly declared that he would rather his mother lie dead without any sensation whatever than live as a goddess in order to hear such things willingly?

Far be it from us to suppose that a Roman senator endowed with the spirit by which he prohibited a theater from being built in the city for brave men would have wished his mother to be worshiped in such a way that she might be propitiated by sacred rites of a kind that would offend a respectable woman merely through their words. Nor would he in any way have believed that the modesty of a praiseworthy woman could be transformed by divinity into its opposite, so that her worshipers would summon her to honors of the sort that, if hurled as insults against anyone while she was living among human beings, would cause her relatives, husband, and children to blush for her unless they closed their ears and withdrew.

Thus this mother of the gods—such a mother that any, even the worst, man would be ashamed to have her—when she sought to take possession of Roman minds, sought an excellent man, not one whom she would make good by admonishing and assisting, but one whom she would deceive by misleading him. She was like the woman of whom it is written: “The woman captures the precious souls of men” (Proverbs 6:26). In this way that mind of great natural ability, exalted as though by divine testimony,

[Note: Several manuscripts read “raised up” rather than “exalted.”]

and truly believing itself to be excellent, would not seek true piety and religion, without which every talent, however praiseworthy, withers and falls through pride. How, then, unless by treachery, could that goddess seek an excellent man, when in her sacred rites she sought things such as excellent men would shrink from admitting into their own banquets?

## Chapter VI — That the Pagan Gods Never Established a Doctrine of Right Living

This is why they took no care for the life and morals of the cities and peoples by whom those divinities were worshiped, allowing them to become filled with such dreadful and detestable evils

[Note: [Col. 0051] Here the manuscripts add *eos* (“them”), though they nevertheless retain it below before the word “to be filled.”]

—not in their fields and vineyards, not in their homes and possessions, nor finally in the body itself, which is subject to the mind, but in the mind itself, in the spirit that governs the flesh—and to become utterly depraved without any terrifying prohibition from those gods.

Or, if they did prohibit such things, let this be shown and established. Let them not parade before us certain whispers breathed into the ears of a very few and handed down as though by a secret religion, by which moral integrity and chastity were supposedly learned. Let places be pointed out or mentioned that were ever consecrated to such gatherings—not places where games were performed with the obscene words and gestures of actors, nor where the Fugalia were celebrated with every license of shameful behavior (truly a “Fugalia,” but a flight from modesty and decency),

[Note: The Fugalia were Roman festivals established in memory of the expulsion of the kings and the liberation of the republic. They were celebrated in February after the Terminalia had been completed.]

but places where the peoples heard what the gods commanded concerning the restraint of greed, the breaking of ambition, and the curbing of luxury; where the wretched learned what Persius rebuked them for needing to learn, when he said:

> Learn, miserable men, and recognize the causes of things:
>
> What are we, or for what future are we born? What order
>
> Has been assigned to us? Where is the gentle turning of the goal,
>
> And from where?
>
> What is the proper measure of money? What is it right to desire?
>
> What stern usefulness does money possess?
>
> How much is fitting to give to one’s country and dear relatives?
>
> Whom has God commanded you to be,
>
> And in what part of human affairs has he placed you?
>
> (*Satire* 3.66–72)

[Note: Our manuscripts read *discite*, omitting the particle *-que*, which is required by the poetic meter. Manuscript 766 reads *agnoscite*, as do the Benedictine Fathers; all the others read *cognoscite*.]

[Note: Several manuscripts read *quidnam venturi* (“for what future we are born”), and some *quonam venturi* (“toward what we are destined to come”).]

[Note: In manuscript B the reading is *quam mollis*. Manuscript 2050 has the same. We preferred the reading of manuscripts 2051, 2052, and 2053.]

[Note: Some manuscripts read *undae*, with a diphthong in the second syllable. This is not inappropriate if the poet perhaps alludes to the turning-post established in the naval combat, toward which the ship had suddenly to turn, as may be seen in Virgil, *Aeneid* 5.]

Let it be stated in what places the precepts of gods who taught such things were customarily recited and frequently heard by the peoples who worshiped them, just as we show that churches have been established for this purpose wherever the Christian religion is spread.

## Chapter VII — Philosophical Discoveries Are Useless Without Divine Authority, Since One Who Is Inclined to Vice Is More Moved by What the Gods Did Than by What Human Beings Discussed

Or perhaps they will remind us of the schools and debates of philosophers. In the first place, these are not Roman but Greek; or, if they are now Roman because Greece too has become a Roman province, they are not precepts of the gods but inventions of human beings, who, endowed with exceptionally keen intellects, made whatever efforts they could through reasoning to investigate what lay hidden in the nature of things, what should be pursued or avoided in morals, what followed by a certain connection in the very rules of reasoning, and what was inconsistent or even contradictory.

Some of them discovered certain great truths insofar as they were divinely assisted; but insofar as they were hindered by human limitations, they went astray. This happened especially because divine providence justly resisted their pride, so that, even by comparison with them, it might display the path of piety that rises from humility to the heights. We shall therefore later have occasion, by the will of the Lord, the true God,

[Note: Lovaniensis reads “the true God and Lord.” The other books lack the connecting particle *and*, so that *true* modifies the noun *Lord*.]

to investigate and discuss this matter.

Nevertheless, if philosophers discovered anything that could suffice for living a good life and attaining blessedness, how much more justly would divine honors be decreed to such men? How much better and more honorably would their books be read in a temple of Plato than the Galli would be castrated in temples of demons, the soft effeminate devotees consecrated, the mad devotees mutilated, and whatever else is customarily celebrated in the sacred rites of such gods—whether cruel, shameful, shamefully cruel, or cruelly shameful?

[Note: The priests of the mother of the gods, Cybele or Berecynthia, were called Galli after the river Gallus, and they were castrated.]

How much more appropriate it would have been, for the instruction of youth in justice, that the laws of the gods be publicly recited than that the laws and institutions of the ancestors be praised to no purpose!

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions read “for instructing youth in justice.”]

For all worshipers of such gods, as soon as lust drives them—“stained,” as Persius says, “with burning poison” (*Satire* 3.37)—look more at what Jupiter did than at what Plato taught or Cato approved. Thus, in Terence, a dissolute young man looks at

> a certain painted panel on the wall, where there was a picture of Jupiter
>
> sending, as they say, a golden shower into Danaë’s lap.
>
> And from this great authority he derives a defense for his own shamefulness,
> boasting that in it he is imitating the god.
>
> “But which god?” he asks.
>
> “The one who shakes the temples of heaven with the greatest thunder.”
>
> “Would I, a little fellow, not do this? Indeed, I did it—and gladly.”
>
> (Terence, *The Eunuch*, act 3, scene 5, lines 36–37, 42–43.)

## Chapter VIII — In Scenic Games the Gods Were Not Offended by the Presentation of Their Shamefulness but Were Appeased by It

But, someone may say, these things are not handed down in the sacred rites of the gods, but in the poets’ stories. I do not wish to say that the mystical rites are more shameful than the theatrical performances—though they are. I say this, which refutes those who deny it: the Romans did not introduce those very games, in which the poets’ fictions reign, into the sacred rites of their gods through ignorant compliance; rather, the gods themselves, by issuing harsh commands and in a certain sense extorting it, caused the games to be produced solemnly for them and consecrated to their honor.
