I touched on this briefly in the first book (chapter 32).

For when a plague was growing more severe, scenic games were first established at Rome by the authority of the pontiffs. Who, then, in conducting his life would not think that he ought to pursue rather the things performed at games established by divine authority than the things written in laws promulgated by human counsel?

If the poets falsely represented Jupiter as an adulterer, surely the gods, being chaste—for such a great crime had been fabricated in human games, not neglected—ought to have become angry and exacted vengeance. These are the more tolerable scenic games: comedies and tragedies, that is, poets’ fictions performed in spectacles, composed with much shamefulness of subject matter but at least without the obscenity of language found in many other performances. Even these, however, boys are compelled by their elders to read and learn among the studies called honorable and liberal.

## Chapter IX — What the Ancient Romans Thought About Restraining Poetic License, Which the Greeks, Following the Judgment of Their Gods, Chose to Leave Free

Cicero testifies in the books he wrote on the Republic—books whose fragments are no longer extant, though some passages are preserved by Seneca, Nonius, Aulus Gellius, Lactantius, and others—what the ancient Romans thought about this. There Scipio,

[Note: This was Scipio Aemilianus, the son of Publius Aemilius, who defeated Perseus, king of Macedonia. He was adopted by the son of Scipio Africanus the Elder, destroyed Numantia and Carthage, and was called Africanus the Younger.]

arguing, says:

> “Comedies could never have approved their own theatrical abuses unless the customs of life had tolerated them.”

The earlier Greeks, for their part,

[Note: Vindobonensis and Lovaniensis read *quidam* (“certain Greeks”).]

maintained a certain consistency with their corrupt opinion. Among them the law even permitted comedy to say openly, by name, whatever it wished about whomever it wished. Thus, as Africanus says in the same books:

> “Whom did it not attack—or rather, whom did it not harass? Whom did it spare? Let us grant that it attacked Cleon, Cleophon, and Hyperbolus, popular men who were wicked and seditious in the state. We can endure this, although it is better that such citizens be marked by a censor than by a poet.”

[Note: [Col. 0054] On Cleon, Cleophon, and Hyperbolus, see Plutarch, *Nicias*, chapters 7 and 9; also Thucydides, book 4 of the *Peloponnesian War*; Cicero, *Brutus* 62; and Aristophanes.]

> “But But for Pericles,
>
> who had governed his state at home and in war for many years with the greatest authority, to be violated in verse and to have such verses performed on the stage was no more fitting than if our Plautus had wished to insult Publius and Gnaeus Scipio, or Caecilius Marcus Cato.”

[Note: Pericles, who held the leading position at Athens for many years in the administration of the state, is known from Plutarch, who wrote his biography, as well as from Thucydides 2, Cicero’s *On the Orator* 3, the *Brutus*, and the *Orator*.]

[Note: Plautus is called “our” by Scipio, who had never seen him, because he was a Latin poet; previously he had been speaking of Greek comic poets.]

[Note: Naevius, nearly the contemporary of Plautus, is said to have died at Utica in Africa, to which he had been driven by the faction of the nobles, especially the Metelli and Scipio Africanus, whom he had attacked in his verses. Aulus Gellius discusses him in 3.3, 6.8, and 8.14.]

[Note: [Col. 0054] Publius and Gnaeus Scipio were brothers and, if Servius is to be believed, twins. In his commentary on *Aeneid* 6, Servius interprets “the two Scipiads, thunderbolts of war” as referring to them. Cicero likewise calls them “the two thunderbolts of empire” in his speech for Cornelius Balbus and “the two bulwarks of war” in the first *Paradox*.]

[Note: Caecilius Statius, a comic poet of Gallic origin, was a companion of Ennius. Cicero mentions him in *Letters to Atticus* 7.3; Velleius in 1.17; and Aulus Gellius in 3.16, 2.23, and 17.21. Some books here and below, in chapter 12, write *Coelius*, but this is incorrect, as is clear from Horace, *Epistles* 2.1.57.]

[Note: The elder Cato is meant, the first of the Porcian family to hold public offices, who lived at the same time as Ennius and Caecilius.]

Then, shortly afterward, he says:

> “Our Twelve Tables, by contrast, although they sanctioned only a very few matters by capital punishment, thought that this too ought to be sanctioned: if anyone had sung an abusive song, or composed a poem that brought disgrace or shame upon another. Excellent. For we ought to have our life placed before the judgments of magistrates and in lawful proceedings, not before the ingenuity of poets; nor ought we to hear an insult unless under a law that permits us to respond and defend ourselves in court.”

[Note: The printed editions read *actitavisset*, but the manuscripts’ *occentavisset* is more accurate; this word also occurs in the surviving fragments of the Twelve Tables. The following explanation is written in the margin of the very old Corbeiensis manuscript: “To *occentare* is to utter an infamous song naming a person. To *occentare* is to sing an opposing song.” Festus gives nearly the same explanation, speaking of “a reproach made loudly and with a kind of melody.”]

[Note: The printed editions read *ac magistratuum*; the particle *ac* is absent from the manuscripts.]

I have thought it appropriate to excerpt these words from Cicero’s fourth book on the Republic, with a few omissions or slight alterations for ease of understanding. They are highly relevant to the matter I am attempting to explain, if I can.

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and several manuscripts read *pertinet* in the singular. Manuscript 766 does likewise.]

He then says other things and concludes this passage in such a way as to show that the ancient Romans disapproved of a living person being either praised or blamed on the stage. But, as I said, the Greeks, although more shamelessly, nevertheless more consistently chose to permit this, since they saw that their gods welcomed and enjoyed insults not only against human beings but also against the gods themselves in scenic stories—whether those insults were invented by poets or whether the gods’ actual crimes were being recalled and performed in theaters, and were regarded by their worshipers as worthy, if only of laughter—and, sadly, not only of imitation.

For it was excessively proud to spare the reputation of the leaders and citizens of the state when the divinities did not wish their own reputation to be spared.

## Chapter X — By What Art of Inflicting Harm the Demons Wish Either False or True Crimes to Be Reported About Them

What is offered in defense—that these things are not spoken about the gods as true, but as false and fabricated—is itself more wicked if one considers the piety owed to religion; but if one considers the demons’ malice, what could be more cunning or more skillful for deception?

When an insult is directed against a good and useful leader of his country, is it not all the more disgraceful the farther it is removed from the truth and the more alien it is to his life? What punishments, then, are sufficient when such a wicked and conspicuous injury is done to God?

But the malicious spirits whom these people consider gods wish even crimes they did not commit to be spoken of them, provided that they may lure human minds into these opinions as into nets and drag them with themselves toward the punishment appointed for them.

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus read *inducant*, “may lure.”]

This is so whether human beings committed these crimes—human beings whom those spirits, rejoicing in human error, are glad to have regarded as gods, and on whose behalf they themselves interpose through a thousand arts of harming and deceiving—or whether the crimes attributed to the divinities were in fact committed by no human beings at all. Those most deceitful spirits gladly accept such fictions about themselves so that their authority may appear sufficiently suitable for transferring people from heaven to earth in order to perpetrate crimes and shameful acts.

Since the Greeks therefore felt themselves to be slaves of such divinities, they in no way thought that they ought to be spared by poets amid so many and such great theatrical insults against those gods. They either wished in this way to make themselves resemble their gods, or feared that, by seeking a more honorable reputation for themselves and thereby preferring themselves to their gods, they would provoke those gods to anger.

## Chapter XI — How Scenic Actors Were Admitted among the Greeks to the Administration of the State Because Those Who Appeased the Gods Were Unjustly Despised by Human Beings

This consistency is also shown by the fact that the Greeks considered the scenic actors of those same stories worthy of considerable honor in the state.

For, as is also recorded in that book on the Republic, Aeschines of Athens, a most eloquent man, after performing tragedies as a young man, entered public life; and Aristodemus, likewise a tragic actor, was repeatedly sent by the Athenians as an ambassador to Philip on matters of the greatest importance concerning peace and war.

[Note: The same printed editions read “worthy of the honor of their own state.”]

[Note: This is also known about Aeschines from Plutarch’s *On the Ten Orators*, in the life of Aeschines, pp. 840–841, where Aristodemus is also mentioned. See Demosthenes, *On the Crown*, and Aulus Gellius 11.9.]

For the Greeks did not think it consistent, when they saw that the same arts and the same scenic games were acceptable to their gods, to count those through whom the games were performed as dishonorable and degraded.

The Greeks acted shamefully, certainly, but entirely consistently with their gods. They did not dare to withdraw the lives of their citizens from the tongues of poets and actors, since they saw that the lives of the gods themselves were being attacked by those same gods’ will and pleasure. Nor did they think that the human beings through whom such performances were enacted in the theaters—performances which they had learned were pleasing to the divinities under whose power they lived—should merely not be despised in the state; they thought that such people should be honored above all.

What reason could they find for honoring priests, because through them victims acceptable to the gods were offered, while regarding scenic performers as dishonorable, through whom that pleasure or honor was presented to the gods—gods who demanded it and became angry if it was not supplied, as the people had learned from their commands?

Especially since Labeo,

[Note: There were three Labeos renowned for their knowledge of civil law. The most learned of them all was Antistius Labeo, who lived under Caesar Augustus and was an expert not only in law but in all antiquity. Augustine is referring to him here. Suetonius mentions him in *Augustus* 54, and Aulus Gellius in 1.12 and 13.10 and 13.12.]

whom they proclaim to have been highly knowledgeable about such matters, distinguishes good divinities from evil divinities by this very difference in worship. He says that evil gods are appeased by killings and gloomy supplications, while good gods are appeased by joyful and pleasant services, such as, he says, games, banquets, and ritual couches.

[Note: See below, book 3, chapter 17.]

We shall discuss the whole matter more carefully later, if God wills. For the present, whether all things are indiscriminately attributed to all the gods as though they were good—for gods ought not to be evil, whereas these spirits, because they are unclean, are all evil—or whether, as Labeo thought, those services are assigned to the former and these to the latter by a definite distinction, the Greeks most appropriately consider both groups worthy of honor: priests, through whom victims are offered, and scenic performers, through whom games are presented.

[Note: [Col. 0056] The manuscripts variously read “consider worthy by honor” or “consider worthy for honor,” omitting *dignos* (“worthy”); our manuscripts read “consider worthy for honor.”] Otherwise they would be convicted either of injuring all their gods, if games are pleasing to all, or, what is more disgraceful, of injuring those whom they consider good, if games are loved only by them.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “they consider worthy of honor”; others, “they consider worthy of honor,” omitting the word *worthy*. Our manuscripts read “they consider worthy of honor.”]

## Chapter XII — By Taking Away from Poets the Freedom to Attack Human Beings Which They Had Given Them against the Gods, the Romans Displayed Better Judgment about Themselves Than about Their Gods

The Romans, however, as Scipio boasts in that discussion of the Republic, did not wish the lives and reputations of their citizens to be subjected to the reproaches and insults of poets. They even decreed that anyone who dared to compose such a poem should suffer capital punishment.

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and nearly all the manuscripts read “also decreeing capital punishment,” without *to be punished*. Lovaniensis has “to be punished.” The scribe of manuscript 766 added *to be punished* between the lines.]

In relation to themselves they established this with sufficient propriety, but in relation to their gods they acted arrogantly and irreligiously. They knew that their gods were not only patient with the insults and curses of poets but even pleased by them; yet they judged themselves, rather than their gods, unworthy of such injuries. They protected themselves from them by law, while mixing such injuries against their gods even into their solemn sacred rites.

Do you really praise this, Scipio—that Roman poets were denied the license to heap reproach upon any Roman, when you see that they spared none of your gods? Did the reputation of your senate seem more valuable to you than that of the Capitol,

[Note: The Curia, the place where the senate met, stands here for the senators; the Capitol, which was the temple of Jupiter, stands for the gods themselves.]

or even that of a single Rome more valuable than that of the whole heaven, so that poets were forbidden by law to exercise an abusive tongue against your fellow citizens, while they hurled such insults against your gods with complete security, no senator, censor, leader, or pontiff preventing them?

Was it evidently disgraceful for Plautus or Naevius to insult Publius and Gnaeus Scipio, or for Caecilius to insult Marcus Cato; yet was it honorable for your Terence

[Note: “Your Terence,” who was an African by nationality but an intimate friend of Scipio, as he was also of Laelius. They are said to have assisted him in writing his plays.]

to incite the depravity of young men by means of the crime of Jupiter Optimus Maximus?

## Chapter XIII — The Romans Ought to Have Understood That Their Gods, Who Desired to Be Worshiped through Shameful Games, Were Unworthy of Divine Honor

But perhaps, if he were alive, he would answer me: How could we have wished those things to go unpunished which the gods themselves wished to be sacred, since they introduced scenic games—where such things are celebrated, spoken, and performed—into Roman customs, and ordered that these games be dedicated and presented to their own honors?

Why, then, were the gods not more readily understood from this to be false gods, utterly unworthy of the divine honors that the state should render? If they were gods whom it would be entirely improper and inappropriate to worship, supposing they desired games to be performed with insults against the Romans, how, I ask, were they thought worthy of worship? How were they not recognized as detestable spirits who, in their desire to deceive, demanded that their crimes be celebrated among their own honors?

[Note: Lovaniensis reads, “how, I ask, were the gods thought worthy of worship?” The word *gods* is absent from the other books.]

Likewise, although the Romans were already oppressed by a harmful superstition to the point of worshiping gods whom they saw to have wished scenic obscenities to be consecrated to them, they nevertheless remembered their own dignity and modesty. They did not honor the actors of such stories in the manner of the Greeks. Rather, as Scipio himself says in Cicero, since they considered the whole theatrical profession and the stage a disgrace,

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and the manuscripts read “considered it a disgrace,” with *in*; the printed editions omit it.]

they wished that this class of people should not merely lack the honor enjoyed by other citizens but should also be removed from their tribe by the censor’s mark.

[Note: To be removed from one’s tribe was a punishment imposed on men of the plebeian or third order. It meant being transferred from a more distinguished tribe to a less distinguished one, as is clear from Livy 45.15. Compare Tertullian, *On the Spectacles* 22.]

A splendid prudence indeed, and one that deserves to be counted among Roman praises—but I wish it had followed itself and imitated itself.

For see: rightly, whoever among Roman citizens chose to be a scenic performer was not merely given no place of honor; he was not even permitted, because of the censor’s mark, to remain in his own tribe.

O spirit eager for civic glory, genuinely Roman!

[Note: “Genuinely Roman,” that is, truly Roman in its eagerness for glory, because the Roman people were exceedingly eager for glory.]

But let me be answered: by what consistent reasoning are scenic performers excluded from every honor, while scenic games are admitted among the honors of the gods? Roman virtue had long been unfamiliar with those theatrical arts,

[Note: For nearly four hundred years. Livy 7.2 reports that the games were introduced in the year 392 from the foundation of the City.]

and, if they had been sought for human pleasure and amusement, they would have entered through the corruption of human morals. The gods demanded that those performances be presented to them. How, then, is the scenic performer through whom a god is worshiped rejected? And how can the actor of that theatrical shame be marked with disgrace if the one who demands it is worshiped?

In this dispute Greeks and Romans contend with one another. The Greeks think that they rightly honor scenic performers because they worship gods who demand the crimes of scenic games. The Romans, however, do not permit scenic performers to dishonor even a plebeian tribe—much less the senatorial Curia.

In this debate, the following reasoning resolves the substance of the question. The Greeks propose: “If such gods are to be worshiped, then such human beings must also be honored.” The Romans assume: “But such human beings must in no way be honored.” The Christians conclude: “Therefore such gods must in no way be worshiped.”

## Chapter XIV — Plato Was Better, Since He Granted No Place to Poets in a Well-Ordered State, Than These Gods, Who Wished to Be Honored through Scenic Games

1. We next ask: the poets themselves, composers of such stories, who are forbidden by the law of the Twelve Tables to damage the reputation of citizens, why are they not considered dishonorable scenic performers when they hurl such shameful insults against the gods? On what principle is it right that the actors of poetic fictions and disgraceful gods should be disgraced, while their authors are honored?

Or perhaps the palm should rather be awarded to the Greek Plato, who, when rationally constructing the kind of state a city ought to be, judged that poets should be expelled from the city as enemies of the truth.

[Note: This is the reading found with great unanimity in the manuscripts. The printed editions read “enemies of the state.”]

Plato could not tolerate insults against the gods, nor did he wish the minds of citizens to be colored and corrupted by fictions.

Now compare Plato’s humanity, which expelled poets from the city lest they deceive its citizens, with the divinity of the gods who demanded scenic games for their own honor. Plato, even if he could not persuade them by argument, nevertheless urged the frivolity and wantonness of the Greeks not to write such things. These gods, by commanding that such things be performed, extorted them from the gravity and modesty of the Romans.

Nor did they merely wish these performances to take place; they wished them to be dedicated to themselves, consecrated to themselves, and solemnly presented to themselves.

[Note: The Lovaniensis edition alone reads “nor yet”; this is less satisfactory.]

To whom, then, would a state more honorably decree divine honors: to Plato, who prohibited these shameful and impious practices, or to demons who delighted in this deception of human beings and to whom Plato could not persuade the truth?

2. Labeo thought this Plato should be reckoned among the demigods [Note: [Col. 0058] According to Varro and others, there are three orders of gods. Some they called highest gods; others middle gods, who are also demigods, begotten from one immortal parent, such as Romulus and Hercules, and so forth. Others, of the third order, were born from two mortal parents and were called heroes.], just as Hercules and Romulus are. He places demigods above heroes, but assigns both groups a place among the divine beings. Nevertheless, I have no doubt that this man whom he calls a demigod ought to be preferred not merely to heroes, but even to the gods themselves.

Roman laws approach Plato’s discussions in this respect: when Plato condemns all poetic fictions, the Romans at least deprive poets of the license to slander human beings; Plato excludes poets from habitation in the city itself [Note: [Col. 0059] The printed editions read, “he drives them away from habitation in the city itself.” The word “drives away” is absent from the manuscripts.], while the Romans at least remove the performers of poetic tales from the fellowship of the state—and, if they dared say anything against the gods who demanded theatrical games, perhaps they would remove them altogether. The Romans therefore could neither receive nor hope to receive laws for establishing good morals or correcting bad ones from gods whom they defeat and convict by their own laws.

Those gods demand theatrical games for their honor; the Romans exclude theatrical performers from every honor. Those gods order the insults against gods to be celebrated in poetic fictions; the Romans restrain the poets’ shamelessness from insulting human beings. That demigod Plato resisted even the lust of such gods and showed what ought to be accomplished according to the natural disposition of the Romans: he did not want poets, whether lying at will or presenting the worst deeds of the gods for miserable human beings to imitate, to live at all in a well-ordered state.

We do not call Plato a god or a demigod; nor do we compare him with any holy angel of the supreme God, any truthful prophet, any apostle, any martyr of Christ, or any Christian human being. The reason for this judgment of ours will, with God’s help, be explained in its proper place. Yet, since they themselves want him to have been a demigod, we consider him preferable—if not to Romulus and Hercules (although no historian or poet has said or invented that Plato killed his brother or committed any disgraceful act [Note: [Col. 0059] That is, he did not kill his brother, as Romulus is said to have done, nor commit any disgraceful act, as historians have reported or poets invented many such acts concerning Hercules.)—then certainly to Priapus, or to some Cynocephalus [Note: [Col. 0059] Lucan refers to Egypt in this connection, Book 8, lines 831–832:

“We have received your Isis into Roman temples,
and half-dog gods, and rattles that stir up mourning.”

], and finally even to Fever [Note: [Col. 0059] I would be endless if I were to cite the ancient passages concerning Fever, which was worshiped among the Romans. See Pliny, Natural History, Book 2, chapter 7; Aelian, Various Histories, Book 12, chapter 11; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3, chapter 25: “We see a shrine of Fever consecrated on the Palatine.” LARCHER.], whom the Romans partly received as foreign deities and partly consecrated as their own.

How, then, could such gods either prevent the immense evils of soul and morals from threatening good people through good precepts and laws, or undertake to uproot those evils once implanted—gods who even took care to sow and increase crimes, wishing the peoples to learn through theatrical celebrations of deeds that were either their own or supposedly their own, so that human depravity might be inflamed of its own accord, as though by divine authority? All this happened while Cicero protested in vain. Speaking of poets, he says [Note: [Col. 0059] Vindelinus, Amerbach, and Erasmus read: “who, speaking of poets, had approached them.”]: “When to them there is added the shouting and approval of the people, as though of some great and wise teacher, what darkness do they spread over them! What fears do they bring upon them! What desires do they inflame!” [Note: [Col. 0059] Similar words are found in the Tusculan Disputations, Book 3.]

## CHAPTER XV—That the Romans established certain gods for themselves not by reason but by flattery

What, then, was the basis there [Note: [Col. 0060] Vindelinus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read “there”; Amerbach and most manuscripts read “in those things.”] for choosing even those false gods: reason, or rather flattery? They considered this Plato, whom they wish to call a demigod, unworthy of any little shrine, although he labored through such extensive discussions to prevent human morals from being corrupted by the evils of the soul that must especially be avoided. Yet they preferred their own Romulus to many gods, although even their more secret doctrine commends him as a demigod rather than a god [Note: [Col. 0060] On this more secret doctrine, by which the sacred name of the guardian spirit and of the City itself was concealed, see Pliny, Natural History, Book 28, chapter 4; Plutarch, Roman Questions, question 62; Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book 3, chapter 9; especially Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities, Book 4, chapter 62; and Valerius Maximus, Book 1, chapter 1, section 13. COQUAEUS.].

For they even established a flamen for him, and this type of priesthood, as the apex [Note: [Col. 0060] The history of the sanctity of the apex—that is, the woolen rod at the top of the flamen’s cap—is recorded by Valerius Maximus, Book 1, chapter 1, section 4: “While Sulpicius was sacrificing, the apex slipped from his head and deprived him of the priesthood.”] attests, was so distinguished in Roman religious practice that they had only three flamines, appointed for three divine beings: the Dialis for Jupiter, the Martialis for Mars, and the Quirinalis for Romulus. For Quirinus [Note: [Col. 0060] Quirinus was so called from the language of the Sabines, from which the Romans were also called Quirites. See Ovid, Book 2 of the Fasti; Livy, Book 2.] was later so named because of the citizens’ goodwill, as though he had been received into heaven.

Thus Romulus was preferred by this honor even to Neptune and Pluto, the brothers of Jupiter, and to Saturn himself, their father: the priesthood that they had assigned to Jupiter as a great distinction, they also assigned to Romulus, and to Mars as his father—perhaps on his account.

## CHAPTER XVI—That, if the gods had any concern for justice, the Romans ought to have received rules of life from them rather than borrowing laws from other men

If the Romans could have received laws for living from their gods, they would not, some years after the founding of Rome [Note: [Col. 0060] Nearly three hundred years after the founding of the City, according to Livy, Book 3, chapters 33–34.], have borrowed the laws of Solon from the Athenians. Yet they did not preserve them as they received them [Note: [Col. 0060] The word “preserved” is absent from the manuscripts. It is also absent from our copies; it was inserted into codex A by a fifteenth-century hand.], but attempted to make them better and more corrected.

Although Lycurgus pretended that he had established laws for the Lacedaemonians on the authority of Apollo, the Romans wisely refused to believe this and therefore did not receive their laws from that source. Numa Pompilius, who succeeded Romulus in the kingship, is said to have established certain laws, although they would by no means have sufficed to govern the state; he also established many religious rites for them. Yet he is not said to have received those same laws from the gods.

Their gods therefore took no care that the evils of the soul, the evils of life, and the evils of morals—which were so great that even their most learned men affirm that states perished from them while their cities still stood [Note: [Col. 0061] See Plautus, The Persian.]—should not befall their worshipers. Indeed, as has been discussed above, they took every care that such evils should increase.

## CHAPTER XVII—On the abduction of the Sabine women and other injustices that flourished in the Roman state even in its celebrated periods

Or perhaps laws were not established for the Roman people by the gods because, as Sallust says, “justice and goodness among them prevailed not more by laws than by nature” (Sallust, On the Conspiracy of Catiline, chapter 9)? I suppose that the Sabine women were abducted according to this justice and goodness. For what could be more just and good than to lure other men’s daughters by means of a spectacle, not receive them from their parents, but carry them off by force, each man as he could?

For if the Sabines acted unjustly in refusing the women when they were requested, how much more unjust was it to carry off women who had not been given? A more just war could have been waged against the people who had refused their daughters when their neighbors and fellow-countrymen requested them in marriage than against those who were reclaiming the women they had lost. In that case [Note: [Col. 0061] The printed editions read, “That, therefore, should rather have happened there, where Mars,” etc. The text has been corrected from the manuscripts.] Mars should rather have assisted his son while he was fighting, so that he might avenge by arms the wrong of marriages refused and in that way obtain the women he desired. For perhaps, by some right of war, the victor might justly have carried off women unjustly refused. But without any right of peace he seized women who had not been given, and waged an unjust war against their parents, who were justly enraged.

This, however [Note: [Col. 0061] Interpreters of this work refer the pronoun “This” to the war mentioned above, which Livy reports was happily concluded at the outset by a treaty when the Sabines, already almost victorious, agreed to it (Book 1, chapter 13). We think, however, that it refers to the Romans’ morals and equity, which Augustine immediately praises, since among them it was never permitted by any law to imitate the deed of their god Romulus in abducting women.], turned out more usefully and more successfully: although the circus spectacle remained as a memorial of that deception [Note: [Col. 0061] Romulus first celebrated the Circus Games at Rome for Neptune the Equestrian, so that he might carry off, especially, the Sabine maidens whom he could not obtain in marriage from the neighboring peoples, after summoning them for the sake of the spectacle. The ancients called these games Consualia, from the name, as they report, of the god Consus, namely, Equestrian Neptune, from whom Romulus had sought help and advice in the difficulty of obtaining marriages. On these matters see Livy, Book 1, chapter 9.], yet the example of the crime did not please that state and empire. The Romans erred more easily in consecrating their god Romulus after that injustice than in permitting, by any law or custom, his deed to be imitated in the abduction of women.

According to this justice and goodness, after King Tarquinius had been expelled with his children—for his son had violently violated Lucretia by rape—Junius Brutus forced Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus [Note: [Col. 0061] After royal power had been expelled, these two, L. Junius Brutus and L. Tarquinius Collatinus, were made the first consuls. Livy, Book 1, records that Collatinus was compelled by his colleague to resign the magistracy because of the Tarquinian name and lineage, and that, after receiving his property, he left Rome and migrated to Lavinium.], the husband of that same Lucretia, his colleague, a good and innocent man, to resign his office because of the name and kinship of the Tarquins, and did not permit him to live in the state. He committed this crime with the support or acquiescence of the people, from whom Collatinus, just as Brutus himself had, had received the consulship.

According to this justice and goodness, Marcus Camillus, an outstanding man of that period, who, after a ten-year war, easily defeated the Veientes, the Roman people’s most formidable enemies, although the Roman army had been repeatedly and disastrously defeated and Rome itself was already doubting and trembling for its safety, captured their exceedingly wealthy city. Yet, through the envy of those who disparaged his valor and the arrogance of the tribunes of the plebs, he was brought to trial. He experienced the city he had liberated as so ungrateful [Note: [Col. 0062] Thus all the manuscripts. In B: “he was brought to trial and experienced it as so ungrateful.” M.] that, certain of his condemnation, he voluntarily went into exile and was even condemned in his absence to a fine of ten thousand asses. Soon he was to become again the avenger of his ungrateful homeland against the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0062] He was called the father of his country, another founder of the City, and another Romulus. He captured Veii, a city of Etruria. Later, falsely accused, he went into exile at Ardea to avoid envy, two years before Rome was captured by the Gauls. Livy, Book 5, chapter 32, says that Camillus was condemned in his absence to a fine of fifteen thousand asses; Plutarch says fifteen thousand asses. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts have “ten thousand” here.].

I am already weary of recalling the many disgraceful and unjust events by which that state was agitated, when the powerful attempted to subject the plebs to themselves, while the plebs refused to submit to them; and when the defenders of both sides acted more from factional passion and a love of victory than from any thought of justice and goodness.

## CHAPTER XVIII—What Sallust’s history reveals about the morals of the Romans, whether restrained by fear or relaxed through security [Note: [Col. 0062] The printed editions read “severity,” incorrectly and contrary to the manuscripts.]

1. I shall therefore exercise restraint and use Sallust himself as my witness. When, in praising the Romans, he said the words from which our present discussion arose—“Justice and goodness among them prevailed not more by laws than by nature”—he was praising the period in which, after the expulsion of the kings, the state grew extraordinarily and greatly within a brief span of its existence. Yet, in the first book of his History and at its very beginning, he admits that even then, when the state had been transferred from kings to consuls, after a short interval [Note: [Col. 0062] Fifteen years later, as can be understood from Livy, Book 2, chapter 21: the 258th year from the founding of the City, marked by the news of Tarquin’s death.], there were injuries inflicted by the powerful, and, because of them, a secession of the plebs from the patricians, as well as other dissensions in the City.

For after he had recalled that the Roman people had conducted themselves with excellent morals and the greatest concord between the Second and Third Punic Wars [Note: [Col. 0062] There were three wars between the Romans and the Carthaginians. The first lasted twenty-two years, in Sicily and afterward in Africa; it began in the year 495 from the founding of the City, according to Pliny, Book 33. The second began twenty-three years later and was fought in Spain, Sicily, Italy, and Africa; it was concluded there in its seventeenth year by Scipio Africanus the Elder, after Hannibal’s defeat. The third began forty-nine years later in Africa and ended in its third year with the destruction of Carthage by Scipio Africanus the Younger.], and had said that the cause of this good order was not love of justice but, while Carthage still stood, fear of an unreliable peace, from which that Nasica did not want Carthage destroyed, so that wickedness might be restrained and those excellent morals preserved by curbing vices through fear, Sallust immediately added:

“But discord, avarice, ambition, and the other evils that commonly arise in prosperous circumstances increased most after the destruction of Carthage.”

Thus he indicated that these evils had also previously been accustomed to arise and increase. Explaining why he had said this, he continues:

“For injuries inflicted by the powerful, and because of them the secession of the plebs from the patricians, as well as other dissensions at home, had existed from the beginning; and no more than after the expulsion of the kings, while fear of Tarquin and the serious war with Etruria [Note: [Col. 0063] Namely, with Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, who wanted Tarquin restored to the kingship and was pressing the Romans with a severe siege. On this matter see Livy, Book 2, chapter 9 and following.] continued, was the state governed by an equitable and moderate law.”

You see how, even during that brief period after the expulsion—that is, the ejection—of the kings, when the state was governed to some extent by an equitable and moderate law, he says that fear was the cause, because they feared the war that King Tarquin, driven from the kingship and the City and allied with the Etruscans, was waging against the Romans.

Pay attention, then, to what he adds:

“Then the patricians began to exercise a servile rule over the plebs, to decide over their lives and backs [Note: [Col. 0063] Vindelinus reads “and quietness toward themselves.” The other books more correctly read “and backs,” that is, beatings and the punishment of rods, by which it was forbidden for the body of a free Roman citizen to be beaten.] in the manner of kings, to drive them from their land, and, excluding everyone else, to exercise sole authority. Oppressed by these cruelties and especially by usury [Note: [Col. 0063] The Loeb edition alone reads “especially by the burden of usury.”], while enduring tribute and military service amid continual wars, the plebs took up arms and occupied the Sacred Mount and the Aventine [Note: [Col. 0063] That secession of the plebs to the Sacred Mount beyond the river Anio took place in the sixteenth year after the expulsion of the kings. There they first created tribunes who would be, as it were, protectors of the plebs. In another secession they first went to the Aventine, which is part of the City. Later, so that the isolation might be greater and consequently terror might be brought upon the City, they are said to have gone to the Sacred Mount. See Cicero, First Speech on behalf of Cornelius; Livy, Book 1, and elsewhere.]; and then established tribunes of the plebs and other rights for themselves. The end of the dissensions and conflict on both sides was the Second Punic War.”

You see from what period onward—that is, a short interval after the expulsion of the kings—the Romans were such as Sallust says, “Justice and goodness among them prevailed not more by laws than by nature.”

2. Moreover, if such were those periods that are proclaimed to have been the finest and best periods of the Roman state, what should we now say or think about the age that followed, when, to use the words of that same historian, “having gradually changed, it became from the finest and best the worst and most criminal” (Sallust, On the Conspiracy of Catiline, chapter 5), namely, after the destruction of Carthage, as he has recalled?

How Sallust himself briefly recalls and describes those times can be read in his History, where he shows that they advanced through how many moral evils, which arose in prosperity, all the way to the civil wars [Note: [Col. 0063] The wars between the patricians and the Gracchi, between Marius and Sulla, and between Caesar and Pompey.] [Note: [Col. 0063] Manuscript 766 reads “proventum.” M.]. “From that time onward,” he says, “the morals of our ancestors were not gradually carried downward, as before, but were precipitated like a torrent. The young were so corrupted by luxury and avarice that it can rightly be said that men were born who could neither possess property themselves nor tolerate others possessing it” [Note: [Col. 0063] That is, they would squander whatever they could seize from others.].

Sallust then says more about Sulla’s vices and the other degradation of the state; and other writers agree with him on these matters, although their style is far inferior.

[Col. 0064] 3. Yet, I think, you see—and anyone who pays attention readily perceives—into what a foul mass [Note: [Col. 0064] The editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read colluviem. This is an error corrected by Vindelinus and the manuscripts.] of the worst morals that state had sunk before the arrival of our heavenly King.

These events took place not only before Christ had begun to teach in the flesh, but even before he had been born of the Virgin. Since they do not dare to attribute to their gods the many and great evils of those times—whether the earlier evils, which could be more easily endured, or the intolerable and dreadful evils after the overthrow of Carthage—although those gods inserted into human minds, through malicious cunning, the opinions from which such vices would grow wild, why do they attribute present evils to Christ? He forbids the worship of false and deceitful gods by the most salutary teaching, and, detesting and condemning these harmful and disgraceful human desires by divine authority, gradually withdraws his family everywhere from the world, which is wasting away and collapsing under these evils, so that he may establish an eternal and most glorious city—not through the applause of vanity, but through the judgment of truth.

## CHAPTER XIX—On the corruption of the Roman state before Christ removed the worship of the gods

Behold the Roman state—not I the first to say this, but their own authors, from whom we learned these matters at such a price, said it long before the coming of Christ—“gradually changed from the finest and best into the worst and most criminal.”

Behold: before the coming of Christ, after Carthage had been destroyed, “the morals of their ancestors were not gradually, as before, but like a torrent, hurled headlong; so greatly was the youth corrupted by luxury and avarice.”

Let them read to us the precepts given by their gods to the Roman people against luxury and avarice. Would that they had merely kept silent about chastity and moderation and had not also demanded from that people disgraceful and shameful practices, to which they procured authority through a false divinity that brought destruction.

Let them read our own writings—through the Prophets, the holy Gospel, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Epistles—so many teachings against avarice and luxury, proclaimed everywhere to peoples gathered for this purpose, delivered with such excellence and divinity, not sounding like the disputations of philosophers, but thundering like oracles and clouds of God.

Yet they do not attribute to their gods the fact that, before Christ’s coming, the state had become the worst and most criminal through luxury, avarice, and savage [Note: [Col. 0064] Vindelinus, Amerbach, and Erasmus read “and theatrical.”] and shameful morals. Instead, whatever affliction its pride and pleasures have suffered in this period, they charge against the Christian religion.

If the kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old and young together (Psalm 148:11–12), every age capable of hearing and both sexes, and even the tax collectors and soldiers addressed by John the Baptist (Luke 3:12–14), were to hear and heed at once the religion’s precepts concerning just and honorable morals, then the state of this present life would be adorned by its prosperity, and it would ascend most blessedly to the summit of eternal life, where it would reign forever.

But because one person hears and another despises, and because more people are friendly toward vices that flatter them wickedly than toward the useful harshness of virtue [Note: [Col. 0065] This alludes to the two paths of virtue and vice that Hesiod imagined in Works and Days, lines 285 and following, and Prodicus in Xenophon, Memorabilia, Book 2, chapter 2. Hence Cicero, On Duties, Book 1, chapter 32.], Christ’s servants are commanded to endure even a very bad and most criminal state, if that is necessary—whether they are kings, princes, judges, soldiers, provincials, rich or poor, free or enslaved, of either sex—and, in that most holy and august court of the angels and heavenly state, where God’s will is law, to secure for themselves a distinguished place even through this endurance.

## CHAPTER XX—What sort of happiness those who blame the times of the Christian religion wish to enjoy, and by what morals they wish to live

But such worshipers and lovers of these gods, who rejoice that they are also imitators of their crimes and disgraces, care nothing that the state is not the worst and most criminal. “Let it merely stand,” they say; “let it flourish, filled with resources and glorious through victories; or, what is more fortunate, let it enjoy secure peace.”

And what is that to us? Indeed, it concerns us all the more if each person continually increases his wealth, so that it may be available for daily outpourings through which every more powerful person may also subject those who are weaker than himself. Let the poor obey the rich for the sake of being filled, and, so that they may enjoy quiet idleness under the rich men’s patronage, let the rich use the poor for their clientage and service.

Let the peoples applaud not those who deliberate about their interests, but those who distribute pleasures. Let no difficult command be imposed, and let no impure practice be forbidden. Let kings care not how good, but how submissive, are those over whom they rule. Let the provinces serve their kings not as governors of morals, but as masters of possessions and providers of their pleasures; let them honor them not sincerely, but fear them wickedly and slavishly.

Let the laws take notice not of what harms another’s life [Note: [Col. 0065] Several manuscripts read “another’s life.” Vindelinus, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read “another’s vineyard.” So too our copies. M.], but of what harms each person’s own life. Let no one be brought before the judges unless he has been troublesome or harmful against another’s property, household, safety, or anything else against that person’s will. As for his own affairs, or with his own people, or with anyone willing, let each person do whatever he pleases.

Let public prostitutes abound, either for everyone who wishes to enjoy them or especially for those who cannot keep private ones. Let the largest and most splendid houses be built; let sumptuous banquets be frequently held. Wherever anyone wishes and is able, let there be playing, drinking, vomiting, and indulgence day and night. Let dances resound everywhere; let theaters seethe with the voices of indecent merriment and every kind of pleasure, whether most savage or most shameful.

Let the person who dislikes this happiness be a public enemy. Whoever attempts to change or remove it, let the free multitude drive him from their ears, overturn him from his seat, and remove him from among the living. Let those gods be considered true who have secured this happiness for peoples and preserved it once secured. [Col. 0066] Let them be worshiped as they wish, let them demand whatever games they wish, which they may hold with or from their worshipers; let them merely ensure that, against such happiness, nothing is feared from an enemy, a plague, or any disaster.

What sane person would compare this state, I will not say with the Roman Empire, but with the household of Sardanapalus? He was once king so devoted to pleasures that he had the following written on his tomb: that, once dead, he possessed only what his lust had consumed by devouring even while he lived [Note: [Col. 0066] Sardanapalus was the last king of the Assyrians. Cicero quotes his epitaph in the Tusculan Disputations, Book 5, chapter 35.].

If these people had such a king indulging them in these practices and opposing no one in them with any severity, they would consecrate a temple and a flamen to him more gladly than the ancient Romans did to Romulus.

## CHAPTER XXI—What Cicero’s judgment was concerning the Roman state

1. But if the person who called the Roman state the worst and most criminal is despised, and if these people care nothing how full it is of the stain and disgrace of the worst and most criminal morals, provided only that it stand and endure, let them hear that it was not, as Sallust relates, made the worst and most criminal, but, as Cicero argues, had already completely perished and no state at all remained.

For he introduces Scipio—the very man who had destroyed Carthage—discussing the state at a time when, through the corruption Sallust describes, it was already on the point of perishing. The discussion takes place at the time when one of the Gracchi had already been killed, from whom Sallust writes that serious seditions began [Note: [Col. 0066] He means Tiberius Gracchus, who was killed by Scipio Nasica, grandson of the man whom the Senate had judged the best citizen, because Tiberius had introduced an agrarian law and wanted his tribunate continued. Meanwhile Scipio Africanus the Younger, of whom he is speaking here, was conducting the war at Numantia.].

His death is mentioned in the same books. At the end of the second book, Scipio had said:

“As in strings, flutes, and song itself and voices, a certain harmony must be maintained from distinct sounds, which trained ears cannot endure if altered or discordant; and although this harmony is produced from the moderation of very dissimilar voices, it is nevertheless concordant and fitting—so, from the highest, lowest, and middle orders interposed among them, the state, through a measured arrangement [Note: [Col. 0066] Vindelinus, Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “measured by arrangement.” Most other manuscripts read “by moderation.”], should resound in the concord of dissimilar elements as do sounds; and what musicians call harmony in song is concord in the state, the closest and best bond of security in every state, and this cannot exist at all without justice.”

After he had discussed at somewhat greater length and more fully how greatly justice benefited the state and how greatly its absence harmed it, Philus [Note: [Col. 0066] Thus also all our manuscripts. Perhaps it should be read “Philus.” M.], one of those present at the discussion, then took up the matter and asked that this very question be treated more carefully and that more be said about justice, because it was already commonly said that a state could not be governed [Note: [Col. 0066] Several books here and below read “conducted” in place of “governed.” So also manuscripts 766, 2051, and 2052. M.] without injustice.

Scipio agreed that this question should be examined and resolved. He replied that he considered nothing further to have been said about the state, nor could the discussion proceed farther, unless it were established not only that the statement “it cannot be governed without injustice” was false, but that this was supremely true: a state cannot be governed without the highest justice [Note: [Col. 0067] So also manuscripts 766, 2051, and 2053. Others read “conducted.” M.] (Book 2, chapter 43).

Since the explanation of this question was postponed until the following day, the matter was argued in the third book amid great contention [Note: [Col. 0067] The manuscripts read “conflict.” Manuscript 2050 reads “contention.” M.]. Philus himself took up the position of those who believed that a state could not be governed [Note: [Col. 0067] So manuscripts 2051, 2052, and 2053; manuscripts 2050 and 766 read “conducted.” M.] without injustice, clearing himself especially so that no one would think he held this view personally. He argued earnestly on behalf of injustice against justice, attempting to show by plausible arguments and examples that justice was disadvantageous to the state, while injustice was beneficial.

Then Laelius, at everyone’s request, undertook to defend justice. He asserted as forcefully as he could that nothing was so hostile to the state as injustice, and that the state could neither be governed nor endure except through great justice [Note: [Col. 0067] Cicero mentions this contest in Laelius, chapter 4.].

2. After this question had been discussed as fully as seemed sufficient, Scipio returned to the matters that had been interrupted. He recalled and commended his brief definition of the state, by which he had said that it was the people’s affair (Book 1, chapter 25). He determined that the people was not every gathering of a multitude, but a gathering united by agreement concerning law and a common interest.

He then showed how useful a definition is in argument and drew from his definitions the conclusion that there is a state—that is, a people’s affair—when it is governed well and justly, whether by one king, a few aristocrats, or the whole people.

But when the king is unjust—whom, following Greek usage, he called a tyrant—or when the aristocrats are unjust, whose agreement he called a faction—or when the people itself is unjust, for which he found no customary name except to call it a tyrant as well—then the state is not merely defective, as had been argued the previous day. Rather, as the reasoning connected with those definitions demonstrated, there is no state at all.

For it would not be the people’s affair when a tyrant or faction [Note: [Col. 0067] Morel, Elements of Criticism, p. 152, reads “a tyrant or a faction.” B and our manuscripts read “a faction.” M.] took control of it; nor would the people itself still be a people if it were unjust, since it would not be a multitude united by agreement concerning law and a common interest, as the people had been defined.

3. Therefore, when the Roman state was such as Sallust describes it, it was not merely the worst and most criminal, as he says, but, according to this reasoning, it was altogether nonexistent. This was made clear by the discussion of the state held among its leading men at that time [Note: [Col. 0067] Cicero introduces as speakers in that discussion Scipio Africanus the Younger, Gaius Laelius, and Lucius Furius Philus.].

Tullius himself, speaking not in Scipio’s words or anyone else’s but in his own [Note: [Col. 0067] Here Vindelinus, Amerbach, and Erasmus add “he testifies”; Lovaniensis reads “he demonstrated.” At this point the manuscripts leave a word to be supplied; “made clear” is required.], says the same thing at the beginning of the fifth book. After first quoting a verse of the poet Ennius, in which he had said:

“By ancient morals and men the Roman state stands,”

Cicero says:

“That verse, whether because of its brevity or its truth, seems to me to have been uttered as if from some oracle. For neither men, unless the state had been so ordered in its morals, nor morals, unless such men had been in charge, could have established or for so long preserved so great a state, ruling so justly and so widely. Therefore, before our memory, ancestral custom itself brought forward outstanding men, and outstanding men preserved the ancient custom and institutions of their ancestors.

“But our age, having received the state like an excellent painting already fading through age, not only neglected to renew it with the same colors with which it had been made, but did not even take care to preserve at least its form and outermost lines, as it were. For what remains of those ancient morals by which he said the Roman state stood, when we see them so worn away through neglect that they are not only not practiced but not even known [Note: [Col. 0068] Several manuscripts read “but now already,” or “and now already.” Our copies read “but now.” M.]?

“For what should I say about the men? The morals themselves have perished through a lack of men; and concerning so great an evil we must not only give an account, but, as though accused of a capital crime, somehow plead our case. Through our vices, not through some accident, we retain the state in name; in reality, however, we lost it long ago.”

4. Cicero acknowledged this—indeed, long after the death of Africanus [Note: [Col. 0068] About seventy years after the death of Africanus, which is assigned to the year 624 from the founding of the City.]—the man whom he made discuss the republic in his books, yet still before Christ’s coming [Note: [Col. 0068] Namely, sixty years before Christ. For between Cicero’s consulship, in which year he published the books *On the Republic*, and the thirty-second year of Augustus’s reign, in which Christ was born, sixty years intervened.]: if such things were heard and said when the Christian religion had been proclaimed and was prevailing, who would not think that they ought to be charged to the Christians? Why, then, did their gods not take care that the republic should not at that time perish and be lost—the republic whose loss Cicero, long before Christ came in the flesh, so mournfully lamented? Let its admirers determine what kind of republic it was even under those ancient men and customs: whether true justice flourished in it, or whether even then it was not alive in its customs but merely painted in colors. Cicero himself, though unaware of it, expressed this when he preferred it. But at another time, if God wills, we shall examine this. For in its proper place I shall endeavor to show that, according to Cicero’s own definitions—briefly set out by Scipio as to what a republic is and what a people is, with many statements also bearing witness, whether Cicero’s own or those of the persons whom he made speak in the same discussion—it was never a republic, because true justice never existed in it [Note: [Col. 0068] See below, Book 19, chapters 21 and 24.]. According to more probable definitions, however, it was a republic in a certain qualified sense [Note: [Col. 0068] Thus the better manuscripts. But Vind. and Er. read *quaedam*, “a certain [one].” Lov. has *quondam*, “formerly.”]; and it was administered better by the earlier Romans than by those who came later. But true justice exists only in that republic whose founder and ruler is Christ—if indeed it pleases us to call it a republic, since we cannot deny that it is the commonwealth of a people. If this name, which elsewhere is used differently, is perhaps too remote from our customary usage, true justice certainly exists in that city of which Holy Scripture says: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God” (Psalm 86:3).

## CHAPTER XXII  
### That the gods of the Romans never took any care that the republic should not perish through corrupt morals

1. But as concerns the present question, however praiseworthy they may say this republic was or is, according to their most learned authorities it had already become utterly depraved and disgraceful long before Christ’s coming; indeed, it no longer existed at all, and had completely perished through its utterly corrupted morals. Therefore, if it was not to perish, its guardian gods ought to have given their worshiping people outstanding rules for living and for moral conduct—the people who honored them in so many temples, through so many priests and kinds of sacrifices, with such manifold and varied rites, so many solemn festivals, and the celebrations of so many great games. Yet in all this the demons did nothing except attend to their own business. They did not care how those people lived; rather, they cared that they should live ruinously, provided that, subjected by fear, they rendered all those services to their honor.

Or, if they did give such rules, let them be produced, displayed, and read: what laws of the gods, given to that state, did the Gracchi [Note: [Col. 0069] Tiberius Gracchus and his brother Gaius. See above, col. 43.] despise when they threw everything into turmoil through seditions; what laws did Marius [Note: [Col. 0069] Marius was a municipal citizen of Arpinum, who was elected consul at Rome seven times and defeated Jugurtha, the Cimbri, and the Teutons. Finally, when he began a civil war with Sulla, he himself was defeated and fled to Africa.] and Cinna [Note: [Col. 0069] After Marius had been defeated, when Sulla departed to wage war against Mithridates, he left the consuls Cornelius Cinna and Gnaeus Octavius in the City. Cinna, eager for revolution, disagreed with his colleague and was driven by him from the City. To avenge this injury, Cinna recalled Marius from Africa, made war upon the City, and at last entered it and filled everything with slaughter.] and Carbo [Note: [Col. 0069] As Cicero writes in Book 9, Letter 21 to Paetus, there were many Carbones of the Papyria family. The one of whom Augustine speaks, Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, followed the Marian faction; defeated by Sulla, he fled to Sicily and was killed at Lilybaeum by Pompey.] despise when they proceeded even to civil wars, undertaken for the most unjust reasons, conducted cruelly, and ended more cruelly still? And what laws did Sulla himself [Note: [Col. 0069] He was, as Cicero says in Book 3 of *On Ends*, the teacher of three destructive vices: luxury, greed, and cruelty.] despise—Sulla whose life, morals, and deeds, as described by Sallust and other historians, who would not shudder to hear? Who would not admit that the republic had then perished?

2. Or perhaps, because of the morals of citizens of this kind, they will dare to oppose, as they usually do in defense of their gods, that line of Virgil:

> All the gods departed, abandoning shrines and altars,  
> the gods by whom this empire had stood?  
> (*Aeneid* 2.351–352)

First, if this is so, they have no reason to complain about the Christian religion, saying that their gods, offended by it, abandoned them; for their ancestors had long before driven so many small gods from the altars of the City by their own morals, as though they were driving away flies.

Nevertheless, where was this crowd of deities when, long before the ancient morals were corrupted, Rome was captured and burned by the Gauls? Or were they perhaps present but asleep? For at that time, when the entire City had fallen into the power of the enemy, only the Capitoline Hill remained; and even it would have been captured had not at least the geese kept watch while the gods slept [Note: [Col. 0070] See Livy, Book 5, chapters 38ff. and chapters 47–48, and Plutarch, *Camillus*.]. Hence Rome had almost fallen into the superstition of the Egyptians, who worship animals and birds, when it celebrated solemn rites for a goose.

But for the moment I am not yet discussing these adventitious evils—evils affecting the body rather than the soul—which arise either from enemies or from some other disaster. I am now speaking of the stain upon morals. When those morals had first been gradually discolored and then plunged forward like a torrent, so great a collapse of the republic occurred—although its roofs and walls remained intact—that their great authorities do not hesitate to say that it was then lost.

The gods had rightly departed, abandoning their shrines and altars, so that the republic might be lost, if the state had despised their instructions concerning a good life [Note: [Col. 0070] Lov. reads: “the gods, whose instructions concerning a good life.” The other books disagree.] and justice. But what sort of gods, I ask, were they, if they did not wish to live with their worshiping people, whom they had not taught to live well while they were living badly?

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### That variations in temporal circumstances depend not on the favor or opposition of demons, but on the judgment of the true God

1. What shall we say, moreover, since they appear to have assisted their desires in being fulfilled and are shown not to have presided over restraining them? For those who helped Marius—a new man and one of obscure origin, the most bloodthirsty author and perpetrator of civil wars—to become consul seven times, and helped him to die an old man during his seventh consulship, so that he would not fall into the hands of Sulla, who was soon to be victorious [Note: [Col. 0070] The printed editions add: “Why did they not also help him to restrain himself from such monstrous crimes?” But this is absent from all Gallican and Roman manuscripts.],—if their gods did not help him in these matters, they admit something substantial: that even without the favor of their gods a human being can attain such great temporal happiness, which they love too much; and that people like Marius can be heaped with and enjoy health, strength, wealth, honors, dignity, and longevity while the gods are angry, while people like Regulus can be tortured and die through captivity, slavery, poverty, sleeplessness, and suffering while the gods are friendly.

If they grant that this is so, they confess, in short, that the gods are of no benefit and are worshiped to no purpose. For if they pressed the people to learn greater opposition to the virtues of the soul and to a morally upright life, whose rewards are to be hoped for after death; if, even in these passing and temporal goods, they neither harm those whom they hate nor benefit those whom they love—why are they worshiped? Why are they sought with such zeal? Why, in difficult and sorrowful times, is it complained that they have departed as though offended, and why is the Christian religion attacked with the most undeserved insults on their account?

But if they possess the power either to benefit or to harm in these matters, why were they present to the worst man, Marius, and absent from the best man, Regulus? Are they thereby shown to be themselves utterly unjust and evil? If they are therefore thought more deserving of fear and worship, let them not be thought so on that account either: Regulus is found to have worshiped them no less than Marius. Nor should a completely wicked life appear desirable merely because the gods are thought to have favored Marius more than Regulus.

For Metellus, the most highly praised of the Romans, who had five sons who were consuls [Note: [Col. 0071] This was Quintus Metellus Numidicus, grandson of Lucius Metellus the pontiff. He is discussed by Pliny, Book 7, chapter 44; Cicero, *On Ends*, Book 5, chapters 27–28; *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 1, chapter 35; and Valerius Maximus, Book 7, chapter 1. All of them present him as an example of supreme happiness. Vives and Coquaeus observe from those authors that he had only four sons. Nevertheless, all the books that I have been able to inspect read “five sons who were consuls.”], was also fortunate in temporal circumstances; whereas Catiline, utterly wicked, was crushed by poverty and, overthrown in the war arising from his crime, was unhappy. Yet the good who worship God are preeminent in the truest and most certain happiness, which can be conferred by God alone.

2. Therefore, when that republic was perishing through corrupt morals, its gods did nothing either to direct or to correct those morals so that it might not perish. Rather, they added to the corruption and depravity of its morals so that it would perish.

Nor should they pretend to be good on the ground that they departed as though offended by the injustice of the citizens. They were plainly there; they are exposed and convicted. They could neither help by giving instruction nor remain concealed by silence.

I omit the fact that Marius, when pitied by the people of Minturnae, was commended to the goddess Marica in her grove, so that she might make everything prosper for him [Note: [Col. 0071] Marius was taken to Minturnae, a town of Campania, while fleeing from Sulla after being defeated in the first civil battle. You will learn from Plutarch’s life of Marius, Velleius, Book 2, Appian, *Civil Wars*, Book 1, and others how he was received by the people of Minturnae.]; and that, returning safe from the depths of despair, he led a cruel army into the City, where his victory was more bloody, more lawless, and more savage than that of an enemy. Let those who wish to know read the accounts of the writers who described it [Note: [Col. 0071] Vind., Am., and Er. read: “let those who wish to know read.”].

But this, as I said, I omit. I do not attribute Marius’s bloody success to some Marica, whoever she may have been; rather, I attribute it to the hidden providence of God, intended to silence their mouths and to free from error those who do not act from partisan zeal but observe these matters intelligently.

For even if demons possess some power in these affairs, they possess only as much as they are permitted by the secret decision of the Almighty. This is so that we may neither esteem earthly happiness too highly—since, as in the case of Marius, it is often granted even to the wicked—nor again judge it to be evil, when we see that many devout and good worshipers of the one true God have, despite the demons’ opposition, been outstanding in it. Nor should we think that these same unclean spirits ought to be won over or feared on account of such earthly goods or evils.

For just as wicked human beings on earth cannot do everything they wish, neither can those spirits, except insofar as they are allowed by the ordinance of Him whose judgments no one fully comprehends and whom no one can justly reproach [Note: [Col. 0071] All manuscripts read *sinitur*, “they are allowed.”].

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the acts of Sulla, in which the demons displayed themselves as his helpers

1. Sulla himself, certainly, lived in times so bad that earlier times, of which he seemed to be the avenger, were longed for by comparison with his own. When he first moved his camp against Marius toward the City [Col. 0072], Livy writes that the entrails at the sacrifice were so favorable to him that the haruspex Postumius offered to have himself held in custody and put to death unless, with the gods’ help, he fulfilled what Sulla had in mind.

Behold, the gods had not departed, abandoning their shrines and altars, since they foretold the outcome of events and took no care to correct Sulla himself. By their predictions they promised great success, and they did not break his evil desire by threatening him.

Then, while he was in Asia conducting the war against Mithridates, a message was delivered to him through Lucius Titius from Jupiter, saying that he would overcome Mithridates; and so it happened. Later, when he was preparing to return to the City and to avenge, with civil bloodshed, the injuries inflicted upon himself and his friends [Note: [Col. 0072] Lov. reads “the injuries that had arisen.” The words “that had arisen” are absent from Vind., Am., Er., and most manuscripts.], the same Jupiter again sent him a message through a certain soldier of the Sixth Legion. He had previously foretold victory over Mithridates, the message said, and now promised to give Sulla the power to recover the republic from his enemies, though not without much bloodshed.

Sulla then asked what appearance the soldier had seen. When the soldier described it, Sulla recognized the appearance he had previously heard about from the man who had brought the message from the same Jupiter concerning victory over Mithridates.

What answer can be given here as to why the gods took care to announce such things as though they were successes, while none of them took care, by warning Sulla, to correct him before he committed such great crimes with his wicked civil arms—crimes that would not merely defile the republic but utterly destroy it?

They are evidently demons, as I have often said and as is known to us from the sacred Scriptures. The events themselves sufficiently show that they were attending to their own business: to be regarded and worshiped as gods, and to receive from those who offered such things what would unite the offerers with them in one utterly evil cause at the judgment of God.

2. Later, when Sulla had come to Tarentum and sacrificed there, he saw on the head of a calf’s liver something resembling a golden crown. The haruspex Postumius then replied that this signified a splendid victory for him and ordered him alone to eat those entrails.

Soon afterward, a slave belonging to a certain Lucius Pontius cried out prophetically: “I come as a messenger from Bellona; the victory is yours, Sulla.” He then added that the Capitol would burn. After saying this, he immediately left the camp. The next day he returned in a more excited state and cried out that the Capitol had burned. In fact, the Capitol had really burned.

It was easy for a demon both to foresee this and to announce it very quickly. Pay close attention, however, to what bears most directly upon the issue: under what sort of gods do those wish to live who blaspheme the Savior who frees the wills of the faithful from the dominion of demons?

The man cried out prophetically, “The victory is yours, Sulla”; and, so that it might be believed that he was crying this out by a divine spirit, he also announced something that was both about to happen and soon did happen, something far away from the place through which that spirit was speaking. Yet he did not cry out, “Spare us your crimes, Sulla”—crimes so horrifying as those which Sulla committed there as victor, he to whom a golden crown, the most illustrious sign of that very victory, appeared on a calf’s liver.

If just gods were accustomed to give signs of this kind, and not wicked demons, they would surely have shown by those entrails evils that were impious and gravely harmful to Sulla himself. For that victory benefited his dignity far less than it harmed his desire for power. It caused him, while greedily pursuing excess and being lifted up and cast down by success, to perish more completely in his morals than he destroyed his enemies in their bodies.

Those gods did not announce to him through entrails, auguries, dreams, or prophecies the things that were truly sad and truly worthy of mourning. They were more afraid that he might be corrected than that he might be defeated. Indeed, they took sufficient care that, victorious and glorious over his fellow citizens, but defeated and captive in his abominable vices, he should through those vices be placed under the power of the demons themselves much more tightly.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### How greatly evil spirits incite human beings to crimes when, in the commission of wickedness, they introduce the supposed divine authority of their example

1. Who, then, could fail to understand or see—unless he has chosen rather to imitate such gods than to be separated from their society by divine grace—how much these evil spirits strive by their example to furnish crimes with what seems to be divine authority? This was even displayed in a broad plain of Campania, where not long afterward the civil armies clashed in a wicked battle: the spirits themselves were first seen to fight among one another [Note: [Col. 0073] Julius Obsequens, *Book on Prodigies*.].

For immense crashes were first heard there; then many people reported that they had seen two armies fighting for several days. When the battle ceased, they also found traces resembling those of human beings and horses, as extensive as could have been imprinted by such a conflict.

If, then, the gods truly fought among themselves, human civil wars are excused. Yet let us consider what the malice or misery of gods of this kind must be. But if they pretended to have fought, what else did they accomplish except that the Romans, by waging civil war against one another, might seem to commit no crime, as though they were following the example of the gods?

Civil wars had already begun, and the execrable slaughter of several [Note: [Col. 0073] The printed editions read *aliqua*, “some.” The manuscripts read *aliquot*, “several,” which refers to *battles* below.] wicked battles had already occurred. Many had already been moved by the fact that a soldier, while stripping the spoils from a slain man, recognized his brother on the stripped corpse; and, cursing civil wars, he killed himself there and joined himself to his brother’s body [Note: [Col. 0073] From Livy, Book 79.].

Therefore, so that people would not grow weary of so great an evil, but rather the passion for wicked arms would increase more and more, the harmful demons [Note: [Col. 0073] The printed editions read “then these demons.” Most manuscripts, including those of better quality, read “the harmful demons.” This reading agrees with the phrase “harmful spirits” in the following chapter, section 1.] whom those people thought should be worshiped and venerated wished to appear to human beings fighting among themselves. Their purpose was that civic feeling should not shrink from imitating such battles, but rather that human crime should be excused by divine example.

By this cunning the evil spirits also ordered that theatrical games—about which I have already said much—should be dedicated and consecrated to them. There the great crimes of the gods were celebrated in theatrical songs and dramatic performances, so that both those who believed that the gods had done such things and those who did not believe it but nevertheless saw that the gods eagerly wished such things to be displayed for them might imitate them without fear.

Thus, lest anyone think that the poets had written insults against the gods rather than something worthy of them wherever they recalled the gods fighting among themselves, the spirits themselves confirmed the poets’ songs in order to deceive human beings. They displayed their battles not only through theatrical performers in the theater but also by exhibiting them themselves in the field before human eyes.

2. We have been compelled to say these things because their own authorities did not hesitate to say and write that the Roman republic had already been destroyed by the worst morals of its citizens, and that nothing remained of it before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

They do not attribute this destruction to their gods, yet they attribute to our Christ the transient evils through which the good cannot perish, whether they live or die. Our Christ continually teaches so many precepts of the best morals against corrupt morals [Note: [Col. 0074] Thus our manuscripts, except 766. B. reads *frequenter*, “frequently,” incorrectly.]; whereas their gods did nothing through any such precepts for the people who worshiped them, or for that republic, to prevent its destruction.
