Indeed, by corrupting those same morals through the harmful authority of their examples, they acted rather so that it would perish.

No one, I think, will now dare to say that the republic did not then perish because

> All the gods departed, abandoning shrines and altars,

as though they were friends of virtue and had been offended by the vices of human beings. For they are convicted of having been present by so many signs in entrails, auguries, and prophecies, through which they eagerly claimed and commended themselves as foreknowers of the future and helpers in battles. If they had truly departed, the Romans would have burned less fiercely for civil wars from their own desires than from the instigation of those gods.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On the secret admonitions of the demons concerning good morals, while every form of wickedness was openly taught in their sacred rites

1. Since these things are so—since disgraceful acts mingled with cruelties, insults against the gods, and crimes, whether revealed or invented at their own demand and, if not performed, provoking their anger, were shown to have been consecrated and dedicated to them in fixed and regular solemnities; and since such things were brought before the eyes of everyone as spectacles to be imitated—what are we to say of those same demons?

They confess themselves to be unclean spirits through pleasures of this kind; by their own disgraceful acts and crimes, whether reported or fabricated, and by demanding that such things be celebrated—extorting them from the shameless and from the modest [Note: [Col. 0074] The edition of Lov. alone reads *expetita*, “requested.”]—they testify that they are authors of a criminal and unclean life. Yet they are said to give, in their shrines and secret inner sanctuaries, certain good precepts concerning morals to some of their consecrated worshipers, as though to a select few [Note: [Col. 0074] Heraldus regards the words “to some, as though to selected ones” as a gloss on Arnobius, Book 5. But they are found in all the manuscripts and fit Augustine’s purpose very well, perhaps alluding to the Manichaean Elect, to whom the more secret teaching of that sect was reserved. For the words that follow, “their consecrated worshipers,” do not refer to morals themselves, as Heraldus thought, as though the phrase were adjectival; rather, they signify people devoted to the gods through religious observance, as throughout this work.].

If this is so, the malice of the harmful spirits must be recognized and exposed as all the more cunning for that very reason. The force of goodness and chastity is so great that every human nature, or nearly every one, is moved by their praise; nor is it so corrupted by shamefulness that it loses every sense of honor.

Therefore, unless the demons’ malignity somewhere transforms itself—as we know from our Scriptures it does—into angels of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), it does not accomplish its work of deception.

Outside, then, unclean impiety resounds around the people with the loudest tumult, while inside, simulated chastity scarcely makes a sound among a few. Shameful things are displayed openly, and praiseworthy things are kept secret. Honor lies hidden, while disgrace is exposed. The evil that is done summons everyone as spectators; the good that is spoken scarcely finds any hearers—as though honorable things ought to be shameful and dishonorable things worthy of boasting.

But where does this happen except in the temples of demons? Where except in the inns of deceit [Note: [Col. 0075] The printed editions add here “to see, blushing,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]? The former is done so that the more honorable, who are few, may be captured; the latter so that the more numerous, who are utterly shameful, may not be corrected.

2. Where and when the consecrated worshipers of Caelestis [Note: [Col. 0075] “The consecrated worshipers of Caelestis,” that is, worshipers of the virgin goddess Caelestis, whose worship was especially widespread among the Africans and Carthaginians. She was discussed above, chapter 4, where see note (b). The interpreters of this work have therefore been mistaken when they have taken the name *Caelestis* here as an ordinary adjective and written observations on the following words about the games of the goddess Flora and about the festivals of Flora, Vesta, and other gods. The entire passage undoubtedly refers to the African goddess Caelestis.] heard precepts of chastity, we do not know. But before the very shrine where we saw that image placed, people streamed together from every direction and stood wherever they could; and we watched the games being performed with the greatest attention, looking now at the procession of prostitutes, now at the virgin goddess; seeing the former worshiped submissively, and obscene acts celebrated before the latter.

There we saw neither bashful performers nor any more modest theatrical display. Every office of obscenity was being carried out. It was known what pleased the virginal deity, and what a more educated matron might carry home from the temple was displayed.

Some more modest women turned their faces away from the impure movements of the performers, yet learned the art of vice [Note: [Col. 0075] The printed editions add here “blushing to see,” which is absent from the manuscripts.] by furtive attention. They were ashamed before human beings, lest they dare to watch immodest gestures with an unrestrained gaze; but they dared much less to condemn with a chaste heart the sacred rites of the goddess whom they venerated.

Yet this was openly offered for learning in the temple, whereas at home at least some privacy was sought for carrying it out. Human modesty was greatly astonished—if any were present there—that people did not freely commit human crimes which they learned religiously from the gods, and that they would have the gods angry unless they also took care to display them.

For what other spirit, secretly stirring the most wicked minds, both urges people to commit adultery and feeds upon the deeds, except the spirit that also delights in such sacred rites—setting up images of demons in temples, loving images of vices in games, whispering words of justice in secret [Col. 0076] to deceive even the few good people, and openly multiplying invitations to wickedness in order to possess the innumerable wicked?

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### With what overthrow of public discipline the Romans consecrated the obscenities of the games to appease their gods

The serious man and would-be philosopher Tullius [Note: [Col. 0076] The printed editions read “the philosopher Tertullius.” Most manuscripts agree on the latter word, though in some it is divided so as to read “the philosopher, thrice Tullius.” The more genuine reading appears to be that of the old Corbie manuscript, *philosophaster Tullius*, “Tullius the would-be philosopher,” a reading reached by conjecture by Ludovicus Vives. Augustine apparently uses this word to mark the emptiness of Cicero’s philosophy, which did not free him from such foolish and sacrilegious errors.]—who was about to become aedile—was shouting in the ears of the City that, among the other duties of his magistracy, he had to appease Mother Flora through the celebration of games [Note: [Col. 0076] *Against Verres*, Act 6.]. These games are accustomed to be celebrated with greater devotion precisely because they are more disgraceful.

Elsewhere, already consul and in the midst of the City’s extreme dangers, he says that games were held for ten days and that nothing pertaining to the appeasement of the gods had been omitted [Note: [Col. 0076] *Against Catiline*, Act 3, chapter 8.]—as though it were not better to provoke such gods by self-restraint than to appease them by luxury, and to challenge them to hostility by moral integrity than to placate them by such deformity.

For the human beings on whose behalf they were appeased could not have inflicted more serious harm through whatever savage cruelty than the gods themselves inflicted when they were appeased by the most shameful vices. In order to avert what was feared from the enemy in the body, the gods were won over by a method through which virtue was conquered in the mind. They would not stand as defenders against the attackers of the walls unless they first became conquerors of good morals.

This was the insolent, impure, shameless, wicked, and unclean appeasement of such deities—a form of appeasement whose performers the native character of Roman virtue deprived of honor, drove out from the tribe, recognized as disgraceful, and made infamous. This, I say, was the shameful appeasement of such deities, to be shunned and detested by true religion; these were the seductive and criminal stories about the gods; these were the dishonorable deeds of the gods, either wickedly and shamefully committed or even more wickedly and shamefully fabricated [Note: [Col. 0076] Thus the manuscripts. In the printed editions, *conficta*, “fabricated,” appears here; and at another place, after *turpiusque*, they had *commissa*, “committed.” Cod. 766 reads: “these dishonorable deeds of the gods, either wickedly and shamefully done, or…”].

The whole City learned these things through its eyes and ears. It saw that such deeds, whether committed or fabricated, pleased the gods, and therefore believed that they ought not only to be displayed to them but also imitated by itself. It did not learn that obscure something presented as good and honorable, which was spoken to so few and so secretly—if indeed it was spoken at all—that it seemed more a matter of fearing that it should become known than of fearing that it should not be done.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### On the health-giving character of the Christian religion

The unjust and ungrateful complain and murmur that human beings are rescued through Christ’s name from the infernal yoke and punitive fellowship of these utterly unclean powers, and transferred from the night of that most destructive impiety into the light of the most health-giving piety. They complain because they are possessed by that wicked spirit more deeply and more tightly [Note: [Col. 0076] The printed editions read “oppressed,” but the manuscripts disagree.]—because the people stream to the churches [Col. 0077] in chaste gatherings, with men and women honorably separated from one another.

There they hear how they ought to live well here for a time, so that after this life they may deserve to live happily and forever; there Holy Scripture and the teaching of justice resound from a higher place in the presence of all, so that those who do these things may hear of their reward and those who do not may hear of their judgment.

Even if some mockers of such precepts come there, all their insolence is either laid aside through a sudden change or restrained by fear or shame. Nothing shameful or disgraceful is set before them to watch and imitate where the precepts of the true God are conveyed, or his miracles recounted, or his gifts praised, or his benefits requested.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### An exhortation to the Romans to cast off the worship of the gods

1. Desire these things instead, O praiseworthy Roman character, O offspring of the Reguli, Scaevolas, Scipios, and Fabricii. Desire these things instead, and distinguish them from that most shameful vanity and that most deceitful malignity of demons.

If anything praiseworthy naturally stands out in you, it is cleansed and perfected only by true piety; by impiety, however, it is destroyed and punished [Note: [Col. 0077] Thus Er. and the manuscripts. Vind., Am., and Lov. read *dispergitur*, “scattered.”].

Now choose what you will follow, so that you may be praised without error not in yourself but in the true God. For at that time popular glory was present to you, but, by the hidden judgment of divine providence, the true religion—which you should have chosen—was absent.

Awake: it is day. As you have awakened in some of your people, whose perfected virtue and sufferings for the true faith we celebrate—people who, fighting everywhere against the most hostile powers and conquering them by dying bravely, have won this homeland for us with their blood.

To this homeland we invite you and exhort you to join the number of its citizens. Its sanctuary, in a sense, is the true remission of sins [Note: [Col. 0077] This alludes to Romulus’s asylum, discussed below, Book 5, chapter 17, at the end.].

Do not listen to your degenerate sons who attack Christ and Christians and accuse these as though they were evil times, while they seek times in which life would not be peaceful but rather iniquity secure. Such things never pleased you even for the sake of an earthly homeland. Now seize the heavenly homeland, for which you will labor very little, and in which you will truly and forever reign.

There you will have neither the Vestal hearth [Note: [Col. 0077] The perpetual fire dedicated to Vesta. Livy writes that if it were extinguished by accident, this was a sign that great evils were impending: Book 5, chapter 52, and Book 28, chapter 11.], nor the Capitoline stone [Note: [Col. 0077] The stone image of Jupiter in the Capitol. From this arose the Romans’ most sacred oath, “By Jupiter the Stone!”], but one true God,

> who will set neither limits nor times to the course of things,  
> and will grant an empire without end.  
> (*Aeneid* 1.278–279)

## 2. Do not seek false and deceptive gods; rather, cast them away and despise them, bursting forth into true freedom. They are not gods, but malign spirits, for whom your eternal happiness is punishment. Juno does not appear to have begrudged the Trojans—from whom you derive your bodily origin—the Roman citadels as much as these demons, whom you still think gods, begrudge everlasting abodes to every race of human beings. And you yourself, in no small measure, have passed judgment on such beings, when you appeased them through theatrical games and wanted the human beings by whom you produced those same games to be infamous. Suffer your freedom to be asserted against the unclean spirits who had imposed upon your necks the obligation to consecrate and celebrate their own disgrace.

You removed the performers of divine crimes from your honors. Entreat the true God to remove from you those gods who delight in their own crimes—whether they are real, which is most disgraceful, or fictitious, which is most malicious. It is good that, of your own accord, you did not wish to admit actors and stage performers to the fellowship of citizenship; awake more fully: the divine majesty is in no way appeased by arts through which human dignity is polluted. By what reasoning, then, do you think that gods who delight in such services should be counted among the number [Note: [Col. 0078] Lov., “in every number.” *Omni* is absent from the other books.] of the holy heavenly powers, when you did not think that the human beings through whom those same services were performed should be counted among any class of Roman citizens?

The heavenly city is incomparably more glorious: there, victory is truth; dignity, holiness; peace, happiness; life, eternity. It has such gods all the less in its fellowship, if you were ashamed to have such people in yours. Therefore, if you desire to reach the blessed city, avoid fellowship with demons. Those who are appeased by disgraceful acts are unworthily worshiped by honorable people. Thus let these beings be removed from your piety [Note: [Col. 0078] So the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “from your fellowship.”] through Christian purification, just as those others were removed from your dignity by censorial condemnation.

As for bodily goods, which alone the wicked wish to enjoy, and bodily evils, which alone they do not wish to suffer—although these demons do not possess even the power over such things that they are thought to possess; and although, if they did possess it, we ought nevertheless to despise these things rather than worship them on their account, and, by worshiping them, be unable to attain those things which they begrudge us—we shall next see that in these matters, too, they have no such power as those who insist that they ought to be worshiped on this account suppose. This, then, will be the limit of this book.

# BOOK THREE

As in the preceding book Augustine showed that the Romans had been continually afflicted, from the founding of the City, by the evils of morals and the soul, so in the present book he shows that they were continually afflicted by bodily disadvantages and external misfortunes, and that the false gods, although they were freely worshiped before the coming of Christ, accomplished nothing toward averting such evils.

[Col. 0079]

## CHAPTER ONE — On the adversities that only the wicked fear, and that the world has always suffered while it worshiped the gods

I think enough has now been said about the evils of morals and of the soul—evils that must be avoided above all—and about how the false gods did nothing to help the people who worshiped them, so that they would not be crushed beneath the heap of those evils; rather, they acted so that the people would be crushed as severely as possible.

Now I see that I must speak of those evils which these people alone do not wish to suffer: famine, disease, war, plunder, captivity, slaughter, and any similar evils that we mentioned in the first book. For the wicked count as evils only those things that do not make people wicked; and they are not ashamed that, amid the goods they praise, they themselves—the praisers—are wicked. They are more upset if they have a bad estate than if they have a bad life, as though the greatest good for a human being were to possess every good except oneself.

But the gods of these people, when they were freely worshiped, did not prevent such evils—the only evils they fear—from befalling them. For when the human race was being worn down, before the coming of our Redeemer, by countless disasters in different places and times, some of them even unbelievable, what other gods did the world worship than these, apart from the one Hebrew people and certain individuals outside that people, wherever by the most hidden and just judgment of God they were found worthy of divine grace [Note: [Col. 0079] Augustine teaches this very point in Letter 102 to Deogratias, no. 15: “‘The salvation’—he says—‘of this religion . . . has never been lacking to anyone who was worthy of it,’ etc.” Explaining this opinion of his in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, no. 19, he says: “If it is examined and asked from what source anyone is worthy, some are not lacking who say, by human will; but we say, by divine grace or predestination.”]?

But, so as not to make this too long, I shall say nothing of the most grievous sufferings of all the other nations everywhere. I shall speak only of what concerns Rome and the Roman Empire—that is, of the city itself and of all the lands either joined to it by association or subject to it by condition—which sufferings they endured before the coming of Christ, when they already belonged, as it were, to the body of its commonwealth.

## CHAPTER TWO — Whether the gods worshiped alike by Romans and Greeks had reasons for allowing Ilium to be destroyed

First, what shall we say of Troy itself, or Ilium, from which the Roman people originated? We must not pass over or conceal what I also touched upon in the first book [Chapter 4]: since it had the same gods and worshiped them, why was it defeated, captured, and destroyed by the Greeks?

“Priam,” they say, “paid the ancestral perjuries of Laomedon” [Note: [Col. 0079] Hence Virgil, *Georgics* 1.502:

> We pay for the perjuries of Laomedontian Troy.]

Then it is true that Apollo and Neptune served that same Laomedon in hired labor, for he is said to have promised them payment and sworn falsely to them. [Col. 0080] I am astonished that Apollo, who was called a prophet, labored at so great a construction without knowing that Laomedon would deny the promised payment. Yet it was no more fitting that Neptune himself, his uncle, Jupiter’s brother and king of the sea, should be ignorant of the future.

For Homer introduces him as prophesying something great concerning the race of Aeneas, from whose descendants Rome was founded [Note: [Col. 0080] The word “founded” is absent from Vind., Am., Er., and the manuscripts. It is not absent from manuscript 2053. M.] [Note: [Col. 0080] The writers do not sufficiently agree either about the date of the City’s founding or about Homer’s age. The more probable opinion is that Homer lived approximately 160 years after the Trojan War and about 1,000 years before Christ, while Solomon was reigning in Judea. Whatever other opinion one may prefer, Homer was earlier than Rome; Cicero also testifies to this in *Tusculan Disputations* 1.1, as does Aulus Gellius in 17.21.]—although the same poet is said to have lived before that city was founded—and says that he even carried him away in a cloud so that Achilles would not kill him (*Iliad* 20.302–305). Virgil acknowledges this:

> He wished to overturn from their foundations

(as he admits in Virgil)

> the walls of perjured Troy, built by his own hands.  
> (*Aeneid* 5.810–811.)

Therefore Neptune and Apollo, such great gods, did not know that Laomedon would refuse them their payment; they were builders of the Trojan walls for nothing, and for an ungrateful man. Let them consider whether it is more serious to believe in such gods than to swear falsely to such gods. Homer himself did not readily believe this, for he represents Neptune fighting against the Trojans but Apollo fighting for the Trojans, although the story relates that both were offended by that perjury.

If, then, they believe the stories, let them be ashamed to worship such divinities. If they do not believe the stories, let them not bring forward Trojan perjuries, or wonder that the gods punished Trojan perjuries but loved Roman ones. For how did Catiline’s conspiracy obtain such a large supply of people in so great and so corrupt a state—people whose hands and tongues were nourished by perjury or civil bloodshed [Note: [Col. 0080] Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 14.]? What else were the repeatedly corrupted senators doing in their judgments, and the people repeatedly doing in their votes or in whatever matters were dealt with before it in public assemblies, except sinning also by perjury [Note: [Col. 0080] That is, the judges gave judgment under oath, and the people were bound by an oath when casting their votes, so that they would not, moved by money or favor, place anything before the welfare of the state.]?

For although their morals were utterly corrupt, the ancient custom of swearing was preserved—not so that fear of religion might restrain them from crimes, but so that perjuries might also be added to their other crimes.

## CHAPTER THREE — That the gods could not have been offended by Paris’s adultery, since it is said to have been common among them

There is therefore no reason why the gods—of whom, as they say, that empire had stood (*Aeneid* 2.352)—should be imagined angry at perjuring Trojans, when they are shown to have been defeated by the victorious Greeks. [Col. 0081] Nor did they grow angry at Paris’s adultery, as some again argue, so as to abandon Troy. For they are accustomed to be the authors and teachers of sins, not their punishers.

“Sallustius says: ‘As I have received it, the city of Rome was founded and initially inhabited by Trojans who, under Aeneas as leader, had fled and wandered about with no settled homes’ (*The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 6).”

If, then, the divinities judged that Paris’s adultery ought to be punished, it ought rather to have been punished in the Romans [Note: [Col. 0081] The printed editions read “in the Trojans.” The manuscripts support the correction.] or certainly in the Romans as well, because the mother of Aeneas [Note: [Col. 0081] Venus.] committed it. But how did they hate that disgraceful act in Paris when they did not hate it in their associate Venus—among other matters, the act she committed with Anchises, from which she bore Aeneas?

Was it because one act was committed with Menelaus indignant, while the other was permitted by Vulcan [Note: [Col. 0081] Venus’s husband.]? The gods, I suppose, do not become jealous of their wives—so little so that they even deign to share them with human beings.

Perhaps I may seem to be mocking the stories and not treating a matter of such weight seriously. Let us therefore not believe, if you please, that Aeneas was Venus’s son. I grant it, provided that Romulus was not Mars’s son either [Note: [Col. 0081] Romulus was the son of Mars and the Vestal Ilia Silvia.]. But if the one is allowed, why not the other? Is it permitted for gods to mingle with human women, but forbidden for human men to mingle with goddesses? A harsh—or rather unbelievable—condition: what was permitted to Mars, under Venus’s law, in intercourse, is not permitted to Venus herself under her own law. Yet both claims have been confirmed by Roman authority. For the later Caesar believed no less in his ancestress Venus [Note: [Col. 0081] He was approximately 700 years later than Romulus. The Julian family traced its ancestry through Iulus, the son of Aeneas, and through Iulus to Venus. Caesar’s own words on this matter are recorded by Suetonius.] than the earlier Romulus believed in Mars as his father.

## CHAPTER FOUR — On Varro’s opinion that it is useful for people to pretend that they were born from the gods

Someone may say: “Do you really believe these things?”

I certainly do not believe them. For even Varro, a highly learned man among them, almost admits—although not boldly or confidently—that these stories are false. Yet he says that it is useful for states for brave men to believe that they were born from the gods, even if this is false: in this way, the human spirit, bearing as it were the confidence of divine descent, may dare more boldly to undertake great deeds, act more vigorously, and, because of that very security, accomplish them more successfully.

When Varro’s opinion is expressed, as best I could, in my own words, you see how broad an opening it creates for falsehood: we may understand that more sacred and almost religious traditions could be fabricated wherever lies about the gods themselves were thought to benefit the citizens.

## CHAPTER FIVE — That it is not credible that the gods punished Paris’s adultery, since they did not avenge it in Romulus’s mother

But whether Venus could bear Aeneas from intercourse with Anchises, or Mars could beget Romulus from intercourse with Numitor’s daughter, let us leave undecided. For almost the same question also arises concerning our Scriptures, where it is asked whether the transgressing angels had intercourse with the daughters of human beings; from this, giants—that is, [Col. 0082] exceedingly large and strong men—were born, and the earth was then filled with them [Note: [Col. 0082] He discusses this question below, book 15, chapter 23.] (Genesis 6:4).

[V.] Let our discussion, then, for the moment be directed to both possibilities. For if the stories repeatedly read among them about Aeneas’s mother and Romulus’s father are true, how can adultery among human beings displease the gods when they tolerate the same things harmoniously among themselves? But if those stories are false, even so they cannot be angry at real human adulteries when they delight in their own fictitious ones.

Furthermore, if the story about Mars is not believed, then the story about Venus should not be believed either; and without the pretext of divine intercourse, Romulus’s mother has no defense. She was, moreover, the Vestal priestess Silvia [Note: [Col. 0082] Vind., Am., and most manuscripts read *Ilia* instead of *Silvia*. Both names belonged to Numitor’s daughter, the mother of Romulus and Remus, who was also called Rhea. Our manuscripts read *ilia*.].

Therefore the gods ought to have avenged that sacrilegious crime against the Romans even more than Paris’s adultery against the Trojans. For the ancient Romans themselves used to bury alive the Vestal priestesses who had been caught in sexual misconduct [Note: [Col. 0082] Livy, books 8 and 22.], whereas they punished adulterous women, even when some sentence was imposed, with no death [Note: [Col. 0082] See Livy 10.31.]. They considered offenses against divine sanctuaries so much more serious that they punished them more severely than offenses against human beds.

## CHAPTER SIX — On Romulus’s fratricide, which the gods did not avenge

I add another point. If human sins displeased those divinities to such an extent that, offended by Paris’s deed, they abandoned Troy to sword and fire, then the killing of Romulus’s brother [Note: [Col. 0082] Remus.] ought to have moved them against the Romans more than the Greek husband [Note: [Col. 0082] Menelaus, the husband of Helen, who was carried off by Paris.] was moved against the Trojans. The fratricide of the nascent city ought to have provoked them more than adultery in the established city.

It is irrelevant to the issue now before us whether Romulus ordered this to be done, or whether Romulus himself did it—a fact that many deny shamelessly, many question out of modesty, and many conceal out of grief. Nor should we linger here in a more careful investigation of the matter through the weighed testimony of many writers. It is publicly established that Romulus’s brother was killed—not by enemies, not by strangers.

If Romulus either committed or ordered this deed, he himself was more the head of the Romans than Paris was of the Trojans [Note: [Col. 0082] Paris was not king, but the son of Priam, king of the Trojans.]. Why, then, did that ravisher of another man’s wife provoke the anger of the gods against the Trojans, while this slayer of his own brother invited the protection of those same gods for the Romans [Note: [Col. 0082] The Trojan gods were transferred to Lavinium through Aeneas, then to Alba through Ascanius, and finally summoned to Rome through Romulus.]?

But if that crime was unrelated to Romulus’s deed or command, then, since it ought certainly to have been avenged, the whole city committed it, because the whole city tolerated it [Note: [Col. 0082] So Am., Er., and the manuscripts. Vind. and Lov. read “consented.”]; and it killed not merely a brother but, what is worse, a father. For each had been a founder, when one was removed by crime and not permitted to rule. [Col. 0083]

There is, I think, no reason to ask what evil Troy had deserved, so that the gods would abandon it to destruction, or what good Rome had done, so that the gods would inhabit it and allow it to grow—unless it was that the gods, defeated there, fled and betook themselves to these people, whom they were likewise to deceive. Indeed, they remained there as well, according to their custom, to deceive those who would again inhabit the same lands; and here they gloried in greater honors by practicing the same arts of deception even more extensively.

## CHAPTER SEVEN — On the destruction of Ilium by Fimbria, Marius’s general

Certainly, when civil wars were already raging, what misery had Ilium committed that it should be destroyed by Fimbria, a thoroughly wicked man of the Marian party, much more savagely and cruelly than once by the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0083] On this matter, see Livy, books 82 and 83; Appian, *Mithridatic War*.]?

At that earlier time many fled from there, and many who were captured at least continued to live in slavery. Fimbria, however, first issued a proclamation that no one was to be spared, and he burned the entire city and all the people in it. Ilium deserved this—not from the Greeks, whom it had provoked by its own injustice, but from the Romans, whose origins it had extended through its own calamity—with those common gods contributing nothing to repel it, or, more truthfully, possessing no power to do so.

Did the gods then also

> All depart, leaving shrines and altars deserted,

the gods by whose power that city had stood, rebuilt after the ancient fires and ruins of the Greeks?

But if they had departed, I ask the reason. As for the townspeople, I find their cause better in proportion as I find the gods’ cause worse. The townspeople had closed their gates against Fimbria in order to preserve their city intact for Sulla; for this reason he became angry and burned them, or rather utterly destroyed them.

Sulla was still the leader of the better civil faction [Note: [Col. 0083] Cicero, *Oration for Caelius*; Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 51.]; he was still attempting to recover the commonwealth by arms; he had not yet met the bad outcomes of these good beginnings. What, then, could the citizens of that city have done better? What more honorably, more faithfully, or more worthy of Roman kinship than to preserve their city for the better cause of the Romans and close their gates against the parricide of the Roman commonwealth?

But let the defenders of the gods consider into what destruction this act turned for them. If the gods had abandoned adulterers and left Ilium to the Greek flames so that a more chaste Rome might arise from its ashes, why did they later abandon that same city, related to the Romans—not rebelling against Rome, its noble daughter, but maintaining the most constant and dutiful allegiance to its more just faction—and leave it to be destroyed, not by the brave men of Greece but by the most vile man among the Romans?

Or, if the gods disliked the cause of Sulla’s party, for whose sake the wretched inhabitants closed their gates while preserving their city, why did they promise and foretell such great benefits to that same Sulla? Are they recognized here too as flatterers of the fortunate rather than defenders of the unfortunate?

Ilium was therefore not destroyed at that time because the gods abandoned it. For the demons, always most vigilant in deceiving, did what they could. Once all the images had been overthrown and burned together with the city, the temple of Minerva alone is reported, as Livy writes, to have remained intact amid so great a ruin [Col. 0084] [Note: [Col. 0084] This passage does not survive in Livy’s book 83, which concerns the destruction of Ilium.]. This was not so that the following words might be said to the gods’ praise:

> Father gods, under whose power Troy has always stood  
> (*Aeneid* 1.702–703),

but so that the following words might not be said in their defense:

> All the gods departed, leaving shrines and altars deserted.

They were permitted to do this—not so that they might be proved powerful, but so that they might be shown to have been present.

## CHAPTER EIGHT — Whether Rome ought to have been entrusted to the Trojan gods

After the lesson provided by Troy itself, with what prudence, then, was Rome entrusted to the Trojan gods for safekeeping?

Someone may say that they had already become accustomed to living in Rome when Ilium fell under Fimbria’s attack. How, then, did Minerva’s image remain standing? Furthermore, if they were in Rome when Fimbria destroyed Ilium, perhaps they were at Ilium when Rome itself was captured and burned by the Gauls. But since they have extremely keen hearing and move with great speed, they quickly returned at the sound of the goose, so that at least they might protect the Capitoline Hill, which remained; as for defending anything else, they were informed of the need to return too late.

## CHAPTER NINE — Whether we ought to believe that the gods provided the peace that existed under Numa’s reign

These gods are also believed to have helped Numa Pompilius, Romulus’s successor, so that he might have peace throughout the whole period of his reign and close the gates of Janus, which are customarily open during wars [Note: [Col. 0084] Macrobius explains why the gates of Janus were open in war and closed in peace, *Saturnalia* 1.9.]. This was supposedly deserved because he established many sacred rites for the Romans.

That man ought indeed to be congratulated for so much leisure, if only he had known how to devote it to beneficial matters and, neglecting his most pernicious curiosity, seek the true God with true piety. But the gods did not grant him that leisure; they might perhaps have deceived him less if they had found him without leisure. For the less occupied they found him, the more they occupied him themselves. Varro reveals what he contrived and by what arts he was able to associate such gods with himself or with that state; if it pleases the Lord, this will be discussed more carefully in its proper place.

For the present, since the question concerns their benefits, peace is a great benefit. But it is a benefit of the true God, who often gives it, like the sun, rain, and other necessities of life, even to the ungrateful and wicked.

But if those gods conferred this great good on Rome or Pompilius, why did they never afterward grant it to the Roman Empire during the more glorious periods themselves [Note: [Col. 0084] Vind., Am., Er., and almost all the manuscripts read “glorious.” The same reading occurs in manuscript 766.]? Were the sacred rites more useful when they were being established than when, once established, they were being celebrated? At that time they did not yet exist, but were being added so that they might exist; afterward, they already existed and were being maintained so that they might be beneficial.

What, then, is the explanation for the forty-three years—or, as others prefer, thirty-nine [Col. 0085] years—spent in such prolonged peace during Numa’s reign [Note: [Col. 0085] Livy, Plutarch, and others give Numa forty-three years, whereas Eutropius, Eusebius, and Cassiodorus report that he reigned only forty-one. Augustine took these figures from Cicero, *On the Republic* 2.14.], and for the fact that afterward, once the sacred rites had been established and the gods themselves—who had been summoned by those rites—had become its guardians and protectors, from the founding of the City until Augustus, after so many years only one year is mentioned as a great marvel, following the First Punic War, in which the Romans were able to close the gates of war?

## CHAPTER TEN — Whether it should have been desired that the Roman Empire be enlarged through such a frenzy of wars, when it could have been both peaceful and secure through the policy by which it grew under Numa

Do they reply that, unless wars continually arose and followed one another without interruption, the Roman Empire could not have been enlarged so far and so widely or become so famous for its great glory?

What a suitable reason: the empire had to be restless in order to be great? Is it not better, in human bodies, to have moderate stature with health than to reach some gigantic size through perpetual suffering and, once one has reached it, not to rest, but to be troubled by greater evils in proportion to the size of one’s limbs?

What evil would it have been—and would it not rather have been a very great good—if the times described by Sallustius had continued, when he says:

> “At the beginning, kings—for this was the first name of power on earth—were divided: some exercised their intellect, others their bodies. Even then human life was conducted without greed; each person was satisfied with his own possessions.”  
> (*The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 2)

Or, for the empire to be enlarged so greatly, was it necessary for what Virgil detests to occur, when he says:

> Until gradually a worse and more degraded age arrived,  
> And the frenzy of war and the desire for possession.  
> (*Aeneid* 8.326–327.)

But plainly the Romans have a just defense for so many wars undertaken and waged: they were compelled to resist enemies who attacked them unjustly, not by greed for acquiring human praise but by the necessity of defending their safety and liberty.

Let this be entirely so. For after their state, as Sallustius himself writes, appeared to have grown sufficiently prosperous and sufficiently powerful in laws [Note: [Col. 0085] In Sallustius, the word is “citizens,” not “laws.”], morals, and territory, as is the case with most mortal things, envy arose from prosperity. “Then neighboring kings and peoples began to test them in war, while only a few of their friends came to their aid; the rest, struck with fear, kept away from dangers” [Note: [Col. 0085] B. reads “kept far away from dangers.” The editions of Sallustius and our manuscripts omit *far*.].

“But the Romans, intent at home and in the field, hurried, made preparations, urged one another on, went to meet the enemy, and defended their liberty, country, and parents with arms. Afterward, when they had driven back the dangers by their courage, they brought aid to their allies and friends and formed friendships more by giving benefits than by receiving them” (*The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 6).

Rome grew appropriately through these practices. But during Numa’s reign, so that the peace might last so long, were wicked men attacking and testing Rome in war, or did none of this happen, so that that peace could continue? [Col. 0086]

For if Rome was being harassed by wars even then, yet no weapons were being brought against weapons, by what means were the enemies calmed without being defeated in battle or terrified by a martial attack? Those same means could always have been used, and Rome could always have ruled peacefully with the gates of Janus closed.

But if this was not within their power, then Rome did not have peace for as long as their gods wished, but for as long as the neighboring peoples all around wished, since they did not provoke Rome by any war—unless perhaps such gods will dare to sell to a human being even what another human being either wished or did not wish.

It does indeed matter, because of their own vice, to what extent these demons are permitted either to terrify or to excite evil minds. But if they could always do this, and if some other, more secret and higher power did not often act otherwise against their efforts, they would always have peace and victories in war at their disposal [Note: [Col. 0086] So Vind., Am., and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read “peace.”], which are almost always brought about through movements of human minds. Yet not only do stories—which lie about many things and scarcely indicate or signify anything true—confess that these events often occurred against their will; Roman history itself also confesses it.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN — On the image of Apollo at Cumae, whose weeping was believed to signify the defeat of the Greeks, whom he could not help

For what other reason was that Apollo at Cumae reported to have wept for four days when war was being waged against the Achaeans and King Aristonicus [Note: [Col. 0086] Julius Obsequens writes that he wept for four days in *On Prodigies*, chapter 87; Livy, however, says for three days and three nights. The Achaeans are not otherwise mentioned as having taken part in the war against Aristonicus.]?

Terrified by this prodigy, the haruspices thought that the image ought to be thrown into the sea. But the elders of Cumae intervened and reported that a similar prodigy had appeared in the same image during the wars of Antiochus and Perses [Note: [Col. 0086] The printed editions read “Persis.” The manuscripts read *Persis*, for which Ludovicus Vives thinks *Persae* should be read, meaning Perses, son of Philip, king of the Macedonians, whom Lucius Aemilius Paulus defeated in the Second Macedonian War. See Plutarch, *Aemilius Paulus*. Manuscript 766 reads *Persis*. The war mentioned here involved the Achaeans; above, their participation in Aristonicus’s war was incorrectly reported.]. Since the outcome had been favorable to the Romans, they testified that, by decree of the Senate, gifts had been sent to that same Apollo.

Then the haruspices, summoned as though they were more expert, replied that Apollo’s weeping image was favorable to the Romans because the Cumaean colony was Greek [Note: [Col. 0086] Strabo 5.4.] and Apollo, by weeping, had signified mourning and disaster for its own land, from which he had been summoned—that is, for Greece itself.

Soon afterward it was announced that King Aristonicus had been defeated and captured. Apollo certainly did not want him to be defeated and grieved over it, and he indicated this through the tears of his stone image.

Thus, although they are fictional, the poems of the poets describe the character of demons not altogether inappropriately, and in ways resembling the truth. In Virgil, Diana grieved for Camilla, and Hercules wept for dying Pallas [Note: [Col. 0086] *Aeneid* 11.836–849.].

Perhaps this is why Numa Pompilius, enjoying peace but not knowing or seeking who had granted it, while he idly considered to which gods he should entrust Rome’s [Col. 0087] safety and kingdom, did not suppose that the true and omnipotent supreme God cared for earthly affairs. Recalling the Trojan gods whom Aeneas had brought over, and observing that they had not been able to preserve for long either the Trojan kingdom or the Lavinian kingdom founded by Aeneas himself, he thought that other gods should be sought—gods whom he might either add to those earlier ones as guardians, like fugitives, or as helpers, like invalids, whether those earlier gods had already crossed over to Rome with Romulus or were destined to cross over at some time when Alba was destroyed.

## CHAPTER TWELVE — How many gods the Romans added to themselves beyond Numa’s establishment, whose multitude did not help them

Yet Rome was not content even with those sacred rites, many as they were, which Pompilius had established there, for Jupiter himself did not yet have his chief temple there [Note: [Col. 0087] *Jovis* is said here in the nominative case, not the genitive.]. King Tarquinius built the Capitol there.

Aesculapius, moreover, made his way from Epidaurus to Rome [Note: [Col. 0087] The printed editions read “went away to Rome.” The older books read “made his way to Rome.” Manuscripts 766, 2050, 2051, and 2052 read “made his way to Rome”; manuscript 2053 reads “made his way to come to Rome.”], so that, as a highly skilled physician, he might practice his art more gloriously in the most famous city [Note: [Col. 0087] Livy records that Aesculapius was brought to the City from Epidaurus, a town in Achaea, book 10, chapter 47.].

The Mother of the Gods also came—I do not know from where—from Pessinus [Note: [Col. 0087] Vind., Am., and Er. read: “But the Mother of the Gods, born I know not where, settled on the Praenestine hill.” Ludovicus Vives thinks that “she settled on the Palatine hill” should be read, because, he says, the Mother of the Gods was placed on the Palatine. But the reading of Lov. and the manuscripts is more reliable: “The Mother of the Gods also came, I know not from where, from Pessinus.” Compare above, book 1, chapter 30, column 42, note (b).].

For it was unworthy that, while her son already presided over the Capitoline Hill, she should still be hiding in an obscure place. Yet if she is the mother of all the gods, she not only followed some of her sons to Rome, but even preceded others who would later follow. I am truly astonished if she gave birth to the Cynocephalus, who came from Egypt much later.

Whether the goddess Fever was also born from her, Aesculapius, her great-grandson, may determine. But wherever she was born, the foreign gods will not, I suppose, dare to call her an obscure goddess, since she is a Roman citizen.

Under the protection of so many gods—who could count them?—native and foreign, heavenly, earthly, infernal, marine, spring, and river gods [Note: [Col. 0087] Many manuscripts read “rain gods.”], and, as Varro says, determinate and indeterminate gods, with males and females in every class of gods, just as among animals—under the protection, then, of so many gods, Rome ought not to have been shaken and afflicted by disasters so great and terrible, of which I shall mention a few out of many.

For by establishing and providing temples, altars, sacrifices, and priests for so many gods, Rome had gathered them together for its protection with the great smoke of its sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0087] “Smoke” signifies the emptiness of sacrifices or the vanity of pride.], as though this were a signal; and by doing so it offended the one supreme true God, to whom alone these rites are properly owed.

It did indeed live more happily with fewer gods. But as it grew larger, it thought that more gods had to be employed, just as a ship requires more sailors in proportion to its size. I suppose it despaired that the few under whose protection it had lived better, in comparison with its worse life, were insufficient to aid its greatness.

For first, under the kings themselves—[Col. 0088] except for Numa Pompilius, about whom I have already spoken—what a great evil of discordant conflict there was, which compelled Romulus’s brother to be killed!

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN — By what right and under what treaty the Romans obtained their first marriages

How could even Juno, who with her Jupiter already

> cherished the Romans as masters of the world  
> and the toga-clad people  
> (*Aeneid* 1.281–282),

nor Venus herself, help her own descendants of Aeneas to obtain marriages by honorable and equitable custom? Such a great calamity arose from this shortage that they seized them by deceit and soon were compelled to fight with their fathers-in-law. Thus the wretched women, not yet reconciled to their husbands after the wrong done to them, were already endowed with the blood of their parents.

But, someone will say, the Romans prevailed in this conflict against their neighbors. At the cost of how many wounds on both sides, and how many deaths among people so closely related and bordering on one another, did those victories come?

Because of the one father-in-law, Caesar, and his one son-in-law, Pompey, after Caesar’s daughter, Pompey’s wife, had died, with how great and how justified an impulse of grief Lucan exclaims:

> Wars more than civil through the Emathian fields,
We sing of the justice granted to crime! (Lucan, Book 1, lines 1–2.) Thus the Romans conquered, so that, with hands made bloody by the slaughter of their fathers-in-law, they might extort pitiable embraces from those men's daughters; nor did those women dare mourn their slain fathers, lest they offend their victorious husbands. While those men were still fighting, the women did not know for whom they should offer their vows [Note: [Col. 0088] See Ovid, *Fasti* 3, lines 205 ff.].

With such marriages Bellona, not Venus, endowed the Roman people [Note: [Col. 0088] So nearly all manuscripts. In B., “endowed” (*dotavit*). M.]; or perhaps that infernal fury Alecto [Note: [Col. 0088] Vind., Am., Er., and the manuscripts: “infernal fury.” So also manuscript 766. M.], with Juno now favoring them, had more power over them than when she had been stirred up at Juno’s prayers against Aeneas [Note: [Col. 0088] *Aeneid* 7, lines 323 ff.]. Andromache was more fortunate in her captivity than those Roman women were in their marriages [Note: [Col. 0088] Andromache, the wife of Hector, was taken to Greece by Pyrrhus after the destruction of Troy and married to him.]: although she was enslaved, Pyrrhus killed no Trojan after embracing her. The Romans, however, were killing their fathers-in-law in battle, even as they embraced their daughters in the bridal chambers.

That victorious woman, once subjected, could grieve the death of her people, but had no reason to fear it; those women, joined to the combatants, feared the deaths of their parents while their husbands advanced, and grieved when they returned; they possessed neither fear freely nor grief freely. For the destruction of citizens, relatives, brothers, and parents, they were either piously tormented or cruelly rejoiced at their husbands’ victories.

To this was added the fact that, as wars alternate in their fortunes, some women lost their husbands by the sword of their parents, while others lost both parents and husbands by the swords of both sides. For those conflicts were not insignificant among the Romans either. Indeed, matters came even to the siege of the city, and the inhabitants defended themselves behind closed gates. When the gates were opened by treachery and the enemy admitted within the walls, a wicked and exceedingly fierce battle between sons-in-law and fathers-in-law was fought in the very forum [Col. 0089] [Note: [Col. 0089] Livy, Book 1, chapters 11–13.]. Those abductors were even defeated; and, often fleeing inside their own houses, they stained their former victories—though those victories themselves were shameful and lamentable—even more grievously [Note: [Col. 0089] He means not victories over the Sabines, but those won over the Caeninenses and others, concerning which see Livy, Book 1, chapter 10.].

Nevertheless, Romulus, now despairing of the courage of his men, asked Jupiter to make them stand; and on that occasion Jupiter acquired the title Stator. There would have been no end to so great an evil unless those abducted women had rushed out with their hair torn, thrown themselves before their parents, and calmed their entirely justified anger—not with victorious weapons, but with submissive filial devotion [Note: [Col. 0089] Livy, Book 1, chapters 12–13.].

Then Romulus was compelled to endure Titus Tatius, king of the Sabines, as his partner in government, being unable to bear an equal partner in rule. But when would he have tolerated this man for long, when he had not tolerated his own brother and twin? Hence, after Tatius too had been killed, Romulus obtained the kingdom alone, so that he might be a greater god [Note: [Col. 0089] According to the consensus of the historians, Tatius was not killed by Romulus but by the Laurentines; they say, however, that Romulus bore the matter less resentfully than was fitting. Livy, Book 1, chapter 14.].

What sort of laws of marriage are these, what provocations to war, what treaties of brotherhood, kinship, alliance, and divinity? What, finally, was the life of the state under so many guardian gods? You see how many and how great things could be said on this subject, if my purpose were not concerned with what remains and my discourse were not hastening on to other matters.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On the impiety of the war that the Romans waged against the Albans, and on the victory gained through the desire to rule

1. What happened next, after Numa, under the other kings? With what great harm, not only to themselves but also to the Romans, were the Albans provoked into war! Evidently Numa’s peace had become worthless because it had lasted so long. How frequent were the slaughter and destruction of the Roman and Alban armies, and the mutual devastation of the two states!

For Alba, which Ascanius, the son of Aeneas, had founded, and which was more nearly Rome’s mother than Troy itself, was challenged to battle by King Tullus Hostilius. It fought, and was afflicted, and afflicted others, until many grew weary of the equal succession of conflicts. Then it was decided to test the outcome of the war through three brothers on each side: three Horatii came forward from the Romans, and three Curiatii from the Albans. Of the three Curiatii, two Horatii were overcome and killed; one Horatius overcame and killed the three Curiatii [Note: [Col. 0089] See Livy, Book 1, chapters 22–30.].

Thus Rome emerged victorious, but in that final contest the disaster was such that of six living men only one returned home. Who suffered loss in both states? Who mourned, except the stock of Aeneas, the descendants of Ascanius, the offspring of Venus, the grandchildren of Jupiter [Note: [Col. 0089] The manuscripts of good authority read “granddaughters of Jupiter.” Or should this refer to the daughter-state and the mother-state, of which he speaks immediately afterward? So also manuscript 766. M.]? For this too was more than a civil war, since a daughter-state fought against its mother-state.

Another savage and dreadful evil was added to this final battle of the three brothers. Since the two peoples had previously been friends—for they were neighbors and related by blood—the sister of the Horatii had been betrothed to one of the Curiatii. After she saw the spoils of her fiancé [Note: [Col. 0089] Several manuscripts read “the betrothal gifts.”] on her victorious brother, she was killed by that same brother because she wept.

The feeling of this one woman seems to me to have been more humane [Col. 0090] than that of the entire Roman people. She was still bound by her pledge to the man who had become her husband—or perhaps, grieving for the very brother who had killed the man to whom he had promised his sister, she had wept without deserving blame. For why does the pious Aeneas, in Virgil, commendably grieve even for an enemy killed by his own hand [Note: [Col. 0090] *Aeneid* 10, lines 821 ff.]? Why did Marcellus, recalling that the Syracusan state, only recently at its height and glory, had suddenly fallen beneath his hands, and considering the common condition of humanity, pity it with tears [Note: [Col. 0090] Above, Book 1, chapter 6.]?

Let us obtain from human feeling this much: that the woman grieved without guilt for her fiancé, killed by her brother, if men have grieved with praise for enemies whom they themselves had conquered. Therefore, while that woman was mourning the death inflicted on her fiancé by her brother, Rome was rejoicing that it had fought against a mother-state with such slaughter and had conquered through the shedding of so much kindred blood on both sides.

2. What is set before me—the name of praise and the name of victory? Let the obstacles of insane opinion be removed, and let crimes be seen naked, weighed naked, and judged naked. Let the cause of Alba be stated, just as the adultery of Troy was stated. No such cause, nothing comparable to it, is found: the only purpose was to rouse the idle men to arms,

> Tullus, and the armies now unused to triumphs

> (*Aeneid* 6, lines 814–815).

Through that fault alone such a crime was committed, a war between allies and kinsmen. Sallustius touches briefly on this great fault in passing. After briefly recalling earlier times, when human life was conducted without greed and each person was content with his own possessions, he says:

> “But afterward, when in Asia Cyrus, and in Greece the Lacedaemonians and Athenians, began to subdue cities and nations, to regard the desire to rule as the cause of war, and to consider the greatest glory to lie in the greatest empire” (*Sallust, Against Catiline*, chapter 2);

and the rest that he himself had undertaken to say. For the present, it is enough for me to have quoted his words up to this point.

This desire to rule agitates and crushes the human race through great evils. Through this desire Rome then celebrated its victory over Alba, and called the praise of its crime glory. “Because the sinner is praised,” says our Scripture, “in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts wickedly is blessed” (Psalm 10:3).

Therefore let deceptive coverings and misleading whitewash be removed from events, so that they may be examined with sincere judgment. Let no one say to me, “That man or the other was great because he fought and conquered this or that man.” Gladiators also fight, and they too win; that cruelty also receives rewards and praise. Yet I think it better to suffer the penalties of any kind of cowardice than to seek the glory of those weapons.

And yet, if gladiators were to enter the arena to fight one another, with one being the son and the other the father, who could endure such a spectacle? Who would not remove it? How, then, could a glorious contest of arms exist between one city that was the mother and another that was the daughter? Or was it different because that arena was not an arena, and the wider fields were filled not with the deaths of two gladiators but with the deaths of many in two peoples; because those contests were not enclosed by an amphitheater but by the whole world; and because an impious spectacle was provided both for the living at that time and for posterity, for as long as the fame of it extends?

3. Nevertheless, those guardian gods of the Roman empire endured the violence of their own devotion and acted as theatrical spectators of such contests, until the sister of the Horatii, because of the three slain Curiatii, was herself added by fraternal steel to the two brothers killed by the other side, so that Rome, which had conquered, would not have fewer deaths as well.

Then, as the fruit of victory, Alba was destroyed. After Ilium, which the Greeks overthrew, and after Lavinium, where Aeneas had established a foreign and fugitive kingdom [Note: [Col. 0091] So the manuscripts agree almost unanimously. But the printed editions read: “where King Latinus had established Aeneas as a foreign and fugitive king.”], those Trojan gods had dwelt there in a third abode. But perhaps, following their custom, they had already migrated from there as well; therefore it was destroyed. Evidently they had departed,

> “all the gods whose empire had stood there, leaving shrines and altars behind.”

They had indeed departed for the third time already, so that it might be confidently believed that Rome would be their fourth home. Alba had displeased them, where Amulius had ruled after expelling his brother [Note: [Col. 0091] Numitor.]; and Rome had pleased them, where Romulus had ruled after killing his brother [Note: [Col. 0091] Remus.].

But before Alba was destroyed, they say that its people were transferred to Rome, so that one state might be formed from the two. Let that have happened so. Nevertheless, that city—the kingdom of Ascanius and the third dwelling of the Trojan gods—was overthrown by the daughter-city, its mother. Yet in order that the remnants of war might fuse the two peoples into one pitiable mass, much blood had first been shed on both sides.

Why should I now recount one by one the same wars repeatedly renewed under the other kings—wars that seemed to have ended in victories, were repeatedly completed through such great slaughter, and were repeatedly resumed after treaties and peace between sons-in-law and fathers-in-law and their descendants? A considerable indication of this calamity was that none of those kings ever closed the gates of war. Therefore, under so many guardian gods, none of them ruled in peace.

## CHAPTER XV  
### What the lives and deaths of the Roman kings were like

1. What, then, were the deaths of those kings themselves? Let the flattering fable take care of Romulus, by which he is said to have been received into heaven. Let certain of their writers take care of the matter, those who said that he was torn apart by the senate because of his ferocity, and that a certain Julius Proculus was brought forward to claim that Romulus had appeared to him and had commanded through him that the Roman people worship him among the gods; and that in this way the people, who had begun to swell with anger against the senate, were restrained and pacified [Note: [Col. 0091] Livy, Book 1, chapter 16, and Dionysius, *Roman Antiquities*, Book 2.].

For a solar eclipse had also occurred, and the ignorant crowd, unaware that it had been caused by the regular course of the sun, attributed it to Romulus’s merits. As though, if that had been the sun’s mourning, it should not rather have been believed that Romulus had been killed, and that the crime itself had been indicated by the withdrawal even of daylight—as in fact happened when the Lord was crucified through the cruelty and impiety of the Jews (Luke 23:45).

That this obscuration of the sun did not occur according to the regular course of the stars is sufficiently shown by the fact that it was then the Passover of the Jews, which is solemnly celebrated at the full moon; whereas a regular solar eclipse occurs only at the end of the lunar cycle.

Cicero also sufficiently indicates that Romulus’s reception among the gods was considered to have happened rather than actually happened. When praising him in his books *On the Republic* (Book 2, chapter 10), in the speech of Scipio, he says:

> “He achieved so much that, when he suddenly disappeared after the sun had been obscured, he was thought to have been placed among the gods; an opinion that no mortal has ever been able to attain without extraordinary glory for his virtue.”

When Cicero says that Romulus suddenly disappeared, this clearly implies either the violence of a storm or the secrecy of a murder and crime. Other writers of theirs also add a sudden storm to the eclipse of the sun, which surely either provided an opportunity for the crime or itself consumed Romulus.

Regarding Tullus Hostilius, the third king after Romulus, who was himself also destroyed by lightning, Cicero says in the same books that he was not believed to have been received among the gods after such a death because perhaps the Romans did not wish to make public what had been approved—that is, accepted as credible—in the case of Romulus, lest they cheapen it by easily attributing the same thing to another [Note: [Col. 0092] On this and what follows, see Livy, Book 1, and Dionysius, Book 3.].

He also says openly in his *Invectives*:

> “We have raised Romulus, who founded this city, to the immortal gods through goodwill and reputation” (*Third Oration against Catiline*, chapter 1),

thus showing that this had not truly happened, but had been proclaimed and spread through goodwill because of Romulus’s merits and virtue.

In the dialogue *Hortensius*, when speaking about regular solar eclipses, he says:

> “So that it produces the same darkness as it produced at the death of Romulus, who met his end through an obscuration of the sun.”

Here he certainly had no fear of speaking of a man’s death, because he was acting more as a disputant than as a eulogist.

2. What dreadful deaths did the other kings of the Roman people have, except Numa Pompilius and Ancus Marcius, who died of illness? Tullus Hostilius, as I have said, the victor over and destroyer of Alba, was burned by lightning together with his entire household. Priscus Tarquinius was killed by the sons of his predecessor. Servius Tullius was murdered through a wicked crime by his son-in-law Tarquinius Superbus, who succeeded him in the kingdom.

Nor did “the gods depart, leaving shrines and altars behind,” after such a great act of parricide against the best king of that people—those gods whom they say were moved by the adultery of Paris to do this to wretched Troy and leave it to be destroyed and burned by the Greeks. On the contrary, Tarquinius himself succeeded his father-in-law after killing him.

Those gods saw this wicked parricide of his father-in-law reigning, and even [Col. 0093] exulting in many wars and victories, and constructing the Capitol from the spoils [Note: [Col. 0093] The printed editions read “from the spoils of war.” “Of war” is absent from the manuscripts and was not necessary to add, since “spoils” means nothing other than booty acquired in war or money collected from the sale of booty. See Aulus Gellius, Book 13, chapter 23; Florus, Book 1, chapter 7, concerning this same Tarquinius: “From the spoils of captured cities he erected a temple.”]. They did not depart, but remained present, and endured their king Jupiter presiding and reigning over them in that most lofty temple—in other words, in the work of a parricide.

For he did not first build the Capitol while innocent and then, after his evil deeds, get driven from the city. Rather, he reached the very kingdom in which he would build the Capitol by perpetrating a monstrous crime. The fact that the Romans afterward expelled him from the kingdom and shut him outside the walls of the city was not because of his own offense against Lucretia, but because of his son’s crime, committed not only without his knowledge but even in his absence. At that time he was besieging the city of Ardea and waging war on behalf of the Roman people. We do not know what he would have done if his son’s outrage had been reported to him.

Nevertheless, without investigating his judgment or testing it, the people deprived him of power; and, after recalling the army, which they ordered to abandon him, they then closed the gates and did not allow him to enter when he returned [Note: [Col. 0093] Livy, Book 1, chapter 57 ff.].

After those most serious wars, in which he weakened the same Romans by stirring up their neighbors against them, he was abandoned by those whose support he had relied on and was unable to recover the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0093] So all the manuscripts. The usual reading was *valuit*.]. He then lived quietly as a private citizen for fourteen years, as is said, in Tusculum, a town near Rome, and grew old with his wife [Note: [Col. 0093] Tarquinius in fact spent several years at Tusculum with his son-in-law Octavius Mamilius; but he died at Cumae in the house of the tyrant Aristodemus, according to Livy, Book 2, chapters 15 and 21.], perhaps with a more desirable death than that of his father-in-law, who was killed through the crime of his son-in-law, with his daughter, as is reported, not unaware of it [Note: [Col. 0093] Livy, Book 1; Valerius, Book 9, chapter 11.].

Yet the Romans did not call this Tarquinius cruel or criminal, but “the Proud,” perhaps because they could not endure his royal arrogance with another form of arrogance. For they despised the crime by which he had killed their excellent king and father-in-law to such an extent that they made him their king. I wonder whether they did not, by this crime, repay so great a crime with an even greater one.

Nor did “the gods depart, leaving shrines and altars behind.” Unless someone should defend those gods in this way: that they remained in Rome so that they could punish the Romans more through punishments than help them through benefits, deceiving them with empty victories and crushing them through the most serious wars.

Such was the life of the Romans under their kings, during the supposedly laudable period of that republic, until the expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus—approximately 243 years. Yet all those victories, purchased with so much blood and at the price of such great calamities, scarcely extended that empire twenty miles from the city [Note: [Col. 0093] So all the manuscripts. In B., “miles” (*milliaria*). M.], an extent that cannot even be compared with the territory of some Getulian city [Note: [Col. 0093] “Getulian,” that is, situated in Getulia, a region of Africa.].

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the first Roman consuls, one of whom drove the other from his country and soon died at Rome, after the most atrocious acts of parricide, struck down by an enemy whom he had wounded

[Col. 0094]

Let us add to this period also the time during which Sallustius says that the state was governed under equitable and moderate law (see above, Book 2, chapter 18), while fear of Tarquinius and the serious war with Etruria continued. For as long as the Etruscans assisted Tarquinius in trying to recover his kingdom, Rome was shaken by a serious war. Therefore Sallustius says that the republic was conducted under equitable and moderate law while fear pressed upon it, not because justice persuaded it.

In that very brief period, how disastrous was the year in which the first consuls were created after the royal power had been expelled! They did not complete their own year. Junius Brutus first drove his colleague, Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, dishonorably from the city; then he himself soon fell in battle, mutually wounded with the enemy [Note: [Col. 0094] With Arruns, the son of King Tarquinius Superbus. Livy, Book 2, chapters 2–8.], after first killing with his own hand his sons and his wife’s brothers, because he had learned that they had conspired to restore Tarquinius.

After Virgil had commendably recalled this deed, he immediately recoiled from it with compassion. For after saying,

> The father will summon his sons, who are fomenting new wars,

> to punishment, for beautiful liberty’s sake,

he then exclaimed and said:

> Unhappy man! However his descendants may regard these deeds.

However, he said, the descendants may regard—elevate and praise—those deeds; the man who killed his sons is unhappy. And as though to console the unhappy man, he added:

> Love of country prevailed, and an immense desire for praise.  
> (*Aeneid* 6, lines 820–823.)

Does it not seem that in this Brutus—who both killed his sons and, struck by the son of Tarquinius whom he himself had wounded, could not survive him, but rather Tarquinius himself survived him—the innocence of his colleague Collatinus was avenged? Collatinus, a good citizen, endured from the expulsion of Tarquinius what Tarquinius the tyrant himself had endured.

For Brutus himself is also said to have been related by blood to Tarquinius. But evidently Collatinus was oppressed by the similarity of his name, since he too was called Tarquinius. He should therefore have been compelled to change his name, not his country. Finally, in his name [Note: [Col. 0094] Vind., Am., and Er. read “if in his name.” In Lov., the words “it would be less” occur not here but below, after “in his name”; “if” is added. This particle is absent from the manuscripts, and the sentence is no less complete—indeed, stronger—without it.] this word could have been reduced, and he could have been called simply Lucius Collatinus.

But for that reason he did not lose what he could have lost without any harm, so that he was ordered to be deprived both of the honor of being the first consul and of citizenship as a good citizen. Is this, then, the detestable injustice of Junius Brutus’s glory, and something of no use to the republic? Was it for the perpetration of this that

> Love of country prevailed, and an immense desire for praise?

After the tyrant Tarquinius had certainly been expelled [Note: [Col. 0094] In some manuscripts of good authority, “the tyrant” is absent.], Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, the husband of Lucretia, was created consul with Brutus [Col. 0095]. How justly the people considered a citizen’s character, not his name! How unjustly [Note: [Col. 0095] The manuscripts read “how impiously.” Perhaps “so impiously” should be read.] Brutus, if he was offended by the name, deprived his colleague of country and honor when he could have deprived him only of his name!

These were the evils and adversities that occurred when that republic was governed under equitable and moderate law. Lucretius too, who had been substituted in Brutus’s place, was carried off by illness before that same year ended. Thus Publius Valerius, who had succeeded Collatinus, and Marcus Horatius, who had been substituted for the deceased Lucretius, completed that funereal and Tartarean year, which had five consuls and in which the Roman republic inaugurated the new honor and power of the consulship.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### What evils afflicted the Roman republic after the beginnings of consular rule, when the gods whom it worshiped did not help it

1. Then, once fear had diminished somewhat—not because the wars had ceased, but because they pressed with less weight—when the period of government under equitable and moderate law had ended, there followed what the same Sallustius briefly explains:

> “Then the fathers exercised a servile authority over the plebeians, deciding concerning their life and backs in the manner of kings, driving them from their fields, and, while the others were excluded, exercising authority alone.”

Oppressed by these cruelties, and especially by debt [Note: [Col. 0095] So Sallustius and manuscript 766. In B., “the plebeian.” M.], while enduring taxation and military service at the same time through continual wars, the plebeians occupied the Sacred Mount and the Aventine under arms; and then they secured tribunes of the plebs and other rights for themselves.

The end of the dissensions and conflict on both sides came with the Second Punic War. [XVII.] Why, then, should I either endure such delays in writing or inflict them on my readers? Sallustius has briefly indicated how wretched that republic was over so long a period, through all those years up to the Second Punic War, when wars from abroad did not cease to disturb it and internal conflicts and civil seditions continued.

Therefore those victories were not solid joys of the blessed, but empty consolations of the wretched, alluring incitements toward undergoing one barren [Note: [Col. 0095] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “terrible.”] evil after another, for those who were in no way at peace.

Let good and prudent Romans not be angry with us because we say these things. Indeed, they should neither be asked nor admonished about this matter, since it is entirely certain that they will not be angry. For we do not say anything more serious or severe than their own authorities say, though we are far inferior to them in style and leisure; yet those authorities themselves labored to learn these works, and compel their sons to labor over them.

But if they are angry, how would they have tolerated me if I said what Sallustius says?:

> “Very numerous disturbances, seditions, and finally civil wars arose, while a few powerful men, for whose advantage most had submitted, sought domination under the honorable name of the fathers or the plebs; and citizens were called good or bad, not according to their merits toward the republic, since all were corrupt, but according to whether each was the richest and strongest in wrongdoing, because he defended the existing order as though he were good.”

Moreover, if those writers of history thought that it belonged to honorable liberty not to keep silent about the evils of their own state, though they were compelled in many places to praise it with great acclaim, because they had no other and truer state in which eternal citizens were to be read about, what ought we to do? Since our hope in God is so much better and more certain, our freedom ought to be correspondingly greater, when they attribute present evils to our Christ in order to alienate weaker and more ignorant minds from the state in which alone one must live eternally and happily.

Nor do we say anything more dreadful about their gods than their own repeatedly cited authorities, whom they read and praise. Indeed, we have taken from those very authorities the things we say, and we are in no way capable of saying either such things or everything that could be said.

2. Where, then, were those gods whom people think should be worshiped for the sake of the small and deceptive happiness of this world, when the Romans—whom those gods sold themselves to through the most mendacious cunning as worthy of worship—were afflicted by such great calamities?

Where were they when the consul Valerius was killed while defending the Capitol, which had been seized [Note: [Col. 0096] Ludovicus Vives thinks that *inscensum*, from *inscendo*, should be read; for the slaves had not burned the Capitol. We believe that *insessum*, “occupied,” should be read, from *insideo*, the verb Livy uses in recounting the event in Book 3. Our manuscripts have *incensum*. M.] by exiles and slaves [Note: [Col. 0096] Livy, Book 3, chapters 15–18.]? He himself could more easily have helped Jupiter’s temple than that crowd of so many gods, together with their greatest and best king, whose temple he had freed, could help him.
