Where were they when the state, exhausted by the thick accumulation of the evils of seditions, was waiting in brief calm for envoys sent to Athens to obtain laws, and was devastated by severe famine and pestilence [Note: [Col. 0096] The same work, chapter 32.]?

Where were they when, once again, as the people were suffering from hunger, they first created a prefect of the grain supply; and when, as that famine grew worse, Spurius Maelius [Note: [Col. 0096] The printed editions read “Aemilius.” The manuscripts read “Maelius,” as does Livy, Book 4, chapters 13–16.], who had distributed grain to the starving multitude, incurred the charge of aspiring to kingship, and was killed by Quintus Servilius, master of the horse, through the insistence of the aged dictator Lucius Quinctius, amid the greatest and most dangerous tumult of the state [Note: [Col. 0096] The same work, Book 4, chapters 12–15.]?

Where were they when, after a great pestilence had arisen, the people had long and severely suffered without remedy under useless gods, and thought it necessary to provide new lectisternia, something it had never done before [Note: [Col. 0096] The manuscripts of Am. and some others, including the very ancient Corbeiensis, read: “The people, wearied for a long time and greatly under useless gods.” They do not add “without remedy,” which is also omitted by Vind. The Regius manuscript, another Corbeiensis, and some other manuscripts read: “Under useless gods, the people, wearied for a long time and greatly, [sought] an empty remedy.” This is not a bad reading; nevertheless, we suspect that the words “an empty remedy,” first written in the margin of the book, later migrated into the text, and that eventually “without remedy” began to be read in their place.] [Note: [Col. 0096] The same work, Book 5, chapter 13.]?

The couches were spread in honor of the gods; from this the sacred—or rather sacrilegious—name was derived.

Where were they when, after the Roman army had suffered frequent and great defeats at Veii through ten consecutive years of unsuccessful fighting, it was finally rescued by Furius Camillus, whom the ungrateful state later condemned [Note: [Col. 0096] The same work, chapters 10–25 and chapter 32.]?

Where were they when the Gauls captured, plundered, and burned Rome, and filled it with slaughter [Col. 0097] [Note: [Col. 0097] Livy, Book 5, chapter 37 ff.]?

Where were they when that notorious pestilence inflicted such a great slaughter that Furius Camillus himself died—he who had first defended the ungrateful republic against the Veientes and later avenged it against the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0097] The same work, chapter 46 ff., and Book 7, chapter 1.]? During that pestilence they introduced theatrical games, another new pestilence—not into the bodies of the Romans, but, what is far more harmful, into their morals [Note: [Col. 0097] See above, Book 1, chapter 32, and Book 2, chapter 8.].

Where were they when another serious pestilence was believed to have arisen from the poisons of married women, whose conduct—of very many women of rank, beyond belief—was found to be more deadly than any pestilence [Note: [Col. 0097] Two of them, Cornelia and Sergia, belonged to patrician families, according to Livy, Book 8, chapter 18, who says that 170 married women were condemned for this crime.]?

Or where were they when the two consuls, together with their armies, were surrounded by the Samnites at the Caudine Forks [Note: [Col. 0097] Lov. reads “the Caudine Forks.” The other books and Livy, Book 9, read “the Caudine Forks.” They are mountain passes in the Caudine valley between Abella and Beneventum, near the town of Caudium in Samnium, not far from Beneventum and Capua.] and were compelled to make a disgraceful treaty with them? Six hundred Roman knights were given as hostages, while the rest, having surrendered their weapons and other possessions and been stripped of their coverings, were sent beneath the enemy’s yoke, each with a single garment [Note: [Col. 0097] Livy, Book 9, chapter 2 ff.]?

Or when, while the others were suffering from a severe pestilence, many in the army too were struck by lightning and died [Note: [Col. 0097] The same work, Book 10, chapter 31.]?

Or when, because of another intolerable pestilence, Rome was compelled to summon and employ Aesculapius from Epidaurus as a physician-god [Note: [Col. 0097] The same work, at the end of chapter 47.]—since perhaps Jupiter, king of all, who had already sat for a long time in the Capitol, had not been allowed to learn medicine because of the many sexual outrages to which he had devoted himself as a young man?

Or when the enemies—the Lucanians, Bruttians, Samnites, Etruscans, and Senonian Gauls—conspired at one time: first their envoys were killed, and then the army was overwhelmed together with its commander, seven tribunes perishing with him and thirteen thousand soldiers?

Or when, after the long and serious seditions at Rome, during which the plebs finally withdrew to the Janiculum in the face of hostile plunder [Note: [Col. 0097] Lov. reads “separation”; the other books read “plunder.” Livy, Book 11, discusses this secession of the plebs to the Janiculum, the mountain now called Montorio.], the calamity of this evil was so dreadful that, because of it—as was customary in extreme dangers—the dictator Hortensius was appointed; and after recalling the plebs, he died while still holding that office, something that had happened to no dictator before and that was a more serious crime for those gods, now that Aesculapius was present?

3. Then so many wars broke out everywhere that, because of a shortage of soldiers, those proletarians were enrolled for military service. They had received this name because they devoted themselves to producing offspring and, owing to their poverty, were unable to serve in the army.

Pyrrhus, king of Greece, then celebrated with enormous glory, was also summoned by the Tarentines and became an enemy of the Romans. When he consulted Apollo about the future outcome, Apollo delivered an ambiguous oracle with considerable cleverness, so that whatever happened, the god himself would be considered divine. For he said:

> I say to you, Pyrrhus, that you are able to conquer the Romans.

Thus, whether Pyrrhus defeated the Romans or the Romans [Col. 0098] defeated Pyrrhus, the prophet could await either outcome without danger.

What disasters, and how dreadful, then befell both armies? In that conflict Pyrrhus nevertheless emerged superior, so that he could now proclaim Apollo divine according to his own interpretation—unless, in the next battle, the Romans departed as the victors.

Amid such great slaughter in the wars, a severe pestilence also arose among women: pregnant women died before giving birth at term. I suppose Aesculapius excused himself by saying that he claimed to be a chief physician [Note: [Col. 0098] The printed editions read “claimed himself to be a chief physician.” The word “himself” is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.], not a midwife.

The animals too died in the same way, so that it was thought that the race of animals was about to perish. What if that memorable winter, raging with such incredible ferocity that dreadful depths of snow remained even in the forum for forty days and the Tiber was frozen solid [Note: [Col. 0098] Some manuscripts read “was delayed.”], had occurred in our own times? What things, and how many, would they have said about it?

What of that enormous pestilence as well—how long it raged, and how many it killed? When it extended into another year with much greater force, the Romans, with Aesculapius present to no avail, resorted to the Sibylline Books [Note: [Col. 0098] Orosius, Book 4, chapter 5.]. In this class of oracles, as Cicero records in his books *On Divination*, people usually place greater trust in interpreters who conjecture ambiguous meanings as they are able or willing to do (Book 2, chapter 54).

It was then declared that the cause of the pestilence was that many people privately held possession of numerous sacred buildings that they had occupied. Thus, for the moment, Aesculapius was freed from the serious charge of incompetence or negligence.

But why had many people occupied those buildings, with no one preventing them, unless it was because prayers had long been offered in vain to such a multitude of gods? In this way the places had gradually been abandoned by their worshipers, so that, as though empty, they could be claimed for human uses without offending anyone.

For if those buildings, diligently sought out and restored at that time as though to calm the pestilence, had not afterward lain hidden, neglected and appropriated in the same way, the fact that Varro, writing about sacred buildings, records so many things that had been forgotten would not be attributed to his great learning. But meanwhile an elegant remedy was arranged—not for driving away the pestilence, but for excusing the gods.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### How many disasters wore down the Romans during the Punic Wars, when the protection of the gods was sought in vain
1. Now, during the Punic Wars, while victory long hung undecided and uncertain between the two empires, and two exceedingly powerful peoples drove their forces against one another, each attacking the strongest and wealthiest, how many lesser kingdoms were crushed? How many great and famous cities destroyed? How many states afflicted, how many ruined? How far and wide were whole regions and lands devastated? How often were each side defeated and then victorious? How many human beings were consumed, whether soldiers engaged in combat or peoples who took no part in arms? What a quantity of ships was overwhelmed in naval battles and sunk amid the variety of storms? If we attempted to recount or even mention these things, we should become nothing other than writers of history ourselves.

Then the Roman state, thrown into great fear, resorted to futile and laughable remedies. On the authority of the Sibylline Books, secular games were restored, [Col. 0099] games whose celebration had been established at intervals of a hundred years but had perished from neglect in more prosperous times. The pontiffs also renewed sacred games for the dead—games themselves abolished in earlier, better years. Naturally, when they were renewed, the dead, enriched by such a great abundance of the dying, took pleasure even in playing: for surely the wretched human beings were staging, through those savage wars and bloody hatreds and victories ending in death on both sides, great games for demons and lavish banquets for the dead.

Nothing truly more pitiable occurred in the First Punic War than the fact that the Romans were defeated in such a way that even that Regulus was captured, the man whom we mentioned in the first and second books (Book 1, chapters 15 and 24; and Book 2, chapter 23)—a truly great man, previously victorious over and conqueror of the Carthaginians. He would even have brought the First Punic War to an end, had he not, through an excessive desire for praise and glory, imposed upon the exhausted Carthaginians harsher terms than they could bear. If that man’s wholly unexpected captivity, utterly disgraceful enslavement, utterly faithful oath, and most cruel death do not compel those gods to blush, then it is true that they are made of bronze and have no blood.

2. Nor were the gravest disasters of that period absent within the walls. For when the Tiber overflowed far beyond its customary level, almost all the level parts of the city were overturned: some places were driven away by the force of the river like a torrent, others were soaked and undermined as though by a long-standing pool. This disaster was then followed by a still more destructive fire. After it had seized the taller buildings around the Forum, it did not spare even the temple of Vesta, its closest familiar dwelling, where the virgins—more condemned than honored—were accustomed to provide it, as it were, with perpetual life through the most diligent replacement of wood. At that time the fire not only lived there but raged.

Terrified by its violence, the virgins could not rescue the fatal sacred objects, which had already oppressed the three cities in which they had been kept [Note: [Col. 0099] He means Ilium, Lavinium, and Alba.]. The pontiff Metellus, forgetting in some measure his own safety, rushed in and carried them away, half-burned himself [Note: [Col. 0099] Livy, Book 19.]. The fire did not recognize even him; or rather, there was no deity there that would not also have fled, had one been present. Thus it was the man who was able to help Vesta’s sacred objects, rather than those objects the man. If they could not drive the fire away from themselves, what help could they provide against those waters and flames for the state whose safety they were thought to protect? The event itself made clear that they were completely powerless.

We would make none of these charges against them if they said that those sacred objects had been established not for the protection of temporal goods but to signify eternal ones—and that therefore, since they were bodily and visible things and happened to perish, nothing was diminished from the realities for whose sake they had been established, and they could be restored for the same purposes. But now, through a remarkable blindness [Note: [Col. 0099] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *miserabili*, “wretched.”], they suppose that it could have been brought about by sacred objects capable of perishing that the earthly safety and temporal prosperity of the state could not perish. Therefore, when it is shown that, even while those sacred objects remained, either the destruction of safety or misfortune descended upon the state, they are ashamed to change an opinion which they cannot defend [Note: [Col. 0100] An old manuscript of Saint-Amand reads: “which they cannot defend, let them not be ashamed.”].

## CHAPTER XIX  
### The affliction of the Second Punic War, in which the strength of both sides was consumed

As for the Second Punic War, it would take far too long to recount the disasters of the two peoples, fighting one another over such great distances and expanses, so that, as even those who undertook not so much to narrate Rome’s wars as to praise the Roman empire admit, the one who conquered more closely resembled the defeated [Note: [Col. 0100] Livy, beginning of Book 21, and Silius Italicus, Book 1.].

For when Hannibal rose from Spain, crossed the Pyrenees, traversed Gaul, and burst through the Alps, his forces increasing through so long a circuit, laying waste or subduing everything, and then, like a torrent, pouring into the jaws of Italy, how bloody were the wars that were fought, how many the battles [Note: [Col. 0100] The manuscripts read: “How bloody the battles that were fought! How often …”—and so also manuscript 766.]! How often were the Romans defeated! How many towns defected to the enemy, how many were captured and crushed! How dreadful were the battles, and how repeatedly glorious for Hannibal through Roman disaster!

What shall I say about the astonishingly horrifying disaster at Cannae, where Hannibal, although exceedingly cruel, is nevertheless reported to have ordered his men to spare the survivors after being sated by the slaughter of so many fiercest enemies [Note: [Col. 0100] The disaster at Cannae, where the Roman army was defeated near the town or village of Cannae in Apulia, is described by Livy, Book 22, chapters 41 and following.]? From there he sent three measures of gold rings to Carthage [Note: [Col. 0100] Livy, Book 23, chapter 12.], so that they might understand that so much Roman rank had fallen in that battle that it was more easily grasped by measure than counted by number; while the slaughter of the rest of the multitude, so much greater in number as it was lower in status [Note: [Col. 0100] The printed editions have *infirmioris*, “weaker.” The manuscripts more correctly have *infimioris*, that is, “of the lowest-ranking multitude,” who had no use for a ring.], lying without rings, was thought better inferred than reported.

Finally, such a shortage of soldiers followed that the Romans collected accused criminals by offering them immunity, granted freedom to slaves, and from these established—not merely supplemented—a shameful army [Note: [Col. 0100] The manuscripts of Ambrosius and Erasmus have *pudendis*, “shameful.”]. Thus arms were lacking for slaves—or, rather, lest we wrong them, for men who had already been made free—to fight on behalf of the Roman republic. Weapons were taken down from the temples, as though the Romans were saying to their gods: “Put away what you have held so long in vain, lest our slaves perhaps be able to make some useful use of it, when you, our deities, have been able to accomplish nothing.”

At that time, when the treasury had also failed to provide the soldiers’ pay, private wealth was brought into public use. Everyone contributed whatever he possessed, so that, apart from their individual gold rings and individual *bullae*—pitiful badges of rank—the Senate itself, and still more the other orders and tribes, retained no gold for themselves [Note: [Col. 0100] Livy, Book 22, chapters 57 and 59–61.]. Who could tolerate such people if, in our own times, they were forced into such poverty, when we can scarcely tolerate them now, although more is being given to actors for excessive pleasure than was then contributed to the legions for the sake of their ultimate survival [Col. 0101]?

## CHAPTER XX  
### The destruction of Saguntum, whose people perished because of their friendship with the Romans, while the Roman gods brought them no aid

But amid all the disasters of the Second Punic War, nothing was more pitiable and more deserving of a lament than the destruction of the Saguntines [Note: [Col. 0101] Saguntum, or Saguntus, was once a very famous city of Hispania Tarraconensis, not far from the place where Valencia now stands. Livy, Book 21, chapters 6–15, describes its destruction by Hannibal.].

This Spanish state, an especially devoted friend of the Roman people, was destroyed while it remained faithful to that people. For this reason Hannibal, having broken the treaty with the Romans, sought pretexts by which to provoke them into war. He therefore besieged Saguntum fiercely. When this was heard at Rome, ambassadors were sent to Hannibal, ordering him to withdraw from the siege. They were disregarded, proceeded to Carthage, and lodged a complaint about the broken treaty; then, having accomplished nothing, they returned to Rome.

While these delays were taking place, that wretched and exceedingly wealthy city, dear both to its own state and to Rome, was destroyed by the Carthaginians in the eighth or ninth month. It is horrifying to read of its destruction, and still more horrifying to write about it. Nevertheless, I shall mention it briefly, for it is highly relevant to the matter at hand.

First it wasted away from hunger; indeed, some are said to have fed even on the corpses of their own people. Then, exhausted in every respect, and unwilling even to fall alive into Hannibal’s hands, it publicly built a huge pyre, blazing into which they hurled themselves and all their people, after slaughtering them with the sword.

Here those gluttonous and worthless gods [Note: [Col. 0101] The manuscripts of Vindobonensis and Ambrosianus have *duelliones*, “war-makers.”] might have done something—those gods who gape after the fat of sacrifices and deceive people in the darkness of false divinations. Here they might have done something: they might have come to the aid of a city most devoted to the Roman people and not allowed it to perish while dying for the preservation of its faith. They themselves, at any rate, had presided when it was joined to the Roman republic by a treaty. Thus, while faithfully preserving what had pleased those very guardians, what it had joined and bound by faith and constrained by oath, it was besieged, overwhelmed, and destroyed by a faithless enemy.

If those gods later frightened Hannibal with storms and lightning when he was near the Roman walls and drove him far away [Note: [Col. 0101] Livy, Book 26, chapter 11.], they should have done something of the kind then, for the first time. I dare say that they could more honorably have raged with storms on behalf of Rome’s friends—who were endangered because they would not break faith with Rome and who at that time had no aid—than on behalf of the Romans themselves, who were fighting for their own interests and were wealthy in comparison with Hannibal.

If, then, they were guardians of Roman prosperity and glory, they would have turned away from Rome so grave a charge as the disaster of Saguntum. But how foolishly do people believe that Rome did not perish when Hannibal was victorious because of those gods who defended it, when they could not come to the aid of Saguntum, lest it perish because of its friendship with Rome? If the Saguntines had been a Christian people, and had suffered something of this kind for the evangelical faith, although they would not have corrupted themselves through sword or fire, nevertheless, if they had suffered destruction for the evangelical faith, they would have suffered it in the hope in which they had believed in Christ—not in hope of a reward lasting for the briefest time, but of unending eternity [Col. 0102] [Note: [Col. 0102] Only the printed editions have “and would possess unending eternity.” Erasmus has *interminatae*, “unbounded.”].

But what will the defenders and apologists of those gods—who are said to be worshiped for this very reason, and whom people are therefore required to worship, so that the prosperity of these fleeting and passing things may be secure—answer us about the Saguntines who perished, except what they answer about the dead Regulus? The difference is that he was one man, while these were an entire state; yet in both cases the cause of death was the preservation of faith. For its sake he wished to return to the enemy, while Saguntum refused to go over to the enemy. Does preserved faith, then, provoke the anger of the gods? Or can individual human beings, and even entire states, perish despite the favor of the gods? Let them choose which they want. If those gods are angry with preserved faith, let them seek faithless people to worship them. But if human beings and states can perish, even when those gods favor them, after suffering many severe torments, then they are worshiped without any useful benefit of this happiness.

Let those therefore cease to complain who think that they have been made unhappy because the sacred objects of their gods have been destroyed. Even while those sacred objects remained, and even while the gods favored them, they could have complained not, as now, about misery, but, like Regulus and the Saguntines, have been horribly tortured and utterly destroyed.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### How ungrateful the Roman state was toward Scipio, its liberator, and what its morals were when Sallust described it as being at its best

Between the Second and the last Carthaginian War, when Sallust said that the Romans acted with the best morals and the greatest concord—for I pass over many matters, considering the limits of the work undertaken—at that very time of the best morals and greatest concord, that Scipio, liberator of Rome and Italy [Note: [Col. 0102] Scipio Africanus the Elder.], distinguished and marvelous finisher of the Second Punic War, so terrible, destructive, and dangerous, victor over Hannibal and conqueror of Carthage, whose life from adolescence is described as devoted to the gods and nurtured among temples [Note: [Col. 0102] Livy, Book 26, chapter 19; and Aulus Gellius, Book 7, chapter 1.], yielded to the accusations of his enemies. Deprived of his country—the country which he had restored safe and free through his own valor—he spent and completed the remainder of his life in the town of Liternum. After his notable triumph, he showed no desire for that city, so much so that he is said to have ordered that, even after his death, no funeral should be held for him in his ungrateful homeland [Note: [Col. 0102] Livy, Book 38, chapters 50–56.].

Then, for the first time, through Gnaeus Manlius [Note: [Col. 0102] Vindobonensis, Erasmus, and the manuscripts have “Gnaeus Manlius.” Our codices have “Gnaeus Mallius.” Livy himself, in Book 39, calls him Gnaeus Manlius Vulso and records that he triumphed over the Gauls who inhabited Asia—namely, Asia Minor—who were called Gallo-Greeks and Galatians.], the proconsul celebrating a triumph over the Gallo-Greeks, Asian luxury crept into Rome, worse than any enemy [Note: [Col. 0102] The same, Book 39, chapter 6.]. Then, for the first time, bronze couches and costly coverings were seen, it is said; then female musicians were introduced into banquets, along with other licentious depravity.

But I have undertaken to speak now of the evils which people suffer intolerably, not of those which they willingly commit. Thus what I mentioned about Scipio is more relevant to the present discussion: that, yielding to his enemies, he died outside the homeland which he had liberated, and that the Roman deities—from whose temples he had driven Hannibal—did not repay him in kind, although they are worshiped solely for the sake of this prosperity.

But because Sallust said that morals were at their best at that time, I thought it necessary to mention the Asian luxury, so that it might be understood that Sallust said this also in comparison with other periods, when morals were worse amid the gravest dissensions. For then—that is, between the Second and last Carthaginian War—the Voconian Law was also passed, forbidding anyone to make a woman an heir, not even an only daughter [Note: [Col. 0103] Livy, Book 41, chapter 34.]. I do not know what could be said or imagined more unjust than this law.

Nevertheless, throughout that interval between the two Punic Wars, the unhappiness was more tolerable. The army was worn down only by wars abroad, but it was consoled by victories; at home, however, no dissensions raged, as they had at other times. But in the last Punic War, by a single assault of the other Scipio, who for this reason also acquired the surname Africanus [Note: [Col. 0103] Africanus the Younger.], the rival of the Roman empire was destroyed from its foundations [Note: [Col. 0103] Livy, Book 51.]. Thereafter the Roman republic was overwhelmed by such great heaps of evils that, being so swiftly overthrown, it is shown to have been harmed more by the prosperity and security of its affairs—from which those evils were accumulated through excessively corrupt morals—than it had formerly been harmed by Carthage, hostile for so long [Note: [Col. 0103] Codex 766 has “would show.”].

Throughout all this period, up to Caesar Augustus—who seems not yet, even in their own opinion, to have wrested from the Romans a glorious liberty, but rather a contentious, destructive, and by then utterly enervated and feeble liberty; to have recalled everything to royal authority; and, as though it had collapsed through diseased old age, to have restored and renewed the republic—in all this period I omit, for the moment, the military disasters arising from one cause or another, and the treaty with Numantia, stained by dreadful disgrace [Note: [Col. 0103] Numantia was a city of Hispania Tarraconensis, made famous by its war with the Romans and finally destroyed by Scipio Africanus. Livy, Book 55, discusses the treaty made with the Numantines by Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, as well as the ill-omened flight of the chickens from their cage.].

For the chickens had flown from their cage and, as they say, had given the consul Mancinus a bad omen [Note: [Col. 0103] Livy, Book 55.], as though during all those years in which that small state had besieged and afflicted the Roman army, and had already begun to be a terror to the Roman republic itself, other men had advanced against it under a bad omen [Note: [Col. 0103] The manuscripts have *processerunt*, “advanced.”].

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Mithridates’ edict ordering all Roman citizens found in Asia to be killed

But these matters, I say, I omit, although I will by no means remain silent about the fact that Mithridates, king of Asia, ordered all Roman citizens traveling throughout Asia and occupied with their business in innumerable numbers to be killed on a single day [Note: [Col. 0103] The same, Book 78.]; and it was done.

What a pitiable spectacle of human affairs that was: suddenly, wherever anyone was found—in the countryside, on the road, in a town, in a house, in a village, in the Forum, in a temple, in bed, at a banquet—he was unexpectedly and impiously slaughtered! What groans belonged to the dying, what tears to those watching, and perhaps even to those striking the blows? What a harsh necessity confronted the hosts—not only of seeing those abominable killings in their own homes but also of carrying them out; their faces suddenly transformed from gentle hospitality to the execution of a hostile act in peacetime, with mutual wounds, if I may put it so [Note: [Col. 0104] The printed editions have “with, so to speak, mutual wounds.” The words “so to speak” are absent from the manuscript tradition; in their place several manuscripts read *repente*, “suddenly.”], when the one struck in body and the one striking in spirit were both wounded?

Had all these people also disregarded omens? When they left their homes for that journey from which there was no return, did they not have household and public gods whom they could consult? If so, then these people have no reason to complain in this matter about our times. In former times the Romans despised such vanities. But if they did consult them, let the answer be what benefit those consultations provided, when such things were permitted merely by human laws, with no one preventing them [Note: [Col. 0104] The printed editions have “such things were permitted.” The manuscripts omit *talia*, “such things.”].

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### The internal evils by which the Roman republic was harassed, preceded by the portent among all the animals that serve human beings

But now let us recall briefly, as far as we can, those evils which, the more internal they were, the more pitiable they proved: civil—or rather uncivil—dissensions; no longer merely seditions, but even civil wars themselves, in which so much blood was shed; where partisan zeal was no longer raging against one another through the disagreements and diverse voices of assemblies [Note: [Col. 0104] The printed editions have *contentionum*, “contentions.” The manuscripts have *concionum*, “assemblies.”], but plainly through sword and weapons.

How much Roman blood did the Social War, the Servile War, and the Civil Wars shed? How much devastation and depopulation did they bring upon Italy? For before the Latin allies rose up against Rome, all the animals subject to human use—dogs, horses, asses, oxen, and every other kind of livestock under human control—suddenly became wild and forgot their domestic gentleness. Abandoning their dwellings, they wandered about free and avoided the approach not only of others but even of their masters, not without death or danger to anyone who dared approach them if he pressed near [Note: [Col. 0104] Julius Obsequens, *On Prodigies*, chapter 114; and Orosius, Book 5, chapter 18.].

What a sign of how great an evil was this, if it was a sign, when the sign itself was so great an evil—and if it was not a sign [Note: [Col. 0104] So all the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “What a sign of how great an evil was this? If this was a sign, and the sign was so great an evil, how great was the evil of which it was a sign?”]! If this had occurred in our times, we should have found these people more rabid than those people found their animals.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### The civil discord stirred up by the seditions of the Gracchi

The beginning of the civil wars [Note: [Col. 0104] The manuscripts read “the beginning of the civil evils,” and so also Codex 766.] was the seditions aroused by the agrarian laws of the Gracchi. They wished to divide among the people the lands which the nobility wrongfully possessed. But daring to tear up so ancient an injustice was extremely dangerous—or rather, as the event itself showed, extremely destructive.

What funerals took place when the elder Gracchus was killed [Note: [Col. 0105] Tiberius Gracchus. See above, Book 2, chapter 21.]? And what funerals took place when his other brother was killed not long afterward? For noble and common people alike were being killed not through laws and the orderly exercise of authority, but amid the tumult and clashes of arms.

After the killing of the other Gracchus [Note: [Col. 0105] Gaius Gracchus. See Plutarch, *Life of the Gracchi*.], the consul Lucius Opimius, who had taken up arms against him within the city and, after crushing and destroying him with his associates, had inflicted a great slaughter of citizens, proceeded with a judicial inquiry to pursue the others. He is said to have killed three thousand people. From this it can be understood how great a multitude of deaths [Note: [Col. 0105] Some codices have “of the dead.” Our codices have “of deaths.”] the confused clash of arms may have produced, when the investigation conducted through the courts, as though after examination, produced so many.

The slayer of Gracchus himself sold his head to the consul for as much gold as the head weighed; for this bargain had preceded the killing. Marcus Fulvius, a former consul, was also killed in it together with his children.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### The temple of Concord, built by decree of the Senate at the site of seditions and massacres

With truly elegant senatorial wisdom, at that very place where the fatal riot had occurred, where so many citizens of every rank had fallen, they built a temple of Concord, so that it might strike the eyes of those addressing the assembly as a witness to the punishment of the Gracchi and pierce their memory.

But what else was this than mockery of the gods: to build a temple for that goddess who, if she had existed in the state, would not have allowed it to collapse, torn apart by such great dissensions? Unless perhaps Concord was guilty of this crime because she had abandoned the hearts of the citizens, and therefore deserved to be confined in that temple as in a prison. For if they wished the building to correspond to the events, why did they not rather construct a temple of Discord there?

Or is there any reason why Concord should be a goddess and Discord not be one, so that, according to Labeo’s distinction, the former is good and the latter evil [Note: [Col. 0105] See above, Book 2, chapter 11.]? He himself seems to have followed no other principle than the observation that at Rome a temple had been established for Fever just as for Health. In the same way, therefore, a temple ought to have been established not only for Concord but also for Discord.

The Romans therefore acted dangerously in choosing to live with so evil a goddess when she was angry, and they did not recall that the destruction of Troy had originated in her offense. For because she had not been invited among the gods, she devised a quarrel among the three goddesses [Note: [Col. 0105] Juno, Pallas, and Venus.] by means of the golden apple [Note: [Col. 0105] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *commentata est*, “she contrived.”]: hence the quarrel of the deities, Venus victorious, Helen carried off, and Troy destroyed.

Therefore, if she was perhaps indignant that she had not deserved to have any temple among the gods in the city, and for that reason was already disturbing the state with such great riots, how much more fiercely could she have been provoked when, at the site of that slaughter [Col. 0106]—that is, at the site of her own work—she saw a temple built for her rival?

These vanities make us laugh, but those learned and wise men grow angry over them. Yet the worshipers of good and evil deities never resolve the question of Concord and Discord, whether they have neglected the worship of these goddesses and preferred to them Fever and Bellona, for whom they established ancient shrines, or whether they worshiped these two as well, since, when Concord departed, raging Discord led them all the way to civil war.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### The various kinds of war that followed the construction of the temple of Concord

They thought that the temple of Concord, a witness to the slaughter and punishment of the Gracchi, should be set before those addressing the assembly as a splendid obstacle to sedition [Note: [Col. 0106] The manuscripts have “to the sedition.”]. How much good this achieved is shown by the worse events that followed.

For afterward the popular speakers labored not to avoid the example of the Gracchi but to surpass it: Lucius Saturninus, tribune of the plebs; Gaius Servilius, praetor; and, much later [Note: [Col. 0106] The manuscripts have “Gaius Servilius, praetor.” All books then read “and much later.” Ludovicus Vives thinks that one should read “and not much later,” since he found only seven years between Saturninus’ tribunate and Marcus Livius Drusus. Livy wrote about Drusus, the author of the Social War, in Book 71; about Saturninus and Servilius Glaucia, the praetor, in Book 69.], Marcus Drusus. From the seditions of all these men arose, first, extremely grave massacres, and then the Social Wars [Note: [Col. 0106] The Social Wars were undertaken against the Romans by their allies and kinsmen—the Etruscans, Latins, Sabines, and others.], through which Italy was severely afflicted and brought to astonishing devastation and depopulation [Note: [Col. 0106] The printed editions have “lamentable.” The manuscripts have “astonishing.” In Book 5, Eutropius, discussing the Social and Civil Wars, counts more than 150,000 people consumed, including 24 former consuls, 7 former praetors, and nearly 300 senators. Orosius, Book 5, chapter 22, agrees, though Velleius reports that many more were killed.].

The Servile War then followed [Note: [Col. 0106] One Servile War occurred before the Social War. Livy, Book 56, writes that it was stirred up by a certain Syrian slave named Eunus and later strengthened when another slave, Cleon, joined forces with him. A later war arose from gladiators. Livy, Book 95, records that seventy-four of them escaped from Lentulus’ gladiatorial school at Capua, and that Chrysum and Spartacus commanded their army. They also had Oenomaus as a commander, according to Florus, Book 3. Augustine here and below, Book 4, chapter 5, means this later war.] [Note: [Col. 0106] On the gladiatorial war, see the epitome of Livy, Book 95; Appian, *Civil Wars*, Book 1, near the end; Florus, Book 3, chapter 20; Plutarch, *Life of Marcus Crassus*, who brought this war to an end; and Orosius.], and then the Civil Wars. In them [Note: [Col. 0106] These words, “in them,” are absent from all our manuscripts.] what battles were fought, how much blood was shed, so that almost all the peoples of Italy, over whom Roman rule exercised the greatest power, were subdued like savage barbarians [Note: [Col. 0106] Lovaniensis has “like barbarity.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts have “like savage barbarism.”]?

Consider how the Servile War, contracted from a very small number—fewer than seventy gladiators—grew to such a large and fierce force; what number of Roman commanders those men overcame; what cities and regions they devastated, and in what manner. Even those who wrote the history could scarcely explain it adequately [Note: [Col. 0106] See below, Book 4, chapter 5.].

Nor was that the only Servile War. Before it, slaves had devastated the province of Macedonia, and afterward Sicily and the coastal regions. Who could express the magnitude and horror of the crimes first committed by brigands and then by powerful pirate wars [Note: [Col. 0107] Livy, Book 99.]?

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### The civil war between Marius and Sulla

When Marius, already stained with civil blood after killing many of the opposing party, had been defeated and had fled the city, and the state had scarcely drawn a little breath, Cinna later prevailed together with Marius—to use Cicero’s words. Then, when the most distinguished men had been killed, the lights of the state were extinguished.

Sulla later avenged the cruelty of this victory—there is no need even to say how great was the reduction of citizens and how great the disaster to the republic (*Against Catiline*, Oration 3, chapter 10, §24). Concerning this vengeance, which was more destructive than if the crimes being punished had been left unpunished, Lucan also says:

> The remedy exceeded all bounds, and followed too far  
> the hand to which the disease had led it; the guilty perished.  
>   
> But when only the guilty could now survive,  
> freedom was granted to hatred, and anger, released  
> from the restraints of the laws, rushed forth.

(*Pharsalia*, Book 2, lines 142–146.) [Note: [Col. 0107] Thus our manuscripts. In manuscript B: “and followed too far the hand to which the disease had led it; the hand perished.” Our codices omit the words “Then freedom was granted to hatred, and anger, released from the restraints of the laws, rushed forth.”]

In that war between Marius and Sulla, apart from those who fell in battle abroad, the streets, squares, Forums, theaters, and temples of the city itself were filled with corpses. It would be difficult to judge when the victors produced more funerals: first, when they fought to win, or afterward, because they had won.

When the Marian victory first took place, after Marius restored himself from exile, killings were carried out everywhere in all directions, and the head of the consul Octavius was placed on the Rostra [Note: [Col. 0107] On this and what follows, see Livy, Book 80; Appian, Book 1 of the *Civil Wars*; Plutarch, *Lives of Marius and Sulla*, and elsewhere.]. Caesar and Fimbria were slaughtered in their own homes [Note: [Col. 0107] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have “were slaughtered by their own people.”], the two Crassi, father and son, were butchered in one another’s sight, Bebius and Numitorius were dragged by a hook and died with their entrails scattered, Catulus escaped the hands of his enemies by taking poison, and Merula, the *flamen Dialis*, opened his veins and offered a sacrifice to Jupiter with his own blood.

Before Marius’ very eyes, those men were repeatedly struck whom he had refused to greet by extending his right hand.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### The character of Sulla’s victory as the avenger of Marian cruelty

Sulla’s victory followed as the avenger of this cruelty. After so much citizen blood had been shed to obtain it, and although the war had ended while enmities remained alive, it raged more cruelly in peacetime.

In addition to the earlier and most recent massacres of the elder Marius, still more serious ones had been added by the younger Marius and Carbo, men of the same Marian party. With Sulla pressing upon them, and despairing not only of victory but of life itself, they filled everything with the slaughter of their own and of others. For, besides the widespread massacre scattered through different places [Col. 0108], even while the Senate was under siege [Note: [Col. 0108] Livy, Book 86.], men were led out to the sword from the very Senate house, as though from a prison.

Mucius Scaevola, the pontiff, was killed while embracing the altar itself, since nothing among the Romans was considered more sacred than the temple of Vesta. He almost extinguished with his own blood that fire which the virgins, through perpetual care, always kept burning.

Sulla then entered the city as victor. In the public villa, where peace itself—not war—was raging, he had struck down seven thousand surrendered men [Note: [Col. 0108] Vindobonensis, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have “infantrymen.” Ambrosianus and the manuscripts have “surrendered men.” Livy, Book 88, supports this reading, except that he reports not seven but “eight thousand surrendered men” slaughtered. Valerius, Book 9, chapter 2, says: “He ordered four legions of the opposing party, who had followed their oath of allegiance, to be butchered in the public villa, which was in the Campus Martius …”]—men who were certainly unarmed—not by fighting but by issuing orders [Note: [Col. 0108] Seneca, *On Clemency*, chapter 12.].

Throughout the city every Sullan was striking down whomever he wished. The funerals could not be counted at all, until someone suggested to Sulla that some people ought to be allowed to live, so that those who had won might have subjects to rule.

Then the license to slaughter, which had been raging everywhere in every direction, was restrained, and amid great rejoicing that tablet was posted containing the names of two thousand men of both distinguished orders, the equestrian and the senatorial, who were to be killed and proscribed. The number was distressing, but the limitation consoled them. There was not as much grief because so many were falling as there was joy because the rest were not afraid.

Yet among some of those condemned to die, even the security of the others, cruel though it was, groaned over the carefully devised forms of death. One man was torn apart without a sword by the hands of men who mangled him—men treating a living human being more savagely than beasts usually tear apart an abandoned corpse [Note: [Col. 0108] Florus calls this man Bebius, Book 3, chapter 21; he must be distinguished from the man mentioned above, chapter 27, as having been killed among the followers of Sulla.].

Another, with his eyes gouged out and his limbs cut off piece by piece, was forced to live—or rather to die—for a long time amid such tortures [Note: [Col. 0108] This was Marius the praetor, a relative of Gaius Marius. Valerius, Book 9, chapter 2; Florus, Book 3, chapter 21.].

Certain noble cities were also put up for sale under the spear [Note: [Col. 0108] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and several manuscripts have “were devastated.” Other books more correctly have “were put up for sale under the spear.” Florus, Book 3, chapter 21, clarifies the passage: “The most splendid municipalities of Italy were sold under the spear: Spoletium, Interamnium, Praeneste, and Fluentia. For Sulmo … just as hostages, by the law and custom of war, are ordered to be led away after being condemned to death, so Sulla ordered the condemned city to be destroyed.” Thus Augustine is not speaking of the people of Praeneste, as Coquaeus thought, but of the people of Sulmo when he says here that an entire city was ordered to be slaughtered.], as though they were country estates. One city, as if a single condemned criminal were ordered to be led away, was ordered to be slaughtered in its entirety.

These things were done in peacetime, after the war—not to hasten the acquisition of victory, but to prevent the victory already won from being despised. Peace competed with war in cruelty, and peace won. War struck down armed men; peace, unarmed ones. War existed so that the one struck might, if able, strike in return; peace existed not so that the one who had escaped might live, but so that, while dying, he would not resist.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### A comparison of the Gothic invasion with the disasters that the Romans suffered either from the Gauls or from the authors of the civil wars
[Col. 0109]

What madness of foreign peoples, what barbarian savagery, can be compared with this victory of citizens over citizens? What did Rome ever see more disastrous, darker, or more bitter—whether the former invasion of the Gauls and the more recent one of the Goths, or the ferocity of Marius, Sulla, and the other most distinguished men on their respective sides, like its own lights turned against its own limbs? The Gauls indeed slaughtered the senate—everyone they could find of it throughout the city, apart from the Capitoline Hill, which alone was defended to some extent; but to those stationed on that hill they at least sold their lives for gold: even if they could not seize them by the sword, they could nevertheless wear them down by siege. The Goths, on the other hand, spared so many senators that it is more astonishing that they killed any at all. But Sulla, while Marius was still alive, occupied the very Capitol, which had been safe from the Gauls, in order to decree slaughter as the victor; and when Marius had escaped by flight, Sulla returned more savage and bloodthirsty, and in the Capitol itself, even through a decree of the senate, deprived so many people of life and property. But when Sulla was absent and the Marian party held power, what was sacred enough for them to spare, when they did not spare Mucius, a citizen, senator, and priest, as he approached the very altar—where, they say, the Roman destiny lay—with pitiable embraces? Finally, Sulla’s last proscription list, leaving aside countless other deaths, slaughtered more senators than the Goths were even able to despoil.

[Note: Plutarch, in his Life of Sulla, writes that Sulla displayed three different lists of proscribed persons within a few days.]

## CHAPTER XXX.—On the succession of wars that preceded Christ’s coming, numerous and most grievous.

With what face, what heart, what shamelessness, what folly—or rather, insanity—do they not attribute those events to their own gods, while attributing these to our Christ? The savage civil wars, more bitter than all foreign wars—as even their authors acknowledge—which not merely afflicted that republic but utterly destroyed it, arose long before Christ’s coming. Through a chain of criminal causes they proceeded from the war of Marius and Sulla to the wars of Sertorius and Catiline—one of whom had been proscribed by Sulla, the other brought up by him.

[Note: “The one proscribed” means Quintus Sertorius, a partisan of Marius, concerning whom see Livy, book 90; “the one brought up” means Catiline, who had attached himself to Sulla.]

From there they proceeded to the war of Lepidus and Catulus, one of whom wished to annul Sulla’s acts while the other wished to defend them.

[Note: Lepidus wished to annul them; Catulus wished to defend them. See Livy, book 90.]

From there they proceeded to the war of Pompey and Caesar. Pompey had been a follower of Sulla and had either equaled or already surpassed his power; Caesar, however, could not tolerate Pompey’s power—not because he possessed it, but because he did not, though after defeating and killing Pompey he surpassed it. From there they reached the other Caesar, later called Augustus, during whose reign Christ was born.

Augustus himself also waged civil wars against many opponents, and in them many distinguished men perished, including Cicero, that eloquent master of the art of governing the republic. A conspiracy of certain noble senators slaughtered Gaius Caesar, the conqueror of Pompey—who had exercised his civil victory mercifully and granted life and rank to his opponents—as though he were seeking royal power, and as though the conspirators were acting on behalf of the republic’s liberty, in the very senate-house. Afterward, Antony, very different in character from him and stained and corrupted by every vice, appeared to aspire to Caesar’s power; Cicero vigorously resisted him [Col. 0110]

in the name of that same supposed liberty of the fatherland.

Then there emerged that other Caesar, a young man of remarkable gifts, the adopted son of that Gaius Caesar. As I have said, he was later called Augustus. Cicero supported this young Caesar, so that his power might be strengthened against Antony, hoping that, once Antony’s domination had been driven out and crushed, he would restore the republic’s liberty. He was so blind and heedless of the future that the very young man whose rank and power he was fostering both permitted Antony, as though in some pact of concord, to have Cicero himself killed, and subjected to his own rule the liberty of the republic for which Cicero had cried out so loudly.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—That those who are not permitted to worship the gods shamelessly attribute present troubles to Christ, although such disasters occurred when those gods were worshipped.

Let those who are ungrateful to our Christ for such great blessings accuse their gods of such great evils. Certainly, when those evils were occurring, the altars of the deities were glowing, breathing out Sabaean incense and fresh garlands; the priesthoods were flourishing and the temples gleaming. Sacrifices were being offered, games were being held, and frenzy was being enacted in the temples, while so much citizens’ blood was being shed by citizens everywhere—not only in other places, but even among the very altars of the gods.

Tullius did not choose a temple in which to take refuge, because Mucius had chosen one in vain. But those who insult the Christian age far more disgracefully either took refuge in places especially dedicated to Christ, or the barbarians themselves led them there so that they might live.

This I know—and anyone who judges without partisan zeal readily acknowledges it with me, to say nothing of the many other matters I have mentioned and the far more numerous matters I have thought too lengthy to mention: if the human race had embraced Christian teaching before the Punic Wars, and if there had followed such a devastation of affairs as the fourth of those wars inflicted upon Europe and Africa, not one of the people we now endure would have failed to attribute such evils to the Christian religion.

As far as the Romans are concerned, their complaints would have been tolerated even less if the acceptance and spread of the Christian religion had been followed by that invasion of the Gauls, that devastation by the Tiber’s flooding and by fire, or those civil wars—which precede every other evil. If other events also occurred that were so incredible that they were counted among prodigies, and if they had happened in Christian times, whom would their people have accused of them except Christians?

I pass over events that were more astonishing than harmful: oxen speaking; unborn infants crying out certain words from their mothers’ wombs; serpents flying; women, hens, and men being transformed into the male sex; and other things of this kind. [Col. 0111]

Whether these accounts in their books—books that are not fictitious but historical—are true or false, they do not bring destruction upon human beings, but astonishment.

But when it rains earth, when it rains chalk, when it rains stones—not stones called by that name as hail is, but stones in the strict sense—these things could certainly cause serious harm. We read in their writers that, when fires from Mount Etna flowed from the very summit of the mountain down to the nearest shore, the sea boiled so violently that rocks were burned and the pitch of ships melted. This was certainly no slight harm, although it was astonishing beyond belief.

They also wrote that, in another eruption of fire, Sicily was so filled with ash, with such force, that the roofs of the city of Catina were buried and crushed, causing them to collapse.

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the edition of Louvain read “they caused to collapse”; the manuscripts read “it caused to collapse.” Erasmus reads “it caused to collapse.”]

Moved by this disaster, the Romans compassionately remitted that year’s tribute from the city. They also recorded that, when Africa was already a province of the Roman people, there was a prodigious multitude of locusts. After consuming the crops and the leaves of the trees, they say that the locusts were driven into the sea in an immense

[Col. 0112]

and immeasurable cloud.

When they had died and been cast back upon the shores, and the air had consequently become corrupted, such a pestilence arose that, in the kingdom of Masinissa alone, eight hundred thousand people are said to have perished, and many more in the lands nearest the shore.

[Note: Although Masinissa had already died, the territory is called his kingdom because his son Micipsa, to whom the Roman people had granted it for his great services, was then governing it.]

At Utica, they affirm that, out of thirty thousand young men who were there, ten thousand remained.

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmus read “men.” The thirty thousand were soldiers stationed at Utica for the defense of all Africa, according to Orosius, who, agreeing with Augustine, calls them “young men.” A little farther below, the old Corbeiensis manuscript and certain others read “ten thousand remained.”]

If such is the sort of nonsense we endure—and to which we are compelled to respond—which of these events would not be attributed to the Christian religion if it were seen occurring in Christian times? Yet they do not attribute these things to their gods, whose worship they demand for the very reason that they may not suffer such events, or lesser ones, although they endured greater ones when those gods were worshipped.

## BOOK FOUR

[Note: Augustine mentions this fourth book and the fifth book of *The City of God* in Letter 169 to Evodius, written toward the end of 415, and testifies in sections 1 and 13 that he began and completed both books in that same year.]

In this book it is proved that the greatness and long duration of the Roman Empire should be attributed not to Jupiter or the pagan gods—each of whom was thought fit to be entrusted with responsibility for scarcely one individual matter, and that only the lowest sort—but to the one true God, the author of happiness, by whose power and judgment earthly kingdoms are established and preserved.

[Col. 0111]

## CHAPTER I.—On the matters discussed in the first book.

[Col. 0111]

When I began to speak of the City of God, I first thought it necessary to answer its enemies. Pursuing earthly pleasures and longing after transient things, they complain against the Christian religion—which alone is a wholesome and true religion—about whatever sorrow they suffer in such things, suffering it through the mercy of God, who admonishes, rather than through his severity in punishing.

And since among them there is also an uneducated populace, they are inflamed more violently against us, as though by the authority of learned men. The ignorant suppose that the unusual events occurring in their own times had never occurred in earlier ages. Those who know that this opinion is false nevertheless strengthen it, by concealing their knowledge, so that they may appear to have just grounds for murmuring against us.

It was therefore necessary to demonstrate, from the books that their own authors recorded for remembrance so that the history of earlier times might be known, that matters were very different from what they suppose. At the same time it was necessary to teach that the false gods whom they either openly worshipped or still secretly worship are the filthiest, most malicious, and most deceitful demons. They take pleasure in their own crimes, whether real or invented, and have wished those crimes to be celebrated in their festivals, so that human weakness might not be recalled from committing condemnable acts while divine authority is offered as though for imitating them.

We have proved these things not from our own conjecture, but partly from recent memory, since we ourselves have seen such things being offered to such deities, and partly from the writings of those who left these accounts to posterity—not as an insult, but as an honor to their gods.

Thus Varro, a man of great learning and authority among them, when he divided his books into works concerning human and divine matters, assigning some to human affairs and others to divine affairs according to the dignity of each subject, placed theatrical games not merely among human matters but among divine matters. Yet surely, if a city contained only good and honorable people, theatrical games ought not to have existed even among human affairs.

He did this, certainly, not on his own authority, but because, having been born and raised at Rome, he found such things among its divine institutions. And since, at the end of the first book, we briefly set out what was to be said next, and have discussed some of those matters in the two books that followed, we recognize that we must now fulfill the expectations of our readers concerning what remains.

## CHAPTER II.—On the matters contained in the second and third books.

[Col. 0112]

We had promised, then, to say certain things against those who attribute the disasters of the Roman republic to our religion, and to recall all the evils—whatever their number and whatever their magnitude—that might occur to us or seem sufficient: the evils endured by that state, or by the provinces belonging to its empire, before their sacrifices were prohibited. Beyond doubt, they would attribute all these things to us if either our religion were already clear to them or it had so prohibited them from their sacrilegious rites.

[Note: Louvain reads “sacrilegious”; the other books differ.]

We have dealt with these matters sufficiently, as I think, in the second and third books: in the second, discussing the evils of character, which should be counted either as the only evils or as the greatest; in the third, discussing those bodily and external evils that only fools dread suffering, although good people often suffer them as well. The former evils, I do not say patiently but willingly, are embraced by those who thereby make themselves evil.

And how little I said about the city itself and its empire—indeed, not even everything down to Caesar Augustus! What if I had wished to recall and enlarge upon those evils that people do not inflict upon one another, such as the devastations and destructions caused by combatants, but that arise from the earthly elements of the world itself?

Apuleius briefly touches upon these in one place in the book he wrote *On the World*.

[Note: This statement is found in Apuleius; what follows is not.]

He says that all earthly things undergo changes, transformations, and destruction. To use his words, he says that through violent earthquakes the earth has split open and swallowed cities together with their inhabitants; that through sudden torrential rains whole regions have been washed away; that places which had previously been connected to the mainland have been made islands by the encroaching waves, while others, through the sea’s withdrawal, have been made accessible on foot; that cities have been overturned by winds and storms; that fires have flashed from the clouds, by which regions of the East were consumed and destroyed; and that in the western regions certain springs and floods produced similar devastation.

Thus, from the summits of Etna, when its craters once poured forth, rivers of flame ran down the slopes like torrents through a divine fire. If I had wished to collect these and similar events recorded in history, when would I have finished recounting what happened in those times, before the name of Christ suppressed the empty practices of those people—practices harmful to true salvation?

[Note: The manuscripts read “any of those empty practices.” Manuscript 766 and manuscript 2050 have this reading; the other manuscripts available to us read “none of those empty practices,” which is incorrect.]

I had also promised to demonstrate what their character was, and for what reason the true God deigned to enlarge their empire, since all kingdoms are in his power; and how little those whom they regard as gods helped them, indeed how greatly they harmed them by deceiving and misleading them.

This, then, is what I now see must be discussed, especially concerning the growth of the Roman Empire. As for the destructive deceit of the demons whom they worshipped as gods, how many evils it introduced into their character has already been said at some length, especially in the second book.

Throughout the three completed books, wherever it seemed appropriate, we also commended the extent to which, even amid the evils of war, God—through the name of Christ, to whom the barbarians showed such honor beyond the custom of warfare—bestowed consolations upon both good and wicked people, just as he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).

## CHAPTER III.—Whether the extent of empire, which is acquired only through wars, should be counted among the goods of the wise or of the happy.

Let us now see what sort of thing it is that they dare attribute the great extent and long duration of the Roman Empire to those gods whom they insist they honor honorably through the services of disgraceful games and the ministries of disgraceful people.

[Note: The printed editions read, “so that their joy may be compared with glass.” The manuscripts of better quality, omitting “their,” read, “so that glass-like joy may be compared”—that is, acquired.]

[Col. 0114]

Yet first I would like to investigate briefly what sort of reason or wisdom it is, when one cannot point to human happiness, always to be found amid the disasters of war and civil or foreign bloodshed—human beings consumed by dark fear and bloody desire—to wish to glory in the magnitude and extent of an empire, in order to procure a joy bright as glass, fragile and feared all the more horribly lest it suddenly shatter.

[Note: The printed editions read, “that is most dear to his relatives,” omitting the particle “when,” which the manuscripts contain.]

To make this easier to judge, let us not lose ourselves in empty boasting and dull the sharpness of our attention with high-sounding words such as “peoples,” “kingdoms,” and “provinces.” Let us instead posit two men—for just as a single letter is one element in speech, so each individual person is, as it were, an element of a state and kingdom, however vast the extent of land it occupies.

Let us imagine one of these two men poor, or rather of moderate means, and the other exceedingly rich—but a rich man anxious with fears, wasting away in grief, burning with desire, never secure, always restless, panting amid continual conflicts of enmity, indeed increasing his estate to an immense degree through these miseries and piling upon those increases equally bitter anxieties.

Let us imagine the man of moderate means with a small and modest household sufficient for him, dearly loved by his own, rejoicing in the sweetest peace with relatives, neighbors, and friends, religious in devotion, kind in spirit, sound in body, frugal in life, chaste in conduct, and secure in conscience.

I do not know whether anyone could be so foolish as to hesitate over which of the two he should prefer. As it is with these two men, so it is with two households, two peoples, and two kingdoms: the rule of equity applies. If it is applied attentively and our judgment is corrected, we shall very easily see where vanity dwells and where happiness dwells.

Therefore, if the true God is worshipped and served through true rites and good morals, it is beneficial for good people to reign far and wide for a long time. This is beneficial not so much to the rulers themselves as to those over whom they rule.

As far as the rulers themselves are concerned, their piety and integrity—which are great gifts of God—are sufficient for true happiness, by which this life is rightly lived and eternal life afterward received. On this earth, therefore, the reign of good people is granted not so much for their benefit as for the benefit of human affairs.

The reign of wicked people, however, harms the rulers more, since they ravage their own souls through the greater license afforded to crimes. It harms those subjected to them through service only if their own conduct is unjust. For the righteous, whatever evils are inflicted by unjust rulers are not punishment for crime but a testing of virtue.

Thus a good person, even if he is a slave, is free; but a wicked person, even if he reigns, is a slave—not merely to one master, but, what is more grievous, to as many masters as he has vices. Concerning these vices, divine Scripture says: “For by whatever anyone has been overcome, to this he has been enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

## CHAPTER IV.—How kingdoms without justice resemble bands of robbers.

[Col. 0115]

When justice is removed, what are kingdoms except great bands of robbers? For what are bands of robbers themselves except little kingdoms?

[Note: The word “themselves” is absent from all our manuscripts.]

A band is composed of human beings; it is governed by the authority of its leader, bound together by an agreement of association, and its plunder is divided according to an established law. When this evil grows through the addition of desperate men until it occupies places, establishes settlements, seizes cities, and subjugates peoples, it openly assumes the name of a kingdom. What gives it this name is not the removal of desire but the addition of impunity.

A certain captured pirate gave Alexander the Great an elegant and truthful answer. For when that king asked the man what he thought he was doing by keeping the sea unsafe, the pirate replied with free insolence: “What you do, when you keep the whole world unsafe. But because I do it with a tiny ship, I am called a pirate; because you do it with a great fleet, you are called an emperor.”

[Note: Nonius Marcellus reports this from Cicero, book 3 of *The Republic*.]

## CHAPTER V.—On the fugitive gladiators whose power was comparable to royal dignity.

I shall therefore omit asking what sort of men Romulus gathered, since it was a great benefit to them that, by being granted a share in the civic community, they were induced to abandon the thought of the punishments they deserved—fear of which was driving them toward greater crimes—so that thereafter they might be more peaceful toward human affairs.

I say this because the Roman Empire itself, already great through the subjugation of many peoples and terrifying to the rest, felt this danger bitterly and feared it deeply, and suppressed it with no small effort in order to avert an immense disaster, when a very small number of gladiators fled from a training school in Campania, assembled a large army, had three commanders, and devastated Italy far and wide and with great cruelty.

[Note: The printed editions read “suppressed”; the manuscripts read “suppressed it,” so that the meaning is that this monstrous servile war was suppressed by the Roman Empire, not without great difficulty.]

[Note: Livy, book 95; Plutarch, *Life of Crassus*; Orosius, book 5, chapter 24; and Augustine above, book 3, chapter 26.]

Let them say which god helped these men, so that from a small and despised band of robbers they rose to a kingdom feared by the already immense Roman forces and fortifications. Or will they deny that the gods helped them because they did not last long?

[Note: They were destroyed in the third year of the servile war by Marcus Licinius Crassus.]

As though any human life lasts a long time! By this reasoning, then, the gods help no one to reign, since everyone dies quickly; nor should what disappears within a short time in each individual—and therefore, one by one, in everyone—be counted a benefit.

For what difference does it make to those who worshipped the gods under Romulus, and who died long ago, that after their deaths the Roman Empire grew so greatly? They are dealing with their own cases among the dead—whether for good or for ill does not concern the present matter.

This should be understood of all those who, through that empire—although it stretches over long periods as mortals die and are succeeded by others—have passed rapidly and hurriedly through the brief days of their own lives, carrying the burdens of their deeds.

[Col. 0116]

But if even benefits lasting the briefest time are to be attributed to the gods’ assistance, then those gladiators were not helped insignificantly. They broke the bonds of their servile condition, fled, escaped, gathered a large and very powerful army, obeyed the counsels and orders of their kings, and became greatly feared by Roman might. They captured many things from several Roman commanders who were unable to defeat them; they won many victories, enjoyed whatever pleasures they wished, and did whatever desire suggested. Finally, until they were conquered—which was accomplished only with the greatest difficulty—they lived in eminence and as rulers.

But let us proceed to greater matters.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the ambition of King Ninus, who was the first to wage war against neighboring peoples in order to rule more widely.

Justin, who followed the Greek—or rather, foreign—historian Trogus Pompeius, and who wrote history not only in Latin, as Trogus did, but also briefly, begins his work with these words:

“At the beginning of human affairs and of the nations and peoples, power was in the hands of kings. They were raised to the summit of this majesty not by popular ambition but by moderation tested among good men. The peoples were bound by no laws; the decisions of their leaders served as laws. It was customary to protect the boundaries of the empire rather than extend them; kingdoms ended within each person’s own fatherland.

“Ninus, king of the Assyrians, was the first of all to change this ancient and almost ancestral custom of the nations through a new desire for power. He was the first to wage war against neighboring peoples and to subdue populations, still inexperienced in resistance, as far as the borders of Libya.”

A little later he says:

“Ninus secured the greatness of the dominion he had sought through continuous possession. After subduing the neighboring peoples, he became stronger as he moved against others through the addition of forces, and each victory over those nearest him became the instrument of the next. In this way he subjugated the peoples of the entire East.”

Whatever degree of reliability either this writer or Trogus may have had—for other, more trustworthy writings show that they sometimes lied—it is nevertheless established among other authors that the Assyrian kingdom was extended far and wide by King Ninus.

It lasted so long that the Roman Empire has not yet reached that age. For, according to those who have followed chronological history,

[Note: Eusebius.]

this kingdom lasted 1,240 years from the first year in which Ninus began to reign, until it was transferred to the Medes.

[Note: Justin, Diodorus, Plutarch, Eusebius, and others wrote about the transfer of power from the Assyrians to the Medes through Arbaces, commander of the Medes, who defeated Sardanapalus. Orosius says that this occurred in the very year in which, among the Latins, Proca—father of Amulius and Numitor, and grandfather of Rhea Silvia, the mother of Romulus—began to reign.

The Medes held power for 350 years, until King Astyages. It was then transferred through Cyrus, son of Cambyses, to the Persians, who held it for 230 years, until Alexander, son of Philip.

Augustine calls Alexander’s kingdom very brief in duration, either because Alexander himself ruled for only a few years after overthrowing the Persian kingdom, or because the Macedonian, or Greek, empire founded by Alexander was maintained by his successors only until the brothers Seleucus and Antiochus—that is, approximately until 246 years before Christ—when, under Arsaces’ seizure of power, the Parthian kingdom arose.

This kingdom lasted until approximately the year 226 after Christ, the fifth year of the reign of Alexander Severus Caesar. At that time, Artaxerxes the Persian, having defeated the Parthians, restored the Persian Empire, which still existed in Augustine’s time.]

[Col. 0117]

But to wage war against neighboring peoples, then proceed against others, and crush and subjugate peoples who had done them no harm, merely out of a desire for dominion—what else should this be called but a great band of robbers?

## CHAPTER VII.—Whether earthly kingdoms are helped or abandoned by the gods during their growth and decline.

If this great and long-lasting kingdom existed without the assistance of the gods, why is the Roman kingdom, extensive in territory and long-lasting in time, attributed to the Roman gods? Whatever the cause was in that case, it is the same here.

But if they insist that the former kingdom too must be attributed to the gods’ assistance, I ask which gods. The nations that Ninus conquered and subdued were not then worshipping different gods. Or, if the Assyrians had their own gods, supposedly more skilled craftsmen in building and preserving an empire, did those gods die when the Assyrians themselves lost their empire? Or, without receiving their promised payment—or having been promised a greater reward elsewhere—did they prefer to pass over to the Medes, and from there once more to the Persians, when Cyrus invited them and promised them something more advantageous?

What nation still endures in its own kingdom, after Alexander of Macedon’s kingdom—great in extent but exceedingly brief in duration—rather than being confined within the narrow bounds of the East? If this is so, then either the gods are faithless, abandoning their own people and passing over to their enemies—which no human being did, as Camillus did not when, after conquering and capturing a hostile city, he found Rome, for which he had won the victory, ungrateful, yet later, forgetting the injury and remembering his fatherland, freed Rome again from the Gauls—or they are not sufficiently strong to deserve being called gods, since they can be overcome by human plans or strength.

Or, if, when they wage war among themselves, it is not gods who are defeated by humans but gods who are defeated by other gods, each belonging to a particular city, then the gods themselves have hostilities among them, which each undertakes on behalf of his own side. A city, therefore, ought not to have worshipped its own gods more than the others, by whom its gods might have been helped.

Finally, whatever this passage, flight, migration, or desertion in battle of the gods may mean, the name of Christ had not yet been preached in those times and regions when those kingdoms were lost and transferred through immense military disasters.

For if, after 1,200 years and more, when the Assyrian kingdom was taken away, the Christian religion had already preached another eternal kingdom there and prohibited the sacrilegious worship of false gods, what else would the foolish people of that nation have said except that the kingdom, preserved for so long, could have perished for no other reason than that its own religion had been abandoned and Christianity received?

Let them observe their own reflection in this voice of vanity, and, if they possess any sense of shame, blush at making similar complaints. The Roman Empire, however, has been afflicted rather than transformed; this also happened to it in times before the name of Christ, and it has been restored from that affliction. Nor should we despair of its restoration in our own times. For who knows God’s will concerning this matter?

## CHAPTER VIII.—Which gods the Romans suppose assisted them in enlarging and preserving their empire, although they believed that scarcely one god could be entrusted with the care of one individual matter.

[Col. 0118]
