Next, if it pleases us, let us ask, from the great multitude of gods whom the Romans worshipped, which god, or which gods, they believe enlarged and preserved that empire. For in so distinguished a work, so full of dignity, they would surely not dare assign any part to the goddess Cloacina,

[Note: Louvain and manuscripts of good quality read “Cluacina.” Other old books, together with Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmus, read “Cloacina.” Lactantius, book 1 of *On False Religion*, chapter 20, says: “Tatius”—that is, the man who reigned with Romulus—“consecrated the image of Cloacina, found in the Great Sewer; and because he did not know whose likeness it was, he gave it a name from the place.” Cyprian agrees in *On the Vanity of Idols*, as does Augustine himself below, chapter 23. There was also a Venus called Cluacina, from *cluere*, “to cleanse,” concerning whom see Pliny, book 15, chapter 29.]

or to Volupia, whose name comes from pleasure; or to Lubentina, whose name comes from lust; or to Vaticanus,

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “Vagitanus.”]

who presides over the cries of infants; or to Cunina, who manages their cradles.

But how could all the names of the gods and goddesses be mentioned in a single book, when they could scarcely contain them in enormous volumes, distributing a particular divine function to each individual matter?

[Note: All our manuscripts read “and goddesses.”]

They did not even think that the care of the fields should be entrusted to one god alone. They assigned the countryside to the goddess Rusina, the mountain ridges to the god Jugatinus,

(a) (b)

the hills to the goddess Collatina, and the valleys to Vallonia.

Nor could they find a single Segetia to whom they might entrust the crops once and for all. As long as the sown grain was beneath the earth, they wanted the goddess Seia to preside over it; when it was already above the earth and forming a crop, the goddess Segetia; and when the grain had been gathered and stored, so that it might be safely preserved, they appointed the goddess Tutilina.

Who would think that Segetia was insufficient for the entire period during which the crop progressed from its first green shoots to its dry ears? Yet it was not enough for those who loved a multitude of gods that the wretched soul should be prostituted to a crowd of demons, disdaining the chaste embrace of the one true God.

They therefore appointed Proserpina over sprouting grain;

(c)

the god Nodutus over the joints and knots of the stalks; the goddess Volutina over the wrapping of the husks; when the husks open so that the ear may emerge, the goddess Patelana;

[Note: The manuscripts have this form; the printed editions have “Patelena.”]

when the crops are leveled with new ears—for they said that to level is *hostire*—the goddess Hostilina;

[Note: All our manuscripts have this passage in the following form: “they said *ostire*, and the goddess Ostilina.”]

when the grain is flowering, the goddess Flora; when it is milky, the god Lacturnus;

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Louvain read “the goddess Lacturcia.” But the old books we follow here are supported by Servius on *Georgics* 1, who, following Varro, calls him the god Lacturnus, not a goddess.]

when it is ripening, the goddess Matuta;

[Note: Vindobonensis and Erasmus read “Matura.” The better manuscripts, together with Louvain, read “Matuta.”]

and when it is weeded—that is, removed from the earth—the goddess Runcina.

I am not mentioning everything, because I am disgusted by what they are not ashamed of.

[Col. 0119]

I have mentioned these very few examples so that it might be understood that they could in no way dare to say that these deities established, enlarged, or preserved the Roman Empire, since each was assigned to a particular function in such a way that nothing universal was entrusted to any one of them.

When, then, could Segetia care for the empire, when she was not permitted to care simultaneously for crops and trees? When could Cunina think about weapons, when her office did not permit her to go beyond the cradles of infants? When could Nodutus help in war, when his responsibility extended not even to the husk of an ear but only to the knot of a joint?

A single person appoints one doorkeeper for his house, and because he is a human being, that is entirely sufficient. These people appointed three gods: Forculus for the doors, Cardea

[Note: All the books have this form. Ludovicus Vives would prefer “Carna.” Ovidius calls the same goddess both Carna and Crane, *Fasti* 6.101–102.]

for the hinges, and Limentinus for the threshold.

[Note: “Cardea”; Ovid, *Fasti*, book 6, verses 101–102, has “Carna.”]

Thus Forculus could not at the same time guard the hinge and the threshold.

## CHAPTER IX.—Whether the greatness and long duration of the Roman Empire should be attributed to Jupiter, whom his worshippers regard as the supreme god.

Leaving aside, or at least setting aside for a while, this multitude of minor gods, we must investigate the function of the greater gods, through which Rome became so great that it ruled so many peoples for so long.

Surely, then, this is Jupiter’s work. They wish him to be king of all the gods and goddesses.

[Note: Some copies read, “They wish him to be the king who completes all things.”]

His scepter indicates this; the Capitol on the lofty hill indicates it. Concerning this god, although it was said by a poet, they proclaim it most fittingly:

“Jupiter is full of all things.” (Virgil, *Eclogue* 3, line 60.) Varro believes that even those who worship one God alone without an image worship this god, though they call him by another name. But if this is so, why was he treated so badly at Rome—as indeed among other nations as well—that an image was made for him? Varro himself so detests this that, although he was oppressed by the perverse custom of so great a state, he nevertheless did not hesitate to say and write that those who introduced images among the peoples both removed fear and added error.

## CHAPTER X — What opinions were followed by those who assigned different gods to different regions of the world

Why is Juno also joined to him as wife, since she is called both his sister and his spouse (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1, line 47)? “Because,” they say, “we understand Jupiter as the ether and Juno as the air; and these two elements are joined together, one being above and the other below.” He, then, is not the one of whom it was said, “Jupiter is full of all things,” if Juno fills some part. Or does each fill both, so that these two spouses are together both in the two elements and simultaneously in each one? Why, then, is the ether assigned to Jupiter and the air to Juno?

[Note: The printed editions read, “if the two themselves”; *if* is absent from the manuscripts.]

Finally, the two of them would have been enough. What is the reason that the sea is assigned to Neptune and the earth to Pluto? And lest these two also remain without spouses, Salacia is added to Neptune and Proserpina to Pluto. For just as Juno, they say, holds the lower part of the sky—that is, the air—so Salacia holds the lower part of the sea and Proserpina the lower part of the earth.

They seek some way to patch up their fables, but do not find one. For if these things were so, the ancients would have taught that there were three elements of the world rather than four, so that the several divine couples might be distributed among the several elements. Yet they have emphatically asserted that the ether is one thing and the air another. Water, whether upper or lower, is in any event water. Suppose it is unlike the other: is it therefore so unlike that it is no longer water? And the lower earth—what else can it be but earth, however great the difference by which it is distinguished?

Moreover, behold: the entire corporeal world has now been filled by these four, or three, elements. Where will Minerva be? What will she hold? What will she fill? For she was established in the Capitolium together with these, although she is not the daughter of both. Or if they say that Minerva holds the upper part of the ether, and that for this reason the poets invented the story that she was born from Jupiter’s head, why then is she not rather appointed queen of the gods, since she is higher than Jupiter? Is it because it was considered unworthy to place a daughter before her father? Why was this same principle of justice not preserved in the case of Jupiter in relation to Saturn? “Because he was defeated,” they say. “So they fought?” “Certainly not,” they answer; “that is the babble of fables.”

Let us not believe the fables, then, and let better things be thought about the gods. Why, therefore, was Saturn not given a seat of honor equal to his son Jupiter’s, even if not higher? “Because Saturn,” they say, “is the length of time.” [Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2, chapter 25.] Those, therefore, who worship Saturn worship time, and the king of the gods, Jupiter, is represented as born from time.

For what disgrace is there in saying that Jupiter and Juno were born from time, if he is the sky and she the earth, since the sky and earth were certainly made? Their learned and wise men also have this in their books—not from poetic inventions, but from the books of philosophers. Virgil says:

> Then the almighty Father, ether, in fruitful rains  
> Descended into the lap of his joyful spouse  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* 2, lines 325–326),

that is, into the lap of the earth or land.

Here too they wish there to be certain distinctions, and within the earth itself they think that Terra, Tellus, and Tellumo are different. [Note: They called Terra the element itself; Tellus, the goddess deriving from the passive force inherent in the earth, as a female; and Tellumo, the god deriving from the active force, as a male. See below, book 7, chapter 23.]

They regard all these as gods, each called by its own name, distinguished by its own functions, and worshiped with its own altars and sacred rites. They also call this same Terra the mother of the gods. Thus the poets would now be inventing more tolerable fictions if, according to these people’s sacred—not poetic—books, Juno were not only Jupiter’s sister and wife, but also his mother. [Note: This is Augustine’s argument: If we believe the Gentile poets—or even their mystical interpretation by which they wrap such stories in allegory—Terra is Juno herself; but Terra is the mother of all the gods; therefore Juno is also Jupiter’s mother. — Coquaeus.]

They wish the same earth to be Ceres and also Vesta, although they frequently assert that Vesta is nothing but fire, associated with the hearths without which a state cannot exist. For this reason, virgins are accustomed to serve her, because, just as nothing is born from a virgin, so nothing is born from fire. This whole vanity should surely have been abolished and extinguished by the one who was born from a Virgin.

For who could tolerate the fact that, although they have attributed so much honor—and, as it were, chastity—to fire, they are sometimes not ashamed even to call Vesta Venus, so that the honored virginity of her attendants is made to disappear? If Vesta is Venus, how did virgins properly serve her by abstaining from sexual acts? Are there perhaps two Venuses, one a virgin and the other a woman? Or rather three: one belonging to virgins, who is also Vesta; another belonging to married women; and another belonging to prostitutes? To this last Venus the Phoenicians gave a gift from the prostitution of their daughters before marrying them to men. [Note: Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 1, chapter 10, from Sanchuniathon, and Athanasius, in his *Oration against the Gentiles*, report this of the Phoenicians; other writers report it of Armenians, Cyprians, and Lydians. — Coquaeus.]

Which of these is the wife of Vulcan? Certainly not the virgin, since she has a husband. But let her not be a prostitute, lest we seem to do an injury to the son of Juno and the associate of Minerva. [Note: Vulcan was the son of Juno by Jupiter, and the associate of Minerva, goddess of the arts, because he was in charge of forging the instruments of the arts. See Plato, *Critias*.]

Therefore she is understood to belong to married women. Yet we do not want them to imitate her in what she did with Mars.

“Again,” they say, “you are returning to the fables.” What kind of justice is this: that they become angry with us because we say such things about their gods, while they do not become angry with themselves, who most gladly watch such crimes of their gods in the theaters? And—what would be incredible unless it were demonstrated by the clearest testimony—these very theatrical crimes of their gods were instituted in honor of those same gods. [Note: Printed editions have *instituta esse*, “were instituted”; the manuscripts differ.]

## CHAPTER XI — On the many gods whom the teachers of paganism defend as one and the same Jupiter

[Note: A few manuscripts read *quotlibet*; most read *quodlibet*.]

However many physical explanations and arguments they may wish to assert, let Jupiter be the soul of this corporeal world, filling and moving the whole mass constructed and compacted from four elements—or however many they prefer. [Note: See below, book 7, chapter 6.] Let him sometimes surrender his parts to his sister and brothers; let him sometimes be the ether, embracing the air—Juno—from above; let him sometimes be the whole sky together with the air, while the earth, as his wife and also his mother—for such a thing is not considered disgraceful among gods—is made fertile by fruitful rains and seeds.

Or, not to run through everything, let him be the one god of whom they think the most renowned poet said:

> For the god passes through all things,  
> Through lands, the regions of the sea, and the deep sky  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* 4, lines 221–222).

Let him himself be Jupiter in the ether, Juno in the air, Neptune in the sea, and Salacia in the lower parts of the sea; Pluto on earth, Proserpina in the lower earth; Vesta on household hearths, Vulcan in the smith’s furnace; in the heavenly bodies—the sun, moon, and stars; Apollo in divination; Mercury in commerce; the Initiator in Janus; the Terminator in Terminus; Saturn in time; Mars and Bellona in wars; Liber in vineyards; Ceres in grain; Diana in forests; Minerva in talents. [Note: Ludovicus Vives observes that some books read *janitor* (“doorkeeper”) rather than *initiator*; nevertheless, every copy he examined, as well as our manuscripts, reads *initiator*. Several manuscripts read *Diespater*; others *Dispater* or *Diispater*.]

Finally, let him also be present in that crowd of so-called plebeian gods: in the name of Liber, let him preside over the seed of men, and in the name of Libera over that of women. [Note: On these matters see below, book 6, chapter 9.] Let him be Diespiter, who brings childbirth to its day; let him be the goddess Mena, whom they placed in charge of women’s menstruation; let him be Lucina, invoked by women in labor.

Let him bring help to those being born by receiving them into the bosom of the earth, and be called Opis. Let him open the mouth in a baby’s cry, and be called the god Vaticanus. Let him raise the child from the earth, and be called the goddess Levana. Let him protect the cradle, and be called the goddess Cunina.

Let him not be another god, but be present in those goddesses who sing the fates of newborns and are called the Carmentes. [Note: According to Aulus Gellius, book 16, chapter 16, there were two Carmentes, named Postverta and Prorsa.]

Let him preside over chance and be called Fortuna. In the goddess Rumina, let him suckle the infant, because the ancients called the breast *ruma*. In the goddess Potina, let him provide drink; in the goddess Educa [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erfurt manuscripts have *Edulica*.], food.

Because of the fear of infants, let him be called Paventia. [Note: Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book 2, chapter 11, has *Paventina*.] From hope that is coming, let him be called Venilia; from pleasure, Volupia; from action, Agenoria; from the impulses by which a person is driven to excessive action, let the goddess Stimula be named.

Let Strenia be the goddess who makes a person energetic. [Note: Thus in the manuscripts here and below, chapter 16; the printed editions have *Strenua*.] Let Numeria teach counting; Camoena, singing. Let him also be the god Consus, by giving counsel, and the goddess Sentia, by inspiring thoughts.

Let him be the goddess Juventas, who, after the *praetexta*, receives the beginnings of youthful age. [Note: An old Faurentian manuscript adds in the interlinear space, “after fifteen years.” The gloss is not inappropriate. The *praetexta* was a toga woven round with purple, worn not only by magistrates but also by boys until puberty, at which time they put on the *toga virilis*.]

Let him also be Fortuna Barbata, who clothes adults with a beard. Yet those who refused to honor them [Note: The printed editions have *voluerit*, “he would have wished”; the manuscripts’ *noluerunt*, “they refused,” is better: the reference is to those who established that a goddess, Barbatam, rather than a god, should be worshiped by adults.] should at least have called this divinity a male god—either Barbatum, from the beard, just as Nodutus was named from knots—or certainly not Fortuna, but, because she has beards, Fortunius.

Let him join spouses together in the god Jugatinus. When the belt is loosened from the virgin bride, let him be invoked, and let her be called the goddess Virginiensis. [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have *Virginensis*.]

Let him be Mutunus or Tutunus, who among the Greeks is Priapus. [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erfurt, and some manuscripts have *Motunus*. Lovanium, with several manuscripts, has *Mutinus*. Most old books have *Mutunus*, supported by Arnobius, book 4, and Lactantius, book 1 of *On False Religion*, chapter 20. Ambrosianus and Erfurt then add, “or Tutinus”; Vindobonensis has “or Tutumus”; a few manuscripts, “or Tuturius”; nearly all the others, “or Tutunus.” The Lovanium editors, following Ludovicus Vives’s conjecture, omitted this. Arnobius, *Against the Gentiles*, book 4: “And because we do not prostrate ourselves in supplication before Mutunus and Tutunus,” and so forth.]

If they are not ashamed that all these things I have mentioned—and whatever I have not mentioned, for I have not thought it necessary to mention everything—are one Jupiter, whether all these are, as some wish, his parts, or his powers, as those think who prefer him to be the soul of the world, a view regarded as belonging to great and highly learned men, then, if these things are so—though for the moment I do not ask what sort of thing that is—what would they lose if they worshiped one God with the wiser economy of a shortcut?

For what part of him would be neglected, when he himself, who is all things, was worshiped? But if it was to be feared that his omitted or neglected parts would become angry, then this whole life is not, as they claim, the life of one living being, containing all the gods as its powers, limbs, or parts. Rather, each part has a life separate from the others, if one can become angry because of another, and one can be appeased while another is provoked.

If it is said that Jupiter as a whole could be offended if his parts were not also worshiped individually and minutely, that is foolishly said. None of them would be omitted when the one who possesses them all was worshiped. To pass over other innumerable examples: when they say that all the stars are parts of Jupiter, and that all live and possess rational souls, and therefore are unquestionably gods, do they not see how many they fail to worship, how many of them they do not build temples for or establish altars to, although they have thought that this should be done for only a very few stars, with sacrifices offered to them individually? [Note: Perhaps read *tam* (“so”) for *tamen* (“nevertheless”).]

If, then, those who are not worshiped individually become angry, do they not fear living, with a whole sky angered, while only a few have been appeased? But if they worship all the stars because they are in Jupiter, then by this shortcut they could offer supplication for all of them in that one god. No one would be neglected, since no one would be despised in the one; whereas, by worshiping certain gods, they would furnish a much larger number of those passed over with a just cause for anger—especially when Priapus, stretched out in shameful nakedness, was placed before those shining from their heavenly seat. [Note: The printed editions add, “when supplication was offered to all in that one”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XII — On the opinion of those who thought that God is the soul of the world and the world the body of God

Does this not move intelligent people—or people of any kind? It does not require exceptional intelligence merely to set aside contentious zeal and consider whether, if the soul of the world is God and the world is related to that soul as a body, there is one living being consisting of soul and body, and whether this god, in a certain bosom of nature, contains everything within himself.

From his soul, by which this entire mass is given life, the lives and souls of all living things are then taken according to the destiny of each thing at birth [Note: The old books read *nascendi* (“of being born”); so too our manuscripts.], so that absolutely nothing remains [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erfurt have *remanere potest*; Lovanium has *remanere posse*. *Posse* is absent from the manuscripts.] which is not part of God. [Note: Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions have *sinus quidam*, “a certain bosom”; the manuscripts have *sinu quodam*, “in a certain bosom.”]

If this is so, who does not see what great impiety and irreligion follow—that whenever someone tramples on something, he tramples on a part of God, and that whenever any living creature is killed, a part of God is slaughtered? I do not wish to mention everything that may occur to those who reflect on this, but which cannot be spoken without shame.

## CHAPTER XIII — On those who assert that only rational living beings are parts of one God

But if they contend that only rational animals, such as human beings, are parts of God, I do not see—if the whole world is God—how they separate beasts from his parts. Yet why struggle against the point? Concerning the rational living being itself, that is, the human being, what more wretched belief can there be than that a part of God is beaten when a boy is beaten?

And who could endure the thought that parts of God become lustful, unjust, impious, and altogether worthy of condemnation, unless he were completely insane? Finally, why does he become angry with those by whom he is not worshiped, when he is not worshiped by his own parts?

It remains, then, that they should say that all the gods have lives of their own, each living for itself, and that none of them is part of anything else; but that all who can be known and worshiped should be worshiped, because they are so numerous that all cannot be worshiped.

Of these, I suppose they think that Jupiter, because he presides as king, established or enlarged the Roman dominion. For if he did not do this, what other god could they believe capable of undertaking so great a work, when all are occupied with their own duties and activities and one does not intrude upon another’s? [Note: Lovanium reads *ne alter* (“lest one”); the other printed editions and the manuscripts differ.] The dominion of human beings, then, could be extended and enlarged by the king of the gods.

## CHAPTER XIV — The enlargement of kingdoms is incongruously attributed to Jupiter, since, if Victory is a goddess as they claim, she alone would suffice for this business

Here I ask first why the kingdom itself is not also some god. Why should it not be so, if Victory is a goddess? Or what need is there of Jupiter himself in this matter, if Victory favors and is propitious, and always goes to those whom she wishes to be victorious?

With this goddess favoring and being propitious—even if Jupiter were idle or occupied with something else—which peoples would remain unsubdued? Which kingdoms would not yield?

Or perhaps they disapprove of the good fighting with the most unjust wickedness and, in order to enlarge their kingdom, voluntarily provoking peaceful neighbors who are doing no wrong into war? If that is how they think, I entirely approve and praise them. [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erfurt read *non displicet* (“does not displease”); the negation was deleted on the authority of the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XV — Whether it is fitting for good men to wish to rule more widely

Let them therefore see whether perhaps it does not belong to good men to rejoice in the extent of a kingdom. The injustice of those against whom just wars were waged helped the kingdom to grow. It would certainly have remained small if the peace and justice of neighboring peoples had provoked no injury by which war was waged against them.

Thus, if human affairs were more fortunate, all kingdoms would be small, rejoicing in harmonious neighborliness. There would be as many kingdoms of peoples in the world as there are houses of citizens in a city.

Accordingly, to wage war and enlarge one’s kingdom by conquering peoples seems to the wicked a happiness, but to the good a necessity. Yet because it would be worse for the unjust to rule over the more just, this too is not improperly called a kind of happiness.

But without doubt it is a greater happiness to have a good neighbor living in harmony with you than to subjugate an evil neighbor in war. It is an evil prayer to wish to have someone whom you hate or fear, so that there may be someone for you to defeat.

If, then, by waging just wars—not impious or unjust ones—the Romans were able to acquire so great an empire, should they also worship foreign injustice as some goddess? We see that it contributed greatly to the breadth of their empire: it made people unjust, so that there would be opponents against whom just wars could be waged and the empire enlarged.

Why, then, should Injustice not also be a goddess—or at least the injustice of foreign peoples—if Fear, Pallor, and Fever deserved to be Roman gods?

With these two—the injustice of others and the goddess Victory—Injustice stirring up the causes of wars and Victory successfully bringing the same wars to an end, the empire grew even while Jupiter was taking a holiday.

For what part would Jupiter have here, when those things that could be considered his gifts are treated as gods, called gods, worshiped as gods, and invoked in their own capacities? He would have some part here too if he himself were called the kingdom, just as Victory is called one.

Or if the kingdom is Jupiter’s gift, why should victory not also be regarded as his gift? It certainly would be, if not a stone in the Capitol, but the true King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 19:16), were recognized and worshiped.

## CHAPTER XVI — Why the Romans, assigning individual gods to all things and all movements, wished the temple of Quiet to be outside the gates

I am greatly astonished that, although they assigned individual gods to individual things and almost to individual movements, they called the goddess Agenoria, who aroused people to action; the goddess Stimula, who goaded them to action beyond measure; and the goddess Murcia, who prevented movement beyond measure and, as Pomponius says, made a person *murcidus*, that is, excessively lazy and inactive. [Note: It is unknown which Pomponius this was: perhaps Atticus; or Lucius Pomponius, writer of Atellan plays; or Gnaeus Pomponius, the orator—all of whom lived in Cicero’s time; or one of those who lived after Cicero, Pomponius Mela or Julius Pomponius; or Pomponius, the tragic poet mentioned by Quintilian; or a jurist. — Ludovicus Vives.]

They called Strenia the goddess who made a person energetic. To all these gods and goddesses they undertook to perform public rites. But Quiet, calling her the one who made people quiet, although she had a temple outside the Colline Gate, they refused to adopt publicly.

Was this an indication of a restless spirit? Or was it rather signified in this way that whoever persisted in worshiping that crowd—not truly of gods but of demons—could not possess quiet? To this quiet the true Physician calls us when he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

## CHAPTER XVII — Whether, if Jupiter possesses supreme power, Victory too ought to be regarded as a goddess

Perhaps they say that Jupiter sends the goddess Victory, and that she, obeying the king of the gods like a subject, goes to those whom he commands and takes her seat on their side.

This can truly be said—not of that Jupiter whom, according to their opinion, they invent as king of the gods, but of the true King of the ages, who sends not Victory, which is no substance, but his angel, and makes victorious whomsoever he wishes. His purpose may be hidden, but it cannot be unjust. [Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovanium have: “His purpose may be hidden; it cannot be unjust.” Manuscript M has the shorter reading.]

For if Victory is a goddess, why is Triumph not also a god? And why is Victory joined to him as wife, brother, or son?

These people have formed such opinions about the gods that, if poets invented such things and we attacked them, they would reply that the inventions of poets were laughable and should not be attributed to real divinities. Yet they themselves did not laugh when they read such ravings not in poets but worshiped them in temples.

They should therefore ask Jupiter concerning everything and offer supplication to him alone. For if Victory is a goddess and is under that king, she could not dare resist him wherever he sent her, but would rather do his will.

## CHAPTER XVIII — How those who think Felicity and Fortune are goddesses distinguish them

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “distinguished them.”]

What shall we say of the fact that Felicity too is a goddess? She received a temple, deserved an altar, and suitable rites were performed for her. She alone, then, should have been worshiped. For where she was present, what good would not be present?

But what does it mean that Fortune is also thought to be a goddess and is worshiped? Is felicity one thing and fortune another? Fortune can be bad, they say; but if felicity were bad, it would no longer be felicity.

Certainly, we ought to regard all gods and goddesses of either sex—if they have sex at all—as good. Plato says this (*Republic* 2), as do other philosophers and eminent governors of states and peoples.

How, then, is the goddess Fortune sometimes good and sometimes bad? Perhaps when she is bad she is not a goddess, but suddenly changes into an evil demon. How many goddesses, then, are there? Clearly as many as there are fortunate people—that is, people of good fortune.

Since at the same time there are also many others experiencing bad fortune, would Fortune, if she were one goddess, be both bad and good at once—one thing for these people and another for those? Or is the goddess who is good always good? Then she is Felicity. Why, therefore, do they use two names?

But this might be tolerated, since one thing is often called by two names. What, then, is the reason for the different temples, different altars, and different rites?

“There is a reason,” they say. “Felicity is what the good possess as a result of preceding merits; but Fortune, which is called good, happens by chance, without any examination of merits, to both good and evil people—and for this reason it is called Fortune.”

How, then, is that good which comes without any judgment both to the good and to the evil? Why is she worshiped, when she is so blind that, falling indiscriminately upon anyone, she commonly passes by her worshipers and clings to those who despise her?

Or if her worshipers accomplish something by which she notices and loves them, then she follows merits; she does not come by chance. Where, then, is that definition of Fortune? Where is the fact that she received her name from chance? [Note: *Ergo*, “therefore,” is absent from all our manuscripts.]

For it is of no use to worship her if she is Fortune. But if she distinguishes her worshipers so as to benefit them, she is not Fortune.

Or does Jupiter also send her wherever he wishes? Let him alone be worshiped, then. Fortune cannot resist him when he commands her and sends her wherever he wishes.

Or let the wicked worship her—those who do not wish to possess the merits by which the goddess Felicity might be invited.

## CHAPTER XIX — On Female Fortune

They attribute so much importance, as though to a divinity, to the one whom they call Fortune that they committed to memory that her image, dedicated by married women and called Female Fortune (*Fortuna Muliebris*) (Livy, book 2), also spoke (Plutarch, *Coriolanus* and *On the Fortune of Rome*), and that it said—not once but twice—that the married women had dedicated it properly.

If this is true, we should not be surprised. For it is not difficult even for wicked demons to deceive in this way. Rather, these people ought to have recognized their arts and cunning from the fact that the goddess who spoke was one who comes by chance, not one who comes in response to merits.

Fortune was talkative, while Felicity was mute. Why else, except so that people would not take care to live rightly, having gained Fortune’s favor, which would make them fortunate without any good merits? [Note: Manuscript B reads, “and for what purpose?”]

Certainly, if Fortune speaks, she would have spoken not merely as a female but rather as a male, so that it would not be thought that the very women who dedicated the image had invented such a miracle through feminine loquacity.

## CHAPTER XX — On Virtue and Faith, which the pagans honored with temples and rites while neglecting other good things that ought likewise to have been worshiped, if divinity was rightly attributed to others

[Note: Perhaps read “to them” rather than “to others.”]

They also made Virtue a goddess. If she were a goddess, she would indeed have deserved precedence over many. But since she is not a goddess, but a gift of God, she should be sought from him, by whom alone she can be given, and the whole crowd of false gods will vanish.

But why is Faith also believed to be a goddess and given a temple and altar? Whoever wisely recognizes Faith makes himself her dwelling place.

How, though, do they know what faith is, whose first and greatest duty is to believe in the true God? But why was Virtue not sufficient? Is faith not included in it? They saw that Virtue ought to be divided into four forms: prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

And since each of these forms has its own parts, faith belongs among the parts of justice. It occupies the highest place among us, provided we understand what it means that “the just shall live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4).

But I am astonished at them, lovers of a multitude of gods. If Faith is a goddess, why did they wrong so many other goddesses by neglecting those to whom they could likewise have dedicated temples and altars?

Why did Temperance not deserve to be a goddess, when some Roman leaders acquired no small glory through her name? Why, finally, is Courage not a goddess—the Courage that was present with Mucius [Note: Mucius was called Scaevola. Livy, book 2, chapter 12.] when he extended his right hand into the flames; that was present with Curtius [Note: Livy, book 7, chapter 6.] when he threw himself headlong into the chasm for his country; that was present with the elder Decius [Note: Livy, book 8, chapter 9.] and the younger Decius [Note: Livy, book 10, chapter 28. On these men see also below, book 5, chapter 18.] when they devoted themselves on behalf of the army?

Whether true courage was present in all these men is not the issue at present. Why did Prudence, why did Wisdom, deserve no place among the divinities? Is it because all are worshiped under the general name of Virtue itself?

Then one God too could be worshiped, whose parts the other gods are thought to be. Yet in that one Virtue there are both Faith and Chastity, which nevertheless deserved altars outside, in their own temples.

## CHAPTER XXI — Since they did not understand that these are gifts of God, they ought at least to have been content with Virtue and Felicity

[Note: The printed editions read: “Since they did not understand the one God, they ought at least to have been content with Virtue.”]

It was not truth but vanity that made these goddesses. For these are gifts of the true God; they themselves are not goddesses.

Nevertheless, where there are Virtue and Felicity, what else is sought? What is sufficient for one whom virtue and felicity are not sufficient for? Virtue embraces everything that must be done; felicity, everything that should be desired.

If Jupiter was worshiped in order to give these things, and if the breadth and endurance of a kingdom are good things, then they too belong to felicity. Why was it not understood that these were gifts of God, not goddesses?

But if they were thought to be goddesses, at least such a vast crowd of other gods would not have been sought. Let them consider the functions of all the gods and goddesses—functions which they invented according to their own opinions—and, if they can, find something that any god could provide for a human being who possesses virtue and felicity.

What instruction would have to be sought from Mercury or Minerva [Note: Mercury presided over eloquence; Minerva over arts and talents.] when virtue possessed everything within itself? The art of living well and rightly was defined by the ancients as virtue. From the Greek term ἀρετή (*aretē*), “virtue,” they therefore thought that the Latins derived the word for “art.” [Note: Donatus, commentary on Terence’s *Andria*, act 1, scene 1, line 4.]

But if virtue could come only to an intelligent person, what need was there for the god Catius the Father, who made people *cati*, that is, sharp-minded, when felicity could bestow this? For being born intelligent is a matter of felicity.

Therefore, even if the goddess Felicity could not be worshiped by someone not yet born, so that, once won over, she might give him this gift, she could grant it to his parents, her worshipers, so that intelligent children might be born to them.

What need was there for women in labor to invoke Lucina? If Felicity were present, they would not only give birth safely but also give birth to good children.

What need was there to commend newborns to the goddess Ops; crying infants to the god Vaticanus; infants lying down to the goddess Cunina; nursing infants to the goddess Rumina; standing children to the god Statilinus; those approaching to the goddess Adeona; those departing to Abeona?

Why invoke the goddess Mens so that they might have a good mind; the god Volumnus and goddess Volumna so that they might have good intentions; the marriage gods so that they might be joined well in marriage? [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and several manuscripts have “the conjugal gods.”]

Why invoke the rural gods so that they might obtain abundant crops, and especially the divine Fructesea herself; Mars and Bellona so that they might wage war well; the goddess Victory so that they might conquer; the god Honor [Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts have *Honorinus*, “the god Honorinus.”] so that they might be honored; the goddess Pecunia so that they might be wealthy; the god Aesculanus [Note: Some manuscripts consistently have *Aescalonus* here and below.] and his son Argentinus so that they might possess bronze and silver money?

They made Aesculanus the father of Argentinus because bronze money first came into use, followed afterward by silver. [Note: Pliny, book 33, chapter 13.]

But I am astonished that Argentinus did not beget Aurinus, since gold followed as well. If these people had possessed such a god, they would have placed Aurinus before his father Argentinus and his grandfather Aesculanus, just as they placed Jupiter before Saturn.

What need, then, was there, for the sake of these goods—whether of mind, body, or external circumstances—to worship and invoke such a crowd of gods? I have not mentioned them all, nor could they themselves provide separate and individual gods for all human goods, item by item, when the one goddess Felicity could have bestowed everything through a great and easy shortcut.

Not only would no other god be sought for obtaining good things; none would be sought even for driving away evils.

Why should the goddess Fessonia be invoked for the weary? [Note: Many old books have *Fossona*.] Why the goddess Pellonia for driving away enemies? Why, in the case of the sick, a physician, Apollo, or Aesculapius—or all of them together when the danger was great?

Why should the god Spinensis be invoked to uproot thorns from the fields? [Note: Vindobonensis, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have *Spinensis*.] Why should the goddess Robigo be entreated not to approach?

With Felicity present and protecting them, either no evils would arise or they would be driven away with the greatest ease.

Finally, since we are discussing the two goddesses Virtue and Felicity: if felicity is the reward of virtue, then it is not a goddess but a gift of God. But if it is a goddess, why should she not also be said to bestow virtue itself, since attaining virtue too is a great felicity?

## CHAPTER XXII — On the knowledge of the gods who ought to be worshiped, which Varro boasts that he has imparted to the Romans

What, then, is the value of what Varro boasts that he provides his fellow citizens as an immense benefit? He not only lists the gods whom the Romans ought to worship; he also says what belongs to each one.

“Just as,” he says, “it is of no use to know the name and appearance of some physician while being ignorant of what a physician is, so it is of no use to know that Aesculapius is a god if you do not know that he helps health and therefore remain ignorant of why you ought to entreat him.” [Note: Thus our manuscripts. B has: “How is it of no use?”]

He confirms this with another comparison, saying that no one can live—not merely live well—if he does not know who is a smith, who a baker [Note: The printed editions read *pictor* (“painter”).], who a plasterer, from whom he can obtain some useful object; whom he should take as an assistant, whom as a guide, and whom as a teacher.

In the same way, he asserts, knowledge of the gods is useful if one knows what force, ability, and power each god possesses in relation to each thing. From this, he says, we can know which god we ought to call upon and invoke for each purpose [Note: Lovanium reads “for the sake of each thing”; *rei* (“thing”) is absent from the other books.], so that we do not behave like mime actors and ask Liber for water or the Water-Nymphs for wine.

A great benefit indeed! Who would not thank him if he were showing the truth, and if he taught human beings to worship the one true God from whom all good things come?

## CHAPTER XXIII — On Felicity, whom the Romans, worshipers of many gods, long failed to honor with divine worship, although she alone was sufficient for everything
1. But what is the point at issue now? If their books and sacred rites are true, and Felicity is a goddess, why was she not established as the sole deity to be worshiped, she who could bestow everything and make people happy at one stroke? For what does anyone desire anything except in order to become happy? Why, finally, did Lucullus, after so many Roman leaders, establish a temple to this great goddess only so late? [Note: [Col. 0129] About the year 666 from the founding of the City; for this is assigned to the consulship of Licinius Lucullus, by whom a temple was established to Felicity because he had successfully waged war against the kings Mithridates and Tigranes.] Why did Romulus himself, wishing to found a happy state, not build a temple especially to her? Nor would he have supplicated the other gods for anything, since nothing would be lacking if she were present. For he himself would neither have first become king nor, as they think, afterward become a god, if he did not have this goddess favorable to him.

Why, then, did he establish for the Romans the gods Janus, Jupiter, Mars, Picus, Faunus, Tiberinus, Hercules, and whatever other gods there were? Why did Titus Tatius add Saturn, Ops, Sol, Luna, Vulcan, Light, and however many others he added—including also the goddess Cloacina—while neglecting Felicity? Why did Numa establish so many gods and goddesses without her? Or perhaps he could not see her amid such a crowd? Certainly King Hostilius himself would not have introduced new gods, Fear and Paleness, to be propitiated, if he had known or worshiped this goddess. For in the presence of Felicity all fear and paleness would not depart because they had been propitiated, but would flee because they had been driven away.

2. Next, what are we to make of the fact that the Roman empire was already growing far and wide, while no one yet worshiped Felicity? Was the empire therefore greater rather than happier? For how could true felicity exist where true piety did not exist? Piety is the truthful worship of the true God, not the worship of so many false gods as there are demons.

But afterward, once Felicity had been admitted into the number of the gods, great unhappiness from civil wars followed. Or was Felicity perhaps justly indignant because she had been invited so late, and not to her honor but rather to her disgrace, so that she was worshiped together with Priapus, Cloacina, Fear, Paleness, Fever, and the rest—not deities deserving worship, but crimes of those who worshiped them?

3. Finally, if such a great goddess was thought worthy of worship amid so disgraceful a crowd, why was she not worshiped more conspicuously than the others? For who could tolerate the fact that Felicity was established neither among the so-called Consentes gods, whom they say are admitted to Jupiter’s council, nor among those whom they call the Select Gods? [Note: [Col. 0130] The printed editions read: “Felicity was established, that is, a temple.” The word “that” is absent from the manuscripts.] A temple ought to have been made for her that would surpass the others both in the eminence of its site and in the dignity of its construction.

For why should anything not be made better than Jupiter himself? What gave Jupiter even his kingship except Felicity—if, indeed, he was happy while he reigned? And felicity is preferable to kingship. No one doubts that it is easy to find a person afraid of becoming king; but no one is found who does not wish to be happy.

Therefore, if the gods could be consulted through augury or in any other manner, they should have been consulted about this matter: whether they wished to yield their place to Felicity. If the sites had already been occupied by other temples or altars, and there were no place where a larger and loftier temple could be built for Felicity, Jupiter himself would even have yielded, so that Felicity might rather possess the very summit of the Capitoline Hill. No one would resist Felicity unless—something impossible—he wished to be unhappy.

If Jupiter were consulted, he certainly would not do what the three gods Mars, Terminus, and Juventas did: they refused in every way to yield their place to their greater king. For, as their writings relate, when King Tarquinius wished to build the Capitol and saw that the place which seemed to him more worthy and suitable had already been occupied by other gods [Note: [Col. 0130] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads, “by alien gods.”], he did not dare to do anything against their decision, believing that they would yield voluntarily to so great a deity and their own ruler. Since many of them were present where the Capitol was to be established, he asked by augury whether they wished to give up the place to Jupiter. All of them wished to withdraw from it except those whom I have mentioned: Mars, Terminus, and Juventas. [Note: [Col. 0131] Livy, book 1, mentions only Terminus. Florus, book 1, and other historians add Juventas, but not Mars.]

For that reason the Capitol was constructed in such a way that these three were also inside it, marked by signs so obscure that scarcely even the most learned people knew this. Jupiter himself, therefore, would in no way despise Felicity, just as he was despised by Terminus, Mars, and Juventas. Indeed, even those who had not yielded to Jupiter would certainly yield to Felicity, who had made Jupiter their king. Or, if they did not yield, they would not do so out of contempt for her; rather, they would prefer to be obscure in Felicity’s house than to stand out in their own places without her.

4. Thus, once the goddess Felicity had been established in the most spacious and lofty place, the citizens would learn from whom aid for every good wish should be sought. And so, with nature itself urging them, they would abandon the superfluous multitude of other gods and worship Felicity alone; they would supplicate her alone; the citizens who wished to be happy—and no one would not wish it—would frequent her temple alone. Thus she herself would be sought from herself, since everyone sought her.

For who would wish to receive anything from any god except felicity, or what he believes contributes to felicity? Therefore, if felicity has power over whom she accompanies—and she does, if she is a goddess—what greater folly is there than to ask felicity from some other god, when one could obtain her from herself?

They ought therefore to have honored this goddess above the other gods even by the dignity of her location. For, as we read in their own writings, the ancient Romans worshiped a certain Summanus [Note: [Col. 0131] Pliny, book 2, chapter 52; Ovid, *Fasti* 6.731–732], to whom they attributed the nocturnal thunderbolts, more than Jupiter, to whom the daytime thunderbolts belonged. But after a distinguished and lofty temple had been built for Jupiter, the multitude flocked to him on account of the temple’s magnificence, so that scarcely anyone can be found who remembers having even read the name of Summanus, which can no longer be heard.

But if Felicity is not a goddess—for, as is true, she is a gift of God—then let the God who can give her be sought, and let the harmful multitude of false gods be abandoned. That multitude is vainly pursued by a multitude of foolish people, who make the gifts of God into gods for themselves and offend the one whose gifts they are through the stubbornness of their proud will.

For someone who worships felicity as though she were a goddess cannot avoid unhappiness if he abandons God, the giver of felicity—just as someone who licks painted bread cannot avoid hunger because he does not ask for real bread from the person who possesses it.

## CHAPTER XXIV—How the Pagans Defend Their Worship of the Divine Gifts Themselves among the Gods

It is worthwhile to examine their arguments. “Surely,” they say, “we are not to believe that our ancestors were so foolish as not to know that these were divine gifts, not gods? But because they knew that such things could be granted only through some god’s generosity, and could not discover the names of the gods who granted them, they called the gods by the names of the things they perceived to be given by them. They derived certain names from those things: thus, from *bellum* (‘war’) they called the goddess Bellona, not war itself; from *cunae* (‘cradle’) Cunina, not a cradle; from *segetes* (‘crops’) Segetia, not crops; from *poma* (‘fruit’) Pomona, not fruit; from *boves* (‘cattle’) Bubona [Note: [Col. 0132] Erasmus reads: “from *boves*, Bobona.” The Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis editions read: “from *boves*, Bubona.” M.], not an ox.

“Or else they used no alteration of the word at all, but called them by the names of the things themselves. Thus Pecunia was called a goddess because she gives money, although money itself was certainly not thought to be a goddess; likewise Virtus, which gives courage; Honor, which gives honor; Concordia, which gives concord; Victoria, which gives victory. So, when Felicity is called a goddess, it is not the thing that is given that is intended, but the divine power from which felicity is given.”

## CHAPTER XXV—On Worshiping the One God Alone, Who, Though His Name Is Unknown, Is Recognized as the Giver of Felicity

Once this explanation has been given to us, we may perhaps persuade more easily those whose hearts are not too hardened of what we wish. For if human weakness has already perceived that felicity can be given only by some god—and this was perceived by people who worshiped so many gods, including their own king Jupiter—then, because they did not know the name of the one from whom felicity was given, they wished to call him by the name of the thing which they believed was given by him [Note: [Col. 0132] The printed editions read, “and therefore.” The manuscripts do not have *et*, “and.”]. They therefore judged sufficiently [Note: [Col. 0132] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead have *indicant*, “they indicate.”] that felicity could not be given by Jupiter himself, whom they already worshiped, but by the one whom they thought ought to be worshiped under the name of Felicity herself.

I firmly affirm that they believed felicity was given by some god whom they did not know. Let him, then, be sought; let him be worshiped; that is enough. Let the tumult of countless demons be rejected. Let that God not be enough for the person who is not satisfied with his gift. I say, let the God who gives felicity not be enough for the one who is not satisfied to receive felicity itself. But whoever is satisfied with it—for a human being has nothing greater to desire—let him serve the one God, the giver of felicity.

He is not the one whom they call Jupiter. For if they recognized him as the giver of felicity, they would certainly not seek another god or goddess from whom felicity might be given, under the name of Felicity herself; nor would they think that Jupiter should be worshiped with such insults. This Jupiter is called the adulterer of other men’s wives [Note: [Col. 0132] So all our manuscripts read. In B., *adulterator*, “seducer.” M.]; he is the shameless lover and abductor of the beautiful boy [Note: [Col. 0132] Ganymede. Homer, *Iliad* 20.] 

## CHAPTER XXVI—On the Theatrical Games Which the Gods Demanded to Be Celebrated for Them by Their Worshipers

“But Homer was inventing these things,” says Cicero [Note: [Col. 0132] *Tusculan Disputations* 1.26], “and transferring human things to the gods; I would rather that divine things were transferred to us.” The serious man rightly disapproved of the poet who fabricated crimes of the gods.

Why, then, are theatrical games—where these things are spoken, sung, and acted—presented as honors to the gods and recorded by the most learned people among sacred matters? Here Cicero should cry out, not against the poets’ inventions, but against the institutions of the ancestors.

Would they not also cry out, “What have we done? The gods themselves demanded that these things be presented as honors to them. They ordered it with dreadful insistence and foretold disaster if it was not done. Because something had been neglected, they punished it with the utmost severity; because what had been neglected was performed, they showed that they were appeased.”

Among their virtues and marvelous deeds the following is certainly recounted. Titus Latinius [Note: [Col. 0133] The printed editions read *Latino*. Some manuscripts read *Latinio*.], a Roman peasant and head of a household, was told in a dream to report to the Senate that the Roman Games should be renewed, because on their first day the gods had evidently been displeased by the grim execution of a certain criminal who had been ordered to be led to punishment before the watching people—gods who were seeking amusement from the games.

When the man who had been warned by the dream did not dare to carry out the order the next day, the same command was given again on the second night, with greater severity. He lost his son because he did not obey. On the third night he was told that a greater punishment threatened him if he did not comply. Even then he did not dare to do so, and he fell into a severe and dreadful illness.

Then, on the advice of his friends, he reported the matter to the magistrates and was carried in a litter into the Senate. Once he had related the dream, he immediately recovered his health and departed on foot, healed. The Senate, astonished by so great a miracle, decreed that the Games should be renewed at four times the expense. [Note: [Col. 0133] Livy, book 2, chapter 36, and Valerius, book 1, chapter 7, section 4, agree with this account; they call him a man of the plebs. Cicero, narrating this very dream in book 1 of *On Divination*, chapter 26, intended to signify this by the expression “Roman peasant.”]

Who would not see, if he has sound judgment, that human beings subjected to wicked demons—whose domination only the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord can remove—were compelled by force to present to such gods things that right judgment could have declared shameful?

In those games, the crimes of the divine beings were repeatedly presented in poetry, even though the games were renewed by order of the Senate because the gods compelled it. In those games the most disreputable actors sang, acted, and pleased the audience with Jupiter as a corrupter of chastity [Note: [Col. 0133] So the manuscripts and the Vindobonensis read. Am., Er., and Lov. instead have *placabant*, “appeased.”].

If that was invented, he would be angry; but if he took pleasure even in fictitious accounts of his own crimes, when would he be worshiped unless one served the devil? Was this the one who founded, expanded, and preserved the Roman empire, though he was more contemptible than any Roman who found such things displeasing? Was this the one who gave felicity, though he was worshiped so unhappily—and became even more unhappily angry if he was not worshiped in that manner?

## CHAPTER XXVII—On the Three Classes of Gods Discussed by the Pontiff Scaevola

It has been recorded in writing that the learned pontiff Scaevola [Note: [Col. 0133] This is the same Scaevola whom Cicero praises in *On the Orator* 1.39 as “the most eloquent of jurists and the most juristic of the eloquent.”] discussed three traditional classes of gods: one belonging to the poets, another to the philosophers, and a third to the leaders of the state.

He says that the first class is frivolous, because many things unworthy of the gods are invented about them. He says that the second does not suit states, because it contains some things that are superfluous and others that it is harmful for the people to know.

There is no great difficulty concerning the superfluous things; even jurists are accustomed to say, “Superfluous things do no harm.” But what are those things that cause harm when made public? “These,” he says, “are not gods: Hercules, Aesculapius, Castor, and Pollux. For learned men have revealed that they were human beings and died according to human condition.”

What else [Note: [Col. 0134] The printed editions read: “What else, except that their cities do not possess true images of those who are gods,” etc. *Quam* (“except”) should be deleted, since it is absent from all the manuscripts and, if added, connects the following words—which belong to the pontiff Scaevola—badly with what immediately precedes.]? Their cities do not possess true images of those who are gods; for the true God has neither sex nor age nor defined bodily members. The pontiff does not want the people to know these things, although he does not think them false [Note: [Col. 0134] Several manuscripts read, “although they do not think them false.” One manuscript, in a second hand, reads, “although he reckons them.”]. He therefore considers it expedient for states to be deceived in matters of religion.

Varro himself does not hesitate to say this in his books *On Divine Matters*. What a splendid religion, to which a weak person seeking deliverance may flee, while he is told that it is expedient for him to be deceived when he seeks the truth by which he may be liberated!

Why Scaevola rejects the poetic class of gods is also not concealed in those same writings: because the poets deform the gods in such a way that they cannot even be compared with good human beings. They make one steal, another commit adultery; they make another say and do things in a different, shameful, and foolish manner; they make three goddesses compete with one another for the prize of beauty, and the two who lost to Venus destroy Troy; they make Jupiter himself transform into a bull or a swan in order to sleep with some woman; they make a goddess marry a human being and Saturn devour his children. In short, nothing can be invented of miracles or vices that is not found there and that is not far removed from the nature of the gods.

O Scaevola, greatest of pontiffs, abolish the games if you can. Instruct the people not to offer such honors to the immortal gods, where it is delightful to admire the gods’ crimes and pleasing to imitate what they can do.

But if the people answer you, “Pontiffs, you introduced these things to us,” ask the gods themselves—at whose instigation you ordered these things—that they not order such performances to be presented to them. If these things are evil and therefore cannot in any way be believed of the majesty of the gods, the insult to the gods is even greater when such things are invented about them with impunity.

But they do not listen to you. They are demons; they teach depravity and delight in disgraceful things. They not only do not regard it as an insult when such things are invented about them; they cannot bear the insult of having those things omitted from their solemn rites.

And if you appeal to Jupiter against them, especially because so many of his crimes are acted out in theatrical games, does he not suffer the greatest insult from you—even if you call him the god Jupiter, by whom this entire world is ruled and governed—when you think that he should be worshiped together with these beings and declare him to be their king?

## CHAPTER XXVIII—Whether the Worship of the Gods Helped the Romans Obtain and Extend Their Empire

In no way, then, could such gods—who are appeased, or rather accused, by such honors, so that the crime is greater in their taking pleasure in false representations than if the truth were told about them—have enlarged and preserved the Roman empire.

For if they could have done this, they would rather have conferred so great a gift upon the Greeks, who worshiped them more honorably and worthily in such divine matters, that is, in theatrical games. The Greeks did not withdraw from the attacks of the poets, by which they saw the gods torn apart; they gave the poets permission to mistreat whatever human beings they pleased, and they did not judge the actors themselves shameful, but considered them worthy even of distinguished honors.

Just as the Romans could possess gold money although they did not worship the god Aurinus, so they could also possess silver and bronze money without worshiping either Argentinus or his father Aesculanus—and likewise with everything else that it is tedious to enumerate.

Thus they could not have possessed their kingdom without the true God, even against his will. But if the false and numerous gods had been ignored or despised, and that one God had been known and worshiped with sincere faith and upright conduct, they would have had a better kingdom here, however great it might have been; and afterward they would have received an everlasting kingdom, whether or not they possessed one here. [Note: [Col. 0135] Lovaniensis reads *incognito*, “unknown,” contrary to the other books.] [Note: [Col. 0135] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead have *post hoc*, “after this.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX—On the False Augury by Which the Strength and Stability of the Roman Kingdom Seemed to Be Indicated

For what are we to make of the claim that the following was a most favorable omen—the one I mentioned shortly before—that Mars, Terminus, and Juventas refused to yield their places to Jupiter, king of the gods?

“For in this way,” they say, “it was signified that the Martian race, that is, the Roman people, would yield the place it occupied to no one; that the Romans would move no one from his boundaries on account of the god Terminus; and that Roman youth, because of the goddess Juventas, would yield to no one.”

Let them therefore consider what sort of king of their gods and giver of their kingdom they have, since these omens set him up as an adversary to whom it was glorious not to yield. Yet, if these things are true, they have nothing at all to fear. For they will not admit that the gods yielded to Christ, who had refused to yield to Jupiter. They could yield to Christ while the boundaries of the empire remained intact, and they could yield their places and, above all, the hearts of believers.

But before Christ came in the flesh, and before, finally, the writings from which we produce these accounts had been composed—yet after that omen had occurred under King Tarquinius—the Roman army was routed several times, that is, turned to flight. This showed the omen false, since Juventas had not yielded to Jupiter. The Martian people were crushed within the City itself when the Gauls prevailed and burst in; and the boundaries of the empire were narrowed when many cities defected to Hannibal.

Thus the splendor of the omens was emptied of meaning. What remained was defiance against Jupiter, not of gods but of demons. For it is one thing not to have yielded; it is another to return from a place to which one had yielded.

Moreover, afterward the boundaries of the Roman empire in the East were altered by the will of Hadrian. For he ceded the three noble provinces of Armenia, Mesopotamia, and Assyria to the Persian empire [Note: [Col. 0135] See Eutropius, book 8, chapter 6]. Thus the god Terminus, who according to them guarded the Roman boundaries and had not yielded his place to Jupiter in that splendid omen, seemed to have feared Hadrian, king of human beings, more than the king of the gods.

When those provinces were recovered at another time, Terminus yielded again in almost our own memory, when Julian [Note: [Col. 0136] Julian the Apostate. See below, book 5, chapter 21], devoted to the oracles of those gods, rashly ordered the ships carrying provisions to be burned. Deprived of supplies, the army was soon reduced to such want—after Julian himself had been killed by an enemy wound—that no one would have escaped, with enemies attacking on every side and the emperor’s army thrown into confusion by his death, unless the boundaries of the empire had been established there by a peace settlement, where they still remain today. They were not fixed with as great a loss as that conceded by Hadrian, but they were nevertheless fixed by a compromise. [Note: [Col. 0136] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Lovaniensis read: “with enemies attacking on every side, the emperor’s army being thrown into confusion by his death.” M.]

Thus, according to a worthless omen, the god Terminus did not yield to Jupiter; yet he yielded to Hadrian’s will, to Julian’s recklessness, and to Jovian’s necessity [Note: [Col. 0136] Jovian, Julian’s successor.].

The more perceptive and serious Romans saw these things, but they had little power against the custom of the state, which had been bound to demonic rites. For even if they sensed that these things were vain, they nevertheless thought that the religious worship owed to God should be offered to the nature of things, which had been established under the rule and dominion of the one true God. They were serving, as the Apostle says, “the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Romans 1:25).

The help of this true God was necessary: help by which holy and truly pious men would be sent to die for the true religion, so that false religion might be removed from the living. [Note: [Col. 0136] The printed editions read: “so that false religion might be removed by the living.” The manuscripts read: “so that false things might be removed from the living.”]

## CHAPTER XXX—What the Worshipers of the Gods of the Nations Themselves Admit They Think About Them

Cicero, an augur, ridicules auguries [Note: [Col. 0136] He himself declares that he was an augur in *On the Laws* 2], and criticizes people who regulate the plans of their lives by the calls of ravens and crows (*On Divination* 2.37).

But this Academic philosopher, who maintains that everything is uncertain, is unworthy of having any authority in these matters. In the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, Quintus Lucilius Balbus argues before him. Although Balbus himself inserts superstitions derived from the nature of things as though they were physical and philosophical teachings, he nevertheless expresses indignation at the institution of images and at the fabulous opinions, speaking as follows:

“Do you not see, then, how reasoning has been drawn from physical matters, discovered rightly and usefully, to fictitious and fabricated gods? This has produced false opinions, confused errors, and almost senile superstitions. For the forms, ages, clothing, and adornments of the gods are known to us. Their families, moreover, marriages, and kinships—all have been transferred to resemble human weakness.

“For they are also represented with disturbed minds; for we have received accounts of the desires, illnesses, and anger of the gods. Nor, as the stories relate, have the gods been free from wars and battles. Not only—as in Homer—when some gods defended two opposing armies on different sides (*Iliad* Υ, lines 67 ff.) but also when they waged their own wars against the Titans or Giants. These things are both said and believed with the greatest foolishness, and they are full of utter emptiness and extreme frivolity” (chapter 28).

Here, at least for the moment, are the admissions of those who defend the gods of the nations.

Then, when he says that these things belong to superstition, but that religion consists in what he himself seems to teach according to the Stoics, he says:

“For not only philosophers but also our ancestors separated superstition from religion. For those who prayed and sacrificed all day so that their children might survive were called superstitious” (see Lactantius, book 4, chapter 28).

Who would not understand that, while fearing the custom of the state, he is trying to praise the religion of the ancestors and separate it from superstition, but cannot discover how to do so? For if those who prayed and sacrificed all day were called superstitious by the ancestors, were not those also superstitious who established—as he criticizes—images of the gods distinguished by different ages and clothing, together with the families, marriages, and kinships of the gods?

When these things are condemned as superstitious, that condemnation necessarily implicates the ancestors who established and worshiped such images. It also implicates Balbus himself, who, however eloquently he strives to free himself, was nevertheless compelled to venerate these things and would not dare even to mutter in a public assembly what he loudly proclaims in this discussion.

Let us therefore, as Christians, give thanks to the Lord our God—not to Heaven and Earth, as Balbus argues, but to the one who made heaven and earth. Through the profound humility of Christ, the preaching of the Apostles, and the faith of martyrs who died for the truth and lived with the truth, he has overthrown these superstitions—which Balbus, as though stammering, scarcely reproves—not only in religious hearts but also in the superstitious temples themselves, through the liberated service of his people.

## CHAPTER XXXI—On the Opinions of Varro, Who, Though He Rejected Popular Belief and Did Not Arrive at Knowledge of the True God, Nevertheless Judged That One God Should Be Worshiped

1. What does Varro himself say—the man whom we regret to have placed theatrical games among divine matters, although not by his own judgment? In many passages he urges people, as though religiously minded, to worship the gods. Does he not nevertheless admit that he does not follow by his own judgment the practices which he recalls as having been established by the Roman state? Indeed, he openly confesses that, if he were establishing a new state, he would without hesitation dedicate the gods and their names according to the pattern of nature instead.

But since he was living among an ancient people, he says that he ought to retain the history of names and titles received from the ancestors, just as it had been handed down, and that he wrote and investigated these matters for the purpose of encouraging the common people to worship them more rather than despise them.

By these words the exceedingly shrewd man sufficiently indicates that he does not reveal everything which would not be contemptible to him but would appear worthy of contempt to the common people if it were not kept silent.

I would have been thought to be merely conjecturing this, if he himself had not plainly said elsewhere, when discussing religions, that many things are true which it is not only unhelpful for the common people to know but which, even when false, it is expedient for the people to regard differently; and that for this reason the Greeks enclosed their initiations and mysteries in silence and within walls.

Here he certainly exposed the entire policy of those who were regarded as wise and by whom states and peoples were governed. Yet the wicked demons are wonderfully delighted by this deception. They possess deceivers and deceived alike, and no one frees us from their domination except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

2. The same exceedingly shrewd and learned author also says that those alone seemed to him to have understood what God is who believed that God is a soul governing the world through motion and reason [Note: [Col. 0138] Concerning these matters, see Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* 1.2.].

Thus, although he did not yet grasp what the truth contains—for the true God is not a soul but the maker and creator even of the soul—nevertheless, if he could have been free from the prejudices of custom, he would have confessed and urged the worship of one God, governing the world through motion and reason. The remaining dispute with him on this matter would have concerned his saying that God is a soul rather than also the creator of the soul [Note: [Col. 0138] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “rather than the creator of the soul.” The other books have, “and the creator of the soul.”].

He also says that the ancient Romans worshiped the gods for more than 170 years without images [Note: [Col. 0138] Plutarch, in his *Life of Numa*, chapter 8, writes that Numa forbade the Romans to suppose that the image of God had the form of a human being or an animal; and that during the first 170 years they did indeed erect temples, but dedicated no bodily images. Compare Pliny, book 34, chapter 4.]. “If this practice had continued,” he says, “the gods would be worshiped more chastely.”

Among others, he calls the Jewish people as a witness to this opinion of his. Nor does he hesitate to conclude that passage by saying that those who first set up images of the gods for peoples both removed fear from their states and added error. He wisely judged that the gods could easily be despised in the stupidity of images.

By saying not that they “transmitted error” but that they “added error,” he clearly wishes it to be understood that error already existed even without images.

Therefore, when Varro says that only those understood what God is who believed him to be a soul governing the world, and when he considers religion more chastely observed without images, who does not see how close he came to the truth? If he had been able to resist so ancient an error, he would surely have judged that the one God, whom he believed governed the world, should be worshiped without an image. Being so near, he might perhaps easily have been warned about the mutability of the soul, so that he would recognize as the true God the immutable nature that had created the soul itself.

Since these things are so, whenever such men inserted in their writings mockeries of the many gods, they were compelled to acknowledge them by a hidden will of God rather than attempting to persuade others of them. Therefore, if we produce any testimonies from those writings, we produce them to refute those who refuse to notice from how great and how wicked a power of demons we are freed by the singular sacrifice of such holy blood poured out and by the gift of the Spirit bestowed.

## CHAPTER XXXII—For What Supposed Advantage the Leaders of the Nations Wanted False Religions to Continue among the Peoples Subject to Them

[Col. 0139]

Varro also says that peoples were more inclined toward the poetic than toward the physical accounts of the generations of the gods. For this reason, he says, the ancestors—the ancient Romans—believed in the sex and generations of the gods and established marriages among them.

This does not seem to have been done for any other reason than that it was the business of men who were regarded as prudent and wise to deceive the people in matters of religion and, in this very thing, not only to worship but also to imitate the demons, whose greatest desire is to deceive.

For just as demons cannot possess anyone unless they have deceived that person by deception, so human rulers—certainly not just, but resembling demons—persuaded the people in the name of religion to accept as true things which they knew to be vain. In this way they bound the people more closely, as it were, to civil society, so that they might similarly possess those subject to them. [Note: [Col. 0139] Most manuscripts read *aptius*, “more suitably.” M. reads likewise in manuscript 766.]

But what weak and uneducated person could escape both the deceitful rulers of the state and the demons?

## CHAPTER XXXIII—That the Times of All Kings and Kingdoms Were Ordered by the Judgment and Power of the True God

That God, therefore, the author and giver of felicity, because he alone is the true God, gives earthly kingdoms both to the good and to the wicked. Nor does he do this rashly or as though by chance—for God is not fortune—but according to an order of events and times that is hidden from us but perfectly known to him. Yet he does not serve as a subject to this order of times; rather, as its Lord, he himself rules, governs, and arranges it.

But he gives felicity only to the good. They may have it or not have it while serving; they may have it or not have it while ruling. Yet felicity will be complete in that life where no one will any longer serve.
