[Note: [Col. 0139] The older and manuscript books all lack the following words, which the editions of Vind., Am., Er., and Lov. place before the next sentence: “And therefore God commonly grants the kingdoms of this world to the good and the wicked, so that the good may not desire them as great gifts of God.” They then repeat the entire sentence: “And therefore earthly kingdoms are given by him both to the good,” etc. The observation of Ludovicus Vives and Latinius concerns not this sentence, as some have thought, but the words prefixed to it: those words are absent from the manuscripts and have slipped from the margin into the text. Our manuscripts also omit them. M.]

And therefore earthly kingdoms are given by him both to the good and to the wicked, so that his worshipers, still immature in the progress of their souls, may not covet these gifts from him as though they were something great.

This is also the mystery of the Old Testament, in which the New was hidden: earthly promises and gifts were given there, for those who understood—and even then possessed spiritual insight, although they did not yet proclaim it openly—to signify what eternity was represented by those temporal things and in which gifts of God true felicity consisted.

## CHAPTER XXXIV—On the Kingdom of the Jews, Which Was Established and Preserved by the One True God So Long as They Remained in the True Religion
Therefore, so that even those earthly goods might be recognized as placed under the power of the one God alone—goods for which those who cannot conceive of anything better hunger—rather than under the power of the many false gods whom the Romans formerly believed ought to be worshiped, God multiplied his people in Egypt from a very small number and delivered them from there by wondrous signs. Nor did those women invoke Lucina when he himself rescued and preserved their infants from the hands of the pursuing Egyptians, who wanted to kill them all, so that their births might be multiplied in marvelous ways and that nation might grow beyond belief. Without the goddess Rumina they suckled; without Cunina they lay in their cradles; without Educa and Potina they took food and drink. Without so many childish gods they were reared; without the gods of marriage they were married; without worship of Priapus they joined themselves to their wives. Without invoking Neptune, the sea opened before them as they crossed it, and overwhelmed their pursuing enemies when the returning waves closed back over them. Nor did they consecrate any goddess Mannia when they received manna from heaven; nor, when a struck rock poured forth water for the thirsty, did they worship Nymphs or Lymphs. Without the frenzied rites of Mars and Bellona they waged wars; and although they did not conquer without victory, they regarded victory not as a goddess but as a gift of their God. Without Segetia they had their crops, without Bubona their cattle, honey without Mellona, apples without Pomona; and, in short, everything for which the Romans thought they had to supplicate such throngs of false gods, they received far more successfully from the one true God. And if they had not sinned against him through impious curiosity, as though seduced by magical arts, by turning away to foreign gods and idols, and finally by killing Christ, they would have remained in that same kingdom—perhaps not more extensive, but happier. And now that they are scattered throughout nearly all lands and peoples is the providence of that one true God: so that, when the images, altars, groves, and temples of the false gods are everywhere overthrown and sacrifices are prohibited, it may be demonstrated from their own books how this had been prophesied long beforehand, lest, when it was read in ours, it should perhaps be thought to have been fabricated by us.

What follows must now be considered in the next volume, and here an end must be given to this lengthy discussion.

# BOOK FIVE

[Note: [Col. 0139] Written in the year 415. At the beginning he deals with the removal of the belief in fate, lest there should eventually be people who wished to attribute to fate the power and growth of the Roman Empire, which he demonstrated in the preceding book could not be attributed to the false gods. He then proceeds to the question of God’s foreknowledge and proves that it does not take away the freedom of our will. Afterwards he speaks about the ancient morals of the Romans, and by what merit of theirs—or by what judgment of God—it came about that the true God himself, whom they did not worship, assisted them in enlarging their empire. Finally, he teaches what should truly be regarded as the happiness of Christian emperors.]

[Col. 0139]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0139]

Since it is evident that happiness is the fullness of all desirable things, and that it is not a goddess but a gift of God, human beings ought therefore to worship no god except the one who can make them happy. Hence, if happiness were a goddess, she alone would rightly be said to deserve worship. Let us now consequently consider for what reason God, who can also grant those goods that even the wicked may possess—and therefore those who are not happy—wished the Roman Empire to become so great and so long-lasting. For since the multitude of false gods whom they worshiped did not accomplish this, we have already said much, and we shall say more wherever it seems appropriate.

## CHAPTER ONE—The cause of the Roman Empire and of all kingdoms is neither accidental nor dependent on the position of the stars

The cause of the greatness of the Roman Empire, therefore, is neither accidental nor fated [Note: [Col. 0141] There were people who thought that one must here resort to an accidental or fated cause. Cicero is a witness in Book Two of *On Divination*, chapter 47: “L. Tarutius Firmanus, our friend,” he says, “a man especially learned in Chaldaean calculations, even traced the natal day of our city back to the Parilia on which we received it as having been founded by Romulus, and said that Rome was born when the moon was in the ascendant; nor did he hesitate to sing its fate. O the immense power of error! Did even the natal day of a city depend on the power of the stars and the moon? Suppose that, in the case of a child, it matters from what configuration of the heavens he first drew breath: could this have any force in the stones or mortar from which the city was made?”], according to the view or opinion of those who call things accidental if they have no causes or do not arise from any rational order, and things fated if they occur by the necessity of some order apart from the will of God and human beings.

Human kingdoms are established wholly by divine providence. If someone therefore attributes them to fate because he calls God’s will or power by the name “fate,” let him retain his opinion but correct his language. Why does he not say at the outset what he will say later, when someone asks him what he means by fate? For when people hear this word, ordinary usage leads them to understand nothing other than the force of the position of the stars, such as it is when someone is born or conceived. Some separate this from God’s will; others affirm that even this depends upon it.

But those who suppose that the stars, without God’s will, determine what we do or what good things we possess or evils we suffer must be rejected by the ears of everyone—not only of those who hold the true religion, but also of those who wish to be worshipers of gods of any kind, even false ones. For what else does this opinion accomplish except that no god at all should be worshiped or invoked? Our present discussion, however, is not directed against such people, but against those who oppose the Christian religion in defense of beings whom they regard as gods.

Those, on the other hand, who make the position of the stars—somehow determining what each person is like and what good or evil happens to him—depend upon God’s will, do great injury to heaven if they think that the stars were given this power by the authority of the supreme God, so that they may willingly make such determinations. They imagine that crimes are decreed in heaven, as though in its most illustrious senate and most splendid curia—crimes for which, if some earthly city had decreed them, it would have deserved to be destroyed by the judgment of the human race.

What judgment is then left to God concerning human actions, when a heavenly necessity is imposed upon them, since he is Lord both of the stars and of human beings? Or, if they do not say that the stars, having received power from the supreme God, determine these things by their own choice, but that in imposing such necessities they altogether carry out his commands, should we then think this about God which they consider utterly unworthy to think about the will of the stars?

But if the stars are said rather to signify these things than to cause them—so that their configuration is, as it were, a form of speech predicting the future rather than producing it (and this was the opinion of no small number of learned men)—mathematicians do not ordinarily speak in this way. They do not, for example, say, “Mars, being so positioned, signifies a murderer,” but, “It makes a murderer” [Note: [Col. 0142] The Vindobonensis, the Ambrosianus, and the Erfurtensis read: “It does not make a murderer.” The word “not” is absent from the other books.]. Nevertheless, let us grant that they do not speak as they ought, and that one should take from philosophers the rule of language for announcing what they think they find in the position of the stars. Why is it [Note: [Col. 0142] So read our manuscripts. Some printed editions have *qui sit* (“how it is”).] that they have never been able to say why, in the lives, actions, circumstances, occupations, arts, honors, and other matters belonging to human life, and even in death itself, there is usually so great a diversity that, in these respects, many outsiders are more alike than the twins themselves, separated by only a very brief interval at birth but conceived in a single intercourse and at the same moment?

## CHAPTER TWO—The similar and dissimilar health of twins

Cicero says that Hippocrates, the most renowned physician, left in writing that, when certain brothers had begun to fall ill at the same time and their illness worsened and improved at the same time, he suspected them of being twins [Note: [Col. 0142] This is not found in the extant books of Cicero or Hippocrates. I suspect that Cicero said it in the little book *On Fate*. Anyone who examines it more closely will find that it has reached our age mutilated, damaged, and full of errors. —LUDOVICUS VIVES.]. The Stoic Posidonius, who was greatly devoted to astrology, used to assert that they had been conceived and born under the same configuration of the stars [Note: [Col. 0142] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 2, *On Divination* 1, and *On Duties* 3.]. Thus, what the physician believed to belong to a very similar bodily constitution, the philosophical astrologer attributed to the power and configuration of the stars that had existed when they were conceived and born.

In this matter the medical conjecture is much more acceptable and, being closer to the facts, more credible. For the parents, while having intercourse, may have been bodily disposed in such a way that the beginnings of the conceptions were affected accordingly, so that, after receiving their subsequent growth from the mother’s body, the children were born with similar health. Then, being nourished in one house on the same foods, and having the same air, location, and water—things which medicine testifies to have great power to affect the body for good or ill [Note: [Col. 0142] Thus the Corbeiensis manuscript. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read *accipiendum* (“must be understood”).]—and being accustomed to the same exercises, they might possess bodies so similar that even toward falling ill they would be moved at the same time by the same causes in the same way.

But to drag the configuration of the sky and stars that existed when they were conceived or born into this equality of illness, when at the same time so many things of the most diverse kinds, with the most diverse conditions [Note: [Col. 0142] Most manuscripts read *effectuum* (“effects”).] and outcomes [Col. 0143], could have been conceived and born in the land of one region subject to the same sky, I do not know what kind of presumption this is.

We know, however, twins who not only have different activities and travels, but also suffer different illnesses. On this matter Hippocrates, as far as I can see, could offer the easiest explanation: different illnesses may have happened to them because of different foods and exercises, which arise not from the body’s constitution but from the will of the mind.

As for Posidonius, or anyone else who asserts the influence of fated stars, it is remarkable if he can find anything to say here without wishing to deceive the minds of the ignorant about matters they do not understand. For what they try to establish from the brief interval of time that separated the twins at birth, because of the small portion of the sky where the indication of the hour is placed—which they call the horoscope—either does not have as much power as the diversity found in the twins’ wills, actions, characters, and circumstances, or else has even more power than the twins’ common lowliness or nobility of birth, the greatest difference of which they place only in the hour at which each was born.

Accordingly, if one is born so quickly after the other that the same part of the horoscope remains, I ask for all the things to be equal—things that can be found equal in no twins. But if the delay of the second changes the horoscope, I ask for different parents, whom twins cannot have.

## CHAPTER THREE—The argument that the mathematician Nigidius took from the potter’s wheel in the question of twins

It is therefore useless to produce that famous story about the potter’s wheel, which they say Nigidius offered in reply when perplexed by this question, and from which he was also called Figulus [Note: [Col. 0143] Aulus Gellius mentions Nigidius in Book 19, chapter 14, and Lucan in Book 1, verses 639 and following.].

For after turning the potter’s wheel with all the force he could, while it was spinning he struck it twice, with the greatest speed, with ink at what was, so to speak, a single point on it. Afterwards, when the motion had stopped, the marks he had made were found far apart on the outer edge of the wheel. “So,” he said, “in the sky’s great swiftness, even if one twin is born after the other with the same speed with which I struck the wheel twice, there is a great distance in the space of heaven. From this,” he said, “come all the differences said to exist in the characters and circumstances of twins.”

This fiction is more fragile than the vessels shaped by that rotation. For if there is so great a difference in heaven—one that cannot be grasped by the constellations—that one twin receives an inheritance and the other does not, why do they dare, after examining the constellations of other people who are not twins, to make predictions concerning that secret which no one can comprehend or mark down according to the moments of those being born?

But if they make such statements about the births of others because those things extend over longer periods of time, while the moments of the small divisions that twins can have between their births are assigned to trivial matters about which mathematicians are not ordinarily consulted—for who consults them about when he should sit, when he should walk, or when and what he should eat?—are we not speaking of these same small intervals when we show that the characters, actions, and circumstances of twins are very numerous and very different?

## CHAPTER FOUR—Esau and Jacob, twins greatly unlike each other in character and actions

Two twins were born in the ancient memory of the patriarchs—speaking of notable persons—in such a way that the younger, following immediately after the elder, held the elder’s heel. There was so much difference in their lives and characters, such disparity in their actions, and such dissimilarity in their parents’ love, that this very difference even made them enemies of one another (Gen. 25:24–34).

Is this explained by saying that while one was walking the other was sitting, while one was sleeping the other was awake, and while one was speaking the other was silent—matters belonging to those tiny intervals that cannot be grasped by those who record the configuration of the stars under which each person is born, from which the mathematicians are consulted?

One underwent mercenary servitude; the other did not serve. One was loved by his mother; the other was not loved. One lost the honor that was held in high esteem among them; the other obtained it. What shall we say about wives, children, and possessions—what great differences there were! [V.] If these matters belong to the tiny intervals of time that separate twins, and are not attributed to the constellations, why are such things announced after the constellations of other people have been examined? But if they are announced because they belong not to incomprehensible instants but to periods of time that can be observed and recorded, what role does that potter’s wheel play here except to send people with hearts of clay spinning around, so that the empty talk of the mathematicians may not be refuted?

## CHAPTER FIVE—The ways in which the mathematicians are proved to profess a vain science

Do not the very men whose illness Hippocrates, examining it medically, suspected to be twins because the illness of both appeared more severe and milder at the same time, sufficiently refute those who wish to attribute to the stars what arose from a similar bodily constitution?

For why were they ill similarly and at the same time—one not earlier and the other later—as they had been born, since plainly both could not be born at the same time? Or, if it made no difference that they fell ill at different times because they were born at different times, why do they insist that the different times of birth matter for differences in other things?

Why could they travel at different times, marry at different times, beget children at different times, and do many other things because they were born at different times, but could not for the same reason fall ill at different times? For if the unequal delay in their births changed the horoscope and introduced difference into other matters, why did the thing that they had in common through the equality of the time of their conception remain in their illnesses?

Or, if the fates of health are determined at conception, while those of other matters are said to be determined at birth, they ought not to say anything about health after examining the constellations of births, since the hour of conception is not available for their examination. But if they predict illnesses without examining the horoscope of conception because the moments of birth indicate them, how could they tell either of the twins, from the hour of his birth, when he would fall ill, when the other, who did not have the same hour of birth, would necessarily have to fall ill at the same time?

Furthermore, I ask: if the interval of time at the birth of twins is so great that their constellations must thereby be different, because of a different horoscope, and for that reason all the other cardinal points are different [Note: [Col. 0145] Manilius discusses these astrological cardinal points in Book 2, verses 908 and following.], with such power assigned to them that their fates are consequently different, how could this happen when the time of their conception cannot be different?

Or, if twins conceived at one moment could have different fates for birth, why could not two people born at one moment have different fates for living and dying? For if the one moment in which both were conceived did not prevent one from being born earlier and the other later, why, if two people are born at one moment, should anything prevent one from dying earlier and the other later?

If conception at one moment allows twins to have different circumstances in the womb, why should birth at one moment not also allow any two people on earth to have different circumstances, so that all the inventions of this art—or rather of this vanity—may be abolished?

What does it mean that people conceived at one time and one moment, under one and the same position of the sky, have different fates leading them to be born at different hours, while two people born together at one moment, under one and the same position of the sky, from two mothers cannot have different fates leading them to different necessities of living or dying?

Or do those conceived not yet have fates that they will be unable to have unless they are born? What, then, is meant by their saying that, if the hour of conception could be discovered, these diviners could foretell many things [Note: [Col. 0145] The printed editions have *divinitus* (“by divine inspiration”). Some manuscripts have *divinius* (“more divinely”); others, and more plausibly, have *divinis*, that is, by mathematicians who profess the art of divination. —Our manuscripts have *divinius*.]? Hence some also proclaim that a certain wise man chose an hour at which to have intercourse with his wife, so that he might beget an extraordinary son.

Finally, this is also why Posidonius, a great astrologer and likewise a philosopher, replied concerning those twin brothers who were ill at the same time: it happened because they had been born at the same time and conceived at the same time. For he added conception precisely so that he could not be told that those who were certainly conceived at exactly the same time might not have been born at exactly the same time. His purpose was that the fact that they were ill similarly and simultaneously should not be explained simply by an equal bodily constitution, but that the same equality of health should also be bound by stellar connections.

If, then, conception has such power to produce equality of fate, their birth ought not to have altered the same fates. But if the fates of twins are altered because they are born at different times, why should we not rather understand that they had already been altered, so that they would be born at different times? Does the will of living people not alter the fates of birth, when the order of births alters the fates of conception?

## CHAPTER SIX—Twins of different sexes

Even in the conception of twins, where certainly the temporal moment of both is the same, how does it happen that under the same fatal constellation one is conceived male and the other female?

We know twins of different sexes, both of whom are still alive and both still vigorous in age. Their bodily appearance is similar to one another insofar as this is possible in different sexes, yet in the direction and purpose of their lives they are so unlike that, apart from the actions which necessarily differ between male and female, he serves in the office of a Count and is almost always away from his home, while she does not leave her ancestral land and her own countryside. Moreover—and this is more incredible if astral fates are believed, but not surprising if human wills and God’s gifts are considered—he is married, while she is a consecrated virgin; he has fathered a large family, while she has not married.

“But surely the power of the horoscope is very great!” I have already discussed sufficiently how little this amounts to. Whatever its power may be, they say that it is effective at birth. Is it effective also at conception, where it is clear that there was a single act of intercourse, and where nature has such power that, once a woman has conceived, she cannot conceive another child at all [Note: [Col. 0146] Aristotle, *History of Animals* 7.4, Pliny, *Natural History* 7.11, and Hippocrates in *On Superfetation* nevertheless teach that a woman can conceive again after one fetus has already been conceived, and that this has sometimes happened.]? Hence the moments of conception in twins must be the same.

Or was one of them changed into a male while being born, or the other into a female, because they were born under different horoscopes?

It could perhaps be said without complete absurdity that certain stellar influences affect only bodily differences, just as we see the seasons of the year vary with the sun’s approaches and withdrawals, and certain kinds of things increase and diminish with the moon’s waxing and waning, such as sea urchins, shellfish, and the extraordinary tides of the ocean. But the wills of the mind are not subjected to the positions of the stars.

Now, when these people also try to bind our actions to the stars, they compel us to ask how their theory can be consistent even in bodily matters. For what is so closely connected with the body as bodily sex? Yet twins of different sexes could be conceived under the same position of the stars.

What, then, could be said or believed more foolishly than that the position of the stars, which was the same for both at the hour of conception, could not bring it about that the one who shared the same constellation would not have a sex different from his brother, while the position of the stars at the hour of their birth could bring it about that he would differ so greatly from him in virginal holiness?

## CHAPTER SEVEN—The choice of the day on which a wife is taken, or on which something is planted or sown in a field

Who could tolerate the notion that, in choosing days, they devise new fates for their own actions? That man was apparently not born in such a way that he would have an extraordinary son, but rather in such a way that he would beget a contemptible one; and therefore a learned man chose the hour at which he would have intercourse with his wife. Thus he made a fate that had not existed, and from his own action [Note: [Col. 0147] The printed editions, contrary to the written books, have *fato* (“by fate”).] something began to be fated that had not been present at his birth.

O singular folly! A day is chosen for taking a wife. I suppose this is because one can enter upon an unsuitable day unless one is careful, and marry unhappily. Where, then, is the claim that the stars have already decreed his fate at birth? Can a human being alter by choosing a day what has already been determined for him, while what he himself determines by choosing a day cannot be altered by another power?

Furthermore, if only human beings, and not everything beneath the sky, are subject to constellations, why do they choose some days [Note: [Col. 0147] The manuscripts read: “Why do they choose days differently?”] suitable for planting vines, trees, or crops, and other days for breeding animals, whether taming them or admitting males to them, so that mares or cows may bear offspring, and for other things of this kind?

But if chosen days are effective for these matters because the position of the stars dominates all earthly bodies, whether living or nonliving [Note: [Col. 0147] The manuscripts do not have the words “whether nonliving.”], according to the differences of temporal moments, let them consider how innumerable things are born, arise, or begin under a single point of time, yet have such diverse outcomes that these observations should appear laughable to any child.

Who is so senseless as to dare say that all trees, all grasses, all beasts, snakes, birds, fish, and worms each have different moments of birth? Yet people commonly bring to the mathematicians, to test their expertise, the constellations of mute animals whose births they carefully observe at home for this investigation. They prefer those mathematicians to all the others who, after examining the constellations, say that what was born was not a human being but an animal.

They even dare to say what kind of animal it is—whether suitable for wool-production, transportation, the plow, or guarding the house. They also test the fates of dogs, and these predictions are given amid the loud cries of astonished admirers.

People become so foolish that they suppose that, when a human being is born, the births of all other things are so held back that not even a fly is born under the same region of the sky as that person. For once they admit this, the reasoning proceeds by gradual and moderate steps from flies to camels and elephants.

Nor do they wish to notice that, when a day has been chosen for sowing a field, so many seeds are placed in the earth at the same time, germinate at the same time, and, once the crop has emerged, grow green, ripen, and turn yellow together. Yet among them rust destroys some ears, birds ravage others, and human beings pluck still others.

What different constellations will they say these had, when they see them having such different outcomes? Or will they regret choosing days for these matters and deny that they belong to a heavenly decree, subjecting only human beings to the stars because God alone has given human beings free wills on earth?

When all these things are considered, it is not without reason believed that, when astrologers remarkably give many true answers, this happens through the hidden instigation of evil spirits. Their concern is to implant and strengthen in human minds these false and harmful opinions about astral fates [Col. 0148], not through any art of marking and examining the horoscope—which does not exist.

## CHAPTER EIGHT—Those who call the connection of causes dependent upon God’s will “fate,” rather than the position of the stars

Those who call “fate” not the configuration of the stars, such as it is when anything is conceived, born, or begun, but the connection and sequence of all causes by which everything that happens comes about, need not be troubled or contend with them very much over a dispute about the word. For they attribute the order of causes itself and a certain connection to the will and power of the supreme God, who is rightly and truly believed both to know everything before it happens and to leave nothing disordered. From him come all powers, although not all wills come from him.

That they call the will of the supreme God himself “fate”—the will whose power extends irresistibly through all things—is proved in this way. These verses belong, unless I am mistaken, to Annaeus Seneca:

> Lead me, supreme Father, ruler of the lofty sky;  
> Wherever you wish, there is no delay in obeying.  
> I am here, ready; make me unwilling, and I shall follow, groaning,  
> And, being bad, I shall endure doing what was permitted to the good.

> Fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling. [Note: [Col. 0148] *Epistle* 107, near the end.]

In the final verse he most clearly called “fates” what above he had called the will of the supreme Father. Seneca says that he is ready to obey it, so that he may be led willingly rather than dragged unwillingly; for, plainly:

> Fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.

The following Homeric verses also support this opinion. Cicero translated them into Latin:

> Such are the minds of human beings, such as the day [Note: [Col. 0148] The printed editions have *qualis* (“such as”). But manuscripts of good reputation have *quali*. Some have *quales* (“such”). In the second verse the Colbertinus manuscript has *astrifero* (“star-bearing”) where another reading has *auctiferas* (“productive”). Neither reading corresponds to the Greek as it now stands:
>
> **Toîos gar noos estin epichthoniôn anthrôpôn,**  
> **Oion ep’ êmar agêsi patêr andrôn te theôn te.**
>
> That is:
>
> “Such is the mind of earthly human beings,  
> As is the day brought forth by the father of human beings and gods.”] that Father Jupiter has illumined with his light over the fruitful lands. [Note: [Col. 0148] *Odyssey* 18.136–137.]

In this question the poetic statement would not itself have authority. But since he says that the Stoics, who assert the power of fate, customarily use these verses from Homer, the discussion concerns not the opinion of that poet but the opinion of those philosophers. For through the verses they bring into the argument concerning fate, they make it perfectly clear what they think fate is, since they call upon Jupiter, whom they regard as the supreme god, and say that the connection of fates depends upon him.

## CHAPTER NINE—God’s foreknowledge and human free will, against Cicero’s definition

### 1

Cicero tries to refute these people in such a way that he does not think he can accomplish anything against them unless he abolishes divination [Note: [Col. 0148] Book 2 of *On Divination*.]. He attempts to abolish it by denying that there is knowledge of future things, and he argues with all his strength that there is no such knowledge at all, either in God or in human beings [Note: [Col. 0149] All our manuscripts read: “either in human beings or in God.” —M.], and that there is no prediction of events.

Thus he denies God’s foreknowledge and tries, through empty arguments and by setting against it certain oracles that can easily be refuted, to overthrow every prophecy clearer than daylight. Yet he does not refute even those oracles themselves. In refuting the conjectures of the mathematicians, however, his argument is effective, because such conjectures really are of a kind that destroy and refute themselves.

Those who establish astral fates are much more tolerable than this man, who abolishes foreknowledge of the future. For it is manifest madness both to confess that God exists and to deny that he knows the future [Note: [Col. 0149] The manuscripts read *praescientiam* (“foreknowledge”). But codices 2050 and 2052 have *praescium* (“one who knows beforehand”).].

Cicero saw this himself and therefore also attempted to assert what is written: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1), though not in his own person. He saw how unpopular and offensive this would be. Accordingly, in the books *On the Nature of the Gods* (Book 3), he made Cotta argue this matter against the Stoics, while, on behalf of Lucilius Balbus, to whom he assigned the defense of the Stoic position, he preferred to render a judgment rather than speak on behalf of Cotta, who maintained that no divine nature exists.

But in the books *On Divination* he openly attacks foreknowledge of the future in his own person. He appears to do all this so that he may avoid admitting that fate exists and preserve free will. For he thinks that, once knowledge of future things is admitted, fate necessarily follows, so that it cannot be denied at all.

But however the tortuous disputes and arguments of philosophers may stand, just as we confess the supreme and true God, so we confess his supreme will, power, and foreknowledge. We do not fear that, because he foreknew that we would do what we do willingly, we therefore do not do it willingly—for his foreknowledge cannot be mistaken. This is what Cicero feared, and therefore he attacked foreknowledge; and what the Stoics feared, and therefore they said that not everything happens by necessity, although they maintained that everything happens by fate.

### 2

What, then, did Cicero fear in the foreknowledge of future things, so that he attempted to undermine it through a detestable argument? Clearly, if all future things are foreknown, they will come in the order in which they were foreknown to come. If they will come in that order, the order of events is certain to God, who foreknows them. If the order of events is certain, the order of causes is certain; for nothing can happen without some efficient cause preceding it. But if the order of causes by which everything that happens comes about is certain, he says, everything that happens happens by fate.

If this is so, nothing is in our power and there is no choice of the will. If we concede this, he says, all human life is overturned: laws are given in vain; rebukes, praise, blame, and exhortations are applied in vain; and no justice establishes rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked.

He therefore does not wish foreknowledge of future things to exist, lest these unworthy, absurd, and destructive consequences follow for human affairs. He constrains the religious mind into this dilemma: it must choose one of two things—either that something lies within our will, or that there is foreknowledge of future things. For he thinks that both cannot exist, but that if one is affirmed the other is removed: if we choose foreknowledge of future things, the freedom of the will is removed; if we choose freedom of the will, foreknowledge of future things is removed.

Thus, as a great and learned man who was exceptionally skilled in safeguarding human life, he chose free will from these two options. To establish it, he denied foreknowledge of future things; and so, while wishing to make human beings free, he made them sacrilegious.

The religious mind, however, chooses both and confesses both, confirming both through the faith of piety.

“How?” he asks. “For if there is foreknowledge of future things, all those consequences will follow that are connected with it, until one arrives at the conclusion that nothing lies within our will. But if something lies within our will, by retracing the same steps one arrives at the conclusion that there is no foreknowledge of future things.”

The entire chain is retraced in this way: If there is freedom of the will, not everything happens by fate. If not everything happens by fate, there is no certain order of causes for everything. If there is no certain order of causes, there is no certain order of events for God who foreknows them, since events cannot happen except through preceding and efficient causes. If the order of events is not certain to God who foreknows them, not everything happens as he foreknew it would happen. But if not everything happens as he foreknew it would happen, he says, then God does not have foreknowledge of all future things.

3. Against these sacrilegious and impious attempts, we affirm both that God knows all things before they happen and that we act by our will in everything which we perceive and know can be done by us only when we are willing. We do not, however, say that everything happens by fate; indeed, we say that nothing happens by fate, since we show that the term “fate,” wherever speakers customarily use it, means the configuration of the stars at the time when each person is conceived or born (for the thing itself is asserted without foundation). But we neither deny nor call “fate” the order of causes in which God’s will has the greatest power—unless, perhaps, we understand fate as derived from *fari*, “to speak,” that is, from speaking [Note: [Col. 0150] Nearly all ancient writers derive the word from *fari*, though in various ways. “What the Parcae establish by speaking,” says Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book 6, §52.]. For we cannot deny that it is written in the Holy Scriptures: “God has spoken once; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy, for you will repay each according to his works” (Psalm 61:12–13).

What is meant by “God has spoken once” is that he has spoken immutably—that is, unchangeably—just as he knows unchangeably all things that are to come and all things that he himself will do. On this account, we could call it “fate” from *fari*, unless this name were already customarily understood in another sense, toward which we do not wish people’s hearts to be inclined.

It does not follow that, if the order of all causes is certain to God, therefore nothing lies within the freedom of our will. For our wills themselves belong to the order of causes, which is certain to God and contained within his foreknowledge, since human wills too are causes of human actions. Thus he who foreknew all the causes of things could certainly not have been ignorant among those causes of our wills, which he foreknew as the causes of our actions.

4. What Cicero himself concedes [Note: [Col. 0151] Vind., Am., and Er.: “argues.”]—that nothing happens unless an efficient cause precedes it—also suffices to refute him in this question (*On Fate*, chapter 10 and following). For what assistance does it give him to say that, although nothing happens without a cause, not every cause is fatal, since there is a chance cause, a natural cause, and a voluntary cause? It is enough that he admits that everything which happens happens only when a cause has preceded it.

We say that those causes which are called chance causes—from which the name “fortune” is also derived—are not nonexistent, but hidden; and we attribute them either to the will of the true God or to that of whatever spirits may be involved. Nor do we in any way separate natural causes from the will of him who is the author and creator of all nature.

Voluntary causes, moreover, belong either to God, or to angels, or to human beings, or to any animals—if, indeed, those movements of animals without reason by which they do things according to their nature are to be called wills [Note: [Col. 0151] At this point the manuscripts read “souls.”]—when they either pursue or avoid something [Note: [Col. 0151] The Lov. edition alone has: “when they pursue or avoid something good or evil.”].

By “the wills of angels” I mean those of good angels, whom we call God’s angels, as well as those of evil angels, whom we call the devil’s angels or demons; and likewise the wills of good and evil human beings. Hence it follows that the efficient causes of everything that happens are voluntary causes alone, belonging, that is, to a nature which is the spirit of life.

This air or wind is also called “spirit”; but since it is a body, it is not the spirit of life. The spirit of life, therefore, which gives life to all things and is the creator both of every body and of every created spirit, is God himself—the uncreated spirit, certainly. In his will resides supreme power. He assists the good wills of created spirits, judges the evil ones, orders them all, and grants power to some while granting it to others not.

For just as he is the creator of all natures, so he is the giver of all powers, not of all wills. Evil wills do not come from him, since they are contrary to the nature which comes from him. Bodies, therefore, are more subject to wills: some to ours, that is, to those of all mortal animals, and more to human wills than to those of beasts; others to the wills of angels. Yet all bodies are subject above all to the will of God, and all wills are subject to him, because they have no power except what he grants.

God, therefore, is the cause of things who makes but is not made. Other causes both make and are made, as do all created spirits, especially rational ones. Bodily causes, however, which are more made than makers, should not be numbered among efficient causes, since they can do only what the wills of spirits accomplish through them.

How, then, does the order of causes—which is certain to God in his foreknowledge—make it so that nothing lies within our will, when our wills themselves have so important a place in that order of causes? Let Cicero argue with those who call this order of causes “fateful,” or rather who designate it by the name of fate, as the Stoics do (*On Fate*, chapters 11–12). We recoil from this, especially because of the term, which is not customarily understood as referring to the true reality.

But when he denies that the order of all causes is most certain and perfectly known to God’s foreknowledge, we detest him more than the Stoics. Either he denies that God exists—which he attempted to do by adopting another person’s role in his books *On the Nature of the Gods*—or, if he confesses that God exists while denying that God foreknows the future, he says nothing other than what that fool said in his heart: “There is no God” (Psalm 13:1). For he who does not foreknow all future things is certainly not God.

Therefore our wills have as much power as God willed and foreknew that they would have. Consequently, whatever power they possess, they possess with complete certainty; and whatever they are going to do, they themselves wholly do, because he whose foreknowledge cannot be deceived foreknew both their future power and their future actions.

Accordingly, if I wished to apply the term “fate” to anything, I would rather say that fate is the will of the weaker subject to the will of the stronger, who holds it in his power, than that our will is taken away by the order of causes which the Stoics, using the name of fate in an unusual but self-chosen manner, call fate.

## CHAPTER X  
### Whether any necessity rules over human wills

1. We need not fear that necessity which, in their fear of it, caused the Stoics to labor at distinguishing the causes of things, placing some beyond necessity and subjecting others to it. Among the things they did not wish to be under necessity, they placed our wills as well, lest our wills be unfree if subjected to necessity.

If our necessity is to be called that which is not in our power but accomplishes what it can even against our will, as the necessity of death does, it is clear that our wills—by which we live rightly or wrongly—are not under such necessity. For we do many things which we certainly would not do if we did not wish to do them. This applies first of all to willing itself: if we wish, it exists; if we do not wish, it does not exist. We would not will if we did not wish to will.

But if necessity is defined as that according to which we say that something must be so or must happen in a certain way, I do not see why we should fear that it takes away the freedom of our will. For we do not place God’s life or God’s foreknowledge under necessity when we say that God must always live and must foreknow all things, any more than his power is diminished when we say that he cannot die or be deceived. Indeed, he is incapable of these things in such a way that, if he could undergo them, he would necessarily possess less power.

He is rightly called omnipotent, although he cannot die or be deceived. He is called omnipotent because he does what he wills, not because he suffers what he does not will; if that happened to him, he would in no way be omnipotent. Thus certain things are impossible for him precisely because he is omnipotent.

Likewise, when we say that, whenever we will, we must will by free choice, we speak the truth without doubt; yet we do not thereby subject free choice to the necessity which removes freedom. Our wills therefore exist, and they themselves do whatever we do by willing—things that would not happen if we did not will them.

Whatever someone unwillingly suffers through the will of another human being nevertheless involves the power of a will: not the will of the person suffering, perhaps, but the power of God [Note: [Col. 0153] Lov. has “the power of God is.” The other books lack the word “is.”]. For if there were only a will without the power to accomplish what it willed, it would be impeded by a more powerful will. Even then it would still be a will, and it would belong not to another but to the one who willed, even if he could not accomplish what he willed.

Therefore, whatever a human being suffers against his will, he ought not to attribute to human wills, angelic wills, or the wills of any created spirit, but rather to him who grants power to those who will.

2. It is not therefore the case that nothing lies within our will because God foreknew what would lie within our will. For he who foreknew this did not foreknow nothing. Moreover, if he who foreknew what would lie within our will foreknew not nothing but something, then surely, even with him foreknowing it, something lies within our will.

We are consequently compelled in no way either to abolish free choice while retaining God’s foreknowledge or, while retaining free choice, to deny that God foreknows the future—which would be impious. We embrace both; we confess both faithfully and truthfully: the one so that we may believe rightly, the other so that we may live rightly. We live badly if we do not believe rightly about God.

Far be it from us, therefore, to deny his foreknowledge in order that we may wish to be free [Note: [Col. 0153] Nearly all the manuscripts have “so that we may will freely.”], since by his help we are—or will be—free.

Accordingly, laws, reprimands, exhortations, praise, and blame are not without purpose. For he foreknew that these too would occur, and they have as much power as he foreknew they would have. Prayers also have power to obtain those things which he foreknew he would grant to those who pray. Rewards for good deeds and punishments for sins have therefore been established justly.

A human being does not sin because God foreknew that he would sin [Note: [Col. 0153] Several manuscripts of good authority, including the Faurentian and Corbeiensian: “For a human being does not fail to sin because God foreknew that he would sin.” The Gervasianus has: “Nor does a human being sin.”]. Rather, it is beyond doubt that he himself sins when he sins, because he whose foreknowledge cannot be deceived foreknew that he would sin—not fate, not fortune, nor anything else. If he does not wish to sin, he certainly does not sin; but if he does not wish to sin, God also foreknew this.

## CHAPTER XI  
### On God’s universal providence, whose laws encompass all things

The supreme and true God, therefore, with his Word and Holy Spirit—these three being one, the one omnipotent God—the creator and maker of every soul and every body; the one by participation in whom all who are happy in truth, not in vanity, are happy; who made the human being a rational animal consisting of soul and body; who, when the human being sinned, neither permitted him to remain unpunished nor abandoned him without mercy; who gave to good and evil alike existence along with stones, seminal life along with trees, sensory life along with animals, and intellectual life along with the angels alone;

from whom come every measure, every form, and every order; from whom come measure, number, and weight; from whom comes whatever naturally exists, whatever its kind and whatever its worth; from whom come the seeds of forms, the forms of seeds, and the movements of seeds and forms;

who gave the flesh its origin, beauty, health, fertility for propagation, arrangement of its members, and the health that comes from their harmony; who gave irrational souls memory, sensation, and appetite, and to rational souls, in addition, mind, understanding, and will;

who has left neither heaven and earth alone, nor angel and human being alone, nor even the organs of a small and contemptible living creature, nor a bird’s tiny feather [Note: [Col. 0154] Our manuscripts have “little feather.” M.], nor a small flower of the grass, nor a leaf of a tree without the harmony of their parts and a kind of peace among them—

this God cannot in any way be believed to have wished the kingdoms of human beings, their dominions and their servitudes, to be outside the laws of his providence.

## CHAPTER XII  
### By what conduct the ancient Romans deserved that the true God, although they did not worship him, should increase their empire

1. Let us therefore examine what Roman conduct, and for what reason, the true God—who holds even earthly kingdoms in his power—deigned to assist in increasing their empire.

To make our discussion of this subject more complete, we wrote the preceding book relevant to it, showing that the gods whom they thought should be worshiped even in trivial matters had no power in this affair. We also discussed, in the earlier parts of the present volume up to this point, the removal of the question of fate, lest anyone who had already been persuaded that the Roman empire had not been extended and preserved by the worship of those gods should attribute it instead to some kind of fate rather than to the supremely powerful will of the highest God.

The ancient and earliest Romans, as far as their history teaches and commends them, although—like other nations, with the single exception of the Hebrew people—they worshiped false gods and sacrificed not to God but to demons, were nevertheless eager for praise, generous with money, and desirous of immense glory and honorable riches (Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 7). They loved glory with the greatest ardor; for its sake they wished to live and did not hesitate to die [Note: [Col. 0154] Several manuscripts have “they wished to conquer.” In B.: “and did not hesitate to die for it” [Col. 0155]. The same is found in manuscripts 2051 and 2053; but manuscript 2052 has: “for its sake they wished to live, and for its sake they did not hesitate to die.” Manuscript 2050 has: “for its sake they wished to live, for its sake they wished to conquer, for its sake they did not hesitate to die.” We have followed the reading of manuscript 766. M.].

They suppressed their other desires beneath this one immense desire. Finally, because serving their own country seemed inglorious while ruling and commanding seemed glorious, they first desired it to be free with all their energy, and then to be mistress.

Hence, unable to endure royal domination, they established annual offices and two magistrates, who were called consuls—from *consulere*, “to deliberate” or “to take counsel”—rather than kings or lords, from ruling and dominating. Indeed, kings seem more properly to have been named from *regere*, “to rule,” just as a kingdom comes from kings and kings, as has been said, from ruling. But royal arrogance was not regarded as the discipline of one who rules or the benevolence of one who gives counsel; it was regarded as the pride of one who dominates.

After King Tarquin was expelled and consuls established, what followed was what the same author included among the praises of the Romans: “After the state had won its freedom, it is incredible to relate how quickly it grew; so great a desire for glory had seized it” [Col. 0155] (Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 7). This eagerness for praise and desire for glory therefore accomplished many remarkable things—laudable and glorious, that is, in human estimation.

2. Sallust also praises the great and distinguished men of his own time, Marcus Cato and Gaius Caesar. He says that for a long time the republic had possessed no one great in virtue, but that in his own memory those two men had possessed immense virtue, though of different character.

Among Caesar’s praises he placed the fact that he desired for himself a great command, an army, and a new war in which his valor might shine forth (*ibid.*, chapters 53–54). Thus it was [Note: [Col. 0155] The editions read *fidebat*. The manuscripts’ authority corrects this to *fiebat*.] part of the wishes of men great in valor to stir unfortunate nations to war and drive Bellona with her bloody scourge, so that there might be a place where their valor could shine. This was surely produced by that eagerness for praise and desire for glory.

Thus, first from love of freedom, then from desire for domination, and from their longing for praise and glory, they accomplished many great things. Their distinguished poet also bears witness to both motives. For he says:

> Nor did Porsenna command that the expelled Tarquin  
> Be received, and he pressed the city with a mighty siege:  
> The sons of Aeneas rushed into battle for freedom.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.646–648)

At that time, therefore, it was a great thing for them either to die bravely or to live free. But once freedom had been won, such a desire for glory had seized them that freedom alone seemed insufficient unless domination too were sought, while it was regarded as a great thing that—as though Jupiter himself were speaking—the same poet says:

> Indeed harsh Juno,  
> Who now troubles sea, earth, and heaven with fear,  
> Will turn her plans toward better things, and cherish with me  
> The Romans, lords of the world, the toga-clad nation.  
> So it has been decreed. An age will come, as the passing  
> Of the years proceeds, when the house of Assaracus will crush  
> Phthia and splendid Mycenae beneath servitude,  
> And will dominate conquered Argos.  
> (*Aeneid* 1.279–285)

Virgil, of course, while introducing Jupiter as if he were predicting the future, was himself recalling events already accomplished and observing the present. I have mentioned these verses in order to show that the Romans valued domination after freedom in such a way that it was counted among their great praises.

The same poet also says that, when he preferred to the arts of other peoples those very arts peculiar to the Romans—the arts of ruling, commanding, subduing, and defeating peoples:

> Others will forge bronze breathing with greater delicacy;  
> I believe they will draw living faces from marble;  
> They will plead cases better and trace the movements  
> Of the heavens with the rod, and tell of the rising stars.  
> But you, Roman, remember to rule peoples with authority.  
> These will be your arts: to impose the custom of peace,  
> To spare the subjected, and to crush the proud.  
> (*Aeneid* 6.847–853)

3. They practiced these arts with greater skill because they gave themselves less to pleasures, to the weakening of mind and body through the pursuit and accumulation of wealth, and to corrupting morals through those riches—by plundering unfortunate citizens and lavishing gifts on disgraceful performers.

When such moral stains [Note: [Col. 0156] Some manuscripts read *labe*: through the common scribal error of omitting a final letter when it is the same as the first letter of the following word, where it sounded more distinctly when pronounced by the reader. A little earlier one should perhaps read *quia tales*; or, at any rate, here “moral stains” are themselves called vicious persons, as Plautus in *Persa*, act 3, scene 3, verse 4, calls a man “the stain of the people,” and Cicero, *Oration for Sestius*, chapter 8, says, “I have something to set against that stain and filth.” Our manuscripts read *labe*. Morel reads thus, *Elementa Critica*, p. 289: “Such moral stains everywhere already prevailed and abounded when Sallust wrote these things and Virgil sang them.” M.] already prevailed and abounded, at the time when Sallust wrote these things and Virgil sang them, men did not seek offices and glory through those arts but through deceit and fraud. Hence Sallust also says:

> At first ambition exercised men’s minds more than avarice, although this vice was nevertheless closer to virtue. For the good and the coward alike desire glory, honor, and power for themselves; but the former, he says, strives by the true path, while the latter, because he lacks good arts, contends by deceit and fraud.  
> (Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 11)

These are the “good arts”: to reach honor, glory, and power through virtue, not through deceitful ambition. Yet both the good and the coward desire them equally; but the former—that is, the good man—strives by the true path. Virtue is the path by which he strives as toward the goal of possession, namely, glory, honor, and power.

That the Romans had this disposition is also indicated by the temples of their gods, which they established very close together: the temples of Virtue and Honor [Note: [Col. 0156] Livy, book 27, chapter 25.]. They treated as gods things that are given by God.

From this it can be understood what end good men wished virtue to have and toward what they directed it: toward honor, certainly. For evil men did not possess virtue, although they desired honor and attempted to obtain it by evil arts—that is, by deceit and fraud.

4. Cato was praised more appropriately. Of him Sallust says: “The less he sought glory, the more it followed him” [Note: [Col. 0156] In Sallust: “the more he attained it.”] (*ibid.*, chapter 54).

For glory—the object of their burning desire—is the judgment of people who think well of others. Virtue is therefore better when it is not content with human testimony but only with the testimony of its own conscience. Hence the Apostle says: “For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). And elsewhere: “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another” (Galatians 6:4).

Glory, honor, and power, which good men desired for themselves and toward which they strove to advance by good arts, ought not to be pursued by virtue; rather, they themselves ought to follow virtue. For virtue is not true virtue unless it tends toward that end where the good of the human being is found, beyond which there is no better good.

Therefore even the honors sought by Cato ought not to have been sought by him; rather, the state ought to have bestowed them on him because of his virtue, although he did not seek them [Note: [Col. 0156] See Plutarch, *Life of Cato the Younger*.].

5. But although Caesar and Cato were two Romans distinguished for virtue in that period, Cato’s virtue appears to have been much closer to truth than Caesar’s. Let us therefore examine what the state was like at that time, and what it had been like earlier, in Cato’s own speech:

> Do not suppose, he says, that our ancestors made the republic great from small beginnings by arms. If that were so, we would have a far more splendid state. We have a greater supply than they had of allies and citizens, as well as of arms and horses. But other things made them great, things which we do not possess: at home, industry; abroad, just command; a mind free in deliberation, subject neither to crime nor to lust.
>
> In place of these we have luxury and avarice; public poverty and private wealth. We praise riches and pursue idleness. There is no distinction between the good and the wicked; ambition possesses all the rewards of virtue.
>
> Nor is this surprising. When each of you separately makes plans for himself, when at home you serve pleasures and here you serve money or favor, the result is an attack upon an empty republic.  
> (Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 52)

6. Whoever hears these words of Cato—or of Sallust—may think that all, or most, of the ancient Romans praised in this way were then such men. That is not so. Otherwise the statements Sallust himself also writes would not be true—those which I recalled in the second book of this work (chapter 18), where he says that from the beginning there had been at home injuries inflicted by the powerful, and, because of them, secessions of the plebs from the patricians and other dissensions; that fair and moderate law had not been observed for any longer after the kings had been expelled than as long as fear of Tarquin remained, until the serious war undertaken against Etruria because of him had come to an end.

Afterward, he says, the patricians exercised a servile domination over the plebs, scourged them in the manner of kings, drove them from their fields, and, while excluding everyone else, alone exercised power. The end of these disputes—while some wished to dominate and others refused to serve—was the Second Punic War [Note: [Col. 0157] Manuscripts 766, 2050, 2052, and 2053 have: “the end was in the Second Punic War.” M.].

For once again, a grave fear began to press upon them, and a greater concern restrained their restless spirits from those disturbances and recalled them to civil concord.

Yet through certain few men who were good in proportion to their own capacity, great affairs were administered; and while those evils were endured and moderated, the foresight of a few good men caused the state to grow. The same historian says that, although he had read and heard many accounts of the remarkable deeds the Roman people had performed at home and in war, on sea and on land, he was pleased to consider what had chiefly sustained such great undertakings.

He knew that the Romans had often engaged the enemy’s great legions with a small force, and that wars had been waged with small armies against wealthy kings. After much reflection, he said that it was clear to him that the outstanding virtue of a few citizens had accomplished everything, and that this was why poverty had overcome riches and the few had overcome the many.

“But after the state was corrupted by luxury and idleness,” he says, “the republic once again sustained the vices of its commanders and magistrates through its own greatness.”

The virtue of the few, then—those who strove toward glory, honor, and power by the true path, that is, by virtue itself—was praised even by Cato. From this came the “industry at home” which Cato mentioned, so that the treasury would be wealthy while private resources remained modest. In contrast, when morals were corrupted, he placed the opposite vice: public poverty and private wealth.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On the love of praise, which, although it is a vice, is considered virtue because it restrains greater vices

Since the kingdoms of the East had long been illustrious [Note: [Col. 0158] Namely, those of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, and others, discussed above, book 4, chapter 7.], God therefore willed that a western kingdom should also arise—later in time, but more illustrious in the breadth and greatness of its empire.

He granted this chiefly to such men as were able to subdue the serious evils of many nations: men who, for the sake of honor, praise, and glory, served their country, in which they sought glory itself, and did not hesitate to place its safety before their own. Because of this single vice—that is, the love of praise—they suppressed their desire for money and many other vices.

For the person who recognizes that the love of praise is also a vice sees more soundly. This did not escape the poet Horace, who says:

> You swell with love of praise; there are certain expiations  
> Which, after thrice reading the book, can restore you.  
> (*Epistles* 1.1.36–37)

In a lyric poem, likewise, to restrain the lust for domination, he sang:

> You will rule more broadly by subduing the greedy spirit  
> Than if you joined Libya to distant Gades  
> And both Carthaginians served a single master.  
> (*Odes* 2.2.9–12)

Nevertheless, those who do not restrain their baser desires through the faith of piety, having received the Holy Spirit, and through love of intelligible beauty are at least better—though not yet holy, still less disgraceful—when restrained by the desire for human praise and glory.

Even Tullius could not conceal this [Note: [Col. 0158] Vind., Am., and Er.: “Even Tullius could not remain silent about this.” Not badly.], in the same books which he wrote *On the Republic*, where he speaks of training the leader of the state, whom he says must be nourished by glory. He then recalls that his ancestors accomplished many remarkable and distinguished deeds from desire for glory.

They therefore not only failed to resist this vice; they even thought it should be aroused and inflamed, believing that it was useful to the republic. Yet Tullius does not conceal this plague even in his philosophical books, where he confesses it as clearly as daylight. When speaking of studies which ought certainly to be pursued for the sake of the true good, not for the display of human praise, he introduced this universal and general judgment:

> Honor nourishes all the arts, and all are inflamed toward the pursuit of glory; but those things which are disapproved by everyone always lie neglected.  
> (*Tusculan Disputations* 1.2)

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On cutting away the love of human praise, since all the glory of the righteous is in God

This desire is therefore resisted better, without doubt, than it is yielded to. For the more completely a person is cleansed of this impurity, the more like God he is. In this life, although it is not eradicated completely from the heart—for it does not cease to tempt even minds that are making good progress—at least the desire for glory should be overcome by love of justice [Note: [Col. 0159] Some manuscripts have “should be overcome by delight in justice.”].

If anything lies neglected because it is disapproved by some or all people, then, provided it is good and right, even the love of human praise itself should blush and yield to the love of truth.

This vice is so hostile to faithful piety—if the desire for glory occupies a greater place in the heart than fear or love of God—that the Lord said: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (John 5:44).

Again, concerning certain people who had believed in him but were afraid to confess him openly, the Evangelist says: “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John 12:43).

The holy Apostles did not act in this way. When they preached the name of Christ in places where it was not merely disapproved—as the poet says, “those things which are disapproved by everyone always lie neglected”—but held in the greatest detestation, they held fast to what they had heard from the good Teacher, who was also the physician of souls:

> “Whoever denies me before human beings, I will deny before my Father who is in heaven and before the angels of God.”  
> (Matthew 10:33; Luke 12:9)

Amid curses and insults, amid the gravest persecutions and cruel punishments, they were not deterred from preaching human salvation by the great uproar of human hostility.

And when they performed and proclaimed divine things and lived divinely, and when immense glory followed in the Church of Christ as hard hearts were, so to speak, conquered and the peace of justice introduced, they did not rest in that glory as though it were the end of their virtue. Rather, they referred that glory too to the glory of God, by whose grace they were what they were. Through this very incentive they kindled in those for whom they cared a love of the one by whose power those people too would become such as the Apostles were.

For, lest they should be good on account of human glory, their Teacher had instructed them, saying:

> “Beware of practicing your righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”  
> (Matthew 6:1)

But again, lest they misunderstand this perversely and fear to please human beings, thereby doing less good by concealing their goodness, he showed the purpose for which their goodness should become known:

> “Let your works shine before human beings, so that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”  
> (Matthew 5:16)

It is not, therefore, so that you may be seen by them—that is, with the intention of turning them toward yourselves, since you are nothing through yourselves—but so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven, and, having been turned toward him, become what you are [Note: [Col. 0159] The editions have “this.” The manuscripts have “these,” that is, the Apostles, about whom he spoke earlier.].

The martyrs followed these Apostles. They surpassed Scaevolas, Curtii, and Decii—not by inflicting punishments upon themselves, but by enduring punishments inflicted upon them; not through a merely apparent virtue, but through true virtue, because through true piety; and they surpassed them also in their countless multitude.

But those earlier men belonged to an earthly state, whose citizens were assigned as the end of all their duties the state’s safety and a kingdom not in heaven but on earth—not eternal life, but the departure of the dying and succession by those who would die. What else could they love except glory, by which they wished, even after death, to live as though in the mouths of those who praised them?

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the temporal reward which God granted to the good conduct of the Romans

Since, therefore, God was not going to give these people eternal life with his holy angels in his heavenly city—to whose fellowship true piety leads, true piety which renders the service of religion, called *latreia* (λατρεία) by the Greeks, to the one true God alone—if he had not granted them even this earthly glory of an outstanding empire, their good practices, that is, their virtues, by which they strove to attain such glory, would have received no reward.

For concerning people who appear to do some good for the sake of being glorified by others, the Lord also says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2).

Thus these Romans despised their private possessions for the sake of the common good, that is, the republic and its treasury; resisted avarice; served their country with free deliberation; and were subject neither to crime according to their laws nor to lust. By all these practices they strove, as by a true path, toward honors, power, and glory.

They were honored among almost all nations; they imposed the laws of their empire on many peoples; and today they are glorious in nearly every nation through literature and history.

They have no reason to complain about the justice of the supreme and true God: they have received their reward.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the reward of the holy citizens of the eternal city, for whom the examples of Roman virtues are useful

The reward of the saints is altogether different, even here, where they endure reproaches for the city of God, which is hated by those who love this world [Note: [Col. 0160] The manuscripts, with broad agreement, have “for the truth.”].

That city is eternal. No one is born there, because no one dies there. There is true and complete happiness—not a goddess, but God’s gift. From there we have received the pledge of faith, while, as pilgrims, we sigh for its beauty.

There the sun does not rise upon the good and the evil (Matthew 5:45); rather, the sun of justice protects the good alone. There there will be no great industry devoted to enriching the public treasury through narrow private resources, because the common treasure is truth.

The Roman empire was therefore extended for the sake of human glory not only so that such a reward might be granted to such men, but also so that the citizens of that eternal city, for as long as they are pilgrims here (2 Corinthians 5:6), might look carefully and soberly upon those examples and see how great a love is owed to their heavenly homeland because of eternal life, if its citizens loved an earthly homeland so greatly for the sake of human glory.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### What benefit the Romans derived from waging wars, and how much they contributed to those whom they conquered
1. For as far as this mortal life is concerned—which is lived and brought to an end within a few days—what difference does it make under whose rule a person destined to die lives, provided that those who rule do not compel him to impious and unjust deeds? Or did the Romans really harm the nations whom they subjugated and imposed their laws upon, except insofar as this was accomplished through the immense slaughter of wars? If it had been done peacefully, the same result would have been achieved with better success; but there would have been no glory for the triumphant. For the Romans themselves also lived under the laws that they imposed upon others. If this had been done without Mars and Bellona [Note: [Col. 0161] Thus more correctly in Lov. and the manuscripts. But Vind., Am., and Er.: “This would have sufficed for the state, except that it displeased Mars and Bellona.”], so that victory too would have had no place—since no one could conquer where no one had fought—would not the Romans and the other nations have had one and the same condition? Especially if what was afterward done with the greatest good will and humanity had immediately been done: that all who belonged to the Roman Empire should receive a share in citizenship and become Roman citizens. Thus what had previously belonged to a few would belong to all; except that the populace, which did not possess its own fields, lived from the public treasury. Its sustenance would have been supplied more graciously by harmonious citizens through good administrators of the state than extracted from the defeated.

2. [Note: [Col. 0161] Here chapter 17 begins in the manuscripts.] For as regards safety and good morals, I entirely fail to see what difference it makes whether some conquered and others were conquered, even as regards the very dignities of human beings [Note: [Col. 0161] The printed editions have “and the very dignities.” The word “and,” absent from the manuscripts, should be deleted, so that the meaning is: “that good morals are the very dignities of human beings.”], apart from that utterly empty arrogance of human glory in which those who burned with an immense desire for it and waged burning wars received their reward. Do their fields not pay taxes? Are they permitted to learn what others are not? Are there not many senators in other lands who do not even know Rome by sight [Note: [Col. 0161] After citizenship was granted to many nations, several from them were also enrolled in the Senate, and there were senators who had never come to Rome, just like other citizens who had never seen Rome. Ludovicus Vives.]? Remove boastfulness, and what are all human beings except human beings? Even if the perversity of the age allowed those who were better to be more honored, even then human honor ought not to be considered a great thing, since smoke has no weight.

Yet let us also make use in these matters of the benefit of the Lord our God. Let us consider how much those who deserved to receive human glory as the reward of such virtues despised, endured, and subdued in their desires for its sake. Let this also help us to crush pride, so that, when the city in which we have been promised that we shall reign is as far removed from this one as heaven is from earth, eternal life from temporal joy, substantial glory from empty praises, the fellowship of angels from the fellowship of mortals, and its light from the light of the sun and moon—the light of the One who made the sun and moon—then the citizens of so great a homeland may not think that they have done anything great if, in order to attain it, they have performed some good work or endured some evil, when those men did so much and endured so much for the sake of this earthly city, which they had already obtained.

This is especially so because the remission of sins, which gathers citizens into the eternal homeland, has something resembling, in a certain shadowy way, that Romulean asylum by which the impunity of every kind of offense gathered together the multitude from which that city was to be founded.

# CHAPTER XVIII

## How Christians ought to be free from boasting if they have done anything for love of the eternal homeland, since the Romans did so much for human glory and an earthly city

[Col. 0162]

1. What great thing, then, is it to despise all the pleasant allurements of this age for the sake of that eternal and heavenly homeland, when Brutus was able even to kill his sons for the sake of this temporal and earthly one [Note: [Col. 0162] Livy, book 2, chapter 5]—something that the other homeland compels no one to do? Yet it is certainly more difficult to kill one’s sons than to do what must be done for this homeland: either to give the poor what seemed destined to be gathered and preserved for one’s children, or, if a trial arises that compels one to do this for faith and justice, to lose it.
