For neither earthly riches—whether they must be lost while we live or possessed after our death by people whom we do not know, or perhaps by people whom we do not wish to possess them—make us or our children happy. God makes people happy; he is the true wealth of minds. But even the poet who praises Brutus bears witness to his unhappiness because he killed his sons. For he says:

> And the father will summon his sons, stirring up new wars,  
> To punishment, for beautiful freedom—  
> Unhappy, however posterity may judge those deeds.

But in the following verse he consoled the unhappy man:

> The love of country conquers, and the immense desire for praise.  
> (*Aeneid*, book 6, lines 820–823.)

These are those two things—freedom and the desire for human praise—that compelled the Romans to remarkable deeds [Note: [Col. 0162] All Gallican manuscripts have *compulit* (“compelled” singular).]. If, then, for the freedom of mortals and the desire for praises sought from mortals, sons could be killed by their father, what great thing is it if, for the true freedom that liberates us from the dominion of iniquity, death, and the devil—not through a desire for human praise but through love of those being liberated—not from King Tarquin but from demons and the prince of demons—sons are not killed, but Christ’s poor are counted among the sons?

2. If another Roman commander, also called Torquatus, killed his son—not because he had fought against his homeland, but even while fighting for his homeland, yet because he had fought against his father’s authority, that is, against what his father, the commander, had ordered—after the enemy had provoked him and youthful ardor had driven him into battle, although he had won, lest the example of disregarded command contain more evil than the glory of a slain enemy contained good [Note: [Col. 0162] Compare above, book 1, chapter 23], why should those boast who, for the laws of the immortal homeland, despise earthly goods, which are loved far less than sons?

If Furius Camillus liberated from the Gauls even his ungrateful homeland, from whose neck he had removed the yoke of the fiercest enemies, the Veientes, and had been condemned by rivals, because he had no preferable place in which he could live in glory [Note: [Col. 0162] The Lov. edition alone has “more gloriously.”] [Note: [Col. 0162] See above, book 2, chapter 17, and book 4, chapter 7], why should a person be exalted as though he had done something great if, after suffering at the hands of carnal enemies in the Church the gravest insult of disgrace, he did not transfer himself to its heretical enemies [Col. 0163] or himself establish some heresy against it, but instead defended it as far as he could from the most destructive perversity of the heretics [Note: [Col. 0163] Some manuscripts have *vanitate* (“vanity”) instead. Manuscripts 766 and 2053 have *pravitate* (“perversity”). M.], since there is no other place—not one in which a person lives in human glory, but one in which eternal life is acquired?

If Mucius [Note: [Col. 0163] Mucius, who was called Scaevola after the destruction of his right hand. Livy, book 2, chapters 12–13, and Plutarch, *Life of Publicola*.], in order to secure peace with King Porsenna, who was pressing the Romans with a very serious war, because he could not kill Porsenna himself mistakenly killed another man in his place, extended his right hand into a blazing altar before Porsenna’s eyes and declared that many men like the one he saw had conspired for Porsenna’s destruction—and Porsenna, terrified by the courage of the man and by the conspiracy of such men, immediately restrained himself from that war by making peace [Note: [Col. 0163] The manuscripts have “without hesitation” instead of “without any delay.”]—who will reckon his merits as a claim upon the kingdom of heaven if, for it, he has expended not one hand, and has done this not voluntarily, but while suffering persecution, by giving his whole body to the flames?

If Curtius, mounted and armed, plunged himself at full speed into the gaping chasm in the earth, obeying the oracle of his gods because they had ordered that what the Romans possessed as the best thing should be sent there—and they could understand nothing else by this than that they excelled in men and arms, so that, evidently, at the command of the gods, an armed man had to hurl himself into that death [Note: [Col. 0163] Curtius. See Livy, book 7, chapter 6; Valerius Maximus, 4.5, chapter 5]—what will someone say that he has done greatly for the eternal homeland if, having suffered an enemy to his faith, he has died not by voluntarily sending himself into such a death, but by being sent there by that enemy, when he has received from his Lord and likewise the King of his homeland the more certain oracle: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28)?

If the Decii devoted themselves, consecrating themselves, as it were, to be killed in explicit terms, so that when they fell and appeased the anger of the gods with their blood the Roman army might be delivered [Note: [Col. 0163] Livy, books 8 and 10], the holy martyrs should in no way be proud as though they had done something worthy for participation in that homeland [Note: [Col. 0163] The Gervasian manuscript has “for the attainment of that homeland.”] where there is eternal and true happiness, if, even to the shedding of their blood, they contended through the faith of charity and the charity of faith, loving not only their brothers for whom their blood was shed [Note: [Col. 0163] “For whom it was shed”: not indeed for their redemption, as Christ’s blood was shed, but as an example of courage. “From the courage of the faithful,” says Leo, *epistle* formerly 83, now 97, “examples of endurance are born, not gifts of righteousness.” Leonard Coquaeus], but also the very enemies by whom it was shed, as they had been commanded?

If Marcus Pulvillus, while dedicating the temple of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, was falsely told by envious men that his son had died, so that, disturbed by the report, he would withdraw and his colleague would thereby obtain the glory of the dedication, and he despised the report to such an extent that he even ordered the body to be cast out unburied [Note: [Col. 0163] Plutarch says this; Livy, however, writes that he ordered the corpse to be carried away], and thus in his heart the desire for glory had conquered the grief of bereavement, what will someone say that he has done greatly for the preaching of the holy Gospel, through which citizens of the heavenly homeland are delivered and gathered from various errors, when the Lord said to one who was concerned about burying his father, “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22)?

If Marcus Regulus, lest he deceive his most cruel enemies by breaking his oath, returned to them from Rome itself, because, as he is said to have replied to the Romans who wished to retain him, after he had served the Africans he could no longer possess there the dignity of an honorable citizen—and the Carthaginians, because he had acted against them in the Roman Senate, killed him with the most grievous tortures [Note: [Col. 0164] Above, book 1, chapters 15 and 24]—are those tortures not to be despised for the faith of that homeland to whose blessedness faith itself leads? Or what shall be rendered to the Lord for all that he has rendered (Psalm 115:12), if for the faith owed to him a person has suffered things such as Regulus suffered for the faith that he owed to his most destructive enemies?

How, then, will a Christian dare to boast of voluntary poverty, so that he may walk more freely through the pilgrimage of this life along the road that leads to the homeland where God himself is true wealth, when he hears or reads that Lucius Valerius, who died during his consulship, was so poor that his burial had to be arranged with money contributed by the people [Note: [Col. 0164] There is an error both in the praenomen and in the year of his death. He was said to have been not Lucius but Publius Valerius Publicola; and he did not die during his fourth consulship, but in the following year, when Verginius and Cassius were consuls, the sixth year after the expulsion of the kings. Livy, book 2, chapter 16; Dionysius, book 5]?

Let him hear or read that Quintius Cincinnatus, possessing only four *iugera* and cultivating them with his own hands, was taken from the plow [Note: [Col. 0164] In B., “brought” instead. M.] to become dictator, an office certainly more honorable than the consulship; and after conquering his enemies and attaining immense glory, he remained in the same poverty [Note: [Col. 0164] Livy, book 3, chapter 26; Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 4, section 7].

Or what great thing will he proclaim that he has done because no reward of this world has seduced him from fellowship with that eternal homeland, when he has learned that Fabricius could not be separated from Roman citizenship by the many gifts promised by Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, including even a fourth part of the kingdom, and preferred to remain there as a private citizen in his poverty?

For although they possessed a commonwealth—that is, the people’s property, the homeland’s property, the common property—so opulent and rich, they themselves were so poor in their homes that one of them, who had already been consul twice, was expelled from that Senate of poor men by a censor’s mark because he was found to possess ten pounds of silver vessels [Note: [Col. 0164] He means Cornelius Rufinus, concerning whom see Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 9; Aulus Gellius, book 4, chapter 8; Livy, book 14]. Thus these very poor men, whose triumphs enriched the public treasury, lived in poverty. Do not all Christians who, following the more excellent calling, make their riches common, according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles—that distribution should be made to each according to each person’s need, and that no one should say that anything is his own, but that everything should be common to them (Acts 2:45; 4:32)—understand that they ought not to be puffed up with boasting for doing this to obtain fellowship with the angels, when those men did nearly the same thing to preserve the glory of the Romans?

[Col. 0165]

3. If these and other examples of this kind are found in their literature, when would they have become known, when would they have been proclaimed with such fame, unless the Roman Empire had been enlarged far and wide by magnificent successes? Accordingly, through that empire, so extensive and so long-lasting, and renowned and glorious through the virtues of so many men, both the reward that those men sought was given to their intention and examples of necessary admonition were placed before us.

Thus, if we do not possess, for the most glorious city of God, virtues of which those virtues are in some fashion likenesses—the virtues that they maintained for the glory of an earthly city—we should be stung by shame; and if we do possess them, we should not be lifted up by pride. For, as the Apostle says, “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

But their way of life was considered sufficiently worthy of human glory and present time. Therefore even the Jews who killed Christ, as the New Testament revealed what had been veiled in the Old, were most appropriately granted the glory of these men. For the purpose was that the one true God should be worshiped not for earthly and temporal benefits—which divine providence grants indiscriminately to the good and the wicked—but for eternal life, everlasting gifts, and fellowship with the heavenly city; and that those who sought and obtained earthly glory through whatever virtues might conquer those who, through great vices, killed and rejected the giver of true glory and the eternal city.

# CHAPTER XIX

## How the desire for glory differs from the desire for domination

There is indeed a difference between the desire for human glory and the desire for domination. For although it is easy for one who takes excessive delight in human glory also ardently to desire to rule, nevertheless those who desire the glory of human praise—provided that it is genuine—take care not to displease those who judge well.

There are many good qualities in character about which many people judge well, even though many do not possess them. Through these moral qualities people strive toward glory and power, or domination. Of such a person Sallust says, “But he strives along the true path.” Yet whoever desires to dominate and rule without the desire for glory—that desire by which a person fears displeasing those who judge well—usually seeks to obtain what he loves even through the most flagrant crimes.

Accordingly, one who desires glory either strives along the true path or, at any rate, contends through tricks and deceptions, wishing to appear good when he is not [Note: [Col. 0165] The printed editions have “to appear what he is not,” omitting *esse* (“to be”), which the manuscripts contain] (Sallust, *Catiline*).

Therefore, for a person who possesses virtues, it is a great virtue to despise glory, because its contempt is visible before God but cannot be disclosed to human judgment. Whatever someone does before human eyes in order to appear a despiser of glory, if it is believed that he does it for greater praise—that is, for greater glory—there is no way for him to show the suspicious minds of others that he is otherwise than they suspect.

But one who despises the judgments of those who praise him also despises the rashness of those who suspect him. Nevertheless, if he is truly good, he does not despise their salvation, since a person who possesses virtues from the Spirit of God has such great righteousness that he even loves his enemies, and loves them in such a way that he wishes his haters or slanderers [Note: [Col. 0166] Thus Vind., Am., Er., and most manuscripts. Lov. has “his whisperers” instead] to become corrected companions—not in an earthly homeland but in the heavenly one.

As for his praisers, although he considers of little account the fact that they praise him, he does not consider of little account what they love. He does not wish to deceive those who praise him, lest he deceive those who love him. Therefore he earnestly strives that the One from whom a person has whatever in him is rightly praised should rather be praised.

But whoever despises glory and craves domination surpasses beasts either in the vices of cruelty or in those of lust. There were some Romans of this kind, for they did not lack the desire for domination even after losing concern for their reputation. History records that many such men existed; but Nero Caesar first attained the summit and, as it were, the citadel of this vice. His lust was so great that, unless one knew it, nothing manly was thought to be feared from him; his cruelty was so great that, unless one knew it, he would not be believed to possess anything gentle.

Yet even such men receive the power to rule only through the supreme providence of God, when he judges human affairs worthy of such rulers. The divine voice speaks openly about this through the wisdom of God: “By me kings reign, and tyrants hold the earth through me” (Proverbs 8:15). But lest tyrants be thought not to be the worst and most wicked kings, but instead to be called “strong” according to the old usage, as Virgil says,

> It will be part of my peace to have touched the hand of the tyrant,

(*Aeneid*, book 7, line 266), it is stated most explicitly elsewhere concerning God: “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the perversity of the people” (Job 34:30).

Accordingly, although I have explained as well as I could why the one true and just God, according to a certain pattern of an earthly city, helped the Romans, who were good in that respect, to attain the glory of so great an empire, there may nevertheless be another, more hidden reason, arising from the different merits of the human race, known more fully to God than to us.

This, however, must be clear to all who are truly devout: no one can possess true virtue without true piety—that is, without the true worship of the true God [Note: [Col. 0166] See below, book 19, chapter 25]; nor is virtue true when it serves human glory.

Nevertheless, those who are not citizens of the eternal city, which in our sacred Scriptures is called the city of God (Psalm 45:5; 47:3, 9, and elsewhere), are more useful to an earthly city when they possess even that kind of virtue than if they possess none at all.

But when people endowed with true piety live well and possess the knowledge required to govern peoples, nothing is more advantageous to human affairs than for them, by God’s mercy, to possess power. Such people attribute whatever virtues they can possess in this life to nothing but God’s grace, because he has given them to those who desire, believe, and ask for them. At the same time, they understand how far they fall short of the perfection of righteousness that exists in the fellowship of those holy angels, to which they strive to conform themselves.

However highly the virtue that, without true piety, serves human glory may be praised and proclaimed, it must in no way be compared with the small beginnings of the saints, whose hope is placed in the grace and mercy of the true God.

# CHAPTER XX

## Human virtues serve human glory as shamefully as they serve bodily pleasure

[Col. 0167]

Philosophers who place the end of human good in virtue itself commonly paint a picture in words to bring shame upon certain philosophers who approve virtues but measure them by the end of bodily pleasure, and who think pleasure desirable for its own sake and virtues for the sake of pleasure. In this picture, pleasure sits on a royal throne like a delicate queen, while the virtues are placed beneath her as servants, attending to her nod and doing what she commands.

She commands prudence to investigate vigilantly how pleasure may reign and remain secure. She commands justice to provide whatever benefits it can in order to acquire friendships necessary for bodily advantages, and to injure no one, lest pleasure be unable to live securely because of offenses against the laws. She commands courage, if pain comes to the body but does not compel it to die, to hold its mistress—that is, pleasure—firmly in the mind, so that by recalling former delights it may soften the stings of present pain. She commands temperance to take only as much food as is sufficient, and, if anything is enjoyable, not to allow some harmful excess to disturb health and seriously offend pleasure—which the Epicureans also place chiefly in bodily health.

Thus the virtues, with all the dignity of their glory [Note: [Col. 0167] Some manuscripts of good authority have “with all the glory of their dignity.” Manuscript 766 has the same reading. Manuscript 2053 has “with all the glory of dignity.” M.], serve pleasure as though she were a certain imperious and dishonorable little woman. They say that nothing is more disgraceful and deformed than this picture, and that nothing is less tolerable to the eyes of good people. They speak truly.

But I do not think that a picture has been given sufficient proper dignity if one is also imagined in which human virtues serve human glory. Glory may not be a delicate woman, but it is inflated and possesses much emptiness. Therefore the solidity and firmness of virtues do not properly serve it, so that prudence provides nothing, justice distributes nothing, courage tolerates nothing, and temperance moderates nothing except what pleases human beings and serves vaporous glory.

Nor will those defend themselves from this disgrace who, while despising the judgments of others as though they were despisers of glory, seem wise to themselves and please themselves. For their virtue, if indeed they possess any, is in another way subjected to human praise; the person who pleases himself is nevertheless a human being.

But one who, through true piety toward God—whom he loves, believes in, and hopes in—pays more attention to the things in which he displeases himself than to whatever things in him may please not so much himself as the truth, attributes nothing by which he can now please to anyone but God’s mercy, fearing to displease him. For the things that have been healed he gives thanks, and for those that still need healing he pours out prayers.

# CHAPTER XXI

## The Roman kingdom was ordained by the true God, from whom all power comes and by whose providence all things are governed

Since these things are so, let us attribute the power to grant kingdoms and empires to no one but the true God, who gives the kingdom of heaven to the devout alone, but gives an earthly kingdom to both the devout and the impious, as it pleases him, who is pleased by nothing unjust.

Although we have said something that he wished to be clear to us, it is nevertheless a great and exceedingly difficult task for us to investigate the hidden matters of human beings and to judge the merits of kingdoms with transparent discernment.

That one true God, who neither abandons the human race in judgment nor in help, gave the Romans a kingdom when he wished and to the extent that he wished. He is the one who gave a kingdom to the Assyrians, and also to the Persians, whose writings maintain that only two gods were worshiped by them, one good and the other evil—not to mention the Hebrew people, about whom I have already said as much as seemed sufficient, who worshiped no god except the one God, even when they ruled.

The same God who gave the Persians crops without the worship of the goddess Segetia, and other gifts of the earth without the worship of all the many gods whom they assigned individually to individual things, or even several to individual things, also gave them a kingdom without the worship of those gods through whose worship they believed they had ruled.

So also among individuals: the one who gave power to Marius gave it to Gaius Caesar; the one who gave it to Augustus gave it also to Nero [Note: [Col. 0168] He pairs two men, one good and one bad: the cruel Marius with the most merciful Gaius Caesar, and the excellent emperor Augustus with the worst, Nero]; the one who gave it to the Vespasians, father and son, most agreeable emperors, gave it also to the most cruel Domitian. And, not to proceed through them one by one, the one who gave it to the Christian Constantine gave it also to the apostate Julian.

Julian’s excellent natural character was deceived by a sacrilegious and detestable curiosity arising from the love of ruling. He was devoted to empty oracles. Trusting in the security of victory, he burned the ships that carried necessary provisions. Then, pressing forward rashly with immoderate daring, he was soon killed as his rashness deserved, and left his army impoverished in hostile territory, so that it could escape from there only if, contrary to the omen of the god Terminus mentioned in the preceding book (chapter 29), the boundaries of the Roman Empire were moved. For the god Terminus yielded to necessity, though he had not yielded to Jupiter.

Certainly the one true God rules and governs these things as he pleases. And if he does so for hidden reasons, are they for that reason unjust?

# CHAPTER XXII

## The duration and outcomes of wars depend upon God’s judgment

So too the very duration of wars depends upon his will and just judgment and mercy, by which he either wears down or consoles the human race, bringing some wars to an end more quickly and others more slowly.

The war against the pirates was completed by Pompey [Note: [Col. 0168] It ended on the fortieth day after Pompey departed from Brundisium. Florus, book 3; Cicero, *For the Manilian Law*]; the Third Punic War was completed by Scipio with incredible speed and brevity of time [Note: [Col. 0168] Livy says that it was entirely finished within the fifth year after it began, book 49. Florus, book 2, says it was completed in four years]. The war of the fugitive gladiators, although many Roman commanders and two consuls were defeated and Italy was horribly battered and devastated, was nevertheless brought to an end in the third year, after much destruction had been suffered [Note: [Col. 0168] Thus Vind., Am., and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. have “was completed.”].

The Picentes, Marsi, and Paeligni—peoples not foreign but Italian—after enduring for a long time a devoted servitude beneath the Roman yoke, attempted to raise their heads into freedom, when many nations had already been subjugated to the Roman Empire and Carthage had been destroyed [Note: [Col. 0168] Compare Livy, books 72–76 and 95–96]. In this Italian war, although the Romans were very often defeated, two consuls and other highly distinguished senators perished, the calamity was nevertheless not prolonged for a very long time [Col. 0169], for its fifth year brought it to an end.

But the Second Punic War weakened and nearly exhausted Roman strength through eighteen years of the greatest losses and calamity to the state [Note: [Col. 0169] Livy, book 30, supports this, as does Florus, book 2. Polybius, book 3, and Orosius, book 4, chapter 20, however, assign only seventeen years to this war]. In two battles [Note: [Col. 0169] One was the battle at Lake Trasimene, the other the battle at Cannae. Livy, book 22; Florus, book 2], nearly seventy thousand Romans fell.

The First Punic War lasted twenty-three years [Note: [Col. 0169] Orosius agrees with Augustine. Polybius, book 1, says that it lasted twenty-four years, because he apparently counts the years from the occasion for beginning the war, whereas the others count from its commencement]. The Mithridatic War lasted forty years [Note: [Col. 0169] Florus, book 3, chapter 5].

And lest anyone suppose that the Romans’ beginnings were stronger for bringing wars to an end more quickly in earlier times—times greatly praised for every virtue—the Samnite War lasted nearly fifty years [Note: [Col. 0169] Eutropius and Orosius count forty-nine years in this war. Florus counts fifty; there are no more if it is ended with the consul Fabius Gurges. Appian, however, counts eighty, and the Samnites themselves say in Livy, book 23, that they waged war against the Roman people for nearly one hundred years]. In that war the Romans were defeated so thoroughly that they were even sent under the yoke.

But because they did not love glory for the sake of justice, but appeared to love justice for the sake of glory, they broke the peace and treaty that had been made [Note: [Col. 0169] See Livy, book 9].

I recall these things because many people ignorant of past events—and some who conceal their knowledge—if they see a war during Christian times dragged out somewhat longer, immediately attack our religion with arrogant insolence, exclaiming that, if it did not exist and the gods were worshiped according to the ancient rite, then by that Roman valor which, with Mars and Bellona helping, brought such great wars rapidly to an end, this war too would be concluded with the greatest speed.

Let those who have read remember how long the wars were, with what varied outcomes [Note: [Col. 0169] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have “with varied results”], and with what mournful disasters the ancient Romans waged them, just as the circle of the earth is accustomed to be tossed about like a stormiest sea by the changing tempest of such evils. And let them, however unwillingly, sometimes admit the truth, rather than destroy themselves with insane tongues directed against God and deceive the ignorant.

# CHAPTER XXIII

## The war in which Rhadagaisus, king of the Goths and a worshiper of demons, was defeated with his enormous forces in a single day

Yet what God did in our own memory, in very recent times, with wonderful mercy, they do not recall with thanksgiving. As far as they can, they try to bury it in the oblivion of all human beings, if that is possible. If we remain silent about it, we too shall be ungrateful.

When Rhadagaisus, king of the Goths, already stationed with a huge and monstrous host in the vicinity of the City, threatened the Roman necks, his army was defeated in a single day with such speed that not a single Roman was, I will not say killed, but even wounded [Note: [Col. 0169] Er. and Lov. have “but not even wounded.” The particle “not” is absent from the other books. It is also absent from our manuscripts. M.]—while far more than one hundred thousand of his army were struck down. He himself, together with his sons [Note: [Col. 0169] Many manuscripts of good authority, both Roman and Gallican, do not have “together with his sons.” Nor do our manuscripts. M.], was soon captured and put to death with the punishment he deserved [Col. 0170] [Note: [Col. 0170] Paulus Aemilius, book 1 of the *History of the Franks*, Orosius, book 7, chapter 37, and others report that there were more than two hundred thousand Goths. This defeat of Rhadagaisus occurred under Honorius, in the year of Christ 406. See Augustine, *Sermon* 105, chapter 10].

For if that impious man, with such great and so impious forces, had entered Rome, whom would he have spared? To what places of the martyrs would he have shown honor? In whose person would he have feared God? Whose blood would he not have shed, whose chastity would he have left untouched?

What cries would these people have raised in honor of their gods, and with what insults would they have boasted that he had won and had been able to accomplish so much because he appeased and invited the gods through daily sacrifices—something that the Christian religion did not permit the Romans to do?

When he was already approaching those places where, by the command of supreme Majesty, he was crushed, and his fame was spreading everywhere, we were told at Carthage that the pagans were believing, spreading, and loudly proclaiming that, because he was protected and assisted by friendly gods to whom he was said to sacrifice almost daily, he could not possibly be defeated by those who performed no such sacrifices to the Roman gods and did not allow anyone else to perform them.

Yet these wretched people do not give thanks for God’s great mercy. When he had determined to chastise human morals, which deserved to suffer even worse things through a barbarian invasion [Note: [Col. 0170] Thus several manuscripts. Some others have “morals deserving worse things,” omitting “to suffer.” The printed editions have “morals deserving something worse”], he tempered his indignation with such gentleness that he first caused that man to be defeated miraculously, lest glory be given to the demons whom he was known to supplicate, to overthrow the minds of the weak. Then [Note: [Col. 0170] The printed editions have “then together with.” The word “together” is absent from the manuscripts] Rome was captured by those barbarians who, contrary to the entire custom of earlier wars, protected those who fled to holy places through reverence for the Christian religion, and who opposed the demons themselves and the rites of the impious sacrifices on which Rhadagaisus had relied in the Christian name, so that they seemed to wage a far more savage war against those rites than against human beings [Note: [Col. 0170] The manuscripts omit “in the Christian name.” All our manuscripts omit it as well. M.].

Thus the true Lord and governor of events both chastised the Romans with mercy and, by the astonishing defeat of those who supplicated demons, showed that those sacrifices were not necessary for the preservation of present circumstances. The result was that those who do not contend stubbornly but attend wisely may understand both that true religion should not be abandoned for present necessities and that it should be held more firmly through the faithful expectation of eternal life.

# CHAPTER XXIV

## What the happiness of Christian emperors is, and how true it is
Nor do we call certain Christian emperors happy merely because they ruled for a longer time, or because, after dying peacefully, they left behind sons who were reigning, or because they subdued the enemies of the state, or because they were able both to guard against and to suppress hostile citizens rising up against them. Some worshipers even of demons, who do not belong to the kingdom of God—to which these men do belong—have been deemed worthy to receive these and other gifts or consolations of this troubled life. This too was done by God’s mercy, lest those who believed in him should desire such things from him as though they were the highest goods. But we call them happy if they rule justly; if, amid the tongues of those who honor them in exalted language and the excessively humble attentions of those who salute them, they are not puffed up, but remember that they are human beings; if they make their power serve his majesty, so as above all to extend the worship of God; if they fear, love, and worship God; if they love more that kingdom in which they do not fear having partners; if they are slow to punish and quick to forgive; if they exercise punishment only as necessity requires for governing and defending the state, and not to satisfy the hatred of enmity; if they grant pardon not to give iniquity impunity, but in hope of correction; if they compensate for what they are often compelled to decree harshly by the gentleness of mercy and the generosity of benefactions; if their luxury is restrained in proportion to the freedom they might have enjoyed; if they prefer to rule their own depraved desires rather than any peoples; and if they do all these things not for the ardor of empty glory, but for love of eternal blessedness; if they do not neglect to offer to their true God, for their sins, the sacrifice of humility, compassion, and prayer. We say that Christian emperors of this kind are happy in hope for the present, and will afterward be happy in reality, when what we await has come.

## CHAPTER XXV.—The Prosperities Which God Granted to the Christian Emperor Constantine

For the good God, lest people who believed that he should be worshiped for the sake of eternal life should think that no one could attain these high positions and earthly kingdoms unless he supplicated demons—for these spirits were thought to have great power in such matters—filled the emperor Constantine, who did not supplicate demons but worshiped the one true God, with such earthly gifts as no one would dare to hope for. He even granted him permission to found a city as a partner of the Roman Empire, as it were a daughter of Rome herself, but without any temple or image of demons.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Constantinople.]

He ruled for a long time.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Orosius, book 7, chapter 26, reports that he ruled for thirty-one years.]

A single Augustus held and defended the entire Roman world; in conducting and waging wars he was most victorious; in crushing tyrants he prospered in every way.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Clearly Maxentius and Licinius.]

He died in advanced old age, from illness and age; he left behind sons who were emperors.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Constantius, Constantine, and Constans.]

But again, lest anyone should become a Christian emperor merely to attain Constantine’s happiness—for each person ought to be a Christian for the sake of eternal life—God removed Jovian much sooner than Julian.

[Note: [Col. 0171] A smaller number of manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read *Jovinianum*. So too all our editions. M.]

He permitted Gratian to be killed by a tyrant’s sword.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Namely, slain by Andragathius, prefect of the tyrant Maximus.]

Yet he permitted it much more gently than he had permitted Magnus Pompey, who worshiped, as it were, the Roman gods.

[Note: [Col. 0171] The printed editions read “namely”; all the manuscripts read “as it were.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171] As Florus writes, book 4, chapter 3: “Slaughtered on the shore of Pelusium, under the authority of a most contemptible king—that is, the ward Ptolemy—and at the counsels of eunuchs, and, so that no evil might be lacking, by the sword of his deserter Septimius, he died before the eyes of his wife and children.” See Livy, book 112.]

For Pompey could not be avenged by Cato, whom he had left, in a manner of speaking, as heir to the civil war; but Gratian, although pious souls have no need of such consolations, was avenged by Theodosius,

[Col. 0172] who captured and killed Maximus while he was at Aquileia,

whom he had made a partner in the empire, although he had a young brother.

[Note: [Col. 0172] Namely, the younger Valentinian, son of the elder Valentinian and Justina.]

He was more eager for faithful fellowship

[Note: [Col. 0172] The printed editions read: “although he had also a brother, more eager for the faith of fellowship.” But the particle “also” is absent from the better manuscripts; on their authority we emend the text to *fide*.]

than for excessive power.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—The Faith and Piety of Augustus Theodosius

### 1

Accordingly, while Gratian was still alive, Theodosius not only preserved the faith he owed him, but even after his death, when Valentinian had been driven out by his murderer Maximus, received the young Valentinian, Gratian’s brother, as a Christian ward into his share of the empire; he guarded him with paternal affection. Although he could easily have taken him away, since the boy had been stripped of every resource, if he had burned more with desire to enlarge his rule than with love of doing good, he instead consoled him through his very humanity and favor, receiving him while preserving his imperial dignity.

Then, when Maximus’ success made him formidable, Theodosius, amid the anxieties of his own cares, did not turn to sacrilegious and unlawful forms of divination. Instead, he sent to John, who lived in the Egyptian desert and whom he had learned, through an increasingly widespread report, to be a servant of God endowed with the spirit of prophecy; from him he received a most certain message of victory.

Soon, after destroying the tyrant Maximus, he restored the boy Valentinian, with the most compassionate reverence, to the portion of the empire from which he had been expelled. When Valentinian was shortly afterward killed, whether by treachery or by some other means or accident, Theodosius, after again receiving a prophetic response and confident through faith, crushed the other tyrant, Eugenius, who had been illegitimately substituted in that emperor’s place. Against his exceedingly powerful army he fought more by prayer than by striking blows.

The soldiers who were present told us that whatever they hurled was torn from their hands, since a violent wind was blowing from Theodosius’ forces against the enemy; it not only carried away with the greatest speed whatever was thrown against them, but also turned their own weapons back against their bodies. Hence the poet Claudian, although alien to the name of Christ, nevertheless said in his praise:

> O one excessively beloved by God, for whom Aeolus pours forth from his caves  
> armed winters; for whom the ether serves as a soldier,  
> and the winds, having sworn their compact, come to the trumpet-call!

[Note: [Col. 0172] Our manuscripts omit: “for whom Aeolus pours forth from his caves armed winters.” M.]

(*In the Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius*, verses 96–98.)

As victor, just as he had believed and foretold, he removed the images of Jupiter, which had been, I know not by what rites, supposedly consecrated and set up in the Alps against him. Because they were made of gold, he cheerfully and graciously gave them to the soldiers who joked about them—which that joy permitted—and said that they wished to be struck by those thunderbolts.

He wished the sons of his enemies, whom the violence of war—not his own command—had carried off,

[Note: [Col. 0172] Most manuscripts read: “whom not by his command”; and some continue, “but the violence of war had carried off,” omitting “but.” Perhaps the reading should be: “whom not he, but the violence of war, had carried off.” Manuscripts 766, 2052, and 2053 read: “whom, not by his command, the violence of war had carried off.” M.]

to become Christians on this occasion, although they were not yet Christians, when they fled to the church; and he loved them with Christian charity. He did not deprive them of their possessions, and increased their honors.

[Col. 0173]

[Note: [Col. 0173] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “but.”] After the victory he allowed no private enmity against his enemies to prevail.

He did not, like Cinna, Marius, Sulla, and others of their kind, wish to bring civil wars to an end once they had already ended; rather, he grieved more that they had arisen than he wished to harm anyone by bringing them to an end.

Amid all these actions, from the very beginning of his reign he did not cease to aid the Church, which was suffering, by the most just and merciful laws against the impious. The heretic Valens, favoring the Arians, had grievously afflicted it; and Theodosius rejoiced more in being a member of that Church than in ruling on earth.

He ordered the images of the Gentiles to be overthrown everywhere, understanding clearly that even earthly gifts lie not in the power of demons but in the power of the true God.

What was more remarkable than his religious humility, when he was compelled to avenge the most serious crime of the Thessalonians, for which he had already promised pardon after bishops had interceded for them, because of the disturbance caused by certain persons who were attached to him? Restrained by ecclesiastical discipline, he performed such penance that, while the people prayed for the emperor, they became more moved by seeing his imperial height prostrate than fearful, because of his sin, of seeing him angry.

These and any similar good works, which it would take too long to recount, he carried with him from this temporal vapor of every human height and eminence. The reward of those works is eternal happiness, whose giver is God to the truly pious alone.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Some manuscripts read “alone,” rather than “to the truly pious.”]

The other heights or supports of this life—like the world itself, light, breezes, lands, waters, fruits, and the human soul, body, senses, mind, and life—he distributes to the good and the wicked alike. Among these is every magnitude of imperial power, which he dispenses according to the governance of the times.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Here, in the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain, this was made chapter twenty-seven, and the following title was added: “Augustine’s invective against the envious, who wrote against the already published books.” But this was attempted without manuscript authority and against the older Vindelinian edition.]

### 2

[XXVII.] I see that I must now also answer those who, having been refuted and convicted by the clearest evidence—which shows that the multitude of false gods contributes nothing to those temporal goods that fools alone desire to possess—try to assert that the gods should be worshiped not for the usefulness of the present life, but for the sake of the life that is to come after death.

To those who wish to worship empty things for the sake of friendship with this world and complain that they are not permitted to indulge their childish sentiments, I think that these five books have provided an adequate answer. After I had published the first three and they had begun to circulate in many hands, I heard that certain people were preparing to write some sort of reply against them. Later I was informed that they had already written it but were looking for a time when they could publish it without danger.

I warn them not to desire what is not good for them. It is easy for anyone who does not wish to remain silent to appear to have answered. For what is more talkative than vanity? Yet vanity cannot thereby do what truth can, merely because, if it wishes, it can shout more loudly than truth.

Let them consider everything carefully. If, perhaps, judging without partisan zeal, they should perceive that their arguments are such as can be shaken rather than overturned by the most shameless loquacity and by a kind of satirical or theatrical frivolity, let them restrain their trifles; and let them choose rather to be corrected by the prudent than praised by the imprudent.

For if they are awaiting an opportunity not for the freedom to speak the truth, but for the license to abuse, may what Tully said of a certain man—who was called happy because he had license to sin—not happen to them:

> O wretched man, to whom it was permitted to sin!

[Note: [Col. 0174] Something similar is said of Cinna in *Tusculan Disputations*, book 5, chapter 19.]

Whoever, therefore, thinks himself happy because he has license to abuse will be much happier if this is entirely forbidden him. Once he has laid aside the emptiness of boastfulness, he can still, at this time, contradict whatever he wishes under the appearance of a desire to offer advice; and, as far as they are able,

[Note: [Col. 0174] The printed editions read *possit*, “may be able.” The manuscripts more correctly read *possunt*, “are able”: understand those who are consulted in friendly debate.]

he can hear honorably, seriously, and freely what he ought to hear from those whom he consults in friendly discussion.

# BOOK SIX

Thus far against those who think that the gods should be worshiped for the sake of this temporal life. Now, however, against those who believe that worship should be offered to them for the sake of eternal life. In the five books that follow, Augustine will refute them, first showing how contemptible a view of the gods Varro himself held, although he was the most highly esteemed writer on pagan theology. According to Varro, he presents three kinds of theology: fabulous, natural, and civil. He then demonstrates that neither the fabulous nor the civil kind contributes anything to the blessedness of the life to come.

[Col. 0173]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0173]

In the five preceding books I seem to have argued sufficiently against those who think that the many false gods—whom Christian truth proves to be useless images, or unclean spirits and harmful demons, or at any rate creatures rather than the Creator—should be venerated and worshiped, for the usefulness of this mortal life and earthly affairs, with that rite and servitude called in Greek *λατρεία* (*latreia*), which is owed to the one true God.

Who does not know that for excessive folly or obstinacy neither these five books nor any other books, however numerous, can be sufficient, since it is regarded as the glory of vanity to yield to no force of truth—to the destruction, naturally, of the person whom so monstrous a vice dominates? Even against all the diligence of a physician, an incurable disease is unconquered, not because of any fault in the physician, but because of the sick person.

Those, however, who weigh and consider what they read, whether without any persistence in their ancient error or without a great and excessive persistence in it, will more readily judge that, in bringing this number of five volumes to completion, we have satisfied the need of the question with more discussion than it demanded rather than with less. They will be unable to doubt that all the resentment which the ignorant try to direct against the Christian religion because of the disasters of this life and the destruction and alteration of earthly affairs—while even learned men, possessed by mad impiety, not only conceal these facts but favor them against their own conscience—is altogether empty of sound thought and reason, and full of the lightest rashness and the most destructive hostility.

## CHAPTER I.—Those Who Say That the Gods Are Worshiped by Them Not for the Present Life but for the Eternal Life

### 1

Now, therefore, since from this point onward the promised order requires that those who contend that the gods of the Gentiles—whom the Christian religion destroys—should be worshiped not for this life but for the life that is to come after death should also be refuted and instructed, I am pleased to take the beginning of my argument from the truthful oracle of the holy Psalm:

> Blessed is the one whose Lord is God, whose hope he is, and who has not turned to vanities and lying madnesses.  
> (Psalm 39:5)

Nevertheless, among all vanities and lying madnesses, philosophers deserve to be heard with far greater tolerance. They disliked those opinions and errors of the peoples who established images for their deities and either invented or believed invented many false and unworthy things about those whom they call immortal gods, mixing what they believed with their worship and sacred rites.

With these people—who, even if they did not openly proclaim such views, at least gave some testimony of disapproval by muttering in their discussions—the question may be treated without excessive impropriety: whether, for the sake of the life that is to come after death, one ought to worship not many gods, whom certain philosophers, superior and more distinguished than the rest, believed to have been made by the one God and placed in exalted positions, but the one God who made every spiritual and bodily creature.

[Note: [Col. 0175] Plato, in the *Timaeus*.]

### 2

But who could tolerate the claim that those gods, some of whom I mentioned in the fourth book,

[Note: [Col. 0175] Chapters 11 and 21.]

and to whom separate offices are assigned for separate minor matters, can provide anyone with eternal life?

Or will those very learned and sharp-minded men, who boast that they have taught, as a great benefit, why one ought to supplicate each god and what should be requested from each—lest, with the most shameful absurdity, like that which commonly occurs humorously in a farce, someone should ask Liber for water and the Nymphs for wine—

[Note: [Col. 0175] The printed editions read *Nymphis*, “the Nymphs”; the manuscripts consistently read *Lymphis*. The Latin letter was formerly altered from the Greek name *Numphe*, by which the ancients called waters or goddesses of the waters.]

be able to recommend to someone supplicating the immortal gods that, when he has asked the Nymphs for wine and they have replied, “We have water; ask Liber for that,” he should properly say, “If you do not have wine, at least give me eternal life”?

What could be more monstrous than this absurdity?

[Note: [Col. 0175] Vindelinus, Amerbach, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read *monstruosius*, “more monstrous.”]

Will those goddesses, laughing—for they are usually quick to laugh—

[Note: [Col. 0175] He alludes to Virgil, *Eclogue* 3, verse 9: “But the Nymphs, readily disposed, laughed.” In that passage, however, *faciles* means ready not to laugh but to grant a hearing.]

if they do not seek to deceive like demons, not answer the petitioner:

> “Human being, do you think that we have life in our power, when you hear that we do not even possess a vine?”

It is therefore the height of shameless folly to ask or hope for eternal life from such gods, who are said to guard the individual parts of this most troubled and short life, and whatever pertains to supporting and sustaining it, in such a way that, if what lies under the protection and power of one is requested from another, the request is so inappropriate and absurd that it seems almost identical with theatrical buffoonery.

When this is done by actors who know what they are doing, they are rightly laughed at in the theater; when it is done by ignorant fools, they are more deservedly mocked in the world.

As to which god or goddess one should supplicate, and for what purpose, the matter has been skillfully discovered and committed to memory by learned men, so far as the gods established by the cities are concerned: what should be requested from Liber, for example; what from the Nymphs; what from Vulcan; and so forth from the others, some of whom I mentioned in the fourth book, while I thought others should be passed over.

Furthermore, if it is an error to ask Ceres for wine, Liber for bread, Vulcan for water, and the Nymphs for fire, how much greater madness must it be understood to be if anyone supplicates any of these for eternal life?

### 3

Therefore, when we were investigating the earthly kingdom and asking which gods or goddesses should be believed capable of granting it to human beings, after everything had been examined it was shown to be far removed from the truth to suppose that even earthly kingdoms could be bestowed by any of these many false deities. Is it not then the most insane impiety to believe that eternal life—which must unquestionably and incomparably be preferred to all earthly kingdoms—can be given to anyone by any one of them?

For such gods did not appear unable to give even an earthly kingdom because they were great and exalted while the kingdom was something small and lowly, unworthy of their concern amid such eminence. However lightly anyone may despise the fleeting heights of an earthly kingdom in view of human frailty, those gods appeared to be such that they seemed utterly unworthy of being entrusted with even these things, whether to give them or to preserve them.

And so, if—as the discussions of the preceding two books have shown—no god from that multitude, whether it consists as it were of plebeian or of aristocratic gods, is fit to give mortal kingdoms to mortals, how much less can any of them make mortals immortal?

### 4

This is further confirmed by the fact that, since we are now dealing with those who think that the gods should be worshiped not for this life but for the life that is to come after death, they should not be worshiped at all even for those things that are attributed to the power of such gods as though divided among them and belonging to each individually—not by the judgment of truth, but by the opinion of vanity—as those maintain who insist that their worship is necessary for the advantages of this mortal life. Against them I have already argued sufficiently, as far as I was able, in the five preceding volumes.

If matters stood as follows: if the very age of those who worshiped the goddess Juventas flourished more splendidly, while her despisers either died during their youthful years or grew cold in youth as though seized by old age; if bearded Fortuna clothed the cheeks of her worshipers more attractively and cheerfully, while we saw those who despised her remain beardless or badly bearded—even then we should most correctly say that these individual goddesses have power only up to this point, being somehow limited by their particular functions.

[Col. 0177]

[Note: [Col. 0177] The printed editions read: “have power to be limited in some way by their functions.” The manuscripts’ reading, *limitatas*, “limited,” should be retained; and the word *posse*, “to have power,” should be understood there in the sense of “to possess force.”]

Consequently, eternal life should not be requested from Juventas, who does not give a beard; nor should anything good after this life be hoped for from bearded Fortuna, whose power in this life is so negligible that she cannot even grant the same age at which a beard appears.

But in fact, since the worship of these goddesses is not necessary even for the very things believed to be subject to their power—for many who worshiped the goddess Juventas did not flourish in that age at all, while many who did not worship her rejoice in the strength of youth; likewise, many who supplicated bearded Fortuna were unable to reach any beard, or even a deformed one, and those who worship her to obtain a beard are mocked by her bearded despisers—is the human heart so foolish that it recognizes the worship of these gods as empty and ridiculous with respect to the temporal and quickly passing gifts over which each is said to preside, yet believes their worship fruitful for eternal life?

Not even those who assigned these temporal functions to them, so that foolish peoples might worship them—for they thought there were too many gods for any one of them to sit idle—dared to say that these gods could give eternal life.

## CHAPTER II.—What We Should Believe Varro Thought about the Gods of the Gentiles, Whose Kinds and Sacred Rites He Exposed as Such That He Would Have Treated Them More Reverently If He Had Kept Entirely Silent about Them

Who investigated these matters more inquisitively than Marcus Varro? Who discovered them more learnedly? Who considered them more attentively? Who distinguished them more sharply? Who wrote about them more diligently and fully?

[Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscripts 2050, 2051, and 2052 read “more plainly and fully.”]

Although he is less pleasing in eloquence, he is so full of learning and judgment that, in every branch of knowledge which we call secular and he calls liberal, this one man teaches the student of facts as much as Cicero delights the student of words.

Indeed, Tully himself gives him such a testimonial that in the *Academic Books* he says that he held the discussion treated there with Marcus Varro, “a man,” he says, “easily the sharpest of all and, without any doubt, the most learned.”

[Note: [Col. 0177] The passage is missing from the surviving books of the *Academic Questions*.]

He does not say “the most eloquent” or “the most fluent,” because in that ability Varro is in fact far inferior. Instead, he says, “easily the sharpest of all.” And in those books—that is, the *Academics*—where he maintains that everything must be doubted, he adds, “without any doubt, the most learned.”

He was so certain of this matter that he removed the doubt which he customarily applied to everything, as though, even while discussing it on behalf of the Academic doubt, he had forgotten that he was an Academic.

In the first book, while praising Varro’s literary work, he says:

> We, wandering and straying in our own city as though foreigners and guests, were led home by your books as by a house, so that at last we might recognize who and where we were. You have disclosed the age of our fatherland; the divisions of time; the laws of sacred rites; the laws of priests; domestic discipline; public discipline;

[Note: [Col. 0177] Cicero has “military discipline.”]

> the seat

[Note: [Col. 0177] The printed editions read “the seats.” Most manuscripts, and Cicero, read “the seat.”]

> of regions and places; and the names, kinds, functions, and causes of all divine and human things.  
> (Cicero, book 1, chapter 3, *Academic Questions*.)

This man, therefore, of such distinguished and exceptional expertise—of whom Terentianus also says briefly in an elegant verse:

> Varro, learned in every respect;

(*On Meters*, in the section on Phalaecian verses),

who read so much that we are astonished that he found time to write anything, and wrote so much that we can scarcely believe anyone could have read it all—this man, I say, so great in intellect and learning, if he had been an opponent and destroyer of the matters he writes about as though they were divine, and had said that they belonged not to religion but to superstition, I do not know whether he would have written so much about them that was worthy of ridicule, contempt, and abhorrence.

But since he worshiped these same gods and judged that they should be worshiped, to such an extent that in that very work of his literary writings he says that he fears they may perish—not through enemy attack, but through the negligence of the citizens—from which ruin he says he is rescuing them and storing and preserving them in the memory of good men through books of this kind, with greater care than Metellus is said to have rescued the Vestal sacred objects from the fire, or Aeneas the household gods from the destruction of Troy; and since, nevertheless, he passes on for later generations matters that the wise and the foolish alike rightly judge should be rejected and that are utterly hostile to the truth of religion—what are we to think except that this acute and highly learned man, though not liberated by the Holy Spirit, was oppressed by the customs and laws of his own state, and yet did not wish to remain silent about what moved him, under the pretext of commending religion?

## CHAPTER III.—Varro’s Division of His Books Composed on the Antiquities of Human and Divine Affairs

He wrote forty-one books of *Antiquities*. He divided them into human and divine matters, assigning twenty-five to human matters and sixteen to divine matters. In this division he followed the principle of assigning the books on human affairs in groups of six to four parts. He intended to address who acts, where they act, when they act, and what they do.

Thus, in the first six he wrote about people; in the second six about places; in the third six about times; and in the fourth six, which were also the final six, he completed the discussion of actions. Four groups of six make twenty-four. But he placed at the beginning one separate book, which first spoke generally about everything.

In the divine matters he likewise preserved the same form of division, insofar as it concerns what is offered to the gods. Sacred rites are offered by human beings in places and at times. He treated these four subjects in groups of three books: he wrote the first three about people, the next about places, the third group about times, and the fourth about sacred rites. Here too he carefully distinguished who offers them, where they offer them, when they offer them, and what they offer.

But because it was necessary to say—and this was especially expected—to whom they offer them, he wrote three final books about the gods themselves, so that five groups of three would make fifteen. There are, however, sixteen books in all, as we have said, because at the beginning of these also he added one separate book that first spoke generally about everything.

Having completed it, he subdivided the first three sections of that fivefold arrangement, which concern human beings, as follows: the first book is about pontiffs; the second about augurs; the third about the *quindecimviri sacris faciundis*, the fifteen men responsible for sacred rites.

[Note: [Col. 0179] Two men responsible for sacred rites had been established by Tarquinius Superbus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes, *Roman Antiquities*, book 4, chapter 62, to preside over the reading of the sacred books, the Sibylline verses, and the interpretation of the fates of the Roman people. When the plebs later insisted that men should be appointed from its own ranks, their number was increased to ten. Five were eventually added, and that number thereafter remained.]

The second group of three, concerning places, was arranged so that one book discussed shrines, another sacred buildings, and the third religious places.

The three that follow these, concerning times—that is, festival days—were arranged so that one dealt with holidays, another with circus games, and the third with theatrical games.

Of the fourth group of three, concerning sacred rites, he assigned consecrations to one, private rites to another, and public rites to the last.

At the end of this procession, as it were, of ritual services, the gods themselves follow in the three remaining books—the gods to whom the whole worship is directed: in the first, the certain gods; in the second, the uncertain gods; and in the final book of all, the principal and select gods.

## CHAPTER IV.—That, According to Varro’s Discussion, Human Affairs Are Found to Be More Ancient Than Divine Affairs among the Worshipers of the Gods

### 1

From what we have already said, and from what will be said hereafter, it is very easy for any person who is not obstinately hostile to himself in his heart to see that eternal life is sought, hoped for, or desired with utter shamelessness in vain throughout this entire sequence of extraordinarily beautiful and subtle divisions and distinctions.

These institutions are either human or demonic—not demonic in the sense of the good demons they call such, but, to speak more plainly, institutions of unclean and unquestionably evil spirits. With remarkable envy, these spirits secretly insert into the thoughts of the impious harmful opinions through which the human soul becomes increasingly empty and unable to be joined and attached to immutable and eternal truth. At times they openly thrust such opinions upon the senses, and by whatever deceptive testimony they can, they confirm them.

Varro himself testifies that he wrote first about human affairs and afterward about divine affairs because cities existed first and these institutions were later established by them.

True religion, however, was not established by any earthly city; rather, it establishes the heavenly city itself. The true God, giver of eternal life, inspires and teaches it to his true worshipers.

### 2

[IV.] Varro, therefore, admits that he wrote first about human affairs and afterward about divine affairs because these divine institutions were established by human beings. His reasoning is as follows:

> “Just as the painter exists before the painted panel, and the craftsman before the building, so cities exist before the things established by cities.”

He says that he would have written first about the gods and afterward about human beings if he were writing about the whole nature of the gods.

As though he is writing about some nature and not the whole nature! Or as though even some nature of the gods, although not the whole, ought not to be prior to human beings!

Moreover, in those three final books, where he carefully explains the certain, uncertain, and select gods, does he not appear to omit any nature of the gods?

What, then, does he mean when he says: “If we were writing about the whole nature of the gods and human beings, we would complete the divine matters before touching the human”?

Either he writes about the whole nature of the gods, or about some part of it, or about none at all. If about the whole, it must unquestionably be placed before human affairs. If about some part, why should that part itself not precede human affairs? Is some part of the gods’ nature unworthy of being placed before the whole of human nature?

But if it is too much to place some divine part before all human affairs, at least it is worthy of being placed before Roman affairs. For he wrote his books on human affairs not in relation to the whole world, but only in relation to Rome.

Nevertheless, he said that he rightly placed these books before the books on divine affairs in the order of composition, just as he placed the painter before the painted panel and the craftsman before the building. He thus most openly confessed that these divine matters, like painting and building, had been established by human beings.

It remains, then, to understand him as having written about no nature of the gods at all. He did not wish to say this openly, but left it for those with understanding to perceive.

Where it is said, “not the whole,” ordinary usage indeed suggests “some”; but it can also mean “none,” since what is none is neither the whole nor some part.

For, as he himself says, if the whole nature of the gods were the subject about which he was writing, it should be placed before human affairs in the order of composition. Even if it were not the whole but only some part, truth itself cries out, even while he is silent, that it should certainly be placed before Roman affairs. Yet he rightly places it afterward; therefore it is nothing.

He did not, then, intend to place human affairs before divine affairs; rather, he did not wish to place false things before true things. In what he wrote about human affairs, he followed the history of events. But what are the matters he calls divine except opinions about empty things?

This is evidently what he wished to indicate by a subtle sign: not only did he write about these matters later than about the others, but he also gave the reason why he had done so. If he had kept silent about that reason, others might perhaps have defended his action differently.

In the very reason he supplied, however, he left nothing for others to conjecture at their discretion, and sufficiently demonstrated that he had placed human beings before human institutions—not human nature before the nature of the gods.

Thus he confessed that he had written his books on divine affairs not about truth, which pertains to nature, but about falsehood, which pertains to error.

He made this clearer elsewhere, as I mentioned in the fourth book:

[Note: [Col. 0179] Chapter 31, section 1.]

he said that he would write according to the pattern of nature if he himself were founding a new city; but because he had found an ancient city already established, he could do nothing except follow its customs.

## CHAPTER V.—The Three Kinds of Theology According to Varro: One Fabulous, Another Natural, and a Third Civil
1. Next, what are we to make of his statement that there are three kinds of theology—that is, of the mode of reasoning that explains the gods—and that one of them is called mythic [Note: Manuscript 766 omits “is called.”], another physical, and the third civil? If Latin usage permitted it, we would call the first kind “fable-making” (*fabulare*); but let us call it “fabulous,” for *mythic* is so called from fables: μῦθος (*mythos*) means “fable” in Greek. The second may now be called “natural,” since common usage also permits that expression. The third Varro himself expressed in Latin, calling it “civil.”

He then says: “They call that mythic which poets chiefly use; that physical which philosophers use; and that civil which peoples use.” The first, he says, “contains many things fabricated contrary to the dignity and nature of the immortals. In it one god is born from a head, another from a thigh, another from drops of blood; in it the gods are said to have stolen, committed adultery, and served human beings. Finally, everything is attributed to the gods that can happen not merely to a human being, but even to the most contemptible human being.” Here, certainly, whenever he could, whenever he dared, whenever he thought it would go unpunished, he made clear—without the obscurity of any ambiguity—how great an insult the most mendacious fables inflicted upon the nature of the gods. For he was speaking not of natural theology, nor of civil theology, but of the fabulous theology, which he thought he could freely condemn.

2. Let us see what he says about the second kind. “The second kind,” he says, “is the one I have explained, about which philosophers have left many books. In these books we find discussion of who the gods are, where they are, what kind and what sort they are; whether the gods have existed from some point in time or from eternity; whether they are made of fire, as Heraclitus believes; or of numbers, as Pythagoras holds; or of atoms, as Epicurus says. And so there are other questions of this sort, which ears can more easily endure within the walls of a school than outside them in the forum.” He found nothing to criticize in this kind, which they call physical and which belongs to philosophers; he merely recorded their disagreements, through which the multitude of opposing schools has arisen. Yet he removed this kind from the forum—that is, from the peoples—and confined it to schools and enclosed rooms. But he did not remove that first, most mendacious and disgraceful kind from the cities.

O devout popular ears—and among them Roman ears as well! They cannot endure what philosophers debate about the immortal gods; but what poets sing and actors perform, although it is fabricated contrary to the dignity and nature of the immortals, and although it can happen not merely to a human being but even to the most contemptible human being, they not only endure but listen to willingly. More than that, they decide that these things also please the gods themselves, and that through them the gods must be appeased.

3. Someone might say: “Let us distinguish these two kinds—the mythic and the physical, that is, the fabulous and the natural—from the civil kind with which we are now concerned; Varro himself distinguished them in this way. Let us now see how he explains the civil kind.”

I understand why the fabulous kind must be distinguished: because it is false, disgraceful, and unworthy. But to wish to distinguish the natural from the civil—what is that other than to admit that the civil itself is defective? For if the former is natural, what objection does it have that it should be excluded? But if what is called civil is not natural, what merit does it have that it should be admitted?

This, surely, is the reason why he wrote first about human affairs and afterward about divine affairs: because in divine affairs he followed not nature [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read “not the nature of the gods.” “Of the gods” is absent from the other editions and from the manuscripts.], but human institutions.

Let us, then, examine the civil theology as well. “The third kind,” he says, “is the kind which citizens in cities, especially priests, ought to know and administer. It consists in determining which gods are to be publicly worshiped, and what sacred rites and sacrifices each person ought to perform” [Note: All Gallican manuscripts, together with several Roman ones, read: “It consists in determining which gods are to be publicly worshiped and what sacred rites and sacrifices each person ought to perform.”].

Let us attend to what follows. “The first theology,” he says, “is especially suited to the theater, the second to the world, and the third to the city.” Who does not see to which he awarded the palm? Clearly, to the second, which he said above belonged to philosophers. For he testifies that this theology pertains to the world, than which they consider nothing more excellent among existing things.

But did he distinguish or join together the two other theologies—the first and the third, namely, those of the theater and of the city? [Note: Louvain reads “and separated them.” Erasmus and the better manuscripts more correctly read “or joined them?” Varro seems to have joined together the theologies that he distinguished by his own arrangement—the first and the third, the fabulous and the civil—by teaching that one pertains to the city and the other to the theater, which is part of the city. Codex 2050 reads “distinguished and joined them.”]

For we see that what belongs to the city cannot necessarily belong to the world, although we see that cities exist in the world. It can happen that, according to false opinions, things are worshiped and believed in a city whose nature exists nowhere in the world or beyond the world. But where is there a theater except in a city? Who established a theater except a city? Why did it establish one except for theatrical games? And where are theatrical games found except among divine matters, about which these books are written with such diligence?

## CHAPTER VI — The mythic, that is, fabulous, theology, and the civil theology, against Varro

1. O Marcus Varro, although you are the most acute of all human beings and, without any doubt, extremely learned, yet you are a human being, not God; nor have you been lifted by the Spirit of God to see and proclaim divine things in truth and freedom. You do indeed perceive how sharply divine matters must be separated from human trifles and falsehoods. Yet you fear offending the deeply corrupt opinions and customs of peoples in their public superstitions—opinions which you yourself perceive to be alien from the nature of the gods, or of such gods as the weakness of the human mind imagines among the elements of this world, when you consider them from every side; and all your literature resounds with this perception.

What can human intelligence do here, however outstanding it may be? What assistance can your extensive and varied human learning provide you in these straits? You wish to worship natural gods, but you are compelled to worship civil ones. You have discovered other gods, the fabulous ones, against whom you can more freely vent what you think [Note: This is why Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 11, calls Varro “the Roman Cynic.” Coquaeus.]; and from them, whether you wish it or not, you pour contamination over these civil gods as well.

You say that the fabulous gods are suited to the theater, the natural gods to the world, and the civil gods to the city—although the world is a divine work, whereas cities and theaters are human works; although the gods laughed at in theaters are the same gods worshiped in temples; and although you present theatrical games to no others than those to whom you sacrifice victims.

How much more freely and subtly you could have divided these matters by saying that some gods are natural and others established by human beings, but that among those established by human beings the poets’ literature has one account and the priests’ another—and that both are so friendly with one another through their fellowship in falsehood that both are pleasing to demons, whereas the teaching of truth is hostile to them.

2. Setting aside for a little while the theology they call natural, about which we must speak later, is it finally pleasing to seek or hope for eternal life from poetic, theatrical, playful, and stage gods? Far from it! Rather, may the true God avert such monstrous and sacrilegious madness.

What? Is eternal life to be sought from those gods who approve of these things and are appeased by them, while their crimes are repeatedly enacted there? No one, I think, is so insane as to rush into such an abyss of frenzied impiety.

Thus no one obtains eternal life either through the fabulous theology or through the civil theology. The former sows its false fabrications by inventing disgraceful things about the gods; the latter reaps them by approving them. The former scatters falsehoods; the latter gathers them. The former attacks divine matters with false accusations; the latter embraces the enactment of those accusations in divine observances. The former makes impious inventions about the gods resound in human songs; the latter consecrates them in the festivals of the gods themselves. The former sings of the crimes and disgraceful acts of the deities; the latter loves them. The former exposes or invents them; the latter either bears witness to what is true or takes pleasure in what is false.

Both are disgraceful and both deserving of condemnation. But the one that is theatrical openly professes public disgrace, while the one that is urban adorns itself with the disgrace of the other. Is eternal life to be hoped for from this source, when our brief and temporal life is polluted by it?

Or does the association of wicked human beings pollute life if they insinuate themselves into our feelings and assent, while the fellowship of demons, who are worshiped through their crimes, does not pollute it? If the things are true, how evil are they! If they are false, how evil is it to approve them!

3. When we say these things, someone ignorant of such matters may perhaps think that only those things about such gods which are unworthy of divine majesty, ridiculous, and detestable are celebrated in poetic songs and theatrical performances, while the sacred rites performed not by actors but by priests are free from and alien to every disgrace.
