If this were so, no one would ever think that theatrical disgrace ought to be celebrated in their honor; nor would the gods themselves ever command such things to be performed for them. But the reason no one is ashamed to perform such things in theaters as a service to the gods is that similar things are performed in temples.

Finally, when the author just mentioned tried to distinguish civil theology from fabulous and natural theology as a third kind of its own, he wanted it to be understood as composed more from both than separated from both. For he says that what the poets write is less than what peoples ought to follow, while what philosophers write is more than what it is useful for the common people to investigate. “These two,” he says, “are so different that nevertheless not a few things have been taken from both kinds for civil purposes. Therefore, whatever we share with the poets, we shall write together with the civil material” [Note: The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “what we share with our own.” Our manuscripts read likewise.], “although our association ought to be greater with philosophers than with poets.”

Thus there is not no association with the poets. And yet elsewhere he says that, concerning the origins of the gods, peoples were more inclined toward the poets than toward the natural philosophers. Here he said what ought to happen; there, what does happen. He said that the natural philosophers wrote for the sake of utility, and the poets for the sake of pleasure. Consequently, the things written by the poets that peoples ought not to follow are the crimes of the gods—things that nevertheless please both peoples and gods. For, as he says, poets write for the sake of pleasure, not utility; yet they write what the gods desire and peoples perform.

## CHAPTER VII — The likeness and concord of the fabulous and civil theologies

1. The fabulous, theatrical, stage theology, full of disgrace and depravity, is therefore brought back into the civil theology. This whole theology, which is rightly judged deserving of blame and rejection, is a part of the civil theology that is considered worthy of worship and observance.

It is not an incongruous part, as I have undertaken to show, nor something alien to the whole body that has been improperly attached and hung upon it. Rather, it is entirely consonant with it and joined to it as a member of the same body in the most fitting manner.

For what else do those images, forms, ages, sexes, and attributes of the gods indicate? Do the poets have a bearded Jupiter and a beardless Mercury, while the pontiffs do not? Did mimers, and not priests as well, give Priapus his enormous genitals? Does he stand to be worshiped in sacred places in any other form than that in which he comes forward to be mocked in theaters?

Are Saturn as an old man and Apollo as a young man merely characters of actors, and not statues in shrines? Why are Forculus, who presides over doors, and Limentinus, who presides over the threshold, male gods, while Cardea, who guards the hinge, is female? Are these not found in books of divine matters—things that serious poets considered unworthy of their songs?

Does the theatrical Diana carry weapons while the urban Diana is simply a virgin? Is the stage Apollo a lyre-player while the Delphic Apollo is free from this art?

But these things are more respectable in comparison with the worse ones. What did they think of Jupiter himself when they placed his nurse in the Capitol? Did they not thereby bear witness to Euhemerus, who wrote that all such gods were human and mortal beings—not with fabulous chatter, but with historical diligence?

When they established the gods called the Epulones, the parasites of Jupiter, at his table, what else did they intend except a sacred mime? For if a mime had said that parasites had been invited to Jupiter’s banquet, he would plainly have seemed to be seeking laughter.

Varro said it—not while mocking the gods, but while commending them. The books in which he wrote this testify that they were books of divine, not human, matters; and he wrote it not while explaining theatrical games, but while unfolding the laws of the Capitol.

Finally, he is defeated by such evidence and admits that, just as they made the gods in human form, so they believed that the gods took pleasure in human pleasures.

2. Nor did the malignant spirits fail to do their part by strengthening these harmful opinions through the deception of human minds.

This is the origin of the story that the idle and holiday-keeping custodian of Hercules played dice with himself, alternating between his two hands and placing Hercules in one and himself in the other. The terms were that, if he himself won, he would provide himself with a dinner from the temple offerings and hire a mistress; but if Hercules won, he would provide the same things, at his own expense, for Hercules’ pleasure.

Then, when he had been defeated by himself as though by Hercules, he gave the god Hercules the promised dinner and the most famous prostitute, Larentina [Note: The editions read “Laurentina.” The better manuscripts read “Larentina.” Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 1, chapter 20, says: “She is Flora, whose festival is the Floralia.”].

After she had slept in the temple, she saw in a dream that Hercules had intercourse with her and told her that, when she left the temple, she would find with the first young man she met the payment that she ought to believe had been paid to her by Hercules.

Accordingly, as she was leaving, the first young man she met was the very wealthy Tarutius. He kept her as his beloved for a long time, and when he died he left her as his heir [Note: The word “left” is absent from the manuscripts.]. Having acquired a very substantial fortune, and not wishing to seem ungrateful for divine payment, she herself named the Roman people as heir to what she thought would be most acceptable to the gods. When she failed to appear, her will was found. For these services, they say, she even earned divine honors.

3. If poets invented these things, or if mimes acted them, they would unquestionably be said to belong to the fabulous theology and would be judged separable from the dignity of the civil theology.

But when such disgraces are revealed not by poets but by peoples; not by mimes but by sacred rites; not by theaters but by temples—that is, when they belong not to fabulous but to civil theology—and are disclosed by so great an author [Note: Manuscript 766 reads “teacher.”], then actors do not portray the gods’ great depravity in their playful arts without reason; rather, priests attempt in vain to portray a nonexistent holiness of the gods as though through sacred rites.

These are the sacred rites of Juno, and they are celebrated on her beloved island of Samos, where she was given in marriage to Jupiter [Note: Manuscripts 766, 2050, and 2053 read “were celebrated.”]. These are the sacred rites of Ceres, at which Proserpina, carried off by Pluto, is sought. These are the sacred rites of Venus, at which her beloved Adonis, the most beautiful young man, is mourned after being killed by a boar’s tusk. These are the sacred rites of the Mother of the Gods, at which the beautiful young Attis, beloved by her and castrated through feminine jealousy, is mourned together with the unhappy human beings who have been castrated and are called Galli.

Since these rites are more deformed than every theatrical obscenity, why do they try to separate the poets’ fabulous inventions about the gods—which supposedly belong to the theater—from the civil theology that they wish to make belong to the city, as though the former were disgraceful and unworthy while the latter were honorable and worthy?

Rather, the actors deserve thanks for sparing human eyes and not exposing in their spectacles everything that is concealed behind the walls of sacred buildings.

What good judgment should we form of their sacred rites, which are hidden in darkness, when what is brought into the light is so detestable? Let them themselves see what they do in secret through the castrated and effeminate men. Yet they have been entirely unable to conceal those same men, unhappily and disgracefully emasculated and corrupted.

Let them persuade whomever they can that they perform something holy through such men—men whom they cannot deny are counted and move among their sacred people [Note: Several manuscripts read “their sacred rites.” Shortly afterward the editions read: “which would never enter either the theater or the chorus of prostitutes, where no castrated man …” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.].

We do not know what they do, but we know through what sort of men they do it. For we know what is done on the stage, where no castrated or effeminate man has ever entered—not even into a chorus of prostitutes—and yet even there disgraceful and infamous persons perform such acts; indeed, they ought not to be performed by honorable people.

What, then, are those sacred rites for whose performance holiness has chosen people whom not even theatrical obscenity admits among its own?

## CHAPTER VIII — The interpretations of natural causes that the pagan teachers attempt to display on behalf of their gods

1. But, they say, these matters have certain “physiological” interpretations—that is, interpretations in terms of natural causes. As though in this discussion we were seeking physiology and not theology; that is, an account not of nature but of God.

Although the true God is God by nature, not by opinion, it does not follow that every nature is God. Human nature, the nature of cattle, trees, and stones all exist, certainly, but none of these is God.

If, when the sacred rites of the Mother of the Gods are being discussed, the starting point of this interpretation is certainly that the mother of the gods is the earth, what more are we seeking, and what other matters are we examining? What could more clearly support those who say that all these gods were human beings? For just as they are earth-born, so the earth is their mother [Note: All the manuscripts read: “For just as they are earth-born, so the earth is their mother.”].

But in true theology the earth is God’s work, not his mother.

However their sacred rites may be interpreted and referred to the nature of things, for men to undergo what belongs to women is not according to nature but contrary to nature. This disease, this crime, this disgrace has a recognized place among those sacred rites, although among the vicious customs of human beings it scarcely has a place even among tortures that must be confessed.

Furthermore, if these sacred rites—which are proved to be more disgusting than theatrical obscenities—are excused and cleansed on the ground that they have their own interpretations by which they are shown to signify the nature of things, why should the poetic accounts not likewise be excused and cleansed? Many have interpreted them in the same manner, to such an extent that some explain even the most monstrous and unspeakable story told about Saturn—namely, that he devoured his own children—as meaning that the passage of time, signified by the name Saturn, consumes whatever it produces; or, as Varro himself thinks, that Saturn pertains to seeds, which fall back into the earth from which they arise. Others interpret this and other matters in other, similar ways.

2. And yet the fabulous theology is called fabulous and, together with all such interpretations, is criticized, rejected, and condemned. It is distinguished as rightly repudiated not only by the natural theology, which belongs to philosophers, but also by the civil theology under discussion, which is asserted to belong to cities and peoples, because it fabricated things unworthy of the gods.

This was evidently done with the intention that, since the keenest and most learned people—those who wrote these things—understood that both the fabulous and the civil theology deserved condemnation, they dared to condemn the former but did not dare to condemn the latter. They therefore set up the former for blame and displayed it as comparable to the latter—not so that the latter might be chosen as preferable to the former, but so that, when the latter was understood to be like the former, both might be rejected. Thus, without endangering those who feared to criticize the civil theology, both could be despised, and what they call natural theology could find a place among better minds.

Both the civil and the fabulous theologies are fabulous, and both are civil. Anyone who prudently examines the vanities and obscenities of both will find both fabulous; anyone who notices that theatrical games belonging to the fabulous theology are included in the festivals of the civil gods and in the divine affairs of the cities will find both civil.

How, then, can the power of granting eternal life be attributed to any of these gods, when their images and sacred rites prove them to be most plainly like the fabulous gods in their forms, ages, sex, attributes, marriages, generations, and rites? In all these matters they either indicate that the gods were human beings, and that sacred rites and ceremonies were established for them according to the life or death of each one, with demons insinuating and reinforcing this error; or else that unclean spirits entered through some opportunity in order to deceive human minds.

## CHAPTER IX — The functions of the individual gods

1. What of the functions of the deities themselves, divided and broken down into such petty details, on account of which they say that prayers ought to be addressed to them according to each one’s particular function? We have already mentioned not all but many of them. Do these functions not correspond more closely to the buffoonery of a mime than to divine dignity? [Note: The editions read “more closely than.” The manuscripts lack the word “more”; Augustine often omits it in similar passages.]

If someone employed two nurses for an infant, one of whom gave nothing but food and the other nothing but drink, just as these people employed two goddesses for this purpose, Educa and Potina, he would plainly seem to be foolish and to be performing something like a mime in his own house.

They wish Liber to have been named from *liberamentum*—“release”—because, through his favor, males are released during intercourse when their seed is emitted. They say that Libera, whom they also consider Venus, performs the same function for females, because they claim that females too emit seed. For this reason, they place the corresponding male bodily part of Liber in the temple, and the female one of Libera. To these they add women assigned to Liber and wine, for the arousal of lust.

Thus the Bacchanalia were celebrated with the utmost madness [Note: This is how our manuscripts read. B has “are celebrated.”]. Varro himself admits that such things could not have been done by the Bacchants except with their minds deranged. Yet afterward they displeased the more sensible senate, which ordered them removed. At least here, perhaps, they finally perceived what unclean spirits can do to human minds when they are regarded as gods.

Certainly such things would not be performed in theaters. There people play rather than rave—although to have gods who take pleasure even in such games is itself akin to madness.

2. What, moreover, are we to make of this? He distinguishes the religious person from the superstitious by saying that the gods are feared by the superstitious person, whereas the religious person reveres them only as parents, not fearing them as enemies. He also says that all the gods are so good that it would be easier for them to spare those who do harm than to injure any innocent person.

Yet he records that, after a woman has given birth, three guardian gods are appointed to prevent the god Silvanus from entering at night and tormenting her. For the purpose of indicating these guardians, three men go around the thresholds of the house at night: first they strike the threshold with an ax, then with a pestle, and third they sweep it with brooms. By giving these signs of cultivation, they prevent the god Silvanus from entering, since trees are neither cut down nor pruned without iron, meal is not prepared without a pestle, and crops are not gathered without brooms.

From these three things three gods are named: Intercidona from the cutting of the ax, Pilumnus from the pestle, and Deverra from the brooms. By means of these guardian gods, the woman who has given birth is protected against the violence of the god Silvanus.

Thus, against the savagery of a harmful god, the protection of good gods would not be sufficient unless there were several of them against one—and against one so harsh, terrifying, and uncultivated, as befits a woodland god—and unless they opposed him with signs of cultivation as though with contrary forces.

Is this the innocence of the gods? Is this their harmony? Are these the health-giving deities of cities—things more deserving of ridicule than the farces of the theater? [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “more deserving of ridicule than the farces of poets and theaters.”]

3. When a male and female are joined together, the god Jugatinus is appointed. Let that be endured. But the bride must be led home, and the god Domiducus is appointed; so that she may be in the house, the god Domitius is appointed; so that she may remain with her husband, the goddess Manturna is added.

What more is required? Let human modesty be spared. Let the rest be carried out by the desire of flesh and blood, with the privacy of modesty secured.

Why is the bedroom filled with a crowd of deities, when even the bridesmen depart from it? And why is it filled with them? Not so that their presence, once considered, might produce greater concern for chastity, but so that the woman, weak in sex and frightened by novelty, may, with their assistance, lose her virginity without any difficulty.

For the goddess Virginiensis is present, as is the god-father Subigus, the mother-goddess Prema, and the goddess Pertunda [Note: This is how Ambrosianus and the manuscripts read. Vindobonensis, Erasmus, and Louvain read “Partunda,” and below “Partundus,” instead of “Pertundus.”], as well as Venus and Priapus [Note: See Arnobius, book 4, and Lactantius, book 1, chapter 20.].

What is this? If the man struggling with that act really needed help from the gods, would not one god—or one goddess—be enough? Surely Venus alone would not be insufficient, since she is said to have received this name because without her power [Note: Our manuscripts read “because without power,” omitting “her.”] a woman does not cease to be a virgin.

If human beings have any sense of shame that the deities lack, when married couples believe that so many gods of both sexes are present and intent upon this act, are they not so embarrassed that the man is less aroused and the woman more resistant?

And certainly, if the goddess Virginiensis is present so that the virgin’s girdle may be loosened; if the god Subigus is present so that she may be subjected to the man; if the goddess Prema is present so that, once subjected, she may be restrained from moving; what is the goddess Pertunda doing there? Let her blush and go outside. Let the husband do something himself.

It is extremely dishonorable that what she is called to perform should be accomplished by anyone except him. But perhaps she is tolerated for this reason: because she is said to be a goddess, not a god.

For if she were believed to be male and were called Pertundus, the husband would seek help against him on behalf of his wife’s chastity even more [Note: Louvain and some manuscripts read “more greatly.” Our manuscripts read “more.”] than the woman who has given birth seeks it against Silvanus.

But why should I say this, when Priapus is also present—an excessively male being [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “excessively masculine”]—upon whose enormous and disgraceful phallus the new bride was ordered to sit, in the most honorable and religious custom of matrons? [Note: Manuscripts 766, 2050, and 2052 read “the new bride was ordered to sit, in the most honorable and religious custom of matrons”; B reads “the new bride is ordered to sit, in the most honorable and religious custom of matrons.” Manuscripts 2051 and 2053 agree with B. Morel reads “the new bride was ordered to sit, with the most honorable and religious face of matrons.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 136.]

4. Let them continue, then, and attempt with whatever subtlety they can to distinguish civil theology from fabulous theology, cities from theaters, temples from stages, the sacred rites of pontiffs from the songs of poets—as honorable things from disgraceful, truthful from deceitful, serious from frivolous, earnest from playful, desirable from rejected things.

We understand what they are doing. They know that the theatrical and fabulous theology depends upon this civil theology and is reflected from it, as from a mirror, in the poets’ songs. Therefore, after displaying this civil theology, which they do not dare condemn, they more freely accuse and criticize its image, the theatrical theology, so that those who recognize what they want may detest this very face of which the theatrical theology is the image.

Yet the gods themselves love it as though they were looking at themselves in the same mirror, so that they may be seen more clearly in both forms for what they are and what sort of beings they are.

For this reason they also compelled their worshipers by terrifying commands to dedicate the uncleanness of the fabulous theology to them, to place it in their festivals, and to include it in divine affairs. In this way they made it more clearly known that they themselves were the most unclean spirits, and they made the theatrical theology—cast aside and rejected—into a member and part of this urban theology, as though it were chosen and approved.

Thus, although the whole is disgraceful and deceitful and contains fictitious gods, one part of it is found in the writings of priests and the other in the songs of poets.

Whether it has other parts is another question. For the present, because of Varro’s division, I believe I have shown sufficiently that both the urban and the theatrical theologies belong to one civil theology.

Since both are alike in disgrace, absurdity, unworthiness, and falsehood, may it be far from religious people either to hope for eternal life from this theology or from that.

5. Finally, Varro himself began to recall and enumerate the gods beginning with the conception of a human being. He began their number [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Louvain read “numbers.” Erasmus and several manuscripts read “number.”] with Janus and carried the sequence through to the death of the aged human being. He concluded the gods pertaining to the human being himself with the goddess Naenia, who is sung about at the funerals of old men.

Then he began to display other gods who pertained not to the human being himself but to the things that belong to human beings, such as food, clothing, and whatever else is necessary for this life. In every case he showed what each god’s function was and why each one ought to be entreated.

Yet throughout this exhaustive account he neither demonstrated nor named any gods from whom eternal life ought to be sought—the one reason why we Christians exist in particular.

Who, then, could be so slow-witted as not to understand that, by explaining and exposing civil theology so carefully, by showing it to resemble the fabulous, unworthy, and disgraceful theology, and by teaching with sufficient clarity that the fabulous theology is a part of it, Varro was preparing a place in human minds only for the natural theology that he says belongs to philosophers?

He did this with such subtlety that he criticized the fabulous theology but did not dare criticize the civil theology openly. Instead, by exposing it, he showed that it deserved criticism. In this way, after both had been rejected by the judgment of those who understood correctly, only the natural theology would remain to be chosen.

We must discuss that theology more carefully in its proper place, with the help of the true God.

## CHAPTER X — The freedom of Seneca, who criticized civil theology more vigorously than Varro criticized fabulous theology

1. The freedom that Varro lacked—the freedom that prevented him from openly criticizing this urban theology, so like the theatrical theology, as he had criticized the other—was not entirely absent from Annaeus Seneca, whom we find, from several indications, to have flourished during the times of our apostles.

It was present in his writing but absent from his life. For in the book that he composed against superstition [Note: This same book is cited by Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 12, but it no longer survives.], he criticized this civil and urban theology much more fully and vigorously than Varro criticized the theatrical and fabulous theology.

When discussing images, he says: “They dedicate sacred and immortal beings, inviolable, in the cheapest and most immobile material. They clothe them in the forms of human beings, wild animals, and fish; some give them mixed sexes in different bodies” [Note: The manuscripts read “sacred, immortal, inviolable”; the editions read “sacred, immortal, and inviolable gods.” Johannes Meursius proposed: “They dedicate [the gods] in the cheapest and most ignoble material; they clothe them in the forms of human beings, wild animals, and fish; some clothe mixed sexes in different bodies.”]. “They call these things deities, which, if they suddenly appeared with a spirit, would be regarded as monsters.”

A little later, after proclaiming natural theology and arranging the opinions of certain philosophers, he posed an objection to himself and said:

“At this point someone says, ‘Shall I believe that heaven and earth are gods, and that there are other gods above the moon and others below it?’ Shall I endure either Plato or the Peripatetic Strato [Note: See Diogenes Laertius, book 5, sections 58 and following.], one of whom made a god without a body and the other without a mind?”

In response to this he says:

“What, then, finally, seem more true to you—the dreams of Titus Tatius, Romulus, or Tullus Hostilius? Tatius dedicated Cloacina as a goddess; Romulus dedicated Picus and Tiberinus; Hostilius dedicated Pavor and Pallor, the most terrifying emotions of human beings—one being the movement of a frightened mind, the other of the body, not even a disease but a color. Will you believe that these are deities and admit them into heaven?”

How freely he wrote about the very rites that are cruelly disgraceful! “One man,” he says, “cuts off his male organs; another cuts his arms” [Note: Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 1, chapter 21.]. “Where do they fear angry gods when they earn their favor in this way? The gods ought not to be worshiped in any manner if they desire even this.”

“So great is the madness of a disturbed mind, driven from its proper seat, that the gods are appeased in the way in which not even the most savage human beings behave, although their cruelty has been handed down in stories. Tyrants tore the limbs of some people, but ordered no one to tear his own limbs. Some were castrated for the pleasure of royal lust, but no one, at the command of a master, injured his own hands so as not to be a man. They cut themselves to pieces in temples and supplicate with their wounds and blood.”

“If anyone has the leisure to look at what they do and what they suffer, he will find them so unseemly for honorable people, so unworthy of the free, and so unlike the sane, that no one would doubt that they were mad if they raved with fewer companions. As it is, the crowd of the insane serves as the defense of their sanity.”

### 2.

But who would believe that the things he records as customarily taking place in the Capitol itself—and condemns with complete fearlessness—are done by anyone except mockers or madmen? For when he had mocked the fact that in the Egyptian rites Osiris is mourned as lost and then, once found, becomes the occasion of great rejoicing—although his loss and discovery are fabricated, the grief and joy are nevertheless genuinely expressed by those who have lost and found nothing[Note: [Col. 0191] The printed editions read: “and then mocked the great joy at its discovery.” The manuscripts read: “and then mocked that it was found with great joy.”]

—he says:

> “Yet this madness has a fixed season. It is tolerable to go mad once a year. I came to the Capitol: I was ashamed of the dementia made public, of what empty madness has assigned to itself as a duty. One man supplies the god with names [Note: [Col. 0191] B reads *numina* (“divine powers”); manuscripts 766, 2051, and 2053 support *nomina* (“names”). M.], another announces the hours to Jupiter; one is a lictor, another an anointer who, by the pointless movement of his arms, imitates someone applying oil. There are women who arrange Juno’s and Minerva’s hair; standing far from the temple, and not merely far from the image, they move their fingers in the manner of women dressing hair. There are women who hold a mirror; there are those who summon the gods to their lawsuits; there are those who present petitions and explain their case to them. A learned chief mime, already a decrepit old man, performed a mime every day in the Capitol, as though the gods were eagerly waiting to watch what human beings had ceased to watch. Every kind of craftsman, having worked for the immortal gods, sits idle there.” [Note: [Col. 0191] B reads *operantium* (“of workers”); following manuscripts 766 and 2053, M. corrects to *operatum* (“having worked”).]

[Note: [Col. 0191] The Vindobonensis, the Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts read *exspectarent* (“were eagerly waiting”), rather than *spectarent* (“were watching”).]

[Note: [Col. 0191] This is how all our manuscripts read. In B., *quem homines desierant*, omitting *illi* (“what human beings had ceased to watch”). M.]

And shortly afterward:

> “Yet these people,” he says, “even if they promise the god a useless service, promise one that is neither shameful nor infamous. Certain women sit in the Capitol who think that Jupiter loves them; they are not frightened even by the regard of Juno—if one is willing to believe the poets—the most wrathful of goddesses.”

### 3.

Varro did not possess this freedom: he dared to criticize only poetic theology; he did not dare to criticize civil theology, which this man has cut to pieces. But if we attend to the truth, the temples in which these things are performed are worse than the theaters in which they are represented. Hence, in these rites of civil theology, Seneca, wishing to act as a wise man, chose rather to treat such matters as parts that he should not possess in the religion of his mind, but should portray in his conduct. For he says:

> “The wise man will observe all these things as though they were commanded by the laws, not as though they were pleasing to the gods.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What of the fact that we also join gods in marriage—and not even in a pious manner, but brothers and sisters? We assign Bellona to Mars, Venus to Vulcan, Salacia to Neptune. Yet we leave some of them unmarried, as though the supply had run out—especially since there are some widows, such as Populonia, Fulgora, and the goddess Rumina” [Note: [Col. 0191] The manuscripts of good authority read *Divarona*.], “for whom I am not surprised that no suitor has appeared. We shall worship that whole ignoble crowd of gods, which long-standing superstition has heaped together over a long age, in such a way,” he says, “that we remember that its worship belongs more to custom than to reality.”

Thus neither those laws nor custom in civil theology established anything because it was pleasing to the gods or pertained to reality. Yet this man, whom philosophy had made almost free [Note: [Col. 0192] This is the reading of several manuscripts. The printed editions have *philosophi quasi liberum fecerunt* (“philosophers made him almost free”).], nevertheless, because he was a prominent senator of the Roman people, worshiped what he criticized, practiced what he condemned, and adored what he blamed. Evidently, although philosophy had taught him something important—namely, that he should not be superstitious in the world—because of the laws of his fellow citizens and the customs of human beings he did not indeed perform the role of an actor in a theater, but imitated one in a temple. His conduct was all the more blameworthy because he performed the falsehoods he acted out in such a way that the people believed he was performing them truthfully; whereas an actor, by playing, would entertain rather than deceive by misleading.

## CHAPTER XI  
### What Seneca Thought about the Jews

Among the other superstitions of civil theology, he also criticized the Jewish rites, especially the Sabbaths, asserting that they practiced them uselessly because, by setting aside every seventh day, they lost almost a seventh of their lives in idleness and suffered harm by failing to do many things that pressed upon them at the proper time.

Yet, although Christians were already at that time extremely hostile to the Jews, he did not dare to mention them in either a favorable or an unfavorable sense, lest he either praise them contrary to the ancient custom of his homeland or criticize them contrary, perhaps, to his own inclination. Speaking of the Jews, however, he says:

> “Meanwhile, the custom of that most criminal nation has grown so powerful that it has now been received throughout all lands: the conquered have given laws to their conquerors.”

He expressed his astonishment in saying this; and, ignorant of what was being accomplished by divine providence, he added a statement that clearly indicated what he thought about the nature of their rites. For he says:

> “Yet they know the reasons for their rite; the greater part of the people do what they do not know the reason for doing.”

But concerning the rites of the Jews—why and to what extent they were instituted by divine authority, and later, when the appropriate time came, were removed by that same authority from the people of God, to whom the mystery of eternal life had been revealed—we have spoken elsewhere, especially when we were arguing against the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 0192] See Book Thirty-Three *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, vol. 8.], and it will be discussed at a more suitable place in this work.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Once the vanity of the pagan gods has been exposed, it cannot be doubted that they can grant eternal life to no one, since they do not even assist temporal life

Now, because of the three theologies that the Greeks call mythical, physical, and political, and that may be called in Latin fabulous, natural, and civil: since eternal life is not to be hoped for either from the fabulous theology—which even the worshipers of its many false gods freely criticized—or from the civil theology, which is shown to be a part of it and is found to be similar to it, or even worse—if what has been said in this volume is not enough for anyone, let that person add what was discussed at length in the earlier books, especially in Book Four, concerning God as the giver of happiness.

For to whom, except to Happiness alone, would human beings have to be consecrated for the sake of eternal life, if Happiness were a goddess? But since it is not a goddess, but a gift of God, to which God should we be consecrated except to the giver of happiness, whom we love with devout charity because he gives eternal life, where true and complete happiness exists?

I think that no one ought to doubt, on the basis of what has been said, that none of those gods is the giver of happiness—those gods who are worshiped with such great shamefulness and who, unless they are worshiped in that manner, grow angry with far greater shamefulness, thereby confessing themselves to be the most unclean spirits.

Moreover, if someone does not give happiness, how can he give eternal life? For we call that life eternal in which happiness is without end. But if the soul lives in eternal punishments, by which the unclean spirits themselves will also be tormented, that is eternal death rather than life. For no death is greater or worse than the death in which death itself does not die.

But because the nature of the soul, by virtue of having been created immortal, cannot exist without some kind of life, its supreme death is alienation from the life of God in the eternity of punishment. Eternal life, therefore—that is, happiness without any end—is given only by the one who gives true happiness.

Since those whom this civil theology worships have been proved unable to give it—not only because of these temporal and earthly matters, as we demonstrated in the preceding five books, but much more because of eternal life, which will exist after death, a matter that we have treated in this one book even with their cooperation—they are not to be worshiped.

But because the force of an age-old habit has roots sunk too deeply, if I seem to anyone to have argued too little about rejecting and avoiding this civil theology, let that person turn his attention to another volume, which, with God’s assistance, is to be joined to this one.

# BOOK SEVEN

## On the Select Gods of Civil Theology: Janus, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Others; and on the Fact That Their Worship Does Not Bring One to the Happiness of Eternal Life

[Col. 0193]

## PREFACE

Those who possess quicker and better minds—minds for which the preceding books are more than sufficient for this undertaking—will have to bear patiently and calmly with me as I labor more diligently to uproot and eradicate the depraved and ancient opinions hostile to the piety of truth, opinions that the long-continued error of the human race has implanted deeply and tenaciously in darkened minds, and as, to the measure of my ability, I cooperate with the grace of him who, as the true God, can accomplish this, relying on his help. For the sake of others, they should not consider superfluous what they already perceive to be unnecessary for themselves.

A matter of very great importance is at stake when the true and truly holy divinity is proclaimed as something to be sought and worshiped: although it also provides us with the supports necessary for the frailty in which we now live, it is to be sought and worshiped not, however, for the transient vapor of mortal life, but for the blessed life, which alone is eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0193] The Vindobonensis and Erasmianus read *non tantum* (“not merely”).]

## CHAPTER I  
### Since it has been established that there is no divinity in civil theology, should we believe that it can be found among the select gods?

This divinity—or, if I may put it so, this *deity*; for our people are no longer reluctant to use this word in order to translate more precisely from the Greek what they call θεότης (*theotēs*)—this divinity or deity is not present in the theology called civil, which Marcus Varro explained in sixteen volumes.

That is, if the sixth book, which we have just completed, has not yet persuaded anyone that the worship of such gods as the cities have instituted, and in the manner in which they have instituted them, does not lead to the happiness of eternal life, then, after reading this book, that person will have no further question concerning what remains to be settled on this matter.

For it may be that someone will at least suppose that the select and preeminent gods whom Varro included in his final volume—and about whom we have said little—should be worshiped for the sake of the blessed life, which is eternal and nothing else.

On this matter I do not say what Tertullian perhaps expressed more wittily than truly:

> “If the gods are selected like onions, then surely the others are judged rejected.” [Note: [Col. 0194] Something similar occurs in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 13.]

I do not say this. For I see that even from among the select some are selected for something greater and more distinguished, just as in military service, once recruits have been selected, some of these too are selected for a more important task involving arms.

When those who are to become leaders are selected in the Church, the others are not thereby rejected, since all good believers are rightly called “the elect.” In a building, foundation stones are selected without rejecting the others, which are assigned to other parts of the structure. Grapes are selected for eating, while the others that we leave for drinking are not rejected.

There is no need to run through many examples, since the matter is clear. Therefore, neither the writer, nor their worshipers, nor the gods themselves are to be blamed simply because certain gods have been selected from among many; rather, we must consider who these gods are and for what purpose they appear to have been selected.

## CHAPTER II  
### Who the select gods are, and whether they are exempt from the offices of the lesser gods

Varro commends these select gods in the structure of a single book: Janus, Jupiter, Saturn, Genius, Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Vulcan, Neptune, the Sun, Orcus, Father Liber, Tellus, Ceres, Juno, the Moon, Diana, Minerva, Venus, and Vesta. There are almost twenty altogether: twelve males and eight females.

Are these deities called select because of their greater administration of affairs in the world, or because they became better known to the peoples and received greater worship?

If they are called select because greater operations are administered by them in the world, we ought not to have found them among that almost plebeian multitude of deities assigned to minor tasks. For Janus himself, first of all, when conception takes place and all those operations begin—operations distributed piecemeal among the minor deities—opens the passage for receiving the seed.

Saturn is there too, on account of the seed itself. Liber [Note: [Col. 0195] Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2, teaches that this Liber is different from Liber Bacchus, son of Jupiter and Semele.] is there, who frees the male by the emission of seed. Libera is there—whom they also wish to be Venus—who confers the same benefit upon the female, so that she too is freed by the emission of seed.

All these belong to those who are called select. But there is also the goddess Mena, who presides over menstrual flows; although she is Jupiter’s daughter, she is nevertheless of no distinction. [Note: [Col. 0195] The printed editions read *providentiam* (“providence”); the manuscripts correct this to *provinciam* (“office”).] The same author assigns this office of menstrual flows in the book on the select gods to Juno herself, who among the select gods is also queen; and here, as Juno Lucina, she presides over the same blood together with Mena, her stepdaughter.

There are also two exceedingly obscure figures—I do not know who they are—Vitumnus and Sentinus. One of them bestows life upon the child in the womb, the other sensation. And surely, although they are of no distinction, they accomplish much more than all those nobles and select gods. For plainly, without life and sensation, what is the whole thing carried in the woman’s womb except some utterly wretched object, comparable to mud and dust?

## CHAPTER III  
### How no reason can be offered for the selection of certain gods, when a more excellent administration is assigned to many inferior ones

### 1.

What reason, then, compelled so many select gods to undertake these minor tasks, where they are surpassed in the distribution of this beneficence by Vitumnus and Sentinus, whom obscure fame keeps hidden?

The select Janus provides the passage, almost a door, for the seed. The select Saturn provides the seed itself. The select Liber provides the emission of that seed for males. Libera, who is Ceres or Venus, provides the same for females. The select Juno—and not she alone, but together with Mena, Jupiter’s daughter—provides the menstrual flows for the growth of what has been conceived.

And obscure and undistinguished Vitumnus provides life; obscure and undistinguished Sentinus provides sensation. These two are more important than those functions to the extent that life and sensation themselves surpass those functions, even as life and sensation are themselves surpassed by intellect and reason. For just as beings that reason and understand are certainly superior to those that live and sense without understanding or reason, like animals, so those endowed with life and sensation are rightly preferred to those that neither live nor sense.

Among the select gods, therefore, Vitumnus the giver of life and Sentinus the giver of sensation ought to have been held in higher esteem than Janus, who admits the seed; Saturn, who gives or sows the seed; and Liber and Libera, who stir or emit the seed—for it is unworthy even to think about those seeds unless they come to life and sensation.

These select functions are not given by the select gods, but by certain unknown gods who, in comparison with the dignity of the others, have been neglected.

If it is answered that Janus has power over all beginnings, and therefore that what opens for conception is rightly attributed to him [Note: [Col. 0195] The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus read *quod aperit conceptum* (“what opens conception”).]; that Saturn has power over all seeds, and therefore the sowing of human beings cannot be separated from his activity; that Liber and Libera have power over all seeds that are to be emitted, and therefore preside over what pertains to the propagation of human beings; and that Juno has power over all things that are cleansed and give birth, and therefore is not absent from the cleansing of women and the births of human beings—then let them consider what they will answer concerning Vitumnus and Sentinus.

Do they wish to grant them power over all things that live and sense? If they do, let them observe how much higher a place they will assign to them. For to be born from seeds belongs to the earth and is from the earth; but they suppose that even the starry gods live and sense.

If, however, they say that only those functions were assigned to Vitumnus and Sentinus that come to life in the flesh and are supported by the senses, why is the god who makes everything live and sense not also the one who gives life and sensation to the flesh, granting this function to births as part of his universal work?

And what need is there for Vitumnus and Sentinus? If the one who universally presides over life and the senses has entrusted these carnal functions, as it were to servants, as the lowest and most remote tasks, to them, are the select gods so bereft of attendants that they could not find anyone to whom they themselves might entrust these tasks, but, with all their nobility—which seemed to make them worthy of selection—were forced to work together with gods of no distinction?

Juno, the select goddess, queen, and sister and wife of Jupiter, is nevertheless *Iterduca* for children, and works together with the undistinguished goddesses Abeona and Adeona. They have also placed there the goddess Mens, who gives children a good mind; yet she is not included among the select gods, as though anything greater could be bestowed upon a human being.

Juno, however, is included because she is *Iterduca* and *Domiduca*, as though it were of any benefit to travel and be brought home if one does not have a good mind. The goddess of this gift these selectors did not place among the select deities.

Indeed, she ought to have been preferred even to Minerva, to whom they assigned memory through these minor operations performed for children. For who would doubt that having a good mind is much better than possessing a memory, however great? No one who has a good mind is evil; yet some of the worst people possess astonishing memories, and are all the worse because they are less able to forget the evil things they think.

Nevertheless, Minerva is among the select gods, while the goddess Mens has been buried beneath the crowd of inferior deities.

What shall I say about Virtue? What about Happiness? We have already said much about them in Book Four [Note: [Col. 0196] Namely, chapters 21 and 23.]. Although they regarded these as goddesses, they were unwilling to give them any place among the select gods, where they gave places to Mars and Orcus—to the one as the agent who causes deaths, to the other as the receiver of the dead.

### 2.

Since, then, in these minor operations—which have been distributed piecemeal among many gods—we see even the select gods working as though a senate were laboring alongside the common people, and we find that certain gods whom no one thought worthy of selection administer things much greater and better than those who are called select, it remains to suppose that they were called select and preeminent not because they administer more distinguished affairs in the world, but because it happened that they became better known to the peoples.

Hence Varro himself also says that, among certain father-gods and mother-goddesses, just as among human beings, lack of distinction had occurred.

If, then, Happiness perhaps ought not to have been among the select gods because those gods attained this distinction not by merit but by chance, at least Fortune should have been placed among them—or rather above them. They say that she is a goddess who distributes gifts to each person not according to a rational arrangement but as things happen at random. [Note: [Col. 0197] Lovaniensis reads *non irrationabili* (“not according to an irrational arrangement”); the other printed editions, supported by the manuscripts, read *non rationabili* (“not according to a rational arrangement”).]

She ought to have held the highest place among the select gods, among whom she displayed most clearly what she could do, since we see that they were selected not by outstanding virtue, not by rational happiness, but by the power of Fortune, recklessly, as their worshipers understand her.

For the eloquent Sallustius perhaps had even these gods in mind when he said:

> “But Fortune certainly rules over everything; she exalts and obscures all things more according to her caprice than according to truth.” [Note: [Col. 0197] *The War against Catiline*, chapter 8.]

For they cannot find a reason why Venus was exalted and Virtue obscured, since the divinities of both were consecrated by them and their merits are not comparable.

Or, if Venus deserved to be ennobled because more people desire her—for more people desire Venus than Virtue [Note: [Col. 0197] “Desire” is understood.]—why was the goddess Minerva exalted and the goddess Pecunia obscured, when avarice attracts more people in the human race than skill? Even among those who practice a craft, one rarely finds a person who does not put his art up for sale in exchange for money; and people always value more highly the thing for the sake of which something is done than the thing that is done for the sake of something else.

If, then, this selection of the gods was made according to the judgment of the foolish multitude, why was the goddess Pecunia not preferred to Minerva, since many craftsmen exist for the sake of money?

But if this distinction belongs to a few wise people, why was Virtue not preferred to Venus, since reason places Virtue far above her?

At least, as I have said, Fortune herself—who, according to those who attribute the greatest power to her, rules over everything and exalts and obscures all things more according to caprice than according to truth—if she had such power even over the gods that, by her reckless judgment, she could exalt whom she wished and obscure whom she wished, ought to have held the foremost place among the select gods, since she has such outstanding power even over the gods themselves.

Or, in order that she might not be there, must we suppose that Fortune herself had no other fortune than an adverse one? She was therefore adverse to herself, since, while making others noble, she was not herself ennobled.

## CHAPTER IV  
### The inferior gods were treated better, since no insults disgrace them, than the select gods, whose great disgraces are celebrated

Any lover of nobility and renown would congratulate these select gods and call them fortunate if he did not see that they had been selected more for insults than for honors. Their very lack of distinction has concealed that lowest crowd, so that they would not be overwhelmed by reproaches.

We do laugh when we see them divided among themselves according to the fabricated ideas of human beings and assigned separate tasks, like petty tax collectors [Note: [Col. 0197] Lovaniensis reads *minutularios*. The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and several manuscripts read *munuscularios*. Other older books have *minuscularios* here and below, in chapter 11.] or like craftsmen in a silversmiths’ quarter [Note: [Col. 0197] This refers to the district of the city inhabited by silversmiths. M.], where a single vessel passes through the hands of many craftsmen before it emerges as a finished product, although one skilled craftsman could have completed it.

Yet it was thought that the multitude of workers could not otherwise be accommodated except by having each of them quickly and easily learn a single part of the craft, lest they all be forced to become fully skilled in one craft slowly and with difficulty.

Nevertheless, scarcely any of the nonselect gods is found who has acquired an infamous reputation through some crime; whereas scarcely any of the select gods is found who has not received upon himself some mark of conspicuous disgrace. The former descended to the lowly tasks of the latter; the latter did not rise to the lofty crimes of the former.

Concerning Janus, I do not readily find anything that pertains to reproach. Perhaps he was such a being that he lived more innocently and kept farther away from crimes and scandals. He received Saturn, who was fleeing, with kindness. He shared the kingdom with his guest, so that they even founded separate cities [Note: [Col. 0198] Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 8, lines 357–358.]: Janus founded Janiculum, Saturn founded Saturnia.

But these people, eager for every kind of disgrace in the worship of the gods, because they found his life less shameful, disfigured him by the monstrous ugliness of his image, sometimes making him two-faced, sometimes even four-faced, as though he were double.

Or perhaps they wished that, since most of the select gods had lost their faces by perpetrating shameful deeds, the more innocent he was, the more “facied” he should appear?

## CHAPTER V  
### On the More Secret Teaching and Physical Explanations of the Pagans

But let us rather listen to their physical interpretations, by which they try to color the shamefulness of their wretched error with the appearance of a higher teaching.

First, Varro commends these interpretations in this way: he says that the ancients fashioned images, emblems, and adornments of the gods so that, when those who had approached the mysteries of the teaching observed them with their eyes, they could see in their minds the soul of the world and its parts—that is, the true gods.

Those who made images of them in human form, he says, seem to have followed this principle: that the human soul, which is in a human body, is very similar to the immortal soul. [Note: [Col. 0198] See Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 5, chapter 13.]

It is as though vessels were set up for the purpose of indicating the gods, and in the temple of Liber a wine vessel were placed to signify wine, by means of that which contains indicating what is contained. In the same way, an image possessing human form signifies the rational soul, because this nature—which they wish their god, or gods, to be—usually dwells in that form as in a vessel.

These are the mysteries of the teaching that this most learned man had penetrated, from which he brought these things into the light.

But, O most acute man, did you lose in these mysteries of teaching the prudence by which you soberly judged that those who first established images for the peoples both removed fear from their fellow citizens and added error, and that the ancient Romans had observed the gods more chastely without images? These men were your authorities, enabling you to dare to say such things against later Romans.

For if those most ancient Romans had also worshiped images, perhaps you would have suppressed in the silence of fear the whole argument about not establishing images—true for the present purpose [Note: [Col. 0198] The printed editions read *veri*; this is corrected from the manuscripts to *verum*.]—and proclaimed these mysteries of teaching more loudly and grandly in such destructive and empty fabrications.

Nevertheless, your soul, so learned and ingenious—which is where we deeply lament you—could not through these mysteries of teaching reach its God [Note: [Col. 0199] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts read *ad Deum suum* (“to its God”); Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *ad Deum summum* (“to the highest God”).], that is, the one by whom it was made, not the one with whom it was made; not the one of whom it is a portion, but the one whose creation it is; not the one who is the soul of all things, but the one who made every soul. Only when he illuminates it can the soul become blessed, provided it is not ungrateful for his grace.

What these mysteries of teaching are like, and how highly they should be valued, the following discussion will show.

For now, this most learned man admits that the soul of the world and its parts are the true gods. From this it is understood that his entire theology—namely, the natural theology to which he attributes the greatest importance—could extend only as far as the nature of the rational soul.

In this book he says very little in advance about the natural theology. We shall see whether, through physiological interpretations, he can refer to this natural theology the civil theology that he wrote last concerning the select gods.

If he can, then the whole thing will be natural theology; and what need was there to add civil theology to it with such careful distinction?

But if the two have been separated by a proper distinction, then, since even the natural theology that pleases him is not true—it reaches as far as the soul, but not as far as the true God who made the soul—how much more base and false is this civil theology, which is chiefly occupied with the nature of bodies! The interpretations themselves, some of which I must necessarily mention, will demonstrate this by the great care with which those people have sought them out and elucidated them. [Note: [Col. 0199] The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and the manuscripts read *necessaria* (“necessary”), rather than *necessario* (“necessarily”).]

## CHAPTER VI  
### On Varro’s Opinion That God Is the Soul of the World, Which Nevertheless Contains Many Souls in Its Parts, Whose Nature Is Divine

Thus, while still introducing the natural theology, Varro says that he thinks the god is the soul of the world, which the Greeks call κόσμος (*kosmos*), and that this very world is god. But just as a wise human being, although composed of body and soul, is nevertheless called wise because of the soul, so the world is called god because of the soul, although it is composed of soul and body.

Here he seems, in some fashion, to confess one God. But, in order to introduce many gods as well, he adds that the world is divided into two parts, heaven and earth; and that heaven is divided in two, into ether and air; while earth is divided into water and soil.

Of these, the ether is the highest, the air second, the water third, and the earth lowest. All these four parts are full of souls: immortal souls in the ether and air, mortal souls in the water and earth.

From the highest circuit of heaven down to the circle of the moon, the ethereal souls are the heavenly bodies and stars; they are not only understood to be the celestial gods but are also visible. [Note: [Col. 0199] The printed editions read *easque* (“and them”); most manuscripts read *eos* (“them,” referring to the heavenly bodies and stars).] Between the orbit of the moon and the summits of the clouds and winds are the aerial souls, but they are seen by the mind, not by the eyes. They are called heroes, household spirits, and genii.

This, evidently, is the natural theology briefly set forth in this introduction—a theology that pleased not only this man but many philosophers. It will have to be discussed more carefully when, with the assistance of the true God, I have completed what remains concerning civil theology as it relates to the select gods.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Whether It Was Reasonable to Separate Janus and Terminus into Two Deities

Janus, then, from whom he began, who exactly is he? The answer is: “He is the world.” This is plainly a brief and clear answer.

Why, then, are the beginnings of things said to belong to him, while their ends belong to another whom they call Terminus? For on account of beginnings and endings, they say that two months were dedicated to these two gods [Note: [Col. 0200] Plutarch, *Numa*.], in addition to the ten months whose first month, extending through December, is March: January to Janus, February to Terminus.

For this reason, they say that the Terminalia are celebrated in February, when the purifying rite takes place that they call *Februum* [Note: [Col. 0200] Several manuscripts of the best authority, together with the Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus, read *Februm*. This is perhaps not incorrect, although Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book 5, reads: “*Februum* among the Sabines means a purification, and in our sacred rites it is a word.”], from which the month received its name [Note: [Col. 0200] Plutarch, in the same work.].

Do beginnings of things, then, belong to the world, which is Janus, while endings do not belong to it, so that another god had to be placed in charge of them? Do they not admit that everything they say happens in this world is also brought to an end in this world?

What sort of vanity is this: to give him half-power in the work, but a double face in his image? Would they not have interpreted this two-faced figure much more elegantly if they had said that he was both Janus and Terminus, assigning one face to beginnings and the other to endings? For the one who performs an action must attend to both.

In every movement of his action, the person who does not consider the beginning does not foresee the end. Hence intention must be joined to memory that looks back and foresight that looks ahead. [Note: [Col. 0200] This is how all the manuscripts read; one of them, however, has *prospicientis* (“of foresight”) instead of *prospiciens* (“foresight”). The printed editions read *necesse est ut memoriae respicienti prospiciens*, and so forth.]

For if someone forgets what he began, how will he discover how to finish it?

If they supposed that the blessed life begins in this world but is completed beyond the world, and therefore assigned to Janus—that is, to the world—the power of beginnings alone, they would certainly have placed Terminus above him and would not have excluded Terminus from the select gods.

Even now, however, since the beginnings and endings of temporal things are handled by these two gods, Terminus ought to have been given greater honor. For there is greater joy when any matter is completed; beginnings, however, are full of anxiety until they are brought to their end. The person who begins something chiefly desires, pursues, awaits, and longs for its completion, and does not rejoice over an undertaking begun unless it is brought to an end.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### For What Reason the Worshipers of Janus Fashioned His Two-Faced Image, Which They Nevertheless Also Wish to Be Seen as Four-Faced

But now let the interpretation of the two-faced image be presented. They say that Janus has two faces, one in front and one behind, because our mouth, when we open it, appears similar to the world. Hence the Greeks also call the palate οὐρανός (*ouranos*, “heaven”); and, he says, certain Latin poets have called the palate “heaven.” From this opening of the mouth there is an entrance outward toward the teeth and inward toward the throat. [Note: [Col. 0201] See Ennius in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2.]

Behold how far the world has been brought on account of the name of our palate, whether Greek or poetic.

But what does this have to do with the soul? What does it have to do with eternal life? This god is worshiped merely because of saliva, for which, partly by swallowing and partly by spitting, the two gates beneath the heaven of the palate are opened.

What could be more absurd than to find no two opposite gates in the world itself through which it might either admit something into itself or send something out from itself, and then wish to construct an image of the world in Janus from our mouth and throat—which have no likeness to the world—on account of the palate alone, which Janus does not resemble?

When they make him four-faced and call him the double Janus, they interpret this as referring to the four regions of the world, as though the world looked outward through each face, just as Janus does through all his faces.

Moreover, if Janus is the world and the world consists of four regions, the image of the two-faced Janus is false [Note: [Col. 0201] After *Jani bifrontis* (“of the two-faced Janus”), the printed editions add: “because, although Janus is read as four-faced, he is never nevertheless found to be four-Janus.” This addition is absent from the manuscripts.].

Or, if it is true for the reason that the whole world is also customarily understood by the names East and West, then, when we name the other two regions, North and South, will anyone therefore call the world double, just as they call that four-faced figure the double Janus?

They have no basis at all for interpreting the four gates—which are open to those entering and leaving—as corresponding to the world, just as, in the case of the two-faced figure, they found at least in the human mouth something to say—unless Neptune should perhaps come to their aid and hold out a fish, whose jaws, in addition to the opening of its mouth and throat, also open to the right and left.

And yet no soul escapes this vanity through so many gates except the soul that hears the Truth saying, “I am the gate” (John 10:9). [Note: [Col. 0201] The printed editions repeat here the addition concerning the two-faced Janus mentioned above; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER IX  
### On the Power of Jupiter and His Comparison with Janus

### 1.

Let them explain whom they wish Jupiter—who is also called Jupiter—to be. [Note: [Col. 0201] *Jovis* and *Jupiter* were originally both used in the nominative; usage eventually established *Jovis* in the oblique cases and *Jupiter* in the nominative.]

“He is a god,” they say, “who possesses power over the causes by which something comes to be in the world.”

How great this is, that most famous line of Virgil testifies:

Happy is he who has been able to learn the causes of things. (Georgics, Book 2, line 490.)

But why is Janus placed before him? Let that exceptionally sharp and learned man answer us. “Because,” he says, “the beginnings belong to Janus, but the highest things belong to Jupiter.” Jupiter is therefore rightly regarded as king of all. For beginnings are surpassed by what is highest: although beginnings precede in time, the highest things surpass them in dignity.

But this would be correctly said if the beginnings and highest points of actions were distinguished, as when the beginning of an action is setting out, while its culmination is arriving; or when the beginning of an action is beginning to learn, while its culmination is acquiring knowledge. Thus, in every case, beginnings are starting points, and culminations are [Note: [Col. 0201] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “and the culminations are.”] endpoints.

But this matter has already been debated between Janus and Terminus. The causes attributed to Jupiter, however, are efficient causes, not effects; nor can they in any way precede in time either completed actions or the beginnings of actions. For the thing that causes is always prior to the thing that is caused. Therefore, if the beginnings of actions belong to Janus, they are not for that reason prior to the efficient causes attributed to Jupiter. For just as nothing comes to be, so nothing begins to come to be unless a causing agent has preceded it.

If the people call this god, in whose power are all the causes of all created and natural things, “Jupiter,” and worship him with such great insults and such criminal accusations, they bind themselves to a more heinous sacrilege than if they believed absolutely that there were no god. It would therefore be better for them to call some other being “Jupiter,” one worthy of disgraceful and shameful honors, attaching to him the empty fiction that they would rather blaspheme—as the stone is said to have been substituted for Saturn, which he was to devour in place of his son—than to call this being a god who thunders and commits adultery, who rules the whole world while wallowing in every kind of sexual outrage, who possesses the highest causes of all created and natural things, yet does not possess good causes of his own.

2. Next I ask what place they now assign among the gods to this Jupiter, if Janus is the world. For Varro defined the true gods as the world-soul and its parts; and consequently, according to them, whatever is not this is certainly not a true god.

Will they therefore say that Jupiter is the world-soul, so that Janus is its body—that is, this visible world? If they say this, there will be no way for them to call Janus a god, since even according to them the body of the world is not a god, but only the world-soul and its parts. Accordingly, the same author says most explicitly that he considers the god to be the world-soul, and this very world to be god; but just as a wise human being, although composed of soul and body, is nevertheless called wise from the soul, so the world is called god from the soul, although it is composed of soul and body.

The body of the world alone, then, is not god; either its soul alone is god, or its body and soul together—but in such a way that it is god not from the body but from the soul. If, then, Janus is the world, and Janus is a god, will they say that Jupiter, in order to be a god, is some part of Janus? They are more accustomed to attribute the universe to Jupiter. Hence the saying:

> All things are full of Jupiter.

[Note: [Col. 0202] Virgil translated this verse in Eclogue 3, line 60, from the beginning of Aratus’s *Phaenomena*. Aratus said that Jupiter is full of all things, in accordance with the Stoic view, who understood the world-soul to permeate the universe. LARCHER.]

Thus, in order for Jupiter to be a god, and especially king of the gods, they cannot regard him as anything other than the world, so that, according to them, he rules over the other gods as over his own parts.

Varro also interprets several verses of Valerius Soranus in this sense, in the book that he wrote separately on the worship of the gods. The verses are these:

> Almighty Jupiter, king of kings, things, and gods,  
> Progenitor and progenitress of the gods, one god and all things.

[Note: [Col. 0202] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erfurtensis read: “king of kings, himself god.”]

In that same book these verses are explained as follows: they believed that the male was the one who emitted seed, and the female the one who received it; and that Jupiter is the world, which emits all seeds from itself and receives them into itself. “For this reason,” he says, “Soranus wrote, ‘Jupiter, progenitor and progenitress’; and, with no less reason, ‘the one and all,’ because the world is one, and all things are in that one.”

## CHAPTER X — Whether Janus and Jupiter are correctly distinguished

Since Janus is the world, and Jupiter is the world, and the world is one, why are Janus and Jupiter two gods? Why do they have separate temples, separate altars, different rites, and unlike images?

If the reason is that the power of beginnings is one thing and the power of causes another, and that the former received the name Janus while the latter received the name Jupiter, then if one human being possessed two powers or two skills in different matters, would they therefore be called two judges or two craftsmen merely because the power of each skill was different?

So too, when one God himself possesses power over beginnings and over causes, must we therefore suppose that he is two gods because beginnings and causes are two things?

If they think this reasonable, let them also say that Jupiter himself is as many gods as the surnames they have given him on account of his many powers. For all the things from which these surnames were derived are many and diverse. I shall mention a few.

## CHAPTER XI — The surnames of Jupiter, which refer not to many gods but to one and the same god

They called him Victor, Unconquered, Helper, Impeller, Stayer, Centumpedus, Supinalis, Beam, Nourisher, Ruminus, and others whose enumeration would be lengthy.

[Note: [Col. 0203] Ambrosianus and Erfurtensis read *Alinus*. See Aristotle, *On the World*, chapter 7. Ludovicus Vives enumerates these and many others.]

They gave these surnames to one god because of different causes and powers, yet they did not thereby force him to be as many gods as there were things involved: because he conquered everything; because no one conquered him; because he brought help to those in need; because he possessed the power to impel, halt, establish, and overturn; because, like a beam, he held together and supported the world; because he nourished all things; and because, as *ruma* means “udder,” he nourished animals.

As we have observed, some of these matters are great and some insignificant; yet he is said to perform both. I think that the causes of things and their beginnings are more closely related to each other—on account of which they wanted one world to be two gods, Jupiter and Janus—than are holding up the world and giving an udder to animals.

[Note: [Col. 0203] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads: “whom they say holds up the world.”] Yet they were not compelled to make two gods on account of these two activities, so greatly different in power and dignity. Rather, one Jupiter was called *Tigillus* for the one and *Ruminus* for the other.

I do not wish to say that providing an udder for suckling animals might have suited Juno more than Jupiter, especially since there was also the goddess Rumina, who could provide assistance or service to him in this task.

For I realize that it could be answered that Juno herself is nothing other than Jupiter, according to those verses of Valerius Soranus in which it is said:

> Almighty Jupiter, father of kings, things, and gods,  
> Progenitor and progenitress of the gods.

Why, then, was he also called Ruminus, when more careful inquiry might reveal that he himself is also that goddess Rumina? If it seemed rightly unworthy of the majesty of the gods for one deity to be assigned responsibility for the node of an ear of grain and another for its husk, then how much more unworthy is it

[Note: [Col. 0204] The printed editions here also read “another”; the manuscripts read “another [goddess],” namely Volutina. See above, Book 4, chapter 8.] for one lowly matter—that animals should be nourished at the breast—to be cared for by the power of two gods, one of whom is Jupiter, himself king of all, and for him to perform this task not at least with his wife, but with some obscure Rumina—unless he himself is also Rumina herself?

[Note: [Col. 0204] The printed editions add here: “he himself, Ruminus”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]

Perhaps *Ruminus* was used for male sucklings and *Rumina* for females? I would say that they did not wish to impose a feminine name on Jupiter, were it not that in those verses he is called both progenitor and progenitress. Moreover, among his other surnames I find that he was also called Pecunia; and among those minor deities we find the goddess Pecunia, whom we mentioned in Book 4, chapter 21.

But since both males and females possess money, let them decide for themselves why he was not called both Pecunia and Pecunius, just as he was called Rumina and Ruminus.

## CHAPTER XII — That Jupiter is also called Pecunia

How elegantly, indeed, did they give the reason for this name! “He is also called Pecunia,” they say, “because everything belongs to him.”

[Note: [Col. 0204] On the word *pecunia*, see Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, no. 6.]

What a great explanation of a divine name! Rather, the one to whom everything belongs is most basely and insultingly called Pecunia. For, in relation to everything contained in heaven and earth, what is money among all the things that human beings possess under the name of money?

Clearly, avarice gave Jupiter this name, so that whoever loves money might seem to love not just any god, but the king of all.

It would be quite different if he were called “Riches,” for riches are one thing and money another. We call people rich, wise, just, and good even when they possess no money or only a little. They are richer in the virtues by which, even amid the necessities of bodily things, what they have is sufficient for them. But we call the avaricious poor: they are always gaping with desire and always in need. They may possess very large sums of money, but however abundant their money, they cannot avoid being in need.

We rightly call the true God rich—not in money, but in omnipotence. Thus people who possess money are called rich, but inwardly they are needy if they are greedy. Likewise, those who lack money are called poor, but inwardly they are rich if they are wise.

What sort of theology, then, ought this to be for a wise person, when the king of the gods has received the name of a thing that no wise person has ever desired?

[Note: [Col. 0204] Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 11.]

For how much more easily, if something conducive to eternal life were taught beneficially in this doctrine, would the god who rules the world be called not “Money” by them but “Wisdom”—whose love purifies one from the filth of avarice, that is, from the love of money?

## CHAPTER XIII — While Saturn and Genius are explained, both are shown to be one Jupiter

[Col. 0205]

But why say more about this Jupiter, to whom perhaps the other gods must be referred, so that the belief in a multitude of gods may prove empty, since this one god himself is all of them?

[Note: [Col. 0205] Several manuscripts read: “since they themselves are all.”]

This is so whether they are thought to be his parts or powers, or whether the force of the soul—which they believe to be diffused through all things—receives, from the parts of this mass from which the visible world arises and from the manifold administration of nature, the names of several gods.
