For what is Saturn? “One of the principal gods,” he says, “in whose power lies dominion over all sowings.” Is this not the interpretation of those verses of Valerius Soranus, according to which Jupiter is the world, which emits all seeds from itself and receives them into itself? He, therefore, is the one in whose power lies dominion over all sowings.

What is Genius? “The god,” he says, “who has been placed in charge of and possesses the power of generating all things.” Whom else do they believe to possess this power than the world, to which it was said: “Jupiter, progenitor and progenitress”?

And when elsewhere he says that Genius is the rational spirit of each individual, and that therefore there is a separate genius for each individual, but that the spirit of the world is god, he brings the matter back to the same point: the spirit of the world is to be believed to be Genius in a universal sense.

This, then, is the one they call Jupiter. For if every genius is a god, and every man’s spirit is a genius, it follows that every man’s spirit is a god. But if the absurdity itself forces them to recoil from this conclusion, it remains for them to say that the genius who is god in a singular and eminent sense is the one whom they call the spirit of the world, and therefore Jupiter.

## CHAPTER XIV — The functions of Mercury and Mars

They could not find a way to refer Mercury and Mars to some part of the world or to some work of God—things that exist in the elements. Therefore, at least, they placed them in charge of human activities, as ministers of speech and warfare.

[Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “ministers.”]

If Mercury possesses power even over the speech of the gods, then he also rules over the king of the gods, if Jupiter speaks according to Mercury’s will or received from him the ability to speak. But this is surely absurd.

If Mercury is said to have been assigned power only over human speech, it is not believable that Jupiter wished to descend to nurse at the breast not only children but also cattle—for which he was surnamed Ruminus—while refusing to take responsibility for our speech, by which we surpass cattle. Consequently, Jupiter and Mercury are the same god.

But if speech itself is said to be Mercury, as the interpretations given about him show—for he is said to have been called Mercury as though “running between” (*medius currens*), because speech runs between human beings [Note: [Col. 0205] In Arnobius, *Against the Pagans*, Book 3: “as though *medicur* [lacuna].”]; and for this reason he is called *Hermes* in Greek, because speech or interpretation, which certainly pertains to speech, is called *hermēneia* (ἑρμηνεία); and for this reason he is also placed in charge of merchandise, because speech mediates between sellers and buyers; and the wings on his head and feet are intended to signify that speech is borne swiftly through the air [Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “For this reason they put wings on his head and feet, wishing to signify …”]; and he is called the messenger because all thoughts are announced through speech—then, if Mercury himself is speech, even by their own admission he is not a god.

Yet they make gods for themselves out of beings who are not even demons, while, by supplicating unclean spirits, they are possessed by those who are not gods but demons.

Likewise, since they could not find any element or part of the world in which Mars might carry out works of any kind belonging to nature, they called him the god of war, although war is a human activity and not something desirable for human beings.

If Felicitas granted perpetual peace, Mars would have nothing to do. But if Mars himself is war, just as Mercury is speech, then—would that it were as clear that war is not a god as it is that Mars is not one, even if war is falsely called a god.

## CHAPTER XV — Certain stars to which the Pagans gave the names of their gods

Unless perhaps those stars are the gods, since they named them after those gods: for they call one star Mercury and another likewise Mars.

But there is also the star they call Jupiter; yet for them the world is Jupiter. There is also the star they call Saturn; yet in addition they assign to him a considerable substance, namely that of all seeds.

There is also the brightest of all, which they call Venus; yet they also want the same Venus to be the Moon, although, concerning that most brilliant heavenly body, they contend among themselves as though over the golden apple—Juno and Venus.

Some say that the morning star is Venus’s, while others say that it is Juno’s; but, as usual, Venus wins. For many more assign that star to Venus, so that scarcely anyone among them can be found who thinks otherwise.

Who, then, would not laugh when they call Jupiter king of all, even though his star is so greatly surpassed in brightness by Venus’s star?

[Note: [Col. 0206] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads “since,” in place of “because.”]

For Jupiter’s star ought to have been brighter than the others to the same degree that Jupiter himself is more powerful.

They reply that it appears so because the star thought to be dimmer is higher and much farther from the earth. If, then, the higher position deserved greater dignity, why is Saturn higher than Jupiter there?

Could the vanity of the myth that makes Jupiter king not reach as far as the stars? And what Saturn could not obtain in his own kingdom or in the Capitol, was he at least allowed to retain in heaven?

[Note: [Col. 0206] Saturn could not obtain it in his own kingdom, since he is said to have been expelled from Crete by his son Jupiter; nor in the Capitol, because although he had occupied the Capitoline Hill, where Saturnia had been founded, that hill later became sacred to Jupiter.]

Why, moreover, did Janus not receive a star? If the reason is that he is the world and all things are in him, then Jupiter is also the world, yet Jupiter has a star. Or did Janus arrange his case as best he could, and, in compensation for the one star he lacks among the constellations, receive so many faces on earth?

Furthermore, if they regard Mercury and Mars as parts of the world only because of their stars, so that they can have them as gods—since speech and war are certainly not parts of the world but human activities—why did they make no altars, sacred rites, or temples for Aries, Taurus, Cancer, Scorpio, and the other signs of this kind, which they count among the heavenly signs and which consist not of individual stars but of several stars?

They say that these signs are placed higher than Mercury and Mars in the highest heaven, where the more constant motion gives the stars their unerring course.

[Note: [Col. 0207] The Lovaniensis edition reads “these,” while other printed editions and the manuscripts read “them.”]

Why, then, did they not regard these signs as gods—not merely among the select gods, but not even among the common or plebeian gods?

## CHAPTER XVI — Apollo, Diana, and the other select gods whom they wanted to be parts of the world

Although they want Apollo to be a diviner and physician, they nevertheless said that he is the sun itself, so that they could place him in some part of the world. They likewise made Diana his sister, the moon, and the protectress of roads.

Hence they want her to be a virgin, because a road produces nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0207] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads “because it produces nothing,” omitting the word “road.”]

For this reason, too, they both have arrows: the two heavenly bodies extend their rays from heaven all the way to the earth.

They want Vulcan to be the fire of the world, Neptune the waters of the world, and Father Dis—that is, Orcus—to be the earthly and lowest part of the world.

They place Liber and Ceres in charge of seeds, Liber over male seeds and Ceres over female seeds; or Liber over liquid and Ceres over the dryness of seeds.

[Note: [Col. 0207] See Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book 3, §§ 59, 66.]

And all this is referred to the world, that is, to Jupiter, who was therefore called “progenitor and progenitress,” because he emitted all seeds from himself and received them into himself.

Indeed, they also want the Great Mother to be the same as Ceres, whom they say is nothing other than the earth; and they also identify her with Juno. Therefore they assign to her the secondary causes of things, although Jupiter was called “progenitor and progenitress of the gods,” because according to them the whole world itself is Jupiter.

They also said that Minerva, because they placed her in charge of human arts, was either the highest ether or even the moon, since they could not find a star in which to place her.

[Note: [Col. 0207] Manuscript 2050 reads “minds” (*mentibus*).]

[Note: [Col. 0207] Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3, chapter 11, translated by us into French in *Démonstrations évangéliques*, vol. 1. M.]

They also thought Vesta herself the greatest of the goddesses for the reason that she is the earth, although they believed that the lighter fire of the world, which serves ordinary human uses, should be assigned to her rather than the more violent fire belonging to Vulcan.

[Note: [Col. 0207] See Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book 1, chapter 12.]

Consequently, they want all these select gods to be this world: in some cases the whole world, and in others parts of it. The whole world is Jupiter; its parts include Genius, the Great Mother, the Sun and Moon—or rather Apollo and Diana.

[Note: [Col. 0207] The manuscripts read: “the Sun or Moon; or rather …”]

Sometimes they make one god into several things, and sometimes several gods into one thing.

One god is several things, as in the case of Jupiter: the whole world is regarded as Jupiter, and so are heaven alone and the star alone.

Likewise, Juno is mistress of the secondary causes, Juno is the air, Juno is the earth, and—if she had defeated Venus—Juno would be the star.

[Note: [Col. 0207] “Had defeated,” presumably in the contest over the morning star, which, as he observed in the preceding chapter, some say belongs to Juno.]

Similarly, Minerva is the highest ether, and Minerva is also the moon, which they believe to be located at the lowest boundary of the ether.

But they make one thing into several gods in this way: Janus is the world, and Jupiter is the world; likewise Juno is the earth, the Great Mother, and Ceres.

## CHAPTER XVII — That Varro himself declared his opinions about the gods to be uncertain

Just as with these examples I have mentioned, so with the rest: they do not explain matters but rather entangle them. As the impulse of their wandering opinion drives them, they leap and recoil here and there, this way and that, so that Varro himself preferred to doubt everything rather than affirm anything.

After completing the first book of the three final books, concerning the certain gods, he began in the second to discuss the uncertain gods and said:

“When I set down uncertain opinions about the gods in this little book, I ought not to be criticized. Anyone who thinks that judgments ought to be made and can be made will make that judgment himself when he has heard me. I can more readily be brought to call into question what I said in the first book than to direct everything I shall write in this book toward some unified conclusion.”

[Note: [Col. 0208] The manuscripts read: “to prescribe everything, so that I may direct some conclusion,” omitting “toward.”]

Thus he made not only the book on the uncertain gods uncertain, but also the book on the certain gods.

Then, in this third book, on the select gods, after prefacing what he thought ought to be said from the standpoint of natural theology, as he was about to enter upon the vanities and mendacious insanities of civil theology—

[Note: [Col. 0208] He alludes to Psalm 39:5.]

—where he was guided not by the truth of things but also constrained by the authority of his ancestors, he said:

“Concerning the public gods of the Roman people, to whom they have dedicated temples and whom they have marked out by adorning them with numerous images, I shall write in this book. But, as Xenophanes of Colophon writes, I shall set down what I think, not what I maintain. For it belongs to a human being to form opinions, but to God to know.”

He therefore timidly promises a discourse concerning matters not comprehended, not firmly believed, but merely conjectured and doubted; he is going to discuss things established by human beings.

For, just as he knew that the world exists, that heaven and earth exist, that heaven shines with stars, that earth is fertile with seeds, and other matters of this kind; and just as he firmly believed that this entire mass and nature is ruled and administered by some invisible and exceedingly powerful force, so he could not affirm that Janus was the world itself, or discover how Saturn was both the father of Jupiter and made subject to the ruling Jupiter, along with other matters of this kind.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The more credible explanation of how the error of Paganism became established

A more credible explanation of these matters is given when the supposed gods are said to have been human beings, and when those who wished to flatter them by calling them gods established sacred rites and ceremonies for each of them according to his character, conduct, deeds, and experiences.

These rites gradually infiltrated human minds, which were like demons and eager for frivolous things, and were spread far and wide.

[Note: [Col. 0208] The printed editions read “they spread them.” The manuscripts provide the corrected reading.]

The rites were embellished by the falsehoods of poets, and deceptive spirits led people astray through them.

For it could more easily have happened that an impious young man, fearing to be killed by his impious father and desiring royal power, drove his father from the kingdom than that Saturn’s son Jupiter overcame his father for the reason given by this interpreter: namely, because the cause belonging to Jupiter precedes the seed belonging to Saturn.

For if this were so, Saturn would never have been prior, nor would he have been Jupiter’s father. A seed is always preceded by its cause, and it is never generated from a seed.

But when people attempt to dignify utterly empty myths—whether stories of human deeds or events—as though they were natural interpretations, even the sharpest minds suffer such great difficulties that we are compelled to grieve over their folly as well.

## CHAPTER XIX — The interpretations by which a rationale for the worship of Saturn is contrived

“Saturn,” he says, “was said to devour whatever was born from him, because seeds returned to the place from which they were born. And the clod of earth that was offered to him to devour in place of Jupiter signifies,” he says, “that people began to cover the crops with human hands by sowing them before the usefulness of plowing had been discovered.”

Saturn, then, ought to have been called the earth itself, not the seeds. For in a certain sense the earth devours what it has produced, when the seeds born from it return to be received back into it.

And what bearing does the claim that he received a clod in place of Jupiter have on the fact that human hands covered seed with a clod? Was the seed therefore not devoured, as the other things were, because it was covered with a clod?

The account is told as though the person who placed the clod there had removed the seed, just as they say that Jupiter was removed from Saturn when the clod was offered to him; rather than that, by covering the seed, the clod caused it to be devoured more thoroughly.

Furthermore, in this interpretation the seed is Jupiter, not the cause of the seed, as was said shortly before.

But what can people do who, when interpreting foolish matters, cannot find anything wise to say?

“He has a sickle,” he says, “because of agriculture.” Yet agriculture did not exist during his reign; and for that reason his period is said to have been earlier, according to the interpretation of the same author’s little tales, because the first human beings lived from the seeds that the earth produced spontaneously.

Or did he receive the sickle after losing his scepter, so that he who had been an idle king in the earliest times became a hardworking laborer when his son was king?

Next, he says that some peoples used to sacrifice children to him, as did the Carthaginians, and that some even sacrificed adults, as did the Gauls, because the human race is the best kind of all seeds.

[Note: [Col. 0209] Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 4, chapter 16, in *Démonstrations évangéliques*, vol. 1. M.]

What need is there to say more about this most savage folly?

Let us rather observe and hold firmly to this: these interpretations do not refer to the true God, a living, incorporeal, and unchangeable nature, from whom blessed life for eternity must be requested. Their limits lie instead in bodily, temporal, mutable, and mortal things.

“The fact,” he says, “that Saturn is said in the myths to have castrated his father Heaven signifies that divine seed belongs to Saturn, not to Heaven.”

This is apparently because nothing is born in heaven from seeds.

But consider: if Saturn is the son of Heaven, he is also the son of Jupiter.

[Col. 0210]

For they assert innumerable times and with great care that Heaven is Jupiter.

[Note: [Col. 0210] The Lovaniensis edition reads “unchangeably,” but the other printed editions and the manuscripts read “innumerably.”]

[Note: [Col. 0210] See Eusebius, cited passage, Book 3, chapters 3 and 10. M.]

Thus matters that do not proceed from truth often overturn themselves without anyone forcing them to do so.

He says that Saturn was called *Kronos* (Κρόνος), a Greek word meaning a span or extent of time; “without time,” he says, “seed cannot be fertile.”

Many other things are said about Saturn, and everything is referred to seed. But surely Saturn alone ought to have been sufficient for seeds with all this power. Why are the other gods required for these matters, especially Liber and Libera, that is, Ceres? Concerning them he again says so much about seed that one would think he had said nothing about Saturn.

## CHAPTER XX — The rites of Ceres of Eleusis

Among the rites of Ceres, those Eleusinian rites are especially celebrated, which were most renowned among the Athenians.

[Note: [Col. 0210] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Lovaniensis read “Eleusina.”]

Varro interprets nothing about them except what concerns grain, which Ceres discovered, and Proserpina, whom she lost when Orcus carried her off.

He says that Proserpina herself signifies the fertility of seeds. When this fertility had failed at a certain time and the earth was grieving under the same sterility, the belief arose that Orcus had carried away the daughter of Ceres—that is, fertility itself—which was called Proserpina from *proserpere*, “to creep or spring forth”—and had detained her in the underworld.

When this event had been publicly mourned, because the same fertility returned, joy arose when Proserpina was restored, and ceremonies were established on that account.

He then says that many things are handed down in her mysteries which concern nothing except the discovery of crops.

## CHAPTER XXI — The obscenity of the rites celebrated for Liber

As for the rites of Liber, whom they placed in charge of liquid seeds—and therefore not only of the liquids of fruits, among which wine holds a kind of primacy, but also of the seeds of animals—it is indeed shameful to say to what obscenity they proceeded because of the length of the discussion; yet, because of the arrogant stupidity of these people, I am not ashamed to say it.

Among the other matters that I am forced to pass over because they are numerous, Varro says that in the crossroads of Italy certain rites of Liber were celebrated with such unrestrained obscenity that the male sexual organ was worshiped in his honor—not in some modestly secluded place, but openly, with depravity rejoicing.

During the festivals of Liber this shameful organ was placed on little carts with great honor and carried first through the countryside to the crossroads, and afterward all the way into the city.

At Lavinium, moreover, an entire month was assigned to Liber. During its days everyone used the most shameful language, until the organ had been carried through the forum and set down in its proper place.

[Note: [Col. 0210] Some manuscripts read *Lavino*. But many manuscripts of good authority read *Lanvino*, perhaps for *Lanuvino*. In Horace, *Odes*, Book 3, ode 27, line 3, one finds *agro Lanuvino*. Sigonius discusses the difference between the towns of Lanuvium and Lavinium in his commentary on Livy, Book 8, chapter 14.]

A most honorable married woman was required to place a crown publicly upon that dishonorable organ.

[Col. 0211]

Thus, apparently, the god Liber had to be appeased for the fertility of seeds; thus fascination was to be driven away from the fields, by forcing a married woman to do in public what not even a prostitute ought to have been permitted to do in a theater if married women were watching.

[Note: [Col. 0211] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erfurtensis, and several manuscripts read “for the outcomes of the seeds.”]

For these reasons Saturn alone was believed unable to suffice for seeds, so that the unclean soul might find opportunities to multiply gods. Deprived, because of its uncleanness, of the one true God, and prostituted among many false gods by its appetite for greater uncleanness, that soul called these sacrileges sacred rites and offered itself to be violated and polluted by crowds of filthy demons.

## CHAPTER XXII — Neptune, Salacia, and Venilia

Neptune already had Salacia as his wife, whom they said was the lower water of the sea. Why was Venilia also added to her, unless it was so that, without any reason grounded in necessary rites, the invitation to demons might be multiplied solely through the lust of a prostituted soul?

But let the interpretation of this distinguished theology be brought forward, an interpretation that may restrain us from such criticism by providing a rationale.

“Venilia,” he says, “is the wave that comes to the shore; Salacia is the wave that returns to the open sea.”

[Note: [Col. 0211] He alludes to Psalm 77:39.]

Why, then, are two goddesses made when there is one wave that comes and returns?

Clearly, it is the same insane lust, surging into many divinities. Although the water that goes and returns is not doubled, the soul is nevertheless further polluted by this occasion of vanity, when two demons are invited—the soul that goes and does not return.

I ask you, Varro—or you who have read such writings by such learned men and boast that you have learned something important—to interpret this, not, I will not say, according to that eternal and unchangeable nature which alone is God, but at least according to the world-soul and its parts, which you consider true gods.

That you made Neptune the part of the world-soul that permeates the sea is an error that is at least somewhat more tolerable. But is a wave coming to the shore and returning to the open sea two parts of the world, or two parts of the world-soul?

Who among you is so foolish as to regard this as wisdom?

Why, then, did they make two goddesses for you, unless your wise ancestors took care—not that more gods should rule you, but that more demons should possess you, since they delight in these vanities and falsehoods?

But why did Salacia, according to this interpretation, lose the lower part of the sea, to which she had been subject as a wife? For when you describe her as the returning wave, you have now placed her on the surface.

Or was it because, having accepted Venilia as a concubine, she angrily shut her husband out of the upper regions of the sea?

## CHAPTER XXIII — The Earth, which Varro confirms to be a goddess because the world-soul that he believes to be god also permeates this lowest part of its body and imparts divine power to it
1. There is, to be sure, one earth, which we see filled with its own animals; yet, since it is itself a great body, the lowest part among the elements and of the universe, why do they wish to make it a goddess? Is it because it is fertile? Why, then, are human beings not rather gods, since by cultivating it they make it more fertile—when they plow it, not when they worship it?

“But,” they say, “the part of the soul of the universe that pervades it makes it a goddess.” As though the soul in human beings were not more evident—there being no question whether it exists—and yet human beings are not regarded as gods. And, what is gravely lamentable, human beings, who are not gods and are themselves superior to those beings, are subjected, in a remarkable and pitiable error, to their worship and adoration.

Indeed, Varro himself, in the same book *On the Selected Gods*, asserts that there are three degrees of soul in the whole of nature. The first passes through all the living parts of the body and has no sensation, but only the power of health necessary for living. He says that this power pervades our body in the bones, nails, and hair; just as, in the universe, trees without sensation are nourished and grow, and in their own way live.

The second degree of soul is that in which sensation exists. This power reaches the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, and sense of touch.

The third degree of soul is the highest, which is called *animus* [mind], in which understanding predominates. He says that all mortals except the human being lack this [Note: [Col. 0212] So read our manuscripts. In B., “which is called *animus*.” M.]. [Note: [Col. 0212] The printed editions add here: “in which, since human beings seem to be like God”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]

He says that this part of the soul of the universe is god, but that in us it is called a Genius. In the universe, however, there are stones and the earth that we see, through which sensation does not pervade, just as it does not pervade the bones and nails of a god. But the sun, moon, and stars—which we perceive and by which the universe itself perceives—are its sensation. The ether, moreover, is its mind. Through the power of the latter, which reaches the stars, it also makes them gods; and through that which pervades the earth, it makes the goddess Tellus; while that which from there pervades the sea and ocean is the god Neptune [Note: [Col. 0212] In earlier editions, after “Genius is called,” the passage read as follows: “Thus, then, establishing three degrees in the soul of the universe, he says that one part of it consists of stones and pieces of wood, and this earth that we see, through which sensation does not pervade; another he calls its sensation, such as the ether; and the third he calls its soul, which evidently reaches the stars. He asserts that this too makes gods, and that through it, when it pervades the earth, it makes the goddess Tellus, while that which from there passes through the sea and ocean is the god Neptune.” The reading we have preferred is found in all or the better-quality manuscripts.]

2. Let him therefore return from this theology, which he thinks natural, and from which, as though for the sake of resting, he emerged exhausted by these labyrinths and winding passages. Let him return, I say—let him return to the civic theology. Here I still hold him; for the moment I am dealing with this matter.

I am not yet saying that, if the earth and stones resemble our bones and nails, they likewise have no understanding, just as they lack sensation; or that, if our bones and nails are said to have understanding for the reason that they are in a human being who possesses understanding, then the person who calls these things gods in the universe is as foolish as one who calls the bones and nails within us human beings. Perhaps these matters should be discussed with the philosophers. For now, however, I still want this man as a politician [Note: [Col. 0212] The printed editions add, “that is, as a civic theologian.” This gloss is absent from the manuscripts.].

For it may be that, although he seems to have wished to raise his head slightly into the apparent freedom of natural theology, nevertheless, while still turning over this book and thinking that he is occupied with it, he also looked back from there toward civic theology. He may have said this so that his ancestors—or other cities—would not be thought to have worshiped Tellus and Neptune without reason.

But this is what I say: if the part of the world-soul that pervades the earth is one, just as the earth is one, why did it not also make one goddess, whom he says is Tellus? And if it did so, where will Orcus be, the brother of Jupiter and Neptune, whom they call Father Dis [Note: [Col. 0213] Above, chapter 16]? Where will be his wife Proserpina, who, according to another opinion set down in the same books, is said to be not the fertility of the earth but its lower part [Note: [Col. 0213] Ibid. See Varro, book 5 of *On the Latin Language*, § 68.]?

If they say that, when the part of the world-soul pervades the upper part of the earth, it makes the god Father Dis, but when it pervades the lower part, it makes the goddess Proserpina, what will that Tellus be? For the whole of what she herself was has thus been divided between these two parts and gods, so that it is impossible to discover what the third part is or where it is—unless someone says that Orcus and Proserpina together are the one goddess Tellus, and that there are no longer three but either one or two. Yet they are called three, regarded as three, and worshiped as three, with their own altars, shrines, rites, images, and priests; and through all this they also defile the soul, prostituted to their deceptive demons, who violate it.

Let it still be answered what part of the earth the part of the world-soul pervades in order to make the god Tellumo. “Not so,” he says, “but the one and same earth has a twofold power: a masculine power, because it produces seeds, and a feminine power, because it receives and nourishes them. Hence Tellus is said to derive her name from the feminine power, and Tellumo from the masculine.”

Why, then, do the pontiffs, as he himself indicates, after adding two others, make a divine offering to four gods—to Tellus, Tellumo, Altor, and Rūsor? Tellus and Tellumo have already been discussed. Why Altor? “Because,” he says, “everything that is born is nourished from the earth.” Why Rūsor? “Because,” he says, “everything returns again to the same place.”

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the surnames of Tellus and their meanings, which, even if they indicated many things, ought not to have confirmed belief in many gods

1. One earth ought therefore, on account of this fourfold power [Note: [Col. 0213] Most and better manuscripts, including Vind. and Am., read “fourfold power” (*quatergeminam vim*).], to have four surnames, not to make four gods—just as there is one Jupiter with so many surnames and one Juno with so many surnames. In all these cases, a plurality of powers is said to belong to one god or one goddess; the plurality of surnames does not produce a plurality of gods.

But surely, just as even the most worthless women whom men have pursued out of lust sometimes become weary of and repent their crowds of lovers, so the soul, made worthless and prostituted to unclean spirits, first multiplied gods for itself, before whom it might be thrown down to be defiled as often as it pleased, and then at times became weary of this as well.

For Varro himself, as though embarrassed by that very crowd, wants Tellus to be one goddess. “They call her,” he says, “the Great Mother. The fact that she has a drum signifies that she is the globe of the earth; the towers on her head signify cities; the seats fashioned around her signify that, while all things move, she herself does not move. The fact that they made the Galli serve this goddess signifies that those who lack seed ought to follow the earth, since everything is found in it.” [Col. 0214]

[Note: [Col. 0214] This note is printed at the foot of column 214, but its callout number, 2, does not appear in the text. “A little later,” most manuscripts read “who make,” rather than “which happens”; the passage is obscure and corrupt.]

“As for their leaping and throwing themselves about before her,” he says, “this teaches those who cultivate the earth not to sit still, since there is always something for them to do. The sound of cymbals, the tossing of tools, the movement of hands, and the clatter produced by this activity signify what occurs in cultivating the field. Hence bronze is used, because the ancients worshiped her with bronze before iron had been discovered.

“They add a lion, untethered and tamed, in order to show that no kind of earth is so remote and exceedingly wild that it ought not to be subdued and cultivated.”

Then he adds and says that Tellus, the Mother, was regarded as several gods because they named her by many names and surnames. “They think Tellus is Ops, because she is improved by work; Mother, because she gives birth to many things; Great, because she produces food; Proserpina, because crops spring forth from her; Vesta, because she is clothed with plants. Thus,” he says, “they not unreasonably bring the other goddesses back to her.”

If, then, she is one goddess—and, if truth is consulted, she is not even that—why go on multiplying her into many? Let these be many names belonging to one goddess, not many goddesses but many names.

Yet the authority of their misguided ancestors weighs upon him and compels Varro himself, after this statement, to waver. For he adds and says: “The opinion of our ancestors concerning these goddesses—that they thought them to be many—does not conflict with this.”

How does it not conflict, when it is one thing for one goddess to have many names and another thing for there to be many goddesses? “It may happen,” he says, “that the same thing is one, while there are several things within it.”

I grant that there can be several things in one human being—but are there therefore several human beings? So there can be several things in one goddess—but are there therefore several goddesses? Still, let them divide, combine, multiply, repeat, entangle, and intertwine things as they please.

2. These are the celebrated mysteries of Tellus and the Great Mother, in which everything is referred to mortal seeds and the practice of agriculture. Can it be that a drum, towers, Galli, the frenzied tossing of limbs, the clatter of cymbals, and the fabrication of lions, all of which are referred to these matters and have this purpose, promise eternal life to anyone? Is it for this reason that the castrated Galli serve this Great Goddess, to signify that those who lack seed ought to follow the earth—as though that very servitude did not rather make them lack seed?

For by following this goddess, do they acquire seed when they lack it, or, by following this goddess, do they lose seed when they possess it? Is this an interpretation, or an object of detestation?

Nor is sufficient attention paid to how greatly the wicked demons have prevailed: they dared not promise these people anything great through these rites, yet they were able to demand things so cruel. If the earth were not a goddess, human beings would work with their hands upon it in order to obtain seed through it; they would not rage against themselves in order to lose their seed on her account. If she were not a goddess, she would become fertile through the hands of others in such a way that she would not compel a human being to become sterile through his own hands.

Now, the fact that during the rites of Liber an honorable matron crowned the male organ, while a crowd watched—and perhaps her husband too stood there, blushing and sweating, if human beings possess any sense of shame [Col. 0215]—and the fact that during wedding celebrations a new bride was ordered to sit upon the shaft of Priapus, are far less contemptible and less trivial [Note: [Col. 0215] Vind., Am., and Er. read “and less shameful.” The alternative is less appropriate.] than this most savage obscenity, or most obscene savagery, in which both sexes are mocked by demonic arts [Note: [Col. 0215] Several manuscripts read “rites”; some read “nets.”] in such a way that neither is destroyed by its own wound.

In the former case, the bewitchment of the fields is feared; here, the amputation of the limbs is not feared. There, the modesty of a new bride is so dishonored that not only is her fertility not taken away, but neither is her virginity; here, virility is amputated in such a way that the person becomes neither a woman nor remains a man.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### What interpretation the teaching of the wise men of Greece discovered concerning the castration of Attis [Note: [Col. 0215] This should be read from the manuscripts as “Attis” rather than “Atys.”]

That Attis [Note: [Col. 0215] In most ancient books the name is written with a double *t*: Attis. Servius discusses his history or myth in book 9 of the *Aeneid*; Arnobius in book 5, and elsewhere.] is not mentioned, nor has Varro sought an interpretation of him, in whose memory the Gallus is castrated [Note: [Col. 0215] See above, book 2, chapter 7; and below, book 6, chapter 7, § 3.].

But the learned and wise Greeks by no means kept silent about an explanation so sacred and distinguished. Because of the springlike appearance of the earth, which is more beautiful than in the other seasons, Porphyry, the eminent philosopher, declared that Attis signifies flowers, and that he was castrated because a flower falls before the fruit (in the book *On the Natural Reason of the Gods*).

They therefore compared not the man himself—or someone like a man—who was called Attis, but his male organs, to a flower. For those organs fell while he himself was alive. Indeed, they did not merely fall, nor were they plucked: they were plainly torn apart. And once that flower had been lost, no fruit followed afterward, but rather sterility.

What, then, is the remainder of the man himself? And whatever remained after he had been castrated, what is it said to signify? To what is it referred? What interpretation is brought forth from it? Or, by contriving these explanations in vain and discovering nothing, do they persuade us that we should instead believe what rumor has spread and committed to writing about a castrated man?

Varro rightly recoiled from this [Note: [Col. 0215] The printed editions read, “he opposed this.” The manuscripts support the correction.], and did not wish to say it; for this did not escape so learned a man.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On the obscenity of the rites of the Great Mother

Likewise, concerning the effeminate men consecrated to that same Great Mother in defiance of all modesty among men and women—men who, until yesterday, with wet hair, whitened faces, flowing limbs, and a feminine gait, went through the streets and alleys of Carthage, even demanding from the people the means by which they might live shamefully [Note: [Col. 0215] The Galli of the Mother of the Gods were permitted to solicit alms from the people by a law passed by Metellus, which Ovid mentions in book 4 of the *Fasti*, lines 350 onward. Cicero, *On the Laws*, book 2, chapter 9, says: “Except for the servants of the Idaean Mother, and those on the proper days, no one is to compel anyone to contribute.” He adds in chapter 16: “We abolished the contribution, except the one we permitted for a few days as belonging to the Idaean Mother; for it fills minds with superstition and empties households.” See Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 13.]—Varro wished to say nothing, and I do not remember ever having read anything by him on the subject.

Interpretation failed, reason blushed, and speech fell silent. The Great Mother surpassed all the gods who were her sons—not in the greatness of her divinity, but in the enormity of her crime. The monstrosity of Janus cannot be compared with this monster. He had mere deformity in his images; she has deformed cruelty in her rites. He had limbs added to stones; she has limbs destroyed in human beings.

This disgrace is not surpassed by all the numerous and enormous acts of adultery attributed to Jupiter himself. He, amid his amorous dealings with women, brought shame upon heaven through a single Ganymede; she, through so many publicly professed effeminate men, both polluted the earth and insulted heaven.

Perhaps we could compare or even prefer Saturn to her in this form of most shameful cruelty, since he is said to have castrated his father. But in the rites of Saturn, human beings could be killed by the hands of others rather than castrated by their own hands.

As the poets relate, he devoured his children, and the natural philosophers interpret this as they please; but, as history records, he killed them. The Romans, however, did not accept the fact that the Carthaginians sacrificed their own children to him. But this Great Mother of the Gods brought castrated men into Roman temples as well, and preserved this savagery and custom, supposedly strengthening Roman power by cutting off the male organs of men.

What are the thefts of Mercury, the wantonness of Venus, and the adulteries and obscenities of the others in comparison with this evil—things we would bring forth from the books if they were not sung and acted every day in the theaters? But what are these things in comparison with so great an evil, whose magnitude was suitable only to the Great Mother?

Especially since those acts are said by the poets to have been invented—as though the poets had also invented the claim that such things are pleasing and acceptable to the gods. For poets to sing or write about them may be audacity or wantonness on the poets’ part. But for such things to be added to divine rites and honors at the command—and through the extortion—of the same divinities, what is this but the crime of the gods? Rather, it is a confession of demons and the deception of wretched people.

Yet the fact that the Mother of the Gods earned worship through the consecration of castrated men was not invented by the poets. They preferred to shudder at it rather than sing of it.

Should anyone be consecrated to these selected gods in order to live happily after death, when, once consecrated to them, he cannot live honorably before death—subject as he is to superstitions so foul and bound to unclean demons?

“But all these things,” he says, “are referred to the universe.” Let him see whether they are not rather referred to what is unclean. What, indeed, cannot be referred to the universe if it is shown to exist in the universe [Note: [Col. 0216] The editions of Vind., Am., and Er. omit this sentence: “What, indeed, cannot be referred to the universe if it is shown to exist in the universe?” In its place they have: “For whoever has this universe as his god is neither religious in mind nor will live honorably or purely.” We, however, seek the mind. Although this reading seemed better to Ludovicus Vives, it evidently arose from an ill-formed gloss on what precedes, “Let him see whether it is not rather referred to what is unclean,” where nothing else needed to be supplied except “spirit,” that is, “demon.”]?

We, however, seek the mind which, trusting in true religion, does not worship the universe as its god, but praises the universe as God’s work, for the sake of God; and, purified from the filth of the world, arrives in purity at God, who created the universe.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On the fictions of the natural philosophers, who neither worship true divinity nor worship it in the manner in which true divinity ought to be worshiped

[Col. 0217]

1. We see that these selected gods have indeed become more widely known than the others—not so that their merits might be brought to light, but so that their disgrace might not remain hidden. It is therefore more credible that they were human beings, as both poetic and historical writings have reported.

For when Virgil says:

> First Saturn came from heavenly Olympus,  
> Fleeing Jupiter’s weapons, an exile with his kingdom taken away  
> (*Aeneid*, book 8, lines 319–320),

and when he continues with matters relevant to this subject, Euhemerus [Note: [Col. 0217] Vind., Am., and some manuscripts read “Homerus.” The other books, however, more correctly read “Euhemerus,” who wrote a sacred history. See above, book 6, chapter 7, § 1.] unfolds the entire history of Saturn—a history that Ennius translated into Latin—we need not linger over it, since those who before us wrote against errors of this kind, whether in Greek or Latin, have said much about the subject.

2. [XXVII.] When I consider the natural philosophies by which learned and clever men attempt to transform these human matters into divine matters, I see that they can be reduced to nothing except temporal and earthly works and corporeal nature—or, even if invisible, nevertheless mutable nature. But this is in no way the true God.

If this were at least carried out through interpretations consonant with religious reverence, it would certainly be lamentable that the true God was not announced and proclaimed through them; yet it might in some measure be tolerated that such foul and shameful things were neither done nor commanded. But now, since, in place of the true God—by whose indwelling alone the soul is happy—it is impious to worship either body or soul, how much more impious is it to worship these things in such a way that neither the worshiper’s body nor soul attains salvation or human dignity?

Therefore, if some element of the universe or some created spirit—even one that is not unclean or evil—is worshiped with temple, priest, and sacrifice, the worship owed to the true God, this is not evil because the things with which it is worshiped are evil, but because those things are the kind of things with which only the One to whom such worship and service are owed ought to be worshiped.

But if, through the foolishness or monstrosity of images, the sacrifices of human beings, the crowning of male private parts, payment for sexual immorality, cutting of limbs, castration, the consecration of effeminate men, and festivals of impure and obscene games, someone claims to worship the one true God—that is, the creator of every soul and body—he does not sin because the one he worships ought not to be worshiped; he sins because, although the One ought to be worshiped, he does not worship him as he ought to be worshiped.

But whoever worships both such things—that is, shameful and criminal things—and not the true God, the maker of soul and body, but some creature, however free from vice it may be—whether soul, body, or soul and body together—sins against God twice over: first, because he worships in place of God something that is not God; and second, because he worships with things of a kind with which neither God himself nor anything other than God ought to be worshiped.

How, and with what shameful wickedness, these people worshiped is obvious. But what or whom they worshiped would be obscure, unless their history bore witness to it—especially since those very foul and shameful things are admitted to have been offered to divinities that demanded them with terrifying force. Thus, with all ambiguity removed, it is clear that wicked and most unclean demons were invited by this entire civic theology to behold foolish images and, through them, to possess foolish hearts [Note: [Col. 0218] Compare *Letter* 102, § 20.].

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### That Varro’s doctrine concerning theology agrees with itself in no part

What, then, is the value of the fact that the most learned and acute Varro attempts, as though through subtle reasoning, to reduce and refer all these gods to heaven and earth? [Note: [Col. 0218] Thus in the manuscripts. But in the printed editions the punctuation here was faulty, and a connective particle was added, giving: “and attempts to refer—and cannot?” “They slip,” etc.] They slip from his hands, spring away, slide down, and fall. For, when he is about to discuss the female gods—that is, the goddesses—he says:

“Since, as I said in the first book concerning places, there are two principles of the gods discerned from heaven and earth, from which the gods are partly called heavenly and partly earthly, just as in the earlier section we began with heaven when we spoke of Janus, whom some have said is heaven and others the universe, so among the females we begin our writing with Tellus.”

I perceive what an affliction such a great burden places upon this intellect. He is led by a certain plausible line of reasoning to think that heaven is what acts and earth what undergoes action, and therefore he attributes masculine power to the former and feminine power to the latter. He does not consider that the one who does these things is rather the one who made both.

For this reason, in the previous book he also interprets the celebrated mysteries of the Samothracians in this way, and promises, with an appearance of extreme religious devotion, that he will explain in writing and send to them matters that are not even known to their own people [Note: [Col. 0218] See book 5 of *On the Latin Language*, § 58.]. He says that there he gathered from many indications that the images signify one thing as heaven, another as earth, and another as the models of things, which Plato calls ideas. He wants Jupiter to be understood as heaven, Juno as earth, and Minerva as the ideas: heaven, from which something is made; earth, from which it is made; and the model according to which it is made.

Here I will not discuss the fact that Plato says that those ideas possess such great power [Note: [Col. 0218] In the *Timaeus* and *Parmenides*.] that, according to them, heaven not only made something but was itself made. This is what I say: in this book of the selected gods, Varro has lost that system of three gods by which he had, as it were, encompassed everything.

For he assigns male gods to heaven and female gods to earth, yet places among the latter Minerva, whom earlier he had placed above heaven itself. Moreover, the male god Neptune is in the sea, which belongs more properly to earth than to heaven. Finally, Dis Pater [Note: [Col. 0218] Several manuscripts read “Father Dis”; others, “Dispater.” Manuscript 766 has “Dis Pater”; manuscripts 2050, 2052, and 2053 have “Dispater.” M.], who in Greek is called Πλούτων (*Ploutōn*), is himself the male brother of both and is declared to be an earthly god, holding the upper earth and having Proserpina as his wife in the lower earth.

How, then, do they attempt to refer the male gods to heaven and the female gods to earth [Note: [Col. 0218] The editions of Vind. and Am. read: “How, then, do they declare that the male gods are in heaven and the female gods on earth, when they again attempt to refer the male gods to earth and the female gods to heaven?”]? What solid, consistent, sober, or determinate element does this argument contain?

Tellus, moreover, is the beginning of the goddesses—the Great Mother, that is, before whom the mad obscenity of the effeminate, the castrated, and those who cut and fling about themselves resounds. What, then, is meant by calling Janus the head of the gods and Tellus the head of the goddesses? In the former case error does not make one head, and in the latter madness does not make a sound one [Note: [Col. 0219] The error refers to the two-faced Janus; the madness refers to the insane priests of the Great Mother.].

Why do they vainly attempt to refer these things to the universe? Even if they could, no pious person worships the universe in place of the true God [Note: [Col. 0219] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “as though the universe, or a work, could be worshiped in place of the true God.”]. Yet the evident truth proves that they cannot do even this. Let them refer these things instead to dead human beings and to the worst demons, and no question will remain.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### That everything which the natural philosophers referred to the universe and its parts ought to have been referred to the one true God

Let us consider in this way how all the things which they refer to the universe, on the basis of their theology of these gods and as though through physical explanations, may be attributed without any scruple of sacrilegious opinion to the true God instead—the God who made the universe, the creator of every soul and every body.

We worship God, not heaven and earth, the two parts of which this universe consists; nor do we worship the soul or souls diffused through every living thing. We worship the God who made heaven and earth and everything that is in them; who made every soul, whether it lives in whatever manner and lacks sensation and reason, or whether it also has sensation, or whether it also possesses understanding.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### With what piety the Creator is distinguished from created things, so that as many gods are not worshiped as there are works of one author

And now, as I begin to review those works of the one true God on account of which these people, while attempting to interpret their most shameful and criminal rites as though honorably, made many false gods for themselves, we worship the God who established beginnings and ends for the natures created by him, both of existing and of moving; who possesses, knows, and orders the causes of things; who created the power of seeds; who implanted the rational soul—what is called the *animus* [mind] [Note: [Col. 0219] So read Vind., Er., and the manuscripts. Our manuscripts likewise read this; B. has “which is called *animus*.” M.]—in whatever living beings he wished; who gave the capacity and use of speech; who granted the gift of foretelling the future to whatever spirits he pleased, and through whichever spirits he pleases himself foretells the future and drives away illnesses; who also governs the beginnings, progress, and ends of wars themselves when the human race must thus be corrected and chastened; who both created and governs the most intense and violent fire of this universe in accordance with the balance of its immense nature; who is the creator and governor of all waters; who made the sun, the brightest of bodily lights, and gave it an appropriate power and movement; who does not withdraw his dominion and power even from the regions below; who provided seeds and nourishment for mortals, whether dry or liquid, assigning them to natures suited to them; who establishes and makes the earth fertile [Note: [Col. 0220] Am., Er., and Lov. read “made fertile.” Vind. and the manuscripts read “makes fertile.”]; who bestows its fruits upon animals and human beings; who knows and orders not only the primary causes but also the secondary ones; who established the moon’s movement [Note: [Col. 0220] Vind., Am., and manuscripts of good quality read “its measure.” Manuscripts 766, 2052, and 2053 likewise have “its measure.” In manuscript 2051 this part of the phrase is absent. M.]; who provides heavenly and earthly paths for changes of place; who granted the human minds he created knowledge of the various arts to assist life and nature; who established the union of male and female for the propagation of offspring; who granted gatherings of human beings the gift of earthly fire for the most convenient uses, so that they might apply it to hearths and lights.

These are certainly the things which the acute and learned Varro labored to distribute among the selected gods through I know not what physical interpretations, whether he received them from elsewhere or devised them himself.

[XXX.] But one true God does and directs all these things—God, that is, wholly present everywhere [Note: [Col. 0220] The printed editions read, “But the same God, wholly present everywhere.” The manuscripts support the correction.], confined by no places, bound by no restraints, divisible into no parts, mutable in no respect, filling heaven and earth with his present power, his nature being in need of nothing [Note: [Col. 0220] The printed editions read, “not being absent.” All the manuscripts read, “not being in need.”].

Thus he administers all the things he created while also allowing those things themselves to exercise and carry out their own movements [Note: [Col. 0220] Compare book 5 against Julian, § 51.]. For although nothing can exist without him, they are not what he is [Note: [Col. 0220] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “although nothing can exist without him, they are nevertheless not in any way what he is.”].

He also does many things through angels; but he makes angels blessed only from himself. Thus, although he sends angels to human beings for certain reasons, he makes human beings blessed not from angels but from himself, just as he makes angels blessed from himself.

From this one true God we hope for eternal life.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### The particular benefits of God enjoyed by the followers of truth, in addition to his general generosity

For, in addition to such benefits as he bestows upon good and evil alike through that administration of nature of which we have said something, we have from him a great and distinctive sign of great love.

Although we are in no way able to offer sufficient thanks for the fact that we exist, that we live, that we behold heaven and earth, and that we possess mind and reason by which we may seek the very one who created all these things, still he did not entirely abandon us when we were weighed down and overwhelmed by sins, turned away from contemplation of his light, and blinded by love of darkness—that is, of iniquity.

He sent us his Word, who is his only Son. By being born and suffering for us in the flesh he assumed, he made us know how highly God valued the human being. Through that unique sacrifice we might be cleansed from all sins; and, with his Spirit’s love poured into our hearts, after overcoming every difficulty, we might come into eternal rest and the ineffable sweetness of contemplating him.

What hearts, what tongues, could claim to be sufficient to give him thanks?

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### That the mystery of Christ’s redemption has never been absent, and has always been proclaimed through different signs

This mystery of eternal life was proclaimed from the beginning of the human race, through certain signs and sacraments suited to the times, by angels whenever it was appropriate [Note: [Col. 0221] Compare book 9 of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, §§ 34–36.].

Then the Hebrew people were gathered into a certain commonwealth that enacted this mystery. There, through some who knew and some who did not know what they were doing, it was foretold that what has been taking place from Christ’s coming until now and will continue thereafter was to come.

Later, that same people was dispersed among the nations for the sake of the testimony of the Scriptures, in which the eternal salvation that would come in Christ had been foretold [Note: [Col. 0221] So correctly read our manuscripts. B. has “after that same people.” M.].

For not only all the prophecies contained in words, and not only the precepts of life that shape conduct and piety [Note: [Col. 0221] Several manuscripts read “confirm conduct and piety.” Manuscript 766 likewise has this reading. M.] and are contained in those writings, but also the sacred rites, priesthoods, tabernacle or temple, altars, sacrifices, ceremonies, feast days, and everything else belonging to that service which is owed to God—and which in Greek is properly called λατρεία (*latreia*)—signified and foretold those things which, on account of the eternal life of the faithful in Christ, we both believe have been fulfilled, see being fulfilled, and trust will be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0221] Augustine discusses these matters more extensively in various places below, beginning with book 17. See also book 4 against Faustus, chapter 2, and book 22, chapter 21.].

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### That only through the Christian religion could the deception of the evil spirits, who rejoice in human error, be revealed

Through this one true religion, therefore, it was possible to reveal that the gods of the nations are the filthiest demons, who, under the pretext of departed souls or under the appearance of worldly creatures, desire to be thought gods; who exult with proud impurity in divine honors and in the same criminal and shameful things; and who begrudge human souls their conversion to the true God.

A human being is freed from their savage and impious domination when he believes in the one who offered an example of such great humility for rising up, as these spirits fell through such great pride.

Among them are not only those of whom we have already said much, along with others of the same kind among the various nations and lands, but also those with whom we are now dealing, as though selected into the senate of the gods—selected, clearly, for the nobility of their crimes, not for the dignity of their virtues.

While Varro attempts to refer their rites to natural explanations, seeking to dignify shameful things, he cannot discover how such explanations fit or correspond to them, because the causes of those rites are not what he thinks—or rather, what he wishes to be thought.

For if not only these causes themselves, but any others of this kind, were present, although they had nothing to do with the true God and the eternal life that must be sought in religion, nevertheless some sort of explanation drawn from the nature of things might somewhat mitigate the offense produced by some apparent obscenity or absurdity in the rites when it was not understood. This is what he attempted in certain theatrical dramas and the mysteries of shrines: he did not acquit the shrines by comparing them with theaters; rather, he condemned the shrines by comparing them with theaters. Nevertheless, he made some attempt to soothe the sense offended by horrific things by offering, as it were, an explanation of natural causes [Note: [Col. 0222] The manuscripts read, “the explanation of the cause soothed.”].

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### On the books of Numa Pompilius, which the senate ordered to be burned lest the reasons for the rites contained in them become known
But by contrast we find—as that most learned man himself has recorded—that the explanations of the rites set forth in the books of Numa Pompilius could in no way be tolerated, nor were they thought worthy either of being made known to religious people by being read or at least of being stored away in writing in darkness. I shall now say what I promised in the third book of this work that I would say in its proper place (chap. 9). For, as we read in Varro’s book *On the Worship of the Gods*:

> “When a certain Terentius had a farm at the Janiculum, and his plowman, passing near the tomb of Numa Pompilius, had uprooted from the earth with his plow his books, in which the explanations of the established rites had been written, he brought them into the City to the praetor. But when the praetor had examined their opening sections, he referred so important a matter to the senate. There, when the leading men had read certain explanations of why each rite had been instituted, the senate approved Numa after his death; and, as religious fathers enrolled, they decreed that the praetor should burn the books.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0222] Some manuscripts read *araret* (“was plowing”) instead of *haberet* (“had”).—Our codices read *haberet*. M.]

[Note: [Col. 0222] See Livy, book 40, chapter 29; Valerius, book 1, chapter 1; Pliny, book 13, chapter 13, or 27; Festus and Plutarch, *Numa*; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book 1, chapter 22.]

Let each person believe what he thinks; or rather, let any distinguished defender of so great an impiety say what insane controversy has suggested ought to be said. For my part, it is enough to point out that the explanations of the rites written by King Pompilius, the founder of the Roman rites, ought to have remained unknown not only to the people and the senate, but even to the priests themselves; and that Numa Pompilius, through illicit curiosity, had reached those secrets of the demons which he himself would indeed write down, so that he would have something to remind him of them by reading. Yet, since he was king and feared no one at all, he dared neither teach them to anyone nor destroy them by erasing them or consuming them in any other way. Thus, what he did not wish anyone to know, lest he teach human beings wicked things, he feared to violate, lest he incur the anger of the demons; and so he buried it where he thought it safe, never imagining that a plow could come near his tomb.

The senate, however, feared to condemn the religious practices of their ancestors and was therefore compelled to approve Numa; yet it judged those books so pernicious that it ordered them not to be buried again, lest human curiosity seek out with much greater eagerness a matter already disclosed, but to be destroyed by flames as accursed records.

[Note: [Col. 0223] In our manuscripts, except 2050, the words “or hydromancy” are absent. MS 2051 has *nycromantia*. M.]

For, since they already thought it necessary to perform those rites, they judged that the state would err more tolerably while ignorant of their reasons than it would be disturbed by knowing them.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—Hydromancy, by which Numa, having seen certain images of demons, was deceived.

Numa himself, to whom no prophet of God and no holy angel was sent, was compelled to practice hydromancy, so that in water he might see images of the gods—or rather, deceptions of demons—from whom he might hear what he ought to establish and observe in the rites. Varro likewise says that this form of divination was brought from the Persians, and records that Numa himself, and later the philosopher Pythagoras, made use of it; he adds that, when blood was employed, they were said to consult the inhabitants of the underworld.  
[Note: [Col. 0223] MS 766 reads *qua* instead of *quo*. M.]

[Note: [Col. 0223] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read *suscitari* (“to be raised up”) instead of *sciscitari* (“to consult”); some manuscripts subsequently read *necromanteian*.]

In Greek it is called *necromancy* (νεκρομαντεία). Whether it is called hydromancy or necromancy, the meaning is the same: the dead are thought to prophesy. Let those who practice such arts see for themselves by what means these things are done. I do not wish to say that even before the coming of our Savior such arts were ordinarily forbidden by the laws of the Gentile cities themselves and punished with the severest penalty. I do not, I say, wish to say this; perhaps such things were then permitted.

Yet Pompilius, whose rites he disclosed, buried the explanations of those rites through these very arts; so greatly did he himself fear what he had learned. The senate burned the books in which those explanations had been revealed. Why, then, does Varro interpret for me, as though they were physical, some other explanations of those rites—explanations which, if those books had contained them, would certainly not have been burned? Or would the fathers enrolled likewise have burned these books of Varro, written and published for Caesar the pontiff?  
[Note: [Col. 0223] See Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book 1, chapter 6.]

Since Numa Pompilius had brought out—that is, carried away—the water from which he practiced hydromancy, he is therefore said to have had the nymph Egeria as his wife, as Varro explains in the book mentioned above.  
[Note: [Col. 0223] Livy, book 1, chapter 19; Ovid, book 3 of the *Fasti*, lines 275–276.]

For this is how historical events are usually turned into fables by being sprinkled with lies. In that hydromancy, then, that most inquisitive Roman king learned both the rites which the pontiffs were to have in their books and their explanations, which he wished no one but himself to know. Thus he caused them, in a certain sense, to die separately with him when he took care that they should be withdrawn from human knowledge and buried.

Either, then, the filthy and harmful desires of demons were written there in such a way that, from them, the whole of that civil theology appeared execrable even to men who had undertaken so many shameful things in the rites themselves; or else all those beings were revealed to be nothing other than dead human beings whom, through the exceedingly long passage of time, almost all the peoples of the Gentiles had come to believe to be immortal gods. The same demons delighted in such rites, presenting themselves as objects of worship in place of those dead men whom they had caused to be regarded as gods, supported by certain attestations of deceptive miracles.

Yet by the hidden providence of the true God it came about that, through the arts by which hydromancy could be practiced, the demons were permitted to disclose all those things to Pompilius, their associate; but they were not permitted to warn him, as he was dying, to burn them rather than bury them. When they had been hidden so that they would not become known, the demons could not prevent either the plow by which the books were unearthed or Varro’s pen, by which what happened in this matter has come down to our memory.

For they cannot accomplish what they are not permitted to accomplish. They are permitted to act according to the merits of those whom, by a profound and just judgment of the supreme God, they are rightly allowed either merely to afflict or even to subject and deceive.

How harmful those writings were, and how alien to the worship of true divinity, may be understood from this: the senate preferred to burn the books that Pompilius had concealed rather than fear what the man feared who had not dared to do this.

Whoever therefore wishes neither to have a blessed life in the future nor even to live a pious life now should seek eternal death through such rites.  
[Note: [Col. 0224] All manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have: “Whoever, therefore, wishes neither to have a happy life in the future nor even to live a pious life now, should seek eternal death through such rites.”]

But whoever does not wish to have fellowship with wicked demons should not fear the harmful superstition by which they are worshiped; rather, let him recognize the true religion by which they are exposed and conquered.

# BOOK EIGHT

He comes to the third kind of theology, called natural theology, and undertakes with the Platonists—who are easily the foremost of the philosophers and approach more closely to the truth of the Christian faith—to examine the question concerning the gods belonging to it, namely, whether the worship of these gods is useful for attaining the blessed life that is to come after death. First he refutes Apuleius and all others who wish worship to be offered to demons as intermediaries and interpreters between gods and human beings. He shows that the demons themselves are subject to vices, and that they have introduced and are entirely favorable to and delighted by whatever good and prudent people shun and condemn: the sacrilegious inventions of poets, theatrical mockeries, the harmful practices and crimes of magical arts. Consequently, they cannot by any means reconcile human beings to the good gods.

[Col. 0223]

## CHAPTER ONE.—The question of natural theology to be examined with philosophers of superior learning.

We now need a much more attentive mind than was required in resolving the preceding questions and explaining the preceding books. For concerning the theology which they call natural, the discussion must be held not with just anyone—for it is neither fabulous nor civil, that is, neither theatrical nor civic; the former boasts of the crimes of the gods, while the latter reveals the gods’ even more criminal desires, and thus belongs rather to wicked demons than to gods—but with philosophers. If we interpret their very name in Latin, it professes a love of wisdom.  
[Note: [Col. 0224] See Cicero, *On Duties*, book 2, chapter 2.]

Moreover, if wisdom is God, through whom all things were made, as divine authority and truth have shown (Wisdom 7:24–27; Hebrews 1:2–3), the true philosopher is a lover of God. But because the reality designated by this name is not present in all who glory in the name—for not everyone called a philosopher is consequently a lover of true wisdom—then, from all whose opinions we have been able to learn through their writings, we must choose those with whom this question may suitably be treated.  
[Note: [Col. 0225] Lactantius, book 3.]

For I have not undertaken in this work to refute the vain opinions of all philosophers, but only those that concern theology—a term which in Greek signifies an account or discourse concerning divinity. Nor have I undertaken to refute the opinions of all of them, but only of those who, while agreeing that divinity exists and that it cares for human affairs, nevertheless do not think that the worship of the one unchangeable God is sufficient for attaining a blessed life, even after death; rather, they think that many others, certainly created and established by that one God, ought for this reason to be worshiped.

These philosophers already surpass Varro’s opinion by their nearness to the truth. For Varro was able to extend the whole of natural theology only as far as this world or its soul. These men, however, confess a God above every nature of soul, a God who made not only this visible world—often called by the name of heaven and earth—but also every soul whatsoever; and who makes rational and intellectual souls, of which the human soul is one kind, blessed through participation in his unchangeable and incorporeal light.

Everyone who has heard even the faintest account of these philosophers knows that they are called Platonists, their name being derived from their teacher Plato. Concerning Plato, therefore, I shall briefly touch upon what I consider necessary for the present question, first recalling those who preceded him in the same branch of learning.

## CHAPTER TWO.—The two kinds of philosophers, namely the Italian and the Ionian, and their founders.

As far as Greek literature is concerned—a language regarded as more illustrious than those of the other nations—two kinds of philosophers are handed down: one Italian, from that part of Italy which was once called Magna Graecia; the other Ionian, in those lands where Greece is still so called. The Italian school had Pythagoras of Samos as its founder, and they also say that the very name “philosophy” originated with him. For previously those who seemed, by a certain mode of praiseworthy life, to excel others were called “wise men.” When asked what profession he followed, he replied that he was a philosopher, that is, a student or lover of wisdom, since to profess oneself wise seemed exceedingly arrogant.  
[Note: [Col. 0225] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book 5, chapter 3.]

The leader of the Ionian school was Thales of Miletus, one of the seven who were called Wise Men.  
[Note: [Col. 0225] He is said below, in book 18, chapter 24, to have lived during the reign of Romulus. The other six Wise Men contemporary with him were Chilo of Lacedaemon, Pittacus of Mytilene, Bias of Priene, Cleobulus of Lindus, Periander of Corinth, and Solon of Athens.]

Those six were distinguished by their manner of life and by certain precepts suited to living well. But Thales, in order to produce successors as well, distinguished himself by investigating the nature of things and committing his discussions to writing. He became especially renowned because, after mastering the calculations of astronomy, he was able to predict eclipses of the sun and moon.  
[Note: [Col. 0226] See Cicero, *On Divination*, book 1, chapter 49.]

Nevertheless, he thought that water was the principle of things, and that from it all the elements of the world, the world itself, and whatever is generated in it came into existence. He assigned no divine mind as the governor of this work, which we behold as so marvelous when we contemplate the world.

Anaximander, his pupil, succeeded him and changed his opinion concerning the nature of things. He did not think that each thing came from one substance, as Thales thought that it came from moisture, but that each thing arose from its own proper principles. He believed that the principles of individual things were infinite, that they generated innumerable worlds and whatever arises in them, and that those worlds were sometimes dissolved and sometimes generated again, each lasting as long as its own age allowed. He too attributed nothing of these works of nature to a divine mind.

Anaximander left Anaximenes as his disciple and successor. Anaximenes assigned all the causes of things to infinite air. He did not deny or remain silent about the gods; yet he believed that the air had not been made by them, but that they themselves had arisen from air.

Anaxagoras, his pupil, perceived a divine mind as the maker of all the things we see. He said that, from infinite matter consisting of particles similar to one another, all the kinds of things were individually produced according to their proper measures and forms, but by the action of a divine mind.  
[Note: [Col. 0226] Vindobonensis, Amerbach, and Erasmus read “dissimilar” instead of “similar.” The same reading occurs again below at the corresponding place.]  
[Note: [Col. 0226] Almost all manuscripts read: “that all things were individually made according to their own and proper [principles].” The Cygirannensis manuscript reads: “that all things were individually made according to their respective and proper [principles].”—Our manuscripts read *fierent* (“were made”) instead of *fieri* (“to be made”), as do most Benedictine codices. M.]

Diogenes also—Diogenes of Apollonia, not the Cynic, whom Cicero discusses in *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1, chapter 12—another pupil of Anaximenes, said that air was indeed the matter of things, from which everything was made; but he held that air possessed divine reason, without which nothing could be made from it.  
[Note: [Col. 0226] Diogenes of Apollonia, not Diogenes the Cynic.]

Archelaus, the pupil and successor of Anaxagoras, followed him.
[Note: [Col. 0226] Vindobonensis, Amerbach, and Erasmus read “dissimilar.”] He too thought that everything consisted of particles similar to one another, from which each thing was made; yet he also said that mind was present, and that by bringing together and dispersing the eternal bodies—that is, those particles—it brought all things into operation. Socrates is said to have been his pupil and Plato’s teacher; for Plato’s sake I have recalled all these matters briefly.

## CHAPTER THREE.—The Socratic discipline.

Socrates, then, is remembered as the first to turn the whole of philosophy toward correcting and shaping morals, whereas before him everyone had devoted the greatest effort to investigating chiefly physical, that is, natural, matters.  
[Note: [Col. 0226] Cicero, *Academic Questions*, book 1, chapter 4; *Tusculan Disputations*, book 5, chapter 4.]
