I do not think it can be determined with certainty whether, in doing this, Socrates directed his mind toward discovering something clear and certain that was necessary for the blessed life because he was weary of obscure and uncertain matters; for the sake of that blessed life alone he seems to have watched and labored with all the diligence of philosophers. Or perhaps, as some more favorably suppose, he did not wish minds polluted by earthly desires to attempt to rise toward divine things.  
[Note: [Col. 0227] MS 766 reads *suspicatur* (“supposes”) instead of *suspicantur* (“suppose”). M.]  
[Note: [Col. 0227] One or two manuscripts add *et* before *conari* (“and to attempt”).]

For he saw that people were seeking the causes of things, causes which he believed to be first and supreme only in the will of the one supreme God. He therefore thought that they could be grasped only by a purified mind. For this reason he judged that one must devote oneself to a life purified by good morals, so that the mind, freed from the burdens of lust, might by its natural vigor raise itself toward eternal things and, with the purity of understanding, behold the nature of incorporeal and unchangeable light, where the causes of all created natures live in stability.  
[Note: [Col. 0227] In Plato, *Phaedo*.]

It is nevertheless established that, in the very moral questions to which he seemed to devote his whole mind, he dealt with and turned over, with remarkable charm and the sharpest wit, the folly of ignorant people who thought they knew something—whether by openly confessing his own ignorance or by concealing his knowledge. Hence, condemned through slanderous accusation stirred up by inflamed hostilities, he was sentenced to death.

Afterward, however, the city of Athens publicly mourned the very man whom it had publicly condemned. The people’s indignation was turned against his two accusers to such a degree that one of them was crushed and died under the force of the multitude, while the other escaped a similar punishment by voluntary and perpetual exile.  
[Note: [Col. 0227] He means Meletus and Anytus. The former was condemned to death, while Anytus was compelled to go into exile. See Plato, *Apology of Socrates*, and Laertius, “Socrates.”]

Socrates therefore left behind so distinguished a reputation in life and death that he acquired many followers of his philosophy, whose eager study was devoted to discussing moral questions, in which the highest good is examined—the good by which a human being can become blessed.  
[Note: [Col. 0227] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “without which a human being cannot become blessed.” Other printed editions and the manuscripts omit *sine* (“without”) and *non* (“not”).]

Since Socrates, while moving everything, asserting and destroying everything, did not make the matter evident, each person took from his discussions whatever pleased him and established the end of the good wherever he thought fit. The end of the good is that which, once someone reaches it, makes him blessed.

The Socratics consequently held such diverse opinions among themselves concerning this end—something scarcely credible as the work of followers of one teacher—that some said the highest good was pleasure, like Aristippus, while others said it was virtue, like Antisthenes. Thus still others held still other opinions; it would take too long to enumerate them.  
[Note: [Col. 0227] See Cicero, *On Ends*, book 2.]

## CHAPTER FOUR.—Plato, the foremost among Socrates’ disciples, who divided all philosophy into three parts.

Among Socrates’ disciples, Plato achieved, not undeservedly, such outstanding glory that he completely overshadowed the others.  
[Note: [Col. 0227] The manuscripts read *quae* (“which”), rather than *qui* (“who”). Among our manuscripts, 766 and 2053 read *quae*; 2050 and 2052 read *qui*. M.]

Although he was an Athenian, born into an honorable position among his fellow citizens, and far surpassed his fellow students in remarkable ability, he nevertheless thought that he himself and the Socratic discipline were insufficient for completing philosophy. Therefore, he traveled abroad as far as he could, wherever the fame of acquiring some distinguished branch of knowledge drew him.

Thus in Egypt he learned whatever was there regarded and taught as important. From there he came to those parts of Italy where the Pythagoreans were celebrated and, after hearing the most eminent teachers of Italian philosophy, very easily grasped whatever then flourished in that school.

Because he loved his teacher Socrates in a singular way, he made Socrates speak in almost all his dialogues, and he tempered with Socrates’ charm and moral discussions even those matters which he had either learned from others or had himself seen with as much understanding as he could bring to them.

Since the pursuit of wisdom is occupied with action and contemplation, so that one part of it may be called active and the other contemplative—the active part pertaining to the conduct of life, that is, to the formation of morals, and the contemplative part to the perception of the causes of nature and of the purest truth—Socrates is remembered as having excelled in the active part, while Pythagoras devoted himself more to contemplation with whatever intellectual powers he possessed.  
[Note: [Col. 0228] Compare book 1 of *The Harmony of the Gospels*, section 12.]

Accordingly, Plato is praised for having perfected philosophy by joining the two. He divided it into three parts: one moral, chiefly concerned with action; another natural, assigned to contemplation; and a third rational, by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. Although the rational part is necessary for both action and contemplation, contemplation especially claims for itself the perception of truth.

This threefold division is therefore not contrary to the distinction by which the whole pursuit of wisdom is understood to consist in action and contemplation.

What Plato thought concerning these parts, or about them—that is, where he recognized or believed the end of all actions, the cause of all natures, and the light of all reasoning to be—I consider too lengthy to explain in detail, and I do not think it should be asserted rashly. For, while Plato makes his teacher Socrates argue in his works, he strives to preserve Socrates’ familiar practice of concealing his knowledge or opinion, because that manner also pleased Plato himself. As a result, Plato’s own opinions concerning great matters cannot easily be discerned.

Nevertheless, from what is read in Plato—whether what he himself said  
[Note: [Col. 0228] The words *sive quae dixit* (“whether what he said”) are omitted in B. M.]  
or what he reports and writes as having been said by others, selecting what appeared to him acceptable—we ought to recall and insert certain matters into this work, either where they support the true religion which our faith embraces and defends, or where they seem contrary to it, insofar as the question concerns one God and many gods, for the sake of the truly blessed life that is to come after death.  
[Note: [Col. 0228] The ancient books read this way. The printed editions instead have: “insofar as the question concerns one God and many gods, whom the discipline of the Catholic religion asserts ought to be worshiped for the sake of the truly blessed life that is to come after death. Perhaps…”]

Perhaps those who are celebrated by a more widespread reputation as having understood and followed Plato more sharply and more truthfully than the other philosophers of the nations may think something of God such that in him are found the cause of existence, the principle of understanding, and the order of living. Of these three, one is understood to belong to the natural part, another to the rational part, and the third to the moral part.

For if human beings were created so that, through what excels in them, they might attain to what excels over all things—that is, the one true and supremely good God, without whom no nature exists, no teaching instructs, and no practice is effective—then let him be sought where all things are secure for us; let him be perceived where all things are certain for us; let him be loved where all things are right for us.  
[Note: [Col. 0229] In place of *secura* (“secure”), some manuscripts have *diserta* (“clearly expressed”), and the Colbertinus has *inserta* (“inserted”). Most others have *certa* (“certain”), a word which they repeat in the following clause after *ipse cernatur*. Nowhere, however, do we find the reading which Ludovicus Vives says belongs to the ancient manuscripts: “Let him be sought where all things are certain for us; let him be perceived where all things are true for us,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER FIVE.—Why the discussion concerning theology should chiefly be held with the Platonists, whose doctrines ought to be preferred to those of all other philosophers.

If Plato therefore said that the wise person is an imitator, knower, and lover of this God, by participation in whom one is blessed, why should we examine the others? None have approached us more closely than these men.  
[Note: [Col. 0229] *On True Religion*, section 7.]

Let that fabulous theology, then, which delights the minds of the impious with the crimes of the gods, yield to them; and let the civil theology also yield. In it, impure demons, devoted to earthly pleasures and deceiving peoples under the name of gods, wished human errors to be regarded as their own divine honors. They roused their worshipers, through the foulest passions, to behold the plays representing their crimes as though attending their worship; and they offered themselves even more delightful spectacles from those very spectators. Whatever is performed in the temples under the appearance of decency is polluted by the obscenity associated with the theaters; and whatever shameful things are performed in the theaters is praised by the disgrace of the temples with which it is compared.  
[Note: [Col. 0229] The printed editions read: “they wished human errors to be regarded as their own divine honors; where they treated their worshipers as ministers of their own vanity, to behold the plays representing their crimes; and through them, rousing others by the foulest passions to their worship,” and so forth. The text has been corrected from the ancient books.]

Let those interpretations also yield which Varro derived from these rites, as though they referred to heaven and earth and the seeds and processes of mortal things. For the rites themselves do not signify what he attempts to insinuate, and therefore truth does not follow his effort. Even if they did signify such things, a rational soul ought not to worship as its god those things which, by the natural order, are beneath it; nor ought it to place before itself, as gods, the things to which the true God has placed it above.

Let those things also yield which Numa Pompilius took care to hide by burying them with himself because they truly belonged to rites of this kind, and which the senate ordered to be burned after they were unearthed by the plow.

Among this class are also the revelations which, if we wish to form a somewhat milder judgment of Numa, Alexander of Macedon wrote to his mother, saying that a certain Leo, a high priest of the Egyptian rites, had disclosed them to him.  
[Note: [Col. 0229] See below, at the end of this book, and book 12, chapter 10, section 2; also Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*.]

There it is reported that not only Picus, Faunus, Aeneas, Romulus, Hercules, Aesculapius, Liber born of Semele, the twin sons of Tyndareus, and whatever other mortals they regard as gods, but even the gods of the greatest nations themselves—whom Cicero seems to touch upon under veiled names in the *Tusculan Disputations* (book 1, chapter 13), namely Jupiter, Juno, Saturn, Vulcan, Vesta, and many others whom Varro attempts to transfer to the parts or elements of the world—were human beings.  
[Note: [Col. 0229] Vindobonensis, Amerbach, and Erasmus read *majores* (“greater”) instead of *majorum* (“of the greatest”). Lovaniensis and the manuscripts have the better reading *majorum*. For Cicero uses this wording in the cited passage, book 1 of the *Academic Questions*.]

Fearing, as though these mysteries had been revealed, the priest also warns Alexander, when asking him to communicate them in writing to his mother, to order that they be consumed by fire.

Therefore, not only should these matters contained in the two theologies—the fabulous and the civil—yield to the Platonic philosophers, who said that the true God is the author of things, the illuminator of truth, and the giver of blessedness; other philosophers too should yield to these men, who have knowledge of so great a God. Such others thought that the principles of nature were bodily, and that the cause and principle of things was to be found in bodies: Thales in moisture, Anaximenes in air, the Stoics in fire, Epicurus in atoms—that is, in extremely small bodies which cannot be divided or perceived—and all the rest whom it is unnecessary to pause to enumerate, whether they said that the cause was simple or composite bodies, lifeless or living bodies, but nevertheless bodies.

Some of them believed that living things could arise from nonliving things, as the Epicureans did; others believed that both living and nonliving things arose from something living, but nevertheless that bodies arose from a body. For the Stoics thought that fire—that is, one of the four elements of which this visible world consists—was living, wise, the maker of the world itself and of everything in it, and that this fire altogether was God.

These men and others like them were able to think only what their hearts, bound by the senses of the flesh, had fancied. They had within themselves what they did not see, and they imagined within themselves what they had seen outside, even when they did not see it but merely thought about it. But in the presence of such thought, this is no longer a body, but the likeness of a body.

That by which this likeness of a body is seen in the mind is neither a body nor the likeness of a body; and that by which it is seen, and by which it is judged whether it is beautiful or deformed, is certainly better than the thing being judged. This is the human mind and the nature of the rational soul, which is certainly not a body. The likeness of a body itself, when it is perceived and judged in the mind of someone thinking, is not a body either. Therefore it is neither earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire—those four bodies called the four elements, of which we see the bodily world composed.

Moreover, if our mind is not a body, how can God, the creator of the mind, be a body? Let these philosophers, then, yield to the Platonists, as has been said. Let those also yield who were ashamed to say that God is a body, but nevertheless thought that our minds are of the same nature as he is. They were not moved by the soul’s great mutability, although it is impious to attribute such mutability to the nature of God.

But they say, “The nature of the soul is changed by the body; in itself it is unchangeable.” They might just as well say, “The flesh is wounded by some body; in itself it is invulnerable.” Absolutely nothing that cannot be changed can be changed by anything. Consequently, what can be changed by the body can be changed by something, and therefore cannot rightly be called unchangeable.

## CHAPTER SIX.—The Platonists’ understanding in that part of philosophy called physics.

These philosophers, whom we rightly see celebrated above the others in reputation and glory, saw that no body is God; and therefore, in seeking God, they transcended all bodies. They saw that whatever is changeable is not the supreme God; and therefore, in seeking the supreme God, they transcended every soul and all changeable spirits.

Then they saw that every form in any changeable thing—whatever that thing is, and whatever its mode of being and nature may be—could come only from him who truly is, because he exists unchangeably.

Thus, whether one considers the body of the whole world, its shapes, qualities, and ordered motion, the elements arranged from heaven down to earth, and whatever bodies are contained in them; or every kind of life—whether the life that nourishes and sustains, as in trees; or the life that both does this and perceives, as in animals; or the life that does all this and understands, as in human beings; or the life that needs no nourishment but merely sustains, perceives, and understands, as in angels—none of these can exist except from him who simply is.

For in him, being is not one thing and living another, as though he could exist without living; nor is living one thing and understanding another, as though he could live without understanding; nor is understanding one thing and being blessed another, as though he could understand and not be blessed. Rather, what living, understanding, and being blessed are for him, that is his being.

Because of this unchangeability and simplicity, they understood that he made all these things and that he himself could not have been made by anyone. For they considered that whatever exists is either a body or a life, and that life is something better than body; and that the form of body is perceptible, while the form of life is intelligible. Accordingly, they preferred intelligible form to perceptible form.

We call those things perceptible which can be sensed by bodily sight and touch; we call those things intelligible which can be understood by the mind’s vision.  
[Note: [Col. 0231] Our manuscripts, except 2052, omit the word *possunt* (“can”). M.]

There is no bodily beauty—whether in the state of a body, as a figure, or in motion, as a melody—about which the mind does not judge. It could certainly not do so unless this form were better in the mind, without the swelling mass, the noise of a voice, or the extent of place or time.

But even there, unless it were changeable, one person would not judge perceptible form better than another person: the more gifted person better than the slower, the more skilled better than the less skilled, the more practiced better than the less practiced; and the same person, as he progresses, would not judge better afterward than before. But whatever admits of more and less is unquestionably changeable.  
[Note: [Col. 0231] The manuscripts read *magis* (“more”). The printed editions read *majus* (“greater”).]

From this, gifted, learned, and practiced people easily concluded that the first form does not exist in those things in which it is shown to be changeable. Since, therefore, both body and mind appeared to them more or less beautiful, and since, if they could lack all form, they would not exist at all, they saw that there is something in which form is first and unchangeable  
[Col. 0232] [Note: [Col. 0232] Supply *species* (“form”).]  
and therefore incomparable. They rightly believed that the principle of things is there: it was not made, and from it all things were made.

Thus, “what may be known of God” he himself manifested to them, since his invisible things were understood and perceived through the things that were made, as were his eternal power and divinity (Romans 1:19–20). From him also all visible and temporal things were created.  
[Note: [Col. 0232] Several manuscripts read *invisibilia* (“invisible things”) instead of *visibilia* (“visible things”). Some have both: “from whom also all invisible and visible things were created.”—MS 766 reads *invisibilia*. M.]

Let this suffice concerning that part which they call physics, that is, natural philosophy.

## CHAPTER SEVEN.—Why the Platonists must be regarded as much superior to the others in logic, that is, rational philosophy.

As for doctrine, where the other branch is concerned—the branch they call logic, that is, rational philosophy—let those who placed the judgment of truth in the bodily senses, and who held that everything learned must be measured by their untrustworthy and deceptive standards, never be thought comparable with them: such men as the Epicureans and any others of that kind. The Stoics themselves are included, for although they greatly loved the skill of disputation, which they call dialectic, they thought that it had to be derived from the bodily senses. From these, they asserted, the mind conceives notions, which they call *ἐννοίαι* (*ennoiai*, “conceptions”), namely, of those things that they explain by definition; from these, they thought, the entire method of learning and teaching is developed and connected.

Here I am often greatly astonished when they say that no one is beautiful except the wise, while using the bodily senses to see this beauty: with what eyes of flesh, then, did they behold the form and splendor of wisdom? These philosophers, whom we rightly place above the others, distinguished the things perceived by the mind from those apprehended by the senses, neither taking away from the senses what they are capable of nor granting them more than they are capable of. They declared that the light of minds by which all things are learned is that same God by whom all things were made.

## CHAPTER VIII.—That the Platonists also hold the leading position in moral philosophy.

There remains the moral branch, which in Greek they call *ἠθικήν* (*ēthikēn*, “ethics”). Here the question concerns the highest good: that to which we refer everything we do, which we desire not for the sake of something else but for its own sake, and which, once attained, leaves us requiring nothing further in order to be happy. It is for this reason that it is called the “end” (*finis*), because we desire other things for its sake, but desire it only for its own sake.

Accordingly, some have said that this happiness-producing good exists in the body, some in the soul, and some in both within the human being.

[Note: Codices 766, 2050, 2051, and 2053 read: “some said that it exists in both for the human being.” M.]

For they saw that the human being consists of soul and body, and therefore believed that one could fare well through either of these two, or through both, by means of some final good through which they would be happy, to which they would refer everything they did, and beyond which they would not seek the object to which it was to be referred.

Hence those who are said to have added a third category of goods, called “external,” such as honor, glory, money, and anything of this sort, did not add it as something final—that is, as something to be desired for its own sake—but for the sake of something else. This category, they held, would therefore be good for the good and bad for the bad.

[Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “But for the sake of another good, by which this category would be good for the good,” and so forth.]

Thus those who sought the human good either from the soul, or from the body, or from both, thought that nothing other than the human being was to be sought from the human being. Those who sought it from the body sought it from the inferior part of the human being; those who sought it from the soul, from the better part; and those who sought it from both, from the whole human being. Whether, then, from some part or from the whole, it was sought from the human being alone.

Nor did these distinctions, merely because there were three of them, produce only three disagreements and philosophical schools; for people formed different opinions about the good of the body, the good of the soul, and the good of both.

[Note: See below, Book XIX, chapter 2.]

Let all these yield, therefore, to those philosophers who did not say that the human being is happy when enjoying the body, or when enjoying the soul, but when enjoying God—not as the soul enjoys the body or itself, nor as a friend enjoys a friend, but as the eye enjoys light, if something analogous may be brought from these things to those.

[Note: The printed editions read: “if something is to be brought to those likenesses.” The manuscripts support the emended reading.]

What this means will become clear elsewhere, insofar as we are able, if God himself assists us.

### [IX.]

For now, it is enough to recall that Plato determined the end of the good to be living according to virtue, and that this can happen only to one who possesses knowledge and imitation of God; nor is there any other reason for being happy. Accordingly, he does not hesitate to say that philosophizing is loving God, whose nature is incorporeal.

From this it follows that the student of wisdom—for that is what “philosopher” means—will be happy when he begins to enjoy God. For although the person who enjoys what he loves is not necessarily immediately happy—many are miserable because they love things that ought not to be loved, and still more miserable when they enjoy them—nevertheless no one is happy who does not enjoy what he loves. Even those who love things that ought not to be loved do not think themselves happy merely by loving them, but by enjoying them.

Whoever, then, enjoys what he loves and loves the true and highest good—who but the most wretched person would deny that such a one is happy? Plato says that the true and highest good is God. Hence he wishes the philosopher to be a lover of God, so that, since philosophy strives toward the happy life, the person who loves God may be happy by enjoying God.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the philosophy that came nearer to the truth of the Christian faith.

Accordingly, whatever philosophers have held these opinions about the highest and true God—that he is the maker of created things, the light by which things are known, and the good by which things are done; that from him come to us the beginning of nature, the truth of doctrine, and the happiness of life—whether they are more suitably called Platonists or give their school any other name; whether only the philosophers of the Ionic school, who were preeminent among them, held these views, as Plato himself did and those who understood him correctly; or whether they were Italians, on account of Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans, and perhaps others who repeatedly held the same opinion; or whether they are found among other nations as well, among those regarded as wise men or philosophers—Atlanteans, Libyans, Egyptians, Indians, Persians, Chaldaeans, Scythians, Gauls, Spaniards, and others—we place all of them above the rest and acknowledge them as nearer to us.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “Libyans.” A few, along with the printed editions, read “Libyan.” Following Leonard Coquaeus, we do not distinguish these from the Atlanteans, whom he observes to have been called Libyans because, as Laërtius reports, Atlas was a Libyan, that famous king of Mauretania who is said to have been the first to investigate the courses of the sun, moon, and stars.]

## CHAPTER X.—The superiority of the religious Christian among the philosophical disciplines.

### 1.

For even if a Christian educated only in ecclesiastical literature is unfamiliar with the name of the Platonists, and does not know whether there have been two kinds of philosophers in the Greek language, the Ionians and the Italians, he is not so deaf to human affairs that he does not know that philosophers either profess the pursuit of wisdom or wisdom itself.

Yet he avoids those who philosophize according to the elements of this world and not according to God, by whom the world itself was made. He is warned by the apostolic command, and faithfully hears the words: “Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the elements of the world” (Colossians 2:8).

Then, lest he suppose that all philosophers are of this kind, he hears the same apostle say of certain people: “Because what is known of God is manifest in them; for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made; and likewise his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:19–20).

And when Paul was speaking to the Athenians, after saying something great about God—something that only a few could understand, namely, that “in him we live and move and have our being”—he added, “As some of your own poets have said” (Acts 17:28).

The Christian also knows how to avoid the errors even of these philosophers. For where it is said that through the things that have been made God manifested his invisible things to them so that they might perceive them intellectually, it is also said that they did not rightly worship God himself, because they assigned to other things the divine honors due only to him: “For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became futile in their reasoning, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Romans 1:21–23).

Here too he meant the Romans, Greeks, and Egyptians—who gloried in the name of wisdom—to be understood. But we shall dispute this matter with them later.

In the point on which they agree with us, namely, that there is one God, the author of this whole universe, who is not only incorporeal above all bodies but also incorruptible above all souls, our beginning, our light, and our good, we place them above the rest.

### 2. [X.]

Nor, if a Christian ignorant of their literature does not use in debate the words he has not learned—so as to call in Latin “natural,” or in Greek “physical,” the branch that treats the investigation of nature; and “rational,” or “logical,” the branch that asks how truth can be perceived; and “moral,” or “ethical,” the branch concerned with conduct and with pursuing good ends and avoiding evil ones—is he therefore unaware that from the one true and best God we possess nature, by which we were made in his image; doctrine, by which we may know him and ourselves; and grace, by which we may be happy through cleaving to him.

This, then, is why we prefer these philosophers to the others: while other philosophers have worn out their intellects and efforts in seeking the causes of things and the proper method of learning and living, these, having come to know God, discovered where the cause of the established universe, the light by which truth is perceived, and the source from which happiness is drunk are to be found.

Whether, therefore, these are Platonists or philosophers of any nation who hold these views about God, they agree with us. But we have preferred to conduct this discussion with the Platonists because their writings are better known. The Greeks, whose language is preeminent among the nations, celebrated them with great acclaim; and the Latins, moved either by their excellence or by their renown, learned them more eagerly and, by transferring them into our language, made them more distinguished and celebrated.

[Note: Three editions—V, Am, and Er—add “or favor.”]

## CHAPTER XI.—How Plato may have acquired the understanding by which he approached Christian knowledge.

Some who are joined to us in the grace of Christ are astonished when they hear or read that Plato held these views about God, and recognize that they agree in many respects with the truth of our religion. For this reason some have thought that, when he went to Egypt, he heard the prophet Jeremiah or read the prophetic Scriptures during that journey. I myself expressed this opinion in some of my books.

[Note: Namely, in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, section 43. See *Retractations*, Book II, chapter 4, section 2.]

But a careful calculation of the chronology contained in historical chronicles indicates that Plato was born nearly one hundred years after the time when Jeremiah prophesied.

[Note: Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, assigns Jeremiah’s prophecy to the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth Olympiads, but Plato’s birth to the fourth year of the eighty-eighth Olympiad. Thus he was born more than one hundred and seventy years after Jeremiah’s prophecy.]

Although Plato lived eighty-one years, from the year of his death until the time when Ptolemy, king of Egypt, requested the prophetic Scriptures of the Hebrew people from Judea and arranged for them to be translated and preserved by seventy Hebrews who also knew the Greek language, approximately sixty years are found to have elapsed.

[Note: Plato died in the first year of the 109th Olympiad. Ptolemy Philadelphus arranged for the sacred writings to be translated from Hebrew into Greek in the 124th Olympiad.]

Therefore, during that journey Plato could neither have seen Jeremiah, who had died so long before, nor read those Scriptures, which had not yet been translated into the Greek language he knew. Unless, perhaps, because he was exceptionally eager for learning, he learned these writings through an interpreter, as he did the Egyptian writings—not in order to translate them in writing, which Ptolemy is said to have obtained as a great favor, though he could have inspired fear by his royal power, but in conversation, so that he might learn as much as he could grasp about their contents.

[Note: Justin Martyr asserts that Plato drew and transcribed very many things from the sacred books of the Hebrews in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*; Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book VI; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book I, chapter 22, section 150, and *Exhortation to the Greeks*, Book II, chapter 1; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XI, chapter 9; and Ambrose, Sermon 18 on Psalm 118. Lactantius, however, says in *On True Wisdom*, Book IV, chapter 2, that Plato, traveling out of love for investigating truth, did not visit the Jews.]

The indications that suggest this possibility are these. The Book of Genesis begins as follows: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the water” (Genesis 1:1–2).

In the *Timaeus*, however—the book Plato composed on the formation of the world—Plato says that in that work God first joined earth and fire.

[Note: Lovaniensis adds here, “and the earth itself to the place of earth”; this is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

It is clear that he assigns the place of heaven to fire.

This opinion therefore bears a certain resemblance to the statement, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Next, he says that the two intermediate elements by which these two extremes would be joined to one another are water and air. Hence it is thought that he understood the statement, “The Spirit of God was borne over the water,” in this way. Paying insufficient attention to the manner in which that Scripture usually speaks of the Spirit of God—and since air too is called “spirit”—he may be thought to have understood four elements as mentioned in that passage.

Again, Plato says that the philosopher is a lover of God. Nothing in those sacred writings burns so strongly with this meaning. Most of all, there is the passage that greatly inclines me, so that I almost agree that Plato was not unfamiliar with those books. When the words of God are conveyed through an angel to holy Moses, and Moses asks the name of the one who commands him to go to the Hebrew people in order to liberate them from Egypt, the answer is given: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14). It is as though, in comparison with the one who truly is because he is unchangeable, those things that have been made mutable do not exist. Plato held this idea with great force and commended it with the greatest care.

[Note: Especially in the dialogues *Parmenides* and *Sophist*.]

I do not know whether this is found anywhere in the books of those who lived before Plato, except where it is said: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to them, ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

## CHAPTER XII.—That the Platonists, although they held sound views about the one true God, nevertheless judged that sacrifices should be offered to many gods.

But whoever taught him these things—whether the books of the ancients who preceded him, or rather, as the apostle says, because “what is known of God is manifest in them; for God manifested it to them: for his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made; and likewise his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:19–20)—I have now had sufficient reason, I think, for choosing the Platonic philosophers as the people with whom to conduct this discussion.

The question we have undertaken concerns natural theology: whether, for the sake of the happiness that is to come after death, sacrifice ought to be offered to one God or to many.

[Note: In the printed editions, after “ought to be offered,” the following words were inserted: “For whether one God or many should be worshiped for the goods of this life.” The ancient books lack these words.]

### [XII.]

I chose these philosophers above all because, the better their understanding of the one God who made heaven and earth, the more glorious and distinguished they are considered among the rest. They have been so preferred by the judgment of later generations that, although Aristotle, Plato’s pupil—a man of outstanding intellect and, in eloquence, inferior indeed to Plato but easily surpassing many—founded the Peripatetic school, so called because he was accustomed to debate while walking, and gathered many disciples into his own sect while his teacher was still alive, excelling through his great reputation; after Plato’s death, Speusippus, his sister’s son, and Xenocrates, his beloved disciple, succeeded him in his school, which was called the Academy, and for this reason they and their successors were called Academics; nevertheless, the most distinguished later philosophers, who chose to follow Plato, did not wish to be called Peripatetics or Academics, but Platonists.

[Note: Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XIV, chapters 4–5.]

Among these were the highly renowned Greeks Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Porphyry. In both languages—that is, Greek and Latin—there was also the distinguished Platonist Apuleius the African. But all these men, and others of the same kind, including Plato himself, thought that sacrifices should be offered to many gods.

[Note: Several manuscripts of good authority read “Xeusippus.”]

## CHAPTER XIII.—On Plato’s view, by which he defined the gods as nothing other than good and friendly to virtue.

Although, then, they disagree with us on many other important matters, on the point I have just stated—which is by no means a small matter, and from which the present question arises—I first ask them to which gods they think this worship should be offered: to good gods, to evil gods, or to both good and evil.

But we have Plato’s own judgment, in which he says that all gods are good and that no god is evil at all (*Laws*, Book X, and *Republic*, Book II). It follows, therefore, that this worship is to be understood as offered to good gods; for gods will not be gods if they are not good.

If this is so—and what else is it fitting to believe about the gods?—then the opinion of those who think that evil gods must be appeased with sacrifices lest they cause harm, while good gods must be invoked so that they may help, is plainly refuted.

[Note: Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, Book II, chapters 39 and 10.]

There are no evil gods; honor in the form of sacrifices, as they say, must therefore be offered to the good. Who, then, are those who love theatrical games and demand that they be joined to divine rites and presented in their honor? Their power does not show them to be nonexistent, but this very inclination clearly shows them to be evil.

For what Plato thought about theatrical games is well known: he judged that the poets themselves should be expelled from the state because they had composed songs so unworthy of the majesty and goodness of the gods.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “and benevolence.”]

Who, then, are these gods who contend with Plato himself over theatrical games? Plato does not permit the gods to be defamed by false accusations; these gods command that their honors be celebrated through the very same accusations.

Finally, when these gods ordered the games to be renewed, demanding obscene acts, they also behaved maliciously: they took away the son of Titus Latinius and inflicted illness on him because he had refused their command, then withdrew the illness when he had fulfilled their orders.

[Note: Above, Book IV, chapter 26.]

Plato, however, does not think that such gods should be feared as so evil. Holding firmly to his position, he does not hesitate to remove from a well-ordered people all the sacrilegious nonsense of the poets, with which those gods take pleasure through their association with impurity.

I have already mentioned that Labeo places this Plato among the demigods.

That same Labeo thinks that evil divinities are appeased by bloody victims and supplications of this kind, while good ones are appeased by games and by things of the sort that are associated with cheerfulness.

What, then, is the meaning of this? Plato, a demigod, judges that amusements which he considers shameful should be taken away, not from demigods but from gods—and good gods at that. The gods themselves refute Labeo’s opinion, for in the case of Latinius they showed themselves not merely wanton and playful, but savage and terrifying as well.

Let the Platonists, then, explain this to us—those who, following the judgment of their founder, regard all gods as good and honorable and as companions of the virtues of the wise, and who consider it impious to think otherwise of any god.

[Note: So read our manuscripts. B has: “The Platonists explain this to us.” M.]

“We shall explain it,” they say.

Let us listen attentively, then.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the opinion of those who said that rational souls are of three kinds: in the celestial gods, the aerial demons, and earthly human beings.

### 1.

“There is,” they say, “a threefold division of all living beings possessing a rational soul: gods, human beings, and demons. The gods occupy the highest place, human beings the lowest, and demons the middle. For the dwelling of the gods is in heaven, that of human beings on earth, and that of demons in the air.

“Just as their places have different degrees of dignity, so too do their natures. Accordingly, the gods are superior to human beings and demons, while human beings are placed below gods and demons, both in the order of the elements and in the distinction of merits.

“Therefore demons, being intermediate, must be ranked below the gods, beneath whom they dwell, but above human beings, above whom they dwell. They share with the gods the immortality of their bodies, but with human beings the passions of their souls.”

[Note: Plato, in the *Epinomis*.]

“Therefore,” they say, “it is not surprising that they delight in the obscenities of games and the inventions of poets, since they are captivated by human emotions, from which the gods are far removed and entirely alien. From this it follows that, by detesting and forbidding poetic inventions, Plato did not deprive the gods—who are all good and exalted—of the pleasure of theatrical games, but the demons.”

### 2.

If this is so, although the same view is also found in others, Apuleius the Platonist of Madaura wrote a single book on this subject alone, giving it the title *On the God of Socrates*. There he discusses and explains what kind of divinity Socrates had attached to him and reconciled to himself in a sort of friendship; it is said to have been accustomed to warn him to desist from an action whenever what he intended to do was not going to turn out favorably.

For Apuleius says very plainly and asserts at length that this was not a god but a demon, carefully examining Plato’s view concerning the sublimity of the gods, the lowliness of human beings, and the intermediate position of demons.

If this is so, how did Plato dare—if not against the gods, whom he removed from every human contamination, then certainly against the demons themselves—to deprive the demons of theatrical pleasures by expelling poets from the city? He could have done so only because, in this way, he admonished the human soul that, although it is still placed in these mortal limbs, it should, for the sake of the splendor of moral integrity, scorn the impure commands of demons and detest their uncleanness.

For if Plato rightly and honorably condemned and prohibited these things, then the demons demanded and commanded them in a thoroughly shameful manner.

Either, therefore, Apuleius is mistaken and Socrates did not have a friend from this class of divinities; or Plato contradicts himself, at one moment honoring demons and at another removing their pleasures from a well-governed state; or Socrates should not be congratulated on his friendship with a demon—a friendship of which Apuleius himself was so ashamed that he entitled his book *On the God of Socrates*, although, according to his own discussion, in which he distinguishes gods from demons so carefully and at such length, he ought to have called it *On the Demon of Socrates*. He preferred to put this point in the discussion itself rather than in the title of the book.

Indeed, through sound teaching, which has shed light on human affairs, all or nearly all people abhor the name “demons,” so that anyone who read the title *On the Demon of Socrates* before encountering Apuleius’s discussion, in which the dignity of demons is commended, would certainly not think that its author was a sane man.

What did Apuleius himself find to praise in demons, except the subtlety and strength of their bodies and the higher location of their dwelling? For when he spoke generally about all of them, he said not only nothing good about their character but a great deal that was evil.

After reading that book, no one is surprised at all that they also wanted theatrical obscenity to form part of divine rites; that, while wishing to be thought gods, they could take pleasure in the crimes attributed to the gods; and that whatever in their worship is either laughed at or inspires horror because of its obscene solemnity or shameful cruelty is consistent with their inclinations.

## CHAPTER XV.—That demons are not superior to human beings either because of their aerial bodies or because of their higher dwellings.

### 1.

Therefore, when considering these matters, let a mind that is truly religious and subject to the true God never suppose that demons are better than itself merely because they possess better bodies.

[Note: Origen grants bodies to demons in *On First Principles*, Book II, chapter 8; Tertullian, in *On the Flesh of Christ*; and many other ancient writers do likewise. Augustine himself does not deny it here. He calls them “aerial and ethereal living beings” in *Against the Academics*, Book I, section 20; Letter 9, section 3; and *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book III, chapter 10, sections 14–15, since in the last passage he says that they are vigorous by the nature of their aerial bodies.]

Otherwise, it would have to place many beasts above itself, since they surpass us in keenness of sense, ease and speed of movement, strength, and the long endurance of their bodies.

What human being can equal eagles and vultures in sight? Who can equal dogs in smell? Who can equal hares, deer, and all birds in speed? Who can equal lions and elephants in strength? Who can equal serpents in longevity—serpents that are even said to cast off old age along with their skin and return to youth?

But just as we are superior to all these creatures through reasoning and understanding, so we ought also to be superior to demons through living well and honorably.

For this reason divine providence has granted certain superior bodily endowments to those beings whom we are plainly superior to, so that what makes us superior to them might be commended to us in this way as something to cultivate with much greater care than the body. We would thus learn to despise the bodily excellence that we know demons possess in comparison with the goodness of life by which we surpass them, while we too are destined to possess immortal bodies—not bodies tormented by the eternity of punishments, but bodies preceded by the purity of souls.

### 2.

As for the height of their location—that demons dwell in the air while we live on earth—it is utterly ridiculous to be so moved by this as to think that they should therefore be placed above us. By this reasoning we would also place all flying creatures above ourselves.

“But,” they say, “when flying creatures become tired from flight or need to restore their bodies with nourishment, they return to earth either for rest or for food; demons do not do this.”

Do they therefore approve of placing flying creatures above us, and demons above flying creatures as well? If that is utterly foolish to believe, there is no reason to think demons worthy of esteem because they inhabit a higher element, so that we ought to subject ourselves to them in religious devotion.

For just as it could happen that aerial birds are not merely not superior to us earthly creatures but are actually subject to us because of the dignity of the rational soul within us, so it could happen that demons, although more aerial in nature, are not therefore better than earthly human beings because air is above earth. Rather, human beings ought to be preferred to them because the hope of godly human beings is in no way comparable with the demons’ despair.

Plato’s own reasoning also sufficiently warns us of this. He interweaves and orders the four elements according to proportion, placing the two intermediate elements—air and water—between the two extremes, highly mobile fire and immobile earth. Thus, just as air is above water and fire above air, so water is above earth. Yet this does not mean that we should assess the merits of living beings according to the rank of their elements.

Apuleius himself, along with the others, calls the human being an earthly creature (*On the God of Socrates*). Nevertheless, the human being is placed far above aquatic creatures, even though Plato places water above earth. We should therefore understand that the same order need not be maintained when the merits of souls are under discussion as appears to exist among the ranks of bodies. It can happen that a better soul inhabits an inferior body, and a worse soul a superior one.

[Note: Our manuscripts read “so that they may understand.” M.]

## CHAPTER XVI.—What the Platonist Apuleius thought about the character and actions of demons.

When the same Platonist spoke about the character of demons, he said that they are agitated by the same disturbances of soul as human beings: they are provoked by injuries, appeased by services and gifts, pleased by honors, delighted by various rites of sacrifice, and troubled if anything in those rites is neglected (*On the God of Socrates*).

Among other things, he also says that divinations by augurs, soothsayers, seers, and dreams belong to them, and that the miracles of magicians also come from them.

[Note: Same work.]

Defining them briefly, he says that demons are, by kind, living beings; in soul, subject to passions; in mind, rational; in body, aerial; and in time, eternal. Of these five characteristics, he says that the first three are shared with us, the fourth is proper to them, and the fifth is shared with the gods.

[Note: Supply “the same.”]

But I see that, of the first three characteristics they share with us, two are also shared with the gods. He says that the gods too are living beings, distributing to each its own element: among earthly creatures he placed us with the other things that live and sense on earth; among aquatic creatures, fish and other swimmers; among aerial creatures, demons; and among ethereal creatures, gods.

[Note: So Erasmus and several manuscripts. Some others, with V and Am, omit “which.” In its place some have “who”; and later, instead of “elements,” they read “element.” The Lovanienses preferred the latter reading without sufficient reason.]

Consequently, the fact that demons are living beings by kind is something they share not only with human beings but also with gods and beasts. The fact that they are rational in mind they share with gods and human beings; that they are eternal in time, with the gods alone; that they are subject to passions in soul, with human beings alone; and that they are aerial in body is peculiar to them alone.

Therefore, that they are living beings by kind is nothing great, since beasts are this as well. That they are rational in mind does not place them above us, since we are rational too. That they are eternal in time—what good is that if they are not happy? Temporal happiness is better than miserable eternity.

That they are subject to passions—how does this place them above us, when we too are subject to passions, and would not be so unless we were miserable? That they are aerial in body—how much should this be valued, when any kind of soul is superior to every body, and therefore religious worship, which is owed from the soul, should in no way be owed to something inferior to the soul?

If, among the characteristics he says belong to demons, he had included virtue, wisdom, and happiness, and said that they possessed these eternally and in common with the gods, he would certainly have named something desirable and worthy of high esteem. Yet even then we ought not to worship them as God on account of these things, but rather worship him from whom we knew they had received them.

How much less are aerial creatures worthy of divine honor when they are rational so that they may be miserable, subject to passions so that they are miserable, and eternal so that they cannot bring their misery to an end?

## CHAPTER XVII.—Whether it is fitting for human beings to worship those spirits from whose vices they ought to be liberated.

### 1.

To leave aside everything else and deal only with what Apuleius said demons share with us—namely, the passions of the soul—if all four elements are filled with their own living beings, fire and air with immortal ones, water and earth with mortal ones, I ask why the souls of demons are agitated by the turmoil and storms of passions.

For this is disturbance, which in Greek is called *πάθος* (*pathos*, “passion”). This is why Apuleius chose to call them “subject to passions in soul,” since the term “passion” is derived from the Greek word *πάθος*.

[Note: Codex 2050 reads this passage as follows: “because the word ‘passion’ is called *pathos* by a word derived from a word; but it would better be called ‘disturbance,’” and so forth. M.]

A passion is a movement of the soul contrary to reason.

[Note: Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book IV, chapter 6: “This,” he says, “is Zeno’s definition: that a disturbance is what he calls *pathos*, a movement of the soul turned away from right reason and contrary to nature.”]

Why, then, are these things found in the souls of demons, when they are not found in beasts? If something similar appears in a beast, it is not a disturbance, because it is not contrary to reason, which beasts lack.

In human beings, however, these disturbances arise from foolishness or misery. We have not yet attained that perfection of wisdom and happiness which is promised to us at the end, when we have been liberated from this mortality.

They say that the gods do not suffer these disturbances because they are not only eternal but also happy. They too, they maintain, possess rational souls, but souls entirely pure from every stain and corruption.

Therefore, if the gods are not disturbed because they are happy rather than miserable living beings, and beasts are not disturbed because they are living beings that can be neither happy nor miserable, it remains that demons are disturbed, like human beings, because they are living beings that are not happy but miserable.

2. [XVII.] By what folly, then—or rather madness—are we subjected through some religion to demons, when through true religion we are freed from that vice by which we are like them? For although Apuleius himself, while he spares them greatly and considers them worthy of divine honors, is nevertheless compelled to admit that demons are stirred by anger, true religion commands us not to be stirred by anger but rather to resist it. When demons are enticed by gifts, true religion commands us not to favor anyone by accepting gifts. When demons are soothed by honors, true religion commands us not to be moved by such things in any way. When demons are haters of some human beings and lovers of others—not by a prudent and tranquil judgment, but with an emotion that he himself calls *passive*—true religion commands us even to love our enemies (Matt. 5:44). Finally, true religion commands us to lay aside every movement of the heart and disturbance of the mind, and all the commotions and storms of the soul, with which he asserts that demons seethe and are tossed about. What cause, then, is there—unless it be pitiable folly and error [Note: [Col. 0242] More manuscripts read *mirabilis*, “remarkable,” rather than *miserabilis*, “pitiable.”—]—for you to make yourself humble by venerating one whom you wish to be unlike in your manner of life, and to worship religiously one whom you do not wish to imitate, when the essence of religion is to imitate the one whom you worship?

## CHAPTER XVIII.—What kind of religion it is in which it is taught that human beings ought to use demons as advocates in order to be commended to the good gods

Apuleius, then, and all who think likewise, have paid them this honor in vain, placing them midway in the air, between the ethereal heaven and earth, so that, since no god mingles with a human being (these are Apuleius’s words)—which they claim Plato said—these beings may carry human prayers to the gods and bring back from the gods the things that have been obtained.

For those who believed such things considered it unworthy that human beings should mingle with gods or gods with human beings; but they considered it worthy that demons should mingle both with gods and with human beings: that they should convey requests made here and bring back grants bestowed there. Thus, supposedly, a chaste man, removed from the crimes of magical arts, is to employ as patrons those through whom the gods may hear him more readily and willingly—gods who love the things he does not love, and by not loving which he becomes more worthy to be heard.

For they love theatrical indecencies, which chastity does not love; they love in the practices of magicians a thousand arts of doing harm (Virgil, *Aeneid* 7.338), which innocence does not love. Therefore, if chastity and innocence wish to obtain anything from the gods, they will not be able to do so by their own merits unless their enemies intervene on their behalf. There is no reason for this man to try to justify poetic fictions and theatrical mockeries. Against such things we have their own teacher, Plato, a man of such great authority among them: what if human shame so ill-deserves well of itself that it not only loves disgraceful things but even considers them pleasing to divinity?

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the impiety of the magical art, which relies on the patronage of wicked spirits

Moreover, against magical arts—about which some people, excessively wretched and excessively impious, even take pleasure in boasting—shall I not summon the very public light as a witness? [Note: [Col. 0243] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “take pleasure in boasting in the name of demons, the very public light,” and so forth.] Why are these practices punished with such severity by the force of the laws, if they are the works of divinities who ought to be worshiped? Or perhaps Christians established these laws by which magical arts are punished?

In what other sense can the celebrated poet’s words be understood, unless it is that these magical practices are unquestionably harmful to the human race?

> I call the gods to witness, dear one, and you, my sister,  
> and your sweet head, that against my will I take up magical arts.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.492–493)

And what he says elsewhere about these arts—

> And I have seen harvested crops transplanted elsewhere.  
> (*Eclogue* 8.99)

—because by this pestilential and criminal doctrine other people’s crops are said to be transferred to other lands: does Cicero not record that the Twelve Tables—that is, the most ancient laws of the Romans—contained a written provision establishing a punishment for anyone who did this? [Note: [Col. 0243] The fragments of the Twelve Tables contain: “Whoever has sung away crops; whoever has sung a harmful spell . . . and you shall not entice away another’s grain.” These laws are mentioned by Pliny, *Natural History* 28.2; Seneca, *Natural Questions* 4.7; Apuleius in the *Apology*; and others.]

Finally, was Apuleius himself accused of magical practices before Christian judges? [Note: [Col. 0243] Apuleius was prosecuted on a charge of magic before Claudius, the prefect of Africa, who was by no means a Christian. See the letters of Marcellinus and Augustine, 136 n. 1 and 138 nn. 18–19.]

If he knew that the practices charged against him were divine and pious, and consistent with the works of divine powers, he ought not merely to have confessed them but also to have professed them, blaming instead the laws by which such practices were prohibited and considered worthy of condemnation, although they ought to have been regarded as marvelous and venerable. In that way he would either have persuaded the judges of his own opinion, or, if they judged according to unjust laws and sentenced him to death for proclaiming and praising such practices, the demons would have repaid his soul with gifts worthy of it, since he would not have feared to surrender his human life for proclaiming their divine works.

In the same way, when our martyrs were charged with the crime of the Christian religion—a religion by which they knew they would become eternally saved and glorious—they did not choose to escape temporal punishments by denying it. Rather, by confessing, professing, and proclaiming it, and by faithfully and courageously enduring everything for it, and dying with pious confidence, they compelled the laws by which it was prohibited to blush and caused them to be changed.

There survives a very extensive and eloquent speech by this Platonic philosopher in which he defends himself against the charge of magical practices, asserting that they have nothing to do with him. He does not wish to appear innocent in any other way than by denying practices that cannot be committed by an innocent person.

Yet all the wonders of the magicians—whom he rightly judges worthy of condemnation—are performed through the teachings and works of demons. Why, then, does he consider demons worthy of honor, asserting that they are necessary for carrying our prayers to the gods, when we ought to avoid their works if we wish our prayers to reach the true God?

Further, I ask what sort of human prayers he thinks are carried by demons to the good gods: magical prayers, or lawful ones? If magical, the gods do not want such prayers; if lawful, they do not want them carried by such beings. But if a sinner who has repented pours out prayers—especially if he has committed some magical act—does he finally receive forgiveness through the intercession of those at whose instigation or with whose favor he fell into guilt and now laments it? Or do the demons themselves, in order to earn pardon for the repentant, first repent of having deceived them? [Note: [Col. 0244] Lovaniensis adds here: “so that they too may afterward receive forgiveness.” This is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

No one has ever said this about demons. For if it were so, they would certainly not dare to seek divine honors, since by repenting they would desire to attain the grace of forgiveness. [Note: [Col. 0244] Our manuscripts read *pervenire*, “to reach,” rather than *pertinere*, “to belong.”]

There is detestable pride in the former; here there is pitiable humility.

## CHAPTER XX.—Whether the good gods more willingly mingle with demons than with human beings

But, they say, an urgent and very compelling reason forces demons to act as intermediaries between gods and human beings, so that they may present to the gods what human beings desire and bring back from the gods what they have obtained. What, then, is this reason, and how great is the necessity? “Because,” they say, “no god mingles with a human being.”

What splendid holiness, then, in a god who does not mingle with a human being who supplicates, but does mingle with an arrogant demon; who does not mingle with a repentant human being, but does mingle with a deceptive demon; who does not mingle with a human being fleeing to divinity, but does mingle with a demon pretending to be divine; who does not mingle with a human being asking for forgiveness, but does mingle with a demon persuading him to wickedness; who does not mingle with a human being who, through philosophical books, drives poets from a well-ordered state, but does mingle with a demon seeking, through the theatrical games of magistrates and priests of the state, the mockeries of poets; who does not mingle with a human being who forbids the invention of crimes committed by the gods, but does mingle with a demon who delights in false crimes committed by the gods; who does not mingle with a human being who punishes the crimes of magicians by just laws, but does mingle with a demon who teaches and practices magical arts; who does not mingle with a human being who flees imitation of the demon, but does mingle with a demon lying in wait to ensnare the human being!

## CHAPTER XXI.—Whether the gods use demons as messengers and interpreters, and whether they are deceived by them either unknowingly or willingly

1. Surely the alleged great necessity for this extreme absurdity and indignity is that the ethereal gods, who care for human affairs, would have no knowledge of what earthly human beings were doing unless the aerial demons reported it to them; for the ether is far from the earth and suspended high above it, whereas the air is contiguous both with the ether and with the earth.

O marvelous wisdom! What else do these people think about the gods, whom they all wish to be supremely good, except that the gods care for human affairs, lest they seem unworthy of worship, yet do not know human affairs because of the distance between the elements, so that demons may be thought necessary—and therefore themselves worthy of worship—because through them the gods can learn what is happening in human affairs and come to the aid of human beings when appropriate?

If this is so, these good gods know a demon through its neighboring body better than they know a human being through his good soul. O necessity greatly to be lamented—or rather vanity to be mocked and detested, lest divinity itself be vain!

For if the gods can see our souls with a soul freed from the impediment of the body, they do not need demons as messengers for this purpose. But if the ethereal gods perceive through their own bodies the bodily signs of souls—such as facial expressions, speech, and movements—and from these infer what the demons report, then they can also be deceived by the demons’ lies. Moreover, if the divinity of the gods cannot be deceived by demons, then what we do cannot be unknown to that same divinity. [Note: [Col. 0245] The word *ab*, “by,” is absent from all our manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0245] Here chapter 21 begins in the manuscripts.]

2. I wish these people would tell me whether the demons reported to the gods that Plato disapproved of the poets’ criminal fictions about the gods, while concealing from them that the demons themselves approved of those fictions; or whether they concealed both things, preferring that the gods remain ignorant of the whole matter; or whether they reported both Plato’s religious prudence toward the gods and their own irreverent lust toward the gods; or whether they wished the gods to be ignorant of Plato’s opinion—that he did not want the gods to be defamed by the poets’ impious license through false accusations—while not being ashamed or afraid to disclose their own wickedness, by which they love theatrical games in which those disgraces of the gods are celebrated.

Let them choose whichever of these four alternatives they please; and in whichever they choose, let them consider how badly they think of the good gods.

If they choose the first, they will have to confess that the good gods were not permitted to dwell with good Plato when he prohibited injuries against them, but did dwell with evil demons when those demons rejoiced in such injuries. Thus the good gods, although they were far removed from the good human being, could know him only through evil demons, whom they could not know despite their proximity. [Note: [Col. 0246] The printed editions read “who were near to them.” The manuscripts omit *sibi*, “to them.” Perhaps the reading should be: “whom, although they were near, they could not know.”]

If they choose the second and say that the demons concealed both things, so that the gods knew neither Plato’s most religious law nor the demons’ sacrilegious delight, what useful knowledge of human affairs can the gods gain through demonic intermediaries when they do not know those things that are decreed in honor of the good gods by the religion of good human beings against the lust of wicked demons?

If they choose the third and reply that through the same demonic messengers the gods learned not only Plato’s opinion, which prohibited injuries against the gods, but also the demons’ wickedness, which rejoiced in such injuries, is this reporting a message or offering an insult? And do the gods hear and know both things in such a way that they not only fail to keep wicked demons—who desire and commit things contrary to the dignity of the gods and the religion of Plato—from approaching them, but even send gifts through those evil relatives to the good Plato, who is far away?

For the series of the elements has linked them together, as though with chains, so that the demons can be joined to those by whom they are accused, while they cannot be joined to the one by whom they are defended: they know both things, but cannot alter the weights of air and earth.

If they choose the fourth, however, it is worse than all the others. Who could endure the claim that, if the demons reported to the gods the poets’ criminal fictions about the immortal gods, the unworthy mockeries of the theaters, and their own most ardent desire and sweetest pleasure in all these things, while remaining silent about Plato’s judgment—formed with philosophical seriousness concerning the best republic—that all these things should be removed, then the good gods are compelled through such messengers to know the evils of the worst beings, not things belonging to others but to the very messengers themselves, while they are not permitted to know the good things of the philosophers, which are contrary to those evils—since the former are insults against the gods, whereas the latter are honors paid to them?

## CHAPTER XXII.—On rejecting the worship of demons, against Apuleius

Since, then, none of these four alternatives may be chosen, lest in any one of them such an evil opinion be held about the gods, it remains that we must in no way believe what Apuleius is trying to persuade us of—and what all other philosophers of the same opinion maintain: namely, that demons stand midway between gods and human beings as messengers and interpreters, carrying our requests from here and bringing back the gods’ assistance from there.

Rather, they are spirits exceedingly eager to do harm, completely alien from justice, swollen with pride, livid with envy, and cunning in deceit. They inhabit the air because, having been cast down from the height of the higher heaven, they have been condemned in advance, by the merit of an offense from which return is impossible, to this place, which suits them, as though to a prison. Yet the fact that the region of air lies above earth and water does not mean that they are superior in merit to human beings. Human beings easily overcome them, not by an earthly body, but by a pious mind that has chosen the true God as its helper. [Note: [Col. 0246] Lovaniensis alone reads *aereus*, “aerial.”] [Note: [Col. 0246] Augustine discusses the dwelling-place of demons in several passages of these books. See also *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*, §33, and *On the Christian Contest*, §3.]

Nevertheless, they lord it over many who are unworthy to share in true religion, as though these people had been captured and subjected to them. To the greater part of such people they have persuaded, through marvelous and deceptive signs—whether of things done or of things foretold—that they are gods.

But to certain people who examined their vices somewhat more attentively and carefully they could not persuade them that they were gods. Instead, they pretended to be messengers between gods and human beings and procurers of benefits. Even so, those people thought that at least this honor ought to be paid them: they did not believe them to be gods, because they saw that they were evil—for they wanted all gods to be good—yet they did not dare to call them altogether unworthy of divine honor, especially lest they offend the peoples, whom they saw serving them through so many rites and temples, in an ancient superstition.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—What Hermes Trismegistus thought about idolatry, and how he could have known that the Egyptian superstitions were to be abolished

1. Hermes the Egyptian, whom they call Trismegistus, had and expressed a different view of these matters. [Note: [Col. 0247] See Lactantius, *Institutes* 1.6, and Cyril, *Against Julian* 1.]

For Apuleius denies that these beings are gods, certainly; but when he says that they occupy a kind of middle position between human beings and gods, so that they are necessary to human beings before the gods themselves, he does not separate their worship from the religion of the heavenly gods.

The Egyptian, however, says that some gods were made by the supreme God and others by human beings. Whoever hears this, as I have stated it, thinks that he is speaking of statues, because they are works of human hands. [Note: [Col. 0247] Lovaniensis reads *quae*, “which,” while other printed editions and the manuscripts disagree.]

But he asserts that visible and tangible statues are, as it were, the bodies of gods; and that certain spirits, invited into them, are present in them and possess some power either to do harm or to fulfill certain desires of those who offer divine honors and acts of worship to them.

He says, then, that to join these invisible spirits to visible objects of bodily matter by some art, so that the statues may be like animated bodies—statues dedicated and subjected to those spirits—is to make gods, and that human beings have received this great and marvelous power of making gods. [Note: [Col. 0247] Manuscript 2050 reads *copulari*, “to be joined,” rather than *copulare*, “to join.”]

I shall set down the words of this Egyptian as they have been translated into our language. [Note: [Col. 0247] The passage Augustine cites below comes from Hermes’s dialogue *Asclepius*, which is identified as having been translated into Latin by Apuleius of Madaura. Learned scholars have observed that the Latinity of Apuleius is lacking here. “The speech is plainly dry and bloodless,” says Larcher, “and having nothing resembling Apuleian fullness; this led Wouverius, Scriverius, and many other learned men to remove it from his writings.”]

“And since,” he says, “our discourse concerns the kinship and fellowship of human beings and gods, understand, O Asclepius, the power and force of the human being. The Lord and Father—or, what is supreme, God—just as he is the maker of the heavenly gods, so the human being is the maker of the gods who are content with human proximity in the temples.” [Note: [Col. 0247] In the dialogue of Mercury and Asclepius, the reading is *conjuncti*, “joined together.”]

And shortly afterward:

“Thus humanity,” he says, “always mindful of its nature and origin, perseveres in that imitation of divinity, so that, just as the Father and Lord made eternal gods to be like himself, humanity likewise fashions its own gods in the likeness of its own appearance.” [Note: [Col. 0247] In *Asclepius*: “always near to its nature and origin.” Lovaniensis reads: “always mindful of its human nature and origin.” The word *humanae*, “human,” is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

When Asclepius, to whom he was speaking most directly, replied and said, “You mean statues, O Trismegistus,” he said:

“Statues, O Asclepius. Do you see to what extent you yourself are still doubtful? [Note: [Col. 0248] The manuscripts read *vides*, without the interrogative particle *-ne*, which appears in the printed editions and in *Asclepius*.] Statues animated, full of sensation and spirit, performing great and such-like things; statues that know the future and foretell it by lot, prophecy, dreams, and many other means; inflicting illnesses on human beings and curing them, bringing sadness and joy according to their merits.” [Note: [Col. 0248] Several manuscripts of better quality read as above. The printed editions read: “foretelling those things which perhaps every prophet might be ignorant of, through many and various means.” *Asclepius* reads: “foretelling all things, perhaps, through prophecy and dreams and many other means.” The reading of our manuscripts is supported by another passage of *Asclepius*: “foretelling certain things by lots and divinations.” The manuscript designated A reads *laetitiamque afferentes*, “bringing joy also.”]

“Do you not know, O Asclepius, that Egypt is an image of heaven—or, more truly, a translation or descent of all the things that are governed and carried out in heaven? And, if it must be said, our earth is more truly the temple of the whole world. Yet, since it is fitting that the wise person should foresee all things, you must not be unaware of this: a future time will come when it will become apparent that the Egyptians have served divinity in vain with devout minds and diligent religious observance, and that all their holy worship will fall uselessly into ruin.” [Note: [Col. 0248] Most manuscripts read as above, and *Asclepius* agrees. The printed editions read: “that they have served divinity with diligent religious observance.” Perhaps the reading should be: “that they have served divinity with devout religious observance.” Manuscripts 766 and 2053 read *divinitate*, “by divinity.”] [Note: [Col. 0248] The words “and all their holy worship will fall uselessly into ruin” belong to Mercury in *Asclepius*, but are absent here from the manuscripts.]

2. Hermes then develops this subject at length.
