He appears to be foretelling the time when the Christian religion, being all the more truthful and holy, will all the more forcefully and freely overthrow every deceitful fiction, so that the grace of the most truthful Savior may free human beings from the gods whom human beings make and subject them to the God by whom human beings were made.

But when Hermes foretells these things, he speaks like a friend of those same demonic deceptions. He does not openly mention the Christian name. Rather, as though the things whose observance preserved the likeness of heaven in Egypt were about to be removed and destroyed, he laments the future in a kind of mournful prophecy.

For he belonged to those of whom the Apostle says that, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks to him, but became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible humanity (Rom. 1:21–23), and the rest, which would take too long to recount.

He says many such things about the one true God, the maker of the world, things of the sort that truth contains. Yet, through that darkening of his heart, I do not know how he descends to this point: although he confesses that the gods are made by human beings, he nevertheless always wishes human beings to be subjected to them, and he laments that these gods will be removed in the future.

As though anything could be more wretched than a human being ruled by his own fictions! Indeed, it is more likely that, by worshiping as gods those whom he himself made, he himself should cease to be a human being— [Note: [Col. 0248] The printed editions read: “since it is more likely that, by worshiping as gods those whom he himself made, he himself should cease to be a human being.” This has been emended according to the older books.]

[Note: [Col. 0249] The note is printed at the foot of column 249, but its callout number, 4, does not appear in the text. “So read Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and all the manuscripts. In B., *quam*.”]

—than that, through his worship, the gods whom human beings made should be gods. For it happens more quickly that a human being, placed in honor, is compared with uncomprehending beasts (Ps. 48:13) than that a human work should be preferred to the work of God made in his image—that is, to the human being himself.

Therefore, a human being rightly falls away from the one who made him when he places above himself what he himself has made.

3. Hermes the Egyptian knew that these vain, deceptive, pernicious, and sacrilegious things were destined to be removed, and he grieved over it; [Note: [Col. 0249] Several manuscripts read *sacrilegia*, “sacrileges.”] but he grieved as shamelessly as he knew it unwisely. The Holy Spirit had not revealed these things to him, as it had to the holy prophets, who, foreseeing them, said with rejoicing: “If a human being makes gods, and behold, they are not gods” (Jer. 16:20).

And elsewhere:

“In that day, says the Lord, I will destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and they will no longer be remembered” (Zech. 13:2).

More particularly concerning Egypt, insofar as it bears on this matter, the holy Isaiah prophesies:

“And the works made by human hands in Egypt will be shaken before him, and their heart will be overcome by them” (Isa. 19:1), and other things of this kind. [Note: [Col. 0249] The printed editions read *vincietur*, “will be bound,” whereas the manuscripts read *vincetur*, “will be overcome.” Isaiah has in Greek *ēttēthēsetai*, “will be defeated/overcome.”]

Those people too belonged to this class who rejoiced when what they knew was going to come had arrived: Simeon and Anna, when Jesus had just been born; Elizabeth, who recognized him even while he was still conceived in the Spirit (Luke 2:25–38; 1:41–45); and Peter, who said, by revelation from the Father, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16).

But the spirits had disclosed to this Egyptian the future times of their own destruction. The same spirits, trembling before the Lord present in the flesh, said: “Why have you come to destroy us before the time?” (Matt. 8:29). They said this either because what was future seemed sudden to them, although they had thought it would occur later, or because they called this their destruction—the destruction by which it happened that, once known, they would be despised.

And this was “before the time,” that is, before the time of judgment, when they will be punished with eternal condemnation together with all the human beings who are held in their fellowship. So speaks the religion that neither deceives nor is deceived—not like this man, who, as though blown about by every wind of teaching from here and there (Eph. 4:14), mixes truth with falsehood and laments as though the religion were destined to perish, though he later admits that it is error.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—How Hermes openly confessed the error of his ancestors, although he nevertheless grieved that it should be destroyed

1. For after saying much on this very subject, he returns to it and again speaks about the gods whom human beings made, as follows:

“But enough has now been said about such matters. Let us return,” he says, “to the human being and to reason, since by a divine gift the human being has been called a rational animal. What has been said about the human being is less astonishing, although it is astonishing. For among all marvelous things, this surpasses admiration: that the human being was able to discover the divine nature and to make it. Since, then, our ancestors were greatly mistaken concerning the nature of the gods, because they were unbelieving and did not pay attention to divine worship and religion, they discovered an art by which they might make gods. To their invention they added a power suited to the nature of the world; and, mingling these things, since they could not make souls, they summoned the souls of demons or angels and placed them in holy images and divine mysteries, so that idols might have the power both of doing good and of doing harm” (p. 99).

I do not know whether the demons themselves, when adjured, would confess in the same way as this man has confessed. “Since,” he says, “our ancestors were greatly mistaken concerning the nature of the gods, because they were unbelieving and did not pay attention to divine worship and religion, they discovered an art by which they might make gods.”

Did he say that they had erred at least moderately, so that they discovered this art of making gods? Or was he content to say, “They were mistaken,” unless he added, “They were greatly mistaken”? This great error, then, and the unbelief of those who did not pay attention to divine worship and religion, discovered an art by which they might make gods.

And yet what great error, unbelief, and turning away from divine worship and religion of mind had discovered—namely, that a human being should make gods by art—this wise man laments as though divine religion were destined to be removed at a future time. See whether he is not compelled, by divine power, to disclose the past error of his ancestors, and, by devilish power, to grieve over the future punishment of the demons. [Note: [Col. 0250] Erasmus and the manuscripts read *et vi diabolica*, “and by devilish power”; Lovaniensis reads *et invidia diabolica*, “and by devilish envy.”] For if their ancestors, by greatly erring concerning the nature of the gods, through unbelief and turning away of mind from divine worship and religion, discovered an art by which they might make gods, what is surprising if this detestable art, having made whatever it made while turned away from divine religion, is removed by divine religion, when truth corrects error, faith rebukes unbelief, and conversion corrects turning away? [Note: [Col. 0250] The printed editions read: “when truth may correct error, faith may rebuke unbelief, and conversion may correct turning away.” The manuscripts read *emendat*, *redarguit*, *corrigit*, “corrects,” “rebukes,” and “corrects.”]

2. For if he had said, without stating the causes, that his ancestors had discovered an art by which they might make gods, it would have been our task, if we possessed any sound and pious understanding, to attend and see that they could never have arrived at this art by which a human being makes gods if they had not strayed from the truth, if they believed things worthy of God, and if they paid attention to divine worship and religion.

And yet, if we ourselves stated that the causes of this art were the great error of human beings, their unbelief, and the turning away from divine religion of a wandering and faithless mind, the shamelessness of those resisting the truth might in some measure be endured. But when the very man who marvels above all other things at the power of this art in human beings—by which they were permitted to make gods—and who grieves that a time will come when all these images of gods instituted by human beings will even be ordered removed by law, nevertheless confesses and expressly states the reasons why people came to this point, saying that his ancestors, through great error and unbelief and by failing to pay attention to divine worship and religion, discovered this art by which they might make gods—what ought we to say, or rather what ought we to do, except give as many thanks as we can to our Lord God, who removed these things by causes contrary to those by which they were instituted?

What the multitude of error instituted, the way of truth removed; what unbelief instituted, faith removed; what turning away from the worship of divine religion instituted, conversion to the one true and holy God removed. [Note: [Col. 0251] Lovaniensis alone reads *divino*, “divine,” in place of *divinae*, “of divine religion.”] And this happened not only in Egypt, which the spirit of demons laments here as though it alone were affected, but throughout the whole earth that sings a new song to the Lord, just as the truly sacred and truly prophetic Scriptures foretold, where it is written:

> Sing to the Lord a new song;  
> sing to the Lord, all the earth.  
> (Ps. 95:1)

The title of this psalm is, “When the house was built after the captivity.” For the house of the Lord, the city of God, which is the holy Church, is being built throughout the whole earth after that captivity in which demons possessed those human beings who, when they believed in God, became like living stones by which the house is built (1 Pet. 2:5).

For it was not because human beings made gods that they themselves were not possessed by those whom they had made, since by worshiping them they were transferred into their fellowship. I mean the fellowship not of foolish idols but of cunning demons. For what are idols except what the same Scripture says: “They have eyes, and do not see” (Ps. 113:5)? [Note: [Col. 0251] Vindobonensis, Erasmianus, and several manuscripts read *videbunt*, “they shall see”; manuscript 766 does likewise.] And whatever similar statement had to be made about objects made of material, however skillfully fashioned, which nevertheless lack life and sensation, is there too. [Note: [Col. 0251] See Letter 102, nn. 18–19.]

But unclean spirits, bound to those same images by that wicked art, had miserably taken captive the souls of their worshipers by bringing them into their own fellowship. Hence the Apostle says:

> We know that an idol is nothing; but what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons.  
> (1 Cor. 10:20)

After this captivity, then, by which human beings were held by wicked demons, the house of God is built throughout the whole earth. Hence that psalm received its title, in which it says:

> Sing to the Lord a new song;  
> sing to the Lord, all the earth.  
> Sing to the Lord and bless his name;  
> proclaim his salvation from day to day.  
> Declare his glory among the nations,  
> his wonders among all peoples.  
> For great is the Lord and greatly to be praised;  
> he is to be feared above all gods.  
> For all the gods of the nations are demons,  
> but the Lord made the heavens.  
> (Ps. 95:1–5)

3. Therefore, the man who grieved that the time would come when the worship of idols and the dominion of demons over those who worshiped them would be removed, instigated by an evil spirit, always wanted this captivity to remain, although, once it had passed, the Psalm sings that a house is being built throughout the whole earth.

Hermes foretold that former event with grief; the Prophet foretold this one with joy. And because the Spirit who sang these things through the holy prophets is victorious, Hermes himself was compelled in marvelous ways to confess that the things he did not want and grieved to see removed had been instituted not by the wise, faithful, and religious, but by the erring, unbelieving, and those turned away from the worship of divine religion.

Although he calls them gods, nevertheless, when he says that they were made by such human beings as we certainly ought not to be, he shows, whether he wishes it or not, that they ought not to be worshiped by those who are not like the people by whom they were made—that is, by the wise, faithful, and religious. At the same time, he shows that the very human beings who made them brought this upon themselves: they acquired as gods beings who were not gods.

For that prophetic word is true:

> If a human being makes gods, and behold, they are not gods.  
> (Jer. 16:20)

When Hermes had called such gods—the gods of such people, made by such people through art—gods, that is, demons bound by some art to the bonds of their desires, and had called them gods made by human beings, he nevertheless did not grant them what the Platonist Apuleius did—about whom we have already said enough and shown how inconsistent and absurd his view is: that they should be interpreters and intercessors between the gods whom God made and the human beings whom that same God made, carrying vows from one side and bringing back gifts from the other.

For it is exceedingly foolish to believe that the gods whom human beings made have greater influence with the gods whom God made than do the human beings whom that same God made. A demon bound to an image by impious art was made a god by a human being—but by such a human being, not by every human being. What sort of god, then, is this one whom a human being would not make unless he were erring, unbelieving, and turned away from the true God?

Moreover, if the demons worshiped in temples, placed by some art into images—that is, visible statues—by those human beings who made gods through this art while they had strayed from and turned away from divine worship and religion, are not messengers or interpreters between human beings and gods, both because of their exceedingly wicked and disgraceful character and because human beings, although erring, unbelieving, and turned away from divine worship and religion, are nevertheless unquestionably better than the beings whom they themselves made gods by art [Note: [Col. 0252] The printed editions read: “and, because of their exceedingly wicked and disgraceful character, human beings themselves also.” The manuscripts correct this reading.]—then it remains that whatever they can do, they can do as demons: either by granting apparent benefits and thereby doing greater harm because they deceive more greatly, or by doing harm openly.

Yet they can do none of these things except when and insofar as they are permitted by the high and hidden providence of God. [Note: [Col. 0252] The words *et quantum*, “and insofar as,” are absent from the manuscripts.] They do not possess great influence with human beings as intermediaries between human beings and gods through the friendship of the gods.

For they cannot be friends of the good gods whom we call holy Angels, rational creatures of the holy heavenly dwelling—whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers. [Note: [Col. 0252] Manuscripts of good quality read *coelestes habitationes*, “heavenly dwellings”; the other reading is less correct, unless perhaps *sanctae*, “holy,” should be read in place of *atque*, “and.”] They are as far removed from them in the affection of their minds as vice is removed from virtue and wickedness from goodness.

## CHAPTER XXV.—On What May Be Common to the Holy Angels and Human Beings

Therefore, by no means should we seek the goodwill or beneficence of the gods—or rather, of the good Angels—through the supposed mediation of demons. We should seek it through similarity of good will, by which we are with them, live with them, and worship with them the God whom they worship, even though we cannot see them with bodily eyes. To the extent that we are wretched through dissimilarity of will and the weakness of our infirmity, to that extent we are far removed from them in the merit of our life, not in the place occupied by our bodies.

For it is not because we dwell on earth in the condition of flesh that we are not joined to them, but if, through uncleanness of heart, we savor earthly things. [Note: [Col. 0252] The printed editions read, “but if through the uncleanness of our heart.” The manuscripts, however, read, “but if uncleanness of heart.”] When we are healed, so that we become what they are, we draw near to them meanwhile by faith, if we believe—with their favor—that we are made blessed by the One by whom they too were made blessed.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—That the Whole Religion of the Pagans Was Consummated in the Worship of Dead Human Beings

### 1

It should certainly be observed how this Egyptian, when he grieved that the time would come when those things would be taken away from Egypt which he admits had been instituted by people greatly deceived and unbelieving and turned away from the worship of divine religion, says among other things:

> “Then this most holy land, the abode of shrines and temples, will be filled with tombs and the dead.”

As if, if those things were not taken away, human beings would not be destined to die, or the dead would have to be laid anywhere other than on earth! And surely, the more time and days passed, the greater would be the number of tombs, because of the greater number of the dead.

But what he seems to grieve is that the memorials of our martyrs would take the place of their temples and shrines—so that those who read these things with minds turned away from us and perverted might suppose that the Pagans worshiped gods in temples, whereas we worship the dead in tombs.

For impious people, in such great blindness, stumble, so to speak, against mountains and refuse to see things that strike their eyes, that they do not notice that throughout all the writings of the Pagans either no gods are found who were not human beings, or they are found only with difficulty, and that divine honors were conferred upon the dead. [Note: [Col. 0253] Earlier editions read: “who were not human beings, yet nevertheless strive to display divine honors to all, as though they had never possessed anything human.” A little later they also read, “to be regarded as empty gods.” The text has been corrected according to the older books.]

I omit what Varro says: that all the dead are regarded by them as Manes-gods. He proves this by those sacred rites that are offered to almost all the dead, in which he also mentions funeral games—as though the greatest proof of divinity were that games are not ordinarily celebrated except for divine powers.

### 2

Hermes himself, the subject now under discussion, in that same book where, as though foretelling the future, he laments and says, “Then this most holy land, the abode of shrines and temples, will be filled with tombs and the dead,” testifies that the gods of Egypt were dead human beings.

For after saying that his ancestors, greatly deceived in their understanding of the gods, unbelieving and inattentive to divine worship and religion, had discovered an art by which they could make gods, he says:

> “To this discovery they added a power corresponding to the nature of the world; and, mixing it with that power—for they could not make souls—they summoned the souls of demons or angels and placed them in sacred images through divine rites, so that by means of these images the idols might possess powers both for doing good and for doing harm.”

Then, as though he were about to prove this by examples, he continues:

> “For your grandfather, Asclepius, the first inventor of medicine, to whom a temple has been consecrated on Mount Libya near the shore of the Crocodiles, in which his worldly man—that is, his body—lies, has returned to heaven, the remainder of him—or rather, his whole being, if a human being is wholly what is perceived through life—being better, and even now granting every kind of assistance to sick human beings by his divine power, which he formerly used to provide through the art of medicine.”

Behold: he said that a dead man was worshiped as a god in the place where he had his tomb. He was false and deceiving in saying that he had returned to heaven.

He then adds another example:

> “Hermes,” he says, “whose ancestral name I bear, residing in his eponymous homeland, does he not assist and preserve all mortals who come from every direction?”

This greater Hermes—that is, Mercury—whom he says was his grandfather, is said to be in Hermopolis, that is, in the city bearing his name. [Note: [Col. 0254] In this twenty-sixth chapter we have removed certain words that had been added in the printed editions, where the text read: “False and deceiving (in saying) that he returned to heaven, (even now granting every kind of assistance to sick human beings). Then he adds another.” A little later it read: “He is said to be in the city bearing his name (buried).” The word “buried,” and the other words enclosed in parentheses, are not found in the manuscripts.]

Behold: he says that two gods were human beings, namely Asclepius and Mercury. Both Greeks and Latins hold the same opinion about Asclepius. Many, however, do not think Mercury was mortal, although this man testifies that Mercury was his grandfather.

“But,” someone may say, “that one is different from this one, although they are called by the same name.” I will not argue greatly over whether that one is different from this one. Yet this one too, like Asclepius, became a god from a human being, according to the testimony of so eminent a man among his own people as this Trismegistus, his grandson.

### 3

He adds still more, saying:

> “As for Isis, the wife of Osiris, how many good things do we know her to provide when favorable, and how much harm she can do when angry?”

[Note: [Col. 0254] The word “wife” is absent from the manuscripts and also from the Asclepius, where the text reads: “As for Isis and Osiris, how many good things we know them to provide when favorable, and how much harm when angry.”]

Then, to show that the gods made by human beings through that art belonged to this same class—and thus to indicate that he believed demons had arisen from the souls of dead human beings, whom human beings, greatly deceived, unbelieving, and irreligious, had placed in images by means of the art they discovered, since those who made such gods could certainly not create souls—after saying of Isis what I have mentioned, namely, how much harm we know her to do when angry, he went on to add:

> “For it is easy for earthly and worldly gods to become angry, since they have been made and composed by human beings from both natures.” [Note: [Col. 0254] In place of “from both natures,” Mercury’s Asclepius has “outside nature also,” a very corrupt reading.]

He says “from both natures,” from soul and body: so that the demon represents the soul, and the image represents the body.

“Hence,” he says, “it came about that these sacred animals were named by the Egyptians, and that in their respective cities the souls of those animals which had been consecrated while alive were worshiped, so that those cities were inhabited according to their laws and called by their names.” [Note: [Col. 0254] This is the reading of the Ambrosian manuscript and the other manuscripts, as well as of the Asclepius. The editions of Louvain read, “those who consecrated them alive”; Erasmus has the same, changing only “these” to “them.”]

Where, then, is that seemingly mournful lament that the Egyptian land, the most holy abode of shrines and temples, would become filled with tombs and the dead? The lying spirit, by whose prompting Hermes spoke these words, was compelled through that very statement to confess that even then the land was already filled with tombs and dead persons whom they worshiped as gods.

But the demons’ grief was speaking through him: they were mourning because their future punishments were about to be inflicted at the memorials of the holy martyrs. For in many such places they are tormented, confess, and are expelled from the bodies of possessed human beings.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the Kind of Honor Christians Pay to the Martyrs

### 1

Yet we do not establish temples, priesthoods, sacred rites, or sacrifices for those same martyrs, because their God—not they themselves—is our God.

Certainly we honor their memorials as those of holy human beings of God, who fought for the truth even to the death of their bodies, so that true religion might become known after false and fabricated religions had been refuted. Even those who previously held this conviction suppressed it through fear.

But who has ever heard a Christian priest standing at an altar constructed for the honor and worship of God, even over the sacred body of a martyr, say in his prayers, “I offer you a sacrifice, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian”? At their memorials, sacrifice is offered to the God who made them both human beings and martyrs and who joined them to his holy Angels in heavenly honor.

Thus, by that celebration, we give thanks to the true God for their victories, and we exhort ourselves to imitate such crowns and palms, invoking the same God for assistance as we renew the memory of the martyrs.

Whatever acts of religious service, therefore, are performed at the places of the martyrs are ornaments of their memorials, not sacred rites or sacrifices offered to the dead as gods. [Note: [Col. 0255] Compare Book 20 Against Faustus, chapter 21.]

Those who bring their meals there also—and this is not done by better Christians, while in many parts of the world no such custom exists—when they have set out the food, pray and then remove it so that they may eat it or distribute some of it to those in need. They wish the food to be sanctified for them through the merits of the martyrs, in the name of the Lord of the martyrs. [Note: [Col. 0255] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions read “there.”] [Note: [Col. 0255] See Book 6 of the Confessions, chapter 2.]

Anyone who knows the one sacrifice that is offered there—the sacrifice of Christians—knows that these are not sacrifices offered to the martyrs. [Note: [Col. 0255] The printed editions read “to God.” The manuscripts, however, have “even” in place of “to God.”]

### 2

We therefore worship our martyrs neither with divine honors nor with human crimes, as those people worship their gods. We offer them neither sacrifices nor turn their disgraceful deeds into their sacred rites.

Concerning Isis, the wife of Osiris and an Egyptian goddess, and concerning their parents—all of whom are said to have been kings—there is a story that, while Isis was sacrificing to those parents, she discovered a crop of barley and showed its ears to her husband the king and to his counselor Mercury. They therefore wish her to be Ceres as well.

What and how many evils are recorded in the secret writings of their mysteries—not by the poets but by those writings themselves—as Alexander writes in a letter to Olympias, his mother, with the priest Leon as his authority, let those read who wish or are able, and let those who have read recall them. [Note: [Col. 0256] See above, chapter 5.] Let them see for what dead human beings, or for what deeds of theirs, sacred rites were instituted as though for gods.

Far be it from them, even if they regard such beings as gods, to dare compare them in any respect with our holy martyrs, whom we do not regard as gods.

For this is why we do not appoint priests for our martyrs or offer sacrifices to them: such things are incongruous, unlawful, and forbidden, and are owed exclusively to the one God. Nor do we entertain them with their own crimes or with the most shameful games in which those people either celebrate the indecencies of their gods, if those gods committed such acts when they were human beings, or invent the pleasures of harmful demons, if they were not human beings.

Socrates would not have had a god from this class of demons, if he had had a God. [Note: [Col. 0256] The words “if he had had a God” are absent from manuscripts 766, 2050, and 2053.] But perhaps such a god was brought to that innocent man, who was alien to the art of making gods, by those who wished to excel in that same art.

What more need be said? No one who is even moderately prudent doubts that these spirits should not be worshiped for the sake of the blessed life that is to follow death.

But perhaps they will say that all the gods are good, whereas some demons are evil and others good. They will maintain that those whom they believe to be good should be worshiped, since through them we attain the blessed life that lasts forever. What this amounts to must now be examined in the following book.

## BOOK NINE

After saying in the preceding book that the worship of demons must be rejected, since they themselves reveal through so many arguments that they are evil spirits, Augustine now confronts in this book those who distinguish among demons, saying that some are evil and others good. Having refuted that distinction, he proves that the office of mediator between human beings and blessedness belongs to no demon at all, but to Christ alone.

[Col. 0255]

## CHAPTER I.—To What Point the Previous Discussion Has Reached, and What Remains to Be Examined

Some have thought that there are both good and evil gods. Others, holding a higher opinion of the gods, have attributed so much honor and praise to them that they did not dare believe any god to be evil.

But those who said that some gods are good and others evil also called demons by the name of gods, although they likewise sometimes, and more rarely, called gods by the name of demons. Thus they admit that even Jupiter himself, whom they wish to be king and prince of the rest, was called a demon by Homer. [Note: [Col. 0256] Plutarch, in the essay *On the Cessation of Oracles*.]

Those, however, who assert that all gods are good, and far superior to those human beings who are considered good, are troubled by the deeds of demons, which they cannot deny. Since they believe that such deeds could in no way be committed by gods whom they all wish to be good, they are compelled to introduce a distinction between gods and demons. Whatever in the works or dispositions of these hidden spirits displeases them—through which the spirits reveal their power in wicked ways—they believe to belong to demons, not gods.

Yet they think that these same demons have been placed midway between human beings and gods, as though no god mingled with humanity in order to carry requests from here and bring back the things obtained there. This is the view of the leading and most distinguished philosophers, the Platonists. With them, as with people of exceptional authority, we have chosen to examine the question whether the worship of many gods contributes to attaining the blessed life that is to follow death.

In the preceding book we asked how demons, who delight in things that good and prudent human beings reject and condemn—namely, sacrilegious, disgraceful, and criminal acts, the poetic fabrications concerning the gods themselves, and the criminal and punishable violence of magical arts—could reconcile good human beings to the good gods as though they were nearer and dearer to those gods. It became clear that they could do so in no way whatsoever.

## CHAPTER II.—Whether Among the Demons, Who Are Inferior to the Higher Gods, There Is Some Class of Good Beings Through Whose Protection the Human Soul Can Attain True Blessedness

Accordingly, as we promised at the end of the previous book, this book must contain a discussion not of the difference—if they wish there to be one—among the gods, whom they all call good, nor of the difference between gods and demons, since they place the gods far above and away from human beings but locate demons between gods and human beings.

Rather, it must discuss the difference among the demons themselves, insofar as this concerns the present question. [II.] For it is common among many people to say that some demons are good and others evil.

Whether this is the opinion of the Platonists or of anyone else, it must by no means be neglected in discussion, lest someone imagine that good demons ought to be followed. Through them, as intermediaries, such a person might seek and strive to be reconciled to gods whom he believes to be all good, so that he might be able to be with them after death. Entangled in and deceived by the fraud of evil spirits, however, he would wander far from the true God, with whom alone, in whom alone, and from whom alone the human soul—that is, the rational and intellectual soul—is blessed.

## CHAPTER III.—What Apuleius Attributes to Demons; Although He Does Not Take Reason Away from Them, He Assigns Them No Virtue

What, then, is the difference between good and evil demons? The Platonist Apuleius, discussing them generally and saying so much about their aerial bodies, said nothing about the virtues of their souls—virtues with which they would have been endowed if they were good.

He therefore kept silent about the cause of blessedness. But he could not keep silent about the evidence of their misery. He confessed that their mind—which he declares to be rational—is not at least imbued and fortified with virtue so as never to yield to the irrational passions of the soul. Instead, like the minds of fools, it too is agitated by turbulent disturbances.

His words on this subject are as follows:

> “From this class of demons,” he says, “poets are accustomed, and not far from the truth, to invent gods as haters and lovers of certain human beings: some they cause to prosper and exalt, while others they oppose and afflict. Accordingly, they also represent them as pitying, becoming indignant, suffering anguish, and rejoicing, undergoing every aspect of the human soul, and fluctuating through every surge of thought with a similar movement of heart and commotion of mind. All these little agitations and storms are far removed from the tranquility of the heavenly gods.” (*Apuleius, On the God of Socrates*)

Is there any doubt in these words that Apuleius said not that some lower parts of their souls, but the very minds of the demons—the minds by which they are rational animals—are disturbed by the storm of passions like a turbulent sea?

Thus they cannot even be compared with wise human beings. Wise human beings, although they endure such disturbances of soul, from which human frailty is not immune, under the conditions of this life, resist them with an untroubled mind. They do not yield to them by approving or carrying out anything that strays from the path of wisdom and the law of justice.

The demons, however, resemble foolish and unjust mortals—not in body but in character—or, rather, they are worse, because they are older and cannot be healed from the punishment they deserve. They too fluctuate in the very sea of the mind, as Apuleius called it, and do not stand firm in any part of the soul through truth and virtue, by which turbulent and wicked affections are resisted.

## CHAPTER IV.—The Opinions of the Peripatetics and Stoics Concerning the Disturbances That Affect the Soul

### 1

There are two philosophical opinions concerning these movements of the soul, which the Greeks call πάθη (*pathē*). [Note: [Col. 0258] The form should be written *pathē*, as the Greek term, on the authority of the manuscripts; this was ordered by the Benedictine Fathers in the Addenda: “which the Greeks call *pathē*.”] Some among us, such as Cicero, call them *perturbationes*, “disturbances” (*On Ends*, Book 3, chapter 20; *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 3, chapter 4; Book 4, chapters 5 and 6, and elsewhere); some call them “affections” or “feelings”; [Note: [Col. 0258] Quintilian, *Institutes of Oratory*, Book 6, chapter 2, section 20.] and some, like Apuleius, translating the Greek more literally, call them “passions.”

Some philosophers therefore say that these disturbances, affections, or passions also occur in the wise person, but in moderated form and subject to reason, so that the sovereignty of the mind imposes laws upon them by which they are reduced to a necessary measure.

Those who hold this view are Platonists or Aristotelians, since Aristotle was Plato’s disciple and founded the Peripatetic school.

Others, such as the Stoics, do not approve of any passions of this kind occurring in the wise person at all.

Cicero, however, in his books *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, proves that these people—that is, the Stoics—contend against the Platonists or Peripatetics more in words than in substance. For the Stoics refuse to call bodily and external things “goods,” calling them instead “advantages,” since they wish no good to belong to a human being except virtue, understood as the art of living well, which exists only in the soul.

The others call these things “goods,” simply and according to ordinary usage; but in comparison with the virtue by which one lives rightly, they call them small and insignificant. Thus, although both groups use different names—“goods” or “advantages”—they nevertheless evaluate the things in the same way. In this dispute, the Stoics appear to take pleasure only in novelty of terminology.

It therefore seems to me that here too, where the question is whether passions of the soul occur in the wise person or whether the wise person is entirely free from them, the controversy concerns words more than things. For, insofar as the substance of the matter is concerned, and not the sound of the terms, I believe that the Stoics themselves think the same as the Platonists and Peripatetics.

### 2

To omit other arguments by which I could show this, and not make the discussion too long, I will mention one especially clear example.

Aulus Gellius, a man of exceptionally refined eloquence and extensive and fluent learning, writes in the books entitled *Attic Nights* [Note: [Col. 0259] The Vindobonensis and the manuscripts read “Agellius.” The Ambrosian manuscript, Erasmus, and Louvain read “A. Gellius.”] that he once sailed with a certain famous Stoic philosopher.

As Aulus Gellius relates more fully and at greater length—though I will touch on it briefly (*Attic Nights*, Book 19, chapter 1)—when the ship was being tossed about with extreme danger by a terrible sky and sea, the force of fear made the philosopher turn pale.

Those present noticed this, watching with the greatest curiosity, even though they were near death, to see whether the philosopher’s mind would be disturbed.

After the storm had passed, as soon as safety provided an opportunity for conversation, or even for idle chatter, one of the people carried by the ship—a wealthy and luxurious Asian—addressed the philosopher, mocking him because he had been frightened and had turned pale, while the Asian himself had remained unafraid in the face of the destruction that threatened them.

The philosopher then repeated the reply of the Socratic Aristippus. When Aristippus had heard the same words from a similar man in a similar situation, he replied that the man had rightly felt no concern for the soul of such a worthless scoundrel, whereas the philosopher ought to have feared for the soul of Aristippus.

After the philosopher had driven off the rich man with this answer, Aulus Gellius later asked him—not in order to provoke him, but to learn—what the reason for his fear had been.

To instruct the man, who was ardently devoted to the pursuit of knowledge, the philosopher immediately brought out from his small bundle a book by the Stoic Epictetus. It contained teachings consistent with the doctrines of Zeno and Chrysippus, whom we know to have been the founders of the Stoics.

Aulus Gellius says that he read in this book that the Stoics held the following view: mental impressions, which they call *phantasiai*, are not under our control; neither whether nor when they enter the mind is within our power. When they arise from terrifying and fearful things, they must necessarily move even the mind of a wise person, so that for a short time he may become frightened with fear or contract with sadness, as though these passions anticipate the work of the mind and reason. [Note: [Col. 0259] This is the reading of most manuscripts. The editions read “when they arise.” A little later, all our manuscripts read “it is necessary”; manuscript B reads “it is necessary that.”]

Yet this does not mean that an opinion of evil is formed in the mind, or that such impressions are approved and assented to. The Stoics wish the matter of assent to remain within our control, and they judge that the difference between the mind of a wise person and that of a fool is this: the fool’s mind yields to these passions and adapts its assent to them, whereas the wise person, although necessarily experiencing them, nevertheless preserves in an unshaken mind a true and stable judgment concerning what he ought rationally to desire or avoid.

I have explained this as well as I could—not indeed more conveniently than Aulus Gellius, but certainly more briefly and, as I think, more clearly. These are the things he says he read in Epictetus’ book and that Epictetus taught and believed according to the doctrines of the Stoics.

### 3

If this is so, there is either no difference or almost no difference between the Stoics’ opinion and that of the other philosophers concerning the passions and disturbances of the soul. Both groups defend the mind and reason of the wise person from their domination.

Perhaps this is why the Stoics say that such passions do not occur in the wise person: they do not cloud or overthrow the wisdom by which he is wise through any error or defect.

Yet these passions do affect the mind of the wise person without destroying the serenity of wisdom, because of those things that they call advantages or disadvantages, although they refuse to call them goods or evils.

Surely, if that philosopher had regarded as worthless the things he perceived he might lose in the shipwreck—such as this life and the safety of the body—he would not have recoiled from the danger so greatly that even his pallor revealed it.

Nevertheless, he could endure that emotional disturbance while maintaining firmly in his mind the judgment that the life and bodily safety threatened by the violence of the storm were not goods capable of making those who possessed them good, as justice does.

As for their claim that these things should not be called goods but advantages, that belongs to a dispute over words, not an examination of realities. What difference does it make whether they are more appropriately called goods or advantages, provided that the Stoic is no less frightened and pale than the Peripatetic at being deprived of them, evaluating them equally even if he does not give them the same name?

If the dangers threatening these goods or advantages forced both groups to commit a disgraceful or criminal act, so that they could not retain them in any other way, both would say that they preferred to lose the things by which the body’s nature is preserved safe and sound rather than commit the acts by which justice is violated.

Thus, when this judgment is firmly established, the mind does not allow any disturbances to prevail against reason, even if they arise in the lower parts of the soul. On the contrary, it rules over them and exercises the sovereignty of virtue by refusing to consent to them and instead resisting them.

Virgil also depicts Aeneas in this way when he says:

> “His mind remains unmoved; his tears roll uselessly.”  
> (*Aeneid* 4.449)

## CHAPTER V.—That the Passions Affecting Christian Minds Do Not Drag Them into Vice but Exercise Virtue

It is not necessary now to demonstrate at length and with painstaking care what divine Scripture teaches about these passions, since Christian instruction is contained in it.

Scripture subjects the mind itself to God, so that God may govern and assist it, and it teaches that the passions must be moderated and restrained by the mind in such a way that they are turned to the uses of justice.

In our discipline, therefore, the question is not so much whether a devout mind becomes angry, but why it becomes angry; nor whether it is sad, but what makes it sad; nor whether it is afraid, but what it fears.

To become angry with someone who sins, so that he may be corrected; to become sorrowful for someone who is afflicted, so that he may be liberated; to fear for someone in danger, lest he perish—I do not know whether anyone could condemn these responses after sound reflection.

The Stoics are also accustomed to condemn mercy. [Note: [Col. 0260] See below, Book 14, chapters 8 and 9.] Yet how much more honorably that Stoic would be disturbed by mercy for a human being who needed to be rescued than by fear of shipwreck!

Cicero spoke far better, more humanely, and more appropriately to the feelings of the devout in his praise of Caesar, where he says:

> “None of your virtues is either more admirable or more pleasing than mercy.”  
> (*Speech for Quintus Ligarius*, chapter 12)

What, then, is mercy except a kind of compassion in our heart for another person’s misery, by which we are compelled, if we can, to come to that person’s aid?

This movement serves reason when mercy is shown in such a way that justice is preserved, whether it is shown by giving to someone in need or by forgiving someone who repents.

Cicero, an excellent speaker, did not hesitate to call mercy a virtue, although the Stoics are not ashamed to number it among the vices. Yet, as the book of the distinguished Stoic Epictetus teaches, according to the doctrines of Zeno and Chrysippus, who held the leading positions in this school, [Note: [Col. 0261] Supply “parts” or “positions.”] they admit passions of this kind into the mind of the wise person, whom they nevertheless wish to be free from all vices.

It follows that they do not regard these passions as vices when they occur in the wise person in such a way that they have no power against the virtue and reason of the mind. Thus the Peripatetics—or even the Platonists—and the Stoics hold one and the same view.

But, as Tully says, “a dispute over words has long tormented the little Greeks, who are more eager for contention than for truth.” (*On the Orator*, Book 1, chapter 11, section 47)

It may still reasonably be asked whether it belongs to the infirmity of the present life that even good people must endure feelings of this kind in their good works, while the holy Angels punish those whom the eternal law of God assigns to punishment without anger, assist the miserable without compassion for misery, and help those whom they love in danger without fear.

Nevertheless, the names of these passions are applied to the Angels according to human linguistic custom, because of a certain similarity in their actions, not because of any weakness in their affections.

God himself, according to the Scriptures, becomes angry, yet is not disturbed by any passion. [Note: [Col. 0261] See Book 1 Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, section 40, and elsewhere.]

In this case, the effect of vengeance is designated by the word, not the turbulent emotion itself.

## CHAPTER VI.—With What Passions Demons Are Agitated, According to Apuleius’ Confession, Although He Claims That Through Their Aid Human Beings Are Assisted by the Gods

Leaving aside for the moment the question concerning the holy Angels, let us see how the Platonists say that the demons placed midway between gods and human beings fluctuate amid these surges of passion.

If they experienced movements of this kind while free from these passions and ruling over them, Apuleius would not have said that they “fluctuate through every surge of thought with a similar movement of heart and commotion of mind.” (*On the God of Socrates*) [Note: [Col. 0261] The printed editions read “did not experience”; this is wrong and contrary to the manuscripts.]

Their very mind, therefore—that is, the higher part of the soul by which they are rational, in which virtue and wisdom would rule over and moderate the passions of the lower parts of the soul if they possessed any virtue and wisdom—their very mind, I repeat, fluctuates in a sea of disturbances, as this Platonist confesses.

The mind of demons is therefore subjected to the passions of lust, fear, anger, and the rest of this kind.

What part of them, then, is free and possessed of wisdom, by which they might please the gods and advise human beings according to the likeness of good moral character, when their mind, enslaved and oppressed by the vices of passion, turns whatever reason it naturally possesses so much more sharply toward deceiving and misleading others, the more strongly the desire to do harm possesses it? [Note: [Col. 0262] This is the reading of the manuscripts of good authority. The Louvain edition omits “moral character”; in its place the Vindobonensis and Ambrosian manuscripts read “of the gods.” Erasmus has “of these” instead of “of good.”]

## CHAPTER VII.—That the Platonists Say the Gods Have Been Disgraced by the Poets’ Fictions Concerning a Contest Between Opposing Allegiances, Although These Features Belong to Demons, Not Gods

But if someone says that the demons whom the poets, not far from the truth, invent as haters and lovers of certain human beings are not drawn from all demons but only from the number of evil demons—for Apuleius said that these fluctuate in the sea of the mind through every surge of thought—how are we to understand this?

When he said this, was he not describing the entire class of demons, rather than some of them—that is, the evil ones—as being placed between gods and human beings on account of their aerial bodies?

For he says that poets invent the following: that they make gods out of this class of demons, give them the names of gods, and, with the unpunished license of fabricated verse, assign from among them friends and enemies to whatever human beings they choose. Yet, he says, they declare the gods to be removed from the character of these demons, as well as from their heavenly dwelling and the abundance of their blessedness. (*On the God of Socrates*)

This, then, is the poets’ fiction: to call those beings gods who are not gods, and, under the names of gods, to make them contend with one another on behalf of human beings whom they love or hate according to their partisan preferences.

He says that this fiction is not far from the truth because beings who are not gods are called by the names of gods, yet are described as demons of the sort they actually are.

Finally, he says that this accounts for the Homeric Minerva who intervened among the assembled Greeks to restrain Achilles. (*Ibid.*)

He therefore wishes that the Minerva in that story be regarded as a poetic fiction because he believes Minerva to be a goddess and places her among the gods whom he believes to be all good and blessed, in the lofty seat of the ether, far removed from intercourse with mortals.

But that one demon favored the Greeks and opposed the Trojans, just as another assisted the Trojans against the Greeks—the latter being mentioned by the same poet under the name of Venus or Mars, whom Apuleius places among the gods, who do not perform such actions, in their heavenly dwellings—and that these demons contended with one another on behalf of those whom they loved and against those whom they hated: this, he admits, the poets said not far from the truth.

For it was of these beings that the poets spoke—beings whom Apuleius testifies to fluctuate through every surge of thought with a movement of heart and commotion of mind like those of human beings—so that they could exercise love and hatred not according to justice, but, like people resembling them in the crowds of spectators at hunts and chariot races, according to the interests of their respective factions, taking one side against another. [Note: [Col. 0262] See the Exposition of Psalm 39, sections 8 and 9, and of Psalm 53, section 10.]

The Platonist philosopher seems to have taken care that, when these things were sung by the poets, they should not be believed to be done by the gods themselves, whose names the poets introduce through fiction, but by the intermediate demons.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The Platonist Apuleius’ Definition of the Heavenly Gods, the Aerial Demons, and the Earthly Human Beings

[Col. 0263]

What of that very definition of demons—is it not worth examining (in which, certainly, he included all of them by determining their nature), when he says that demons are animals in genus, passive in soul, rational in mind, aerial in body, and eternal in time (ibid.)? Among these five characteristics, he said absolutely nothing [Note: [Col. 0263] Perhaps, “by which.”] that demons might appear to share with at least good human beings but not with the wicked. For when he embraced human beings in a somewhat fuller description, speaking of them in their proper place as the lowest and earthly beings—having first spoken of the heavenly gods—he wished, by commending the two ultimate divisions, the highest and the lowest [Note: [Col. 0263] The printed editions read *ad ultimum*, “at last.” They are corrected from the older books, whose reading is confirmed by the statement below, section 12, concerning “the two ultimate divisions of nature,” that is, the highest and the lowest.], to speak in third place of the intermediate demons:

“Human beings,” he says, “shining in reason [Note: [Col. 0263] The manuscripts display remarkable variation here. Vind., Am., and manuscripts of good authority read *gaudentes*, “rejoicing.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *plaudentes*, “applauding.” Certain other manuscripts read *ferventes*, “burning,” and some *fruentes*, “enjoying.” But the Colbertine manuscript, as in Apuleius, more probably has *cluentes*, that is, “excelling.”], powerful in speech, immortal in souls, mortal in limbs, light and anxious in minds, brutish and vulnerable in bodies, unlike in character, alike in error, obstinate in boldness, persistent in hope, fruitless in labor, subject to fickle fortune, mortal individually yet perpetual as a whole species, changeable through offspring succeeding one another, fleeting in time, slow in wisdom, swift in death, and querulous in life, inhabit the earth” (*On the God of Socrates*).

When he said here [Note: [Col. 0263] Vind., Am., and most manuscripts read *hinc*, “hence.”] so many things applicable to the majority of human beings, did he also fail to mention what he knew applied only to a few, when he said “slow in wisdom”? If he had omitted this, he could in no way have properly completed the description of the human race with such concentrated care. Yet when he praised the excellence of the gods, he affirmed that in them there supremely exists the very blessedness which human beings wish to attain through wisdom.

Therefore, if he had wished some demons to be understood as good, he would also have included something in their description by which they might be thought to share either some portion of blessedness with the gods or some kind of wisdom with human beings. But in fact he mentioned no good belonging to them by which the good might be distinguished from the wicked. Although he also spared a freer expression of their wickedness—not so much lest he offend the demons themselves as lest he offend their worshipers, among whom he was speaking—he nevertheless indicated to the wise what they ought to think about them. For he entirely separated from the passions of the gods, whom he wished to be believed wholly good and blessed, and, as he himself says, from all their disturbances, joining them only through the eternity of their bodies; while he most plainly insisted that demons were like human beings, not like the gods, in soul. And he did not connect them with human beings through the good of wisdom, of which human beings too may partake, but through the disturbance of passions, which rules the foolish and wicked, whereas the wise and good so govern it that they would rather not have it than conquer it.

For if he had wished demons to be understood as sharing with the gods the eternity of their souls rather than [Col. 0264] of their bodies, he certainly would not have excluded human beings from participation in this matter, since, like a Platonist, he undoubtedly holds that human souls are eternal. Thus, when describing this class of living beings, he said that human beings possess “immortal souls and mortal limbs.” Consequently, if human beings do not share eternity with the gods because they are mortal in body, demons possess it for precisely the opposite reason: they are immortal in body.

## CHAPTER IX

### Whether the friendship of the heavenly gods can be provided for human beings through the mediation of demons

What, then, are these mediators between human beings and the gods, through whom human beings seek access to the friendship of the gods, when they share with human beings the worse element that is better in a living creature—namely, the soul—and share with the gods the better element that is worse in a living creature—namely, the body?

Since a living creature, that is, an animal, consists of soul and body, and the soul of these two is certainly superior to the body—even when vicious and weak, it is still superior to the healthiest and strongest body, since its nature is more excellent and is not reduced below the body by the stain of vices, just as even dirty gold is valued more highly than silver or lead, however pure—these mediators of gods and human beings, through whose interposition human things are joined to divine things, have with the gods an eternal body, but with human beings a vicious soul. It is as though the religion by which human beings wish to be joined to the gods through demons were established in the body rather than in the soul.

What wickedness or punishment, then, has suspended these false and deceptive mediators upside down, as though by the head, so that they share the lower part of a living creature, namely the body, with those above, but the higher part, namely the soul, with those below; and, joined to the heavenly gods in the servile part, are wretched with earthly human beings in the ruling part?

The body is a servant, as Sallustius also says: “We use the soul more for command, the body more for service.” He added: “The one is common to us with the gods, the other with the beasts” (*Sallustius, On the Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 1), since he was speaking of human beings, whose body, like that of beasts, is mortal.

But these beings whom the philosophers have presented to us as mediators between us and the gods [Note: [Col. 0264] Several manuscripts of good authority read *prodiderunt*, “have handed down” or “have declared.”] can indeed say of soul and body: “The one is common to us with the gods, the other with human beings.” But, as I have said, they are as though bound and suspended upside down: possessing a servile body with the blessed gods and a ruling soul with miserable human beings [Note: [Col. 0264] The word *habentes*, “possessing,” is absent from the manuscripts.], exalted in their lower part and cast down in their higher.

Hence, even if someone should think that they possess eternity with the gods because their souls are not separated from their bodies by death, as happens with earthly animals, one must not for that reason regard their body as the eternal vehicle of the honored, but as the eternal bond of the condemned [Note: [Col. 0264] Vind., Am., and Erasmus read *damnandorum*, “of those being condemned.”].

## CHAPTER X

### That, according to Plotinus’ view, human beings are less wretched in mortal bodies than demons in eternal ones

[Col. 0265]

Plotinus, who lived in times close to our own [Note: [Col. 0265] This is the reading of Am. and the manuscripts. Vind., Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have *vicinus*, singular, “close.” The philosopher Plotinus died near the beginning of the reign of Aurelian, that is, around the year 270 after Christ, as can be understood from Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*.], is praised for having understood Plato more excellently than the others [Note: [Col. 0265] Compare book 3 of *Against the Academics*, section 41.]. When discussing human souls, he says: “The merciful Father was making mortal bonds for them” (*Enneads* 4.3.12).

Thus he judged that the very fact that human beings are mortal in body belongs to the mercy of God the Father, so that they might not be held forever by the misery of this life. The wickedness of demons was judged unworthy of this mercy: in the misery of a soul subject to passions, it received not a mortal body, as human beings did, but an eternal one.

They would indeed be happier than human beings if they possessed with them a mortal body but with the gods a blessed soul. They would be equal to human beings if, together with their wretched soul, they had at least been granted a mortal body like theirs—provided, nevertheless, that they acquired some measure of piety, so that they might find rest from their hardships at death. But now they are not merely no happier than human beings, since their soul is wretched; they are also more wretched because of the perpetual bond of their body.

He did not wish it to be understood that, by advancing through some discipline of piety and wisdom, demons could become gods, since he expressly said that demons are eternal.

## CHAPTER XI

### On the Platonists’ opinion that the souls of human beings become demons after leaving their bodies

He says, indeed [Note: [Col. 0265] Apuleius, namely, in *On the God of Socrates*.], that human souls are demons, and that human beings become Lares if they have deserved well; Lemures, if they have deserved ill, or Larvae; but that they are called Manes gods if it is uncertain whether their merits were good or evil.

If one pays even a little attention, who does not see what an abyss this opinion opens for the pursuit of depraved conduct? For however wicked human beings may have been, they become all the worse the more eagerly they desire to cause harm, whether they think that they will become Larvae or, as gods, Manes. They even imagine that after death they are invited by certain sacrifices, as though by divine honors, so that they may inflict harm. For he says that Larvae are harmful demons made from human beings.

But this raises another question. He says that the blessed are called in Greek *eudaimones* (εὐδαίμονες) because they possess good souls—that is, good demons—thereby also affirming that human souls are demons.

## CHAPTER XII

### On the three pairs of opposites by which, according to the Platonists, the nature of demons and human beings is distinguished

But now we are discussing those beings whom he described in their own nature as intermediate between gods and human beings: animals in genus, rational in mind, passive in soul, aerial in body, and eternal in time.

After first separating the gods, placed in the lofty heavens, from human beings, placed on the lowest earth, both by location and by the dignity of their nature, he concluded as follows:

“For the present,” he says, “you have two kinds of living creatures: gods differing greatly [Col. 0266] from human beings in the loftiness of their dwelling, the perpetuity of their life, and the perfection of their nature; with no close communication between them, since so great an interval of elevation divides their highest habitations from the lowest [Note: [Col. 0266] In Apuleius: “since so great an interval of elevation divides them.”]; and since life there is eternal and unfailing, while here it is transitory and fragmentary; and since those intellects are exalted to blessedness, whereas these are cast down into misery” (*On the God of Socrates*).

Here I see three contrary pairs mentioned concerning the two ultimate divisions of nature, namely, the highest and the lowest. For the three admirable qualities he proposed concerning the gods, he repeated in other words so as to set against them three corresponding opposites in human beings.

The three qualities of the gods are these: loftiness of place, perpetuity of life, and perfection of nature. He repeated these in other words so as to oppose to them three characteristics of the human condition:

“When,” he says, “so great an interval of elevation divides the highest habitations from the lowest”—because he had said “loftiness of place.”

“And since life there,” he says, “is eternal and unfailing, while here it is transitory and fragmentary”—because he had said “perpetuity of life.”

“And since those intellects,” he says, “are exalted to blessedness, whereas these are cast down into misery”—because he had said “perfection of nature.”

Thus he posited three qualities of the gods: lofty place, eternity, and blessedness; and their three opposites in human beings: lowest place, mortality, and misery.

## CHAPTER XIII

### How demons, being neither blessed with the gods nor miserable with human beings, are intermediate between the two without sharing either side

1. Since he placed demons between these three qualities of the gods and the three of human beings, there is no dispute concerning place. Between the lofty and the lowest, an intermediate place is most appropriately understood and designated.

The remaining two pairs require more careful attention, to determine either how they are shown to be foreign to demons or how they are distributed among them in the manner demanded by their intermediate position. Yet they cannot be foreign to them. For just as we say that an intermediate place is neither the highest nor the lowest, so, since demons are rational animals, we cannot rightly say that they are neither blessed nor miserable, as though they were plants or cattle, which lack sensation or reason. Whatever beings possess reason in their minds must necessarily be either miserable or blessed.

Likewise, we cannot rightly say that demons are neither mortal nor eternal. For all living things either live forever or bring their life to an end through death. Yet he said that demons are eternal in time. What, then, remains except that these intermediates possess one of the two highest qualities and one of the two lowest?

For if they possess both qualities from the lower pair, or both from the higher pair, they will not be intermediate, but will either recoil or settle toward one side or the other [Note: [Col. 0266] Almost only the Lovaniensis edition has *resilient* and *recumbent*, future forms: “will recoil” and “will settle.”].

Since, as has been shown, they cannot lack both qualities, they will mediate by receiving one from each side. And because they cannot possess from the lower pair the eternity that is absent there, they possess this one quality from the higher pair. Therefore, the other quality needed to complete their intermediate position can only be misery.

2. [XIII.] Thus, according to the Platonists, the lofty gods possess either blessed eternity or eternal blessedness; [Col. 0267] weak human beings possess either mortal misery or miserable mortality; and intermediate demons possess either miserable eternity or eternal misery.

Nor did the five qualities he included in the definition of demons show them to be intermediate, as he had promised. For he said that they possess three qualities with us: that they are animals in genus, rational in mind, and passive in soul; one with the gods: that they are eternal in time; and one peculiar to themselves: that they are aerial in body.

How, then, are they intermediate when they possess one quality with the highest and three with the lowest? Who cannot see that, having abandoned the middle position, they incline and sink toward the lowest?

Yet intermediates can plainly also be found in such a way that they possess one distinctive quality, namely an aerial body, just as those at the extremes possess one distinctive quality each: the gods an ethereal body, and human beings an earthly one. The other two qualities are common to all: that they are animals in genus and rational in mind.

For when he himself spoke of gods and human beings, he said: “You have two kinds of living creatures.” And these people do not ordinarily describe the gods as anything other than rational in mind.

Two qualities remain: that they are passive in soul and eternal in time. Of these, they possess one with the lowest and the other with the highest, so that their intermediate position, balanced according to proportional reason, is neither raised to the highest nor depressed into the lowest.

This, then, is that miserable eternity of demons, or eternal misery. The one who said that they are passive in soul would also have said that they are miserable, had he not been ashamed on behalf of their worshipers [Note: [Col. 0267] The printed editions have *pro eorum cultoribus*, “on behalf of their worshipers.” The manuscripts omit *pro*, “on behalf of.”]. Moreover, since the world is governed by the providence of the supreme God—as they themselves also admit—and not by random chance, their eternal misery would never exist unless there were great wickedness.

3. If, then, the blessed are rightly called *eudaimones*, the demons whom these philosophers have placed midway between human beings and the gods are not *eudaimones*. What, then, is the place of good demons, who, above human beings and below the gods, provide assistance to the former and service to the latter?

For if they are good and eternal, they are certainly also blessed. But eternal blessedness does not allow them to be intermediate, since it makes them greatly like the gods and greatly separates them from human beings.

Therefore, these philosophers will vainly attempt to show how good demons, if they are both immortal and blessed, can rightly be established as intermediates between immortal and blessed gods and mortal and miserable human beings. Since they possess both qualities with the gods—namely, blessedness and immortality—and none of these qualities with miserable and mortal human beings, how are they not rather removed from human beings and joined to the gods than placed midway between the two?

They would then be intermediate if they too possessed two qualities of their own, not sharing both qualities with either side, but one quality with each of the two sides. Thus, a human being is something intermediate, but between beasts and angels: since a beast is an irrational and mortal animal, while an angel is rational and immortal, the human being is intermediate—lower than angels, higher than beasts—possessing mortality with beasts and reason with angels, a mortal rational animal.

So, when we seek an intermediate between blessed immortals and miserable [Col. 0268] mortals, we must find something that is either blessed but mortal or miserable but immortal.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Whether human beings, although mortal, can be happy with true blessedness

Whether a human being can be both blessed and mortal is a major question among human beings. Some have looked upon their condition too humbly and denied that a human being can possess blessedness so long as he lives as a mortal; others have exalted themselves and dared to say that mortals can be blessed if they possess wisdom.

But if this is so, why are these very people not rather placed as intermediates between miserable mortals and blessed immortals, possessing blessedness with the blessed immortals and mortality with miserable mortals? For if they are blessed, they envy no one—what is more miserable than envy?—and therefore, as far as they can, they provide for miserable mortals so that they may attain blessedness [Note: [Col. 0268] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have *consulant*, “let them provide.”], and so that they too may be able to become immortal after death and be joined to immortal and blessed angels.

## CHAPTER XV

### On the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus

1. But if—as is argued with much greater credibility and probability—all human beings, so long as they are mortal, must also be miserable, a mediator must be sought who is not merely human but also God, so that the blessed mortality of this mediator, intervening, may lead human beings from mortal misery to blessed immortality.

He had to become mortal, but he ought not to remain mortal. He became mortal not through any weakening of the divinity of the Word, but by assuming the weakness of flesh. Yet he did not remain mortal in that flesh, which he raised from the dead, since this is the fruit of his mediation: that those for whose liberation he became mediator should not themselves remain forever in the death of the flesh.

Accordingly, the mediator between us and God had to possess both a mortality that passes away and a blessedness that remains: so that through what passes away he might correspond to those who must die, and through what remains he might transfer the dead to it.

Good angels, therefore, cannot be intermediates between miserable mortals and blessed immortals, since they too are both blessed and immortal. But evil angels can be intermediates, because they are immortal with the former and miserable with the latter.

Opposed to them is the good Mediator, who, against their immortality and misery, both chose to be mortal for a time and was able to remain blessed for eternity. Thus, lest their boast of immortality seduce into misery, through the humility of his death and the kindness of his blessedness he destroyed both their proud immortality and their harmful misery in those whose hearts he cleansed through faith in him and liberated from their most filthy domination.

2. A mortal and miserable human being, therefore, separated by a great distance from immortals and the blessed, what mediator should he choose by whom he may be joined to immortality and blessedness?

Whatever can attract him in the immortality of demons is miserable [Col. 0269]; whatever can offend him in the mortality of Christ is no longer present. There, then, eternal misery must be avoided; here, death need not be feared, since it could not be eternal, and eternal blessedness must be loved.

For an immortal and miserable mediator interposes himself for this purpose: to prevent passage to blessed immortality, since what impedes remains—that is, misery itself. But the mortal and blessed mediator interposed himself for this purpose: that, once mortality had passed away, he might make mortals immortal by raising from the dead, as he demonstrated in himself, and make the miserable blessed, from which condition he himself never departed.

One, then, is the evil mediator who separates friends; another is the good mediator who reconciles enemies. There are many mediators who separate because the multitude that is blessed becomes blessed through participation in the one God. Through deprivation of that participation, the miserable multitude of evil angels opposes itself as an impediment rather than interposes itself as an aid to blessedness. By its very multitude it somehow makes such a disturbance that it becomes impossible to reach that one blessed-making good.

To bring us to it, we needed not many mediators but one—and that very one whose participation makes us blessed: the Word of God, not made, through whom all things were made.

Yet he is not mediator merely because he is the Word. For the Word, supremely immortal and supremely blessed, is far from miserable mortals. He is mediator through the fact that he became human. By that very fact he shows that, for reaching that good which is not only blessed but also makes blessed, we ought not to seek other mediators through whom we might suppose that stages of ascent must be constructed. For the blessed and blessed-making God, by becoming a participant in our humanity, provided a short route to participation in his divinity.

He does not free us from mortality and misery by leading us to immortal and blessed angels in such a way that through participation in them we too become immortal and blessed; rather, he leads us to that Trinity through participation in which the angels too are blessed.

Therefore, when he wished to be below the angels in the form of a servant, so that he might be mediator (Philippians 2:7), he remained above the angels in the form of God: the same one who in what is lower is the way of life, and in what is higher is life itself.

## CHAPTER XVI

### Whether the Platonists reasonably defined the heavenly gods as avoiding earthly contamination and not mingling with human beings, while demons assist human beings in attaining the friendship of the gods

For it is not true that the same Platonist says Plato declared: “No god mingles with a human being.” He says that this is the chief proof of their sublimity: that they are not contaminated by any contact with human beings (*Apuleius, On the God of Socrates*).

He therefore admits that demons are contaminated. Consequently, they cannot cleanse those by whom they are contaminated, and all become equally unclean: demons through contact with human beings, and human beings through worship of demons.

Or, if demons can be touched by and mingle with human beings without being contaminated, they are clearly better than the gods, since the gods would be contaminated if they mingled with human beings. For this is said to be the chief quality of the gods: that, being sublimely separated, they cannot be contaminated by human contact.

[Col. 0270]

As for the supreme God, creator of all things, whom we call the true God, he asserts that Plato praises him as the only one who cannot be comprehended even slightly by any speech or expression because of the poverty of human language. Yet, he says, wise men scarcely attain an understanding of this God after they have removed themselves from the body as far as the strength of their soul permits—and even then the understanding sometimes appears to them like a white light flashing amid the deepest darkness with the speed of a lightning flash (*On the God of Socrates*).

If, therefore, the truly supreme God above all things is present to the minds of the wise by a certain intelligible and ineffable presence—even if only occasionally, even if only like a white light flashing with the speed of a lightning flash—when they have removed themselves from the body as far as permitted, and if he cannot be contaminated by them, why are these gods placed far away in a lofty region lest they be contaminated by human contact?
