As though it were enough merely to see those ethereal bodies, by whose light the earth is illuminated as much as is necessary [Note: [Col. 0270] Erasmus and Venetus read: “as though those ethereal bodies could be contaminated by human touch alone, and not also by sight.” M.]. Moreover, if the stars are not contaminated when they are seen—and he calls all visible stars gods—and if demons are not contaminated by the sight of human beings, although they are seen at close range, perhaps they would be contaminated by human voices, though not by the sharpness of human eyes. For this reason they have demons as intermediaries, through whom human voices may be reported to the gods, from whom they are far away, so that the gods may remain entirely uncontaminated?

What shall I say now about the remaining senses? The gods could not be contaminated by smell if they were present, nor could demons when they are present be contaminated by the vapors of living human bodies, if they are not contaminated by the stench of so many sacrificial corpses [Note: [Col. 0270] See below, book 10, chapter 11, section 2.].

As for the sense of taste [Note: [Col. 0270] Vind., Am., Erasmus, and most manuscripts read *sensu*, “by the sense.”], they are under no necessity of replenishing their mortal condition, so that hunger would drive them to seek food from human beings.

Touch, however, is within their power. For although contact appears to derive its name chiefly from this sense, nevertheless, if they wished, they could mingle with human beings to the extent of seeing and being seen, hearing and being heard. But what necessity is there for touching? Human beings would not dare desire this when enjoying the sight or conversation of gods or good demons. And if curiosity advanced so far that they wished to touch them, how could anyone touch unwillingly a god or a demon who cannot even be seized by one who catches a sparrow?

2. By seeing, therefore, by presenting themselves to sight, and by speaking and hearing, the gods could mingle bodily with human beings. If demons mingle in this way and are not contaminated, while the gods would be contaminated if they mingled, then they call demons uncontaminable and gods contaminable.

But if demons too are contaminated, what benefit do they provide human beings for a blessed life after death? Once contaminated, they cannot cleanse human beings so that, purified, they may join them to uncontaminated gods, between whom and human beings these demons have been placed as intermediaries.

Or, if they provide no such benefit, what advantage does the friendly mediation of demons offer human beings? [Col. 0271] Is it that after death human beings do not pass through demons to the gods, but that both groups live together in a contaminated state, and therefore neither is blessed?

Unless someone should say that friendly demons cleanse their friends after the manner of sponges or similar objects, so that the demons themselves become dirtier in proportion as human beings become cleaner through them as though they were wiping cloths.

But if this is so, the gods mingle with demons who are more contaminated than they are—the very demons whose proximity and contact with human beings the gods avoided lest they be contaminated.

Or perhaps the gods can cleanse demons contaminated by human beings without being contaminated by them, while they could not do the same for human beings? Who could think such things except one deceived by the most deceitful demons?

And what if seeing and being seen causes contamination? Human beings see the gods whom he calls visible (*On the God of Socrates*), the brightest lights of the world (*Virgil, Georgics* 1.5–6), and the other stars; while demons are safer from this contamination by human beings because they cannot be seen unless they wish it.

Or if it is not being seen but seeing that causes contamination, let them deny that human beings are seen by those brightest lights of the world whom they consider gods, since their rays extend all the way to the earth. Yet their rays, diffused through every kind of unclean thing, are not contaminated; whereas the gods would be contaminated if they mingled with human beings, even if contact were necessary for providing assistance. For the earth is touched by the rays of the sun and moon, yet their light does not contaminate it.

## CHAPTER XVII

### To attain the blessed life, which consists in participation in the supreme good, human beings need not a mediator such as a demon, but one such as Christ

I am greatly astonished at such learned men, who judged that all corporeal and sensible things must be subordinated to incorporeal and intelligible things, yet, when blessed life is at issue, make mention of bodily contacts.

Where is that saying of Plotinus in which he declares: “We must flee, then, to our dearest homeland, and there is the Father, and there is everything”? “What,” he asks, “then, is the fleet or the means of flight? To become like God” (*Enneads* 1.6.8; 2.3).

If, therefore, the more like God someone becomes, the nearer he is to him, no other distance from God exists than unlikeness to him. The human soul is more unlike that incorporeal, eternal, and unchangeable being in proportion as it is more desirous of temporal and mutable things.

[XVII.] To heal this condition, since mortal and unclean things below cannot be suited to the immortal purity that is supreme, a mediator is indeed necessary. But he must not be one who has an immortal body close to the highest things while possessing a diseased soul like the lowest—one who, because of that disease, envies our healing rather than helping us to be healed. He must be one who, joined to us below through the mortality of his body, provides truly divine assistance for cleansing and liberating us through the immortal justice of his spirit [Note: [Col. 0271] Most manuscripts read: “through the justice of an immortal spirit.”], by which he remained among the highest things—not through distance of place, but through the excellence of likeness.

[Col. 0272]

Surely this uncontaminable God did not fear contamination from the human being with whose nature he clothed himself, or from the human beings among whom he lived in human form [Note: [Col. 0272] Some manuscripts, though not of better authority, read: “among whom the human being lived.”].

For these are not minor truths that he demonstrated salutarily through his incarnation: that true divinity cannot be contaminated by flesh, and that demons must not therefore be thought better than we are because they do not possess flesh [Note: [Col. 0272] Compare book 13 of *On the Trinity*, section 22.].

This is he whom holy Scripture proclaims as “the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). But this is not the place to speak, with due adequacy to our ability, of his divinity, by which he is always equal to the Father, and of his humanity, by which he became like us.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### That the deceit of demons, while promising a way to God through their mediation, strives to turn human beings away from the way of truth

Those false and deceptive mediators, the demons, who through the impurity of their spirits are plainly wretched and malicious in many manifestations, and who nevertheless attempt, through the intervals of bodily places and the lightness of aerial bodies, to draw us away and turn us aside from the progress of our souls, do not provide a way to God; rather, they obstruct us so that the way may not be followed [Note: [Col. 0272] Lovaniensis has *et non viam*, “and do not provide a way.” The conjunction *et*, “and,” is absent from the other books.].

Even along the bodily way itself—which is utterly false and full of error, and on which justice does not travel, since we must ascend to God not through bodily elevation but through spiritual, that is, incorporeal, likeness—the friends of demons arrange an order of elemental stages, placing aerial demons as intermediaries between the ethereal gods and earthly human beings. They nevertheless think that the chief quality of the gods is that, because of this distance of place, they are not contaminated by human contact.

Thus they believe that demons are contaminated by human beings rather than that human beings are cleansed by demons, and that the gods themselves could have been contaminated had they not been protected by the loftiness of their dwelling.

Who is so unhappy as to think himself cleansed by such a way, in which contaminating human beings are said to contaminate demons, the demons themselves are contaminated, and the gods are contaminable? Would he not rather choose the way on which contaminating demons are avoided, and on which human beings are cleansed from contamination by the uncontaminable God [Note: [Col. 0272] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads: “and by the unchangeable God.”], so that they may enter into fellowship with uncontaminated angels?

## CHAPTER XIX

### That even the worshipers of demons no longer use the name “demons” to signify anything good

But lest we appear to be disputing even about words, since some of these people—so to speak, demon-worshipers, among whom is Labeo—maintain that the same beings whom they call demons are called angels by others, I now see that I must say something about good angels. These people do not deny that such beings exist, but prefer to call them good demons rather than angels.

We, however, in accordance with the language of Scripture, according to which we are Christians, read that angels are partly good and partly evil [Note: [Col. 0273] [[Col. 0273] This note is printed at the foot of column 272, but its callout number, 1, does not appear in the text.] Manuscript 766: “but let anyone …” M.], but we never read of good demons. Wherever this name occurs in those Scriptures—whether they are called *demons* or *demonia*—it signifies only malignant spirits.

The people everywhere have followed this manner of speaking so thoroughly that even among those called pagans, who insist that many gods and demons ought to be worshiped, there is scarcely anyone so literate and learned that he would dare praise even his own servant by saying, “You have a demon” [Note: [Col. 0273] Coquaeus notes that Tertullian, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 3, should be consulted. M.]. Anyone who wished to say this to another cannot doubt that it would be understood only as an intended insult.

What reason, then [Note: [Col. 0273] Manuscripts 766 and 2050 read *non*, “not.”], compels us, after offending the ears of so many people—indeed, by now almost everyone, accustomed to hearing this word only in a bad sense—to explain what we have said, when by using the name “angels” we could avoid the same offense that might arise from the name “demons”?

## CHAPTER XX

### On the kind of knowledge that makes demons proud
Although even the origin of this name, if we look to the divine Books, contributes something very worthy of understanding. For they are called *daemones* (δαίμονες), since—this being a Greek word—they are named from knowledge. [Note: [Col. 0273] Plato, in the *Cratylus*, reports that *daimones* are so called as though *daêmones*, that is, “skilled” and “knowing about things.” See Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book 2.] But the Apostle, speaking by the Holy Spirit, says: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1). This is rightly understood in no other way than that knowledge is beneficial when love is present; without love, however, it puffs up—that is, it raises one into the pride of an utterly empty kind of swelling. Thus in the demons there is knowledge without love, and therefore they are so puffed up, that is, so proud, that they have undertaken to have the divine honors and the service of religion— which they know to be owed truly to God—offered to themselves, and, as far as they can and among those with whom they can, they continue to do so. [Note: [Col. 0273] Vind. and the manuscripts read *satis egerint*. Likewise elsewhere, *satis ago* is consistently used for *satago*.] Against the pride of the demons, then, by which the human race was possessed in accordance with its deserts, the humility of God, which appeared in the form of a servant [Note: Vind., Am., Er., and several manuscripts: “which appeared in Christ.” Some ancient books likewise read: “which appeared in Christ.” —So also the Corbie manuscript. But A, B, and C read as in the printed text.], possesses such power that human souls, swollen with the filth of arrogance and made like the demons by pride, but not by knowledge, do not understand it.

## CHAPTER XXI — How the Lord wished to become known to the demons

The demons themselves knew this in such a way that they said to the same Lord, clothed in the weakness of flesh: “What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us before the time?” [Note: All manuscripts: “Have you come to destroy us?” omitting “before the time.”] (Mark 1:24; also Matt. 8:29). It is clear from these words that they possessed both great knowledge and no love. For they feared their punishment from him; they did not love justice in him. Yet he became known to them only as much as he wished; and he wished only as much as was fitting. [Col. 0274]

But he became known not as he was known to the holy angels, who enjoy a participated eternity according to that in which he is the Word of God [Note: Compare Book 4 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, §§40, 50; see also the following chapter]; rather, he became known to them in the manner in which he had to be made known in order to terrify them—those from whose tyrannical power, in a certain sense, he was going to free the predestined for his kingdom and glory, always truthful and truly everlasting.

Thus he became known to the demons not through that which is eternal life, the unchangeable light that illumines the godly, to the sight of which hearts are cleansed through the faith that is in him; but through certain temporal effects of his power and signs of his most hidden presence, which could be more perceptible to the angelic senses even of wicked spirits than to human weakness. Finally, when he judged that these manifestations should for a little while be restrained and concealed himself somewhat more deeply, the prince of the demons was uncertain about him and tempted him, investigating whether he was the Christ, insofar as he himself permitted himself to be tempted, so that he might make the humanity he bore conform to an example for our imitation.

After that temptation, when the angels—as it is written—ministered to him (Matt. 4:3–11), plainly good and holy angels, and therefore objects of fear and trembling to unclean spirits, the demons increasingly came to know how great he was, so that, when he commanded, no one dared resist him, however contemptible the weakness of his flesh might appear in him.

## CHAPTER XXII — The difference between the knowledge of the holy angels and that of the demons

To these good angels, then, all knowledge of bodily and temporal things, by which the demons are puffed up, is worthless—not because they are ignorant of such things, but because the love of God, by which they are sanctified, is precious to them. In comparison with that beauty—not merely incorporeal, but also unchangeable and ineffable—with holy love of which they burn, they despise all things that are below it and are not what it is, themselves included among those things, so that from the whole of their goodness they may enjoy that Good from which they are good.

For this reason they also know temporal and mutable things more certainly, because they behold their principal causes in the Word of God, through whom the world was made—causes by which some things are approved, some rejected, and all things ordered. The demons, however, do not contemplate in the Wisdom of God the eternal and, so to speak, pivotal causes of times; rather, through their greater experience of certain signs hidden from us, they foresee far more future events than human beings do. Sometimes they also announce their own plans in advance. In short, these beings are often deceived; the angels never are.

For it is one thing to conjecture temporal things from temporal things, and mutable things from mutable things, and to introduce into them the temporal and mutable mode of one’s own will and ability—which has been permitted to the demons for a definite reason. [Note: Several manuscripts read *molum*; so also Codex 2051. M.] It is another thing to foresee changes of times in the eternal and unchangeable laws of God, which live in his Wisdom, and to know the will of God—which is both the surest and the most powerful of all [Note: So Erasmus and the manuscripts. But Vind., Am., and Lov. read: “which is the most powerful of all, of the divine Spirit,” etc.]—through participation in his Spirit. This has been granted to the holy angels by right discernment.

Therefore they are not only eternal but also blessed. The good by which they are blessed is God, by whom they were created. For they enjoy, without turning away, participation in and contemplation of him.

## CHAPTER XXIII — The name “gods” is falsely attributed to the gods of the nations, although by the authority of the divine Scriptures it is shared by the holy angels and righteous human beings

### 1

If the Platonists prefer to call these beings gods rather than demons, and to number them among those whom their author and teacher Plato, in the *Timaeus*, writes to have been created gods by the supreme God, let them say what they wish; we need not struggle with them over a dispute about words.

For if they say that these beings are immortal, yet made by the supreme God, and that they are blessed—not through themselves, but by cleaving to him by whom they were made—they are saying what we say, whatever name they give them. That this is the view of the Platonists, whether of all or of the better ones, can be found in their writings.

Indeed, concerning the very name by which they call such an immortal and blessed creature “gods,” there is almost no disagreement between us and them, because in our sacred Scriptures also it is written: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken” (Ps. 49:1); and elsewhere: “Give thanks to the God of gods” (Ps. 135:2); and elsewhere: “A great King above all gods” (Ps. 94:3).

But where it is written, “He is terrible above all gods,” the reason for this statement is shown immediately afterward. For it continues: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:4–5). Thus he said “above all gods,” but gods of the nations—that is, those whom the nations regard as gods, who are demons. He is therefore terrible: under the terror of him the demons said, “Have you come to destroy us?” (Mark 1:24).

But where he is called “God of gods,” he cannot be understood as the God of demons; and where he is called “a great King above all gods,” far be it from us to understand this as “a great King above all demons.” The same Scripture, however, also calls human beings in the people of God gods: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6).

The God of these gods, therefore, may be understood as the one called “God of gods”; and the great King above these gods may be understood as the one called “a great King above all gods.”

### 2

Nevertheless, when we are asked: If human beings are called gods because they belong to the people of God, whom God addresses through angels or through human beings, how much more are immortals worthy of this name, since they enjoy the blessedness to which human beings desire to attain by worshiping God?—what shall we answer except that the sacred Scriptures expressly call human beings “gods” rather than those immortal and blessed beings with whom we are promised that we shall be equal in the resurrection, lest, because of their excellence, unbelieving human weakness should dare to establish one of them as a god for us? [Col. 0276]

This is easy to avoid in the case of human beings. Human beings in the people of God ought to have been called gods more explicitly, so that they might become certain and confident that the one called “God of gods” is their God. For although those immortal and blessed beings who are in heaven are called gods [Note: Coquaeus observes that Origen, in Homily 8 on Exodus, teaches this from the sacred Scriptures.], they are nevertheless not called “gods of gods,” that is, gods of the human beings established in the people of God, to whom it was said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

Hence the Apostle says: “Although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:5–6).

### 3

There is therefore no need to dispute greatly about the name, since the matter itself is so clear that it leaves no room for doubt. But as for our saying that angels have been sent from the number of those immortal and blessed beings to announce God’s will to human beings [Note: The particle *autem* is absent only from the Lov. edition.], this does not please the Platonists, because they believe that this ministry is carried out not by those whom they call gods—that is, immortal and blessed beings—but by demons, whom they dare to call immortal only, not also blessed; or at least by beings so immortal and blessed that they are nevertheless good demons, not gods placed in a higher rank and removed from human contact.

Although this may seem to be a dispute about a name, the name “demons” is nevertheless so detestable that we must distance ourselves from it by every means with regard to the holy angels.

This book, then, may now be brought to a close with our understanding that those immortal and blessed beings—whatever they may be called [Note: Printed editions read *quomodolibet*; the manuscripts read *quodlibet*.]—who nevertheless have been made and created, are not intermediaries by whom miserable mortals, separated from them by both conditions, may be led to immortal blessedness. Those who are intermediaries, sharing immortality with their superiors but misery with their inferiors, are miserable because of the deserts of their wickedness; and because they do not possess blessedness, they can envy it in us rather than bestow it.

Therefore the friends of demons have nothing worthy to bring us that would make us worship them as helpers; rather, we ought to avoid them as deceivers. As for those whom they regard as good, and therefore not only immortal but also blessed, and whom they think should be worshiped under the name of gods with sacred rites and sacrifices in order to obtain a blessed life after death—whatever such beings may be, and whatever name they may deserve—we shall discuss more carefully in the following book that they do not wish, through such religious service, anyone other than the one God to be worshiped, by whom they were created and through participation in whom they are blessed.

# BOOK TEN

In this book Augustine teaches that good angels do not wish the divine honor called the worship of *latria*, and rendered through sacrifices, to be offered except to the one God, whom they themselves also serve. He then discusses against Porphyry the beginning and the way of the soul’s purification and liberation.

[Col. 0277]

## CHAPTER I — The Platonists also defined that true blessedness is bestowed on angels and human beings by the one God; but it must be asked whether those whom they therefore believe should be worshiped wish sacrifices to be offered only to the one God, or also to themselves

### 1

It is the firm conviction of all who can in any way use reason that all human beings wish to be blessed. But while human weakness searches for who the blessed are, or from where blessedness comes, many great controversies have arisen, in which philosophers have worn away their studies and leisure. To bring these controversies forward and discuss them would be both lengthy and unnecessary.

If the reader recalls what we did in Book Eight when choosing the philosophers with whom the question of the blessed life that will exist after death was to be examined—whether we can attain it by religious worship and sacrifices offered to the one true God, who is also the maker of the gods, or by serving many gods through religion and sacrifices—he will not expect us to repeat the same things here, especially since, if he happens to have forgotten them, he can support his memory by rereading them. [Note: Several manuscripts read “help.” Our manuscripts read “support.”]

We chose the Platonists, deservedly the most distinguished of all philosophers, because, although they could understand, insofar as they were able [Note: The particle *sicut* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Vind., Am., and Er. editions; the following *ita* is then to be understood as “therefore.”], that the immortal and rational—or intellectual—soul of a human being cannot be blessed except by participating in the light of that God by whom both the soul itself and the world were made, they nevertheless deny that anyone can attain what all human beings desire—that is, the blessed life—unless he cleaves in pure and chaste love to that one supremely good God who is unchangeable.

But because they too, whether yielding to the vanity and error of the nations or—as the Apostle says—“becoming futile in their speculations” (Rom. 1:21), thought, or wished to be thought, that many gods should be worshiped, and because some of them even judged that divine honors through sacred rites and sacrifices should be offered to demons, a matter to which we have already responded in considerable part, we must now examine and discuss, insofar as God grants it, how those immortals and blessed beings established in heavenly dwellings, dominions, principalities, and powers—whom the Platonists call gods, and some of whom they call either good demons or angels along with us—are to be understood as wishing religion and piety to be observed by us.

To put it more plainly: do they wish us to perform sacred rites and sacrifices to them also, or only to their God, who is also our God? Do they wish us to consecrate some of our possessions—or ourselves—in the rites of religion?

### 2

For this is the worship owed to divinity—or, if it must be stated more precisely, to deity. Because I have no sufficiently suitable Latin word by which to express it in a single term, whenever necessary I indicate in Greek what I mean. Our translators have rendered *latria* (λατρεία), wherever it occurs in the sacred Scriptures, as “service.” But the service owed to human beings—the service according to which the Apostle commands servants to be subject to their masters (Eph. 6:5)—is customarily called by another Greek name. [Note: Namely, *douleia*, as in the Greek of the passage from the Apostle cited above: *hoi douloi*, “servants.” Augustine makes the same distinction frequently: in *Questions on Exodus*, Question 94; “*Douleia*,” he says, “is owed to God as Lord, but *latria* to God as God.” Likewise in *Questions on Genesis*, Question 61; in *Against Faustus*, Book 15, §9; Book 20, §21; in Letter 102, §20; and elsewhere.]

But according to the usage of those who composed the divine utterances for us, *latria* either always, or so frequently that it is practically always, denotes that service which pertains to the worship of God. Therefore, if it is called simply “worship,” it does not seem to be owed to God alone. For we are also said to worship human beings whom we regularly honor either by remembrance or by presence. And not only are those things worshiped to which we subject ourselves with religious humility; certain things subject to us are also said to be worshiped.

For from this word come the terms “farmers,” “tenants,” and “inhabitants.” The gods themselves are called *heaven-dwellers* (*coelicolas*) for no other reason than that they dwell in heaven—not, of course, by venerating it, but by inhabiting it, as though they were certain colonists of heaven. They are not like those called colonists who, because of agriculture, owe a condition of service to the native soil under the authority of its possessors. [Note: This word was not in use among the ancient Greeks. The divine James describes *threskeia* in his Epistle, chapter 1, verse 27. Sophocles, *Philoctetes*, 1440–1444: “But remember this: practice piety toward the gods; for Father Zeus counts all other things secondary. Piety does not die with mortals; whether they live or die, it never perishes.” —Larcher.]

Rather, as a great author of Latin eloquence said:

> There was an ancient city, which Tyrian colonists held.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.12)

He called them colonists from inhabiting, not from agriculture. Hence cities founded by larger cities, like swarms of peoples, are called colonies.

Accordingly, it is entirely true in a certain proper sense of this word that worship is owed to God alone. But because the worship of other things is also spoken of, the worship owed to God cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word.

### 3

Even “religion” itself, although it seems more distinctly to signify not the worship of just anyone but the worship of God—whence our translators rendered by this name what is called *threskeia* (θρησκεία) in Greek—nevertheless does not avoid ambiguity when the question concerns the worship of the deity. For in the Latin usage of speech, not only among the uneducated [Note: The printed editions read “not only among the uneducated.” The word “only” is absent from the manuscripts.], but also among the most learned, “religion” is said to be owed to human kinships, affinities, and every kind of relationship. Thus we cannot confidently say that religion is nothing other than the worship of God, since the word seems improperly to be removed from its meaning of observance toward human relationships.

“Piety” also is ordinarily understood properly as the worship of God, which the Greeks call *eusebeia* (εὐσέβεια). Yet it is also said to be practiced dutifully toward parents. In ordinary popular usage, this word is also frequently applied to works of mercy. I think this happened because God chiefly commands such works and testifies that they please him either as sacrifices or in preference to sacrifices.

From this custom of speech it has come about that God himself is also called pious (2 Chron. 30:9; Sirach 11:13; Judith 7:20). The Greeks, certainly, do not call God *eusebein* in any usage of their language; nevertheless, even their common people use *eusebeia* for mercy. Therefore, in certain passages of the Scriptures, so that the distinction might be clearer, they preferred to say not *eusebeia*, which is formed from good worship, but *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια), which sounds as though it is formed from the worship of God. [Note: Compare the *Enchiridion*, Book II, chapter 2, concerning Job 27:28.]

We cannot express either of these with one Latin word. What is called *latria* in Greek and translated into Latin as “service”—but service by which we worship God; or what is called *threskeia* in Greek and “religion” in Latin—but religion directed by us toward God; or what they call *theosebeia*, while we cannot express it in one word but can call it “the worship of God”—this, we say, is owed only to that God who is the true God and who makes his worshipers gods (Ps. 81:6; John 10:34–35).

Therefore, whatever immortal and blessed beings exist in heavenly habitations, if they do not love us and do not wish us to be blessed, they are certainly not to be worshiped. But if they love us and wish us to be blessed, surely they wish this from the same source from which they themselves are blessed. Or are they blessed from one source and we from another?

## CHAPTER II — What Plotinus the Platonist thought about heavenly illumination

But in this question we have no conflict with these more excellent philosophers. They saw and explained abundantly in their writings, in many ways, that they become blessed from the same source as we do: through a certain intelligible light, which is God to them, and which is other than those whom it illuminates, so that they may shine and, through participation in it, remain perfected and blessed.

Plotinus, often and at length explaining Plato’s view, asserts that even the soul which they believe to be the soul of the universe is blessed from no other source than ours. He says that this light is something which the soul itself is not, but by which it was created, and by whose intelligible illumination it shines intelligibly.

He also offers an analogy from those incorporeal beings to these visible [Note: The word “visible” is absent from most manuscripts.] and immense bodies of heaven, as though that light were the sun and the soul were the moon. For they believe that the moon is illuminated by the opposition of the sun.

Thus that great Platonist says that the rational soul—or rather, it should be called intellectual, since he understands the souls of the immortals and blessed to belong to this category, and he does not doubt that they dwell in heavenly habitations [Col. 0280]—has no nature above it except God, who fashioned the world and by whom the soul itself was made. Nor is the blessed life and the light of understanding truth provided to those heavenly beings from any other source than the one from which it is provided to us.

In this he agrees with the Gospel, where we read:

> There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light. The true light was present, which illumines every human being coming into this world.

This distinction sufficiently shows that a rational or intellectual soul, such as John possessed, cannot be light for itself, but shines through participation in another, true light. John himself also confesses this when, bearing witness to him, he says: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:6–9, 16).

## CHAPTER III — Concerning the true worship of God, from which the Platonists deviated, although they understood him to be the creator of the universe, by worshiping angels, whether good or evil, with divine honor

### 1

Since these things are so, if the Platonists—or anyone else who has held such views—knew God and glorified him as God and gave thanks, they would not become futile in their speculations, nor would they partly become authors of the errors of the nations and partly lack the courage to resist them. They would certainly confess that one God, the God of gods, must be worshiped by those immortal and blessed beings as well as by us mortal and miserable beings, so that we may become immortal and blessed. He is both our God and theirs.

### 2 [IV]

To him we owe the service called *latria* in Greek, whether in the various sacraments or in ourselves. We are all together his temple, and each of us individually is a temple (1 Cor. 3:16–17), because he deigns to dwell both in the concord of all and in each individual. He is not greater in all than in each, since he is neither expanded by mass nor diminished by division.

When our heart is raised toward him, it is his altar. We appease him through his Only-Begotten as priest. We slaughter bloody victims for him when we contend for his truth even to the point of bloodshed. We burn for him the sweetest incense [Note: All our manuscripts read: “we burn him with the sweetest incense.”] when we blaze before him with pious and holy love. We vow and restore to him his gifts in us and ourselves. On the festivals and appointed days, we devote and consecrate to him the remembrance of his benefits, lest ungrateful forgetfulness creep in through the passage of time. We sacrifice to him the offering of humility and praise upon the altar of the heart, burning with fervent love. [Note: Several manuscripts read “fervent” in the accusative; some read “of fervent love.”]

In order to see him, insofar as he may be seen, and to cleave to him, we are cleansed from every stain of sins and evil desires and consecrated in his name. [Note: Some books read “in his name” in the dative: “to his name.”] He himself is the source of our blessedness; he himself is the end of every desire.

Choosing him—or rather choosing him again, for we had lost him by neglecting him—we seek him again, and hence religion is said to have been so called [Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2, chapter 28, thinks that *religion* was named from *relegere*, “to reread” or “to review”: “Those who carefully considered and, as it were, reread everything pertaining to the worship of God were called religious from *relegere*. But Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book 4, chapter 28, prefers to derive *religion* from *religare*, “to bind.” See *Retractions*, Book 1, chapter 13, §9.]—and by loving him we move toward him, so that when we reach him we may rest. We are blessed because we are perfected by that end.

Our good, concerning whose end there is great dispute among philosophers, is nothing other than cleaving to him. Through the incorporeal embrace—if it may be called such—of this one being, the intellectual soul is filled and made fruitful with true virtues. We are commanded to love this good with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength. By this good we ought both to be led by those who love us and to lead those whom we love.

Thus the two commandments are fulfilled on which all the Law and the Prophets depend: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:37–40).

For in order that human beings might know how to love themselves, an end was established for them to which they should refer everything they do in order to be blessed. For one who loves himself does not wish to be anything other than blessed. This end is to cleave to God (Ps. 72:28).

When someone who knows how to love himself is commanded to love his neighbor as himself, what else is commanded except that, as far as he can, he should commend to his neighbor the love of God? [Note: See Letter 155, especially §§11 and following.]

This is the worship of God; this is true religion; this is right piety; this is the service owed to God alone.

Therefore, whatever immortal power, however great its virtue, if it loves us as itself loves itself, wishes us to be subject to the one to whom it itself is subject and by whom it is blessed, so that we may be blessed. [Note: Compare *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 1, §30.] If it does not worship God, it is miserable because it is deprived of God. But if it worships God, it does not wish to be worshiped as God.

For it rather supports that divine judgment and favors the powers of love concerning which it is written: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, unless it be to the Lord alone” (Exod. 22:20).

## CHAPTER IV — That sacrifice is owed to the one true God

To say nothing for now of the other matters pertaining to the religious service by which God is worshiped, there is certainly no human being who would dare say that sacrifice is owed to anyone except God. [Note: The printed editions read: “except to God—or to the Lord—alone.” The word “alone” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Many things, finally, have been appropriated from divine worship for the honoring of human beings, whether through excessive humility or through destructive flattery. Yet those to whom such honors are offered are still regarded as human beings, who are said to deserve worship and veneration; and if much more is added, adoration. But who has judged that sacrifice should be offered except to one whom he either knew, thought, or imagined to be a god?

How ancient the worship of God through sacrifice is is sufficiently indicated by those two brothers, Cain and Abel: God rejected the sacrifice of the elder but looked upon that of the younger with favor. [Note: Compare Letter 102, §17, Question 3, and the following chapters, 5 and 6.]

## CHAPTER V — Concerning the sacrifices that God does not require, but commanded to be observed as signs of what he does require

Who would be so foolish as to think that God needs, for some purpose, the things offered in sacrifices? Since divine Scripture bears witness to this in many places, it will suffice, to avoid prolixity, to recall the brief statement from the Psalm: “I said to the Lord, You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2).

Therefore God is not to be thought to need not only cattle or any other corruptible and earthly thing, but not even human righteousness itself. Everything by which God is rightly worshiped benefits the human being, not God.

For no one would say that he benefited a spring by drinking from it, or the light by seeing it. [Note: All manuscripts read “consulted it” rather than “benefited it.”] Nor is it to be understood otherwise when sacrifices of this kind [Note: The manuscripts read “other” (*alia*) rather than “such” (*talia*).] were offered by the ancient fathers in the form of animal victims—sacrifices that the people of God now reads about but does not perform [Note: Vind., Am., and Er. read: “which the people of God lawfully does not perform.”]—than that those things signified the things carried out in us, so that we may cleave to God and provide for our neighbor’s good with the same end in view. [Note: Lov. reads “for this end only”; *only* is absent from the other books.] Therefore a visible sacrifice is the sacrament, that is, the sacred sign, of an invisible sacrifice.

Hence the repentant person—or the prophet himself seeking to have God favorable toward his sins—says through the prophet: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; you will not delight in whole burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” [Note: In Greek: *ouk exoudenōsei*, “he will not despise.”] (Ps. 50:18–19).

Let us observe how, where he said that God did not desire sacrifice, he there showed what sacrifice God did desire. He does not desire the sacrifice of slaughtered cattle, but he desires the sacrifice of a contrite heart. Thus, by the sacrifice which he says he does not desire, that sacrifice is signified which he has stated that he does desire.

He said that God did not desire those things in the sense in which foolish people are thought to believe that God desires them as objects of his own pleasure. For if God did not wish the sacrifices he desires—one of which is a contrite and humbled heart in the grief of repentance—to be signified by those sacrifices which people thought he desired as pleasing to himself [Note: Most manuscripts read “by sacrifices offered to him.”], he certainly would not have commanded in the old Law that such sacrifices be offered.

Therefore they had to be changed at the proper and appointed time, lest people should believe that the sacrifices themselves were desired by God—or at least acceptable in themselves to us—rather than the things signified by them.

Hence, in another place in another Psalm, he says: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49:12–13). It is as though he were saying: “Certainly, if I needed such things, I would not ask them from you, since I have them under my power.”

Then, adding what those things signify, he says: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (ibid. 14–15).

Likewise, through another prophet: “With what shall I approach the Lord? With what shall I take hold of my exalted God? Shall I approach him with whole burnt offerings, with year-old calves? Will the Lord accept thousands of rams, or tens of thousands of fat goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my impiety, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul? It has been declared to you, human being, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: to do justice [Note: The word “and righteousness,” added in the Lov edition, is absent here from the other books and from the sacred Scripture], to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?” (Micah 6:6–8).

In the words of this prophet, both matters have been distinguished and it has been sufficiently declared that God does not require those sacrifices in themselves, but that by them are signified the sacrifices he does require.

In the Epistle entitled “to the Hebrews” [Note: Ludovicus Vives says that this manner of citation indicates that the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews is uncertain. Nevertheless, Augustine unhesitatingly numbers it among Paul’s fourteen Epistles in Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, §13. Indeed, several manuscripts of good reputation—the Corbie manuscript, the Colbert manuscript, and others—do not read “entitled,” but “written.”], it says: “Do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is pleased” [Note: The printed editions read: “God is appeased.” The manuscripts read: “God is pleased,” which corresponds no less appropriately to the Greek *euaresteitai ho theos*, “God is reconciled.”] (Heb. 13:16).

Accordingly, where it is written, “I desire mercy” [Note: The printed editions read: “I desire mercy more.” The word “more” is absent from the manuscripts] “rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6), nothing other than the preference of one sacrifice over another should be understood. For what everyone calls “sacrifice” is a sign of the true sacrifice. But mercy is the true sacrifice; hence the statement recalled shortly before: “With such sacrifices God is pleased.”

Therefore, whatever is read as having been divinely commanded in many ways concerning sacrifices in the ministry of the tabernacle or temple is referred to the signification of love of God and neighbor [Note: Vind., Am., Er., and the manuscripts read: “to signifying.”]. For on these two commandments, as it is written, all the Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40).

## CHAPTER VI — Concerning the true and perfect sacrifice
Therefore, every work that is performed [Note: [Col. 0283] Most manuscripts read *quo agitur* (“by which it is performed”).], so that we may cling to God in holy fellowship, being directed, of course, toward that end of the good by which we can truly be blessed, is a true sacrifice. Hence even the mercy by which assistance is given to another, if it is not done for God’s sake, is not a sacrifice. For although it is performed or offered by a human being, sacrifice is nevertheless a divine thing; thus the ancient Latins also called the human being himself, consecrated in God’s name [Note: [Col. 0283] The printed editions read *nomini* (“to the name”). This is corrected from the manuscripts and from another similar passage above, chapter 3.] and vowed to God, insofar as he dies to the world in order to live for God, a sacrifice. For this too belongs to the mercy that each person exercises toward himself. Therefore it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclesiasticus XXX, 24).

When we discipline our body also through temperance [Note: [Col. 0283] Our manuscripts read *cum temperantia castigamus* (“when we discipline with temperance”). M.], if we do this for God’s sake, as we ought, so that we may not present our members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but as weapons of righteousness to God (Romans VI, 13), it is a sacrifice. Exhorting us to this, the Apostle says: “Therefore I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational service.”

If, then, the body—which the soul uses as something inferior, as a servant or as an instrument—is a sacrifice when its good and proper use is referred to God, how much more is the soul itself a sacrifice when it refers itself to God, so that, kindled by the fire of his love, it loses the form of worldly desire and is re-formed in subjection to him as its unchangeable form; thus pleasing him by receiving from his beauty? The same Apostle adds this immediately afterward: “And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is—what is good and pleasing and perfect” (Romans XII, 1–2).

Since, therefore, true sacrifices are works of mercy, whether toward ourselves or toward our neighbors, which are referred to God; and since works of mercy are performed for no other reason than that we may be freed from misery, and consequently that we may be blessed—and this happens only through that good of which it is said, “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Psalm LXXII, 28)—it follows that the whole redeemed city itself, that is, the congregation and fellowship of the saints, is offered to God as a universal sacrifice through the great Priest, who also offered himself in his passion for us, so that we might be the body of so great a Head according to the form of a servant.

For he offered this form, and in this form he was offered, because according to this form he is mediator, in this form he is priest, and in this form he is sacrifice. When, therefore, the Apostle had exhorted us to present our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, our rational service, and not to be conformed to this age but to be transformed in the renewal of our minds, so as to prove what the will of God is—what is good, pleasing, and perfect, and that we ourselves are the whole sacrifice—he says:

“For by the grace of God given to me I say to everyone among you not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, as God has allotted to each a measure of faith. For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another, having different gifts according to the grace that has been given to us” (Romans XII, 3–6).

This is the sacrifice of Christians: many are one body in Christ. The Church also continually celebrates this through the sacrament of the altar, familiar to the faithful, where it is shown to her that, in the very thing which she offers [Note: [Col. 0284] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “that in the offering which she offers.”], she herself is offered.

## CHAPTER VII—That the holy angels’ love for us is such that they wish us to be worshipers not of themselves, but of the one true God

It is rightly the case that those established in the heavenly dwelling places—immortal and blessed, rejoicing in participation in their Creator, made firm by his eternity, assured by his truth, and made holy by his gift—love us mortals and wretched beings mercifully, so that we may become immortal and blessed. They do not want us to sacrifice to them [Note: [Col. 0284] Several manuscripts read *sacrificari* (“to be sacrificed”).], but to him whose sacrifice they know themselves to be, together with us.

With them we are one city of God, of which it is said in the Psalm: “Glorious [Note: [Col. 0284] Here and in other places, manuscripts of good quality read *Gloriosissima* (“most glorious”).] things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm LXXXVI, 3). One part of this city is a pilgrim among us; the other part assists us among them.

For from that heavenly city, where God’s intelligible and unchangeable will is the law, from that heavenly court, so to speak—for care (*cura*) is exercised there concerning us—the Holy Scripture was sent down to us through the ministry of angels [Note: [Col. 0285] Compare *Expositions on the Psalms* 90, sermon 2, no. 1.], and there we read: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated, unless it is to the Lord alone” (Exodus XXII, 20).

So many miracles have borne witness to this Scripture and this law, with such commandments, that it is sufficiently clear to whom they wish us to sacrifice—those immortal and blessed beings who wish us to be what they themselves are.

## CHAPTER VIII—On the miracles that God, even through the ministry of angels, has graciously employed in support of the faith of the devout, according to his promises

For if I were to recall events so ancient, I would seem to be going over them at greater length than is appropriate: the miracles that were performed in witness to God’s promises, by which, thousands of years beforehand, he foretold Abraham that all nations would have blessing in his seed (Genesis XVIII, 18).

For who would not marvel that Abraham’s wife, a barren woman, bore him a son at an age of old age when she could no longer give birth, being no longer fertile [Note: [Col. 0285] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. The printed editions read: “at an age when she could neither give birth nor be fertile.”] (Genesis XXI, 2); and that, at the sacrifice of this same Abraham, a flame produced from heaven ran between the divided victims [Note: [Col. 0285] In *Retractions* II, chapter 43, section 2, Augustine says: “It should not have been listed as a miracle at Abraham’s sacrifice that a flame produced from heaven ran between the divided victims, since this was shown to him in a vision.”] (Genesis XV, 17)?

Or who would not marvel that the heavenly destruction of Sodom was foretold to this same Abraham by angels whom he had received as guests in human form, and through whom he had received God’s promises concerning the offspring to come (Genesis XVIII, 20, 14); and that, when the destruction was already imminent, his brother’s son Lot was wondrously rescued from Sodom by those same angels; while his wife, looking back on the way and suddenly being transformed into salt (Genesis XIX, 17, 26), gave a great sacramental warning that no one on the road of his deliverance ought to desire what lies behind?

What, indeed, and how great were the things wondrously accomplished through Moses for the people of God in Egypt, when they were being rescued from the yoke of slavery? The magicians of Pharaoh—that is, of the king of Egypt who oppressed that people under his domination—were permitted to perform certain marvels so that they might be overcome all the more wondrously. They performed them through magical arts and incantations, to which evil angels, that is, demons, are devoted. Moses, however, acting with far greater power because with greater justice in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth, and with angels serving him, easily overcame them (Exodus VII–VIII, 7).

Finally, when the magicians failed during the third plague, the ten plagues were completed through Moses according to a great arrangement of mysteries; through them Pharaoh’s and the Egyptians’ hardened hearts yielded and allowed the people of God to depart (Exodus VIII–XII). Soon, however, Pharaoh regretted this, and when they tried to pursue the departing Hebrews, the Hebrews passed through the divided sea on dry land, while the water, returning from both sides upon itself, covered and overwhelmed the Egyptians (Exodus XIV).

What shall I say about those miracles that occurred with astonishing divine power while the same people were being led through the wilderness: waters that could not be drunk losing their bitterness when wood was thrown into them, as God had commanded, and satisfying the thirsty (Exodus XV, 23–25); manna coming down from heaven for the hungry; and, although a measure had been established for those gathering it, whatever anyone gathered beyond that measure rotting when worms appeared, while twice as much gathered before the Sabbath remained undefiled by any decay because gathering on the Sabbath was not permitted; when they desired to eat meat, the camp being filled with birds, although it seemed impossible for any supply to suffice for so great a people, and the heat of their desire being extinguished by the disgust of satiety (Exodus XVI; Numbers XI, 31–34);

enemies who confronted them, barred their passage, and fought them being struck down while Moses prayed and extended his hands in the form of a cross, without any Hebrew falling (Exodus XVII, 8–16); seditious persons among the people of God, separating themselves from the fellowship divinely ordered, being swallowed alive when the earth opened, as a visible example of invisible punishment (Numbers XVI, 23–34); a rock struck with a staff pouring forth abundant streams for so great a multitude (Exodus XVII, 6–7; Numbers XX, 8–11); and the deadly bites of serpents—the most just punishment of sinners—being healed by a bronze serpent raised up on wood and looked upon, so that relief might be given to the afflicted people and, with death destroyed by death, the likeness of crucified death might be signified (Numbers XXI, 6–9).

When, later, the erring people began to worship this serpent, which had been preserved in memory of the event, as though it were an idol, King Hezekiah, serving God with religious authority, crushed it with great praise for his devotion (2 Kings XVIII, 4).

## CHAPTER IX—On unlawful arts concerning the worship of demons, in which the Platonist Porphyry is involved, approving some things and seeming to disapprove others

### 1

These and many other things of this kind—which it would be far too lengthy to recount in full—were done to commend the worship of the one true God and to prohibit the worship of many false gods. They were done with simple faith and the confidence of devotion, not through incantations and spells composed by the criminal art of curiosity, which is called magic, or by the more detestable name *goetia*, or by the more respectable name *theurgy* [Note: [Col. 0286] *Goetia* is a kind of magic performed by raising the dead; it is so called from the lamentation around tombs. *Theurgy*, meaning something like “divine operation,” is the name given to the practice by which gods or demons are invoked through particular sacrifices and ceremonies considered good by pagans.].

Those who attempt to distinguish these practices in this way want some people devoted to unlawful arts to appear condemnable—people whom the common crowd also calls sorcerers, for they say that these belong to *goetia*—while others are to appear praiseworthy, to whom they assign *theurgy*. Yet both groups are bound by the deceptive rites of demons under the names of angels [Note: [Col. 0286] Here the ninth chapter begins in the manuscripts.].

### 2

For Porphyry too promises, with some hesitation and in a kind of embarrassed argument, a certain purification of the soul through theurgy; yet he denies that this art can provide anyone’s return to God. Thus he may be seen wavering, through alternating judgments, between the vice of sacrilegious curiosity and the profession of philosophy.

At one moment he warns that this art is to be avoided as deceptive, dangerous in the very act of its practice, and prohibited by law [Note: [Col. 0286] See below, chapter 28.]; at another, yielding as though to its praisers [Col. 0287], he says that it is useful for cleansing a part of the soul—not the intellectual part, through which the truth of intelligible things, which have no bodily likenesses, is perceived, but the spiritual part, through which the images of bodily things are apprehended [Note: [Col. 0287] You will find a very similar distinction in *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis* XII, sections 50–51, namely, the distinction among intellectual, spiritual, and bodily vision.].

He says that this spiritual part is made suitable and fit, through certain theurgic consecrations called *teletae* [Note: [Col. 0287] *Teletae* were called certain complete expiations and sacrifices, lacking nothing.], for receiving spirits and angels and for seeing gods. Yet he admits that from these theurgic *teletae* no purification comes to the intellectual soul that would make it fit to see its God and to discern what truly exists [Note: [Col. 0287] Nearly all manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have, only at this point, *vera sunt* (“are true”), except Erasmus, who also has *vera* (“true”) at another place below instead of *vere* (“truly”).].

From this it can be understood what sort of gods, or what kind of vision, he says is produced by theurgic consecrations—a vision in which things that truly exist are not seen.

Finally, he says that the rational soul—or, as he prefers to call it, the intellectual soul—can escape into the heavenly realm [Note: [Col. 0287] The manuscripts read *in sua* (“into its own”); a few have *insuper* (“above”).—Our codices read *in sua*. M.], even if its spiritual part has not been purified by any theurgic art. Yet he says that the spiritual part is purified by a theurgist only to such an extent that it does not thereby attain immortality and eternity.

Although, therefore, he distinguishes angels from demons, describing the regions of demons as aerial and those of angels as ethereal or empyrean; and although he advises that one should use the friendship of some demon, by whose conveyance anyone might be lifted a little from the earth after death, while he maintains that another way leads to the heavenly fellowship of angels, he nevertheless bears witness, in a kind of explicit confession, that the fellowship of demons must be avoided. He says that after death the soul, while paying the penalty for its sins, recoils from the worship of the demons by whom it had been deceived.

Nor could he deny that the very theurgy which he commends as a means of reconciling angels and gods is practiced among such powers—powers that either envy the soul’s purification or serve the arts of the envious. In support of this point he reports a complaint of some Chaldean or other:

“A good man in Chaldaea,” he says, “complains that the results he sought for the purification of the soul have been frustrated despite great effort, because a man powerful in the same matters, moved by envy, had bound the powers invoked by sacred prayers so that they would not grant the requests. Therefore,” he says, “the one bound them, and the other did not release them.”

From this indication, he said, it appears that theurgy is a discipline for accomplishing both good and evil, among gods as well as among human beings; that gods too suffer and are brought into those disturbances and passions which Apuleius commonly attributes to demons and human beings, although he separates the gods from them by the elevation of their ethereal dwelling and asserts Plato’s view in that distinction.

## CHAPTER X—On theurgy, which promises false purification to souls through the invocation of demons

[Col. 0288]

Behold now another Platonist, Porphyry, whom they report to be more learned. Through some unknown theurgic discipline, he says that even the gods themselves are bound by passions and disturbances, since they could be adjured and terrified by sacred prayers so that they would not provide purification for the soul. They could be so terrified by the one commanding evil that, through the same theurgic art, they could not be released from that fear by the one requesting good, nor set free to bestow the benefit [Note: [Col. 0288] See below, chapter 11, section 2.].

Who would not see that all this is the invention of deceptive demons, unless he were their most wretched slave and alienated from the grace of the true liberator? For if such things were being done among good gods, the one benefiting the soul’s purification would surely have greater power there than the malicious obstructer. Or if the person on whose behalf the matter was undertaken seemed unworthy of purification to just gods, they ought not to have denied it because they were terrified by an envious power, nor, as he himself says, because they were hindered through fear of a stronger divinity, but by free judgment.

It is astonishing that that kindly Chaldean, who wished to purify the soul through theurgic rites, did not find some higher god who could either terrify the terrified gods even more and compel them to do good, or restrain the one terrifying them, so that they might do good freely. This would be so, at least, if the good theurgist lacked sacred rites by which he might first purify the very gods whom he invoked as purifiers of the soul from that plague of fear.

For what reason could a more powerful god be summoned to terrify them, but not one by whom they might be purified? Is there a god who hears the envious person and instills fear in the gods so that they may not do good, but no God who hears the benevolent person and removes fear from the gods so that they may do good?

O splendid theurgy! O purification of the soul worthy of praise! There unclean envy commands more than pure benevolence obtains. Rather, this is the deception of malignant spirits, which must be avoided and detested, and a saving teaching that must be heard.

For when those who perform these filthy purifications through sacrilegious rites see, as this writer reports, certain images of angels or gods of marvelous beauty—as though with a purified spirit, if indeed they see anything of the kind—this is what the Apostle means when he says that “Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians XI, 14).

For those phantasms belong to him who, desiring to entangle the wretched souls of many false gods through deceptive rites and to turn them away from the worship of the true God—the only worship by which they are cleansed and healed—is described, as was said of Proteus:

“He changes himself into every form” (Virgil, *Georgics* IV, line 411),

pursuing with hostility, coming to the aid of them deceitfully, and harming them in both ways.

## CHAPTER XI—On Porphyry’s letter to Anebontes the Egyptian, in which he asks to be instructed about the diversity of demons

### 1

This Porphyry showed better judgment when he wrote to the Egyptian Anebontes. There, adopting the appearance of one consulting and inquiring, he both exposes and overturns sacrilegious arts.

There he indeed rejects all demons, whom he says, through lack of understanding, draw in moist vapor and therefore exist not in the ether but in the air beneath the moon, and even in the globe of the moon itself [Note: [Col. 0289] The Louvain edition omits *in* here, and shortly afterward *et malitias*. All the other books have both.]. Yet he does not dare to attribute to all demons all the deceptions, wickednesses, and absurdities that rightly disturb him. For he calls some demons “benevolent,” following the customary usage of others, even though he admits that all are generally unintelligent.

He wonders not only that gods are attracted by victims, but also that they are compelled and forced to do what human beings want. He asks how, if gods are distinguished from demons by their bodies and incorporeality, the sun and moon and the other visible things in heaven—which he does not doubt are bodies—are to be considered gods; and, if they are gods, how some can be called benevolent and others malevolent; and how they can be joined to incorporeal beings, since they themselves are corporeal.

He also asks, as though in doubt, whether in diviners and those who perform certain marvels the souls are more powerful [Note: [Col. 0289] The manuscripts, instead of *potentiores* (“more powerful”), have *passiones* (“passions”) after *loco*.—Better. M.] or whether some spirits come from outside through whom these things can be accomplished. He leans rather toward the view that they come from outside, because, with stones and herbs employed, they bind certain things, open closed doors, or perform some similar marvel.

Hence he says that some people believe there is a certain kind of being whose proper function is to hear, by nature deceptive, assuming every form and taking many shapes, pretending to be gods, demons, and the souls of the dead. This, they believe, is what brings about all the things that appear good or evil. Yet in matters that are truly good it provides no assistance; indeed, it neither knows them, but sometimes reconciles things badly, falsely accuses, and obstructs diligent followers of virtue. It is full of rashness and arrogance, delights in odors, is captivated by flattery, and displays the other characteristics associated with this class of deceptive and malicious spirits that come from outside into the soul and deceive human senses, whether asleep or awake.

Porphyry does not assert these things as convictions of his own; rather, he suspects or questions them so tentatively that he attributes the assertions to others. For it was difficult for so great a philosopher either to know the whole fellowship of the devil or to denounce it confidently, whereas a Christian old woman does not hesitate to know it [Note: [Col. 0289] The manuscripts read *nec cunctatur esse* (“nor does she hesitate that it exists”).—More accurately. M.] and detests it with complete freedom.

Unless perhaps he was reluctant to offend both the man to whom he was writing, Anebontes, as a most distinguished priest of such rites, and the other admirers of such practices as divine works belonging to the worship of the gods.

### 2

Nevertheless, he proceeds and mentions, as though making inquiries, matters that, when soberly considered, can be attributed only to malicious and deceptive powers.

For he asks why, after beings are invoked as though they were better, they are commanded as though they were worse, so that they may carry out unjust human orders; why, when touched by a sexual act, they do not hear the person who invokes them, although they themselves do not hesitate to lead anyone into any incestuous intercourse; why they declare that their priests ought to abstain from living creatures, lest they be polluted by bodily vapors [Col. 0290], while they themselves are enticed by other vapors and by the odors of sacrifices; and why, although the inspector is forbidden contact with corpses, these rites are often celebrated with corpses.

He asks what it means that a person subject to any vice directs threats not at a demon or at some dead soul, but at the sun itself, the moon, or any heavenly being, and falsely terrifies them in order to force the truth from them. For he threatens that he will make the heavens collide and makes other threats impossible for a human being to carry out, so that the gods, like the most foolish children, terrified by false and ridiculous threats, may accomplish what is commanded [Note: [Col. 0290] Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* V, chapters 8–10, *Démonstrations évangéliques*, volume 1. M.].

He also says that a certain Chaeremon, an expert in such rites—or rather, sacrileges—wrote about what was reported to be practiced among the Egyptians, whether concerning Isis or her husband Osiris. These rites were said to have great power to compel the gods to do what was commanded, whenever the person who compelled them by spells threatened to reveal or destroy the rites; he even terrifyingly declared that he would scatter the limbs of Osiris if they neglected to do what they were ordered.

Porphyry rightly marvels that such empty and insane things could be threatened by a human being against gods—not just any gods, but the heavenly beings shining with the light of the stars—and that the human being could compel them by force, without these threats being ineffective, bringing them to do whatever he wished.

Yet rather than truly marveling and asking the causes of such events, he gives it to be understood that those spirits perform them whose kind he earlier described under the name of another’s opinion. They are not deceptive by nature, as he put it, but by vice: they pretend to be gods and the souls of the dead. As for demons, they do not merely pretend to be them, as he himself says; they plainly are demons.

And as for his view that powers suitable for carrying out various effects are manufactured on earth by human beings through herbs, stones, living creatures, particular sounds and words, certain figures and fabrications, and even through movements of the stars observed in the course of the heavens, all of this belongs to those same demons—deceivers of souls subject to them—who provide themselves with pleasurable entertainments from human error.

Either Porphyry, genuinely doubting and investigating these matters, nevertheless mentions them so that they may be exposed and refuted, and so that they may be shown to belong not to those powers that favor us in attaining blessed life but to deceptive demons; or, if we take a more favorable view of the philosopher, he wished in this way not to offend the Egyptian, who was devoted to such errors and thought he knew great things, with the proud authority of a teacher, nor to disturb him through an open adversarial dispute. Instead, by the humility of one who asks questions and wishes to learn, he wanted to turn him toward considering these matters and to show him how contemptible, or even how deserving of avoidance, they are.

Finally, near the end of the letter, he asks to be taught by him what the way to blessedness is according to Egyptian wisdom. As for those whose intercourse with the gods was directed toward finding a runaway slave, acquiring an estate, arranging a marriage, conducting trade, or something of that kind, he says that they appear to have cultivated wisdom in vain if they disturbed the divine mind over such matters.

He also says that those very divinities with whom they conversed, even if they foretold the truth about other matters, were nevertheless neither gods nor benevolent demons, since they offered no secure or sufficiently reliable instruction concerning blessedness; rather, they were either the being called “the Deceiver” or merely a human fabrication.

## CHAPTER XIII—On the miracles that the true God performs through the ministry of the holy angels

Since such great and extraordinary things are performed through these arts that they exceed the entire range of human ability, what remains except that those things which appear to be wondrously foretold or done as though by divine power, yet are not referred to the worship of the one God—to whom alone it is blessed to cling simply, as even the Platonists confess and testify in many ways—should prudently be understood as the mockeries and seductive hindrances of malicious demons, which must be avoided through true devotion?

[XII.] Whatever miracles, moreover, are performed either through angels or in whatever manner by such divine action that they commend the worship and religious service of the one God, in whom alone blessed life exists, we must believe to be performed by those who love us according to truth and devotion, or through them, with God himself working in them.

For we must not listen to those who deny that the invisible God performs visible miracles, since, even according to their own view, he made the world, which they certainly cannot deny is visible. Whatever, therefore, is wondrously done in this world is surely less than the whole world itself—that is, heaven and earth and everything in them—which God certainly made.

But just as he who made it is hidden and incomprehensible to human beings, so too is the manner in which he made it. Although the miracles of visible natures have become commonplace through the frequency with which we see them, nevertheless, when we contemplate them wisely, they are greater than the most unusual and rarest things. For a human being is a greater miracle than any miracle performed through a human being [Note: [Col. 0291] See sermon 126, no. 4.].

Therefore God, who made visible heaven and earth, does not disdain to perform visible miracles in heaven or on earth, by which he may stir the soul—still devoted to visible things—to worship him, who is invisible. Where and when he performs such miracles rests with him, in whose unchangeable counsel lie the times that have already been established for all future things.

For while moving temporal things, he is not moved temporally; he does not know what is to be done in a manner different from how he knows what has been done; nor does he hear those who invoke him in a manner different from how he sees those who will invoke him. For when his angels grant a hearing, he himself grants it in them, as in his true, non-manufactured temple, just as he does in his holy human beings; and his commands are fulfilled temporally [Note: [Col. 0291] Thus the manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads: “As in all his saints, whose commands are fulfilled temporally.”], having been seen in his eternal law.

## CHAPTER XIII—On the invisible God, who often made himself visible, not according to what he is, but according to what those who saw him were able to bear

Nor should it be disturbing that, although he is invisible, he is often said to have appeared visibly to the patriarchs. Just as the sound by which a thought established in the silence of understanding is heard is not identical with the thought itself [Col. 0292], so the appearance in which God was seen, while he remained established in an invisible nature, was not what he himself was [Note: [Col. 0292] Compare *Questions on Exodus* 101.].

Nevertheless, he himself was seen in that bodily appearance, just as the thought itself is heard in the sound of the voice. Nor were they unaware that they were seeing the invisible God in a bodily appearance that was not himself. For Moses spoke with the one who was speaking, yet said to him: “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself, so that I may see you knowingly” [Note: [Col. 0292] Concerning these matters, see *Questions on Exodus* 151 and Letter 147, section 20.] (Exodus XXXIII, 13).

Since, therefore, it was necessary for the law of God to be given with awe in the proclamations of angels—not to one person or to a few wise men, but to an entire nation and a great people—great events took place before that same people on the mountain, where the law was given through one man, while the multitude witnessed the fearful and terrifying things that occurred.

For the people of Israel did not believe Moses in the same way as the Lacedaemonians believed their Lycurgus when he said that he had received the laws he established from Jupiter or Apollo. When the law was given to the people, commanding that the one God be worshiped, the creature was visibly shown, before that very people and through wondrous signs and movements of things, insofar as divine providence judged sufficient, to be serving the Creator in order that this same law might be given [Note: [Col. 0292] The Louvain edition reads *dandam docentem* (“teaching in order that it might be given”). *Docentem* is absent from the other printed editions and from our manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER XIV—On worshiping the one God not only for eternal but also for temporal benefits, because all things lie within the power of his providence

Just as the proper education of one human being progresses through certain stages of time, so too did the proper education of the human race belonging to the people of God advance through successive periods, as though through stages of life, so that it might rise from temporal things to grasp eternal things and from visible things to invisible things.
