Thus, even at the time when visible rewards were divinely promised, the one God was nevertheless commended as the one to be worshiped, lest the human mind, even for the earthly benefits of this passing life, submit to anyone other than the true Creator and Lord of the soul.

Whoever denies that everything which angels or human beings can provide for human beings lies within the power of the one Almighty is insane. The Platonist Plotinus certainly discusses providence, and demonstrates that it extends from the supreme God—whose beauty is intelligible and ineffable—down to these earthly and lowest things by pointing to the beauty of little flowers and leaves. He confirms that all these things, as though added on and very swiftly perishing, could not possess the most fitting proportions of their forms unless they were formed from that place where intelligible and unchangeable form persists, possessing all things simultaneously (*Enneads* III, book 2, chapter 13).

The Lord Jesus showed this in the passage where he says: “Consider the lilies of the field [Note: [Col. 0292] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions add here, “how they grow,” and below read “in every” instead of “in such.”], they do not labor or spin. But I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?” (Matthew VI, 28–30).

Therefore the human soul, still weak through earthly desires, rightly grows accustomed to expect from the one God alone those very inferior and earthly goods that it desires temporally and that are necessary for this passing life, though they are to be despised in comparison with the eternal benefits of that other life. In this way it does not depart from his worship even in its desire for these things, and may reach him through contempt for them and turning away from them.

## CHAPTER XV—On the ministry of the holy angels, by which they serve God’s providence

Thus divine providence was pleased to order the course of time so that, as I have said and as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, the law concerning the worship of the one true God might be given through the proclamations of angels (Acts VII, 53).

In these proclamations the very person of God also appeared—not through his substance, which always remains invisible to corruptible eyes, but visibly through certain signs, by means of a creature subject to the Creator. He also spoke syllable by syllable, through the brief passing intervals of time, in the sounds of human language.

In his own nature, however, he neither begins nor ceases to speak—not bodily, but spiritually; not sensibly, but intelligibly; not temporally, but, so to speak, eternally [Note: [Col. 0293] The beautiful statements in *Expositions on the Psalms* XLIV, no. 5, return to this subject.]. His ministers and messengers, who enjoy his unchangeable truth and are immortally blessed, hear him more purely—not with the ear of the body but with the mind. What they hear him command in ineffable ways, and what must be brought down into these visible and sensible things, they carry out without hesitation and without difficulty.

This law was given through the distribution of times [Note: [Col. 0293] Augustine composed book four of *Against Faustus* concerning this law.]. At first, as has been said, it contained earthly promises, through which eternal things were signified; many celebrated these through visible sacraments, while few understood them.

Nevertheless, the worship of the one God is commanded there with the clearest testimony, both of words and of all things—not of one among the crowd, but of him who made heaven and earth, every soul, and every spirit that is not what he himself is. He made them; they were made, and in order to exist and remain in good condition they depend upon him by whom they were made.

## CHAPTER XVI—Whether, for attaining blessed life, we should believe those angels who demand that they be honored with divine worship, or those who command that sacred service be rendered not to themselves but to the one God
1. Which angels, then, do we judge should be believed concerning the blessed and everlasting life? Those who wish to be worshiped with the rites of religion, demanding that sacred honors and sacrifices be offered to them by mortals; or those who say that all this worship is owed to the one God, creator of all things, and command that it be rendered to him in true piety—he in whose contemplation they themselves are blessed, and promise that we too shall be blessed? For the vision of God is a vision of such great beauty, and so worthy of love, that Plotinus [Col. 0294] does not hesitate to call anyone most wretched who, without it, is endowed with and abounds in every other good (*Enneads* I.6.7).

Since, then, certain angels summon us by wondrous signs to worship this one God, while others summon us to worship themselves with *latria*—and since the former forbid these others to be worshiped, whereas the latter do not dare to forbid worship of him—let the Platonists answer; let all philosophers answer; let the theurgists, or rather the *periurgists* [Note: Some manuscripts have *perturgi*; others, *perteurgi*; others, *periurgi*.] answer—for all those arts deserve the latter name more properly.

Finally, let human beings answer, if any awareness of their own nature, in which they were created rational, still lives in them to any degree [Note: Some manuscripts have *illius*, “of that one.”]: let them answer, I say, whether sacrifices should be offered to those gods or angels who command that sacrifices be offered to themselves, or to the one to whom those who forbid sacrifice to both themselves and those others command that it be offered. If neither group performed any miracles, but merely issued commands—the one group that sacrifice should be offered to them, the other forbidding this but commanding sacrifice to the one God alone—piety itself ought sufficiently to discern which of these things proceeded from the arrogance of pride and which from true religion.

I will say more. If only those who demand sacrifices for themselves moved human minds by miraculous deeds, while those who forbid this and command that sacrifice be offered to God alone did not deign to perform such visible miracles at all, surely their authority should be preferred, not by the judgment of the bodily senses, but by reason of the mind. But when God has acted to commend the utterances of his truth, making, through these immortal messengers who proclaim not their own arrogance but his majesty, miracles greater, more certain, and more conspicuous, so that weak and pious people would not be more easily persuaded by those who demand sacrifices for themselves—because they display certain astonishing things to their senses—who could be so foolish as not to choose the truth to follow, when he finds in it greater things to admire?

2. I am not speaking of those miracles of the gentile gods that history commends which occur at hidden intervals of time through the causes of the world itself, although established and ordered under divine providence—such as unusual births among animals and an extraordinary appearance of things in heaven and on earth, either merely terrifying or also harmful, which are said to be procured and mitigated by demonic rites through the most deceptive cunning of those demons [Note: Vindobonensis, Amerbach, and the manuscripts have *daemonicis*.] Rather, I mean those events which plainly appear to be accomplished by their force and power: for example, the report that the images of the Penates, which Aeneas carried away from Troy in his flight, migrated from place to place [Note: Above, Book I, chapter 3.]; that Tarquinius cut a whetstone with a razor [Note: At the command of Tarquinius, Actius Navius cut it, as Cicero testifies, *On Divination* I.17 and *On the Nature of the Gods* II, as does Livy I.35 and others.]; that the Epidaurian serpent clung as a companion to Aesculapius when he sailed to Rome [Note: See Livy, epitome of Book 11; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.622 ff.; Valerius Maximus I.8.2.]; that the ship carrying the image of the Phrygian mother, rendered immovable by the combined efforts of so many men and oxen [Col. 0295], was moved and drawn by a single little woman after she had tied it with her belt [Note: So Vindobonensis, Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis has *alligata*, “having been tied.”]—as evidence of her chastity [Note: That woman was Claudia Quinta, according to Cicero, *On His Response to the Haruspices*; Ovid, *Fasti* IV.295 ff.; and Livy XXIX.14.]; or that a Vestal virgin [Note: Valerius Maximus VIII.1.5 calls her Tuccia.] whose chastity was under investigation removed the accusation by carrying water from the Tiber in a sieve filled with water, without its leaking through.

These events, and others of the same kind, are in no way to be compared in power and magnitude with those we read of as having occurred among the people of God—much less with those things which the laws even of the peoples who worshiped such gods judged worthy of prohibition and punishment, namely, magical or theurgic practices. Most of these practices deceive the senses of mortals through an imaginary trickery that exists only in appearance, as when the moon is supposedly brought down until, as Lucan says, “being nearer, it foams upon the herbs set beneath it” (*Pharsalia* VI.503). Some, however, even if they seem to equal certain deeds of pious people in their operation, are shown to be incomparably inferior to ours by the very end that distinguishes them.

For among those practices, the more eagerly many gods are sought for worship in sacrifice, the less worthy they are of worship. In ours, by contrast, the one God is commended—he who demonstrates, both by the testimony of his Scriptures and by the later removal of those very sacrifices, that he has no need of such things. If, then, angels demand sacrifice for themselves, those who do not demand it for themselves but for God, the creator of all things, whom they serve, are to be preferred to them. In this they show how sincerely they love us: through sacrifice they seek to subject us not to themselves but to him, in whose contemplation they themselves are blessed, and to whom they desire us to attain, from whom they themselves have not departed.

But if angels who wish sacrifices to be offered not to one God but to many do not want them offered to themselves, but to those gods whose angels they are, even so those who are angels of the one God of gods are to be preferred to them. They command that sacrifice be offered to him in such a way that they forbid it to any other, whereas none of the others forbids sacrifice to the one to whom these angels command it to be offered.

Moreover, if—as their proud deceit more clearly indicates—they are neither good angels nor angels of good gods, but evil demons who wish sacrifices to be offered not to the one supreme God alone but to themselves, what greater protection against them should be chosen than the one God, whom the good angels serve? They command us to serve him through sacrifice, even though we ourselves ought to be his sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XVII

### Concerning the Ark of the Testimony and the miracles of the signs divinely performed to commend the authority of the Law and the promise

Accordingly, the law of God, which was given through angelic proclamations, in which the one God of gods was commanded to be worshiped with religious rites while all others were forbidden, was placed in the Ark, which was called the Ark of the Testimony. This name sufficiently signifies that the God worshiped through all those things was not ordinarily enclosed or confined in a place. Although his responses and certain signs were given to human senses from the location of that Ark, the meaning was that testimonies of his will were being offered from it.

The law itself was written on stone tablets and, as I have said, placed in the Ark. [Col. 0296] During the time of the wandering in the wilderness, the priests carried it with due reverence together with the Tabernacle, which was likewise called the Tabernacle of the Testimony. It was a sign that during the day a cloud appeared, shining like fire at night (Exodus 13:21); when the cloud moved, the camps moved, and where it stopped, the camps were set up (ibid. 40:34–35).

Great testimonies of miracles were given to that law, apart from those I have mentioned and apart from the voices that came from the place of the Ark. When the same Ark crossed the Jordan as they entered the promised land, the river, standing still upstream while flowing away downstream, provided both it and the people with a dry passage (Joshua 3:16–17). Then, when the same Ark had been carried around seven times the first hostile city they encountered—a city that, following the custom of the nations, worshiped many gods—the walls suddenly fell, attacked by no hand and struck by no battering ram (ibid. 6:20).

After this, when they were already in the promised land and the same Ark had been captured by their enemies because of their sins, those who had captured it honorably placed it in the temple of their god, whom they worshiped above the others. They departed and closed the doors; when the temple was opened the next day, they found the image to which they had offered worship fallen down and horribly broken.

Then, driven by portents and punished even more grievously, they returned the Ark of the divine testimony to the people from whom they had taken it. How was it returned? They placed it on a cart, harnessed to it young cows from whom they had taken their suckling calves, and allowed them to go wherever they wished, wishing thereby also to test the divine power. But the cows, without a human guide or driver, persistently followed the road to the Hebrews and were not called back by the lowing of their hungry offspring; thus they brought back to their own worshipers a great sacrament (1 Samuel 4–6).

These things, and others of the same kind, are small in God’s sight but great for terrifying and healthfully instructing mortals. If philosophers, and especially the Platonists, are praised for having understood more correctly than others—as I mentioned shortly before—that divine providence also governs these weak and earthly things, on the testimony of the many beauties produced not only in the bodies of animals but also in plants and grass, how much more clearly do these events testify to divinity, which are performed at the time of its proclamation, where the religion is commended that forbids sacrifice to all heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings and commands it to God alone—he who alone makes those who love him and are loved by him blessed?

This religion establishes appointed times for such sacrifices and declares that they are to be changed for the better through a better priest. It testifies that God does not desire these things themselves, but signifies other and greater things through them—not so that he himself may be exalted by these honors, but so that we, set aflame by the fire of his love, may be stirred to worship him and cling to him, which is beneficial to us, not to him.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Against those who deny that the miracles by which the people of God were instructed should be believed in the ecclesiastical books

Will someone say that these miracles are false, that they never occurred, but were deceitfully written down? Whoever says this, if he denies altogether that any writings should be believed concerning these matters [Col. 0297], may also say that no gods care about mortal affairs. For the gods did not persuade people that they should be worshiped in any other way than through the effects of wondrous deeds, and the history of the nations also bears witness to these deeds—nations whose gods were able to display themselves as wondrous rather than useful.

Accordingly, in this work of ours, of which we now have the tenth book in hand, we have not undertaken to refute those who deny that any divine power exists or maintain that the gods do not care about human affairs. Rather, we have undertaken to refute those who prefer their gods to our God, the founder of the holy and most glorious city, not knowing that he himself is also the invisible and unchangeable creator of this visible and mutable world, and the truest giver of blessed life—not from the things he created, but from himself.

For his most truthful prophet says: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28). Among philosophers there is a question about the end of the good, toward which all duties are to be directed. This man did not say, “For me, it is good to abound in riches”; or “to be distinguished by purple and scepter, or to excel by a diadem”; or, as some philosophers were not ashamed to say, “For me, bodily pleasure is good”; or, as those who seemed to speak more appropriately, as though they were better, “For me, the virtue of my mind is good.” Instead, he says: “For me, it is good to cling to God.”

He had been taught this by the one to whom alone sacrifice should be offered, as even his holy angels warned by their testimony through miracles [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “his angels warned by the testimony of legal sacrifices.”]. Thus he himself had become his sacrifice: seized and set aflame by an intelligible fire, he burned, and was carried by holy desire into his ineffable and incorporeal embrace.

But if the worshipers of many gods—whatever they suppose their gods to be—believe that miracles were performed by those gods, whether on the authority of civic histories or of magical books, or, as they consider more respectable, of theurgic books, what reason is there for their refusing to believe those writings in which these events are said to have occurred, writings that deserve so much greater faith in proportion as the one to whom they command sacrifice alone is greater above all?

## CHAPTER XIX

### What is the meaning of the visible sacrifice that true religion teaches should be offered to the one true and invisible God

Those who think that visible sacrifices are suitable for other gods, but invisible sacrifices for the invisible God—greater sacrifices for the greater and better sacrifices for the better, such as the services of a pure mind and good will—surely do not understand that the former are signs of the latter, just as spoken words are signs of things.

Therefore, just as in prayer and praise we direct meaningful words to him to whom we offer in our hearts the very realities signified by those words, so in offering sacrifice let us know that a visible sacrifice should be offered to no one other than him whose invisible sacrifice we ourselves ought to be in our hearts.

Then all the angels and higher powers, who are more powerful in goodness and piety, favor us and rejoice with us, and assist us according to their strength toward this very end. But if we wish to offer these things to them, they do not gladly accept them; and when they are sent to human beings in such a way [Col. 0298] that their presence can be perceived, they most openly forbid it.

There are examples in the sacred writings. Some people thought that the honor owed to God should be offered to angels, either by worshiping or sacrificing to them; they were forbidden to do so by the angels’ own warning and were commanded to offer it to him to whom alone they knew it was lawful to offer it (Judges 13:16; Revelation 22:8–9).

Holy human beings of God imitated the holy angels. When Paul and Barnabas performed a miracle of healing in Lycaonia, they were thought to be gods, and the Lycaonians wished to sacrifice victims to them. They humbly rejected this and announced to them the God in whom they should believe (Acts 14).

The deceitful spirits arrogantly demand this for themselves for no other reason than that they know it is owed to the true God. For they do not truly rejoice, as Porphyry and some others think, in the odors of corpses. They have an abundance of odors everywhere, and if they wanted more, they could provide them for themselves. Therefore, the spirits that arrogate divinity to themselves delight not in the smoke of any body but in the mind of the supplicant, once deceived and subjected, so that they may rule over it, blocking the way to the true God and preventing a human being from becoming his sacrifice while being sacrificed to anyone other than him.

## CHAPTER XX

### Concerning the supreme and true sacrifice, which he himself became as Mediator of God and human beings

Hence that true Mediator, who, by taking the form of a servant, became the mediator between God and human beings—the human being Christ Jesus—although in the form of God he receives sacrifice together with the Father, with whom he is one God, nevertheless in the form of a servant preferred to become a sacrifice rather than receive one, lest anyone, on this account, suppose that sacrifice should be offered to any creature.

By this he is both priest: himself offering, and himself the offering. He wished the sacrifice of the Church to be the daily sacramental sign of this reality. Since the Church is the body of the head himself, through him it learns to offer itself [Note: Vindobonensis and Amerbach read: “He wished the sacrifice of the Church to be daily; since he himself is the head of his body, and it itself is the body of its head, it is accustomed to be offered both through him and he through it. Of this true sacrifice…”].

The ancient sacrifices of the saints were manifold and varied signs of this true sacrifice: the one sacrifice was represented through many, as though one reality were spoken of in many words, so that it might be commended at length without becoming tedious [Note: Compare Book I against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, §38.]. All false sacrifices have yielded to this supreme and true sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XXI

### How power was given to demons for the glorification of the saints through their endurance of suffering [Note: The printed editions have: “the saints who have already endured suffering.” The manuscripts support the emended reading.], by which they conquered the aerial spirits not by appeasing them but by remaining in God

At appointed and limited times, power was also permitted to demons so that, by stirring up the human beings whom they possess, they might tyrannically wage hostility against the city of God and take sacrifices from those who offer them and demand them from those who willingly give them; indeed, by violently persecuting people, they might extort sacrifices even from the unwilling. This is found to be not only harmless but useful to the Church [Col. 0299], so that the number of martyrs may be completed (Revelation 6:11) [Note: Coquaeus here cites Tertullian, *Apology* 50: “The more we are cut down by you, the more numerous we become; the blood of Christians is seed.” And in *To Scapula* 5: “Know that this sect is built up all the more when it seems to be struck down.”].

The city of God counts these people among its citizens as more illustrious and honored the more courageously they fight against the sin of impiety, even to the point of bloodshed [Note: The printed editions have: “against the impiety of the powers.” The other reading, found in all the manuscripts, is preferable, for Augustine clearly alludes to Hebrews 12:4: “You have not yet resisted to the point of bloodshed in your struggle against sin.”].

If ecclesiastical usage allowed it, we would call these our Heroes by a much more fitting name. For this name is said to have been derived from Juno, who is called *Hera* (Ἥρα) in Greek; and therefore, according to the myths of the Greeks, some son of hers was called *Heros*. The myth seems to signify allegorically that the air is assigned to Juno, where they wish heroes to dwell with demons; by this name they call the souls of the dead who possess some merit.

But, by contrast, our martyrs would be called heroes, if, as I have said, ecclesiastical usage permitted it—not because they had fellowship with demons in the air, but because they conquered those same demons, that is, the aerial powers. In them they also conquered that very Juno, whatever she is thought to signify—a figure whom poets introduce, not altogether inappropriately, as hostile to virtues and envious of brave men who seek heaven.

Yet Virgil again unhappily submits and yields to her: although Juno says in his poem,

> “I am defeated by Aeneas!”  
> (*Aeneid* VII.310),

Virgil has Helenus warn Aeneas himself, as though by religious counsel, saying:

> “Sing your vows gladly to Juno, and by suppliant gifts  
> overcome the mighty lady.”  
> (*Aeneid* III.438–439)

From this opinion Porphyry—although he states it not as his own view but that of others—says that a good god or spirit does not come into a human being unless the evil one has first been appeased [Note: Compare Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food* II.39.]. It is as though evil divinities were stronger among them than good ones, since evil powers obstruct the assistance of the good unless they are appeased and allow it; and the good cannot benefit anyone against the will of the evil, whereas the evil can cause harm without the good being able to resist them.

This is not the way of true and truly holy religion. Our martyrs do not conquer Juno—that is, the aerial powers that envy the virtues of the pious—in this manner. If customary speech permitted the expression, our heroes overcome Hera not by suppliant gifts but by divine virtues. Scipio Africanus, for example, is more appropriately surnamed Africanus because he conquered Africa by virtue than if he had appeased his enemies with gifts so that they would spare him.

## CHAPTER XXII

### From where the saints receive power against demons, and from where true purification of the heart comes

By true piety, the people of God drive out the aerial power hostile and opposed to piety by exorcizing it, not by appeasing it. They conquer all the temptations of its hostility by praying to their God [Col. 0300] against it—not by praying to it [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “all its temptations and adversities.”].

For it conquers or subjugates no one except through participation in sin. It is conquered, therefore, in the name of him who assumed a human being and lived without sin, so that in him, the priest and the sacrifice, the remission of sins might take place—that is, through the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, through whom, after the purification of sins, we are reconciled to God.

Human beings are separated from God only by sins. In this life the purification of our sins does not occur through our own power but through divine mercy: through his forgiveness, not through our strength. For even that slight degree of virtue which is called ours has been granted to us by his goodness. We would attribute much to ourselves in this flesh if we did not live under pardon until we lay it aside.

Therefore grace was bestowed upon us through the Mediator so that, though polluted by sinful flesh, we might be cleansed through the likeness of sinful flesh. By this grace of God, through which he has shown us his great mercy, we are governed in this life by faith, and after this life we shall be brought by that same grace to complete perfection through the vision of unchangeable truth.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### Concerning the principles in which the Platonists profess that the purification of the soul consists

Porphyry also says that it was answered by divine oracles that we are not purified by the initiation rites (*teletae*) of the moon and sun. This was intended to show that a human being cannot be purified by the *teletae* of any gods. For whose *teletae* can purify, if those of the moon and sun do not—gods whom they regard as the foremost among the celestial gods?

Finally, he says that the same oracle explicitly stated that the principles are able to purify, lest, when it had been said that the *teletae* of the sun and moon do not purify, they should suppose that the *teletae* of some other god among the multitude could purify.

As a Platonist, we know what he means by “principles.” He speaks of God the Father and God the Son, whom in Greek he calls the paternal intellect, or paternal mind [Note: Compare below, chapter 28.]. Concerning the Holy Spirit he says either nothing or nothing openly, although I do not understand whom else he could call the middle between these two.

For if he wished, like Plotinus, to have the nature of the soul understood as a third entity, when he discusses the three principal substances (*Enneads* V.1), he would surely not have called it the middle between these two—that is, between the Father and the Son. Plotinus places the nature of the soul below the paternal intellect (ibid., chapter 6, and elsewhere); but when Porphyry says “middle,” he does not place it below but between them.

Clearly, he said what he could, or what he wished, in a way that corresponds to what we call the Holy Spirit: the Spirit not of the Father alone or of the Son alone, but of both. Philosophers speak freely, and in matters most difficult to understand they do not fear offending religious ears. For us, however, it is lawful to speak according to a definite rule, lest freedom of language generate an impious opinion even about the realities signified by the words.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Concerning the one true principle, which alone purifies and renews human nature [Note: The printed editions have *solam*, “alone” in the feminine; the manuscripts more correctly have *solum*, agreeing with *principium*.]

We do not, then, speak of two or three principles [Col. 0301] when we speak of God, just as we are not permitted to speak of two or three gods. Although, when speaking of each individually—whether of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—we confess each one to be God, we nevertheless do not say, as the heretics called Sabellians do [Note: In discussing this heresy, Coquaeus writes, among many other things: “They all suppose that Sabellius was the first author of this heresy. Yet Epiphanius, in heresy 57, reports that Noetus, the teacher of Sabellius, devised it before him, as he had devised many other heresies.”], that the Father is the same person as the Son, or that the Holy Spirit is the same person as the Father and the Son. Rather, the Father is the Father of the Son, the Son is the Son of the Father, and the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son is neither the Father nor the Son.

The statement, therefore, was correct that a human being is purified only by the principle, even though among them the principles were expressed in the plural.

[XXIV.] But Porphyry, subject to the envious powers of which he was ashamed and which he feared to criticize openly, did not wish to understand that the Lord Christ is the principle by whose incarnation we are purified. He despised him in the very flesh that he assumed for the sake of our purification—a great sacrament that he failed to understand because of the pride which the true and gracious Mediator cast down by his humility.

In this mortality he revealed himself to mortals, whereas the malicious and deceitful mediators, by not possessing such mortality, exalted themselves more proudly and promised unfortunate human beings deceptive assistance, as though immortals to mortals.

Thus the good and true Mediator showed that sin is evil, not the substance or nature of flesh. Human flesh, together with the human soul, could be assumed without sin, possessed, laid aside in death, and changed for the better in resurrection. Nor is death itself, although it was the punishment of sin—which he nevertheless endured for us without sin—to be avoided by sinning; rather, if the opportunity is given, it is to be endured for the sake of justice.

He could therefore release sins by dying because he both died and did not die for his own sin [Note: The manuscripts read “and not for sin,” with *his own* left to be supplied.].

That Platonist did not recognize him as the principle; for if he had recognized him, he would have recognized the purifier. Neither flesh nor the human soul is the principle, but the Word through whom all things were made.

Flesh does not cleanse by itself, but through the Word by whom it was assumed, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). For when he spoke mystically of eating his flesh, and those who did not understand were offended and withdrew, saying, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?”, he replied to those who remained: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (ibid. 6:61, 64).

The principle, therefore, having assumed soul and flesh, cleanses both the soul and the flesh of believers. For when the Jews asked who he was, he replied that he was the principle (ibid. 8:25).

We could never have perceived this—carnal, weak, burdened with sins, and enveloped in the darkness of ignorance—unless we were cleansed and healed by him through that which we were and were not. We were human beings, but we were not righteous [Note: Compare Letter 140, §10.]. In his incarnation, however, human nature existed, but it was righteous, not sinful [Col. 0302].

This is the mediation by which a hand was extended to those who had fallen and were lying prostrate. This is the seed ordained through the angels, through whose proclamation the law was also given (Galatians 3:19)—the law that commanded the one God to be worshiped and promised that this Mediator would come.

## CHAPTER XXV

### That all the saints, both under the time of the Law and in earlier ages, were justified through the sacrament and faith of Christ

Through faith in this sacrament, the righteous of ancient times were also able to be purified by living piously—not only before the law was given to the Hebrew people, for they were not without God or his angelic preachers, but also during the time of the law itself, although it appeared to contain carnal promises in figures of spiritual realities [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *viderentur*, “appeared,” in the plural. Other books have *videretur*, “appeared,” with the law as the subject.], on account of which it is called the Old Testament. At that time there were also prophets through whom, as through the angels, the same promise was proclaimed.

Among their number was the one whose great and divine statement concerning the end of human good I mentioned shortly before: “For me, it is good to cling to God.” In that psalm the distinction between the two Testaments, as they are called—the Old and the New—is sufficiently made clear.

Because he saw the wicked abounding in carnal and earthly promises, he says that his feet had almost been moved and his steps nearly poured out into a fall, as though he had served God in vain, since he saw those who despised him flourishing in the happiness he had expected from God. He says that he had labored to investigate this matter, wishing to understand why it was so, until he entered the sanctuary of God and understood their end—those whom, in his error, he had considered happy.

Then he understood that they had been cast down because they exalted themselves, as he says, and that they had failed and perished because of their iniquities. The whole height of their temporal happiness had become for them like the dream of one awakening, who suddenly finds himself deprived of the deceptive joys he had imagined.

And because they seemed important to themselves in this earth, or earthly city, he says: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.” That it was nevertheless beneficial for him to seek even earthly things only from the one true God, in whose power all things are, he makes sufficiently clear when he says: “I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you.”

He said “like a beast,” clearly because he did not understand. He should have desired from God those things that could not be common to him and the wicked, not those things in which he saw them abounding and therefore thought that he had served God in vain, since those who refused to serve him possessed them as well.

“Yet I am always with you”: even in desiring such things, he had not sought other gods. Thus he continues: “You have held the hand of my right hand” [Note: Lovaniensis has “my right hand,” while the other books disagree.], “and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me”—as though all those things belonged to the left, since when he saw the wicked abounding in them, he almost fell.

“What is there for me in heaven,” he says, “and apart from you what have I desired on earth?” [Col. 0303] He reproved himself and rightly found fault with himself, because, although he possessed so great a good in heaven—as he later understood—he had sought from his God on earth a passing, fragile, and in some sense earthy happiness.

“My heart and my flesh failed,” he says, “God of my heart”—a good failure, in which he passed from lower things to higher. Hence another psalm says: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:3). And another says: “My soul has failed for your salvation” (Psalm 118:81).

Yet when he had spoken of both—that is, of the failing heart and flesh—he did not add, “God of my heart and my flesh,” but “God of my heart.” For through the heart the flesh is cleansed. Hence the Lord says: “Cleanse the things within, and the things without will be clean” (Matthew 23:26).

He then calls God himself his portion, not something from God but God himself: “God,” he says, “is the God of my heart, and God is my portion forever.” Among the many things chosen by human beings, God himself pleased him as the one to be chosen.

“For behold,” he says, “those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you”—that is, everyone who wishes to be the prostitute of many gods.

Hence follows the statement for whose sake the other points from the same psalm have also seemed worth discussing: “But for me, it is good to cling to God”—not to go far away, not to commit fornication among many.

To cling to God will be perfect when everything that must be liberated has been liberated. For now, however, what follows is being fulfilled: “To place my hope in God.” For hope that is seen is not hope. “Who hopes for what he sees?” says the Apostle. “But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

Established in this hope, let us now do what follows, and let us too, according to our small measure, be angels of God—that is, his messengers—announcing his will and praising his glory and grace. Thus, after saying, “To place my hope in God,” he adds: “That I may announce all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm 72).

This is the most glorious city of God. It knows and worships one God. The holy angels announced it; they invited us to share in its fellowship and wished us to be its citizens. They are not pleased that we worship them as our gods, but that with them we worship their God and ours. Nor are they pleased that we offer sacrifices to them, but that together with them we ourselves become a sacrifice to God.

Anyone who considers these things without malicious obstinacy will have no doubt that all the immortal and blessed beings who do not envy us—for if they envied us, they would not be blessed—but instead love us so that we too may be blessed with them, favor and assist us more when we worship with them the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, than if we worshiped them themselves through sacrifices.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Concerning Porphyry’s inconsistency as he fluctuates between confessing the true God and worshiping demons

[The supplied source ends here, at the heading of Chapter XXVI.]

I do not know how else to explain it (so far as I can judge), but Porphyry was ashamed before his theurgist friends [Note: [Col. 0303] The editions read “for his theurgist friends”; *for* is absent from the manuscripts.]. For he had some understanding of these matters, but he did not openly defend them against the worship of many gods [Note: [Col. 0304] The editions read, “but he did not openly defend the true God against the worship of many gods.” The words “the true God” are a gloss, absent from the manuscripts. Therefore “he defended” must refer to those things which Porphyry understood to some extent.]. He said, moreover, that there are some angels who descend and pronounce divine messages to theurgic human beings, while there are others who, on earth, declare the things belonging to the Father and reveal his height and depth. Are we then to believe that these angels, whose ministry is to declare the Father’s will, wish us to submit to anyone except the one whose will they announce to us? Hence this Platonist himself rightly advises that they should be imitated rather than invoked.

We therefore need not fear that, by refusing to sacrifice to them, we shall offend the immortal and blessed beings who are subject to the one God. For what they know is owed to the one true God alone—and by cleaving to him they themselves are blessed—they certainly do not wish to have offered to themselves, either through any representative symbol or through the very thing signified by the sacraments. Such arrogance belongs to demons, proud and wretched; entirely different is the piety of those who are subject to God and blessed by cleaving to no one else but him. In order that we too may receive this good, they ought to favor us with sincere kindness, not claim that we should be subjected to them, but announce the one under whom we may be joined with them in peace.

Why do you still tremble, philosopher, and hesitate to speak freely against powers that are hostile both to true virtues and to the gifts of the true God? You have already distinguished the angels who announce the Father’s will from those angels who, brought down by some unknown art, descend to theurgic human beings [Note: [Col. 0304] The editions read, “You have already said that the angels who announce the Father’s will are different from those angels who descend to theurgic human beings.” Here we follow the manuscripts, though their reading is difficult.]. Why do you still honor the latter by saying that they pronounce divine messages? What divine messages do they pronounce, when they do not announce the Father’s will? They are surely the ones whom an envious man has bound by sacred incantations, so that they could not provide the soul’s purification; nor could they be released from those bonds and restored to their own power by the Good One who, as you say, desires to purify [the soul].

Do you still doubt that these are evil demons? Or do you perhaps pretend not to know it because you do not wish to offend the theurgists from whom, deceived by curiosity, you learned these pernicious and insane doctrines as though they were a great benefit [Note: [Col. 0304] Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 4, chapters 9–10.]? Do you dare to raise this envious force—not a power but a pestilence—and not merely a mistress, but, as you admit, rather a slave of the envious—beyond this air into heaven, and to place it among your gods, even the stellar gods? Or do you thereby also disgrace the stars themselves with these reproaches?

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On Porphyry’s impiety, by which he surpassed even Apuleius’ error

How much more humanely and tolerably your fellow Platonist Apuleius went astray! He held that only the demons assigned to the region below the moon are agitated by the diseases of the passions and the disturbances of the mind. He honored them, certainly, but whether willingly or unwillingly, he confessed this about them. Yet, with as much argument as he could muster, he separated the higher gods of heaven, belonging to the ethereal regions—whether visible, such as the sun, moon, and the other lights there, which he saw shining before his eyes, or invisible, as he supposed them—from every stain of these disturbances [Note: [Col. 0305] The editions read, “free from these disturbances.” The word “free” is absent from the manuscripts.] (*On the God of Socrates*) [Note: [Col. 0305] This is how our manuscripts read. In one manuscript: “he distinguished them.”].

But you learned from Chaldean teachers [Note: [Col. 0305] The editions add “your.”]—not from Plato—to exalt human vices into the ethereal or empyrean heights of the universe and into the heavenly firmaments, so that your gods might pronounce divine messages to the theurgists. Yet by the intellectual life you make yourself superior to these divine messages, so that, as a philosopher, you evidently consider the purifications of theurgic art entirely unnecessary for yourself. Nevertheless, you impose them upon others, thereby paying your teachers what appears to be their reward: you lead those who cannot philosophize toward practices which you confess to be useless for yourself, since you are capable of higher things.

Thus all those who are removed from the virtue of philosophy—which is exceedingly arduous and belongs to very few—are, under your authority, driven to seek theurgic human beings, by whom they may be purified, not in their intellectual soul but at least in their spiritual soul. And since the multitude of those who are unwilling to philosophize is incomparably greater, more people are compelled to go to your secret and illicit teachers than to the Platonic schools.

For this is what the most unclean demons promised you, pretending to be ethereal gods and making you their herald and angel [Note: [Col. 0305] Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 4, chapter 4]: that, once purified in the spiritual soul by theurgic art, they would not return to the Father, but would dwell above the aerial regions among the ethereal gods.

The multitude of human beings for whose liberation from the dominion of demons Christ came does not hear these promises. In him they possess the most merciful purification of their mind, spirit, and body. For this reason he assumed the whole human being without sin, in order to heal the whole of which a human being consists from the plague of sins.

Would that you too had known him and had entrusted yourself more safely to him for healing, rather than to your own virtue—which is human, fragile, and weak—or to your most pernicious curiosity. He would not have deceived you, since even your oracles, as you yourself write, confessed him to be holy and immortal [Note: [Col. 0305] See below, book 19, chapter 23.]. Of him also the most distinguished poet, speaking poetically because he spoke under the veiled identity of another person, yet truthfully if you refer his words to Christ himself, said:

> Under your guidance, if any traces of our crime remain,  
> They shall be canceled, and the lands shall be freed from perpetual fear.  
> (*Eclogue* 4.13–14)

For he said what may also apply to those who have made great progress in the virtue of justice: because of the weakness of this life, traces of crimes may remain, even when the crimes themselves do not. These traces are healed only by that Savior of whom this verse was spoken.

Virgil himself indicates, almost at the beginning of that *Eclogue*, that he did not say this on his own authority, when he writes:

> The final age of the Cumaean song has now arrived.  
> [Col. 0306]

It is therefore unmistakable that this was spoken by the Cumaean Sibyl.

But those theurgists—or rather, those demons—who fashion likenesses and images of gods pollute rather than purify the human spirit with the falsehood of phantasms and the deceptive mockery of empty forms. For how can they purify the human spirit when they themselves possess an unclean one? Otherwise, they would not have been bound by the incantations of an envious man, nor would they, through fear or a similar envy, have refused or suppressed the empty benefit they appeared ready to provide [Note: [Col. 0306] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads “were ready to provide.”].

It is enough that you say that the intellectual soul—that is, our mind—cannot be purified by theurgic purification, and that even the spiritual soul, namely, the part of our soul inferior to the mind, which you assert can be purified by such an art, cannot by that art be made immortal and eternal. Christ, however, promises eternal life. Therefore the world runs to him—even though you are indignant, astonished, and stunned by it.

What benefit is there in the fact that you could not deny that human beings go astray through theurgic discipline, that this blind and foolish doctrine deceives very many, and that it is an unquestionable error to run to angelic princes and powers by performing rites and prayers? And then, as though you did not wish to appear to have wasted your effort in learning these things [Note: [Col. 0306] This is how the manuscripts read. The editions have “in teaching these things.”], you send people to the theurgists, so that their spiritual soul may be purified—people who do not live according to their intellectual soul?

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### Through what persuasions Porphyry was blinded and could not recognize true wisdom, which is Christ

You therefore send people into certain error. Nor are you ashamed of so great an evil, even though you profess yourself a lover of virtue and wisdom [Note: [Col. 0306] The editions read, “you profess yourself a lover of virtue and wisdom.” The word “yourself” is absent from the manuscripts.]. If you had truly and faithfully loved wisdom, you would have recognized Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, and you would not, swollen with the pride of empty knowledge, have recoiled from his saving humility [Note: [Col. 0306] Porphyry was first a Christian, but later deserted and opposed the faith. Compare Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 23.].

Yet you also admit that the spiritual soul can be purified without theurgic arts and without the *teletae*—the initiatory rites whose useless study you undertook—with the virtue of continence. At times you even say that the *teletae* do not raise the soul after death, so that they appear to offer no benefit after the end of this life even to the soul you call spiritual. Yet you turn these matters over in many ways and repeat them, as I think, for no other reason than to appear an expert even in such things, to please those curious about illicit arts, or to make them curious about such arts yourself.

Still, it is well that you say this art must be feared either because of the dangers imposed by the laws or because of the practice itself [Note: [Col. 0306] “Because of the dangers imposed by the laws,” since civil laws established penalties for magical art; “or because of the practice itself,” since it is a dangerous undertaking unless properly performed. For demons are provoked and inflict great evils upon the inexperienced practitioner of incantations, as many examples have shown; they love complete impiety, from which return to piety is difficult. Therefore they drive people toward it by terrors. —Ludovicus Vives.]. Would that, at least, the wretched should hear this from you and withdraw from it, lest they be swallowed up there, or not approach it at all.

You certainly say that ignorance, and the many vices arising from it, cannot be purified by any *teletae*, but only by the *patrikos nous* (πατρικὸς νοῦς), that is, the paternal mind or intellect, which is conscious of the Father’s will [Note: [Col. 0307] Eugubinus discusses the paternal mind at length from the Platonists in book 1 of *On Perennial Philosophy*. For them it is also called *ho epekeina nous* (“the intellect beyond”). He reports Porphyry’s own view of the divine or paternal mind in chapter 11. —Coquaeus.].

But you do not believe that this is Christ. For you despise him because of the body he received from a woman and because of the disgrace of the cross, deeming yourself fit, after despising and rejecting the lowly things, to pluck lofty wisdom from higher things.

Yet he fulfills what the holy Prophets truthfully foretold about him:

> I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,  
> and reject the understanding of the intelligent.  
> (Isaiah 29:14)

He does not destroy and reject in them his own wisdom, which he himself gave them, but the wisdom arrogated by those who do not possess him. Therefore, after recalling this prophetic testimony, the Apostle continues:

> Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish? For since the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, God was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching. For the Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.  
> (1 Corinthians 1:19–25)

Those who are wise and strong in their own virtue despise this as foolish and weak. But this is the grace that heals the weak—not those who proudly boast of their false blessedness, but those who humbly confess their true misery.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### On the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the impiety of the Platonists is ashamed to confess

1. You proclaim the Father and his Son, whom you call the paternal intellect or mind, and the one between them, whom we think you mean to call the Holy Spirit and whom, according to your custom, you call three gods [Note: [Col. 0307] See below, book 19, chapter 23.]. Although you use undisciplined language, you nevertheless see, however dimly and as if through certain shadows of a thin imagination, what must be sought. But you do not wish to recognize the incarnation of the immutable Son of God, through which we are saved so that we may reach what we believe and, however partially, understand.

Thus you see, however imperfectly—though from a distance and with clouded vision—the homeland in which we must remain, but you do not possess the way by which we must go.

Nevertheless, you acknowledge grace, since you say that reaching God through the virtue of understanding has been granted to only a few. You do not say, “A few were pleased,” or “A few desired it,” but, when you say that it has been granted, you unquestionably confess God’s grace rather than human sufficiency.

You use this word even more explicitly when, following Plato’s opinion [Note: [Col. 0307] In the *Phaedo* and the *Epinomis.], you yourself do not hesitate to say that in this life a human being cannot in any way attain the perfection of wisdom, but that for those who live according to the intellect whatever is lacking can, through God’s providence and grace, be completed after this life.

If only you had known God’s grace through Jesus Christ our Lord, and had been able to see that his incarnation itself—by which he assumed a human soul and body—is the supreme example of grace. But what am I to do? I know that I speak in vain to one who is dead. Yet as far as you are concerned—and as far as those who esteem you are concerned, who love you either with whatever love of wisdom they possess or through curiosity about arts that you ought not to have learned—I may perhaps not be speaking in vain. It is to these people, rather than to you, that I address my appeal.

God’s grace could not have been commended more graciously than by the fact that the one and only Son of God, remaining immutable in himself, assumed a human being [Note: [Col. 0308] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and several manuscripts read, “was clothed with a human being.” These same books later have “through the mediation of the human being, by which one might come to him.” Our manuscripts likewise have this reading.], and offered human beings the hope of his love through the mediation of a human being, by whom human beings might come to him—he who was so far removed from mortals as immortal, from the mutable as immutable, from the impious as just, and from the wretched as blessed.

And because he naturally implanted in us the desire to be blessed and immortal, he remained blessed while assuming mortality, so that he might grant us what we love; and by enduring what we fear, he taught us to despise it.

2. But in order for you to accept this truth, humility was necessary—a virtue that is with the greatest difficulty persuaded upon your necks. What, especially for people of your kind of wisdom, is said to be incredible? What, I ask, is incredible to you when it is said that God assumed a human soul and body?

You attribute so much to the intellectual soul—which is certainly a human soul—that you say it can become consubstantial with that paternal mind whom you confess to be the Son of God. What, then, is incredible if one intellectual soul, in an ineffable and singular manner, was assumed for the salvation of many?

As for the body, we know by the testimony of our very nature that the soul is joined to it, so that the human being may be whole and complete. If this were not something utterly familiar, it would surely be more incredible. For it is easier to accept in faith that, although the human is joined to the divine and the mutable to the immutable, spirit is joined to spirit—or, to use the terms customary among you, the incorporeal to the incorporeal—than that a body is joined to the incorporeal.

Or perhaps the unusual birth of a body from a virgin offends you? This ought not to offend you; indeed, it ought rather to lead you to embrace piety, since one who is wondrous was wondrously born.

Or is it the fact that, after laying down that very body in death and transforming it for the better through resurrection, he raised it above, now incorruptible and no longer mortal [Note: [Col. 0308] This is how the manuscripts read. The editions have, “and immortal.”]? Perhaps you refuse to believe this because you observe Porphyry, in the very books from which I have quoted—those he wrote *On the Return of the Soul*—so frequently commanding that every body must be fled if the soul is to remain blessed with God.

But he himself should rather have been corrected in this view, especially since, concerning the soul of this visible world and its immense corporeal mass, you hold such incredible opinions together with him. For, on Plato’s authority (*Timaeus*), you say that the world is an animal, and a supremely blessed animal, which you also wish to be everlasting.

How, then, will it never be separated from its body and never lack blessedness, if every body must be fled in order for the soul to be blessed? You also acknowledge that this sun and the other stars are bodies—not only in your books, since all human beings readily see and admit this with you—but you further assert, with what you consider a higher expertise, that they are supremely blessed animals and everlasting together with these bodies.

What, then, is the reason that, when Christian faith is urged upon you, you forget or pretend not to know what you are accustomed to argue and teach? Why, because of your opinions—opinions that you yourselves contradict—do you refuse to be Christians, unless it is because Christ came humbly and you are proud?

What the bodies of the saints will be like in the future resurrection may at some point be discussed more carefully among the most learned students of the Christian Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0309] This is how our manuscripts 2050 and 2052 read; one manuscript has “somewhat more carefully.”]. We nevertheless have no doubt that they will be everlasting, and that they will be such as Christ showed by his own resurrection as an example [Note: [Col. 0309] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads, “like the body Christ displayed as an example of his resurrection.”].

Whatever their nature, however, since they are proclaimed to be wholly incorruptible and immortal, and in no way to impede the soul’s contemplation by which it is fixed upon God—and since you too say that immortal bodies exist among the heavenly beings, belonging immortally to the blessed—why do you suppose that every body must be fled in order for us to be blessed, so that you may appear to flee the Christian faith as though rationally? Is it perhaps shameful to be corrected? That too is a vice belonging only to the proud.

It is evidently shameful for learned men, disciples of Plato, to become disciples of Christ—Christ who taught a fisherman by his Spirit to understand and say:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made in him was life, and the life was the light of human beings; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

A certain Platonist used to say, as we were accustomed to hear from the holy elder Simplicianus, who later presided as bishop over the Church of Milan [Note: [Col. 0309] See *On the Predestination of the Saints*, no. 4, and *Confessions*, book 8, chapter 2, no. 4.], that this beginning of the holy Gospel whose title is *According to John* ought to be written in letters of gold and displayed in the most prominent places throughout all the churches.

But that divine teacher was despised by the proud because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1–5, 14). It is not enough for the wretched that they are sick unless, even in their sickness, they exalt themselves and are ashamed of the medicine by which they could be healed. For they do not act in this way so that they may be lifted up, but so that, by falling, they may be afflicted more grievously.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### How much of Platonic doctrine Porphyry rejected and corrected by dissenting from it

If it is considered disgraceful to correct anything after Plato, why did Porphyry himself correct certain matters, and not insignificant ones [Col. 0310]? It is completely certain that Plato wrote that human souls, after death, are transferred even into the bodies of beasts [Note: [Col. 0310] Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 13, chapter 16, in the French version, *Démonstrations évangéliques*, volume 1.].

This doctrine was held by Porphyry’s teacher [Note: [Col. 0310] Earlier editions read, “Plato, the teacher, held this doctrine.” Later, Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus continue: “and yet it rightly displeased Porphyry, Plato’s disciple.” The Lovaniensis has, “and Plotinus, Porphyry’s disciple, nevertheless…” The older books, which here agree most closely with one another, restore the passage. Plotinus certainly followed Plato’s opinion concerning the return of souls into any bodies in *Enneads* 3.4.2. Porphyry himself writes that he came to Rome from Greece in the tenth year of the emperor Gallienus, when Plotinus was about fifty-nine years old, and that he listened to him for five years.]—and by Plotinus (*Enneads* 3.4.2). Yet it rightly displeased Porphyry. He thought that human souls return into human bodies, not those they had left behind, but different and new ones.

He was presumably ashamed to believe that, after being transformed into a mule, a mother might carry her son; yet he was not ashamed to believe that, after being transformed into a young woman, a mother might perhaps marry her son. How much more honorably may we believe what the holy and truthful angels taught, what the Prophets spoke under the impulse of God’s Spirit, what the Savior himself—whose coming was foretold by messengers sent before him—taught, and what the Apostles, sent to fill the world with the Gospel, proclaimed? How much more honorably, I say, may we believe that souls return once to their own bodies than that they return repeatedly to different bodies?

Nevertheless, as I have said, Porphyry was corrected to a considerable degree in this opinion, so that at least he held that human souls could be cast only into human beings and did not hesitate to abolish the prisons of beasts.

He also says that God gave the soul to the world for this purpose: that, having come to know the evils of matter, it might return to the Father and never again be held polluted by contact with such things. Although he holds something inappropriate here—for the soul was given to the body rather to do good, since it would not learn evils if it did not do them—he nevertheless corrected, and not in a minor matter, the opinion of the other Platonists by confessing that, once cleansed from all evils and established with the Father, the soul would never again suffer the evils of this world.

By this opinion he certainly removed what is regarded as especially Platonic: that just as the dead always arise from the living, so the living always arise from the dead (Plato, *Phaedo*). He also showed to be false what Virgil appears to have said in Platonic fashion: that purified souls, sent to the Elysian fields—a name by which the joys of the blessed seem to be indicated in the form of a fable—are summoned to the river Lethe [Note: [Col. 0310] See Plato, book 10 of the *Republic*], that is, to forgetfulness of what has gone before:

> Namely, that they may forget and revisit the vault of heaven above,  
> And begin once more to wish to return into bodies.  
> (*Aeneid* 6.750–751)

Porphyry rightly rejected this, since it is truly foolish to believe that, from a life which cannot be blessed unless it is completely certain of its own eternity, souls should desire the corruption of mortal bodies and return from there to these things [Note: [Col. 0310] Some manuscripts read “this thing.”]—as though the highest purification brought about a desire for pollution.

For if being perfectly cleansed causes them to forget all evils, while forgetfulness of evils causes a desire for bodies in which they will again become entangled in evils, then surely supreme happiness will be the cause of unhappiness, perfection of wisdom the cause of folly, and complete purification the cause of uncleanness [Note: [Col. 0311] This is how the manuscripts read. The editions have “purity.”].

Nor will the soul be blessed in truth for as long as it exists in a place where it must be deceived in order to be blessed. For it will not be blessed unless it is secure. But in order to be secure, it will always falsely suppose that it will remain blessed, since at some point it will also become wretched. If falsehood is the cause of its joy, how will it rejoice in truth?

Porphyry saw this and said that the purified soul therefore returns to the Father, so that it may never again be held polluted by contact with evils.

[XXXI.] It was therefore falsely supposed by some Platonists that there is a necessary cycle in which souls continually depart and return to the same things. Even if this were true, what good would it do to know it? Unless, perhaps, the Platonists dared to set themselves above us because in this life we would not know what they, in another and better life, having been most purified and wise, would have failed to know—and would become blessed by believing falsely.

If it is absurd and foolish to say this, then Porphyry’s opinion must certainly be preferred to that of those who imagined cycles of souls alternating endlessly between blessedness and misery. If this is so, behold: the Platonist disagrees with Plato for the better. Behold: he saw what Plato did not see, and after such a great and eminent teacher he did not recoil from correction, but preferred truth to a human being.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### Against the argument of the Platonists, by which they assert that the human soul is coeternal with God

Why, then, should we not rather believe the divine authority concerning matters that human ingenuity cannot investigate? That authority says that the soul itself is not coeternal with God but was created, although it did not previously exist.

The Platonists, unwilling to believe this, seemed to offer themselves a sufficient reason: unless something had always existed beforehand, it could not thereafter exist eternally.

Yet concerning the world and the gods whom, according to Plato, God made within the world (*Timaeus*), he says quite openly that they began to exist and have a beginning, while nevertheless asserting that they will not have an end but will remain forever through the exceedingly powerful will of the Creator.

They found a way to understand this: the beginning, they say, is not a beginning in time but a beginning of dependence. For, they say, if a foot had always existed in dust from eternity, a footprint would always have been beneath it; yet no one would doubt that the footprint was made by the one who trod upon it, nor would one be prior to the other, although one was made by the other.

So too, they say, the world and the gods created within it both always existed, since the one who made them always existed, and yet they were made.

But if the soul always existed, must its misery also be said to have always existed? Further, if something in it that had not existed eternally began to exist in time, why could it not have happened that the soul itself began to exist in time, although previously it had not existed?

Moreover, its blessedness also, after its experience of evils, became more secure and destined to remain without end, as Porphyry himself admits. It therefore unquestionably began in time and nevertheless will always exist, although previously it did not.

The entire argument is therefore dissolved by which it is supposed that nothing can exist without an end in time unless it has no beginning in time. For the soul’s blessedness has been discovered: although it had a beginning in time, it will not have an end in time.

Therefore human weakness must yield to divine authority. Let us believe, concerning true religion, those blessed and immortal beings who do not seek for themselves the honor which they know is owed to their God, who is also ours. They do not command us to offer sacrifice except to him alone—to him to whom we too, together with them, as I have often said and must often say, ought to be sacrifice, offering ourselves through that priest who, in the human nature he assumed, according to which he also willed to be a priest, deigned even to become a sacrifice for us unto death [Note: [Col. 0312] Some manuscripts of no better authority read, “in the form which he assumed, according to which…” This is also the reading of manuscript 2050.].

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### On the universal way of liberating the soul, which Porphyry failed to find because he sought it wrongly, and which Christian grace alone opened

1. This is the religion that contains the universal way of liberating the soul, since no soul can be liberated except by this way. For this is, in a certain sense, the royal way: the one way that leads to a kingdom secure not in the unstable elevation of time but in the steadfastness of eternity.

When Porphyry says, near the end of the first book of *On the Return of the Soul*, that no one particular sect had yet been received which contains a universal way of liberating the soul [Note: [Col. 0312] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus read, “that no sect had yet been received into one particular sect.” Most manuscripts likewise read thus, but differ from those editions immediately afterward, reading “which” rather than “that.”—Our manuscripts have the same reading.]—whether from some genuinely true philosophy, or from the customs and discipline of the Indians, or from the teachings of the Chaldeans, or from any other way—and that this same way had not yet come to his knowledge through historical investigation, he unquestionably confesses that some such way exists, but that it had not yet come to his knowledge.

Thus whatever he had learned with the greatest diligence concerning the liberation of the soul, and whatever he seemed to himself—or rather to others—to know and possess, was not sufficient for him. For he felt that some exceedingly authoritative source was still lacking, one which he ought to follow in so important a matter.

When he says that no sect had yet come to his knowledge from some genuinely true philosophy which contains a universal way of liberating the soul, he sufficiently shows, in my judgment, either that the philosophy in which he philosophized is not genuinely true, or that it does not contain such a way. And how can a philosophy be genuinely true if it does not contain this way? For what other way is there that is universal for liberating the soul except the way by which all souls are liberated, so that without it no soul is liberated?

When he adds, “or from the customs and discipline of the Indians, or from the teachings of the Chaldeans, or from any other way,” he testifies in the clearest terms that this universal way of liberating the soul is not contained either in what he learned from the Indians or in what he learned from the Chaldeans. Yet he could not fail to mention that he had received divine oracles from the Chaldeans, since he refers to them so constantly.

What, then, does he wish us to understand as the universal way of liberating the soul that had not yet been received, whether from some truly genuine philosophy or from the teachings of those peoples who were regarded as possessing great knowledge of divine matters—because among them curiosity about discovering and worshiping various angels had greater influence—and that had not yet come to his knowledge through historical inquiry?

What is this universal way except one that is not peculiar to each nation but divinely bestowed as a common possession upon all nations?

This man, who was certainly not lacking in intelligence, did not doubt that such a way existed. For he did not believe that divine providence could leave the human race without this universal way of liberating the soul.

He does not say that it does not exist. He says only that this great good and great aid had not yet been received and had not yet come to his knowledge. Nor is this surprising. Porphyry lived at a time when this universal way of liberating the soul—which is none other than the Christian religion—was being permitted to be attacked by worshipers of idols and demons and by earthly kings [Note: [Col. 0313] Porphyry lived under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, who persecuted the Christians with the most unjust hatred.], on account of the affirmation and consecration of the number of martyrs—that is, witnesses to the truth—through whom it would be demonstrated that all bodily evils must be endured for the sake of faith, piety, and the commendation of truth.

Porphyry therefore saw these things and imagined that, through such persecutions, this way would soon perish, and for that reason he did not think it was the universal way of liberating the soul. He did not understand that the very thing which troubled him and which he feared to endure in his choice belonged rather to the confirmation of this way and to its stronger commendation.

## 2.

This, then, is the universal way of liberating the soul—that is, the way granted by divine mercy to all nations. Its knowledge has already come, and will yet come, to all to whom it is destined; and neither ought it nor will it be permissible for anyone to say to it, “Why now? And why so late?” For the purpose of the one who sends it cannot be penetrated by human intelligence. This too was perceived by that man when he said that this gift of God had not yet been received and had not yet come to his knowledge. He did not, therefore, judge it untrue merely because it had not yet been received into his faith or had not yet reached his knowledge.

This, I say, is the universal way of liberating believers, concerning which faithful Abraham received the divine oracle: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). He was indeed a Chaldean by nation; but in order that he might receive such promises, and that from him the seed might be propagated which was ordained through angels in the hand of the Mediator (Galatians 3:19), in whom this universal way of liberating the soul was to exist—that is, the way given to all nations—he was commanded to depart from his country, his kindred, and his father’s house (Genesis 12:1). Thus he himself was first freed from the superstitions of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 0313] Compare below, Book 16, chapter 12.]. By following and worshiping the one true God, he faithfully believed him who made these promises.

This is the universal way of which it is said in the sacred prophecy:

> May God have mercy on us and bless us;  
> may he cause his face to shine upon us and have mercy on us,  
> so that we may know your way on earth,  
> your salvation among all nations.  
> (Psalm 66:2–3)

Accordingly, long afterward, having assumed flesh from the seed of Abraham, the Savior himself said of himself: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

This is the universal way concerning which it was prophesied so long beforehand:

> In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be manifest, established on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall come to it, and many peoples shall enter and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he shall announce his way to us, and we shall walk in it.” For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.  
> (Isaiah 2:2–3)

[Note: [Col. 0314] The older books omit the words “of the house of the Lord.”]

That way, therefore, belongs not to one nation but to all nations. The law and word of the Lord did not remain in Zion and Jerusalem; rather, they went forth from there in order to spread throughout the whole world.

For this reason, after his resurrection, the Mediator said to his frightened disciples:

> It was necessary that what is written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled.

Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them:

> It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.  
> (Luke 24:44–47)

This, then, is the universal way of liberating the soul. The holy angels and holy prophets signified it and foretold it—first among the few people whom they were able to find receiving God’s grace, and especially among the Hebrew people, whose commonwealth was in a certain sense itself consecrated—as a prophecy and foreshadowing of the city of God that was to be gathered from all nations. They signified it through the tabernacle, the temple, the priesthood, and the sacrifices, and they foretold it in certain utterances that were clear, though in many others mystical.

When the Mediator himself was present in the flesh, and his blessed apostles were already revealing more openly the grace of the New Testament, they made clear what had been signified somewhat more obscurely in earlier times, in accordance with the distribution of the ages of the human race, as God in his wisdom chose to order it.
