The signs bore witness to the marvelous works of God, of which I have already mentioned a few above.

For there appeared not only angelic visions, and were heard not only the words of heavenly ministers. Rather, when people acting in simple piety according to the word of God were present, unclean spirits were driven from human bodies and minds; bodily defects and illnesses were healed; wild animals of land and water, the birds of the air, trees, the elements, and the stars obeyed divine commands; the underworld yielded; and the dead returned to life. These signs are apart from the Savior’s own particular and singular miracles, especially those of his birth and resurrection. In the one, he displayed only the mystery of his mother’s virginity; in the other, he also displayed an example of the resurrection of those who will rise at the end.

This way purifies the whole human being and prepares the mortal for immortality in all the parts of which it consists. For, lest a different purification be sought for that part which Porphyry calls “intellectual,” another for that which he calls “spiritual,” and yet another for the body itself, the most truthful and powerful purifier and savior took up the whole human being.

Apart from this way—which was never absent from the human race, partly when these future things were foretold and partly when events already accomplished were announced—no one has been liberated, no one is being liberated, and no one will be liberated.

## 3.

But when Porphyry says that the universal way of liberating the soul had not yet reached his knowledge through historical acquaintance, what history can be found either more illustrious than this, which has attained such an eminent authority throughout the whole world, or more trustworthy—one in which past events are narrated in such a way that future events are also foretold, many of which we see fulfilled, and from which we confidently hope that what remains will without doubt be fulfilled?

For Porphyry, or any of the Platonists, cannot despise, even in this way, divination and prediction concerning, as it were, earthly matters and things belonging to this mortal life—as they rightly do in other prophecies and in divinations of whatever kinds or arts.

[Note: [Col. 0315] The older books read *vaticinantibus* (“soothsayers”) instead of *vaticinationibus* (“prophecies”).] For they deny that such things are worthy of being attributed to great men or regarded as great—and rightly so. Either they arise from the foreknowledge of lower causes, as in the art of medicine, where by certain preceding signs many things that will happen to a person’s health are foreseen [Note: [Col. 0315] The manuscripts read *eventura*; the printed editions read *venturae*.]; or unclean demons announce beforehand the things they have arranged. They in a certain way claim for themselves the right to direct the minds and desires of wicked people toward actions corresponding to them, and to exercise this right in the lowest material of human frailty.

[Note: [Col. 0315] The printed editions read: “and in the minds and desires of any wicked people they balance words corresponding to actions, or actions corresponding to words, so that they may in a certain way claim for themselves a right in the weak material of human frailty.” This is corrected according to the manuscripts, which read as follows: “whose right—that is, the right of their actions—in directing the minds and desires of wicked people toward actions corresponding to them—that is, corresponding to those same depraved desires—they in a certain way claim for themselves, and in the lowest material of human frailty.”]

[Note: [Col. 0315] See the book *On the Divination of Demons*, section 3 and following.]

Holy men, walking in this universal way of liberating souls, did not concern themselves with making such predictions as though they were great prophecies, although these matters too were not hidden from them and were often foretold by them, in order to establish faith in things that could not be disclosed to mortal understanding or quickly brought to experience. Rather, the things they announced as future, insofar as God’s will was granted to them to know it, were truly great and divine.

Christ was to come in the flesh; and the things accomplished in him with such clarity and fulfilled in his name—the repentance of human beings and the conversion of their wills to God, the forgiveness of sins, the grace of righteousness, the faith of the devout, and the multitude of believers throughout the world in the true divinity; the overthrow of the worship of idols and demons; the testing through temptations; the purification of those who make progress and their liberation from every evil; the day of judgment; the resurrection of the dead; the eternal condemnation of the fellowship of the wicked; and the eternal kingdom of the most glorious city of God, which enjoys the sight of its God in immortality—all these things were foretold and promised in the Scriptures of this way. We see so many of them fulfilled that, with right devotion, we are confident that the remaining things too will come to pass.

Those who do not believe in the uprightness of this way, which leads to the vision of God and eternal union with him, as it is preached and affirmed in the truth of the holy Scriptures, may attack it, because they do not understand it; but they cannot defeat it [Note: [Col. 0316] Compare Letter 137 to Volusianus.].

## 4.

Therefore, in these ten books, although we have done less than the expectation of some people concerning us had anticipated, nevertheless, for the sake of the zeal of others, we have satisfied them insofar as the true God and Lord has deigned to assist us, refuting the objections of the wicked, who prefer their gods to the Creator of the holy city about which we have undertaken to speak.

Of these ten books, the first five were written against those who think that the gods should be worshiped for the sake of the good things of this life; the last five against those who believe that the worship of the gods should be maintained for the sake of the life that will exist after death.

Accordingly, as I promised in the first book, I shall now explain, insofar as God assists me, what I judge should be said about the origin, progress, and appointed ends of the two cities which, in this present age, we have said are in some way interwoven and mingled with one another.

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Note: [Col. 0315] Written in the year of Christ 416 or 417.]

The second part of this work begins here [Note: [Col. 0315] “The second part of this work,” Augustine says in *Retractations* 2.43.2, “is contained in twelve books. The first four of these contain the origin of the two cities, one of which is God’s and the other this world’s; the next four their course or progress; and the final three their appointed ends.” Augustine was working on this eleventh book when, at his request, Paulus Orosius began writing his books of *Histories*, in the year of Christ 416 or 417. Orosius himself praises him in his preface as “persisting in completing the eleventh book against the pagans; for,” he says, “as soon as the ten rays of these books, rising from the watchtower of ecclesiastical clarity, were lifted up, they shone throughout the whole world.”]

This is the second part of the work, concerning the origin, progress, and appointed ends of the two cities, the earthly and the heavenly. In this first book Augustine demonstrates how the beginnings of these same cities preceded the creation of the world in the distinction between the good and evil angels; on that occasion he discusses the creation of the world, which is described in the sacred Scriptures at the beginning of Genesis.

[Col. 0315]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On that part of the work in which the beginnings and ends of the two cities, that is, the heavenly and earthly cities, begin to be demonstrated

We call the city of God the city to which that Scripture bears witness which, not through the accidental movements of minds but plainly through the supreme ordering of providence, has by its divine authority surpassed all the writings of all nations and subjected to itself every kind of human intelligence [Note: [Col. 0317] Compare *On Christian Doctrine* 2.63.].

For it is written there: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 87:3). And in another psalm we read: “Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, on his holy mountain, making the rejoicing of the whole earth abundant.” A little later in the same psalm: “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God founded it forever” (Psalm 48:2–3, 9).

Again, in another psalm: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God; the Most High sanctified his tabernacle. God is in its midst; it shall not be moved” (Psalm 46:5–6).

From these and similar testimonies—which it would take too long to recount in full—we have learned that there is a city of God whose citizens we desire to be, through that love which its Founder has inspired in us [Note: [Col. 0317] Most manuscripts read *concupivimus*, “we have desired.” Some read *concupimus*, “we desire.”].

The citizens of the earthly city prefer their gods to the Founder of this holy city, not knowing that he is the God of gods—not of false gods, that is, of the wicked and proud, who, deprived of his unchangeable light shared by all and therefore reduced to a certain impoverished power, pursue their own private powers, so to speak, and seek divine honors from subjects whom they have deceived—but of the devout and holy gods, who prefer to subject themselves to the one God rather than to have many subject to them, and who prefer to worship God rather than to be worshiped as God.

Against the enemies of this holy city we have replied in the ten preceding books, insofar as we were able, with the assistance of our Lord and King.

Now, recognizing what is expected of me and not forgetting my obligation, I shall undertake, relying everywhere upon the assistance of that same Lord and King, to discuss, insofar as I am able, the origin, course, and appointed ends of the two cities—the earthly and the heavenly—which, during this intervening age, we have said are in some way interwoven and mingled with one another. First I shall explain how the beginnings of these two cities preceded the distinction among the angels.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### On knowing God, to whose knowledge no human being comes except through the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ

It is a great and exceedingly rare achievement to rise by the attention of the mind above the whole bodily and incorporeal creation, considered and recognized as mutable, and to arrive at the unchangeable substance of God, and there to learn from God himself that he alone made every nature that is not what he is.

For God does not speak with a human being through some bodily creature, making himself heard in bodily ears while airy spaces are struck between the one who sounds and the one who hears; nor does he speak through some spiritual creature formed in the likeness of bodies, as in dreams or in any similar manner. Even in that case he speaks, as it were, to bodily ears, because he speaks, as it were, through a body and as though an interval of bodily places intervened. Such visions are indeed very similar to bodies [Col. 0318]. But he speaks through the truth itself, if anyone is capable of hearing with the mind and not with the body.

He speaks to that part of the human being which is better than the other parts of which a human being consists, and which God alone surpasses. For when a human being is rightly understood—or, if this cannot be understood, at least believed—to have been made in the image of God, that person is plainly closer to the supreme God in the part by which he surpasses his lower parts [Note: [Col. 0318] “Parts” is to be supplied.], which he shares even with animals.

But because the mind itself, which naturally possesses reason and understanding, has been weakened by certain dark and longstanding vices, not only for clinging to and enjoying the unchangeable light but also for enduring it [Note: [Col. 0318] Vindicianus, Erasmus, and one manuscript read “for enjoying, through merit, the unchangeable light.” The Ambrosian edition reads “for enduring, through merit, the unchangeable light.” Three manuscripts read “for enjoying the unchangeable light.” The same reading appears in Manuscript 2050 M.], until it is renewed and healed day by day and becomes capable of such great happiness, it first had to be imbued and purified by faith.

So that it might walk more confidently toward the truth, the truth itself, God the Son, assuming humanity without consuming or abolishing divinity, established and founded that faith, so that for the human being the way to God might be through the human being who is God. For this is the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

He is mediator insofar as he is human [Note: [Col. 0318] The printed editions read, “insofar as he too is human.” The manuscripts omit “too”; one manuscript has *est*, “is,” in its place.]; and for this reason he is also the way. For if there is a way between the one who is journeying and the destination toward which he is journeying, there is hope of arriving. But if the way is absent or unknown, what benefit is there in knowing where one ought to go?

There is one most secure way against all errors: that the same person be both God and human. Where one goes, he is God; by which one goes, he is human.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### On the canonical authority of Scripture, composed by the divine Spirit

First through the prophets, then through himself, and afterward through the apostles, he spoke as much as he judged sufficient; and he also established the Scripture called canonical, possessing the highest authority. From it we have faith concerning matters which it is not expedient for us to be ignorant of and which we are not capable of knowing by ourselves.

For if we can know through our own testimony those things that are not remote from our senses, whether our inner or even our outer senses—and they are therefore called “present,” because we say that they are before our senses, just as things available to the eyes are before our eyes—then, plainly, concerning things that are remote from our senses, since we cannot know them through our own testimony, we seek other witnesses and believe those from whose senses we do not believe that such things are or have been remote.

Thus, just as concerning visible things that we have not seen we believe those who have seen them, and likewise concerning other matters belonging to each of the bodily senses, so concerning those things that are perceived by the soul and mind—for the mind itself is rightly called a sense, from which the word “judgment” (*sententia*) also derives—that is, concerning invisible things remote from our inner sense [Note: [Col. 0318] The Louvain edition reads “outer sense,” contrary to the other printed editions and the manuscripts], we ought to believe those who have learned that these things are arranged in that incorporeal light or who behold them as they abide there.

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### On the creation of the world: that it is not timeless, nor ordered by a new decision of God, as though he later wished what he had previously not wished

[Col. 0319]

### 1.

The greatest of all visible things is the world; the greatest of all invisible things is God. We see that the world exists; we believe that God exists. But that God made the world, we trust no one more safely than God himself.

Where have we heard him? For the present, nowhere better than in the holy Scriptures, where his prophet said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1).

Was this prophet present when God made heaven and earth? No. But the Wisdom of God was present [Note: [Col. 0319] Proverbs 8:27: “When he prepared the heavens, I was there,” and so forth.], through whom all things were made, who transfers herself also into holy souls and establishes them as friends of God and prophets (Wisdom 7:27), and who silently recounts his works inwardly to them. God’s angels also speak to them—those who always behold the face of the Father (Matthew 18:10)—and announce his will to those to whom it is appropriate.

This prophet was one of them: he said and wrote, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” He is such a suitable witness through whom we should believe God that, by the same Spirit of God through whom he learned that these things had been revealed to him, he also foretold so long beforehand the faith that would be ours.

### 2.

But what pleased the eternal God to make heaven and earth at that time, when he had not made them before [Note: [Col. 0319] Compare *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* 1.3 and *Confessions* 11.10, 12, and 30.]?

Those who say this, if they wish the world to be eternal, without any beginning, and therefore do not want it to appear to have been made by God, are excessively estranged from the truth and are mad with the deadly disease of impiety.

For apart from the prophetic utterances, the world itself, through its supremely ordered mutability and movement and through the most beautiful appearance of all visible things, proclaims in a certain silent way both that it was made and that it could have been made only by God—ineffably and invisibly great, and ineffably and invisibly beautiful.

But those who confess that it was indeed made by God, yet do not want it to have a beginning in time, but rather a beginning of its creation, saying that it has always been made in some scarcely intelligible manner, do say something by which they seem to defend God against accidental rashness: they do not want it believed that the thought of making the world suddenly came to him, although it had never occurred to him before, or that a new will arose in him, since he is altogether unchangeable.

Yet I do not see how this reasoning can stand concerning other things, especially the soul. If they contend that the soul is coeternal with God, they will in no way be able to explain where its new misery came from, since it had never previously existed throughout eternity.

If they say that its misery and blessedness have always alternated, they must also say that they will always alternate [Note: [Col. 0319] Erasmus reads, “that nature always alternates.” Several manuscripts read, “that nature has always alternated.” Some read, “that nature has always been alternated.”]. From this follows the absurdity that, even when the soul is called blessed, it is not blessed in this respect: if it foresees its future misery and degradation, then it is not truly blessed; but if it does not foresee them and does not expect to become degraded and miserable, while it always considers itself blessed, then it is blessed by a false opinion. Nothing more foolish than this can be said.

If, however, they think that the soul’s misery has alternated with blessedness throughout the infinitely long ages of the past, but that now, once liberated, it will not return to misery, they are nevertheless compelled to admit that it was never truly blessed, but is only now beginning to be so through a new and non-deceptive blessedness. Consequently, they will admit that something new has happened to it, something great and glorious which had never happened throughout eternity.

If they deny that God had eternally held the cause of this novelty in his plan, they will at the same time deny that he is the author of its blessedness, which is impious beyond expression. But if they say that God himself devised a new plan so that the soul might thereafter be blessed forever, how will they show that he is free from the very mutability that displeases them?

Furthermore, if they confess that the soul was created in time but will never perish thereafter—so that it has a beginning, like a number, but no end [Note: [Col. 0320] The printed editions read, “like a true thing.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “like a number.” A number indeed has a beginning from unity, but has no end in which it stops of itself, since however much is added, a greater number can always be formed.]—and therefore that, once it has experienced miseries and been liberated from them, it will never afterward be miserable, they will certainly not doubt that this occurs while God’s plan remains unchangeable.

Let them therefore believe that the world too could have been made in time, without thereby supposing that God changed his eternal plan and will in making it.

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### That one should no more think of infinite stretches of time before the world than of infinite places

Next, those who agree that God is the creator of the world, yet ask what answer should be given concerning the time of the world, should consider what answer they themselves give concerning its place.

For one may ask why it was made at that particular time and not earlier, just as one may ask why it was made here, where it is, and not elsewhere.

If they imagine infinite stretches of time before the world, during which it seems to them that God could not have remained inactive, let them similarly imagine infinite expanses of place outside the world. If someone says that the omnipotent God could not have been inactive there, will it not follow that they must be compelled, with Epicurus, to dream of innumerable worlds [Note: [Col. 0320] The manuscripts read *cogantur* (“they are compelled”); the printed editions read *cogatur* (“he is compelled”).]?

The only difference would be that Epicurus asserts that worlds are generated and dissolved by the accidental movements of atoms, whereas these people would say that they were made by God—if they refuse to allow him to remain inactive throughout the boundless immensity of places extending on every side outside the world, and if they also deny that those worlds, as they think of this one, can be dissolved for any reason.

For we are dealing with people who agree with us that God is incorporeal and the creator of all natures that are not what he is. It would be too unworthy to admit others into this religious discussion—especially since, among those who think that the worship of many gods must be offered, these philosophers have surpassed the rest in distinction and authority for no other reason than that, although by a considerable distance, they are nevertheless closer to the truth than the others.

[Note: [Col. 0320] The Louvain edition omits “especially since, among those,” and consequently joins the words incorrectly: “It would be too unworthy to admit others into this religious discussion, who think that the worship of many gods must be offered. These philosophers have surpassed the rest,” etc.; as though those with whom it does not seem unworthy to discuss religion—undoubtedly the Platonists—did not themselves think that ritual worship should also be rendered to many other gods.]

Or perhaps they will say that the substance of God, which they neither enclose nor define nor extend through space, but which—as is worthy of a conception of God—they confess to be wholly present everywhere in incorporeal presence, is absent from such vast spaces outside the world and occupies only the one place—and, in comparison with that infinity, so very small a place—in which the world exists? I do not think they will proceed to such empty talk.

Since, then, they say that there is one world, immense indeed in bodily magnitude but finite and bounded in its place, and that it was made by the activity of God, let them answer for themselves concerning the infinite places outside the world: why does God cease from his work in them? They must give the same answer concerning the infinite times before the world: why did God cease from his work in them?

And just as it does not follow that God established the world in this place rather than elsewhere by chance instead of by divine reason—since this place could have been chosen among the equally infinite spaces open everywhere without any superior merit, although no human being can comprehend the divine reason by which it was done [Note: [Col. 0321] Vindicianus, Ambrose, and Erasmus add *natura*, “by nature,” after *comprehendere*; the Louvain edition has *mens*, “mind.” This is superfluous, since in the older books the word *ratio*, “reason,” is left to be supplied]—so it does not follow that we should think something accidental happened to God because he created the world at that time rather than at an earlier one. For the earlier times had equally passed by through an infinite stretch into the past, and there would have been no difference by which one time could have been preferred to another.

If they say that human beings think emptily when they imagine infinite places, since there is no place beyond the world, the answer is that in the same way human beings think emptily when they imagine past times in which God was inactive, since there is no time before the world [Note: [Col. 0321] Compare *Confessions* 11.13 and following.].

## CHAPTER SIX  
### That the creation of the world and of time have one beginning, and that neither precedes the other

For if eternity and time are rightly distinguished—and there is no time without some mutable change of movement, whereas in eternity there is no change—who does not see that there would have been no times if no creature had been made that changed something by some movement? When one thing gives way to and succeeds another—things that cannot exist simultaneously—time would follow according to intervals of shorter or longer duration.

Since God, in whose eternity there is absolutely no change, is the creator and ordainer of times, I do not see how it can be said that he created the world after stretches of time, unless one says that some creature already existed before the world, through whose movements time could pass [Note: [Col. 0321] Compare *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* 5.12.].

But if the sacred and most truthful Scriptures say that “in the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), so that he is understood to have made nothing beforehand—for if he had made something before all the other things he made, that would more properly be called what he made “in the beginning”—then without doubt the world was not made in time but with time.

For what is made in time is made both after some time and before some time: after what is past and before what is future. But there could have been nothing past, because there was no creature whose mutable movements could produce the passage of time.

The world was made with time, if a mutable movement was made along with its creation, as the order of the first six or seven days also seems to show. In those days evening and morning are named, until everything that God made during those days was completed on the sixth day, and on the seventh day, through a great mystery, God’s resting is commended.

What kind of days these were is either exceedingly difficult or even impossible for us to imagine; how much more difficult, then, to express?

## CHAPTER SEVEN  
### On the nature of the first days, which are said to have had evening and morning before the sun was made

We see that the days familiar to us have evening only from the setting of the sun and morning only from its rising. But the first three of those days passed without the sun, which is reported to have been made on the fourth day.

At first, light was made by the word of God, and God is said to have separated it from darkness and to have called that light “day,” while he called the darkness “night” (Genesis 1:4). But what sort of light that was, and through what alternating movement it operated, and what kind of evening and morning it produced, is remote from our senses. Nor can we understand it as it actually is, although it must be believed without any hesitation.

For either it is some bodily light, whether in the higher regions of the world, far from our sight, or the source from which the sun was afterward kindled; or by the name “light” the holy city was signified, in the holy angels and blessed spirits, of which the apostle says: “The Jerusalem above is our eternal mother in the heavens” (Galatians 4:26).

He also says elsewhere: “For you are all sons of light and sons of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness” (1 Thessalonians 5:5).

[Note: [Col. 0322] The manuscripts read: “Yet we may perhaps understand, at least to some extent, the evening and morning of this day appropriately; for the knowledge of creation, in comparison …” The printed editions read: “There is, however, also an evening and morning of this day, at least to some extent; for the knowledge of creation, in comparison …”]

Nevertheless, we may perhaps be able to understand, at least to some extent and appropriately, the evening and morning of this day. For the knowledge of creation, in comparison with the knowledge of the Creator, becomes in a certain sense evening; and it likewise becomes light and turns into morning when it is referred to the praise and love of the Creator. It does not turn into night, where the Creator is not abandoned for the love of creation.

Finally, when Scripture counted those days in order, it nowhere inserted the word “night.” It does not say anywhere, “Night was made,” but rather, “There was evening, and there was morning, one day” (Genesis 1:5). Likewise on the second day and the others.

For the knowledge of creation in itself is, so to speak, more faded than when creation is known in the Wisdom of God, as in the art by which it was made. Therefore it can more fittingly be called evening than night. Yet, as I have said, when it is referred to the praise and love of the Creator, it returns to morning.

When this occurs in the knowledge of creation itself, it is one day; when it occurs in the knowledge of the firmament—which was called heaven and was placed between the lower and upper waters—it is the second day; when it occurs in the knowledge of the earth and sea and all things that grow, which are rooted in the earth, it is the third day; when it occurs in the knowledge of the greater and lesser lights and of all the stars, it is the fourth day; when it occurs in the knowledge of all the aquatic animals and flying creatures made from the waters, it is the fifth day; and when it occurs in the knowledge of all terrestrial animals and of the human being himself, it is the sixth day [Note: [Col. 0323] Compare the books *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, especially Books 1 and 4.].

## CHAPTER EIGHT  
### What sort of divine rest is to be understood, when God rested on the seventh day after the works of the six days

When God rests on the seventh day from all his works and sanctifies it, this must by no means be understood childishly, as though God had grown weary through working—he who spoke and they were made (Psalm 148:5), by an intelligible and everlasting word, not by a sounding and temporal one.

Rather, God’s rest signifies the rest of those who rest in God, just as the joy of a house signifies the joy of those who rejoice in the house, even if it is not the house itself but something else that makes them joyful.

How much more is this true if the same house, through its beauty, makes its inhabitants joyful, so that it is called joyful not only in that manner of speaking by which what contains is signified through what is contained—as when we say, “The theaters applaud” and “the meadows bellow,” when it is people who applaud in the theaters and cattle that bellow in the meadows—but also in the manner by which the cause is signified through its effect, as when a letter is called joyful because it signifies the joy of those whom it makes joyful when they read it?

Accordingly, when prophetic authority most fittingly tells us that God rested, it signifies the rest of those who rest in him and whom he himself causes to rest [Note: [Col. 0323] “Aristobulus,” Eusebius writes in *Preparation for the Gospel* 13.12, “reported that God is said to have rested on the seventh day because, having created all things, he implanted rest in them—that is, enduring stability, permanence, and an established, fixed, and unchangeable order—or because whatever he had determined to make was completed exactly as he had ordained.” COQUAEUS.].

Prophecy also promises this to the human beings to whom God speaks and for whose sake it was written: after the good works that God performs in them and through them, if in this life they first approach him in some manner through faith, they too will have eternal rest in him. This was also represented by the sabbath rest prescribed by the law among the ancient people of God, about which I think it should be discussed more carefully in its proper place.

## CHAPTER NINE  
### What should be held concerning the creation of the angels according to the divine testimonies
Now, since I have undertaken to speak of the origin of the holy city, and first thought that I should say what concerns the holy angels—for they constitute a large part of this city, and one all the more blessed because it has never lived as a stranger—I shall explain, insofar as seems sufficient, what divine testimonies are available on this subject, with God’s help. When Sacred Scripture speaks of the creation of the world, it does not explicitly say whether the angels were created, or in what order. But if they have not been passed over, they are signified either under the name of heaven, where it is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), or rather under the name of this light of which I am speaking.

I do not think, however, that they were passed over, on the grounds that it is written that God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made, while the book itself begins in this way: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” so that he seems to have made nothing before heaven and earth. Since, therefore, he began with heaven and earth, and since the earth itself, which he first made, was—as Scripture subsequently declares—invisible and unformed, and since, before light had yet been made, there was necessarily darkness over the abyss, that is, over a certain undifferentiated mixture of earth and water (for where there is no light, there must be darkness), and since thereafter all things were arranged by being created, as is related to have been completed over six days, how could the angels have been passed over as though they were not among God’s works, from which he rested on the seventh day?

That the angels are God’s work is not omitted here, but it is not stated explicitly; elsewhere, however, Holy Scripture bears witness to this in the clearest terms. For in the hymn of the three men in the furnace, after it had been said, “Bless all the works of the Lord, O Lord,” in the enumeration of those same works the angels are also named (Dan. 3:57–58). And in the Psalm we sing:

> Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. 148:1–5).

Here too it is stated most plainly by divine authority that the angels were made by God. For after they have been mentioned among the other heavenly things, the statement concerning everything follows: “He spoke, and they were made.” Who, then, would dare to suppose that the angels were made after all those things that are enumerated as having been made over the six days?

[Note: [Col. 0324] The Lov. edition alone reads “after all these common things.” A little later it has the same reading, on equal authority, while all the other books disagree.]

But if anyone is so foolish as to think so, that folly is refuted by a Scripture of equal authority, where God says, “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me with a loud voice” (Job 38:7, according to the Septuagint). The angels, therefore, already existed when the stars were made. But the stars were made on the fourth day. Shall we then say that the angels were made on the third day? Far from it. It is obvious what was made on that day: the earth was separated from the waters, and those two elements received distinct forms according to their kinds, while the earth produced whatever is rooted and fixed in it.

On the second day, then? Not that either: for at that time the firmament was made between the upper and lower waters, and it was called heaven; and in that firmament the stars were made on the fourth day. Clearly, then, if the angels belong among the works of God of those days, they are that light which received the name “day.” And in order that its unity might be commended, it was not called the first day, but “one day.”

[Note: [Col. 0324] The Greek theologians hold that spiritual things preceded bodily things, and that the Creator of the world used them, as it were, as ministers in producing the remaining things; Plato followed this opinion in his account of the world’s creation. Saint Jerome, following Gregory his teacher and his fellow Greeks, judged that spiritual things came before bodily things. Basil and Dionysius, however, as well as nearly all Greeks and Latins, Ambrose, Bede, Cassiodorus, and this Augustine, maintain that all things were produced by God simultaneously; this seems to agree with Ecclesiasticus 18:1: “He who lives forever created all things together.” —LUD. VIVES.]

Nor is there another second day, or third, or any of the others; rather, that same one day was repeated in order to complete the number six or seven, on account of the sixfold or sevenfold knowledge: the sixfold knowledge, namely, of the works God made, and the sevenfold knowledge of God’s rest.

[Note: [Col. 0325] See below, chapters 30 and 31.]

For when God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, if the creation of the angels is rightly understood in this light, they were certainly made participants in the eternal light, which is itself the immutable Wisdom of God, through whom all things were made, whom we call the only-begotten Son of God. Thus, illuminated by the light in which they were created, they became light, and they were called “day” by their participation in the immutable light and day, which is the Word of God, through whom both they and all things were made.

For the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9), also enlightens every pure angel, so that the angel is light not in himself but in God. If an angel turns away from him, the angel becomes impure, as are all those who are called unclean spirits: no longer light in the Lord, but darkness in themselves, deprived of participation in the eternal light. For there is no nature that is evil; rather, the loss of the good has received the name “evil.”

## CHAPTER X — On the simple and immutable Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the one God, for whom quality is not one thing and substance another

**1.** Only that which is good is simple, and therefore only that which is good is immutable: this is God. From this good all good things were created, but they are not simple, and therefore they are mutable. I say “created,” that is, made, not begotten. For what is begotten from the simple good is likewise simple, and is what that from which it was begotten is; these two we call the Father and the Son. And the two together with the Holy Spirit are one God: that Spirit of the Father and the Son who, by a certain proper signification of this name, is called the Holy Spirit in Sacred Scripture.

He is other than the Father and the Son, because he is neither the Father nor the Son. But I said “other,” not “another thing,” because he too is equally simple, equally good, immutable, and coeternal. And this Trinity is one God; nor is it therefore not simple because it is a Trinity. For we do not call this nature of the good simple because in it there is only the Father, or only the Son, or only the Holy Spirit; nor because this is merely a Trinity of names without the subsistence of the persons,

[Note: [Col. 0325] Am., Er., and certain manuscripts read “without substance.”]

as the Sabellian heretics thought.

[Note: [Col. 0325] In this place Vind., Am., and Er. add: “The Father who begot is simple, and the Son who was begotten is likewise simple, and he is what that from which he was begotten is.” But these words are absent from Lov. and the manuscripts.]

Rather, it is called simple because what it has, that it is—except where each person is spoken of relatively in relation to another. For the Father certainly has the Son, yet he himself is not the Son; and the Son has the Father, yet he himself is not the Father. Whatever, therefore, is said of a person in relation to that person himself, and not to another, is what that person has: just as he is said to be living in relation to himself, possessing life, and himself being that very life.

[Note: [Col. 0325] The manuscripts read *vivus* (“alive”) rather than *vivens* (“living”).]

[Note: [Col. 0325] Compare below, chapter 24 of this book.]

**2.** For this reason, therefore, that nature is called simple in which having something does not mean possessing something that can be lost, or in which the one who has is not one thing and what is had another—like a vessel with some liquid, a body with a color, air with light or heat, or a soul with wisdom. None of these is what it has: a vessel is not the liquid, nor a body the color, nor air the light or heat, nor a soul wisdom. Hence they can also be deprived of the things they have and be changed into other states or qualities: the vessel can be emptied of the moisture with which it is full, the body can lose its color, the air can become dark or cold, and the soul can become foolish.

But even if a body is incorruptible, such as is promised to the saints in the resurrection, it does indeed possess the unlosable quality of incorruption; yet, while its bodily substance remains, it is not identical with incorruption itself. For incorruption is wholly present in each of its parts, neither greater in one place nor less in another; no part is more incorruptible than another. The body itself, however, is greater as a whole than in a part; and when one part of it is larger and another smaller, the larger part is not therefore more incorruptible than the smaller.

The body, then, is one thing: it is not wholly present everywhere in itself. Incorruption is another: it is wholly present everywhere in the body, because every part of an incorruptible body, though unequal to the other parts, is equally incorruptible. For, to give an example, a finger is smaller than the whole hand, but the hand is not therefore more incorruptible than the finger. Thus, although hand and finger are unequal, the incorruptibility of the hand and of the finger is equal. Accordingly, although incorruptibility is inseparable from an incorruptible body, the substance by which the body is called a body is one thing, and its quality, by which it is called incorruptible, is another. Therefore, even in this case, it is not identical with what it has.

The soul itself also, even if it is always wise, as it will be when it is freed forever, will nevertheless be wise through participation in immutable wisdom, which is not identical with the soul itself.

[Note: [Col. 0326] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “as it will be when it is freed forever from its present misery; for although it will then be wise forever, it will nevertheless be so through participation in immutable wisdom,” and so forth.]

For even if air were never deprived of the light infused into it, it would still be one thing, and the light by which it is illuminated another. I do not say this as though air were the soul, as certain people thought who were unable to conceive of an incorporeal nature.

[Note: [Col. 0326] Diogenes, following Aristotle, *On the Soul*, book 1, chapter 2; Andremus and Anaximenes, following Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 9.]

Yet these things bear a certain similarity to those things, despite their great difference, so that it may reasonably be said that an incorporeal soul is illuminated by the incorporeal light of the simple wisdom of God just as a body of air is illuminated by bodily light. And just as air grows dark when deprived of this light—for the darkness of all bodily places is nothing other than air lacking light—

[Note: [Col. 0326] Compare book 1, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, no. 7.]

so the soul grows dark when deprived of the light of wisdom.

**3.** Accordingly, those things that are principally and truly divine are called simple because in them quality is not one thing and substance another, nor are they divine, wise, or blessed through participation in something else. Yet in Holy Scripture the Spirit is called “manifold” wisdom (Wisdom 7:22), because he contains many things; but what he has, he is, and all those things are one. For there are not many wisdoms, but one wisdom, in which are immense and infinite treasures of intelligible things.

[Note: [Col. 0327] Several manuscripts read: “in which are certain infinite and finite treasures belonging to it.” Others read: “in which are certain infinite treasures and treasures belonging to it that are finite.” Manuscript 2050 reads: “and infinite treasures belonging to it.” —M.]

In these treasures are all the invisible and immutable principles of things, including those of visible and mutable things, which were made through that wisdom. For God did not make anything without knowing it—a statement that cannot rightly be made even of just any human craftsman. Moreover, if he made all things knowingly, he made the things that he knew. From this there comes to mind something marvelous but nevertheless true: this world could not be known to us unless it existed, but it could not exist unless it were known to God.

## CHAPTER XI — Whether we should believe that those spirits who did not remain in the truth also participated in the blessedness that the holy angels have possessed from the beginning of their existence

Since these things are so, those spirits whom we call angels were not, for any interval of time, previously darkness; but as soon as they were made, they became light.

[Note: [Col. 0327] See below, book 12, chapter 9.]

They were not created merely so that they might exist in some fashion and live in some fashion; they were also illuminated so that they might live wisely and happily. Some angels turned away from this illumination and did not obtain the excellence of wise and blessed life, which is undoubtedly eternal and certain and secure in its own eternity. Yet they retain rational life, even though foolishly lived, in such a way that they cannot lose it, even if they wish to.

But who can determine to what extent they participated in that wisdom before they sinned? How shall we say that they were equal in participation in it to those who are truly and fully blessed because they are in no way deceived about the eternity of their blessedness? If they had been equal in it, these others too would likewise have remained blessed in its eternity, because they would likewise have been certain.

For eternal life cannot truthfully be called eternal in the same way as life of any duration if it is going to have an end. Life is so called simply because it involves living, whereas eternal life is so called because it has no end. Therefore, although not everything eternal is immediately blessed—for penal fire too is called eternal—nevertheless, if truly and perfectly blessed life is eternal and nothing else, the life of those angels was not such, since it was destined at some time to end, and therefore was not eternal, whether they knew this or, in ignorance, thought otherwise. If they knew it, fear prevented them from being blessed; if they did not know it, error did so.

But if they were ignorant of this in such a way that they did not trust false or uncertain beliefs, and did not incline with firm assent in either direction as to whether their good would be everlasting or would at some point have an end, then that very hesitation concerning so great a happiness lacked the fullness of blessed life that we believe exists in the holy angels.

Nor do we restrict the term “blessed life” to such narrow meanings that we say only God is blessed.

[Note: [Col. 0328] The ancients defined blessedness as a perfect condition, complete in every respect with all goods; this seems to apply only to God, through participation in whom angels and holy human beings are blessed. —LUD. VIVES.]

Yet he is so truly blessed that no greater blessedness can exist. In comparison with him, what or how much is it that blessed angels possess, in the highest blessedness that can exist among angels?

## CHAPTER XII — On the comparison between the blessedness of the righteous, who do not yet possess the reward of the divine promise, and that of the first human beings in paradise before sin

Nor do we think that, insofar as rational or intellectual creatures are concerned, only those beings should be called blessed.

[Note: [Col. 0328] Three editions, Vind., Am., and Er., read: “For we do not think that even those beings, compared with such great blessedness, should be called blessed insofar as rational or intellectual creatures are concerned.” The wording should be emended in accordance with Lov. and the manuscripts.]

For who would dare deny that those first human beings in paradise were blessed before sin?

[Note: [Col. 0328] See the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, no. 26, volume 10.]

This is so even though they were uncertain how long their blessedness would last, or whether it would be eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0328] See book 11, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, nos. 24–25.]

It would have been eternal had they not sinned. For today we not improperly call blessed those whom we see leading this life justly and devoutly, with hope of future immortality, without a conscience ravaged by sin, readily obtaining divine mercy for the sins of this weakness. Although they may be certain of the reward of their perseverance, they are nevertheless found to be uncertain about perseverance itself. For what human being knows that he will persevere to the end in the practice and progress of righteousness, unless he is made certain of this by some revelation from the one who, through a just and hidden judgment concerning this matter, instructs not everyone but deceives no one?

Accordingly, insofar as present good is concerned, the first human being in paradise was more blessed than any righteous person in this mortal weakness. But insofar as future hope is concerned, anyone amid any bodily torments is more blessed if it is manifest to him—not by opinion but by certain truth—that he will possess forever, without any affliction, the fellowship of the angels in participation in the supreme God, than that human being was in his great happiness in paradise, uncertain of his own fall.

[Note: [Col. 0328] Compare throughout the books *On the Gift of Perseverance* and *On Rebuke and Grace*.]

## CHAPTER XIII — Whether all the angels were created in one condition of blessedness, so that those who fell could not know that they would fall, while those who remained standing received foreknowledge of their perseverance after the fall of the others

Accordingly, it is now not difficult for anyone to see that blessedness is produced by the conjunction of both things that intellectual nature desires through a rightly directed purpose: namely, that it enjoy the immutable good, which is God, without any distress, and that it neither hesitate, through any doubt, nor be deceived, through any error, about remaining in him forever.

We piously believe that the angels of light possess this. By a corresponding line of reasoning we conclude that the sinful angels, who through their perversity were deprived of that light, did not possess it even before they fell.

[Col. 0329] Yet if they lived before sin, they must certainly be believed to have possessed some blessedness, even if not foreknowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0329] Compare book 11, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, nos. 21–34, and the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, no. 10.]

Or, if it seems harsh to believe that, when the angels were made, some were created in such a way that they did not receive foreknowledge either of their perseverance or of their fall, while others were created in such a way that they knew with the most certain truth the eternity of their blessedness, we may suppose that all were created with equal happiness from the beginning and remained so until those who are now evil fell by their own will from that light of goodness.

Without a doubt, however, it is much harsher now to suppose that the holy angels are uncertain about their own eternal blessedness and ignorant of themselves of what we have been able to know about them through the Holy Scriptures. For what Catholic Christian is ignorant that no new devil will ever arise from among the good angels, just as this devil will never again return to the fellowship of the good angels?

The Truth promises in the Gospel to the holy and faithful that they will be equal to the angels of God (Matt. 22:30); they are also promised that they will enter eternal life (ibid. 25:46). But if we are certain that we will never fall from that immortal blessedness, while they are not certain, then we shall already be superior to them, not equal. Since, however, the Truth does not deceive, and we shall be equal to them, they too are certainly assured of their eternal blessedness.

The others, because they were not certain of it—for their blessedness was not eternal and therefore could not be something of which they were certain, since it was destined to have an end—must either have been unequal to them, or, if they were equal, after the fall of the others they must have received certain knowledge of their own everlasting blessedness.

Unless perhaps someone says that what the Lord says about the devil in the Gospel—“He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44)—should be understood to mean not only that he was a murderer from the beginning, that is, from the beginning of the human race, from which there was of course a human being whom he could kill by deceiving him, but also that from the beginning of his own creation he did not stand in the truth. On this interpretation, he was never blessed with the holy angels, because he refused to be subject to his Creator and, through pride, took delight as though in a private power of his own.

[Note: [Col. 0329] Vind., Am., Er., and several manuscripts read “and through his own pride.” Elsewhere the printed editions read “exalted,” whereas the better manuscripts have “delighted.”]

Thus he became false and deceptive, because he can never escape the power of the Almighty, and because, by pious submission, he refused to hold what truly is, while through proud exaltation he seeks to pretend to be what he is not.

[Note: [Col. 0329] Some codices read “he seeks, through the exaltation of pride, to pretend.” Manuscript 2050 reads “he seeks, through pride and exaltation, to pretend.” —M.]

On this view, what the blessed apostle John also says is understood: “The devil sins from the beginning” (1 John 3:8)—that is, from the time he was created he rejected righteousness, which no will can possess except one that is pious and subject to God.

Whoever accepts this opinion does not share the view of those heretics, namely the Manichaeans, and whatever other plagues think similarly, that the devil has a certain nature of evil proper to himself, as though from some opposing principle. They are so foolishly deluded that, although they share with us the authority of these Gospel words, they do not notice that the Lord did not say, “He was alienated from the truth,” but “He did not stand in the truth.” By this he intended us to understand that the devil fell away from the truth: if he had stood in it, he would have become a participant in it and remained blessed with the holy angels.

[Note: [Col. 0330] Compare book 11, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, no. 27 and following.]

## CHAPTER XIV — In what manner of expression it was said of the devil that he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him

He then added an indication, as though we had asked how it could be shown that he did not stand in the truth, and said, “Because truth is not in him.” Yet truth would be in him if he had stood in it.

The expression, however, is in a less usual form. For the words “He did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him” (John 8:44) seem to say that the reason he did not stand in the truth is that truth is not in him, whereas the reason truth is not in him is rather that he did not stand in the truth.

There is a similar expression in the Psalm: “I cried out, because you have heard me, O God” (Ps. 16:6). It would seem that it ought to have been said, “You have heard me, O God, because I cried out.” But after saying, “I cried out,” as though someone had asked him how he could show that he had cried out, he demonstrated the intensity of his cry from the effect of God’s hearing him, as though he were saying: “I show from this that I cried out: you have heard me.”

## CHAPTER XV — What should be understood concerning the statement, “The devil sins from the beginning”

They do not understand that when John says of the devil, “The devil sins from the beginning” (1 John 3:8), if this is natural, it cannot in any way be sin.

[Note: [Col. 0330] Manuscripts of good authority read: “They do not understand that, if his nature is such, it cannot in any way be sin.” Several others read: “if it is natural.” Vind., Am., and Er. report the passage with an expanded gloss: “They do not understand—those who wish to assert from this that there is a nature of sin—that no sin whatever is natural.”]

But what answer can be given to the prophetic testimonies? Isaiah, speaking under the figurative person of the prince of Babylon and indicating the devil, says: “How has Lucifer fallen, he who used to rise in the morning?” (Isa. 14:12). Or what answer can be given to Ezekiel: “You were in the delights of the paradise of God; you were adorned with every precious stone”? There it is understood that he was at some time without sin.

[Note: [Col. 0330] Compare book 11, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, no. 32.]

A little later it is said to him more explicitly: “You walked without blemish in your days” (Ezek. 28:13–14). If these passages cannot more appropriately be understood in another way, then we must also take the statement “He did not stand in the truth” to mean that he was in the truth but did not remain in it.

And the statement “The devil sins from the beginning” should not be thought to mean that he sinned from the beginning of his creation, but from the beginning of sin, which began with his own pride.

Nor should what is written in the book of Job, when the devil is being discussed, be understood in this way: “This is the beginning of the creature of the Lord, which he made to be mocked by his angels” (Job 40:14, according to the Septuagint). The Psalm seems to agree with this when it says, “This dragon whom you formed to be mocked by him” (Ps. 103:26). It should not be understood as though we are to think that he was created such that the angels would mock him from the beginning, but rather that he was assigned to this punishment after his sin.

[Note: [Col. 0331] See book 11, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, nos. 29–30 and 34–35.]

His beginning, therefore, is the Lord’s creation. For there is no nature, even among the lowest and most insignificant animals, that he did not establish—he from whom come every measure, every form, and every order, without which no thing can be found or conceived. How much more, then, is this true of the angelic creature, which surpasses all the other things God created in the dignity of its nature?

## CHAPTER XVI — On the degrees and distinctions of creatures: utility evaluates them in one way, the order of reason in another

Among those things that exist in some fashion but are not what God is, from whom they were made, living things are placed above nonliving things—for example, things that possess the power of reproduction or even of desire above those that lack such movement. Among living things, those possessing sensation are placed above those that do not, as animals above trees. Among things possessing sensation, those possessing understanding are placed above those that do not, as human beings above cattle. Among things possessing understanding, immortal things are placed above mortal things, as angels above human beings.

These are placed above one another according to the order of nature. But there is another and different mode of evaluation according to the use each thing has, so that we prefer certain things lacking sensation to certain things possessing sensation—indeed, if we had the power, we might wish to remove them entirely from the order of nature—whether because we do not know what place they occupy in it, or because, even if we know, we place them after our own advantages.

For who would not rather have bread than mice in his house, or coins than fleas? But what wonder is this, when even in the valuation of human beings, whose nature is certainly of such great dignity, a horse is often purchased at a higher price than a slave, and a gem than a maidservant?

The reason of one who considers things with freedom of judgment differs greatly from the necessity of one who is in need, or the pleasure of one who desires. Reason considers what each thing is worth in itself within the ranks of things, whereas necessity considers what it seeks for the sake of what; and reason seeks what appears true to the light of the mind, whereas pleasure seeks what pleasantly flatters the bodily senses.

[Note: [Col. 0331] Our manuscripts read *cogitat* (“considers”) rather than *cogitet* (“may consider”).]

[Note: [Col. 0331] Our manuscripts read *exspectat* (“awaits”) rather than *exquirat* (“investigates”).]

But in rational natures a certain force, as it were, of will and love has such power that, although angels are superior to human beings according to the order of nature, good human beings are preferred to evil angels according to the law of justice.

## CHAPTER XVII — The vice of evil is not nature but contrary to nature; in sinning, the Creator is not the cause, but the will

Because of nature, therefore, not because of the devil’s evil, we rightly understand the statement, “This is the beginning of the creature of the Lord” (Job 40:14, according to the Septuagint). For undoubtedly, wherever there is the vice of evil, an uncorrupted nature preceded it.

Vice is so contrary to nature that it can do nothing except harm the nature to which it belongs. Accordingly, it would not be a vice to depart from God if it were not more proper to the nature whose vice it is to be with God. Therefore even an evil will is a great testimony to the goodness of nature.

But just as God is the best creator of good natures, so he is the most just governor of evil wills, so that when those wills make evil use of good natures, he himself makes good use even of evil wills. Thus he caused the devil—good by his creation, evil by his will, and placed in a lower order—to be mocked by his angels; that is, he caused his temptations to benefit the saints whom the devil desires to harm.

And because, when God created him, he was certainly not ignorant of the devil’s future malignity, and foresaw the good he himself would bring from that malignity, the Psalm says, “This dragon whom you formed to be mocked by him” (Ps. 103:26). Thus, in the very fact that he formed him, although he formed him good through his goodness, God is understood already, through his foreknowledge, to have prepared how he would make use of him even in his evil condition.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On the beauty of the universe, which through God’s ordering is made more splendid even by the opposition of contraries

For God would not have created anyone—not to speak of angels, but even of human beings—whom he foreknew would become evil, unless he likewise knew for what good purposes he would employ them, and thus adorn the order of the ages, like a most beautiful poem, with certain antitheses.

The figures called *antitheses* are highly fitting ornaments of expression; in Latin they are called *opposita* (“opposites”), or, more precisely, *contraposita* (“contraposed”).

[Note: [Col. 0332] Several manuscripts of no inferior authority read: “which, as they are called in Latin, are opposites.”]

This term is not customary among us, although Latin speech—and indeed the language of every people—also employs these same ornaments of expression. The apostle Paul explains this figure beautifully in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says:

> Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor; through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers, yet truthful; as unknown, yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined, yet not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing everything (2 Cor. 6:7–10).

Just as these contraries set against contraries lend beauty to speech, so the beauty of the ages is composed by the opposition of contraries through a certain eloquence—not of words but of things. This is stated most explicitly in the book of Ecclesiasticus, in the following manner:

> Good is set against evil, and life against death; so the sinner against the godly. And so look upon all the works of the Most High: two and two, one opposite the other (Eccli. 33:15).

## CHAPTER XIX — What seems to be meant by the statement, “God divided between the light and the darkness”

Although the obscurity of divine speech is useful also for this reason—that it produces many truths and brings them into the light of knowledge, when one person understands it in one way and another in another—nevertheless, what is understood in an obscure passage must be supported either by the testimony of manifest facts or by other passages that are not at all doubtful. This may occur when, in treating many matters, we arrive at what the writer understood; or when that understanding itself remains hidden, but the occasion of treating a profound obscurity gives rise to the statement of other truths.

[Note: [Col. 0333] Several manuscripts read “in the beginning” here and in the other occurrence. The printed editions are supported by the Greek translation of the Septuagint, *eis archas* (“for beginnings”).]

It does not seem to me an absurd interpretation of God’s works if, when that first light was made, the angels are understood to have been created, and a division is understood to have taken place between the holy angels and the unclean angels, where it is said: “And God divided between the light and the darkness; and God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.”

Only he could make this distinction who could also foresee, before they fell, that they would fall, and that, deprived of the light of truth, they would remain in dark pride. For between the day and night best known to us—that is, between this light and these darknesses—God commanded the familiar lights of heaven, perceptible to our senses, to divide them: “Let there be lights,” he said, “in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth and to divide between the day and the night.”

And shortly afterward:

> And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the beginning of the day, and the lesser light to rule the beginning of the night; and the stars. And God placed them in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth, to rule the day and the night, and to divide between the light and the darkness (Gen. 1:4–5, 14, 16–18).

[Note: [Col. 0333] Several manuscripts read here, and in the other place, “at the beginning.” The printed editions are supported by the Greek translation of the Septuagint, *eis archas* (“for beginnings”).]

But between that light which is the holy fellowship of the angels, shining intelligibly through the illumination of truth, and the darkness opposed to it—that is, the utterly dark minds of the evil angels who have turned away from the light of righteousness—only he could divide who could not be ignorant or uncertain that the future evil would arise not from nature but from the will.

## CHAPTER XX — On the statement made after the separation of the light and darkness: “And God saw that the light was good”

Finally, we must not pass over in silence the fact that after God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, it immediately follows: “And God saw that the light was good”—not after he separated the light from the darkness, called the light day and the darkness night, lest he seem to have given testimony of his approval to such darknesses together with the light.

Where the darknesses are blameless—those between which the lights of heaven divide this light visible to our eyes—the words “And God saw that it was good” are introduced not before, but afterward:

> And he placed them, he says, in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth, to rule the day and the night, and to separate between the light and the darkness. And God saw that it was good.

Both things were pleasing, because both are without sin.

But where God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, and “God saw that the light was good,” and afterward it follows, “And God separated between the light and the darkness; and God called the light day, and the darkness he called night” (Gen. 1:3–5, 17–18), the words “And God saw that it was good” are not added. Otherwise both would have been called good, although one of them was evil—not by nature, but through its own vice. Thus only the light was pleasing there to the Creator; the angelic darknesses, although they had to be ordered, were not nevertheless to be approved.

## CHAPTER XXI — On the eternal and immutable knowledge and will of God, by which all the things he made have always been pleasing to him as things to be made in the manner in which they were made
What else, then, is to be understood by the statement repeated throughout, “God saw that it was good,” except the approval of the work according to the art by which it was made, namely, the Wisdom of God? Yet God did not learn that it was good only when it had been made [Note: [Col. 0334] This, of course, was what the Manichaeans objected. Compare Book 1 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, no. 13.], so that nothing would have been made if it had been unknown to him. Therefore, when he sees that it is good—a thing which would certainly not have been made had he not seen it before it was made—he teaches that it is good; he does not learn this.

Plato, indeed, dared to say more: namely, that God was uplifted by joy when the universe had been completed (*Timaeus*). Yet even he was not so foolish as to think that God had been made happier by the novelty of his work. Rather, he wished to show that what had been made pleased its craftsman, just as what was to be made had already pleased him in his art—not that God’s knowledge changes in any way, so that things which do not yet exist produce one thing in it, things which already exist another, and things which have existed another [Note: [Col. 0334] Thus Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts; Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *fiant*, “are made.”]. For he does not, as we do, foresee what will be, observe what is present, or look back upon what has passed; rather, he sees in a certain other way, altogether and profoundly different from the customary course of our thoughts [Note: [Col. 0334] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “widely and”; the other books, “profoundly and.”]. He does not see by a thought changed from one thing to another, but sees everything in an entirely unchangeable manner. Thus, although things that occur temporally are not yet when future, are already when present, and no longer are when past, he comprehends them all in a stable and eternal present. Nor does he see them one way with his eyes and another with his mind—for he is not composed of mind and body—nor one way now, another way previously, and another way afterward. For his knowledge, unlike ours, is not altered by the variation of the three times, namely, the present, past, and future; with him there is “no change, nor shadow of alteration” (James 1:17).

His attention does not pass from one thought to another, since in his incorporeal vision all that he knows is present at once. He knows temporal things without any temporal notions of his own, just as he moves temporal things without any temporal movements of his own. Therefore, he saw that what he made was good in the very place where he saw that it was good to make it. Nor, because he saw the thing after it had been made, did he double or in any way increase his knowledge, as though his knowledge had been less perfect before he made what he saw. He would not have worked so perfectly unless his knowledge had been equally perfect, receiving no addition from his works.

Accordingly, if it were merely necessary for us to be told who made the light, it would have been enough to say, “God made the light.” But if we were to be told not only who made it, but also through what he made it, it would have been sufficient to say, “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light,” so that we might know that God made the light, and made it through the Word. But because three things about a creature chiefly needed to be made known to us—who made it, through what he made it, and why he made it—the text says: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good.” If, then, we ask who made it, the answer is: God. If we ask through what he made it: “He said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” If we ask why he made it: “Because it was good.” No author is more excellent than God, no art more effective than God’s Word, and no cause better than that a good God should create something good.

[Col. 0335]

Plato too declares this to be the most just cause for creating the world: that good works might be made by a good God (*Timaeus*)—whether he had read this, or perhaps learned it from those who had read it; whether, by his exceptionally keen intellect, he had perceived the invisible things of God through the things that were made; or whether he himself had learned it from those who had perceived these things.

## CHAPTER XXII — Concerning those who find certain things displeasing within the universe of things well created by the good Creator, and who suppose that there is some evil nature

Yet certain heretics failed to see this cause—that is, the goodness of God as the reason for creating good things—a cause so just and suitable that, when carefully considered and devoutly pondered, it settles every dispute among those investigating the origin of the world. They are offended by many things because these do not suit the needy, fragile mortality of this flesh, which already proceeds from a just punishment: fire, for example, or cold, or a wild beast, or something of that kind. They do not consider how vigorous such things are in their own places and natures, how beautifully they are arranged in order, how much adornment they contribute to the universe according to their proportions, as though to a commonwealth [Note: [Col. 0335] Some manuscripts read “positions.”], or how much usefulness they provide even for us, if we use them appropriately and intelligently. Thus even poisons, harmful when applied improperly, become health-giving medicines when used appropriately. Conversely, even the things in which they take pleasure—food, drink, and this light—are experienced as harmful when used immoderately and at the wrong time [Note: [Col. 0335] Sound manuscripts read *importuno*, “inopportunely”; the printed editions, “importunately.”] [Note: [Col. 0335] Against the Manichaeans. See Book 1 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, nos. 25–26.].

Therefore divine providence admonishes us not to condemn things foolishly, but diligently to seek their usefulness. Where our intelligence or weakness fails, we should believe that their usefulness is hidden, just as there were certain things we could scarcely discover. For the very concealment of their usefulness is either an exercise in humility or a crushing of pride. In fact, no nature at all is evil; and the name “evil” signifies nothing except the privation of good. From earthly things up to heavenly things, and from visible things up to invisible things, some goods are better than others; they are unequal for this purpose: that all things might exist.

God, however, is so great an artist [Note: [Col. 0335] Several manuscripts read “the greatest.”] in great things that he is not lesser in small ones. These small things are not to be measured by their magnitude—for they have none—but by the wisdom of their craftsman. Thus, in the visible form of a human being, if one eyebrow is shaved away, how nearly nothing is taken from the body, yet how much is taken from its beauty; for beauty consists not in bulk, but in the symmetry and proportion of the limbs [Note: [Col. 0335] The Vindobonensis, the Ambrosianus, and several manuscripts read *visibili*, “visible”; the printed editions have *visibilis*.].

Nor is it surprising that those who think that some nature is evil, having arisen and been propagated from a certain contrary principle, refuse to accept this reason for the creation of things: that a good God created good things. They believe instead that he was driven by the utmost necessity to repel the evil rebelling against him in these worldly exertions, and that he mingled his good nature with evil in order to restrain and overcome it. They suppose that this nature, most shamefully polluted, most cruelly enslaved and oppressed, is cleansed and liberated only with great toil—and not entirely; rather, [Col. 0336] whatever part of it could not be purified from that defilement is to become the covering and bond of the defeated and imprisoned enemy [Note: [Col. 0335] Manuscript 2051 reads “of repelling”; manuscript 2050, “with evils being repelled”; in B the word *repellendi* is wholly absent.].

The Manichaeans would not thus rave—or rather, would not thus go insane—if they believed God’s nature to be, as it is, unchangeable and wholly incorruptible, incapable of being harmed by anything. They would then understand, with Christian soundness of mind, that the soul, which could be changed for the worse by its will and corrupted by sin, and thereby deprived of the light of unchangeable truth, is not a part of God, nor of that nature which belongs to God [Note: [Col. 0336] Several manuscripts read, “which God is.”], but was created by him and is vastly unlike its Creator.

## CHAPTER XXIII — Concerning the error in which Origen’s teaching is censured

1.
