Yet it is even more astonishing that some who believe with us that there is one source of all things, and that no nature which is not what God is could exist except from that Creator, nevertheless refused to accept this reason for making the world—so good and simple a reason—in a good and simple manner: that the good God created good things, and that after God there should be things which were not what God is, but were nevertheless good, since a good God alone could make them.

They say that souls, not indeed parts of God but made by God, sinned by withdrawing from their Creator; and that, according to the varying degrees of their sins, they deserved different stages of descent from the heavens to the earth and different bodies, as though these were bonds. They say that this is the world and that this was the reason the world was made—not so that good things might be created, but so that evil things might be restrained.

For this reason Origen is rightly censured. In the books he calls *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*—that is, *On Principles*—he held and wrote this view. Here I am astonished beyond what can be expressed that a man so learned and practiced in ecclesiastical literature failed first to notice how contrary this was to the intention of this Scripture, which possesses such great authority. Throughout the works of God it adds, “And God saw that it was good”; and, after completing them all, it says, “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1). It intended no other cause for the making of the world to be understood than that good things should be made by a good God.

If no one had sinned, the world would have been adorned and filled solely with good natures. And because there is sin, it does not follow that everything has been filled with sins, since by far the greater number of beings in heaven preserves the order of its nature. Nor, because an evil will refused to preserve the order of nature, has it escaped the laws of the just God who orders all things well. For just as a painting is beautiful when black is placed in its proper position, so the universe of things, if someone could behold it, is beautiful even with sinners included, although their deformity disgraces them when considered in themselves.

2. [Col. 0337]

Next, Origen—and all who hold this view—should have recognized that, if the opinion were true, and the world had been made so that souls might receive bodies according to the merits of their sins, as prisons in which they would be punished, then the higher and lighter bodies should have been given to those who sinned less, and the lower and heavier ones to those who sinned more. Demons, for whom nothing is worse, should therefore have received earthly bodies, since nothing is lower or heavier, rather than human beings—even bad ones—having them [Note: [Col. 0337] The manuscripts read, “even good ones.” The Vindobonensis and Ambrosianus likewise read “even good ones” here, but in a later passage these two printed editions add “even good ones” after “rather than bad ones.”].

But now, so that we might understand that the merits of souls are not to be weighed by the qualities of their bodies, the worst demon is aerial, whereas a human being—even though now evil—is far less and more mildly evil, and nevertheless received an earthly body before sin.

What could be said more foolishly than that God the craftsman provided the sun so that there would be one sun in one world, not for the sake of the beauty of its adornment or even the health of bodily things [Note: [Col. 0337] Compare the book addressed to Orosius against the Priscillianists and Origenists, no. 11.], but rather because one soul had sinned in such a way that it deserved to be imprisoned in such a body? Consequently, if it had happened that not one soul but two—or rather, not two but ten or a hundred—had sinned in a similar and equal manner, this world would have had a hundred suns. Their not doing so would then have been due not to the craftsman’s wondrous provision for the health and beauty of bodily things, but rather to the fact that the sinning of a single soul had progressed to such an extent that it alone deserved such a body.

It is plainly not the progress of souls—about which they do not know what they are talking—but the progress of those very people who hold such opinions that must be restrained, as being far removed from truth and merit.

These three things, then, which I commended above—who made each creature, through what he made it, and why he made it—are required in every creature. The answers are: God, through the Word, because it is good [Note: [Col. 0337] The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and manuscripts read, “because it is good.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “because he is good.”]. Whether the Trinity itself is indicated to us here in mystical depth—namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—or whether something arises that prevents this from being understood as the meaning of this passage of Scripture, is a question requiring extensive discussion; nor should we force ourselves to explain everything in a single volume.

## CHAPTER XXIV — Concerning the divine Trinity, which has scattered indications of its meaning throughout all its works

We believe, hold, and faithfully proclaim that the Father begot the Word, that is, Wisdom, through whom all things were made: the only-begotten Son, one from One, eternal from the co-eternal, supremely good and equally good. We also believe that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son, and that he too is consubstantial and co-eternal with both.

Thus the whole is a Trinity because of the distinct property of the persons, and one God because of the inseparable divinity, just as he is one omnipotent God because of the inseparable omnipotence. Yet when each person is considered individually, each is answered to be God and omnipotent; when all are considered together, they are not three gods or three omnipotent beings, but one omnipotent God. There is in the three such inseparable unity as has willed itself to be proclaimed in this way.

Whether the Holy Spirit, because he is common to both, may rightly be called the goodness of both the good Father and the good Son, I do not dare rashly to pronounce [Col. 0338]. Yet I shall more readily dare to call him the holiness of both—not as though he were a quality belonging to both, but as himself also their substance and the third person in the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0338] The manuscripts read *ipsum*, “himself”; the printed editions read *ipsam*, “itself.”]. I am led to this more plausibly because, although the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, he alone is properly called the Holy Spirit, as though he were the substantial and consubstantial holiness of both.

But if divine goodness is nothing other than holiness, then it is certainly an exercise of careful reasoning, not a rash act of presumption, to understand that the same Trinity is suggested to us in God’s works by a certain hidden manner of speaking, intended to exercise our attention: who made each creature, through what he made it, and for what purpose he made it.

The Father is indeed understood in the Word’s saying, “Let there be.” Whatever was made when he spoke was unquestionably made through the Word. In the statement, “God saw that it was good,” it is sufficiently signified that God made what was made neither from necessity nor from any need of his own advantage, but solely from goodness—that is, because it is good. This is said after the thing has been made in order to indicate that the thing made corresponds to the goodness for which it was made. If this goodness is rightly understood as the Holy Spirit, the whole Trinity is disclosed to us in its works.

From this comes the origin, formation, and blessedness of the holy city that is above, in the holy angels. If one asks where it comes from: God founded it. If one asks how it is wise: it is illuminated by God. If one asks how it is happy: it enjoys God. Subsisting, it is given proportion; contemplating, it is illumined; cleaving, it rejoices. It exists, sees, and loves; it flourishes in God’s eternity, shines in God’s truth, and rejoices in God’s goodness.

## CHAPTER XXV — Concerning the threefold discipline of the whole of philosophy

As far as can be understood, philosophers have wished the discipline of wisdom to be threefold—or rather, they were able to observe that it was threefold. For they did not establish it as such; rather, they discovered that it was so. One part is called physics, another logic, and the third ethics. Their names have now become common in the writings of many, so that they are called natural, rational, and moral; we also briefly touched upon them in Book 8 (Chapter 4 and following).

This does not mean that it follows that these philosophers conceived something concerning the Trinity according to God in these three divisions [Note: [Col. 0338] The Vindobonensis and most manuscripts read, “not because it follows.”]. Although Plato is said to have been the first to discover and commend this division, he regarded God as the author of all natures, the giver of intelligence, and the inspirer of the love by which one lives well and happily.

Certainly, when different people hold different opinions about the nature of things, the method of investigating truth [Note: [Col. 0338] Sound manuscripts read “of finding”; the printed editions, “of investigating.”], and the end of the good to which we ought to refer everything we do, their whole concern nevertheless revolves around these three great and general questions. Thus, although each person pursues different things in each of them, and their opinions are various and divergent, no one doubts that there is some cause of nature, [Col. 0339] some form of knowledge, and some supreme end of life.

There are also three things considered in every human craftsman when he produces something: nature, instruction, and practice. Nature is judged by talent, instruction by knowledge, and practice by its fruit. I am not unaware that, strictly speaking, fruit belongs to the one who enjoys, and use to the one who uses. The difference appears to be that we are said to enjoy a thing which delights us in itself, without reference to anything else, whereas we use a thing which we seek for the sake of something else [Note: [Col. 0339] See Book 1 of *On Christian Doctrine*, nos. 3–5, and near the end of Book 10 of *On the Trinity*, no. 12.].

Accordingly, temporal things should be used rather than enjoyed, so that we may deserve to enjoy eternal things. Not like the perverse, who wish to enjoy money but use God, since they do not spend money for God’s sake, but worship God for the sake of money.

Nevertheless, in the manner of speaking that custom has more widely established, we both use fruits and enjoy uses. Fruits are indeed now properly called the produce of fields, which we all use temporally. In accordance with this custom, then, I shall call “use” those three things that I said must be considered in a human being: nature, instruction, and use [Note: [Col. 0339] The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and manuscripts read “custom”; Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “manner.”].

For the attainment of a blessed life, philosophers devised the threefold discipline I mentioned: the natural discipline, because of nature; the rational discipline, because of instruction; and the moral discipline, because of use.

If, then, our nature came from ourselves, we would certainly have generated our own wisdom as well, and would not need to acquire it through instruction—that is, by learning from elsewhere. Our love too, proceeding from us and directed back toward us, would suffice for living happily, and we would need no other good to enjoy. But now, because God is the author of our nature, which exists at all, we must unquestionably have him as our teacher if we are to think truly; and we must also have him as the giver of inward sweetness if we are to be happy.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Concerning the image of the supreme Trinity, which is found in a certain manner even in the nature of the human being who has not yet been made blessed

Even in ourselves we recognize the image of God—that is, of that supreme Trinity—although it is not equal, but very far and greatly distant from it; although it is not co-eternal and, to say everything more briefly [Note: [Col. 0339] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads *dicatur*, “may be said”; the others read *dicitur*, “is said.”], is not of the same substance as God. Nevertheless, among the things made by God, nothing is by nature closer to God. This image still needs to be perfected by reformation, so that it may also possess the closest likeness [Note: [Col. 0339] Here the principal manuscripts begin Chapter 27.].

For we both exist, and know that we exist, and love that we exist and know [Note: [Col. 0339] The manuscripts read “and love that being”; the printed editions, “and our being.”]. In these three things I have mentioned, no plausible falsehood disturbs us. We do not grasp them, as we do things outside us, through any bodily sense—for example, colors by seeing, sounds by hearing, odors by smelling, flavors by tasting, and hard and soft things by touching. We also turn over in thought and retain in memory the images of these sensible things, images that are similar to them though no longer bodily; through these images we are stirred toward desire for such things.

But without any deceptive play of fantasies or phantasms [Col. 0340], I am absolutely certain that I exist, that I know this, and that I love it. I fear none of the arguments of the Academics who say, “What if you are deceived?” For if I am deceived, I exist. One who does not exist certainly cannot be deceived; therefore I exist if I am deceived. Since I exist if I am deceived, how can I be deceived about my existence, when it is certain that I exist if I am deceived? Therefore, because I would exist even if I were deceived, I am unquestionably not deceived in knowing that I exist.

It follows that I am not deceived in knowing that I know this. For just as I know that I exist, so I also know that I know this very thing. And when I love these two things, I add to the things I know a third thing—the love itself—which is likewise not of lesser value. For I am not deceived in loving myself when I am not deceived about the things I love. Indeed, even if those things were false, it would still be true that I love false things. For how could I rightly be reproved and rightly forbidden to love false things if it were false that I loved them? But when those things are also true and certain, who could doubt that their love, when they are loved, is itself true and certain?

Indeed, no one is so disposed as not to wish to exist, just as no one is so disposed as not to wish to be happy. For how could someone be happy if he did not exist?

## CHAPTER XXVII — Concerning essence and knowledge, and the love of both

1. Existence itself is so pleasing by a certain natural force that even those who are miserable do not wish to perish. Although they recognize themselves as miserable, they wish not themselves to be removed from things, but rather their misery. Even those who seem most miserable to themselves, and plainly are so—judged miserable not only by the wise, because they are foolish, but also by those who think themselves happy, because they are poor and beggars—if someone offered them immortality by which their misery itself would not die, while proposing that, if they did not wish to remain in the same misery forever, they would instead exist nowhere and perish altogether, would certainly rejoice with gladness and would always choose to exist in that way rather than not to exist at all.

Their most familiar experience bears witness to this. Why do they fear death and prefer to live in that distress rather than bring it to an end through death, unless it is sufficiently evident how nature recoils from nonexistence? Therefore, when they know that they are destined to die, they desire, as a great benefit, that this mercy be granted them: that they may live somewhat longer in the same misery and die later. They plainly indicate, then, with what gratitude they would receive even such immortality as had no end to their poverty.

What shall we say? Do all animals, even irrational ones—which have not been given the ability to think about these things—from immense dragons down to tiny worms, not show by every movement available to them that they wish to exist and therefore flee destruction? What shall we say? Do trees and all shrubs, which have no sense by which to avoid destruction through deliberate movement, not nevertheless drive their roots deeper into the earth so that they may send the safe shoot of their crown into the air, [Col. 0341] draw nourishment, and thus preserve their own existence in some fashion [Note: [Col. 0340] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and some manuscripts read “fasten the roots deeper in the earth”; other old books read “fasten another root in the earth”; Erasmus and Lovaniensis, “fasten other roots in the earth.”]?

Finally, do bodies themselves—which possess not only no sense, but not even any life of the seed—nevertheless not leap upward, descend downward, or remain balanced in between, so as to preserve their essence wherever, according to nature, they are able to exist?

2. How greatly human nature loves knowledge, and how unwilling it is to be deceived, can be understood from this: anyone of sound mind prefers to lament than to rejoice in madness. This is a great and wondrous power among mortals, one found in no living beings other than human beings [Note: [Col. 0341] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “human beings,” contrary to the other printed editions and manuscripts; manuscript 2050 reads “a human being.”]. Some animals have eyesight much sharper than ours for gazing upon this light, but they cannot touch that incorporeal light by which our mind is, in a certain manner, illumined, so that we can judge rightly about all these things. To the extent that we grasp it, to that extent we are able to do so.

Nevertheless, in the senses of irrational animals there exists, although in no way knowledge, at least a certain likeness of knowledge. The other bodily things are called sensible not because they sense, but because they are sensed. What resembles senses in trees is that they are nourished and reproduce [Note: [Col. 0341] The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and manuscripts read “produce offspring”; Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “are produced.”].

Yet both these things and all bodily things have hidden causes within nature. They offer their forms—which make the structure of this visible world beautiful—to the senses to be sensed, as though, since they cannot know, they seemed to wish in some way to become known.

We apprehend them through bodily sensation, but we do not judge them by bodily sensation. For we possess another sense of the inner person, far superior to this one, by which we sense what is just and unjust: the just through an intelligible form, and the unjust through its privation. The sharpness of the pupil, the opening of the ear, the passages of the nostrils, the taste of the throat, and no bodily touch whatsoever contribute to the operation of this sense.

There I am certain both that I exist and that I know this, and I am equally certain that I love these things and that I love myself.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Whether we ought also to love the love by which we love existence and knowledge, so that we may draw closer to the image of the divine Trinity

We have said enough about those two things—essence, that is, existence, and knowledge—including how greatly they are loved in us and how, in the other things below us, a certain likeness of them, though differing, is also found, insofar as the plan of this work appeared to require. But we have not yet discussed whether the love by which they are loved is itself also loved.

It is loved. We prove this from the fact that, among human beings who are loved more rightly [Note: [Col. 0341] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads *quod hominibus quae rectius amantur*; the text reads *quod in hominibus qui rectius amantur*.], love itself is loved more. For a good man is not rightly called good because he knows what is good, but because he loves it.

Why should we not also feel, even in ourselves, that we love the love by which we love whatever good we love? There is also a love by which what ought not to be loved is loved. [Col. 0342]

The person who loves the love by which what ought to be loved is loved hates that other love in himself.

Both loves can exist in one person. This is good for a human being: that, as the love by which we live well grows, the love by which we live badly should diminish, until it is healed completely and everything by which we live is changed into the good.

If we were animals, we would love bodily life and what belongs to its senses; that would be our sufficient good, and when things were well with us according to this, we would seek nothing else. Likewise, if we were trees, we could love nothing, since they possess no sentient movement; nevertheless, we would seem to desire that by which we might be more fertile and more abundantly fruitful. If we were stones, waves, wind, flame, or something of this sort, without any sense or life at all, we would nevertheless possess something like a desire for our proper places and order. For, as it were, the movements of bodies are the weights of their loves, whether they strive downward by heaviness or upward by lightness. A body is carried by weight just as a soul is carried by love, wherever it is carried [Note: [Col. 0342] See Book 13 of the *Confessions*, chapter 9.].

Since, then, we are human beings created in the image of our Creator, whose true eternity, eternal truth, and eternal and true love constitute the divine reality—and since this itself is the eternal, true, and beloved Trinity, neither confused nor divided—we observe that the things below us would neither exist in any way nor be contained in any form nor seek or preserve any order unless they had been made by him who supremely exists, who is supremely wise, and who is supremely good.

Thus, running through all that he has made with wondrous stability, we gather, as it were, certain traces of him, impressed more deeply in some places and less deeply in others. But when we contemplate his image in ourselves, we should rise, like the younger son of the Gospel returning to himself (Luke 15:18), so that we may return to him from whom we had departed by sinning [Note: [Col. 0342] The printed editions read “and”; the older books differ.].

There our existence will have no death, our knowledge no error, and our love no offense. Now, however, although we hold these three things of ours with certainty, and do not rely upon other witnesses for them, but experience them as present and behold them with our innermost and most truthful vision, nevertheless, so long as we do not know of ourselves what their future will be, whether they will ever cease, and where they will lead if they are directed well or badly, we either seek or possess other witnesses concerning them. Why there ought to be no doubt about the trustworthiness of those witnesses will be discussed more carefully in a later place.

In this book, however, concerning the city of God—which does not wander in the mortality of this life, but is always immortal in heaven, that is, concerning the holy angels who cleave to God—we have already said that God first divided them from those who abandoned the eternal light and became darkness. With his help, let us explain as best we can what we have begun.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Concerning the knowledge of the holy angels, by which they know the Trinity in its very divinity, and by which they behold the causes of works first in the art of the worker rather than in the works of the craftsman themselves

[Col. 0343]

For those holy angels do not learn God through sounding words, but through the very presence of immutable truth, that is, his only-begotten Word. They know the Word himself, the Father, and their Holy Spirit; they know that this is an inseparable Trinity, that its individual persons are one substance, and yet that all are not three gods but one God. They know these things more intimately than we know ourselves.

They also know the creation better there—that is, in the wisdom of God, as in the art by which it was made—than in itself. Consequently they know themselves better there than in themselves, though they know themselves also in themselves. For they were made, and are something other than he who made them. There, therefore, they know as it were by daytime knowledge; but in themselves, as it were by evening knowledge, as we have already said above (Chapter 7). For it makes a great difference whether something is known in the reason according to which it was made, or in itself. Thus the straightness of lines or the truth of figures is known one way when it is apprehended by the intellect, another when it is drawn in dust [Note: [Col. 0343] The whole theory of lines and surfaces is known more certainly and better from mathematical principles than from a drawing, which is never so exact as to set the thing itself before the eyes as it is. A line which is the shortest from point to point, as Euclid says, or all lines from the centre to the circumference being equal, is understood more accurately from geometrical precepts than from a drawing, not merely in dust, but even by Parrhasius or Apelles. LUDOVICUS VIVES.]. So too justice is known one way in immutable truth, another in the soul of a just person.

Then likewise the other things: the firmament between the higher and lower waters, which was called heaven; the gathering of waters below and the uncovering of the earth, and the establishment of herbs and trees; the creation of sun, moon, and stars; the animals from the waters—namely birds, fish, and swimming beasts; all things whatsoever that walk and creep upon the earth; and man himself, who would excel all things on earth. All these things are known by the angels one way in the Word of God, where they have their unchangeably abiding causes and reasons—that is, the reasons according to which they were made—and another way in themselves: there by clearer knowledge, here by more obscure knowledge [Note: [Col. 0343] The manuscripts read “there by clearer, here by more obscure.”], as it were, of art and of works. Yet when these works are referred to the praise and worship of their Creator himself, morning, as it were, dawns in the minds of those who contemplate them.

## CHAPTER XXX — Concerning the perfection of the number six, which is the first completed by the sum of its parts

These things are narrated as completed in six days because of the perfection of the number six, repeated six times on the same day; not because God required a delay of time, as though he could not create all things at once, which would thereafter carry on time through fitting motions, but because the perfection of works is signified by the number six.

For the number six is the first completed by its parts: namely, its sixth part [Col. 0344], its third, and its half, which are one, two, and three; added together, they make six. In this consideration of numbers, those are to be understood as parts which can be stated as what fraction they are, such as a half, a third, a fourth, and so on, denominated from some number.

For example, because four is a part of the number nine, it cannot therefore be said what fraction of it it is. But one can: it is its ninth part; and three can: it is its third part. Yet these two parts together, the ninth and the third—that is, one and three—fall far short of its whole sum, which is nine.

Likewise, in ten, four is some part of it, but it cannot be said what fraction it is. One can: it is its tenth part. It also has a fifth, which is two, and a half, which is five. But these three parts—the tenth, fifth, and half, that is, one, two, and five—added together do not complete ten; for they are eight.

But the parts of the number twelve, added together, exceed it. For it has a twelfth, which is one; a sixth, which is two; a fourth, which is three; a third, which is four; and a half, which is six. One, two, three, four, and six make not twelve but more, namely sixteen.

I thought this should be mentioned briefly in order to commend the perfection of the number six, which, as I said, is the first perfected when its parts are reduced to a sum. God completed his works in this number [Note: [Col. 0344] Compare Book 4 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, nos. 2–7, and Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, nos. 7–9.]. Therefore the principle of number is not to be despised. Those who consider carefully many passages of the holy Scriptures see how greatly it is to be valued. Nor was it without reason that it was said in praise of God: “You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight” (Wisdom 11:21).

## CHAPTER XXXI — Concerning the seventh day, in which fullness and rest are commended.

On the seventh day, that is, on the same day repeated seven times—a number that is itself perfect in another respect—the rest of God is commended, in which sanctification first resounds (Gen. II, 2–3) [Note: [Col. 0344] Compare *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 5, nos. 1–3, and book 4, nos. 31–37.]. Thus God did not wish to sanctify this day in any of his works, but in his rest, which has no evening. For no creature exists such that it too, being known in one way in the Word of God and in another way in itself, produces a different kind of knowledge, as it were diurnal in one case and vespertine in the other [Note: [Col. 0344] That is, the rest of God, which is not any creature.]. Concerning the perfection of the number seven, much could indeed be said; but this book is already quite lengthy, and I fear that, having found an opportunity, we may seem to wish to display our little knowledge more frivolously than usefully. We must therefore observe a due measure and seriousness, lest, while speaking at length about number, we be judged to neglect measure and weight.

It is enough, then, to point out that the ternary is the first number wholly odd, and the quaternary the first number wholly even; from these two the number seven is composed. [Col. 0345] For this reason it is often put for the whole, as in: “The righteous man falls seven times, and rises again” (Prov. XXIV, 16)—that is, however often he falls, he will not perish. This was intended to be understood not of iniquities, but of tribulations that lead to humility. And likewise: “Seven times a day I will praise you” (Ps. CXVIII, 164). Elsewhere this is expressed in another way: “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII, 2). Many similar statements are found in the divine authorities, in which, as I have said, the number seven customarily stands for the totality of a given thing.

For this reason the Holy Spirit is also often signified by this same number [Note: [Col. 0345] Compare *Sermon* 8, no. 13.], of whom the Lord says: “He will teach you all truth” (John XVI, 13). There is the rest of God, by which one rests in God. For in the whole—that is, in complete perfection—there is rest; but in part there is labor. Therefore we labor so long as we know in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be abolished (I Cor. XIII, 9–10). This is why we also search these Scriptures with labor.

But the holy angels [Note: [Col. 0345] The manuscripts omit the particle *ad* (“to”); some of these have “to the fellowship and assembly.”], whose fellowship and assembly we long for during this most laborious pilgrimage, have, just as they possess the eternity of remaining, so also the ease of knowing and the blessedness of resting. For they help us without difficulty, since, with pure and free spiritual movements, they do not labor.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—Concerning the opinion of those who hold that the creation of the angels preceded that of the world

But lest anyone argue and say that it is not the holy angels who are signified by what is written, “Let there be light,” and “there was light,” but either suppose or teach that whatever corporeal light there was was then made for the first time; and that the angels were made earlier—not merely before the firmament, which was made between the waters and the waters and called heaven, but before that which is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; and that the words “In the beginning” were not spoken as though this were made first, since he had made the angels beforehand, but because he made all things in Wisdom, which is his Word, and Scripture itself called him “the beginning,” just as, when the Jews asked him who he was, he replied in the Gospel that he was “the beginning” (John VIII, 25)—I will not engage in controversy on the contrary side, especially because I take great pleasure in the fact that the Trinity is commended even at the very opening of the holy book of Genesis.

For when it is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” so that the Father is understood to have made them in the Son, as the Psalm attests, where we read, “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24), the Holy Spirit is most appropriately mentioned shortly afterward as well. For after it had been said what kind of earth God first made, or what mass or material for the future construction of the world he designated by the name “heaven and earth,” the text continues and adds: “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss”; then, so that the mention of the Trinity might be completed, it says: “And the Spirit of God was hovering over the water” (Gen. I, 1–3).

Therefore, let each person understand this as he wishes, since it is so profound that, for the exercise of readers who do not depart from the rule of faith, it can generate many interpretations. Let no one, however, doubt that the holy angels dwell in exalted abodes [Note: [Col. 0346] The editions read “in the abodes of heaven.” The word “of heaven” is absent from the manuscripts.], not indeed coeternal with God, but nevertheless secure and certain of their own everlasting and true happiness. Teaching that his little ones belong to their fellowship, the Lord says not only, “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Matt. XXII, 30); he also shows what contemplation the angels themselves enjoy when he says: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (ibid. XVIII, 10).

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Concerning the two different and unequal societies of angels, which are not inappropriately called by the names “light” and “darkness”

That certain angels sinned and were thrust down into the lowest regions of this world, which is like a prison to them, where they are held until their final condemnation on the day of judgment, the apostle Peter clearly shows when he says that God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, thrusting them into prisons of the darkness of the underworld [Note: [Col. 0346] The Ambrosian edition, Erasmus, and Louvain read “of hell.” Vindobonensis and the manuscripts have *infert*.], handed them over to be reserved for punishment at the judgment (II Pet. II, 4).

Who, then, would doubt that God divided these from those, whether by foreknowledge or by action? And who would deny that the former are rightly called “light,” since we who still live by faith and still hope for their equality, though we do not yet possess it, have already been called light by the Apostle: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8)? Those deserters, on the other hand, are plainly called darkness, as surely recognize those who either understand or believe that they are worse than unbelieving human beings.

Therefore, even if another light is to be understood in this passage of the book, where we read, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light,” and other darknesses are signified in what is written, “God divided the light from the darkness” (Gen. I, 3–4), we have nevertheless judged that these two angelic societies are represented: one enjoying God, the other swelling with arrogance [Note: [Col. 0346] Vindobonensis, the Ambrosian edition, and several manuscripts read *typo*, “with arrogance.”] [Note: [Col. 0346] Augustine uses the same word in *Confessions* III, 3, and VII, 9, to express pride and arrogance.]; one to whom it is said, “Worship him, all his angels” (Ps. XCVI, 8); the other whose prince says, “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. IV, 9); one burning with the holy love of God, the other smoking with the unclean love of its own exaltedness.

And since, as it is written, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6; I Pet. V, 5), one dwells in the heavens of heavens, while the other, cast down from there, rages in this lowest aerial heaven; one is tranquil in luminous devotion, the other turbulent in dark desires; one, at God’s command, mercifully helps and justly punishes, while the other, in its arrogance, burns with the desire to subjugate and harm; one serves God’s goodness, so that it may assist as much as he wills [Note: [Col. 0346] Thus the manuscripts read. The editions have *bonitatis*, “of goodness.”]; [Col. 0347] the other is restrained by God’s power, lest it harm as much as it wills; the former mocks the latter, so that, against its will, it benefits through its persecutions; the latter envies the former when it gathers its own pilgrims.

We have therefore judged that these two angelic societies, different and opposed to one another—one good by nature and upright in will, the other good by nature but perverse in will—are declared by other, clearer testimonies of the divine Scriptures and are signified in this book, whose name is Genesis, by the names “light” and “darkness.” Even if the one who wrote this passage perhaps intended something else, it has not been useless to examine the obscurity of this interpretation. For although we have been unable to discover the intention of the author of this book, we have nevertheless not departed from the rule of faith, which is sufficiently known to the faithful through the other sacred Scriptures of the same authority [Note: [Col. 0347] All our manuscripts, except Codex 2050, read *abhorruimus*, “we recoiled.”].

For although bodily works of God are mentioned here, they undoubtedly possess some likeness to spiritual realities, in accordance with which the Apostle says: “For you are all sons of light and sons of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness” (I Thess. V, 5). But if that writer too intended this, our purpose has reached the more complete conclusion of the discussion: namely, that a man of such exceptional and divine wisdom—or rather, that the Spirit of God through him—should not be believed to have omitted the angels when recounting the works of God, which he says were all completed on the sixth day.

Whether the words “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” were written because he made them first, or, as is more fittingly understood, “In the beginning” because he made them in the only-begotten Word, by these names the universal creation is signified: either spiritual and corporeal, which is more credible, or the two great parts of the world, containing all created things. Thus he first set forth the whole of creation, and afterward unfolded its parts according to the mystical number of the days.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—Concerning the view that, in the establishment of the firmament, angels are signified by the name of the waters that were divided, and concerning the view that some waters were not created

Although some have thought that, in a certain sense, peoples of angels are signified by the name “waters” [Note: [Col. 0347] Augustine himself appears to have held this view in *Confessions* XIII, 15 and 32. But he rejected it in *Retractions* II, 6, no. 2. Origen held the same opinion; Epiphanius criticized it in his *Letter to John of Jerusalem*, as did Jerome in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem.], and that this is what is meant by, “Let there be a firmament between the water and the water” (Gen. I, 6)—so that the angels are understood above the firmament [Col. 0348], while below it are either these visible waters, or the multitude of evil angels, or the nations of all human beings—then, if this is so, the place where the angels were made is not indicated there, but the place where they were divided.

Some even deny that the waters were made by God, which is an exceedingly perverse and impious absurdity, because nowhere is it written, “God said, ‘Let there be waters’” [Note: [Col. 0348] This heresy is also mentioned in *On Heresies*, heresy 76, though its author is not named. Theodoret attributes it to the Audians in book 4 of *Heretical Fables*. Epiphanius, on the contrary, notes among other things that the heretics of heresy 54, the Sampsaeans, worshiped water and regarded it as a kind of god. Coquaeus.]. They could, with similar absurdity, say the same about the earth: for nowhere do we read, “God said, ‘Let there be earth.’”

“But,” they say, “it is written, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth.’” Therefore water too must be understood there, since both are comprehended under one name. For the sea belongs to him, as it is written in the Psalm, “and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land” (Ps. XCIV, 5) [Note: [Col. 0348] Vindobonensis, Erasmus, and Louvain omit *terram*, “land.” The more authoritative manuscripts have it, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The Ambrosian edition also has it, but with the addition: “and the dry land, that is, the earth, his hands formed.”].

But those who wish angels to be understood by the name of the waters above the heavens are moved by the weights of the elements, and therefore do not think that the fluid and heavy nature of water could have been established in the higher regions of the world. According to their principles, if they themselves could make a human being, they would not place phlegm—which in Greek is called *phlegma* (φλέγμα), and which performs the function of water among the elements of our body—in the head.

For the head is the seat of phlegm, most appropriately, in accordance with God’s work; but according to their conjecture it is placed there so absurdly that, if we did not know this and it were similarly written in this book that God had placed fluid, cold, and therefore heavy moisture in the highest part of all the other parts of the human body, these weighers of the elements would certainly not believe it. And if they were subject to the authority of the same Scripture, they would judge that something else had to be understood from it.

But since, if we carefully investigate and discuss each point written in that divine book concerning the constitution of the world, many things would have to be said and we would have to depart far from the purpose of the work undertaken; and since we have now discussed, as much as seemed sufficient, those two different and opposing societies of angels, in which there are also the beginnings of the two cities among human affairs, about which I have undertaken to speak next, let us close this book at last.

# BOOK TWELVE

In this book Augustine first investigates the angels—namely, whence some have a good will and others an evil will, and what was the cause of the blessedness of the good angels and the misery of the evil angels. He then treats of the creation of humankind and teaches that humanity was created not from eternity but in time, and by no other author than God.

[Col. 0347]

## CHAPTER I.—Concerning the one nature of the good and evil angels

### 1

Before I speak of the creation of humankind, where the origin of the two cities will become apparent insofar as it concerns the race of rational mortals, just as it already seems to have become apparent in the angels in the preceding book, I see that I must first say certain things about the angels themselves. These will demonstrate, as far as we are able, how neither inappropriate nor incongruous it is to speak of a fellowship between human beings and angels, so that we should rightly speak not of four cities—two of angels and as many of human beings—but rather of two cities, that is, societies: one constituted among the good, the other among the evil, not only among angels but also among human beings.

### 2

There can be no doubt that the contrary desires of the good and evil angels arose not from different natures and principles—for the good God created and formed both as the author of all substances—but from their wills and desires. Some steadfastly persist in the common good of all, which is God himself for them, and in his eternity, truth, and love; others, taking greater pleasure in their own power, as though they themselves were their own good, flowed away from the higher, common, beatifying good toward their own concerns. They made the arrogance of exaltation stand in place of the highest eternity, the cunning of vanity in place of the most certain truth, and partisan striving in place of undivided love; thus they became proud, deceitful, and envious.

The cause of their blessedness, therefore, is adherence to God. Accordingly, the cause of the misery of the others must be understood in the opposite way: it is failure to adhere to God. Thus, when it is asked why the former are blessed, the correct answer is, “Because they adhere to God”; and when it is asked why the latter are miserable, the correct answer is, “Because they do not adhere to God.”

There is no good of a rational or intellectual creature by which it is blessed except God. Thus, although not every creature can be blessed—for wild animals, wood, stones, and whatever is of this kind neither attain nor receive this gift—the creature that can be blessed cannot do so from itself, because it was created from nothing, but from the one by whom it was created. For it is blessed when it possesses this good, and miserable when it loses it. But he who is blessed by a good that is not another but himself cannot be miserable, because he cannot lose himself.

### 3

We therefore say that there is no immutable good except the one true and blessed God. The things he made are indeed good, because they are from him; nevertheless, they are changeable, because they were made not from him but from nothing. Although, therefore, they are not the highest things—for God is a greater good than they are—they are nevertheless great changeable goods, capable of adhering to the immutable good and thereby becoming blessed. So much is this their good that without it they must be miserable.

Nor are the other things in the universe of creation thereby better because they cannot be miserable. We should not say that the other members of our body are better than the eyes because they cannot become blind. Just as a sentient nature, even when it suffers pain, is better than a stone, which cannot suffer pain in any way, so a rational nature, even when miserable, is superior to one that lacks reason or sensation and therefore cannot be subject to misery.

Since this is so, this nature—which was created with such excellence that, although it is changeable, it can nevertheless attain blessedness by adhering to the immutable good, that is, to the highest God, and which cannot satisfy its need except by being blessed, and cannot be sufficient for the satisfaction of that need unless God is its possession—plainly commits a fault by failing to adhere to him. Every fault harms nature, and therefore is contrary to nature.

This nature, then, differs from the one that adheres to God not by nature but by fault. Yet by this very fault the nature itself is shown to be very great and highly praiseworthy. For whatever fault is rightly censured is undoubtedly an indication that the nature is praiseworthy. The correct condemnation of a fault consists in the fact that by it a praiseworthy nature is dishonored.

Thus, when blindness is called a fault of the eyes, it is shown that sight belongs to the nature of the eyes; and when deafness is called a fault of the ears, it is demonstrated that hearing belongs to their nature. So, when the fault of the angelic creature is said to be its failure to adhere to God, this most clearly declares that it is fitting for its nature to adhere to God.

Who could worthily conceive or express how great is the praise of adhering to God, so that one may live by him, receive wisdom from him, rejoice in him, and enjoy so great a good without death, error, or distress? Accordingly, even by the fault of the evil angels, whereby they do not adhere to God, it is sufficiently shown—since every fault harms nature—that God created their nature so good that not being with God is harmful to it.

## CHAPTER II.—No essence is contrary to God, because, in relation to him who supremely is and always is, whatever is not appears wholly different [Note: [Col. 0350] Some manuscripts read “different in every respect.”]

These things have been said so that, when we speak of apostate angels, no one may suppose that they could have had a different nature, as though from another principle, or that God was not the author of their nature. The more clearly anyone understands what God said through the angel when he sent Moses to the children of Israel—“I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14)—the more readily and easily he will escape the impiety of this error.

Since God is the highest essence—that is, since he supremely is—and is therefore immutable, he gave being to the things he created from nothing, but not supreme being, as he himself has it. He gave more being to some and less to others, and thus arranged the natures of essences in degrees.

For just as, from that which is “to know” (*sapere*), the word “wisdom” (*sapientia*) is derived, so from that which is “to be” (*esse*) the word “essence” (*essentia*) is derived. This is indeed a new term, not used by the ancient authors of the Latin language, but now customary in our time, so that our language would not lack the term that the Greeks call οὐσία (*ousia*). The word was formed by translating the word directly, so that it might be called *essentia*.

Accordingly, no nature is contrary to that nature which supremely is, through whose action all things that are exist, except that which is not. For non-being is contrary to that which is. Therefore no essence is contrary to God—that is, to the highest essence and the author of all essences, of whatever kind they may be.

## CHAPTER III.—Concerning the enemies of God, who are enemies not by nature but by a contrary will; and since this will harms them, it harms a good nature—for if a fault does not harm, it is not a fault

Those who oppose God’s rule not by nature but by their faults are called enemies of God in the Scriptures. They are entirely unable to harm him, but they harm themselves. They are enemies in their will to resist, not in the power to inflict injury.

For God is immutable and wholly incorruptible. Therefore the fault by which those called his enemies resist God is evil not for God but for themselves. This is so for no other reason than that it corrupts the good of their nature.

Nature, then, is not contrary to God; fault is. For what is evil is contrary to good [Note: [Col. 0351] Some manuscripts read: “but fault, because it is evil, is contrary to good.”]. Who, then, would deny that God is supremely good? Fault, therefore, is contrary to God, as evil is contrary to good.

But the nature that fault corrupts is also good; hence fault is certainly contrary to this good as well. Yet evil is contrary to God only as evil to good, whereas to the nature it corrupts it is not merely evil but also harmful. For no evils are harmful to God, but only to changeable and corruptible natures—which are nevertheless good, as the very faults themselves testify.

If those natures were not good, faults could not harm them. For what do faults do by harming them except remove their integrity, beauty, health, virtue, and whatever good is customarily taken away or diminished in a nature by fault? If all good were entirely absent, a fault would do no harm by removing nothing good, and therefore would not be a fault. For that something should be a fault and yet do no harm is impossible.

It follows that, although a fault cannot harm the immutable good, it nevertheless cannot harm anything except what is good, because it exists only where it does harm. This too may be stated as follows: a fault can exist neither in the highest good nor anywhere except in some good.

Therefore only good things can exist somewhere; evil things alone exist nowhere. For even those natures that have been corrupted by the fault of an evil will are evil insofar as they are faulty, but good insofar as they are natures. And when a faulty nature is undergoing punishment, apart from the fact that it is a nature, even this is good in it: that it is not unpunished. For this is just, and everything just is undoubtedly good.

No one suffers punishment for natural faults, but for voluntary ones. Even when a fault has been strengthened by habit or excessive development and has grown in as though naturally, it took its beginning from the will. For we are now speaking of the faults of a nature in which there is a mind capable of intelligible light, by which the just is distinguished from the unjust.

## CHAPTER IV.—Concerning the nature of irrational or lifeless things, which in its own kind and order does not depart from the beauty of the universe

As for the faults of cattle, trees, and other changeable and mortal things, which lack intellect, sensation, or life altogether, and whose dissoluble nature is thereby corrupted, it is ridiculous to regard them as deserving condemnation. These creatures received from the will of the Creator such a mode of being that, by yielding and succeeding one another, they complete, in their own kind, the lowest beauty of the times, in harmony with the parts of this world.

Earthly things were not, after all, to be made equal to heavenly things; nor should these have been absent from the universe because those are better. Therefore, in the places where such things ought to exist, when one thing arises as another fails, when lesser things yield to greater, and when the things surpassed are transformed into the qualities of those that surpass them, there is an order of transitory things.

The beauty of this order does not delight us because, being woven into a part of it in accordance with the condition of our mortality, we cannot perceive the whole, to which the parts that offend us belong with sufficient fitness and beauty. Therefore, since we are less capable of contemplating this order, we are most rightly commanded to believe in the providence of the Creator, lest we dare, through the rashness of human vanity, to criticize in any respect the work of so great an artist.

Even the non-voluntary and non-penal faults of earthly things, if we consider them wisely, commend the natures themselves, of which there is not one whose author and creator is not God. For what displeases us in a fault is that by it something is taken away which pleases us in the nature—except that human beings often dislike the natures themselves when they become harmful to them, because they consider not the natures but their own advantage. So it was with those animals whose abundance chastised the pride of the Egyptians.

In this way they could also criticize the sun, since judges order certain wrongdoers or debtors to be exposed to the sun [Note: [Col. 0352] This is a kind of punishment directed more toward disgrace than toward the torture of suffering, although it is not without its own torment. In Spain, procuresses are subjected to it: they are fastened in wooden collars and smeared with honey, so that flies, bees, and wasps swarm upon them. Ludovicus Vives.].

Nature, therefore, considered in itself, not in relation to our convenience or inconvenience, gives glory to its maker. The nature of eternal fire is likewise unquestionably praiseworthy, although it will be punitive for the condemned impious. For what is more beautiful than fire, blazing, vigorous, and luminous? What is more useful than fire, warming, healing, and cooking? Yet nothing is more troublesome than that which burns.

The very same thing, applied in one way [Note: [Col. 0352] Vindobonensis, the Ambrosian edition, and Erasmus read *poenaliter*, “punitively.”], is destructive, while applied appropriately it is found to be most beneficial. For who could adequately express in words its uses throughout the whole world? Nor should we listen to those who praise light in fire but condemn its heat, judging not from its nature but from their own convenience or inconvenience. They want to see; they do not want to be burned. But they pay little attention to the fact that the very light which certainly pleases them can, through incompatibility, harm weak eyes, and that in the heat which displeases them certain animals can, through compatibility, live in health [Note: [Col. 0352] See below, book 21, chapter 4.].

## CHAPTER V.—That the Creator is praiseworthy in every kind and mode of nature

All natures, then, because they exist and therefore possess their own mode, their own form, and a certain peace proper to them, are undoubtedly good. When they are where they ought to be according to the order of nature, they preserve, insofar as they have received it, their own being.

Those that have not received everlasting existence change for the better or worse according to the use and movement of things to which they are subject by the law of the Creator, moving by divine providence toward the outcome contained in the reason governing the universe. Thus even the degree of corruption that leads changeable and mortal natures to destruction does not make what was cease to be in such a way that something that ought to be does not subsequently arise from it.

Since this is so, God, who supremely is, and from whom every essence that does not supremely exist was made—for it ought not to be equal to him, since it was made from nothing, and could not exist at all if it had not been made by him—is not to be criticized because of the offense of any faults, but is to be praised in the contemplation of all natures.

## CHAPTER VI.—What is the cause of the blessedness of the good angels, and what is the cause of the misery of the evil angels

The truest cause of the blessedness of the good angels is therefore found to be that they adhere to him who supremely is. When the cause of the misery of the evil angels is sought, the fitting answer is that they turned away from him who supremely is and turned toward themselves, who do not supremely exist. And what is this fault called other than pride? “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X, 15).

They therefore did not wish to preserve their strength for him (Ps. LVIII, 10). They would have been greater if they had adhered to him who supremely is; but by preferring themselves to him, they preferred what is less.

This was the first defect, the first poverty, and the first fault of that nature which was created so as not to be supreme, yet to be capable of possessing blessedness by enjoying him who supremely is. When it turned away from him, it did not become nothing, but became less; and for that reason it became miserable.

If the efficient cause of this evil will is sought, nothing is found. For what makes the will evil, when the will itself makes the evil deed? Accordingly, an evil will is the efficient cause of an evil deed, but nothing is the efficient cause of an evil will.

For if there is some thing, it either has a will or does not have one. If it has one, it certainly has either a good will or an evil will. If it has a good will, who would be so foolish as to say that a good will makes an evil will? For, if that were so, a good will would be the cause of sin—than which nothing more absurd can be imagined.

But if this thing that is thought to make the will evil itself has an evil will, I in turn ask about the thing that made it; and, so that there may be some limit to the inquiry, I seek the cause of the first evil will. For it is not the first evil will if an evil will made it [Note: [Col. 0353] Vindobonensis, Ambrosian, and Louvain read: “which no will, even an evil one, made.” The manuscripts correct the text.]. Rather, that is the first will which nothing made. For if something preceded it from which it was made, that preceding will is the first, since it made the other.

If it is answered that no thing made it and that therefore it always existed, I ask whether it existed in some nature. If it existed in no nature, it did not exist at all. But if it existed in some nature, it corrupted and damaged that nature, and thereby deprived it of a good. Therefore an evil will could not exist in an evil nature, but in a good yet changeable nature, one that could be harmed by this fault.

For if it did not harm, it was certainly not a fault, and therefore it should not be called an evil will. But if it did harm, it harmed by taking away or diminishing some good. Thus an everlasting evil will could not have existed in something in which a natural good had preceded, a good that the evil will could remove by harming it.

[Col. 0354] If, then, it was not everlasting, I ask who made it. It remains to say that the evil will was made by the thing in which there was no will. I ask whether this thing was superior, inferior, or equal.

If it was superior, it was certainly better. How, then, could it have had no will rather than a good will? The same can plainly be said if it was equal [Note: [Col. 0354] Thus the manuscripts read. The editions have: “The same can plainly be said if it was equal.”]. For when two beings are equally good in will, one does not make the other’s will evil.

It remains, then, that an inferior thing, in which there was no will, made the will of the angelic nature that first sinned evil. But whatever this inferior thing may be, down to the lowest earth, since it is a nature and essence, is undoubtedly good, possessing its own mode and form in its own kind and order.

How, then, can a good thing be the efficient cause of an evil will? How, I ask, can good be the cause of evil? When the will turns away from what is higher and turns toward lower things, it becomes evil—not because the thing toward which it turns is evil, but because the turning itself is perverse. Therefore the inferior thing did not make the will evil; rather, the will itself, which was made, perversely and disorderly desired the inferior thing [Note: [Col. 0354] All the manuscripts read *quia*, “because.”].

For if two people, equal in disposition of mind and body, see the beauty of one body, and one of them is moved, upon seeing it, to enjoy it illicitly, while the other remains steadfast in a chaste will, what do we suppose is the cause of an evil will arising in one but not in the other?

What thing made that will evil in the one in whom it arose? Surely not the beauty of that body, for it did not produce the evil will in both, since it appeared equally before the sight of both. Is it the flesh of the one who looked? Why not also that of the other? Or is it the mind? Why not that of both? We have said that both were equal in mind and body.

Should we say that one of them was tempted by the secret suggestion of an evil spirit? But surely he consented to that suggestion and to whatever persuasion it involved by his own will. It is this consent, this evil will that he applied to the one who was wrongly persuading him, whose cause we are seeking.

And, so that this obstacle too may be removed from the question: if both are tempted by the same temptation, and one yields and consents to it while the other remains as he had been, what else is apparent except that one wished to fall away from chastity and the other did not? From where did this arise except from their own wills, when the bodily and mental disposition of both was the same?

The same beauty was seen equally by the eyes of both, and the same secret temptation pressed equally upon both. Therefore, if those who wish to know what thing made the evil will in one of them look carefully, nothing presents itself.

If we say that he himself made it, what was he before the evil will except a good nature, whose author is God, who is the immutable good? Therefore, whoever says that the one who consented to the tempter and persuader, while the other did not, made for himself an evil will to use illicitly the beautiful body that had been equally present for both to see—although before that sight and temptation both had been alike in mind and body—should ask whether he made it because he is a nature or because he was made from nothing.

He will find that the evil will did not begin from the fact that he is a nature, but from the fact that the nature was made from nothing. For if nature is the cause of an evil will, what else are we compelled to say except that evil is made by good and that good is the cause of evil, since an evil will is made by a good nature?

But how can it happen that a good nature, although changeable, should make something evil before it has an evil will—that is, should make the evil will itself?

## CHAPTER VII.—That the efficient cause of an evil will is not to be sought for
No one, then, should seek an efficient cause of an evil will; for it is not efficient but deficient, since the process is not an effecting but a defecting. To defect from that which supremely is to that which is less is precisely to begin to have an evil will. As for wishing to discover the causes of these defections—which, as I have said, are not efficient but deficient—that is like wishing to see darkness or hear silence. Yet both are known to us: the one only through the eyes, the other only through the ears—not in their actual form, to be sure, but in the privation of form. Let no one, therefore, ask me to know what I know that I do not know, unless perhaps he wishes to learn not to know what must be known to be unknowable. For those things that are known not in their form but in the privation of their form are, if one may say or understand it, known by not knowing, so that by knowing they are not known. For when the visual faculty of the bodily eye moves through bodily forms, it sees darkness nowhere except where it has begun not to see. In the same way, the perception of silence belongs not to any other sense but only to the ears; yet silence can be perceived in no way except by not hearing. Thus our mind, by understanding, does indeed behold intelligible forms; but where they fail, it learns by not knowing. For who understands his offenses? (Ps. XVIII, 13 [XIX, 12]).

## CHAPTER VIII.—On the perverse love by which the will defects from the immutable good to a mutable good

I know this: God’s nature can never, nowhere, and in no respect defect; and that those things can defect which have been made from nothing. Yet, insofar as they exist and do good (for then they do something), they have efficient causes [Note: [Col. 0355] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus read: “then they do something when they have efficient causes.” Lovaniensis reads: “then, when they do something, they have efficient causes.” The particle *when*, absent from the manuscripts, should be removed.]; but insofar as they defect and thereby do evil—for what do they then do except produce vanity?—they have deficient causes [VIII.]. I also know that an evil will occurs in something that would not occur if it did not will it; and therefore just punishment follows defects that are not necessary but voluntary. One does not defect toward evils but defect evilly—that is, not toward evil natures, but evilly because, contrary to the order of natures, one defects from what supremely is to what is less.

For avarice is not a defect of gold, but of a human being who perversely loves gold, having abandoned justice, which ought incomparably to have been preferred to gold. [Col. 0356] Nor is lust a defect of beautiful and pleasurable bodies, but of a soul that perversely loves bodily pleasures, having neglected temperance, by which we are joined to things spiritually more beautiful and incorruptibly more pleasurable. Nor is boastfulness a defect of human praise, but of a soul that perversely loves to be praised by human beings, having scorned the testimony of conscience. Nor is pride a defect of the one who grants power, or of power itself, but of a soul that perversely loves its own power, despising the more just power of one who is more powerful. Accordingly, whoever perversely loves the good of any nature, even if he attains it, becomes evil in relation to that good and wretched because deprived of a better one.

## CHAPTER IX.—Whether the holy angels have the same one whom they have as the creator of their nature also as the author of their good will, through the love poured into them by the Holy Spirit

1. Since, then, there is no natural—or, if the expression is permissible, essential—efficient cause of an evil will—for the evil of mutable spirits begins with it, by which the good of their nature is diminished and corrupted; and such a will is produced only by defection, by which God is abandoned, while the cause of this defection itself necessarily fails—if we say that there is likewise no efficient cause of a good will, we must take care lest the good will of the good angels be believed not to have been made but to be coeternal with God.

Since they themselves were made, how can it be said that their good will was not made? Moreover, because it was made, was it made together with them, or did they previously exist without it? But if it was made together with them, there is no doubt that it was made by the one by whom they too were made; and as soon as they were made, they clung to the one by whom they were made, through the love with which they were made. They are distinguished from the company of the others by this: these remained in that same good will, while those were changed by defecting from it—that is, by an evil will, precisely in that they defected from the good one. They would not have defected from it if they had not willed to do so [Note: [Col. 0356] The manuscripts read as translated. The printed editions, however, have: “by the very fact that they defected from the good; from which they would not have defected if they had indeed willed to do so.”].

But if the good angels previously existed without a good will and made it in themselves without God’s working in them, then they were made better by themselves than by him. Far be it from us to believe this. For what were they without a good will except evil? Or, if they were not evil for the reason that no evil will was present in them—for they had not defected from one they had not yet begun to possess—at least they were not yet such, not yet as good as they began to be when they had a good will.

Or, if they could not make themselves better than the one who had made them—for no one makes anything better than he does—then surely they could not have had the good will by which they would become better unless the Creator’s assistance had worked in them. And when their good will effected this: that they turned not toward themselves, who were less, but toward him who supremely is, clinging to him and living wisely and happily by participation in him—what else is shown except that every good will would have remained helpless in mere desire unless he who had made the good nature capable of him had made it better from himself by filling it, first making it more eager by awakening it?

[Col. 0357] 2. This too must be examined: if the good angels made a good will in themselves, did they make it with some will or with none? If with none, then they certainly did not make it. If with some, was that will evil or good? If evil, how could an evil will have been the producer of a good will? If good, then they already had it. And who had made this will except the one who created them with a good will—that is, with a chaste love by which they would cling to him—creating their nature and granting them grace at the same time [Note: [Col. 0357] The printed editions read “in them.” The word *in* is absent from the manuscripts.]?

Hence we must believe that the holy angels never existed without a good will—that is, without the love of God. But those who, although created good, nevertheless became evil, did so by their own evil will. Their good nature did not make that evil will, except when it voluntarily defected from the good, so that the cause of evil is not the good but defection from the good. Either they received a lesser grace of divine love than those who remained steadfast in it, or, if both were created equally good, then, when these fell through an evil will, the others, receiving greater assistance, reached that fullness of blessedness from which they became utterly certain that they would never fall—as we have already discussed in the book that follows this one (ch. 13).

We must therefore confess, with due praise of the Creator, that it can be said not only of holy human beings but also of the holy angels that the love of God has been poured into them through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to them (Rom. V, 5); and that the following statement is the good not only of human beings but first and above all of the angels: “But for me, to cling to God is good” (Ps. LXXII, 28 [LXXIII, 28]). Those who share this good possess, both with the one to whom they cling and with one another, a holy fellowship; and they are one city of God, and likewise his living sacrifice and his living temple.

The part of this city that is gathered from mortal human beings in order to be joined to the immortal angels—now journeying as a mortal community on earth, or resting, among those who have died, in the hidden receptacles and dwelling places of souls—having been created by the same God, must now be discussed as to how it arose, just as was said concerning the angels. For according to the faith of Holy Scripture, which rightly possesses marvelous authority throughout the world, the human race took its beginning from one human being whom God first created; and Scripture foretold in advance, with true divinity, that all the nations would believe it, among the other truths that it proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0357] Compare *Enchiridion*, no. 9.].]

## CHAPTER X.—On the falsity of that history which assigns many thousands of years to past times

1. Let us therefore set aside the conjectures of people who do not know what they are saying about the nature or origin of the human race. For some, just as they believed concerning the world itself, suppose that human beings have always existed [Note: [Col. 0357] Basil, *First Homily on the Hexaemeron*: “Some profane men asserted that human nature was eternal; others that human beings were first born in Attica, others in Arcadia, others in Egypt.” To these they also added the Scythians. COQUAEUS.].

Hence Apuleius too, when describing this kind of living creature, says: “Individually mortal, yet collectively perpetual in the universal race” (*On the God of Socrates*).

When they are asked, if the human race has always existed, how their history can truly narrate who were the inventors of which things, who first established the liberal disciplines and other arts, or from whom this or that region, part of the earth, or island first began to be inhabited, they reply that through floods and conflagrations, occurring at fixed intervals of time [Note: [Col. 0358] See Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book 3, chapters 27ff.; and Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2.], not indeed all but most of the earth is so devastated that human beings are reduced to a tiny number, from whose offspring the former multitude is restored; and thus it is repeatedly restored and established as though for the first time, although what had been interrupted and extinguished by those immense devastations is actually being restored. But they maintain that a human being absolutely cannot exist except from a human being. They say what they suppose, not what they know.

2. They are also deceived by certain utterly false writings, which they claim to contain many thousands of years in their history of the ages [Note: [Col. 0358] See Cicero, *On Divination*, book 1, chapter 19, and Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 7, chapter 14.], whereas from the Sacred Scriptures we reckon that fewer than six thousand years have yet elapsed since the creation of humanity [Note: [Col. 0358] Eusebius, whom Augustine follows in his chronological arrangement, reckons 5,611 years from the creation of the world to the capture of Rome by the Goths, calculating according to the Septuagint interpreters. From the Hebrew text, Bede places 4,377 years between creation and the reign of Honorius and the younger Theodosius, when the Goths captured the City. LUDOVICUS VIVES.].

Not to discuss at length how the vanity of those writings in which far more thousands of years are reported may be refuted, and how no reliable authority for this matter can be found in them, consider that letter of Alexander the Great to his mother Olympias [Note: [Col. 0358] See above, book 8, chapter 5.]. In it he reports an account by an Egyptian priest, which the priest had drawn from writings held sacred among them and which included kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0358] The manuscripts read as translated. The printed editions have: “it also contains kingdoms.”] also known to Greek history.

In that letter, the Assyrian kingdom exceeds five thousand years; in Greek history, however, it has approximately 1,300 years from the reign of Belus himself, whom that Egyptian also places as king at the beginning of the same kingdom. As for the empire of the Persians and Macedonians down to Alexander himself, to whom the letter was addressed, the Egyptian assigns it more than eight thousand years; whereas among the Greeks, the period of the Macedonians down to Alexander’s death is found to be 485 years, and that of the Persians, until it ended with Alexander’s victory, is reckoned as 233 years [Note: [Col. 0358] See the note above on book 4, chapter 7.].

These figures, then, are far smaller than those of the Egyptians; even if multiplied by three, they would not equal them [Note: [Col. 0358] Our manuscripts read *aequarent* (“would equal them”). M.]. For the Egyptians are said once to have had years so short that they ended after four months [Note: [Col. 0358] See Pliny, *Natural History*, book 7, chapter 48; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 2, chapter 12; and Augustine himself below, book 15, chapter 12.]. Thus one fuller and truer year, such as the year now possessed both by us and by them, contained three of their ancient years.

But even so, as I have said, the Greek history does not agree with the Egyptian in its reckoning of time. Therefore the Greek account should rather be trusted, because it does not exceed the number of years contained in our writings, which are truly sacred.
