Moreover, if this letter of Alexander, which became especially well known, departs so greatly from credible historical chronology, how much less should we believe those writings that people have wished to produce as filled with fabulous antiquities [Note: [Col. 0359] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and several manuscripts read *voluerunt* (“they wished”).] in opposition to the authority of the most widely known and divine books—books that foretold that the whole world would believe them, and that the whole world, just as they foretold, did believe; books that demonstrate, through the truth with which their prophecies of the future are fulfilled, that they truly narrated the past?

## CHAPTER XI.—On those who do not consider this world eternal, but suppose either that there are innumerable worlds or that the same single world is perpetually born and dissolved through a fixed cycle of ages

Others, however, who do not consider this world eternal—whether they suppose that there are innumerable worlds rather than only this one, or that there is indeed only one but that it arises and perishes innumerably at fixed intervals of the ages [Note: [Col. 0359] See Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 2, chapter 9, and below, book 18, chapter 41, section 2.]—must necessarily admit that the human race existed before there were human beings who generated it.

For just as those people suppose that floods and conflagrations do not occur throughout the whole world and therefore insist that a few human beings always remain, from whom the former multitude may be restored, so these others cannot suppose that, when the world perishes, some human beings remain in the world [Note: [Col. 0359] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts read: “so these others can suppose that, when the world perishes, something of humanity remains in the world.”]. Rather, just as they believe that the world itself is reborn from its own matter, so they suppose that within it the human race arises from its elements, and then that the offspring of mortals springs from parents, just as do the offspring of other animals.

## CHAPTER XII.—What should be said to those who complain that the first creation of humanity was so late

What I replied when the question concerned the origin of the world—to those who refuse to believe that it did not always exist but began to exist, as Plato also most openly acknowledges (*Timaeus*), although some believe that he thought otherwise than he says—I should also reply concerning the first creation of humanity, on account of those who are similarly troubled by the question why humanity was not created through countless and infinite former ages, and why it was created so late that the Sacred Scriptures indicate that fewer than six thousand years have elapsed since it began to exist [Note: [Col. 0359] Above, book 11, chapter 5.].

If the shortness of the period troubles them, because the number of years since humanity was created seems to them so small according to our authoritative writings, let them consider that nothing is long-lasting when it has an endpoint, and that all spans of the ages, when compared with boundless eternity, should not be judged small but nonexistent. Accordingly, even if it were said that five or six thousand years had passed, or sixty thousand, or six hundred thousand, or sixty times that number, or six hundred times that number, or six hundred thousand times that number since God made humanity—or if this total were likewise multiplied by as many times again that no name for the number remained—one could still ask why he had not made humanity earlier.

For the eternity without beginning during which God refrained from creating humanity is so vast that, if any immense and ineffable quantity of time were compared with it—though that quantity were bounded by an end and limited to a definite span—it ought not even appear as large as a drop of water, however small, compared with the whole sea, even with the ocean that surrounds the earth. In the case of those two things, one is indeed extremely small and the other incomparably vast, but both are finite. The span of time that proceeds from some beginning and is confined by some endpoint, however great its extent, when compared with that which has no beginning, should—I do not know whether to say—be counted as nothing rather than as something very small.

For if, proceeding backward from the end, the shortest moments are subtracted one by one, the number gradually diminishing, even if it is so immense that no word can name it as one goes backward, eventually the subtraction will reach the beginning—just as if you subtracted the days of a human being from the day in which he now lives back to the day on which he was born.

But if, in a span that began from no beginning, one subtracts backward—not individual minute moments, nor quantities of hours, days, months, or even years, but spans as great as the entire sum of years that no reckoner can now express, though that sum is consumed by the minute subtraction of moments—and if these immense spans are subtracted not once, twice, or many times, but continually, what happens, what is being done, when one never reaches a beginning that is entirely nonexistent?

Therefore, what we now ask after five thousand and more years [Note: [Col. 0360] The printed editions read “and more besides.” The word “more” is absent from the manuscripts.] could also be asked by later generations after six hundred thousand times as many years, with the same curiosity, if human mortality continued to arise and perish for so long and ignorant weakness continued to persist. Those who lived before us could have raised this question in the very recent period following humanity’s creation. Indeed, the first human being himself, either on the following day or later on the very day after he had been made, could have asked why he had not been made earlier. And whenever he had been made earlier, he would not then, now, or later have found different grounds for this controversy about the beginning of temporal things.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On the revolution of the ages, by which some philosophers believed that, once the ages had been enclosed within a fixed limit, all things would always return to the same order and the same appearance

1. The philosophers of this world thought that they could or should dissolve this problem in no other way than by introducing cycles of time, through which they asserted that the same things had always been renewed and repeated in the nature of things, and would continue to be so without end through the cycles of the ages that come and pass—whether these cycles occurred while the world remained in existence, or whether the world arose and perished at fixed intervals, always displaying as though new the same things that had already passed and those that were yet to come.

They cannot by this utter mockery free the immortal soul, even after it has acquired wisdom, as it proceeds without end toward a false blessedness and returns without end to true misery. For how can that be true blessedness whose eternity is never trusted, while the soul either, in its utter ignorance, does not know the misery that is to come, or, in its unhappiness, fears it even in the midst of blessedness?

Or, if the soul proceeds from miseries to blessedness without ever returning to them again, then something new occurs in time that has no end in time. Why, then, should the world not also be new? Why should the human being made in the world not also be new? Thus those supposed cycles, discovered by false wisdom and false sages, may be avoided by the straight path of sound doctrine.

2. Some people also wish the words read in the book of Solomon called Ecclesiastes to be understood as referring to these cycles, returning to the same things and bringing everything back to the same state:

“What is that which has been? The same that shall be. And what is that which has been done? The same that shall be done; and there is nothing new under the sun. Is there anything of which one may say, ‘See, this is new’? It has already existed in the ages that were before us” (Eccles. I, 9–10).

They wish this to be understood as referring to cycles returning to the same things and recalling everything to the same state [Note: [Col. 0361] So Origen, *On First Principles*, book 3, chapter 5, and there, book 2, chapter 3.]. But Solomon either spoke of the things about which he had been speaking above—namely, of generations going and others coming, of the courses of the sun, and of the flows of streams—or certainly of all kinds of things that arise and perish.

There were human beings before us, there are some with us, and there will be others after us; and the same is true of each kind of animal and plant. Even monsters themselves, which are born contrary to ordinary usage, although they differ from one another and some are said to have occurred only once, nevertheless, insofar as they are generally wonders and monsters, have existed and will exist; nor is it new or recent for a monster to be born under the sun.

Some, however, have understood these words as though that wise man wished it to be understood that everything had already been made in God’s predestination, and therefore nothing is new under the sun.

But it is far from the true faith to believe that Solomon’s words signify those cycles by which, as these people suppose, the same cycles of times and temporal things are repeated, so that, for example, just as in this age the philosopher Plato taught his disciples in the city of Athens, in the school called the Academy [Note: [Col. 0361] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and many manuscripts read *Academica*.], so through countless former ages, at very long but nevertheless fixed intervals, the same Plato, the same city, the same school, and the same disciples were repeated, and through countless subsequent ages will be repeated. Far be it, I say, from us to believe this.

For Christ died once for our sins; but rising from the dead, he dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. VI, 9). And after the resurrection we shall always be with the Lord (I Thess. IV, 16), to whom we now say what the sacred Psalm admonishes us: “You, Lord, shall preserve us and guard us from this generation forever.”

I consider the following words to fit these people well: “The wicked walk around” (Ps. XI, 8–9 [XII, 8–9])—not because their life will return through the cycles they imagine, but because their path is now one of such error, that is, of false doctrine.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the temporal creation of the human race, which God established neither through a new plan nor through a changeable will

What wonder is it, then, if those who wander in these cycles find neither an entrance nor an exit? They do not know either the beginning from which the human race and our mortality began or the end by which they will be closed, since they cannot penetrate the depth of God. For although he is eternal and without beginning, he began time from some beginning and made in time the human being whom he had never previously made—not, however, by a new and sudden plan, but by an immutable and eternal purpose.

Who can investigate this unsearchable depth and search out what cannot be scrutinized, according to which God created temporal humanity in time, before whom no human being had ever existed, not by a changeable will, and multiplied the human race from one person?

When the Psalm itself had first said, “You, Lord, shall preserve us and guard us from this generation forever,” and then had struck back at those whose foolish and impious doctrine preserves no eternity of liberation and blessedness for the soul, immediately adding, “The wicked walk around”—as though someone had said to it: “What, then, do you believe, think, and understand? Is it to be supposed that God suddenly decided to make the human being whom he had never made throughout the infinite eternity of the past, although nothing new can happen to him and nothing mutable exists in him?”—it immediately replied, speaking to God himself: “According to your depth you have multiplied the children of human beings” (ibid.).

Let human beings think what they suppose, and hold and debate whatever pleases them, he says; “according to your depth,” which no human being can know, “you have multiplied the children of human beings.” It is very deep indeed to investigate [Note: [Col. 0362] Lovaniensis and a few manuscripts read “it is very deep to investigate.”], both that God has always existed [Note: [Col. 0362] The manuscripts read “and has always existed,” omitting “God.”] and that he wished first, at a particular time, to make the human being whom he had never made, without changing his plan or will.

## CHAPTER XV.—Whether God, being always God, must also be understood always to have been Lord, so that there was always a creature over which he ruled; and how what is said always to have been created cannot be called coeternal

[Col. 0363]

1. Just as I do not dare to say that the Lord God was at some time not Lord [Note: [Col. 0363] See book 5, *On the Trinity*, no. 17.], so I must not doubt that humanity never existed previously and that the first human being was created at a certain time.

But when I consider what he was always Lord of, if a creature did not always exist, I am afraid to assert anything, because I also look at myself and recall that it is written: “Who among human beings can know the counsel of God? Or who can think what the Lord wills? For the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our plans uncertain. For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 13–15).

Among the many things I think about in this earthly dwelling [Note: [Col. 0363] Here Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus add “they press me down.” Lovaniensis lacks the addition, but nevertheless corrupts the sense by incorrect punctuation of the following words.]—certainly many, because I cannot discover the one thing that is true, whether among them or beyond them, which perhaps I do not think of—if I were to say that there had always been a creature over which the one who is always Lord ruled, so that he was never not Lord, but that now one creature and now another existed through different spans of time, in order that we might not say that any creature was coeternal with the Creator, which sound faith and reason reject, I would have to take care lest it be absurd and alien to the light of truth to say that a mortal creature, through successive periods of time, had always existed, one passing away and another succeeding it, while the immortal creature did not begin to exist until our age was reached—when the angels too were created, if that light which was first made rightly signifies them—or rather that heaven of which it is said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1).

Yet they did not exist before they were made, lest, if they are said always to have existed as immortals, they be believed coeternal with God.

But if I say that the angels were not created in time, but existed before all times, and that God was their Lord, since he was never anything other than Lord, I will also be asked whether, if they were made before all times, they could always have existed.

Perhaps the answer may seem to be: “How could they not always have existed, when that which exists at every time may properly be said always to exist?” They existed at every time to such an extent that they were made before all times—if time began from heaven, and they already existed before heaven.

But if time existed even before heaven, then it did not exist in hours, days, months, and years—for it is clear that these dimensions of temporal intervals, which are ordinarily and properly called times, began from the movement of the heavenly bodies. Hence, when God established them, he said: “Let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years” (ibid., 14). Rather, time existed in some mutable movement in which one thing passed earlier and another later [Col. 0364] [Note: [Col. 0364] The manuscripts read as translated. The printed editions have: “one thing passed earlier and another succeeded later.”], because they cannot exist simultaneously.

If, therefore, something of this kind existed before heaven in the movements of the angels [Note: [Col. 0364] Compare the discussion in book 8 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, no. 39.], and therefore time already existed, and if the angels had been moving temporally from the moment they were made, then they too existed at every time, since time was made together with them.

Who, then, would say, “That which existed at every time did not always exist”?

2. But if I answer this, I will be told: “How, then, are they not coeternal with the Creator, if he always existed and they always existed? How can they be called created if they are understood always to have existed?”

What answer can be given to this? Should we say that they always existed because they existed at every time, having been made together with time or together with the times, and yet were created?

For we will not deny that time itself was created, although no one doubts that time always existed at every time. For if time did not exist at every time, was there then a time when there was no time? What utterly foolish person would say this?

We can rightly say: “There was a time when Rome did not exist; there was a time when Jerusalem did not exist; there was a time when Abraham did not exist; there was a time when humanity did not exist,” and so forth. Finally, if the world was made not at the beginning of time but after some time had passed, we can say: “There was a time when the world did not exist.”

But “There was a time when no time existed” is as inappropriate to say as if someone said, “There was a human being when no human being existed,” or, “There was this world when this world did not exist.” For if one thing and another are understood, it can somehow be said: “There was another human being when this human being did not exist.” Thus we can rightly say: “There was another time when this time did not exist.” But who, however foolish, would say: “There was a time when no time existed”?

Therefore, just as we say that time was created, although it is said always to have existed because time existed at every time, so it does not follow that, if the angels always existed, they were not created. They are said to have always existed because they existed at every time; and they existed at every time because time itself could in no way exist without them. For where there is no creature whose mutable movements cause times to pass, time cannot exist at all.

Accordingly, even if the angels always existed, they were created; and even if they always existed, they are not therefore coeternal with the Creator. He always existed in immutable eternity; they were made. But they are said always to have existed because they existed at every time, and time could in no way exist without them. Yet time, because it passes through mutability, cannot be coeternal with immutable eternity.

Accordingly, even if the angels’ immortality does not pass away in time—neither having been past, as though it no longer existed, nor being future, as though it did not yet exist—their movements, by which times pass, move from the future into the past. Therefore they cannot be coeternal with the Creator, of whose movement one cannot say either that what has been is no longer, or that what will be does not yet exist.

3. Therefore, if God was always Lord, he always had a creature serving under his dominion; yet that creature was not begotten from him but made by him from nothing, and it was not coeternal with him. He existed before it, although no time existed without it—not preceding it through an interval that passed [Note: [Col. 0365] Only Lovaniensis reads “passing.” Shortly afterward it also reads, “how the Creator was always Lord.”], but preceding it through an abiding perpetuity [Note: [Col. 0365] See *Confessions*, book 11, chapter 13, no. 16, and chapter 16, at the beginning.].

But if I give this answer to those who ask how the Creator was always Lord, if the serving creature did not always exist, or how it was created and not rather coeternal with the Creator, if it always existed, I fear that I may more easily be judged to be asserting what I do not know than teaching what I do know.

I therefore return to what our Creator wished us to know. As for those things that he has either permitted wiser people to know in this life or reserved for the fully perfected to know in the other life, I confess that they are beyond my powers. But I have thought that these matters should be treated without affirmation, so that those who read them may see from what dangers of inquiry they ought to abstain, and may not consider themselves capable of everything. Rather, let them understand how obediently they must follow the Apostle’s salutary command, where he says:

“I say, through the grace that has been given to me, to everyone among you: do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think with sober judgment, as God has allotted to each the measure of faith” (Rom. XII, 3) [Note: [Col. 0365] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and the manuscripts read “through the grace of God that has been given to me”; the words “of God” are absent from the main text.].

For if an infant is nourished according to his strength, he will grow and be able to receive more; but if he exceeds the capacity of his strength, he will fail before he grows.

## CHAPTER XVI.—How the eternal life promised by God to humanity before the eternal ages is to be understood
What ages passed before the human race was established, I confess that I do not know; nevertheless, I have no doubt that absolutely no creature is coeternal with the Creator. The Apostle also speaks of eternal ages—not future ones, but, what is even more astonishing, past ones. For he says: “In hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal ages” [Note: [Col. 0365] The Greek reads *pro tōn chronōn aiōniōn*, which the Vulgate translates *ante tempora saecularia* (“before the ages of the world”), while the version translated by Jerome has *ante tempora aeterna* (“before eternal ages”); for the Greek *aiōn* can be rendered in Latin as *saeculum* (“age”) or *aeternum* (“eternal”), as Augustine observes in *Against the Priscillianists*, no. 5. Hence, at Romans 16:25, the Greek *chronois aiōniois* is rendered in the Vulgate itself as *temporibus aeternis* (“eternal times”). Jerome, explaining the passage in the Epistle to Titus, says: “Before these times of the world, therefore, one must believe that there was a certain eternity of ages . . . Six thousand years of our world have not yet been completed: what eternities were there before? How many ages? How many origins of ages must we suppose there were? Before all these times . . . God the Father promised that the Word of his wisdom, and his very Wisdom, and the life of those who were to believe, would come into the world.” Augustine’s interpretation in *Against the Priscillianists*, no. 6, is shorter and easier: namely, that the Apostle called those times eternal which have no time preceding them. Compare also *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 1, no. 4, and *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 72.]; “but in his own times he manifested his Word” (Titus 1:2–3). Behold: he says that there were eternal times in the past, although they were not coeternal with God. For if before eternal times he not only existed but also promised eternal life [Col. 0366]—which he manifested in his own times, that is, at the appropriate times—what else was this than his Word? For this is eternal life. But how did he promise it, since he surely promised it to human beings, who did not yet exist before eternal times, unless it was already fixed in his eternity, and in his Word itself, coeternal with him, by predestination—that which was to come about in its own time?

## CHAPTER XVII.—What sound faith maintains concerning God’s unchangeable plan or will, against the arguments of those who wish God’s works, repeated from eternity, always to return through the same cycles of ages

1. I also have no doubt that before the first human being was created, no human being had ever existed—not that the same individual had revolved through certain cycles some unknown number of times, nor that some other person of similar nature had existed. Nor do the arguments of philosophers deter me from this faith. Their sharpest argument is thought to be this: they say that no infinite thing can be encompassed by any knowledge; and therefore, they claim, God possesses within himself all the finite explanations of all the finite things he makes [Note: [Col. 0366] The printed editions have *fecit* (“he made”); the manuscripts have *facit* (“he makes”).]. His goodness, however, must not be thought ever to have been inactive, lest his activity be temporal while his inactivity had previously been eternal—as though he had regretted his earlier beginningless inactivity and therefore begun his work. Consequently, they say, the same things must always be repeated, and the same things must always pass through repetition: either while the world remains subject to change—although it has never not existed and was nevertheless made without a beginning of time—or with its origin and dissolution likewise repeated, and always to be repeated, through those cycles. Otherwise, if God’s works were said to have begun at some point, he would seem to have condemned in some way his earlier beginningless inactivity as inert and idle, and therefore displeasing to him, and on that account to have changed. But if he is said always to have worked on temporal things, though on different things at different times, and thus eventually to have reached the making of a human being whom he had never made before, then he would seem to have made what he made not through knowledge—which they think cannot encompass anything infinite—but with a kind of accidental inconsistency, as though he made things when they happened to occur to him.

Moreover, if those cycles are admitted, they say, by which the same temporal things are repeated either while the world remains, or while the world itself inserts its recurring origins and dissolutions into those same cycles, then neither idle leisure—especially over so long a duration without beginning—nor thoughtless recklessness in his works is attributed to God. For if the same things are not repeated, no knowledge or foreknowledge of his can encompass them when they are varied through infinite diversity.

2. If reason could not refute these arguments by which the impious try to turn our simple piety away from the straight road, so that we may walk in a cycle with them, faith ought to mock them. Moreover, with the help of the Lord our God, manifest reason shatters these revolving circles fabricated by their opinion. They go astray above all because they prefer to walk in a false circle rather than along a true and straight path: they measure the wholly unchangeable divine mind, capable of encompassing any infinity and numbering all innumerable things without any alternation of thought, by their own human, mutable, and narrow minds. Thus what the Apostle says happens to them: “For comparing themselves with themselves” [Note: [Col. 0367] The Vulgate differs; but Augustine here, and in *Psalm 34* and *Against Faustus*, book 22, chapter 47, follows the Greek reading, *kai sygkrinontes heautous heautois ou syniousin* (“and comparing themselves with themselves, they do not understand”). The editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain have *semetipsos non intelligunt* (“they do not understand themselves”). But the Vindobonensis and the manuscripts, agreeing with the Greek, lack the word *semetipsos* (“themselves”).], “they do not understand” (2 Corinthians 10:12).

For since they do whatever comes into their minds to be done by a new decision—for they possess mutable minds—they are plainly thinking not of God, whom they cannot conceive, but of themselves in his place; and so they compare not him with themselves, but themselves with themselves—not with him, but with themselves. We, however, must not believe that God is affected one way when he is inactive and another way when he is at work, since he cannot be said to be affected as though something occurred in his nature that had not existed before. Whoever is affected suffers, and everything that suffers something is mutable. Therefore, his inactivity must not be imagined as idleness, laziness, or inertia, just as his work must not be imagined as labor, exertion, or industry. He knows how to act while at rest, and how to rest while acting. He can apply an eternal plan to a new work—not a new plan—and he did not begin to do what he had not done because he repented that he had previously ceased.

But even if he first ceased and afterward worked—which I do not know how a human being could understand—this certainly means that the “earlier” and “later” occurred in things that first did not exist and later existed. In him, however, one will did not follow another and change or remove it; rather, by one and the same eternal and unchangeable will, he both brought about that the things he created should not exist earlier, for as long as they did not exist, and that they should exist later, when they began to exist. In this way, he perhaps wondrously shows to those who are able to perceive such things how little he needed them, but created them out of gratuitous goodness, since without them, from an eternity without beginning, he remained in no lesser blessedness.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—Against those who say that things which are infinite cannot be encompassed even by God’s knowledge

As for the other claim they make—that infinite things cannot be encompassed even by God’s knowledge—they are left with no choice but to dare say this and plunge themselves into that deep abyss of impiety: that God does not know all numbers. That numbers are infinite is absolutely certain. For no matter at what number you suppose an end should be made, that number itself—not merely increased by one, but however large it may be and however great a multitude it may contain within the very rational structure and knowledge of numbers—can be not only doubled but multiplied. Yet each number is bounded by its own properties, so that no one of them can be equal to any other. Thus they are unequal and different from one another; each individually is finite, and all together are infinite.

Does God, then, fail to know all numbers because they are infinite [Note: [Col. 0367] Erasmus and the manuscripts have this reading. The Vindobonensis, Amerbach, and Louvain editions have *nescit omnipotens Deus* (“God Almighty does not know”).]? Does God’s knowledge reach only to a certain sum of numbers [Col. 0368] and leave the rest unknown? Who, even in the utmost madness, would say this? Nor will these people dare to despise numbers and say that they do not belong to God’s knowledge, since Plato, among them, commends God with great authority as having fashioned the world through numbers (*In Timaeo*); and among us it is written of God: “You have ordered all things by measure and number and weight” (Wisdom 11:21). The prophet likewise says of him: “He brings forth the world in number” [Note: [Col. 0368] The printed editions have *Qui profert numero saeculum* (“who brings forth the world in number”); the manuscripts have *Qui profert numerose saeculum* (“who brings forth the world numerously”). The passage is Isaiah 40:26 according to the Septuagint: *ho ekpherōn kat’ arithmon ton kosmon autou* (“he who brings forth his world according to number”).] (Isaiah 40:26, according to the Septuagint). And the Savior says in the Gospel: “All the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matthew 10:30).

Therefore, let us not doubt that every number is known to him “whose understanding is without number,” as the Psalm says (Psalm 146:5). Thus the infinity of number—although there is no number of infinite numbers—is nevertheless not incomprehensible to him whose understanding is without number. Accordingly, if whatever is comprehended by knowledge is bounded by the comprehension of the knower, then surely every infinity is, in some ineffable manner, finite for God, because it is not incomprehensible to his knowledge.

Why, then, if the infinity of numbers cannot be infinite for God’s knowledge, by which it is comprehended, should we little human beings presume to set limits to his knowledge? Why should we say that unless the same temporal things are repeated through the same cycles of time, God cannot either foreknow all that he made in order to make it, or know it after he has made it? His wisdom is simply manifold and uniformly multiform; by an incomprehensible comprehension it comprehends all incomprehensible things, so that if he should always wish to make whatever new and dissimilar things follow upon preceding things [Note: [Col. 0368] Only the Louvain edition has *consequuntur* (“follow”).], he could not possess them as disordered or unforeseen. Nor would he foresee them from the immediately preceding time; his eternal foreknowledge would contain them.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Concerning the ages of ages

Whether he does this in such a way [Note: [Col. 0368] The Louvain edition has *Quod ut ita faciat* (“that he may do this in such a way”). The other printed editions and the manuscripts have *Quod utrum ita faciat*, namely, “whether he does this in the manner stated at the end of the preceding chapter.”] and whether what are called “the ages of ages” are joined together in continuous connection, advancing as different ages through an ordered dissimilarity—while only those who are liberated from misery remain without end in their blessed immortality—or whether “the ages of ages” are so called because the ages abide in the unshaken stability of God’s wisdom, as though they brought about the ages of these things that pass away with time, I do not dare to determine [Note: [Col. 0368] See Jerome, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 1, verse 5.].

Perhaps, indeed, one could say “an age” for what are “ages,” so that “the age of the age” means nothing other than “the ages of ages,” just as “the heaven of heaven” means nothing other than “the heavens of heavens.” For God called the firmament above which are the waters “heaven” (Genesis 1:8), and yet the Psalm says: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4).

Which of these two alternatives is correct—or whether something else concerning the ages of ages can be understood beyond these two—is a most profound question [Col. 0369]. It does not obstruct what we are now doing if the matter is deferred for the time being without discussion, whether we can determine something about it or whether the very process of more careful investigation makes us more cautious, so that amid such great obscurity of things we do not rashly dare to affirm anything.

For now, we are arguing against the opinion that asserts those cycles through which the same things are thought necessarily to be repeated at recurring intervals of time. Whichever of those interpretations of “the ages of ages” is true, it has no bearing on these cycles. For whether “the ages of ages” are ages in which the same things are not repeated, but one proceeds from another in the most orderly connection, while the blessedness of the liberated remains completely secure without any return to misery; or whether “the ages of ages” are eternal things ruling over temporal things as masters over subjects, those cycles that turn the same things around have no place. They are especially refuted by the eternal life of the saints (Matthew 25:46).

## CHAPTER XX.—Concerning the impiety of those who assert that souls who share in the highest and true blessedness will return again and again, through cycles of time, to the same miseries and labors

1. What pious ears could endure the claim that, after a life passed through so many and such great calamities—if this is even to be called life, since it is rather death, and so grievous that the death which frees us from it is feared because of love for this death [Note: [Col. 0369] Compare Cicero, *The Dream of Scipio*, chapter 3.]—after such great, numerous, and dreadful evils have finally been expiated and ended through true religion and wisdom, souls will at last reach the sight of God and become blessed through contemplation of incorporeal light by participation in his unchangeable immortality, which we burn with love to attain, only to find it necessary at some point to abandon it; and that those who abandon it, cast down from that eternity, truth, and happiness, will be entangled in Tartarean mortality [Note: [Col. 0369] The Louvain edition alone has *immortalitati* (“immortality”).], shameful folly, and execrable miseries—where God is lost, truth is hated, and happiness is sought through filthy wickedness—and that this will happen again and again, without end, at fixed intervals and measures of the earlier and later ages; and all this so that God may know his works through defined cycles continually going and returning through our false blessednesses and true miseries, eternal by alternating but unceasing revolution, since otherwise he could neither cease from making nor, by knowing, investigate things that are infinite?

Who could hear this? Who could believe it? Who could endure it? If these things were true, they would not merely be more wisely left unspoken; they would also—as best I can express what I wish—be more wisely unknown. For if we will not remember these things there, and will therefore be blessed, why is our misery here made heavier by knowing them? But if we shall necessarily know them there, then at least let us not know them here, so that our expectation here may be happier than our attainment there of the highest good. Here, eternal life is awaited as something to be attained; there, it would be known as blessed but not eternal, since it would eventually be lost.

[Col. 0370] 2. But if they say that no one can reach that blessedness unless, during the education provided by this life, he has learned about these cycles in which blessedness and misery alternate in turn, how then can they admit that the more someone loves God, the more easily he will reach blessedness, when they teach doctrines that make love itself grow sluggish? For who would love less warmly and less ardently someone whom he thinks he must necessarily abandon, and against whose truth and wisdom he will take his stand, precisely when he has reached the full knowledge of him that his capacity permits, in the perfection of blessedness? No one can faithfully love even a human friend whom he knows he will in the future become an enemy.

But far be it from us to accept as true what threatens us with a true misery that will never end but will repeatedly and endlessly be interrupted by intervals of false blessedness. For what could be more false and deceptive than that blessedness in which we either do not know that we shall become miserable amid so great a light of truth, or fear it at the summit of supreme happiness? If we shall be ignorant of the coming calamity, then our misery here is better informed, since here we know that blessedness will come. But if the impending disaster will not be hidden from us there, then a miserable soul passes its time more happily while awaiting blessedness, after which it will be lifted up into blessedness, than a blessed soul does while awaiting misery, after which it will be cast back into misery. Thus the hope of our unhappiness is happy, and the hope of our happiness unhappy. Since here we suffer present evils and there fear those impending, it follows that we could always be more truly miserable than ever blessed.

3. But since these things are false, as piety cries out and truth proves—true happiness is indeed promised to us, a happiness whose secure possession will always be retained and never interrupted by any unhappiness—let us follow the straight way, which is Christ for us, and with him as guide and savior turn the path of faith and our mind away from the empty and foolish cycle of the impious.

If the Platonist Porphyry refused to follow the opinion of his fellow Platonists concerning these cycles and the souls’ ceaseless alternations of going and returning, whether moved by the emptiness of the matter itself or already showing reverence for Christian times—and, as I recalled in the tenth book, chapter 30, preferred to say that the soul was given over to the world in order to learn about evils, so that, once liberated and purified from them, it would suffer nothing of the kind thereafter when it returned to the Father—how much more ought we to detest and avoid this falsehood hostile to the Christian faith?

With these cycles emptied and defeated, no necessity compels us to think that the human race did not have a beginning in time merely because, through certain unknown cycles, nothing in the world is new that had not previously existed at fixed intervals and would not exist again afterward. For if a soul is liberated without returning to miseries, as no soul was ever previously liberated, something occurs in it that had never occurred before [Note: [Col. 0370] Some manuscripts have: “something occurs in it that had never occurred to it.”]—and something very great indeed, namely, an eternal happiness that never ends. If such novelty occurs in an immortal nature, repeated by no cycle and never to be repeated by any cycle, [Col. 0371] why is it claimed that novelty cannot occur in mortal things?

If they say that no novelty of blessedness occurs in the soul because it returns to the state in which it had always been, then certainly the liberation itself is new, since it is liberated from a misery in which it had never previously been; and the novelty of misery itself occurred in one who had never before experienced it. But if this novelty does not enter into the order of things governed by divine providence [Note: [Col. 0371] The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions have *ordine* (“in the order”) rather than *ordinem* (“into the order”).], but occurs by chance instead, where are those determined and measured cycles in which nothing new happens, but the same things that existed are repeated?

But if this novelty too is not excluded from the ordering of providence, whether the soul was given [Note: [Col. 0371] The Vindobonensis, Amerbach, and Erasmus editions have: “Whether the soul was exalted or had fallen.” The Louvain edition has: “Whether the soul was given or came from itself.” The manuscripts have the better reading: “Whether the soul was carried forth or had fallen.” The reference is evidently to two opinions: some taught that souls were given and sent into bodies by God, while others thought that they had fallen from heaven into bodies through their own fault to undergo punishment.] or had fallen, then things can occur that had never happened before and nevertheless are not alien to the order of things.

If the soul could bring upon itself through ignorance a new misery that was not unforeseen by divine providence, so that providence included this misery as well within the order of things and did not imprudently free the soul from it, with what rashness born of human vanity do we dare deny that divinity can make things new—not new for itself, but new for the world—which it had never made before and had never at any time had unforeseen?

But if they say that liberated souls will indeed not return to misery, yet that when this happens nothing new occurs in the world because different souls have always been liberated, are being liberated, and will be liberated, let them at least grant this: that new souls come into existence, for which there is both a new misery and a new liberation. For if they say that the souls are ancient and eternal in the past, and that new human beings are made from them each day, from whose bodies they are liberated—if they have lived wisely—in such a way that they never return to miseries, they will consequently have to say that the souls are infinite in number.

For however large the finite number of souls might have been, it could not suffice through infinite ages of the past for human beings always to be produced from it, whose souls would continually have to be liberated from this mortality and would never thereafter return to it. Nor will they in any way explain how, in things which they wish to be finite so that they may be known to God [Note: [Col. 0371] The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions have: “which they do not wish to be known to God because they are infinite.”], there can be an infinite number of souls.

4. Therefore, since those cycles have now been exploded—cycles through which the soul was thought necessarily to return to the same miseries—what remains more consistent with piety than to believe that it is not impossible for God both to make new things that he has never made before and, through ineffable foreknowledge, to have no mutable will?

As for whether the number of liberated souls that will never again return to miseries can always increase, let those who argue so subtly about restricting the infinity of things consider that question. We, however, bring our reasoning to an end from both sides. If that number can increase, what reason is there to deny that something could have been created which had never previously been created, if the number of liberated souls—which had never previously existed—not only came into existence once but will never cease coming into existence?

But if there must be a determinate number of liberated souls that will never return to misery, and this number will not increase thereafter, then whatever that number may be, it certainly never existed before. It could not, surely, grow and reach the limit of its quantity without some beginning; and that beginning had never previously existed in this manner. Therefore, in order that this might exist, the human being was created—before whom no human being existed.

## CHAPTER XXI.—Concerning the creation of one first human being, and of the human race in him

Having explained, as far as we could, this extremely difficult question—difficult because of God’s creating something new without any novelty in his will—it is not hard to see that what was done was much better: that the human race should multiply from one human being whom God first created, rather than begin from several.

For although he established some animals as solitary and, in a certain sense, isolated—that is, animals that prefer solitude, such as eagles, kites, lions, wolves, and whatever creatures are like them—and others as gregarious, preferring to live gathered together in herds, such as doves, starlings, deer, does [Note: [Col. 0372] He uses *damulas* as a diminutive because the animal is timid and neither wild nor tame. LUD. VIVES.], and other creatures of this kind, nevertheless he did not propagate either class from single individuals, but commanded several to exist together.

But the human being, whose nature he was forming as in some way intermediate between angels and beasts—so that, if submissively obedient to his Creator as his true Lord, he guarded his commandment with pious obedience, he would pass into angelic fellowship and obtain blessed immortality without the intermediary of death [Note: [Col. 0372] According to Coquaeus, this touches upon the Pelagian heresy; concerning it, see *On Heresies*, heresy 88.] and without any end; but if, using free will proudly and disobediently, he offended the Lord his God, he would be condemned to death, live like a beast as a slave of lust, and be destined after death for eternal punishment—God created as one individual, not to be left alone without human society, but so that through this arrangement the unity of that society and the bond of concord might be more strongly commended to him. Human beings would thus be bound together not only by similarity of nature but also by the affection of kinship. For God did not even choose to create the woman who was to be joined to the man in the same way as he created the man himself, but made her from him, so that the entire human race might be diffused from one human being.

## CHAPTER XXII.—That God foreknew that the human being whom he first created would sin, and likewise foresaw how great a people of the devout he would transfer from his offspring into angelic fellowship

God was not unaware that the human being would sin and, already subject to death, would propagate descendants destined to die. Nor was he unaware that mortals would progress in the enormity of sinning to such an extent that beasts lacking rational will would live more safely and peacefully among their own kind than human beings, although the beginnings of the former sprang forth in greater numbers from the waters and the earth [Col. 0373] [Note: [Col. 0373] Amerbach and most manuscripts have *plurimum* (“in very great number”).] than the human race, which was propagated from one individual to commend concord among human beings. For lions have never waged wars against lions, nor dragons against dragons, as human beings have against one another.

But he also foresaw that, by his grace, a people of the devout would be called to adoption, justified through the remission of sins, and joined in eternal peace to the holy angels by the Holy Spirit, once the last enemy, death, had been destroyed. For this people it would be beneficial to consider that God had established the human race from one human being in order to commend to human beings how pleasing to him is unity even among many.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—Concerning the nature of the human soul, created in the image of God

Therefore God made the human being in his own image. He created in him a soul such that, through reason and understanding, he would surpass all terrestrial, aquatic, and flying animals, which do not possess a mind of this kind.

And when he had formed the man from earthly dust and had given him the soul I have described—whether by breathing into him a soul he had already made, or rather by making it through the act of breathing [Note: [Col. 0373] Compare *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 7, no. 35.]—and had willed that the breath he made by breathing—for what else is breathing than making breath?—should be the human soul, he also made the man’s wife as a helper in procreation, taking a bone from his side, as God.

These things must not be imagined according to the custom of fleshly craftsmanship, as we see artisans fashioning from some earthly material, with bodily limbs, whatever forms their skill can produce. The hand of God is the power of God, who also invisibly works visible things. But those who measure God’s power and wisdom—which knows how to make even seeds themselves without seeds—from these familiar and daily works regard these things as mythical rather than true [Note: [Col. 0373] Amerbach has *ipsa certa facere* (“to make the very certain things”); several manuscripts have *ipsa quoque facere* (“to make these things also”).]. Since they do not understand the things established at the beginning, they think about them faithlessly—as though these very things that they know, if narrated to people who had never experienced them, would seem less incredible. Indeed, many people attribute even these things more to bodily natural causes than to the works of the divine mind.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—Whether angels can be called creators of any creature, however small

We have no business in these books with those who do not believe that the divine mind makes or cares for such things. But those who believe their Plato—that all mortal animals were made not by the supreme God who fashioned the world, but by lesser gods whom he himself created, with his permission or command, and that among these animals the human being holds a preeminent place and is akin even to the gods (*In Timaeo*)—if they rid themselves of the superstition by which they seek the grounds on which they might seem justified in offering sacred rites and sacrifices as though to their creators, will easily rid themselves also of this erroneous opinion.

For it is not permissible to believe or say that the creator of any nature, however small and mortal, is anyone other than God—and this even before the matter can be understood. As for the angels, whom they more readily call gods, even if they contribute their activity, whether commanded or permitted, to the things generated in the world, nevertheless we do not call them creators of animals any more than we call farmers creators of crops and trees.

## CHAPTER XXV.—That every nature and every form of the whole creation is formed solely by God’s work

There is one kind of form that is applied externally to any bodily material, as potters, smiths, and craftsmen of that kind work; they also paint and fashion forms resembling the bodies of animals. But there is another kind that possesses its efficient causes internally, proceeding from the secret and hidden decision of living and intelligent nature. This kind not only makes the natural forms of bodies but also makes the souls of living beings themselves, while they are not yet made.

The first kind of form should be attributed to all sorts of craftsmen; the second, however, belongs only to the one craftsman, Creator and Founder, God, who made the world itself and the angels without any world and without any angels.

By the divine and, so to speak, productive power—which does not know how to be made but knows how to make—the roundness of the heavens and the roundness of the sun received their form when the world was made. By that same divine and productive power, which does not know how to be made but knows how to make, the roundness of the eye and the roundness of an apple received their form. So too did the other natural shapes that we see in all things that are born, shapes not applied externally but produced by the Creator’s innermost power, who said: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24), and whose wisdom “reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1).

What kind of ministry the angels, having been made first, provided to the Creator as he made the rest, I do not know. I do not dare attribute to them what perhaps they cannot do, nor ought I detract from [Note: [Col. 0374] Most manuscripts have *denegare* (“deny”) rather than *derogare* (“detract from”).] what they can do. Nevertheless, I attribute the creation and establishment of all natures—by which it comes about that natures exist at all—to that God, with whose favor even the angels know, with thanksgiving, that they themselves owe their existence to him.

Therefore, we do not call farmers creators of any fruits when we read: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7). Nor do we call the earth itself a creator, although it appears to be the fertile mother of all things, bringing forth shoots and holding them fixed by their roots, since we likewise read: “God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body” (the same, 15:38).

Similarly, we ought not to call the woman the creator of her own childbearing, but rather him who said to one of his servants: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). And although the soul of a pregnant woman, affected in one way or another, may be able to clothe the fetus, as it were, with certain qualities, as Jacob caused livestock to be born with varied colors through variegated rods (Genesis 30:37), it did not itself make the nature that is born, any more than that nature made itself.

Therefore, whatever bodily or seminal causes are applied to generate things—whether through the activities of angels, human beings, or any animals, or through the union of males and females—and whatever desires or movements of the mother’s soul may be able to add something of shape or color to tender and soft conceptions, it is the supreme God alone who makes the very natures that are affected in one way or another within their own kind.

His hidden power, penetrating all things with undefiled [Note: [Col. 0375] The printed editions have *incommutabili* (“unchangeable”) rather than *incontaminabili* (“undefiled”).] presence, makes whatever exists in any way exist, to whatever extent it exists. For unless he makes it so, it could not be this or that, but could not exist at all [Note: [Col. 0375] Compare *On the Trinity*, book 3, nos. 13–16.].

Therefore, in the kind of form that craftsmen impose externally upon bodily things, we say that the city of Rome and the city of Alexandria had as their founders not the craftsmen and architects, but the kings by whose will, plan, and command they were built—Rome having Romulus, Alexandria Alexander. How much more, then, must we say that God alone is the founder of natures, since he makes nothing from material that he himself did not make, and has no workers except those whom he himself created? If he were to withdraw his power of fabrication, so to speak, from things, they would no longer exist, just as they did not exist before they were made.

But by “before” I mean in eternity, not in time. For who else is the creator of times except the one who made the things whose movements cause times to pass?

## CHAPTER XXVI.—Concerning the opinion of the Platonists, who thought that angels were created by God but were themselves the creators of human bodies
Thus Plato wanted the lesser gods, made by the supreme God, to be the makers of the other animals, so that they might receive their immortal part from him, but themselves attach the mortal part to it (*Timaeus*). Accordingly, he did not want them to be the creators of our souls, but of our bodies. Since Porphyry says that, for the purification of the soul, every body must be avoided, and since, together with his Plato and the other Platonists, he holds that those who have lived immoderately and dishonorably return to mortal bodies in order to undergo punishment—Plato, indeed, even to the bodies of beasts, but Porphyry only to those of human beings [Note: [Col. 0375] Compare above, Book 10, chapter 30]—it follows that they must say that these gods, whom they want us to worship as our parents and creators, are nothing other than the makers of our fetters and prisons; not our instructors, but our imprisoners and binders in wretched workhouses and grievous chains.

Either, then, the Platonists should stop threatening souls with punishments in these bodies, or they should not proclaim as gods to be worshiped those whose activity in us they urge us, as far as we can, to flee and escape—although both claims are utterly false. For souls do not undergo punishment in this way when they return to this life; and, among all living beings, whether in heaven or on earth, there is no creator except the one by whom heaven and earth were made.

For if there is no reason for living in this body except disgraceful punishments, how does the same Plato say that the world could not have been made most beautiful and best in any other way than by being filled with every kind of animal—that is, with immortal and mortal beings (*Timaeus*)? But if our formation, by which we have been created mortal, is a divine gift, how can it be a punishment to return to these bodies, that is, to divine benefits? And if God, as Plato constantly asserts, held in eternal intelligence the forms of all animals, just as he held those of the entire world, how could he not himself have created everything? Or would he have refused to be the craftsman of certain things whose creation was known to his ineffable and ineffably praiseworthy mind?

## CHAPTER XXVII — That in the first man there arose the entire fullness of the human race, in which God foresaw which portion would be honored with reward and which condemned to punishment

1. The true religion, therefore, rightly [Note: [Col. 0376] Thus all our manuscripts. In B., *quae* is absent. M.] recognizes and proclaims him as the creator of the whole universe and also of all animals—that is, of souls as well as bodies. Among earthly creatures, man was made preeminent by him in his image, for the reason I have stated, and perhaps for some other greater reason that remains hidden. He was made one, but he was not left alone. For no species is more discordant through vice and more social by nature than this one.

Human nature could not more suitably speak either against the vice of discord, warning that it should not arise, or for its healing once it had arisen, than by recalling that parent whom God therefore chose to create as one, from whom the multitude would be propagated, so that through this reminder unity might also be preserved in harmony among the many. The fact that the woman was made for him from his side also sufficiently signifies how dear the union of husband and wife ought to be.

These works of God are certainly unusual because they are the first. Those who do not believe these things ought not to believe in any miracles either; for if such things were produced by the customary course of nature, they would not be called miracles. Yet what is born under so great a governance of divine providence, even if its reason remains hidden, is born for no purpose. A sacred psalm says: “Come and see the works of the Lord, who has set miracles upon the earth” (Ps. XLV, 9). Why, then, the woman was made from the man’s side, and what this first miracle, in a certain sense, prefigured, I shall explain elsewhere, insofar as God assists me.

2. [XXVII.] Now, since this book must be brought to a close, let us suppose that in this first man, who was made at the beginning, the two societies in the human race—almost two cities—had already arisen, not yet in manifest reality, but in God’s foreknowledge. From him would come human beings who would be joined, some to evil angels in punishment, others to good angels in reward, by God’s hidden but nevertheless just judgment. For since it is written, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10), neither can his grace be unjust nor his justice cruel.

# BOOK THIRTEEN

In this book it is taught that death in human beings is punitive and arose from Adam’s sin.

[Col. 0377]

## CHAPTER I — The fall of the first man, through which mortality was contracted

Having dealt with the exceedingly difficult questions concerning the origin of our age and the beginning of the human race, the order of the subject now requires us to discuss the fall of the first man—or rather, of the first human beings—and the origin and propagation of human death.

For God did not create human beings in the manner in which he created the angels, so that even if they sinned they could in no way die. Rather, he created them so that, after they had fulfilled the duty of obedience, angelic immortality and blessed eternity would follow without the intervention of death; but that disobedience would be punished by death through a most just condemnation. We have already said this in the preceding book (chapter 21).

## CHAPTER II — The death that can befall the soul, which in some manner will always live, and the death to which the body is subject

But I see that I must discuss the very nature of death somewhat more carefully. Although the human soul is truly said to be immortal, it too has a certain kind of death. It is called immortal because, in some manner, however slight, it does not cease to live and perceive; the body, on the other hand, is called mortal because it can be deprived of all life and does not live at all by itself.

The death of the soul, therefore, occurs when God abandons it, just as the death of the body occurs when the soul abandons it. Thus the death of both things—that is, of the whole human being—occurs when the soul, abandoned by God, abandons the body. For then the soul does not live from God, nor the body from the soul.

This kind of death of the whole human being is followed by that which the authority of the divine utterances calls the “second death” (Rev. II, 11; XXI, 8). The Savior signified this when he said: “Fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

Since this does not occur until the soul has been so joined to the body that they are separated by no division, it may seem strange how the body is said to be killed by a death in which it is not abandoned by the soul, but remains animate, conscious, and tormented. For in that final and eternal punishment, which must be discussed more fully in its proper place, the death of the soul is rightly so called, because it does not live from God. But how can the death of the body be so called, when it lives from the soul? For otherwise it could not experience the bodily torments that will exist after the resurrection.

Is it because every kind of life is some good, whereas pain is an evil, and therefore the body should not be said to live when the soul is present in it not as the cause of living but of suffering? The soul, then, lives from God when it lives well; for it cannot live well unless God is at work within it, producing what is good. The body, however, lives from the soul when the soul lives in the body, whether the soul itself lives from God or not.

The life of the impious in their bodies is not the life of their souls but the life of their bodies. Even dead souls—that is, souls abandoned by God—can impart this life to their bodies, since their own limited life, by which they are also immortal, has not ceased.

Yet in the final condemnation, although the human being does not cease to perceive, because this perception is neither sweet with pleasure nor healthful in repose, but punitive through pain, it is more appropriately called death than life. It is called the second death because it follows the first, by which joined natures are separated—whether God and the soul, or the soul and the body.

Of the first death of the body, therefore, it can be said that it is good for the good and bad for the bad. The second, however, is certainly neither the possession of any good people nor good for anyone [Note: [Col. 0378] Compare Sermon 65].

## CHAPTER III — Whether the death that passed to all human beings through the sin of the first human beings is also the punishment of sin for the saints

A question necessarily arises that must not be concealed: Is the death by which soul and body are separated truly good for the good? [Note: [Col. 0378] On this question compare St. Jerome, Letter 24, on the death of Lea, and Letter 25, to Paula, on the death of her daughter Blesilla. COQUAEUS.]

For if it is, how can it be maintained that death itself is also the punishment of sin? The first human beings would certainly not have suffered it if they had not sinned. How, then, can that be good for the good which could not occur except to the bad? But again, if it could occur only to the bad, it ought not to be good for the good, but nothing at all. For why should there be any punishment where there was nothing to punish?

We must therefore admit that the first human beings were so constituted that, if they had not sinned, they would have experienced no kind of death. But those same first sinners were punished with death in such a way that everything arising from their stock was also held subject to that same punishment [Note: [Col. 0378] Some manuscripts: “is held subject.”]. For nothing other than what they themselves had been would be born from them.

Because of the magnitude of that fault, condemnation changed nature for the worse, so that what had preceded punitively in the first sinful human beings would also follow naturally in all who were born thereafter. For a human being does not come from a human being in the same way that a human being comes from dust. Dust was the material from which the human being was made; a human being, however, is the parent from whom a human being is begotten. Therefore, what earth is, flesh is not, although flesh was made from earth. But what the human parent is, the human offspring also is.

In the first human being, through the woman, the whole human race that would pass into descendants was present when that marital union received the divine sentence of its condemnation. And what the human being became—not when he was created, but when he sinned and was punished—this he begot, insofar as concerns the origin of sin and death.

He was not reduced by sin or punishment to the childish dullness and weakness of mind and body that we see in infants. God willed these conditions to be like the beginnings of the young of animals, whose parents he had cast down into a bestial life and death, as it is written: “When man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to the beasts without understanding and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII, 13).

Yet we also see infants weaker than the tenderest young of other animals in the use and movement of their limbs and in the perception by which they seek and avoid things—as though human power rose so much higher above the other living creatures precisely because its impulse, like an arrow stretched by a bow, had been drawn back and held in reserve.

The first man, therefore, did not fall or get driven by unlawful presumption and just condemnation into these childish beginnings. Rather, human nature was so corrupted and changed in him that he was forced to endure within his members the disobedience of desire resisting him, and was bound by the necessity of dying. Thus he begot what he had become through vice and punishment: beings subject to sin and death.

If infants are released from this bond of sin through the grace of the Mediator, they can suffer only that death which separates the soul from the body; but, once freed from their obligation to sin, they do not pass into that other punishment, the second death, which is without end.

## CHAPTER IV — Why death, that is, the punishment of sin, is not removed from those who have been absolved from sin through the grace of regeneration

If someone is troubled by the question why they suffer even death itself, if death too is the punishment of sin, when their guilt has been abolished through grace, this question has already been treated and resolved in another work of ours, which we wrote on the baptism of infants [Note: [Col. 0379] These are the three books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, whose title is supplemented by the words “and on the Baptism of Infants” in Book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 33].

There it was said that the soul is left to experience separation from the body, even though the bond of guilt has already been removed, because if bodily immortality immediately followed the sacrament of regeneration, faith itself would be weakened. Faith exists precisely when what is not yet seen in reality is awaited in hope [Note: [Col. 0379] Compare Book 2, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, nos. 49–55].

Through the strength and struggle of faith, at least in those of more mature age, the fear of death also had to be overcome. This was especially evident in the holy martyrs. Their struggle would have no victory and no glory—indeed, it could not be a struggle at all—if, after the washing of regeneration, the saints could no longer suffer bodily death.

When infants are to be baptized, who would not therefore hasten to the grace of Christ so that they might not be separated from the body? In that case faith would not be proved by an invisible reward; indeed, it would no longer be faith, since one would immediately seek and receive the reward of one’s work.

But now, through the greater and more marvelous grace of the Savior, the punishment of sin has been turned to the service of righteousness. At that time it was said to the human being, “You shall die if you sin.” Now it is said to the martyr, “Die, so that you may not sin.” At that time it was said, “If you transgress the commandment, you shall die” (Gen. II, 17). Now it is said, “If you refuse death, you will transgress the commandment.”

What was then to be feared so that sin might not be committed must now be accepted so that sin may not be committed. Thus, through God’s ineffable mercy, the punishment of vices itself passes into the weapons of virtue, and even the punishment of the sinner becomes the merit of the righteous.

At that time death was acquired through sinning; now righteousness is fulfilled through dying. This, however, applies to the holy martyrs, to whom the persecutor presents the alternatives either of abandoning the faith or of enduring death. The righteous prefer, by believing, to suffer what the first wicked suffered by refusing to believe. If those earlier people had not sinned, they would not have died; but these will sin unless they die. Those died because they sinned; these do not sin because they die.

Through the guilt of the former, it came about that punishment was reached; through the punishment of the latter, it comes about that guilt is not reached. This is not because death, which was previously an evil, has become some kind of good; rather, God has granted such great grace to faith that death—which is plainly opposed to life—has become the instrument by which one passes into life.

## CHAPTER V — Just as the wicked make bad use of the law, which is good, so the righteous make good use of death, which is evil

When the Apostle wished to show how powerful sin is for doing harm when grace does not come to our aid, he did not hesitate to call even the law by which sin is prohibited the “power of sin.” “The sting of death,” he says, “is sin; and the power of sin is the law” (1 Cor. XV, 56).

This is entirely true. Prohibition increases the desire for an illicit act when righteousness is not loved in such a way that the pleasure of sinning is overcome by the delight of righteousness. But only divine grace enables true righteousness to be loved and to give delight.

Yet lest the law be thought evil because it was called the power of sin, he himself, in another passage where he addresses this sort of question, says: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. What, then, that which is good, was made death to me?” “By no means. But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment” (Rom. VII, 12–13) [Note: [Col. 0380] Printed editions: “the sinful one or sin.” The manuscripts read: “sinful or sin.” In Greek: ἁμαρτωλὸς ἢ ἁμαρτία (*hamartōlos ē hamartia*), “sinful or sin.”].

He said “exceedingly,” because transgression is added when, through an increased desire to sin, the law itself is also despised.

Why have we thought this worth mentioning? Clearly because, just as the law is not evil when it increases the desire of sinners, so death is not good when it increases the glory of those who endure it: the one is abandoned for the sake of iniquity and makes transgressors, while the other is accepted for the sake of truth and makes martyrs.

Accordingly, the law is good because it prohibits sin; death, however, is evil because it is sin’s wage. But just as the unjust make bad use not only of evil things but also of good things, so the righteous make good use not only of good things but also of evil things.

Thus the wicked make bad use of the law, although the law is good; and the good die well, although death is evil.

## CHAPTER VI — The evil of general death, by which the union of soul and body is separated

[Col. 0381]

Therefore, as regards bodily death—that is, the separation of the soul from the body—when those who are called dying suffer it, it is good for no one. The force by which the two things that had been joined and bound together in the living person are torn apart has a harsh sensation and is contrary to nature, so long as it lasts, until all sensation arising from the union of soul and flesh is taken away.

Sometimes, however, a single blow to the body or a sudden seizure of the soul interrupts the entire distress and, because of its speed, does not permit it to be felt. Whatever it is in the dying that, with painful sensation, takes away sensation, when it is endured piously and faithfully, increases the merit of patience but does not remove the name of punishment.

Thus, although death is unquestionably the punishment of the one who is born, perpetuated through the propagation of the first human being, nevertheless, if it is paid for piety and righteousness, it becomes the glory of the one who is reborn. And although death is the repayment of sin, it sometimes obtains that nothing be repaid to sin.

## CHAPTER VII — The death accepted for confessing Christ by those who have not been regenerated

For whoever dies in confession of Christ without having received the washing of regeneration receives as much benefit toward the forgiveness of sins as if he had been washed in the sacred font of Baptism.

The one who said, “Unless anyone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 5), made an exception for these people in another statement, where he said no less generally: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X, 32). And elsewhere: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (ibid. XVI, 25).

This is why it is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV, 15). For what is more precious than a death by which all sins are forgiven and merits are increased still more abundantly?

Those who, because they could not postpone death, were baptized and departed from this life with all their sins erased do not possess as great a merit as those who, although they could have postponed death, did not postpone it for this reason: they preferred to end their life by confessing Christ rather than reach his Baptism by denying him.

If they had done so, even the sin by which they had denied Christ through fear of death would have been forgiven them in that washing—the same washing in which the crime of those who had killed Christ was also forgiven. But without an abundance [Note: [Col. 0381] Erasmus and the manuscripts read this way. Vindelinus and Amerbachius: “But when not unless through an abundance.” Lovaniensis: “But when only through an abundance.”] of the grace of that Spirit who “breathes where he wills” (John III, 8), how could they love Christ so greatly that, in such peril to their lives and with such hope of forgiveness, they could not deny him?

The precious death of the saints, for whom Christ’s death had been sent and granted beforehand with such great grace that they did not hesitate to expend their own lives in order to gain him, therefore showed that what had previously been established as the punishment of the sinner had been turned to this use, so that from it a more abundant fruit of righteousness might arise.

Death, then, should not be considered good because it has been turned to such great benefit—not by its own power, but by divine assistance.
