What was then set before human beings as something to fear, so that sin might not be committed, is now set before them as something to be accepted, so that sin may not be committed, that what has been committed may be erased, and that the palm of righteousness, due to a great victory, may be awarded.

## CHAPTER VIII — That in the saints the acceptance of the first death for the sake of truth is the release from the second death

If we consider the matter more carefully, even when someone dies faithfully and commendably for the sake of truth, death is being avoided. A portion of it is accepted precisely so that the whole of it may not befall him and so that the second death, which will never end, may not be added.

The separation of the soul from the body is accepted so that, when the soul has been separated from God, it may not also be separated from the body, and so that, once the first death of the whole human being has been completed, the eternal second death may not follow.

Therefore, as I said, death, when those who are dying suffer it and when it causes them to die, is good for no one, but it is endured commendably for the sake of retaining or attaining a good. When those who are now called dead are in it, however, it is not absurd to say that it is bad for the wicked and good for the good. The souls of the pious, separated from the body, are at rest; the souls of the impious suffer punishments, until their bodies rise again for eternal life in the case of the former and for eternal death, which is called the second death, in the case of the latter.

## CHAPTER IX — Whether the time in which the sense of life is taken away should be said to belong to the dying or to the dead

But should the time during which souls separated from the body are either in good things or in evils be called “after death” or rather “in death”? For if it is after death, then it is not death itself—which has been completed and passed away—but the soul’s present life after death, whether good or bad, that is good or bad.

Death was bad for them when it existed—that is, when they were suffering it, while they were dying—because they were undergoing a heavy and painful sensation, which the good use well. But once death has been completed, how can it be either good or bad when it no longer exists?

Moreover, if we attend still more carefully, neither will that appear to be death in which we said that the dying experience a heavy and painful sensation. For as long as they perceive, they are certainly still alive; and if they are still alive, they should be said to be before death rather than in death, because when death comes it removes all bodily sensation, which is painful as death approaches.

Accordingly, it is difficult to explain how we call them “dying” when they are not yet dead but are already being shaken by the final and deadly affliction as death approaches. Even if they are rightly called dying, when the death that now threatens arrives, they are called not dying but dead.

There is therefore no dying person except one who is living. For when someone is at that extreme point of life at which those are whom we say are giving up their soul, whoever has not yet been deprived of the soul is still alive. The same person, then, is simultaneously dying and living—but approaching death and departing from life [Note: [Col. 0382] The manuscripts read: “departing from life.”]. Yet he is still in life because the soul is present in the body; he is not yet in death because the soul has not yet departed from the body.

But if, once the soul has departed, he is not then in death but rather after death, when can anyone be said to be in death? For there will be no dying person if no one can be simultaneously dying and living; as long as the soul is in the body, we cannot deny that the person is living. Or, if someone should rather be called dying while his body is already undergoing the process of dying, and if no one can simultaneously be living and dying, I do not know when he is living.

## CHAPTER X — The life of mortals, which should be called death rather than life

From the moment anyone begins to exist in this mortal body, the process of death is continually taking place in him [Note: [Col. 0383] A large part of what Augustine says in this chapter is taken from Seneca, in various passages. LUD. VIVES.]. The mutability of this condition throughout the entire time of the present life—if it should be called life—works toward the arrival of death.

No one exists who is not closer to death after a year than he was before that year, closer tomorrow than today, today than yesterday, a little later than now, and now than a little earlier. Whatever time is lived is subtracted from the span of life; and each day what remains becomes less and less. Thus the whole of this life is nothing other than a journey toward death, in which no one is permitted either to stand still even briefly or to proceed somewhat more slowly. All are driven by the same motion and pushed forward by an approach that differs for no one.

A person whose life was shorter did not pass his days more quickly than one whose life was longer. Since equal moments were carried away equally from both, one had a nearer destination and the other a more distant one, toward which both ran at an equal speed. It is one thing to have traveled a greater distance and another to have walked more slowly. Therefore, the person whose passage through time extends farther toward death does not proceed more slowly but completes more of the journey.

If each person begins to die—or, what is the same thing, to be in death—from the moment death itself begins to take place in him, that is, from the moment life begins to be subtracted, then, when this subtraction has been completed, he will already be after death, not in death. Clearly, therefore, from the moment he begins to exist in this body, he is in death.

For what else takes place in each day, hour, and moment until the death that was in progress is completed, and the time after death begins—the time that was “in death” while life was being subtracted? Thus a human being is never in life from the moment he exists in this body, which is more a dying body than a living one, if he cannot be simultaneously in life and in death.

Or is he rather simultaneously in life and in death: in life, certainly, in which he lives until it is wholly taken away; but in death, because he is already dying as life is taken away? If he is not in life, what is being taken away until its complete exhaustion? But if he is not in death, what is the taking away of life itself? It is not without reason that, once life has been entirely taken away from the body, he is said to be after death, since death existed while life was being taken away.

For if, once life has been taken away, the human being is not in death but after death, when—unless it is while life is being taken away—will he be in death?

## CHAPTER XI — Whether anyone can be both living and dead at the same time

[Col. 0384]

1. But if it is absurd to say that a human being is already in death before he reaches death (for to what does he draw near by passing through the periods of his life, if he is already in it?), especially since it is highly unusual to say that one is simultaneously living and dying, when one cannot be simultaneously awake and asleep, we must ask when he is dying. For before death comes, he is not dying but living; when death has come, he will be dead, not dying. The former, therefore, is still before death; the latter is already after death. When, then, is he in death? (For then he is dying.) Thus, just as there are three expressions—before death, in death, after death—so three corresponding terms must be supplied: living, dying, and dead. Yet it is most difficult to determine when he is dying, that is, in death, where he is neither living, which is before death, nor dead, which is after death, but dying, that is, in death.

For as long as the soul is in the body, especially if sensation is also present, the human being, who consists of soul and body, undoubtedly lives; and therefore he must still be said to be before death, not in death. But when the soul has departed and taken away all bodily sensation, he is said to be dead and after death. Thus the point at which he is dying, or in death, disappears between the two: for if he still lives, he is before death; if he has ceased to live, he is already after death. Therefore one never apprehends him as dying, that is, in death.

Likewise, in the passage of time the present is sought and not found, because it has no duration through which one passes from the future into the past. Must we not then consider whether, by this reasoning, bodily death might be said not to exist? For if it exists, when does it exist—since it is in no point, and no one can be in it? For if one lives, it does not yet exist, because that is before death, not in death; but if one has already ceased to live, it no longer exists, because that too is after death, not in death. Yet again, if there is no death before or after, what is meant by the expressions “before death” and “after death”? These too are said vainly if there is no death.

And would that we had lived well in Paradise, so that death truly did not exist. But now it not only exists, but is so distressing that it can neither be explained by any manner of speech nor avoided by any reasoning.

2. Let us therefore speak according to customary usage [Note: [Col. 0384] Lovaniensis: “the usage of the Scriptures.” “Of the Scriptures” is absent from the other books.]; for we ought not to speak otherwise. Let us say “before death,” before death occurs, as it is written: “Before death, call no one blessed” (Ecclus. XI, 30). Let us also say, when it has occurred: “After his or her death, this or that happened.” And let us speak of the present time as best we can, as when we say, “That dying man made his will, and while dying left this or that to these persons and those”; although he could not do this at all except while living, and did it rather before death than in death.

Let us also speak as divine Scripture speaks, which does not hesitate to say that the dead too are in death, not after death. Hence: “For in death there is none who remembers you” (Ps. VI, 6). Until they rise again, they are rightly said to be in death, just as one is said to be in sleep until he wakes; although we call those in sleep sleeping, yet [Note: [Col. 0385] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “not.”] we cannot similarly call those who are already dead dying. For they are no longer dying who, as regards the bodily death now under discussion, have already been separated from their bodies.

But this is what I said cannot be explained by any manner of speech: how those who are dying are said to live, or how those already dead, even after death, are said still to be in death. For how are they after death if they are still in death? Especially since we do not call them dying, as we call those in sleep sleeping, those in sickness sick, those in pain suffering, and those in life living; whereas the dead, before they rise again, are said to be in death, yet cannot be called dying.

Hence I think it has happened neither inappropriately nor incongruously—though not through human contrivance, perhaps by divine judgment—that the Latin word *moritur* (“dies”) could not be declined even by grammarians according to the rule by which other such words are declined. From *oritur* (“arises”), for example, comes the past-tense expression *ortus est* (“has arisen”); and similar words are inflected by past participles. But if, from *moritur*, we seek a past-tense expression, the usual answer is *mortuus est* (“is dead”), with a doubled *u*. For *mortuus* is said as *fatuus*, *arduus*, *conspicuus*, and similar words are said: they are not past-tense forms, but, being nouns, are declined without reference to time. Yet the noun is used in place of a past participle, as though to decline what cannot be declined. It has therefore fittingly happened [Note: [Col. 0385] Many manuscripts read: “is used. Not unfittingly, therefore, it has happened,” etc.] that, just as what it signifies cannot be declined in action—that is, avoided—so the word itself cannot be declined in speech [Note: [Col. 0385] He plays on the ambiguity of *declinari*: it cannot be declined in action, that is, avoided; nor can it be inflected through grammatical moods in speech. LUD. VIVES.].

Yet through the aid of the grace of our Redeemer it can be brought about that we may at least avoid the second death. For that death is more grievous and the worst of all evils: it does not occur through the separation of soul and body, but rather through the union of both in eternal punishment. There, conversely, human beings will be neither before death nor after death, but always in death; and therefore they will never be living, never dead, but dying without end. For a human being will never be worse off in death than where death itself will be without death.

## CHAPTER XII — What death God threatened to the first human beings if they transgressed his command

When, therefore, it is asked what death God threatened the first human beings if they transgressed the command received from him and did not keep obedience—whether the death of the soul, of the body, of the whole human being, [Col. 0386] or the one called the second death—the answer must be: all of them. For the first consists of two deaths; the second consists wholly of them all. For just as the whole earth consists of many lands and the whole Church of many churches, so the whole of death consists of all deaths. The first death consists of two: one of the soul and the other of the body. Thus the first death of the whole human being occurs when the soul, without God and without the body, undergoes punishments for a time; but the second occurs where the soul, without God and with the body, undergoes eternal punishments.

Therefore, when God said to that first human being whom he had placed in Paradise, concerning the forbidden food, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II, 17), that threat encompassed not only the earlier part of the first death, in which the soul is deprived of God; nor only the later part, in which the body is deprived of the soul; nor only the whole first death itself, in which the soul, separated from both God and body, is punished; but every kind of death down to the last, which is called the second death, after which there is no other.

## CHAPTER XIII — What punishment the transgression of the first human beings first experienced
After the transgression of the command had taken place, immediately, when divine grace had departed, they were ashamed of the nakedness of their bodies. Therefore they covered their private parts with fig leaves, which perhaps were the first things discovered by them in their agitation (Gen. 3:7). These members had previously been the same, but they had not been private parts. Thus they experienced a new movement in their disobedient flesh, as though a corresponding punishment for their disobedience. For the soul, which had taken pleasure in its own freedom in a perverse way and had disdained to serve God, was being deprived of its former mastery over the body. And because it had abandoned its higher Lord according to its own will, it did not retain its lower servant according to its own will; nor did it possess the flesh as wholly subject to it, as it could always have done had it itself remained subject to God. Then the flesh began to desire against the spirit (Gal. 5:17), with which conflict we were born, drawing the origin of death and bearing in our members and corrupted nature the struggle—or victory—of that first transgression.

## CHAPTER XIV.—What sort of man was made by God, and into what condition he fell through the choice of his own will

For God, the author of natures, created man upright, not of course the author of vices. But man, voluntarily corrupted and justly condemned, generated descendants who were corrupted and condemned. For we were all in that one man when we were all that one man who fell into sin through the woman who had been made from him before sin. The individual form in which each of us would live had not yet been created and distributed to us separately; but there already existed the seminal nature from which we were to be propagated. Because this nature had been corrupted through sin, bound by the chain of death, and justly condemned, man could not be born from man in any different condition. Accordingly, from the evil use of free will arose this whole succession of calamity, which, through humanity’s corrupted origin—as through a corrupted root—leads the human race, by an interconnected series of miseries, all the way to the end of the second death, which has no end, except for those who are freed by the grace of God.  
[Col. 0386] [Note: Some manuscripts read “death.”]

## CHAPTER XV.—That Adam, by sinning, first abandoned God before he was abandoned by God; and that the first death of the soul was its departure from God

Therefore, even if in the words “You shall surely die” we understand only that death which occurs when the soul is abandoned by its life, which is God—for it was not abandoned so that it might abandon, but it abandoned so that it might be abandoned, since its will is prior to evil, while the will of its Creator is prior to its good, whether in creating it when it did not exist or in restoring it when it had fallen and perished—[Col. 0387] [Note: The manuscripts read, “because it had fallen and perished.”]—if, then, we understand God to have announced this death when he said, “On the day when you eat from it, you shall surely die,” as though he had said, “On the day when you abandon me through disobedience, I shall abandon you through justice,” then clearly the other deaths that were certainly to follow were also announced in that death.

For when the disobedient movement arose in the flesh of the disobedient soul, on account of which they covered their private parts, one death was experienced: that in which God abandoned the soul. This was signified by his words when he said to the man who, in irrational fear, was hiding himself, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). He was not asking because he was ignorant, but admonishing by reproach, so that the man might consider where he was—in a condition in which God was not.

But when the soul itself abandoned the body, which had been corrupted by age and worn out by old age, the second death came into experience. God, still punishing sin, had said of this to the man, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (ibid., 19). Thus from these two deaths was completed that first death which belongs to the whole man, and which is followed at the end by the second death unless man is freed by grace.

For the body that is from the earth would not return to the earth except by its own death, which occurred when it was abandoned by its life—that is, by the soul. Hence it is clear among Christians who truly hold the catholic faith that even the death of the body was inflicted upon us not by the law of nature—by which God made no death for man—but as the desert of sin. For God, avenging sin, said to the man in whom we were all then present, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

[Col. 0387] [Note: Manuscripts of good authority read “of man.” Thus manuscript 2051.]

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the philosophers who do not think that the separation of the soul from the body is punitive, although Plato represents the supreme God as promising the lesser gods that they will never be stripped of their bodies

### 1.

But the philosophers, against whose calumnies we defend the city of God—that is, his Church—think that they wisely ridicule our claim that the soul’s separation from the body must be counted among its punishments. They hold, namely, that the soul’s perfect blessedness comes to it when, completely stripped of every body, it returns to God simple, solitary, and in a certain sense naked.

If I found nothing in their writings with which this opinion could be refuted, I would have to argue at greater length in order to demonstrate that it is not the body itself but the corruptible body that is burdensome to the soul. Hence the statement from our Scriptures that we cited in the preceding book (book 15): “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). By adding “corruptible,” Scripture clearly indicated that it is not every kind of body, but the kind that was made such by the punishment following sin, which weighs down the soul. Even if it had not added that word, we ought to understand nothing else.

But since Plato most explicitly declares that the gods made by the supreme God possess immortal bodies, and represents that very God by whom they were made as promising them, as a great benefit, that they will remain forever with their bodies and will not be separated from them by any death, what is one to make of these men? Do they pretend not to know what they know in order to attack the Christian faith? Or do they prefer, in contradiction to themselves, to say things that oppose their own position, while never ceasing to oppose us?

These, indeed, are Plato’s words, as Cicero translated them into Latin.  
[Col. 0388] [Note: In the little book entitled *On the Universe*, which is part of Plato’s *Timaeus*. Compare below, book 22, chapter 26, and volume 5, sermon 241, section 8.]

In these words Plato represents the supreme God addressing the gods whom he had made and saying:

“You who have been born from the generation of the gods, consider from what works I am the father and maker. These are indissoluble against my will.”  
[Note: Printed editions read “indissoluble at my command.” The manuscripts, as in Cicero, read “against my will.” Perhaps this should be “not against my will.” For in Plato’s *Timaeus* the Greek is *emou ge thelontos*—“if I so will,” literally, “with my willing.”]

“Although everything bound together can be dissolved, it is not the part of a good being to wish to dissolve what has been bound by reason.”  
[Note: Printed editions read “it is good.” The manuscripts read “it is the part of a good being,” in agreement with Cicero and Plato’s Greek, *kalou*—“of the good.”]

“But since you have come into being, you cannot be immortal and indissoluble in yourselves. Yet you will certainly not be dissolved, nor will any fate of death destroy you, nor will they be stronger than my plan, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those bonds by which you were joined when you were generated.”  
[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “nor will they ever.”]

Behold: Plato says that the gods are mortal through the union of soul and body, yet immortal by the will and plan of the God by whom they were made. If, then, it is a punishment for souls to be joined to any kind of body, why does God, addressing them as though they were anxious that they might perhaps die—that is, be separated from the body—make them secure of their immortality? He does not do so because of their nature, as though it were compacted rather than simple, but because of his unconquerable will, by which he is powerful enough to ensure that beings who have come into existence do not perish and that what has been joined together is not dissolved, but continues incorruptibly.

### 2.

Whether Plato speaks truly about the stars is another question. We must not immediately grant him that these spheres of light, or little globes shining with bodily light above the earth by day or by night, live by means of certain souls of their own—souls that are intellectual and blessed. He persistently asserts the same thing concerning the universe itself, as though it were one enormous animal containing all other animals.  
[Col. 0388] [Note: Plato says this frequently in the *Timaeus* and the *Epinomis*.]

But, as I said, this is another question, which we have not undertaken to examine now. I have mentioned this one point against those who glory in being called or being Platonists, yet are ashamed to be Christians lest a name they share with the common crowd should make cheap the pride of the cloak-wearers—a pride all the more inflated because they are so few. [Col. 0389] [Note: By “cloak-wearers” he means philosophers. Hence Aulus Gellius, 9.2, says of a man who falsely professed philosophy by his grooming and dress: “I see a beard and a cloak; I do not yet see a philosopher.”] Seeking something to criticize in Christian teaching, they attack the eternity of bodies, as though these things were mutually contradictory: that we should seek the soul’s blessedness and yet wish it always to remain in a body, as though bound to a wretched chain.

Yet Plato, their author and teacher, says that the supreme God granted to the gods made by him the gift that they should never die—that is, that they should never be separated from the bodies with which he joined them.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Against those who assert that earthly bodies cannot be made incorruptible and eternal

### 1.

These men also contend that earthly bodies cannot be everlasting, although they do not doubt that the earth itself is an everlasting member of their god—not indeed of the supreme god, but of the great god whom they identify with the whole of this world—and that it is placed at the center.

Since, then, this supreme god made for them another being whom they regard as a god—namely, this world, which Plato in the *Timaeus* says is to be preferred to the other gods beneath it—and since they consider this world to be animate, containing, as they claim, a rational or intellectual soul within so vast a bodily mass; and since they hold that its four elements have been established as members of its body, set and arranged in their proper places, and wish their union to be indissoluble and eternal so that this great god of theirs may never die, what reason is there for the earth to be eternal as a central member in the body of the greater animal, while the bodies of other earthly animals cannot be eternal if God so wills?

“The earth,” they say, “must be returned to the earth from which the bodies of earthly animals were taken.” Thus, they say, those bodies must necessarily be dissolved and die, and in this way be restored to the stable and eternal earth from which they had been taken.

If someone should similarly make the same claim about fire and say that the bodies taken from the universal fire in order to make heavenly animals must be returned to it, would not the immortality that Plato, as though speaking for the supreme God, promised to such gods be destroyed by the force of this argument? Or does this not happen there because God does not will it—God whose will, as Plato says, is overcome by no force?

What, then, prevents God from accomplishing the same thing with earthly bodies, since Plato confesses that God can ensure that beings who have come into existence do not perish, that things which have been joined together are not dissolved, that things taken from the elements are not returned to them, and that souls placed in bodies never abandon them but enjoy immortality and everlasting blessedness with them?  
[Col. 0389] [Note: Some manuscripts read “bound” instead of “joined.”]

Why, then, could he not make earthly bodies immortal? Is God powerful only as far as Christians believe, and not as far as Platonists wish? Clearly the philosophers were able to know the plan and power of God, while the prophets were not? For, on the contrary, the Spirit of God taught his prophets to proclaim his will, insofar as he deigned to reveal it, whereas human conjecture deceived the philosophers in their attempt to understand it.

### 2.

Yet they ought not to have been deceived to such an extent—not merely through ignorance but even more through obstinacy—[Col. 0390] [Note: The manuscripts read “but even more”; the printed editions read “indeed even more.”]—that they should openly contradict themselves. On the one hand, they assert with great argumentative force that, in order to be blessed, the soul must flee not merely an earthly body but every body whatsoever; on the other, they say that the gods possess supremely blessed souls while nevertheless being bound to eternal bodies: the heavenly gods to bodies of fire, and Jupiter’s soul—Jupiter whom they identify with this world—to all the bodily elements through which this entire mass rises from earth to heaven.

For Plato thinks that this soul extends and spreads from the innermost center of the earth—which geometers call the center—through all its parts to the highest and farthest reaches of heaven, by means of musical numbers. Thus this world is the greatest, most blessed, and eternal animal, whose soul possesses the perfect happiness of wisdom and does not abandon its own body; and whose body lives forever from that soul and cannot dull or retard it, although it is not simple but compacted from so many and such various bodies.

Since they allow these things on the basis of their own conjectures, why do they refuse to believe that, by divine will and power, earthly bodies can be made immortal, so that souls living in them may not be separated by any death or weighed down by any of their burdens, but may live eternally and happily?  
[Col. 0390] [Note: Compare book 6 of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, sections 36–37.]

They assert that God can do this for their gods in bodies of fire, and for Jupiter himself, their king, in all the bodily elements. For if every body must be fled by the soul in order for it to be blessed, let their gods flee from the spheres of the stars; let Jupiter flee from heaven and earth. Or, if they cannot, let them be judged miserable.

But these men want neither alternative. They do not dare grant their gods separation from bodies, lest they appear to worship mortal beings; nor do they grant them deprivation of blessedness, lest they admit that their gods are unhappy.

Therefore, not every body must be fled in order to attain blessedness, but corruptible, troublesome, burdensome, dying bodies—not bodies such as God’s goodness made for the first human beings, but such as the punishment of sin compelled them to be.

[Col. 0390] [Note: Compare sermon 241, section 67.]

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On earthly bodies, which philosophers assert cannot exist in heaven because what is earthly is said by its natural weight to be drawn toward the earth

“But,” they say, “it is necessary that the natural weight of earthly bodies either hold them in the earth or force them toward the earth; and therefore they cannot exist in heaven.”  
[Col. 0390] [Note: Compare the book *On Faith and the Creed*, section 13.]

The first human beings were indeed on the earth, in a wooded and fruitful place that received the name paradise. But since this too must be answered—whether on account of Christ’s body with which he ascended into heaven, or on account of the bodies that the saints will have in the resurrection—let them consider earthly weights somewhat more carefully.

If human art can make vessels from metals that immediately sink when placed in water, and can make them float by certain methods, how much more credibly and effectively can some hidden mode of God’s operation—by whose almighty will, Plato says, beings that have come into existence do not perish and things that have been joined together cannot be dissolved—enable earthly masses to be supported? God can do this much more wonderfully with incorporeal beings joined to corporeal ones than with any corporeal things joined to any other corporeal things. He can ensure that earthly bodies are not depressed by weight into the depths, and can grant souls that are perfectly blessed the ability to place their earthly yet already incorruptible bodies wherever they wish and to move them wherever they wish, with the greatest ease of position and motion.

If angels can do this—seizing earthly animals from wherever they wish and setting them wherever they wish—should we believe either that they cannot do it without effort or that they feel the burden? [Col. 0391] [Note: “Without effort” is absent from the manuscripts.] Why, then, should we not believe that the spirits of the saints, perfected and blessed by God’s gift, can carry their bodies without any difficulty wherever they wish and set them wherever they wish?

For just as, with earthly bodies, we are accustomed to experience their weight when carrying loads, so that the greater the quantity, the greater the heaviness—more pounds pressing more than fewer—the soul nevertheless carries the members of its flesh more lightly when they are robust in health than when they are wasted by illness. [Col. 0391] [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “more lightly.”] And although a healthy and vigorous person is more burdensome to another who carries him than a thin and sick person, [Col. 0391] [Note: Vindobonensis and the manuscripts read “sound” (*salvus*).] he himself is more agile in moving and carrying his own body when he has greater bodily mass in good health than when, in disease or famine, he has the least strength.

Thus, even in the case of earthly bodies, though they are still corruptible and mortal, what matters is not the weight of their quantity but the manner of their bodily condition. And who could express in words how great the difference is between the present condition that we call health and the immortality that is to come?

Let philosophers, then, not refute our faith on the basis of the weights of bodies. I do not wish to ask why they do not believe that an earthly body can exist in heaven, since the whole earth is suspended in nothingness. Perhaps, indeed, an argument concerning the very center of the world, because all heavier things converge upon it, might appear more plausible.

I say this: if the lesser gods, to whom Plato entrusted the making even of man among the other earthly animals, were able—as he says—to remove the quality of burning from fire while leaving the quality of shining that flashes through the eyes (ibid.), shall we hesitate to grant this power to the supreme God? Plato granted to the will and power of that God that beings which have come into existence should not die, and that things so diverse and unlike—corporeal and incorporeal—joined together should not be separated by any dissolution.

Can God not remove corruption from human flesh to which he grants immortality, while leaving its nature, preserving the harmony of its form and members, and taking away the slowness caused by weight?

But concerning the faith in the resurrection of the dead and their immortal bodies, we must discuss the matter more carefully, if God wills, at the end of this work.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Against the doctrines of those who do not believe that the first human beings would have been immortal if they had not sinned

[Col. 0392]

Let us now explain what we undertook to say about the bodies of the first human beings. Neither this death—which is said to be good for the good—nor merely by a few who understand or believe, but by all known, namely the separation of the soul from the body, by which the body of a living creature that was plainly alive plainly dies, could have happened to them unless it followed the desert of sin.

Although there can be no legitimate doubt that the souls of righteous and devout people live in repose after death, it would nevertheless have been far better for them to live with their bodies in good health.  
[Col. 0392] [Note: Compare book 12 of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, section 68, and the *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 14, section 2.]

Indeed, even those who in every respect consider existence without a body to be the highest blessedness are refuted by a judgment that contradicts their own opinion. For no one would dare to place those wise men of theirs—whether they are going to die or have already died, that is, whether they are without bodies or are about to abandon their bodies—above the immortal gods, to whom, according to Plato, the supreme God promises the great gift of indissoluble life, namely eternal fellowship with their bodies.

The same Plato considers human beings to be treated most favorably if they have lived this life devoutly and justly, so that, separated from their bodies, they may be received into the bosom of those gods who never abandon their own bodies (in the *Phaedo* and *Phaedrus*):

> Surely, forgetful of these things, let them look again upon the vaults above,  
> And begin once more to wish to return into bodies.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.750–751.)

Virgil is praised for having expressed this from Platonic doctrine. For Plato thinks that the souls of mortals can neither remain forever in their own bodies, but are dissolved by the necessity of death, nor endure perpetually without bodies. Rather, by alternating turns, he thinks that the living continually become dead and the dead living.

He holds that the wise differ from other human beings in this respect: after death they are carried to the stars, where each rests somewhat longer in the star suited to him, and then, having forgotten his former misery and overcome by the desire to possess a body, returns to the labors and hardships of mortals. Those who have led a foolish life, however, are immediately sent back into bodies suited to their deserts, whether human or animal (in the *Phaedrus*).

Thus he places even good and wise souls in this most wretched condition: bodies are not assigned to them with which they might live forever and immortally, so that they can neither remain in bodies nor endure eternal purity without them.

We have already said in the earlier books—especially book 10, chapter 30—that Porphyry, in the Christian era, became ashamed of this Platonic doctrine. He not only removed the bodies of animals from human souls, but also wished the souls of the wise to be freed from bodily bonds in such a way that, fleeing every body, they might remain blessed forever with the Father.

Therefore, lest he appear to be defeated by Christ, who promises the saints everlasting life, Porphyry too placed purified souls in eternal happiness without any return to their former miseries. But, in opposing Christ, he denied the resurrection of incorruptible bodies and asserted that souls would live forever not only without earthly bodies but without any bodies whatsoever.

[Col. 0393] [Note: See below, book 22, chapter 27.]

Yet even with this opinion, whatever its character, he did not at least instruct them not to submit in religious service to gods who possess bodies. Why was this, unless he did not believe that souls, although joined to no body, were better than those gods?

Therefore, if these men will not dare—and I do not think they will dare—to place human souls above gods who are supremely blessed and yet established in eternal bodies, why do they consider it absurd that the Christian faith proclaims that the first human beings were created in such a way that, if they had not sinned, they would not have been released from their bodies by any death? Instead, having been granted immortality as the reward of preserved obedience, they would have lived forever with their bodies; and that the saints will have such bodies in the resurrection—the very bodies in which they labored here—that neither corruption nor difficulty can affect their flesh, nor pain and unhappiness their blessedness?

## CHAPTER XX.—That the flesh of the saints, which now rests in hope, is to be restored to a better condition than that of the first human beings before sin

Accordingly, the souls of the departed saints do not now regard as grievous the death by which they were separated from their bodies, because their flesh rests in hope, however much it may seem to have suffered insults without any remaining sensation.

For, contrary to Plato’s view, they do not desire bodies to be obliterated through forgetfulness.  
[Col. 0393] [Note: So read Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the better manuscripts. Erasmus reads “bodies forgetfulness”; the Louvain edition, “forgetfulness of bodies.”]

Rather, because they remember what has been promised to them by him who deceives no one—who even gave them assurance concerning the preservation of the hairs of their heads (Luke 21:18)—they eagerly and patiently await the resurrection of the bodies in which they endured many hardships, knowing that they will suffer nothing of that kind in them thereafter.

For if they did not hate their flesh when, because of its weakness, they restrained it by spiritual authority as it resisted their mind (Eph. 5:29), how much more will they love it when it too becomes spiritual?  
[Col. 0393] [Note: Several manuscripts read “as it resisted.”]

Just as the spirit serving the flesh may appropriately be called carnal, so the flesh serving the spirit will rightly be called spiritual—not because it will be changed into spirit, as some think on the basis of what is written, “The natural body is sown; the spiritual body shall rise” (1 Cor. 15:42), [Col. 0393] [Note: Origen, in the books *On First Principles* (*peri Archôn*), says that every bodily creature will be changed into spiritual bodies, and that all substance will be transformed into one most pure body, purer than every splendor, and such as the human mind cannot now conceive. “And afterward,” he says, “God will be all in all,” so that all bodily nature may be reduced to that substance which is better than all others, namely the divine substance, than which none is better. Ludovicus Vives.] but because it will be subjected to the spirit with the highest and wondrous ease of obedience, so that, with every experience of distress, every corruptibility, and every sluggishness removed, it will possess the most secure will of indissoluble immortality.  
[Col. 0393] [Note: Some books read “capacity” instead of “ease.”] [Note: Manuscript 2051 reads “up to the fullness of immortality”; manuscript 2050, “up to the fulfillment of immortality.”]

For it will not merely be unlike what it now is in any excellent state of health;  
[Col. 0394] it will not even be like what it was in the first human beings before sin.

Although they would not have died had they not sinned, they nevertheless used food as human beings, while still bearing earthly bodies that were natural, not yet spiritual. Although these bodies would not grow old through age and thus be driven by necessity toward death—their condition was wonderfully preserved for them by the tree of life, which stood in the middle of paradise together with the forbidden tree—they nevertheless consumed other foods besides the fruit of the one tree that had been forbidden.

That tree was not evil in itself; it was forbidden in order to commend the good of pure and simple obedience, which is a great virtue in a rational creature established under the Creator and Lord. For where no evil was touched, if the forbidden thing was touched, the only sin was disobedience.

Thus they were nourished by the other things they consumed, so that their natural bodies would not experience any distress through hunger or thirst. [Col. 0394] [Note: Some manuscripts read, “Therefore it was sustained”; manuscript 2051, “Therefore it was sustained by the things they consumed.”] They tasted the fruit of the tree of life so that death would not somehow steal upon them from elsewhere, or so that, worn out by old age after the passage of time, they would not perish. The other foods were as nourishment; that tree was as a sacrament.

Thus the tree of life in the bodily paradise may be understood in the same way as Wisdom, the mother of all good things, in the spiritual—that is, intelligible—paradise, concerning which it is written, “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Prov. 3:18).  
[Col. 0394] [Note: Only the Louvain edition adds “to all.”]

## CHAPTER XXI.—On the paradise in which the first human beings lived: how, without compromising the truth of the historical account concerning a bodily place, something spiritual may rightly be understood through its symbolism

Accordingly, some people refer the whole paradise in which, according to the truth of sacred Scripture, the first human beings, the parents of the human race, are said to have lived, to intelligible things. They transform those trees and fruit-bearing plants into virtues and ways of life.  
[Col. 0394] [Note: Philo the Jew, at the end of *On the Creation of the World* and in the first book of the *Allegories of the Law*, interprets Moses’ account of paradise solely mystically and allegorically and considers that it ought not to be understood in any other way. Origen likewise does so in his works on Genesis and in book 4, chapter 2, of *On First Principles*. Coquaeus.]

They act as though those visible and bodily things did not exist, but had been described or written in that form merely to signify intelligible things. As though paradise could not have been bodily because it can also be understood spiritually. As though there were not two women, Hagar and Sarah, and from them two sons of Abraham, one from a slave woman and the other from a free woman, because the Apostle says that the two Testaments were prefigured in them (Gal. 4:22–24). Or as though water did not flow from a rock when Moses struck it (Exod. 17:6; Num. 20:11) because Christ can also be understood there through a figurative meaning, as the same Apostle says, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

Therefore no one forbids us to understand paradise as the life of the blessed; its four rivers as the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice; its trees as all useful disciplines; the fruits of the trees as the conduct of the devout; the tree of life as Wisdom herself, the mother of all good things; and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as the experience of transgressing the command.

God established punishment for sinners rightly and justly, but man does not experience it for his own good.

These things may also be understood in the Church, so that we may regard them more properly as prophetic signs anticipating future realities: paradise itself as the Church, as we read of it in the Song of Songs (Song 4:13); the four rivers of paradise as the four Gospels; the fruit-bearing trees as the saints; their fruits as their works; the tree of life as the Holy of Holies, namely Christ; and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as the proper exercise of the will.

For man cannot use his own will without harm when he despises the divine will. Thus he learns the difference between clinging to the good that is common to all and taking pleasure in what is his own. Loving himself, he is handed over to himself, so that, filled with fears and sorrows, he sings in the Psalm—provided that he perceives his evils—“My soul within me is troubled” (Ps. 41:7). Once corrected, he says, “I will keep my strength toward you” (Ps. 58:10).

Let these things be said, and any others that may more suitably be said, about understanding paradise spiritually, with no one forbidding it—provided that the historical truth of that account is also believed, commended as it is by a completely trustworthy narrative of events.

## CHAPTER XXII.—On the bodies of the saints after the resurrection, which will be spiritual in such a way that the flesh will not be changed into spirit

The bodies of the righteous, therefore, which will exist in the resurrection will need neither any tree by which they may be enabled not to die from sickness or from growing old through age, nor any other bodily foods by which the slightest distress of hunger and thirst may be avoided. They will be clothed with the sure and altogether inviolable gift of immortality, so that they will eat only if they wish, by possibility and not by necessity.

Angels too have done this when they appeared visibly and tangibly—not because they needed food, but because they wished and were able to do so, in order to accommodate themselves to human beings through a certain human-like condescension appropriate to their ministry.  
[Col. 0395] [Note: Compare Letter 102, section 6.]

For we must not believe that the angels ate only in appearance when human beings received them as guests (Gen. 18; Tob. 11), although, to those who did not know that they were angels, they appeared to eat with a need like ours.

Hence the angel says in the Book of Tobit, “You saw me eating, but you saw only with your eyes” (Tob. 12:19). That is: you thought that I was taking food because I needed to restore my body, as you do.

But if something else concerning angels can perhaps be argued more plausibly, Christian faith certainly has no doubt concerning the Savior himself: after the resurrection, although already possessing spiritual flesh, he nevertheless took food and drink with his disciples (Luke 24). It is not the ability to eat and drink, but the need to eat and drink, that will be removed from such bodies.

Therefore they will be spiritual—not because they will cease to be bodies, but because they will subsist through the life-giving spirit.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—What is to be understood by the natural body and the spiritual body; and who die in Adam, while others are made alive in Christ
1. For just as these bodies, which have a living soul but not yet a life-giving spirit, are called “animal bodies” [Col. 0396]—yet they are not souls, but bodies—so those bodies are called “spiritual.” But far be it from us to believe that they will become spirits; rather, they will be bodies possessing the substance of flesh, yet suffering no carnal sluggishness or corruption because of the life-giving spirit. Then the human being will be heavenly, not earthly—not because the body formed from earth will no longer be the same body, but because, by a heavenly gift, it will become such that it is suited even to inhabiting heaven, not by losing its nature but by changing its quality.

The first man, however, was “from the earth, earthly” (I Cor. XV, 47), and was made a living soul, not a life-giving spirit; this latter condition was reserved for him as the reward of obedience. Therefore it is beyond doubt that his body, which needed food and drink so that it would not suffer hunger and thirst, and which was preserved from the necessity of death and maintained in the flower of youth—not by that complete and indissoluble immortality, but by the tree of life—was not spiritual but animal. Nevertheless, he would certainly not have died unless, by transgressing, he had fallen under the sentence pronounced and threatened by God.

And although he was not denied food even outside paradise, nevertheless, when he had been excluded from the tree of life, he would have been handed over to the passage of time and to old age, and destined for an end [Note: [Col. 0396] Thus the manuscripts of the best quality. The printed editions, however, read: “he would have been brought more slowly to an end by time and old age.”]—in that life alone which, even in an animal body, he could have possessed perpetually in paradise, until he became spiritual through the merit of obedience, if he had not sinned.

Therefore, even if we understand that the manifest death by which the soul is separated from the body was also signified in what God had said, “On the day you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Gen. II, 17), it should not for that reason seem absurd that they were not separated from the body on the very day on which they ate the forbidden and deadly food. For on that day their nature was changed and corrupted for the worse, and, through their most just separation from the tree of life, the necessity of bodily death was also established in them—the necessity with which we are born.

For this reason the Apostle does not say, “The body will be dead because of sin,” but says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.” Then he adds: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. VIII, 10–11). Thus the body that is now a living soul will then become a life-giving spirit; yet the Apostle calls it dead because it has already been bound by the necessity of dying.

At that earlier time, however, it was a living soul, though not a life-giving spirit, in such a way that it could not rightly be called dead, because it could not have acquired the necessity of dying except through the commission of sin. But since God, by saying “Adam, where are you?” signified the death of the soul, which occurred when he abandoned God, and by saying “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 9, 19), signified the death of the body, which occurs when the soul departs from it [Note: [Col. 0396] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “when it departs.”], we should not suppose that he said nothing about the second death because he wished it to remain concealed on account of the dispensation of the New Testament [Col. 0397], in which the second death is most plainly declared. His purpose was that this first death, which is common to all, should first be shown to have come from that sin which, having been committed in one man, became common to all. The second death, however, is certainly not common to all, because of those who are called according to the purpose [Note: [Col. 0397] The printed editions read, “the saints who are called,” and below, “to be conformed.” The manuscripts have neither “the saints” nor “to be conformed”; these words are also absent from the Greek text of the Apostle.], whom, as the Apostle says, he foreknew and predestined “to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII, 28–29), and whom by the grace of God, through the Mediator, he delivered from the second death [Note: [Col. 0397] In some manuscripts the twenty-third chapter begins here.]

2. The Apostle speaks in this way about the first man’s having been made an animal body. For, wishing to distinguish what is now animal from what will be spiritual in the resurrection, he says: “It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body.” Then, to prove this, he says: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one.” And to show what an animal body was, he says: “Thus it is written: ‘The first man was made a living soul.’”

In this way, therefore, he wished to show what an animal body is, although Scripture did not say of the first man, who was called Adam, when his soul was created by the breath of God, “The man was made an animal body,” but rather, “The man was made a living soul” (Gen. II, 7). Thus, in what is written, “The first man was made a living soul,” the Apostle wished the human body to be understood as animal.

He showed how the spiritual body should be understood by adding, “But the last Adam became a life-giving spirit”—unquestionably signifying Christ, who rose from the dead in such a way that he could no longer die at all. Finally, he continues and says: “But not first the spiritual, but the animal; afterward, the spiritual.” Here he declared much more plainly that he had indicated the animal body in the statement that the first man was made a living soul, and the spiritual body in the statement, “The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.”

The animal body comes first—the kind possessed by the first Adam, although he would not have died unless he had sinned; the kind we now possess, insofar as his nature was changed and corrupted in him after he sinned, so that it acquired the necessity of dying; and the kind Christ himself first deigned to possess for our sake, not from necessity but by power. Afterwards there will be the spiritual body, such as has already gone before in Christ as our head, and such as will follow in his members at the final resurrection of the dead.

3. The Apostle then adds the clearest distinction between these two men, saying: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, such are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven” (I Cor. XV, 42–49).

The Apostle presented this in such a way that it is now accomplished in us according to the sacrament of regeneration, as he says elsewhere: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galat. III, 27). In reality, however, it will be completed then, when what is now animal in us through birth has become spiritual through resurrection. To use his own words, “We have been saved in hope” (Rom. VIII, 24).

We have put on the image of the earthly man through the propagation of transgression and death, which birth has brought upon us. But we put on the image of the heavenly man through the grace of forgiveness and eternal life, which regeneration grants us only through the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Tim. II, 5). He is to be understood as the heavenly man because he came from heaven to be clothed with a body of earthly mortality, so that he might clothe it with heavenly immortality.

He calls the others heavenly because by grace they become his members, so that with them Christ is one, as head and body [Note: [Col. 0398] This view was held by Origen, *On First Principles*, book 1, chapter 3; Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 5; Cyprian, *Letter to Jubaianus*; Cyril, book 9 on John, chapter 47; Basil, on Psalm 48; Ambrose, *On Paradise*; Philaster; and others. Compare book 2 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, sections 10–11.]

In the same Epistle he states this still more clearly: “By a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 21–22)—now, of course, in the spiritual body, which will be a life-giving spirit.

This does not mean that all who die in Adam will be members of Christ—for among them many more will be punished by the second death forever—but the words “all” and “all” are used because, just as no one dies in an animal body except in Adam, so no one is made alive in a spiritual body except in Christ.

Accordingly, we must by no means suppose that at the resurrection we will have a body such as the first man had before sin. Nor should the statement, “As was the earthly, such are the earthly,” be understood according to what came about through the admission of sin. We must not imagine that before he sinned he had a spiritual body, which was changed into an animal body as a punishment for sin.

To think this is to pay insufficient attention to the words of so great a teacher, who says: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one,” and then adds, “As it is written, ‘The first man Adam was made a living soul.’” Was this made after sin, when this is the first condition of the human being, concerning which the blessed Apostle took this testimony from the Law in order to demonstrate the animal body?

## CHAPTER XXIV  
How that breathing should be understood by which the first man was made a living soul, and also that which the Lord performed when he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit”

1. For this reason some have thought, with insufficient consideration, that in the passage which reads, “God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Gen. II, 7), the soul was not then given to the first man, but that the soul already present in him was made alive by the Holy Spirit. They are moved by the fact that, after the Lord Jesus had risen from the dead, he breathed upon his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22). Thus they suppose that something similar occurred then, as though the Evangelist had continued here by saying, “And they became living souls.”

If this had indeed been said, we would understand that the Spirit of God is a certain life of souls, without which rational souls must be regarded as dead, although their presence makes bodies appear to live. But the words of the book itself clearly testify that this is not what happened when the human being was created. They read as follows: “And God formed the man, dust from the earth” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ludovicus Vives: The Septuagint translated this, *Kai eplasen ho Theos ton anthrōpon, choun labōn apo tēs gēs*: “And God fashioned the man, taking dust from the earth.” I suspect that one word is missing at this point in Augustine’s text, so that it should read either, “God fashioned the man, taking dust from the earth,” or, with an ablative, “God fashioned the man, with dust taken from the earth.” Laurinus’s codex has *pulvere* (“with dust”). Yet in the Chaldean Targum it reads, “God created the man, dust from the earth.”]

Some, thinking that this should be interpreted more plainly, said, “And God fashioned the man from the clay of the earth.” For it had been said above, “A spring rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth” (Gen. II, 6), so that “clay” might be understood as earth combined with moisture. For immediately after this statement comes: “And God formed the man, dust from the earth,” as the Greek manuscripts have it, from which this Scripture was translated into Latin [Note: [Col. 0399] He indicates that the Churches formerly used a Latin translation from the Greek Septuagint, which was later succeeded by Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew.]

Whether one says “formed” or “fashioned”—the Greek word is *eplasen* (ἔπλασεν)—it makes no difference to the matter; nevertheless, “fashioned” is more exact. But those who preferred “formed” thought that ambiguity should be avoided, since in Latin usage it became customary to say that people “fashion” things when they compose something by means of deceitful imitation [Note: [Col. 0399] Several manuscripts read, “when they imitate and compose.”]

This man, then, formed from the dust of the earth or from clay—for it was moistened dust—this man, I say, or, to express it more exactly as Scripture speaks, this “dust from the earth,” the Apostle teaches was made an animal body when it received a soul. “And this man became a living soul”: that is, this fashioned dust became a living soul.

2. “He already had a soul,” they say; “otherwise he would not be called a man, since a man is not body alone or soul alone, but one constituted from soul and body.” This is true: the soul is not the whole human being, but the better part of the human being; nor is the body the whole human being, but the lower part. Yet when both are joined together, the name “human being” applies to them; and the individual parts do not lose that name even when we speak of them separately.

Who, for example, is forbidden by ordinary speech to say, “That man has died, and now he is at rest or in punishment,” when this can be said of the soul alone? Or, “That man was buried in such-and-such a place,” when this can refer only to the body? Will they say that divine Scripture does not usually speak in this way [Col. 0400]? On the contrary, it bears witness to us on this point so clearly that, even when these two things are joined and the human being is alive, it calls each separately by the name “human being”: it calls the soul the inner human being and the body the outer human being (II Cor. IV, 16), as though there were two human beings, although together they are one human being.

We must therefore understand in what respect the human being is said to be made in the image of God, and in what respect he is said to be earth and to return to earth. The former is said with reference to the rational soul, which God, by breathing—or, if that expression is more suitable, by inspiring—placed in the human being, that is, in the human body. The latter is said with reference to the body, which God fashioned from dust and to which he gave a soul, so that it might become an animal body, that is, a human being made into a living soul.

3. Therefore, in what the Lord did when he breathed and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he plainly wished this to be understood: that the Holy Spirit is not only the Spirit of the Father, but also the Spirit of the Only-Begotten himself. For that same Spirit is the Spirit of both Father and Son, with whom the Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is not a creature but the Creator.

That bodily breath proceeding from the mouth of flesh was not the substance and nature of the Holy Spirit. Rather, it was a sign by which we should understand, as I have said, that the Holy Spirit is common to the Father and the Son: they do not each have a separate spirit, but there is one Spirit belonging to both.

In the Holy Scriptures this Spirit is always called by the Greek word *pneuma* (πνεῦμα), just as the Lord called him here when, signifying him by the breath of his bodily mouth, he gave him to his disciples. In all the passages of the divine utterances I have never encountered him called anything else.

But where we read, “And God fashioned the man, dust from the earth, and breathed—or inspired—into his face the breath of life,” the Greek does not use *pneuma* (πνεῦμα), which is ordinarily used of the Holy Spirit, but *pnoē* (πνοή). This word is more frequently used of a creature than of the Creator. For this reason some Latins, to preserve the distinction, preferred to call it not “spirit” but “breath.”

The same word occurs in Greek in that passage from Isaiah where God says, “I made every breath” (Isa. LVII, 16, according to the Septuagint), plainly signifying every soul. What is called *pnoē* in Greek, our translators have rendered sometimes as “breath,” sometimes as “spirit,” and sometimes as “inspiration” or “breathing in,” even when it is said of God [Note: [Col. 0400] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “sometimes they also translated it as ‘soul.’] But *pneuma* is never translated except as “spirit”: whether the human spirit, of which the Apostle says, “For who knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in that person?” (I Cor. II, 11); or the spirit of an animal, as it is written in Solomon’s book, “Who knows whether the spirit of a human being goes upward into heaven and the spirit of an animal goes downward into the earth?” (Eccl. III, 21); or this bodily spirit, which is also called wind—for this is the word used where the Psalm sings, “Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy spirit” (Ps. CXLVIII, 8); or the uncreated Creator, as in the Lord’s words in the Gospel, “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0401], where he signifies him by the breath of his bodily mouth.

The same applies to the words, “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19), where the Trinity itself is commended most excellently and clearly; and to the statement, “God is spirit” (John IV, 24); and to many other passages of the sacred Scriptures.

In all these scriptural testimonies, so far as the Greek is concerned, we see not *pnoē* (πνοή) written but *pneuma* (πνεῦμα); and so far as the Latin is concerned, not “breath” but “spirit.” Therefore, in the statement, “He inspired,” or, if it should be said more exactly, “He breathed into his face the breath of life,” even if the Greek had used *pneuma* rather than *pnoē*, as it does there, it still would not follow that we must understand the Spirit who is properly called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity. For, as has been said, it is clear that *pneuma* is used not only of the Creator but also of a creature.

4. “But,” they say, “when he had said ‘spirit,’ he would not have added ‘of life’ unless he had wished the Holy Spirit to be understood there; and when he had said, ‘The man became a soul,’ he would not have added ‘living’ unless he meant the life of the soul, which is bestowed upon it by the gift of God’s Spirit. Since the soul lives according to its own mode of life, why was ‘living’ added unless that life was intended which is given to it through the Holy Spirit?”

What is this but an attempt to argue carefully from human suspicion while attending carelessly to the Scriptures? For what difficulty would there have been in not going any farther, but reading a little earlier in the same book: “Let the earth produce a living soul” (Gen. I, 24), when all the land animals were created? Then, after a short interval, still in the same book, what difficulty would there have been in noticing what is written: “And everything that had the breath of life, and everything that was upon the dry land, died” (Gen. VII, 22), when it was indicating that everything living on the earth had perished in the flood?

If, then, we find both a living soul and the breath of life even in animals, as divine Scripture habitually speaks; and if, in this very passage where it says, “Everything that had the breath of life,” the Greek has used not *pneuma* but *pnoē*: why do we not say, “Why was ‘living’ added, since a soul cannot exist without living?” Or, “Why was ‘of life’ added, when he had said ‘spirit’?”

Rather, we understand that Scripture, according to its customary manner, spoke of “the breath of life” and “a living soul” when it wished animals—that is, animated bodies—to be understood, bodies in which this manifest bodily sensation was present through the soul.

In the creation of the human being, however, we forget how Scripture habitually speaks, even though it spoke here according to its own manner. It wished to indicate that, although the human being received a rational soul—which was not created as other flesh is produced by water and earth, but was created by God’s breathing—he was nevertheless made in such a way that, in the animal body which becomes a living body through the soul within it, he lived as those animals lived of which it said, “Let the earth produce a living soul.”

It likewise says that they had within them the breath of life [Col. 0402]; and here too the Greek did not say *pneuma* but *pnoē*: plainly not the Holy Spirit, but their soul, expressed by that name.

5. “But,” they say, “the breath of God is understood to have come forth from God’s mouth. If we believe it was a soul, it will follow that we must confess it to be of the same substance as God and equal to that Wisdom which says, ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclus. XXIV, 5).”

Wisdom did not in fact say that she was breathed forth from God’s mouth, but that she came forth from his mouth. Just as we can make breath—not from our own nature as human beings, but from the surrounding air which we draw in and draw back out by breathing—when we blow, so almighty God could make breath not from his own nature, nor from some underlying creature, but even from nothing. By inserting it into the human body, he is most suitably said to have inspired or breathed it into the body: the incorporeal Creator making the incorporeal breath, the immutable the mutable, because the uncreated made the created.

Nevertheless, so that those who wish to speak about the Scriptures may learn that they fail to notice the expressions of Scripture, let them hear or read that it is not only something equal and of the same nature that is said to come forth from God’s mouth. For God says: “Because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III, 16).

6. There is therefore no reason for us to resist the Apostle, who speaks with complete clarity. Distinguishing the animal body from the spiritual body—that is, the body in which we are now from the one in which we will be—he says: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise. If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one, as it is written: ‘The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.’ But not first the spiritual, but the animal; afterward, the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, such are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven” (I Cor. XV, 44–49).

We have already spoken above about all these apostolic words. The animal body in which the Apostle says the first man Adam was made was formed not so that it could not die at all, but so that it would not die unless the man sinned. The spiritual and immortal body that will be in a life-giving spirit will not be able to die at all.

The soul was created immortal. Although it is said to have died through sin, because it lacks a certain kind of life—namely, the Spirit of God, by which it could also have lived wisely and happily—it nevertheless does not cease to live according to its own particular, though wretched, life, because it was created immortal.

The same is true of the apostate angels. Although they are dead in a certain sense because of their sin, since they abandoned the fountain of life, which is God, by drinking from whom they could have lived wisely and happily, they could not die in such a way as to cease altogether to live and perceive, because they were created immortal. Thus, after the final judgment, they will be cast into the second death in such a way that even there they will not be deprived of life, since they will not be deprived of perception when they are in pain.

But human beings who belong to the grace of God, citizens of the holy angels who remain in blessed life, will be clothed with spiritual bodies in such a way that they will neither sin nor die any longer. Yet they will be clothed with an immortality which, like that of the angels, cannot be taken away by sin: the nature of the flesh will remain, but no carnal corruption or sluggishness will remain at all.

7. A question now necessarily follows, which must be examined and, with the help of the Lord God of truth, resolved. If the lust of disobedient members arose in those first human beings from the sin of disobedience, after divine grace had abandoned them; if this was why they opened their eyes to their nakedness—that is, why they directed their attention to it with excessive curiosity—and, because the shameless movement resisted the authority of the will, covered their private parts: how would they have propagated children if they had remained, without transgression, as they were created?

But since this book must also be brought to a close, and so great a question ought not to be compressed into the narrow limits of this discourse, let it be deferred, with a more suitable arrangement, to the book that follows [Note: [Col. 0404] Thus Erasmus and several manuscripts. Others read, “it is deferred with a more suitable arrangement.”]

## BOOK FOURTEEN [Note: [Col. 0403] This book is cited in book 1 of *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, written around the year 420.]

Again concerning the sin of the first man, from which Augustine teaches that the cause of carnal life and vicious affections flowed; especially showing that the shameful evil of lust was the reciprocal punishment of disobedience, and investigating how, if the human being had not sinned, he would have propagated children without lust.

[Col. 0403]

## CHAPTER I  
All would have fallen through the disobedience of the first man into the perpetuity of the second death, unless the grace of God had delivered many

We have already said in the preceding books that God wished to establish the human race from one human being, so that it would be joined not only by a likeness of nature but also by a certain bond of kinship into a harmonious unity through the bond of peace. Nor would this race have been destined to die in each of its individual members, unless the first two—one of whom was created from no one, the other from him—had earned this by disobedience.

They committed so great a sin that human nature was changed for the worse, and the obligation of sin and the necessity of death were transmitted even to their descendants. The reign of death dominated human beings so completely that it would have driven them all headlong into the second death, whose punishment has no end, unless the undeserved grace of God had delivered some from it.

Thus it came about that, although so many and such great nations throughout the world live according to different rites and customs and are distinguished by a manifold variety of languages, weapons, and clothing, there exist nevertheless no more than two kinds of human society, which according to our Scriptures we may rightly call two cities.

One is the society of those who wish to live according to the flesh, the other of those who wish to live according to the spirit, each in the peace proper to its own kind; and when they attain what they desire, they live in the peace proper to their own kind.

## CHAPTER II  
How the carnal life is to be understood—not as arising only from vices of the body, but also from vices of the soul

1. We must first see, then, what it means to live according to the flesh and what it means to live according to the spirit. Anyone who looks at what we have said at first sight, either without remembering or without sufficiently considering how the Holy Scriptures speak, might think that the Epicurean philosophers lived according to the flesh because they placed the highest human good in bodily pleasure [Col. 0404], along with any others who in whatever way have thought that the good of the body is the highest good of the human being.

The same person might think that the whole mass of people who do not philosophize according to some doctrine or in that manner, but are inclined toward lust and know how to rejoice only in the pleasures they grasp through bodily senses, live according to the flesh; and that the Stoics, who place the highest human good in the soul, live according to the spirit, since what is the human soul except spirit?

But according to the way divine Scripture speaks, both groups are shown to live according to the flesh. For it calls not only the body of an earthly and mortal animal “flesh”—as when it says, “Not all flesh is the same flesh, but one is the flesh of human beings, another the flesh of animals, another of birds, another of fish” (I Cor. XV, 39)—but uses the significance of this name in many other ways.

Among these various modes of expression, it often calls the human being himself, that is, human nature, “flesh,” using the figure of speech in which the whole is signified by a part [Note: [Col. 0404] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “signifying the whole by a part.” The word “signifying” is absent from other printed editions and from the manuscripts, so that the sense is: “using the figure of speech called ‘the whole by a part.’”]

Such is the statement, “By works of the law no flesh will be justified” (Rom. III, 20). What did he wish to be understood except “no human being”? A little later he says this more plainly: “No one is justified by the law” [Note: [Col. 0404] Lovaniensis reads, “By the law no human being will be justified.” Other printed editions and the manuscripts read, “No one is justified by the law,” or “will be justified.”] (Galat. III, 11); and to the Galatians: “Knowing that a human being is not justified by works of the law” (Galat. II, 16).
