In this sense we understand, “And the Word became flesh” (John I, 14): that is, “a human being.” Some who did not understand this correctly [Note: [Col. 0404] The Apollinarists.] thought that Christ lacked a human soul. Just as a part is understood from the whole when Mary Magdalene’s words are read in the Gospel: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John XX, 13), although she was speaking only of Christ’s flesh, which she thought had been taken away from the tomb where it had been buried, so also the whole is understood when a part is named “flesh,” as in the passages mentioned above.

2. Since divine Scripture therefore calls various things “flesh” in many ways—ways that would take too long to investigate and collect—in order that we may discover what it means to live according to the flesh, which is certainly evil, although the nature of flesh itself is not evil, let us carefully examine that passage of the Epistle which the Apostle Paul wrote to the Galatians. He says:

“The works of the flesh are manifest, namely, adulteries, fornications, uncleanness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, animosities, dissensions, factions, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Galat. V, 19–21).

When this entire passage of the apostolic Epistle is considered insofar as it seems sufficient for the present matter, it can resolve the question of what it means to live according to the flesh.

Among the works of the flesh which he said were manifest and which, after listing them, he condemned, we find not only those that pertain to the pleasure of the flesh—such as fornications, uncleanness, licentiousness, drunkenness, and revelries—but also those which display vices of the soul unrelated to bodily pleasure.

Who would not understand idolatry, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, animosities, dissensions, factions, and envies to be vices of the soul rather than of the flesh? It can happen that, because of idolatry or the error of some faction, a person abstains from bodily pleasures. Yet even then, although that person may appear to restrain and suppress the lusts of the flesh, apostolic authority proves that he lives according to the flesh; and it shows that, in abstaining from bodily pleasures, he performs condemnable works of the flesh.

Who does not hold enmities in the soul? Or who speaks in such a way that he says to an enemy, or to someone he considers an enemy, “You have an evil flesh toward me,” rather than, “You have an evil disposition toward me”? Finally, just as, if someone heard the word “carnalities,” so to speak, he would undoubtedly attribute it to the flesh, so no one doubts that animosities belong to the soul. Why, then, does the Teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth call all these things, and things like them, works of the flesh, unless he wishes the human being himself to be understood by the name “flesh,” using that manner of speech in which the whole is signified by a part?

## CHAPTER III  
The cause of sin proceeded from the soul, not from the flesh; and the corruption contracted through sin is not sin but punishment

1. If anyone says that the flesh is the cause of the vices found in the evil conduct of human beings, because the soul, affected by the flesh, lives in this way, that person certainly has not carefully considered the whole of human nature. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15).

Accordingly, the same Apostle, speaking of this corruptible body, concerning which he had shortly before said, “Although our outer human being is being corrupted” (II Cor. IV, 16), says: “We know that if our earthly house of habitation is dissolved [Note: [Col. 0405] The printed editions read, “this earthly house of habitation.” The word “this” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.], we have a building from God, a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, longing to be clothed with our dwelling that is from heaven, if indeed, once clothed, we shall not be found naked [Note: [Col. 0405] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions read, “if indeed clothed,” omitting “once.”]. For we who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. V, 1–4).

We are therefore burdened by the corruptible body, and, knowing that the cause of this burden is not the nature and substance of the body but its corruption, we do not wish to be stripped of the body but to be clothed with its immortality. Then, too, there will be a body [Note: [Col. 0406] “Body” is to be supplied.], but because it will not be corruptible, it will not burden us.

The corruptible body therefore now weighs down the soul, and “the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15). Nevertheless, those who think that all the evils of the soul have arisen from the body are in error [Note: [Col. 0406] Here the third chapter begins in the manuscripts.]

2. Although Virgil seems to explain the Platonic position in brilliant verses, saying,

> Their vigor is fiery, and their origin heavenly,  
> So far as harmful bodies do not weigh them down,  
> And earthly limbs and mortal members do not dull them;

and although, wishing it to be understood that the four familiar disturbances of the soul—desire, fear, joy, and grief, as though they were the origins of all sins and vices—arise from the body, he adds and says:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice, and do not see the heavens, ...

They look upward, shut in by darkness and a blind prison (Aeneid, book 6, lines 730–734). Yet our faith holds otherwise. For the corruption of the body, which weighs down the soul, is not the cause of the first sin but its punishment; nor did corruptible flesh make the sinful soul, but the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible. Although certain inducements to vice—and vice-laden desires themselves—arise from this corruption of the flesh, not all the vices of an evil life are nevertheless to be attributed to the flesh, lest we thereby absolve the devil from all of them, since he has no flesh. For although the devil cannot be called a fornicator or a drunkard, or anything else of this kind that belongs to the pleasures of the flesh—since he is also the hidden persuader and instigator of such sins—he is nevertheless supremely proud and envious. This viciousness so took possession of him that on account of it he was destined to eternal punishment in the prisons of this murky air.[^c0040-1]

Yet these vices, which hold supremacy in the devil, the Apostle attributes to the flesh, although it is certain that the devil does not possess flesh. For he says that enmities, strife, rivalries, animosities, and envies are works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20–21). The head and origin of all these evils is pride, which reigns in the devil without flesh. Who, moreover, is more hostile to the saints than he? Who is found to be more contentious, more vehement, more rivalrous, or more envious against them? Since he possesses all these qualities without flesh, how are these works of the flesh unless they are the works of the human being whom, as I have said, he calls by the name “flesh”? For it was not by possessing flesh—which the devil does not possess—but by living according to himself, that is, according to humanity, that the human being became like the devil. The devil too wished to live according to himself when he did not stand in the truth, so that he might speak falsehood not from God but from himself; and he is not only a liar but also the father of falsehood (John 8:44). He was the first to lie, and from the one from whom sin began, falsehood also began.

## CHAPTER IV — What It Means to Live According to Humanity and What It Means to Live According to God

### 1

When a human being therefore lives according to humanity and not according to God, he is like the devil. For even an angel had to live not according to the angel but according to God, in order to stand in the truth and speak truth from God, not falsehood from himself. Elsewhere the same Apostle says of the human being: “But if the truth of God has abounded through my falsehood” (Romans 3:7). He said “my falsehood,” but “the truth of God.” [The manuscripts read “our falsehood.”]

When, therefore, a human being lives according to truth, he does not live according to himself but according to God. For it is God who said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). But when he lives according to himself—that is, according to humanity—and not according to God, he certainly lives according to falsehood. This is not because the human being himself is falsehood, since God, who is certainly not the author and creator of falsehood, is his author and creator; but because the human being was made upright so that he would live not according to himself but according to the one by whom he was made—that is, so that he would make the will of that one, rather than his own, his will. Not to live in the manner in which he was made to live—that is falsehood.

For he wishes to be blessed even though he does not live in such a way that he can be blessed. What is more false than this desire? Hence it can rightly be said that every sin is falsehood. Sin is committed only by that desire by which we wish things to go well for us, or do not wish them to go badly for us. Thus it is falsehood when, although something is done so that things may go well for us, it instead causes things to go badly for us; or when, although something is done so that things may be better for us, it instead makes them worse for us. And why is this so, unless it is because a human being can fare well through God, whom he abandons by sinning, but not through himself, according to whom he sins by living?

### 2

What we have said, then—that two cities, different and opposed to one another, arose because some lived according to the flesh and others according to the spirit—can also be expressed by saying that some live according to humanity and others according to God. For Paul says most plainly to the Corinthians: “Since there is rivalry and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to humanity?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

To walk according to humanity is therefore to be carnal, since “humanity” is understood from “flesh,” that is, from a part of the human being. He had called these same people “animal” earlier and “carnal” later, saying:

“For who knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we,” he says, “have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God. We also speak of these things, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. But the animal human being does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:11–14). [The printed editions and manuscripts read *sed docti spiritus* (“but taught by the Spirit”), except the old Colbertinus manuscript, which reads *sed doctis spiritu* (“but in words taught by the Spirit”), in accordance with the Greek ἀλλ᾽ ἐν διδακτοῖς; the Vulgate instead has *sed in doctrina* (“but in teaching”).]

To such people—that is, to the animal—he says shortly afterward: “And I, brothers, was unable to speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal people” (ibid. 3:1). The same principle is understood from this manner of speaking: the whole is signified by a part.[^c0040-2] For the whole, which is the human being, can be signified both by “soul” and by “flesh,” which are parts of the human being. Thus an animal human being is not one thing and a carnal human being another; rather, both are the same: a human being living according to humanity.

In the same way, it is human beings who are signified both where it is written, “By works of the law no flesh will be justified” (Romans 3:20), and where it is written, “Seventy-five souls went down with Jacob into Egypt” (Genesis 46:27). In the first passage “every human being” is signified by “all flesh,” and in the second seventy-five human beings by “seventy-five souls.” [This follows the edition of the Septuagint. Our Vulgate counts no more than seventy souls, although Acts 7:14 has seventy-five souls; see below, book 16, chapter 40.] What is said as “not in words taught by human wisdom” could have been said as “not in words taught by carnal wisdom,” just as what is said, “You walk according to humanity,” could have been said, “You walk according to the flesh.”

This becomes still clearer in what follows: “When one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollo,’ are you not human beings?” (1 Corinthians 3:4). What he had expressed by “You are animal” and “You are carnal,” he expressed more plainly by “You are human beings.” This means: “You live according to humanity, not according to God”; if you lived according to God, you would be gods.

## CHAPTER V — On the Nature of Body and Soul: The Opinion of the Platonists Is More Tolerable Than That of the Manichaeans, but the Platonists Too Are Rejected Because They Attribute the Causes of Vices to the Nature of the Flesh

It is therefore unnecessary, in order to insult the Creator, to accuse the nature of the flesh on account of our sins and vices. In its kind and order it is good. But to abandon the good Creator and live according to a created good is not good, whether one chooses to live according to the flesh, according to the soul, or according to the whole human being, who consists of soul and flesh—and who can therefore be signified both by the name of soul alone and by the name of flesh alone.

For whoever praises the nature of the soul as the highest good and accuses the nature of the flesh as evil is plainly pursuing the soul in a carnal manner and fleeing the flesh in a carnal manner, because he judges this by human vanity, not by divine truth.

The Platonists do not rave as the Manichaeans do, detesting earthly bodies as though their nature were evil,[^c0040-3] since they attribute to God the Craftsman all the elements from which this visible and tangible world has been composed, together with their qualities. Nevertheless, they think that souls are affected by earthly limbs and dying members in such a way that from these arise for them the diseases of desires, fears, joy, and sorrow. These four—whether “perturbations,” as Cicero calls them,[^c0040-4] or “passions,” as most people call them, rendering the Greek word literally[^c0040-5]—contain all the viciousness of human conduct.

If this is so, what are we to make of Aeneas in Virgil, when, having heard from his father in the underworld that souls would return again to bodies, he wonders at this opinion and exclaims:

> O father, must we think that some souls from here  
> rise upward to heaven,  
> and return again to sluggish bodies?  
> What so dreadful a desire for light is this?  
> (Aeneid, book 6, lines 719–721.)

Does this so dreadful a desire still remain in those souls’ celebrated purity, arising from earthly limbs and dying members? Does he not assert that they have been cleansed of all such bodily pestilences, as he calls them, when they begin again to wish to return into bodies?

Hence it follows that, even if the matter were as they hold—which is altogether absurd, namely, that the purification and pollution of souls alternately going and returning continually succeed one another—it could not truthfully be said that all blameworthy and vicious movements of souls grow upon them from earthly bodies. For according to them, that “dreadful desire,” as the distinguished poet says, is so far from arising from the body that it compels the soul to be in a body after it has been purified from every bodily pestilence[^c0040-6] and established outside every body.

Therefore, even by their own admission, the soul is affected not only by flesh, so that it desires, fears, rejoices, and grieves,[^c0040-7] but can also be stirred to these movements from itself.

## CHAPTER VI — On the Quality of the Human Will, Under Whose Judgment the Affections of the Soul Are Considered Either Wrong or Right

What matters is the quality of a human being’s will. If it is wrong, these movements will be wrong; but if it is right, they will be not only blameless but even praiseworthy.

For the will is present in all of them; indeed, all of them are nothing other than wills. For what is desire and joy except the will consenting to the things we want? And what are fear and sorrow except the will dissenting from the things we do not want? [The manuscripts read *consensione* (“by consenting”); below, *in dissensione* (“in dissenting”).]

When we consent by seeking what we want, the will is called desire; when we consent by enjoying what we want, it is called joy. Likewise, when we dissent from what we do not want to happen, such a will is fear; but when we dissent from what happens against our will, such a will is sorrow.

In general, according to the variety of things that are sought or avoided, just as a human being’s will is attracted or offended, so it changes and turns toward one or another of these affections.

Accordingly, a human being who lives according to God and not according to humanity must be a lover of the good. It follows that he must hate evil. Since no one is evil by nature, but whoever is evil is evil through vice, the person who lives according to God ought to have “perfect hatred” (Psalm 138:22) toward the wicked: he must neither hate the human being because of the vice nor love the vice because of the human being, but hate the vice and love the human being. Once the vice has been healed, everything that ought to be loved will remain, and nothing that ought to be hated.

## CHAPTER VII — That “Love” and “Affection” Are Found Indiscriminately in Sacred Scripture Both in Good and in Evil

### 1

Whoever is resolved to love God and to love his neighbor—not according to humanity but according to God—as he loves himself, is plainly said to possess, on account of this love, a good will, which in the language more usual in the sacred Scriptures is called *charity*. Yet “love” too is used according to those same sacred Scriptures.

For the Apostle says that the person chosen to govern the people must be a lover of the good (1 Timothy 3:1–10). And when the Lord himself questioned the Apostle Peter, after saying, “Do you love me more than these?” Peter replied, “Lord, you know that I love you.” Again the Lord asked not whether Peter loved, but whether he had affection for him; and again Peter replied, “Lord, you know that I love you.” In the third question the Lord himself did not say, “Do you have affection for me?” but “Do you love me?” The Evangelist then says: “Peter was grieved because he said to him a third time, ‘Do you love me?’” Yet the Lord had not said “Do you love me?” three times, but twice “Do you have affection for me?” and once “Do you love me?”

From this we understand that when the Lord said, “Do you have affection for me?” he said nothing other than “Do you love me?” Peter, however, did not change the word for this one thing, but said even a third time, “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you” (John 21:15–17).

### 2

I have recalled this because some people think that affection or charity is one thing and love another. They say that affection is to be understood in a good sense, and love in a bad sense.[^c0040-8]

It is nevertheless entirely certain that even the authors of secular literature did not speak in this way. Let philosophers determine whether, or by what method, they distinguish these terms. Their books sufficiently show, however, that they value love in good things and toward God himself.

It was necessary to make clear that the Scriptures of our religion, whose authority we place before every other kind of writing, do not mean one thing by “love” and another by “affection” or “charity.” We have already shown that “love” can be used in a good sense. But lest anyone suppose that love can be spoken of both in good and in evil, whereas affection is to be spoken of only in good, let him consider what is written in the Psalm: “But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6). And consider the words of the Apostle John: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15).

Here in one passage “affection” is found both in good and in evil.

As for “love” in evil—for we have already shown it in good—let no one demand an example; let him read what is written: “For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money” (2 Timothy 3:2).

A right will, therefore, is a good love, and a perverse will is an evil love. Love that eagerly seeks to possess what is loved is desire; love that possesses and enjoys it is joy; love that flees what opposes it is fear; and when what it flees occurs, the resulting feeling is sorrow. Thus these things are evil if the love is evil and good if the love is good.

Let us prove what we say from Scripture. The Apostle desires to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). And: “My soul desired to long for your judgments”—or, if expressed more appropriately, “My soul longed to desire your judgments” (Psalm 118:20). And: “The desire for wisdom leads to the kingdom” (Wisdom 6:21).

Yet custom has established this manner of speech: if “desire” or “longing” is mentioned without stating what is desired, it can be understood only in an evil sense.

Joy is found in good: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Psalm 31:11); “You have given joy to my heart” (Psalm 4:7); and “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 15:11).

Fear is found in good in the Apostle, where he says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12); “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11:20); and “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:3).

As for sorrow—which Cicero more often calls “distress”[^c0040-9] and Virgil “pain,” when he says, “They grieve and rejoice” (since I preferred to say “sorrow,” because “distress” or “pain” is more commonly used of bodies)—the question is more difficult: can sorrow be found in good?

## CHAPTER VIII — On the Three Perturbations Which the Stoics Wanted to Exist in the Soul of the Wise Person, Excluding Pain or Sorrow, Which the Soul’s Virtue Should Not Experience

### 1

The Stoics wished there to be three things which the Greeks call *eupatheiai* (εὐπάθειαι), but which Cicero called “constancies” in Latin, corresponding to the three perturbations in the soul of the wise person: in place of desire, will; in place of joy, gladness; in place of fear, caution. But in place of distress or pain—which, to avoid ambiguity, we have preferred to call sorrow—they denied that anything could exist in the soul of the wise person.

They say that will seeks the good, which the wise person does; gladness is over an attained good, which the wise person attains everywhere; caution avoids evil, which the wise person ought to avoid. But sorrow is over an evil that has already occurred, and they think that no evil can happen to the wise person. Therefore they said that nothing corresponding to sorrow could exist in his soul.

They thus speak as though they deny that anyone except the wise person can will, rejoice, or exercise caution, while the foolish person can only desire, be glad, fear, and be sorrowful. According to Cicero, the former are three “constancies”; according to most others, the latter are four “passions.” In Greek, as I have said, the former three are called *eupatheiai* (εὐπάθειαι), while the latter four are called *pathē* (πάθη), “passions.”

When I carefully investigated as far as I could whether this language agrees with the sacred Scriptures, I found the Prophet saying, “There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 57:21, according to the Septuagint), as though the wicked might be glad rather than rejoice over evil, since “rejoicing” properly belongs to the good and pious.

Likewise, the Gospel says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7:12). This appears to be said as though no one could wish for anything evil or shameful, but could only desire it. Hence, because of customary usage, some interpreters added “good things” and translated it: “Whatever you wish people to do to you in good things, do the same to them.” They thought it necessary to guard against anyone wishing people to do dishonorable things to him—not to mention more disgraceful matters, but certainly luxurious banquets—in which he might think that, if he did similar things for them, he would be fulfilling this commandment.

But in the Greek Gospel from which the Latin was translated, “good things” does not appear. Rather, it reads: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.” I believe this is because, in saying “you wish,” he already intended good things to be understood. For he did not say, “You desire.”

### 2

Yet our language must not always be restrained by these precise distinctions; sometimes we must use them, and when we read the words of those whose authority it is not permissible to resist, they must be understood in the sense where a sound meaning cannot otherwise be found.[^c0040-10] Such are the examples we have cited, partly from the Prophet and partly from the Gospel.

Who does not know that the wicked exult in gladness? Yet the Lord says, “There is no rejoicing for the wicked.” Why, unless because “rejoicing” has another meaning when the word is used in its proper and exact sense?

Again, who would deny that people are rightly commanded to do to others whatever they desire others to do to them, lest they mutually delight one another through the disgrace of unlawful pleasure? Yet the commandment is most wholesome and true: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.” And why is this so, unless because in this passage “will” is used in a special sense and cannot be understood in evil?

In the more usual form of speech, which ordinary language most frequently employs, it certainly would not be said, “Do not wish to tell every lie” (Ecclesiasticus 7:14), unless there were also an evil will, distinguished from the will praised by the angels when they said, “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The addition of “good” is superfluous if the will can be nothing but good.

What great praise of charity would the Apostle have expressed by saying that it “does not rejoice over iniquity” (1 Corinthians 13:6), unless wickedness also rejoiced? Even among authors of secular literature, these words are used without such a distinction.

Cicero, the most distinguished of orators, says: “I wish, Conscript Fathers, to be merciful” (First Oration against Catiline, chapter 2). Because he used the word in a good sense, would anyone be so perversely educated as to insist that he ought to have said not “I wish” but “I will”?

On the other hand, in Terence a disreputable young man, burning with insane desire, says: “I want nothing else except Philumena.” That this wish was lust is sufficiently shown by the reply placed in the mouth of his older servant. [Some books read “wiser servant.”] The servant says to his master:

> How much better it would be for you to take pains  
> to remove this love from your heart  
> than to say things that only inflame your desire in vain.  
> (Andria, act 2, scene 1, lines 6–8.)

That Virgil too used “gladness” in an evil sense is shown by the verse in which he summarized these four perturbations with the greatest brevity:

> Hence they fear and desire, they grieve and rejoice.  
> (Aeneid, book 6, line 733.)

The same author also says, “The mind’s evil joys” (ibid., lines 278–279).

### 3

Therefore both the good and the evil will, exercise caution, and rejoice; or, to express the same thing in other words, both the good and the evil desire, fear, and rejoice. [The printed editions added “fear” after “exercise caution,” incorrectly: Augustine is using Stoic terminology, which recognized only three affections or *eupatheiai*, assigning caution in place of fear.] But the former do so well, the latter badly, according as their will is right or perverse.

Sorrow too—the feeling which the Stoics thought could not be found in the soul of the wise person—is found in good, especially among our people. For the Apostle praises the Corinthians because they had been sorrowful according to God.

Perhaps someone will say that the Apostle congratulated them because they had been sorrowful in repentance, and that such sorrow can belong only to those who have sinned. For he says:

“I see that that letter, although it grieved you for a time, now makes me rejoice—not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved unto repentance. For you were grieved according to God, so that you suffered no loss through us. For sorrow according to God produces repentance leading to salvation, not to be regretted; but the sorrow of the world produces death. For behold, this very thing—that you were grieved according to God—how much earnestness it has produced in you” (2 Corinthians 7:8–11). [Vindobonensis and Ambrosianus omit “not to be regretted”; the other books retain it, corresponding to the Greek ἀμεταμέλητον (*ametamelēton*). Augustine does not normally omit this word; see Sermon 254, §2.]

The Stoics could therefore answer on behalf of their position that sorrow appears useful for this purpose: that a person may regret having sinned. But they would say that it cannot exist in the soul of the wise person because no sin falls upon him for which he might be sorrowful in repentance, nor any other evil whose endurance and experience could make him sorrowful.

They also say that Alcibiades—forgive me if my memory does not deceive me about the man’s name—when he thought himself blessed, wept while Socrates argued with him and demonstrated that he was miserable because he was foolish.[^c0040-11] His foolishness, therefore, was the cause of this useful and desirable sorrow: the sorrow by which a human being grieves that he is what he ought not to be. The Stoics, however, say that the wise person, not the fool, cannot be sorrowful.

## CHAPTER IX — On the Perturbations of the Soul, Whose Affections the Life of the Righteous Possesses in a Right Form

### 1

As far as this question concerning the perturbations of the soul is concerned, we have already answered these philosophers in the ninth book of this work, showing that they are more eager to quarrel over words than over things, and more concerned with contention than with truth (chapters 4–5).

Among us, however, in accordance with the sacred Scriptures and sound doctrine, the citizens of the holy city of God, living according to God during their pilgrimage in this life, fear and desire, grieve and rejoice. Because their love is right, all these affections are right in them.

They fear eternal punishment and desire eternal life. They grieve in reality,[^c0040-12] because they still groan within themselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of their body (Romans 8:23). They rejoice in hope, because the saying that is written will be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54).

Likewise, they fear sinning and desire perseverance; they grieve over sins and rejoice in good works. In order to fear sinning, they hear: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). In order to desire perseverance, they hear what is written: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (ibid. 10:22). In order to grieve over sins, they hear: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). In order to rejoice in good works, they hear: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Likewise, according as their weakness or strength may be, they fear being tempted and desire to be tempted; they grieve in temptations and rejoice in temptations. In order to fear being tempted, they hear: “If anyone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself lest you too be tempted” (Galatians 6:1). In order to desire to be tempted, they hear a certain strong man of the city of God saying: “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Psalm 25:2). In order to grieve in temptations, they see Peter weeping (Matthew 26:75); in order to rejoice in temptations, they hear James saying: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations” (James 1:2).

### 2

They are moved by these affections not only on their own account but also on account of those whom they desire to be freed: they fear that they may perish, grieve if they perish, and rejoice if they are freed.

Let us recall above all that excellent and powerful man who glories in his weaknesses (2 Corinthians 12:5), the man through whom we Gentiles came into the Church of Christ—the Teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth—who labored more than all his fellow apostles (1 Corinthians 15:10), and instructed the people of God through many Epistles, not only those whom he saw present but also those whom he foresaw would exist in the future.

That man, I say, the athlete of Christ,[^c0040-13] taught by Christ, anointed by Christ (Galatians 1:12), crucified with Christ (ibid. 2:19), glorified in Christ, made a spectacle in the theater of this world to angels and human beings (1 Corinthians 4:9), lawfully fighting the great contest and pursuing the prize of the heavenly calling toward what lies ahead (Philippians 3:14)—we gladly behold him with the eyes of faith: rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep (Romans 12:15), having battles outside and fears within (2 Corinthians 7:5), desiring to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), longing to see the Romans so that he might have some fruit among them as among the other Gentiles (Romans 1:11, 13), showing zeal for the Corinthians and, through that very zeal, fearing that their minds might be led astray from the chastity that is in Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2–3), having great sorrow and continual pain in his heart on account of the Israelites (Romans 9:2), because, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God (ibid. 10:3), and declaring not only his sorrow but also his mourning over certain people who had sinned previously and had not repented of their impurity and fornications (2 Corinthians 12:21). [Most manuscripts read “awaiting him”; some read “we behold.”]

### 3

If these movements and affections, arising from love of the good and holy charity, are to be called vices, then let us allow what are truly vices to be called virtues. [Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts read “truly”; Erasmus and the Lovaniensis edition read “really.”]

But when these affections follow right reason and are employed where appropriate, who would dare call them diseases or vicious passions? Accordingly, the Lord himself, having deigned to live a human life in the form of a servant, though he had absolutely no sin, adopted these affections wherever he judged that they should be adopted.

For since his body was truly human and his soul truly human, his human affection was not false. Thus, when the Gospel reports that he was angry and grieved over the hardness of the Jews’ hearts (Mark 3:5); that he said, “I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe” (John 11:15); that, about to raise Lazarus, he even shed tears (ibid. 11:35); that he desired to eat the Passover with his disciples (Luke 22:15); and that, as his passion approached, his soul was sorrowful (Matthew 26:38), these things are certainly not falsely reported.

Rather, for the sake of a definite dispensation, he took these movements into his human soul when he wished, just as he became human when he wished.

### 4

Therefore, and this must be acknowledged, even when we possess these affections in a right manner and according to God, they belong to this life, not to the future life for which we hope; and often we yield to them even against our will.

Thus, although we may be moved not by blameworthy desire but by praiseworthy charity, we sometimes weep even when we do not want to. We possess these affections, therefore, because of the weakness of the human condition. The Lord Jesus did not possess them in this way, for even his weakness was subject to his power.[^c0040-14]

But while we bear the weakness of this life, if we have none of these affections at all, then we are not living rightly. For the Apostle censured and detested certain people whom he also said were “without affection” (Romans 1:31). The sacred Psalm likewise condemned those of whom it says: “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none” (Psalm 68:21).

To feel no sorrow at all while we are in this place of misery, as one of the learned men of this world perceived and said,[^c0040-15] does not come without a great price: inhumanity of soul and insensibility of body.

Accordingly, if the condition called *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια) in Greek—“impassibility,” if it could be rendered in Latin—is to be understood as a state in which one lives without these affections that arise contrary to reason and disturb the mind, then it is plainly good and greatly to be desired. But even this condition does not belong to the present life.

For it is not the voice of just any people, but especially of the pious, the very just, and the holy, who say: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). This *apatheia* will therefore exist when there is no sin in a human being.

For now, however, one lives well enough if one lives without crime. But whoever thinks he lives without sin is not acting so as to have no sin; rather, he is acting so as not to receive forgiveness.

If *apatheia* is instead to be called the condition in which no affection whatsoever can touch the soul,[^c0040-16] who would not judge such insensibility worse than every vice?

It may therefore rightly be said that perfect blessedness will exist without the stimulus of fear and without any sorrow. But who, unless utterly estranged from the truth, would say that love and joy will not exist there?

If *apatheia* means that no fear terrifies and no sorrow afflicts,[^c0040-17] then it must be avoided in this life if we wish to live rightly—that is, according to God. In the blessed life promised to us as eternal, however, it is plainly to be hoped for.[^c0040-18]

### 5

The fear of which the Apostle John says, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and whoever fears is not perfect in love” (1 John 4:18), is not the same kind of fear as that which the Apostle Paul had when he feared that the Corinthians might be deceived by the serpent’s cunning (2 Corinthians 11:3). Charity possesses this fear—indeed, only charity possesses it.

Rather, John is speaking of the kind of fear that is not in love, about which the Apostle Paul himself says: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again into fear”[^c0040-19] (Romans 8:15).

But that chaste fear which endures forever and ever (Psalm 18:10), if it will also exist in the future age—for how else can it be understood to endure forever and ever?—is not fear that terrifies us away from an evil that can occur. It is fear that holds us in the good that cannot be lost.

For where the love of an attained good is unchangeable, the fear of avoiding evil is, if one may put it so, secure. By the name “chaste fear” is signified that will by which we must wish not to sin and avoid sin—not through the anxiety of weakness, lest we perhaps sin, but through the tranquility of charity.

Or, if no kind of fear at all can exist in that most certain security of perpetual and blessed joys, then “The chaste fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” was said in the same way as “The patience of the poor will not perish forever” (Psalm 9:19). For patience itself will not be eternal, since it is necessary only where evils must be endured. Rather, what is reached through patience will be eternal.

In the same way, perhaps chaste fear is said to endure forever and ever because what fear itself leads to will endure.

6. Since this is so, and since a righteous life must be led by which one may arrive at the blessed life, all these affections are righteous in the righteous life and perverse in the perverse one. The blessed life, however—and likewise the eternal one—will have love and joy that are not only righteous but also secure; it will have no fear or sorrow. From this it now becomes in some measure apparent what sort of people the citizens of the City of God ought to be during this pilgrimage, living according to the spirit and not according to the flesh—that is, according to God and not according to man—and what sort they will be in that immortality toward which they are journeying. The city, then—that is, the society—of the ungodly, who live not according to God but according to man, and who, in the worship of false divinity and contempt for the true, follow the teachings of men or demons, is shaken by these perverse affections as by diseases and disturbances. And if it has any citizens who seem able to control such movements and, as it were, moderate them, they are so proud and exalted in their impiety that, by this very fact, their swellings are greater in proportion as their pains are lesser. And if some, through a vanity as much more monstrous as it is rarer, should become so enamored of this condition in themselves that they are aroused and uplifted by no affection whatsoever, and bent or inclined by none, they lose their entire humanity rather than attain true tranquility. For something is not therefore righteous because it is hard, nor is it therefore healthy because it is insensible.

[Note: [Col. 0417] Physicians, when they cannot restore health to certain afflicted members, induce insensibility, so that they deprive them of all sense of pain—not because they are healthy, but so that they feel nothing. LUDOVICUS VIVES.]

## CHAPTER X  
### Whether We Should Believe That the First Human Beings, Placed in Paradise, Were Affected by No Disturbances before They Sinned

But whether the first man—or the first human beings, for they were a married couple—had, before sin, in their animal body such affections as we shall not have in our spiritual body once all sin has been purged and brought to an end, is a question not unreasonably raised. For if they had them, how were they blessed in that celebrated place of blessedness, namely, paradise? Who can be called absolutely blessed if he is affected by fear or sorrow? What, moreover, could those human beings have feared or grieved over amid such an abundance of such great blessings, where death was not feared, nor any ill health of the body; where nothing was lacking that a good will might attain, and nothing was present that could offend the flesh or spirit of a human being living happily?

There was undisturbed love of God, and among the married couple, living together in faithful and sincere fellowship; and from this love there was great joy, since what was loved did not cease to be available for enjoyment. There was the tranquil avoidance of sin, and while it remained, no other evil whatever that could cause sorrow rushed upon them.

Or perhaps they desired to touch the forbidden tree in order to eat from it, but feared death; and therefore desire and fear already disturbed those human beings even in that place? Far be it from us to suppose this, where there was no sin at all. For it is not no sin to desire what God’s law prohibits and to abstain from it through fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness. Far be it from us, I say, to suppose that before any sin there was already such a sin there, so that they would commit with respect to the tree what the Lord says concerning the woman: “Whoever has looked upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

How happy, then, were the first human beings, who were agitated by no disturbances of spirit and afflicted by no bodily inconveniences! The whole human society would have been equally happy if neither they had committed the evil that they transmitted even to their descendants, nor anyone from their stock had committed iniquity deserving condemnation. And while this happiness continued [Note: [Col. 0417] Some manuscripts: “thus.”], until the number of the predestined saints was completed through that blessing in which it was said, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28), another and greater blessing would have been given, such as was given to the blessed angels: a state in which there would already be certain security that no one would sin and no one would die. The life of the saints would then have been such, after no experience of labor, sorrow, or death, as it will be after all these things, when the dead are raised and their bodies restored in incorruption.

## CHAPTER XI  
### On the Fall of the First Human Being, in Whom Nature Was Well Created and Can Be Restored Only by Its Author

1. But because God foreknew everything, and therefore could not have been ignorant that man would also sin, we ought to affirm the holy city according to what He foreknew and ordained [Note: [Col. 0418] In the Louvain edition, *eam* (“it”) is omitted.], not according to what could not come within our knowledge because it was not part of God’s ordering. For man could not disturb the divine plan by his sin, as though he had compelled God to change what He had decreed. God, by foreseeing, anticipated both things: both what the man whom He Himself created good would become—that is, how evil he would be—and what good He Himself would bring about from him even in that condition.

For although God is said to change His decrees—and hence, by a figurative manner of speaking, God is also read in the sacred Scriptures to have repented (Gen. 6:6; 1 Kings 15:11)—this is said with reference to what man had hoped for or what the order of natural causes was carrying forward, not with reference to what the Almighty had foreseen that He Himself would do.

Thus God made man, as it is written, “upright” (Eccl. 7:30), and therefore of good will. For he would not be upright if he did not possess a good will. Good will, then, is God’s work, since with it man was made by Him. But the first evil will, because it preceded all evil works in man, was rather a kind of falling away from God’s work toward his own works than any work in itself. And the works were evil because they were according to man himself and not according to God; thus the will itself was like an evil tree producing those works as evil fruits, or the man himself insofar as he was of evil will.

Moreover, although an evil will is not according to nature but against nature, because it is a defect, it nevertheless belongs to the nature whose defect it is—for it cannot exist except in a nature. It belongs, however, to the nature that He created from nothing, not to the nature that the Creator begot from Himself, as He begot the Word through whom all things were made. For even though God fashioned man from the dust of the earth, that same earth and every earthly material are altogether from nothing; and He gave the soul, which was also made from nothing, to the body when man was made.

Yet good so overcomes evil that, although evils are permitted to exist to demonstrate how wisely provident the Creator’s justice can make use even of them, good can exist without evil—as does God Himself, true and supreme, and all the heavenly invisible and visible creation above this darksome air [Note: [Col. 0418] Only the Louvain edition reads *invisible*, omitting “visible.”]—whereas evil cannot exist without good, because the natures in which evils exist, insofar as they are natures, are certainly good.

Evil is removed, moreover, not by taking away some nature that had been added, or some part of it, but by healing and correcting what had been corrupted and depraved. The will, therefore, is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. Such freedom was given by God; once lost through its own fault, it cannot be restored except by Him who was able to give it. Hence Truth says: “If the Son makes you free, then you will be truly free” (John 8:36). This is the same as if He had said: “If the Son saves you, then you will be truly saved.” For He is liberator in the same respect in which He is savior.

2. Man therefore lived according to God in paradise, both bodily and spiritually. For paradise was not bodily because of bodily goods and not spiritual because of the goods of the mind; nor was it spiritual in such a way that man enjoyed it through inward senses but not bodily in such a way that he enjoyed it through outward senses. It was plainly both, because of both.

[Note: [Col. 0419] Compare above, Book XIII, chapter 21.]

But afterward, when that proud angel—and consequently envious—through the same pride had turned from God toward himself, choosing to rejoice in subjects with a kind of tyrannical arrogance rather than to be subject, he fell from the spiritual paradise. (I have discussed his fall and that of his companions, who from being angels of God became his angels, sufficiently, insofar as I could, in Books XI and XII of this work.) Desiring, by his baneful cunning [Note: [Col. 0419] Vindobonensis, Amelianus, Erfurtensis, and some manuscripts read *malesuasa*; most manuscripts, *malesuadenda*. Louvain more aptly reads *malesuada*, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.276: “baneful hunger.”], to creep into the human senses through a cunning suited to his purpose, and envying the man because he himself had fallen while the man still stood, he chose the serpent in the bodily paradise as the animal through which he might speak. There, together with those two human beings, male and female, the other terrestrial animals also moved about, subject to them and harmless. The serpent was a slippery animal, moving in winding coils and suited to the work it was to perform.

Employing the serpent, subjected to himself through an angelic presence and a superior nature by spiritual malice, as an instrument, he deceitfully addressed the woman [Note: [Col. 0419] Many manuscripts read *fallaciam*, “deceit.”]. He began, naturally, with the inferior part of that human union, so that he might proceed gradually to the whole. He did not suppose that the man could easily be made to believe an error or be deceived through his own error, but that, while yielding to another’s error, he could be deceived.

For just as Aaron was not induced to consent to the erring people in making an idol, but yielded under constraint (Exod. 32:3–5), and it is not credible that Solomon thought through error that idols should be served, but that he was compelled to those sacrileges by feminine blandishments (1 Kings 11:4), so we must believe that the man, in relation to his own woman—one to one, human being to human being, husband to wife—did not believe her as one speaking truthfully and thus become deceived into transgressing God’s law, but obeyed her through their bond of fellowship.

For the Apostle did not say without reason, “And Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived” (1 Tim. 2:14): unless it was because she accepted what the serpent said to her as though it were true, while he did not wish to be separated from his sole companion, nor from their fellowship in sin. Yet he was no less guilty; rather, he sinned knowingly and deliberately [Note: [Col. 0419] Erfurtensis and the manuscripts read *si sciens*, “if knowingly.”].

Hence the Apostle does not say, “He did not sin,” but, “He was not deceived.” Indeed, he shows this when he says, “Through one man sin entered the world,” [Note: [Col. 0419] The printed editions read “he shows that Adam himself sinned.” *Peccasse* (“sinned”) is absent from the manuscripts.] and shortly afterward more plainly: “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5:12, 14). He intended those to be understood as deceived who do not think that what they are doing is sin; but Adam knew. Otherwise, how would it be true that Adam was not deceived?

Yet, inexperienced in divine severity, he could be mistaken in thinking that what had been committed was pardonable. Thus, in the respect in which the woman was deceived, he was not deceived; but he was mistaken about how what he was about to say should be judged: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me some of the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12).

[Note: [Col. 0420] So the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The printed editions have, “whom you gave me as a companion.”]

Why say more? Although both were not deceived in believing, both were nevertheless seized in sinning and entangled in the devil’s snares.

## CHAPTER XII  
### On the Nature of the First Sin Committed by Man

If anyone is troubled by the question why human nature is not changed by other sins in the way it was changed by the transgression of those first two human beings—so that it became subject to such corruption as we see and feel, and through this corruption subject to death [Note: [Col. 0420] Amelianus, Erfurtensis, and Louvain read “and to death”; “and” is absent from the manuscripts.], and was disturbed and tossed by so many and such great affections, mutually opposed to one another, whereas it certainly was not like this in paradise before sin, even though it was in an animal body—if anyone is troubled by this, as I have said, he ought not therefore to think that the first sin was slight or small because it was committed in eating food that was not evil or harmful, except insofar as it was forbidden.

For God would not create or plant anything evil in that place of such great happiness. But obedience was commended in the commandment; and in a rational creature this virtue is, in a certain sense, the mother and guardian of all virtues, since the creature was made in such a way that it is beneficial for it to be subject to God, but destructive for it to make its own will, rather than the will of Him by whom it was created.

This commandment—not to eat from one kind of food, when such an abundance of other food lay before them—was so slight to observe and so brief to retain in memory, especially since desire had not yet resisted the will. The punishment that afterward followed its transgression was therefore incurred with proportionately greater injustice, the more easily obedience could have guarded against it.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### That in Adam’s Transgression an Evil Will Preceded the Evil Act

1. They began to be evil in secret, so that they would fall into open disobedience. For they would not have reached the evil act unless an evil will had preceded it. But what could be the beginning of an evil will except pride? [Note: [Col. 0420] Manuscripts 2050 and 2051 read *quid*, “what.”] “For pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15).

What, then, is pride except the desire for a perverse elevation? For a perverse elevation is to abandon the one to whom the mind ought to cling as its principle and, in a certain sense, to make and be its own principle. This happens when a person is too pleased with himself. He is pleased with himself in this way when he falls away from that unchangeable good which ought to have pleased him more than he pleased himself.

This falling away is voluntary. For if the will had remained stable in love of the higher, unchangeable good—from which it was illumined so that it might see and kindled so that it might love—it would not have turned away from it toward self-pleasing, and thus become darkened [Note: [Col. 0421] Nearly only the Louvain edition reads *intenebresceret*, “would become darkened.”] and chilled, so that either the woman would believe that the serpent had spoken the truth or the man would place his wife’s will before God’s command and think himself a transgressor deserving pardon if he did not abandon his life’s companion even in fellowship in sin.

The evil act, then—that transgression by which they ate the forbidden food—was not committed except by those who were already evil. For “a bad fruit would not be produced except by a bad tree” (Matt. 7:18). But for the tree to become bad was contrary to nature, since it could happen only through the fault of the will, which is contrary to nature. Yet nature could not be corrupted by defect unless it had been made from nothing. Thus, insofar as it is a nature, it derives its being from the fact that it was made by God; but insofar as it falls away from Him who is, it derives this from the fact that it was made from nothing. [Note: [Col. 0421] The better manuscripts read “from Him who is”; Vindobonensis, Amelianus, and Erfurtensis read “from that which it was made,” while Louvain reads “from Him by whom it was made.”]

Man did not fall in such a way that he became absolutely nothing; rather, by being inclined toward himself, he became less than he was when he clung to Him who supremely is. Therefore, when he abandoned God and existed in himself—that is, pleased himself—he did not become nothing, but approached nothingness. Hence, according to the sacred Scriptures, the proud are also called by another name: “those who please themselves” (2 Pet. 2:10).

It is good to have one’s heart above; yet not directed toward oneself, which is pride, but toward the Lord, which is obedience—and obedience cannot belong except to the humble. There is, therefore, something in humility that wonderfully raises the heart, and something in exaltation that casts the heart down. This seems contrary: that exaltation should be downward and humility upward. But devout humility makes one subject to what is higher; nothing is higher than God, and therefore humility exalts, because it makes one subject to God.

Exaltation, however, when it is a vice, by the very fact that it rejects subjection [Note: [Col. 0421–0422] Most manuscripts omit *quo* (“by which”); after “subjection,” Vindobonensis continues, “falls from Him,” omitting “and.”], falls from Him above whom nothing exists; and by this very fact it becomes lower. Thus it fulfills what is written: “You cast them down when they were exalted” (Ps. 72:18). He did not say, “When they had become exalted,” as though they were first exalted and afterward cast down; rather, “When they were being exalted,” they were then cast down. For the very act of being exalted is already to be cast down.

Therefore, since humility is especially commended now in the City of God and to the City of God as it journeys through this world, and is especially proclaimed in its King, who is Christ; and since the vice opposed to this virtue, the vice of exaltation, is taught by the sacred Scriptures to rule especially in its adversary, who is the devil: plainly this is the great distinction by which the two cities of which we speak are distinguished—one the society of godly human beings, the other of ungodly human beings, each together with the angels belonging to it, in whom one kind of love of God preceded, and the other kind of love of self.

2. Once the sin had become manifest and open, when what God had forbidden had been done, the devil would not have seized man unless he had already begun to please himself. This is why the statement “You will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5) also delighted him. They could have become better by clinging through obedience to the supreme and true principle, rather than by making themselves their own principle through pride.

Created gods are gods not through their own truth [Note: [Col. 0422] Vindobonensis and the manuscripts read *veritate*, “truth”; Amelianus, Erfurtensis, and Louvain read *virtute*, “power.”] but through participation in the true God. Yet by desiring more [Note: [Col. 0422] The printed editions read “man, by desiring more”; “man” is absent from the manuscripts.], man became less: while he loved to be self-sufficient [Note: [Col. 0422] Vindobonensis, Amelianus, and the manuscripts read *diligit*, “loves”; Erfurtensis and Louvain read *delegit*, “chooses.”], he fell away from Him who truly sufficed for him.

That evil, then, by which man, when he pleased himself as though he too were light, turned away from the light which, if it pleased him, would itself make him light—that evil, I say, preceded in secret the evil that was perpetrated openly. For it is true, as it is written: “The heart is exalted before ruin, and it is humbled before glory” (Prov. 16:18).

That ruin which occurs in secret plainly precedes the ruin that occurs openly, while the former is not thought to be ruin. Who considers exaltation a ruin, when already present in it is the falling away by which the Most High has been abandoned? But who does not see that it is ruin when there is an evident and undeniable transgression of the commandment?

For this reason God forbade the act: once it had been committed, no appearance of justice could defend it. And I dare [Note: [Col. 0422] The printed editions read “And therefore I dare”; *ideo* (“therefore”) is absent from the manuscripts.] to say that it is beneficial for the proud to fall into some open and manifest sin by which they become displeasing to themselves, since they had already fallen by pleasing themselves. [Note: Compare *On Nature and Grace against the Pelagians*, §§26, 27, 32.]

Peter was healthier for displeasing himself when he wept than for pleasing himself when he presumed (Matt. 26:75, 33). The sacred Psalm also says: “Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord” (Ps. 82:17)—that is, they will seek to please you as they seek your name, having pleased themselves while seeking their own.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On the Pride of the Transgression, Which Was Worse Than the Transgression Itself

There is, however, a worse and more condemnable pride: that by which even in manifest sins a refuge of excuse is sought. So those first human beings said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate”; and the man said: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me some of the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:13, 12).

Here there is nowhere the sound of a request for pardon, nowhere an appeal for healing. Although they do not deny what they committed, as Cain did (Gen. 4:9), pride nevertheless still seeks to attribute to another what it did wrongly: the woman’s pride attributes it to the serpent, the man’s pride to the woman.

But where there is an open transgression of the divine command, this is accusation rather than true excuse. For they did not commit the act for that reason—that the woman acted at the serpent’s persuasion and the man at the woman’s prompting—as though anything should have been preferred to God, to whom they ought either to have believed or submitted.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the Justice of the Retribution Received by the First Human Beings for Their Disobedience

1. God was therefore despised: He who had commanded them, who had created them [Note: [Col. 0422] The printed editions read “who had created the human being, who had made him in His image.” The manuscripts omit “the human being” and “him.”], who had made them in His image, who had placed them over the other animals, who had established them in paradise, who had provided an abundance of all things and safety, who had burdened them with neither many nor great nor difficult commands, but had supported their salutary obedience with one very brief and very light command—by which He reminded that creature, for whom free service was beneficial, that He was its Lord.

A just condemnation followed, and a condemnation of such a kind that the human being who, by guarding the commandment, was destined to become spiritual even in the flesh became also carnal in mind [Note: [Col. 0423] The printed editions read “and because”; the manuscripts read “and.”]; and he who had pleased himself through his pride was, by God’s justice, given over to himself. Yet not in such a way that he was altogether in his own power [Note: [Col. 0423] Vindobonensis, Amelianus, and Erfurtensis read “not as he desired, that he should be in his own power”; Louvain reads “not as he desired,” while *affectabat* (“desired”) is absent from the manuscripts that read “not thus.”]: disagreeing even with himself, he was to endure a harsh and wretched servitude under the one to whom he had consented by sinning [Note: [Col. 0423] Manuscript 2051 reads *qui* (“who”); Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 89, argues that this is the correct reading.], in place of the freedom he had desired.

He died in spirit willingly and was destined to die in body unwillingly; a deserter from eternal life, he was condemned to eternal death unless grace should set him free.

Whoever thinks such a condemnation excessive or unjust plainly does not know how great the iniquity of sin was where there was such ease in not sinning. For just as Abraham’s great obedience is rightly praised because he was commanded to kill his son, an exceedingly difficult thing (Gen. 22:2), so the disobedience in paradise was all the greater because what was commanded involved no difficulty.

And just as the obedience of the second man is more worthy of praise because he became obedient even unto death (Phil. 2:8), so the disobedience of the first man is more detestable because he became disobedient even unto death. For when a great punishment for disobedience had been announced, and the Creator had commanded something easy, who can adequately explain how great an evil it is not to obey in an easy matter, under the command of such great authority and the threat of such a terrifying penalty?

2. Finally, to put it briefly: in the punishment of that sin, what was repaid to disobedience except disobedience? For what other misery belongs to man than that his own disobedience should be directed against himself, so that, because he did not want what he was able to do, he should now want what he is unable to do? [Note: This reverses Terence, *Andria* 2.1.5–6: “Since what you wish cannot be done, wish what can be.”]

In paradise, even if he could not do everything before sin, whatever he could not do he did not want to do; and therefore he could do everything he wanted. But now, as we recognize in his descendants and as divine Scripture testifies, “man has become like vanity” (Ps. 144:4).

Who can enumerate how many things he wants that he cannot do, while his own spirit—that is, his own will—and the flesh that is inferior to it do not obey him? Against his will, his spirit is often disturbed, his flesh suffers, grows old, and dies; and we endure whatever else we would not endure against our will if our nature obeyed our will in every way and in all its parts.

But the flesh suffers something by which it is prevented from serving. What difference does it make from where this comes, provided that, through the justice of the ruling God [Note: [Col. 0423] Some manuscripts read “through the justice of the condemning God.”], whom we refused to serve as subjects, our flesh—which had been subject to us—causes us trouble by not serving us, although by not serving God we have been able to cause trouble for ourselves, not for Him?

For He does not need our bodily service in the way that we need the service of the body. Therefore what we receive is our punishment, not His punishment for what we have done.

The pains that are called pains of the flesh belong to the soul in the flesh and arise from the flesh. For what does the flesh by itself, without the soul, either suffer or desire? But when the flesh is said to desire or suffer, it is either the human being himself, as we have discussed, or something belonging to the soul that is affected by the body’s experience—something harsh, producing pain, or something gentle, producing pleasure.

The pain of the flesh, however, is merely an offense to the soul arising from the flesh, and a kind of disagreement with its condition; just as the soul’s pain, which is called sorrow, is disagreement with things that have happened against our will. Sorrow is often preceded by fear, which is also in the soul, not in the flesh. But the pain of the flesh is not preceded by any such fear of the flesh that is felt in the flesh before the pain.

Pleasure, however, is preceded by a certain appetite, felt in the flesh as its desire, such as hunger and thirst, and what is more customarily called lust in the genital organs, although this is a general term for every desire.

The ancients also defined anger itself as nothing other than the desire for revenge.

[Note: [Col. 0424] Compare Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book III, chapter 5, and Book IV, chapter 9.]

Yet sometimes, when there is no possibility of revenge [Note: [Col. 0424] Some manuscripts read “and”; so do ours, except manuscript 2050.], a human being becomes angry even with inanimate things, as when, in anger, he smashes a pen that is writing badly or breaks a reed pen.

This too, although more irrational, is nevertheless a kind of desire for revenge, and, so to speak, a sort of shadow of retribution, whereby those who do evil may suffer evil.

There is therefore a desire for revenge, which is called anger; a desire to possess money, which is called greed; a desire to win by any means, which is called obstinacy; and a desire for glory, which is called boastfulness. There are many and varied desires, some of which even have their own proper names, while others do not.

For who could readily say what the desire to rule is called, although civil wars themselves testify how greatly it prevails in the minds of tyrants?

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the Evil of Lust, Whose Name Applies to Many Vices but Is Properly Assigned to the Obscene Movements of the Body

Although there are desires for many things, nevertheless, when lust is mentioned without specifying what it is lust for, the mind generally thinks of nothing except that desire by which the obscene parts of the body are aroused.

This desire claims for itself not only the whole body and not only the exterior but also the interior, and it moves the whole human being, joining and mingling an affection of the soul with an appetite of the flesh, so that pleasure follows—pleasure greater than which there is none among bodily pleasures. At the very moment when its climax is reached, almost all the sharpness and, as it were, wakefulness of thought is overwhelmed.

What friend of wisdom and holy joys, living a married life but, as the Apostle instructed, knowing how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the disease of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thess. 4:4–5), would not, if he could, beget children without this lust? In this duty of sowing offspring as well, would he not wish that the members created for this work should serve the mind in response to the command of the will, just as all the other members are each assigned to their respective functions, rather than being driven by the heat of lust?

But even the lovers of this pleasure, whether in marital intercourse or in the impurities of vice, are not aroused whenever they wish. Sometimes that unwelcome movement occurs when no one asks for it; sometimes it abandons one who longs for it, and, while desire burns in the mind, the body is cold.

Thus, in a wondrous way, lust does not serve not only the will to beget but even the desire to indulge; and although it usually opposes the mind that restrains it in every respect, it sometimes even divides against itself, so that when the mind is aroused, lust does not follow itself in arousing the body.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the Nakedness of the First Human Beings, Which They Saw as Shameful and Embarrassing after Sin

It is rightly this lust of which we are most ashamed; and the members themselves, which, by a certain right of their own, so to speak, move or do not move not wholly at our discretion [Note: [Col. 0425] Vindobonensis, Amelianus, and most manuscripts read “are moved or are not moved”; Erfurtensis reads “move or do not move.”], are rightly called *pudenda* (“shameful parts”), though they were not such before man’s sin.

For as it is written, “They were naked, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. 2:25)—not because their nakedness was unknown to them, but because nakedness was not yet shameful. Lust did not yet move those members against the will, nor did the flesh, by its own disobedience, in a certain sense bear witness against the disobedience of man.

For they were not created blind, as the uninstructed common people suppose. The man saw the animals, after all, and gave them names (Gen. 2:20); and of the woman it is written: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes to look upon” (Gen. 3:6).

Their eyes were therefore open, but they were not open for this purpose—that is, they were not attentive to recognizing what the garment of grace provided for them—because they did not know that their members could resist their will.

When that grace was removed, so that disobedience might be punished by a corresponding disobedience, there appeared in the movement of the body a certain shameless novelty, from which nakedness became indecent; and this made them attentive and rendered them ashamed.

Hence, after they had violated God’s command by open transgression, it is written of them: “The eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings” (Gen. 3:7).

“The eyes of both were opened,” he says—not in order to see, for they had seen before, but in order to distinguish between the good they had lost and the evil into which they had fallen.

Hence the tree itself, because it would produce this knowledge if it were touched for eating against the prohibition, received from that circumstance the name “the tree of knowing” good and evil.

[Note: [Col. 0425] The printed editions have scientiae, “of knowledge.” The manuscripts have sciendi, “of knowing.”]

For after the distress of disease has been experienced, the pleasantness of health also becomes more evident.

They therefore knew that they were naked: they had been stripped, that is, of the grace by which it came about that the nakedness of their bodies did not shame them because no law of sin resisted their minds.

This, then, they learned—something they would more happily have remained ignorant of if, believing and obeying God, they had not committed the act that forced them, through infidelity and disobedience, to experience its harm.

Therefore, ashamed of the disobedience of their flesh, as though of a punishment bearing witness to their disobedience, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings—namely, coverings for the genital organs. Some interpreters have rendered these as succinctoria, “girding coverings.”

[Note: [Col. 0426] In the Septuagint, perizômata, “coverings.”]

Campestria is indeed a Latin word, but it was so called because young men who exercised naked in the field covered their shameful parts. Hence the common people call those who are girded in this way campestrati, “wearers of campestria.”

What lust, in disobedience, moved against the will condemned by the fault of disobedience [Note: [Col. 0426] The better manuscripts read *culpa*, “fault”; the printed editions read *culpam*, “fault” in the accusative.], modesty now modestly covered. From this all nations, since they are descended from that stock, retain so deeply implanted in them the practice of covering their shameful parts that some barbarians do not even bathe with those parts naked, but wash while wearing their coverings.

[Note: [Col. 0426] See Herodotus, Book I, chapter 10; Plato, Republic, Book V, p. 452. LARCHER.]

Even through the shadowy wildernesses of India, when certain men practice philosophy naked—whence they are called Gymnosophists, “naked philosophers”—they nevertheless use coverings for their genitals, although they lack coverings for the rest of their limbs.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### On the Shame of Intercourse, Not Only in General but Also in Marriage
The act itself, however, which is performed through such lust, occurs not only in various forms of fornication, where hiding places are required to evade human judgments, but also in the use of prostitutes, which the earthly city has made a licit disgrace. [Note: [Col. 0426] Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Fabiola*, addressed to Oceanus, says: “The laws of the Caesars are one thing, those of Christ another; Papinianus commands one thing, our Paul another. Among them, the reins of immorality are loosened for men, and once only fornication and adultery have been condemned, lust is freely permitted in brothels and with slave girls—as though dignity, rather than the will, made the fault.”] Although what is done is something that no law of that city prosecutes, permitted and unpunished lust nevertheless avoids public view; and natural modesty has provided brothels themselves with secrecy. Immodesty could more easily lack the restraints of prohibition than shamelessness remove the hiding places of that disgrace. Yet even the shameful themselves call this a disgrace; although they are lovers of it, they do not dare to be its exhibitors.

What of marital intercourse, which, according to the prescriptions of the marriage Tables, takes place for the purpose of producing children? Is it not itself, although lawful and honorable, in need of a bed removed from observers? Does it not send out all servants, and even the groomsmen themselves, and anyone whom some necessity had permitted to enter, before either spouse begins to caress the other? And since, as someone has said, the greatest authority of Roman eloquence [Note: [Col. 0426] Lucan adorns Cicero with this title in Book 7, verses 62–63, and Augustine likewise uses it in Book 4 of *On Christian Doctrine*, no. 34.] says that all rightly performed actions wish to be placed in the light [Note: [Col. 0426] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 2, chapter 26.], that is, they desire to be known: [Col. 0427] this rightly performed act desires to be known in such a way that it nevertheless blushes to be seen.

For who does not know what spouses do with one another so that children may be conceived? After all, wives are taught with such public ceremony that this should be done; yet when the act by which children are conceived is taking place, even the children themselves, if any have already been born from it, are not permitted to be witnesses. Thus this rightly performed act seeks the light of minds for its own knowledge, yet shuns the eyes. Why is this, unless because what is fitting by nature is performed in such a way that what is shameful accompanies it as punishment?

## CHAPTER XIX — That the Parts of Anger and Lust Are Moved So Viciously That They Must Be Restrained by the Brakes of Wisdom—A Condition Absent from the Health of Nature Before Sin
