This is why even those philosophers who came closer to the truth [Note: [Col. 0427] The Platonists, as he discusses frequently above.] confessed that anger and lust are vicious parts of the soul, because they are moved turbulently and disorderly, even toward things that wisdom does not forbid to be done [Note: [Col. 0427] Vind., Am., Er., and our manuscripts read *perpetrari vetat*, “forbids it to be done,” omitting the negative particle.]; and consequently that they require a governing mind and reason. They claim that this third part of the soul is stationed, as it were, in a citadel to govern those others, so that, while it commands and they serve, justice may be preserved in a human being throughout every part of the soul.

These parts, then—which they admit to be vicious even in a wise and self-controlled person, so that the mind may restrain, curb, and call them back from the things toward which they are unjustly moved, and permit them to act only in accordance with what the law of wisdom allows—anger, for example, toward the exercise of just correction, and lust toward the duty of propagating offspring: these parts, I say, were not vicious in paradise before sin. For they were not moved toward anything against the upright will, so that it would be necessary for reason to hold them back as though with governing reins. The fact that they are now moved in this way, and that those who live temperately, justly, and piously regulate them—sometimes more easily, sometimes with greater difficulty—by restraining and curbing them [Note: [Col. 0427] The manuscripts read “and by resisting.”], is certainly not health arising from nature, but sickness arising from guilt.

But why is it that the actions of anger and of the other emotions in various words and deeds are not concealed by modesty in the way that the actions of lust, performed through the genital organs, are? The reason is surely that, in the other cases, it is not the emotions themselves that move the bodily members, but the will, once it has consented to them; and the will entirely governs their use. Whoever speaks a word in anger, or even strikes someone, could not do so unless the tongue and hand were moved, so to speak, at the command of the will; and these members move by that same will even when there is no anger.

But lust has in a certain sense enslaved the genital parts of the body to its own authority, so that they cannot be moved if lust is absent, and unless it rises either spontaneously or when aroused. This is what causes shame; this is what, in its embarrassment, avoids the eyes of those watching. A human being more readily endures a crowd of spectators when he is unjustly angry with another person than even one person’s gaze when he is rightly joining himself to his wife.

## CHAPTER XX — On the Utterly Empty Shamefulness of the Cynics

[Col. 0428]

Those canine philosophers—that is, the Cynics—did not see this, putting forward against human modesty nothing but a canine opinion, that is, an unclean and shameless one. Since what takes place with one’s wife is just, they held that it ought not to be a source of shame when done openly, and that marital intercourse should not be avoided in any street or public square.

Natural modesty nevertheless overcame the opinion of this error. For although they say that Diogenes once did this boastfully, thinking that his school would become more distinguished if his shamelessness were fixed more memorably in human minds, the Cynics later ceased to do it. Modesty prevailed, so that people were ashamed before other people, rather than error prevail, so that people might desire to be like dogs.

Therefore, concerning the man—or those men—reported to have done this, I think that they exposed the movements of the intercourse to the eyes of people who did not know what was happening beneath the cloak [Note: [Col. 0428] The reading *tegeretur*, “was covered,” occurs only in the Louvain edition. Shortly afterward most manuscripts read *praesente conspectu*, “in the presence of spectators.”], rather than that such pleasure could have been carried out while human eyes were pressing upon them. For there the philosophers were not ashamed to be seen wishing to have intercourse, where lust itself would have been ashamed to rise.

Even now we see that there are Cynic philosophers: these are the men who not only wrap themselves in a cloak but also carry a staff. Yet none of them dares to do this; and if any had dared, they would have been overwhelmed—not to mention the blows of those throwing stones—at least by the spittle of those who spat upon them.

Human nature is therefore unquestionably, and rightly, ashamed of this lust. For in its disobedience—since it subjected the genital organs of the body to its own movements alone and snatched them away from the authority of the will—it sufficiently reveals what was repaid to that human being for his first disobedience. This was fittingly displayed especially in the part through which human nature itself is generated, since that nature was changed for the worse by that first and great sin. No one is freed from the bondage of that sin unless what was committed for the common ruin when all were present in one person, and punished by God’s justice, is atoned for in individuals by God’s grace.

## CHAPTER XXI — On the Blessing of the Increase of Human Fertility Before Sin, Which Transgression Would Not Have Removed, and to Which the Disease of Lust Was Added

Far be it from us, then, to believe that the married couple placed in paradise would have fulfilled through this lust—because of which they covered those same organs in shame—what God said in his blessing: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). This lust arose after sin; after sin, nature, no longer shameless, experienced, noticed, blushed at, and covered it, having lost the authority to which the body had obeyed in every respect.

Yet that blessing of marriage—that married people should increase, multiply, and fill the earth—remained even among those who sinned. Nevertheless, it was given before they sinned, so that it might be understood that the procreation of children belongs to the glory of marriage, not to the punishment of sin.

But now people, plainly ignorant of the happiness that existed in paradise, suppose that children could not have been begotten except through what they have experienced—that is, through the lust at which we see even the propriety of marriage blush. Some entirely reject and faithlessly mock the divine Scriptures, where it is read that after sin they were ashamed of their nakedness and covered their private parts [Note: [Col. 0429] The Manichaeans, evidently, who rejected the writings of the Old Testament. Compare *On the Usefulness of Believing*, addressed to Honoratus, no. 4.]. Others, although they accept and honor the Scriptures, nevertheless do not wish the words “Increase and multiply” to be understood according to bodily fertility [Note: [Col. 0429] He refutes those who interpreted these words spiritually; he also recalls this interpretation in *On the Good of Marriage*, no. 2. At one time he himself was not far removed from the same opinion, as is clear from his discussions in Book 1 of *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans*, no. 30, and in Book 13 of the *Confessions*, chapter 24. In this passage, however—and rightly—he interprets the words literally. COQUAEUS.], because something similar is also said with reference to the soul: “You will multiply me in my soul by your power” [Note: [Col. 0429] This is the reading of the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The printed editions read, “You will multiply strength in my soul.”] (Ps. 137:4).

Thus they understand “And fill the earth, and rule over it,” which follows in Genesis, to mean that the earth is the flesh, which the soul fills by its presence and over which it rules especially when it is multiplied in strength. They maintain that bodily offspring could not then be born without lust—which arose after sin, was observed, confused, and veiled—any more than they can now; nor would offspring have been born in paradise, but outside it, as in fact happened. For after they had been expelled from there, they came together for the begetting of children and gave birth to them.

## CHAPTER XXII — On Marital Union, Instituted and Blessed by God in the Beginning

We, however, have no doubt whatsoever that, according to God’s blessing—“increase and multiply and fill the earth”—marriage is a gift, instituted by God from the beginning before human sin, when he created male and female. That the sexes are bodily is, of course, evident. God’s blessing itself was added to this work. For after Scripture had said, “He made them male and female,” it immediately added: “And God blessed them, saying, Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and rule over it” (Gen. 1:27–28), and so forth.

Although all these words can appropriately be referred also to a spiritual understanding, it is nevertheless greatly absurd to resist the clear meaning that male and female should be understood not as some analogous reality within a single human being—for in that person one thing rules and another is ruled—but as they are most evidently seen in bodies of different sexes, created in order that by producing offspring they might increase, multiply, and fill the earth [Note: [Col. 0429] In the printed editions, after “and fill the earth,” there is an additional phrase: “To this statement, so evident …” It is absent from the manuscripts.].

For the Lord was not asked about the spirit that commands and the flesh that obeys; or about the rational soul that rules and the irrational desire that is ruled; or about the contemplative virtue that excels and the active virtue that is subordinate; or about the intellect of the mind and the sensation of the body. Rather, he was asked plainly about the marital bond by which the two sexes are mutually bound to one another—whether it was lawful to dismiss one’s wife for any reason, since Moses had permitted the Israelites, because of the hardness of their hearts, to give a certificate of divorce. He answered:

“Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0430] Vind., Am., and Er. read “he who made man from the beginning.” The word “man” is absent from Louvain and the manuscripts, as well as from the Greek text of the Gospel and even from the Latin text in the Corbie Bibles of the Vulgate version.] made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’? Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:4–6).

It is therefore certain that male and female were originally instituted in the same way that we now see and know two human beings of different sexes. Yet they are called one, either because of their union or because of the origin of the woman, who was created from the man’s side. The Apostle too, on the basis of this first example that preceded by God’s institution, admonishes each individual man to love his wife (Eph. 5:25; Col. 3:19).

## CHAPTER XXIII — Whether Generation Would Also Have Taken Place in Paradise if No One Had Sinned, or Whether the Institution of Chastity There Would Have Fought Against the Act of Lust

### 1

Whoever says that they would not have had intercourse and would not have begotten children unless they had sinned—what is he saying except that, for the number of the saints, human sin was necessary? If, by not sinning, they would have remained alone because, as they think, they could not have begotten children unless they had sinned, then sin was certainly necessary so that there might not be only two righteous people but many.

If this is absurd to believe, we should instead believe that the number of the saints sufficient to complete that most blessed city would have been just as great even if no one had sinned as the number now gathered by God’s grace from the multitude of sinners, until the children of this age beget and are begotten (Luke 20:34).

### 2

Therefore, if sin had not existed, those marriages worthy of paradise’s happiness would have produced beloved offspring and would not have possessed shameful lust [Note: [Col. 0430] See *On Original Sin*, nos. 40–43.]. But how this could have happened cannot now be demonstrated by an example. Nevertheless, it ought not to seem incredible that even one member could have served the will without this lust, just as so many members now serve it.

Do we not move our hands and feet, when we wish, toward the actions to be performed by those members, without any resistance and with as much ease as we see both in ourselves and in others—especially in craftsmen of every kind of bodily work, where skill, being more agile, has been added to a weaker and slower nature? Why should we not believe that, if lust had not existed—the lust repaid for the sin of disobedience—those members could likewise have served human beings obediently at the command of the will for the work of begetting children?

Does not Cicero, in his books *On the Republic*, when discussing the differences among forms of rule and drawing an analogy for this matter from human nature, say that the bodily members are commanded as children are, because of their readiness to obey, while the vicious parts of the soul are restrained like slaves under a harsher authority? In the natural order, the soul is certainly placed above the body, yet the soul itself commands the body more easily than it commands itself.

Nevertheless, this lust about which we are now speaking is all the more shameful because, in its case, the soul neither commands itself effectively enough to prevent desire altogether, nor commands the body completely enough for the private parts to be moved by the will rather than by lust. If this were so, they would not be private parts [Note: [Col. 0431] Louvain reads, “they would not be private parts at all.” “At all” is absent from the other books.].

But now the soul is ashamed that the body resists it, although the body is subject to it as an inferior nature. In the other emotions, when the soul resists itself, it is less ashamed because, when it is defeated by itself, it defeats itself—although disorderly and viciously, since it is defeated by those parts that ought to be subject to reason, and therefore, as has been said, by its own parts and by itself. For when the soul defeats itself in an orderly manner, so that its irrational movements are subjected to mind and reason—provided that mind and reason themselves are subject to God—that is a matter of praise and virtue.

Yet the soul is less ashamed when it does not obey itself in its vicious parts than when the body, which is distinct from it and beneath it, and whose nature does not live without it, does not yield to it when it wishes and commands.

### 3

But when other members are held in check by the command of the will, without which those members aroused by lust against the will cannot accomplish what they desire, chastity is preserved—not because the pleasure of sin has been lost, but because it has not been permitted.

This resistance, this opposition, this quarrel between will and lust—or, more precisely, the sufficiency of the will and the neediness of lust—would certainly not have existed in paradise if culpable disobedience had not been punished by punitive disobedience. Rather, those members would have served the will, just as all the others did [Note: [Col. 0431] All the manuscripts read: “the members would have served the will, just as all the others served it.”].

Thus “the genital field” [Virgil, *Georgics*, Book 3, verse 136] would have sown the vessel created for this work, just as the hand now sows the earth. And although modesty now resists us when we wish to discuss this matter more carefully, compelling us to ask beforehand for the pardon of chaste ears, there would have been no reason for this restraint. Speech would have ranged freely, without any fear of obscenity, over everything that the mind considering such members might comprehend; nor would the words themselves have been called obscene. Whatever was said about them would have been as honorable as what we say when speaking about other parts of the body.

Whoever therefore approaches these writings with immodesty should flee from guilt, not from nature; let him condemn the deeds of his own shamefulness, not the words required by our subject. In these matters a chaste and religious reader or listener readily forgives me, while I refute unbelief—not arguing from faith concerning things not experienced, but from the perception of things that have been experienced.

The person who does not recoil from the Apostle when he condemns the horrifying crimes of women who “exchanged the natural use for that which is against nature” (Rom. 1:26) reads these words without offense—especially since we are not now recalling and condemning, as he did, blameworthy obscenity, but, in explaining as far as we can the effects of human generation [Col. 0432] [Note: [Col. 0432] The Louvain edition alone reads *affectibus*, “emotions,” rather than *effectibus*, “effects.”], we nevertheless avoid obscene words, as he did.

## CHAPTER XXIV — That Innocent People Remaining in Paradise by the Merit of Their Obedience Would Have Used Their Genital Organs for the Generation of Offspring in the Same Way as the Other Members Are Used at the Command of the Will

### 1

The man, therefore, would have sown offspring, and the woman would have received it, with their genital organs moved when and as much as the task required by the will, not aroused by lust.

For we do not move only those members that are articulated by bones joined together, such as the feet, hands, and fingers. We also move those that are relaxed in soft sinews whenever we wish, agitating and extending them, producing length by stretching, bending them by twisting, and hardening them by contracting them. Such are the parts in the mouth and face that the will moves as far as it can.

Finally, the lungs themselves—the softest of all the viscera, apart from the marrow, and for that reason enclosed within the cavity of the chest—serve the will, like the bellows of smiths or musical instruments, for drawing in and releasing breath and for emitting or modulating the voice: in breathing, speaking, shouting, and singing.

I omit the fact that certain animals have been naturally endowed with the ability, if they sense something to be driven away at any place on the covering with which their entire body is clothed, to move only the spot where they sense it. They shake off not only flies that have settled upon them but even spears lodged in the skin [Note: [Col. 0432] Vind., Am., and Er. read “ears of grain.”] by trembling the skin.

Is it because a human being cannot do this that the Creator could not have bestowed it upon whatever animals he wished? In the same way, human beings could have possessed obedience even in their lower members, which they lost through their disobedience. It was not difficult for God to create a human being in such a way that, even in his flesh, that member would be moved only by his will which now cannot be moved except by lust.

### 2

We know the natures of certain human beings to be very different from those of others and astonishing in their rarity. They can do with their bodies certain things that others cannot possibly do and scarcely believe when they hear of them.

Some can move either one ear or both at once. Some, while keeping their heads motionless, draw all the hair covering the head down toward the forehead and pull it back again whenever they wish. Some, after lightly handling their stomachs, bring forth intact from within themselves, as though from a sack, whatever they choose from among an astonishing quantity and variety of things they have swallowed.

Some imitate and reproduce the voices of birds, cattle, and all sorts of other people so exactly that, unless they are seen, they cannot be distinguished at all. Some emit from below, without any breaking of wind [Note: [Col. 0432] The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions read “without any shame.”], so many sounds at will that they seem to sing even from that part.

I myself have experienced that a person can sweat whenever he wishes. It is well known that some people cry when they wish and shed tears abundantly.

There is something much more incredible, however, which many of our brothers have experienced within very recent memory. There was a certain presbyter named Restitutus [Col. 0433] in the parish of the Church of Calama [Note: [Col. 0433] The Calama mentioned here is not the town of Phoenicia, as Ludovicus Vives thought, but a town in Africa situated between Hippo and Cirta, of which Augustine speaks very frequently.].

Whenever he wished—for those who desired to witness the marvelous event would ask him to do it—he imitated the voices of almost any person lamenting. Then he withdrew so completely from his senses and lay so like a dead man that he felt nothing when pinched or pricked, and sometimes was even burned by applied fire without sensing any pain, except afterward from the wound.

That he did not move his body by resistance but by lack of sensation was shown by the fact that, as in a corpse, no breathing was found. Yet afterward he reported that, if people spoke more loudly, he heard their voices as though from far away.

Since the body, even now, in certain people—although they live this wretched life in corruptible flesh—serves them so wonderfully in many movements and sensations beyond the ordinary mode of nature, what reason is there for us not to believe that, before the sin of disobedience and the punishment of corruption, human members could have served the human will in propagating offspring without any lust?

Human beings were therefore handed over to themselves because, by pleasing themselves, they abandoned God; and, by not obeying God, they could not obey themselves. From this comes the more evident misery by which a human being does not live as he wishes. For if he lived as he wished, he would consider himself happy; yet even then he would not be happy if he lived shamefully.

## CHAPTER XXV — On True Happiness, Which Temporal Life Does Not Possess

Although, if we examine the matter more carefully, no one lives as he wishes unless he is happy, and no one is happy unless he is just. But even the just person does not live as he wishes unless he has reached the place where he can no longer die, be deceived, or be offended, and where it is certain that he will always remain so.

This is what nature desires, and it will not be fully and perfectly happy unless it obtains what it desires. But now, what human being can live as he wishes when living itself is not within his power? He wishes to live but is compelled to die. How, then, does one live as one wishes if one does not live as long as one wishes? And if one wishes to die, how can one live as one wishes if one does not wish to live?

If one wishes to die not because one does not wish to live, but in order to live better after death, then one still does not live as one wishes, but reaches what one wishes by dying.

But suppose that he does live as he wishes, because he has forced himself and commanded himself not to wish what he cannot have, and to wish what he can have, as Terence says:

> Since what you wish cannot be done,  
> Wish what can be done.  
> (*Andria*, Act 2, Scene 1, verses 5–6.)

Is he happy for that reason, because he is patiently miserable? A happy life, unless it is loved, is not possessed. And if it is loved and possessed, it must necessarily be loved above all other things, since everything else that is loved must be loved for its sake.

If it is loved as much as it deserves to be loved—for a person is not happy if he does not love the happy life itself as it deserves—then it is impossible for someone who loves it in this way not to wish it to be eternal. It will therefore be happy when it is eternal.

## CHAPTER XXVI — That We Should Believe That the Happiness of Those Living in Paradise Could Have Fulfilled the Duty of Begetting Without a Shameful Desire

[Col. 0434]

The human being therefore lived in paradise as he wished, so long as he wished what God had commanded. He lived enjoying God, from whom he was good because goodness itself made him good. He lived without any want, possessing forever the power to live in this way.

Food was present so that he would not hunger; drink, so that he would not thirst; the tree of life, so that old age would not dissolve him. Nothing corrupting, whether in the body or arising from the body, inflicted any annoyance upon any of his senses. No internal illness was feared, nor any external blow. There was complete health in the flesh and complete tranquility in the soul [Note: [Col. 0434] The manuscripts read “in the mind.”].

Just as there was no heat or cold in paradise, so no disturbance of the good will arose in its inhabitant from desire or fear [Note: [Col. 0434] The manuscripts read “occurred.”]. There was nothing sad and nothing frivolously joyful. True joy [Note: [Col. 0434] Some manuscripts read “true” in the masculine form; our manuscripts read “true.”] was perpetually maintained from God, toward whom love burned from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5). Between the spouses there was a faithful partnership grounded in honorable love, a harmonious vigilance of mind and body, and an effortless observance of the commandment.

No weariness exhausted the one at leisure; no sleep pressed upon the unwilling [Note: [Col. 0434] A similar description of the earthly paradise occurs in Basil the Great, *Homily on Paradise*, and in John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book 2, chapter 11. COQUAEUS.].

Amid such ease of circumstances and happiness of human beings, far be it from us to suspect that offspring could not have been planted without the disease of lust. Rather, those members would have been moved by the command of the will as the other members were, and, without the seductive stimulus of heat, with tranquility of mind and body and without any corruption of integrity, the husband would have poured his seed into his wife’s womb [Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 8, verse 406].

The fact that this cannot be proved by experience does not mean that it should not be believed. Those bodily parts would not then have been activated by turbulent heat, but by spontaneous power, as necessity required. In this way, male seed could have been introduced into the wife’s womb while the integrity of the female genital organs remained intact, just as now menstrual blood can flow from a virgin’s womb while that same integrity remains intact. The one could have been introduced by the same passage by which the other can be expelled.

Just as the female organs would be relaxed for childbirth not by groans of pain but by the impulse of maturity, so for impregnation and conception the two natures would have been joined not by the desire of lust but by voluntary use.

We are now speaking about things that cause shame. Therefore, although we conjecture as best we can what they might have been like before they became objects of shame, our discussion must nevertheless be restrained more by the modesty that holds us back than aided by eloquence, of which we possess little.

For since not even those who could have experienced what I am describing ever experienced it—because, with sin intervening first, they deserved exile from paradise before they could come together in the peaceful exercise of their will for the work of sowing offspring—how can these things now come before the human senses when they are mentioned, except through the experience of turbulent lust rather than through a conjecture about peaceful will?

This is why modesty hinders the speaker, [Col. 0435] although reason does not fail the thinker.

Nevertheless, the omnipotent God, the supreme and supremely good creator of all natures, helper and rewarder of good wills, abandoner and condemner of evil wills, and arranger of both, certainly did not lack a plan by which he could fill his city with the predetermined number of citizens in his wisdom, drawing them even from the condemned human race.

He would distinguish them not by merits—for the entire mass had been condemned as though in a corrupted root—but by grace. And in those who were set free, as well as in those who were not, he would show what he bestows upon them.

For each person recognizes that he has been rescued from evils by gratuitous rather than owed goodness when he is exempted from the fellowship of those with whom he would justly share a common punishment.

Why, then, would God not create those whom he foresaw would sin, since in them and through them he could show both what their guilt deserved and what his grace would grant? And under that creator and governor, why would the perverse disorder of sinners overturn the right order of things?

## CHAPTER XXVII — On Sinners—Angels and Human Beings—Whose Perversity Does Not Disturb God’s Providence

Therefore sinners—angels and human beings—do nothing that can hinder “the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 110:2). For the one who distributes everything wisely and omnipotently to each person knows how to make good use not only of the good but also of the evil.

Accordingly, since God made good use of the evil angel, who, because of the merit of his first evil will, was so condemned and hardened that he would no longer have a good will, why would he not permit the first human being—who had been created upright, that is, with a good will—to be tempted by him?

The human being had been so constituted that, if he relied upon God’s help, he would overcome the evil angel; but if, arrogantly pleasing himself, he abandoned God his creator and helper, he would be overcome. He would have good merit in a will made upright by divine assistance, but evil in a will made perverse by abandoning God.

Even his trust in God’s help could not exist without God’s help; yet it was still within his power, by pleasing himself, to withdraw from these benefits of divine grace. Just as living in this flesh without the assistance of food is not within one’s power, while not living in it is within one’s power—as those who kill themselves demonstrate—so living well without God’s help was not within his power even in paradise. But living badly was within his power, although happiness would not continue and the most just punishment would follow.

Since God was not ignorant of this future human fall, why should he not have allowed him to be tempted by the malice of the envious angel? He was in no way uncertain that the human being would be overcome; rather, he already knew that, through the human being’s offspring, aided by his grace, that same devil would be overcome by the greater glory of the saints.

Thus it happened that nothing future was hidden from God, yet his foreknowledge did not compel anyone to sin. Through the experience that followed, he also demonstrated to rational angelic and human creatures the difference between each person’s own presumption and God’s protection.

For who would dare to believe or say that it was not in God’s power to prevent either an angel or a human being from falling? But he preferred not to take this power away from them, and thus to show both how much evil their pride could produce and how much good his grace could accomplish.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — On the Character of the Two Cities, the Earthly and the Heavenly

Two loves, then, created two cities: the earthly city, namely, love of self even to contempt of God; and the heavenly city, love of God even to contempt of self [Note: [Col. 0436] In Book 11 of *On Genesis Literally*, no. 20, he promised the work *The City of God* in these words: “These two loves, one of which is holy and the other unclean, one social and the other private … distinguished two cities founded among the human race … Concerning these two cities we shall perhaps discuss more fully elsewhere, if the Lord wills.”].

The earthly city glories in itself, while the heavenly city glories in the Lord. The earthly city seeks glory from human beings; for the heavenly city, God, who bears witness to its conscience, is its greatest glory. The earthly city lifts its head in its own glory; the heavenly city says to its God, “You are my glory and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. 3:4).

In the earthly city, the lust to dominate rules among its rulers and among the nations it subjugates. In the heavenly city, those who govern serve one another in love: the leaders by caring for those under them, and the subjects by obeying. The earthly city loves its own strength in its powerful people; the heavenly city says to its God, “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17:2).

Thus, in the earthly city, its wise people—living according to the human standard—have pursued either bodily goods, or goods of the soul, or both. Or, although they were able to know God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him. Instead, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise—that is, exalting themselves in their own wisdom under the rule of pride—they became fools. They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents.

They became leaders or followers in the worship of such images, and they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever (Rom. 1:21–25).

But in the heavenly city there is no human wisdom except piety, by which the true God is rightly worshiped. It awaits its reward in the fellowship of the saints—not only of human beings but also of angels—so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28).

# BOOK FIFTEEN

After treating in the four immediately preceding books the origin of the two cities, the earthly and the heavenly, Augustine now adds an equal number of books concerning the course of those same cities. He approaches the subject by treating the principal events of sacred history that relate to it, beginning in this fifteenth book with the events recorded in Genesis from Cain and Abel up to the Flood.

[Col. 0437]

## CHAPTER I — On the Two Orders of Human Generation, Advancing from the Beginning Toward Different Ends

[Col. 0437]

1. Many people have formed many opinions, spoken many words, and committed many things to writing concerning the blessedness of paradise—or paradise itself—and concerning the life there of the first human beings, as well as their sin and punishment. We too, in accordance with the holy Scriptures—or with what we have read in them or have been able to understand from them—in conformity with their authority, have spoken of these matters in the preceding books. If, however, these questions are pursued in greater detail, they give rise to discussions of many kinds and forms, which would have to be woven through more volumes than the nature of this work and the time available require. We do not have so much leisure that we ought to linger over everything that idle and scrupulous people may ask—people readier to question than more capable of understanding [Note: [Col. 0437] Codex 258 has *scripulosi* (“scrupulous”) for *scrupulosi*. M.].

I nevertheless believe that we have already done enough concerning the great and difficult questions about the beginning either of the world [Note: [Col. 0437] Lov. has “about the beginning or about the end of the world.” “About the end” is absent from the editions of Vind., Am., and Er., and from the better manuscripts, and ought to be absent, since Augustine soon says that he must speak later about the end.], or of the soul, or of the human race itself. We have divided the human race into two kinds: one consisting of those who live according to human nature, the other of those who live according to God. These we also call, mystically, two cities—that is, two societies of human beings. One of them is predestined to reign eternally with God; the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil. But that is their end, about which we must speak later.

Now, since enough has been said about their origin—whether in the angels, whose number is unknown to us, or in the first two human beings—it seems to me that we must now undertake the course of these two cities, beginning from the time when those two began to beget children and continuing until human beings cease to beget them. For this entire period, or age, in which the dying depart and the newborn succeed them, is the course of the two cities about which we are speaking.

2. Cain, therefore, was born first from those two parents of the human race, belonging to the city of human beings; Abel was born later, belonging to the city of God. For just as in one human being we experience what the Apostle says: “Not first the spiritual, but the animal, and afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46)—and therefore, since each person arises from a condemned lineage [Note: [Col. 0437] Some manuscripts have “born from Adam” (*ex Adam nata*).], must first be evil and carnal from Adam, but, if he makes progress by being reborn into Christ [Note: [Col. 0437] Lov. alone has “in Christ” (*in Christo*).], will afterward be good and spiritual—so it was in the whole human race. When these two cities first began to advance through birth and death, the citizen of this age was born first; the one who was a stranger in this age, belonging to the city of God, was born afterward: predestined by grace, chosen by grace, by grace a stranger below, by grace a citizen above.

For, as far as he himself is concerned, he arises from the same mass, which in its origin is wholly condemned. But God, like a potter—for the Apostle introduces this comparison not foolishly but wisely [Note: [Col. 0438] Or rather, he borrowed it from Isaiah 45:9 and Jeremiah 18:3 ff. COQUAEUS.]—made from the same mass one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:21). The vessel for dishonor was made first, and afterward the one for honor. For in the one human being also, as I have already said, what is rejected comes first: from this we must necessarily begin, though we need not remain there; afterward comes what is approved, toward which we advance and where, once we arrive, we remain.

Accordingly, not every evil person will become good, but no one will be good who was not evil. Yet the sooner anyone is changed for the better, the sooner he causes to be named in himself what he has grasped, and covers over the earlier name with the later one. Thus it is written of Cain that he built a city (Gen. 4:17); Abel, however, as a stranger, did not build one. For the city of the saints is above, although here it gives birth to citizens in whom it dwells as a stranger until the time of its kingdom arrives. Then it will gather all of them, risen in their bodies, when the promised kingdom is given to them: there they will reign with their Prince, the King of the ages, without any end of time.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the children of the flesh and the children of the promise

A certain shadow and prophetic image of this city served on earth to signify it rather than to present it, at the time when it was necessary for it to be displayed. It too was called the holy city, appropriately because it was a signifying image—not the expressed reality, as it will be in the future. Concerning this serving image, and concerning the free city that it signifies, the Apostle speaks to the Galatians as follows:

“Tell me,” he says, “you who desire to be under the law, have you not heard the law?” [Note: [Col. 0438] Several manuscripts, following the Vulgate, have “have you not read the law?” Others, with the editions, have “have you not heard the law?” The Greek is *ton nomon ouk akouete*—that is, “have you not heard the law?” Only our manuscript 2050 agrees with the Vulgate. M.]

“For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the one who was by the slave woman was born according to the flesh; while the one who was by the free woman was born through the promise. These things are an allegory” [Note: [Col. 0438] Compare Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, no. 15.].

“For these are two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai [Note: [Col. 0439] Thus all the editions, following the Greek *apo orous Sina*, “from Mount Sinai.” The manuscripts are likewise, except for a few that, following the Vulgate, have “on Mount Sinai.”], producing slavery, which is Hagar [Note: [Col. 0439] So the manuscripts. The editions instead have “which is Agar” (*quae est Agar*).]. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which is joined [Note: [Col. 0439] Lov. has “which is joined” (*quae conjuncta est*); the other editions and most manuscripts differ.], to the Jerusalem that now exists; for it is enslaved with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all” [Note: [Col. 0439] Vind. and several manuscripts, following the Greek *heôs esti mêtêr pantôn hêmôn*, have “which is the mother of us all.” Er. and Lov. have “which is our mother.”].

“For it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband.’ But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac. But just as at that time the one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one who was born according to the spirit, so it is now. But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman.’ Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, by the freedom with which Christ freed us” (Gal. 4:21–31).

This way of understanding, descending from apostolic authority, opens up for us how we ought to receive the Scriptures of the two Testaments, the Old and the New. For a certain part of the earthly city was made an image of the heavenly city—not by signifying itself, but another city—and for that reason it was enslaved. It was established not for its own sake but to signify another; and, with the other signification preceding, it too was made a prefiguration of what was prefigured.

Hagar, the slave woman of Sarah, and her son were therefore a kind of image of this image. And because the shadows were to pass away when the light came, Sarah, the free woman who signified the free city—and whom that shadow in turn served to signify in another way—said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman will not be heir with my son Isaac,” as the Apostle says, “with the son of the free woman.”

We therefore find in the earthly city two forms: one displaying its own presence, the other serving by its presence to signify the heavenly city. Nature, corrupted by sin, gives birth to citizens of the earthly city; grace, freeing nature from sin, gives birth to citizens of the heavenly city. Hence the former are called “vessels of wrath,” and the latter “vessels of mercy” (Rom. 9:22–23).

This too was signified in Abraham’s two sons: Ishmael, who was born according to the flesh by the slave woman called Hagar, and Isaac, who was born according to the promise by the free woman Sarah. Both indeed came from Abraham’s seed; but custom, displaying nature, gave birth to the one, while the promise, signifying grace, gave the other. In the one case human practice is displayed; in the other, divine beneficence is commended.

## CHAPTER III  
### On Sarah’s barrenness, which God’s grace made fruitful

Sarah was barren. In despair of offspring, and desiring at least to have by her slave woman what she saw she could not have from herself, she gave the slave woman to her husband to be made fruitful by the man from whom she had wished but had been unable to bear a child. Thus she even in this way exacted her due from her husband, exercising her right over another woman’s womb.

Ishmael was therefore born as human beings are born, through the union of the two sexes, according to the customary law of nature. For this reason he is said to have been born “according to the flesh.” This does not mean that these benefits are not gifts of God, or that God does not bring them about—God whose creative wisdom, as it is written, “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). But where the gift of God was to be signified—a gift freely bestowed by grace upon human beings without their deserving it—it was fitting that the son should be given in a manner not owed by the processes of nature.

For nature no longer promised children from such a union of male and female as could have existed between Abraham and Sarah at that age, especially with the woman’s added barrenness. She could not bear even then, when it was not that age lacked fecundity, but that fecundity lacked age. The fact, therefore, that the fruit of posterity was not owed to nature in such a condition signifies that human nature, corrupted by sin and consequently justly condemned, deserved no true happiness in the future.

Isaac, therefore, rightly signifies, as born through the promise, the children of grace, citizens of the free city, companions in eternal peace. There the love will not be of one’s own private will, so to speak, but a love rejoicing in the common and unchangeable good and making one heart out of many—that is, perfectly harmonious [Note: [Col. 0440] Vind., Am., and Er. have “made perfectly harmonious” (*perfecte facta concors*).]—through the obedience of love.

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the conflict and peace of the earthly city

The earthly city, which will not be eternal—for once it has been condemned to the final punishment, it will no longer be a city—has its own good here below, in fellowship with which it rejoices, insofar as joy over such things is possible. Since this good is not of such a kind that it causes no distress to those who love it, this city frequently divides against itself through quarrels, wars, and battles, seeking victories that are either deadly or at least mortal.

For whatever part of itself rises in war against another part seeks to be victorious over nations, although it is captive to vices. If it wins, it is lifted up more proudly—even with a deadly victory [Note: [Col. 0440] The editions have “even so a deadly victory” (*etiam sic mortifera*). “So” is absent from the manuscripts.]. But if, reflecting on its condition and the common chances of life, it is distressed more by what may happen in adversity than it is puffed up by what has happened in prosperity [Note: [Col. 0440] Manuscript 2051 has “by what has happened” (*provenerunt*). M.], that victory is merely mortal. For it cannot always continue to rule those whom it has been able to subjugate by victory.

Yet it is not right to say that the goods desired by this city are not goods, since it too is better, in its own human sphere. It desires a certain earthly peace amid earthly concerns; for it desires to reach that peace by waging war. If it wins and no one remains to resist, there will be peace—the peace that the opposing parties did not have when, in wretched need, they fought over things they could not possess together. To this peace laborious wars aspire; this peace is attained by what is considered a glorious victory.

But when those who were fighting for the more just cause win, who would doubt that the victory ought to be celebrated and that a desirable peace has come about? These are goods, and without doubt they are gifts of God. But if, while better goods belonging to the heavenly city are neglected—where victory will be secure in eternal and supreme peace—these goods are desired in such a way that they are either believed to be the only goods or loved more than those believed to be better, misery must follow and the misery already present must increase.

## CHAPTER V  
### On the first founder of the earthly city, a fratricide, whose impiety the founder of the Roman city matched by killing his brother

The first founder of the earthly city was therefore a fratricide. Overcome by envy, he killed his own brother, a citizen of the eternal city who was living as a stranger on this earth. It is therefore no wonder that, much later, in the founding of the city that was destined to become the head of this earthly city of which we are speaking and to rule over so many nations, an image of the same kind corresponded to this first example and, as the Greeks call it, archetype (*archétypos*, ἀρχέτυπος).

For there too, as a certain poet recalled the crime itself:

> “The first walls were drenched with a brother’s blood.”  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* 1.95.)

Thus Rome was founded, as Roman history records, when Remus was killed by his brother Romulus—except that in this case both were citizens of the earthly city. Both sought glory from the establishment of the Roman state; but they could not both possess glory as great as either could have possessed had there been only one. For he who wished to glory in domination would necessarily dominate less if his power were diminished by a living partner.

Thus, so that one might possess the whole dominion, the partner was removed; and by crime there grew for the worse what would have been less—and better—if innocence had remained.

Cain and Abel, however, did not both have a similar desire for earthly possessions between themselves. The one who killed the other did not envy him because his own dominion would become narrower if both ruled—for Abel was not seeking domination in the city his brother was founding. Rather, it was that diabolical envy by which the wicked envy the good, and for no other reason [Note: [Col. 0441] Vind., Am., and Er. have “there is no other reason.” The word *est* (“is”) has been wrongly added; the preceding words, “that diabolical envy,” are put in the ablative, and the verb must be supplied: “he envied.”] than that the latter are good while the former are evil.

For a possession of goodness is in no way diminished by the addition or continued presence of a partner. Indeed, goodness is a possession which the undivided love of partners possesses more broadly the more harmoniously [Note: [Col. 0441] Nearly all the manuscripts have this reading. Vind., Am., and Er. instead have: “Indeed, the possession of goodness becomes broader the more harmoniously the undivided love of the partners possesses it.” Lov. has: “Indeed, the possession of goodness becomes greater the more broadly and harmoniously the undivided love …”].

In the end, the person who does not want to possess this good in common will not possess it; and he will find it greater in proportion as he has been able to love his companion there more greatly.

What arose between Remus and Romulus showed how the earthly city is divided against itself; what arose between Cain and Abel demonstrated the enmity between the two cities themselves, the city of God and the city of human beings.

The wicked therefore fight among themselves; likewise, the good and the wicked fight among themselves. But good people, if they are perfect, cannot fight among themselves. Those who are making progress but are not yet perfect can do so, however, in such a way that each good person fights against the other on that side on which he also fights against himself.

For even in one human being “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). Thus spiritual desire can fight against another person’s carnal desire, or carnal desire against another person’s spiritual desire, just as the good and wicked fight among themselves; or, certainly, the carnal desires themselves of two good people who are not yet perfect can fight among themselves, just as the wicked fight among themselves, until the health of those who are being healed is brought to its final victory.

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the illnesses that, as punishment for sin, the citizens of the city of God also suffer during their pilgrimage in this life, and from which God heals them

This illness—that is, that disobedience about which we discussed in Book Fourteen (chapters 1, 11, and elsewhere)—is the punishment of the first disobedience, and therefore it is not nature but a defect. For this reason it is said to those who are making progress in goodness and living by faith during this pilgrimage: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2) [Note: [Col. 0442] Compare *On Eighty-Three Questions*, question 71.].

Elsewhere it is said: “Correct the restless, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone. See that no one repays anyone evil for evil” (1 Thess. 5:14–15).

Again, in another place: “If a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch over yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1).

And elsewhere: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26).

And in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone” [Note: [Col. 0442] “Alone” (*solum*) is absent from the manuscripts.] (Matt. 18:15).

Again, concerning sins by which many people are offended, the Apostle says: “Rebuke those who sin in the presence of all, so that the others may also have fear” (1 Tim. 5:20).

For this reason many commands are also given concerning granting forgiveness to one another, and with great care, for the sake of maintaining peace, without which no one will be able to see God (Heb. 12:14). There is that terrifying example in which a servant is ordered to repay a debt of ten thousand talents that had been forgiven him, because he had not forgiven his fellow servant a debt of one hundred denarii. Having set forth this comparison, the Lord Jesus added and said: “So also will your heavenly Father do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matt. 18:35).

In this way the citizens of the city of God, who are pilgrims on this earth [Note: [Col. 0442] Lov. alone has “on this earthly land” (*in hac terrena*).], are healed, sighing for the peace of their heavenly homeland. The Holy Spirit works inwardly so that the medicine applied outwardly may have effect. Otherwise, even if God himself, using a creature subject to him, addresses human senses in some human form—whether the bodily senses or those which we possess in dreams and which resemble the bodily senses—if he does not govern and move the mind by inward grace, all preaching of the truth is useless to a human being.

God does this while distinguishing vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath, by a dispensation that he himself knows, one that is very hidden but nevertheless just. For, with his help in wondrous and hidden ways, when sin dwelling in our members—which is now rather the punishment of sin—does not reign in our mortal body, so that we obey its desires, and when we do not offer our members to it as weapons of iniquity, as the Apostle commands (Rom. 6:12–13), it is turned toward the mind that, under God’s governance, does not consent to evil, and it will have that mind governing it more peacefully now; afterward, once perfect health [Note: [Col. 0443] Vind. and Am. have “and, governing it, will possess it more peacefully now, afterward perfect health.” A little later, where the text has *regnabit* (“will reign”), almost only Lov. has *regnantem* (“reigning”).] and immortality have been received, the human being will reign without any sin in eternal peace.

## CHAPTER VII  
### On the cause and persistence of Cain’s crime, whom not even God’s word recalled from the deed he had conceived

1. But what benefit did it bring him that God spoke to Cain, as we have explained as best we could, in the manner [Note: [Col. 0443] Vind., Am., Er., and several manuscripts have “in the way” (*eo modo*).] in which he used to speak with the first human beings through a subject creature, as their companion, in a form suited to them [Note: [Col. 0443] Compare Book 8 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, no. 37, and Book 9, nos. 3 and 4.]? Did he not, even after the divine warning, carry out the crime he had conceived of killing his brother?

For when God had distinguished between their sacrifices, looking favorably upon the one and with disfavor upon the other—a distinction that must have been made known through some visible attesting sign—and had done this because the latter’s works were evil while his brother’s were good, Cain became very sad and his face fell.

For it is written:

“And the Lord said to Cain, ‘Why have you become sad, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be at peace: for his turning is toward you, and you will rule over him’” (Gen. 4:6–7, according to the Septuagint).

In this warning that God gave to Cain, the statement, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?” has generated many interpretations because it is not clear why or in what sense it was said. Each interpreter of the divine Scriptures attempts to explain it according to the rule of faith.

A sacrifice is offered rightly when it is offered to the true God, to whom alone sacrifice must be offered. But it is not divided rightly when the places, times, the things themselves that are offered, the person who offers, the one to whom it is offered, or those to whom what has been offered is distributed for eating are not rightly distinguished. Here, then, we may understand “division” as discernment:

- when something is offered where it ought not to be offered, or what ought to be offered there is offered elsewhere;
- when something is offered at a time when it ought not to be offered, or what ought to be offered at another time is offered then;
- when something is offered that ought never and nowhere to have been offered;
- when a person keeps for himself the better things of the same kind than those he offers to God;
- or when a profane person, or anyone who ought not to partake, is made a participant in what has been offered.

In which of these respects Cain displeased God cannot easily be discovered.

But since the Apostle John, speaking about these brothers, says: “Not like Cain, who was from the evil one and killed his brother. And for what reason did he kill him? Because his works were evil, but his brother’s were righteous” (1 John 3:12), it may be understood that God did not look favorably upon his offering because in this very act he was dividing wrongly: he was giving God something of his, but keeping himself for himself.

All those do this who follow not God’s will but their own—who, that is, live not with an upright but with a perverse heart—and yet offer God a gift by which they think he can be bought off, so that he may not help them in healing their depraved desires but in fulfilling them.

This is characteristic of the earthly city: to worship God or the gods so that, with their assistance, it may rule in earthly victories and peace—not from the love of serving others, but from the desire to dominate. The good use the world in order to enjoy God; the wicked, by contrast, wish to use God in order to enjoy the world, though they at least believe that he exists or that he cares for human affairs. There are others who are much worse, who do not even believe this.

When Cain learned that God had looked favorably upon his brother’s sacrifice but not upon his own, he ought certainly to have changed and imitated his good brother, not, in his pride, to have envied him. But he became sad, and his face fell.

God especially reproved this sin: sorrow at another’s goodness, and at that of a brother. In reproving him, he asked: “Why have you become sad, and why has your face fallen?” God saw that he envied his brother, and he was reproving this.

For human beings, whose hearts are hidden from one another, it could have been uncertain and entirely ambiguous whether that sorrow arose from his own wickedness—which he had learned displeased God—or from grief over his brother’s goodness, which had pleased God when he looked upon his sacrifice.

But God, explaining why he had not accepted Cain’s offering, showed that Cain himself deserved displeasure rather than his brother undeservedly, since Cain was unjust in dividing wrongly—that is, in living wrongly—and unworthy of having his offering approved; yet he was even more unjust because he freely hated his righteous brother [Note: [Col. 0444] So our codices. In B., “rather than that his brother should undeservedly displease him.” M.].

2. Nevertheless, God did not dismiss him without a holy, just, and good command: “Be at peace,” he says; “for his turning is toward you, and you will rule over him.”

His brother? Certainly not. Over what, then, if not over sin? For he had said, “You have sinned,” and then added, “Be at peace; for his turning is toward you, and you will rule over him.”

This may indeed be understood in such a way that the turning of sin ought to be toward the human being, so that he knows that he ought to attribute to no one but himself the fact that he sins. This is the healing medicine of wholesome repentance, and an appropriate request for forgiveness: where it says, “His turning is toward you,” we should not supply “it will be,” but “let it be”—that is, the words are a command, not merely a prediction.

Each person will then rule over sin if, instead of defending it, he subjects it to himself through repentance. Otherwise he will serve the sin that rules him if he gives his patronage to what has happened [Note: [Col. 0444] Lov. has “to what is approaching” (*accedenti*). Other books have *accidenti*.].

But if “sin” is understood as carnal desire itself, of which the Apostle says, “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17), and among the fruits of the flesh he also mentions envy—the envy by which Cain was goaded and inflamed toward his brother’s destruction—then “it will be” is rightly supplied: “For its turning will be toward you, and you will rule over it.”

For when that carnal part has been stirred—the part that the Apostle calls sin when he says, “It is not I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:17)—a part of the soul that even philosophers say is defective, not one that ought to drag the mind along but one that the mind ought to govern and restrain from unlawful actions by reason—when, then, it has been stirred toward committing some wrong, if one keeps still [Note: [Col. 0445] So the manuscripts. The editions instead have “if one gives in” (*acquiescatur*).] and obeys the Apostle’s command, “Do not offer your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Rom. 6:13), it is turned, subdued and conquered, toward the mind, so that reason rules over it as its subject.

This is what God commanded Cain, who was inflamed against his brother by the torches of envy and wished to remove the one whom he ought to have imitated.

“Be at peace,” he said: “hold your hands back from crime; do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires, and do not offer your members as weapons of iniquity to sin. Its turning is toward you: when it is not helped by being indulged, but is restrained by remaining at peace. And you will rule over it: when it is not permitted to act outwardly, it becomes accustomed even inwardly not to be moved, under the power of the mind that governs and benevolently directs it.”

Something similar is said in the same divine book about the woman. After the sin, when God questioned and judged them, sentences of condemnation were pronounced upon the serpent—the devil—and upon the woman and her husband themselves.

For when he had said to her, “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning, and in sorrows you will bear children,” he then added: “And your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you” (Gen. 3:16).

What was said to Cain about sin, or about the defective desire of the flesh, is said in this passage about the sinful woman. Here we must understand that the husband, in governing his wife, ought to resemble the mind governing the flesh.

For this reason the Apostle says: “He who loves his wife loves himself; for no one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:28–29). These things must be healed, as our own things, not condemned as something alien.

But Cain received that command of God as a transgressor. For as the defect of envy grew stronger, he ambushed and killed his brother [Note: [Col. 0445] Several manuscripts have “ambushed his brother.”].

Such was the founder of the earthly city. How he also signified the Jews, by whom Christ was killed—the shepherd of human sheep, whom Abel, the shepherd of sheep, prefigured—since this is a matter belonging to prophetic allegory, I will refrain from discussing now. I recall having said certain things about it against Faustus the Manichaean [Note: [Col. 0445] Namely, Book 12, chapters 9 and following.].

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Why Cain founded a city at the beginning of the human race

1. Now I must defend the historical account, lest Scripture appear incredible when it says that a city was built by one human being at a time when, after a brother had killed his brother, no more than four—or rather three—men seem to have been on the earth: the first human being, the father of all; Cain himself; and his son Enoch, after whom the city itself was named.

But those who are troubled by this consider too little that the writer of this sacred history did not need to name all the human beings who could have existed at that time, but only those whom the plan of the work required him to mention.

The purpose of that writer, through whom the Holy Spirit was accomplishing this work, was to reach Abraham through the succession of certain generations propagated from one human being, and thereafter, through Abraham’s seed, to reach the people of God. In that people, distinguished from the other nations, everything was prefigured and foretold that was foreseen in the Spirit as to come concerning the city whose kingdom will be eternal, and concerning its King and likewise its founder, Christ.

At the same time, the other society of human beings, which we call the earthly city, was not to be omitted; it was to be mentioned to the extent necessary for the city of God to become clear even by comparison with its adversary.

Since, therefore, divine Scripture, when it also records the number of years that those human beings lived, concludes in this way: “And he begot sons and daughters, and all the days of so-and-so, or of such-and-such, which he lived, were so many years, and he died” (Gen. 5:4–5, and elsewhere)—are we, because it does not name those sons and daughters, not to understand that during the many years in which they lived at that first age of this world many human beings could have been born, by whose communities even many cities could have been founded?

Rather, it belonged to God, under whose inspiration these things were written, to arrange and distinguish these two societies at the beginning by their different generations, so that the generations of human beings—that is, of those living according to human nature—would be traced separately from the generations of the sons of God, that is, of those living according to God, down to the Flood.

There the separation and mingling of the two societies are narrated. Their separation is shown by the fact that the generations of each are recorded separately: one from Cain the fratricide, the other from the man called Seth, who too was born from Adam in place of the brother whom Cain had killed.

Their mingling is shown by the fact that, when the good had declined into worse, all had become such that they were destroyed by the Flood, except for one righteous man named Noah, his wife, his three sons, and the same number of daughters-in-law. These eight human beings deserved to escape in the ark from the destruction of all mortal beings.

2. Therefore, where it is written, “Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and he was building a city in the name of his son Enoch,” it does not follow that Enoch should be thought to have been his first son.

Nor should this be inferred from the statement that he knew his wife, as though he had then first joined himself to her in intercourse. For the same Scripture says this not only of Adam, the father of all, at the time when Cain was conceived—Cain whom he appears to have had as his firstborn—but later as well: “Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth” (Gen. 4:17, 25).

From this it is understood that Scripture commonly speaks in this way, even though whenever we read in it that human beings were conceived, it does not always mean that the two sexes were then joining together for the first time.

Nor is it necessarily an argument that we should regard Enoch as his father’s firstborn merely because the city was named after him. It is not unreasonable that, although he had other children, his father loved Enoch more than the others for some reason.

Judah, after all, was not the firstborn from whom Judea and the Jews were named. But even if this son was born first to the founder of that city, it should not for that reason be thought that the city received his name from his father at the time of his birth. For a city could not then have been established by one person, since a city is nothing other than a multitude of human beings bound together by some bond of fellowship.

Rather, when that man’s family had grown so numerous that it already possessed the size of a people, it could certainly have happened that he both established a city and gave the established city the name of his firstborn.

For the life of those human beings was so long that, among those mentioned there whose years are not omitted, the one who lived the shortest time before the Flood reached seven hundred and fifty-three years [Note: [Col. 0447] This is Lamech, according to the Septuagint, Genesis 5:31.]. Several lived beyond nine hundred years, although no one reached one thousand.

Who, then, would doubt that during the lifetime of one human being the human race could have multiplied so greatly that there would have been enough people to establish not one city but many [Note: [Col. 0447] Our fathers’ memory preserved the recollection of a village in Spain with nearly one hundred houses, whose inhabitants were all descended from an old man who was still living, so that there was no longer a term of kinship by which he could be called by the name of his descendant. For in our language we do not ascend beyond *abavus*. LUD. VIVES.]?

This can very easily be inferred from the fact that from one Abraham, in little more than four hundred years, so great a multitude of the Hebrew nation was produced that, at the departure of that people from Egypt, six hundred thousand men [Note: [Col. 0447] Our manuscripts have “six hundred thousand men”; except codex 2050, which reads “six hundred and sixty thousand men.” M.] of military age are reported to have existed (Exod. 12:37).

We may leave aside the nation of the Idumeans, which did not belong to the people of Israel and was begotten by Esau, Israel’s brother and Abraham’s grandson, as well as the other peoples [Note: [Col. 0447] Supply “peoples.”] born from Abraham’s seed but not begotten through his wife Sarah.

## CHAPTER IX  
### On the long life of human beings before the Flood, and on the greater size of human bodies
For this reason, no prudent assessor of events would doubt that Cain could have founded not merely some city, but even a large one, since the life of mortals was prolonged to so great a length [Note: [Col. 0447] See Pliny, *Natural History*, book 7, chapters 49–50.]—unless perhaps some unbeliever should raise against us, on the basis of the sheer number of years, the question of whether people really lived as long then as is written in our authorities [Note: [Col. 0447] Vind., Am., Er., and several manuscripts read *in auctoritatibus nostris*, “in our authorities.”], and deny that this should be believed. For they likewise do not believe that bodies then were far larger than they are now. Hence their most distinguished poet, Virgil [Col. 0448], speaking of a huge stone that a brave man [Note: The Lov. edition alone reads *fortissimus*, “a very brave man.”] of those times, fighting, both tore from the boundary of a field, ran with, whirled around, and hurled,

> “Scarcely could twelve chosen men  
> Raise it upon their necks—  
> men with such bodies as the earth now produces.”

he says [Note: [Col. 0448] Er. and Lov. read *Vix illud*, “Scarcely could twelve men lift that.” But the other printed editions and manuscripts read *Vix illum*, “Scarcely could twelve men lift him.” It may refer either to the stone or to the boundary marker mentioned immediately beforehand by Virgil.] (*Aeneid*, book 12, lines 899–900), thereby indicating that the earth was then accustomed to produce larger bodies. How much more so, therefore, in the more recent ages of the world, before that famous and widely reported flood?

Yet the magnitude of ancient bodies is generally proved to unbelievers by graves stripped bare through age, the force of rivers, or various accidents, where bones of the dead of incredible size have appeared, or from which they have fallen. I myself, not alone but with several others, saw on the shore at Utica a human molar so enormous that, if it were cut up bit by bit into the dimensions of our teeth, it seemed to us capable of producing a hundred of them. But I would believe that it belonged to some giant. For besides the fact that all bodies then were much larger than ours, giants greatly surpassed the rest. So also in later times, including our own, there have indeed been rare individuals who exceeded the size of others by a great deal, though such people have almost never been entirely absent.

Pliny the Elder, a most learned man, testifies that, as the course of the ages advances further and further, nature bears smaller bodies. He also reports that Homer often lamented this in verse—not mocking these statements as poetic fictions, but accepting them as historical testimony, like a writer recording natural marvels (*Natural History*, book 7, chapter 16). But, as I said, discoveries of bones, which endure because of their lasting nature, generally reveal the bodily size of the ancients even many centuries later.

The number of years lived by each person who existed in those times cannot now be tested by any comparable evidence. Yet for that reason faith in this sacred history should not be diminished. The more shamelessly we refuse to believe its narratives, the more clearly we see that its prophecies have been fulfilled.

The same Pliny also says [Note: [Col. 0448] See Pliny, *Natural History*, book 7, chapter 49.] that there still exists a people among whom people live for two hundred years. If, then, places unknown to us are believed still to exist where human lives last for periods we have not experienced, why should it not also be believed that such periods existed in the past? Is it credible that something exists somewhere which does not exist here, but incredible that something once existed which does not exist now?

## CHAPTER X — On the difference by which the numbers of years appear to disagree between the Hebrew and our codices

Therefore, although there appears to be some difference between the Hebrew and our codices [Note: By “our codices” he means the Latin codices then used by the Church, translated from the Greek version of the Septuagint; “the Hebrew codices” are those translated from the Hebrew Scripture. Compare book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, sections 16 and 22.] in the actual number of years—and I do not know how this came about—nevertheless the difference is not so great that the two disagree about those people having lived for such long periods [Col. 0449]. For the first man himself, Adam, is found in our codices to have lived two hundred and thirty years before he fathered the son who was called Seth, whereas in the Hebrew codices he is said to have lived one hundred and thirty years (Genesis 5:3). But after he fathered him, he is read as having lived seven hundred years in our codices, and eight hundred in theirs (ibid., 4). Thus, in both, the total sum agrees.

Then, through the successive generations, before the person who is said to have been born was born, his father is found among the Hebrews to have lived one hundred years fewer; but after that person himself was born, one hundred years fewer are found in our codices than in the Hebrew ones. Thus on both sides the total agrees. In the sixth generation the two codices nowhere disagree. In the seventh, where Enoch is said not to have died but to have been transferred because he pleased God, there is the same discrepancy as in the preceding five generations: one hundred years before he fathered the son mentioned there. Thus the totals likewise agree. For, before his transfer, he lived according to both codices three hundred and sixty-five years (ibid., 21–23).

The eighth generation does contain some variation, but it is smaller and unlike the others. Methuselah [Note: [Col. 0449] The manuscripts read *Mathusalam*. Later, only the Lov. edition has *quippe cum genuit Enoch*, “since he fathered Enoch.” The other books more correctly have *quippe quem*, “for he whom.”], whom Enoch fathered, lived, according to the Hebrews, not one hundred years fewer but twenty more before he fathered the one who follows in the succession; these years are again added in our codices after he fathered him, and in both the total of all the years corresponds (ibid., 25–27).

Only in the ninth generation—that is, in the years of Lamech, Methuselah’s son and Noah’s father—does the total differ, though not by much. For Lamech is found to have lived twenty-four years more in the Hebrew codices than in ours. Before he fathered the son called Noah, he has six years fewer in the Hebrew codices than in ours; but after he fathered him, he has thirty more in those same codices than in ours (ibid., 28–31). Thus, subtracting those six years, twenty-four remain, as stated.

## CHAPTER XI — On the years of Methuselah, whose age appears to exceed the flood by fourteen years

From this discrepancy between the Hebrew codices and ours arises that most famous question: Methuselah is calculated to have lived fourteen years after the flood [Note: [Col. 0449] See Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.], although Scripture records that, of all who were then on the earth, only eight people escaped the destruction of the flood in the ark (1 Peter 3:20), and Methuselah was not among them.

According to our codices, Methuselah lived one hundred and sixty-seven years before he fathered the one whom he called Lamech. Then Lamech himself lived one hundred and eighty-eight years before Noah was born from him; together these amount to three hundred and fifty-five years. To these are added Noah’s six hundred years, in which year of his life the flood occurred (Genesis 7:6). These make nine hundred and fifty-five years from Methuselah’s birth to the year of the flood [Col. 0450].
