The total years of Methuselah’s life are calculated as nine hundred and sixty-nine: for after living one hundred and sixty-seven years and fathering the son called Lamech, he lived another eight hundred and two years. Together these, as we have said, make nine hundred and sixty-nine years (Genesis 5:25–27). Thus, subtracting nine hundred and fifty-five years from Methuselah’s birth to the flood, fourteen remain, during which he is believed to have lived after the flood.

For this reason some suppose that he was with his father, who had been transferred, for a certain time—not on earth, where it is established that all flesh was destroyed which nature does not permit to live in the waters—and that he lived there until the flood had passed. They are unwilling to detract from the authority of the codices which the Church accepted as more authoritative, and they believe that the Jewish codices, rather than ours, lack what is true. For they do not admit that the error could more likely have occurred among the translators than that something false should exist in the language from which Scripture itself was translated into ours through the Greek.

They say, however, that it is not credible that the translators of the Septuagint, who translated at the same time and with one mind, could have erred, or that, where they had no interest in doing so, they would have wished to lie. But they claim that the Jews, while envying us because the Law and the Prophets passed to us through translation, altered certain things in their codices so that the authority of our Scriptures might be diminished.

Let each person accept this opinion or suspicion as he thinks best. It is nevertheless certain that Methuselah did not live after the flood, but died in that same year, if what is found concerning the number of years in the Hebrew codices is true. What I think about those translators of the Septuagint I shall discuss more carefully in its proper place, when, with the Lord’s help, we come to mention those periods as fully as the needs of this work require [Note: [Col. 0450] Below, book 18, chapters 42–44].

For the present, it is sufficient for the question at hand that, according to both codices, the people of that age lived such long lives that, within the lifetime of one who was first born from the two parents whom the earth alone then possessed, the human race could multiply to the point of establishing even a city [Note: [Col. 0450] Thus our codices. In B., *ut possit*, “so that he can.”].

## CHAPTER XII — On the opinion of those who do not believe that the people of the earliest ages lived as long as is written

### 1

For those who think that the years of those times were reckoned differently must not be listened to in any way—that is, as though they were so short that ten of them were reckoned as one of our years. Therefore, they say, whenever anyone hears or reads that someone lived nine hundred years, he should understand ninety: ten of their years constituted one of ours, and ten of ours constituted one hundred of theirs.

Accordingly, they suppose that Adam was twenty-three years old when he fathered Seth, and that Seth himself was twenty [Note: [Col. 0450] Supply: “years.”] years and six months old when Enos was born from him—years which Scripture calls two hundred and five. For, as those whose opinion we are explaining conjecture, they divided one year of the kind we now have into ten parts, and called those parts years. One of these parts contains the square of six, because God completed his works in six days so that he might rest on the seventh. I discussed this matter as best I could in the eleventh book (chapter 8).

Six times six, the number that produces the square of six, makes thirty-six days. Multiplied by ten, these reach three hundred and sixty, that is, twelve lunar months. Because of the remaining five days by which the solar year is completed, and the quarter-day by which, when multiplied by four in the year called leap year, one day is added, the ancients subsequently added days so that the number of years might be accounted for; the Romans called these intercalary days.

Thus Enos, whom Seth fathered, was nineteen years old when his son Cainan was born from him—years which Scripture calls one hundred and ninety (Genesis 5:9, according to the Septuagint). And thereafter, through all the generations in which the years of people before the flood are mentioned, almost no one is found in our codices who fathered a son when he was one hundred years old or younger, or even one hundred and twenty, or not much older. Rather, those who fathered children at the youngest age are reported to have been one hundred and sixty years old, or more.

For, they say, a man who was ten years old could not father children—although those years were called one hundred years by those people. But at sixteen years puberty is mature and already suitable for begetting offspring; that age was called one hundred and sixty years by those times.

To make it not incredible that a year was then reckoned differently, they add what is found in the histories of many writers: that the Egyptians had a year of four months [Note: [Col. 0451] See Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 2, chapter 12], the Acarnanians one of six months, and the Lavinians one of thirteen months.

After Pliny the Elder had recorded that it had been written that one man lived one hundred and fifty-two years, another ten years more [Note: Several manuscripts read *alios*, “others.”], others had lives of two hundred years, others of three hundred, some reached five hundred, others six hundred, and some even eight hundred, he thought that all these things arose from ignorance about the times. “Some,” he says, “designated one year in summer and another in winter; others by the four seasons, like the Arcadians, whose years were three months long.” He added that at times the Egyptians, whose short years we have said above consisted of four months, bounded the year by the moon’s completion. “Thus,” he says, “among them people are reported to have lived even a thousand years each” [Note: [Col. 0451] Pliny, book 7, chapter 49].

### 2

With arguments that seemed plausible, certain people, without destroying faith in this sacred history but attempting to reinforce it so that it would not be incredible that the ancients are reported to have lived so many years, persuaded themselves—and do not think that they persuaded themselves imprudently—that the year was then called such a very small period of time that ten of their years constituted one of ours, and ten of ours constituted one hundred of theirs.

But the falsity of this is demonstrated by extremely clear evidence. Before I do so, it seems to me that I should not remain silent about what suspicion might be more credible [Col. 0452].

Certainly, we could refute and disprove this assertion from the Hebrew codices, where Adam is found to have been not two hundred and thirty but one hundred and thirty years old when he fathered his third son (Genesis 5:3). If those years are thirteen of ours, he undoubtedly fathered his first son when he was eleven years old or not much older. Who can beget children at that age according to the customary and universally familiar law of nature?

But let us set him aside, since perhaps he could have done so even when he was created. For it is not credible that he was made as small as our infants are. But his son was not two hundred and five, as we read, but one hundred and five when he fathered Enos (ibid., 6); and according to these people he was therefore not yet eleven years old.

What shall I say about his son Cainan, who, while he is found to have been one hundred and seventy years old in our codices, is read in the Hebrew codices as having been seventy when he fathered Mahalaleel (ibid., 12)? Who begets a child at seven years of age, if seventy years were then called what seven years are now?

## CHAPTER XIII — Whether, in counting the years, the authority of the Hebrews or of the translators of the Septuagint should be followed

### 1

But when I say this, the response will immediately be made that it is a Jewish falsehood—a matter sufficiently discussed above—for the translators of the Septuagint, men deservedly celebrated, could not have lied.

If I ask what is more credible: that the Jewish people, spread so far and wide, could have conspired by common agreement to write this falsehood and, while envying others their authority, deprived themselves of the truth; or that seventy men, who were themselves Jews, stationed in one place because the Egyptian king Ptolemy had summoned them for this work, envied foreign peoples the truth itself and did this by a shared plan—who would not see which alternative is more readily and easily believed?

But surely no prudent person will believe either that the Jews, whatever their perversity and wickedness, could have exerted so much power over so many codices dispersed so far and wide, or that those seventy memorable men shared one plan to withhold the truth from the nations out of envy.

It is therefore more credible to say that, when these texts first began to be copied from Ptolemy’s library, something of this kind could have happened in a single codex—that is, in the first copy made from it—from which it then spread more widely; and there could indeed have been a copyist’s error [Note: [Col. 0452] The manuscripts read *sed*, “but.”].

This is not absurd to suspect in the question concerning Methuselah’s lifespan, and also in the other case where the total does not agree by twenty-four years. But in those cases where the same pattern of error continues, so that before the son who belongs in the succession is born, one version has an additional one hundred years while another lacks them; and after the son is born, the years that were lacking are present, while those that were present are lacking, so that the total agrees—and this occurs in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and seventh generations—the error itself appears to possess a certain, if one may call it so, consistency [Col. 0453]. It does not smell of chance, but of deliberate effort.

### 2

Therefore, let that difference in the numbers, which are arranged one way in the Greek and Latin codices and another way in the Hebrew codices—where this equal pattern of one hundred years being added beforehand and later subtracted is not continued through so many generations—be attributed neither to Jewish malice nor to the diligence or prudence of the translators of the Septuagint, but to the error of the copyist who first received the task of copying the codex from the library of the king mentioned above.

Even today, when numbers do not contribute to anything that can easily be understood or that appears useful to learn, they are copied carelessly and corrected even more carelessly. Who would think that he needed to learn how many thousands of men each of the tribes of Israel could have contained? It is not thought to be useful; and how few people are there who recognize the depth of its usefulness?

But here, where through so many connected generations one hundred years are present in one place and absent in another, and after the son who had to be mentioned is born they are absent where they had been present and present where they had been absent, so that the total agrees, clearly the person who did this wished to persuade people that the ancients lived for so many years because they called very short periods years. He attempted to demonstrate this from the maturity of puberty, at which age people were capable of begetting children. He therefore thought that, in those one hundred years, ten of ours should be understood, lest unbelievers refuse to accept that people had lived so long; and thus he added one hundred years wherever he did not find an age suitable for begetting children, and, after sons had been born, subtracted those same years so that the total would agree.

In this way he wished to make the ages suitable for begetting offspring appear credible, while nevertheless not defrauding the total number of years lived by each person. The fact that he did not do this in the sixth generation is itself what more strongly suggests that he did it where the matter we are discussing required it, because he did not do it where it did not.

For in that generation he found, among the Hebrews, that Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years before he fathered Enoch (Genesis 5:18). According to the theory of short years, these amount to sixteen years and somewhat less than two months—a period already suitable for begetting. Therefore, it was not necessary to add one hundred short years, making our twenty-six years, nor to subtract after Enoch’s birth the years that had not been added before his birth. Thus it happened that in this case there was no variation between the two codices.

### 3

But again it raises the question why, in the eighth generation, before Lamech was born from Methuselah, the Hebrew codices read one hundred and eighty-two years [Note: [Col. 0453] Some manuscripts omit *duo*, “two”; in its place *septem*, “seven,” seems to be the correct reading. For this is what appears in the Hebrew text at Genesis 5:25, whereas the translators of the Septuagint have one hundred and sixty-seven years at that point. Our codices have “two.”], while twenty fewer are found in our codices, where one hundred are usually added; and after Lamech was born, the missing years are restored to complete the total, which does not differ in either codex.

For if he wished one hundred and seventy years to be understood as seventeen, on account of the maturity of puberty, then he should no more have subtracted anything than he should have added anything. He had found an age suitable for begetting children, and this was the reason why in other cases he added those one hundred years where he did not find such an age.

We might reasonably think that this subtraction of twenty years had happened by chance through a copying error, if he had not subsequently taken care to restore them, as he had earlier subtracted them, so that the total would remain intact. Or should we perhaps think that it was done more craftily, in order to conceal the deliberate practice by which one hundred years were usually added first and later subtracted? For here, too, where it was unnecessary, something similar occurred: a small number was first subtracted and afterward restored, though it was not one hundred years.

However this may be understood—whether one believes that it happened in this way or not, whether ultimately it was so or was not so—I would have no doubt that the correct procedure is this: whenever something different is found in the two codices, since both cannot be true with respect to the historical facts, preference should be given to the language from which the translation into the other language was made by the translators.

For in three Greek codices, one Latin codex, and one Syriac codex, all agreeing among themselves, Methuselah was found to have died six years before the flood [Note: [Col. 0454] Compare *Questions on Genesis*, question 2.]

## CHAPTER XIV — On the equality of the years, which passed in the same spans of time in the earliest ages as they do now

### 1

Let us now see how it can be clearly demonstrated that the years reckoned in the extremely long lives of those people were not so short that ten of them constituted one of ours, but were of the same length as the years we now have—that is, years completed by the sun’s circuit.

It is written that the flood occurred in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life. Why, then, is it read there: “And the waters of the flood came upon the earth in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month” (Genesis 7:10–11, according to the Septuagint) [Note: Printed editions read *vitae*, “of [the] life”; the manuscripts read *in vita*, “in [the] life,” following the Greek Septuagint.], if that smallest year—the kind of which ten make one of ours—had thirty-six days?

Such a tiny year, if it received that name according to the ancient custom, either has no months, or its month is three days long, so that it has twelve months. How, then, could it be said here, “In the six-hundredth year, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month,” unless months existed then such as those we have now? For how otherwise could it be said that the flood began on the twenty-seventh day of the second month?

Then, at the end of the flood, we read:

> “And the ark came to rest in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat. The waters, however, were diminishing until the eleventh month; and in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains appeared” (ibid. 8:4–5).

If, therefore, those were months of the same kind, the years too were certainly of the same kind as ours. For months of three days could not have twenty-seven days. Or if one-thirtieth of three days was then called a day, so that everything was reduced proportionally, then that great flood, which is recorded as having occurred for forty days and nights, did not last even four of our days. Who could tolerate such absurdity and folly?

Let this error, then, be removed—the error that wishes by a false conjecture to support the credibility of our Scriptures in such a way as to undermine it elsewhere. Indeed, a day was then just as long as it is now, determined by twenty-four hours passing through day and night; a month was just as long as it is now, bounded by the moon’s beginning and completion; and a year was just as long as it is now, completed by twelve lunar months, with five days and a quarter added because of the solar cycle.

The six-hundredth year of Noah’s life was therefore a year of the same length as ours [Note: All manuscripts read *quanti anni*; printed editions have the erroneous *tantus anni*.]; its second month and the twenty-seventh day of that month were when the flood began. During that flood, forty days of uninterrupted, violent rain are recorded (Genesis 7:12)—days that did not consist of two hours and a little more, but of twenty-four hours, completed through day and night.

Consequently, those ancient people lived for years as long as the years in which Abraham later lived for one hundred and seventy-five years [Note: [Col. 0455] Most manuscripts have one hundred and seventy, omitting five.] (ibid. 25:7), his son Isaac for one hundred and eighty (ibid. 35:28), and his son Jacob for nearly one hundred and fifty (ibid. 27:28); and as long as the one hundred and twenty years lived by Moses at a somewhat later period (Deuteronomy 34:7), and as long as people even now live for seventy or eighty years, or not much more, of whom it is said: “And beyond this is toil and pain” (Psalm 89:10).

### 2

That variation in numbers which is found between the Hebrew codices and ours does not disagree with this conclusion about the longevity of the ancients. If it contains something so different that both versions cannot be true, the truth of the historical events must be sought from the language from which what we have was translated.

Although this resource is available everywhere to those who wish to use it, it is not without significance [Note: [Col. 0455] This means: “It is not empty or without mystery and purpose.” Ludovicus Vives.] that no one has dared to correct the translators of the Septuagint from the Hebrew codices in the many passages where they appear to say something different. For that difference was not considered a copying error, nor do I in any way think that it should be so considered.

Rather, where there is no copyist’s error, we should believe that, through the divine Spirit, they wished to say something differently—where the sense would be consistent with and proclaim the truth—not in the manner of translators [Note: The manuscripts read *munere*, “office/duty,” in place of *more*, “manner.”], but with the freedom of prophets. Hence apostolic authority is found to use not only the Hebrew Scriptures but also the Septuagint itself when it cites testimonies from Scripture.

I have promised to discuss this more carefully in a more suitable place, if God helps me. For now, I shall deal with what lies before us. There can be no doubt that the man who was first born from the first man could, while people lived so long, establish a city—certainly an earthly one, not the city called the City of God. It is for the purpose of writing about that city that we have taken upon ourselves the labor of this great work.

## CHAPTER XV — Whether it is credible that the men of the first age abstained from intercourse until the age at which they are reported to have fathered children

[Col. 0456]

### 1

Someone may therefore say: Is it really to be believed that a man intending to beget children, without having made a commitment to continence, abstained from sexual intercourse for one hundred years or more—or, according to the Hebrews, not much less than that, namely eighty, seventy, or sixty years—or that, if he did not abstain, he was unable to beget any offspring?

This question can be answered in two ways. Either puberty was proportionally later in the same degree as the length of the whole life was greater; or—and this seems more credible to me—the sons mentioned here were not the firstborn, but those whom the order of succession required in order to reach Noah, from whom in turn we see that Abraham was reached. Thereafter the succession continued to a definite point in time, for as much of the course of the most glorious city, wandering in this world and seeking its heavenly homeland, as had to be marked by the generations being mentioned.

What cannot be denied is that Cain was born first of all from the union of male and female. For Adam would not have said at his birth what he is recorded as having said—“I have acquired a man through God”—unless that child had first been added by birth to those two as a human being.

Abel followed him. His elder brother killed him, and he first displayed, in a certain prefiguration [Note: [Col. 0456] Lov. has *praefigurationem*, “a prefiguration,” while the other printed editions and the manuscripts disagree.], the fate of the City of God as a pilgrim: it would suffer unjust persecutions from the impious, who were, in a sense, earthborn—that is, lovers of an earthly origin and people who enjoyed the earthly happiness of the earthly city.

But it is not apparent how old Adam was when he fathered them. After this, the genealogies are arranged separately: one from Cain, the other from the one whom Adam fathered in succession to the brother whom Cain killed. He called his name Seth, saying, as it is written: “For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed” (Genesis 4:1, 25).

Since these two lines of descent—one from Seth and the other from Cain—set forth, in distinct orders, the two cities of which we are speaking, one heavenly and wandering on earth, the other earthly, either longing or clinging to earthly things as though they were its only joys, no age is stated for any descendant of Cain, even though his line is counted from Adam through the eighth generation, when he fathered the one who is mentioned after him.

The Spirit of God did not wish to mark the times of the generations of the earthly city before the flood, but preferred to do so in the case of the heavenly city, as though its generations were more worthy of remembrance.

When Seth was born, however, the years of his father are not left unmentioned; but Adam had already fathered other children. Would anyone dare assert that Cain and Abel were his only children? Because they alone are named on account of the order of the generations that needed to be recorded, it does not follow that they alone were born from Adam at that time.

For when, with the names of all the others covered in silence, Adam is nevertheless read to have fathered sons and daughters, who would presume to say how numerous this offspring was, if he wishes to avoid the charge of rashness [Col. 0457]? Adam could indeed, after Seth was born, have said by divine inspiration, “God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel,” because Seth was destined to fulfill Abel’s holiness—not because he was the first to be born after Abel in chronological order.

Furthermore, it is written: “Seth lived two hundred and five years,” or, according to the Hebrews, “one hundred and five years,” “and he fathered Enos.” Who could assert, except someone thoughtless, that Enos was Seth’s firstborn? We would then rightly marvel and ask how Seth had remained free from marriage for so many years without any intention of continence, or how, though married, he had fathered no child—especially since it is also written of him: “And he fathered sons and daughters, and all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years, and he died” (Genesis 5:4–8).

The same is then said successively of those whose years are mentioned: it is not concealed that they fathered sons and daughters. It is therefore entirely unclear whether the one who is said to have been born was the firstborn. Indeed, since it is not credible that those fathers, living for such a long time, were either still immature or lacked wives or children, it is likewise not credible that these were the first sons born to them.

But when the sacred historian was intent on reaching, through the succession of generations and through marked periods, the birth and life of Noah, in whose time the flood occurred, he mentioned not the children who were firstborn to their parents, but those who entered into the order of succession.

### 2

To make this clearer by example, I shall insert something that will leave no one in doubt that what I am saying could have happened. The evangelist Matthew, wishing to commend the genealogy of the Lord’s flesh to memory through a succession of ancestors, began with Abraham and aimed first at reaching David. He says: “Abraham begot Isaac.” Why did he not say Ishmael, whom Abraham begot first? Then he says: “Isaac begot Jacob.” Why did he not say Esau, who was his firstborn? Clearly, because through them he could not reach David.

He continues: “Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.” Was Judah the firstborn? He says: “Judah begot Phares and Zara” (Matthew 1:2–3). Neither of these twins was Judah’s firstborn, for he had already fathered three sons before them.

Matthew therefore retained in the genealogy those through whom he could reach David, and from David reach the point toward which he was directing the genealogy. From this it can be understood that the ancient people before the flood likewise were represented not by their firstborn, but by those through whom the successive order of generations led to the patriarch Noah. Thus we need not be wearied by the obscure and unnecessary question of their allegedly late puberty.

## CHAPTER XVI — On the law of marriage, and how the first unions differed from marriages that followed
1. Since, after the first union of the man made from dust and his wife made from the man’s side, the human race required the joining of males and females in order to multiply through procreation—and since there were no human beings except those born from those two—men took their sisters as wives. This was all the more ancient because necessity compelled it, and therefore later became all the more blameworthy when religion prohibited it. [Col. 0458]

For the most proper principle of charity was observed: human beings, for whom harmonious fellowship was useful and honorable, were to be bound together by the ties of different relationships. No one person was to have many such relationships concentrated in himself, but each relationship was to be distributed among separate persons; thus, for the more diligent establishment of social life, many people would possess many distinct relationships.

[Note: The Amsterdam and Louvain editions read “in one [woman]” (*in una*) instead of “in one [person]” (*in uno*); the reading is corrected from Vindocinensis, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. The Louvain edition alone reads *colligendam* (“to be bound together”) for *colligandam* (“for binding together”).] A father and a father-in-law, for example, are the names of two different relationships. Thus, when each person has one father and another person as his father-in-law, charity extends itself more abundantly.

But Adam was necessarily both father and father-in-law to his sons and daughters when brothers and sisters were joined in marriage. Likewise Eve, his wife, was both mother and mother-in-law to the children of both sexes. If there had been two women, one the mother and the other the mother-in-law, social affection would have been bound together more richly. Finally, the sister herself, who also became a wife, held two relationships in one person.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “who” (*quae*) rather than “which” (*quod*).] If these had been distributed individually—one person being a sister and another a wife—the number of human relationships would have increased.

But this could not happen then, when there were no human beings apart from the brothers and sisters born from those first two. It therefore had to happen as soon as it became possible: when an abundance of people existed, wives were to be taken from among those who were no longer sisters; and not only was there then no necessity that this should occur, but if it did occur, it would be wrong.

For if even the grandchildren of the first human beings, who could already take their cousins as wives, had married their sisters, then one person would have possessed not two but three relationships. These ought to have been distributed individually, so that a more numerous kinship might be bound together by charity. One man would then be father, father-in-law, and maternal uncle to his sons—the sons, that is, of his sister and wife. His wife would likewise be mother, paternal aunt, and mother-in-law to those same common children. Those children would not only be brothers and spouses to one another, but also cousins, since they would be the children of siblings.

All these relationships, which in one person connected three people, would connect nine if they were distributed individually: one person would have one sister, another wife, another cousin, another father, another maternal uncle, another father-in-law, another mother, another paternal aunt, and another mother-in-law. In this way the social bond would not be confined within a small number of people, but would spread more broadly and abundantly through frequent relationships.

2. As the human race grew and multiplied, we see that even among the impious worshipers of many false gods this principle has been observed. Although fraternal marriages may be permitted by perverse laws, better custom nevertheless prefers to recoil from the permission itself. Though it was entirely permissible to take sisters in marriage in the earliest times of the human race, people now shun it as though it could never have been permitted.

Custom has very great power either to attract or to offend the human mind. When custom restrains immoderate desire in this matter, it is rightly judged wicked to tear it apart and corrupt it. [Col. 0459]

[Note: Printed editions read *designari*. Several manuscripts more aptly read *dissignari*, that is, “to be torn apart and broken up.” Thus in Terence, *Adelphoe*, act 1, scene 2, where Eugraphius reads *dissignavit* for *designavit* in “What has he just broken up?” and says that *dissignare* properly means to break something sealed by laws.]

For if it is unjust to cross the boundary of fields out of greed for possession, how much more unjust is it, through lust for intercourse, to overturn the boundary of morals? Even in our own times we have experienced how rarely marriages between cousins occurred, because their degree of kinship is close to that of siblings, although the law permitted them. Divine law had not forbidden it, and human law had not yet done so.

[Note: The law enacted by Theodosius forbidding marriages between cousins is praised by Aurelius Victor in his account of Theodosius and by Ambrose in Book 8, Letter 66. Augustine may perhaps allude to that law later in the words, “But who would doubt that at this time even marriages between cousins have more properly been prohibited?” Theodosius’s law has not survived to the present; another law concerning the same matter does survive, attributed to Constantius and enacted at Rome during the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus, in the Theodosian Code, Book 2, On Incestuous Marriages. Cassiodorus Senator, Book 7 of the *Variae*, chapter 46, shows that the emperors formerly granted permission for a cousin to be a legitimate wife.]

Nevertheless, even a permitted act was shunned because of its proximity to what was forbidden. Intercourse with a cousin seemed almost like intercourse with a sister, because cousins themselves are called brothers on account of such close blood relationship, and are almost siblings.

The ancient fathers were religiously concerned that kinship, gradually separating itself through successive degrees, should move farther away and cease to be kinship. They therefore sought to bind it again in marriage while it was still not far removed, as though calling back what was fleeing. Hence, when the world was already full of human beings, men did not take as wives women born of the same father or mother, or of both parents, but they did love to take wives from their own wider family.

But who would doubt that at the present time marriages between cousins have more properly been prohibited—not only for the reasons we have discussed, namely, to multiply relationships, so that one person should not possess two relationships when two persons could possess them and thereby increase the number of kinships, but also because, somehow, human modesty contains something natural and praiseworthy? A person to whom kinship requires reverent honor restrains himself

[Note: The manuscripts read *consobrinorum* (“of male cousins”); printed editions read *consobrinarum* (“of female cousins”). Printed editions read *verecundum* (“modest”); the manuscripts read *reverendum* (“requiring reverence”).] from that person as an object of sexual desire, even though she may be capable of bearing children; indeed, we see that marital chastity itself blushes at such desire.

3. The union of male and female, insofar as it concerns the mortal human race, is a kind of seedbed of the city. But the earthly city requires generation alone, whereas the heavenly city also requires regeneration, so that it may escape the guilt of generation.

Whether there was some bodily and visible sign of regeneration before the Flood—and, if there was, what kind it was, as circumcision was later commanded to Abraham (Genesis 17:10–11)—sacred history does not say. [Note: Compare *Against Julian*, Book 5, §45.] It does, however, plainly state that even those most ancient human beings offered sacrifice to God. This was clear in the case of the first two brothers, and Noah, after the Flood, when he had come out of the ark, is recorded to have offered sacrifices to God (Genesis 8:20).

We have already spoken of this matter in the preceding books: arrogant demons, claiming divinity for themselves and desiring to be believed gods, demand sacrifice for themselves and rejoice in such honors for no other reason than that they know true sacrifice is owed to the true God.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the two fathers and rulers born from one parent

Since Adam was the father of both lines—that is, of the line belonging to the earthly city and of the line belonging to the heavenly city—Abel was killed, and in his killing a remarkable sacrament was signified. Then two fathers of the respective races came into being: Cain and Seth. In the sons of these men, whose names needed to be recorded, the distinguishing signs of these two cities among the mortal human race began to appear more clearly.

Cain fathered Enoch, and in Enoch’s name he founded a city: the earthly city, that is, not a pilgrim city in this world, but one resting in the temporal peace and happiness of this world. Cain is interpreted as “Possession”; hence, when he was born, either his father or his mother said, “I have acquired a man through God” (Genesis 4:1).

Enoch, however, means “Dedication.” The earthly city is dedicated where it is founded, because here it possesses the end toward which it aims and aspires.

Seth, on the other hand, is interpreted as “Resurrection,” and his son Enos is interpreted as “Man”—not in the same way as Adam, for that name too is interpreted as “Man,” but as a common word in that language, Hebrew, for male and female. For Scripture says of Adam: “Male and female he made them, and he blessed them, and he called their name Adam” (Genesis 5:2). Thus there is no doubt that the woman was called Eve by her proper name, while Adam, which means “Man,” was the name of both.

Enos, however, is interpreted as “Man” in such a way that those acquainted with that language assert that a woman cannot be called by this word, as though he were “the son of resurrection,” where “they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Luke 20:35). For there will be no generation there, once regeneration has brought people to that place.

For this reason, I think it should not be overlooked that in the generations descended from the one called Seth, although sons and daughters are said to have been fathered, no female born there is specifically named. In the generations descended from Cain, however, at the very end to which they extend, the last female born is named.

[Note: The manuscripts read *dicantur* (“are said”); printed editions read *dicatur*. Most manuscripts read *pertenduntur* (“are extended”) for *protenduntur*. Compare Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis*, question 47. —Coquaeus.]

Thus we read:

> Methusael fathered Lamech; and Lamech took two wives, the name of one being Adah and the name of the second Zillah. Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and keep livestock. The name of his brother was Jubal; he was the one who demonstrated the psaltery and the lyre. Zillah also bore Tubal; he was a worker in bronze and a hammerer of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal was Naamah.  
> (Genesis 4:18–22)

[Note: Some manuscripts have “Noemina.”]

The generations descended from Cain extend this far. In all, counting Adam himself, there are eight generations from Adam: seven down to Lamech, who had two wives, and the eighth generation is found in his sons, among whom a woman is also mentioned.

This elegantly signifies that the earthly city would possess carnal generations until its end—generations produced by the union of males and females. Hence, in a circumstance found nowhere else before the Flood apart from Eve, the wives of that man who is here called the last father are expressed by their proper names.

Just as Cain, whose name means “Possession,” the founder of the earthly city, and his son Enoch, in whose name the city was founded and whose name means “Dedication,” indicate that this city has both an earthly beginning and an earthly end, where nothing more is hoped for than what can be seen in this age, so we must examine

[Note: Printed editions read *quam quod* (“than that which”); *quod* is absent from the manuscripts.] what this sacred history says about Seth, who is separately recorded as the father of a line of generations.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### What is signified in Abel, Seth, and Enos that appears to pertain to Christ and his body, that is, the Church

“And Seth,” it says, “was born a son, and he called his name Enos; this man hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God” (Genesis 4:26).

The testimony of truth surely cries out. The man who is the son of resurrection lives in hope; in hope lives the city of God while it is a pilgrim here, the city born from faith in the resurrection of Christ.

From those two men—Abel, whose name means “Lamentation,” and his brother Seth, whose name means “Resurrection”—the death of Christ and his life from the dead are symbolized. From this faith the city of God is born: that is, the man who hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God.

“For by hope we were saved,” the Apostle says. “But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

Who, then, would think that this is unrelated to the depth of the sacrament? Did Abel not hope to call upon the name of the Lord God, whose sacrifice Scripture records as having been so acceptable to God? Did Seth himself not hope to call upon the name of the Lord God, concerning whom it was said, “For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel” (Genesis 4:25)?

Why, then, is something understood to be common to all the godly attributed particularly to him, unless it was necessary that in the one who is first recorded as having arisen from the father of the generations separated toward the better part—that is, toward the heavenly city—there should be a prophetic prefiguration of the man, that is, of the human society, which does not live according to man in the reality of earthly happiness, but according to God in hope of eternal happiness?

It does not say, “This man hoped in the Lord God,” or, “This man called upon the name of the Lord God,” but, “This man,” it says, “hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God.”

What does “hoped to call upon” mean except that it is a prophecy of the people who would arise and, according to the election of grace, call upon the name of the Lord God? This is what the Apostle understands concerning this people, which belongs to God’s grace, when another prophet says: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Romans 10:13; Joel 2:32).

The very statement, “He called his name Enos,” which means “Man,” followed by, “This man hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God,” sufficiently shows that man ought not to place his hope in himself. For, as we read elsewhere, “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5). Therefore he ought not to place hope even in himself, if he is to be a citizen of the other city—the city not dedicated according to the son of Cain in the present age, as this mortal age passes away, but in the immortality of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### The meaning shown by Enoch’s translation

This line too, whose father is Seth, contains the name of dedication in the generation that is seventh from Adam, counting Adam himself. For Enoch, whose name means “Dedication,” was born seventh from Adam.

He is the one who was translated, because he pleased God, and he occupies a notable place in the order of the generations: the seventh from Adam, corresponding to the day on which the Sabbath was consecrated.

From Seth himself, the father of these generations distinguished from Cain’s line, Enoch is sixth—just as man was made on the sixth day, when God completed all his works.

But the translation of this Enoch prefigured the delay of our dedication. That dedication has already taken place in Christ our head, who rose in such a way that he would not die again and was himself translated. Another dedication of the entire house remains, however. Christ himself is its foundation, and it is postponed until the end, when there will be a resurrection of all, and they will no longer die.

Whether it is called the house of God, the temple of God, or the city of God, it is the same thing, and this does not conflict with Latin usage. Virgil, for example, calls the most powerful city the house of Assaracus, intending the Romans, who derive their origin from Assaracus through the Trojans. He also calls them the house of Aeneas (*Aeneid* 1.284; 3.97), because, under Aeneas’s leadership, the Trojans came to Italy and Rome was founded by them.

That poet imitated the sacred Scriptures, in which the house of Jacob is said to be the great people of the Hebrews.

## CHAPTER XX  
### How Cain’s succession is closed in eight generations from Adam, and how Noah is found to be the tenth among the descendants of the same father, Adam

1. Someone may say: If the author of this history intended, in recording the generations from Adam through his son Seth, to reach Noah, under whom the Flood occurred and from whom the line of those being born was again taken up until it reached Abraham, from whom the evangelist Matthew begins the generations that lead to Christ, the eternal King of the city of God, what did he intend in the generations from Cain, and to what point did he wish to bring them?

The answer is: to the Flood, by which the whole race of the earthly city was destroyed, though it was restored through the sons of Noah. For this earthly city and the society of people living according to man could not fail to exist until the end of this age, concerning which the Lord says, “The children of this age beget and are begotten” (Luke 20:34).

Regeneration, however, leads the pilgrim city of God in this age into the other age, whose children neither beget nor are begotten. Here, therefore, being born and begetting are common to both cities, although the city of God even here has many thousands of citizens who abstain from begetting children. The other city also has some who imitate them, though they are in error.

[Note: The manuscripts read: “but that city too has [such persons] by a certain imitation, though in error.” Printed editions expand the wording: “but that city too has some citizens like these, by a certain imitation, though in error.”]

For even those who, straying from this faith, have founded various heresies belong to that city: they live according to man, not according to God. The Gymnosophists of India, who are said to philosophize naked in the solitudes of India, are also its citizens, and they abstain from begetting.

[Note: Compare above, Book 14, chapter 17, at the end.]

This is not a good thing, however, unless it is done according to faith in the highest good, which is God.

No one is found to have done this before the Flood. Even Enoch himself, the seventh from Adam, who is reported to have been translated rather than to have died, fathered sons and daughters before his translation; among them was Methuselah, through whom the line of the generations to be recorded continued.

2. Why, then, are so few successions recorded in the generations from Cain, if they had to be brought down to the Flood, and if there was no long period before puberty during which people remained without offspring for a hundred years or more?

If the author of this book did not intend to reach some person to whom the sequence of generations necessarily had to lead—as, in the generations descended from Seth, he intended to reach Noah, from whom the necessary succession would again proceed—why was it necessary to omit the firstborn sons in order to reach Lamech, in whose sons that sequence ends, in the eighth generation from Adam and the seventh from Cain? It would seem as though something were to be connected from that point, leading either to the Israelite people, in whom earthly Jerusalem also provided a prophetic figure of the heavenly city, or to Christ according to the flesh, who is “God blessed above all forever” (Romans 9:5), the builder and ruler of the heavenly Jerusalem. Yet the entire offspring of Cain was destroyed by the Flood.

It may therefore be supposed that the firstborn were recorded in this same order of generations.

Why, then, are there so few? There could not have been so few generations down to the Flood if the fathers did not remain free from begetting until their hundredth year, unless puberty was then correspondingly delayed in proportion to that longevity. For even if they were thirty years old when they began to father children, eight times thirty—since there are eight generations counting Adam and the sons of Lamech—amounts to 240 years. Is it credible, then, that they did not beget children during all the remaining time until the Flood? For what reason did the author of this account not wish to record the generations that followed?

According to our manuscripts, the years from Adam to the Flood amount to 2,262.

[Note: Some manuscripts have 2,250. Eusebius, Jerome, Bede, and others, following the manuscripts of the Septuagint, calculate 2,242 years. One manuscript, no. 2050, has 2,272.]

Even if we believe the smaller number to be more accurate, let 240 years be subtracted from 1,656 years. Is it credible that the offspring of Cain could have remained without generations for 1,400 years and more, the years that remain until the Flood?

3. Whoever is troubled by this should remember that, when I asked how it could be believed that those ancient men were able to abstain from begetting children for so many years, the question was resolved in two ways: either by assuming late puberty in proportion to such a long life, or by understanding that the sons mentioned in the generations were not firstborn, but those through whom the author of the book could reach the person he intended—just as, in the generations of Seth, he reached Noah.

Accordingly, in the generations of Cain, if no person appears whom the author intended to reach, and to whom it was necessary to arrive through those recorded rather than through the firstborn, the explanation of late puberty remains. They would therefore have become physically mature and capable of begetting somewhat after their hundredth year, so that the sequence of generations would proceed through the firstborn and reach the number of years required by the Flood.

It is also possible that, for some more hidden reason unknown to me, the sequence of generations was carried down to Lamech and his sons in order to commend this city, which we call earthly; then the author of the book ceased recording the others that could have existed down to the Flood.

[Note: I believe that only the generations of Cain that were to be punished for fratricide were enumerated. Josephus writes in this way in *Jewish Antiquities* 1.2.1: “When Cain was offering sacrifice and asking that he not incur anger on account of it, he relaxed the harsher punishment of homicide and decreed that he was accursed, declaring that his offspring would be punished down to the seventh generation.” Cain himself also lived until that time, and the narrator did not wish to omit the end of his life by means of his genealogy. —Ludovicus Vives.]

That may also be the reason why the order of generations was not carried through the firstborn: it may not be necessary to assume such late puberty among those people. The same city that Cain founded in the name of his son Enoch could have ruled widely and possessed kings—not several at the same time, but one in each generation, succeeding one another as those who reigned fathered them.

The first of these kings could have been Cain himself; the second, his son Enoch, in whose name the city was founded where he was to reign; the third, Gaidad, whom Enoch fathered; the fourth, Manihel, whom Gaidad fathered; the fifth, Methusael, whom Manihel fathered; and the sixth, Lamech, whom Methusael fathered—Lamech being the seventh from Adam through Cain.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone has *ibi* (“there”), and shortly afterward *ubi regnaret* (“where he might reign”), for *ubi regnaretur* (“where rule was exercised”). Some manuscripts read Mevia; others, Maviael; the Septuagint has Maleleel.]

It did not necessarily follow that the firstborn sons of reigning kings would succeed their fathers. Rather, succession might go to those whom merit in ruling, because of virtue useful to the earthly city, or some chance, might identify; or, by a kind of hereditary right of royal succession, especially to the son whom the father loved above his other children.

[Note: Our manuscripts read “that the firstborn sons of kings”; manuscript B reads “that the firstborn [should succeed] to the kingdom.”]

The Flood could have occurred while Lamech was still alive and reigning, so that it would find and destroy him, along with all the other human beings except those who were in the ark. Nor is it surprising if, with various numbers of years interposed, the two lines did not have an equal number of generations through the long period from Adam to the Flood: seven through Cain, but ten through Seth. For, as I have already said, Lamech is the seventh from Adam, and Noah the tenth.

For this reason, not one son of Lamech is mentioned, as in the preceding generations, but several: it was uncertain who would have succeeded him after his death if time for reigning had remained between Lamech and the Flood.

4. However the matter may stand—whether the sequence of generations from Cain proceeded through firstborn sons or through kings—it seems to me that one point must by no means be passed over in silence. When Lamech was found to be the seventh from Adam, so many of his children were counted that the number eleven was completed, and by this number sin is signified.

Three sons and one daughter are added. The wives, however, may signify something else, not what now needs to be emphasized. At present we are speaking about generations; from whom those women were born is left unmentioned.

Since the Law is proclaimed by the number ten, from which the memorable Decalogue takes its name, the number eleven, because it exceeds ten, clearly signifies transgression of the Law and therefore sin.

This is why, in the Tabernacle of the Testimony, which was like a movable temple during the journey of God’s people, eleven curtains of haircloth were commanded to be made (Exodus 26:7).

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “a walking temple” (*templum deambulatorium*).]

In goats’ hair there is a remembrance of sins, because of the goats destined for the left hand. We confess and prostrate ourselves in goats’ hair, as though saying what is written in the Psalm: “My sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:5).

The offspring from Adam through the wicked Cain therefore ends with the number eleven, by which sin is signified. That number is closed by a woman, the sex from which the beginning of sin arose, through which we all die.

It also happened that the pleasure of the flesh, which would resist the spirit, followed. For Lamech’s daughter herself, Naamah, is interpreted as “Pleasure.”

Through Seth, from Adam to Noah, the legitimate number ten is indicated. To Noah three sons are added. When one falls, two are blessed by their father, so that, with the reprobate removed and the approved sons added to the number, the number twelve is also signified. Twelve is notable both in the number of the patriarchs and in that of the Apostles, because of the parts of seven, one multiplied by the other. For three times four, or four times three, produces twelve.

With these matters established, I see that we must consider and mention how these two lines, which by their distinct generations signify two cities—one of those born from the earth and the other of those born again—were later mixed and confused in such a way that the entire human race, except for eight people, deserved to perish in the Flood.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Why, after Enoch, the son of Cain, has been mentioned, the whole account of his generation is continued down to the Flood, whereas, after Enos, the son of Seth, has been mentioned, the narrative returns to the beginning of the human creation

First, we must observe how, when the generations from Cain were being enumerated, after the descendant who came before all the others—the one in whose name the city was founded, namely Enoch—had been mentioned, the rest were connected in sequence down to the end of which I have spoken, until that race and its entire offspring were destroyed by the Flood.

When, however, one son of Seth, Enos, had been mentioned, before the remaining generations were added down to the Flood, a kind of division is inserted, and it is said:

> This is the book of the birth of human beings. On the day when God made Adam, he made him in the image of God. Male and female he made them, and he blessed them, and he called their name Adam, on the day when he made them.  
> (Genesis 5:1–2)

It seems to me that this was inserted so that the reckoning of time might begin again from Adam himself. The writer did not wish to make this reckoning in the earthly city, as though God mentioned that city in such a way that he did not count it.

But why does the narrative return here to this recapitulation after the son of Seth has been mentioned—the man who hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God—unless the two cities had to be set forth in this manner? [Col. 0466] One is represented through a murderer and extends to a murderer, for Lamech also confesses to his two wives that he has committed homicide (Genesis 4:23). The other is represented through the man who hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God.

For this is the whole and supreme task of the city of God that is a pilgrim in this world during its mortal existence: it had to be commended through one man whom the resurrection of the one who was killed brought forth.

That one man is the unity of the entire heavenly city—not yet complete, but destined to be completed through this prophetic prefiguration already set before us.

Let the son of Cain—that is, the son of Possession, possession of what except the earthly?—have a name in the earthly city, which was founded in his name. He belongs to those of whom it is sung in the Psalm: “They have called their names in their lands” (Psalm 48:12). For this reason what is written in another Psalm follows them: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing” (Psalm 72:20).

But let the son of Seth—that is, the son of Resurrection—hope to call upon the name of the Lord God. He prefigures the society of human beings that says: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God” (Psalm 52:10).

Let him not seek the empty glories of a famous name on earth: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not turned toward vanities and lying insanities” (Psalm 39:5).

[Note: Printed editions read *falsas* (“false”); the manuscripts read *mendaces* (“lying, deceitful”), as Augustine regularly does.]

Thus, once the two cities have been set forth—one existing in the reality of this age and the other in hope in God—and once they have emerged, as if through the common door of mortality opened in Adam, so that they might run forth and extend themselves toward their distinct and proper ends, the reckoning of time begins.

[Note: The manuscripts read *procurrant* (“run forth”); printed editions read *percurrant* (“run through”).]

In this reckoning other generations are added, after a recapitulation from Adam. From his origin, condemned as a single mass handed over to deserved condemnation, God made some vessels of wrath for dishonor and others vessels of mercy for honor (Romans 9:23), rendering to the former what was owed in punishment and giving to the latter by grace what was not owed.

Thus, even from comparison with the vessels of wrath, the heavenly city, which is a pilgrim on earth, may learn not to trust in the freedom of its own will, but to hope to call upon the name of the Lord God.

For the will exists in a nature made good by the good God but made mutable by the immutable God, because it was made from nothing. From the good it can turn aside to do evil, and this occurs through free choice; and from evil it can turn toward doing good, which does not occur without divine assistance.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### The fall of the sons of God, captivated by love of foreign women, whereby all except eight people deserved to perish in the Flood

As the human race advanced and increased through this freedom of the will, a mingling took place, and through shared wickedness a certain confusion of the two cities arose.

This evil again found its cause in the female sex—not, indeed, in the way it had at the beginning. Those women did not, at that time, seduce men through deception and persuade them to sin. Rather, women who had been wicked in their ways from the beginning, in the earthly city—that is, in the society of those born from the earth—were loved by the sons of God, citizens of the other city, which is a pilgrim in this world, because of their bodily beauty (Genesis 6:1ff.).

This beauty is indeed God’s gift. But he grants it also to the wicked, so that it may not appear to be a great good to the good.

Having abandoned the great good proper to the good, they fell toward a lesser good, which is not proper to the good but common to the good and the wicked. Thus the sons of God were captivated by love of the daughters of men, and, in order to enjoy them as wives, they declined into the customs of the earthly society, abandoning the piety they had preserved in the holy society.

So bodily beauty—created by God, certainly, but a temporal, carnal, and inferior good—is wrongly loved when God, the eternal, inward, and everlasting good, is set aside. In the same way, justice is abandoned and gold is loved by the greedy—not because of any sin belonging to gold, but because of the human being.

The same is true of every creature. Since every creature is good, it can be loved both rightly and wrongly: rightly, when the proper order is preserved; wrongly, when the order is disturbed.

I expressed this briefly in verse in a certain praise of the Creator:

[Note: All the manuscripts read this wording. Printed editions read: “someone expressed it briefly in verses in a certain praise of the Creator.”]

> These are yours; they are good, because you, being good, created them.  
> Nothing in them is ours except what we do by loving sinfully,  
> Neglecting order, and loving in place of you what was created by you.

But if the Creator is truly loved—that is, if he himself is loved, and nothing else is loved in his place that is not himself—he cannot be loved wrongly.

Indeed, love itself must be loved in the proper order, so that what ought to be loved is loved well and there may be in us the virtue by which we live rightly.

Therefore it seems to me that the brief and true definition of virtue is: “the order of love.” For this reason the bride of Christ, the city of God, sings in the holy *Song of Songs*: “Set love (*caritas*) in order within me” (Song of Songs 2:4).

[Note: Compare *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 1, §28.]

When the order of this charity—that is, of affection and love—was disturbed, the sons of God neglected God and loved the daughters of men.

These two names sufficiently distinguish the two cities. For those men were also, by nature, sons of men; but through grace they had begun to bear another name.

In the same Scripture in which the sons of God are said to have loved the daughters of men, those same sons are also called angels of God. Hence many people think that they were not human beings but angels.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Whether it should be believed that angels of spiritual substance, captivated by love of beautiful women, entered into marriages with them, from which giants were born
1. We left this question, mentioned in passing in the third book of this work (chapter 5), unresolved: whether angels, since they are spirits, can physically have intercourse with women. For it is written, “He makes his angels spirits”—that is, he makes those who are spirits by nature his angels by assigning them the office of announcing. For the word called *angelos* (ἄγγελος) in Greek, rendered *angelus* in Latin declension, means “messenger” in Latin. But whether he subsequently added something about their bodies when he said, “and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103:5), or whether his ministers are meant to burn with love as with a spiritual fire, is uncertain.

Nevertheless, the same most truthful Scripture testifies that angels appeared to human beings in such bodies that they could not only be seen but also touched. And since there is a very widespread report—and many affirm that they have learned this either by their own experience or from those whose experience is trustworthy—that Silvans [Note: [Col. 0468] Our manuscripts read *non esset* (“would not be”). M.], and Fauns [Note: [Col. 0468] Here Lovaniensis adds “Panes,” which is absent from the other printed editions and manuscripts.], whom the common people call incubi, have often behaved wickedly toward women and desired and accomplished intercourse with them [Note: [Col. 0468] Above, book 6, chapter 9, section 2.]; and that certain demons, whom the Gauls call *Dusii*, continually attempt and accomplish this uncleanness—indeed, so many make such assertions that to deny it seems shameless—I do not dare to define whether some spirits, embodied in the airy element (for this element can be perceived by bodily sense and touch even when it is stirred by a fan), might also experience such lust, so that, in whatever manner they can, they might mingle with women who perceive them.

Yet I would in no way believe that God’s holy angels could at that time have fallen in such a way. Nor do I think that the apostle Peter was speaking of them when he said, “For if God did not spare the angels who sinned, but thrust them into the prisons of darkness and delivered them to be held for judgment” (2 Peter 2:4); rather, he was speaking of those who first apostatized from God and fell with their prince, the devil, who by the envy and deceit of the serpent cast down the first human being [Note: [Col. 0468] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read “deceived.”].

That human beings were also called angels of God is abundantly attested by the same holy Scripture. For it is written even of John, “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way” (Mark 1:2). The prophet Malachi was also called an angel by a particular grace—that is, by a grace specially granted to him (Malachi 2:7).

2. Yet what troubles some people is that, from those who were called angels of God and from the women whom they loved, we read that not human beings of our race but giants were born. But surely bodies of human beings greatly exceeding our ordinary size—which I also mentioned above (chapter 9)—have been born in our own times. Was there not, a few years ago, when the destruction of the city of Rome perpetrated by the Goths was approaching, a woman in Rome who greatly surpassed all others in a kind of gigantic stature, together with her father and mother? Crowds came from everywhere to see her, and what chiefly aroused wonder was that neither of her parents was even as tall as the tallest people we are accustomed to see.

Giants, therefore, could have been born even before the sons of God—who were also called angels of God—mingled with the daughters of men, that is, with those living according to the human condition: namely, the sons of Seth with the daughters of Cain. For the canonical Scripture speaks in this way in the book where we read these things; its words are:

“And it came to pass, after human beings began to multiply upon the earth, and daughters were born to them, that the angels of God, seeing the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. And the Lord God said: ‘My spirit shall not remain in these human beings forever, because they are flesh. Their days, however, shall be one hundred and twenty years.’ Now giants were upon the earth in those days; and afterward, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and they bore children for themselves, those were the giants, men renowned from of old” [Note: [Col. 0469] The particle *autem* (“however”), omitted in the printed editions, is found in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint.] [Note: [Col. 0469] This passage of Genesis, misunderstood by Lactantius (*Divine Institutes*, book 2, chapter 15), Sulpicius Severus (*Sacred History*, book 1, chapter 2), and several others, gave rise to tales that angels mingled with women; many of the ancients followed this error. LARCHER.] (Genesis 6:1–4).

These words of the divine book clearly indicate that giants were already upon the earth in those days when the sons of God took wives from the daughters of men, loving them because they were beautiful—that is, fair. For it is the custom of this Scripture to call those who are physically handsome “good.” But giants were also born after this had happened. For it says: “Now giants were upon the earth in those days; and afterward, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men.” Therefore, both before and afterward, they existed in those days.

But when it says, “and they bore children for themselves,” it sufficiently shows that previously, before the sons of God fell in this way, they bore children for God, not for themselves—that is, not under the rule of sexual desire, but in the service of the duty of propagation. They were not producing a family for their own pride, but citizens of the city of God, to whom, as angels of God, they might announce that they should place their hope in God (Psalm 77:7). They would thus resemble the one who was born from Seth, the son of resurrection, and who hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God. In that hope they and their descendants would be co-heirs of eternal goods and, under God the Father, brothers of the sons.

[Col. 0470] 3. Scripture itself declares without any ambiguity that they were not angels of God in such a way that they were not human beings, as some think, but that they were undoubtedly human beings. For after it had first been said that the angels of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose, it immediately added: “And the Lord God said: ‘My spirit shall not remain in these human beings forever, because they are flesh.’”

They had been made angels and sons of God through the Spirit of God; but by turning toward lower things they are called human beings according to nature, not grace. They are also called flesh: deserters from the spirit and, by deserting, themselves deserted.

The Seventy translators called these beings both angels of God and sons of God. Not all manuscripts, however, contain this reading; some have nothing except “sons of God.” Aquila, whom the Jews place before the other translators, rendered the phrase not “angels of God” or “sons of God,” but “sons of gods” [Note: [Col. 0470] Aquila lived under the emperor Hadrian. Although he had initially adopted the Christian name and was being drawn away by the Apostles and the Lord’s disciples from mathematical and astrological studies, to which he was excessively devoted, he nevertheless persisted in those vain studies and was expelled from the Church. Consequently, abandoning Christianity, he turned to Judaism and later learned the Hebrew language with great zeal, intending—as Epiphanius testifies—to attack the translation of the Seventy and distort the prophecies concerning Christ, interpreting them so that they appeared to concern anything rather than Christ. COQUAEUS.].

Both readings, however, are true. For they were sons of God, under whom as Father they were also brothers of their own fathers; and they were sons of gods, because they had been begotten by gods, with whom they themselves were also gods, according to the Psalm: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81:6).

The Seventy translators are rightly believed to have received a prophetic spirit, so that if they changed anything by its authority and said what they were translating in a form different from the original, no one would doubt that this too had been spoken by divine inspiration. Nevertheless, the Hebrew text is said to be ambiguous at this point, so that it could be translated either “sons of God” or “sons of gods.”

4. Let us therefore set aside the tales of those writings called apocryphal, because their hidden origin was not clear to the fathers, through whom the authority of the truthful Scriptures has reached us in an entirely certain and well-known succession. Even if some truth is found in these apocryphal writings, they possess no canonical authority because of the many falsehoods they contain.

We cannot deny that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, wrote certain divine things, since the apostle Jude says this in his canonical Epistle (Jude 14). But it is not without reason that his writings are not included in the canon of Scripture preserved in the temple of the Hebrew people through the successive diligence of the priests. They were judged suspect because of their antiquity, and it could not be discovered whether these were truly things that he had written [Note: [Col. 0470] The printed editions add, “But why this is so”; this is absent from all the manuscripts.], since no trustworthy custodians could be found who had preserved them properly through an unbroken succession.

Therefore, the writings circulated under his name, which contain these tales about giants—claiming that they did not have human fathers—are rightly judged by prudent people not to be his. The same applies to many writings circulated under the names of other prophets and to more recent writings circulated by heretics under the names of the Apostles [Col. 0471]. All these have been removed from canonical authority by careful examination under the designation “apocryphal.”

Accordingly, according to the Hebrew and Christian canonical Scriptures, there is no doubt that many giants existed before the Flood, and that they were citizens of the earthly society of human beings. The sons of God, who according to the flesh were descended from Seth, abandoned righteousness and turned toward this society. Nor is it surprising that giants could also be born from them. For not all were giants; but certainly there were many more then than in all subsequent times after the Flood.

The Creator chose to create them for this reason as well: to show that a wise person, who is blessed by spiritual and immortal goods far better and more enduring, and by goods proper to the good rather than common to the good and evil, ought not to value highly not only bodily beauty but also bodily size and strength. Another prophet, commending this point, says:

“There were those giants, famous men, who from the beginning were of great stature, knowing war. The Lord did not choose them, nor did he give them the way of knowledge. They perished because they did not possess wisdom; they were destroyed because of their lack of understanding” (Baruch 3:26–28).

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### How we should understand the Lord’s statement concerning those who were destined to perish in the Flood: “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”

When God said, “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years” (Genesis 6:3), this should not be understood as though it had been foretold that thereafter human beings would not live beyond one hundred and twenty years, since we find that even after the Flood some lived beyond five hundred. Rather, we should understand that God said this when Noah was near the end of his five hundredth year—that is, when he was living through his four hundred and eightieth year—which Scripture, according to its custom, calls “five hundred,” often designating the greater part by the name of the whole.

For in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, the Flood occurred (Genesis 7:11). Thus the one hundred and twenty years foretold were to be the remaining years of life for the human beings who were to perish; when they had elapsed, they would be destroyed by the Flood.

Nor is it without reason that the Flood is believed to have occurred only after those who were unworthy of such a death were no longer found on earth—a death by which punishment was inflicted on the wicked. This does not mean that such a kind of death could harm good people who would one day die in any event. Nevertheless, none of those whom Holy Scripture records as descended from the seed of Seth died in the Flood.

The divine account gives the cause of the Flood in this way:

“And the Lord God, seeing that the wickedness of human beings had multiplied upon the earth, and that everyone [Note: [Col. 0471] The printed editions read, “and that each one”; the manuscripts read, “and every one,” in accordance with the Septuagint: *kai pas tis*.] continually thought carefully in his heart about evil, considered that he had made human beings upon the earth, and reconsidered, and God said: ‘I will wipe out the human being whom I have made from the face of the earth, from human being to beast, and from creeping things to the birds of the sky, because I am angry that I made them’” [Note: [Col. 0471] The manuscripts read *deleam* (“I will wipe out”), rather than the printed *delebo* (“I will wipe out”).] (Genesis 6:5–7).

## CHAPTER XXV  
### Concerning the wrath of God, which does not disturb his unchangeable tranquility by any agitation

The wrath of God is not a disturbance of his mind, but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin. His “considering” and “reconsidering” signify the unchangeable plan by which mutable things are changed. For God does not repent of any deed as a human being does; his decision concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.

But if Scripture did not use such expressions, it would not in some manner make itself more familiar to every kind of human being, whom it wishes to benefit: frightening the proud, rousing the negligent, exercising those who seek, and nourishing those who understand. It would not do this if it did not first bend down and, in a sense, descend to those who lie below.

When it also announces the destruction of all earthly animals and birds, it declares the magnitude of the future catastrophe. It does not threaten irrational living creatures with destruction as though they themselves had sinned.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### How the ark that Noah was commanded to make signifies Christ and the Church in every respect

1. Now, when God commands Noah, a righteous man—and, as truthful Scripture speaks of him, perfect in his generation (Genesis 6:9)—to make an ark in which he might be saved from the devastation of the Flood together with his own people, that is, his wife, sons, and daughters-in-law, and with the animals that entered the ark at God’s command, this is undoubtedly a figure of the city of God journeying through this world, namely the Church, which is saved through the wood on which the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, hung (1 Timothy 2:5).

Even the measurements of its length, height, and breadth signify the human body, in the truth of which he was foretold and came to human beings [Note: [Col. 0472] Several manuscripts read *ipsius* (“of itself”) rather than *ipsae* (“the measurements themselves”). Manuscript 2051 agrees. M.]. For the length of the human body from the crown of the head to the feet is six times its breadth, which extends from one side to the other, and ten times its height, measured from the back to the belly.

Thus, if you measure a person lying on his back or face down, he is six times as long from head to feet as he is broad from right to left or from left to right, and ten times as long as he is high from the ground. Hence the ark was made three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
