That it received a door in its side plainly signifies the wound made when the side of the crucified man was pierced by a spear (John 19:34). Through this opening those who come to him enter, because from it flowed the sacraments by which believers are initiated.

That it was commanded to be made from squared timbers signifies the stable life of the saints on every side: however you turn a square, it will stand. The other things said about the construction of the same ark are likewise signs of ecclesiastical realities.

[Col. 0473] 2. It would take too long to pursue these matters now. We have already done so in the work we wrote against Faustus the Manichaean (book 12, chapter 14), who denied that anything concerning Christ had been prophesied in the books of the Hebrews.

It is certainly possible for one person to explain these matters more suitably than another, provided that the things being said are all referred to the city of God of which we are speaking, journeying through this wicked age as through a flood. The interpreter must not wish to stray far from the intention of the person who wrote these things.

For example, someone might interpret the statement written here, “You shall make it with lower chambers, second chambers, and third chambers” (Genesis 6:16) [Note: [Col. 0473] The printed editions read *facies ea* (“you shall make these”), but the manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, read *facies eam* (“you shall make it”). Some of them have *bicameratam et tricameratam* (“with two chambers and three chambers”).], not as I interpreted it in that work (book 4, chapter 16): namely, that the Church is gathered from all nations and is called “two-chambered” because of the two kinds of human beings, circumcision and uncircumcision—whom the Apostle also calls Jews and Greeks in another manner (Romans 3:9)—and “three-chambered” because all nations were restored after the Flood from the three sons of Noah.

Instead, he might say something else that is not foreign to the rule of faith. Since Noah wished the ark to have not only lower dwellings but also upper ones, and called these “second chambers,” and also dwellings above the upper ones, which he called “third chambers,” so that a third habitation rose upward from the bottom, the three things commended by the Apostle—faith, hope, and charity—may be understood here (1 Corinthians 13:13).

The threefold fruitfulness of the Gospel may also be understood, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold (Matthew 13:8): conjugal chastity dwelling in the lowest level, widowhood above it, and virginity above that. If anything better can be understood and said according to the faith of this city, the same principle should be applied.

I would say this also concerning the other matters that must be explained here: although they are discussed in different ways, they must nevertheless be brought back to the one harmony of the catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Concerning the ark and the Flood: neither should we agree with those who accept only the history without allegorical meaning, nor with those who defend only the figures while rejecting the historical truth

1. No one should think either that these things were written without purpose, or that what is to be sought here is merely the truth of events without any allegorical meanings; nor, conversely, that these events did not happen at all, but are only figures expressed in words; nor that, whatever these things may be, they do not pertain to the prophecy of the Church.

For who but someone of perverse mind would claim that books preserved through thousands of years with such religious devotion and such careful observance of ordered succession were written in vain? Or who would look only for historical events in a passage where, to omit everything else, if the number of animals required the ark to be made so large, what required two unclean animals and seven clean animals to be brought in (Genesis 7:2), when both kinds could have been preserved in equal numbers [Note: [Col. 0473] Compare book 12 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapters 38 and 15.]? Or was God, who commanded them to be preserved for the restoration of the race, unable to restore them in the way he had established?

2. Those who maintain that these things did not happen but are only figures signifying other realities first argue that so great a Flood could not have occurred that, as the waters rose, they surpassed the highest mountains by fifteen cubits. They appeal to the summit of Mount Olympus, above which, they claim, clouds cannot gather [Note: [Col. 0474] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read “climb.” Later the manuscripts read: “because it is already so high that it is heaven.” Our manuscripts, except 2050, have *sublime* (“high”) rather than *sublimis* (“high”), and manuscript 253 has *quam* (“than”) rather than *jam* (“already”). M.], because it is so high—almost as high as heaven—that the denser air in which winds, mists, and rains are generated is not found there [Note: [Col. 0474] He is speaking of Olympus in Thessaly, ten stadia high, as Plutarch says in *Aemilius Paulus* (chapter 15). Its summit is believed to rise above the place where clouds and winds are formed; Solinus writes that the ashes of sacrifices remain there throughout the year without being scattered by the wind or dissolved by rain (*Polyhistor*, chapter 9). Franciscus Philelphus calls this a fable, claiming that he climbed the mountain to investigate so remarkable a matter. LUD. VIVES.].

They do not consider that the thickest of all the elements—earth—could be there. Or do they deny that the summit of the mountain is earth? Why, then, do they insist that earth could rise into those regions of heaven but water could not, when these measurers and weighers of the elements declare that water is above and lighter than earth?

What reason, then, do they offer for saying that heavier and lower earth invaded the place of the tranquil heavens for so many years, while lighter and higher water was not permitted to do the same, at least for a short time?

3. They also say that the ark could not contain so many kinds of animals in both sexes, two of the unclean and seven of the clean. They seem to count only three hundred cubits of length and fifty of breadth [Note: [Col. 0474] The printed editions add “thirty in height.” Shortly afterward, to make the lower dimensions correspond with the upper, they read that the ark measured nine hundred cubits in length, one hundred and fifty in breadth, and ninety in height. The manuscripts correct this: they properly contain no mention there of cubits of height, since height cannot be multiplied in the same way as length and breadth without compromising the truth of Scripture.].

They do not consider that there was just as much space in the upper levels, and again just as much in the uppermost levels; therefore, when those cubits are multiplied by three, they amount to nine hundred by one hundred and fifty.

If we also consider what Origen not inelegantly argued (*Homily 2 on Genesis*), namely, that Moses, the man of God [Note: [Col. 0474] The word “of God” is absent from several manuscripts, though not all.], educated—as it is written—in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22), who cherished geometry, may have meant geometric cubits, which they assert were each equivalent to six of our cubits, who would not see how much the ark’s size could contain?

As for their argument that an ark of such magnitude could not have been fastened together, they make a most foolish accusation. They know that immense cities have been built, yet they fail to consider the one hundred years during which that ark was constructed.

Unless, perhaps, stone can adhere to stone merely by being joined with lime, so that a wall can be carried around for thousands of cubits, while wood cannot adhere to wood by means of wooden pegs, *epiros* [Note: [Col. 0474] Joannes Meursius once thought that *epigros* should be read here, following Isidore, whose *Etymologies* 19.19 says: “*Epigri* and nails are what make wood adhere to wood.” Later, in his *Glossary*, he said it should be corrected to *epiuros*, from the Greek word *epiouros*, meaning “joint” or “framework.” [Col. 0475] Coquaeus: “Perhaps *epiuros* should be read, from the Greek word *epiouros*, which signifies a wooden peg.” M.], and nails, and with bitumen as glue, so that an ark could be built extending far and wide in straight rather than curved lines.

No human effort would launch it upon the sea; rather, when the waters came, the waves would lift it. By the natural order of weights—and by divine providence more than human skill—it would remain afloat and be guided, so that it would not suffer shipwreck anywhere [Note: [Col. 0475] So all our manuscripts. Manuscript B reads “so that it might be built.” M.].

4. A question is also often raised with great subtlety concerning the smallest creatures—not only animals such as mice and lizards, but also such creatures as locusts, beetles, flies, and finally fleas: whether the ark contained more of them than the number specified, since God gave the command; or whether it was necessary to include them because other animals needed to be fed.

First, those whom this troubles should be reminded that the statement “the things that creep upon the earth” should be understood in such a way that it was not necessary to preserve in the ark creatures that can live in water—not only submerged creatures such as fish, but also those that float upon it, such as many birds.

Furthermore, when it says, “There shall be male and female,” this plainly refers to the restoration of the species. Consequently, it was not necessary for those creatures to be there that can be born without sexual intercourse from various things or from the decay of things. Or, if they were there, as they commonly are in houses, they could have been present without any fixed number.

Alternatively, if the sacred mystery being enacted, and the figure of so great a reality in actual events, could not otherwise be fulfilled unless everything that could not naturally live in water were there in that definite number, then this was not the concern of that human being—or of those human beings—but of God. Noah did not capture and bring them inside; he permitted them to come and enter. For this is the force of the statement, “They shall enter to you” (Genesis 6:19–20): not by human action, but by God’s command.

It should therefore be believed that creatures lacking sex were not there. For it is prescribed and defined: “There shall be male and female.” Some creatures are born without sexual intercourse from various things, yet afterward engage in intercourse and reproduce, such as flies. Others have no male or female at all, such as bees. As for creatures that have sex but do not produce offspring, such as mules and hinnies, it would be surprising if they were there, rather than it being sufficient for their parents—the equine and asinine kinds—to have been there, along with any other creatures that produce a kind through the mingling of different species. But if this too belonged to the mystery, then they were there. For this kind also has male and female.

5. Some people are also troubled by the kinds of food that the animals could have had there. Since some animals are thought to eat nothing but flesh, they ask whether food for them was included in addition to the specified number, because the necessity of feeding other animals required it, or whether, as is more reasonable to believe, there could have been foods besides flesh that suited them all [Note: [Col. 0476] Compare *Questions on Genesis*, question 6.].

For we know how many animals whose food is flesh also eat grains and fruits, especially figs and chestnuts. What, then, is surprising if that wise and righteous man, also divinely instructed concerning what suited each creature, prepared and stored appropriate nourishment for every kind without meat?

What is there that hunger could not compel them to eat? Or what could God not make pleasant and wholesome—God who, by divine power, could even have granted them life without food—unless it suited the fulfillment of the figure of so great a mystery that they should also be fed? [Note: [Col. 0476] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads *facultate* (“by power”); the other editions read *facilitate* (“with ease”).]

No one is permitted to suppose that the many signs represented by these events do not pertain to the prefiguring of the Church, unless he is contentious. For the nations have already filled the Church, and the clean and unclean are contained within a kind of bond of its unity until the appointed end is reached. From this one most evident fact, there can be no legitimate doubt concerning the other things that are sometimes expressed more obscurely and are more difficult to recognize.

Since these things are so, no one who is even moderately reasonable can deny that they were written down neither in vain nor without meaning when they happened, that they are not merely verbal figures without corresponding events, or that they are unrelated to what the Church signifies [Note: [Col. 0476] Manuscript 258 reads “the Church of God.” M.]. Rather, we must believe that they were wisely committed to memory and writing, that they happened, that they signify something, and that this something itself pertains to the prefiguration of the Church.

At this point the book must be brought to a close, so that the course of both cities—the earthly city, namely, that of those living according to the human condition, and the heavenly city, that of those living according to God—may be investigated after the Flood and thereafter in the events that follow.

# BOOK SIXTEEN

In its first part [Note: [Col. 0475] See book 18, chapter 1], from the first chapter through the twelfth, the progress of both cities, the heavenly and the earthly, is presented according to sacred history, from Noah to Abraham. In its latter part, the progress of the heavenly city alone is discussed, from Abraham to the kings of the Israelites.

[Col. 0475]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### Whether after the Flood, from Noah to Abraham, any families living according to God are to be found

[Col. 0475]

Whether, after the Flood, the traces of the holy city as it advanced continued unbroken, or whether they were interrupted by intervening periods of impiety, so that no human being remained who worshiped the one true God, is difficult to discover with certainty from the speaking Scriptures. For in the canonical books, after Noah—who, together with his wife, his three sons, and an equal number of daughters-in-law, was deemed worthy to be rescued from the devastation of the Flood through the ark—we do not find anyone’s piety explicitly praised by divine speech until Abraham, except that Noah, by prophetic blessing, commends two of his sons, Shem and Japheth, seeing and foreseeing what was to happen in the distant future.

Hence it also happened that he cursed his middle son—that is, the one younger than the firstborn but older than the last—who had sinned against his father, not in the son himself but in his own grandson, with these words: “Cursed be the boy Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers.” Canaan had been born from Ham, who had not covered his sleeping father’s nakedness but rather exposed it.

Accordingly, what follows also adds the blessing of the two eldest and youngest sons: “Blessed be the Lord God of Shem, and Canaan shall be his servant; may God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” (Genesis 9:25–27). Just as Noah’s planting of the vineyard, his becoming drunk from its fruit, the uncovering of his nakedness while he slept, and all the other things done and written there are pregnant with prophetic meanings and veiled by coverings [Note: [Col. 0477] See those meanings in book 12 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapters 22 and following.].

## CHAPTER TWO  
### What was prophetically prefigured in the sons of Noah

1. But now that the outcome of these matters has been attained in their descendants, what was hidden has become sufficiently clear. Who, observing these things carefully and intelligently, would not recognize Christ in them?

Shem, from whose seed Christ was born in the flesh, is interpreted as “Named.” What is more named than Christ, whose name now resounds everywhere, so that in the Song of Songs, with prophecy itself leading the way [Note: [Col. 0477] The manuscripts read *praecedente* (“preceding”) rather than the printed *praecinente* (“singing before”).], he is compared to poured-out ointment (Song of Songs 1:2)? In his dwellings—that is, in the churches—the multitude of the nations dwells. For Japheth is interpreted as “Enlargement.”

Ham, on the other hand, whose name is interpreted as “Hot” [Note: [Col. 0477] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “Cunning”; shortly afterward they have “a cunning race.” They also read, “but with the spirit of deceitful cunning, which are accustomed, etc.”], the middle son of Noah, as though distinguishing himself from both and remaining between them, belonging neither to the first fruits of Israel nor to the fullness of the Gentiles—what does he signify except the hot-headed race of heretics?

Their hearts burn not with the spirit of wisdom but with impatience, by which the inward parts of heretics usually seethe [Note: [Col. 0477] The manuscripts read “their beginnings” rather than “their hearts.”], and they disturb the peace of the saints. Yet these things contribute to the benefit of those who make progress, according to the Apostle’s statement: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19).

Hence it is also written, “An instructed son will be wise, but he will use the foolish as a servant” (Proverbs 10:4, according to the Septuagint). For many things belonging to the catholic faith, when they are provoked by the hot [Note: [Col. 0477] Erasmus reads “hot”; the other printed editions, with most manuscripts, read “cunning.” Manuscript 253 reads “hot.” M.] agitation of heretics so that they can be defended against them, are examined more diligently, understood more clearly, and proclaimed more earnestly. A question raised by an adversary becomes an opportunity for learning.

Not only those who are openly separated from the Church, but also all who boast of the Christian name and live destructively [Col. 0478], may reasonably be seen as prefigured by Noah’s middle son. They announce the passion of Christ, signified by that man’s nakedness, in their profession, but dishonor it by their evil conduct. Of such people it was said, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:20).

Therefore Ham was cursed in his son, as in his fruit—that is, in his work. Accordingly, his son Canaan is also fittingly interpreted as “Their movement.” For what else is this than their work?

Shem and Japheth, on the other hand, as circumcision and uncircumcision—or, as the Apostle calls them in another way, Jews and Greeks—yet called and justified, having in some manner come to know their father’s nakedness, by which the passion of the Savior was signified, took a garment, placed it upon their backs [Note: [Col. 0478] Several manuscripts read “their two backs.”], entered backward, and covered the nakedness of their father; they did not see what they covered out of reverence (Genesis 9:23).

In a certain sense, in the passion of Christ we both honor what was done for us and turn away from the crime of the Jews. The garment signifies the sacrament; the backs signify the memory of past events. For the Church celebrates the passion of Christ as already accomplished, at the time when Japheth dwells in the tents of Shem and the evil brother is among them; it does not still look forward to it as something future.

2. Thus the wicked brother, in his son—that is, in his work—is a child, that is, a servant, of his good brothers, when the good knowingly make use of the wicked either for the exercise of patience or for the advancement of wisdom. For, as the Apostle testifies, there are those who proclaim Christ insincerely: “But whether from pretext,” he says, “or in truth Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice” (Phil. 1:18).

He himself planted the vineyard of which the Prophet says, “The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7), and he drank of its wine. This may mean the cup of which he says, “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22), and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid. 26:39), by which he plainly signifies his passion. Or, since wine is the fruit of the vine, it may rather signify that from that vine—that is, from the race of the Israelites—he assumed flesh and blood for us, so that he could suffer. “And he became drunk,” that is, he suffered; “and he was uncovered” (Gen. 9:21). For there his weakness was uncovered, that is, manifested, of which the Apostle says, “Although he was crucified from weakness” (2 Cor. 13:4). Hence the same Apostle says, “The weakness of God is stronger than human beings, and the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25).

When it had said, “And he was uncovered,” Scripture added, “in his house.” It elegantly shows that he was destined to suffer crucifixion and death from the people of his own flesh and from those of his own household—namely, the Jews. The wicked proclaim this passion of Christ outside, merely in the sound of their voice; for they do not understand what they proclaim. The good, however, possess so great a mystery in the inner person, and inwardly honor in their heart the weakness and foolishness of God, which is stronger and wiser than human beings. The figure of this is that Ham went out and reported it outside, whereas Shem and Japheth entered in order to veil it—that is, to honor it; this they did inwardly.

3. We investigate these divine secrets of Scripture as best we can, one more and another less appropriately, yet faithfully holding firmly to this: that the events narrated and written down did not occur without some foreshadowing of future things, and that they are to be referred to none other than Christ and his Church, which is the city of God. From the beginning of the human race, proclamation of this city has never been absent, and we see it fulfilled in every respect.

After Noah’s two sons had been blessed and the one in their midst cursed, mention of certain righteous people who worshiped God devoutly is thereafter omitted for more than a thousand years.

[Note: [Col. 0479] Thus the Vindobonensis, American, and manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain instead read: “there is silence.”]

I do not believe that such people were lacking. But if all had been mentioned, the account would have become excessively long; and this would have been more historical diligence than prophetic foresight. The sacred writer of these books—or rather, the Spirit of God through him—therefore pursues those matters by which not only past events are narrated but future events are also foretold, though these nevertheless pertain to the city of God. For whatever is said here about people who are not its citizens is said for this purpose: that, by comparison with them as their opposite, the city may either advance or stand out.

Certainly, not everything whose occurrence is narrated should be thought to signify something. But because certain things signify something, even those that signify nothing are attached to them. Only the plowshare cuts the earth; but for this to be possible, the other parts of the plow are also necessary. Likewise, in harps and similar musical instruments, only the strings are fitted for producing song; yet, so that they can be fitted, the other components of the instrument’s framework are also present. These are not struck by the singers, but the parts that, when struck, resound are joined to them. Thus, in prophetic history, certain things are also narrated that signify nothing, but the things that signify something adhere to them and are, in a certain manner, bound to them.

**CHAPTER III.—On the generations of Noah’s three sons**

1. The generations of Noah’s sons must therefore now be considered, and what seems necessary to say about them must be added to this work, in which the progress through time of both cities—the earthly and the heavenly—is displayed. They begin to be mentioned with the youngest son, who was called Japheth.

[Note: [Col. 0479] The manuscripts read: “For they begin to be mentioned.”]

Eight sons of his are named.

[Note: [Col. 0479] Augustine followed the Greek manuscripts, which add an eighth son of Japheth named Elisa; consequently, they count fifteen descendants of Japheth. But neither the Hebrew Scripture, nor the Chaldean paraphrase, nor the Complutensian Greek translation contains this Elisa; nor, finally, do those Greek manuscripts used by Jerome contain him, as is clear from his Hebrew Questions on Genesis. COQUAEUS.]

His grandsons were seven, from two of his sons: three from one and four from the other. Thus the total is fifteen.

The sons of Ham, Noah’s middle son, were four; his grandsons were five from one of his sons; and two great-grandsons came from one grandson. Their total is therefore eleven. After these have been enumerated, the account returns, as it were, to the beginning and says: “Chus, however, begot Nebroth.”

[Note: [Col. 0479] The old books consistently write it this way, as do the Septuagint manuscripts: Nebroth. In printed editions, however, it is Nemroth.]

“He began to be a giant upon the earth. He was a giant hunter before the Lord God. Therefore they say, ‘As Nebroth was a giant hunter before the Lord.’ And the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, Orech, Archad, and Chalanne in the land of Sennaar. From that land Assur went out and built Nineveh, and the city of Robooth, and Chalach, and Dasem, between Nineveh and Chalach: this is the great city.”

This Chus, the father of the giant Nebroth, is named first among the sons of Ham, although his five sons had already been counted, along with two grandsons. Either he begot this giant after his grandsons had been born, or—and this is more probable—Scripture spoke of him separately because of the giant’s eminence. For it also mentioned his kingdom, whose beginning was that most famous city Babylon, together with the cities or regions mentioned beside it.

But what is said—that Assur went out from that land, that is, from the land of Sennaar, which belonged to Nebroth’s kingdom, and built Nineveh and the other cities listed afterward—happened much later. The account touches on it on this occasion because of the renown of the Assyrian kingdom, which Ninus, son of Belus, wonderfully enlarged. He was the founder of the great city Nineveh, whose name was derived from his own, so that it was called Nineveh from Ninus.

Assur, from whom the Assyrians derive their name, was not among the sons of Ham, Noah’s middle son; rather, he is found among the sons of Shem, who was Noah’s eldest son. It therefore appears that those who later possessed the kingdom of that giant, proceeded from it, and founded other cities arose from the offspring of Shem. The first of these was called Nineveh after Ninus.

The account then returns to another son of Ham, who was called Mesraim, and mentions the peoples he begot—not as individual people but as seven nations. From the sixth, as though from a sixth son, a nation is said to have arisen called the Philistines; thus there are eight. The account then returns again to Canaan, the son in whom Ham was cursed, and eleven peoples descended from him are named. Then, after certain cities have been mentioned, it says how far they extended. Thus, counting the sons and grandsons, thirty-one descendants are recorded from the offspring of Ham.

2. It remains to mention the sons of Shem, Noah’s eldest son. The narrative, which began with the youngest, reaches him gradually through the sequence of generations. But the point at which Shem’s sons begin to be mentioned contains an obscurity that must be illuminated by explanation, since it is highly relevant to the matter we are investigating.

The text reads as follows: “And to Shem also was born Heber, the father of all the sons, the elder brother of Japheth.” The order of the words is: “And Heber was born to Shem, even to him”; that is, Heber was born to Shem himself, who is the father of all his sons.

[Note: [Col. 0480] The word “his” is absent in editions 253 and 258. M.]

Thus Scripture intended Shem to be understood as the patriarch of all who arose from his stock and whom it is about to mention, whether sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, or descendants arising from them thereafter. Shem did not, of course, beget this Heber; rather, Heber appears as the fifth in the sequence of ancestors. Shem, among his other sons, begot Arphaxat; Arphaxat begot Cainan; Cainan begot Sala; Sala begot Heber.

[Note: [Col. 0481] All our manuscripts read: “Not therefore.”]

It was certainly not without reason that Heber alone is first named among the descendants coming from Shem, and is preferred even to sons, although he is a fifth-generation grandson, unless what has been handed down is true: that the Hebrews were named from him, as though they were Heberites. There may also be another opinion, however, according to which they seem to have been called from Abraham, as though they were Abrahamites.

[Note: [Col. 0481] Compare Book 2 of the Retractions, chapter 16.]

But surely this is true: they were called Heberites from Heber and afterward, with one letter removed, Hebrews. The Hebrew language could be possessed only by the people of Israel, in whom the city of God both dwelt as a stranger among the saints and was prefigured in every respect through sacramental signs.

Thus six sons of Shem are first named. Then four grandsons were born from one of them. Another of Shem’s sons begot his grandson, and from that grandson a great-grandson was born, and from him a great-great-grandson, who is Heber.

Heber begot two sons, one of whom he called Phalech, which means “Dividing.” Scripture then adds and explains the reason for the name: “For in his days the earth was divided.” What this means will become clear later.

The other son born to Heber begot twelve sons. Thus all those descended from Shem number twenty-seven.

In total, therefore, all those descended from Noah’s three sons—fifteen from Japheth, thirty-one from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem—number seventy-three. Scripture then continues:

“These are the sons of Shem, according to their tribes, according to their languages, in their regions and in their nations.”

And again, concerning them all:

“These are the tribes of the sons of Noah, according to their generations and according to their nations. From these the islands of the nations were scattered over the earth after the flood.”

From this it is inferred that there were then seventy-three—or rather, as will later be demonstrated, seventy-two—nations, not seventy-three people. For earlier, when the sons of Japheth had been mentioned, the account concluded in this way:

“From these the islands of the nations were separated in their land, each according to his language, in their tribes and in their nations.”

3. In one passage, the nations are mentioned more explicitly among Ham’s sons, as I showed above. Mesraim begot those called the Ludim, and in the same way the others up to seven nations. After all had been enumerated, the account concludes:

“These are the sons of Ham, according to their tribes, according to their languages, in their regions and in their nations” (Gen. 10).

Many sons are therefore not mentioned because, by being born, they joined other nations, while they themselves were unable to establish nations. For what other reason, when eight sons of Japheth are enumerated, are descendants said to have been born from only two of them? When four sons of Ham are named, why are descendants added from only three? And when six sons of Shem are named, why is the posterity of only two attached to them? Did the others remain without sons? Far from it. They simply did not produce nations for which they would have deserved to be mentioned, because as they were born they were added to other nations.

**CHAPTER IV.—On the diversity of languages and the beginning of Babylon**

[Col. 0482]

Although these nations are said to have existed in their own languages, the narrator nevertheless returns to the time when there was one language among all people, and from that point explains what happened so that the diversity of languages arose.

“And the whole earth,” it says, “had one lip and one voice for all.”

[Note: [Col. 0482] Louvain reads “of the earth.” Other printed editions and the manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek, read “the earth.”]

“And it came to pass, when they moved from the East, that they found a plain in the land of Sennaar and dwelt there. And one man said to his neighbor, ‘Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire.’ And the bricks became for them stone.”

[Note: [Col. 0482] Louvain reads “stones”; the other books and the Septuagint disagree.]

“And bitumen was their clay. And they said, ‘Come, let us build for ourselves a city and a tower whose top will reach up to heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves,’

[Note: [Col. 0482] The printed editions read “may go”; the manuscripts read “will be,” in agreement with the Septuagint’s *estai*.]

[Note: [Col. 0482] The manuscripts read, “and let us make our name.”]

“before we are scattered over the face of the whole earth. And the Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of men had built. And the Lord God said, ‘Behold, there is one race and one lip among all; and this is what they have begun to do. Now nothing of all that they attempt will fail for them. Come, let us descend and confuse their language there, so that each may not hear the voice of his neighbor.’ And the Lord scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they ceased building the city and the tower. Therefore its name was called Confusion, because there the Lord confused the lips of the whole earth; and from there the Lord God scattered them over the face of the whole earth” (Gen. 11:1–9).

This city, which was called Confusion, is Babylon, whose marvelous construction is also celebrated by the history of the nations. Babylon, after all, means “Confusion.” From this it is inferred that the giant Nebroth was its founder, as had been briefly indicated above, when Scripture, speaking of him, said that the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon—that is, the city that held the chief place among the other cities, where the royal dwelling was located as in a metropolis.

Yet the city was not completed to the extent that arrogant impiety had imagined. For an excessive height had been planned, said to reach heaven, whether this referred to the single tower that they were especially building among the others, or to all the towers, which are signified by a singular number just as “a soldier” signifies thousands of soldiers, or as “a frog” and “a locust” signify the multitude of frogs and locusts in the plagues by which the Egyptians were struck through Moses (Exod. 10:4 and elsewhere; Ps. 77:45).

But what could human and empty presumption have accomplished? However high a mass it might raise toward heaven against God, when would it surpass all the mountains? When would it escape the expanse of this cloudy air? Finally, what harm could any spiritual or bodily exaltation do to God, however great?

Humility constructs a safe and true road to heaven, lifting the heart upward to the Lord, not against the Lord, just as this giant is called a hunter “against the Lord” (Gen. 10:9).

Some who failed to understand this were deceived by an ambiguity in the Greek and did not translate the phrase as “against the Lord” but as “before the Lord.” For *enantion* means both “before” and “against.” This is the word used in the Psalm: “Let us weep before the Lord, who made us” (Ps. 94:6). It is also the word used in the Book of Job, where it is written, “You have burst forth in fury against the Lord” (Job 15:13, according to the Septuagint). Thus this giant must be understood as a hunter against the Lord.

What, then, is signified by the name “hunter,” except a deceiver, oppressor, and destroyer of earthly animals? With his peoples, therefore, he raised a tower against the Lord, by which impious pride was signified.

The evil intention is rightly punished even when the intended outcome does not follow. But what was the character of the punishment? Since the authority of a commander resides in language, pride was condemned precisely there, so that the one who had refused to understand in order to obey God’s command would not be understood when commanding a human being.

Thus that conspiracy was dissolved: each person withdrew from the one whom he did not understand and joined himself only to one with whom he could speak. The nations were divided by languages and scattered across the earth, as God willed, who accomplished this by hidden and incomprehensible means.

**CHAPTER V.—On the Lord’s descent to confuse the language of those building the tower**

What is written—“And the Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of men had built”—means that they were not sons of God but a society living according to human standards, which we call the earthly city.

[Note: [Col. 0483] Only the Louvain edition reads “however.”]

God is not moved from place to place, since he is always wholly present everywhere. He is said to descend when he does something on earth that, having been accomplished miraculously beyond the ordinary course of nature, in some way manifests his presence. Nor does he learn by seeing at a particular time, since he can never be ignorant of anything. Rather, he is said to see and know at a particular time what he causes to be seen and known.

That city was not seen in the manner in which God caused it to be seen when he revealed how displeasing it was to him. Yet it may also be understood that God descended to that city because his angels, in whom he dwells, descended. Thus what is added—“And the Lord God said, ‘Behold, there is one race and one lip among all,’” and the rest, followed by, “Come, and let us descend and confuse their language there” (Gen. 11:5–7)—may be a recapitulation, showing how what had been said, “The Lord descended,” was accomplished.

For if he had already descended, what does “Come, and let us descend and confuse” mean—understood as spoken to the angels—unless he descended through the angels, being present in the descending angels? And he does not say, “Come, and you who descend, confuse,” but, “Let us confuse their language there,” showing that he works through his ministers in such a way that they themselves are also God’s fellow workers, as the Apostle says: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. 3:9).

**CHAPTER VI.—What sort of speech is to be understood when God speaks to the angels**

[Col. 0484]

1. When the human being was made, the statement “Let us make man” could also have been understood of the angels, since it does not say, “Let me make.” But because it follows, “in our image,” and it is not permissible to believe that the human being was made in the image of angels, or that the image of angels and of God is the same, the plurality of the Trinity is rightly understood there.

Yet because the Trinity is one God, even after it had said, “Let us make,” Scripture says, “And God made man in the image of God” (Gen. 1:26–27). It does not say, “The gods made,” or “in the image of the gods.”

The same Trinity could also be understood here, as though the Father had said to the Son and the Holy Spirit, “Come, and let us descend and confuse their language there,” if there were anything that prevented the angels from being understood. It is more fitting, rather, to understand that the angels come to God through holy movements—that is, through pious thoughts—by which they consult the unchangeable Truth, as though it were the eternal law in that heavenly court.

For they are not truth in themselves. Rather, as participants in the Truth of their Creator, they move toward it as toward the fountain of life, so that they may receive from it what they do not possess from themselves. Their movement is stable, by which they come and do not depart.

[Note: [Col. 0484] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “And therefore their movement is stable.”]

[Note: [Col. 0484] The manuscripts read: “because they do not depart.”]

God does not speak to the angels in the same way that we speak to one another, or to God, or to angels, or that the angels speak to us, whether God speaks to us through them. He speaks in his own ineffable manner, while this is indicated to us in our manner.

God’s sublime speech, before the creation of his work, is the unchangeable rationale of that work itself. It has no resounding and passing sound, but an eternal power that remains and operates in time. By this he speaks to the holy angels, while we are far removed from them and are addressed in another way. When we too receive some such speech through our inner ears, we draw near to the angels.

I therefore need not continually explain in this work the ways in which God speaks. Either unchangeable Truth itself speaks ineffably to rational creatures’ minds, or it speaks through a changeable creature—whether through spiritual images to our spirit or through bodily voices to the bodily sense.

2. The statement, “And now nothing of all that they attempt will fail for them” (ibid. 11:6), was not spoken as a confirmation, but as a question, in the manner in which threats are often expressed, as a certain poet says:

“Will they not bring out their weapons, and the whole city follow?”
(Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.592.)

It should therefore be understood as though he had said: “Will not everything they attempt fail for them?” But if it is expressed in this way, the threatening tone is not conveyed. For the sake of those who are slower to understand, we have therefore added a particle—namely, “lest”—so that we might say, “Will they not?” since we cannot write down the voice of the speaker.

From those three men, the sons of Noah, seventy-three—or rather, as the argument will demonstrate, seventy-two—nations and as many languages began to exist throughout the earth, and as they increased they also filled the islands.

The number of nations, however, grew much greater than the number of languages. For in Africa we know of many barbarian peoples who share one language. And who could doubt that human beings, as the human race multiplied, were able to cross by ship and inhabit the islands?

**CHAPTER VII.—Whether every kind of beast, even on islands most remote from the mainland, received its origin from the number preserved in the ark from the flood**

There is a question concerning every kind of beast that is not under human care and is not born from the earth like frogs, but propagates solely through the union of male and female, such as wolves and other animals of this sort. How could such animals have existed after the flood, when all that was not in the ark was destroyed, if they were not reproduced from those whose kinds the ark preserved in both sexes?

They may indeed be thought to have swum to the islands, but only to islands nearby. Some islands, however, are situated so far from the mainland that no beast seems to have been able to swim to them. If human beings captured these animals and brought them with them, establishing their kinds wherever they lived, it is not unbelievable that this could have happened through the pursuit of hunting. Nevertheless, whether by God’s command or permission, it should not be denied that they could also have been transported through the work of angels.

But if they arose from the earth according to their original origin, when God said, “Let the earth bring forth a living soul” (Gen. 1:24), it becomes much clearer that all kinds of animals were in the ark not so much for the purpose of restoring the animals as for representing the various nations on account of the sacrament of the Church—if the earth produced many animals on islands to which they could not have crossed.

**CHAPTER VIII.—Whether certain monstrous races of human beings arose from Adam’s offspring or from the sons of Noah**

1. It is also asked whether certain monstrous races of human beings, which the histories of the nations report, should be believed to have descended from the sons of Noah—or rather from that one man from whom they too arose. Some are said to have had one eye in the middle of the forehead; others to have had the soles of their feet turned backward behind their legs; others to have possessed the nature of both sexes, with the right breast male and the left female, and, engaging in intercourse alternately, both to beget and to give birth.

[Note: [Col. 0485] The manuscripts read: “engaging in intercourse with one another alternately.”]

Others are said to have had no mouths and to live only by breathing through their nostrils.

[Note: [Col. 0485] The printed editions add: “having inhaled and exhaled breath.” The words “having inhaled and exhaled” are absent from the manuscripts.]

Others are said to be a cubit tall; the Greeks call them Pygmies, from *pygme*, “cubit.”

[Note: [Col. 0485] “Pygmies” means, as it were, “cubit-tall.”]

Elsewhere, women are said to conceive at the age of five and not to live beyond their eighth year. It is also reported that there is a race in which each person has only one leg, with no bending at the knee, and possesses marvelous speed. They are called Sciopods because, lying on their backs during the heat, they protect themselves from the sun with the shade of their feet.

[Note: [Col. 0485] “Sciopods” means, as it were, “shade-footed.”]

Some are said to have eyes without necks, located in their shoulders. And there are other races of human beings—or almost human beings—painted in mosaic on the maritime colonnade of Carthage, drawn from books as examples of a more curious history.

What shall I say of the Cynocephali, whose doglike heads and actual barking testify that they are beasts rather than human beings?

[Note: [Col. 0486] “Cynocephali” means, as it were, “dog-headed.”]

But it is not necessary to believe that every race said to exist actually does. Nevertheless, whoever is born anywhere as a human being—that is, a rational mortal animal—whatever bodily form, color, movement, sound, power, bodily part, or natural quality he may possess that is unusual to our senses, no believer will doubt that he derives his origin from that one first-created ancestor.

It is nevertheless evident what nature has established in the majority and what is marvelous because of its rarity.

2. The explanation given for monstrous human births among us can also be given for certain monstrous nations. God is the Creator of all things; he himself knows where and when anything ought to be created, or ought to have been created, knowing by what likeness or diversity of parts he composes the beauty of the whole.

But someone who cannot perceive the whole is offended, as though by the deformity of a part, because he does not know what it fits with or to what it is related.

We know that human beings are born with more than five fingers on their hands and feet. This is a smaller deviation than that one.

[Note: [Col. 0486] Most manuscripts read: “than any deviation.”]

Yet far be it from anyone to be so foolish as to suppose that the Creator made an error in the number of human fingers, although he does not know why the Creator did this. So even if a greater difference should arise, he knows what he has done, and no one can justly criticize his work.

At Hippo-Diarrhytum there is a man who appears to have crescent-shaped soles, with only two toes on each, and hands of the same kind.

[Note: [Col. 0486] There were two Hippos in Africa: Hippo-Regius, surnamed Bona, and Hippo-Diarrhytus, which some believe is now called Bizerte. Augustine was bishop not of this Hippo, as Ludovicus Vives thought, but of the other, Hippo-Regius.]

If such a race existed, it would be added to that curious and marvelous history. Are we therefore to deny that this man descended from that one who was first created? Androgynes, whom people also call hermaphrodites, are very rare, but it is difficult for them to be absent from the course of time. In them both sexes appear in such a way that it is uncertain from which they ought rather to take their name. Nevertheless, ordinary usage has prevailed in naming them from the better sex, that is, the male. For no one has ever called them *Androgynaecae* or *Hermaphroditae*.

[Note: [Col. 0486] The Vindobonensis and American manuscripts read “Androgenas”; Erasmus and several manuscripts read “Androgynas.”]

Some years ago, certainly within our own memory, a double human being was born in the East: the upper members were double, while the lower were single. There were two heads, two chests, and four hands; but one abdomen and two feet, as in a single person. He lived long enough for his fame to draw many people to see him.

Who, however, could mention all the human births that differ greatly from those from whom it is absolutely certain they were born?

Therefore, just as these cannot be denied to derive their origin from that one man, so whatever nations are reported to have diverged in bodily differences from the ordinary course of nature—which most people, indeed almost all, follow—must be acknowledged to derive their stock from that same one first father, provided that they fall within this definition: that they are rational mortal animals. This is so, however, only if the reports concerning the variety of those nations and their great difference from one another and from us are true.

For if we did not know that monkeys, apes, and sphinxes were not human beings but beasts, those historians, boasting of their curiosity, could falsely represent them to us as certain races of human beings with impunity.

But if those about whom such marvels have been written are human beings, what if God wished to create certain nations in this way so that, in the case of those monsters that plainly arise among us from human beings, we would not think that his wisdom—which shapes human nature—had erred, as though it were the craft of some less perfect artisan?

[Note: [Col. 0487] The manuscripts read “ought.”]

It should not therefore seem absurd to us that, just as there are certain human monsters among individual nations, so there may be certain monstrous nations within the human race as a whole.

Therefore, to conclude this question gradually and cautiously: either the things written about certain nations are entirely nonexistent; or, if they exist, those beings are not human; or, if they are human, they descend from Adam.

**CHAPTER IX.—Whether we should believe that the lower part of the earth, opposite our habitation, has inhabitants called Antipodes**

As for the claim that there are Antipodes—that is, human beings on the opposite side of the earth, where the sun rises when it sets for us, who tread with their feet opposite to ours—there is no reason to believe it.

[Note: [Col. 0487] Pliny writes that there was a great dispute between educated people and the common crowd concerning the existence of the Antipodes (*Natural History* 2.65). The common reason for denying them was doubtless the same as Lactantius’s, in *Institutes* 3.24, where he calls it “foolish” to believe that there are human beings whose footprints are higher than their heads, or that things which lie here hang upside down there, with crops and trees growing downward, and so forth. He says that the origin of this error was among philosophers, who believed that the world was round. Augustine also thought that the Antipodes should be denied, but not for Lactantius’s reasons. Rather, he denied them lest he be compelled to admit human beings who did not descend from Adam, which contradicts Scripture. Hence Pope Zachary, in Letter 10 to Boniface, written in the year 748, calls it a perverse and wicked teaching that of a certain Virgilius, who asserted that another world and other human beings existed beneath the earth.]

Those who make this claim do not say that they learned it from any historical knowledge; rather, they conjecture it as though by reasoning, because the earth hangs suspended within the vault of heaven, and the world has the same place both as its lowest point and as its center. From this they suppose that the other part of the earth, which is below, cannot be without human inhabitants.

They do not consider that even if the world is believed to have a globular and round shape—or if this is demonstrated by some argument—it does not follow that the earth on that side is also free of the mass of waters. And even if it is free of them, it does not immediately follow that it must have human inhabitants.

For Scripture in no way lies. It gives credibility to its accounts of past events because its prophecies are fulfilled. It would be utterly absurd to say that some human beings could have crossed from this side to that by traversing the immense expanse of the ocean, so that the human race could also have been established there from that one first man.

Therefore, among those peoples who then existed and are gathered as divided into seventy-two nations and as many languages, let us seek, if we can find it, that city of God living as a stranger on earth, which was brought down to the time of the flood and the ark and is shown to have continued in the sons of Noah through their blessings, especially in the eldest, who was called Shem. For Japheth was blessed in such a way that he would dwell in the houses of that same brother of his.

**CHAPTER X.—On the generation of Shem, in whose descendants the order of the city of God proceeds toward Abraham**
1. The sequence of generations from Shem himself must therefore be maintained, so that it may show the city of God after the Flood, just as the sequence of generations from him who was called Seth showed it before the Flood. For this reason, after divine Scripture had displayed the earthly city in Babylon—that is, in confusion—it returns by recapitulation to the patriarch Shem and begins from him the generations leading down to Abraham, mentioning also the number of years after which each person belonging to this sequence fathered a son, and how long he lived. Here, certainly, we must recognize what I promised earlier, so that it may become clear why it is said concerning the sons of Eber: “The name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided” (Gen. 10:25). For what else should be understood by the earth’s being divided except a diversity [Note: [Col. 0488] Vind., Am., Er.: *diversitatem*, “diversity.” Several manuscripts: *diversitates*, “diversities.”] of languages?

Leaving aside, then, the other sons of Shem who are irrelevant to this matter, those are joined together in the order of the generations through whom one can arrive at Abraham, just as before the Flood those were joined through whom one would arrive at Noah—through the generations [Note: [Col. 0488] Ms. 258: *per generationes*, “through generations.” M.] that were propagated from that son of Adam who was called Seth.

Thus this sequence of generations begins:

> “And these are the generations of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old [Note: [Col. 0488] Printed editions: “Shem, son of Noah, was one hundred years old.” But the ancient books, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, omit “son of Noah” and “was.” Compare the *Book of Expressions on Genesis* at this verse.] when he fathered Arphaxad, in the second year after the Flood. And Shem lived five hundred years after he fathered Arphaxad, and he fathered sons and daughters, and he died” (ibid. 11:10–11).

So Scripture proceeds through the others, saying in what year of his life each fathered a son belonging to this order of generations, which extends to Abraham, and indicating how many years he subsequently lived and that he fathered sons and daughters. Thus we may understand how populations could increase, and not childishly become fixated on the few people who are mentioned, wondering how such vast regions of land and kingdoms could have been filled by Shem’s descendants—especially because of the Assyrian kingdom, from which that Ninus, conqueror [Note: [Col. 0488] Vind., Am., and some manuscripts: *dominator*, “ruler.”] of the peoples of the East, ruled everywhere with immense success and passed on to his descendants an exceedingly broad and firmly established kingdom destined to endure for a long time.

2. But, so that we do not linger longer than necessary, we record in this order only the year of life in which each person in this sequence of generations fathered his son, not how many years each lived, so that we may both calculate the number of years from the passing of the Flood to Abraham and, because of those matters [Note: [Col. 0489] Vind., Am., Er., and several manuscripts: *et praeter illa*, “and besides those matters.”] that necessity compels us to discuss at length, touch briefly and in passing upon the others.

In the second year after the Flood, Shem, being one hundred years old, fathered Arphaxad. Arphaxad, being one hundred thirty-five years old, fathered Cainan; and Cainan, being one hundred thirty years old, fathered Sala. Sala himself was likewise that many years old when he fathered Eber. Eber was one hundred thirty-four years old when he fathered Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided. Peleg himself lived one hundred thirty years and fathered Reu; Reu, one hundred thirty-two years, and fathered Serug; Serug, one hundred thirty years, and fathered Nahor; Nahor, seventy-nine years, and fathered Terah; and Terah, seventy years, and fathered Abram (Gen. 10:26), whom God afterward called Abraham by a change of name (ibid. 17:5).

Thus, according to the Vulgate edition—that is, the edition of the Septuagint translators—there are 1,072 years from the Flood to Abraham. In the Hebrew manuscripts, however, far fewer years are said to be found; their proponents offer either no explanation or one of extreme difficulty.

3. When, then, we seek the city of God among those seventy-two nations, we cannot assert that, at the time when they had “one language” (ibid. 11:1), that is, one mode of speech, the human race had already become alienated from the worship of the true God, so that true piety remained only in these generations descended from Shem through Arphaxad and extending to Abraham. Rather, from that pride involved in building a tower up to heaven—which signifies impious arrogance—the city, that is, the society, of the impious became apparent [Note: [Col. 0489] Printed editions: “the earthly city became apparent.” “Earthly” is absent from the manuscripts.].

Whether it did not exist before this, whether it was hidden, or whether instead both societies had continued—the pious society in the two sons of Noah who were blessed and in their descendants, and the impious society in the one who was cursed and in his offspring, among whom there also arose the giant hunter against the Lord—cannot easily be determined. Perhaps, and this is certainly more credible, even then there were already despisers of God among the descendants of those two sons, before Babylon began to be established, and worshipers of God among the descendants of Ham. Nevertheless, we must believe that neither kind of human being was ever absent from the earth.

For even when it is said, “They have all turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one,” in both Psalms where these words occur we also read: “Will they not know, all the workers of iniquity, who devour my people as they eat bread?” Thus even then there was a people of God. Therefore, when it is said, “There is none who does good, not even one,” this is said of the sons of men, not of the sons of God. For it was stated beforehand: “God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood or sought God” (Ps. 13:3–4, 2; Ps. 52:4–5, 3). What follows then demonstrates that all the sons of men—that is, those belonging to the city that lives according to man and not according to God—are reprobate.

## CHAPTER XI  
### That the language originally used among human beings was the one later called Hebrew from the name of Eber, and that it remained in his family when the diversity of languages arose

[Col. 0490]

1. Therefore, just as the fact that there was one language shared by all did not mean that sons of perdition were absent—for before the Flood also there was one language, and yet everyone except the one household of Noah deserved to be destroyed by the Flood—so, when the nations were punished and divided because of the deservedly greater arrogance of their impiety through the diversity of languages, and the city of the impious received the name of confusion, that is, was called Babylon, the house of Eber was not absent, where the language that had previously belonged to everyone remained.

Thus, as I mentioned above, when the sons of Shem began to be enumerated, each of whom fathered a separate nation, Eber was mentioned first, although he was his great-grandson—that is, although he is found to have arisen fifth from him. Since this language remained in his family [Note: [Col. 0490] See below, book 18, chapter 39.], while the other nations were divided among different languages, that language—which is reasonably believed to have previously been common to the human race—was thereafter called Hebrew.

At that time it was necessary to distinguish it from the other languages by a proper name, just as the others too were called by proper names. When it was still one, however, it was called nothing other than human language, or human speech, by which alone the entire human race spoke.

2. Someone might say: If in the days of Peleg, the son of Eber, the earth was divided through languages—that is, if the people who were then on the earth were divided—then, rather, the language that had previously been common to all ought to have been named from Eber himself.

But it must be understood that Eber gave his son the name Peleg, which is interpreted as “Division,” for this reason: he was born at the time when the earth was divided through languages, that is, at that very time. This is what is meant by the statement, “In his days the earth was divided” (Gen. 10:25). For unless Eber were still alive when the multitude of languages arose, the language that was able to remain with him would not have received its name from him [Note: [Col. 0490] There is no unanimous opinion on this matter. For in their *Chronicle*, which they call *Seder Olam*, that is, “Order of the World,” the Hebrews state that the division of languages took place at the end of Peleg’s life, namely, in the 340th year after the Flood, ten years before Noah’s death. Peleg was born in the 101st year after the Flood and lived 209 years. The Hebrews therefore maintain that Eber was a prophet, since by prophetic inspiration he foresaw long beforehand the future division of languages and consequently gave his newborn son this name. St. Jerome appears to agree with this view in the *Hebrew Traditions*, affirming that Eber gave his son his name by a kind of prophecy, that is, from the future event of the division of languages. The same opinion also appears to be held by St. Chrysostom, *Homily 30 on Genesis*. — COQUAEUS.].

For this reason, it must be believed that this was itself the first common language, since that multiplication and alteration of languages arose as a punishment; and certainly the people of God had to exist outside this punishment. Nor is this language without significance—the language Abraham retained [Note: [Col. 0490] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “Nor is it without significance that he retained this language, that is, the language Abraham retained.”] and was not able to transmit to all his sons, but only to those who, propagated through Jacob and coming together as the people of God in a more marked and distinguished way, were able to possess God’s covenants and the lineage of Christ.

Nor did Eber himself spread this same language throughout all his descendants, but only through that line whose generations extend to Abraham. Therefore, even though it is not explicitly stated that there was a pious kind of human being when Babylon was being founded by the impious, this obscurity was not intended to deprive the seeker of an answer, but rather to exercise his attention.

When we read that originally there was one language for all, and that Eber is mentioned before all the sons of Shem, although he arose fifth from him, and when the language is called Hebrew—the language which the authority of the patriarchs and prophets preserved not only in their speech but also in the sacred writings—then, when we ask where, during the division of languages, the language that had previously been common could have remained, and when we know without doubt that wherever it remained, the punishment brought about by the alteration of languages was not present there, what else suggests itself except that it remained among the people from whom it received its name?

And does it not provide a considerable indication of that people’s righteousness that, while the other nations were punished by the alteration of languages, such a punishment did not reach this one?

3. But another question still troubles us: How could Eber and his son Peleg have produced separate nations if one language remained with both of them? Certainly there is one Hebrew nation propagated from Eber down to Abraham, and thereafter through him, until the people of Israel became great. How, then, did all the sons mentioned of Noah’s three sons produce separate nations, if Eber and Peleg did not each produce one?

The more probable explanation is surely that the giant Nimrod also produced his own nation, but because of the excellence of his rule and stature he was named separately and more prominently, so that the number of seventy-two nations and languages might remain. Peleg, however, was mentioned not because he produced a nation—for his nation is that same Hebrew nation, and its language is the same—but because of the notable time in which he lived, since in his days the earth was divided.

Nor should we be troubled by how the giant Nimrod could have reached the age at which Babylon was founded, confusion was made among the languages, and the nations were divided as a result. It does not follow that, because Eber is sixth from Noah while Nimrod is fourth, they could not have lived until that time. This could have happened because people lived longer where there were fewer generations and fewer years where there were more generations; or because they were born later where there were fewer generations and earlier where there were more.

It must certainly be understood that, when the earth was divided, not only had the other sons of Noah’s sons already been born—those who are mentioned as the fathers of nations—but they were also old enough to have numerous families worthy of being called nations. Therefore, it must in no way be supposed that they were born in the order in which they are mentioned.

Otherwise, how could the twelve sons of Joktan, who was another son of Eber and the brother of Peleg, already have produced nations if Joktan was born after his brother Peleg, as he is mentioned after him—especially since the earth was divided at the time when Peleg was born? We must therefore understand that Peleg, though mentioned first, was born much later than his brother Joktan, whose twelve sons already had families so large that they could be divided into distinct languages.

Thus one who was later in age could be mentioned earlier, just as the sons fathered by Japheth—the youngest of Noah’s three sons—are mentioned first; then the sons of Ham, who was the middle son; and finally the sons of Shem, who was the first and eldest.

Some of the names of those nations remained, so that even today it is apparent from where they were derived, as with the Assyrians from Assur and the Hebrews from Eber. Others were altered by the passage of time, so that scarcely even the most learned people, searching through the ancient histories, have been able to discover the origins of all—or even of some—of those nations.

For although the Egyptians are said to have arisen from Ham’s son who was called Mizraim, no corresponding origin of the name is apparent here; nor is one apparent for the Ethiopians, who are said to belong to that son of Ham who was called Cush. And if everything is considered, more names appear to have been changed than to have remained.

## CHAPTER XII  
### On the decisive point in time represented by Abraham, from whom a new order of the sacred succession is woven

Now let us consider the progress of the city of God beginning also from that decisive point in time represented by the patriarch Abraham. From him knowledge of the city begins to become more evident, and the divine promises are read more clearly—promises that we now see fulfilled in Christ.

As we have learned from the testimony of sacred Scripture, Abraham was born in the region of the Chaldeans (Gen. 11:28), a land that belonged to the Assyrian kingdom [Note: [Col. 0492] Our codices: “belonged to the Assyrian kingdom.” M.].

Among the Chaldeans, impious superstitions were already prevailing at that time, as among the other nations. There was therefore one household—that of Terah—from which Abraham was born, and in which the worship of the one true God remained; and, as is credible, in which alone the Hebrew language also remained. Yet even this household, like the more clearly defined people of God in Egypt, is reported by Joshua to have served foreign gods in Mesopotamia (Josh. 24:2), while the other descendants of Eber gradually flowed into other languages and other nations.

Therefore, just as through the waters of the Flood Noah’s one household remained for the restoration of the human race, so, in the flood of many superstitions throughout the whole world, one household—that of Terah—remained, in which the planting of the city of God was preserved.

Finally, just as there, after the generations had been enumerated up to Noah together with the number of years and the cause of the Flood had been set forth, before God began to speak to Noah about building the ark, it is said, “Now these are the generations of Noah” (Gen. 6:9), so here too, after the generations from him who was called Shem, Noah’s son, had been enumerated down to Abraham, a similarly significant point is inserted, so that it may be said:

> “These are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram and Nahor and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot. And Haran died in the presence of Terah his father in the land in which he was born, in the region of the Chaldeans. And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves: the name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran” (Gen. 11:27–29).

This Haran was the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah, who is believed to have been Sarah herself [Note: [Col. 0493] “Sarah” is absent from Ms. 258. M.], Abraham’s wife [Note: [Col. 0493] This is related by Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 1, chapter 7; by the Hebrews in the book *Seder Olam*, chapter 2; and finally by Jerome in the *Hebrew Traditions*. — COQUAEUS.].

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Why, in the migration of Terah, by which he left the Chaldeans and crossed into Mesopotamia, no mention was made of his son Nahor

Next it is narrated how Terah left the region of the Chaldeans with his household, came into Mesopotamia, and settled in Harran; but one of his sons, whose name was Nahor, is passed over, as though he had not taken him with him. For the account runs as follows:

> “And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son, and led them out from the region of the Chaldeans to go into the land of Canaan; and he came to Harran and settled there” (ibid. 11:31).

Nahor and his wife Milcah are nowhere mentioned here. Yet later, when Abraham sent his servant to obtain a wife for his son Isaac, we find it written:

> “And the servant took ten camels from his master’s camels, and from all his master’s goods with him; and he arose and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor” (ibid. 24:10).

This and other testimonies of this sacred history show that Nahor, Abraham’s brother, also went out from the region of the Chaldeans and established his dwelling in Mesopotamia, where Abraham had lived with his father.

Why, then, did Scripture not mention him when Terah departed from the Chaldean nation with his household and settled in Mesopotamia, where not only Abraham his son but also Sarah his daughter-in-law and Lot his grandson are mentioned as having been taken along? Why, we may ask, except perhaps because Nahor had departed from the piety owed to his father and brother, adhered to the superstition of the Chaldeans, and later emigrated from there either in repentance or after suffering persecution because he was regarded with suspicion?

For in the book entitled *Judith*, when Holofernes, the enemy of the Israelites, asked what nation that was and whether he should wage war against it, Achior, the commander of the Ammonites [Note: [Col. 0493] Manuscripts: “Ammanites”; below also, “Ammanites,” in place of “Ammonites.”], answered him as follows:

> “Let our lord hear a word from the mouth of his servant, and I will tell you the truth about the people who inhabit this mountainous land beside you [Note: [Col. 0493] The Lov. edition: “this mountainous land.” But the manuscripts: “this mountainous land beside you,” in accordance with the Greek, *tēn oreinēn tautēn*.]; and no falsehood will come from the mouth of your servant. For this people is descended from the Chaldeans, and earlier they inhabited Mesopotamia, because they did not wish to follow the gods of their fathers, who were honored in the land of the Chaldeans. They turned aside from the way of their ancestors and worshiped the God of heaven, whom they had come to know; and they drove them from the presence of their gods and fled into Mesopotamia, where they lived for many days. Then their God told them to leave their dwelling and go into the land of Canaan, and there they settled” (Judith 5:5–9).

And so forth, as Achior the Ammonite narrates. From this it is clear that the household of Terah suffered persecution from the Chaldeans on account of the true piety by which they worshiped the one and true God.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On the years of Terah, who completed the term of his life at Harran

After Terah died in Mesopotamia, where he is said to have lived 205 years, God’s promises made to Abraham begin to be indicated. For it is written:

> “And the days of Terah in Harran were 205 years, and Terah died in Harran” (Gen. 11:32) [Note: [Col. 0494] The Lov. edition: “And all the days of Terah were …” “All” is absent from the other books and from the Greek Septuagint.].

This should not be understood as though he spent all these days there, but because he completed all the days of his life there—namely, 205 years. Otherwise, it would be unknown how many years Terah lived, since it is not stated in what year of his life he came to Harran; and it is absurd to suppose that in this sequence of generations, where the number of years each person lived is carefully recorded, the number of years of this one man’s life alone was not entrusted to memory.

The years of certain people whom the same Scripture mentions are omitted because they do not belong to this sequence, in which the reckoning of time is woven together through the succession of those who beget and those who are begotten. But this sequence, which proceeds from Adam to Noah and from there to Abraham, contains no one without the number of years of his life.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the time of Abraham’s departure, when, in accordance with God’s command, he left Harran

1. After the death of Terah, Abraham’s father, Scripture goes on to read: “And the Lord said to Abram, ‘Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s household,’” and so forth. But because this follows in the wording of the book, it should not for that reason be thought to have followed next in the sequence of events. For if this is the case, an insoluble problem results.

After these words of God addressed to Abraham, Scripture says:

> “And Abram departed as the Lord had spoken to him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Harran” (ibid. 12:1, 4).

How can this be true if he left Harran after his father’s death? For, as was stated above, Terah was seventy years old when he fathered Abraham. If the seventy-five years of Abraham’s age at the time he left Harran are added to that number, the result is 145 years. Thus Terah was 145 years old when Abraham left that Mesopotamian city, since Abraham was then in the seventy-fifth year of his life; consequently, his father, who had fathered him in his seventieth year, was, as stated, 145 years old.

Therefore Abraham did not leave after his father’s death—that is, after the 205 years during which his father lived. Rather, the year of Abraham’s departure from that place, since it was his seventy-fifth, was undoubtedly his father’s 145th year, for his father had fathered him in his seventieth year.

Accordingly, we must understand that Scripture returned, in its customary manner, to a time that the narrative had already passed over. Thus, earlier, after mentioning the sons of Noah’s sons, it said that they were “in their nations and according to their languages” (Gen. 10:31), and yet afterward, as though this too followed in the order of time, it said: “Now the whole earth had one language and one speech” (ibid. 11:1).

How, then, could they have been according to their nations and according to their languages if there was one language for all? Only because the narrative returned by recapitulation to something that had already occurred.

So here also, after it had been said, “And the days of Terah in Harran were 205 years, and Terah died in Harran” (ibid. 11:31), Scripture returns to what it had passed over so that it might first complete what had been begun concerning Terah:

> “And the Lord said,” it says, “to Abram, ‘Go out from your land,’” and so forth.

After these words of God it adds:

> “And Abram departed as the Lord had spoken to him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Harran.”

This therefore happened when his father was in the 145th year of his life, for then Abraham was in his seventy-fifth [Note: [Col. 0495] Compare *Questions on Genesis*, question 26.].
