This problem has also been solved in another way: Abraham’s seventy-five years when he left Harran may be reckoned from the time when he was delivered from the fire of the Chaldeans, not from the time when he was born—as though he should be regarded as having been born at that point [Note: [Col. 0495] This solution is offered by Jerome, derived from Hebrew tradition, according to which Abraham was thrown by the Chaldeans into a fire that he refused to worship and was divinely delivered from it.].

2. But blessed Stephen, when relating these events in the Acts of the Apostles, says:

> “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Harran, and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you.’”

According to Stephen’s words, God did not speak to Abraham after the death of his father, who certainly died in Harran, where his son also lived with him; rather, God spoke to him before he lived in that city, although he was already in Mesopotamia. Thus he had already departed from the Chaldeans.

When Stephen adds, “Then Abraham went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Harran,” this does not show [Note: [Col. 0495] The word “show” is absent from the manuscripts.] what happened after God spoke to him—for God spoke to him while he was in Mesopotamia, and therefore he did not leave the land of the Chaldeans after those words of God—but refers to the whole period he calls “then,” that is, from the time when Abraham left the Chaldeans and lived in Harran.

Likewise, when Stephen continues, “And from there, after his father died, he settled him in this land in which you now dwell, and your fathers” (Acts 7:2–4), he does not say, “After his father died, he left Harran,” but rather, “from there he settled him here, after his father died.”

We must therefore understand that God spoke to Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Harran; that Abraham nevertheless reached Harran with his father, retaining within himself God’s command; and that he left from there in his own seventy-fifth year, which was his father’s 145th year.

Stephen says that Abraham was settled in the land of Canaan after his father’s death, not that he departed from Harran after his father’s death, because his father was already dead when Abraham purchased the land and began there to possess his own property.

When God says to Abraham, who was already established in Mesopotamia—that is, who had already left the land of the Chaldeans—“Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father’s household,” this is not said so that he might remove his body from a place he had already left, but so that he might detach his mind from it.

For he had not departed from it in spirit if he remained held by the hope and desire of returning; and that hope and desire had to be cut away by God’s command and help, with Abraham’s obedience. It is not implausible to suppose that, after Nahor had later followed his father, Abraham then fulfilled the Lord’s command by leaving Harran with his wife Sarah and Lot, his brother’s son.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the order and character of God’s promises made to Abraham

Now we must consider God’s promises made to Abraham. In them the oracles of our God [Note: [Col. 0496] So the manuscripts. The Lov. edition instead reads: “of our Lord Jesus Christ.”], that is, of the true God, concerning the people of the pious [Note: [Col. 0496] Some codices: “of the impious.”] begin to appear more clearly—the people foretold by prophetic authority.

The first promise is read as follows:

> “And the Lord said to Abram: ‘Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s household, and go into the land that I will show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you, and in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.’”

We must therefore note that two things were promised to Abraham. The first was that his seed would possess the land of Canaan, which is signified where it says, “Go into the land that I will show you,” and, “I will make you into a great nation.” The second, far more excellent, concerned not carnal but spiritual offspring, through which he is the father not of the one Israelite nation alone but of all the nations that follow the footsteps of his faith. This began to be promised in the words, “In you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.”

Eusebius supposes that this promise was made in the seventy-fifth year of Abraham’s life, as though Abraham left Harran immediately after it was made, since Scripture cannot be contradicted where it says, “Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Harran” (Gen. 12:1–4).

But if this promise was made in that year, Abraham was already staying in Harran with his father. For he could not leave there unless he had first lived there. Is Stephen, then, to be contradicted when he says, “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Harran” (Acts 7:2)?

Rather, we must understand that everything happened in the same year: God’s promise before Abraham lived in Harran, his residence in Harran, and his departure from there. This is so not only because Eusebius, in his *Chronicles*, reckons from the year of this promise and shows that the departure from Egypt occurred after 430 years, when the Law was given, but also because the apostle Paul mentions this (Gal. 3:17).

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the three outstanding kingdoms of the nations, one of which—the Assyrian—already stood preeminent when Abraham was born

At that same time there were prominent kingdoms of the nations, among which the earthly city—that is, the society of human beings living according to man—stood out most conspicuously under the rule of the fallen angels. These were three kingdoms: those of the Sicyonians, the Egyptians, and the Assyrians. But the Assyrian kingdom was far more powerful and distinguished.

For that king Ninus, son of Belus, had subjected the peoples of all Asia except India. By “Asia” I mean not the region that is one province of greater Asia, but the whole continent called Asia, which some placed as one of two divisions and most as one of the three divisions of the entire world, so that the whole consists of Asia, Europe, and Africa. They did not make these divisions equally.

For the region called Asia extends from the south through the east to the north; Europe extends from the north to the west; and from there Africa extends from the west to the south. Thus Europe and Africa appear to occupy one half of the world, while Asia alone occupies the other half. But those two regions were made into separate parts because between them the waters that divide the lands enter from the Ocean and form the great sea known to us.

Therefore, if the world is divided into two parts, East and West, Asia will be in one, and Europe and Africa in the other.

Of the three kingdoms that were then preeminent, the kingdom of the Sicyonians was not subject to the Assyrians, since the Sicyonians were in Europe. But how was the kingdom of the Egyptians not subject to them, when the Assyrians held all Asia except, as is reported, the Indians?

In Assyria, therefore, the rule of the impious city had prevailed. Its capital was Babylon, whose name—“Confusion”—is most fitting for the earthly city. At that time Ninus was reigning, after the death of his father Belus, who had first ruled there for sixty-five years. His son Ninus, who succeeded his deceased father in the kingdom, reigned for fifty-two years and was forty-three years into his reign when Abraham was born—approximately 1,200 years before the founding of Rome, as though it were another Babylon in the West.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### On God’s renewed address to Abraham, by which the land of Canaan is promised to him and his seed

Abraham therefore left Harran in the seventy-fifth year of his life and in the 145th year of his father’s life. With Lot, his brother’s son, and Sarah, his wife, he proceeded into the land of Canaan and reached Shechem, where he again received a divine oracle, concerning which it is written:

> “And the Lord appeared to Abraham and said to him, ‘To your seed I will give this land’” (Gen. 12:7).

Nothing is promised here concerning that seed through which he became the father of all nations, but only concerning that seed through which he is the father of the one Israelite nation; for this land was possessed by that seed.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On Sarah’s chastity, preserved by God in Egypt, when Abraham had said that she was his sister and not his wife

After building an altar there and invoking God, Abraham departed from that place and settled in the wilderness. From there he was compelled by famine to go into Egypt. There he called his wife his sister (Gen. 12:7–19), without lying. She was indeed also his sister, since she was related to him by blood, just as Lot, because he was his brother’s son, was also called his brother through the same kinship.

Thus he kept silent about the fact that she was his wife but did not deny it, entrusting the protection of his wife’s chastity to God and, as a human being, avoiding human snares. For if he failed to avoid a danger that could be avoided, he would be tempting God rather than hoping in God. We have said enough on this matter against Faustus the Manichaean (book 22, chapter 36).

In the end, what Abraham had confidently expected from the Lord came to pass. For Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who had taken her as his wife, was severely afflicted and returned her to her husband (Gen. 12:20). Far be it from us to believe that she was polluted by intercourse with another man; it is much more credible that Pharaoh was not permitted to do this because of the great afflictions that befell him.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the separation of Lot and Abraham, which they arranged while preserving their affection
Therefore, when Abraham returned from Egypt to the place from which he had come, Lot, his brother’s son, separated from him and went into the land of Sodom, without any breach of affection. For they had become wealthy and had begun to possess many herdsmen with their flocks; when these quarreled with one another, they avoided in this way a contentious dispute among their households. For, human nature being what it is, some quarrel might also have arisen between Abraham and Lot themselves. Accordingly, these are Abraham’s words to Lot, by which he forestalled this evil:

“Let there be no quarrel between me and you, nor between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, because we are brothers. Is not the whole land before you? Separate from me: if you go to the left, I will go to the right; or if you go to the right, I will go to the left” (ibid. XIII, 8–9).

Perhaps from this there arose among human beings the peaceful custom that, when something belonging to the earth must be divided, the elder divides and the younger chooses.

[Note: [Col. 0498] See Seneca, *Excerpta Controversiarum*, book 6, chapter 3.]

## CHAPTER XXI.—On God’s third promise, by which he promises Abraham and his seed the land of Canaan forever

When, therefore, they had departed and Abraham and Lot were living separately because the support of their households required it, not because of any disgraceful quarrel—and Abraham was in the land of Canaan, while Lot was in Sodom—the Lord said to Abraham in a third oracle:

“Look up with your eyes and see from the place where you now are, toward the north, the southwest, the east, and the sea; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed forever, and I will make your seed like the sand of the earth. If anyone can count the sand of the earth, your seed also shall be counted. Rise, walk through the land in its length and breadth, for I will give it to you” (Gen. XIII, 14–17).

Whether this promise also includes the one by which he was made the father of all nations is not plainly evident. For the words, “I will make your seed like the sand of the earth,” can be understood as referring to this; they are expressed in the figure that the Greeks call *hyperbole*, which is figurative, not literal. Yet no one who has studied Scripture doubts that Scripture habitually uses this and the other figures of speech. This figure—that is, this manner of expression—occurs when what is said is far greater than what is signified by the saying.

For who does not see how incomparably greater is the number of grains of sand than could be the number of all human beings from Adam himself to the end of the world? How much more, then, than the seed of Abraham—not only that which belongs to the Israelite nation, but also that which exists and will exist throughout the whole world among all nations according to the imitation of faith? That seed, in comparison with the multitude of the ungodly, is certainly small in number. Yet even these few constitute an innumerable multitude, which is signified figuratively by the sand of the earth.

To be sure, this multitude promised to Abraham is not innumerable to God, but to human beings; to God, not even the sand of the earth is innumerable. Since, therefore, not merely the Israelite nation but the whole seed of Abraham—where the promise also exists—is compared more fittingly to the multitude of the sand, not according to the flesh but according to the spirit of his many children, the promise of both matters may here be understood to have been made.

[Note: [Col. 0499] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “where the explicit promise exists.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499] Compare *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book 22, chapter 89.]

We said that this was not plainly evident because the multitude of that one nation, which was born according to the flesh from Abraham through his grandson Jacob, also increased so greatly that it filled almost every part of the world. Thus it too could be compared figuratively to the multitude of the sand, since this nation alone is innumerable to human beings.

No one, certainly, doubts that the land signified is that land alone called Canaan. But the words, “I will give it to you and to your seed forever,” can trouble some if they understand “forever” to mean “for eternity.” If, however, they take “forever” here in the sense in which we faithfully understand it—that the beginning of the future age arises from the end of the present age—they will not be troubled. For although the Israelites have been expelled from Jerusalem, they nevertheless remain in other cities of the land of Canaan and will remain there until the end; and since the whole of that land is inhabited by Christians, it too is part of Abraham’s seed.

## CHAPTER XXII.—On Abraham’s defeat of the enemies of Sodom, when he rescued Lot from captivity and was blessed by Melchizedek the priest

After receiving this response of promise, Abraham moved away and remained in another place of the same land, namely, near the oak of Mamre, which was at Hebron (Gen. XIII, 18).

After enemies had invaded Sodom, when five kings were waging war against four, and Lot too had been captured after the Sodomites were defeated, Abraham rescued him. He took three hundred and eighteen of his household-born servants with him into battle and won a victory for the kings of Sodom.

[Note: [Col. 0500] The printed editions read, “a victory *over* the kings.” The word *over* is absent from the manuscripts and ought to be absent: the victory was won for the kings of Sodom, against their enemies.]

He was unwilling to take any spoils, although the king for whom he had won the victory offered them to him. But at that time he was blessed by Melchizedek, who was priest of God Most High (ibid. XIV, 1–20). Much and important material has been written about him in the Epistle entitled *To the Hebrews*, which many say was written by the apostle Paul, while others deny this (Heb. VII).

For there, for the first time, appeared the sacrifice that is now offered to God by Christians throughout the whole world; and what was said much later through the prophet to Christ, who was still to come in the flesh, is fulfilled:

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

Not, of course, according to the order of Aaron; that order was destined to be removed when the realities that had been prefigured by those shadows began to shine forth.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—On the word of the Lord to Abraham, by which he is promised descendants multiplied according to the number of the stars; and how, believing, he was justified while still uncircumcised

At that time also the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision. When God promised him protection and a very great reward, Abraham, concerned about his descendants, said that a certain Eliezer, his household servant, would become his heir. Immediately an heir was promised to him—not that servant, but one who would come forth from Abraham himself—and again an innumerable seed, not like the sand of the earth but like the stars of heaven (Gen. XV, 1–5).

Here it seems to me that descendants exalted by heavenly blessedness are more particularly promised. For as regards multitude, what are the stars of heaven in comparison with the sand of the earth, unless someone says that the comparison is similar to the extent that the stars too cannot be counted? For it must be believed that not all of them can be seen. The more sharply someone looks, the more he sees; and therefore it is rightly thought that some remain hidden even from those with the keenest sight, apart from those stars said to rise and set in the remotest part of the world, on the opposite side from us.

Finally, whatever people boast that they have comprehended and recorded the total number of the stars—such as Aratus or Eudoxus, or any others—this book’s authority disregards them.

Here, moreover, that famous sentence is set down, which the Apostle recalls to commend God’s grace:

“Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV, 6; Rom. IV, 3; Gal. III, 6).

This was so that circumcision might not boast and refuse admission to faith in Christ for the uncircumcised nations. For when this occurred—when Abraham’s faith was reckoned to him as righteousness—he had not yet been circumcised.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On the significance of the sacrifice that Abraham was commanded to offer when he asked to be taught about what he had believed

[Note: [Col. 0501] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “what he might believe.”]

[Col. 0501]

### 1

While God was speaking to him in the same vision, he also said to him:

“I am God who brought you out from the region of the Chaldaeans, to give you this land, so that you may be its heir.”

When Abraham asked by what means he would know that he would be its heir, God said to him:

“Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a pigeon.”

He took all these for him, divided them through the middle, and placed the pieces opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds.

And, as it is written, birds descended upon the divided bodies, and Abram sat beside them. Around sunset a dread fell upon Abram, and behold, a great dark fear fell upon him. And it was said to Abram:

“Know with certainty that your seed will be a sojourner in a land not its own; they will enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation that they serve. Afterward they will come out here with much property. But you will go to your fathers, nourished in peace, in a good old age.”

[Note: [Col. 0501] The Septuagint interpreters have *trapheis*, “nourished,” in ancient manuscripts; nevertheless, in the Complutensian edition they have *tapheis*, “buried.”]

“In the fourth generation they will return here. For the sins of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure.”

When the sun had already gone down, a flame appeared; and behold, a smoking furnace and flaming torches passed between those divided pieces. On that day the Lord God made a covenant with Abram, saying:

“To your seed I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”

### 2

All these things were divinely done and spoken in the vision. To discuss each of them in detail would be lengthy and would exceed the purpose of this work. What we must know is this: after it had been said that Abraham believed God and that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, he did not fail in faith when he said, “Lord and Ruler, by what means shall I know that I shall be its heir?” (Gen. XV, 7–21).

The inheritance of that land had been promised to him. He did not say, “From where shall I know?” as though he still did not believe; rather, he said, “By what means shall I know?” so that some likeness might be supplied for the matter he had believed, by which its mode might be recognized.

Similarly, the Virgin Mary’s question, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” does not express disbelief. She was certain that what was to happen would happen; she was asking how it would happen.

[Note: [Col. 0501] Ambrose uses this example of the holy Virgin for the same matter in *On Abraham the Patriarch*, book 2, chapter 8. More may be compared there with this chapter. COQUAEUS.]

When she had asked this, she heard: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

[Note: [Col. 0501] All our manuscripts omit the words, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” M.]

Finally, here too a likeness was supplied from the animals—the heifer, the she-goat, and the ram, together with the two birds, the turtledove and the pigeon—so that he might know by these signs what would happen, although he no longer doubted that it would happen.

Therefore, whether the heifer signifies the people placed under the yoke of the law, the she-goat the same people destined to become sinful, and the ram the same people also destined to reign—these animals are called three-year-old because there are notable divisions of time from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, and from Abraham to David, who, after Saul had been rejected, was the first to be established in the kingdom of the Israelite nation by the Lord’s will; and in this third period, extending from Abraham to David, that people grew to maturity as though passing through a third age—or whether these things signify something more appropriate, I would nevertheless have no doubt that spiritual people are prefigured by the addition of the turtledove and the pigeon.

For this reason it was said, “But he did not divide the birds”: carnal people are divided among themselves, but spiritual people are in no way divided. They may withdraw from the busy dealings of human beings, like the turtledove, or live among those dealings, like the pigeon; yet each bird is simple and harmless.

This signifies that even within the Israelite people, to whom that land was to be given, there would be undivided sons of the promise and heirs of the kingdom who would remain in eternal blessedness.

[Note: [Col. 0502] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “who would remain.”]

The birds descending upon the divided bodies signify not something good, but the spirits of this air, seeking a kind of food for themselves from the division of carnal people. Abraham’s sitting beside them signifies that, even amid those divisions of carnal people, true believers would persevere to the end.

[Note: [Col. 0502] Vindicianus, Amerbachius, and Erasmus add after “those divisions of carnal people”: “there are some spiritual persons.” The manuscripts do not have this; but most of them read *men* where the printed editions have *true*.]

The dread that fell upon Abraham around sunset, and the great dark fear, signifies the great disturbance and tribulation that will come upon the faithful near the end of this age. Concerning this the Lord said in the Gospel:

“For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning” (Matt. XXIV, 21).

### 3

The words spoken to Abraham—“Know with certainty that your seed will be a sojourner in a land not its own; they will enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years”—were most plainly prophesied concerning the people of Israel, who were to serve in Egypt.

This does not mean that the people would spend four hundred years in that same servitude under their Egyptian oppressors; rather, within those four hundred years it was foretold that this would occur. Just as it is written of Terah, Abraham’s father, “The days of Terah in Harran were two hundred and five years” (Gen. XI, 32)—not because all those years were spent there, but because the period was completed there—so here too it is inserted: “They will enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years,” because that number was completed in the same affliction, not because the whole period was spent there.

The years are called four hundred on account of the completeness of the number, although they are somewhat more—whether they are reckoned from the time when this was promised to Abraham, or from the time when Isaac was born, on account of Abraham’s seed concerning which these things were foretold.

For, as we already said above, from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when the first promise was made to him, until Israel’s departure from Egypt, there were four hundred and thirty years. The Apostle refers to them as follows:

“This is what I mean,” he says: “the law, which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to abolish the promise” (Gal. III, 17).

Those four hundred and thirty years could therefore be called four hundred, since they are not much more; how much more so when several years of that number had already passed at the time when those things were shown and spoken to Abraham in the vision, or when Isaac was born to his father at the age of one hundred, twenty-five years after the first promise? At that point four hundred and five of those four hundred and thirty years still remained, yet God wished to call them four hundred.

No one will doubt that the remaining words spoken by God in the prophecy also pertain to the Israelite people.

[Note: [Col. 0503] Compare *Questions on Exodus*, question 47.]

### 4

The further words—“When the sun had already gone down, a flame appeared; and behold, a smoking furnace and flaming torches passed between those divided pieces”—signify that at the end of the age carnal people will be judged by fire.

Just as the affliction of the City of God, such as is believed never previously to have occurred and which is expected under Antichrist, is signified by Abraham’s dark fear around sunset—that is, as the end of the age approaches—so, at sunset, that is, at the very end, the day of judgment is signified by this fire. It will separate those who are to be saved through fire from those who are to be condemned in fire.

[Note: [Col. 0503] Vindicianus, Amerbachius, and Erasmus read “the end of the age.”]

The covenant made with Abraham next clearly reveals and names the land of Canaan itself, together with eleven nations in it, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.

It is not, therefore, from the great river of Egypt—that is, the Nile—but from the small river that separates Egypt from Palestine, where the city of Rhinocorura is situated.

[Note: [Col. 0503] Compare *Questions on Joshua*, question 21.]

## CHAPTER XXV.—On Hagar, Sarah’s slave woman, whom Sarah herself wished to be Abraham’s concubine

From this point the times of Abraham’s sons follow: one was born from Hagar the slave woman, and the other from Sarah the free woman. We have already spoken of them in the preceding book (chapter 3).

As for what actually happened, no accusation whatsoever should be brought against Abraham on account of this concubine.

[Note: [Col. 0503] Faustus the Manichaean did make such an accusation. See book 22 against him, chapter 30.]

He used her to beget offspring, not to gratify lust; and he did not act insultingly, but rather in obedience to his wife. She believed that her barrenness would be consoled if, since she could not conceive by nature, she made the fertile womb of her slave her own by her will. She thus used the right expressed by the Apostle’s words, “Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. VII, 4), by having the woman bear from another what she herself could not bear.

There is here no lustful desire and no disgraceful wickedness. The wife gives the slave woman to her husband for the sake of offspring; the husband receives her for the sake of offspring. From both of them is sought not the indulgence of vice but the fruit of nature.

Finally, when the pregnant slave woman became proud over her barren mistress, and Sarah, in the suspicion characteristic of women, attributed this rather to her husband, Abraham there too showed that he was not a lover who had enslaved himself to a woman but a free father, and that in Hagar he had preserved the chastity of Sarah his wife. He had fulfilled not his own pleasure but her will: he had accepted, not requested; approached, not hesitated; sown, not loved.

For he said:

“Behold, your slave woman is in your hands; use her as you please” (Gen. XVI, 6).

O manly man in his use of women, temperate with his wife, obedient with his slave woman, and intemperate with no one!

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On God’s testimony to Abraham, by which, in his old age, he promises him a son from barren Sarah, appoints him father of nations, and seals the promise by the sacrament of circumcision

### 1

After this Ishmael was born from Hagar. Someone might have thought that in him the promise had been fulfilled—the promise made when Abraham wished to adopt his household servant as his heir—when God said:

“This one shall not be your heir; but the one who will come forth from you, he shall be your heir” (Gen. XV, 4).

Therefore, so that he would not think this promise fulfilled in the son of the slave woman, when he was already ninety-nine years old the Lord appeared to him and said:

“I am God; be pleasing in my sight, and be without blame, and I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.”

And Abram fell upon his face. And God spoke to him, saying:

“And I—behold, my covenant is with you; and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations. Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, because I have appointed you father of many nations. I will increase you exceedingly, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come forth from you. I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your seed after you. And I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you are a sojourner, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession, and I will be their God.

“And you shall keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations.”

[Note: [Col. 0504] Thus all our manuscripts. In B, *you* is absent, and instead of “throughout their generations” it reads “throughout the generations.” M.]

“And this is the covenant that you shall keep between me and you, and between your seed after you throughout their generations: every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin. It shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. Every male among you throughout your generations who is eight days old shall be circumcised. Every household servant and every purchased servant from any foreigner’s son who is not of your seed shall surely be circumcised—the servant born in your house and the purchased servant. My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant.

“And the uncircumcised male, who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

[Note: [Col. 0504] The printed editions read, “my covenant.” *My* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Septuagint.]

And God said to Abraham:

“Your wife Sara shall not be called Sara, but Sarra shall be her name.”

[Note: [Col. 0505] Thus the manuscripts according to the Septuagint. The printed editions, however, read: “Sarai your wife shall not be called Sarai [or: ‘Sarai any longer’], but Sarra shall be her name.”]

“I will bless her and give you a son from her. I will bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of nations shall come from him.”

And Abraham fell upon his face, and he laughed, and said in his heart:

“If a son will be born to one who is one hundred years old, and if Sarra, who is ninety years old, will give birth?”

And Abraham said to God:

“May Ishmael live before you.”

But God said to Abraham:

“Yes, behold, Sarra your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, to be God to him.”

[Note: [Col. 0505] The Leuven edition reads, “and I will be his God.” Erasmus reads, “and may I be his God.” Vindicianus and Amerbachius more correctly read, “that I may be his God.” Nevertheless, the manuscripts read, “to be God to him.” The Greek Septuagint has *einai autō Theos*, “to be God to him.”]

“And with regard to Ishmael, behold, I have heard you: behold, I have blessed him, and I will enlarge him, and I will multiply him exceedingly.”

[Note: [Col. 0505] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “I will make him great.”]

[Note: [Col. 0505] Our manuscripts read, “and I will multiply him exceedingly.” A little later they read, “and I will make him into a great nation.” M.]

“He shall beget twelve nations, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarra shall bear to you at this time in the following year” (Gen. XVII, 1–21).

### 2

Here the promises concerning the calling of the Gentiles in Isaac—that is, in the son of the promise—are more explicit. This signifies grace, not nature, because a son is promised from an old man and an old barren woman.

Although God also brings about the ordinary course of natural procreation, wherever the work of God is evident—where nature has been impaired and ceased—there grace is understood more clearly.

And because this was to occur not through generation but through regeneration, circumcision was commanded at the time when a son was promised from Sarah. By commanding that all be circumcised—not only sons but also household servants and purchased servants—God testifies that this grace pertains to all.

For what else does circumcision signify than nature renewed after its old condition has been stripped away?

[Note: [Col. 0505] Compare *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 29.]

And what else does the eighth day signify than Christ, who rose on the eighth day—after the completed week, that is, after the Sabbath?

[Note: [Col. 0505] Compare *On Original Sin*, section 30.]

The names of the parents are changed; everything resounds with newness; and in the Old Testament the New is veiled. For what else is called the Old Testament than the concealment of the New? And what else is called the New than the revelation of the Old?

Abraham’s laughter was the joyful exultation of one giving thanks, not the mockery of one who doubted. His words in his heart—“If a son will be born to one who is one hundred years old, and if Sarra, who is ninety years old, will give birth?”—do not express doubt but wonder.

If anyone is troubled by the words, “I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you are a sojourner, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession,” and asks how this has been fulfilled or is still expected to be fulfilled, since no earthly possession can be everlasting for any nation, let him know that our translators render as “everlasting” what the Greeks call *aiōnion* (αἰώνιον), derived from *aiōn* (αἰών). In Greek, *aiōn* means “age.”

The Latins did not dare to translate it as *saeculare*, “belonging to the age,” lest they direct the sense toward something quite different. For many things are called *saecularia*, “worldly” or “belonging to the present age,” which are carried out in this age in such a way that they pass away even within a short time. But what is called *aiōnion* either has no end or extends to the end of this age.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the male who, if he is not circumcised on the eighth day, perishes, because he has broken God’s covenant

It may also be asked how we ought to understand what is said here:

“The male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

This cannot be the fault of the infant whose soul, he says, will perish; nor has the infant himself broken God’s covenant, but rather the adults who failed to ensure that he was circumcised.

The answer is that even infants have all broken that one covenant—not according to the individual character of their own lives, but according to the common origin of the human race—in which all sinned (Rom. V, 12).

Many covenants of God are mentioned, apart from those two great covenants, the Old and the New, as anyone may discover by reading. The first covenant, made with the first human being, is surely this:

“On the day when you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II, 17).

Hence it is written in the book called *Ecclesiasticus*:

“Every flesh grows old like a garment.”

“For the covenant from the age: You shall surely die.”

[Note: [Col. 0506] The printed editions read: “The covenant of this world is that those who transgress God’s commandments shall surely die.” The passage in the ancient books has been freed from a gloss and restored. It is taken from Ecclesiasticus XIV, 18, according to the Septuagint. In the Vulgate it is joined to verse 12 and appears as follows: “The covenant of this world: he shall surely die.”]

Since the more explicit law was given later, and the Apostle says, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. IV, 15), how can what is read in the Psalm be true—“I have considered all the sinners of the earth transgressors” (Ps. CXVIII, 119)—unless all who are held bound by some sin are guilty of transgressing some law?

Therefore, if infants too—as true faith maintains—are born sinners not individually but originally, and for this reason we confess that they need the grace of the forgiveness of sins, then, in the manner in which they are sinners, they are also recognized as transgressors of that law which was given in paradise. Thus both statements are true: “I have considered all the sinners of the earth transgressors,” and, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

Accordingly, since circumcision was a sign of regeneration, and since generation, on account of original sin by which God’s first covenant was broken, rightly destroys the infant unless regeneration sets him free, these divine words must be understood as though they said:

“Whoever has not been regenerated, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken God’s covenant,”

when he too sinned in Adam together with all the others.

For if it had said, “Because he has broken *this* covenant of mine,” it would have forced us to understand the statement only of this circumcision. But since it did not specify what kind of covenant the infant had broken, it is permissible to understand it as referring to that covenant whose breaking could pertain to an infant.

If someone insists that the statement refers only to this circumcision—that the infant broke God’s covenant in it because he was not circumcised—let him seek some mode of expression by which it may not absurdly be understood that the infant broke the covenant because, although it was not broken by him, it was broken in him.

Even so, it must be observed that the soul of the uncircumcised infant perishes unjustly through no negligence of its own, except by the obligation of original sin.

[Note: [Col. 0507] Vindicianus, Amerbachius, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read “justly.”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the changing of the names of Abraham and Sarah, who, although they could not beget children because of her barrenness and both their old age, received the gift of fertility

After so great and so clear a promise had been made to Abraham—“I have appointed you father of many nations”; “I will increase you exceedingly, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come forth from you”; “I will give you a son from Sarra”; “I will bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of nations shall come from him”—a promise that we now see fulfilled in Christ, from that time onward those spouses are no longer called in Scripture by the names by which they had previously been called, Abram and Sara. Instead, just as we have called them from the beginning, and as they are now called by everyone, they are called Abraham and Sarra.

The reason for Abraham’s name being changed is given:

“Because,” he says, “I have appointed you father of many nations.”

Thus Abraham is to be understood to signify this. Abram, the name by which he was formerly called, is interpreted as “exalted father.”

No reason is given for Sara’s changed name. But, according to those who have written interpretations of the Hebrew names contained in these sacred Scriptures, Sara is interpreted as “my princess,” whereas Sarra means “virtue.”

Hence it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

“By faith Sarah herself also received strength for the conception of offspring.”

[Note: [Col. 0507] The Navarra manuscript reads, “for conception,” while the other books disagree. The Greek is *eis katabolēn*, “for the laying down” or “conception” of seed.]

Both were elderly, as Scripture testifies; but she was also barren and had already ceased to menstruate. For this reason she could no longer give birth, even if she had not been barren.

If a woman is of such advanced age that her customary menstrual flow still occurs, she may bear a child by a young man but not by an older man; although that older man may still be able to beget a child by a young woman. Thus Abraham was able to beget children by Keturah after Sarah’s death, because he found her of vigorous age.

This, then, is what the Apostle presents as remarkable, and for this reason he says that Abraham’s body was already dead (Rom. IV, 19): at that age he could not beget a child by every woman who might still have had some final capacity for giving birth.

We must therefore understand that his body was dead with respect to something, not with respect to everything. For if it were dead with respect to everything, old age would no longer be the old age of a living man but the corpse of a dead one.

This question is sometimes resolved in another way: Abraham later begot children by Keturah because the gift of begetting, which he had received from the Lord, remained even after the death of his wife.

But the explanation that we have followed seems preferable to me. A hundred-year-old man in our own time cannot beget a child by any woman; but this was not the case then, when people still lived so long that one hundred years did not yet make a man decrepit with old age.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—On the three men or angels in whom the Lord is indicated to have appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre
Again God appeared to Abraham by the oak of Mamre in the form of three men, whom there can be no doubt were angels, although some think that one of them was the Lord Christ, asserting that he was visible even before assuming flesh [Note: [Col. 0508] Thus taught Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 6; *Against the Jews*, chapter 9; *Against Marcion*, book 2, chapter 27, and book 3, chapter 9, as well as elsewhere; Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 6, and book 4, chapter 26; Clement of Rome, *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 21; Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*; and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 2. Augustine’s opinion, however, is more probable; he also presents it in *On the Trinity*, book 2, no. 21, and *Against Maximinus*, book 2, chapter 26, §§5–6. Ambrose ultimately agrees with him, *On Abraham*, book 1, chapter 5. COQUAEUS.]. It is indeed within the power of the divine, invisible, incorporeal, and immutable nature to appear, without any change in itself, even to mortal eyes—not through what it is, but through something subject to it. And what is not subject to it?

Nevertheless, if they confirm that one of these three was Christ because, after seeing three, Abraham addressed one in the singular—for thus it is written: “And behold, three men stood above him; and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the door of his tent, and worshiped upon the ground, and said: Lord, if I have found favor before you” (Gen. XVIII, 1–3), and so forth—why do they not also observe that two of them came so that the Sodomites might be destroyed, while Abraham was still speaking to one, calling him Lord and interceding that the just man should not be destroyed together with the wicked in Sodom?

Lot, moreover, received those two in such a way that he too addressed one of them in the singular as Lord [Note: [Col. 0508] The Louvain edition alone reads: “in his conversation with them he addressed the two as Lord in the singular.”]. For after saying to them in the plural, “Behold, lords, turn aside into the house of your servant,” and the other words recorded there, we nevertheless read afterward: “And the angels took his hand, and the hand of his wife, and the hands of his two daughters, in that the Lord spared him” [Note: [Col. 0508] The particle *in* is absent from the printed editions, but is found in all the manuscripts according to the Septuagint.]. And it came to pass, as soon as they had brought him outside, that they said: “Save your life; do not look back, nor remain in all the surrounding region; save yourself on the mountain, lest you also be taken.” But Lot said to them: “I beg you, Lord, because your servant has found mercy before you,” and what follows. Then, after these words, the Lord himself answered him in the singular, although he was present in the two angels, saying: “Behold, I have regarded [Note: [Col. 0509] The printed editions read *I have had mercy*. The manuscripts have the more accurate *I have regarded*, for the Greek in the Septuagint is *ethaúmasa*, which here perhaps means “I have looked upon” or “I have shown regard.”] your face” (Gen. XIX, 2–21), and so forth.

It is therefore much more credible that Abraham, in the three men, and Lot, in the two, recognized the Lord, to whom they spoke using the singular number even when they considered them to be men. For they did not receive them in any other way than as though they were mortals in need of human refreshment; rather, there was certainly something in which they excelled, even though they appeared as men, so that those who offered them hospitality could not doubt that the Lord was in them, just as he is accustomed to be in the prophets. For this reason they sometimes addressed the men themselves in the plural and sometimes addressed the Lord in them in the singular [Note: [Col. 0509] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “and sometimes addressed them in the plural as lords, sometimes in the singular as the Lord who was in them.”].

Scripture testifies that they were angels, not only in this book of Genesis, where these events are narrated, but also in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where, in praising hospitality, it says: “Through it, some, without knowing it, received angels as guests” (Hebr. XIII, 2).

Through those three men, then, when the son of Isaac was again promised to Abraham through Sarah, a divine answer was also given in these words: “Abraham shall be a great and numerous nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him” (Gen. XVIII, 18) [Note: [Col. 0509] The Louvain edition reads: “so that it might be said to Abraham, ‘He shall be a great and numerous nation.’” The other printed editions and the manuscripts agree with the Septuagint.]. Here two things were promised, in the briefest yet fullest manner: the nation of Israel according to the flesh, and all the nations according to faith.

## CHAPTER XXX—On Lot’s Deliverance from Sodom and the Destruction of the Same City by Heavenly Fire; and on Abimelech, Whose Desire Could Not Harm Sarah’s Chastity

After this promise, Lot was delivered from Sodom, and a fiery rain came from heaven; the entire region of that impious city was turned to ashes. There, sexual violations of males had become as prevalent as the laws ordinarily permit the license of other acts [Note: [Col. 0509] Compare above, book 14, chapter 18, at the beginning.].

Yet this punishment of theirs was also an image of the future divine judgment. For what does it mean that those who were being rescued were forbidden by the angels to look back, unless it means that, if we are thinking of escaping the final judgment, we must not in our minds return to the former life from which the grace of regeneration strips us? Finally, Lot’s wife, when she looked back, remained behind and was changed into salt (Gen. XIX); to faithful people she provided a kind of seasoning by which they might acquire the wisdom to avoid such an example.

Afterward Abraham again did at Gerar, before Abimelech, the king of that city, what he had done in Egypt concerning his wife, and she was likewise returned to him untouched. There Abraham, when the king rebuked him for remaining silent about his wife and calling her his sister, explained what he had feared and added this: “Indeed, she is truly my sister by my father, but not by my mother” (Gen. XX, 2) [Col. 0510]. For Sarah was Abraham’s sister by his father, through whom she was also his relative. She was of such great beauty that even at that age she could be loved.

## CHAPTER XXXI—On Isaac’s Birth According to the Promise, and on His Name, Given from the Laughter of Both Parents

After these events, a son was born to Abraham from Sarah, according to God’s promise, and he named him Isaac, which means “Laughter.” For the father had laughed when the child was promised to him, marveling with joy; and the mother had laughed when he was again promised through the three men, doubting with joy. Yet the angel reproved her because that laughter, although it arose from joy, was nevertheless not accompanied by complete faith (Gen. XVIII, 12–15). Later, after being confirmed in faith by the same angel, she was strengthened.

The child therefore received his name from this event. Sarah showed that her laughter had not been laughter of derision and reproach but of celebration and joy when, after Isaac’s birth and his receiving of that name, she said: “The Lord has made laughter for me; whoever hears of it will rejoice with me” (ibid. XXI, 6).

After some time, the slave woman was expelled from the household with her son, and those two women signify, according to the Apostle, the two covenants, the old and the new; Sarah, that woman, represents the Jerusalem above, that is, the city of God (Gal. IV, 26) [Note: [Col. 0510] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *that woman’s* instead.].

## CHAPTER XXXII—On Abraham’s Obedience and Faith, by Which He Was Tested through the Offering of His Son for Sacrifice, and on Sarah’s Death

1. Amid these events, all of which it would take too long to recount, Abraham was tested concerning the sacrifice of his beloved son Isaac himself, so that his devout obedience might be made known throughout the ages—not to God. For not every testing should be condemned, since that testing by which proof is produced should also be welcomed [Note: [Col. 0510] He explains this in *Questions on Genesis*, question 57, and *Questions on Exodus*, question 58. Ambrose, *On Abraham the Patriarch*, book 1, chapter 8: “God tests in one way, the devil in another: the devil tests in order to overthrow; God tests in order to crown.” COQUAEUS.].

Often the human mind cannot otherwise become known to itself unless, when a kind of temptation questions it, it answers itself concerning its own strength—not by words but by experience. If in that process it recognizes God’s gift, then it is devout; then it is made firm by the strength of grace rather than puffed up by the emptiness of boasting.

Abraham would certainly never have believed that God took pleasure in human victims, although, when a divine command thunders forth, one must obey rather than argue. Nevertheless, Abraham deserves praise for believing that his son would rise again immediately after being sacrificed. For God had said to him, when he was unwilling to fulfill his wife’s wish that the slave woman and her son be cast out: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.” And there it follows and is said: “But I will make the son of this slave woman into a great nation” [Note: [Col. 0510] The printed editions omit *him*. It is nevertheless found in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint.], “because he is your offspring” (Gen. XXI, 12–13).

How, then, was it said, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called,” when God also called Ishmael his offspring? Explaining what “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” means, the Apostle says: “That is, those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as offspring” [Col. 0511] [Note: [Col. 0511] Erasmus and the Louvain edition read: “the children of the promise are counted as offspring,” with other printed editions and the manuscripts differing.]. Thus, for the children of the promise to be Abraham’s offspring, they are called “in Isaac”—that is, they are gathered together in Christ, who calls them by grace [Note: [Col. 0511] The Louvain edition alone reads *in Christ*, rather than *in Christ who calls*.].

The devout father therefore faithfully held to this promise, since it had to be fulfilled through the one whom God commanded to be killed. He did not doubt that the one who could be given when he was not expected could be restored to him after being sacrificed. This is how it was understood and explained in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “By faith,” it says, “Abraham, when tested, offered Isaac” [Note: [Col. 0511] Some manuscripts read: “By faith, Abraham offered Isaac.” Manuscripts 2050, 2051, and 2053 read: “By faith, Abraham did not spare Isaac.” M.], “and offered his only son, he who had received the promises, to whom it had been said, ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be called,’ reasoning that God could also raise him from the dead.” Therefore it adds: “For this reason he also received him back as a likeness” (Hebr. XI, 17–19).

A likeness of whom, unless of the one of whom the same Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32)? For this reason Isaac, like the Lord carrying his cross, himself carried the wood to the place of sacrifice on which he was to be laid.

Finally, since Isaac was not to be killed, after the father had been forbidden to strike, what was that ram by whose sacrifice the offering was fulfilled through symbolic blood? Indeed, when Abraham saw it, it was caught by its horns in a thicket. Whom, then, did it signify, unless Jesus, crowned with Jewish thorns before he was sacrificed?

2. But let us hear the divine words spoken through the angel. Scripture says:

“And Abraham stretched out his hand to take the sword, to kill his son. And the angel of the Lord called him from heaven and said: Abraham! And he said: Here I am. And he said: Do not lay your hand upon the boy, nor do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God” [Note: [Col. 0511] The printed editions read: “that you fear your God.” The manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, more correctly have: “that you fear God.”], “and you have not spared your beloved son for my sake.”

“Now I know,” it says—that is, “now I have caused it to be known”; for God did not previously lack this knowledge.

Then, after the ram had been sacrificed in place of his son Isaac, Abraham, as we read, called the name of that place “The Lord has seen,” so that people say today, “On the mountain the Lord appeared.” Just as “Now I know” means “Now I have caused it to be known,” so here “The Lord has seen” means “The Lord has appeared”—that is, “He caused himself to be seen.”

And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your beloved son for my sake, unless I bless you, blessing you, and multiply your offspring, multiplying it, like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is beside the shore of the sea. And your offspring shall possess by inheritance the cities of its enemies” [Note: [Col. 0511] The printed editions add *their own*, which is absent from the manuscripts and the Septuagint.]; “and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. XXII, 10–18).

In this way, after the holocaust that signified Christ, the promise concerning the calling of the nations in Abraham’s offspring was confirmed even by God’s oath. He had often promised it, but had never before sworn it. What, indeed, is the oath of the true and truthful God except a confirmation of the promise and a kind of rebuke to the unbelieving?

3. After this Sarah died in the one hundred twenty-seventh year of her life (Gen. XXIII, 1), and in the one hundred thirty-seventh year of her husband’s life. He was ten years older than she, as he himself said when a son was promised to him through her: “If a son will be born to me at a hundred years, and if Sarah will give birth at ninety years” (ibid. XVII, 17).

Then Abraham bought a field in which he buried his wife. Thus, according to Stephen’s account, he was settled in that land, since he began there to be a possessor (Acts VII, 4)—namely, after the death of his father, who is reckoned to have died two years earlier.

## CHAPTER XXXIII—On Rebecca, the Granddaughter of Nahor, Whom Isaac Took as His Wife

Then, when Isaac was forty years old, he took Rebecca, the granddaughter of his paternal uncle Nahor, as his wife—specifically in the one hundred fortieth year of his father’s life, three years after his mother’s death.

When a servant was sent by Isaac’s father into Mesopotamia to bring her, what else was signified when he said to the servant, “Place your hand under my thigh, and I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and the Lord of earth, that you will not take for my son Isaac a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites” (Gen. XXIV, 2–3), except that the Lord, the God of heaven and the Lord of earth, was to come in the flesh drawn from that thigh?

Are these small indications of the truth foretold, which we see fulfilled in Christ [Note: [Col. 0512] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “indications of the truth, which we may see fulfilled in Christ.”]?

## CHAPTER XXXIV—What Is to Be Understood in the Fact That Abraham Took Keturah as His Wife after Sarah’s Death

What, then, does it mean that Abraham took Keturah as his wife after Sarah’s death [Note: [Col. 0512] Jerome, in his *Hebrew Traditions*, reports the opinion of the Hebrews, who thought that Keturah was Hagar herself. COQUAEUS.]? Far be it from us to suspect incontinence, especially at that advanced age and in that holiness of faith.

Were children still being sought, when, by God’s promise, Abraham’s faith had already firmly embraced such a great multiplication of descendants from Isaac, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the earth? But surely, if Hagar and Ishmael, according to the Apostle’s interpretation, signified the carnal people of the Old Testament (Gal. IV, 24), why should Keturah and her sons not also signify those who are carnal yet consider themselves to belong to the New Testament?

Both women, after all, are called Abraham’s wives and concubines; Sarah, however, is never called a concubine [Note: [Col. 0512] The printed editions add: “but only a wife.”]. For when Hagar was given to Abraham, it is written: “And Sarah, Abram’s wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her slave woman, after Abram had dwelt ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife” [Note: [Col. 0513] The word *her* is absent from the printed editions but is found in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint.] (Gen. XVI, 3).

Concerning Keturah, whom he took after Sarah’s death, we read: “And Abraham, adding to his household, took a wife whose name was Keturah.” Behold, both are called wives; yet both are also found to have been concubines, as Scripture later says: “And Abraham gave all that he possessed to Isaac his son; but to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he was still alive, eastward, to the land of the East” (ibid. XXV, 1, 5–6).

The sons of concubines therefore possess certain gifts, but they do not attain the promised kingdom—neither heretics nor carnal Jews—for there is no heir except Isaac. “Those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. IX, 8), of whom it was said: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI, 12).

I do not see why Keturah, taken after the death of his wife, should also have been called a concubine except because of this mystery. But whoever does not wish to understand these matters through such symbolic meanings should not bring an accusation against Abraham. For what if this too was provided as an answer to future heretics who would oppose second marriages [Note: [Col. 0513] The Cataphrygians considered second marriages to differ in no respect from fornication, as Augustine writes in *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*, heresy 26.], so that in the father of many nations himself it might be demonstrated that remarriage after the death of one’s spouse is not a sin?

“And Abraham died when he was one hundred seventy-five years old” (ibid. XXV, 7) [Note: [Col. 0513] Here and in the following passage, *five* is absent from the manuscripts.]. He therefore left his son Isaac at the age of seventy-five—the son whom he had fathered at a hundred.

## CHAPTER XXXV—What the Divine Response Signified Concerning the Twins Still Enclosed in Rebecca Their Mother’s Womb

Let us now see how, through Abraham’s descendants, the ages of the city of God unfold. From Isaac’s first year of life until the sixtieth, in which his sons were born, the following memorable event occurred.

When Isaac asked God that his barren wife might bear children, and the Lord granted what he requested, she conceived, and the twins enclosed within her womb struggled with one another. Troubled by this distress, she questioned the Lord and received the answer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your belly; one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (ibid., 23).

The Apostle Paul wants this to be understood as a great demonstration of grace, because, before they had been born and before they had done anything good or evil, the younger was chosen without any good merits, while the elder was rejected (Rom. IX, 11–13). Insofar as original sin is concerned, they were plainly equal; insofar as individual conduct is concerned, neither had any.

But the plan of the present work does not permit us to speak at greater length about this matter, and we have already said much about it elsewhere. As for the statement, “The elder shall serve the younger,” almost none of us has understood it in any other way than that the greater people of the Jews would serve the lesser Christian people.

And indeed, although this may appear to have been fulfilled in the nation of the Idumaeans, which descended from the elder son who had two names—for he was called both Esau and Edom, from which the Idumaeans derived their name—because that nation was later to be overcome by the people descended from the younger, namely the Israelites, and was to become subject to them, nevertheless it is more appropriately believed that this prophecy, in which it was said, “One people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger,” was directed toward something greater.

And what is this except what is clearly fulfilled in Jews and Christians?

## CHAPTER XXXVI—On the Oracle and Blessing Which Isaac Received, No Otherwise Than His Father Had Received Them, by Merit of the Same Belovedness

Isaac also received an oracle such as his father had received on several occasions. Of this oracle it is written:

> There was a famine upon the land, apart from the famine which had previously occurred in Abraham’s time. And Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar. And the Lord appeared to him and said: “Do not go down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell you, and sojourn in this land; and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and to your offspring I will give all this land, and I will establish my oath which I swore to Abraham your father; and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give all this land to your offspring, and in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because Abraham your father obeyed my voice and kept my precepts, my commandments, my ordinances, and my statutes” (Gen. XXVI, 1–5).

This patriarch had neither another wife nor any concubine, but was content with the progeny of two twins begotten from one union. He too feared danger on account of his wife’s beauty while he lived among foreigners, and did what his father had done: he called her his sister and concealed that she was his wife. For she was related to him by both paternal and maternal blood; yet when the foreigners [Note: [Col. 0514] The manuscripts read “foreigners.”] learned that she was his wife, she also remained untouched.

We must not, however, for that reason prefer him to his father because he had known no woman besides his one wife. The merits of his father’s faith and obedience were undoubtedly greater—so great that God says that he does the good things he does for this man on Abraham’s account: “In your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because Abraham your father obeyed my voice and kept my precepts, my commandments, my ordinances, and my statutes.” And again in another oracle: “I am the God of Abraham your father; do not fear, for I am with you, and I have blessed you and will multiply your offspring for Abraham your father’s sake” (ibid., 24).

Thus we may understand how chastely Abraham did what, to unchaste people seeking precedents in the Holy Scriptures for their wickedness, seems to have been done from lust. We may also learn from this not to compare people with one another on the basis of individual good qualities, but to consider the whole person in each case. Someone may have something in life and conduct by which he surpasses another, and that thing may be far more excellent than what gives the other an advantage over him.

Accordingly, although continence is preferred to marriage, a married believer is nevertheless better than a continent unbeliever. An unbeliever is not merely less worthy of praise, but is utterly to be detested. Let us suppose both to be good [Note: [Col. 0515] Thus the manuscripts with great agreement. The printed editions read: “But a continent unbeliever is not merely less worthy of praise because, though he does not believe, he is continent; rather, he is far more to be blamed because, though continent, he does not believe. Let us therefore suppose both to be good.”]. Even then, the married man who is more faithful and obedient to God is certainly better than the continent man of lesser faith and obedience; but if all else is equal, who would doubt that the continent person is to be preferred to the married one [Note: [Col. 0515] Manuscripts 2050 and 2058 read “is to be preferred.”]?

## CHAPTER XXXVII—On Those Things Mystically Prefigured in Esau and Jacob

The two sons of Isaac, Esau and Jacob, grew up together. The primacy of the elder was transferred to the younger by agreement and mutual consent, because the elder immoderately desired the lentils which the younger had prepared [Note: [Col. 0515] The Louvain edition alone reads: “because the elder immoderately desired the lentils which the younger had prepared.”], and for that price, with an oath interposed, sold his birthright to his brother. Here we learn that in eating a person is to be blamed not for the kind of food, but for immoderate greed.

Isaac grew old, and through old age his eyes lost their sight. He wished to bless his elder son, but unknowingly blessed the younger in his place: Jacob presented himself to his father’s hands in place of his elder brother, who was hairy, having fitted himself with kidskins as though bearing another’s sins. Lest this deceit of Jacob be thought fraudulent deceit, rather than a great mystery being sought in it, Scripture had previously said: “Esau was a man skilled in hunting, a man of the field; but Jacob was a simple man, dwelling at home” (Gen. XXV, 29–34; XXVII). Some of our writers have translated this “without deceit.” Whether it is called without deceit, simple, or more properly without pretence—the Greek is *aplastos* (ἄπλαστος)—what is the deceit of a man without deceit in receiving this blessing? What is the deceit of the simple man, the pretence of one who does not lie, unless it is a profound mystery of truth?

What, then, is the blessing itself? “Behold,” he says, “the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field, which the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven, and of the richness of the earth, and abundance of grain and wine. May nations serve you, and rulers worship you; and may you become [Note: [Col. 0515] The manuscripts read “and may you become.”] lord of your brother, and the sons of your father shall worship you. Cursed be he who curses you, and blessed be he who blesses you.”

Jacob’s blessing, therefore, is the proclamation of Christ among all nations. This is happening; this is being done. The Law and Prophecy are Isaac [Note: [Col. 0515] Erasmus and Louvain read “are in Isaac”; *in* is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]: even through the mouth of the Jews Christ is blessed by that Law and Prophecy as though by one who does not know, because it is itself not known. By the fragrance of Christ’s name the world is filled like a field. His is the blessing of the dew of heaven—that is, of the rain of divine words—and of the richness of the earth—that is, of the gathering of peoples. His is the abundance of grain and wine: the multitude which grain and wine gather in the sacrament of his body and blood [Col. 0516]. Nations serve him, and rulers worship him. He is lord of his brother, because his people rule the Jews. The sons of his father worship him—that is, the sons of Abraham according to faith—because he too is a son of Abraham according to the flesh. Whoever curses him is cursed, and whoever blesses him is blessed.

Christ, I say, is blessed even from the mouth of Jews, though they are in error yet nevertheless chant the Law and Prophets: that is, he is spoken of truly; but another is thought to be blessed, whom they in their error await. Behold, when the elder son returned to claim the promised blessing, Isaac was terrified; realizing with astonishment that he had blessed one in place of another, he inquired who he was. Yet he did not complain that he had been deceived. Indeed, when a great sacrament was at once revealed inwardly to his heart, he checked his indignation and confirmed the blessing. “Who, then,” he says, “has hunted game for me, brought it to me, and I have eaten of everything before you came, and I have blessed him—and he shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVII, 27–29, 33)? Who would not here expect an angry curse, if these events were taking place not by heavenly inspiration but in a merely earthly manner? O events accomplished, yet accomplished prophetically; on earth, yet from heaven; through human beings, yet by God! If each item, so fruitful in great mysteries, were examined, many volumes would have to be filled; but the proper limits of this work compel us to hasten on to other matters.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII—On Jacob’s Being Sent into Mesopotamia to Take a Wife, on the Vision He Saw in Sleep on the Way, and on His Four Women, Though He Had Sought One Wife

1. Jacob was sent by his parents into Mesopotamia to take a wife there. These are the words of his father who sent him: “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites. Arise, flee into Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, the father of your mother, and take a wife for yourself from there, from the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother. May my God bless you, increase you, and multiply you; and you shall become assemblies of nations. May he give you the blessing of Abraham your father [Note: [Col. 0516] The Greek Bibles read *patros mou*, “my father.”], to you and your offspring after you, so that you may become heir of the land of your sojourning which God gave to Abraham” (Gen. XXVIII, 1–4).

Here we now understand that Jacob’s offspring was separated from Isaac’s other offspring, which came through Esau. For when it was said, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (ibid. XXII, 12), the offspring belonging to the city of God was certainly intended; from it was separated Abraham’s other offspring, which was in the son of the slave woman and which was to be in the sons of Keturah. But concerning Isaac’s two twin sons it was still uncertain whether that blessing belonged to both or to one of them, and, if to one, which one it was. This is now made clear when Jacob is prophetically blessed by his father and told: “You shall become assemblies of nations, and may he give you the blessing of Abraham your father.”

2. As Jacob proceeded into Mesopotamia, he received in a dream an oracle which is recorded as follows:

> Jacob went out from the Well of the Oath and set out for Haran; he came to a place and slept there, for the sun had set. He took stones from the place, put them under his head, and slept in that place; and he dreamed. And behold, a ladder was set upon the earth, and its top reached heaven; and the angels of God were ascending and descending upon it. And the Lord leaned upon it and said: “I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; do not fear. The land upon which you sleep [Note: [Col. 0517] Erasmus and Louvain read “through which you sleep”; the other printed editions and the manuscripts correct them.], I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the sand of the earth, and shall spread abroad to the Sea, to the South, to the North, and to the East; and all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your offspring. And behold, I am with you, guarding you in every way by which you go; and I shall bring you back to this land, for I shall not leave you until I have done all that I have spoken to you.” And Jacob awoke from his sleep and said: “The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” And he was afraid and said: “How terrible is this place! This is [Note: [Col. 0517] The printed editions read “this place is not”; the manuscripts read “this is,” in accordance with the Greek *touto*.] nothing but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.” Jacob arose, took the stone which he had placed there [Note: [Col. 0517] Louvain has “had placed under himself.” The manuscripts read “had placed there”; the Septuagint has *ekei*.] under his head, set it up as a pillar, poured oil upon its top, and called the name of that place the House of God (Gen. XXVIII, 10–19).

This belongs to prophecy. Jacob did not pour oil over the stone in an idolatrous manner, as though making it a god; for he neither worshipped that stone nor offered sacrifice to it. But because the name Christ derives from *chrism*—that is, from anointing—something here was certainly prefigured that belongs to a great sacrament. The Savior himself is understood to recall this ladder to our memory in the Gospel. After he had said of Nathanael, “Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit”—for Israel had seen this vision, and he is Jacob—he says in the same place: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John I, 47, 51).

3. Jacob therefore went into Mesopotamia to take a wife from there. Divine Scripture indicates how it happened that he had four women, by whom he begot twelve sons and one daughter, though he desired none of them unlawfully. He had come to take one woman as his wife (Gen. XXIX); but when another had been substituted for the other, he did not dismiss the one with whom he had unknowingly slept at night, lest he seem to have made a mockery of her. And at a time when no law forbade several wives for the purpose of multiplying offspring, he also took her to whom alone he had already pledged faith of future marriage. Since she was barren, she gave her maidservant to her husband, so that she might receive children from her; her elder sister, though she had borne children, followed this example because she desired to multiply her progeny.

Jacob is not recorded as having sought any woman but one, nor as having had intercourse with several except in the duty of begetting children, with marital right preserved; he would not have done even this unless his wives, who had lawful authority over the body of their husband [Col. 0518], had demanded that it be done. Thus he begot twelve sons and one daughter by four women. Then he entered Egypt through his son Joseph, who had been sold by his envious brothers and taken there, and was exalted there.

## CHAPTER XXXIX—Why Jacob Was Also Given the Name Israel

Jacob, as I said a little earlier, was also called Israel; the people descended from him more especially bore that name. This name was given him by the angel with whom he wrestled as he returned from Mesopotamia, an angel who bore a most evident type of Christ. Jacob’s prevailing over him was certainly by the angel’s will, so that the mystery might be prefigured; it signifies Christ’s passion, in which the Jews seemed to prevail over him. Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from the same angel whom he had overcome; and thus the giving of this name was a blessing.

Israel means “Seeing God.” This will be the final reward of all the saints. The same angel touched Jacob, as though he were prevailing, on the breadth of his thigh and thus made him lame (Gen. XXXII, 24–29). Thus Jacob was one and the same man, blessed and lame: blessed in those from that people who believed in Christ, and lame in the unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0518] Compare *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm XLIV, no. 20.]. For the breadth of the thigh is the multitude of the race. There are, indeed, more in that stock of whom it was prophetically said: “And they limped from their paths” (Ps. XVII, 46).
