## CHAPTER XL—How Jacob Is Said to Have Entered Egypt with Seventy-Five Souls, Though Most of Those Who Are Mentioned Were Born at a Later Time
They are therefore reported to have entered Egypt together with Jacob himself—seventy-five persons (Gen. 46:27, according to the Septuagint, and Acts 7:14)—counting Jacob himself together with [Note: [Col. 0518] The particle *cum* (“with”) is absent from the manuscripts.] his sons. In this number only two women are mentioned: one daughter and one granddaughter. But a careful examination of the matter does not indicate that so large a number existed among Jacob’s descendants on the day or in the year when he entered Egypt. For among them Jacob’s great-grandsons are also mentioned, although they could in no way have existed at that time. Jacob was then 130 years old, while his son Joseph was thirty-nine. Since it is clear that Joseph married in his thirtieth year or later, how could he have had great-grandsons within nine years by the sons born to him by that same wife?

Since Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph’s sons, did not yet have sons, but Jacob found them in Egypt as children younger than nine years old, how are not only their sons but even their grandsons counted among the seventy-five who entered Egypt with Jacob? For Machir, son of Manasseh and grandson of Joseph, is mentioned there; and Machir’s son, that is, Gilead, grandson of Manasseh and great-grandson of Joseph. There is also the son born to Ephraim, Joseph’s other son, namely Utalaam [Note: [Col. 0519] Some manuscripts of good quality read *Tutalaam* or *Uttalaam*. In the Septuagint, however, the name is *Sutalaam*. Immediately afterward, before “Joseph’s grandson,” the printed editions read: “There is also Bareth, son of that Utalaah, that is, Ephraim’s grandson.” This has been corrected on the authority of ancient books, supported by the Septuagint edition, except that the latter has *Edom* for *Edem*, and *Sutalaae* for *Utalaae*.], Joseph’s grandson; and Edem, son of that Utalaam, grandson of Ephraim and great-grandson of Joseph (Gen. 50:22; Num. 26:29 ff.). These could in no way have existed when Jacob came into Egypt, when he found Joseph’s sons, his grandsons and the grandfathers of these men, as children younger than nine years.

Rather, Jacob’s entry into Egypt, when Scripture records him as entering with seventy-five persons, was not one day or one year, but the entire period during which Joseph lived, through whom it came about that they entered. For Scripture speaks of Joseph in this way:

“And Joseph dwelt in Egypt, he and his brothers, and all his father’s household; and Joseph lived 110 years, and Joseph saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation.”

That is the great-grandson who was the third generation from Ephraim. For by “the third generation” he means son, grandson, and great-grandson. Then it continues:

“And the sons of Machir, son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s thighs” (Gen. 50:22).

Here too, this is that grandson of Manasseh and great-grandson of Joseph. They are expressed in the plural, as Scripture customarily does. Scripture even called Jacob’s one daughter “daughters,” just as in the usage of the Latin language children are called *sons* in the plural, even when there is no more than one [Note: [Col. 0519] Thus in Latin one son is called *liberi* (“children”), as Gellius writes, *Attic Nights*, book 2, chapter 13. He also cites a statement by the historian Sempronius Asellio, who spoke of Tiberius Gracchus’s only son as *liberos*. Herennius the jurist confirms the same in book 50 of the *Digest*. LUD. VIVES.].

Since, then, Joseph’s prosperity was foretold in that he would be able to see his great-grandsons, they must in no way be thought to have already existed in the thirty-ninth year of their great-grandfather Joseph, when his father Jacob came to him in Egypt.

What misleads those who do not examine the matter carefully enough is that it is written: “Now these are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt together with Jacob their father” (ibid. 46:8). This is said because the seventy-five are counted together with him, not because all of them were already together when he himself entered Egypt. Rather, as I have said, the whole period of his entry is understood: the period during which Joseph lived, through whom he is understood to have entered.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### On the blessing that Jacob promised to his son Judah

Accordingly, on behalf of the Christian people, among whom the city of God is a pilgrim on earth, if we seek Christ’s flesh in Abraham’s seed, after removing the sons of the concubines, Isaac appears. If in Isaac’s seed we remove Esau, who is also Edom, Jacob appears, who is also Israel. If from Israel’s own seed we remove the others, Judah appears, because Christ arose from the tribe of Judah.

Therefore, when Israel was about to die in Egypt and was blessing his sons, let us hear how he prophetically blessed Judah:

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies; your father’s sons shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you have risen. Reclining, you have slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub: who will rouse him? A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things reserved for him come; and he himself is the expectation of the nations [Note: [Col. 0520] The printed editions read, “and he himself will be the expectation of the nations.” *Will be* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint.], binding his foal to the vine, and his she-ass’s foal to the *cilicium* [Note: [Col. 0520] In Greek the phrase is *tē eliki*. Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, book 1, translated it *ad helicem*, that is, “to the branch.”]. He will wash his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are bright from wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Gen. 49:8–12).

I explained these words in my dispute against Faustus the Manichaean (*Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book 12, chapter 42). I think it sufficient to show how clearly the truth of this prophecy shines forth: in it Christ’s death is foretold by the word “sleeping,” and power, rather than necessity, is signified in death by the name “lion.” He himself proclaims this power in the Gospel, saying:

“I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me; rather, I lay it down of myself and take it up again” (John 10:18, 17).

Thus the lion roared; thus he fulfilled what he said. To this power belongs what is added concerning his resurrection: “Who will rouse him?” That is, no human being will do so, but he himself, who also said of his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (ibid. 2:19).

The kind of death itself—that is, the exaltation of the cross—is understood in the one word he says: “You have risen.” But what he added, “Reclining, you have slept,” the evangelist explains when he says, “and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (ibid. 19:30). Or else his burial is recognized in it, in which he lay down sleeping; and from it no human being raised him, as he himself raised some others and the prophets raised certain people, but he rose by himself as from sleep.

His robe, moreover, which he washes in wine—that is, cleanses from sins in his own blood, whose sacrament those who have been baptized know—and what does the addition “and in the blood of the grape his garment” signify except the Church? And “his eyes are bright from wine”: his spiritual people are intoxicated by his cup, of which the Psalm sings, “How splendid is your intoxicating cup!” (Ps. 22:5). And “his teeth are whiter than milk”: this is what the little ones drink from the Apostle—words that nourish them, since they are not yet capable of solid food (1 Cor. 3:2).

He, therefore, is the one in whom the promises reserved for Judah were contained. Until he came, rulers—that is, kings—never failed Israel from that stock. “And he himself is the expectation of the nations”: this is clearer when seen than when explained.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### On Joseph’s sons, whom Jacob blessed by the prophetic crossing of his hands

Just as Isaac’s two sons, Esau and Jacob, provided a figure of the two peoples, the Jews and the Christians—although, as regards descent according to the flesh, the Jews did not come from Esau but the Idumeans, nor did the Christian nations come from Jacob but rather the Jews [Note: [Col. 0520] Compare *Letter* 196, to Asellicus.]—for the figure served only to signify what was said, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23), so it also happened with Joseph’s two sons. The elder represented the Jews, while the younger represented the Christians.

When Jacob blessed them, placing his right hand upon the younger, whom he had at his left, and his left upon the elder, whom he had at his right, this seemed grievous to their father. He admonished his father as though correcting his error and showing which of them was the elder. But Jacob did not wish to change his hands; instead he said:

“I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people, and he too shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations” (Gen. 48:19).

Here too he indicates those two promises [Note: [Col. 0521] The printed editions read *demonstrant* (“they indicate”). The manuscripts support the correction *demonstrat* (“he indicates”).]. One shall become “a people,” the other “a multitude of nations.” What could be clearer than that these two promises contain the Israelite people and the whole world in Abraham’s seed—the one according to the flesh, the other according to faith?

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### On the times of Moses, Joshua son of Nun, and the Judges, and thereafter of the Kings, of whom Saul was the first, but David was pre-eminent both sacramentally and deservedly

1. After Jacob’s death, and Joseph’s as well, during the remaining 144 years until the people departed from the land of Egypt, that nation grew in an astonishing manner, even though it was worn down by such severe persecutions that at one point the male children born among them were killed, when the Egyptians, amazed and alarmed at the people’s excessive increase, were afraid of them.

Then Moses, rescued by stealth from the slaughterers of the children, reached the royal household, while God was preparing great things to be accomplished through him. He was nourished and adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter—this was the name of all the kings in Egypt—and he grew into such a man that he himself led that nation, which had been wondrously multiplied, out from the harshest and most oppressive yoke of slavery that it endured there—or rather, God did so through him, having promised this to Abraham.

First, he fled from there because, while defending an Israelite, he had killed an Egyptian and had become frightened [Note: [Col. 0521] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions say: “For it is reported that he first fled from there to the land of Midian because, while defending an Israelite, he had killed an Egyptian, and, frightened, he fled,” or “might flee.”]. Later, divinely sent, he overcame Pharaoh’s resisting magicians by the power of God’s Spirit.

Then through him ten memorable plagues were inflicted upon the Egyptians, since they refused to release God’s people: water turned into blood; frogs and gnats; flies; the death of livestock; ulcers; hail; locusts; darkness; and the death of the firstborn.

Finally, when the Egyptians pursued the Israelites into the Red Sea after, broken by so many and such great plagues, they had at last allowed them to depart, the Egyptians were destroyed. As the Israelites went away, the sea was divided and made a path for them; but when the pursuing Egyptians entered, the returning wave submerged them.

Afterward, for forty years, under Moses’ leadership, God’s people were driven through the desert [Note: The manuscripts read “in the desert.”]. At that time the Tabernacle was called the Tabernacle of Testimony, where God was worshiped through sacrifices that foretold future things. The Law had already been given on the mountain with great terror, for the divinity was attested by the clearest miraculous signs and voices.

This took place as soon as they had departed from Egypt and the people had begun to be in the desert, on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been celebrated through the sacrifice of the sheep [Col. 0522] [Note: Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *quae* (“which”) instead of *qui* (“who”).]. That Passover so clearly prefigured Christ, announcing through the sacrificial victim that he would pass from this world to the Father—for in Hebrew *Pascha* is interpreted “Passage” (Exod. 12:11)—that, when the New Testament was being revealed, after Christ our Passover had been sacrificed, the Holy Spirit came from heaven on the fiftieth day.

In the Gospel he is called the finger of God (Luke 11:20), so that he might recall our memory to the remembrance of the first prefigured event, since those tablets of the Law are also reported to have been written by the finger of God (Exod. 31:18).

2. After Moses’ death, Joshua son of Nun governed the people, brought them into the promised land, and divided it among them. Under these two remarkable leaders, wars were also waged with the greatest success and in a wondrous manner. God testified that these victories came to them not so much because of the merits of the Hebrew people as because of the sins of the nations whom they conquered.

After these leaders came the Judges, once the people had been settled in the promised land. Thus the first promise made to Abraham began meanwhile to be fulfilled: the promise concerning one nation, namely the Hebrew nation, and the land of Canaan—not yet the promise concerning all nations and the whole world, which the coming of Christ in the flesh, and not observance of the old Law but faith in the Gospel, was to fulfill.

A prefiguration of this was made in the fact that it was not Moses, who had received the Law for the people on Mount Sinai, but Joshua—whose name was also changed by God’s command so that he would be called Jesus—who brought the people into the promised land.

During the time of the Judges, according as the people’s sins and God’s mercy prevailed in turn, prosperity and adversity in war alternated.

3. From there the time of the Kings was reached. Saul was the first to reign. After he was rejected and struck down in battle, and his line was cast aside so that kings would not arise from it, David succeeded to the kingdom. Christ is especially called his son.

With David a certain turning point occurred, and in a way the beginning of the youth of God’s people. A kind of adolescence of this people extended from Abraham himself up to David. For Matthew the evangelist did not mention the generations without reason in such a way as to emphasize this first interval of fourteen generations, from Abraham specifically to David (Matt. 1:17).

A human being begins to be able to beget children from adolescence. Therefore Matthew took the beginning of the generations from Abraham, who was also appointed father of the nations when he received his changed name. Before him, therefore, there was, as it were, the childhood of this kind of people of God, from Noah to Abraham himself. Thus the first language [Note: Several manuscripts read, “and therefore the language,” omitting *first*. Other ancient books read, “and therefore in the language,” or “and therefore from here the language.”] was discovered, namely Hebrew.

For after infancy a person begins to speak in childhood; infancy is so called because a person cannot yet speak (*fari*). That first age is wholly submerged in oblivion, just as the first age of the human race was wiped out by the Flood. For how few people are there who remember their infancy?

Therefore, in this course of the city of God, just as the preceding book contained one and the same first age, so this book contains two ages, the second and the third. In the third age, because of the three-year-old heifer, the three-year-old she-goat, and the three-year-old ram (Gen. 15:9), the yoke of the Law was imposed, an abundance of sins appeared, and the beginning of the earthly kingdom arose. Yet spiritual people were not absent there; their sacrament was represented in the turtledove and the pigeon (ibid.).

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

In this book the course of the city of God is discussed during the times of the Kings and Prophets, from Samuel and David to Christ; and the prophecies committed to sacred writings concerning those times, about Christ and the Church in the books of Kings, Psalms, and Solomon, are expounded.

[Col. 0523]

## CHAPTER I  
### On the times of the Prophets

The city of God, advancing through the sequence of the ages, will show how the promises of God made to Abraham are fulfilled. God promised that to Abraham’s seed would belong both the Israelite nation according to the flesh and all nations according to faith.

Since the preceding book ended with the kingdom of David, we now take up, beginning from that same kingdom, the remaining matters that seem sufficient for the work undertaken.

The entire period beginning when the holy Samuel started to prophesy and continuing until the people of Israel were led captive into Babylon, and from there, after seventy years, when the Israelites returned according to the prophecy of the holy Jeremiah (Jer. 25:11) and God’s house was restored, is the period of the Prophets.

Although we may not improperly call the patriarch Noah himself—during whose days the whole earth was destroyed by the Flood—and others before and after him, down to the time when kings began to exist among God’s people, “prophets,” because through them certain future events concerning the city of God and the kingdom of heaven were either signified in one way or another or foretold—especially since we read that some of them were explicitly called prophets, such as Abraham (Gen. 20:7) and Moses (Deut. 34:10)—nevertheless these are particularly and chiefly called the days of the Prophets: from the time when Samuel began to prophesy.

At God’s command, Samuel first anointed Saul, and after Saul was rejected, David himself as king. From David’s line the others would succeed one another, for as long as it was proper for them to succeed one another in that way.

If I wished to recall everything foretold by the Prophets about Christ, while the city of God passed through these times as its members died and were succeeded by others born after them, the discussion would extend without limit.

First, Scripture itself, which arranges in sequence the Kings and their deeds and events and seems to occupy itself, with historical diligence, in narrating accomplished facts, will be found—if it is considered with the assistance of God’s Spirit—to be intent either more, or certainly no less, on foretelling future events than on declaring past ones.

Who does not know, if he considers these matters even moderately, how laborious and extensive it would be to investigate this by close examination and demonstrate it through exposition, and how many volumes such a task would require [Col. 0524] [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmianus read *indigeat* (“requires”); the Louvain edition reads *dignum* (“worthy”). But the manuscripts of better quality read *indiguum* (“in need of”).]?

Moreover, the very things that unquestionably belong to prophecy are so numerous in their references to Christ and the kingdom of heaven, which is the city of God, that a more extensive discussion would be needed to disclose them than the scope of this work demands.

Therefore, if I am able, I will so moderate my style that, with God’s will, in completing this work I will neither say everything that remains nor omit what is sufficient.

## CHAPTER II  
### When God’s promise concerning the land of Canaan was fulfilled—the land which carnal Israel also received as a possession

In the preceding book we said that from the beginning God made two promises to Abraham. The first was that his seed would possess the land of Canaan. This is signified where it is said: “Go into the land that I will show you, and I will make you into a great nation.” The other was far more excellent: not concerning carnal but spiritual seed, through which he is the father not of one Israelite nation but of all the nations that follow the footsteps of his faith. This began to be promised in the words: “And in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:1–3).

We showed by many other testimonies afterward that these two promises had been made.

The seed of Abraham, that is, the people of Israel according to the flesh, was already in the promised land. There it had begun to reign, not only by holding and possessing the cities of its enemies but also by having kings. God’s promises concerning that people had already been fulfilled to a considerable extent—not only those made to the three patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and whatever others had been made in their times, but also those made through Moses himself.

Through Moses the same people had been freed from Egyptian slavery, and through him all the former events had been revealed during the time when he led the people through the wilderness.

Neither through the distinguished leader Joshua, by whom that people was brought into the promised land, and who, after conquering the nations, divided the land among the twelve tribes as God had commanded, and then died; nor throughout the entire period of the Judges had God’s promise concerning the land of Canaan been fulfilled—that promise extending from a certain river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates [Col. 0525] [Note: Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead say: “that that people would rule from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.”] (Gen. 15:18).

Yet it was not still being prophesied as something future; rather, it was being awaited for fulfillment.

It was fulfilled through David and his son Solomon, whose kingdom was extended over as great a territory as had been promised. For they subdued all those peoples and made them tributaries.

Thus the seed of Abraham according to the flesh—that is, in the land of Canaan—had been established under these kings in the promised land, so that nothing remained for the earthly promise of God to be fulfilled except that, insofar as temporal prosperity was concerned, the Hebrew nation should continue in that same land through the succession of its descendants in an undisturbed condition until the end of this mortal age, if it obeyed the laws of the Lord its God.

But because God knew that it would not do this, he also used its temporal punishments to discipline his few faithful people within it and to admonish those who would later exist among all the nations—those whom, after the New Testament had been revealed, he was going to admonish through the incarnation of Christ, in whom he would fulfill the other promise [Note: The printed editions read: “among all the nations whom he would admonish through them.” The manuscript reading has been adopted.].

## CHAPTER III  
### On the threefold significance of the Prophets, which refers sometimes to the earthly Jerusalem, sometimes to the heavenly Jerusalem, and sometimes to both

1. Accordingly, just as those divine oracles to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and whatever other signs or prophetic sayings were given in the earlier sacred writings, were made in this way, so also the other prophecies from this period of the Kings partly concern the nation descended from Abraham according to the flesh, and partly that seed of his in which all nations are blessed as co-heirs of Christ through the New Testament, to possess eternal life and the kingdom of heaven.

Some, therefore, refer to the slave woman who gives birth to slaves—that is, to the earthly Jerusalem, which is in slavery with her children. Others refer to the free city of God, that is, the true and eternal Jerusalem in heaven, whose children are human beings living according to God and making their pilgrimage on earth. But some passages are understood to belong to both: properly to the slave woman, and figuratively to the free woman.

2. The utterances of the Prophets are therefore found to be threefold, since some concern the earthly Jerusalem, some the heavenly Jerusalem, and some both.

I see that what I am saying must be demonstrated by examples.

The prophet Nathan was sent to rebuke King David for a grave sin and to foretell the evils that would follow from it (2 Sam. 12). Who would doubt that such matters and similar ones—whether spoken publicly, that is, for the salvation or benefit of the people, or privately, when each person sought divine utterances for his own affairs and learned something future for the purposes of temporal life—belonged to the earthly city?

But where it is read:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel: after those days, says the Lord, I will give [Note: The manuscripts read *dando* (“giving”). The Septuagint has *didous dōsō*, “giving, I will give.”] my laws into their mind, and I will write them upon their hearts, and I will see them [Note: The words “and I will see them” are absent from the Latin and Greek Bibles.], and I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Jer. 31:31–33; Heb. 8:8–10),

the heavenly Jerusalem is undoubtedly being prophesied. There God himself is the reward; to possess him and to belong to him is there the supreme and complete good [Note: Thus all our manuscripts read. In manuscript B it is “the supreme good for it.” M.].

The same matter belongs to both when Jerusalem is called the city of God and a future house of God is prophesied in it, and that prophecy appears to be fulfilled when King Solomon builds that most distinguished temple. These events occurred in the earthly Jerusalem according to the historical account, but they were also figures of the heavenly Jerusalem.

This kind of prophecy, as it were, constructed and mixed from both elements, is especially powerful in the canonical books of the ancient writings, which contain narratives of historical events. It has greatly exercised and continues to exercise the minds of those who investigate the sacred Scriptures, so that they seek to discover what is signified allegorically for the seed of Abraham according to faith by what is read as historically foretold and fulfilled in Abraham’s seed according to the flesh.

Indeed, some have thought that in those same books there is nothing either foretold and fulfilled, or fulfilled although not foretold, that does not by figurative meaning suggest something concerning the heavenly city of its God and its children, who are pilgrims in this life.

But if this is so, the utterances of the Prophets—or rather, of all those Scriptures that are included under the name of the Old Testament—will be twofold, not threefold. For nothing there will belong solely to the earthly Jerusalem if everything said and fulfilled concerning it or on its account signifies something that also refers to the heavenly Jerusalem by allegorical prefiguration. There will therefore be only two kinds: one concerning the free Jerusalem, and the other concerning both.

In my view, however, those who think that no historical events in this kind of literature signify anything beyond what happened in the manner in which they happened are greatly mistaken. But those who maintain that absolutely everything there is wrapped in allegorical meanings venture greatly [Note: Compare throughout the books *Against Faustus the Manichaean*.].

For this reason I said that the utterances are threefold, not twofold. I do not mean to blame those who have been able, while preserving the historical truth in the first place, to draw out from any historical event a spiritual meaning of understanding.

But when things are said in such a way that they cannot apply to events accomplished or to be accomplished by human or divine action, what believer would doubt that they were not said in vain? Who would not refer them to spiritual understanding, if able to do so, or admit that they must be referred by someone who is able?

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the prefigured change of the Israelite kingdom and priesthood, and on the things prophesied by Hannah, Samuel’s mother, in the role of the Church

1. When the course of the city of God reached the time of the Kings—when, after Saul had been rejected, David first obtained the kingdom in such a way that his descendants afterward reigned in the earthly Jerusalem through a long succession—it gave, through an event [Note: Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *rei gestae* (“of the event”) instead. And below, two editions, Erasmus and Louvain, read *rerum mutationem* (“the change of things”) instead of *de rerum mutatione* (“concerning the change of things”).] that signified and foretold what should not be passed over in silence, a figure of the future change concerning the two covenants, the old and the new. In this change the priesthood and the kingdom were altered through the new and eternal priest and king, who is Christ Jesus.

For Samuel, substituted in God’s service after the priest Eli had been rejected, exercising both the office of priest and that of judge, and David, established as king after Saul had been cast aside, prefigured what I am saying.

Hannah herself, Samuel’s mother, who had first been barren and afterward rejoiced in fertility, also seems to have prophesied something else when she poured out her joyful thanksgiving to the Lord. With the same devotion with which she had vowed the child, she returned him to God after he was born and weaned.

For she says:

“My heart has been confirmed in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God. My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies; I have rejoiced in your salvation. For there is none holy like the Lord, and there is none just like our God; there is none holy besides you. Do not boast proudly [Note: The printed editions read “do not boast,” omitting *proudly*, which all the manuscripts add. The word is absent from manuscripts 2051, 258, and 253. M.], and do not speak lofty things; let no boastful speech proceed from your mouth. For the Lord is a God of knowledge, and a God who prepares his designs. He has made the bow of the mighty weak, and the weak have girded themselves with strength. Those who were full have been reduced, while the hungry have crossed the land. For the barren woman has borne seven, while she who had many children has become weak. The Lord puts to death and gives life; he brings down to the underworld and brings back. The Lord makes people poor [Note: Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have “the Lord makes a person poor.” The Greek has *ptōchizei*.] and makes rich; he humbles and exalts. He raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dung heap, to seat him with the mighty of the people [Note: Thus Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint. Erasmus and Louvain have “of his people,” and shortly afterward “giving him.”], giving them the seat of glory as an inheritance; giving a vow to the one who makes a vow, and blessing the years of the just; for a man is not strong through strength. The Lord will weaken his adversary; the Lord is holy. Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, and let not the rich man boast in his riches; but let the one who boasts boast in understanding and knowing the Lord, and in doing judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth. The Lord has ascended into the heavens and thundered; he himself will judge the ends of the earth, because he is just [Note: The sacred Bibles omit “because he is just.” Some Greek copies and Theodoret have *dikaios ōn*, “being just.”]; and he gives strength to our kings, and he will exalt the horn of his Christ” (1 Sam. 2:1–10, according to the Septuagint).

2. Are these words really to be thought the words of one little woman, rejoicing in the son born to her? Is the human mind so turned away from the light of truth that it does not perceive that the sayings poured forth by this woman exceed the measure of a woman?

But whoever is appropriately moved by the events themselves, which have already begun to be fulfilled even in this earthly pilgrimage, does he not direct his attention, look, and recognize that through this woman—whose name, Hannah, is interpreted as “His Grace”—the Christian religion itself, the city of God itself, whose king and founder is Christ, and finally the grace of God itself spoke in the prophetic spirit? The proud are alienated from this grace so that they fall, while the humble are filled with it so that they rise. This is what the hymn chiefly resounded.

Unless someone should perhaps say that this woman prophesied nothing, but merely praised God in exultant proclamation on account of the son for whom she had prayed and whom she had obtained.

What, then, does she mean when she says:

“He has made the bow of the mighty weak, and the weak have girded themselves with strength; those who were full have been reduced, while the hungry have crossed the land; for the barren woman has borne seven, while she who had many children has become weak”?

Had she herself borne seven, although she had been barren? She had only one child when she said these things. Nor afterward did she bear seven—or six, with Samuel as the seventh—but three sons and two daughters (1 Sam. 2:20).

Moreover, at a time when no one yet reigned among that people, from where did she derive what she placed at the end: “He gives strength to our kings, and he will exalt the horn of his Christ,” unless she was prophesying?

### 3.

Let the Church of Christ, the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring, say what it recognizes as having been prophesied about itself so long beforehand through the mouth of this devout mother:

“My heart is established in the Lord, and my horn is exalted in my God.”

Truly the heart is established, and truly the horn is exalted, because it is not in itself but in the Lord its God. “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies,” because even amid the constrictions of persecutions the word of God has not been bound, nor has it been bound in those who proclaim it.

“I rejoiced,” she says, “in your salvation.” This is Christ Jesus, whom the aged Simeon, as we read in the Gospel, embracing as a little child [Note: [Col. 0528] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *parvulum*, “a very little child.”], recognizing as great, said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30). Let the Church therefore say: “I rejoiced in your salvation.”

“For there is none holy like the Lord, and there is none righteous like our God”—holy and sanctifying, righteous and justifying. “There is none holy besides you,” because no one becomes holy except through you.

Finally, it follows: “Do not boast proudly [Note: [Col. 0528] All our books omit the word *proudly*. M.], and do not speak lofty things, nor let grandiloquence come forth from your mouth. For God is the Lord of knowledge.” He knows you, even where no one knows [Note: [Col. 0528] Thus the ancient books, except some, which read: “He knows you, and where no one is.” The printed editions have: “He, and no one knows what he knows.”]: “for whoever thinks that he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Galatians 6:3).

These words are spoken to the adversaries of the city of God who belong to Babylon, who presume upon their own strength and glory in themselves, not in the Lord. Among them are also the carnal Israelites, citizens of the earthly Jerusalem, earthborn men, who—as the Apostle says—“being ignorant of the righteousness of God,” that is, of the righteousness that God, who alone is righteous and justifies, gives to human beings, “and wishing to establish their own,” that is, as though acquired by themselves and for themselves, not bestowed upon them by him, “are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3). This is because they are proud, thinking that they can please God through what is their own, not through what is God’s—God who is the God of knowledge and therefore also the judge of consciences, seeing there “the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 93:11), if they are human and do not come from him.

“And preparing,” she says, “his designs.” What designs can we understand these to be, except that the proud should fall and the humble rise? For he carries out these designs when he says: “The bow of the mighty has been weakened, and the weak have been girded with strength.”

The bow has been weakened—that is, the resolve of those who seem so powerful to themselves that, through human sufficiency and without God’s gift and assistance, they can fulfill divine commandments. The weak, by contrast, are girded with strength; their inner voice is: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6:3).

### 4.

“Those who were full of bread,” she says, “have become diminished, and the hungry have crossed the land.” Who are to be understood as those “full of bread,” except those same supposedly powerful people, namely the Israelites, “to whom the oracles of God were entrusted” (Romans 3:2)?

But among that people the sons of the slave woman have become diminished. The Latin expression is somewhat deficient, but it nevertheless conveys well that those who were greater have become lesser: for even in those breads—that is, in the divine utterances, which at that time the Israelites alone among all the nations had received—they savor earthly things.

The nations, however, to whom that law had not been given, after they came through the New Testament to those divine utterances, crossed the land in great hunger, because they savored heavenly rather than earthly things.

And as though the reason for this were being asked, she says: “Because the barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children has become weak.” Here everything that was being prophesied became clear to those who recognized the number seven, by which the perfection of the universal Church was signified.

For this reason the apostle John also writes to seven churches (Revelation 1:4), thereby showing that he was writing to the fullness of one Church. And in the Proverbs of Solomon, Wisdom had earlier prefigured this when she “built herself a house and supported it with seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1).

The city of God was barren among all the nations before this offspring, which we see [Note: [Col. 0529] The printed editions, against the manuscripts, have: “through whom we see it made fruitful.”], came forth. We also see that earthly Jerusalem, which had many children, has now become weak. For whoever among the children of the free woman was in it constituted its strength; but now, because there is the letter there and not the spirit, it has lost its strength and become weak.

### 5.

“The Lord puts to death and gives life”: he put to death the woman who had many children, and gave life to this barren woman who bore seven.

Although it may more suitably be understood that he gives life to the very people whom he has put to death. For he repeats this, as it were, when he adds: “He leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

To those to whom the Apostle says, “If you have died with Christ [Note: [Col. 0529] In the sacred Bibles: “If you have risen with Christ.”], seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God: set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth,” they are salutarily put to death by the Lord. These are the ones who are hungry and have crossed the land.

“For you have died,” he says: this is how God salutarily puts them to death. Then it follows: “And your life is hidden [Col. 0530] with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:1–3): this is how God gives life to those same people.

But did he lead these same people down to the underworld and bring them back? Without controversy among the faithful, we see both of these things fulfilled rather in him, our Head, with whom the Apostle said that our life is hidden in God.

For when God “did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32), in this way he certainly put him to death. And because he raised him from the dead, he gave the same one life again. And because in prophecy his voice is recognized as saying, “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Psalm 15:10), he led the same one down to the underworld and brought him back.

By this poverty of his we have been enriched. For “the Lord makes poor and enriches.” To understand what this means, let us hear what follows: “He humbles and exalts”—certainly, he humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

What is read elsewhere, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), is contained throughout this speech, whose name is interpreted as “His grace.”

### 6.

Now, as for what is added, “He raises the poor man from the earth,” I understand this better of no one than of him who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might be enriched, as was said shortly before (2 Corinthians 8:9).

For he raised him from the earth so quickly that his flesh did not see corruption. Nor will I dissociate from him what is added: “And he lifts the needy man from the dung heap.” The needy man is the same as the poor man [Note: [Col. 0530] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “is the same as the poor man.”].

The dung heap from which he was lifted is most rightly understood as the Jewish persecutors. The Apostle, after saying that he had persecuted the Church, says of their number: “The things that were gains to me, these I have counted as losses for Christ; indeed, I count everything as loss, and even as dung, so that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:7–8).

From the earth, therefore, that poor man was raised above all the rich; and from that dung heap, that needy man was lifted above all the wealthy, so that he might sit with the powerful of the people, to whom he said: “You will sit upon twelve thrones.”

“And giving them the seat of glory as their inheritance.” For those powerful men had said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 19:28, 27); they had made this vow with the greatest determination [Note: [Col. 0530] The printed editions have *potentissimi*, “with the greatest power”; the manuscripts differ.].

### 7.

But from where did they receive this, except from him of whom it is immediately said here: “Giving a vow to the one who vows”?

Otherwise they would have belonged to those powerful people whose bow was weakened. “Giving,” she says, “a vow to the one who vows.” No one would make any right vow to the Lord unless he received from him what he was to vow.

It follows: “And he blessed the years of the righteous,” so that he may live without end with the one to whom it is said: “Your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101:28).

There the years stand firm; here they pass away—or rather, perish. Before they come, they do not exist; when they have come, they will not exist, because they come together with their end.

Of these two things, then—“giving a vow to the one who vows” and “blessing the years of the righteous”—one is what we do, and the other is what we receive. But this second thing is not received from God the giver unless, with him as our helper, the first is accomplished, because “a man is not strong through his own strength.”

“The Lord will make his adversary weak” [Col. 0531]—namely, the one who envies the person making a vow and resists him, so that he may not be able to fulfill what he vowed.

From the ambiguous Greek this can also be understood as “his own adversary” [Note: [Col. 0531] In Greek, namely, *antidikon autou*.]. For when the Lord begins to possess us, the adversary who had been ours becomes his, and is conquered by us [Note: [Col. 0531] Some books have: “will become his, and will be conquered by us.”—Thus manuscripts 2051 and 253. M.]. But this does not happen through our strength, because “a man is not strong through his own strength.”

The Lord, therefore—the holy Lord—will make his adversary weak, so that he may be conquered by the saints whom the holy Lord, the Holy One of holy ones, has made holy.

### 8.

Accordingly, “Let the wise man not glory in his wisdom, let the mighty man not glory in his might, and let the rich man not glory in his riches; but let the one who glories glory in this: to understand and know the Lord, and to practice judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0531] These words are found in the Vulgate, Jeremiah 9:23–24.].

A person understands and knows the Lord to no small degree when he also understands and knows that it is given to him by the Lord to understand and know the Lord.

“For what do you have,” says the Apostle, “that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)—that is, as though the source of your glory came from yourself.

He practices judgment and righteousness who lives rightly. And he lives rightly who obeys God’s commands. The end of the commandment—that is, the goal toward which the commandment is directed—is “love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5, 15).

Moreover, this love, as the apostle John testifies, is from God (1 John 4:7). To practice judgment and righteousness, therefore, is from God.

But what does “in the midst of the earth” mean? Surely those who live at the ends of the earth are not forbidden to practice judgment and righteousness. Who could say that? Why, then, is “in the midst of the earth” added?

If it were not added and it merely said “to practice judgment and righteousness,” the command would apply more obviously to both kinds of people, those living inland and those living by the sea.

But lest anyone should think that after the end of the life lived in this body there remains time in which to practice judgment and righteousness—things that one failed to practice while in the flesh—and thus that one might escape divine judgment, “in the midst of the earth,” it seems to me, means while each person lives in the body.

For in this life each person carries his own earth, which, when the person dies, the common earth receives and will certainly return to him when he rises again.

Therefore, “in the midst of the earth”—that is, while our soul is enclosed in this earthly body—judgment and righteousness must be practiced, so that this may benefit us afterward, when each person will receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10).

When the Apostle says “through the body,” he means through the time during which one lived in the body. For if someone blasphemes with an evil and impious mind, and does not carry out the blasphemy through any bodily members, he will not for that reason be guiltless because he did not perform it by bodily movement, since he performed it during the time in which the body also existed.

In this way the following passage in the Psalm can also suitably be understood: “But God our King, before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 73:12). The Lord Jesus is understood as our God who exists before the ages, because through him the ages were made; he worked [Note: [Col. 0531] The printed editions have *operatus est*. We have deleted *est*, following the manuscripts.] our salvation [Col. 0532] in the midst of the earth when the Word became flesh and dwelt in an earthly body (John 1:14).

### 9.

After it had been prophesied in these words of Hannah how the one who glories should glory—not in himself, certainly, but in the Lord—and after the recompense that will occur on the day of judgment had been signified, the text says: “The Lord ascended into the heavens and thundered; he himself will judge the ends of the earth, because he is righteous.”

It most fully maintained the order of the confession of the faithful. For the Lord Christ ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

For who ascended, as the Apostle says, except the one who also descended into the lower parts of the earth? “The one who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fulfill all things” (Ephesians 4:9–10).

Through his clouds, therefore, he thundered—the clouds that he filled with the Holy Spirit after he had ascended. Concerning these clouds he threatened the servants of Jerusalem, that is, the ungrateful vineyard, through the prophet Isaiah, lest they receive rain from them (Isaiah 5:6).

The words “He himself will judge the ends of the earth” are equivalent to saying, “Even the ends of the earth.” For the one who will certainly judge all human beings will not judge only some other regions.

But “the ends of the earth” are better understood as the ends of the human being. For those things that are changed for better or worse in the intervening time will not be judged; rather, judgment will concern the state in which the person being judged is found at the end.

For this reason it is said: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). Therefore, whoever steadfastly practices judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth will not be condemned when the ends of the earth are judged.

“And he gives,” she says, “strength to our kings,” so that he may not condemn them when judging them. He gives them the strength by which, as kings, they rule the flesh and conquer in him the world—he who shed his blood for them.

“And he will exalt the horn of his Christ.” How will Christ exalt the horn of his Christ? Of the one of whom it was said above, “The Lord ascended into the heavens,” and who was understood to be the Lord Christ, it is said here that he will exalt the horn of his Christ.

Who, then, is the Christ of his Christ? Or will he exalt the horn of each of his faithful, just as this same woman said at the beginning of her hymn: “My horn is exalted in my God”?

All those anointed with his chrism may rightly be called *christs*; yet all of them, together with their Head, constitute one Christ.

Thus Hannah prophesied—Hannah, the mother of Samuel, a holy and greatly praised man. In him, at that time, the change of the old priesthood was represented in figure; and it has now been fulfilled, when she who had many children became weak, so that the barren woman who bore seven might have a new priesthood in Christ.

## CHAPTER V  
### On the matters prophetically spoken by the man of God to Eli the priest, signifying that the priesthood established according to Aaron was to be taken away

### 1.

But the man of God sent to Eli the priest speaks more clearly to Eli himself. His name is not stated, but from his office and ministry he is without doubt understood to have been a prophet [Note: [Col. 0532] “The Jews say that this man of God was Phinehas, whom they also suppose to have been Elijah,” says Jerome in his *Hebrew Traditions* on the First Book of Kings. LUD. VIVES.].

For it is written:

“And a man of God came to Eli and said: Thus says the Lord: Revealing [Note: [Col. 0533] The Louvain edition omits *Revealing*; it is found in the other printed editions, in most manuscripts, and in the Greek Septuagint.] I revealed myself to the house of your father when they were slaves in the land of Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh. And I chose the house of your father from all the tribes of Israel for myself to exercise the priesthood, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, and to carry the ephod. And I gave to the house of your father all the fire-offerings of the sons of Israel for food.

“Why, then, did you look with an impudent eye upon my incense and my sacrifice, and honor your sons above me, to bless the firstfruits of every sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0533] Manuscripts: “to bless the firstfruits of the name of the sacrifice.”] in Israel in my presence?

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: I said, Your house and the house of your father will walk before me forever. And now the Lord says: Far be it; but those who honor me I will honor, and the one who despises me will be despised.

“Behold, the days are coming, and I will destroy your seed and the seed of your father’s house, and there will not be an elder for you in my house all your days. And I will destroy your man from my altar, so that his eyes may fail and his soul may waste away; and everyone who remains [Note: [Col. 0533] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “everyone who will remain.”] of your house will fall by the sword of men.

“And this will be the sign for you, which will come upon these two sons of yours, Hophni and Phinehas: both will die on one day.

“And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do everything that is in my heart and in my soul. And I will build him a faithful house, and he will walk before my Christ all his days.

“And whoever remains in your house will come to worship him for a piece of silver, saying: Throw me into one part of your priesthood, so that I may eat bread” (1 Samuel 2:27–36).

### 2.

This prophecy cannot be said to have been fulfilled in Samuel, in which the change of the old priesthood was foretold with such clarity.

Although Samuel was not from a tribe other than the one appointed by the Lord to serve at the altar, he was nevertheless not one of the sons of Aaron [Note: [Col. 0533] See *Retractations*, book 2, chapter 43, §2.], whose descendants had been designated as the source of the priests.

Accordingly, in this historical event also the same change that was to take place through Christ Jesus was foreshadowed. It belonged properly to the Old Testament, but figuratively to the New; it was itself a prophecy through an event, not through a word, signifying by what happened what the Prophet said in words to Eli the priest.

For afterward there were priests from the family of Aaron, such as Zadok and Abiathar during the reign of David (2 Samuel 15), and others thereafter, before the time came when what had been foretold so long beforehand concerning the change of the priesthood had to be accomplished through Christ.

But who now, looking upon these things with faithful eyes, does not see that they have been fulfilled? There is no tabernacle, no temple, no altar, no sacrifice, and therefore no priest remaining among the Jews, although God’s law had commanded that priests be appointed for them from the seed of Aaron.

This too is recalled here, when the prophet says: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I said, Your house and the house of your father will walk before me forever. And now the Lord says: Far be it; but those who honor me I will honor, and the one who despises me will be despised.”

The fact that he names “the house of his father” shows that he is not speaking of Eli’s immediate father, but of Aaron, who was the first priest appointed and from whose descendants the others were to follow. The preceding words demonstrate this, where he says: “I revealed myself to the house of your father when they were slaves in the land of Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh, and I chose the house of your father from all the tribes of Israel to exercise the priesthood.”

Who was the father of this man [Note: [Col. 0534] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Who was the father of this man.”] in that Egyptian slavery, from which, after they had been liberated, he was chosen for the priesthood, except Aaron?

It was therefore of Aaron’s stock that he said in this passage that priests would no longer exist—a fact that we now see fulfilled. Let faith keep watch: the realities are present, visible, tangible, and thrust before the eyes of those who refuse to see.

“Behold,” he says, “the days are coming, and I will destroy your seed and the seed of your father’s house, and there will not be an elder for you in my house all your days. And I will destroy your man from my altar, so that his eyes may fail and his soul may waste away.”

Behold, the days that were foretold have now come. There is no priest according to the order of Aaron. And whenever a man from his lineage sees the sacrifice of the Christians prevailing throughout the world, while that great honor has been taken away from him, his eyes fail and his soul wastes away with the decay of grief.

### 3.

What follows properly concerns the house of this Eli, to whom these words were spoken:

“And everyone who remains of your house will fall by the sword of men. And this will be the sign for you, which will come upon these two sons of yours, Hophni and Phinehas: both will die on one day.”

This sign, therefore, was made as a sign of the change of the priesthood from this man’s house; by that sign the change of the priesthood from the house of Aaron was signified.

The death of this man’s sons signified the death not of human beings but of the priesthood itself descended from the sons of Aaron.

What follows, however, already concerns the priest whose figure Samuel represented by succeeding this man [Note: [Col. 0534] “This man,” namely, Eli.]. Accordingly, what follows is spoken of Christ Jesus, the priest of the New Testament:

“And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do everything that is in my heart and in my soul; and I will build him a faithful house.”

That house is the eternal and heavenly Jerusalem.

“And he will walk,” he says, “before my Christ all his days.” “He will walk” means “he will dwell,” just as he had said above concerning the house of Aaron: “I said, Your house and the house of your father will walk before me forever.”

When he says, “He will walk before my Christ,” this must be understood of the house itself, not of that priest who is Christ himself, the Mediator and Savior. His house, therefore, will walk before him.

“Will walk” can also be understood as passing from death to life throughout all the days during which this mortality is carried on until the end of the present age.

When God says, “Who will do everything that is in my heart and in my soul,” we should not suppose that God has a soul, since he is the creator of the soul. Rather, this is said of God figuratively, not literally, just as “hand,” “feet,” and the other members of the body are said of him.

And lest anyone believe on this account that human beings were made in the image of God in the form of this flesh, wings are also attributed to him, which human beings certainly do not have. It is said to God: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16:8), so that human beings may understand that these expressions are spoken of that ineffable nature not with proper terms but with transferred ones.

### 4.

What is added—“And whoever remains in your house will come to worship him”—is not properly said of the house of this Eli, but of the house of Aaron, from which people remained until the coming of Jesus Christ, and from which even now there are still some remaining.

For concerning the house of this Eli it had already been said above: “And everyone who remains of your house will fall by the sword of men.”

How, then, could it truly be said here, “And whoever remains in your house will come to worship him,” if it is true that no one would remain from it after the avenging sword, unless he intended those who belong to the lineage—but to the entire priesthood according to the order of Aaron?

Therefore, if this concerns those predestined remnants of which another prophet said, “The remnant will be saved” (Isaiah 10:22), and of which the Apostle says, “So therefore at the present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5), then, since it is rightly understood of such remnants, whoever it is who was said to remain “in your house” surely believes in Christ.

Thus in the time of the Apostles many from that people believed; nor are there now lacking those who, although very rarely, nevertheless believe. In them is fulfilled what this man of God immediately went on to add: “He will come to worship him for a piece of silver.”

Whom is he to worship, except that supreme priest who is also God? For under the priesthood according to the order of Aaron people did not come to the temple or altar of God in order to worship the priest.

What, then, does “for a piece of silver” mean except the brevity of the word of faith, concerning which the Apostle recalls the saying: “The Lord will accomplish and abbreviate his word upon the earth” (Romans 9:28; Isaiah 10:23)?

That silver signifies the utterance of the word is attested by the Psalm, where we sing: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Psalm 11:7).

### 5.

What, then, does the one who comes to worship the priest of God and God the priest say?

“Throw me into one part of your priesthood, so that I may eat bread.”

“I do not wish to be placed in the honor of my fathers, which no longer exists. Throw me into a part of your priesthood. For I have chosen to be despised in the house of God” (Psalm 83:11). I desire to be some sort of member, however insignificant and small, of your priesthood.

Here he calls the people itself the priesthood, whose priest is the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. To this people the apostle Peter says: “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9) [Note: [Col. 0535] The Louvain edition adds: “in Christ.” It also adds: “And again, he says, present your bodies as a living sacrifice.” The other books omit “in Christ.” Some manuscripts, together with Vind., Am., and Er., add another passage from the Epistle to the Romans 12:1: “And again, he says, present your bodies,” and so forth.].

Although some have translated *sacrificii tui*, “of your sacrifice,” rather than *sacerdotii tui*, “of your priesthood,” this nevertheless signifies the same Christian people.

Hence the apostle Paul says: “We, though many, are one bread and one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

What he added—“so that I may eat bread”—also elegantly expresses the kind of sacrifice itself, concerning which the priest himself says: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52).

This is the sacrifice, not according to the order of Aaron but according to the order of Melchizedek. Let whoever reads understand.

This brief and salutarily humble confession—“Throw me into a part of your priesthood, so that I may eat bread”—is the piece of silver, because it is both brief [Note: [Col. 0536] Only the Louvain edition has: “because it is also brief.”] and the utterance of the Lord dwelling in the heart of the believer.

Because he had said above that he gave the house of Aaron food from the victims of the Old Testament, where he says, “I gave to the house of your father all the fire-offerings of the sons of Israel for food”—for these had been the sacrifices of the Jews—he therefore says here, “so that I may eat bread,” which is the sacrifice of Christians in the New Testament.

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the Jewish priesthood and kingdom, which, although said to have been established forever, do not remain; so that other things are understood, whose eternity is promised [Note: [Col. 0536] The Louvain edition has *statura*, “stature,” rather than *statuta*, “established.”] [Note: [Col. 0536] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “so that other things are understood which are promised as eternal.”]

### 1.

Since these things were then foretold with such profound significance and now shine forth with such clarity [Note: [Col. 0536] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “now shine forth with as much clarity.”], someone may nevertheless not unreasonably be troubled and say:

“How can we be confident that everything foretold in those books as yet to come will come to pass [Note: [Col. 0536] Vind. and Am. read: “How can we be confident that all things may agree?” Er. and Louvain read: “How can we be confident that all things will come to pass?” The manuscripts have *venire*, “to come.”], if this very statement divinely spoken there—‘Your house and the house of your father will walk before me forever’—could not be fulfilled?

“For we see that that priesthood has been changed, and what was promised to that house cannot even be hoped for as something that will ever be fulfilled, because what succeeds it after its rejection and alteration is instead proclaimed to be eternal.”

Whoever says this does not yet understand, or does not remember, that the priesthood itself according to the order of Aaron was established as a shadow of the future eternal priesthood. Therefore, when eternity was promised to it, the promise was not made to the shadow and figure itself, but to what was foreshadowed and represented through it.

But lest anyone think that the shadow itself would remain, its change also had to be prophesied.

### 2.

In the same way, the kingdom of Saul himself, who was certainly rejected and cast aside, was a shadow of the future kingdom that would remain in eternity.

That oil with which he was anointed, from which he was called *christus*—“anointed”—must be understood mystically, and recognized as a great sacrament. David himself revered it so greatly that his heart struck him with fear when, hidden in a dark cave into which Saul had also entered under the pressure of natural necessity, he secretly cut off a small piece from the back of Saul’s garment, so that he would have something by which to show how he had spared him when he could have killed him, and thus remove from Saul’s mind the suspicion that led him, thinking holy David his enemy, to persecute him fiercely.

Therefore, lest he be guilty of violating so great a sacrament in Saul, he was afraid even because he had touched his garment in this way.

For it is written:

“And David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of his cloak. But he said to the men who were with him and who urged him to kill Saul, delivered into his hands: ‘Far be it from me before the Lord that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, or lay my hand upon him, for he is the Lord’s anointed’” (1 Samuel 24:6–7).

Such reverence, therefore, was shown to this shadow of the future, not on account of the shadow itself but on account of what it prefigured.

Hence, when Samuel said to Saul, “Because you have not kept my commandment, which the Lord commanded you—otherwise the Lord would now have prepared your kingdom over Israel forever—but now your kingdom will not stand for you; and the Lord will seek for himself a man according to his heart, and the Lord will command him to be ruler over his people, because you did not keep what the Lord commanded you” (1 Samuel 13:13–14), this is not to be understood as though God had prepared Saul himself to reign forever and afterward had refused to keep that promise because Saul sinned.

God did not fail to know that Saul would sin. Rather, he had prepared his kingdom so that it would be a figure of the eternal kingdom.

Therefore he added: “And now your kingdom will not stand for you.” What was signified in Saul stood and will stand; but it will not stand for Saul, because he himself was not to reign forever, nor was his offspring, so that the statement “forever” might at least seem to be fulfilled through descendants succeeding one another.

“And the Lord will seek,” he says, “for himself a man”—whether signifying David or the Mediator of the New Testament himself, who was represented in the chrism with which David himself and his descendants were anointed.

God does not seek a man for himself as though he did not know where that man was. Rather, he speaks through a human being in the manner of human beings, because by speaking in this way he also seeks us.

For we were already known not only to God the Father but also to his Only-Begotten Son, who came “to seek what had been lost” (Luke 19:10), so completely that in him we were chosen “before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4).

Thus, by saying “he will seek for himself,” he meant, “he will have him as his own” [Note: [Col. 0537] Thus, with strong agreement, the ancient books. The printed editions have: “Therefore he said, ‘He will seek for himself,’ as though he were saying that the one whom he already knows to be his own and familiar to himself he will show to others to be his. Hence…”].

In Latin this word takes a prefixed preposition and becomes *acquirit*, “he acquires,” which makes its meaning quite clear. Yet even without the additional preposition, *quaerere*, “to seek,” can be understood as “to acquire”; from this come the words for gains and profit.

## CHAPTER VII  
### On the disruption of the Israelite kingdom, by which the perpetual division of spiritual Israel from carnal Israel is prefigured

### 1.

Again Saul sinned through disobedience, and again Samuel said to him by the word of the Lord:

“Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king over Israel.”

And again, for the same sin, when Saul confessed it, begged forgiveness, and asked Samuel to return with him so that he might appease God, Samuel said:

“I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king over Israel.”

And Samuel turned his face to leave. Saul seized the edge of his cloak, and it tore. Samuel said to him:

“The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today, and he will give it to your neighbor, who is better than you; and Israel will be divided in two. He will not turn back, nor will he repent, for he is not like a human being, that he should repent. He threatens, and does not remain” (1 Samuel 15:23–29).

The man to whom it is said, “The Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king over Israel,” and, “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today,” reigned over Israel for forty years [Note: [Col. 0538] This is also taught below, book 18, chapter 20, and we read it likewise in Acts 13:21. In the Books of Kings the years of Saul’s reign are not recorded, as they are for the kings who followed. Josephus, at the end of book 6 of the *Antiquities*, says: “Saul reigned while Samuel was alive for eighteen years, and after his death for twenty-two”—from which the total of forty years is obtained. The common opinion, however, followed by Eusebius and Sulpicius Severus, is that Samuel’s years are included within the forty years during which Saul is said to have reigned, because sacred chronology yields only forty years from the death of Eli the high priest, who judged Israel, until the beginning of David’s reign. Nevertheless, there is no agreement about precisely how many years Saul lived after Samuel’s death, or even how many years he lived from the beginning of his reign. COQUAEUS.], namely, for as long a period of time as David himself.

He heard this at the beginning of his reign, so that we may understand that it was said for this reason: no one from his lineage was to reign. And let us turn our attention to the lineage of David, from which, according to the flesh, arose the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

## 2.

But Scripture does not have what is read in many Latin manuscripts, “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand”; rather, as we have found it set down in the Greek manuscripts, “The Lord has torn the kingdom from Israel from your hand,” so that “from your hand” is to be understood as referring to “from Israel.” This man, therefore, figuratively represented the person of the people of Israel, which people was destined to lose its kingdom, while Christ Jesus our Lord would reign through the New Testament—not carnally, but spiritually.

When it is said of this kingdom, “And he will give it to your neighbor,” the reference is to kinship according to the flesh: for Christ is from Israel according to the flesh, as was Saul. But what has been added, “good above you,” may indeed be understood as “better than you,” and some have interpreted it in this way. It is better, however, to understand “good above you” as meaning that, because he is good, he is therefore above you [Note: [Col. 0538] In the Louvain edition, “above you” is omitted.], in accordance with that other prophetic statement: “Until I place all your enemies beneath your feet” (Psalm 109:1). Among these enemies is Israel, from which Christ, its persecutor, took away the kingdom.

Nevertheless, there was also an Israel “in whom there was no deceit” (John 1:47), something like the grain among that straw. For the Apostles came from there, as did so many martyrs, the first of whom was Stephen; and from there came so many churches, which the apostle Paul mentions as glorifying God at his conversion (Galatians 1:24).

## 3.

I have no doubt that what follows must be understood with reference to this matter: “And Israel will be divided into two”—namely, into Israel hostile to Christ and Israel adhering to Christ; into Israel belonging to the slave woman and Israel belonging to the free woman. For these two kinds were at first together, just as Abraham was still attached to the slave woman, until she who had been barren was made fruitful through Christ’s grace and cried out, “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Genesis 21:10).

Because of Solomon’s sin, during the reign of his son Rehoboam, we know that Israel was divided into two and continued in that condition, with each part possessing its own kings, until that entire nation was overthrown and deported by the Chaldeans in a great devastation. But what has this to do with Saul? If some such thing had been threatened, it ought rather to have been threatened to David himself, whose son Solomon was.

Finally, the Hebrew nation is not now divided among itself; rather, it is dispersed throughout the world indiscriminately in the fellowship of the same error. But that division which God, under the person of Saul—who represented that kingdom and people—threatened against the kingdom and people is shown to be eternal and unchangeable by the addition: “And he will not turn back, nor will he repent, for he is not like a man, that he should repent.” He threatens, and does not persist—that is, a man threatens and does not persist, but not God, who does not repent as a man does.

Wherever Scripture says that God repents, a change in circumstances is signified, while divine foreknowledge remains unchangeable. Wherever he is said not to repent, this means that he does not change [Note: [Col. 0539] Only the Louvain edition has “this means that he is not changed.”].

## 4.

Clearly, through these words a judgment was divinely pronounced concerning this division of the people of Israel, and it was wholly perpetual. For whoever from among them has passed over to Christ, or is passing over, or will pass over, was not, according to God’s foreknowledge, of that Israel—not according to the one and same nature of the human race.

In fact, all Israelites who adhere to Christ and persevere in him will never be with those Israelites who persist in being his enemies until the end of this life. They will remain forever in the division here foretold. For the Old Testament, “generating slavery from Mount Sinai” (Galatians 4:24), is of no benefit except insofar as it bears witness to the New Testament. Otherwise, as long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts; but whenever anyone passes over from there to Christ, the veil will be taken away (1 Corinthians 3:15–16).

The very intention of those who pass over is changed from the old covenant to the new, so that no longer does anyone seek to receive a carnal happiness, but a spiritual one. For this reason the great prophet Samuel himself, before he anointed Saul king, when he cried out to the Lord for Israel and the Lord heard him, and when he was offering burnt offerings [Note: [Col. 0539] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed editions have *holocaustum* (“burnt offering”); Erasmus adds *simul* (“at the same time”).], while foreigners were approaching for battle against the people of God, the Lord thundered against them. They were thrown into confusion, stumbled before Israel, and were defeated.

Samuel took one stone and set it between the new and old Mizpah [Note: [Col. 0539] The printed editions have *Masphat*. The older books, as in the Septuagint, have *Massephat*.] and called its name Ebenezer, which in Latin means “Stone of the helper” [Note: [Col. 0539] The printed editions have “Stone of help.” The manuscripts have “of the helper,” as does the Septuagint, *toēthor*.]. And he said, “Thus far the Lord has helped us” (1 Samuel 7:5–12).

*Mizpah* is interpreted as “intention.” That stone of the helper is the mediator, the Savior, through whom one must pass from the old Mizpah to the new—that is, from the intention by which a false, carnal happiness was expected in a carnal kingdom, to the intention by which, through the New Testament, the truest spiritual happiness is expected in the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0540]. Since nothing is better than this, God helps us thus far.

# CHAPTER VIII  
## Concerning the promises made to David in his son, which are found nowhere in Solomon but are fulfilled completely in Christ

## 1.

Now I see that it must be shown what God promised to David himself, who succeeded Saul in the kingdom and whose change prefigured that final change for the sake of which all things were divinely spoken and written. This bears upon the matter we are discussing.

When many prosperous things had happened to King David, he conceived the plan of building a house for God—namely, that most renowned temple which was later constructed by his son, King Solomon. While he was considering this, the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, so that he might convey it to the king.

After God had said that David himself would not build a house for him, and that for so long a time he had not commanded anyone among his people to build him a house of cedar, he continued:

“And now you shall say this to my servant David: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I took you from the sheepfold, that you might be leader over my people Israel [Note: [Col. 0540] Here the particle *in*, before *Israel*, is restored from the manuscripts; it corresponds to the Greek *epi* in the Septuagint.]. And I was with you in all the things through which you went, and I destroyed all your enemies from before you, and I made you renowned according to the name of the great ones who are upon the earth.

“And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant it, and it will dwell apart, and it will no longer be disturbed; and the son of iniquity will not again humble it, as from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies.
