“And the Lord will announce [Note: [Col. 0540] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions here and in chapter 12 have, “and the Lord announced.”] to you that you will build a house for him. And when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers [Note: [Col. 0540] The printed editions omit “and.” The manuscripts have it in accordance with the Septuagint; for “you sleep,” some read “you will sleep.”], I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your body, and I will prepare his kingdom. He will build a house for my name, and I will establish his throne forever.

“I will be his father, and he will be my son. And if iniquity comes upon him [Note: [Col. 0540] The Louvain edition alone has, “And when his iniquity comes.” All our manuscripts likewise have this reading, except 2050. M.], I will reprove him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. But I will not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from those from whom I removed it from before my face [Note: [Col. 0540] The printed editions have, “from those from whom I removed my face.” But the reputable manuscripts Gervasianus, Colbertinus, and others agree with the Greek Septuagint, *aph’ōn apestēsa ek prosōpou mou*.].

“And his house will be faithful, and his kingdom before me forever, and his throne will be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:8–16).

## 2.

Anyone who thinks that this great promise was fulfilled in Solomon is greatly mistaken. He notices the statement, “He will build a house for my name,” since Solomon built that famous temple, but he does not notice: “His house will be faithful, and his kingdom before me forever.”

Let him therefore attend and observe Solomon’s house, full of foreign women worshiping false gods, and Solomon himself—once wise—at some point led by them into that same idolatry and overthrown. Let him not dare to think that God either falsely promised this or was unable to foresee that such a Solomon and such a house would come to be.

Nor ought we to doubt this, even if we did not now see these things fulfilled in Christ our Lord, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), lest we vainly and foolishly seek some other person here, as the carnal Jews do. For they themselves understand so clearly that the son promised in this passage to King David was not Solomon that, although the one who was promised has already been revealed with such clarity, they still profess, in their astonishing blindness, to await another.

A certain image of the future reality was indeed present in Solomon: he built the temple, possessed peace in accordance with his name—for *Solomon* means “peaceful” in Latin—and was wonderfully praiseworthy at the beginning of his reign. But even in his own person, under the shadow of the future, he himself announced Christ our Lord; he did not present him.

Therefore certain things were written about him as though these predictions had been made about him, while Holy Scripture, prophesying also through historical events, in a certain way sketches in him the figure of future things. Besides the books of sacred history, where he is reported to have reigned, Psalm 71 is also inscribed with his name. In it many things are said which cannot at all apply to him, but which fit the Lord Christ with the utmost clarity [Note: [Col. 0541] Vindelinus, Ambrosius, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have “with the greatest clarity.”], so that it plainly appears that in Solomon some kind of figure was shadowed, whereas in Christ the reality itself was presented.

For it is known within what boundaries Solomon’s kingdom was enclosed; nevertheless, in that psalm we read, to mention nothing else: “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:8). We see this fulfilled in Christ. For he began his rule from the river, where, after being baptized by John, and with John pointing him out, he began to be recognized by the disciples, who called him not only Teacher but also Lord [Note: [Col. 0541] Compare the *Letter against the Donatists*, *On the Unity of the Church*, §22.].

## 3.

Nor did Solomon begin to reign while his father David was still alive for any other reason—a circumstance that happened to none of those kings—except that this too should make sufficiently clear that he is not the one whom this prophecy indicates [Note: [Col. 0541] Compare Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book 4, chapter 13, §24 and following.]. The prophecy speaks to David:

“And when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your body, and I will prepare his kingdom.”

How, then, because of what follows—“He will build a house for my name”—will Solomon be thought to have been the one prophesied, rather than, because of what precedes—“When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you”—understanding that another peaceful one was promised, who was foretold as being raised up not before David’s death, as Solomon was, but afterward?

However long afterward Jesus Christ was to come, there is no doubt that he had to come after the death of King David, to whom he was promised, since he was to build a house for God—not of wood and stones, but of human beings, such as the house we rejoice that he is building. To this house the Apostle says, speaking to Christ’s faithful: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

# CHAPTER IX  
## How similar the prophecy concerning Christ in Psalm 88 is to the promises made through Nathan’s prophecy in the Books of Kings

For this reason, in Psalm 88, whose title is “An understanding belonging to Ethan the Israelite,” God’s promises to King David are recalled, and certain statements there resemble those set down in the Book of Kings. Thus we read:

“I swore to David my servant: I will prepare your offspring forever.”

And again:

“Then you spoke in a vision to your sons, and you said: I have placed help upon a mighty one, and I have exalted one chosen from my people. I found David my servant; with my holy oil I anointed him. For my hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him.

“The enemy will not prevail against him, and the son of iniquity will not again inflict harm upon him. And I will cut down his enemies before him, and I will put to flight those who hate him. My truth and my mercy will be with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted.

“And I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. He will call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation. And I will make him my firstborn, exalted among the kings of the earth.

“Forever I will preserve my mercy for him, and my covenant will remain faithful to him. And I will establish his offspring forever and ever [Note: [Col. 0542] Manuscripts 2050 and 2051 have “his seat.” M.], and his throne as the days of heaven” (Psalm 88:4–5, 20–30).

All these statements are understood of the Lord Jesus when they are rightly understood, under the name of David, because of the form of a servant which that same Mediator assumed from the seed of David through the virgin.

Immediately something is also said concerning the sins of his sons, resembling what is set down in the Book of Kings and more readily understood as referring to Solomon. There we read, in the Book of Kings:

“And if his iniquity comes upon him, I will reprove him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men; but I will not remove my mercy from him” (2 Samuel 7:14–15).

The word “blows” signifies strokes of correction. Hence we have the statement, “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 104:15). What else does this mean than, “Do not injure them”?

But in the Psalm, when he was speaking as though about David, so that he might say something similar there also, he says:

“If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their offenses with scourges. But I will not scatter my mercy from him” (Psalm 88:31–34).

He did not say “from them,” although he was speaking of his sons and not of David himself; he said “from him,” which, properly understood, amounts to the same thing. For no sins could be found in Christ himself, who is the head of the Church, that would require him to be divinely chastised with the mercy preserved through human correction. Rather, such sins are found in his body and members, which are his people.

For this reason the Book of Kings calls it “his iniquity,” while the Psalm calls it “the iniquity of his sons,” so that we may understand that what is said of his body is, in a certain manner, said of him. For this reason, when Saul was persecuting his body, which is his faithful people, Christ himself said from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Then, in what follows in the Psalm, he says:

“I will not violate my truth, nor profane my covenant, and I will not reject what proceeds from my lips. Once I swore by my holiness: I will not lie to David”—that is, “I will certainly not lie to David”; Scripture often speaks in this way.

He then adds what he will not lie about, saying:

“His offspring will remain forever, and his seat will be like the sun in my sight, and like the full moon forever; and he will be a faithful witness in heaven” (Psalm 88:34–38).

# CHAPTER X  
## How different the events in the kingdom of earthly Jerusalem were from what God had promised, so that it might be understood that the truth of the promise belonged to the glory of another King and kingdom

After such powerful confirmations of the promise, lest anyone think that it had been fulfilled in Solomon—as though it were hoped for but could not be found—the Psalm continues:

“But you have rejected and brought to nothing, O Lord” (Psalm 88:39).

This happened to Solomon’s kingdom in his descendants, even to the overthrow of earthly Jerusalem itself, which had been the seat of that kingdom, and especially to the destruction of the temple that had been built by Solomon [Note: [Col. 0543] Concerning the overthrow of the kingdom, Josephus writes in *Jewish Antiquities*, book 10, chapter 11: “And this was the end of the kings of David’s line, who thereafter reigned twenty-one in number; that span of time contains five hundred and fifteen years, with an additional six months and seven days, counting the twenty years of Saul, the first king, who belonged to another tribe. If these are subtracted, from David to the last year of Zedekiah there elapsed four hundred and ninety-four years and six months.” Josephus likewise writes that the temple was burned four hundred and seventy years after it had been built, with an additional six months and ten days; Zonaras follows him. Eusebius and Cedrenus count four hundred and forty-two years; the Hebrews, four hundred and eighty-three years; and others give still different figures. COQUAEUS.].

But lest this make it seem that God had acted contrary to his promises, the Psalm immediately adds:

“You have delayed your Christ” (Psalm 88:39).

Therefore it is not that Solomon, nor David himself, if the Lord’s Christ was delayed. Although all kings consecrated with that mystical anointing were called his christs—not only those from King David onward, but also Saul, who was the first king anointed over that same people (1 Samuel 24:7), for David himself calls him “the Lord’s anointed”—there was nevertheless one true Christ, whose figure those kings bore through their prophetic anointing.

According to the human opinion of those who thought that he should be understood in David or Solomon, he was deferred for a long time; but according to God’s arrangement, he was being prepared to come at his proper time.

Meanwhile, while he was delayed, what happened to the kingdom of earthly Jerusalem, where he was supposedly going to reign? The Psalm goes on to say:

“You have overturned [Note: [Col. 0543] Several manuscripts have “You have turned away.” The Greek is *Katestrepsas*.] the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his holiness upon the earth. You have destroyed all his walls; you have made his fortifications a source of terror. All who passed along the road plundered him; he became a reproach to his neighbors. You have exalted the right hand of his enemies; you have gladdened all those who hate him. You have turned away the help of his sword, and you have not aided him in battle. You have removed him from purification; you have struck his seat down to the ground. You have shortened the days of his seat; you have covered him with confusion” (Psalm 88:40–46).

All these things came upon the slave woman Jerusalem, in which some sons of the free woman also reigned, holding that kingdom in a temporary administration, while they possessed the kingdom of the heavenly Jerusalem as its sons, in true faith and hope in the true Christ.

The historical record, if it is read, shows how these things came upon that kingdom.

# CHAPTER XI  
## Concerning the substance of the people of God, which exists in Christ through the assumption of flesh; he alone had the power to rescue his soul from the underworld

After these prophecies, the Prophet turns to prayer; but the prayer itself is also prophecy:

“How long, O Lord, will you turn away forever?” (Psalm 88:47)

The words “your face” are understood, just as in the statement, “How long will you turn your face away from me?” (Psalm 12:1). For this reason some manuscripts do not have “will you turn away” here, but “will you be turned away,” although the passage may also be understood as saying, “You turn away your mercy,” which you promised to David.

But what does “forever” mean except “until the end”? This end must be understood as the final time, when that people too will believe in Christ Jesus. Before that end, the distressing events lamented above had to take place.

For this reason the Psalm continues:

“Will your anger burn like fire? Remember what my substance is.”

Nothing is better understood here than Jesus himself, the substance of his people, from whom his flesh takes its nature. For, it says, “You did not establish all the sons of men in vain” (Psalm 88:48).

Unless there were one Son of Man as the substance of Israel, through whom many sons of men would be liberated, all the sons of men would indeed have been established in vain.

Now the whole human race, through the sin of the first man, has fallen from truth into vanity. Hence another Psalm says: “Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow” (Psalm 143:4). Yet God did not establish all the sons of men in vain, because he liberates many from vanity through the mediator Jesus. Those whom he foresaw would not be liberated he nevertheless established—not in vain—for the benefit of those who are to be liberated and for the contrast between the two opposing cities, within the beautiful and most just ordering of the whole rational creation.

Then the Psalm continues:

“Who is the man who will live and not see death? Who will rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld?” (Psalm 88:49)

Who is this except that substance of Israel from the seed of David, Christ Jesus? Of him the Apostle says that, having risen from the dead, he no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6:9).

Thus he will live and not see death, although he did die; but he rescued his soul from the hand of the underworld, to which he had descended in order to release the bonds of the underworld for certain persons [Note: [Col. 0544] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “because he had descended to the underworld to release the bonds of certain sins.”].

He rescued it by that power of which he says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

# CHAPTER XII  
## To whose person the petition for the promised things is to be understood as belonging, concerning which the Psalm says, “Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?” and so forth

But concerning the remaining words of this Psalm, which run as follows:

“Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth? Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have held in my bosom from many nations; the reproach with which your enemies reproached, O Lord, the reproach concerning the exchange of your Christ”—

it may rightly be asked whether these words were spoken from the person of those Israelites who desired that the promise made to David should be restored to them, or rather from the person of Christians, who are Israelites not according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

These words were spoken or written in the time of Ethan, whose name appears in the title of this Psalm; and that was the time of David’s reign. Therefore the Prophet would not say, “Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?” unless the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0545] The manuscripts have “prophecy.”] were assuming the person of those who were to exist much later, for whom the time when these promises were made to King David would be ancient.

The “many nations” may be understood as referring to the time when Christians were persecuted and reproached for Christ’s passion, which Scripture calls an “exchange,” because by dying he became immortal.

The “exchange of Christ” may also be understood as something reproached to the Israelites, because although he was expected to be theirs, he became the possession of the nations. Many nations that believed in him through the New Testament now reproach them for this, while they themselves remain in the old covenant. Thus the words “Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants” are spoken because, since the Lord does not forget them but rather has mercy on them, they too will believe after this reproach.

But the interpretation I offered first seems more suitable to me. These words do not fit the enemies of Christ, who are reproached because Christ passed over to the nations and abandoned them: “Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants.” Such Jews should not be called servants of God.

Rather, the words fit those who, while suffering severe humiliations in persecutions for Christ’s name, could remember that an exalted kingdom had been promised to David’s seed and could say, out of desire for it—not in despair, but by asking, seeking, and knocking:

“Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth? Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have held in my bosom from many nations”—

that is, “I have patiently endured it in my inmost being.”

“The reproach with which your enemies reproached, O Lord; the reproach concerning the exchange of your Christ”—not believing it to be an exchange, but an annihilation [Note: [Col. 0545] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “but a consummation.”].

What else does “Remember, O Lord” mean than “Have mercy, and, in return for my patiently endured humiliation, restore the exalted state which you swore to David in your truth”?

If, however, we assign these words to the Jews [Col. 0546], they could have been spoken by those servants of God who, after earthly Jerusalem had been conquered, were led into captivity before Jesus Christ was born in the flesh. They understood the exchange of Christ to mean that through him one should faithfully await not an earthly and carnal happiness such as had appeared for a few years in the reign of King Solomon, but a heavenly and spiritual happiness.

At that time, the unbelief of the nations, ignorant of this, exulted and taunted the people of God for being captive. What else did it reproach them with than the exchange of Christ—unknowingly reproaching what the faithful understood?

Accordingly, the words with which this Psalm concludes fit the whole people of God who belong to the heavenly Jerusalem, whether those who were hidden in the Old Testament before the New was revealed, or those who, after the New Testament had been revealed, are now openly seen to belong to Christ:

“Blessed be the Lord forever; let it be, let it be” (Psalm 88:50–53).

For the blessing of the Lord in David’s seed is not to be hoped for merely for a time, as it appeared in the days of Solomon, but forever. It is in this most certain hope that the words “Let it be, let it be” are spoken. The repetition of these words confirms that hope.

Understanding this, David says in the Second Book of Kings, from which we digressed to this Psalm:

“And you have spoken concerning the house of your servant for a distant future.”

A little later he therefore says:

“Now begin, and bless the house of your servant forever” (2 Samuel 7:19, 29), and so forth. For he was then about to beget a son from whom his descendants would be carried forward to Christ, through whom his house would become eternal, and that same house would be the house of God.

It is called the house of David because of David’s lineage; but it is the house of God because it is the temple of God, made of human beings and not stones. There the people will dwell with God and in their God forever, and God will dwell with the people and in his people, so that God will fill his people and the people will be filled with their God, when God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28)—himself the reward in peace, who is strength in battle.

Therefore, when Nathan’s words say, “And the Lord will announce to you that you will build a house for him,” David’s words later say:

“For you, Lord Almighty, God of Israel, have revealed this to your servant’s ear, saying, ‘I will build a house for you’” (2 Samuel 7:11, 27).

We too build this house by living well, while God helps us to live well, because “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

When the final dedication of this house comes, then what God spoke here through Nathan will take place:

“And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant it, and it will dwell apart, and it will no longer be disturbed; and the son of iniquity will not again humble it, as from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel” (2 Samuel 7:10–11).

# CHAPTER XIII  
## Whether the truth of the promised peace can be attributed to the times that unfolded under Solomon

Anyone who hopes for this great good in this world and on this earth reasons foolishly. Or will anyone think that it was fulfilled in the peace of Solomon’s kingdom?

Scripture commends that peace, as an image of the future, with exalted praise. But this suspicion is vigilantly ruled out by what follows immediately after the words, “The son of iniquity will not again humble him”:

“As from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Before kings began to exist there, judges had been appointed over that people, from the time when it received the promised land. Yet the son of iniquity—that is, a foreign enemy—certainly humbled it at intervals, during which the narrative records that periods of peace alternated with wars. Some periods of peace there are found to have lasted longer than Solomon’s, although he reigned for forty years.

Under the judge called Ehud, for example, there were eighty years of peace (Judges 3:30). Therefore, far from us be the belief that Solomon’s times were foretold in this promise—much less the times of any other king. None of them reigned in such great peace as Solomon; nor did that nation ever possess the kingdom in such a way that it was free from anxiety about being subjected to enemies. For, amid such instability in human affairs, no people has ever been granted such security that it need not fear hostile attacks in this life.

The place of such peaceful and secure habitation as is promised here is therefore eternal, and it belongs to the eternal, in the mother Jerusalem that is free. There the people of Israel will truly exist. For this name is interpreted as “Seeing God” [Note: [Col. 0547] That is, *Israel*.]. Out of desire for this reward, the faithful life must be lived in this troubled pilgrimage.

# CHAPTER XIV  
## David’s concern for the arrangement and mystery of the Psalms

As the city of God proceeded through the ages, David first reigned in the earthly Jerusalem, which was a shadow of the future. David was a man skilled in songs, who loved musical harmony not for ordinary pleasure but with faithful devotion, and who employed it in the service of his God, the true God, as a mystical representation of a great reality.

The rational and measured concord of diverse sounds, joined together in harmonious variety, suggests the unity of a well-ordered city. In fact, nearly all his prophecy is contained in the Psalms, of which the book we call the Psalter contains one hundred and fifty.

Some wish to maintain that only those Psalms whose titles bear David’s name were composed by David. Others think that only those preceded by the words “Of David” were composed by him, while those whose titles have “To David” were composed by others and adapted to David’s person.

This opinion is refuted by the Gospel voice of the Savior himself, where he says that David, in the Spirit, called Christ his Lord (Matthew 22:43). For Psalm 109 begins:

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Psalm 109:1).

Certainly this same Psalm does not have “Of David” in its title, but “To David,” as do many others.

It seems more credible to me that those who attribute all one hundred and fifty Psalms to David’s work are correct, and that he marked some of them with the names of others who represented something relevant to the subject, while he wished the rest to have no human name in their titles. The Lord inspired him to arrange this variety, although it is hidden, yet not without purpose.

Nor should the fact that the names of certain prophets who lived long after the time of King David are inscribed on some Psalms in that book move us to reject this view. The things said in those Psalms appear to be spoken by those prophets. For the prophetic Spirit could certainly reveal to the prophetic king David even the names of future prophets, so that something fitting their persons might be sung prophetically—just as King Josiah, who would arise and reign more than three hundred years later, was revealed by name to a certain prophet who also foretold his future deeds (1 Kings 13).

# CHAPTER XV  
## Whether everything prophesied in the Psalms concerning Christ and the Church should be adapted to the structure of this work

I now see that I am expected at this point in the book to explain what David prophesied in the Psalms concerning the Lord Jesus Christ or his Church. But I am prevented from doing this in the manner that the expectation itself seems to demand—although I have already done so once—not by lack of material, but rather by its abundance.

I am forbidden, in order to avoid excessive length, to set everything down. Yet I fear that, if I select only certain passages, I may seem to many who know them to have omitted what is more necessary. Moreover, a testimony that is produced ought to have the support of the entire Psalm’s composition, so that nothing contradicts it—even if not every part supports it. Otherwise we may seem, in the manner of those who make patchwork poems, to be plucking verses from a great song and adapting them to the matter we wish to establish, although the song was written not about that matter but about something entirely different [Note: [Col. 0548] The manuscripts have, “or certainly that there is nothing.”] [Note: [Col. 0548] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “as though from a backward song.”].

To show this in any Psalm, the whole Psalm must be expounded. The size of the task is sufficiently indicated both by the works of others and by our own volumes in which we have done this. Let anyone who wishes and is able read those works. He will find how many things, and how great, King David, who was also a prophet, prophesied concerning Christ and his Church—concerning the King, that is, and the city he founded.

# CHAPTER XVI  
## Concerning the things pertaining to Christ and the Church that are stated openly or figuratively in Psalm 44
1. For however distinctive and clear prophetic utterances may be concerning any subject, it is necessary that figurative expressions also be mixed with them. These especially impose upon teachers the laborious task of discussion and interpretation, for the sake of those who are slower to understand. Some passages, nevertheless, display Christ and the Church at first sight, as soon as they are spoken, even though what is less readily understood in them remains to be explained at leisure. Such is the following passage in the same book of the Psalms:

> “My heart has uttered a good word; I declare my works to the king.  
> My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe.  
> You are more beautiful in form than the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.  
> Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one.  
> In your appearance and your beauty, advance, prosper, and reign.  
> Because of truth, meekness, and righteousness; and your right hand shall lead you wondrously.  
> Your arrows are sharp, most powerful.  
> Peoples shall fall beneath you, in the heart of the king’s enemies.  
> Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.  
> You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.  
> Myrrh, resin, and cassia are from your garments, from the ivory houses; from them the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (Psalm 44:2–10).

[Note: [Col. 0548] The printed editions add *tuum* (“your”); it is absent from the manuscripts and from the Septuagint.]

[Note: [Col. 0549] The printed editions read *potentissime* (“most powerful one”), and shortly afterward *in corda* (“into the hearts”). Here and in the other passages below, the manuscripts agree with the version Augustine follows in his *Exposition on Psalm 44*.]

Who, however slow, would not recognize here the Christ whom we proclaim and in whom we believe, when he hears of God, whose throne is forever and ever, and of one anointed by God—plainly with the kind of anointing by which God anoints, not with visible but with spiritual and intelligible chrism? For who is so uneducated in this religion, or so deaf to the fame of Christ, spread so far and wide, that he does not know that Christ is named from *chrisma*, that is, from anointing? Once Christ the king has been recognized, one may now inquire at leisure how the remaining expressions here stated figuratively are to be understood: how he is “more beautiful in form than the sons of men,” with a beauty all the more to be loved and admired because it is less a bodily beauty; what his sword and arrows are; and what the other expressions are that are set forth not literally but figuratively, since he reigns because of truth, meekness, and righteousness.

2. Next, let him contemplate Christ’s Church, joined to her spiritual husband by so great a bond and by divine love. Of her it is said in what follows:

> “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, wrapped in varied attire.  
> Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.  
> For the king has desired your beauty, because he himself is your Lord God.  
> The daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts; the rich among the people shall entreat your countenance.  
> All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in golden fringes, wrapped in varied attire.  
> Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you.  
> They shall be brought with joy and rejoicing; they shall be led into the temple of the king.  
> In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth.  
> They shall remember your name throughout every generation and generation.  
> Therefore peoples shall confess you forever, and for ages of ages” (Psalm 44:10–18).

I do not suppose anyone could be so foolish as to believe that some little woman is here being praised and described—namely, the wife of him to whom it was said:

> “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.  
> You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions”—

that is, Christ above Christians. For these are his companions, from whose unity and concord among all nations this queen is formed. Thus another psalm says of her, “The city of the great King” (Psalm 47:3).

She is spiritually Zion, a name which, interpreted in Latin, means “watchtower” or “contemplation” (*speculatio*). For she contemplates the great good of the age to come, since her intention is directed toward it. She is likewise Jerusalem, in the same spiritual sense, concerning which we have already said much. Her enemy is the city of the devil, Babylon, which is interpreted as “Confusion.” Yet from this Babylon the queen is liberated through regeneration among all nations and passes from the worst king to the best King—that is, from the devil to Christ. For this reason it is said to her, “Forget your people and your father’s house.”

The Israelites who belong to that impious city by flesh alone, not by faith, are also its portion; they too are enemies of this great King and of his queen. When Christ came to them and was killed by them, he became rather the possession of others, whom he had not seen in the flesh. Hence our King himself says through the prophecy of a certain psalm:

> “You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people; you will establish me at the head of the nations.  
> A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Psalm 17:44–45).

[Note: [Col. 0550] The manuscripts read *in capite gentium* (“at the head of the nations”).]

This people of the nations, whom Christ did not know by bodily presence, but which believed in Christ when he was announced to it—so that it was rightly said of it, “At the hearing of the ear it obeyed me,” because “faith comes from hearing” (Romans 10:17)—this people, added to the true Israelites both in flesh and in faith, is the city of God. It also gave birth to Christ according to the flesh, when the people of God existed only in those Israelites. For the virgin Mary belonged to that people, in whom Christ assumed flesh in order to become human.

Of this city another psalm says:

> “A man shall call Zion ‘Mother,’ and a man was made in her; and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5).

Who is this Most High except God? Therefore Christ, who is God, founded that city in the patriarchs and prophets before he became human in it through Mary.

Since, then, it had long before been said prophetically to this queen, the city of God, what we now see fulfilled—“In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth”—for throughout the earth her sons are appointed as her leaders and fathers, while peoples run to her with the confession of eternal praise for ages of ages [Note: [Col. 0550] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions of Vinding, Amelote, and Erasmus read: “her leaders and princes, while they confess.” Lovaniensis reads: “her leaders and fathers are princes, while they confess.” Shortly afterward, where the text has *cum confessione* (“with confession”), some manuscripts have *confessionem* (“confession”); others, with Vinding, Amelote, and Erasmus, have *confessione*, omitting *cum*.]

[Note: [Col. 0550] Compare *Exposition on Psalm 44*, §32.]—there can be no doubt that whatever is obscurely expressed here in figurative language, however it may be understood, must correspond to these most evident realities.

## CHAPTER XVII — On what concerns Christ’s priesthood in Psalm 109, and what concerns his passion in Psalm 21

The same is true of the psalm in which Christ is proclaimed most openly as priest, just as here he is proclaimed as king:

> “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.”

Christ’s sitting at the right hand of God the Father is believed, not seen. Nor does it yet appear that his enemies have been placed beneath his feet; this is being accomplished and will appear at the end. This too is now believed and afterward will be seen.

But what follows is so clear that it is denied not only unbelievingly and disastrously, but even shamelessly:

> “The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion, and rule in the midst of your enemies.”

[Note: [Col. 0550] The printed editions omit *et* (“and”). The manuscripts here, as also Augustine’s *Exposition on Psalm 109*, retain it.]

For the enemies themselves admit that the law of Christ, which we call the Gospel, was sent forth from Zion, and we recognize it as the rod of his power. That he rules in the midst of his enemies is likewise attested by those very people among whom he rules: they gnash their teeth, waste away, and are powerless against him.

Then, shortly afterward, the psalm says:

> “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent.”

By these words it signifies that what follows will be immutable:

> “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:1, 2, 4).

Since there is now nowhere a priesthood and sacrifice according to the order of Aaron, while everywhere there is offered, under Christ the priest, what Melchizedek brought forth when he blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18 ff.), who can be permitted to doubt of whom these words are spoken?

Accordingly, when they are rightly understood, the more obscure things placed in the same psalm refer to these manifest realities. We have done this in our popular sermons [Note: [Col. 0551] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead have: “how they are rightly understood has been made known in our popular sermons.”].

So also in the psalm where Christ prophetically speaks of the humility of his passion, saying:

> “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones.  
> They themselves looked upon me and gazed.”

[Note: [Col. 0551] The printed editions read *pedes meos* (“my feet”). *Meos* is absent from the manuscripts.]

By these words he plainly signified his body stretched out on the cross, his hands and feet fastened and pierced by the blows of the nails, and in this way he presented himself as an object for them to examine and gaze upon. He adds:

> “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Psalm 21:17–19).

The Gospel narrative tells how this prophecy was fulfilled (Matthew 27:35). Then the other things said there less openly are rightly understood, especially when they agree with what has been made so manifest. For those things which we believe have not yet taken place but which we now behold as present are also seen throughout the whole world, just as they were foretold long ago in the same psalm. A little later it says:

> “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord; and all the families of the nations shall worship before him. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21:28–29).

## CHAPTER XVIII — On Psalms 3, 40, 15, and 67, in which the Lord’s death and resurrection are prophesied

1. The oracles of the Psalms were by no means silent concerning his resurrection. For what else is sung in the third psalm in his person?

> “I lay down and slept; I awoke, because the Lord will sustain me” (Psalm 3:6).

[Note: [Col. 0551] So the manuscripts read, in agreement with the Septuagint. The printed editions have: “and I awoke, because the Lord sustained me.”]

Could anyone be so foolish as to think that the prophet wished to tell us something remarkable merely by saying that he slept and awoke, unless this sleep were death and the awakening resurrection, which had to be prophesied in this way concerning Christ?

This is shown much more clearly in Psalm 40, where, as is customary, things that were to come are narrated in the person of the same Mediator as though they had already happened. What was going to happen was already, in God’s predestination and foreknowledge, as though accomplished, because it was certain [Note: [Col. 0552] Ludovicus Vives notes that an old copy does not contain *quia certa erant* (“because they were certain”), and it appears to have been added by someone as a marginal explanation. Nevertheless, all the books we have examined contain it.].

> “My enemies spoke evil against me: When will he die, and his name perish?  
> And if he entered in order to see, his heart spoke vain things; he gathered iniquity to himself.  
> He went out and spoke to the same purpose.”  
> All my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evil.  
> They established an iniquitous word against me: Surely one who sleeps will not rise again?”

[Note: [Col. 0552] The old Corbie manuscript reads: “and they spoke.”]

Here these words are certainly arranged so that they are understood to mean nothing other than if he had said, “Surely one who dies will not rise again?” The preceding words show that his enemies had contemplated and planned his death, and that this was carried out by the one who entered in order to see and went out in order to betray him. Who would not recognize here Judas, who became his betrayer from among his disciples?

Since they were going to do what they plotted—that is, kill him—he showed that they would kill him in vain, because he would rise again, and he added this verse as though he were saying: “What are you doing, foolish men? Your crime will be my sleep. Surely one who sleeps will not rise again?”

Yet he indicates in the following verses that they would not commit so great a crime with impunity:

> “Indeed, the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified his heel against me”—that is, trampled upon me.  
> “But you, O Lord, have mercy on me, raise me up, and I shall repay them” (Psalm 40:6–11).

Who could now deny this, seeing that after Christ’s passion and resurrection the Jews were utterly uprooted from their dwelling places by the devastation and destruction of war [Note: [Col. 0552] Besides the Fathers, Rabbi Samuel Marochianus demonstrates that this was punishment for the crime committed against Christ in his book *On the Advent of the Messiah*. — Coquaeus.]? For he was killed by them, rose again, and meanwhile repaid them with a temporal discipline, except for what he reserves for those who have not been corrected, when he judges the living and the dead.

The Lord Jesus himself, showing this very betrayer to the apostles by offering him the morsel of bread (John 13:26), also recalled this verse of the psalm and said that it had been fulfilled in him:

> “He who ate my bread magnified his heel against me.”

But the words “in whom I hoped” do not suit the head; they suit the body. For the Savior himself did not fail to know him, of whom he had already said, “One of you is a devil” [Note: [Col. 0552] In some manuscripts two passages are cited here as follows: “One of you will betray me,” and “One of you is a devil.” The former is from John 13:21.].

He is accustomed, however, to transfer to himself the person of his members and to attribute to himself what belongs to them, because head and body are one Christ. Hence the Gospel says:

> “I was hungry, and you gave me food.”

Explaining this, he says:

> “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:35, 40).

Thus he said that he had hoped for what his disciples at that time had hoped concerning Judas, when he had been numbered among the apostles.

2. The Jews, however, do not hope that the Christ whom they expect will die. Therefore they do not think that the one whom the Law and the Prophets announced is our Christ; instead, they fabricate some Christ of their own, whom they imagine to be exempt from the suffering of death. Accordingly, with astonishing vanity and blindness, they insist that the words we have quoted signify not death and resurrection but sleep and awakening.

But Psalm 15 also cries out to them:

> “For this reason my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh also will rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15:9–10).

Who would say that his flesh rested in such hope that, while his soul was not abandoned in the underworld but quickly returned to it and revived him, it would not be corrupted as corpses ordinarily are—unless he were the one who rose on the third day? They certainly cannot say this of the prophet and king David.

Psalm 67 also cries out:

> “Our God is the God of salvation, and the Lord’s are the exits from death” (Psalm 67:21).

[Note: [Col. 0553] In the printed editions: “and the Lord, the Lord’s exits from death.” *Domini* (“of the Lord”) is not repeated in the manuscripts or in the Septuagint.]

[Note: [Col. 0553] Lest anyone be misled, *exitus* is nominative plural—*hai diexodoi tou thanatou*—not singular genitive. — Ludovicus Vives.]

What could be said more openly? Jesus is the Lord who is the God of salvation, for his name is interpreted as “Savior” or “Salutary.” The reason for this name was given when, before he was born from the virgin, it was said:

> “She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

Since his blood was poured out for the remission of sins, it was certainly not fitting that he should have other exits from this life than through death. Therefore, after it had been said, “Our God is the God of salvation,” it immediately adds, “And the Lord’s are the exits from death,” so that it might be shown that by dying he would accomplish salvation.

Yet the wording “and the Lord’s” is wonderfully expressed, as though it said: “Such is this mortal life that even the Lord himself could not depart from it in any other way than through death.”

## CHAPTER XIX — On Psalm 68, in which the Jews’ persistent unbelief is declared

But since the Jews do not yield at all before such manifest testimonies of prophecy, even though the events have been brought to such a clear and certain fulfillment [Note: [Col. 0553] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have: “do not believe.”], what is written in the psalm that follows is surely fulfilled in them.

For when, in that psalm also, the things concerning Christ’s passion were prophetically spoken in his person, there was recalled what became evident in the Gospel:

> “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68:22; Matthew 27:34, 48).

Then, as though immediately after such a meal and such provisions, he added:

> “Let their table before them become a snare, and a retribution, and a stumbling block.  
> Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see; and make their back continually bent” (Psalm 68:23–24),

and the remaining words, which were spoken not as a wish but prophetically in the form of a wish.

What wonder, then, if they do not see these manifest things, whose eyes have been darkened so that they may not see? What wonder if they do not look upward toward heavenly things, whose back is continually bent so that they remain bowed toward earthly things [Note: [Col. 0554] Vinding, Amelote, and some manuscripts read *suscipiunt* (“receive”) instead of *suspiciunt* (“look upward”).]?

By these expressions transferred from the body, the vices of their minds are signified.

Let this much be said about the Psalms—that is, about the prophecy of King David—so that there may be some limit. Let those who read these things, and already know all of them, forgive me; and let them not complain about those matters which they either understand or suppose that I may have omitted, perhaps because they are more firmly established.

## CHAPTER XX — On David’s kingdom and merit, and on his son Solomon; and on the prophecy concerning Christ found either in the books attributed to Solomon or in those certainly written by him

1. David therefore reigned in earthly Jerusalem, the son of the heavenly Jerusalem, and was greatly praised by divine testimony. For his sins were overcome by such devotion through the saving humility of repentance that he is unquestionably among those of whom he himself says:

> “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1).

After him his son Solomon reigned over the whole same people. As was said above, he began to reign while his father was still alive. He had good beginnings but a bad end. Prosperity, which wears down the minds of the wise [Note: [Col. 0554] He imitates Sallust in *The War against Catiline*, chapter 11, where these words also occur: “For prosperity wears down the minds of the wise.”], harmed him more than the wisdom itself benefited him—wisdom that is memorable even now and henceforth, and that was then praised far and wide.

He too is found to have prophesied in his books, three of which have been received as canonical: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Two others, one called Wisdom and the other Ecclesiasticus, have, because of a certain similarity of style, acquired the customary attribution to Solomon. The more learned, however, do not doubt that they are not his; nevertheless, the Church, especially in the West, received them into authoritative use from ancient times [Note: [Col. 0554] See Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, section 13, and the *Speculum*.].

In one of them, called the Wisdom of Solomon, Christ’s passion is most openly prophesied. For the impious men who killed him are recalled as saying:

> “Let us surround the righteous man, because he is unpleasant to us and opposed to our works; he reproaches us for sins against the law and brings disgrace upon us for the sins of our discipline.  
> He professes to have knowledge of God and calls himself a son of God.  
> He has become a reproach to our thoughts.  
> He is burdensome even to see, because his life is unlike that of others and his ways are changed.  
> We are regarded by him as worthless, and he keeps away from our ways as from impurities.  
> He prefers the end of the righteous and boasts that he has God as his father.  
> Let us see, then, whether his words are true, and let us test what will happen to him, and we shall know what his end will be.  
> For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his enemies.  
> Let us question him with insults and torture, so that we may know his reverence and test his patience.  
> Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, for, according to his words, there will be regard for him.”

> “Thus they thought, and they were deceived; for their wickedness blinded them” (Wisdom 2:12–21).

In Ecclesiasticus, the future faith of the nations is foretold in this manner:

> “Have mercy on us, O God, ruler of all things, and send your fear over all the nations.  
> Raise your hand over foreign nations, and let them see your power.  
> Just as you were sanctified before them in us, so may you be magnified before us in them, so that they may acknowledge you, just as we have acknowledged you, because there is no God besides you, O Lord” (Ecclesiasticus 36:1–5).

We see this prophecy, expressed in the form of a wish and prayer, fulfilled through Jesus Christ. But against those who contradict us, testimonies that are not written in the Jewish canon are not brought forward with equal firmness.

2. In the three books known to be Solomon’s, and which the Jews also hold to be canonical, a laborious discussion is necessary to show that whatever of this kind is found in them pertains to Christ and the Church. If undertaken now, it would extend us beyond what is appropriate.

Nevertheless, what is read in Proverbs, where impious men are said to speak as follows:

> “Let us unjustly hide the righteous man in the earth; let us swallow him alive like the underworld, and remove his memory from the earth; let us seize his precious possession” (Proverbs 1:11–13),

is not so obscure that it cannot be understood, without laborious explanation, of Christ and his possession, the Church. For the Lord Jesus himself also indicated something similar in the Gospel parable, when he showed that the wicked tenants said:

> “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matthew 21:38).

Likewise, the passage in the same book which we touched upon earlier, when we were discussing the barren woman who bore seven children (above, chapter 4, section 4), has habitually been understood as referring to Christ and the Church as soon as it is uttered by those who know Christ to be the Wisdom of God:

> “Wisdom built herself a house and supported it with seven pillars.  
> She sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine in the bowl, and prepared her table.  
> She sent her servants, calling with a noble proclamation to the bowl, saying: Whoever is foolish, let him turn to me.  
> And she said to those lacking sense: Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Proverbs 9:1–5).

Here we certainly recognize the Wisdom of God—that is, the Word coeternal with the Father—building for herself a house of human flesh in the virgin’s womb and joining the Church to it as members to a head; sacrificing the victims of the martyrs; preparing a table with wine and bread, where the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek also appears; and calling the foolish and those lacking sense because, as the Apostle says, “God chose the weak things of this world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

To these weak ones she nevertheless says what follows:

> “Abandon foolishness, so that you may live; and seek wisdom, so that you may have life” (Proverbs 9:6).

To become a participant in that table is itself to begin to possess life.

In another book, called Ecclesiastes, it says:

> “There is no good for a person except to eat and drink” (Ecclesiastes 8:15).

What can this more credibly be understood to mean than participation in this table, which the priest and Mediator of the New Testament himself provides according to the order of Melchizedek from his body and blood? That sacrifice succeeded all the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which were offered as a shadow of what was to come. For this reason we also recognize the voice of that same Mediator speaking prophetically in Psalm 39:

> “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you fashioned a body for me” (Psalm 39:7).

For in place of all those sacrifices and offerings his body is offered and administered to those who participate.

That this Ecclesiastes, in its repeated and strongly emphasized statements about eating and drinking, does not mean the pleasures of bodily feasting is sufficiently shown where it says:

> “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of drinking.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of feasting” (Ecclesiastes 7:3, 5).

But I think the passage in this book that concerns the two cities—one belonging to the devil and the other to Christ—and their kings, the devil and Christ, deserves greater mention:

> “Woe to you, land, whose king is a boy and whose princes eat in the morning.  
> Blessed are you, land, whose king is the son of the freeborn, and whose princes eat at the proper time, in strength and not in confusion” (Ecclesiastes 10:16–17).

He called the devil a boy because of the foolishness, pride, rashness, insolence, and the other vices that commonly abound in that age. Christ, however, is called the son of the freeborn—that is, of the holy patriarchs who belong to the free city, from whom he was descended according to the flesh.

The princes of that city eat in the morning, that is, before the proper hour, because they do not await the fitting time, which is true happiness in the age to come. They desire to be blessed hastily by the splendor of this age [Note: [Col. 0556] Several manuscripts read: “desiring to be blessed by the speed of this age.”].

The princes of Christ’s city patiently await the time of true blessedness. The passage says, “in strength and not in confusion,” because hope does not deceive them. Concerning this the Apostle says, “Hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5:5). The Psalm also says:

> “Indeed, those who await you shall not be put to shame” (Psalm 24:3).

[Note: [Col. 0556] Lovaniensis reads: “Indeed, all those who await you.” *Universi* (“all”) is absent from the other books.]

Finally, the Song of Songs is a kind of spiritual pleasure belonging to holy minds, in the marriage of that King and queen of the city—that is, Christ and the Church. This pleasure is wrapped in allegorical coverings so that it may be desired more ardently, be unveiled more delightfully, and reveal the bridegroom, to whom it is said in the same Song:

> “Equity has loved you” (Song of Songs 1:3).

And the bride hears there:

> “Love is in your delights” (Song of Songs 7:6).

[Note: [Col. 0556] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *Tacite* (“silently”).]

We pass over many things in silence, out of concern to bring this work to an end.

## CHAPTER XXI — On the kings after Solomon, whether in Judah or in Israel

The other kings after Solomon are scarcely found to have prophesied, through any riddles in their sayings or deeds, concerning Christ and the Church, whether in Judah or in Israel.

These were the names given to the parts of that people after it was divided, by God’s judgment, on account of Solomon’s offense, in the time of his son Rehoboam, who succeeded his father in the kingdom. The ten tribes received by Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, who was established as their king in Samaria, were properly called Israel, although that had been the name of the entire people. The two tribes—Judah and Benjamin—which, for David’s sake, remained subject to the city of Jerusalem so that the kingdom of his lineage might not be completely eradicated, were called Judah, because that was the tribe from which David came.

Benjamin was the other tribe belonging to the same kingdom, as I have said; from it came Saul, who was king before David. But these two tribes together were called Judah, as has been said, and by this name they were distinguished from Israel, which properly designated the ten tribes possessing their own king [Note: [Col. 0557] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *quae* (“which”). The other manuscripts more correctly read *quod*, referring to the name “Israel.”].

The tribe of Levi, because it was priestly and devoted to the service of God rather than to that of kings, was counted as a thirteenth tribe. Joseph, one of the twelve sons of Israel, produced not one tribe, as each of the others did, but two: Ephraim and Manasseh. Nevertheless, the tribe of Levi also belonged more closely to the kingdom of Jerusalem, where the temple of God was located and served by it.

After the people had been divided, Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, first reigned in Jerusalem as king of Judah, while Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, reigned in Samaria as king of Israel. When Rehoboam wished to pursue the divided portion by war as though it were a tyranny, the people were forbidden to fight against their brothers. God declared through a prophet that he had caused this division (1 Kings 12:24). From this it became clear that in this matter there had been no sin either on the part of the king of Israel or on the part of the people, but that the will of God, who was exacting vengeance, had been fulfilled.

Once they had recognized this, both sides remained at peace with one another. The division had been one of kingship, not of religion.

## CHAPTER XXII — On Jeroboam, who profaned the people subject to him through the impiety of idolatry, although God did not cease to inspire prophets among them and to preserve many from the crime of idolatry

[Note: [Col. 0557] In the earlier printed editions: “to inspire prophecies.”]

But Jeroboam, king of Israel, perversely refusing to believe the God whom he had proved truthful by the kingdom promised and granted to him, feared that if the people went to the temple of God in Jerusalem—for according to the divine law the whole nation had to go there for the purpose of offering sacrifices—they would be won over by the king of Judah and restored to the royal stock of David.

He therefore established idolatry in his kingdom and, through a wicked impiety, deceived the people of God, binding them with himself to the worship of images. Yet God did not entirely cease reproving not only that king but also his successors and imitators in impiety, as well as the people themselves, through the prophets.

For there arose there also those great and illustrious prophets who performed many wonders: Elijah and his disciple Elisha. When Elijah said there, “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they are seeking my life” (1 Kings 19:10), he received the answer that seven thousand men were there who had not bent the knee before Baal.

## CHAPTER XXIII — On the varying condition of the two Hebrew kingdoms, until both peoples were led into captivity at different times, and Judah was afterward restored to its kingdom, which finally passed into Roman power

In the kingdom of Judah, which belonged to Jerusalem, prophets likewise continued to appear during the reigns of the succeeding kings, as God was pleased to send them either to foretell what was necessary or to rebuke sins and command righteousness.

For there too, although far fewer than in Israel, there were kings who gravely offended God by their impieties and were punished, together with a similar people, by moderate scourges [Note: [Col. 0558] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *simul* (“together”). Vinding, Amelote, and the manuscripts more correctly read *simili* (“similar”).]. The merits of the pious kings there are also praised at considerable length.

In Israel, on the other hand, we read of kings who were all rejected, though some were more and others less wicked. Both divisions, therefore, as divine providence commanded or permitted, were raised up by various successes and oppressed by adversities. They were afflicted not only by foreign wars but also by civil wars among themselves, so that, when the causes were evident, the mercy or anger of God might be made manifest.

At length, as his indignation increased, that entire nation was conquered by the Chaldeans. It was not only overthrown in its own dwellings but also, for the greater part, transferred to the lands of the Assyrians: first the portion called Israel, consisting of the ten tribes, and afterward Judah as well, after Jerusalem and that most renowned temple had been destroyed. In those lands it spent seventy years in captivity.

After that time it was released and restored the temple that had been destroyed. Although many of its people continued to live in foreign lands, it no longer had two divisions of the kingdom, with two different kings in the separate portions. Rather, there was one ruler in Jerusalem, and all of them, wherever they might be and from whatever place they could come, went at appointed times to the temple of God that was there.

Even then, however, it did not lack enemies from other nations who attacked and conquered it. For Christ found them already tributary to the Romans.

## CHAPTER XXIV — On the prophets who were either the last among the Jews or whom the Gospel history reports around the time of Christ’s birth
Throughout all that time, from their return from Babylon, after Malachi, Haggai, and Zechariah, who prophesied then, and Ezra, they had no prophets until the Savior’s coming, except for another Zechariah, the father of John, and his wife Elizabeth, when Christ’s birth was already near; and, after he had been born, the aged Simeon and Anna, a widow already advanced in years, [Col. 0559] and John himself, the last of them. As a young man, he pointed out Christ, already a young man, not by predicting him as one who was still to come, but nevertheless by revealing him, unknown as he was, through prophetic knowledge. For this reason the Lord himself says: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Matt. 11:13).

But the prophecy of these five is known to us from the Gospel, where the Virgin herself, the Lord’s mother, is also found to have prophesied before John (Luke 1:46–55). Yet the wicked Jews do not accept the prophecy of these people; those among them who believed the Gospel in countless numbers did accept it. For it was then that Israel was truly divided into two, by that division which had been foretold through the prophet Samuel as irrevocable for King Saul. The wicked Jews nevertheless also accept Malachi, Haggai, Zechariah, and Ezra as the last authors admitted to canonical authority. Their writings exist, as do those of others who, amid the great multitude of prophets, wrote very few works that acquired canonical authority. [Note: [Col. 0560] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “prophesied.”]

Of their predictions, insofar as they concern Christ and his Church, I see that some ought to be inserted in this work. This will be done more conveniently, with the Lord’s help, in the following book, so that we do not burden this already very lengthy one any further.

# BOOK EIGHTEEN [Note: [Col. 0559] Written about the year 426. See below, ch. 54.]

He discusses the course of the earthly city from the time of Abraham to the end of the world together with the heavenly city, and touches upon prophecies concerning Christ, both those of the Sibyls and, above all, those of the sacred Prophets who wrote from the beginning of the Roman kingdom onward: Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, Micah, and those who followed.

[Col. 0559]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On the matters discussed in the seventeen books up to the time of the Savior

[Col. 0559]

I promised that I would write about the origin, course [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscripts 2050, 2051, and 258 read “progress.” M.], and appointed ends of the two cities—one belonging to God, the other to this world, in which the former is now a pilgrim, insofar as the human race is concerned—after I had first refuted, insofar as his grace assisted me, the enemies of the city of God, who prefer their gods to its founder, Christ, and who, in a most destructive envy, fiercely begrudge Christians their existence. I did this in the first ten books.

Of the threefold undertaking I have just mentioned, the origin of both cities was arranged in the four books that followed the tenth [Note: [Col. 0559] In the Lovaniensis edition: “in the tenth,” less well.]; then came their course from the first man to the Flood in one book, the fifteenth of this work; and from there to Abraham both cities proceeded once again, in their historical periods as well as in our writings. But from Abraham, the father, to the time of the Israelite kings—where we completed the sixteenth volume—and from there to the Savior’s coming in the flesh, to which the seventeenth book extends, only the city of God seems to have proceeded in my [Note: [Col. 0559] The Amiens and Lovaniensis editions read “in the midst.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts read “in my.”] [Col. 0559] writing.

Yet in this world it did not proceed alone; rather, both cities, as they had proceeded together from the beginning, certainly varied the course of time within the human race. I did this, however, so that from the time when God’s promises began to become clearer up to his birth from the Virgin—in whom [Note: [Col. 0559] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads “in whom.”] what had first been promised was to be fulfilled—the city that belongs to God might appear more distinctly as it proceeded without interruption from the opposition of the other city, although until the revelation of the New Testament it proceeded not in the light but in the shadow.

Now, therefore, I see that what I had interrupted must be resumed, so that I may touch, as much as seems sufficient, on how the other city also proceeded from the time of Abraham, in order that readers may compare the two with one another.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### On the kings and periods of the earthly city, whose reckoning from Abraham’s origin corresponds with the periods of the saints

1. The society of mortals, spread everywhere throughout the earth and bound together by a certain fellowship of one and the same nature despite the greatest diversity of places, pursues its various interests and desires. Since what is sought either suffices for no one or not for everyone—for it is not the same thing—it is frequently divided against itself, and the stronger part crushes the weaker. For the defeated yields to the victorious, preferring domination, or even a certain kind of liberty, to peace and safety; so much so that those who preferred death to servitude have been objects of great wonder.

For in almost every nation this voice of nature has in some way resounded: those who were conquered preferred to be subjected to their victors rather than destroyed by warfare and devastation in every direction. Hence it came about—not without the providence of God, in whose power it lies whether each person is subjected to another in war or subjects another—that some were endowed with kingdoms and others made subject to rulers.

But among the many kingdoms of the earth into which the society concerned with earthly advantage or desire is divided—which, in a universal term, we call the city of this world—we see two kingdoms that have far surpassed the others in renown: first that of the Assyrians, then that of the Romans, ordered and distinguished from each other both in time and in place. For as the former came first and the latter afterward, so the former arose in the East and the latter in the West. Indeed, the end of the former was immediately the beginning of the latter [Col. 0560] [Note: See below, ch. 27.]. I might call the other kingdoms and kings appendages of these two.

2. Ninus was already the second king of the Assyrians, having succeeded his father Belus, the first king of that kingdom, when Abraham was born in the land of the Chaldeans [Col. 0561] [Note: He said above, in book 16, chapter 17, that Abraham was born in the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign, following the Chronicle of Eusebius. Others, rejecting this, assign Abraham’s birth to the twenty-third year of Semiramis.].

At that time the kingdom of the Sicyonians was also very small. From it that supremely learned man Marcus Varro began his account when writing on *The Origin of the Roman People*, as though from an ancient period. For from the kings of the Sicyonians he proceeded to the Athenians, from them to the Latins, and from the Latins to the Romans. Yet, before the foundation of Rome, these peoples are remembered as exceedingly insignificant in comparison with the Assyrian kingdom.

Sallust, the Roman historian, also acknowledges that the Athenians were especially renowned in Greece, though more by reputation than in reality. Speaking of them, he says:

> “The achievements of the Athenians, as I judge them, were sufficiently extensive and magnificent; yet they were somewhat less than they are reputed to have been. But because great talents in writing arose there, the deeds of the Athenians are celebrated throughout the world as the greatest. Thus the virtue of those who performed them is considered as great as illustrious talents were able to exalt it in words” (*The War with Catiline*, ch. 8).

This city also gained no small glory from literature and philosophy, since such studies flourished there above all. But as far as imperial power is concerned, in the earliest times no kingdom was greater than that of the Assyrians, nor one so widely and extensively spread. For it is said that King Ninus, son of Belus, subdued all Asia—which is said to be one-third of the entire world in number of its parts, but half of it in size—as far as the borders of Libya [Col. 0561] [Note: See below, ch. 22; and above, book 16, ch. 17, and book 4, ch. 6.].

He did not rule only over the Indians in the eastern regions; yet after his death his wife Semiramis attacked them in war. Thus it came about that all the peoples or kings in those lands were subject to the Assyrian kingdom and authority and carried out whatever was commanded.

Abraham, therefore, was born among the Chaldeans in that kingdom during the time of Ninus. But because Greek affairs are much better known to us than Assyrian affairs, and because those who investigated the antiquity of the Roman people traced the sequence of times through the Greeks to the Latins, and then to the Romans, who themselves are also Latins, we ought, where necessary, to mention the Assyrian kings, so that it may be apparent how Babylon, as it were the first Rome, proceeded as a pilgrim together with the city of God in this world.

The events that ought to be inserted into this work for the sake of comparing the two cities—namely, the earthly and the heavenly—should be drawn chiefly from Greek and Latin sources, where Rome itself is, as it were, a second Babylon.

3. When Abraham was born, the second kings were Ninus among the Assyrians and Europs among the Sicyonians [Col. 0561] [Note: Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*.]; their first kings had been Belus in the former kingdom and Aegialeus in the latter.

When Abraham had departed from Babylon and God promised him that a great nation would arise from him and that in his seed all nations would be blessed, the Assyrians had their fourth king and the Sicyonians their fifth. Among the Assyrians, the son of Ninus reigned after his mother Semiramis, who is said to have been killed by him after she dared to commit incest with her son.

Some think that she founded Babylon [Col. 0562], though she could certainly have restored it [Note: Diodorus, Justin, and others assert that Babylon was built by Semiramis. Josephus, Eusebius, Marcellinus, and others say that she merely restored it and enclosed it within an immense circuit of walls, counted among the wonders of the world, said to have extended for 480 stades.]. When and how it was founded, we explained in the sixteenth book (ch. 4).

The son of Ninus and Semiramis, who succeeded his mother in the kingdom, is called by some Ninus himself, but by others Ninyas, a name derived from that of his father [Note: The printed editions have *Ninyum*. But the manuscripts, together with Eusebius, have *Ninyam*.].

At that time Telxion held the kingdom of the Sicyonians [Note: The printed editions have *Telexion*. The manuscripts have *Telxion*, or *Telsion*.]. During his reign, conditions there were so peaceful and happy that after his death they worshiped him as a god, offering sacrifices and celebrating games said to have been instituted for him first.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### Under which kings Isaac was born to Abraham, at the age of one hundred, from the promise, and under which Isaac, at the age of sixty, had the twins Esau and Jacob by Rebekah

During the reign of these kings, Isaac, Abraham’s son, was also born according to God’s promise. His mother Sarah, who was barren and already an old woman, had lost hope of offspring. At that time Arrius was the fifth king of the Assyrians [Note: Eusebius’s *Chronicle* has *Analius*. From our manuscripts and from several Benedictine manuscripts we restore *Arrius*. [*Aralius*.] M.].

When Isaac was sixty, twins, Esau and Jacob, were born to him; his wife Rebekah bore them while their grandfather Abraham was still alive and was 160 years old. After completing 175 years, Abraham died while Xerxes—the earlier king of that name, also called Baleus [Note: Eusebius has *Balaneus*.]—was reigning among the Assyrians, and Thuriacus among the Sicyonians, whom some write as Thurimachus [Note: Several manuscripts have *Thirimacus*. Eusebius has *Thiramachus*.]. They were the seventh kings.

The kingdom of the Argives also arose at the same time as Abraham’s grandsons; Inachus was its first king. It should certainly not be omitted that Varro reports that the Sicyonians also used to sacrifice at the tomb of their seventh king, Thuriacus.

When the eighth kings were reigning—Armamitre among the Assyrians, Leucippus among the Sicyonians, and Inachus, the first of the Argives—God spoke to Isaac and promised him the same two things he had promised his father: namely, the land of Canaan to his offspring and the blessing of all nations in his offspring.

These same promises were also made to his son, Abraham’s grandson, who was first called Jacob and later Israel, when Belocus was reigning as the ninth Assyrian king, Phoroneus, son of Inachus, as the second king of the Argives, and Leucippus still among the Sicyonians.

During these times, Greece under Phoroneus, the Argive king, became somewhat more distinguished through the establishment of laws and courts. Yet when Phegous, the younger brother of Phoroneus, died, a temple was established at his tomb in which he was worshiped as a god and oxen were sacrificed to him.

I believe that they considered him worthy of so great an honor because, in the portion of the kingdom assigned to him—for their father had distributed territories to both brothers in which they would reign while he was alive—he had established shrines for the worship of the gods and had taught people to observe the divisions of time by months and years, and how their contents should be measured and counted [Col. 0563].

At this new phenomenon, ignorant people were amazed, and after his death they either imagined or wished him to have become a god.

Io is also said to have been the daughter of Inachus. She was later called Isis and worshiped in Egypt as a great goddess. Others, however, write that she came from Ethiopia into Egypt as queen, and that because she ruled widely and justly and introduced many useful practices and letters to the Egyptians, divine honor was paid to her after she died there—such honor that anyone who said she had been a human being became liable to capital punishment.

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### On the times of Jacob and his son Joseph

When Baleus was reigning as the tenth king of the Assyrians, and Messapus as the ninth king of the Sicyonians—whom some also report as Cephisos [Note: Some manuscripts have *Cephisus*.]—if indeed one man bore two names and they did not instead mistakenly regard one name as belonging to another man whom they recorded in their writings under the other name—and when Apis was the third king of the Argives, Isaac died at the age of 180 and left his twin sons at the age of 120.

The younger of them, Jacob, who belonged to the city of God about which we are writing, while the elder was certainly rejected, had twelve sons. His brothers sold one of them, Joseph, to merchants traveling into Egypt, while their grandfather Isaac was still alive [Note: Compare *Questions on Genesis*, question 122.].

Joseph stood before Pharaoh when, after the humiliation he had endured, he was exalted, being thirty years old.
