For by divinely interpreting the king’s dreams, he foretold that seven years of abundance would come, whose overwhelming plenty would be consumed by another seven barren years that would follow. For this reason the king placed him over Egypt after releasing him from prison, into which the integrity of his chastity had cast him.

He had firmly preserved that integrity before a mistress who loved him wickedly and who lied to her master, who wrongly believed her; when she seized him as he fled, leaving his garment in her hands, he did not consent to the violation.

In the second year of the seven barren years, Jacob came into Egypt with all his household to his son, being 130 years old, as he himself replied when the king questioned him (Gen. 47:9). Joseph was then thirty-nine: thirty years, namely, the age he had when the king honored him, plus the seven years of abundance and two years of famine.

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### On Apis, king of the Argives, whom the Egyptians worshiped under the name Serapis with divine honor

At this time Apis, king not of the Egyptians but of the Argives, crossed by ship into Egypt. After he died there, he became Serapis, the greatest of all the Egyptian gods.

Varro gave a very simple explanation of why he was called Serapis rather than Apis after his death. The chest in which a dead person is placed—which everyone now calls a sarcophagus [Note: *Sarcophagon*, that is, “flesh-eating”; in Greek *soros*, meaning a chest or urn.]—is called *soros* in Greek. Since people began to venerate him as buried there before his temple had been built, he was at first called, as it were, Soros-Apis, or Sorapis; then, with one letter changed, as often happens, he was called Serapis [Note: For an assessment of these etymologies, see Jablonski, *Pantheon Aegyptiorum*, book 2, ch. 5, §8, who will teach you better. LARCHER.].

It was also decreed concerning him that anyone who said he had been a human being would suffer capital punishment. And since almost every temple in which Isis and Serapis were worshiped also contained an image that seemed, by pressing a finger to its lips, to give a sign that silence should be maintained, Varro thinks that this meant that people were to keep silent about their having been human beings.

The ox which Egypt, deceived by astonishing folly, nourished in luxurious abundance in his honor was called Apis, not Serapis, because they worshiped it alive without a sarcophagus. When that ox died, they searched for and found a calf of the same color, marked in the same way with certain white spots, and believed that something marvelous and divinely arranged for them had occurred.

It was not difficult for demons, in order to deceive them, to display the appearance of such a bull to a cow that alone could see it while she was conceiving and pregnant, so that the mother’s desire might attract whatever would already appear bodily in her offspring—just as Jacob, by means of variegated rods, brought it about that variegated sheep and goats were born (Gen. 30:37–42). For what human beings can display to animals that are conceiving by means of real colors and bodies, demons can very easily display by means of fictitious forms.

## CHAPTER SIX  
### During whose reign among the Argives and whose among the Assyrians Jacob died in Egypt

Apis, then, the king not of the Egyptians but of the Argives, died in Egypt. His son Argus succeeded him in the kingdom; from his name the Argives and their city Argos received their names. Under the earlier kings, neither the place nor the people yet bore this name.

While Argus was reigning among the Argives, Erato among the Sicyonians, and Baleus still among the Assyrians, Jacob died in Egypt at the age of 147. As he was dying, he blessed his sons and his grandsons through Joseph and most openly prophesied Christ, saying in his blessing of Judah:

> “The prince shall not fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until the things reserved for him come; and he himself is the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10).

Under Argus, Greece began to use crops and to have grainfields in cultivation, after seeds had been brought in from elsewhere. Argus, too, began after his death to be regarded as a god and was honored with a temple and sacrifices.

While he was reigning, this honor had previously been bestowed on a private individual, a certain Homogyros, who had been struck by lightning, because he was the first to yoke oxen to a plow.

## CHAPTER SEVEN  
### Under which kings Joseph died in Egypt

When Mamitus was reigning as the twelfth king of the Assyrians [Note: The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erfurt manuscripts have *Hermascus*. Some manuscripts have *Amythus*. Others, with the Lovaniensis, have *Mamitus*, following Eusebius, who nevertheless places him not as the twelfth but as the eleventh Assyrian king; then he places Manchaelus as the twelfth, Iphereus as the thirteenth, and Mamytas as the fourteenth. In the following chapter Augustine gives Saphrus in place of him.], Plemaeneus as the eleventh king of the Sicyonians [Note: More manuscripts have *Plemmeus*. Eusebius calls him *Plenneus*.], and Argus still remained king among the Argives, Joseph died in Egypt at the age of 110 (Gen. 50:25).

After his death, the people of God, growing astonishingly, remained in Egypt for 145 years: peacefully at first, until those who had known Joseph died; afterward, because their increase was envied and regarded with suspicion, they were afflicted by persecutions and oppressed by the intolerable labors of slavery until they were liberated from there [Note: The printed editions add after *persecutionibus*: “he was afflicted by countless [persecutions],” which is absent from the manuscripts.]. Yet even amid these persecutions they increased through a divinely bestowed fruitfulness.

In Assyria and Greece, the same kingdoms continued throughout this period.

## CHAPTER EIGHT  
### Under which kings Moses was born, and what religion of the gods arose during the same period

When Saphrus was reigning as the fourteenth king of the Assyrians, Orthopolis as the twelfth king of the Sicyonians, and Criasus as the fifth king of the Argives, Moses was born in Egypt. Through him the people of God were freed from Egyptian slavery, in which they had to be disciplined in such a way as to desire the aid of their Creator.

Some believe that Prometheus lived during the reigns of these kings [Note: Thus Eusebius speaks in the *Chronicle*, expressing the opinion of others: “According to the opinion of some,” he says, “Prometheus lived in these times, from whom they say that human beings were made; and in fact, since he was wise, he transformed their wildness and excessive ignorance into humanity and knowledge.”]. They say that he formed human beings from clay because he is said to have been an excellent teacher of wisdom; yet it is not shown who the wise men of his time were.

His brother Atlas is said to have been a great astrologer [Note: The old books consistently write *Atlans*.]. Hence fable found an occasion to invent that he carried the heavens, although a mountain is called by his name, and its height seems rather to have given rise to the popular belief that it supported the sky.

Many other fabulous tales also began to be invented in Greece during those times. But until Cecrops became king of the Athenians—under whose reign that city also received its name, and under whose reign God led his people out of Egypt through Moses—some dead people were included among the gods through the blind and vain custom and superstition of the Greeks.

Among these were Melantomice, the wife of King Criasus [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erfurt manuscripts have *Melancomice*. The Lovaniensis has *Melantonice*.]; their son Phorbas, who became the sixth king of the Argives after his father; Iasus, the son of the seventh king Triopas; and the ninth king, Sthenelas—also written Stheneleus or Sthenelus, for the name appears variously in different authors.

Mercury is also said to have lived during these times, the grandson of Atlas through his daughter Maia, as more popular writings also proclaim. He became famous for his knowledge of many arts, which he also handed down to human beings. For this merit they wished, or perhaps believed, that he had become a god after his death.

Hercules is said to have lived later, though he belonged to those times of the Argives. Some, however, place him earlier than Mercury; I think they are mistaken. But regardless of when they were born, serious historians who committed these ancient matters to writing agree that both were human beings and that, because they conferred many benefits on mortals for the more advantageous conduct of this life, they deserved divine honors from them.

Minerva, however, was much more ancient than these. For in the time of Ogygus she is said to have appeared as a maiden beside the lake called Tritonis; hence she was also called Tritonia. She was the inventor of many works and was believed to be a goddess all the more readily because her origin was less known.

The story that she was born from Jupiter’s head, sung by poets and found in fables, must be applied to poetry and fiction, not to history and actual events.

Although historians do not agree about when Ogygus himself lived—during whose time a great flood also occurred, though not the greatest flood, in which no human beings escaped except those who could have been in the ark, a flood known to neither Greek nor Latin history [Note: Josephus writes in book 1, chapter 4, of *The Jewish Antiquities*, and Eusebius, following him, in book 9, chapters 11 and 12, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, that there were nevertheless pagan historians who remembered that greatest and universal flood and Noah’s ark: namely, Berossus of Babylon, Mnaseas, Nicolaus of Damascus, and Hieronymus of Egypt. But the writings of those pagans belong to barbarian histories, not to the Greek or Latin histories of which Augustine is speaking. LUD. VIVES.]—nor do they agree whether it was greater than the flood that later occurred in the time of Deucalion.

For Varro began the book I mentioned above from that point and proposed nothing more ancient, from which he could proceed to Roman affairs, than the flood of Ogygus—that is, the flood that occurred in Ogygus’s time.

Our own chroniclers, first Eusebius and then Jerome, who certainly followed earlier historians in this opinion, report that the flood of Ogygus occurred more than 300 years afterward, when Phoroneus was already reigning as the second king of the Argives.

But whenever it occurred, Minerva was already worshiped as a goddess when Cecrops was king of the Athenians. Under that king the city itself is also said either to have been restored or to have been founded.

## CHAPTER NINE  
### When the city of the Athenians was founded, and what cause Varro gives for its name

Varro gives the following explanation of why it was called Athens—a name certainly derived from Minerva, who is called Ἀθηνᾶ (*Athēnā*) in Greek.

When an olive tree suddenly appeared there and water burst forth in another place, these portents disturbed the king, who sent to the Delphic Apollo to ask what should be understood and what should be done. Apollo replied that the olive signified Minerva, the water Neptune, and that it lay within the power of the citizens to decide after which of the two gods, whose signs these were, the city should be called.

After receiving this oracle, Cecrops summoned all the citizens of both sexes to cast their votes—for at that time it was customary in those places for women also to participate in public deliberations. When the multitude had been consulted, the men voted for Neptune and the women for Minerva. Since one more woman was found than there were men, Minerva won.

Then Neptune, angered, devastated the Athenians’ lands with surging marine waves. For it is not difficult for demons to scatter waters wherever they wish. To appease his anger, the same author says that the Athenians imposed three punishments on the women [Col. 0567]: they were not to cast votes thereafter; none of their children was to receive the mother’s name; and no one was to call them Athenians.

Thus that city, the mother and nurse [Note: [Col. 0567] Manuscripts: “mother or nurse.”] of liberal learning and of so many great philosophers—the city than which Greece had nothing more renowned or distinguished—received the name Athens while demons mocked them over a dispute between the sea and a woman, and over a woman’s victory through women [Note: [Col. 0567] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads “feminine.”]. The city was compelled by the offended defeated party to punish the victory of the female victor, fearing Neptune’s waters more than Minerva’s weapons.

For among the women who were punished in this way, Minerva, who had won, was also defeated. She did not come to the aid of her supporters, so that, after losing the power to vote and having their children alienated from their mothers’ names, they could not even be called Athenians or claim the name of the goddess whom the men had made victorious by casting their votes.

What and how much could be said on this subject [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *suffragium*, “vote.” From this it is sufficiently clear what and how much could be said.], if the discourse were not hastening on to other matters?

## CHAPTER TEN  
### What Varro relates about the naming of the Areopagus and about the flood of Deucalion

Nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0567] The manuscripts read: “And nevertheless.”], Marcus Varro does not wish to give credence to fabulous inventions concerning the gods, lest he think something unworthy of their majesty. For this reason he does not wish the Areopagus [Note: The manuscripts consistently have, instead of *Areopagon*, *Areon pagon* or *Arion pagon*.], where the apostle Paul disputed with the Athenians (Acts 17:19ff.), and from which the city’s magistrates were called Areopagites, to have received its name from the fact that Mars—called Ἂρης (*Arēs*) in Greek—was accused of homicide and, when judged by twelve gods in that place, was acquitted by six votes, because whenever the votes were evenly divided, acquittal was customarily preferred to condemnation.

Against this opinion, which was much more widely known, Varro attempts to establish another explanation of the name from obscure literary knowledge, so that the Athenians may not be thought to have called the Areopagus, from the name of Mars and a district, the “district of Mars,” as though this were an insult to the divinities, whom he considers incapable of lawsuits or judgments.

He declares that what is said about Mars is no less false than the story about the three goddesses—Juno, Minerva, and Venus—who are said to have competed before the judge Paris for superiority in beauty, in order to obtain the golden apple; and whose quarrels are sung and danced amid theatrical applause in order to appease the gods, who delight in these supposed crimes of theirs, whether true or false.

Varro does not believe these stories, lest he attribute to the nature or character of the gods something incongruous. Yet, while giving not a fabulous but a historical explanation of the name Athens, he inserts into his writings such a great dispute between Neptune and Minerva about which of their names the city should bear that, when they contended through the display of portents, even Apollo, when consulted, did not dare to judge between them. Instead, just as Jupiter sent the dispute of the three goddesses mentioned above to Paris, so Apollo sent this one to human beings for decision.

Minerva won by the votes, and in the punishment of her female supporters was defeated: she had been able to obtain Athens against her male adversaries but could not have her female friends called Athenaeans.

In these times, Varro writes, when Cranaus, Cecrops’s successor, was reigning among the Athenians, there was a flood. According to our writers Eusebius and Jerome, however, it occurred while Cecrops was still reigning. It was called the flood of Deucalion [Note: Orosius, book 1, chapter 9, writes that Deucalion’s flood occurred 800 years before the foundation of the City, when Amphictyon was reigning at Athens; he was the third ruler after Cecrops.], because he was reigning in the regions where it occurred most severely.

This flood did not reach Egypt or the regions adjoining it [Note: Plato, in the *Timaeus*.].

## CHAPTER ELEVEN  
### When Moses led the people out of Egypt, and when Jesus Nave, who succeeded him, died, in the reigns of which kings

Moses therefore led the people of God out of Egypt at the end of the reign of Cecrops, king of the Athenians, when Ascatades was reigning among the Assyrians, Marathus among the Sicyonians [Note: Many manuscripts have *Maratheus*. Eusebius has *Marachius*.], and Triopas among the Argives.

After he had led the people out, Moses gave them the law received from God on Mount Sinai. This is called the Old Testament because it contains earthly promises; the New Testament, through Jesus Christ, was to follow, promising the kingdom of heaven.

This order had to be maintained, just as in every human being who advances toward God the process described by the Apostle takes place: “The spiritual was not first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual”; for, as he says—and it is true—“The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” [Note: The word *heavenly* is absent from manuscript 258. M.] (1 Cor. 15:46–47).

Moses ruled the people in the wilderness for forty years and died at the age of 120 [Note: Compare the frequent references elsewhere, especially book 19 against Faustus the Manichaean.]. He too had prophesied Christ through the figures of carnal observances in the tabernacle, the priesthood, the sacrifices, and many other mystical and numerous commandments.

Jesus Nave succeeded Moses and settled the people whom he had led into the Promised Land, after the nations who occupied those regions had been defeated by divine authority. After ruling the people for twenty-seven years following Moses’ death [Note: Scripture does not establish with sufficient certainty the number of years Joshua presided over the people of God; hence the various opinions on this matter. Josephus, in book 5, chapter 1, of *The Jewish Antiquities*, thinks that he presided for twenty-five years; Eusebius says twenty-seven or twenty-eight, as do most Hebrews. Sulpicius, in book 1, chapter 23, of his *Sacred History*, and Augustine follow the same view, apparently because in the manuscripts of the Septuagint there was no Ahialon, who is said in Judges 12:11–12 to have judged Israel for ten years. Those years had been assigned to Joshua in order to make up the total of 480 years from the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt to the building of the Temple, which is given in 1 Kings 6:1. Yet it seems possible to infer from Scripture that Joshua spent seven years conquering the land of Canaan and as many more dividing it. Hence some Hebrews assign him fourteen years; and it is probable that he survived for three or four years and thus governed the commonwealth for seventeen or eighteen years. COQUAEUS.], he too died.

At that time Amyntas was reigning as the eighteenth king of the Assyrians [Col. 0569], Corax as the sixteenth king of the Sicyonians, Danaus as the tenth king of the Argives, and Erichthonius as the fourth king of the Athenians.

## CHAPTER TWELVE  
### On the rites of false gods that the kings of Greece instituted for them during those times, reckoned from the exodus of Israel from Egypt to the death of Jesus Nave
During this period—that is, from the departure of Israel from Egypt up to the death of Joshua, through whom that same people received the promised land—sacred rites were instituted for false gods by the kings of Greece. These rites recalled, through solemn celebration, the memory of the Flood and of humanity’s deliverance from it, as well as the wretched life of those who, at that time, migrated now to the heights, now to the lowlands. For they also interpret the ascent and descent of the Luperci along the Sacred Way [Note: The Sacred Way, described in some fashion by Varro in *On the Latin Language*, was so called because a treaty was struck there between Romulus and Tatius, king of the Sabines. This road was steep; hence the ascent and descent of the Luperci—priests, or those who performed rites for the god Pan—along it.] as signifying, they say, people who, because of the inundation of the waters, sought the mountain summits and, when the waters had again receded, returned to the lowlands.

During this period Dionysus, also called Liber Pater and regarded as a god after his death, is said to have shown the vine to his host in Attica. At that time musical games were instituted for the Delphic Apollo, in order to appease his anger, which they thought had afflicted the regions of Greece with infertility because they had not defended his temple, which King Danaus burned when he invaded those same lands in war. They were instructed by his oracle to establish these games [Note: The Louvain edition reads “they were instructed by the oracle”; *his* is omitted in other printed editions and in the manuscripts.].

In Attica, King Erichthonius was the first to institute games for him—not for him alone, but also for Minerva. At these games olive oil was set out as the prize for the victors, since they say that Minerva discovered its fruit, just as Liber discovered wine.

During those years Europa is said to have been carried off by Xanthus, king of the Cretans, whose name we find reported differently in other authors [Note: He is called Asterius in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, where he is said to have fathered Rhadamanthus, Sarpedon, and Minos by Europa.]. From her were born Rhadamanthus, Sarpedon, and Minos, whom popular tradition more commonly declares to have been sons of Jupiter by that same woman. But the worshipers of such gods assign what we have said about the king of the Cretans to historical truth [Note: The Louvain edition reads “they assign it to truth.” *They assign* is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]; whereas what the poets sing about Jupiter, what the theaters resound with, and what the peoples celebrate, they assign to the vanity of fables, so that there might be material for games held to appease the deities, even when those false deities were being charged with crimes.

During this period Hercules was held in high repute in Tyre [Note: Most manuscripts read “in Syria.” But if this is the Hercules who was burned on Mount Oeta, he would be the Argive Hercules, and the reading should be *in Tirynthia*, which is a city in the Peloponnese near Argos, where Hercules was raised. —Ludovicus Vives.]. But evidently he was another, not the one of whom we spoke above. For, according to a more hidden history, there are said to have been several Liber Pater figures and several Her- culeses.

This Hercules, whose twelve immense deeds they enumerate—among which they do not include the killing of the African Antaeus, since that deed belongs to another Hercules—they report in their writings to have set himself on fire on Mount Oeta, because, although he had overcome monsters with his strength, he could not endure the disease from which he suffered.

At that time Busiris, whether king or rather tyrant, sacrificed his guests to his gods [Note: Several manuscripts read, “Busirius sacrificed his own guests to his gods instead.”]. They say that he was the son of Neptune by Libya, daughter of Epaphus. Yet let no one believe that Neptune committed this violation, lest the gods be accused; let it instead be attributed to the poets and the theaters, so that there may be something by which the gods can be appeased.

Vulcan and Minerva are said to have been the parents of Erichthonius, king of the Athenians, in whose final years Joshua is found to have died. But since they wish Minerva to have been a virgin, they say that, during the dispute between the two, Vulcan, aroused, poured out his semen upon the earth, and that a human being was born from it; for this reason the child received such a name. In Greek, *eris* (ἔρις) means “dispute,” and *chthōn* (χθών) means “earth”; from these two words the name *Erichthonius* was compounded.

Yet, as must be admitted, more learned writers refute this account and remove it from the stories told about their gods. They say that this fabulous notion arose from the fact that, in the temple of Vulcan and Minerva—which the two shared at Athens—a child was found exposed and wrapped in a serpent. The serpent signified that he would become great; and because the temple was shared, while his parents were unknown, he was called the son of Vulcan and Minerva. Nevertheless, the fable rather than this historical account indicates the origin of his name.

But what is this to us? Let this account instruct religious people in truthful books [Note: The manuscripts read, “But what is this to us? Let this instruct religious people in truthful books.” The printed editions instead read, “But what is this to us, since these things instruct religious people in truthful books?”]; let that account delight unclean demons in deceptive spectacles. Yet those religious people worship them as gods; and when they deny these stories about them, they cannot purge them of every crime, since, at their demand, they provide games in which shameful things are enacted—things which they deny as though they were wise. These false and shameful gods are appeased there; and although the fable sings of a crime falsely attributed to the deities, to take pleasure in a false crime is nevertheless a real crime.

## CHAPTER XIII — The kind of fables that arose at the time when Judges began to rule over the Hebrews

After the death of Joshua, the people of God had Judges. During their time, humiliations arising from labor on account of their sins alternated among them with prosperous consolations because of God’s mercy.

During this period fables were invented about Triptolemus: that, at Ceres’ command, he was carried by winged serpents and, flying over the lands in need, brought them grain; about the Minotaur: that a beast had been enclosed in the Labyrinth, and that when people entered it they could not get out because of the inextricable confusion; about the Centaurs: that the natures of horses and humans had been joined together; about Cerberus: that he was the three-headed dog of the underworld; about Phrixus and his sister Helle: that they flew while being carried by a ram; about the Gorgon: that she had hair made of snakes and turned those who looked upon her into stones; about Bellerophon: that he rode a winged flying horse, which was called Pegasus; about Amphion: that by the sweetness of his lyre he soothed and drew stones; about the craftsman Daedalus and his son Icarus: that, fitting wings to themselves, they flew; about Oedipus: that he compelled a certain monster, called the Sphinx, a four-footed creature with a human face, to destroy itself by its own plunge after he solved the supposedly insoluble riddle that it used to pose [Note: The printed editions read “a four-footed creature.” The manuscripts read “a four-footed creature” in the accusative form.]; about Antaeus, whom Hercules killed: that he was the son of Earth and therefore, whenever he fell upon the earth, would customarily rise stronger; and whatever other stories I may perhaps have omitted.

These fables, extending as far as the Trojan War—the point at which Marcus Varro ended the second book of his account of the Roman people’s origin—were fashioned by human ingenuity from the opportunity provided by histories containing events that truly occurred, in such a way that they were not attached to the gods as reproaches.

Moreover, whoever invented the story that the most beautiful boy Ganymede was carried off by Jupiter for sexual violation—an outrage committed by King Tantalus and attributed by the fable to Jupiter—or that Danaë’s intercourse was sought through a shower of gold, by which it is understood that the woman’s chastity was corrupted by gold—whether these things, which occurred or were fabricated in those times, were committed by others and falsely attributed to Jupiter, it is impossible to say how much evil they presumed upon human hearts, since people could patiently endure such lies, which they nevertheless embraced willingly. Indeed, the more devotedly they worshiped Jupiter, the more severely they ought to have punished those who dared to say such things about him.

Yet now they are not angry with those who invented these stories; rather, they feared that the gods themselves would be angry if such fictions were performed even in the theaters [Note: The manuscripts read “but unless”—that is, “but they feared that the gods would be angry unless such fictions were performed.”].

During this period Latona gave birth to Apollo—not the one whose oracles, as I said above, were customarily consulted, but the one who served Admetus together with Hercules [Note: We restore this reading from five of our manuscripts and from all those consulted by the Benedictine Fathers. They nevertheless retained in the text of the older editions the reading: “but the one whom they say, together with Hercules, pastured the herds of King Admetus.” That reading is certainly erroneous, since mythographers nowhere associate Hercules with Apollo in the role of herdsman. Therefore the words “together with Hercules,” in Augustine’s thought, indicate not companionship in servitude but the period during which Apollo lived. —M.]. Yet he was believed to be a god, so that many, indeed almost everyone, thought there had been only one Apollo [Note: According to Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 3, chapter 23, some people held that there were several Apollos.].

Then Liber Pater also waged war in India. He had many women in his army, who were called Bacchae—not so much famous for courage as for frenzy. Some writers indeed say that this Liber was defeated and bound; others that he was killed in battle by Perseus, and they do not conceal where he was buried [Note: Eusebius writes as follows on this matter in the *Chronicle*: “Bacchus, engaging in battle with Perseus, is killed, as the poet Dinarchus—not the rhetorician—writes. Whoever wishes may still behold the tomb of Bacchus at Delphi, beside the golden Apollo.” From Cyril, *Against Julian*, book 10, we learn that the poet Dinarchus mentioned here by Eusebius described the deeds of Bacchus in verse. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 1, chapter 21, reports that Bacchus was killed in battle by Perseus and, during the reign of King Perseus in Macedonia, was enrolled among the gods. The same Clement relates Bacchus’ death differently in book 2 of the *Paedagogue*: he was torn apart by the Titans, boiled in cauldrons, and then placed on spits and roasted over a fire. Pallas, however, at Jupiter’s command, snatched Bacchus’ heart and limbs from the executioners’ hands; afterward Apollo was ordered to bury them on Mount Parnassus near Delphi.].

Nevertheless, under the name of this supposed god, the Bacchanalian rites—or rather sacrileges—were instituted by unclean demons. After so many years, the senate was so ashamed of their frenzied obscenity that it prohibited them from existing in the city of Rome [Note: Livy, book 39, chapter 18, reports that these obscenities were prohibited not only in Rome but throughout Italy. Hence Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 6: “The consuls, by authority of the senate, expelled Liber Pater with his mysteries not only from the City but from all Italy.” See above, book 6, chapter 9, note 1.].

During those times Perseus and his wife Andromeda, after they had died, were believed to have been received into heaven, to such an extent that they did not blush or fear to mark their images among the stars and call them by their names [Note: Codex 258 reads “they did not fear,” omitting the word “not.” —M.].

## CHAPTER XIV — The theological poets

During the same period there arose poets who were also called theologians, because they composed poems about the gods. But these gods, although they may have been great men, were nevertheless human beings; or they were the elements of this world, which the true God made; or they were appointed among principalities and powers according to the Creator’s will and their own merits [Note: The printed editions read “and not according to their own merits.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.]. And if they sang anything about the one true God amid many vain and false things, by worshiping other beings with him that are not gods and rendering them the service owed to God alone, they did not serve him rightly. Nor could they themselves refrain from the disgrace of their fabulous gods [Note: After the word “refrain,” the printed editions add: “They are said to have belonged to their number.” This sentence is absent from the older books.]: Orpheus, Musaeus, and Linus.

In truth, these theologians worshiped gods; they were not worshiped as gods. Yet the city of the impious regularly places Orpheus in charge of infernal rites, or rather sacrileges, in some strange fashion.

The wife of King Athamas [Note: Several manuscripts read “Adamantes.”]—whose name was Ino—and her son Melicertes perished by a voluntary plunge into the sea, and, in human opinion, were enrolled among the gods, as were other human beings of their time [Note: The printed editions add here “among whom were,” which is absent from the manuscripts.], Castor and Pollux. The Greeks called Melicertes’ mother Leucothea, and the Latins called her Matuta; yet both peoples regarded her as a goddess.

## CHAPTER XV — The decline of the kingdom of the Argives, at the time when Picus, son of Saturn, first received his father’s kingdom among the Laurentines

During this period the kingdom of the Argives came to an end and was transferred to Mycenae, from which Agamemnon came. The kingdom of the Laurentines arose, where Picus, son of Saturn, first received the kingdom, while Deborah, a woman, was judging the Hebrews. Yet through her the Spirit of God was acting, for she was also a prophetess. Her prophecy, in Judges 5, is less explicit than would allow us to demonstrate without lengthy exposition that it was spoken concerning Christ.

The Laurentines, then, were already reigning in Italy; from them the Roman origin after the Greeks is derived with greater clarity. Nevertheless, the Assyrian kingdom still endured, where Lampares was the twenty-third king, when Picus first began to rule the Laurentines.

As for Saturn, the father of this Picus, let the worshipers of such gods see what they think of him, since they deny that he was human. Others also wrote that he himself ruled in Italy before his son Picus; and Virgil, in more widely known verses, says:

> He gathered that untutored race, scattered over the high mountains,  
> Established laws, and chose that the land be called Latium,  
> Since he had lain hidden and safe within those shores;  
> And, as they say, golden ages existed under that king.  
> (*Aeneid* 8.321–325.)

But let them consider these poetic fictions, and let them insist instead that Picus’ father was Sterces. They say that this most skilled farmer discovered how to fertilize fields with animal dung; from his name, *stercus* (“manure”) was derived. Some say that he was called Stercutius. Whatever reason they may have had for wishing to call him Saturn, they certainly made this Sterces or Stercutius a god on account of agriculture. They likewise received his son Picus into the number of such gods, asserting that he was a distinguished augur and warrior.

Picus fathered Faunus, the second king of the Laurentines. He too is, or was, a god to them. Before the Trojan War they conferred divine honors upon these dead men.

## CHAPTER XVI — Diomedes enrolled among the gods after the destruction of Troy, and his companions said to have been changed into birds

After Troy had been destroyed—a destruction sung everywhere and familiar even to children, and made especially famous and widespread by its magnitude and by the excellence of the languages in which writers described it—and after the deed had been accomplished while Latinus, son of Faunus, was reigning, from whom the kingdom began to be called Latin and the Laurentines ceased to rule, the victorious Greeks, abandoning ruined Troy and returning to their own lands, were torn apart and crushed by various terrible disasters. Yet they too increased the number of their gods from among their own people.

For they also made Diomedes a god. They say that, because a divinely inflicted punishment was imposed, he did not return to his people; and they confirm—not by poetic and fabulous falsehood, but by historical testimony—that his companions were changed into birds. Their supposed god could neither restore them to human nature himself, nor, as a newly admitted heavenly being, obtain this from his king Jupiter.

They even say that he has a temple on the island of Diomedea, not far from Mount Garganus, which is in Apulia. They report that these birds fly around and inhabit the temple with such remarkable obedience that they fill their beaks with water and sprinkle it. If Greeks, or people descended from Greeks, come there, the birds are not only quiet but also fawn upon them; but if they see foreigners, they fly at their heads and wound them with blows so severe that they even kill them. For they are said to be armed with hard, large beaks, quite adequate for such battles [Note: The word “beak” is absent from the manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER XVII — What Varro reported concerning the incredible transformations of human beings

To support this claim, Varro recalls other matters no less incredible concerning that most famous sorceress Circe, who also changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts; and concerning the Arcadians, who, chosen by lot, swam across a certain pool and there were changed into wolves, living with similar wild animals in the deserts of that region. If they did not eat human flesh, then after nine years, when the pool had been renewed, they were changed back into human beings.

Finally, he explicitly names a certain Demaenetus, who, after tasting some of the sacrificial offering that the Arcadians were accustomed to make to their god Lycaean, was changed into a wolf and, in the tenth year, restored to his original form. He then practiced boxing [Note: The printed editions read “he practiced for boxing.”] and won in the Olympic contest.

The historian thinks that this is the only reason why the name Lycaean was given in Arcadia to Pan Lycaeus and Jupiter Lycaeus: namely, because of this transformation of human beings into wolves, which they thought could occur only through divine power. For “wolf” is *lykos* (λύκος) in Greek, from which the form of the name Lycaeus is evident.

He also says that the Roman Luperci arose, as it were, from the seed of those mysteries.

## CHAPTER XVIII — What should be believed concerning transformations that seem to occur in human beings through demonic art

1. But perhaps those who read these things expect us to say something about such extensive demonic deception [Note: After “perhaps expect,” the printed editions add: “what Christians ought to do when miracles are claimed to occur among the idols of the nations.” This annotation was transferred from the margin into the text, for the text lacks it in the older books.]. And what shall we say except that we must flee from the midst of Babylon? This prophetic command, in Isaiah 48:20, is to be understood spiritually, so that we flee from the city of this world—which is certainly the society of impious angels and human beings—by advancing toward the living God with the steps of faith that work through love.

For the greater the power of demons over these lower things that we see, the more firmly we must cling to the Mediator, through whom we ascend from the depths to the heights. If we say that such things are not to be believed, there are still people who assert either that they have heard such things with complete certainty or that they have experienced them themselves.

When we were in Italy, we too heard such stories about a certain region of those parts. They said that women who kept inns and had been initiated into these evil arts used to give cheese to whatever travelers they wished or were able to affect; the travelers would immediately be changed into pack animals and carry whatever was necessary, and, once their work had been completed, would return to themselves. Yet their minds did not become bestial; their rational and human minds remained intact. Apuleius either indicated or invented that the same thing had happened to him in the books he entitled *The Golden Ass*: after taking poison, he became a donkey while his human mind remained.

2. These things are either false or so unusual that they reasonably should not be believed. Yet we must believe with the utmost firmness that almighty God can do everything he wishes, whether in punishment or in granting benefits. Demons, however, do not operate according to the full power of their nature—for their nature too is angelic, although it is evil through its own fault—except in what he has permitted, whose judgments are many and hidden, but never unjust.

Nor do demons create natures, if they perform anything of the kind about which this question turns. Rather, they alter in appearance the things created by the true God, so that they seem to be what they are not. I would therefore not believe that, by any art or power of demons, the mind alone—or even the body—can truly be converted into the limbs and features of beasts. But I would believe that the human phantasy, which even in thought or dreaming is varied through countless kinds of things, and which, although it is not a body, nevertheless takes on forms resembling bodies with marvelous speed, can, when the bodily senses of a person are asleep or overwhelmed, be conveyed in some ineffable manner to the perception of others in a bodily shape.

Thus the bodies of the people themselves may lie somewhere, alive indeed, but with their senses sealed far more heavily and intensely than in sleep; while the phantasy, as though embodied in the form of some animal, appears to the senses of others, and the person himself may also seem to himself to be such a creature, just as he might seem to himself to be such in a dream, and to carry burdens. If those burdens are real bodies, they are carried by demons, so that human beings may be deceived, some seeing real bodies of burdens and others false pack animals.

For a certain man named Praestantius reported that this had happened to his father: he had taken that poison in cheese in his own house and had lain on his own bed as though sleeping, yet he could not be awakened in any way. After several days, Praestantius said, his father seemed to awaken and related, as though they were dreams, what he had suffered: namely, that he had become a horse and, among other pack animals, had carried grain to soldiers—grain called Raetian because it was transported to the Raetians [Note: The Louvain edition reads “to the nets.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts more correctly read “to the Raetians,” that is, to the provinces of the Raetians, or, as others write, the Rhaetians.].

It was discovered that the event had occurred as he related it, although it seemed to him to be a dream.

Another man reported that, at night in his own house, before he went to rest, he had seen a very familiar philosopher come to him and explain certain Platonic doctrines which, when previously asked, he had refused to explain. When this same philosopher was asked why he had done in the other man’s house what he had refused to do when asked in his own, he replied: “I did not do it; I dreamed that I did.” Thus, by means of a phantasmal image, what one man saw in a dream was presented to the other while he was awake.

3. These things have come to us not through just anyone—people whom we might think it shameful to believe—but through the reports of people whom we would not suppose to have lied to us.

Accordingly, what is said of human beings, and has been committed to writing, namely, that they are customarily changed into wolves by the Arcadian gods, or rather demons [Note: This is how all the manuscripts read. The printed editions read “Arcadians.”], and what Virgil says—

> By her spells Circe changed the companions of Ulysses  
> (*Eclogue* 8.70)—

seems to me to have been able to happen according to the manner I have described, if it happened at all.

As for the Diomedean birds, since their kind is said to continue through successive generations, I believe that they were not made from transformed human beings, but were substituted after the human beings had been secretly removed, just as a hind was substituted for Iphigenia, the daughter of King Agamemnon. For such tricks could not have been difficult for demons permitted to act by God’s judgment. But because that maiden was later found alive, it was easily recognized that a hind had been substituted for her [Note: In support of this teaching, a similar story appears in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 7, chapter 4: “While a solemn victim was being sacrificed by the Gentiles at Caesarea, it happened that, through the operation of a demon, it was snatched away with such speed that it seemed to have been carried up into heaven. But when a certain man named Astyrius asked God not to allow people to be deceived in this way, their eyes were opened, and they saw that the victim had been carried to nearby marshes and was stuck there.” —Coquaeus.].

But because Diomedes’ companions nowhere suddenly reappeared and were afterward seen nowhere, they are believed to have been changed into those birds—birds secretly brought from other places where that species exists, transported to those locations, and suddenly substituted in their place—although avenging evil angels had destroyed them [Col. 0576].

That the birds bring water in their beaks to Diomedes’ temple and sprinkle it, that they show affection to those of Greek descent and pursue foreigners—this is not difficult to understand as occurring at the instigation of demons. It is in the demons’ interest to persuade people that Diomedes was made a god, so that, in defiance of the true God, they may cause many to worship false gods and to serve dead human beings who, even while alive, did not truly live: serving them with temples, altars, sacrifices, and priests—things which, when rightly ordered, are owed to the one living and true God alone.

## CHAPTER XIX — Aeneas came to Italy at the time when Labdon was judging the Hebrews

At that time, after Troy had been captured and destroyed, Aeneas came to Italy with twenty ships carrying the survivors of the Trojans. Latinus was reigning there, Menestheus among the Athenians [Note: This is how the Vindobonensis, the Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts read, in agreement with Eusebius. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “Mnestheus.”], Polyphides among the Sicyonians, and Tautanes among the Assyrians [Note: The Vindobonensis, the Ambrosianus, and several manuscripts read “Antanes” or “Autanes.”]. Among the Hebrews, however, Labdon was Judge.

After Latinus died, Aeneas reigned for three years, with the same kings remaining in the places mentioned above, except that Pelasgus was now king of the Sicyonians, and Samson was Judge of the Hebrews. Since Samson was extraordinarily strong, he was thought to be Hercules.

But because Aeneas disappeared when he died, the Latins made him a god. The Sabines likewise enrolled their first king, Sancus—or, as some call him, Sanctus—among the gods [Note: The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmus read “Xanthus, or, as some call him, Xanthius.” The Louvain edition reads “Sangus” in the first place, where most manuscripts have “Sancus,” and some have “Sanccus.” Ovidius calls him Sanctus in *Fasti* 6.217–218. In Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 1, chapter 15, section 8, the reading is “Sancus.” In one edition of Lactantius, Vives read “Sangus.”].

During the same period Codrus, king of the Athenians, deliberately exposed himself to be killed by the Peloponnesians, the city’s enemies, without their recognizing him. And it happened. In this way, they say, he saved his homeland. For the Peloponnesians had received an oracle that they would overcome the Athenians only if they did not kill their king. He therefore deceived them by appearing in the clothing of a poor man and provoking them to kill him during a quarrel. Hence Virgil says:

> And the quarrels of Codrus  
> (*Eclogue* 5.11) [Note: This is how all our manuscripts read. Manuscript B has “And,” less correctly.]

The Athenians worshiped him as a god with the honor of sacrifices.

Silvius, the fourth king of the Latins and son of Aeneas—not by Creusa, by whom Ascanius was born and who ruled there third, but by Lavinia, daughter of Latinus, whom Aeneas is said to have had as a posthumous son—was reigning at the time when Oneus was king of the Assyrians, Melantho was the sixteenth king of the Athenians [Col. 0577]. But while Eli the priest was Judge of the Hebrews, the kingdom of the Sicyonians came to an end; it is said to have lasted for nine hundred and fifty-nine years.

## CHAPTER XX — The succession of the royal order among the Israelites after the period of the Judges

Soon afterward, while the same rulers were reigning in the places mentioned, the kingdom of the Israelites, when the period of the Judges had ended, began with King Saul. At that time Samuel was prophet.

From that period onward the kings of the Latins began to be called Silvii. The first to be called Silvius was Aeneas’ son; thereafter, while they received their own personal names, this surname was also retained, just as much later those who succeeded Caesar Augustus were called Caesars after Caesar.

After Saul was rejected, so that no one from his line would reign, and after his death, David succeeded to the kingdom forty years after the beginning of Saul’s rule [Note: According to the sacred writings, 2 Samuel 2:10, and according to Josephus, Saul reigned for that many years. Eupolemus, however, who wrote a history of the Hebrews, gives only twenty-one. —Ludovicus Vives.].

Then the Athenians ceased to have kings after Codrus’ death and began to have magistrates to administer the commonwealth [Note: Namely, archons. —M.].

After David, who himself also reigned for forty years, his son Solomon became king of the Israelites. He founded that most renowned temple of God at Jerusalem. During his reign Alba was founded among the Latins; afterward, in the same Latium, kings began to be called not Latins but Albans.

Solomon was succeeded by his son Rehoboam, under whom that people was divided into two kingdoms, and each part began to have its own king.

## CHAPTER XXI — The kings of Latium, whose first was Aeneas and whose twelfth, Aventinus, was made a god

After Aeneas, whom they had made a god, Latium had eleven kings, none of whom became a god. Aventinus, however, who follows Aeneas in the twelfth place, was defeated in battle and buried on the mountain that is still called by his name; he was added to the number of such gods as they used to make.

Others did not wish to write that he was killed in battle but said that he disappeared. They also said that the mountain was not named from him, but from the arrival of birds it was called the Aventine [Note: See Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book 5, section 43.].

After him no one in Latium was made a god except Romulus, the founder of Rome. Between him and Aventinus, however, two kings are found. The first of them I shall express in Virgil’s verse [Note: This is how all our manuscripts read. Manuscript B has “I shall say,” less correctly.]:

> That nearest one was Procas, glory of the Trojan race.  
> (*Aeneid* 6.767)

Since Rome was already, in a sense, being born during his reign, the Assyrian kingdom—the greatest of all kingdoms—then reached the end of its extraordinary duration. It was transferred to the Medes after approximately 1,305 years, counting even the time of Belus, who fathered Ninus and was the first king there, content with a small dominion.

Procas reigned before Amulius. Moreover, Amulius made his brother Numitor’s daughter, named Rhea and also called Ilia, the mother of Romulus, a Vestal virgin. They say that she conceived twins by Mars, thereby honoring or excusing her violation in this manner, and adducing as evidence the fact that a she-wolf nursed the exposed infants.

They think that this species of animal belongs to Mars, so that the she-wolf is believed to have offered her breasts to the little ones because she recognized them as the children of her master Mars. Yet there are also those who say that, while the abandoned children lay crying, they were first gathered up by some prostitute and suckled at her breasts. Prostitutes were called *lupae* (“she-wolves”), which is why their disreputable places are still called *lupanaria*. They say that the children later came into the care of the shepherd Faustulus and were raised by his wife Acca.

Even if God wished to aid, through a nursing wild animal, those infants from whom so great a city was destined to be founded, after they had been divinely rescued from the water, in order to expose the cruelty of the king who had ordered them to be thrown into it, what is surprising about that?

Numitor, Romulus’ grandfather, succeeded his brother Amulius to the Latin kingdom. Rome was founded in the first year of Numitor’s reign; consequently, he reigned thereafter together with his grandson Romulus.

## CHAPTER XXII — Rome was founded at the time when the Assyrian kingdom collapsed and Hezekiah was reigning in Judah [Note: The printed editions here read “in Judaea.” The manuscripts read “in Judah,” as do the printed editions themselves in the following chapter.]

To avoid delaying over many matters, the city of Rome was founded like another Babylon and like a daughter of the earlier Babylon. Through it God was pleased to subdue the world and bring it into a single political community governed by laws, pacifying it far and wide.

For there were already powerful and courageous peoples, nations trained in warfare, which would not easily yield and which had to be overcome through immense dangers, considerable devastation on both sides, and dreadful labor.

When the Assyrian kingdom subdued nearly all Asia, although this was accomplished by warfare, it could not have been achieved through very harsh and difficult wars, because the peoples were still inexperienced in resistance and were neither so numerous nor so powerful. Indeed, after that greatest and universal Flood, when only eight human beings escaped in Noah’s ark, little more than a thousand years had passed when Ninus subdued all Asia except India. Rome, however, did not conquer with such speed and ease the many peoples of both East and West whom we see subjected to Roman rule. As it gradually grew stronger and extended itself in every direction, it found those peoples already powerful and warlike.

Therefore, at the time Rome was founded, the people of Israel had been in the promised land for 718 years. Of these, twenty-seven belonged to Joshua; afterward came 329 years of the period of the Judges. From the beginning of the kings there had been 362 years.

At that time Achaz was king in Judah—or, according to those who calculate differently, Hezekiah, who succeeded him. It is certain that Hezekiah, an exceptionally good and devout king, reigned during the time of Romulus.

In that part of the Hebrew people which was called Israel, Hoshea had begun to reign [Note: This conflicts with the chronological calculations. Joshua ruled for fourteen years. The elders or Judges ruled for 410 years. Saul was chosen king in 1068 BC. Rome was founded in 753 BC. Achaz was not king in Judah, much less Hezekiah, who had not yet been born at that time. Jotham, son of Uzziah, was reigning. —Larcher.].

## CHAPTER XXIII — The Erythraean Sibyl, who among the other Sibyls is known to have sung many clear things about Christ
At the same time, some report that the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied. Varro records that there were several Sibyls, not just one [Note: Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 1, chapter 6, reports that Varro counted ten Sibyls.].

This Erythraean Sibyl certainly composed some explicit statements about Christ—something we too had earlier read in Latin, in badly formed and unmetrical Latin verses, through the incompetence of I know not what translator, as we later discovered. For the very distinguished Flaccianus, who had also been proconsul, a man of exceptionally fluent speech and extensive learning, when we were discussing Christ, produced for us a Greek manuscript, saying that it contained poems of the Erythraean Sibyl. In one place he showed that the arrangement of the letters at the beginnings of the verses was such that these words could be read in it: Ἰησοῦς Χρειστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτὴρ, that is in Latin, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” The following verses, whose initial letters yield the meaning just mentioned, as someone translated them into Latin verses that were extant and metrical [Note: Printed editions have *latinis exstantibus* (“existing Latin verses”). This is corrected from the manuscripts.], contain this:

**Ι** The sign of judgment [Note: The Lovaniensis edition alone reads *signo* (“by a sign”).]: the earth will grow wet with sweat.

**Η** From heaven the King will come, destined to be through the ages;

**Σ** Present in the flesh, plainly, to judge the world.

**Ο** From there the unbelieving and the faithful alike will see God,

[5] **Υ** The Most High, with the saints, when the age itself has reached its end.

**Σ** Thus souls will be present together with the flesh, which he himself judges [Note: Here *judicat* (“judges”) is restored on the authority of the manuscripts; the text in B reads *judicet* (“may judge”). The author of the *Oration against the Jews*, Appendix to vol. 8, also uses *judicat*.];

**Χ** When the world lies uncultivated amid dense thickets.

**Ρ** At once men will reject their images, and every treasure as well;

**Ε** Fire will burn the lands, the sea, and the heavens,

[10] **Ι** Searching out the gates of gloomy Tartarus and breaking them open.

**Σ** For free light will be granted to all the flesh of the saints,

**Τ** But eternal fire will consume the guilty [Note: All our manuscripts read *aeterna* (“eternal [fire]”); B has *aeternum*. The author of the *Oration* mentioned above, Appendix to vol. 8, reads *aeternaque* (“and eternal”).].

**Ο** Revealing hidden deeds, then each person will speak

**Σ** Of secrets, and God will disclose hearts to the light.

[15] **Θ** Then there will also be mourning, and all will gnash their teeth.

**Ε** The sun’s radiance will be taken away, and the choir of stars will perish.

**Ο** The heaven will be rolled up [Note: The printed editions read *Solvetur* (“will be loosed”), but the manuscripts read *Volvetur* (“will be rolled up”), so that its initial V corresponds to the Greek vowel Ο, as above in the fourth verse.], and the moon’s splendor will pass away.

**Υ** He will cast down the hills and raise the valleys from below.

**Υ** Nothing sublime or lofty will remain among human things.

[20] **Ι** Now the mountains are made level with the plains, and all the blue waters of the sea

**Ο** Will cease; the shattered earth will perish.

**Σ** Thus alike the springs and the rivers will be scorched by fire.

**Σ** But then the trumpet will send down a mournful sound from on high

**Ω** Upon the world, lamenting wretched crime and its varied sufferings;

[25] **Τ** And the earth, splitting open, will reveal Tartarean chaos.

**Η** And here the kings will stand before the Lord, every one of them,

**Ρ** And a stream of fire and sulfur will fall from the heavens [Note: Erasmus and the Lovaniensis edition read *Decidet* (“will fall”). Better are Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts: *Recidet* (“will fall back”); for the initial letter of this verse must be the same as the final letter of the Greek name *Sōtēr*.].

In these Latin verses, translated somehow from the Greek, the meaning produced when the letters at their beginnings are joined together could not appear in the places where the Greek letter **Υ** occurs, because Latin words could not be found that both began with that letter and suited the sense. These are three verses: the fifth, the eighteenth, and the nineteenth [Note: Erasmus and the Lovaniensis edition read *harum trium* (“of these three”); the other printed editions and the manuscripts more correctly read *horum trium*, namely, of the three verses just mentioned—the fifth, eighteenth, and nineteenth.]. Therefore, if, when joining the letters at the beginnings of all the verses, we do not read the written letters of these three verses, but instead remember the letter **Υ**, as though it were placed in those same positions, the five words “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior” are expressed—but in Greek, not Latin.

There are twenty-seven verses, a number that produces a solid cube. For three times three makes nine; and when those nine are again multiplied by three, so that a figure rises from breadth into height, they reach twenty-seven.

Now, if you join the initial letters of these five Greek words—Ἰησοῦς Χρειστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτὴρ, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior” in Latin—the result is Ἰχθύς, that is, “Fish.” In this name Christ is mystically understood, because in the abyss of this mortality, as in the depth of the waters, he was able to remain alive—that is, without sin.

### 2.

This Sibyl—whether Erythraean or, as some more firmly believe, Cumaean—has nothing in her entire poem, of which this is a very small excerpt, that pertains to the worship of false or manufactured gods. On the contrary, she speaks against them and against their worshipers in such a way that she seems to belong among those who pertain to the City of God.

Lactantius also inserts into his work certain prophecies of the Sibyl concerning Christ, although he does not identify which Sibyl she was. But what he set down separately I have judged should be presented together, as though it were one extended passage, although he mentioned it in several short sections:

“Later he will come into the unjust hands of unbelievers. They will strike God with unholy hands and spit poisonous spittle from their polluted mouths. Yet he will simply offer his holy back to the blows” [Note: Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 4, chapter 18, records these words in Greek:

> Εἰς ἀνόμους χεῖρας καὶ ἀπίστων ὕστερον ἥξει.  
> Δώσουσιν δὲ Θεῷ ῥαπίσματα χερσὶν ἀνάγνοις,  
> Καὶ στόμασιν μιαροῖσι πτύσματα φαρμακόεντα.  
> Δώσει δ᾽ εἰς μάστιγας ἁπλῶς ἁγνὸν τότε νῶτον.

“Later he will come into lawless and unbelieving hands. They will give God blows with unclean hands and, with filthy mouths, poisonous spittle. Then he will simply give his pure back to the whips.”].

“And receiving blows upon the face, he will remain silent, so that no one may recognize who he is, or from where he came to speak to the dead; and he will be crowned with a crown of thorns” [Note: In the same place Lactantius, after a short interval:

> Καὶ κολαφιζόμενος σιγήσει, μή τις ἐπιγνῶ  
> Τίς λόγος, ἤ πόθεν ἦλθεν, ἵνα φθιμένοισι λαλήσῃ  
> Καὶ στέφανον φορέσει τὸν ἀκάνθινον.

“And while being struck upon the face he will be silent, lest anyone recognize who he is, or from where he came, so that he might speak to the dead; and he will wear a crown of thorns.”].

“But for food they gave him gall, and for his thirst vinegar; they will display this table of inhospitality” [Note: Shortly afterward Lactantius, in the same place:

> Εἰς δὲ τὸ βρῶμα χολὴν, κ᾽ εἰς δίψαν ὄξος ἔδωκαν,  
> Τῆς ἀφιλοξενίης ταύτην δείξουσι τράπεζαν.

“And for food they gave gall, and for thirst vinegar; they will display this table of inhospitality.”].

“For you yourself, beginning in folly, did not understand your God, playing with the thoughts of mortals; instead, you crowned him with thorns and mixed the dreadful gall” [Note: Lactantius says in the same place that these verses belong to another Sibyl:

> Αὐτὴ γὰρ σὺ ἄφρων τὸν σὸν θεὸν οὐκ ἐνόησας,  
> Παίζοντα ἐν θνητοῖσι νοήμασιν, ἀλλὰ κ᾽ ἀκάνθαις  
> Ἔστρεψας στεφάνῳ, φοβερήν τε χολὴν ἐκέρασας.

“For you yourself, foolish one, did not understand your own God, playing with mortal thoughts; instead, with thorns you twisted a crown for him and mixed the terrifying gall.”].

“But the veil of the temple will be torn, and at midday there will be an exceedingly dark night for three hours” [Note: Lactantius, book 4, chapter 19:

> Ναοῦ δὲ σχισθήσεται πέτασμα, καὶ ἤματι μέσσῳ  
> Νὺξ ἔσται σκοτόεσσα πελώριος ἐν τρισὶν ὥραις.

“And the veil of the temple will be torn, and in the middle of the day there will be a monstrous, dark night for three hours.”].

“And he will die by death, having taken sleep for three days; then, having returned from the dead to the light, he will come first, showing the beginning of resurrection by having been recalled” [Note: In the same place, somewhat later:

> Καὶ θανάτου μοῖραν τελέσει τρίτον ἦμαρ ὑπνώσας·  
> Καὶ τότ᾽ ἀπὸ φθιμένων ἀνακύψας εἰς φάος ἥξει,  
> Πρῶτος ἀναστάσεως κλητοῖ ἀρχὴν ὑποδείξας.

“And he will fulfill the portion of death, having slept through the third day; then, having risen from the dead, he will come into the light, first showing the beginning of resurrection to those called.”].

Lactantius used these Sibylline testimonies piecemeal, at intervals throughout his discussion, as the points he intended to prove seemed to require them. We have joined them into a single sequence without inserting anything, taking care to distinguish them only by headings, provided that later copyists do not neglect to preserve them. Some have indeed written that the Erythraean Sibyl lived not in the time of Romulus but during the Trojan War.

## CHAPTER XXIV—That the Seven Sages flourished during the reign of Romulus; that at that time the ten tribes called Israel were led captive by the Chaldaeans; and that Romulus, after his death, was granted divine honors

During the reign of Romulus, Thales of Miletus is said to have lived [Note: The chronological calculations are remarkably confused. Thales was born under the archon Damasias, as can be seen in Diogenes Laertius, book 1, §22, in the first year of the thirty-fifth Olympiad, according to Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, book 1, p. 12—that is, in the 115th year after the founding of the City. Ancus Martius was then reigning. LARCHER.], one of the Seven Sages, who, after the theological poets—among whom Orpheus was the most celebrated of all—were called Σοφοί, which in Latin means “Sages.”

At the same time the ten tribes that, in the division of the people, were called Israel were defeated by the Chaldaeans and led captive into those lands [Note: The Israelites were taken into servitude in the fourth year of the fourteenth Olympiad, in 721 before the birth of Christ, the thirty-third year after the founding of the City, while Romulus was still reigning. LARCHER.]. The two tribes called by the name of Judah remained in the land of Judaea and retained their royal seat at Jerusalem.

When Romulus died and had himself disappeared, the Romans enrolled him among the gods—as is also commonly known. This practice had already ceased to such an extent, and afterward was done only through flattery rather than error, in the age of the Caesars, that Cicero attributes to Romulus, with great praise [Note: See below, book 22, chapter 6.], the distinction of having deserved these honors not in primitive and uneducated times, when people were easily deceived, but in an already polished and learned age—although the subtle and penetrating loquacity of the philosophers had not yet grown hot and sprung forth.

Even if later ages did not establish dead human beings as gods, they nevertheless did not cease worshiping and treating as gods those established by the ancients. Indeed, they increased the enticement of empty and impious superstition with images, which the ancients did not possess [Note: See above, book 4, chapter 31, section 2, and note (b), column 138.]. This was brought about by unclean demons in their hearts, who also deceived them through fraudulent oracles, so that even the mythical crimes of the gods—which in a more civilized age were no longer invented—were nevertheless shamefully acted out in theatrical performances for the service of those same false divinities [Col. 0582].

Numa then reigned after Romulus. Although he thought that the state should certainly be fortified by the multitude of false gods, he himself did not deserve, after death, to be enrolled in that same crowd—as though he were thought to have packed heaven so densely with a multitude of divinities that no room could be found there for him.

While he was reigning at Rome, and while among the Hebrews the reign of Manasseh had begun—the impious king by whom the prophet Isaiah is said to have been killed [Note: Manasseh, king of Judah, began to reign in 698 before the birth of Christ, in the seventeenth year of Numa Pompilius’ reign. LARCHER. Jerome writes, on the basis of the most certain Hebrew tradition, that Isaiah was sawn in two with a wooden saw by Manasseh; he adds: “Hence many of our writers refer to Isaiah’s passion the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning the sufferings of the saints: ‘They were sawn in two.’” COQUAEUS.]—they say that the Sibyl of Samos lived.

## CHAPTER XXV—Which philosophers shone during the reign of Tarquinius Priscus among the Romans and of Zedekiah among the Hebrews, when Jerusalem was captured and the Temple overthrown

While Zedekiah was reigning among the Hebrews and Tarquinius Priscus among the Romans—the latter having succeeded Ancus Martius—the Jewish people were led captive to Babylon, Jerusalem was overthrown, and the Temple constructed by Solomon was destroyed. For the Prophets, rebuking them for their crimes and impieties, had foretold that these things would befall them, especially Jeremiah, who even specified the number of years (Jeremiah 25:11).

At that time Pittacus of Mytilene, another of the Seven Sages, is said to have lived [Note: Pittacus was born in 652 before the birth of Christ, as can be calculated from Suidas; he died in 550. See Lucian, *On Long-Lived Persons*, §18. LARCHER.]. Eusebius writes that the five others who, together with Thales—mentioned above—and Pittacus, make up the number seven, lived at the time when God’s captive people were held in Babylonia. They are Solon of Athens, Chilon of Lacedaemon, Periander of Corinth, Cleobulus of Lindus, and Bias of Priene [Note: The manuscripts have *Chilon*; and below, *Periandrus* instead of *Periander*.].

All seven, called Sages, flourished after the theological poets because they surpassed other men in a certain praiseworthy way of life and contained various moral precepts in the concise form of maxims. They left no literary monuments to posterity, except that Solon is said to have given the Athenians certain laws. Thales, however, was a physicist and left books containing his doctrines [Note: On the contrary, Thales committed nothing to writing. See Themistius, *Oration* 26, p. 317 B–C. LARCHER.].

During this period of the Jewish captivity [Note: In 607 before the birth of Christ, after Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem, he imposed tribute on King Jehoiakim; from this began the seventy years of captivity. LARCHER.], Anaximander, Anaximenes, and Xenophanes, all physicists, also flourished. At that time Pythagoras also lived; from him philosophers began to be so called [Note: Compare above, book 8, chapter 2, and below, chapter 37, and elsewhere.].

## CHAPTER XXVI—That at the time when, after seventy years had been completed, the Jewish captivity was ended, the Romans too were freed from royal domination

At about the same time Cyrus, king of the Persians, who also ruled the Chaldaeans and Assyrians, released part of the Jewish captives and had fifty thousand of them return to restore the Temple [Note: In 538 before the birth of Christ, Cyrus granted the Jews by decree a return to their homeland. LARCHER.]. They laid only the first foundations and constructed the altar. But when enemies attacked, they were wholly unable to continue building, and the work was postponed until the time of Darius.

At about the same time the events recorded in the Book of Judith also took place [Note: The events of Judith should be assigned to 634 before the birth of Christ, as Montfaucon proved in his work entitled *History of Judith*. LARCHER.]. The Jews, it is said, did not receive this book into the canon of Scripture. Under Darius, king of the Persians, when the seventy years foretold by the prophet Jeremiah had been completed, freedom was restored to the Jews and their captivity ended, while Tarquinius, the seventh king of the Romans, was reigning. After he was expelled, the Romans themselves also began to be free from the rule of kings.

Up to this time the people of Israel had Prophets. Although there were many of them, only the canonical writings of a few are preserved both among the Jews and among us [Note: Some manuscripts read “canonical Scripture.”]. I promised, at the conclusion of the preceding book, that I would set down some of these in this book; and I now see that this must be done.

## CHAPTER XXVII—The times of the Prophets whose oracles are contained in books, and who then prophesied much about the calling of the Gentiles, when the Roman kingdom began and the Assyrian kingdom declined

To understand their times, let us go back a little into the preceding period. At the beginning of the book of the prophet Hosea, who is placed first among the Twelve, it is written:

“The word of the Lord that came to Hosea in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (Hosea 1:1).

Amos also writes that he prophesied in the days of King Uzziah; he adds Jeroboam, king of Israel, who lived during the same days (Amos 1:1). Isaiah, son of Amoz—or of the prophet mentioned above, or, as is more commonly reported, of another man of the same name who was not a prophet—also places at the beginning of his book the same four kings named by Hosea, and states at the outset that he prophesied during their reigns.

Micah likewise mentions the same period of his prophecy after the days of Uzziah. For he names the three kings who followed and whom Hosea also named: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1). From their writings it is found that these prophets prophesied together at the same time.

Jonah is added to them during the reign of the same King Uzziah, and Joel when Jotham, who succeeded Uzziah, had already begun to reign. We were able to discover the times of these two prophets in the Chronicles, not in their own books, because they say nothing about their dates.

These days extend from Proca, king of the Latins, or from the earlier Aventinus, to Romulus, already king of the Romans [Note: The printed editions read *Romanum*. The manuscripts have *Romanorum*.], or even to the beginning of the reign of his successor, Numa Pompilius. For Hezekiah, king of Judah, reigned until that time. Thus, during those years, these prophets burst forth together like springs of prophecy, when the Assyrian kingdom declined and the Roman kingdom began.

For just as, at the beginning of the Assyrian kingdom, Abraham appeared, to whom exceedingly clear promises were made concerning the blessing of all nations in his seed, so, at the beginning of the western Babylon—under whose imperial rule Christ was destined to come—the prophetic oracles that fulfilled those promises were to be disclosed, not only by being spoken but also by being written, as testimony to so great a future event.

Although prophets had almost never been lacking among the people of Israel since kings first began to rule there, they had been intended only for Israel, not for the Gentiles. But when that prophetic Scripture was being composed which would one day benefit the Gentiles, it was fitting that it should begin when the city that would rule the Gentiles was being founded [Note: The printed editions read *incipere* (“to begin”). The manuscripts more correctly read *inciperet* (“should begin”).].

## CHAPTER XXVIII—What Hosea and Amos prophesied that accords with the Gospel of Christ

The prophet Hosea speaks all the more deeply the more laboriously he is penetrated. Something must nevertheless be drawn from him and included here in fulfillment of our promise. He says:

“And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hosea 1:10).

The Apostles also understood this prophetic testimony as referring to the calling of the Gentile people, who formerly did not belong to God (Romans 9:26). And because this Gentile people is spiritually among the sons of Abraham, and therefore is rightly called Israel, he continues:

“And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel shall be gathered together into one, and they shall appoint for themselves one leader, and shall come up from the earth” (Hosea 1:11).

If we wished to explain this further, the prophetic savor would be dulled. Yet let that cornerstone be recalled, together with the two walls, one from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles (Ephesians 2:14–15, 20–22). Let them be recognized as the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel, resting together upon their one leadership and rising from the earth.

The same prophet testifies that these carnal Israelites [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and most manuscripts read *carnaliter* (“carnally”); all our manuscripts have this reading.], who now refuse to believe in Christ, will later believe—that is, their descendants, since these people will certainly pass by death into their own place. He says:

“For the children of Israel shall sit many days without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an altar, without a priesthood, without manifestations.”

Who does not see that the Jews are now in this condition? But let us hear what follows:

“And afterward the children of Israel shall return, and shall seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall be astonished at the Lord and at his goodness in the last days” (Hosea 3:4–5, according to the Septuagint).

Nothing is clearer than this prophecy, when Christ is understood to be signified by the name of King David [Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read, “by which David … is understood to be Christ.”], who, as the Apostle says, was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3).

This prophet also foretold Christ’s resurrection on the third day, as it was appropriate for it to be foretold in the lofty language of prophecy:

“He will heal us after two days; on the third day we shall rise” (Hosea 6:3).

In accordance with this the Apostle says to us:

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Colossians 3:1).

Amos likewise prophesies concerning such matters:
