“Prepare yourself,” he says, “to call upon your God, O Israel; for behold, I am he who establishes thunder, creates the spirit, and announces his Christ among men” (Amos 4:12–13, according to the Septuagint).

And in another place:

“On that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that has fallen, and I will rebuild its fallen parts; I will raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that the remnant of men may seek me, and all the nations upon whom my name has been invoked, says the Lord who does these things” (Amos 9:11–12, according to the Septuagint).

## CHAPTER XXIX—What Isaiah foretold concerning Christ and the Church

### 1.

Isaiah the prophet is not among the book of the Twelve Prophets, who are called “Minor” because their sayings are brief in comparison with those who are called “Major” because they composed lengthy volumes. Isaiah belongs to the latter group. Because his prophetic period was the same, I add him to the two prophets mentioned above.

Among the things he reproved as wicked, the righteous things he commanded, and the evils he foretold for the sinful people, he also prophesied much more than the other prophets concerning Christ and the Church—that is, concerning the King and the city he founded—so much so that some called him an evangelist rather than a prophet [Note: Thus Jerome, *Letters* 103, to Paulinus, and 117, to Paula and Eustochium, in the preface to his commentary on this prophet; and Cyril, *Oration 1 on Isaiah*. COQUAEUS.].

But, because of the need to bring the work to an end, I shall set down one passage here from among many. Speaking in the person of God the Father, he says:

“Behold, my servant shall understand, and he shall be exalted and greatly glorified. Just as many shall be astonished at you, so your appearance shall be without honor among men, and your glory shall be without honor among men. Thus many nations shall be astonished at him, and kings shall shut their mouths; for those to whom nothing was announced concerning him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.

“Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced him before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground. He had neither appearance nor glory. We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his appearance was without honor, failing before all the sons of men [Note: In the Septuagint, “before the sons of men.” Likewise, a little earlier they have “without honor from the sons of men” rather than “without honor from men.”].

“A man placed under a blow and knowing how to bear weakness; because his face was turned away, he was dishonored and not esteemed. He bears our sins [Note: The Lovaniensis edition omits “our.”] and suffers for us. We considered him to be in pain, under a blow and in affliction. But he was wounded because of our iniquities and weakened because of our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruising we were healed.

“All we like sheep have gone astray; each man has gone astray from his own way, and the Lord delivered him up for our sins. Though he was afflicted, he did not open his mouth [Col. 0586] [Note: Here the Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmianus, and the manuscripts omit “his.” Below, instead of *tondet* (“shaves”), they have *tonderet* (“would shave”).]. Like a sheep he was led to sacrifice, and like a lamb before the one who shaves it, so he did not open his mouth.

“In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who will declare his generation? For his life will be taken from the earth. Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death. And I will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And the Lord wills to cleanse him from the blow.

“If you give your soul for sin, you shall see a long-lived seed [Note: The Septuagint reads: “If you give for sin, your soul shall see a long-lived seed.”]. And the Lord wills to take his life away from pain, to show him light, to form his understanding, to justify the righteous man who serves many well; and he himself shall bear their sins [Note: The printed editions have *portavit* (“bore”). The manuscripts have *portabit* (“will bear”). The Greek has *anoisei* (“will bear”).].

“Therefore he himself shall inherit many, and he shall divide the spoils of the mighty, because his soul was delivered to death, and he was reckoned among the wicked. He himself bore the sins of many, and for their sins he was delivered up” (Isaiah 52:13–15; 53:1–12, according to the Septuagint).

This concerns Christ.

### 2.

Now let us hear what follows concerning the Church:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not give birth, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.

“Enlarge the place of your tent and your curtains; fix them firmly [Note: The printed editions read, “and fix the stakes of your folds.” The manuscripts correct this to “and your curtains,” omitting *stakes*, in accordance with the Septuagint, which reads *kaì tôn aulaiòn sou* (“and of your curtains”). This may be rendered in Latin as *et aulaeorum tuorum*, though *aulaea* is also known as a feminine noun from Quintus Curtius, book 8—if that passage itself is free from corruption.], do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. Extend still farther to the right and to the left. Your seed shall inherit nations, and you shall inhabit deserted cities.

“Do not fear, because you have been put to shame; do not be ashamed, because you have been reproached. For you shall forget eternal shame and shall not remember the reproach of your widowhood. For the Lord who made you—the Lord of hosts is his name—and he who redeemed you, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:1–5), and so forth.

Let this be enough. Several things in it deserve explanation, but I think those passages suffice that are so clear that even enemies are compelled, unwillingly, to understand them.

## CHAPTER XXX—What Micah, Jonah, and Joel prophesied in agreement with the New Testament

### 1.

The prophet Micah, presenting Christ under the figure of a great mountain, speaks as follows:

“It shall be in the last days: the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, prepared upon the tops of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills. Peoples shall hasten to it, and many nations shall go and say:

‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob. He will show us his way, and we shall walk in his paths, because the law shall go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. He will judge among many peoples and rebuke mighty nations, even those far away’” (Micah 4:1–3).

This prophet also foretells the place in which Christ was born:

“And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephratha, you are very small to be among the thousands of Judah; from you one shall come forth for me to be ruler in Israel. His origin is from the beginning, from the days of eternity. Therefore he will give them up until the time when she who is in labor gives birth [Note: This follows the manuscripts according to the Septuagint. The printed editions read, “until the time when she who is in labor shall give birth.”], and the remnant of his brothers shall return to the children of Israel. He shall stand, see, and shepherd his flock in the strength of the Lord, and they shall dwell in the honor of the name of the Lord their God, because now he shall be magnified to the ends of the earth” (Micah 5:2–4, according to the Septuagint).

### 2.

The prophet Jonah prophesied Christ not so much by words as by a certain suffering of his own—indeed more clearly than if he had cried out in words about Christ’s death and resurrection. For why was he received into the belly of the sea creature and restored on the third day, except to signify that Christ would return from the depths of hell on the third day?

### 3.

Everything Joel prophesies requires explanation in many words if what pertains to Christ and the Church is to be made clear. Yet I will not omit one passage that the Apostles also recalled when the Holy Spirit came down upon the assembled believers, as Christ had promised (Acts 2:17–18):

“And it shall be after this: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh. Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your elders shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Indeed, upon my male servants and my female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit” (Joel 2:28–29).

## CHAPTER XXXI—What is found foretold in Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk concerning the salvation of the world in Christ

### 1.

Three of the Minor Prophets—Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk—neither state their own dates nor are their prophetic periods found in the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome [Note: Jerome writes in his commentary on Obadiah: “The Hebrews say that this is the man who, under King Ahab and the most impious Jezebel, fed one hundred prophets in caves, those who had not bent the knee before Baal,” and so forth. He therefore lived in the time of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, when Tiberius was king of the Latins. Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 9, chapter 11, §3, writes that the prophet Nahum lived during the time of Jotham, king of Judah. Finally, concerning the prophet Habakkuk, Daniel 14:32–38 says that he carried his meal from Judaea to Babylon for Daniel; Jerome notes that he prophesied during the Babylonian captivity and that his prophecies were directed toward Babylon.].

Obadiah is indeed placed by them alongside Micah, but not in the section where the dates are recorded at which Micah is known from his writings to have prophesied. I think this happened through the careless error of those who copied the labors of others. We could not find the other two mentioned in the copies of the Chronicles that we possessed. Nevertheless, since they are included in the canon, they too must not be passed over by us.

Obadiah, as far as the length of his writing is concerned, is the shortest of all the Prophets. He speaks against Idumaea, the nation of Esau, the elder of the twin sons of Isaac and grandsons of Abraham, the one who was rejected [Note: The printed editions read: “He speaks against the nation of Idumaea, that is, Esau, one of the two …” This has been corrected according to the ancient manuscripts.].

If, however, we understand Idumaea to stand for the Gentiles, by that manner of speech in which the whole is understood from a part, we can recognize Christ in what he says, among other things:

“On Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and it shall be holy” [Note: This follows the manuscripts according to the Septuagint. The printed editions read, “To Mount Zion.”] (Obadiah 17).

And near the end of the prophecy:

“And those who have been saved shall go up from Mount Zion to defend Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall belong to the Lord” (Obadiah 17, 21, according to the Septuagint).

This is plainly fulfilled when those saved from Mount Zion—that is, from Judaea—believers in Christ, among whom the Apostles are especially recognized, went up to defend Mount Esau. How could they defend it except by saving through the preaching of the Gospel those who believed, so that they might be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God? He expressed this in succession by adding: “And the kingdom shall belong to the Lord.”

Mount Zion signifies Judaea, where salvation and holiness were foretold as future; holiness is Christ Jesus. Mount Esau, however, is Idumaea, through which the Church of the Gentiles was signified. As I have explained, those saved from Mount Zion defended it, so that the kingdom might belong to the Lord. This was obscure before it happened; but once it has happened, what believer does not recognize it?

### 2.

The prophet Nahum—or rather God speaking through him—says:

“I will destroy the carved and cast images; I will make your burial place, because the feet of the one who evangelizes and announces peace are swift upon the mountains.

“Celebrate your festivals, Judah; fulfill your vows, because they shall no longer continue to pass into old age. It is finished, it is consumed, it is taken away [Note: The Lovaniensis edition omits “it is taken away,” which is found in the other printed editions and in the manuscripts].

“He has gone up who breathes upon your face, rescuing you from tribulation” (Nahum 1:14–15; 2:1, according to the Septuagint).

Let the reader who remembers the Gospel recall who has ascended from the underworld and breathed upon the face of Judah—that is, upon the Jewish disciples—the Holy Spirit [Note: The printed editions read, “recall” (or “recalls”) “the Holy Spirit”; the punctuation of the words is faulty and has been corrected from the manuscripts.]. These things pertain to the New Testament, whose festivals are renewed spiritually in such a way that they cannot pass into old age.

Moreover, through the Gospel we now see the carved and cast images—that is, the idols of false gods—destroyed and consigned to oblivion as though to a tomb; and we recognize that this prophecy has also been fulfilled in this matter.

### 3.

Of whom other than Christ’s future coming can Habakkuk be understood to speak when he says:

“And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision plainly on a tablet, so that the one who reads it may grasp it; for the vision is still for its appointed time, and it will arise at the end and not in vain. If it delays, wait for it, because he who comes will certainly come and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:2–3)?

## CHAPTER XXXII—Concerning the prophecy contained in the Prayer and Canticle of Habakkuk
In his prayer, together with the Canticle—to whom but the Lord Christ does he say: “Lord, I have heard your report, and I was afraid; Lord, I considered your works, and I trembled”? What is this other than an ineffable wonder at humanity’s foreknown, new, and sudden salvation?

“Between two living creatures you will be known”: what is this other than either between the two Testaments, or between the two thieves, or between Moses and Elijah conversing with him on the mountain?

“As the years approach, you will be known” [Col. 0589]: you will be revealed at the coming of the appointed time. This requires no explanation. [Note: This is the manuscript reading. In the printed editions, after “you will be revealed,” one reads: “Since this is self-evident, it need not be explained; but what follows, ‘When it is troubled,’ etc., must be explained”—except that in Lovaniensis, after “what follows,” the words “must be explained” are absent.] “When my soul is troubled, you will remember mercy in your anger”: what is this other than that he figuratively represented in himself the Jews, whose nation he belonged to? When, greatly angered and troubled, they crucified Christ, he, remembering mercy, said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

“God will come from Theman, and the Holy One from the shadowy and densely wooded mountain.” In this passage, where it says “he will come from Theman,” others have translated it “from the South” or “from the Southwest.” [Note: Besides the Septuagint, Jerome says, “Aquila, Symmachus, and the fifth edition retained the Hebrew word itself. Only Theodotion explained what Theman meant, saying, ‘He will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Pharan.’” Jerome likewise writes in *Hebrew Places*: “Theman was the region of the princes of Edom in the land of Gebal, taking its name from Theman, son of Eliphaz, son of Esau; but even to this day there is a village called Theman, five miles distant from the city of Petra … It should be known, however, that every southern region is called Theman by the Hebrews.” —Ludovicus Vives.]

This signifies the south, that is, the warmth of charity and the splendor of truth. [Col. 0589] As for the shadowy and densely wooded mountain, although it can be understood in many ways, I would more willingly take it as the height of the divine Scriptures in which Christ was prophesied. For there are many shadowy and obscure things there to exercise the mind of the seeker. He comes from there when one who understands finds him there.

“His power covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise”: what is this other than what is also said in the Psalm, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Psalm 56:6)? [Note: Lovaniensis has “above all the heavens”; “all” is absent from the other books.]

“His brightness will be like light”: what is this other than that his fame will enlighten believers?

“Horns are in his hands”: what is this other than the trophy of the cross?

“And he established the firm love of his strength”: this requires no explanation.

“Before his face the word will go, and it will come forth into the open country behind his feet”: what is this other than that he was foretold before he came here, and proclaimed after he returned from here?

“He stood, and the earth was shaken”: what is this other than that he stood to give help, and the earth was shaken to believe?

“He looked, and the nations melted”: that is, he had mercy and made the peoples repent.

“The mountains were crushed by violence”: that is, by miracles exerting force, the pride of the exalted was crushed.

“The everlasting hills flowed down”: that is, they were humbled for a time so that they might be raised up forever.

“I saw his everlasting entrances because of his labors”: that is, I saw the labor of charity, not without the reward of eternity.

“The tents of the Ethiopians will tremble, and the tents of the land of Midian”: that is, the nations, suddenly terrified by the report of your wonders, even those who are not under Roman jurisdiction, will become part of the Christian people. [Note: Only the Lovaniensis edition has *repentino*, “suddenly”; the other editions have *repente*.]

“Are you angry at the rivers, Lord, or is your fury against the rivers, or your assault against the sea?” This is said because he does not now come to judge the world, but so that the world may be saved through him (John 3:17).

“For you will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation”: that is, your evangelists will carry you, being governed by you; and your Gospel is salvation for those who believe in you. [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “because.”]

“You will bend your bow intently over the scepters, says the Lord”: that is, you will threaten your judgment even against the kings of the earth.

“The earth will be split by the rivers”: that is, as the words of those who preach you flow in, the hearts of human beings will be opened to confession. To them it was said: “Tear your hearts, and not your garments” (Joel 2:13).

“What does ‘They will see you, and the peoples will grieve’ mean, unless it is that they should become blessed through mourning?”

“What does ‘Scattering the waters by your advance’ mean, unless it is that, by walking among those who proclaim you everywhere, you scatter the streams of doctrine here and there?” [Note: The Lovaniensis edition has “You will scatter the waters in your advance.” The reading is corrected from other printed editions and manuscripts, supported by the Septuagint.]

“What does ‘The abyss gave its voice’ mean? Did the depth of the human heart express what it thought of him? ‘The height of its imagination’ is an explanation of the preceding line, for the height is the abyss. When he says ‘of its imagination,’ one must supply ‘it gave its voice’: that is, it expressed what we have said it thought of him. For imagination is a vision which it neither held back nor concealed, but poured forth by confession.

“The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order”: that is, Christ ascended into heaven, and the Church was ordered beneath its king.

“Your arrows will go forth into the light”: that is, your words will be sent forth not into concealment but into public view.

“Into the brightness of the flashing of your weapons”: “your arrows will go forth” must be supplied. For he had said to his disciples: “What I tell you in darkness, say in the light” (Matthew 10:27).

“By threatening you will diminish the earth”: that is, by threatening, you will humble human beings.

“And in fury you will cast down the nations”: because, in avenging, you will strike down those who exalt themselves.

“You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones”; [Note: The manuscripts have *facias*, “that you may save.”] “You cast death upon the heads of the wicked”: none of this requires explanation. [Note: This reading, according to the Septuagint, was also followed by Tertullian in Book 4 of *Against Marcion*, chapter 39. Jerome should be consulted concerning the other interpretations.]

“You raised up bonds as far as the neck.” Here “bonds” can also be understood in a good sense, as the bonds of wisdom, so that the feet may be placed in its fetters and the neck in its collar. [Note: The printed editions have *ut vinciantur*, “so that they may be bound.” The manuscripts more aptly have *ut injiciantur*, “so that they may be placed.”]

“You cut them off in astonishment of mind”: let us supply “the bonds.” He raised up the good bonds and cut off the evil ones, concerning which it is said to him: “You broke my bonds” (Psalm 115:16)—and this “in astonishment of mind,” that is, wonderfully.

“The heads of the mighty will be moved by it”: “by it,” namely, by astonishment. [Note: Here we repeat *in ea*, “by it,” following the manuscripts; it was omitted by the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

“They will open their mouths like one eating secretly.” Certain powerful Jews came to the Lord, astonished at his deeds and words, and, hungering for the bread of his teaching, ate secretly because of fear of the Jews, as the Gospel revealed them (John 19:38).

“And you sent your horses into the sea, disturbing many waters”: these are nothing other than the many peoples. For some would not be converted through fear and others persecute in fury unless all were thrown into confusion.

“I watched, and my belly trembled at the sound of the prayer of my lips; trembling entered my bones, and beneath me my condition was disturbed.” He fixed his attention on what he was saying and was himself terrified by the prayer he poured forth prophetically, in which he saw future events.

[Col. 0591] When many peoples had been thrown into confusion, he saw the tribulations threatening the Church. Immediately he recognized himself as one of its members and said: “I will rest on the day of tribulation,” as belonging to those who are “joyful in hope and patient in tribulation” (Romans 12:12).

“‘That I may ascend,’ he says, ‘to the people of my pilgrimage’”: that is, withdrawing from the wicked people of his carnal kinship, who did not make pilgrimage in this world or seek the heavenly homeland.

“‘For,’ he says, ‘the fig tree will not bear fruit, and there will be no births in the vines; the work of the olive will lie, and the fields will produce no food. The sheep have failed to provide food, and cattle are no longer in the stalls.’”

He saw that nation which was destined to kill Christ would lose the abundance of spiritual resources, which he represented prophetically through earthly fertility. And because that nation suffered such divine anger because, “ignorant of God’s righteousness, it sought to establish its own” (Romans 10:3), he immediately says: “But I will rejoice in the Lord; I will exult in God my Savior. The Lord God is my strength; he will set my feet for completion; he will place me upon the heights, that I may triumph in his song” (Habakkuk 3)—that song, namely, of which something similar is said in the Psalm: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps; he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God” (Psalm 39:3–4).

He therefore triumphs in the Lord’s song who delights in praising him, not himself, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31). Certain manuscripts seem to me to have the better reading, “I will rejoice in God my Jesus,” rather than those which, wishing to render the expression in Latin, omitted the name itself, whose utterance is dearer and sweeter to us.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### On Christ and the calling of the Gentiles, which Jeremiah and Zephaniah foretold by the prophetic Spirit

1. Jeremiah the prophet is one of the greater prophets, like Isaiah, not one of the lesser, concerning whose writings I have already presented some material. He prophesied while Josiah was reigning in Jerusalem and Ancus Marcius among the Romans, when the captivity of the Jews was already approaching. [Note: Jeremiah first became known through the letter he wrote to those who were living in captivity at Babylon. This letter was written in the year 599 before the birth of Christ; but it was already the fifteenth year after Josiah had fallen in battle against Necho, king of Egypt, namely in the year 611. At that time Tarquinius Priscus was king of the Romans. —Larcher.]

He continued his prophecy until the fifth month of the captivity, as we find in his writings. Zephaniah, one of the lesser prophets, is associated with him. For he too says that he prophesied in the days of Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1), but he does not say how long he continued.

Jeremiah therefore prophesied not only in the time of Ancus Marcius but also in that of Tarquinius Priscus, whom the Romans had as their fifth king. For when that captivity occurred, Tarquinius had already begun to reign.

Thus, prophesying about Christ, Jeremiah says: “The Spirit of our face, the Lord Christ, was captured in our sins” (Lamentations 4:20), briefly showing both that our Lord is Christ and that he suffered for us.

In another passage he says: “This is my God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. He found the whole way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38). Some attribute this testimony not to Jeremiah but to his secretary, who was called Baruch; nevertheless, it is more commonly attributed to Jeremiah. [Note: The manuscripts, following the Greek Septuagint, read “on earth”; the printed editions read “in the lands.”]

Again the same prophet speaks of him: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; and he will reign as king, and will be wise, and will execute judgment and righteousness on the earth. In those days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely; and this is the name by which they will call him: The Lord our Righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:5–6).

He also spoke in this way about the future calling of the Gentiles, which we now see fulfilled: “Lord, my God and my refuge in the day of troubles, to you the nations will come from the ends of the earth and say: Truly our fathers possessed lies, idols in which there is no profit” (Jeremiah 16:19).

Because the Jews would not recognize him, although he had to be killed by them, the same prophet signifies this as follows: “The heart is heavy in every respect, and he is a man; and who will know him?” (Jeremiah 17:9, according to the Septuagint).

The passage I placed in Book 17 concerning the New Testament, whose mediator is Christ, also belongs to this prophet (chapter 3). For Jeremiah himself says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Jacob” (Jeremiah 31:31), followed by the other words recorded there.

2. For the present, I shall set down these prophecies concerning Christ from the prophet Zephaniah, who prophesied together with Jeremiah:

“Wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection, for the future; because my judgment is that I may gather the nations and assemble the kingdoms” (Zephaniah 3:8).

And again: “The Lord is terrifying over them, and he will destroy all the gods of the earth; and every island of the nations will worship him from its own place” (Zephaniah 2:11).

A little later he says: “Then I will transform the language of the peoples, and in his offspring, so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke; from the borders of the rivers of Ethiopia they will bring sacrifices to me. On that day you will not be confounded by all your inventions which you wickedly committed against me; for then I will remove from you the offenses of your wrongdoing. You will no longer continue to exalt yourself upon my holy mountain. I will leave in you a meek and humble people, and those who remain of Israel will fear the name of the Lord” (Zephaniah 3:9–13, according to the Septuagint). [Note: Vindobonensis, Amerbach, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “and his offspring,” omitting “in.” Some manuscripts have “On that day you will be confounded,” without the negative particle; others read “in Israel.” The Greek has τοῦ Ἰσραήλ, “of Israel.”]

These are the remnant concerning which it is prophesied elsewhere, as the Apostle also recalls: “If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved” (Isaiah 10:22; Romans 9:27). For these remnants of that nation believed in Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### On the prophecy of Daniel and Ezekiel, which agrees concerning Christ and the Church

1. During the Babylonian captivity itself Daniel and Ezekiel [Col. 0593] first prophesied, two more of the greater prophets. [Note: The older books consistently spell the latter name *Hiezechiel*.] Daniel even defined by a number of years the time when Christ was destined to come and suffer. It would take too long to demonstrate this by calculation, and others have already done so.

Concerning his power and glory [Note: A few manuscripts read “and the Church”; nearly all the others, “and glory.”] he spoke as follows: “I was watching in a night vision, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven. He came to the Ancient of Days, and was presented before him. To him was given dominion, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13–14). [Note: Lovaniensis has “and a son,” whereas the manuscripts more correctly have “like a son.”]

2. Ezekiel likewise signifies Christ prophetically by David, because he assumed flesh from David’s offspring. On account of that form of a servant by which [Note: Most manuscripts read “because.”] he became human, the same Son of God is also called God’s servant. Thus, speaking prophetically in the person of God the Father, he foretells him:

“I will raise up over my sheep one shepherd who will feed them, my servant David; he himself will feed them, and he himself will be their shepherd. I, the Lord, will be their God, and my servant David will be prince in their midst. I, the Lord, have spoken” (Ezekiel 34:23–24).

In another passage he says:

“There will be one king ruling over all, and there will no longer be two nations, nor will they be divided any longer into two kingdoms. They will no longer defile themselves with their idols, their abominations, or any of their iniquities. I will save them from all their dwellings in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. They will be my people, and I will be their God. My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd over all of them” (Ezekiel 37:22–24).

## CHAPTER XXXV

### On the prophecy of the three prophets, namely Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi

1. Three of the lesser prophets remain: Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who prophesied at the end of the captivity. Haggai prophesies Christ and the Church with this rather explicit brevity:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet once more, it is a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land; I will shake all nations, and the Desired One of all nations will come” (Haggai 2:7–8).

We see this prophecy partly already fulfilled and partly expected to be fulfilled at the end. For he shook heaven by the testimony of angels and stars when Christ was incarnate. He shook earth by the great miracle of the virgin birth itself. He shook sea and dry land when Christ is proclaimed both in the islands and throughout the whole world. Thus we see all nations shaken toward faith. But the following words, “and the Desired One of all nations will come,” are awaited with reference to his final coming. [Note: Justin Martyr likewise interpreted this passage as referring to Christ’s second coming, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*. Compare below, chapter 48. —Coquaeus.] For, in order that he might be desired by those awaiting him, he first had to be loved by those believing in him.

2. Zechariah says concerning Christ and the Church:

“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King will come to you, righteous and savior; he himself poor, and riding upon a she-ass [Note: Vindobonensis, Amerbach, and the manuscripts read “a donkey.”], and upon a colt, the son of a she-ass. His power is from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth” (Zechariah 9:9–10). [Note: Lovaniensis reads “to the ends of the world”; “world” is absent from the other books.]

The Gospel records when this occurred, when the Lord Christ used an animal of this kind on his journey; there too this prophecy is recalled in part, insofar as seemed sufficient for that passage (Matthew 21).

Elsewhere, addressing Christ himself in the Spirit of prophecy concerning remission of sins through his blood, he says: “You too, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zechariah 9:11). Various meanings may be held, even in accordance with the right faith, concerning what he intends by this pit. [Note: Jerome, Cyril, and St Thomas explain it as the limbo of the fathers, where their souls were held until Christ’s passion finally set them free; all recent writers follow them. —Coquaeus.] To me, however, it seems best to signify nothing other than the somehow dry and barren depth of human misery, where there are no streams of righteousness, but the mire of iniquity. For the Psalm also says of this: “He drew me up from the pit of misery and from the miry mud” (Psalm 39:3).

3. Malachi, prophesying the Church which we see spread abroad through Christ, says most explicitly to the Jews in the person of God:

“I have no pleasure in you, and I will not receive a gift from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a clean offering will be sacrificed and offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord” (Malachi 1:10).

When they see this sacrifice now offered to God everywhere from the rising of the sun to its setting through Christ’s priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, and cannot deny that the Jews’ sacrifice—to whom it was said, “I have no pleasure in you, nor will I accept a gift from your hands”—has ceased, why do they still await another Christ, when what they read as prophesied and see fulfilled could not have been fulfilled except through him?

For shortly afterward he says of him in the person of God:

“My covenant with him was of life and peace; I gave it to him, that he might fear me with fear and stand in awe before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth; he walked with me uprightly in peace and turned many from iniquity [Note: Thus most manuscripts, following the Septuagint; the printed editions read, “he will walk with me and turn many from iniquity.”], for the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord Almighty” (Malachi 2:5–7).

Nor is it surprising that Christ Jesus is called the angel of Almighty God. For just as he is called servant because of the form of a servant in which he came to human beings, so he is called angel because of the Gospel which he announced to human beings. For, if we translate these Greek words, *Evangelium* means “good announcement,” and *angelus* means “messenger.”

Again he says of him:

“Behold, I send [Col. 0595; Note: Manuscript 258 reads “I shall send.”] my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come into his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he comes, says the Lord Almighty [Note: The printed editions read “the Lord God Almighty”; “God” is absent from the manuscripts.]; and who will endure the day of his entrance, or who will stand at his appearing?” (Malachi 3:1–2).

In this passage he foretold both Christ’s first and second coming: the first, namely, where he says, “and suddenly the Lord will come into his temple,” that is, into his flesh, of which he said in the Gospel, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19); the second where he says, “Behold, he comes, says the Lord Almighty; and who will endure the day of his entrance, or who will stand at his appearing?”

But by saying, “the Lord whom you seek, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire,” he certainly signified that the Jews too seek and desire Christ according to the Scriptures they read. Yet many of them did not recognize that the one whom they sought and desired had come, blinded in their hearts by their preceding deserts.

Certainly, by “covenant,” which he names here, or above where he says, “My covenant was with him,” or here where he calls him the angel of the covenant, we must without doubt understand the New Covenant, in which eternal things are promised, not the old, in which temporal things are promised. Many weak persons, holding these temporal things to be great, and serving the true God for the reward of such things, are troubled when they see the impious abound in them.

Therefore, in order to distinguish the eternal blessedness of the New Covenant, which will be given only to the good, from the earthly happiness of the old, which is often given even to the evil, the same prophet says:

“Your words have weighed heavily upon me, says the Lord, and you have said, ‘In what have we spoken against you?’ You have said: ‘Everyone who serves God is vain; and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinances and walked in supplication before the face of the Lord Almighty? And now we call foreigners blessed; all who do iniquity are built up; they opposed God and were saved.’”

Those who feared the Lord spoke these things, each to his neighbor; and the Lord took notice and heard, and wrote a book of remembrance before him for those who fear the Lord and revere his name. This book signifies the New Covenant.

Finally, let us hear what follows:

“They shall be mine, says the Lord Almighty, for the day [Note: The printed editions read “on the day”; the manuscripts read “for the day,” following the Greek Septuagint.] on which I act, as a possession; and I will choose them as a man chooses [Note: Our manuscripts read “chose.”] his son who serves him. Then you will turn and see between the righteous and the unrighteous, between one who serves God and one who does not serve. For behold, the day comes, burning like an oven, and it will consume them; all foreigners and all who do iniquity shall be stubble, and the day which comes will burn them up, says the Lord Almighty, and neither root nor branch will be left to them. But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings; you will go out and leap like calves released from bonds; [Col. 0596] and you will tread down the wicked, and they shall be ashes beneath your feet on the day on which I act, says the Lord Almighty” (Malachi 3:13–18; 4:1–3).

This is the day called the day of judgment, of which, if God wills, we shall speak more fully in its proper place.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### On Ezra and the books of Maccabees

After these three prophets—Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi—Ezra also wrote at the same time as the liberation of the people from Babylonian bondage. He is regarded more as a writer of historical events than as a prophet; so also is the book called Esther, whose historical event, to God’s praise, is found not far from these times.

Unless perhaps Ezra is to be understood to have prophesied Christ in this: when a question arose among certain young men as to what had the greatest power in affairs, and one said kings, another wine, and the third women, who often ruled kings, that same third man nevertheless showed truth to be victorious over all things (3 Ezra 3:9 ff.). [Note: The Third Book of Ezra, in which this history occurs, contains events preceding the books of Ezra and Nehemiah and therefore among the Greeks is both canonical and First Ezra. Origen cites it as canonical in Homily 9 on Joshua; Athanasius in Book 3 against the Arians; Cyprian in Letter 74 to Pompeius and in *On the Singularity of Clerics*, chapter 21; and Augustine seems here not obscurely to regard it as canonical, since he judges that its statement can be called a prophecy of Christ. —Coquaeus.]

On consulting the Gospel, we recognize Christ to be truth.

From this time, after the temple was restored among the Jews, they had not kings but rulers, down to Aristobulus. [Note: On the death of the high priest Hyrcanus, his son Aristobulus succeeded him and was the first to assume the diadem, in 104 before Christ’s birth. Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, Book 13, chapter 19. —Larcher.]

The calculation of their times is found not in the holy Scriptures called canonical but in other writings, among which are the books of the Maccabees. [Note: See Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, no. 13, and Book 1 against the Letter of Gaudentius, no. 38.] These are not held as canonical by the Jews but by the Church, because of the powerful and marvelous sufferings of certain martyrs who, before Christ came in the flesh [Note: The manuscripts read “in flesh.”], contended for God’s law even to death and endured evils most grave and terrible.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### That prophetic authority is found to be older than every origin of Gentile philosophy

Accordingly, in the time of our prophets, whose writings have now reached the knowledge of almost all nations, the philosophers of the Gentiles, who were called even by that name, did not yet exist. [Note: All manuscripts continue after “nations”: “and, much more, the philosophers of the Gentiles were later than them.”]

The name began with Pythagoras of Samos, who began to excel and become known at the time when the Jews’ captivity was ended. [Note: According to Diogenes Laertius, Pythagoras flourished in the sixtieth Olympiad. Eusebius places him in his *Chronicle* at the sixty-third Olympiad and writes in Book 10, chapter 4, of the *Preparation for the Gospel* that he flourished in the sixty-second Olympiad, when Jesus son of Josedec was high priest among the Hebrews and Zerubbabel was ruler, when Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi prophesied and Servius Tullius reigned among the Romans. Iamblichus writes that he came to Italy about the sixty-second Olympiad; Cicero, *Tusculan Questions*, Book 1, says this occurred while Tarquinius Superbus was ruling, and in Book 4 reports that he was in Italy in the same times in which Junius Brutus freed his country. According to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, Pythagoras died in the fourth or fifth year of the seventieth Olympiad, that is, about 498 before Christ, having lived eighty or ninety years, as Diogenes Laertius reports.]

All the more, therefore, the other philosophers are found to have lived after the prophets. For Socrates of Athens himself, master of all those who then shone most brightly and holding primacy in the branch called moral or active, is found in the chronicles to have lived after Ezra. [Note: Diogenes Laertius writes that Socrates was born in the fourth year of the seventy-seventh Olympiad, falling in 468 before Christ, and died in the first year of the ninety-fifth Olympiad, in his seventieth year.]

Plato too was born not long afterward, and far surpassed Socrates’ other disciples. [Note: As Diogenes Laertius writes from Apollodorus, Plato was born in the eighty-eighth Olympiad and died in the first year of the one hundred and eighth Olympiad, 348 before Christ, at the age of eighty-one.]

If we add their predecessors, who were not yet called philosophers—the seven Sages, and then the natural philosophers who succeeded Thales and imitated his pursuit of investigating the nature of things, namely Anaximander, Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, and some others—even they do not precede all our prophets in antiquity. For Thales, after whom the others came, is reported to have flourished in the reign of Romulus, [Note: Lovaniensis alone reads “flashed forth.”] when the stream of prophecy burst forth from the springs of Israel in writings that would flow through the whole world.

Only those theological poets—Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, and any other among the Greeks—are found earlier in years than these Hebrew prophets whose writings we hold in authority. Yet neither did they precede in time our true theologian Moses, who truthfully proclaimed the one true God and whose writings now stand first in the canon of authority. Thus, so far as the Greeks are concerned, among whom the literature of this age flourished most vigorously, they have nothing on the basis of which to boast of their wisdom, by which our religion, in which true wisdom is found, might seem, if not superior, at least older.

Yet, as must be admitted, not indeed in Greece but among barbarian nations such as Egypt, there had already existed before Moses some learning that was called their wisdom. Otherwise it would not have been written in the holy books that Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22), namely at the time when he was born there and, after being adopted and reared by Pharaoh’s daughter, was also liberally educated.

But neither could Egyptian wisdom precede our prophets’ wisdom in time, since Abraham too was a prophet (Genesis 20:7). What wisdom could there have been in Egypt before Isis—whom, once dead, they judged should be worshipped as a great goddess—had handed letters down to them? Isis, moreover, is said to have been the daughter of Inachus, who first began to reign over the Argives, when Abraham’s grandchildren are already found to have been born.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### That the ecclesiastical canon has not received certain writings of the saints because of their excessive antiquity, lest falsehoods be inserted among truths on their occasion

[Col. 0598]

If, indeed, I go back to much more ancient times, before that great flood there was certainly our patriarch Noah, whom I would not without reason also call a prophet, since the very ark which he made and in which he escaped with his household was a prophecy of our times.

What of Enoch, the seventh from Adam? Is he not also declared to have prophesied in the canonical Epistle of the apostle Jude (Jude 14)? Their excessive antiquity caused their writings not to be held in authority either among the Jews or among us, because they seemed liable to be suspected, lest false things be produced as true. [Note: Compare above, Book 15, chapter 23, no. 4.]

For certain writings said to be theirs are indeed put forward by persons who, according to their own inclination, believe everywhere whatever they wish. But the purity of the canon did not receive them—not because it rejects the authority of those men who pleased God, but because these writings are not believed to be theirs.

Nor should it seem surprising that writings produced under the name of such great antiquity are held suspect, since in the very history of the kings of Judah [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “Judaea.”] and the kings of Israel, which contains the events whose truth we believe on the authority of that canonical Scripture, very many things are mentioned which are not explained there and are said to be found in other books written by the prophets; and in some places the names of those prophets themselves are not concealed (1 Chronicles 29:29; 2 Chronicles 9:29).

Yet these books are not found in the canon received by the people of God. I confess that the reason for this escapes me, unless I suppose that those very persons to whom the Holy Spirit revealed what ought to have authority in religion may have been able to write some things, as human beings, by historical diligence and others, as prophets, by divine inspiration.

These were distinguished in such a way that the former might be judged attributable to themselves, but the latter to God speaking through them; and thus the former would belong to the abundance of knowledge, the latter to religious authority. In that authority the canon is preserved.

Apart from it, writings that are now produced even under the name of ancient prophets [Note: Our manuscripts read “true prophets.”] do not contribute even to that store of knowledge, because it is uncertain whether they belong to those whose names they bear. Consequently they are not believed, especially those in which some things are read even contrary to the faith of the canonical books; this makes it entirely plain that they are not those persons’ writings.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### On the Hebrew letters, which have never ceased to exist in the distinctive character of their own language
Therefore, it is not to be believed, as some suppose, that only the Hebrew language was preserved through the man called Eber, from whom the name “Hebrews” derives, and that from him it came down to Abraham, while the Hebrew letters began with the Law given through Moses. Rather, through that succession of fathers, the language, together with its letters, was preserved. [Note: For many writers—for example, Cyril, Against Julian, book 7, p. 231, D, and Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book 1, chapter 23, §153—state that Moses was the first wise man and the first to transmit letters and grammar to the Jews, and that the Phoenicians received them from the Jews, and the Greeks from the Phoenicians. Augustine, however, does not accept this; he holds that, just as the Hebrew language existed before the Flood, so Hebrew characters too must have been discovered. What Josephus writes seems to confirm this view. In book 1, chapter 3, of The Antiquities of the Jews, speaking of the sons of Seth, he says: “They devised the science of the stars and the knowledge of heavenly things. But, lest their discoveries should slip from human memory and perish before they were known, knowing that Adam had foretold that there would be a twofold universal destruction of things—one by fire, the other by flood—they raised two columns and inscribed their discoveries upon each: so that, if the brick column should happen to be destroyed by the flood, the stone column, surviving, might provide humankind with the opportunity to learn and might display for examination what it contained inscribed upon it. Moreover, the stone column dedicated by them still exists in our own time in the land of Syria.” COQUAEUS.]

Finally, Moses appointed in the people of God those who were to preside over the teaching of letters, before they knew any letters of the divine Law. Scripture calls them γραμματοεισαγωγεῖς, which may be rendered in Latin as *inductors* or *introducers of letters*, because they “induce” them—that is, they in some way introduce them into the hearts of those learning, or rather introduce the learners themselves into them.

Therefore, let no nation boast vainly of the antiquity of its wisdom over our Patriarchs and Prophets, who possessed divine wisdom. For not even Egypt—which is accustomed falsely and emptily to boast of the antiquity of its teachings—is found to have preceded, by whatever wisdom it possessed, the wisdom of our Patriarchs. No one will dare say that they were highly skilled in the wondrous disciplines before they knew letters—that is, before Isis came there and taught them those disciplines.

Moreover, what was their celebrated teaching, which was called wisdom, except chiefly astronomy, and whatever else among such disciplines is usually more useful for exercising the intellect than for enlightening minds with true wisdom? As for philosophy, which professes to teach something by which human beings become happy: around the time of Mercury, whom they called Trismegistus, studies of this kind flourished in those lands—certainly long before the wise men or philosophers of Greece, but nevertheless after Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph; indeed, after Moses himself. For it is reported that, at the time when Moses was born, that great astrologer Atlas was living—the brother of Prometheus, maternal grandfather of the elder Mercury, and grandfather of this Mercury Trismegistus. [Note: Atlas lived in the year 1638 before Christ, according to Eusebius; Moses, according to Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 10, chapters 9, pp. 483–484, was born in 1609 before Christ. Thus twenty-nine years intervened between Atlas and Moses. LARCHER.]

## CHAPTER XL—On the Egyptians’ most mendacious vanity, which assigns one hundred thousand years to the antiquity of their knowledge

In vain, therefore, certain men chatter in the extremity of their presumption, saying that more than one hundred thousand years have been counted from the time when Egypt grasped the science of the stars. In what books did they find this number, when they learned letters from their teacher Isis scarcely two thousand years ago?

Varro is no insignificant authority in history, and he reported this fact in a manner that does not conflict with the truth of the divine writings. Since not yet six thousand years have been completed from the first human being, who was called Adam, how can we regard as anything but objects of ridicule those who try to persuade us of such divergent periods of time, so contrary to this established truth?

For whom should we trust more in recounting the past than the one who also foretold the future—things that we now see as present? Indeed, the very disagreement among historians provides us with reason to believe him rather, since his history does not contradict the divine history that we hold.

Moreover, when the citizens of the impious city, scattered throughout the world, read that highly learned men—none of whose authority appears contemptible—disagree among themselves about events removed from the memory of our age, they do not know whom they ought to believe. We, however, in the history of our religion, supported by divine authority, do not hesitate to judge whatever resists it utterly false, whatever may be the case with other writings of secular authors. Whether those writings are true or false, they contribute nothing that enables us to live rightly and happily.

## CHAPTER XLI—On disagreements among philosophical opinions, and on the agreement of the canonical Scriptures in the Church

### 1

But, leaving historical knowledge aside, why did the philosophers themselves—from whom our discussion proceeded to these matters, and who seem to have labored in their studies for no other purpose than to discover how one ought to live in order to attain happiness—disagree, both teachers with pupils and fellow pupils with one another, except because they sought these things as human beings, by human senses and human reasoning?

There may also have been an ambition for glory, by which each person wished to appear wiser and more perceptive than another, not bound in some way to another’s judgment but the inventor of his own doctrine and opinion. Yet even if I concede that some, or even many, of them were torn away from their teachers or fellow students by their love of truth, so that they might contend for what they believed to be the truth—whether it was so or not—what does human misery accomplish, or toward what goal and by what path does it strive to attain happiness, if divine authority does not lead it?

Finally, may it be far from us to suppose that our authors, in whom the canon of the sacred writings is not without reason fixed and brought to its conclusion, disagree with one another in any respect. [Note: The reasoning is as follows: All philosophers contend with one another and are often opposed to one another; the sacred writers do not disagree among themselves. Philosophers disagree because human beings are prone to error; the sacred authors never disagree because the Holy Spirit speaks through their mouths. LARCHER.]

Accordingly, when they wrote those things, believing that God had spoken either to them or through them, not merely a few chatterers in contentious disputes at schools and gymnasia, but so many great multitudes among the learned and unlearned, in the fields and in the cities, believed them.

They ought indeed to have been few, lest what was to be held as religious should be cheapened by its multitude; yet they were not so few that their agreement should fail to be remarkable. For among the multitude of philosophers, who by literary labor also left behind records of their doctrines, one would not easily find any among whom all the things they thought were in agreement. To demonstrate this would make this work too long.

### 2

What founder of any sect, however, was so approved in this city devoted to demons that the others who held different and opposing opinions were rejected? Were not the Epicureans flourishing openly at Athens, asserting that human affairs did not belong to the care of the gods, while the Stoics, holding contrary opinions, argued that those affairs were governed and protected by the gods as helpers and guardians?

I therefore wonder why Anaxagoras was prosecuted because he said that the sun was a burning stone, thereby plainly denying that it was a god, when Epicurus flourished in glory in that same city and lived securely—not only denying that the sun or any of the stars was a god, but also maintaining that neither Jupiter nor any god at all dwelt in the world, to whom human prayers and supplications might reach.

Was not Aristippus there, placing the highest good in bodily pleasure, and Antisthenes there, asserting instead that a human being becomes happy through virtue of soul? These were two distinguished philosophers, both followers of Socrates, who placed the highest end of life in aims so different and mutually opposed; one even declared the state something to be avoided by the wise, while the other said it was to be administered. Each gathered disciples to follow his own sect.

Indeed, openly, in the prominent and famous colonnade, in the gymnasia, in little gardens, and in public and private places, they contended in crowds, each for his own opinion: some asserting that there was one world, others innumerable worlds; some that the one world had come into being, others that it had no beginning; some that it would perish, others that it would exist forever; some that it was governed by divine mind, others by chance and accident.

Some held that souls were immortal, others that they were mortal. Of those who held them immortal, some said that souls passed into animals, others that they did not. Of those who held them mortal, some said that souls perished immediately with the body, others that they lived afterward for a short time or a longer time, but not forever.

Some placed the end of the good in the body, others in the soul, others in both, and others added external goods to those of soul and body. Some thought that one should always trust the bodily senses, others that one should not always do so, and others never.

What people, what senate, what public authority or dignity of the impious city ever undertook to judge these and almost innumerable other disagreements among philosophers, approving and accepting some while disapproving and rejecting others? Did it not instead keep indiscriminately and confusedly within its bosom all these controversies among men who disagreed—not about fields and houses, or any pecuniary matter, but about the things by which people either live miserably or happily?

And even if some true things were being said there, they were said with the same license as the false. It was therefore not without reason that such a city received the mystical name of Babylon. For Babylon is interpreted as “Confusion,” as we remember having already said. [Book 16, chapter 4, and elsewhere.] Nor does it matter to the devil, its king, with what mutually opposed errors those quarrel who are rightly possessed by many different forms of impiety alike.

### 3

But that nation, that people, that city, that commonwealth, those Israelites to whom the utterances of God were entrusted, in no way confused false prophets with true Prophets with equal license. [Note: The manuscripts read, “with equality of license.”] Rather, they recognized and held as the truthful authors of the sacred Scriptures those who were in agreement with one another and disagreed in nothing.

They were the people’s philosophers—that is, lovers of wisdom; its wise men, its theologians, its prophets, its teachers of righteousness and piety. Whoever was wise and lived according to them was wise and lived not according to human beings but according to God, who spoke through them.

If sacrilege was forbidden there, God forbade it. If it was said, “Honor your father and your mother,” God commanded it. If it was said, “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not murder; you shall not steal” (Exodus 20:12–15), and other things of this kind, it was not human mouths but divine oracles that uttered them.

Whatever certain philosophers, amid the false opinions they held, were able to see as true, and tried to establish by laborious disputations—that God made this world and that he himself governs it with the greatest providence; matters concerning the excellence of virtues, love of country, fidelity in friendship, good works, and everything pertaining to upright conduct—was commended to the people in that city through prophetic, that is, divine voices, although spoken through human beings. These truths were not hammered in through contests of argument, so that anyone who came to know them would fear to despise not human ingenuity but the utterance of God.

## CHAPTER XLII—By what dispensation of God’s providence the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament were translated from Hebrew into Greek, so that they might become known to the Gentiles

One of the kings of the Ptolemies [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read *Ptolomaeorum*; and consistently *Ptolomeus* instead of *Ptolemaeus*.] of Egypt also sought to know and possess these sacred writings.

After the magnificent but very short-lived power of Alexander the Macedonian, who was also called the Great, by which he had subdued all Asia—indeed, almost the whole world—partly by force and arms, partly by terror, and during which, among the other regions of the East, he entered and occupied Judaea, Alexander died. His companions divided that vast kingdom among themselves—not to possess it peacefully, but rather to scatter it, laying waste everything through wars. Egypt then began to have kings of the Ptolemaic line. The first of these, the son of Lagus, transferred many captives from Judaea to Egypt.

After him came another Ptolemy, who was called Philadelphus. He allowed all those whom his predecessor had brought there in subjection to return free. In addition, he sent royal gifts to the temple of God and requested from Eleazar, then the high priest, the Scriptures, which he had evidently heard proclaimed as divine by widespread report. For this reason he desired to possess them in the library that he had made exceptionally famous.

When that high priest sent him the Hebrew Scriptures, Ptolemy afterward requested interpreters as well. Seventy-two were provided: six men from each of the twelve tribes, highly learned in both languages, Hebrew and Greek. Custom has now established that their translation be called the Septuagint.

It is reported that their words displayed such marvelous, astonishing, and wholly divine agreement that, although they sat separately, each by himself, for this task—for Ptolemy had wished to test their reliability—in no word that had the same meaning and equivalent force, nor in the order of the words, did one differ from another. It was as though there were one interpreter: what all had translated was one and the same. For in truth the Spirit was one in them all. [Note: Coquaeus collected passages from other Fathers and from Philo the Jew concerning this matter; some are found in note b to chapter 15, or no. 22, of book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, where Augustine reports the same things. Jerome, compared with that account, regards these claims as “a lie,” since they are so extravagantly embellished in the book *On the History of the Translation of the Septuagint*, which circulated under the name of Aristaeus and was formerly attributed to Josephus. Louis Vives had already said of it: “Fabricated, I think, by some more recent writer.” This tale concerning the seventy-two interpreters has long since been rejected by scholars. “We do not call them the authors of the Greek translation,” say the Sangenovefani in their theses of 23 July 1704, “whom the deceitful Aristaeus advertises.” HARDUINUS. “Old wives’ tales, supported by no suitable authority, devised by Jews and Christians.” LARCHER.]

For this reason they had received so remarkable a gift from God: the authority of those Scriptures was commended in this way as well—not as human writings, but as what they actually were, divine writings—and this would benefit the Gentiles who would one day believe. We now see that this has happened.

## CHAPTER XLIII—On the authority of the Septuagint interpreters, which, without detriment to the honor of the Hebrew style, is to be preferred to all interpreters

Although there were also other interpreters who translated those sacred utterances from Hebrew into Greek—such as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, and also that translation whose author is unknown and which, for that reason, is called the Fifth Edition without the interpreter’s name [Note: Aquila, a man half-Jewish and half-Christian, published his translation under Hadrian, around the year 130 after Christ, more than four hundred years after the Septuagint edition. Symmachus, a proselyte, wrote his under Aurelius or Severus, around the year 200 after Christ. Theodotion, at first a Marcionite and later a Jew, completed his before Symmachus, not far from the time of Commodus, around the year 180. Augustine, following Epiphanius and others, mentions him after Symmachus, perhaps because in Origen’s *Hexapla* Symmachus’s edition had been placed before Theodotion’s, next to Aquila’s edition, while Theodotion’s stood afterward. Besides the Fifth Edition discovered at Jericho, which Augustine mentions here, a Sixth Edition discovered at Nicopolis is also celebrated; both were reportedly inserted into the same Origenian *Hexapla* in fifth and sixth place. Augustine, however, seems not to have known that Sixth Edition.]—nevertheless the Church received this translation, the Septuagint, as though it alone existed, and the Greek Christian peoples use it, most of whom do not know whether any other translation exists.

It was also from this Septuagint translation that what the Latin Churches possess was translated into Latin. [Note: Compare book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, nos. 21 and following.]

Yet in our own times there was the presbyter Jerome, a highly learned man and skilled in all three languages, who translated these same Scriptures into Latin not from Greek but from Hebrew. Although the Jews admit that his learned labor is accurate, they contend that the Septuagint interpreters erred in many places. Nevertheless, the Church of Christ judges that no one should be preferred to the authority of so many men, chosen by Eleazar, then the high priest, for this very work.

For even if one divine Spirit had not appeared in them, and if the seventy-two learned men had compared the words of their translation with one another in the human manner so that whatever pleased them all would remain, no single interpreter ought to have been preferred to them. But when so great a sign of divinity appeared in them, whoever else truthfully translates those Scriptures from Hebrew into any other language either agrees with those Septuagint interpreters, or, if he does not appear to agree, a prophetic depth must be believed to be present there.

For the Spirit who was in the Prophets when they spoke those words was the very same Spirit in the seventy-two men when they translated them. By divine authority, that Spirit could cause them to say something else, as though that prophet had spoken both things, because the same Spirit was saying both; and he could say the same thing differently, so that, even if the words were not identical, the same meaning might become evident to those who understood rightly. He could omit something and add something, thereby showing also that the interpreter’s service to the words was not human servitude in that work, but rather the divine power that filled and governed the interpreter’s mind.

Some people thought that Greek manuscripts of the Septuagint translation ought to be corrected from Hebrew manuscripts. Yet they did not dare to remove what the Hebrew manuscripts did not contain but the Septuagint had supplied. They merely added what was found in Hebrew but absent from the Septuagint, marking these additions at the beginnings of the same verses with certain signs shaped like stars; these signs they call asterisks.

Conversely, what the Hebrews did not have but the Septuagint did have, they marked in a similar manner at the beginnings of the verses with horizontal strokes, like the marks used in writing unciae. Many Greek and Latin manuscripts bearing these signs have been widely circulated. [Note: Lovaniensis reads, “Greek and Latin.” Other printed editions and manuscripts do not have the word “Greek.”]

What has not been omitted or added, but expressed differently—whether it produces another meaning that is itself not discordant, or appears to explain the same meaning in another way—cannot be discovered unless both sets of manuscripts are examined.

Therefore, if—as is proper—we look for nothing else in those Scriptures except what the Spirit of God said through human beings, then whatever is in the Hebrew manuscripts and is not found among the Septuagint interpreters, the Spirit of God did not wish to say through these interpreters but through those Prophets. Whatever is found among the Septuagint interpreters but is absent from the Hebrew manuscripts, the same Spirit preferred to say through these interpreters rather than through those, thereby showing that both groups were prophets.

For in this manner he said one thing through Isaiah, another through Jeremiah, and another through one prophet or another; or he said the same thing differently through one and through another, as he wished. Whatever is found in both, the one and the same Spirit wished to say through both—but in such a way that the former preceded by prophesying, while the latter followed prophetically by interpreting them.

For just as among the former, who spoke true and harmonious things, there was one Spirit of peace, so among the latter—who did not confer with one another, yet interpreted everything as though with one mouth—the same one Spirit appeared.

## CHAPTER XLIV—What is to be understood concerning the destruction of the Ninevites, whose announcement extends over forty days in the Hebrew text but is confined to three days in the Septuagint

[Col. 0605]

But someone may say: “How shall I know what the prophet Jonah said to the Ninevites—whether, ‘Three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,’ or, ‘Forty days’ (Jonah 3:4)?”

For who does not see that both could not at that time have been said by the Prophet who had been sent to terrify the city by announcing its impending destruction? If its destruction was to occur on the third day, certainly not on the fortieth; if on the fortieth, certainly not on the third.

If, therefore, I am asked which of these Jonah said, I think it was rather what is read in the Hebrew text: “Forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

The Septuagint interpreters, translating much later, could have said something else that nevertheless pertained to the matter and converged upon one and the same meaning, although under another significance. They thereby admonished the reader, without rejecting either authority, to rise above the history and seek the reasons for which the history itself was written.

Those events took place in the city of Nineveh, but they also signified something that exceeds the measure of that city. So too the event that the Prophet himself remained for three days in the belly of the sea-monster signified another who was to remain for three days in the depths of hell—the Lord of all the Prophets.

Accordingly, if that city is rightly understood as prophetically representing the Church of the Gentiles, overthrown through repentance so that it would no longer be what it had been, then—since this happened through Christ in the Church of the Gentiles, of which Nineveh bore the figure—whether through forty days or through three days, the same Christ was signified.

Through forty days, because he spent that number of days with his disciples after the resurrection and then ascended into heaven; through three days, because he rose on the third day. It is as though the Septuagint interpreters, who were themselves also prophets, awakened from sleep the reader who wished to cling to nothing except the history of events and said, in a manner of speaking: “Seek him in the forty days, in which you will also be able to find the three days; you will find the former in his ascension, the latter in his resurrection.”

For this reason both numbers could most appropriately signify him: one was spoken through the prophet Jonah, the other through the prophecy of the Septuagint interpreters, yet by one and the same Spirit.

I avoid prolonging the discussion by demonstrating this through many examples in which the Septuagint interpreters are thought to differ from the Hebrew truth, but, when properly understood, are found to agree with it. Therefore I too, following as far as I can in the footsteps of the Apostles—for they themselves placed prophetic testimonies from both sources, that is, from the Hebrew and from the Septuagint—have judged that both authorities should be used, since both are one and divine.

But now let us pursue, as best we can, what remains.

## CHAPTER XLV—That after the restoration of the temple the Jews ceased to have prophets, and from then until the birth of Christ were afflicted by continual adversities, so that it might be shown that the construction of another temple had been promised by prophetic utterances

[Col. 0606]

### 1

After the Jewish nation began to have no Prophets, it undoubtedly became worse—at precisely the time when, after the captivity in Babylonia, it hoped that it would become better once the temple had been restored.

For that carnal people understood in this way what had been foretold through the prophet Haggai, who said, “Great shall be the glory of this latter house, more than of the former.” A little earlier he showed that this had been spoken concerning the New Testament, when he openly promised Christ, saying, “And I will move all nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Haggai 2:10, 8).

In that passage the Septuagint interpreters, by prophetic authority, gave another meaning more suited to the body than to the head—that is, more suited to the Church than to Christ: “The chosen things of the Lord shall come from all the nations,” that is, human beings, concerning whom Jesus himself says in the Gospel, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14).

Through such chosen people of the nations, the house of God is built by the New Testament with living stones, far more glorious than that temple which was constructed by King Solomon and restored after the captivity.

For this reason, from that time onward that nation had neither Prophets and was afflicted with many calamities by foreign kings, including the Romans, so that it would not suppose that Haggai’s prophecy had been fulfilled in that restoration of the temple.

### 2

For not long afterward, when Alexander arrived, it was subdued. [Note: Josephus, book 11 of *The Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 8.] Although no devastation occurred, since they did not dare resist him and therefore received him as subjects with great ease after he had been placated, the glory of that house was nevertheless not as great as it had been under the free rule of their own kings.

Alexander did indeed offer sacrifices in the temple of God, but he was not converted to worship him with true piety; rather, in impious vanity, he thought that God should be honored along with his false gods.

Next, Ptolemy the son of Lagus, as I mentioned above, transferred captives from there to Egypt after Alexander’s death. His successor, Ptolemy Philadelphus, generously released them from there. Through him it came about, as I related shortly before, that we possess the Scriptures of the Septuagint interpreters.

After that they were crushed by the wars described in the books of the Maccabees. Then they were captured by the king of Alexandria, Ptolemy, who was called Epiphanes. [Note: Compare the same author, book 12, chapter 3.] Afterward, by Antiochus, king of Syria, they were compelled through many and most grievous evils to worship idols. The temple itself was filled with the sacrilegious superstitions of the nations. Yet their most vigorous leader Judas, who was also called Maccabaeus, drove out the commanders of Antiochus and cleansed it of all that contamination of idolatry. [Note: Ibid., the cited book, chapters 7 and 8, and 1 Maccabees 6.]

### 3

Not long afterward, a certain Alcimus, although unrelated to the priestly line, was made high priest through ambition, contrary to what was lawful. [Note: 1 Maccabees 7, and Josephus, book 12 of *The Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 15.]

Then, after approximately fifty years—during which they nevertheless had no peace, although they achieved some successes—Aristobulus was the first among them to assume the diadem and become both king and high priest. [Note: Compare above, chapter 36.]

Previously, from the time they returned from the Babylonian captivity and the temple was restored, they had had not kings but commanders or rulers. Although a king may also be called a ruler because of his ruling authority, and a commander because he leads an army, not every ruler or commander can immediately be called a king, as Aristobulus was.

Alexander succeeded him, himself also king and high priest, and is reported to have ruled cruelly over his own people. [Note: Compare Josephus, book 13, chapter 12.] After him, his wife Alexandra became queen of the Jews. [Note: Josephus, the same work, chapter 16.] From her time onward, and thereafter, more serious evils followed them.

For the sons of this Alexandra, Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, fighting among themselves for sovereignty, summoned Roman forces against the Israelite nation. Hyrcanus asked the Romans for assistance against his brother. [Note: Josephus, book 14, chapters 3 and following.]
