By that time Rome had subdued Africa and Greece and was ruling widely over other parts of the world as well. It was as though, unable to bear itself, it had broken itself by its own magnitude. For it had reached serious domestic uprisings, then civil wars among its allies, and soon civil wars within Rome itself. It had so weakened and worn itself down that a change in the form of government was impending, by which it would be ruled by kings.

Pompey, therefore, the illustrious leader of the Roman people, entered Judaea with an army, captured the city, and opened the temple—not with the devotion of a suppliant, but by the right of a conqueror. He approached the Holy of Holies, which no one except the high priest was permitted to enter, not as a worshiper but as a profaner.

After confirming Hyrcanus in the high priesthood and imposing Antipater upon the subjected nation as its guardian—men whom they then called procurators—he led Aristobulus away with him in chains. [Note: This occurred in the second year of the 179th Olympiad, during the consulship of Marcus Tullius Cicero and Gaius Antonius, according to Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 14, chapter 4, §3; sixty-three years before the birth of Christ. LARCHER.]

From that time the Jews also began to be tributaries of the Romans.

Afterward Cassius [Note: Perhaps *Crassus* should be read, for when he was marching against the Parthians he plundered the temple of 8,000 talents, that is, 43,200,000 pounds in our currency. Josephus reports this in *Antiquities*, book 14, chapter 7. These events took place in the year 53 before the birth of Christ. Cassius, however, after Caesar was killed, came to Syria and imposed a tribute of 700 talents upon Judaea, that is, 3,780,000 pounds in our currency, in the year 43 before Christ. Josephus relates this in the same work, chapter 11, §2. LARCHER.] also plundered the temple.

Then, after a few years, they also merited having a foreign king, Herod, under whose reign Christ was born. [Note: Herod obtained the kingdom of Judaea by decree of the Senate in the year 40 before Christ. Christ is believed to have been born in the fourth year of the 194th Olympiad, in the 753rd year from the founding of the City. Hence the Christian era begins in the following year, 754. In reality, however, he was born in the second year of the 193rd Olympiad, shortly before Decimus Laelius Balbus and Gaius Antistius Vetus entered the consulship, in the 748th year from the founding of the City—that is, five years, nine months, and seven days before the common era. Hence the author of the book entitled *The Art of Verifying Dates* must be corrected, since he was not sufficiently careful concerning the reckoning of the Olympiads. The second year of the 193rd Olympiad began in June, around the summer solstice; therefore six months of that second year had not yet elapsed. Rome, moreover, was founded in October, in the third year of the sixth Olympiad, according to Tarrutius, whom Varro follows; see Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, book 9, chapter 54. LARCHER.]

For the fullness of time had already come, signified by the prophetic Spirit through the mouth of the patriarch Jacob, where he says: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10).

Therefore a Jewish ruler from the Jews did not fail until this Herod, whom they first received as a foreign king. The time had therefore come for him to come to whom it had been reserved, as was promised in the New Testament, so that he himself would be the expectation of the nations.

But it could not happen that the nations would await his coming—as we see them awaiting him, to come to execute judgment in the glory of his power—unless they had first believed in him when he came to undergo judgment in the humility of suffering.

## CHAPTER XLVI—On the birth of our Savior, insofar as the Word became flesh; and on the dispersion of the Jews among all nations, as had been prophesied
Therefore, when Herod was reigning in Judaea, while among the Romans the constitution of the state had already been changed, and Caesar Augustus was ruling and through him the whole world had been pacified, Christ was born in accordance with the preceding prophecy (Micah V, 2) at Bethlehem of Judaea: a manifest man from a human virgin, a hidden God from God the Father. For thus the prophet had foretold: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah VII, 14; Matthew I, 23; Luke I, 31).

To commend God in himself, he performed many miracles, some of which the Gospel Scripture records, insofar as it seemed sufficient for proclaiming him. The first of these is that he was born so wondrously; the last, that he ascended into heaven with his body, raised from the dead.

But the Jews, who killed him and refused to believe in him because it was necessary for him to die and rise again, were devastated still more unhappily by the Romans and, utterly uprooted from their kingdom—where foreigners already ruled over them—and dispersed throughout the lands (since indeed they are found everywhere). Through their own Scriptures they bear witness to us that we did not fabricate the prophecies concerning Christ, for many of them, considering those prophecies both before his Passion and especially after his resurrection, believed in him. Of these it was foretold: “Although the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isaiah X, 22).

[Note: Printed editions read: “they were uprooted and dispersed throughout the lands. Since indeed they are found everywhere, and through their own Scriptures, etc.” The wording has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

The others, however, were blinded; concerning them it was foretold: “Let their table before them become a snare, and a retribution, and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and make their back continually bent” (Psalm LXVIII, 23–24).

Thus, since they do not believe our Scriptures, their own Scriptures—which they read while blind—are fulfilled in them. Unless, perhaps, someone should say that Christians fabricated those prophecies concerning Christ which are produced under the name of the Sibyl, or of others, if there are any such that do not pertain to the Jewish people.

[Note: Idle-minded men among the earliest Christians fabricated the Sibylline oracles concerning Christ. LARCHER.]

For us, those prophecies are sufficient which are brought forth from the books of our enemies. We recognize that, by possessing and preserving those same books against their will for the sake of this testimony, they too have been dispersed among all nations, wherever the Church of Christ is spreading.

For a prophecy in the Psalms—which they also read—was uttered beforehand concerning this matter, where it is written: “My God, his mercy shall prevent me. My God has shown me among my enemies” [Note: Printed editions read “from my enemies.” But the manuscripts have “among my enemies,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint.], “slay them not, lest at any time they forget your law; scatter them by your power” (Psalm LVIII, 11–12).

God therefore demonstrated to the Church, in the Jews who are its enemies, the grace of his mercy, because, as the Apostle says, “their trespass is salvation for the Gentiles” [Note: Vindelinus, Amerbach, and Erasmus read, “salvation is among the Gentiles.” The manuscripts do not have *is among*.] (Romans XI, 11).

And for that reason he did not slay them—that is, he did not destroy in them what they are as Jews—even though they were defeated and oppressed by the Romans, lest, having forgotten the law of God, they should be of no value for the testimony with which we are concerned. Therefore it was not enough for him to say, “Slay them not, lest at any time they forget your law,” unless he also added, “Scatter them”; for if, with this testimony of the Scriptures, they existed only in their own land and not everywhere, the Church, which is everywhere, could not have them in all nations as witnesses to the prophecies that had been uttered beforehand concerning Christ.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### Whether, before the Christian era, there were any people outside the Israelite race who belonged to the fellowship of the heavenly city

Therefore, if some foreigner—that is, someone not descended from Israel and not received by that people into the canon of the sacred writings—is read to have prophesied something concerning Christ, and if this has come or should come to our knowledge, it may be mentioned by us as an additional confirmation. This is not because it is necessary, even if absent, but because it is not implausibly believed that there were also among other nations people to whom this mystery was revealed and who were moved to foretell it—whether they were participants in the same grace or strangers to it but instructed by evil angels, whom we know also confessed the Christ who was present, though the Jews did not acknowledge him.

Nor do I think that the Jews themselves would dare to maintain that, from the time when the Israelite stock began, after its elder brother had been rejected, no one except Israelites belonged to God. For there truly was no other people who could properly be called the people of God. But they cannot deny that there were among other nations certain people who belonged, not by an earthly association but by a heavenly fellowship, to the true Israelites, citizens of the heavenly homeland.

If they deny this, they are very easily refuted by the holy and wondrous man Job, who was neither a native nor a proselyte—that is, a newcomer to the people of Israel—but descended from the people of Idumaea, was born there, and died there. Yet he is so praised by the divine utterance that, in justice and piety, no person of his time is made equal to him (Job I; Ezekiel XIV, 20).

Although we do not find the period of his life in the Chronicles, we nevertheless gather from his book—which the Israelites, on account of its merit, received into canonical authority—that he lived three generations after Israel.

[Note: See Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, book 1, chapters 5 and 6.]

I do not doubt that divine providence arranged matters so that, through this one example, we might know that even among other nations there could have been people who lived according to God, pleased him, and belonged to spiritual Jerusalem.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “Israel.”]

Yet no one should be believed to have been granted this except one to whom the one Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, was divinely revealed. He was foretold to the ancient saints as one who would come in the flesh, just as his coming has been announced to us, so that one and the same faith through him might lead to God all who have been predestined for the city of God, the household of God, and the temple of God.

But whatever prophecies of the grace of God through Christ Jesus are produced from other sources may be thought by Christians to have been fabricated. Therefore nothing is more effective for refuting outsiders who dispute this matter, and for making them our own if they are rightly minded, than to produce the divine predictions concerning Christ that are written in the books of the Jews. Torn away from their own homes and dispersed throughout the whole world for the sake of this testimony, they have caused the Church of Christ to grow everywhere.

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
### The prophecy of Haggai, who said that the glory of the house of God would be greater than it had formerly been, was fulfilled not in the rebuilding of the temple but in the Church of Christ

This house has a greater glory than that first house, which had been constructed of wood and stones and other costly materials and metals. Haggai’s prophecy, therefore, was not fulfilled in the restoration of that temple. From the time it was rebuilt, it is never shown to have possessed as much glory as it had in the time of Solomon; rather, it is shown first to have had its glory diminished by the cessation of prophecy, and then to have been brought low by the great disasters of that nation, down to its final destruction by the Romans, as the matters mentioned above testify.

[Note: Nevertheless, this prophecy can be understood according to its proper sense. For Haggai says, “I will fill this house with glory,” on account of the presence of Christ the Redeemer, who often lived in that temple. LARCHER.]

This house, which belongs to the New Testament, is certainly of that much greater glory in proportion as the living stones are better—the believers who are renewed and built into it. It was therefore signified through the restoration of that temple, because the renewal of that building signifies in prophetic language the other Testament, which is called the New.

When God therefore said through the prophet just mentioned, “And I will give peace in this place” (Haggai II, 10), what is signified by the signifying place must be understood through it. Since the Church, which was to be built through Christ, was signified by the restoration of that place, nothing else should be understood by the words, “I will give peace in this place,” except, “I will give peace in the place signified by this place.”

For all signs seem in some way to assume the persons of the things they signify. Thus the Apostle said, “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians X, 4), because that rock, of which this was said, clearly signified Christ.

The glory of this house of the New Testament is therefore greater than that of the house of the former, Old Testament; and its greater glory will appear when it is dedicated. Then will come “the Desired One of all nations” (Haggai II, 8), as it is read in the Hebrew. For previously his coming was not yet desired by all nations. They did not know whom they ought to desire, because they had not believed in him.

Then also, according to the translators of the Septuagint—for this too is a prophetic meaning—“the things chosen of the Lord from all nations” will come. For then only the chosen will truly come, of whom the Apostle says, “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians I, 4).

For the architect himself, who said, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XXII, 14), will show that the house has been built from the chosen—not from those who came when called only to be cast out from the banquet, but from the elect—and that it will thereafter fear no collapse.

At present, however, when even those who will be separated by winnowing, as grain from the threshing floor, fill the churches, the glory of this house does not appear as great as it will appear then, when whoever is there will always be there.

## CHAPTER XLIX  
### The indiscriminate multiplication of the Church, in which many reprobate are mingled with the elect in this age

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “uncertain.”]

In this evil age, in these evil days, when the Church, through present humiliation, is preparing for future exaltation and is being trained by the goads of fear, the torments of suffering, the burdens of toil, and the dangers of temptation—rejoicing in hope alone, whenever it rejoices soundly—many reprobate are mingled with the good. Both are gathered together, as it were, into the Gospel net (Matthew XIII, 47), and in this world, as in the sea, both swim indiscriminately enclosed in nets until they reach the shore, where the evil will be separated from the good and God will be all in all among the good, as in his temple (1 Corinthians XV, 28).

Accordingly, we now recognize the voice of the one who spoke in the Psalm and said, “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Psalm XXXIX, 6). This has happened from the time when he first announced and spoke through the mouth of his forerunner John, and then through his own mouth, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew III, 2; IV, 17).

He chose disciples, whom he also named Apostles (Luke VI, 13), born in humble circumstances, without honor, and uneducated, so that whatever greatness they possessed or accomplished, he himself might be and accomplish in them. Among them he had one who was evil, but whom he used well: thereby fulfilling the arrangement of his Passion and providing his Church with an example of the evils it must endure.

After the holy Gospel had been sown as far as his bodily presence required, he suffered, died, and rose again. By his Passion he showed what we must endure for the truth; by his resurrection, what we must hope for in eternity—apart from the height of the sacrament by which his blood was poured out for the remission of sins.

He lived on earth with his disciples for forty days and, while they watched, ascended into heaven. Ten days later he sent the promised Holy Spirit.

[Note: The printed editions add “of his Father,” but the ancient books do not.]

When the Spirit came upon those who believed, its greatest and most necessary sign was that each of them spoke in the languages of all nations. Thus it signified that the Catholic Church would one day exist throughout all nations and speak in every language.

## CHAPTER L  
### The preaching of the Gospel, which was made clearer and more powerful through the sufferings of its preachers

Then, in accordance with that prophecy, “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah II, 3), and in accordance with the predictions of the Lord Christ himself—when, after his resurrection, he opened the understanding of his disciples, who were astonished with him, so that they might understand the Scriptures, and said to them, “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and remission of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV, 46–47)—and when, again, in response to their question concerning his final coming, he answered and said, “It is not yours to know the times or moments” [Note: The manuscripts do not have “or moments.”] “which the Father has placed in his own authority; but you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts I, 7–8):

The Church first spread from Jerusalem. When many had believed in Judaea and Samaria, it went on to other nations through those who announced the Gospel—those whom he had prepared for the word like lamps and kindled with the Holy Spirit. For he had said to them, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew X, 28). So that they would not be cold with fear, they burned with the fire of love.

Finally, through them—not only through those who had seen and heard him before his Passion and after his resurrection, but also, after their death, through their successors—the Gospel was preached throughout the whole world amid terrible persecutions, various tortures, and the deaths of martyrs. God bore witness through signs, wonders, various powers, and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Thus the peoples of the nations, believing in him who was crucified for their redemption, venerated with Christian love the blood of the martyrs, which had been poured out by the devil’s fury. Even the kings whose laws had laid waste to the Church were salutarily subjected to that name which they had tried to remove cruelly from the earth, and they began to persecute the false gods on whose account they had previously persecuted the worshipers of the true God.

## CHAPTER LI  
### How the Catholic faith is also strengthened through the dissensions of heretics

1. When the devil saw the temples of demons being abandoned and the human race running to the name of the liberating Mediator, he stirred up heretics who, under the Christian name, resisted Christian doctrine. They acted as though they could be tolerated indiscriminately, without any correction, in the city of God, just as the city of confusion indiscriminately tolerated philosophers who held opinions diverse and opposed to one another.

Therefore, if people in the Church of Christ hold some diseased or perverse opinion and, when corrected, stubbornly resist being sound and upright in their thinking, refusing to amend their destructive and deadly doctrines and persisting in defending them, they become heretics. Once they have gone out, they are counted among the enemies who exercise the Church.

Even in this way they benefit the true Catholic members of Christ, though to their own detriment, while God uses even evil things well and all things work together for good for those who love him [Note: Several manuscripts of sound quality read *cooperatur*, “works together.” The reference is to the Apostle’s passage, Romans VIII, 28, where the Greek is *synergei*. This can be translated either way, depending on whether it is referred to God (*Theon*) or to “all things” (*panta*).] (Romans VIII, 28).

All the Church’s enemies, whatever error blinds them or wickedness corrupts them, if they receive the power to afflict the body, exercise its patience; if they oppose it merely by holding evil opinions, they exercise its wisdom; and so that enemies may also be loved, they exercise its goodwill or even its beneficence, whether they are dealt with by persuasive teaching or by discipline that inspires fear.

Accordingly, the devil, the prince of the impious city, by stirring up his own vessels against the city of God as it journeys in this world, is not permitted to harm it. Through divine providence, consolation is provided to it in prosperity, so that it will not be broken by adversity, and discipline in adversity, so that it will not be corrupted by prosperity. Thus each is tempered by the other, so that we recognize in the Psalm the voice that arose from nowhere else: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have brought joy to my soul” (Psalm XCIII, 19).

Hence also comes the Apostle’s saying, “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans XII, 12).

2. For what the same teacher says—“All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” [Note: Our manuscripts have *patiuntur*, “suffer,” except manuscript 2050. The printed editions have *patientur*, “will suffer.”] (2 Timothy III, 12)—must not be thought capable of being absent at any time.

For even when those outside are not raging and tranquility appears to exist—and truly does exist [Note: Erasmus and some manuscripts read, “and truly is useful.”] and brings a great deal of consolation, especially to the weak—there are nevertheless people inside, indeed many of them, who torment the hearts of those living devoutly by their corrupt behavior. Through them the Christian and Catholic name is blasphemed; and the dearer that name is to those who wish to live devoutly in Christ, the more they grieve that, because of the wicked who are placed within, it is loved less than the minds of the devout desire.

Heretics themselves, when they are considered to possess the Christian name, the Christian sacraments, the Scriptures, and the profession of faith, cause great grief in the hearts of the devout. Many who wish to be Christians are forced to hesitate because of their dissensions, and many slanderers find in them material for blaspheming the Christian name, since they too are called Christians in some manner.

Through these and similar corrupt behaviors and errors of human beings, those who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution, even when no one is attacking or troubling their bodies. They suffer this persecution not in their bodies but in their hearts. Hence the voice says, “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart.” It does not say, “In my body.”

But again, because the unchanging divine promises are remembered, as well as the Apostle’s statement, “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy II, 19), and, “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed” [Note: The printed editions read “to be conformed.” The word “to be” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.] “to the image of his Son” (Romans VIII, 29), and none of these can perish, the Psalm therefore continues, “Your consolations have brought joy to my soul.”

The very grief that is produced in the hearts of the devout, when they are persecuted by the behavior of bad or false Christians, benefits those who grieve, because it proceeds from the love by which they do not want those people to perish or to impede the salvation of others. Finally, great consolations also arise from their correction, which flood the souls of the devout with as much joy as their destruction had tortured them with grief.

Thus, in this age and in these evil days, the Church journeys onward—not only from the time of Christ’s bodily presence and that of his Apostles, but from Abel himself, whom his wicked brother first killed as a righteous man, and thereafter until the end of this age—amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God.

## CHAPTER LII  
### Whether it should be believed, as some think, that, once the ten persecutions have been completed, none remains except the eleventh, which will occur in the time of Antichrist

1. Accordingly, I do not think that one should rashly say or believe what has seemed, or seems, to some: that the Church will suffer no more persecutions until the time of Antichrist than the number it has already suffered—that is, ten—and that the eleventh and final persecution will be from Antichrist.

They count the first as having been under Nero [Note: Vindelinus, Amerbach, and some manuscripts omit “which occurred.”], the second under Domitian, the third under Trajan, the fourth under Antoninus, the fifth under Severus, the sixth under Maximinus, the seventh under Decius, the eighth under Valerian, the ninth under Aurelian, and the tenth under Diocletian and Maximian.

[Note: The first persecution was under Nero, in the year of Christ 64; the second under Domitian, in 93; the third under Trajan, in 107; the fourth under Hadrian, in 118, or rather under Antoninus, in 162; the fifth under Severus, in 202; the sixth under Maximinus, in 235; the seventh under Decius, in 250; the eighth under Valerian, in 257; the ninth under Aurelian, in 27; the tenth under Diocletian and Maximian, in 302. LARCHER.]

Because there were ten plagues of the Egyptians before the people of God began to leave that land, they think those plagues should be referred to this interpretation, so that the final persecution of Antichrist may appear like the eleventh plague, through which the Egyptians perished in the Red Sea while they pursued the Hebrews with hostile intent and the people of God crossed over on dry ground.

[Note: Orosius, *History*, book 7, chapter 27, and Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book 2, chapter 33, also hold this view.]

But I do not think that the events which took place in Egypt prophetically signified these persecutions. Although the individual plagues have been compared with the individual persecutions by those who hold this view with great refinement and ingenuity, the comparison arises not from the prophetic Spirit but from human conjecture, which sometimes reaches the truth and sometimes is mistaken.

2. What, then, will those who hold this opinion say about the persecution in which the Lord himself was crucified? In which number will they place it?

If they exclude this one and think that the count should concern only those persecutions directed against the body, not the one in which the head itself was attacked and killed, what will they do about the persecution that took place after Christ ascended into heaven? It occurred at Jerusalem, where blessed Stephen was stoned, where James the brother of John was killed with the sword, where the Apostle Peter was imprisoned for execution and liberated by an angel, where the brothers were driven away and scattered from Jerusalem, and where Saul—who later became the Apostle Paul—was ravaging the Church.

There he himself, after beginning to preach the faith he had persecuted, suffered what he had inflicted, whether in Judaea or among other nations, wherever he preached Christ with the greatest fervor.

Why, then, do they think the count should begin with Nero, when by Nero’s time the Church had already grown amid the most savage persecutions—of which it would take too long to speak in full—and had reached his reign? If they think that persecutions carried out by kings must be counted, Herod was a king, and even after the Lord’s ascension he carried out a very severe persecution.

What, moreover, will they answer concerning Julian, whom they do not include among the ten? Was he not a persecutor of the Church when he forbade Christians to teach and study the liberal arts? Under him Valentinian the Elder, who was the third emperor after him, proved himself a confessor of the Christian faith and was deprived of military service.

[Note: Julian the Apostate barred Christian teachers of rhetoric and grammar from teaching, as Ammianus records in book 22, chapter 10, near the end. For Valentinian’s removal from military service, see Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 13. LARCHER.—Compare also Ammianus, book 26, chapter 10, near the end; Eutropius and others.]

I omit what Julian had begun to do at Antioch, had he not recoiled in astonishment at the freedom and cheerfulness, amid rending claws and tortures, of one exceptionally faithful and steadfast young man singing psalms. After many had been seized for torture, this youth was the first to be tortured throughout the entire day; Julian feared to shame himself more disgracefully in the others.

[Note: When Julian ordered the Christians to transfer the tomb of the martyr Babylas elsewhere, they sang a Psalm in the emperor’s hearing, beginning, “When Israel went out of Egypt” (Psalm CXIII). Julian became enraged and ordered them to be brought back in large numbers and tortured the following day. Sallustius, to whom he had entrusted the task, seized a certain young man named Theodore first. After various kinds of torture had been applied, the young man remained from the beginning of daylight until the eleventh hour with a cheerful and happy expression, sweetly singing the hymn and Psalm that the Church had sung the previous day.

When Sallustius saw this, he ordered him returned to custody and went to the emperor in amazement, urging him not to continue torturing the Christians, since it would bring glory to them but shame and disgrace to the emperor. When Julian heard the matter in full, he abandoned his undertaking.

Eusebius testifies that he met this Theodore at Antioch and asked him whether he had suffered on the rack. “Not at all,” he replied, “for a young man in a white garment stood beside me, repeatedly pouring cold water over me and wiping away my sweat with a dazzlingly white cloth, so that it was actually more painful when I was taken away from there.”

“Hail, young man of such wondrous courage, most worthy of the remembrance of all ages; be gracious and kindly disposed toward us, and bring it about that both young and old may desire to emulate you.” LUDOVICUS VIVES.]

Finally, in our own memory, did Valens, the Arian brother of the aforementioned Valentinian, not ravage the Catholic Church through the eastern provinces in a great persecution?

[Note: Compare Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 2, and Orosius, book 7, chapter 33. See also Augustine, book 2, *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, no. 206.]

What sense does it make not to consider that the Church, bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, can suffer persecution from kings in some nations while not suffering it in others? Unless, perhaps, persecution is not to be counted when the king of the Goths persecuted Christians in Gothia itself with extraordinary cruelty, when there were no Christians there except Catholics, many of whom were crowned with martyrdom. We heard this from certain brothers who had been children there at that time and who recalled without hesitation that they had witnessed it.

[Note: This refers to the persecution raised by Athanaric, king of the Goths, against Christians in the year of the Lord 370, of which Jerome speaks in his *Chronicle* and Orosius in book 7, chapter 32. Epiphanius also discusses it, *Heresy* 70. COQUAEUS.]

What about Persia now? Has persecution not burned so fiercely against the Christians there—if indeed it has now ceased—that some fugitives from that country have reached even Roman towns?

[Note: This persecution arose around the year of Christ 420, under Isdigerdes, king of the Persians, as Theodoret records in book 5, chapter 38 of his *Ecclesiastical History*; or rather under Vararanes, his son, according to Socrates, book 7, chapter 18, and Nicephorus, book 14, chapter 19. Cassiodorus also discusses the same persecution in book 10, chapter 30 of his *Tripartite History*.]

As I consider these matters and others like them, it does not seem that the number of persecutions by which the Church must be exercised should be fixed. But, on the other hand, it is no less rash to assert that some persecutions by kings will occur in addition to that final one, about which no Christian has any doubt.

Accordingly, we leave this question open, asserting or denying neither side, but merely restraining people from the presumptuous boldness of affirming either alternative.

## CHAPTER LIII  
### The hidden time of the final persecution

1. That final persecution, which will come from Antichrist, Jesus himself will certainly destroy by his presence. For it is written that he will kill him “with the spirit of his mouth” and “abolish him by the brightness of his presence” (2 Thessalonians II, 8).

The question is often asked: When will this happen? It is entirely inappropriate. For if it were beneficial for us to know this, from whom could the disciples have asked more appropriately than from God himself, their teacher? They did not remain silent about it in his presence; rather, they asked him directly, saying, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” [Note: The printed editions read, “If at this time you will restore the kingdom of Israel.” But Augustine, as has already been observed elsewhere, customarily reads, “Will you at this time restore the kingdom of Israel?” The excellent Colbertinus manuscript has the same reading here.]

But he said, “It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts I, 6–7).

They certainly asked him about the time, not about the hour, day, or year, when they received this answer. It is therefore futile for us to attempt to calculate and define the years that remain for this age, when we hear from the mouth of Truth that it is not ours to know this.

Nevertheless, some have said that four hundred years, others five hundred, and still others even a thousand, might be completed from the Lord’s ascension to his final coming. It would take too long to demonstrate how each of them supports his opinion, and it would not be necessary. They employ human conjectures; none of them produces anything certain from the authority of canonical Scripture.

But he who says, “It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority,” loosens and commands the fingers of all who calculate about this matter to rest.

[Note: On the method of counting by the fingers, see Herodotus, book 6, chapter 63; Pliny, *Natural History*, book 34, chapter 7; Juvenal, *Satire* 10, line 248; Alexander ab Alexandro, book 1, chapter 14, p. 114. LARCHER.]

2. Since this is an evangelical statement, it is not surprising that it did not restrain the worshipers of many false gods from inventing, through the responses of the demons whom they worship as gods, that the duration of the Christian religion had been fixed for a certain period.

When they saw that Christianity could not be destroyed by so many and such great persecutions, but had rather acquired astonishing growth through them, they devised—I know not what—Greek verses, as though poured forth by a divine oracle in response to someone consulting it. In those verses they indeed make Christ innocent of the charge of what they regarded as sacrilege, but then add that Peter had performed magic, so that the name of Christ would be worshiped for three hundred and sixty-five years and, when that stated number of years had been completed, would immediately come to an end.

[Note: Baronius refers this to the year of the Lord 313. A similar oracle, fabricated by a pagan, is found in Prosper, part 3, *On Predictions*, chapter 38. COQUAEUS.]

O learned hearts! O literate minds [Note: The Louvain edition alone has “of the literate,” instead of “literate”] worthy of believing these things about Christ, which you refuse to believe in Christ—that his disciple Peter did not learn magical arts from him, but that, while Christ himself was innocent, his disciple became a magician; that by his magic arts Peter preferred Christ’s name to his own, through great labors and dangers, and finally through the shedding of his own blood!

If Peter, being a magician, caused the world to love Christ in this way, what did the innocent Christ do to cause Peter to love him in this way? Let them answer themselves, then, if they can, and understand that it was through heavenly grace that the world came to love Christ for the sake of eternal life—through the same grace by which Peter came to love Christ both in order to receive eternal life from him and to suffer for him even unto temporal death.

Moreover, who are these gods who can foretell such things but cannot avert them, submitting so completely to one magician and one magical crime, by which, as they claim, an infant of one year was killed, torn apart, and buried according to an impious rite?

[Note: Tertullian shows in his *Apology*, near the beginning, that the murder of infants was customarily falsely and shamelessly charged against Christians. The Cataphrygians and Pepuzians—two groups belonging to an especially depraved and desperate heresy—did in fact habitually pierce the tender body of an infant in all its limbs, so that, after the blood had been pressed out, flour might be kneaded with it and used to make bread for the Eucharist, as Augustine relates in *On Heresies*, heresies 26 and 27. LUDOVICUS VIVES.]

Thus they allowed a sect hostile to themselves to grow strong for so long a time, to overcome the dreadful cruelties of so many and such great persecutions—not by resisting but by suffering—and finally to reach the overthrow of their images, temples, sacred rites, and oracles.

Finally, what god is this—not our God, certainly, but theirs—who was either enticed by so great a crime or compelled to bring these things about? For those verses say that Peter defined these matters by magical art not at the command of some demon but of a god.

Such is the god possessed by those who do not possess Christ.

## CHAPTER LIV  
### The most foolish lie of the pagans, by which they invented that the Christian religion would last no longer than three hundred and sixty-five years
1. I would collect these and many similar points if the year itself had not yet elapsed—the year that the fabricated prophecy promised and deluded vanity believed. But since, from the time when the worship of Christ’s name was instituted through his bodily presence and through the Apostles, three hundred and sixty-five years have already been completed, what more do we seek from which this falsehood may be refuted? Even if we do not place the beginning of this matter at Christ’s birth, because as an infant and child he had no disciples, nevertheless, when he began to have them, Christian teaching and religion undoubtedly became known through his bodily presence—that is, after he had been baptized in the river Jordan through the ministry of John. For on this account that prophecy had gone before concerning him: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8).

But since, before he had suffered and risen from the dead, faith had not yet been established for everyone—for it was established in Christ’s resurrection (thus the apostle Paul speaks to the Athenians, saying: “He now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, by the man in whom he has established faith for all, raising him from the dead” [Acts 17:30–31])—we make our starting point in resolving this question from that event; especially because it was then also that the Holy Spirit was given, as it was fitting that he should be given after Christ’s resurrection in that city from which the second law, that is, the New Testament, was to begin. The first law was given from Mount Sinai through Moses; this is called the Old Testament. Concerning the one that was to be given through Christ it had been foretold: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). Hence he himself also said that repentance was to be preached in his name among all nations, but beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47).

There, therefore, the worship of this name began, so that people might believe in Jesus Christ, who had been crucified and had risen. There this faith blazed up through such remarkable beginnings [Note: [Col. 0618] Lov., “grew warm” (*incaluit*): other printed editions and manuscripts disagree.], that several thousand people, converted to Christ’s name with astonishing eagerness, sold their possessions so that they might be distributed to the needy, and, with holy purpose and the most ardent charity, attained voluntary poverty; and amid Jews roaring and thirsting for blood they prepared themselves to contend for the truth even unto death—not by armed power, but by a more powerful endurance.

If this was accomplished by no magical arts [Col. 0619], why do they hesitate to believe that the same thing could have been accomplished throughout the whole world by the same divine power by which it was accomplished here? But if Peter had already performed that magic so that at Jerusalem such a multitude of people might be inflamed to worship Christ’s name—people who had either nailed him to the cross after seizing him or mocked him as he hung there—then one must inquire from which year the three hundred and sixty-five years were completed.

Christ therefore died when the two Gemini were consuls, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0619] Tertullian, in *Against the Jews*, chapter 8: “‘Tiberius,’ he says, ‘Caesar held power for twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty days; in the fifteenth year of his reign Christ suffered, being about thirty years old when he suffered.’” A little later: “The suffering of this destruction was completed within the period of the seventy weeks under Tiberius Caesar, when Rubellius Geminus and Fusius Geminus were consuls, in the month of March, at the season of Passover, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.” Lactantius, following him in book 4, chapter 10, of the *Institutes*, assigns the same year of Tiberius’s reign and the same consuls, and varies only concerning the day—perhaps because of scribal error—which resulted in some manuscripts reading “the tenth day before,” others “the seventh day before,” and still others, more correctly, “the eighth day before the Kalends of April,” which is the same as “the eighth day before the Kalends of April,” as can be shown by many examples from Cicero. Augustine likewise asserts that Christ suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, or on March 25, in book 83 of the *Questions*, question 56, and in book 4 of *On the Trinity*, section 9; and with him John Chrysostom, in his sermon *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*; Gregory of Tours, book 10, at the very end; Bede, in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 47; and others. Eusebius, however, in the *Chronicle*, and Epiphanius, in heresy 51, assign the Lord’s passion to the eighteenth year of Tiberius. The Gospel favors this opinion: for in Luke 3:1 Christ’s baptism by John and the beginning of his preaching are referred to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, and it is clear that Christ preached the kingdom of God for three complete years from that point before he suffered. But Dionysius Petavius, in *On the Doctrine of Time*, book 12, chapter 12, maintains that Eusebius and Epiphanius did not calculate Tiberius’s years according to Roman custom: “For,” he says, “those Fathers began the years from the local origin of their cities, namely from the autumn preceding that summer in which Augustus died”; and consequently “they begin to reckon Tiberius’s eighteenth year from the autumn of Julian year 75.” Petavius himself therefore writes in *The Reckoner of Time*, part 1, book 5, that Christ died when Tiberius was consul for the fifth time and Sejanus was consul, on March 23. Baronius, Ludovicus Vives, Leonardus Coquaeus, and others, however, say that it was when Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Camillus Scribonianus were consuls. Finally, there is another opinion, no less approved by learned men, which assigns Christ’s passion to the nineteenth year then in progress of Tiberius, corresponding to Julian year 78, and to the year in which Phlegon, the writer on the Olympiads, according to Eusebius, assigns the eclipse of the sun—year 4 of Olympiad 202—when Severus Sulpicius Galba and Lucius Cornelius Sulla were consuls, and on April 3.]

He rose on the third day, as the Apostles also established by their own senses [Note: [Col. 0619] Vind. Am. and several manuscripts: “his Apostles” (*Apostoli sui*).]. Then, after forty days, he ascended into heaven. Ten days later—that is, on the fiftieth day after his resurrection—he sent the Holy Spirit. Then, while the Apostles preached him, three thousand people believed. Thus, as we believe and as the truth maintains, the worship of that name began through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit; but, as impious vanity fabricated or imagined, through Peter’s magical arts.

Soon afterward, when a remarkable sign had also been performed, a certain beggar who had been lame from his mother’s womb—so lame that others carried him and set him at the temple gate to ask for alms—leaped up healed at Peter’s word in the name of Jesus Christ [Col. 0620], and five thousand people believed. Thereafter, through further and further accessions, the Church of believers grew.

Thus the day from which that year itself began can also be determined: namely, when the Holy Spirit was sent, that is, on the Ides of May. Accordingly, by counting the consuls, three hundred and sixty-five years are found to have been completed by the same Ides, during the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus. Then, in the following year, when Mallius Theodorus was consul—when, according to that oracle of demons or human fabrication, the Christian religion ought already to have ceased to exist—it was unnecessary to investigate what may perhaps have happened in other parts of the world.

Meanwhile, what we know is that in the famous and eminent city of Carthage in Africa, Gaudentius and Jovius, counts of the Emperor Honorius, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, overturned the temples of the false gods and smashed their images. From that time until the present, for nearly thirty years [Note: [Col. 0620] Leonardus Coquaeus, on this passage, says: “Up to the year of Christ 429, the twenty-second year of Theodosius the Younger, when Augustine was writing this.” From the same passage Baronius, under the year 426, section 17, thinks that this book was written in 429, since nearly thirty years are here reckoned from the consulship of Mallius Theodorus, which fell in the year 399. But the prefixed expression *ferme* (“nearly”) clearly indicates that Augustine is using a rounded number, although it is not complete and three or four years are lacking, as is understood below, book 22, chapter 8.] who does not see how greatly the worship of Christ’s name has grown, especially after many of those who had been turned away from the faith as though by that true prophecy became Christians and, when the same number of years had been completed, saw that prophecy to be empty and laughable?

We, therefore, who are and are called Christians, do not believe in Peter, but in the one in whom Peter believed; we have been built up by Peter’s sermons about Christ, not poisoned by magical incantations; nor have we been deceived by sorceries, but aided by his benefits. Christ, Peter’s teacher in the doctrine that leads to eternal life, is himself also our teacher.

2. But let us now finally bring this book to a close, having discussed up to this point and demonstrated as much as seemed sufficient what the mortal course is, from beginning to end, of the two cities—the heavenly and the earthly—intermingled with one another. The earthly city has made for itself whatever false gods it wished, from whatever source, even from among human beings, in order to serve them by sacrificing to them. The heavenly city, however, which is a pilgrim on earth, does not make false gods; rather, it is itself made by the true God, whose true sacrifice it is.

Both cities, nevertheless, make equal use of temporal goods or suffer equal affliction from temporal evils, though their faith, hope, and love are different, until they are separated in the final judgment and each receives its own end—an end that has no end. The ends of both cities must now be discussed.

# BOOK NINETEEN

In this book the ends of both cities, the earthly and the heavenly, are discussed. The opinions of philosophers concerning the ends of good and evil are reviewed—philosophers who vainly attempted to establish happiness for themselves in this life. While they are refuted at greater length, it is shown what the happiness and peace of the heavenly city, or Christian people, are, and what kind of happiness and peace can be possessed here or hoped for in the future.

[Col. 0621]

## CHAPTER ONE

That Varro perceived that, in the question debated by philosophical disputation concerning the ends of goods and evils, there could be two hundred and eighty-eight schools.

1. Since I see that I must next discuss the proper ends of both cities, namely the earthly and the heavenly, I must first set forth—so far as the plan for bringing this work to completion permits—the arguments of mortals by which they have attempted to make happiness for themselves amid the unhappiness of this life. In this way it may become clear how our hope, which God has given us, differs from their vain pursuits, and what the reality itself—that is, the true happiness he will give—really is, not only by divine authority but also with the aid of reason, insofar as we can employ it for the sake of unbelievers.

Philosophers have disputed much and in many ways concerning the ends of goods and evils. They pursued this question with the greatest intensity, attempting to discover what makes a person happy. For the end of our good is that for the sake of which other things are to be desired, while it is desired for its own sake; and the end of evil is that for the sake of which other things are to be avoided, while it itself is avoided for its own sake.

By “the end of good,” therefore, we now mean not that by which it is consumed so that it no longer exists, but that by which it is perfected so that it is complete. And by “the end of evil,” we mean not that by which it ceases to exist, but that to which it proceeds by causing harm. These ends, then, are the highest good and the highest evil.

Those who professed the study of wisdom amid the vanity of this age labored greatly, as I have said, to discover these ends and to attain the highest good in this life while avoiding the highest evil. Yet, although they wandered in different ways, nature’s boundary did not allow them to deviate so far from the path of truth that some did not place the ends of goods and evils in the mind, others in the body, and others in both.

From this threefold, as it were, general division of schools, Marcus Varro, in his book *On Philosophy*, carefully and subtly examined such a great variety of doctrines that, by applying certain distinctions, he very easily arrived at two hundred and eighty-eight schools—not schools that already existed, but that could exist.

2. To explain this briefly, I must begin with what he himself noticed and set down in the book just mentioned. There are four things that people desire naturally, without a teacher, without any assistance from instruction, and without the discipline or art of living called virtue—which is undoubtedly learned. They desire either pleasure, by which the bodily senses are moved delightfully; or tranquility, by which each person suffers no bodily discomfort; or both together, which Epicurus nevertheless calls by the single name “pleasure”; or, universally, the primary things of nature, among which these are included, along with others—whether in the body, such as the integrity of the limbs and its health and soundness, or in the mind, such as the qualities, whether small or great, found in human talents [Col. 0622].

These four things, then—pleasure, tranquility, both together, and the primary things of nature—are present in us in such a way that either virtue, which instruction later implants, must be desired for their sake; or they must be desired for the sake of virtue; or both must be desired for their own sake.

Thus twelve schools arise from this arrangement, since each of the four is tripled. Once I have demonstrated this in one case, it will not be difficult to find it in the others.

When bodily pleasure is either subordinated to the virtue of the mind, preferred to it, or joined to it, there is a threefold variation of schools. It is subordinated to virtue when it is taken up for the use of virtue. For it belongs to the duty of virtue both to live for one’s country and to beget children for one’s country; neither of these can be done without bodily pleasure. Without it, neither food nor drink is taken in order to live, nor is intercourse undertaken in order that generation may be extended.

But when pleasure is preferred to virtue, pleasure itself is desired for its own sake, while virtue is thought necessary for its sake—that is, so that virtue may do nothing except attain or preserve bodily pleasure. This is a debased life, since virtue serves pleasure as its mistress; although in no way should this be called virtue. Nevertheless, this appalling disgrace has also had certain philosophers as its patrons and defenders.

Pleasure is joined to virtue when neither is desired for the sake of the other, but both are desired for their own sake. Therefore, just as pleasure—whether subordinated to virtue, preferred to it, or joined to it—produces three schools, so tranquility, both together, and the primary things of nature are each found to produce three others. For according to the variety of human opinions, they are at one time subordinated to virtue, at another preferred to it, and at another joined to it. Thus the number of schools reaches twelve.

But this number is again doubled when one further distinction is added: namely, that of social life. For whoever follows one of these twelve schools surely does so either for himself alone or also for the sake of another, to whom he ought to wish what he wishes for himself. Accordingly, there are twelve schools of those who think that each of these positions should be held for themselves alone, and another twelve of those who decide that philosophy should be practiced in this or that way not only for themselves but also for others, whose good they desire as their own.

These twenty-four schools are again doubled by adding the distinction derived from the New Academics [Note: [Col. 0622] See below, section 3.], and they become forty-eight. For anyone may hold and defend each of those twenty-four schools as certain, as the Stoics defended the view that the good of a human being, by which he becomes happy, consists solely in virtue of the mind. Another may hold it as uncertain, as the New Academics defended it, since it seemed to them not certain but nevertheless probable.

Thus twenty-four schools arise from those who think that these positions should be followed as certain because of their truth, and another twenty-four from those who think that the same positions should be followed, although uncertain, because of their probability.

Again, since anyone may follow each of these forty-eight schools in the manner of the other philosophers, while another may follow it in the manner of the Cynics, this distinction too doubles them, and they become ninety-six.

Finally, since people can uphold and follow each of these schools in such a way that they either love an unoccupied life, like those who wished and were able to devote themselves solely to the study of doctrine; or an active life, like those who, while philosophizing, were nevertheless deeply occupied with administering the state and governing human affairs; or a life moderated from both kinds, like those who allotted alternating periods of their lives partly to learned leisure and partly to necessary activity—because of these distinctions the number of schools can also be tripled and brought to two hundred and eighty-eight.

3. I have set out these matters from Varro’s book, as briefly and clearly as I could, explaining his views in my own words. But how, after refuting the others, he chooses one—the one he wishes to be that of the Old Academics, whom he wants to appear to have possessed certain doctrines from Plato, their founder, down to Polemo, who was the fourth after him to preside over his school, which was called the Academy [Note: [Col. 0623] Several manuscripts: “Academic.”]—and how he distinguishes them from the New Academics, for whom everything is uncertain, a philosophical school that began with Arcesilaus, the successor of Polemo [Note: [Col. 0623] Compare Cicero, *On the Orator*, book 3, chapter 18]; and how he regards that school, namely, that of the Old Academics, as free from both doubt and every error, would take a long time to demonstrate in full. Nevertheless, the matter must not be omitted altogether.

First, therefore, he removes all those distinctions that multiplied the number of schools. He thinks that they must be removed because the end of good is not found in them. For he does not think that any philosophical school should be called a school if it does not differ from the others by having different ends of good and evil. Since there is no reason for a human being to philosophize except in order to be happy, and what makes a person happy is itself the end of good, there is therefore no reason for philosophizing except the end of good. Consequently, any position that pursues no end of good should not be called a philosophical school.

When, therefore, the question concerns social life—whether the wise person should maintain it so that he desires and cares for the highest good, by which a person becomes happy, for his friend just as he does for himself, or whether he does everything solely for the sake of his own happiness—the question is not about the highest good itself, but about whether a companion is to be accepted or not accepted as a participant in this good, not for his own sake, but so that one may rejoice in his good as in one’s own.

Likewise, when the question concerns the New Academics, for whom everything is uncertain—whether matters in which one should philosophize are to be regarded in this way, or whether, as other philosophers have thought, we ought to regard them as certain—the question is not what is to be pursued as the end of good, but whether the truth of the good itself, which seems to be worth pursuing, is or is not to be doubted. To express this more clearly: the question is whether it should be pursued in such a way that the person who pursues it says that it is true, or in such a way that the person who pursues it says that it seems true to him, even if it should perhaps be false. In either case, both pursue one and the same good.

In the distinction introduced from the dress and customs of the Cynics, the question likewise is not what the end of good is, but whether the person who pursues the true good—whatever he considers true and worth pursuing—should live in that dress and according to those customs. Finally, there were people who, although they pursued different final goods—some virtue, others pleasure—nevertheless maintained the same dress and customs, from which they were called Cynics [Note: [Col. 0624] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “from which” (*ex quo*).]. Therefore, whatever it was that distinguished Cynic philosophers from the others contributed nothing to the choice and pursuit of the good by which they would become happy. For if it made any difference to this matter, the same dress would surely compel them to pursue the same end, and a different dress would prevent them from pursuing the same end.

## CHAPTER TWO

How, after removing all the distinctions that are not schools but questions, Varro arrives at a threefold definition of the highest good, one of which nevertheless must be chosen.

In those three ways of life as well—one consisting of active leisure, but leisure devoted to the contemplation or investigation of truth; another consisting of activity in managing human affairs; and a third moderated from both kinds—when the question is which should preferably be chosen, the controversy does not concern the end of good. Rather, it concerns which of these three makes it more difficult or easier to attain or retain the end of good.

For when a person reaches the end of good, it immediately makes him happy. But in learned leisure, public activity, or the alternation of both, no one is immediately happy. Many people can live in any of these three ways and yet go astray in pursuing the end of good by which a person becomes happy.

The question concerning the ends of goods and evils, then, is one thing; it is this that constitutes each philosophical school. The questions concerning social life, the hesitation of the Academics, the dress and diet of the Cynics, and the three ways of life—leisure, activity, and the life moderated from both—are other questions. None of these concerns a dispute about the ends of goods and evils.

Therefore, since Marcus Varro reached two hundred and eighty-eight schools by applying these four distinctions—social life, the New Academics, the Cynics, and the threefold division of life—and since other distinctions could similarly be added, we must remove them all, because they introduce no question concerning the pursuit of the highest good and therefore are neither schools nor to be called schools. We return to those twelve in which the question is what the human good is, upon attaining which a person becomes happy, so that Varro may show one of them to be true and the others false [Col. 0625].

When that threefold division of life is removed, two parts of this number are subtracted, and ninety-six schools remain. When the distinction added from the Cynics is removed, they are reduced by half and become forty-eight. Let us also remove what was added from the New Academics; again half remains, namely twenty-four. Let what had been added concerning social life likewise be removed, and twelve remain—the distinction that had doubled them to make twenty-four.

Concerning these twelve, then, no one can say why they should not be regarded as schools. For nothing else is sought in them than the ends of goods and evils. Once the ends of goods have been discovered, the ends of evils follow by contrast.

These become twelve schools because the four things—pleasure, tranquility, both together, and the primary things of nature, which Varro calls “the first things” [Note: [Col. 0625] See Cicero, *On Ends*, book 2, chapter 11, and book 5, chapter 7]—are each tripled.

For each of these four is at one time subordinated to virtue, so that it appears desirable not for its own sake but for the duty of virtue; at another it is preferred to virtue, so that virtue is thought necessary not for its own sake but in order to attain or preserve these things; and at another it is joined to virtue, so that both virtue and these things are believed desirable for their own sake. Thus they produce three times the number four and reach twelve schools.

Of those four things Varro removes three—pleasure, tranquility, and both together—not because he disapproves of them, but because those primary things of nature contain within themselves both pleasure and tranquility. What need, then, is there to make three things out of these two—two when pleasure or tranquility is desired separately, and a third when both are desired together—since the primary things of nature contain both of them and many other things besides?

He therefore thinks that the discussion should carefully concern the three schools, to determine which is preferably to be chosen. For true reason permits no more than one to be true, whether it is found among these three or somewhere else, as we shall see later.

For now, let us discuss, as briefly and plainly as we can, how Varro chooses one of these three. These three schools arise when either the primary things of nature are to be desired for the sake of virtue, or virtue for the sake of the primary things of nature, or both—that is, both virtue and the primary things of nature—are to be desired for their own sake.

## CHAPTER THREE

Concerning the three schools that seek the highest human good, and which Varro declares should be chosen, following the view of the Old Academy under the leadership of Antiochus.

1. He attempts to persuade us in the following manner concerning which of these three positions is true and ought to be followed.

First, since philosophy seeks the highest good not of a tree, an animal, or a god, but of a human being, he thinks that one must ask what a human being himself is. For he holds that there are two things in human nature: body and soul. He has no doubt that, of these two, the soul is better and far more excellent. But he asks whether the soul alone is the human being, so that the body is related to it as a horse is to a rider [Note: [Col. 0625] The printed editions add here “he thinks it must be asked,” whereas in the manuscripts the phrase is left to be understood with *he has no doubt*.].

For a rider is not “human being and horse,” but human being alone; nevertheless, he is called a rider because of the way he is related to a horse. Or is the body alone the human being, related in some way to the soul as a cup is to a drink? For a cup is not called “the cup” together with the drink that the cup contains; rather, the cup alone is so called, although it is so called because it is suited to containing the drink.

Or is a human being neither soul alone nor body alone, but both together, with one of them—whether soul or body—being a part, while the whole consists of both, so that he is a human being? It is as when we call two yoked horses a team: whether the right-hand or the left-hand horse is a part of the team, but we do not call either one, however it may be related to the other, a team; we call both together a team.

Of these three possibilities he chooses the third. He believes that a human being is neither soul alone nor body alone, but soul and body together. Accordingly, he says that the highest good of a human being, by which he becomes happy, consists of the goods of both components—namely, of soul and body.

For this reason he thinks that the primary things of nature are to be desired for their own sake, and that virtue itself, which instruction implants as an art of living, is the most excellent good among the goods of the soul.

Therefore, when this virtue—that is, the art of conducting life—has received the primary things of nature, which existed without it but nevertheless existed even when they still lacked instruction, it desires all things for its own sake and itself as well. It uses and enjoys both all these things together and itself, with the aim of taking delight in and enjoying them all, more or less according to the fact that some are greater and others lesser in relation to one another. Yet it rejoices in all of them, and, if necessity demands, despises some lesser things for the sake of attaining or preserving greater ones.

Among all goods, whether of soul or body, virtue places nothing above itself. For it makes good use both of itself and of the other goods that make a person happy. But where virtue itself is absent, however many goods there may be, they are not the goods of the one who possesses them [Note: [Col. 0626] The printed editions read “they are not his good”; the manuscripts more correctly read “they are not his good,” with the dative sense “not good for him.”]. Consequently, they should no longer be called that person’s goods, since, when he uses them badly, they cannot be useful to him.

This life of a human being, then, which enjoys virtue and the other goods of soul and body without which virtue cannot exist, is called happy. If it also enjoys other goods, without which virtue can exist, whether some or many, it is happier. But if it enjoys all of them, so that no good of soul or body is entirely lacking, it is happiest.

For life is not the same thing as virtue, since not every life but only a wise life is virtue; nevertheless, some kind of life can exist without any virtue, whereas virtue cannot exist without any life. I would say the same concerning memory and reason, and anything else of this kind in a human being. These exist even before instruction, but without them no instruction can exist; consequently, neither can virtue, which is surely learned.

Running well, possessing a beautiful body, being strong with great physical power, and other things of this kind are such that virtue can exist without them, and they themselves without virtue. Nevertheless, they are goods. According to these philosophers, virtue also loves them for its own sake and uses and enjoys them, as is fitting for virtue [Note: [Col. 0626] The printed editions read: “and that they themselves are good without virtue; nevertheless, according to these philosophers, etc.” The text has been corrected from the manuscripts.].

[Col. 0627]

2. They also declare this happy life to be social: it loves the goods of its friends for their own sake just as it loves its own, and wishes for them, on account of themselves, what it wishes for itself. This applies whether they are in the household, such as a spouse, children, and other members of the household; or in the place where the household is located, namely the city, as with those who are called citizens; or throughout the whole world, as with the nations joined to it by human society; or in the universe itself, which is designated by the name of heaven and earth, as they say the gods are, whom they wish to be friends of the wise person, whom we more familiarly call angels.

Concerning the ends of goods and, by contrast, of evils, they deny that there can be any doubt at all. They assert that this is the difference between themselves and the New Academics. Nor does it matter to them whether anyone philosophizes, regarding these ends—which they consider true—in the dress and manner of life of a Cynic or in any other dress and manner of life.

Of the three ways of life—leisure, activity, and what is composed from both—they assert that the third pleases them. Varro says that the Old Academics thought and taught these things, with Antiochus as their authority, Antiochus being the teacher of Cicero and of Varro himself. Cicero, however, wishes him to appear to have been more of a Stoic in many respects than an Old Academic [Note: [Col. 0627] This Antiochus was of Ascalon and taught Cicero, Varro, Lucullus, and many other distinguished Romans. He followed the Old Academy, but in such a way as to incline toward the school of Zeno. He maintained that it should not so much be called a new Stoic discipline as a correction of the ancient Academy. For this reason Antiochus’s view on this and many other matters, especially on the highest good, was strongly approved by Marcus Brutus, who attended the lectures of his brother, and by the other Stoics. —Lud. Vives.].

But what does that matter to us? We ought rather to judge the matters themselves than consider it a great achievement to know what each person thought about them.

## CHAPTER FOUR

What Christians think concerning the highest good and the highest evil, against the philosophers who said that the highest good was in themselves and for themselves.

1. If, then, we are asked what the city of God would answer when questioned about each of these matters, and first what it thinks concerning the ends of goods and evils, it will answer that eternal life is the highest good and eternal death the highest evil. Therefore, in order to attain the one and avoid the other, we ought to live rightly.

For this reason it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4; Gal. 3:11). We do not yet see our good, and therefore must seek it by believing; nor does right living come from ourselves unless the one who gave us the faith by which we believe that he will help us assists us as we believe and pray.

But those who thought that the ends of goods and evils were found in this life—placing the highest good either in the body, or in the soul, or in both; and, to express the matter more fully, either in pleasure, or in virtue, or in both; either in tranquility, or in virtue, or in both; either in pleasure and tranquility together, or in virtue, or in both; either in the primary things of nature, or in virtue, or in both—wished, with astonishing vanity, to be happy here and to make themselves happy by themselves.

The Truth mocked them through the prophet, who said: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings”; or, as the apostle Paul quoted this testimony: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile” (Ps. 93:11; 1 Cor. 3:20).

[Col. 0628] **2.** For who, with however great a stream of eloquence, is sufficient to explain the miseries of this life? How Cicero lamented, as best he could, in his *Consolation* over the death of his daughter; but how little was he able to do? For how can those things that are called the first goods of nature, whether in what condition, where, or how, be so well situated in this life that they do not fluctuate amid uncertain accidents? What pain contrary to pleasure, what disturbance contrary to tranquility, cannot befall the body of a wise man? Certainly the amputation or debility of limbs attacks a person’s soundness; deformity, beauty; weakness, health; fatigue, strength; torpor—or slowness—mobility. Is there any of these that cannot invade the flesh of a wise man?

The body’s posture and movement, too, when they are seemly and appropriate, are counted among the first goods of nature. But what if some illness shakes the limbs with trembling? What if the spine of the back bends so far that the hands must be placed upon the ground and makes a human being, in a certain sense, quadrupedal? Will it not overturn every appearance and dignity of bodily posture and movement?

What of the mind’s own primordial goods, as they are called, where they place the first two on account of grasping and apprehending truth—sense and understanding? But how much and what sort of sense remains if, to say nothing of other things, a person becomes deaf and blind? And where will reason and intelligence withdraw, where will they be put to sleep, if someone is made insane by some disease? When the frenzied say or do many absurd things, usually alien to their good purposes and character—indeed contrary to their good purposes and character—whether we think of such things or see them, if we consider them appropriately, we can scarcely hold back our tears, or perhaps cannot hold them back at all.

[Note: [Col. 0628] The Louvain edition alone omits “or perhaps cannot.”]

What shall I say of those who suffer the attacks of demons? Where is their understanding, hidden or buried, when an evil spirit uses both their soul and their body according to its own will? And who can be confident that this evil cannot befall a wise man in this life?

Moreover, what is the quality or extent of the apprehension of truth in this flesh, when, as we read in the truthful book of Wisdom, “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things” (Wisdom 9:15)?

Again, is not the impulse or appetite for action—if that is the correct Latin name for what the Greeks call *ὁρμήν* (*hormēn*, “impulse”)—itself the force by which even the pitiable movements and actions of the insane are carried out, when sense is perverted and reason put to sleep? For they also assign this impulse among the first goods of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0628] Compare Cicero, *On Ends*, book 5, chapter 6, and *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2, chapter 22.]

**3.** Moreover, virtue itself, which is not among the first goods of nature, since it comes afterward, introduced by instruction, although it claims for itself the summit of human goods—what does it do here except wage perpetual war against vices, not external but internal ones, not belonging to others but plainly ours and our own? This is especially true of what the Greeks call *σωφροσύνη* (*sōphrosynē*) and the Latins call temperance, by which carnal desires are restrained lest they drag the consenting mind into every kind of disgrace.

[Note: [Col. 0629] See Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book 3, chapter 8.]

For it is not the case that there is no vice, since, as the Apostle says, “The flesh desires against the spirit”; and the virtue opposed to this vice is present when, as the same Apostle says, “the spirit desires against the flesh.” “For these,” he says, “oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17).

But what do we wish to do when we wish to attain the end of the highest good, except that the flesh should not desire against the spirit and that this vice, against which the spirit desires, should not exist in us? Although in this life we wish for this, we are unable to accomplish it. Let us at least accomplish this much with God’s help: that we do not yield to the flesh desiring against the spirit, with the spirit succumbing, and that we are not dragged by our consent into committing sin.

Far be it from us, then, while we remain in this internal war, to believe that we have already attained the blessedness to which we wish to arrive by conquering. And who is so wise as to have absolutely no struggle against desires?

**4.** What of that virtue called prudence? Does it not, with all its vigilance, distinguish good things from evil, so that no error may creep in when the former are pursued and the latter avoided? Thus it also testifies that we are still in evils, or that evils are still in us. For it teaches us that it is evil to consent to sin, and good not to consent to desire in the matter of sinning.
