Yet temperance accomplishes that good which prudence teaches us: not to consent to evil. Neither prudence nor temperance removes this evil from the present life.

What of justice, whose duty is to assign to each person what belongs to him [Note: [Col. 0629] Justice is defined in the *Institutes*, under the title “On Justice and Law,” as follows: “The perpetual and constant will to assign to each person what belongs to him.” Coquaeus.]—from which a certain just order of nature comes about in the human being, so that the soul is subject to God and the flesh to the soul, and therefore both soul and flesh to God? Does it not show that it is still laboring in this work rather than resting at the completion of the work?

For the less the soul conceives of God in its very thoughts, the less it is subject to God; and the more the flesh desires against the spirit, the less it is subject to the soul. Therefore, as long as this weakness, this plague, this sickness remains in us, how shall we dare to call ourselves already saved? And if we are not yet saved, how shall we dare to call ourselves already blessed with that final blessedness?

Now the virtue whose name is courage, however great its wisdom may be, is a most evident witness to the human evils that it is compelled to endure with patience. I am astonished at the boldness with which the Stoic philosophers insist that these evils are not evils, although they admit that, if they become so great that the wise man either cannot or ought not to endure them, he is compelled to inflict death upon himself and depart from this life.

[Note: [Col. 0629] In Cicero, *On Ends*, book 3, and *Tusculan Disputations*, book 1.]

Yet such is the stupefaction of pride in these people, who think that the end of the good lies here and that they are made blessed by themselves, that they are not ashamed to call this life blessed even when their wise man—that is, the man whom they describe with astonishing vanity—even if blinded, deafened, or struck dumb, weakened in his limbs, tortured by pains, or afflicted by any other evil of this kind that can be said or imagined, is driven by it to inflict death upon himself.

[Col. 0630] O blessed life, which seeks the aid of death in order to be ended! If it is blessed, let us remain in it; but if it is fled because of these evils, how is it blessed?

[Note: [Col. 0630] All manuscripts omit “If, however, because of these evils it is fled, how is it blessed?” and connect what follows immediately after “let us remain in it”: “How are these not evils?”]

Or how are these not evils, which overcome the good of courage and compel courage not merely to yield to them but even to rave, so that it both calls the same life blessed and persuades us to flee it? Who is so blind as not to see that, if it were blessed, it ought not to be fled?

But if they admit that it ought to be fled because of the weight of the weakness by which it is oppressed, what reason is there, then, why, with the neck of pride broken, they do not also admit that it is miserable?

[Note: [Col. 0630] Several manuscripts of good authority read: “But with the weakness openly acknowledged, they admit that it ought to be fled; what reason, then, is there?”]

I ask you: did that Cato [Note: [Col. 0630] Cato of Utica.] kill himself through patience, or rather through impatience? He would not have done so unless he had impatiently endured Caesar’s victory. Where is courage? It yielded, plainly; it succumbed, plainly; it was conquered to such a degree that it abandoned, deserted, and fled from the blessed life. Or was that life not already blessed? It was therefore miserable. How, then, were those things not evils which made life miserable and something to be fled?

**5.** Therefore even those who have admitted that these things are evils—such as the Peripatetics and the ancient Academics, whose school Varro defended—speak more tolerably; but their error too is astonishing: although these evils may be so severe that they must be fled by means of death inflicted by the person who suffers them, they nevertheless insist that the life of the sufferer is blessed.

“The torments and sufferings of the body are evils,” he says, “and they are worse in proportion to their greatness. To be free from them, one must flee this life.”

“Which life, I ask?”

“This one,” he replies, “which is weighed down by such great evils.”

Then surely it is blessed amid those very evils because of which you say it ought to be fled? Or do you call it blessed because you are permitted to depart from these evils by death?

What if, then, by some divine judgment, you were held in those evils, neither permitted to die nor ever allowed to be without them?

[Note: [Col. 0630] The Louvain edition alone reads “you might be released by death.”]

Then at least you would call such a life miserable. It is not miserable, therefore, merely because it is quickly abandoned, since, if it were eternal, even you yourself would judge it miserable. It should not, then, be considered free of misery merely because it is brief—or, more absurdly, called blessed precisely because its misery is brief.

Great is the force of those evils which compel a human being—even, according to them, a wise one—to take away from himself what makes him human. For they say, and rightly say, that this is in a certain sense nature’s first and greatest voice: that a human being should be reconciled to himself, and therefore naturally flee death, being so friendly to himself that he wishes and strongly desires to be an animal and to live in this union of body and soul.

[Note: [Col. 0630] In the manuscripts: “wishes, strongly, and desires.”]

[Note: [Col. 0630] Cicero, *On Duties*, book 4, chapter 4; and *On Ends*, book 3, chapter 5, and book 5, chapter 9.]

Great is the force of those evils by which this sense of nature is conquered—the sense by which death is avoided in every way, with all powers and efforts—and conquered so completely that what was being avoided is desired and sought, and, if it cannot come from elsewhere, is inflicted by the human being upon himself.

[Col. 0631] Great is the force of those evils which make courage homicidal—if it may still be called courage when it is so overcome by these evils that it cannot, through patience, preserve the human being whom, like virtue, it undertook to govern and protect, but is itself compelled to kill him as well.

Certainly the wise man ought also to endure death patiently, but death that comes from elsewhere. According to these philosophers, however, if he is compelled to inflict it upon himself, they must plainly admit that the evils which compel him to do this are not only evils but intolerable evils.

The life, therefore, which is either weighed down by the burdens of such great and serious evils or exposed to their accidents would in no way be called blessed if those who say these things, just as they yield to unhappiness when conquered by evils that grow heavier and inflict death upon themselves, would likewise deign to yield to truth when conquered by sound reasoning in their search for the blessed life. They should not think that, in this mortality, they ought to enjoy the end of the highest good—where the virtues themselves, than which nothing certainly better or more useful is found in a human being here, are more powerful aids against the force of dangers, labors, and pains precisely in proportion as they are greater testimonies to misery.

For if they are true virtues—and they cannot exist except in those who possess true piety—they do not claim that they can ensure that the people in whom they exist suffer no miseries. True virtues are not liars, so as to make such a claim. Rather, they ensure that human life, which is compelled to be miserable amid so many and such great evils of this age, may be blessed through hope of the age to come, just as it is also saved through hope.

For how is a life blessed that is not yet saved? Hence the Apostle Paul says—not of imprudent, impatient, intemperate, and unjust people, but of those who lived according to true piety and therefore possessed true virtues:

“For by hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

Therefore, just as we have been saved in hope, so we have been made blessed in hope; and just as we do not yet possess salvation in the present but await it in the future, so we do not yet possess blessedness in the present but await it in the future. And we await it through patience, because we are in evils that we must patiently endure until we reach those good things in which everything will exist that may delight us ineffably, and nothing will remain that we must endure.

Such salvation, which will exist in the age to come, will itself also be final blessedness. Since these philosophers do not see that blessedness and refuse to believe in it, they try to fabricate for themselves here a thoroughly false one, with a virtue that is as much more deceitful as it is more arrogant.

# CHAPTER V  
## On social life, which, although greatly to be desired, is often overturned by many disturbances

That they wish the wise person to live a social life, we approve much more strongly. For how would this City of God—concerning which we are now, as it happens, occupied with the nineteenth book of this work—either have begun in its origin, advanced in its course, or reached its appointed ends, if there were no social life among the saints?

But who could enumerate, or sufficiently assess, how many and how great are the evils with which human society abounds amid the misery of this mortality? Let them hear, among their comic poets, a man saying, with the feeling and agreement of all humanity:

> “I married a wife—what misery I saw there! Children were born—  
> another care.”  
> (*Terence, The Brothers*, act 5, scene 4, lines 13–14.)

And what of those things that the same Terence lists among the evils of love—injuries, suspicions, enmities, war, and peace again (*The Eunuch*, act 1, scene 1, lines 14–16)? Have they not filled human affairs everywhere? Do they not often occur even in the honorable loves of friends? Are human affairs not everywhere full of these things, where we experience injuries, suspicions, enmities, war, and certain evils, while peace is an uncertain good because we do not know the hearts of those with whom we wish to maintain it—and even if we could know them today, we would certainly not know what they would be like tomorrow?

Who are accustomed, or ought, to be more closely united than those who are even enclosed together in one household? And yet who is secure because of this, when such great evils have so often arisen from their hidden treacheries, and have been all the more bitter because the peace was all the sweeter—the peace that was believed genuine when it was being most cunningly feigned?

For this reason what Tullius says touches every heart and compels a groan:

> “There are no more concealed treacheries than those which lie hidden under the pretense of duty or under some name of relationship. For one who is openly an adversary can easily be avoided by taking precautions; but this hidden, internal, domestic evil not only arises [Note: [Col. 0632] In Cicero: “not only does not arise.”] but also overwhelms one before one can foresee and investigate it.”  
> (Cicero, *Against Verres*, act 2, book 1, chapter 15.)

For this reason that divine saying too—“A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matthew 10:36)—is heard with great anguish of heart. For even if someone is so courageous that he bears with equanimity what a falsely assumed friendship contrives against him, or so vigilant that he avoids it through prudent foresight, nevertheless, when he discovers that such people are faithless and utterly wicked, he must be grievously tormented by the evil of those people, if he himself is good—whether they have always been evil and pretended to be good, or have changed from goodness into this wickedness.

If, then, the household—the common refuge amid these evils of the human race—is not secure, what of the city? The greater it is, the fuller is its forum of civil and criminal lawsuits, even when its often turbulent and bloody seditions and civil wars are at rest. From the outcomes of such wars cities are sometimes free; from their dangers, never.

# CHAPTER VI  
## On the error of human judgments when the truth lies hidden

What shall we think of the judgments human beings pass on human beings—the judgments that cannot be absent from cities remaining in whatever degree of peace—how miserable and lamentable they are? For those who judge cannot see the consciences of the people whom they judge. Hence they are often compelled to seek the truth in the torture of innocent witnesses concerning a case belonging to someone else.

What happens when each person is tortured in his own case? When it is asked whether he is guilty, he is tormented, and an innocent person pays the most certain penalties for an uncertain crime—not because he is discovered to have committed it, but because it is not known that he did not commit it.

Thus the ignorance of the judge is often the calamity of the innocent. And what is more intolerable, more deserving of lamentation and, if possible, of being watered with fountains of tears? Because the judge tortures the accused for this reason—that he may not unknowingly kill an innocent person—it happens, through the misery of ignorance, that he kills the person tortured and innocent—the very person whom he tortured so as not to kill an innocent person.

For if, according to the wisdom of these philosophers, he chooses to flee this life rather than endure those torments any longer, he says that he committed what he did not commit. After he has been condemned and killed, the judge still does not know whether he killed a guilty or an innocent person—the very person whom he tortured so as not to kill an innocent person unknowingly. Thus he tortured an innocent person in order to know, and killed him while still not knowing.

In these shadows of social life, will that wise judge sit, or will he not sit?

[Note: [Col. 0633] Our manuscripts read: “or will he not dare?”]

He will certainly sit. Human society constrains him and drags him into this office, which he considers it a religious crime to abandon. Yet he does not consider it a religious crime that innocent witnesses are tortured in cases belonging to others; that those who are accused, often overcome by the force of pain and confessing false things about themselves, are punished even though they are innocent, once they have been tortured while innocent; that, even if they are not punished by death, they often die during the tortures or as a result of them; that sometimes even those who bring accusations—perhaps wishing to benefit human society so that crimes do not go unpunished—are condemned by a judge who does not know the truth, when, because the witnesses are lying and the accused endures the torture with monstrous firmness and does not confess, they are unable to prove what they allege, even though what they allege is true.

[Note: [Col. 0633] The Louvain edition alone reads: “What of the fact that,” and continues with the following.]

He does not count all these many and great evils as sins. For the wise judge does not do these things out of a desire to harm, but out of the necessity of not knowing; and nevertheless, because human society compels him, he does them out of the necessity of judging as well.

This, then, is what we call human misery, even if it is not the wise person’s wickedness. But does he torture the innocent out of the necessity of not knowing and judging, punish the innocent, and find it insufficient that he is not guilty unless he is also blessed?

How much more thoughtfully and humanely he recognizes the misery in this necessity, hates it in himself, and, if he is piously wise, cries out to God: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Psalm 25:17)!

[Note: [Col. 0633] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erfurtensis read: “How much more thoughtfully and humanely he recognizes the human being in this necessity, and hates this misery in himself.”]

# CHAPTER VII  
## On the diversity of languages, by which human society is divided, and on the misery of wars, including those called just

After the city or town comes the world, in which they place the third stage of human society, beginning with the household, proceeding from there to the city, and then advancing to the world. This, like a gathering of waters, is more filled with dangers in proportion to its size.

In it, first of all, the diversity of languages alienates one human being from another. For if two people meet one another and are compelled by some necessity not to pass by but to remain together, while neither knows the language of the other, mute animals—even of different species—more easily form an association with each other than those two human beings do. For when they cannot communicate to one another what they feel, so great a similarity of nature contributes nothing toward joining human beings together, merely because of the diversity of language. Thus a person is more willing to be with his dog than with a foreign human being.

But an effort was made so that the imperial city might impose not only its yoke but also its language upon the nations it had subdued through the peace of political association, by which there would not be a shortage but even an abundance of interpreters.

True—but through how many and how great wars, with what slaughter of human beings and what shedding of human blood, was this acquired? And when these had ended, the misery of the same evils was not ended. For although foreign nations have not been, and are not, lacking as enemies against whom wars have always been and are being waged,

[Note: [Col. 0634] So read our manuscripts. The B recension reads: “nor are enemies lacking.”]

nevertheless the very extent of the empire gave birth to wars of a worse kind—namely, social and civil wars—which shake the human race more miserably, whether when war is being waged so that eventually there may be rest, or when people fear that it may rise again.

If I wished to express, as would be fitting, the many and manifold disasters and harsh and dreadful necessities of these evils, although I could in no way do so as the subject requires, who could set a limit to such a lengthy discussion?

“But,” they say, “the wise man will wage just wars.”

As though, if he remembers that he is a human being, he would not much more deeply grieve that the necessity of waging just wars had fallen to his lot. For unless they were just, he ought not to wage them; and consequently, for the wise man there would be no wars at all. The injustice of the opposing party imposes upon the wise man the necessity of waging just wars.

[Note: [Col. 0634] Compare *Questions on Joshua*, question 10.]

That injustice is certainly something a human being must grieve over, because it belongs to human beings, even if no necessity of waging war were to arise from it.

Whoever considers these evils—so great, so dreadful, so savage—with grief should acknowledge misery. But whoever either suffers them without grief of soul or reflects upon them and nevertheless considers himself blessed is thereby much more miserable, because he has lost the human sense.

# CHAPTER VIII  
## That the friendship of good people cannot be secure while it is necessary to tremble at the dangers present in this life

But if a certain ignorance resembling madness does not befall us—although in the miserable condition of this life it often does, so that someone is believed to be a friend who is an enemy, or an enemy who is a friend—what consoles us in this human society, so full of errors and hardships, except an unfeigned faith and the mutual love of true and good friends?

The more numerous such friends we have, and the more places in which we have them, the farther and more widely we fear that some evil may befall them amid the great heaps of evils in this age. For we are not merely anxious that they may be afflicted by hunger, wars, diseases, or captivity, or that in the same slavery they may suffer things that we are not even capable of imagining; we are also anxious—and this fear is much more bitter—that they may be changed into treachery, malice, and wickedness.

And when such things occur—so much more often, of course, the more numerous they are and the more places in which they live—

[Note: [Col. 0635] Here most manuscripts omit “and the more places in which they live.”]

and are brought to our knowledge, who can perceive with what lashes our heart is scourged, except one who experiences such things?

We would rather hear that they were dead, although we cannot hear even this without pain. For if their life delighted us because of the consolations of friendship, how could their death bring us no sadness?

Let whoever forbids this sadness forbid, if he can, friendly conversations; let him prohibit or cut off friendly affection; let him tear apart the bonds of all human relationships with the cruel insensibility of his mind. Or let him judge that we should use them in such a way that no sweetness from them should suffuse the soul.

But if this is entirely impossible, how could it happen that the death of someone whose life is sweet to us would not be bitter?

Hence there is also mourning, a kind of wound or sore—not belonging to an inhuman heart—for which dutiful consolations are applied as a remedy.

It is not, therefore, that there is nothing to heal merely because the better the soul is, the more quickly and easily the wound is healed in it. Since the life of mortals is afflicted, now more gently and now more harshly, even by the deaths of those most dear to us, especially those whose services are necessary to human society, we would nevertheless rather hear or see those whom we love dead than fallen away either from faith or from good morals—that is, dead in their very soul.

The earth is full of this immense source of evils. Hence it is written: “Is not human life a temptation upon the earth?” [Note: [Col. 0635] The Vulgate reads “a military service” (*militia*).] (Job 7:1). And for this reason the Lord himself says: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18:7); and again: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

Thus, when good friends die, we rejoice for them, and although their death grieves us, their death itself consoles us more certainly, because they have escaped the evils by which even good people in this life are either crushed, corrupted, or endangered in both ways.

# CHAPTER IX  
## On the friendship of the holy Angels, which cannot be manifest to human beings in this world because of the deceitfulness of the demons, among whom those have fallen who thought that many gods should be worshiped

In the society of the holy Angels—which those philosophers who wished the gods to be our friends placed fourth, as though advancing toward the world from the earthly globe and thereby in some way embracing heaven—we by no means fear that such friends may grieve us either by their death or by their corruption.

But because they do not mingle with us with the familiarity with which human beings mingle with one another—something that also belongs to the hardships of this life—and because Satan, as we read, “transfigures himself as an angel of light” [Note: [Col. 0636] The printed editions read “into an angel.” The manuscripts read “as an angel,” as Augustine does elsewhere.] (2 Corinthians 11:14), in order to test those who need either to be instructed in this way or, by a just judgment, to be deceived, great is God’s mercy that is necessary to prevent someone who thinks he has good Angels as friends from having evil demons as pretended friends and suffering them as enemies all the more harmful because they are more cunning and deceitful.

And for whom is this great mercy of God necessary, except for great human misery, which is oppressed by such great ignorance that it is easily deceived by their simulation?

It is certain that those philosophers in the impious city who said that the gods were their friends fell among evil demons, to whom the entire city is subjected and with whom it will suffer eternal punishment. For from their sacred rites—or rather, their sacrileges—by which they thought these beings should be worshiped, and from the filthy games in which their crimes are celebrated, by which they thought these beings should be appeased, it is sufficiently clear who these beings are, since they are the very authors and enforcers of such great and shameful acts.

# CHAPTER X  
## What fruit is prepared for the saints from overcoming the temptation of this life

But neither are the holy and faithful worshipers of the one true and supreme God secure from their deceptions and manifold temptations. For in this place of weakness and in these evil days, even this anxiety is not useless, so that the security where peace is utterly full and certain may be sought with more fervent desire.

For there the gifts of nature will exist—that is, the gifts bestowed upon our nature by the Creator of all natures—not only good but also everlasting; not only in the soul, which is healed [Note: [Col. 0636] The printed editions read “will be healed.” The manuscripts read “is healed.”] through wisdom, but also in the body, which will be renewed through resurrection.

There virtues will not be struggling against any vices or evils whatsoever, but will possess as the reward of victory the everlasting peace that no adversary will disturb.

[Note: [Col. 0636] Compare book 14 of *On the Trinity*, no. 12.]

For that is final blessedness; that is the end of perfection, which has no end that brings it to completion.

Here, however, we are indeed called blessed when we possess peace—however little of it can be possessed here in a good life. But when this blessedness is compared with the blessedness that we call final, it is found to be altogether misery.

Therefore, when mortal human beings possess in mortal things such peace as can exist here, virtue uses its good things properly, if we live rightly. But when we do not possess it, virtue also makes good use of the evils that a human being suffers.

Yet virtue is true only when it refers both all the good things of which it makes proper use, and whatever it does in the good use of good and evil things, and itself also, to that end where such and so great a peace will be ours that nothing better or greater can exist.

# CHAPTER IX  
## On the blessedness of eternal peace, in which the end of the saints—that is, true perfection—is found

[Col. 0637]

Therefore we may say that the ends [Note: [Col. 0637] Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “the end.” The other books read “the ends.”] of our goods are peace, just as we have said that they are eternal life. This is especially so because, in the holy Psalm, the City of God itself, concerning which this most laborious discussion of ours is being conducted, is addressed in these words:

> “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion.  
> For he has strengthened the bars of your gates;  
> he has blessed your children within you.  
> He has appointed your boundaries as peace”  
> (Psalm 147:12–14).

For when the bars of its gates have been made fast, no one will enter it and no one will leave it. Thus we should understand its boundaries as the peace that we wish to show to be final.

The mystical name of the city itself, Jerusalem, as we have already said, is interpreted as “Vision of peace.” But because the name peace is also frequently used for these mortal things, where there is certainly no eternal life, we have preferred to call the end of this city, where its highest good will be found, eternal life rather than peace.

Concerning this end the Apostle says: “But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and your end is eternal life” (Romans 6:22).

But again, because eternal life may also be understood by those who are not familiar with the Holy Scriptures as the life of the wicked—or, according to certain philosophers, on account of the immortality of the soul—or even, according to our faith, on account of the interminable punishments of the ungodly, who certainly could not be tormented forever unless they also lived forever—the end of this city, in which it will possess its highest good, must be called either peace in eternal life or eternal life in peace, so that it may be more easily understood by everyone.

So great is the good of peace that even in earthly and mortal things nothing is usually heard with greater pleasure, nothing desired with greater longing, and finally nothing better can be found.

If we wish to speak about it at somewhat greater length, we will not, I think, burden our readers, both because of the end of this city about which we are speaking and because of the very sweetness of peace, which is dear to everyone.

# CHAPTER XII  
## That even the savagery of those who wage war and all human unrest desire to reach the end of peace, without whose pursuit no nature exists
1. For whoever looks with me, however imperfectly, at human affairs and our common nature acknowledges that, just as there is no one who does not wish to rejoice, so there is no one who does not wish to have peace. [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice editions read this passage as follows: “For whoever looks with me, however imperfectly, at human affairs and our common nature acknowledges this. For just as there is no one who does not wish to rejoice, so there is no one who does not wish to have peace.” M.] Since even those who desire wars desire nothing other than victory, they therefore seek to reach glorious peace by waging war. For what else is victory than the subjection of those who resist? When this has been accomplished, there will be peace. Thus wars too are waged with peace as their objective, even by those who strive to exercise military valor by commanding and fighting. Hence it is clear that peace is the desirable end of war. Every human being, even when waging war, seeks peace; no one seeks war by making peace. Indeed, those who wish to disturb the peace in which they live do not hate peace, but wish to change it according to their own will. They do not therefore wish there to be no peace, but that the peace should be the one they want. Finally, even if they separate themselves from others through sedition, they achieve nothing unless, with those very associates and conspirators of theirs, they maintain some kind of peace. Accordingly, even brigands, in order to be more violently and safely hostile to the peace of others, wish to have peace among their companions. But even if one man were so overwhelmingly powerful, and so wary of his accomplices, that he entrusted himself to no associate, [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads *consocios*. So manuscripts 258 and 2050. M.] and, lying in ambush alone, overpowered and killed whomever he could and carried off their booty, he would nevertheless maintain some sort of shadow of peace with those whom he could not kill and whom he wanted to remain unaware of what he was doing. In his own house, moreover, with his wife and children, and with any others he has there, he certainly strives to be at peace. For he is undoubtedly pleased when they obey his every command. If they do not, he becomes angry, reproves, and punishes them; and, if necessary, he establishes peace in his household even by savagery. He perceives that this peace cannot exist unless the others in that domestic society are subjected to a certain principle—namely, to himself as the head of his household. Therefore, if he were offered the servitude of many, whether of a city or a nation, so that they served him in the way he wished to be served at home, he would no longer hide as a brigand in secret places, but would exalt himself openly as a king, while the same desire and wickedness remained in him.

Everyone, then, wishes to have peace with those whom he wants to live according to his own will. Even with those against whom they wage war, they wish, if they can, to make them their own and, once they have been subjected, to impose upon them the laws of their peace.

2. But let us imagine someone of the sort celebrated by poetic and fabulous narrative—someone whom, perhaps because of his very unsociable savagery, they preferred to call half-human rather than human. [Note: Cacus is intended here; see Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.185–275.] Although, therefore, the realm of this man was the solitude of a dreadful cave, and his wickedness so individual [Note: Most manuscripts read “as if” (*tanquam*).] that his name was derived from it—for “bad” is called *kakos* (κακός) in Greek, and that was what he was called—no wife would bring him and take away sweet conversation; he would not play with little children or command older ones; he would enjoy no conversation with a friend; and in this respect he would have been not a little happier than his father Vulcan, because Vulcan himself had not begotten such a monster. He would give nothing to anyone, but would take from anyone whatever he wanted, whenever he could, and as much as he wanted. [Note: Some manuscripts read “whatever he wished,” omitting “and”; others read “whom,” or “when” / “whenever he wished.” Apart from a few, they retain the printed reading, “and as much as he wished.”] Nevertheless, in his very solitary cave, whose ground, as it is described, was “always warm with freshly shed blood” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.195–196), he wanted nothing other than peace—peace in which no one would trouble him and no force or terror would disturb his repose.

Finally, he wanted to have peace with his own body; and as long as he had it, he was content. For he commanded his obedient limbs; and, in order to pacify with as much speed as possible his mortality, which was rebelling against him through want, and the sedition of hunger, which was arousing itself to separate and expel the soul from the body, he seized, killed, and devoured whatever he could. Savage and brutal though he was, he nevertheless provided for the peace of his own life and safety with savage and brutal determination. Thus, if he had wished to have with others the peace that he worked so hard to maintain in his cave and within himself [Note: The manuscripts read *satis agebat* (“worked hard enough”); the printed editions have *satagebat*.], he would not have been called wicked, a monster, or half-human. Or perhaps the shape of his body and the vomiting of black fires kept him away from human society; perhaps he was savage not from a desire to harm but from the necessity of living.

But this man either did not exist or—and this is more credible—was not as he is portrayed by poetic fiction. For unless Cacus were excessively condemned, Hercules would be insufficiently praised. Such a man, or half-man, is therefore, as I have said, better believed not to have existed, like many of the poets’ inventions. Even the fiercest wild animals, from which he possessed part of his savagery—for he too is called “half-wild” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.267)—preserve their own kind through a certain peace: by mating, producing offspring, giving birth, caring for their young, and nourishing them, although most of them are unsociable and solitary wanderers—not, of course, like sheep, deer, doves, starlings, and bees, but like lions, foxes, eagles, and owls.

What tigress, after all, does not murmur gently to her cubs and caress them with peaceful ferocity? What kite, however solitary in flying around for plunder, does not form a mate-pair, build a nest, brood its eggs, feed its young, and preserve with as much peace as it can a domestic partnership, so to speak, with its mother of the household? How much more, then, is a human being borne, as it were, by the laws of his nature toward entering into fellowship and peace with other human beings, and toward securing peace for all as far as he is able?

Even wicked people wage war for the peace of their own, and all, if they can, wish to make others their own, so that everyone and everything may serve one person. How could this happen unless they consent to his peace, whether by loving or fearing him? [Note: The printed editions read “unless they consent *to* his peace”; *to* is absent from the manuscripts.] Thus pride perversely imitates God. It hates equality with its associates under God, but wants to impose its own domination upon its associates in God’s place. It therefore hates God’s just peace and loves its own unjust peace; yet it cannot in any way fail to love some kind of peace. No vice, after all, is so contrary to nature that it destroys even nature’s faintest traces.

3. Thus a person who knows how to prefer what is right to what is wrong and what is ordered to what is perverse sees the peace of the wicked in comparison with the peace of the righteous, and does not judge that it ought to be called peace. Yet what is perverse must necessarily be at peace in some respect, and with some part of things, and arise from some part of things—in the elements of which it consists—for otherwise it would not exist at all.

Suppose, for example, that someone is hanging upside down. The position of his body and the arrangement of his limbs are certainly perverse, because what nature requires to be above is below, and what it wants below has been placed above. This perversity has disturbed the peace of the flesh [Note: The manuscripts read “has disturbed”; the printed editions read “will disturb.”] and is therefore painful. Nevertheless, the soul is at peace with its body and strives for its well-being, and therefore there is someone who feels pain. If the soul, excluded by the body’s troubles, departs, then, as long as the joining of the limbs remains, what is left is not without some peace among its parts; and therefore there is still something that hangs there.

The earthly body, moreover, presses toward the earth and resists the bond by which it is suspended; it strives toward the order of its own peace and, as it were, asks in the voice of its weight for a place in which to rest. Once lifeless and without any sensation, it nevertheless does not depart from the natural peace of its order, whether it possesses that peace or is carried toward it.

If medicines and treatment are applied so that the corpse’s form is not allowed to dissolve and fall apart [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “are not allowed” (*sinant*).], a certain peace still joins the parts to one another and attaches the entire mass to what is earthy and appropriate to it, and thus to a peaceful place. But if no care is taken to preserve it [Note: Our manuscripts read *condendi* (“preserving”).], and it is left to the natural course, it is, as it were, in turmoil for as long as its conflicting elevations and movements are at variance with our senses. This is what is perceived in putrefaction, until it becomes compatible with the elements of the world and gradually, little by little, disperses into their peace.

Nevertheless, nothing is in any way removed from the laws of that supreme Creator and Ordainer, by whom the peace of the universe is administered. Even if small animals arise from the corpse of a larger animal, by the same law of the Creator each small body serves its own little creatures in the peace of their well-being. [Note: Vindobonensis and Ambrosianus read “its own animals”; some manuscripts read “of its own animal.”] Even if the flesh of the dead is devoured by other animals, throughout all things they find the same laws, spread everywhere for the preservation of each mortal species: laws that make what is fitting at peace with what is fitting, wherever those remains are carried, whatever things they are joined to, and whatever things they are converted and changed into.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On the universal peace that, amid every disturbance, cannot be taken away by the law of nature, while under a just judge each person reaches by ordered disposition what he has deserved by his will

1. The peace of the body is the ordered proportion of its parts. The peace of the irrational soul is the ordered rest of its appetites. The peace of the rational soul is the ordered agreement of knowledge and action. The peace of body and soul is the ordered life and health of a living creature. The peace of mortal humanity with God [Note: The printed editions read “with immortal God.” “Immortal” is absent from the manuscripts.] is the ordered obedience, in faith, to the eternal law. The peace of human beings is ordered concord. The peace of a household is the ordered concord of command and obedience among those living together. The peace of a city is the ordered concord of command and obedience among its citizens. The peace of the heavenly city is the most perfectly ordered and harmonious fellowship in enjoying God and one another in God. The peace of all things is the tranquility of order. Order is the arrangement that assigns to equal and unequal things their proper places.

Accordingly, the wretched, since insofar as they are wretched they are certainly not at peace, lack the tranquility of order in which there is no disturbance. Yet because they are wretched deservedly and justly, they cannot, even in their very misery, exist outside order; they are not joined to the blessed, but are separated from them by the law of order. Since they are without disturbance, they are fitted together with whatever things they are in, with whatever degree of correspondence; and thus there is in them some tranquility of order, and therefore some peace.

They are wretched, however, because even if they do not suffer while enjoying some security, they are not where they ought to be secure and free from suffering. They would be still more wretched if they did not have peace with the very law by which the natural order is administered. When they suffer, the disturbance of peace has occurred in the respect in which they suffer; yet peace still remains in that respect in which neither pain burns nor the structure itself is dissolved.

Thus, just as there is a certain life without pain, while pain cannot exist without some life, so there is a certain peace without any war, while war cannot exist without some peace—not insofar as it is war, but insofar as it is carried on by or within things that possess some nature. They could not exist at all if they did not subsist through some kind of peace.

2. There is therefore a nature in which no evil exists, or even in which evil cannot exist; but there cannot be a nature in which no good exists. Accordingly, even the nature of the devil, insofar as it is a nature, is not evil; perversity makes it evil. Thus he did not stand in the truth (John 8:44), but did not escape the judgment of truth. He did not remain in the tranquility of order, yet he did not thereby escape the power of the Ordainer.

The good of God that exists in him by nature does not remove him from God’s justice, by which he is ordered in punishment. There God does not pursue the good that he created, but the evil that the devil committed. He does not take away everything he gave to nature, but removes some things and leaves others, so that there may be one who suffers over what he removes. [Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read “what he removed.”] Pain itself is testimony both to the good that has been taken away and to the good that remains. If some good had not remained, he could not grieve over the good he had lost.

For the one who sins is worse if he rejoices in the loss of righteousness. But the one who is tormented, if he gains no good from it, suffers the loss of well-being. Since both righteousness and well-being are good, and the loss of good ought to produce grief rather than joy—unless it is compensated by something better, and the righteousness of the soul is better than the health of the body—it is certainly more fitting that the unjust person grieve in punishment than that he rejoiced in wrongdoing.

Therefore, just as joy over an abandoned good in sin is evidence of an evil will, so pain over a lost good in punishment is evidence of a good nature. Whoever grieves over the loss of the peace of his nature grieves by reason of certain remnants of peace, through which nature remains friendly to him. This is rightly brought about in the final punishment: the unjust and impious are to lament in torment the loss of their natural goods, perceiving that their taker is the most just God, whom they despised as the most gracious giver.

God, therefore, the wisest creator and most just ordainer of all natures, who established the human race as the greatest ornament of earthly things, gave human beings certain goods suited to this life: temporal peace, in proportion to mortal life, in its health, safety, and fellowship with its own kind; and whatever things are necessary either to preserve or recover this peace, such as whatever is suitably and appropriately available to the senses—light, night [Note: Morel, in *Elementa Critica*, p. 153, judges that this should be read on the authority of the manuscripts. In manuscript B the reading is “this visible light, breezes,” etc.], breathable air, drinkable water, and whatever is appropriate for feeding, clothing, caring for, and adorning the body.

He gave these goods according to a most equitable arrangement: whoever, as a mortal, uses such goods properly, goods adapted to the peace of mortals, receives greater and better goods—namely, the peace of immortality itself, together with the glory and honor appropriate to it, in eternal life for the enjoyment of God and of one’s neighbor in God. But whoever uses them wrongly receives neither the former nor retains the latter.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On the order and law, whether heavenly or earthly, by which human society is served even through domination, and which is itself served through such service

Every use of temporal things, then, is referred in the earthly city to the enjoyment of earthly peace; in the heavenly city it is referred to the enjoyment of eternal peace.

Accordingly, if we were irrational animals, we would desire nothing except the ordered proportion of the body’s parts and the rest of our appetites. We would desire nothing, therefore, except bodily repose and an abundance of pleasures, so that the peace of the body might benefit the peace of the soul. For if bodily peace is absent, the peace of the irrational soul is also hindered, because it cannot attain rest from its appetites. Both together, however, benefit the peace that soul and body possess between them—namely, ordered life and health.

Just as animals show that they love bodily peace when they flee pain, and that they love peace of soul when they pursue pleasure to satisfy their appetites, so, by fleeing death, they clearly indicate how greatly they love the peace by which soul and body are united.

But because the human being possesses a rational soul, he subjects all that he shares with beasts to the peace of the rational soul, so that he may contemplate something with his mind and act according to that contemplation. Thus there may be in him the ordered agreement of knowledge and action, which we have called the peace of the rational soul.

He ought therefore to will neither to be troubled by pain, nor disturbed by desire, nor dissolved by death, so that he may know something useful and order his life and conduct according to that knowledge. But lest, through the weakness of the human mind, he fall into the ruin of some error precisely through his pursuit of knowledge, he needs divine instruction, which he obeys with certainty, and assistance, so that he may obey freely.

And because, as long as he is in this mortal body, he is away from the Lord, he walks by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:6–7). Accordingly, he refers every peace—of body, of soul, or of body and soul together—to that peace which mortal humanity has with immortal God, so that there may be in him the ordered obedience, in faith, to the eternal law.

Now, since the Teacher God gives the two chief commandments—love of God and love of neighbor—in which a human being finds three objects of love, God, oneself, and one’s neighbor—and since the person who loves himself does not err when he loves God—it follows that he should also guide his neighbor toward loving God, for he is commanded to love his neighbor as himself.

He should do this for his wife, his children, his household members, and all other people whom he can assist; and he should wish, if he should happen to be in need, to be assisted by his neighbor in the same way. Thus, insofar as it depends on him, he will be at peace with every human being, with the peace of human beings—that is, with ordered concord. Its order is first that he harm no one, and then that he also benefit anyone he can.

His first concern, therefore, is for his own people. He has a more convenient and accessible opportunity to assist them, either by the order of nature or by that of human society. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for the members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8).

From this, then, domestic peace also arises: the ordered concord of command and obedience among those living together. Those who provide assistance command, as the husband commands the wife, parents their children, and masters their servants. Those who receive assistance obey, as wives obey their husbands, children their parents, and servants their masters.

But in the household of a just person who lives by faith and is still away from that heavenly city, those who command also serve those whom they appear to command. They do not command from a desire to dominate, but as a duty to provide care; not from the pride of ruling, but from the mercy of providing for others.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On natural freedom and servitude, whose first cause is sin, whereby a person of evil will, even if he is not another human being’s slave, is the slave of his own desire

The natural order prescribes this; God created humanity in this way. For he says: “Let them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth” (Genesis 1:26). He did not wish the rational creature, made in his image, to rule except over irrational creatures: not human over human, but human over animals.

For this reason, the first righteous men were established as shepherds of animals rather than kings of human beings, so that God might thereby indicate both what the order of creatures requires and what the desert of sinners demands. The condition of servitude is rightly understood as having been imposed upon the sinner. Accordingly, nowhere in Scripture do we read of a slave before the just Noah punished his son with this term (Genesis 9:25). This name, therefore, was earned by guilt, not by nature.

The origin of the word “slaves” in the Latin language is believed to derive from the fact that those who could lawfully be killed under the law of war became slaves when the victors spared them; they were called *servi* from *servare*, “to preserve.” Yet even this occurs only because of the merit of sin. For even when a just war is waged, one fights against the opposing party on account of sin. [Note: Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and several manuscripts read “one fights against sin on the contrary side.” Erasmus and certain other manuscripts read “one fights against contrary sin.” Our codices read “one fights against sin on the contrary side.” M.]

Every victory, moreover, even when it comes to the wicked, humbles the defeated by divine judgment, either correcting their sins or punishing them. The man of God Daniel bears witness to this: while held in captivity, he confesses his own sins and those of his people to God, and in devout grief testifies that these were the cause of that captivity (Daniel 9:5–19).

The first cause of servitude, then, is sin, so that one human being might be subjected to another by the bond of his condition. This occurs only by the judgment of God, with whom there is no injustice, and who knows how to distribute different punishments according to the merits of those who offend.

As the heavenly Lord says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). Thus many religious people serve wicked masters, though they do not serve free persons: “For by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

It is certainly happier to serve a human being than desire, since, to say nothing of other things, the most savage domination of all—desire for domination itself—lays waste the hearts of mortals. In the peace-order by which some human beings are subjected to others, humility benefits those who serve, just as pride harms those who dominate.

No one, however, is by nature—as God first created humanity—a slave of another human being or of sin. But punitive servitude is ordered by that law which commands the natural order to be preserved and forbids it to be disturbed. For if that law had not been violated, there would be nothing to be restrained by punitive servitude.

Therefore the Apostle also admonishes slaves to be subject to their masters and to serve them sincerely and willingly (Ephesians 6:5), so that, if they cannot become free from their masters, they may themselves in a certain sense make their servitude free—not by serving with deceptive fear, but with faithful love—until iniquity passes away, every principality and human power is abolished, and God is all in all.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the equal right of ruling

Therefore, even if our righteous fathers had slaves, they administered domestic peace in such a way that, with respect to these temporal goods, they distinguished the lot of children from the condition of slaves; but, for the worship of God, in whom eternal goods are to be hoped for, they cared equally and lovingly for every member of their household.

The natural order prescribes this so clearly that the name “father of the household” arose from it and became so widely used that even those who rule unjustly take pleasure in being called by it. True fathers of households, however, care for all within their household as for children, so that they may worship and win the favor of God. They desire and hope to reach the heavenly household, where the duty of commanding mortals will not be necessary, because in that immortal blessedness the duty of providing care will no longer be necessary.

Until that destination is reached, fathers ought to regard their exercise of rule as a greater obligation than servants regard their service as something to be endured. If someone in a household opposes domestic peace through disobedience, he is reproved—by word, by blows, or by any other kind of just and lawful punishment, insofar as human society permits—for the benefit of the one who is reproved, so that he may be refitted to the peace from which he had broken away.

For just as it is not kindness to assist someone in such a way that he loses a greater good, so it is not innocence to spare him and allow him to fall into a worse evil. It therefore belongs to the duty of the innocent not only to inflict evil upon no one, but also to restrain from sin or punish sin, so that either the one punished may be corrected by experience or others may be frightened by the example.

Since a human household ought to be the beginning or a small part of the city, and every beginning is referred to an end of its own kind, while every part is referred to the integrity of the whole of which it is a part, it is sufficiently clear that domestic peace must be referred to civic peace—that is, that the ordered concord of command and obedience among those living together must be referred to the ordered concord of command and obedience among citizens.

Thus it follows that a father of a household must take his instructions from the law of the city and govern his household in such a way that it is adapted to the city’s peace. [Note: Most manuscripts read “adapted.”]

## CHAPTER XVII  
### From what source the heavenly society has peace with the earthly city, and from what source it has discord

But the household of people who do not live by faith pursues earthly peace through the things and advantages of this temporal life. The household of people who live by faith, however, awaits the eternal things promised for the future and uses earthly and temporal things as a traveler uses them: not things by which it may be captured and turned away from its journey toward God, but things by which it may be supported in bearing more easily, and in no way increasing, the burdens of the corruptible body, which weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15).

Therefore the use of the things necessary for this mortal life is common to both kinds of people and to both households [Note: The printed editions add “believers and unbelievers”; without these words, it is nevertheless clear that “both kinds of people” means those who live by faith and those who do not.], but the purpose for which each uses them is its own and very different.

Likewise, the earthly city, which does not live by faith, desires earthly peace and fixes the concord of command and obedience among its citizens upon this: that there should be a certain human settlement concerning the things belonging to mortal life.

The heavenly city—or rather that part of it which is traveling through this mortal state and lives by faith—must also use this peace until the mortality for which such peace is necessary has passed away. Accordingly, while it conducts the captive life of its pilgrimage within the earthly city, having already received the promise of redemption and the spiritual gift as a pledge, it does not hesitate to obey the laws of the earthly city by which the affairs suited to sustaining mortal life are administered. Since mortality itself is common to both, concord between the two cities is thereby preserved in matters pertaining to it.

But because the earthly city had certain wise men of its own, whom divine discipline rejects—men who either suspected or, deceived by demons, believed that many gods had to be reconciled to human affairs, with different matters assigned in some fashion to their different functions: to one the body, to another the soul [Note: The printed editions read “to another, the soul,” and subsequently use the accusative consistently: neck, learning, anger, desire, forests, money, navigation, and so forth. These are corrected from the Reims manuscript.]; within the body, to one the head, to another the neck, and so on, each part to a different deity; likewise within the soul, to one intelligence, to another learning, to another anger, to another desire; and among the things connected with life, to one cattle, to another grain, to another wine, to another oil, to another forests, to another money, to another navigation, to another wars and victories, to another marriages, to another births and fertility, and to others the remaining things—

while the heavenly city knew that only one God should be worshiped and that he alone should be served with that service called *latreia* (λατρεία) in Greek and owed exclusively to God, and judged this by faithful devotion [Note: See above, Book 5, chapter 45, and Book 6, chapter 1]—it followed that it could not share the laws of religion with the earthly city. It had to dissent from it on this account and become a burden to those who held different opinions, enduring their anger, hatred, and attacks of persecution, unless it sometimes repelled the spirit of its opponents by the terror of its multitude and always by divine assistance.

Thus, while traveling on earth, this heavenly city calls citizens from every nation and gathers its traveling society in every language. It does not concern itself with whatever is diverse in customs, laws, and institutions by which earthly peace is either acquired or maintained. It neither abolishes nor destroys any of these things; rather, it preserves and follows them, for although they differ among different nations, they are nevertheless directed toward one and the same end, earthly peace, provided that they do not hinder the religion by which the one supreme and true God is taught to be worshiped.

The heavenly city therefore uses earthly peace during its pilgrimage and, in matters belonging to the mortal nature of human beings, preserves and pursues the settlement of human wills insofar as this can be granted without violating piety and religion. It refers that earthly peace to heavenly peace—which is truly peace, and is the only peace that rational creation ought to possess and call peace: the most perfectly ordered and harmonious fellowship in enjoying God and one another in God.

When that destination is reached, there will not be mortal life but fully and certainly vital life; nor will there be an animal body which, while it is being corrupted, weighs down the soul, but a spiritual body, free from every want and wholly subject in every respect to the will.

It possesses this peace while traveling by faith, and lives justly by this faith, referring to the attainment of that peace everything good that it does toward God and neighbor, since the life of the city is necessarily social.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### How different is the uncertainty of the New Academy from the steadfastness of Christian faith

As for the distinction Varro introduced concerning the New Academics, for whom everything is uncertain, the city of God utterly detests such doubt as madness. It possesses, concerning things that it grasps with mind and reason, a knowledge that is most certain, even though it is small on account of the corruptible body that weighs down the soul—for, as the Apostle says, “we know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9).

It also trusts the senses in the evident perception of each thing, senses which the soul uses through the body, since the person who never thinks that they should be trusted is deceived more disastrously.

It also trusts the holy Scriptures, both Old and New, which we call canonical. From them faith itself was conceived, by which the righteous person lives (Habakkuk 2:4), and by which we walk without doubt for as long as we are away from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6). While this faith remains safe and certain, we doubt without just reproach concerning certain matters that have not come to our knowledge through sense or reason [Note: Some manuscripts read “we perceive” rather than “we have perceived.”], that have not been made clear to us through canonical Scripture, and that have not reached our awareness through witnesses whom it would be absurd not to believe. [Note: Compare Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 17. Coquaeus.]

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On the dress and conduct of the Christian people

Certainly it makes no difference to this city by what dress or manner of life—provided it is not contrary to the divine commandments—each person follows this faith by which one reaches God. Thus, even when philosophers become Christians, they are compelled to change not their dress or manner of living, which hinders religion in no way, but their false doctrines.

Accordingly, it gives no concern to the distinction Varro introduced from the Cynics, provided that no one acts disgracefully or intemperately. [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “they act.”]

Of the three kinds of life—leisure, activity, and a combination of the two—anyone may, while preserving the faith, lead a life in any one of them and reach eternal rewards. Yet it matters what one holds through love of truth and what one devotes through the duty of charity.

No one should be so given to leisure that, in that leisure, he does not consider the benefit of his neighbor; nor so devoted to activity that he does not seek the contemplation of God. In leisure, a lazy inactivity ought not to provide pleasure, but rather the investigation or discovery of truth, so that each person may progress in it, retain what he has discovered, and not begrudge it to another. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “and, having discovered it, may not begrudge it to another.”]

In activity, one ought not to love honor or power in this life, since all things are vanity under the sun; but one should love the work itself that is carried out through that honor or power, if it is done rightly and usefully—that is, if it contributes to the salvation of those subject to one, a salvation according to God. We have discussed this above (chapter 6).

For this reason the Apostle says: “Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work” (1 Timothy 3:1). He wished to explain what the episcopate is, since the name refers to a work, not an honor. The word is Greek and derives from the fact that the person placed in charge watches over those placed under him, caring for them. For *epi* (ἐπί) means “over,” while *skopos* (σκοπός) means “attention”; therefore *episkopein* (ἐπισκοπεῖν), if we wish, may be rendered in Latin as *superintendere*, “to oversee.” [Note: Jerome likewise translates *episkopountes* in Letter 8 to Evagrius as “overseeing.” Coquaeus.] Thus a person should understand that he is not a bishop if he loves to preside but not to benefit.

Accordingly, charity for truth seeks holy leisure, while the necessity of charity undertakes just work. If no one imposes this burden, one should devote oneself to receiving and contemplating truth; but if it is imposed, it must be accepted because of the necessity of charity. [Note: Compare Letter 48, section 2.] Even so, however, the delight of truth must not be abandoned entirely, lest that sweetness be withdrawn and this necessity overwhelm one.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That the citizens of the saints are blessed through hope during the time of this life
For this reason, since the supreme good of the City of God is eternal and perfect peace—not the peace through which mortals pass by being born and dying, but that in which immortals remain, suffering absolutely nothing adverse—who could deny that life to be supremely blessed, or, in comparison with it, judge this present life, however full it may be of goods of soul, body, and external things, to be anything but utterly miserable? Nevertheless, whoever possesses this present life in such a way as to direct its use toward that final end, which he loves with the greatest ardor and hopes for with the greatest faithfulness, may not absurdly be called blessed even now—more because of that hope than because of present reality. But present reality without that hope is a false happiness and a great misery, for such a person does not make use of the true goods of the soul. For true wisdom is not that which fails to direct toward the end in which God will be “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28), with certain eternity and perfect peace, the intention governing those things which one prudently discerns, courageously undertakes, temperately restrains, and justly distributes.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Whether, according to Scipio’s definitions in Cicero’s dialogue, the Roman republic ever existed

1. Therefore this is the appropriate place for me to explain, as briefly and clearly as I can, what I promised in the second book of this work that I would demonstrate (chap. 21, §4): namely, that, according to the definitions Scipio employs in Cicero’s books *On the Republic*, the Roman republic never existed.

For he briefly defines a republic as “the affair of the people.” If this definition is true, the Roman republic never existed, because it was never the affair of the people—which he intended as the definition of a republic. He defined a people as an assembly of a multitude united by agreement concerning law and by a common interest.

What he means by agreement concerning law he explains in the course of his discussion, thereby showing that a republic cannot be governed without justice. Where, therefore, true justice is absent, law cannot exist either. For whatever is done according to law is certainly done justly; whereas what is done unjustly cannot be done according to law. One must not call or regard as laws the unjust enactments of human beings, since even they say that law is what has flowed from the source of justice. It is false, moreover, that familiar claim made by some who think incorrectly: that law is whatever is useful to the one who possesses greater power.

[Note: Thrasymachus defined justice in this way in Plato’s first book *On the Republic*. Socrates refutes this definition.]

Consequently, where true justice is absent, a community of human beings united by agreement concerning law cannot exist, and therefore neither can a people, according to Scipio’s—or Cicero’s—definition. And if there is no people, there is no affair of the people, but only the affair of some sort of multitude that does not deserve the name of a people.

Thus, if a republic is the affair of a people, and if there is no people where there is no association through agreement concerning law, while there is no law where there is no justice, it follows beyond doubt that where justice is absent, there is no republic.

Justice, moreover, is that virtue which assigns to each person what is his or her due. What sort of justice, then, is that of a human being who takes human beings away from the true God and subjects them to unclean demons? Is this assigning to each what is his due? If someone takes a piece of land away from the person who bought it and hands it over to someone who has no legal claim to it, he is unjust; but is someone just who takes himself away from the ruling God, by whom he was made, and serves evil spirits?

2. In those same books *On the Republic*, justice is defended against injustice with the greatest vigor and force. Earlier, when the case for injustice had been argued against justice, and it had been claimed that a republic could neither stand nor grow except through injustice, this was presented as the strongest argument: that it is unjust for human beings to be subject to the rule of other human beings. Yet, unless an imperial city, whose republic is great, follows this injustice, it cannot rule over provinces.

The reply from the side of justice was that such servitude is just because it benefits those people, and, when rightly imposed, is undertaken for their benefit—that is, when the wicked are deprived of the freedom to inflict wrongs. Once subdued, they will be better off, because, while unsubdued, they were worse off. To reinforce this argument, a noble example, as though taken from nature, was added, in these words: “Why, then, does God rule over man, the mind over the body, reason over desire and the other vicious parts of the soul?”

This example plainly teaches that servitude is beneficial in certain cases, and that serving God is beneficial to everyone. The mind that serves God rightly rules the body; and, within the mind itself, reason, subject to the Lord God, rightly rules desire and the other vices.

What, then, is to be thought of as justice in a human being who does not serve God? For one who does not serve God can in no way justly rule the body with the mind, or the vices with human reason.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “the other vices.”]

And if there is no justice in such a human being, there is certainly none in a community composed of such human beings. Here, then, there is not that agreement concerning law which makes a multitude of human beings into a people, whose affair is called a republic.

What shall I say about the common interest, by which, according to this definition, an association of human beings is also united and is called a people? Indeed, if one pays careful attention, there is no true advantage for living beings who live impiously. Everyone who does not serve God, but serves demons—and all the more impiously because, although they are utterly unclean spirits, they wish to be sacrificed to as gods—is living in this way.

Nevertheless, what we have said about agreement concerning law should be sufficient to show that, according to this definition, there is no people whose republic can be said to exist where justice is absent.

If they say that the Romans served not unclean spirits but good and holy gods in their republic, must we repeat again the things we have already said—indeed, said more than sufficiently? Who could have reached this point through the preceding books of this work and still doubt that the Romans served evil and impure demons, unless he were exceedingly foolish or shamelessly contentious?

But, leaving aside the character of those whom they worshiped with sacrifices, it is written in the law of the true God: “Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be destroyed, except to the Lord alone” (Exod. 22:20). Thus the one who gave this command with so grave a threat did not wish sacrifice to be offered either to good gods or to evil gods.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Whether the God whom Christians serve is the true God, and whether sacrifice ought to be offered to him alone

But someone may reply: Who is this God, and on what grounds is he shown to be worthy of obedience by the Romans, so that they should worship no other gods with sacrifices besides him?

It is a sign of great blindness still to ask who this God is. He is the God whose prophets foretold the things that we see. He is the God from whom Abraham received the answer: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). That this was fulfilled in Christ, who according to the flesh arose from that seed, is recognized, whether they wish it or not, by those very people who remain enemies of this name.

He is the God whose divine Spirit spoke through those whose prophecies and fulfillments I presented in the preceding books, through the Church that we see spread throughout the entire world.

He is the God whom Varro, the most learned of the Romans, considers to be Jupiter, although he does not know what he is saying.

[Note: Compare Book 1 of *The Harmony of the Gospels*, §30.]

I thought this worth mentioning because a man of such learning could neither suppose that this god did not exist nor regard him as insignificant. He believed him to be the one whom he considered the supreme God.

Finally, he is the God whom Porphyry, the most learned of philosophers, although a bitter enemy of Christians, acknowledges as the great God—even through the oracles of those whom he considers gods.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### What Porphyry says the oracles of the gods answered concerning Christ

1. In the books which he calls *ἐκ λογίων φιλοσοφίας* (*On Philosophy from Oracles*), in which he sets forth and records what are, as it were, divine responses concerning matters belonging to philosophy—

[Note: Most manuscripts have *eglogion philosophias*, for which the printed editions had incorrectly substituted *theologiōn philosophias*.]

[Note: Theodoret and Eusebius frequently cite these books under the title *On Philosophy from Oracles*, as is correct in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 4, chapter 6. In Eusebius’s *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book 3, chapter 6, and in several passages of Theodoret, the title is incorrectly rendered *On Selected Philosophy*. Both Augustine here and Eusebius in the eloquent passage just cited explain the reason for the title and the subject of the work.]

—I shall set down the very words of Porphyry, as they have been translated from Greek into Latin.

“To one who asked,” he says, “which god he might appease in order to call his wife back from Christianity, Apollo gave this answer in verse.”

The following are presented as Apollo’s words:

> You might sooner write letters upon water,  
> or, blowing up your light feathers, fly through the air like a bird,  
> than call back the mind of your polluted and impious wife.

[Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read *inflans* (“blowing”), whereas the manuscripts have *adinflans*.]

> Let her proceed as she wishes, persisting in empty deceptions  
> and in her most deceptive lamentations, singing of a dead God—

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads *Peragat* (“let her carry on”) rather than *Pergat* (“let her proceed”).]

[Note: The old Regius codex reads: “persisting, lamenting a dead God through deceptions, and singing.” Most of the other manuscripts read: “persisting and lamenting a dead God through deceptive devices, singing,” except for another Corbie manuscript, which reads: “Let her proceed as she wishes through empty deceptions, singing of a dead God. Singing of him whom the judges …”]

> whom the judges who thought rightly condemned,  
> and whom the worst kind of death, bound with iron amid beautiful things, killed.

Then, after these verses of Apollo—which were translated into Latin without preserving the meter—Porphyry added:

“In these words he exposed the evasiveness of their irremediable judgment, saying that the Jews accept God more than these people do.”

[Note: The older books omit the word *tergiversationem* (“evasion”); several have *irremediabilem sententiam* (“an irremediable judgment”), while others have *irremediabili sententiae* or *irremediabile sententiae*.]

There you have him, dishonoring Christ and placing the Jews above Christians, while admitting that the Jews accept God. This is how he interpreted Apollo’s verses: Apollo says that Christ was killed by judges who thought rightly, as though those judges had judged justly and Christ deserved to be punished.

Let the lying prophet of Apollo [Note: namely, the Pythia] see what he said about Christ, and let Porphyry see what he believed—or perhaps let Porphyry himself fabricate the claim that the prophet said what he did not say. We shall later see how consistent the oracles themselves are with one another.

Here, however, he rightly says that the Jews, as those who accepted God, judged Christ by deciding that he ought to be subjected to the worst death. The God of the Jews, then, to whom he bears witness, ought to have been obeyed when he said: “Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be destroyed, except to the Lord alone” (Exod. 22:20).

But let us come to clearer evidence and hear how great a God he says the God of the Jews is.

Again, in response to the question he put to Apollo—whether the word or reason, or the law, was better—he says that Apollo replied in verse. He then adds Apollo’s verses, of which I shall quote as much as is sufficient:

> “The God who generates,” he says, “and the king before all things,

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads: “the God who is the generating king and the king before all things.”]

[Note: In Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 23, the verse appears in Greek as follows:  
> Ἠδὲ Θεὸν βασιλῆ καὶ γεννητῆρα πρὸ πάντων  
> “And the God who is king and begetter before all things.”]

> whom heaven, earth, and sea tremble before,  
> whom the hidden depths of the underworld and the divine powers themselves dread;  
> whose law is the Father, whom the exceedingly holy Hebrews honor.”

[Note: A similar oracle is mentioned by Justin in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*. When someone asked which men had ever been religious, the oracle answered:

> Μοῦνοι Χαλδαῖοι σοφίην λάχον ἠδ᾽ ἄρ᾽ Ἑβραῖοι,  
> Αὐτογένητον ἄνακτα σεβαζόμενοι Θεὸν ἁγνῶς.

That is:

> “The Chaldeans alone, and likewise the Hebrews, obtained wisdom,
