> reverently worshiping God, the king born from himself.”

COQUAEUS.]

By this oracle of his god Apollo, Porphyry called the God of the Hebrews so great that the divine powers themselves dread him. Since, then, this God said, “Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be destroyed,” I am amazed that Porphyry himself did not tremble, and did not fear being destroyed for sacrificing to the gods.

2. This philosopher also says good things about Christ, as though he had forgotten the insult of his own which we mentioned shortly before, or as though his gods had cursed Christ in their sleep and, upon waking, had recognized that he was good and praised him appropriately.

Finally, as though he were about to produce something astonishing and incredible, he says:

“Beyond all expectation, what we are about to say will certainly seem so to some people. For the gods pronounced Christ most pious and said that he had become immortal, and they remembered him with favorable praise. But they say that the Christians are polluted, defiled, and entangled in error, and they employ many such blasphemies against them.”

He then adds what are presented as the oracles of gods blaspheming against Christians.

After this he says:

“When those who asked concerning Christ whether he is a god inquired, Hecate answered: ‘You know that, after the body, an immortal soul proceeds onward; but, cut off from wisdom, it is always in error. That soul belongs to a man outstanding in piety; they worship it while alienated from the truth.’”

Then, weaving his own words together with those of this supposed oracle, he says:

“Thus she called him a most pious man, and said that his soul, like the souls of other pious people, had been granted immortality after death.”

[Note: The older books read *immortalitate dignatam* (“deemed worthy of immortality”). In Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book 3, chapter 6, the Greek is *apothanatisthênai* (“to be made immortal”).]

“And she said that Christians worship this soul in ignorance.”

[Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read *errantes* (“in error”) instead of *ignorantes* (“in ignorance”).]

“But when they asked, ‘Why, then, was he condemned?’ the goddess answered by oracle: ‘The body is always exposed to torments that weaken it, but the soul of the pious dwells in a heavenly seat. That soul, however, fatefully caused other souls—whom fate had not allowed to obtain gifts from the gods or knowledge of immortal Jupiter—to become entangled in error. Therefore they are hated by the gods, because he fatefully caused those to become entangled in error whom it was not fated to know God or receive gifts from the gods. He himself, however, being pious, departed into heaven like the pious. Therefore you shall not blaspheme against him, but shall pity the madness of those people, since from this there arose in them a ready and precipitous danger.’”

[Note: The same passage appears in Greek in Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book 3, chapter 6.]

3. Who is so foolish as not to understand either that these oracles were fabricated by a clever man, and one most hostile to Christians, or that they were answered in a similar fashion by impure demons? Their purpose, plainly, was that, because they praise Christ, they might therefore be believed to condemn Christians truthfully, and thus, if possible, block the way of eternal salvation, in which each person becomes a Christian.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads: “They do not believe that anything is contrary to their many-shaped cunning to do harm.”]

For they recognize that nothing conflicts with their many-shaped cunning to do harm if people believe them when they praise Christ, provided that they also believe them when they condemn Christians. Their aim is to make someone who believes both things a praiser of Christ of such a kind that he does not wish to become a Christian; and thus, although Christ is praised by them, he does not liberate that person from the dominion of these demons.

They praise Christ in such a way that anyone who believes him to be as they proclaim him is not a true Christian, but a Photinian heretic, who knows Christ to be merely human and not also God.

[Note: Compare *On Heresies*, heresies 44–45.]

For this reason such a person cannot be saved through Christ, nor avoid or escape the snares of these demons who speak lies.

We, however, can approve neither Apollo when he condemns Christ nor Hecate when she praises him. Apollo wants Christ to be believed unjust, since he says that Christ was killed by judges who thought rightly; Hecate calls him a most pious man, but only a man.

Yet the purpose of both is one and the same: they do not want human beings to be Christians. For unless people become Christians, they cannot be rescued from the power of these beings.

But this philosopher—or rather those who believe such supposed oracles directed against Christians—should first make Hecate and Apollo agree with each other about Christ, if they can, and make them either both condemn him or both praise him. Even if they could do so, we would still avoid these deceitful demons, whether they condemned or praised Christ.

But since their god and goddess disagree about Christ, one condemning him and the other praising him, people who think rightly certainly do not believe them when they blaspheme against Christians.

4. In praising Christ, whether Porphyry or Hecate says that Christ himself fatefully gave Christians over to becoming entangled in error. Yet in doing so he also reveals the causes of that error, as he understands them.

Before I explain those causes from his words, I first ask whether, if Christ fatefully gave Christians over to entanglement in error, he did so willingly or unwillingly. If willingly, how is he just? If unwillingly, how is he blessed?

But let us now hear the causes of the error itself.

“There are,” he says, “lowly earthly spirits, subject in a certain place to the power of evil demons.”

[Note: The editions read *loco terreno quodam* (“in a certain earthly place”); the manuscripts omit *terreno*.]

“These,” he continues, “were the demons from whom the wise Hebrews, one of whom was this Jesus, warned the religious, forbidding them to occupy themselves with those demons, as you heard in the divine oracles of Apollo mentioned above.

[Note: The printed editions add “oracles” after “Apollo”; it is absent from the manuscripts.] Rather, they commanded them to venerate the heavenly gods, and above all to venerate God the Father.

“This is also what the gods command, and we have shown above how they urge people to turn their minds toward God and everywhere command them to worship him.

“But the uneducated and those of impious nature, to whom fate truly did not grant the reception of divine gifts or the knowledge of immortal Jupiter, refusing to listen either to the gods or to divine men, rejected all the gods. Yet they did not hate the prohibited demons; instead, they revered them.

“While pretending to worship God, they do not perform the things by which God is worshiped.”

[Note: So all the manuscripts. The editions instead read: “They chose not merely not to pursue the prohibited demons with any hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending that they worship God …”]

“For God, being the Father of all, needs nothing. But it is good for us when we worship him through justice, chastity, and the other virtues, making life itself a prayer to him through imitation and inquiry concerning him. For inquiry purifies,” he says; “imitation deifies by producing affection for him.”

He rightly praised God the Father and stated the character by which he should be worshiped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these commandments, in which the life of the saints is either censured or praised.

[Note: Several manuscripts read *sive imperatur* (“whether it is commanded”). Ludovicus Vives approves this reading and rejects the other, saying: “The prophets do not censure the life of the saints.” Augustine is speaking of the life of the saints on earth, which was not entirely free from fault. He appears to be indicating two kinds of commandments: those concerning the avoidance of evil, which is censured even in the conduct of those who worshiped the true God, and those concerning the doing of good, which is praised in those same people.]

But in the case of Christians he errs—or rather, he slanders—as much as the demons whom he supposes to be gods desire. It would be easy for anyone to recall the shameful and disgraceful acts performed in theaters and temples in the service of the gods, and to consider what is read, said, and heard in churches, or what is offered to the true God, and from this to understand where the structure of morals lies and where its ruin lies.

But who told or inspired him—unless it was a diabolical spirit—to utter such an empty and blatant lie: that Christians revere the demons whom the Hebrews forbade them to worship, rather than hating them?

Yet the God worshiped by the wise men of the Hebrews also forbids sacrifice to the holy heavenly angels and powers of God, whom, as most blessed citizens in this mortal pilgrimage of ours, we venerate and love. In the law that he gave to his Hebrew people he thunders the command, stating it with a very grave threat: “Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be destroyed.”

And lest anyone suppose that sacrifice was forbidden only to the worst and earthly demons—the “lowly” or “lesser” spirits mentioned by this writer—because these beings too are called gods in the sacred Scriptures, though not gods of the Hebrews but of the nations (as the translators of the Septuagint clearly expressed in the Psalm, saying, “For all the gods of the nations are demons,” Ps. 95:5), lest, then, anyone should suppose that sacrifice to these demons was forbidden while sacrifice to heavenly beings, whether to all or to some, was permitted, he immediately added: “except to the Lord alone,” that is, “except to the Lord only.”

Otherwise someone might think that when he says “except to the Lord alone,” he means the sun, believing that sacrifice ought to be offered to it.

[Note: The Louvain edition reads *putet*; the other editions and the manuscripts have *putat*. Augustine adds that the meaning of this passage is very easily found in the Greek Scriptures, where Exodus 22:20 is expressed unambiguously as *Kyriō monō* (“to the Lord alone”).]

5. The God of the Hebrews, then, to whom even this very learned philosopher bears such great testimony, gave a law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language—not obscure or unknown, but already proclaimed among all nations. In that law it is written: “Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be destroyed, except to the Lord alone.”

What need is there to search out many passages on this subject in his law and in his prophets? Indeed, the task is not to search for hidden or rare sayings, but to collect and set forth in this discussion passages that are clear and abundant. Through them it becomes brighter than daylight that the true and supreme God wished sacrifice to be offered to no one except himself alone.

Let this one saying of that God be heard, feared, and obeyed—a saying brief, or rather weighty, threatening, but true—from the God whom the most learned proclaim so excellently [Note: Most manuscripts read “most excellent”]:

[Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “may become apparent”; the other editions and the manuscripts read “becomes apparent.”]

“Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be destroyed, except to the Lord alone.”

He does not say this because he needs anything, but because it is beneficial for us to belong to him.

For this reason it is sung in the sacred writings of the Hebrews: “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Ps. 16:2).

[Note: The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and manuscripts read *Huic* (“to him”) rather than *Hinc* (“for this reason”).]

We ourselves are his most distinguished and excellent sacrifice—that is, we are his city. [Note: The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmus read “this is” rather than “we are.”] We celebrate the mystery of this reality in our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we discussed in the preceding books (Book 10, chapter 6, and elsewhere).

The Hebrews, through their prophets, uttered divine oracles rebuking the sacrifices that they offered as shadows of what was to come, which would cease, and proclaiming the one sacrifice that the nations from the rising to the setting of the sun would offer—as we already see happening. From these prophecies we have cited as many as seemed sufficient and have scattered them throughout this present work.

Therefore, where there is not this justice—that the one supreme God rules, according to his grace, over a city obedient to him, so that it sacrifices to no one except to him alone—and where, consequently, among all the human beings belonging to that same city and obeying God, the mind rightly and faithfully rules the body and reason rules the vices according to a legitimate order; and where, just as one just person, so an assembly and people of just persons lives by the faith that works through love, by which a human being loves God as God ought to be loved and his neighbor as himself—there is no community of human beings united by agreement concerning law and by a common interest.

For if this community does not exist, there is no people, if this is the true definition of a people. Therefore there is no republic either, because the republic is not the affair of the people where the people itself does not exist.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### By what definition it is clear that not only the Romans but also other kingdoms may rightly claim the name of a people and a republic

But if a people is defined not in this way but in another—for example, if a people is said to be “a community of rational beings united by a harmonious association in the things they love”—then, in order to determine what sort of people each one is, we must examine what it loves.

Nevertheless, whatever it may love, if it is a community of a multitude not of animals but of rational creatures, and if it is united by a harmonious association in the things it loves, it is not improperly called a people. It is better in proportion as it is united in better things, and worse in proportion as it is united in worse things.

According to this definition, the Roman people is a people, and its affair is without doubt a republic. What that people loved in its earliest period and what it loved later, and by what character it reached its bloodiest seditions and then its social and civil wars, breaking and corrupting the very harmony that is, in a certain sense, the salvation of a people—history bears witness. We have set forth much about this in the preceding books.

Nevertheless, I would not for that reason say either that it was not a people or that its affair was not a republic, so long as there remained a community of a rational multitude united by harmonious association in the things it loved.

What I have said about this people and this republic should likewise be understood and taken as said about the Athenians or any other Greeks; about the Egyptians; about that earlier Babylon of the Assyrians, when they held empires, whether small or great, in their public affairs; and about any other nation whatsoever.

For, in general, the city of the impious, over which God does not rule as it obeys him—so that it offers sacrifice only to him and so that within it the mind rightly and faithfully rules the body and reason rules the vices—lacks the truth of justice.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### That true virtues cannot exist where true religion does not exist

Even if the mind appears commendably to rule the body and reason to rule the vices, if the mind and reason themselves do not serve God as God has commanded them to serve him, they do not rightly rule the body and the vices at all.

For what sort of mastery over the body and the vices can belong to a mind that does not know the true God and is not subjected to his rule, but has prostituted itself to the most vicious demons who corrupt it?

Accordingly, the virtues that a person seems to possess—virtues by which he rules the body and the vices in order to acquire or retain something—are, unless he refers them to God, themselves vices rather than virtues.

For although some people think that virtues are then true and honorable when they are referred to themselves and sought for no other reason, even then they are inflated and proud. Therefore they must be judged not virtues but vices.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads: “and therefore not virtues, virtues, but vices,” with the repetition as printed.]

[Note: See *On the Trinity*, Book 13, §§25–26, and Book 14, §3.]

For just as what makes the flesh live does not come from the flesh but is above the flesh, so what makes a human being live blessedly does not come from the human being but is above the human being—not only above the human being, but also above every heavenly power and virtue.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### Concerning the peace of the people alienated from God, which the people of God uses for piety while it is a pilgrim in this world

Therefore, just as the life of the flesh is the soul, so the blessed life of a human being is God. Of him the sacred writings of the Hebrews say: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 144:15).

Miserable, then, is the people alienated from this God. Yet even that people loves a certain peace of its own, which is not to be condemned. It will not possess this peace in the end, because it does not use it well before the end.

Nevertheless, it is also in our interest [Note: The manuscripts read “our” rather than “our interest”] that it possess this peace for the time being in this life, because, so long as the two cities are intermingled, we too make use of the peace of Babylon. From that city the people of God is liberated through faith in such a way that, for the present, it remains a pilgrim among its inhabitants.

For this reason the Apostle also admonished the Church to pray for its kings and those in high positions, adding: “so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and charity” (1 Tim. 2:2).

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “and chastity,” in accordance with the Vulgate and the Greek, *kai semnotēti* (“and dignity” or “reverence”).]

The prophet Jeremiah, when he foretold to the ancient people of God the captivity [Note: “that was to come” is absent from the manuscripts] and divinely commanded them to go obediently into Babylon, serving their God even through this endurance, likewise instructed them to pray for that city, saying: “For in its peace your peace shall be” (Jer. 29:7)—that is, the temporal peace which, for the time being, is shared by the good and the wicked alike.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Concerning the peace of those who serve God, whose perfect tranquility cannot be attained in this temporal life

Our own peace, however, is both here with God through faith and will be with him eternally through sight. But here, whether it is the common peace or our own particular peace, it is such that it is rather a consolation amid misery than the joy of blessedness.

Even our justice, although it is true because of the end of the true good toward which it is directed,

[Note: The older books read “because of the end of the true good.”]

is nevertheless so constituted in this life that it consists more in the remission of sins than in the perfection of virtues.

[Note: This passage should not be understood as though our justice consisted solely in the remission of sins. Rather, as Bellarmine also observes in Book 2 of *On Justification*, chapter 13, it does not exclude the perfection of virtues but places the remission of sin before it. The meaning is that our justice, which consists partly in the remission of sin and partly in the perfection of virtues, consists more in the remission of sin than in the perfection of virtue, because we are able to achieve the former more fully than the latter. In this sense Jerome too, in Book 2 *Against the Pelagians*, maintains that true justice exists in us, although it is not altogether perfect; perfect, however, is the remission of sins. From Coquaeus.]

The prayer of the whole City of God, which is a pilgrim on earth, bears witness to this. Through all its members it cries out to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

This prayer is not effective on behalf of those whose faith is dead without works (James 2:17, 26), but on behalf of those whose faith works through love (Gal. 5:6).

For although reason is subject to God, it does not in this mortal condition, and in this corruptible body that weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), rule the vices perfectly. Therefore such a prayer is necessary for the just.

Indeed, although reason is given command over the vices, it does not command them without conflict. Something of weakness inevitably slips into this struggle even for one who fights well—whether the vices have been defeated and brought under control, or whether one rules over such enemies—so that sin is committed, if not through an easy action, at least through a slipping word or a fleeting thought.

Therefore, as long as the vices are being ruled, there is no complete peace. Those that resist are fought in a perilous battle, while those that have been conquered are not yet celebrated in secure leisure as a triumph, but are still held down under a vigilant rule.

In these temptations, concerning all of which the divine utterances briefly say, “Is not human life a temptation upon the earth?” (Job 7:1, according to the Septuagint), who would presume to live in such a way that he did not need to say to God, “Forgive us our debts,” except a proud person?

And not a great person, but an inflated and swollen one, against whom the one who grants grace to the humble sets himself in justice. Therefore it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5).

Here, then, justice in each person consists in this: that God rules the obedient human being, the mind rules the body, and reason rules the vices, even when they resist—either by subduing them or by resisting them; that one asks God himself both for the grace of merits and for pardon of sins; and that thanksgiving is offered for the good things received.

In that final peace, toward which this justice must be directed and for the sake of attaining which this justice must be possessed, nature will have been healed through immortality and incorruption and will have no vices. Nothing will resist any one of us, either from another person or from ourselves. It will therefore not be necessary for reason to rule vices, since no vices will exist.

God will rule the human being, and the mind will rule the body. The pleasure and ease of obedience there will be as great as the happiness of living and reigning.

This will be eternal both in all and in each individual, and its eternity will be certain. Therefore the peace of this blessedness—or the blessedness of this peace—will be the supreme good.

[Note: The editions read “in all human beings.” The manuscripts omit *hominibus* (“human beings”).]

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### The end toward which the outcome of the wicked is to come
Those, however, who do not belong to this city of God will have, by contrast, everlasting misery, which is also called the second death (Rev. II, 11; XX, 6; XXI, 8): for neither can the soul be said to live there, since it will have been alienated from the life of God, nor the body, since it will be subject to everlasting pains. For this reason that second death will be harsher, because it will not be able to be ended by death.

But since misery seems contrary to blessedness, death to life, and war to peace, it is rightly asked, just as peace has been proclaimed and praised as the end of the good, what kind or sort of war can, by contrast, be understood as existing at the end of the wicked. Whoever asks this should consider what is harmful and destructive in war, and will see that it is nothing other than the opposition and conflict of things against one another. What war, then, can be imagined more grievous and bitter than one in which will is so opposed to suffering, and suffering to will, that such enmity is ended by the victory of neither; and in which the force of pain so conflicts with the very nature of the body that neither yields to the other? Here, when such a conflict occurs, either pain conquers and death takes away sensation, or nature conquers [Note: [Col. 0658] Lov., “or enduring nature conquers.” Other printed editions and the manuscripts lack the word *enduring*.], and health removes the pain. There, however, pain remains in order to afflict, and nature endures in order to feel: for neither fails, precisely so that the punishment may not fail.

Since the good and the wicked will pass through judgment to these respective ends—the good to the end that is to be desired, and the wicked to the end that is to be avoided—I shall discuss this judgment, insofar as God grants it, in the following volume.

# BOOK TWENTY

On the Last Judgment, and on the Testimonies of Both the New and the Old Instrument by Which It Is Announced as Future

[Col. 0657]

## CHAPTER I

That although God judges at all times, this book is properly to discuss His Last Judgment

[Col. 0657]

1. Since we are going to speak about the day of God’s last judgment, insofar as He grants it, and defend it against the impious and unbelieving, we must first set down divine testimonies as though laying the foundation of a building. Those who do not wish to believe them attempt to oppose them with false and deceptive human arguments, either contending that the testimony drawn from the sacred Scriptures signifies something else, or denying altogether that it was spoken by God. For I do not think there is any mortal who, once he has understood these things as they were spoken and has believed that they were spoken by the supreme and true God through holy souls, would not yield and assent to them—whether he admits this with his mouth, or, because of some vice, is ashamed or afraid to admit it; or whether, with an obstinacy resembling madness, he tries to defend, with the utmost contentiousness, what he knows or believes to be false against what he knows or believes to be true.

2. What the whole Church of the true God therefore holds in its confession and profession—namely, that Christ will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead—we call the final day of divine judgment, that is, the last time. For how many days this judgment will extend is uncertain; but no one who has read those writings even somewhat carelessly is unaware that, in the manner of the sacred Scriptures, a day is customarily used for a period of time.

We call it the day of God’s judgment and add “last” or “final” because He judges even now, and has judged from the beginning of the human race: He expelled the first human beings, perpetrators of a great sin, from paradise and separated them from the tree of life. Indeed, when He did not spare the sinning angels (II Peter II, 4), whose prince, having himself been overthrown by himself, overthrew human beings through envy, He unquestionably judged. Nor is the most wretched life of demons and human beings, both in this airy heaven and on earth, filled as it is with errors and afflictions, without His profound and just judgment.

Yet even if no one had sinned, He would still, by a good and righteous judgment, retain the whole rational creation in eternal blessedness, because of its most steadfast adherence to its Lord. He also judges not only universally concerning the race of demons and human beings, so that they are miserable because of the merit of their first sins, but also concerning the individual deeds that they perform by the choice of their will. For even the demons ask not to be tormented (Matt. VIII, 29); and certainly they are neither spared unjustly nor tormented unjustly, each according to his wickedness. Human beings likewise generally pay, openly or secretly, divinely imposed penalties for their deeds, whether in this life or after death—although no human being acts rightly unless aided by divine assistance, and no demon or human being acts wickedly unless permitted to do so by the same and most just divine judgment.

As the Apostle says, “There is no injustice with God” (Rom. IX, 14); and, as he says elsewhere, “The judgments of God are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable” (ibid. XI, 33). In this book, therefore, I shall discuss not those first judgments of God, nor these intermediate ones, but the Last Judgment itself, insofar as He grants it: the time when Christ will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead. This day is properly already called the day of judgment, because then there will be no room for the ignorant complaint: why is that unjust man happy, and why is that just man unhappy? For then the true and complete happiness of all the good, and the deserved and supreme unhappiness of all the wicked, will be made manifest.

## CHAPTER II

On the Variety of Human Affairs, Which Cannot Be Said to Lack God’s Judgment, Although It Cannot Be Searched Out

[Col. 0660]

Now we are learning to endure with equanimity the evils suffered by the good, and not to value highly the goods attained by the wicked. Thus, even in those matters in which divine justice does not appear, divine teaching is salutary. For we do not know by what judgment of God this good man is poor and that wicked man is rich; why this person rejoices, whom we think ought to be tormented by grief because of his ruined character; why that person is saddened, whom a praiseworthy life persuades us ought to rejoice; why an innocent man leaves the court not only unavenged but condemned, either oppressed by the judge’s injustice or overwhelmed by false testimony, while his criminal opponent, not only unpunished but even vindicated, mocks him; why the impious enjoys excellent health while the devout wastes away in illness; why perfectly healthy young men engage in robbery, while infants who could not harm anyone even by a word are afflicted by various terrible diseases; why a person useful to human affairs is carried off by premature death, while those who seem as though they ought never even to have been born live on for a very long time; why a man full of crimes is raised to honors, while darkness hides from view a blameless man of humble station—and so on. Who could collect or enumerate such things?

If these matters displayed a consistent pattern even in their apparent absurdity—if, in this life, in which human beings, as the sacred Psalm says, have become like vanity and whose days pass like a shadow (Ps. CXLIII, 4), only the wicked obtained these fleeting and earthly goods, while only the good suffered such evils—this could be referred to God’s just, or even benevolent, judgment. Those who were not going to attain the eternal goods that make people blessed would thus either be deceived by temporal goods because of their wickedness, or be consoled by them through God’s mercy; and those who were not going to suffer eternal torments would either be afflicted by temporal evils for whatever sins, however many or slight, they had committed, or be disciplined through evils for the completion of their virtues.

But now, when not only are the good in evil circumstances and the wicked in good circumstances—something that appears unjust—but when evils often befall the wicked and goods come to the good as well, the judgments of God become even more inscrutable (Rom. XI, 33), and His ways unsearchable. Although, therefore, we do not know by what judgment God either does or permits these things to occur—He with whom are supreme virtue, supreme wisdom, and supreme justice, with no weakness, rashness, or injustice—we nevertheless profitably learn not to value highly either the goods or the evils that we see to be common to good and wicked people alike. Instead, we should seek those goods that belong to the good, and above all flee those evils that are proper to the wicked.

When we come to that judgment of God whose time is now properly called the day of judgment, and sometimes the day of the Lord, not only will whatever is then judged be shown to be altogether just, but also whatever has been judged from the beginning and whatever will still be judged up to that time. It will also be made manifest how justly God judges when, for now, so many—and almost all—of His just judgments are hidden from the understanding and minds of mortals; although in this matter the faith of the devout is not unaware that what is hidden is just.

## CHAPTER III

What Solomon Discussed in Ecclesiastes Concerning the Things Common to the Good and the Wicked in This Life

Solomon, the wisest king of Israel, who reigned in Jerusalem, began the book called Ecclesiastes—which is also held by the Jews among the canonical books of sacred Scripture—in this way:

“Vanity of those who are vain” [Note: [Col. 0661] Here and immediately afterward in the same chapter, the printed editions read *vanity of vanities*. The manuscripts consistently have *vanity of those who are vain*. Compare Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 7, §3.], says Ecclesiastes; “vanity of those who are vain, and all is vanity. What abundance has a human being in all his labor by which he labors under the sun?” (Eccles. I, 2–3).

As he connected the rest of his discussion with this statement, recalling the afflictions and errors of this life and the passing away of time, in which nothing solid or stable is retained, he also lamented, in a certain sense, within that vanity of things under the sun, that although there is an abundance of wisdom over folly, as there is an abundance of light over darkness, and although the wise man’s eyes are in his head while the fool walks in darkness, nevertheless the same event overtakes them all (ibid. II, 13–14)—namely, in this life that is lived under the sun. He was evidently indicating those evils that we see to be common to good and wicked alike.

He also says that the good suffer evils as though they were wicked, while the wicked obtain goods as though they were good, speaking as follows:

“There is,” he says, “a vanity that has occurred upon the earth: there are righteous people upon whom what is due to the wicked has come, and there are wicked people upon whom what is due to the righteous has come. I said that this also is vanity” (ibid. VIII, 14).

The wisest man devoted this entire book to making known, as much as seemed sufficient, this vanity—not for any other reason than that we might desire the life that has no vanity under this sun, but truth beneath Him who made this sun. In this vanity, then, would not a human being, made like that same vanity, fade away by God’s just and righteous judgment?

Yet during the days of his vanity it makes a very great difference whether he resists or obeys the truth, and whether he is without true devotion or shares in it—not because of acquiring the goods or avoiding the evils of this life, which pass away in vanity, but because of the future judgment, through which good things will remain without end for the good, and evil things without end for the wicked.

Finally, this wise man concluded his book by saying:

“Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole human being: for God will bring every deed into judgment concerning everything despised, whether good or evil” (ibid. XII, 13–14).

What could have been said more briefly, more truly, or more profitably? “Fear God,” he says, “and keep his commandments, for this is the whole human being.” Whoever exists is this: namely, a keeper of God’s commandments. For whoever is not this is nothing. He is not being remade according to the image of truth, but remains in the likeness of vanity.

“For God will bring every deed”—that is, whatever a human being does in this life—“into judgment concerning everything despised,” that is, concerning everyone who appears contemptible here and therefore is not seen; because God sees that person too, neither despises him nor passes him by when He judges.

## CHAPTER IV

That, in Discussing the Last Judgment of God, He Will First Produce Testimonies from the New Testament and Then from the Old

I therefore intend to set forth testimonies concerning this Last Judgment of God from the sacred Scriptures. I must first select them from the books of the New Instrument, and afterward from the Old. For although the old writings are earlier in time, the new are to be preferred in dignity, since the former are heralds of the latter. The new testimonies will therefore be presented first; and, to establish them more firmly, the old will also be brought forward.

In the old writings are the Law and the Prophets [Note: [Col. 0662] Only the Lov. edition reads *prophecies*.]; in the new are the Gospel and the apostolic Letters. The Apostle says:

“For through the law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been manifested without the law, attested by the Law and the Prophets: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” [Note: [Col. 0662] Earlier editions read, “for all who believe in him.” The words “in him” are absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.] (Rom. III, 20–22).

This righteousness of God belongs to the New Testament, and it has testimony from the old books—that is, from the Law and the Prophets. The matter itself must therefore be set forth first, and the witnesses introduced afterward.

Jesus Christ Himself also demonstrated that this order was to be observed, saying:

“An educated scribe in the kingdom of God is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. XIII, 52).

He did not say, “Old things and new”—which He certainly would have said if He had preferred to preserve the order of time rather than the order of merit.

## CHAPTER V

By What Sayings of the Lord the Future Divine Judgment at the End of the Age Is Declared

1. When the Savior Himself rebuked the cities in which He had performed great miracles but which had not believed, and preferred foreigners to them, He said:

“Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.”

A little later, to another city He said:

“Amen I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you” (Matt. XI, 22, 24).

Here He most clearly proclaims that the day of judgment will come.

Elsewhere He says:

“The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. The Queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (ibid. XII, 41–42).

Here we learn two things: that judgment will come, and that it will come with the resurrection of the dead. When He said this about the Ninevites and the Queen of the South, He was plainly speaking about the dead, whom He nevertheless foretold would rise on the day of judgment. He did not say “they will condemn” because they themselves would judge, but because this generation would rightly be condemned by comparison with them.

2. Again, elsewhere, when He was speaking about the present mixture of good and wicked people and their subsequent separation, which will certainly occur on the day of judgment, He used the image of sown wheat and weeds sown over it. Explaining it to His disciples, He said:

“He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is the world [Note: [Col. 0663] The printed editions read, “the field is this world,” and below, “these are the sons of the wicked one.” The manuscripts do not have *this* or *these*.]; the good seed, however, are the sons of the kingdom; the weeds are the sons of the wicked one; the enemy who sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the consummation of the age, and the harvesters are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send His angels, and they will gather from His kingdom all scandals and those who practice iniquity, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XIII, 37–43).

Here He did not name the judgment or the day of judgment, but expressed it much more clearly by the events themselves and foretold that it would occur at the end of the age.

3. Likewise He said to His disciples:

“Amen I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of His majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid. XIX, 28).

Here we learn that Jesus will judge with His disciples. Hence elsewhere He said to the Jews:

“If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges” (ibid. XII, 27).

Nor, because He said that they would sit upon twelve thrones, should we think that only twelve human beings will judge with Him. By the number twelve a certain totality of judges is signified, because the number seven generally signifies universality, and its two parts—three and four—multiplied by one another make twelve. For four times three and three times four are both twelve; and perhaps some other numerical relation involving twelve may also be found that is relevant here [Note: [Col. 0663] See the *Exposition on Psalm XLIX*, §9.].

Otherwise, since we read that the apostle Matthias was appointed in the place of Judas the betrayer (Acts I, 26), the Apostle Paul, who labored more than all of them (I Cor. XV, 10), would have no place from which to judge. Yet he clearly shows that he belongs with the other saints among the number of judges when he says:

“Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (ibid. VI, 3).

The same consideration applies to those who are to be judged in relation to this number twelve. For because it was said, “judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth, will not therefore be judged by them; nor will they judge only that people and not the other nations.

When He says “in the regeneration,” He undoubtedly wishes the resurrection of the dead to be understood by the name of regeneration. For our flesh will be regenerated through incorruption just as our soul has been regenerated through faith.

4. I pass over many passages that appear to speak of the Last Judgment in such a way that, when carefully considered, they are found to be ambiguous or to belong more properly to something else: either to that coming of the Savior by which He comes throughout this whole period in His Church—that is, in His members, gradually and piece by piece, since the whole Church is His body—or to the destruction of earthly Jerusalem. For when He speaks about that destruction, He often speaks as though He were speaking about the end of the age and about that last and great day of judgment. Thus it is entirely impossible to distinguish the reference unless everything that the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—have similarly said about this matter is compared with one another. One of them, for example, explains more obscurely what another sets forth more plainly, so that it may become clear from what source the statements belonging to one matter are drawn.

I made some effort to do this in a letter that I wrote in reply to Hesychius, a man of blessed memory and bishop of the city of Salona. The title of that letter is *On the End of the Age* (Letter 199).

5. I shall therefore say here what is read in the Gospel according to Matthew concerning the separation of the good and the wicked through Christ’s most immediate and final judgment.

“When the Son of Man comes,” He says, “in His majesty, and all the angels with Him, then He will sit upon the throne of His majesty, and all nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will place the sheep at His right hand, but the goats at His left.

“Then the King will say to those who are at His right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.’

“Then the righteous will answer Him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You, or thirsty and give You drink? And when did we see You a stranger and welcome You, or naked and clothe You? Or when did we see You sick or in prison and come to You?’

“And the King will answer and say to them, ‘Amen I say to you, insofar as you did this for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me.’

“Then,” He says, “He will also say to those who are at His left hand, ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels.’”

He then similarly lists for them the things that they did not do, which He remembered the others doing. When they likewise ask when they saw Him in such need, He answers that what was not done for His least ones was not done for Him. Concluding His discourse, He says:

“And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV, 31–46).

The evangelist John, however, most explicitly relates that He foretold that the judgment would take place at the resurrection of the dead. For after saying:

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him,”

He immediately added:

“Amen, amen I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes Him who sent me has eternal life and will not come into judgment, but has passed [Note: [Col. 0664] Several manuscripts here read, “has not come, but has passed.” The printed editions have, “will not come, but will pass.” The editions are not consistent in the passages that follow. Compare *Treatise 22 on John*.] from death into life” (John V, 22–24).

Here He said that His faithful will not come into judgment. How, then, will they be separated through judgment from the wicked and stand at His right hand, unless in this passage He used “judgment” to mean condemnation? For those who hear His word and believe Him who sent Him will not come into such judgment.

## CHAPTER VI

What the First Resurrection Is and What the Second Is

1. He then adds and says:

“Amen, amen I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. For just as the Father has life in Himself, so He has also given the Son to have life in Himself” (John V, 25–26).

He is not yet speaking of the second resurrection, that of bodies, which will take place at the end, but of the first, which is occurring now. To distinguish it, He says, “The hour is coming, and now is.” This is not the resurrection of bodies but of souls.

For souls too have their own death in impiety and sins. According to this death, those people were dead of whom the same Lord says, “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII, 22), so that those dead in soul might bury the dead in body.

Therefore, with reference to those dead in soul through impiety and iniquity, He says: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” By “those who hear” He means those who obey, who believe, and who persevere to the end.

Here He made no distinction between the good and the wicked. For it is good for all to hear His voice and live, passing from the death of impiety into the life of devotion [Note: [Col. 0665] Vind., Am., and the manuscripts read this way. Lov. has, “and to pass into the life of devotion from the death of impiety.”].

Of this death the Apostle Paul says:

“Therefore all have died, and He died for all” [Note: [Col. 0665] The printed editions read, “one died for all.” The word *one* is absent from the manuscripts.], so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for Him who died for them and rose again (II Cor. V, 14–15).

All, therefore, were dead in sins, without exception, whether through original sins or through sins added by the will, whether through ignorance or through knowing and failing to do what is just. And for all the dead, the one who was alive died—one who had absolutely no sin—so that those who live through the forgiveness of sins might no longer live for themselves but for Him who died for all [Note: [Col. 0665] Several manuscripts do not have the words “for all.”] because of our sins and rose again because of our justification.

Thus, believing in Him who justifies the ungodly, justified from impiety and made alive as though from death, we may belong to the first resurrection, which is now taking place [Note: [Col. 0665] Am. and Er. read, “which is now the resurrection of souls.” The other books lack the word *of souls*, which was added to explain this passage. Similarly, shortly afterward, in §2, these editions and Vind. read, “through which one now passes from the death of souls to the life of virtues,” whereas Lov. and the manuscripts have only, “through which one now passes from death to life.”].

For only those who will be blessed eternally belong to this first resurrection. To the second resurrection, which he is about to discuss, he will show that both the blessed and the miserable belong. The first is the resurrection of mercy; the second, of judgment. Hence it is written in the Psalm:

“I will sing of mercy and judgment to You, Lord” (Ps. C, 1).

2. Concerning this judgment he then adds and says:

“And He gave Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man.”

Here He shows that He will come to judge in the flesh in which He had come to be judged. This is why He says, “because He is the Son of Man.”

Then, adding the passage under discussion [Col. 0666], He says:

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear His voice [Note: [Col. 0666] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions instead have, “the voice of the Son of God.”], and those who have done good will come forth into the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil into the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 27–29).

This is the judgment which shortly before, as in the present passage, He had used to mean condemnation, saying:

“Whoever hears my word and believes Him who sent me has eternal life and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life” (ibid., 24).

That is, by belonging to the first resurrection, through which one now passes from death to life, he will not come into condemnation, which He signified by the term “judgment,” just as also in this passage, where He says, “Those who have done evil into the resurrection of judgment”—that is, of condemnation.

Let him therefore rise in the first resurrection who does not wish to be condemned in the second. “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (ibid., 25)—that is, they will not come into the condemnation called the second death. Into this death, after the second resurrection—which will be the resurrection of bodies—those who do not rise in the first resurrection, which is the resurrection of souls, will be cast.

For the hour will come—where He does not say “and now is,” because it will be at the end of the age, that is, at the final and greatest judgment of God—when all who are in the tombs will hear His voice and come forth (ibid., 28).

He did not say, as He did concerning the first resurrection, “and those who hear will live.” For not all will live with that life which, because it is blessed, is the only life properly so called. Of course, they could not hear and come forth from the tombs with their flesh resurrected without possessing some kind of life.

But why not all will live He teaches in what follows:

“Those who have done good,” He says, “will come into the resurrection of life”—these are the ones who will live. “But those who have done evil will come into the resurrection of judgment”—these are the ones who will not live, because they will die the second death.

For they did evil because they lived badly; and they lived badly because they did not come back to life in the first resurrection, which is now taking place, or because, after coming back to life in it, they did not remain in it to the end.

Thus, just as there are two regenerations, of which I have already spoken above—one according to faith, which now takes place through Baptism, and the other according to the flesh, which will take place in its incorruption and immortality through the great and final judgment—so there are also two resurrections.

The first is now occurring and is the resurrection of souls; it does not permit a person to come into the second death. The second is not now occurring but will take place at the end of the age; it is not the resurrection of souls but of bodies. Through the final judgment it will send some into the second death and others into that life which has no death.

## CHAPTER VII

What Is Written in John’s Apocalypse Concerning the Two Resurrections and the Thousand Years, and What May Reasonably Be Thought Concerning Them

1. The same evangelist John spoke about these two resurrections in the book called the Apocalypse, in such a way that its first resurrection was not understood by some of our people and was even turned into certain ridiculous [Col. 0667] fables.

For the apostle John says in the book just mentioned:

“And I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a chain in his hand. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss; and he shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were finished. After this he must be released for a short time.

“And I saw thrones, and those seated upon them, and judgment was given. And the souls of those who had been killed because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God, and of any who had not worshiped the beast or his image and had not received his mark upon their forehead or their hand, [Note: [Col. 0667] The printed editions read, “judgment was given to them, and the souls of those who had been killed because of …” This is plainly the reading of the Vulgate and the Greek text of Revelation XX. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts here omit *to them* and have, “And the souls of those who had been killed.” Augustine will later explain this very reading in chapter 9.] reigned with Jesus for a thousand years. The rest of them did not come to life until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a part in this first resurrection. Over these the second death has no authority, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with Him for a thousand years” (Rev. XX, 1–6).

Those who, because of these words of the book, have supposed that the first resurrection will be bodily were especially moved, among other considerations, by the number one thousand years. They imagined that the saints must then observe a sabbath of such duration, a holy rest after six thousand years of labor, counted from the creation of the human being and from the time when, because of the merit of that great sin, humanity was sent away from the happiness of paradise into the afflictions of mortality.

Since it is written, “One day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day” (II Peter III, 8), they imagined that, once six thousand years had been completed as though they were six days, a kind of seventh-day Sabbath would follow in the final thousand years, so that the saints might rise for the celebration of this Sabbath.

This opinion would be in some measure tolerable if some spiritual delights were believed to be present in that Sabbath for the saints through the Lord’s presence. For even we once held such an opinion [Note: [Col. 0667] As may be seen in Sermon 259, elsewhere numbered 19 among the Sirmondian sermons.].

But when they say that those who rise at that time will devote themselves to immoderate bodily feasts, in which there will be so much food and drink that they will not merely observe no moderation but even exceed the limits of credulity itself, such notions can be believed only by people who are carnal. Those who are spiritual call those who believe such things *Chiliasts*, using the Greek term Χιλιασταί; translating the word literally, we may call them *Milliarii*, “Millenarians.”

It would take too long to refute them point by point. Rather, we must now show how these Scriptures are to be understood.

### 2.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself says: “No one can enter the house of a strong man and seize his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark 3:27). He wished the strong man to be understood as the devil, because the devil was able to hold the human race captive; and his goods, which Christ was going to seize, were to be his faithful people, whom the devil possessed in various sins and acts of impiety.

Therefore, so that this strong man might be bound, this apostle saw in the Apocalypse an angel descending from heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a chain in his hand. “And he seized,” he says, “that dragon, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years”—that is, he restrained and curbed his power to deceive and possess those who were to be liberated.

As far as I can see, the thousand years may be understood in two ways. Either this event takes place in the final thousand years—that is, in the sixth millennium of years, as on the sixth day, whose latter periods are now passing; and afterward there will follow the Sabbath, which has no evening, namely, the rest of the saints, which has no end. In that case he called the final part of this millennium, as of a day, which remained until the end of the age, “a thousand years,” according to the manner of speech by which a part is signified by the whole.

Or certainly he used “a thousand years” for all the years of this age, so that the fullness of time itself might be indicated by a complete number. For the number one thousand produces the solid square of the number ten. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, which is already a square figure, but a plane one. In order for it to rise in height and become solid, one hundred is again multiplied tenfold, and the result is one thousand.

Moreover, if one hundred is sometimes used for the whole—as in the promise made by the Lord to the one who abandons all his possessions and follows him: “He will receive a hundredfold in this age” (Matthew 19:29; Mark 10:30)—the Apostle, explaining this in a sense, says: “As having nothing, yet possessing all things” (2 Corinthians 6:10), because it had already been said [Note: [Col. 0668] Here the particle *ante* (“previously”) does not indicate the preceding words of Paul, as some have thought, but earlier times. For the saying cited, “The whole world of wealth belongs to a faithful man,” was spoken by Solomon in Proverbs; there, in chapter 17 after verse 6, it is found in the Septuagint, not in the Vulgate. It is cited by Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 2, and by other ancient writers cited in volume 2, on Epistle 153, section 26.]: “The whole world of wealth belongs to a faithful man” [Note: [Col. 0668] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *remanet* (“remains”) instead of *remanebat* (“remained”).]—how much more is one thousand used for the whole, where there is the solidity of the tenfold square?

Hence that passage in the Psalm is also better understood in this way: “He has remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations” (Psalm 104:8)—that is, for all generations.

### 3.

“And he sent him,” it says, “into the abyss”: clearly, he sent the devil into the abyss. By this name is signified the innumerable multitude of the impious, whose hearts are exceedingly deep in their wickedness against the Church of God. This does not mean that the devil was not there before; rather, he is said to have been sent there because, excluded from believers, he began to possess the impious more fully.

For the devil possesses more completely the one who is not only alienated from God but also gratuitously hates those who serve God.

“And he shut him in,” it says, “and sealed him over him, so that he would no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were ended.” “He shut him in” means that he forbade him to go out—that is, he prohibited him from transgressing the imposed limit. The addition “and sealed him” seems to me to signify that God wished it to remain hidden who belong to the devil’s portion and who do not. This is entirely concealed in the present age: for it is uncertain whether the one who appears to be standing will fall, and whether the one who appears to be lying fallen will rise.

By this bond and confinement, therefore, the devil is prevented and restrained from deceiving those nations that belong to Christ, whom previously he was deceiving or holding captive. For God chose them before the foundation of the world to rescue them from the power of darkness (Ephesians 1:4) and transfer them into the kingdom of the Son of his love [Note: [Col. 0669] So read several manuscripts of good authority. The printed editions have *claritatis suae* (“of his brightness”) instead of *charitatis suae* (“of his love”).] (Colossians 1:13), as the Apostle says.

For who among the faithful does not know that the devil still deceives nations and draws them with him into eternal punishment—but not those predestined to eternal life? Nor should it disturb us that the devil often deceives even those who, already regenerated in Christ, walk in the ways of God.

“For the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19): none of these does the devil deceive into eternal condemnation. The Lord knows them as God, to whom even future things are not hidden—not as a human being, who sees another human being only for the present (if indeed he sees him, since he does not see his heart), and who does not even see for himself what that person will later become.

For this purpose, then, the devil has been bound and shut up in the abyss: so that he might no longer deceive the nations from which the Church consists, whom he previously held deceived before the Church existed. For it was not said that he should not deceive anyone, but “that he should no longer deceive the nations”; by these, without doubt, he wished the Church to be understood.

“Until the thousand years are ended,” he says—that is, either the portion remaining of the sixth day, which consists of a thousand years, or all the years during which this age is thereafter to run its course.

### 4.

Nor should the statement “that he should no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years are ended” be understood as though afterward he would deceive precisely those nations from which the predestined Church consists, whose deception he has been prevented from effecting by that bond and confinement.

Either the statement is expressed according to a manner of speech found several times in Scripture, as in the Psalm: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God until he has mercy upon us” (Psalm 122:2). For when he has had mercy, the eyes of his servants will not cease to be directed toward the Lord their God.

Or certainly the order of the words is this: “And he shut him in and sealed him over him until the thousand years are ended.” As for the phrase inserted—“so that he should no longer deceive the nations”—it is independent of the connection of that order and should be understood separately, as if it had been added afterward. The whole sentence would then read: “And he shut him in and sealed him over him until the thousand years are ended, so that he should no longer deceive the nations”—that is, he shut him in until the thousand years were ended for this purpose: that he should no longer deceive the nations.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### On the Binding and Release of the Devil

### 1.

“After this,” he says, “he must be released for a short time” (Revelation 20:3).

If the devil’s being bound and confined means that he cannot deceive the Church, will his release therefore mean that he can? By no means. The Church, predestined and chosen before the foundation of the world, will never be deceived by him. Of it was said: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

And yet the Church will exist even at the time when the devil is to be released [Note: [Col. 0669] The printed editions read, “and yet here will be the Church.” The word *Ecclesia* (“Church”) is absent here from the manuscripts.], just as from the time it was established it has existed and will exist at every moment—in those members who succeed one another through birth and death.

For shortly afterward he says that the devil, once released, will draw the nations whom he has deceived throughout the whole world into war against the Church, and that the number of its enemies will be like the sand of the sea.

“And they went up,” he says, “over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city; and fire came down from heaven from God and consumed them. And the devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet also were [Note: [Col. 0670] The printed editions have *et pseudoprophetae* (“and the false prophets”). The reading is corrected from the manuscripts.]; and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever” (Revelation 20:8–10).

But this already pertains to the final judgment. I have mentioned it here so that no one might suppose that, during the short period in which the devil will be released, the Church will not exist on earth—either because he will not find it here when he is released or because he will destroy it when he persecutes it by every means.

Thus, throughout the entire period embraced by this book—from Christ’s first coming to the end of the age, when his second coming will occur—the devil is not bound in such a way that the meaning of his binding throughout the interval called by the number one thousand years is simply that he cannot deceive the Church, since even when released he will certainly not deceive it.

For plainly, if being bound means being unable to deceive, or being forbidden to deceive, what will being released mean except being able, or being permitted, to deceive? But may that never happen.

Rather, the devil’s binding means that he is not permitted to exercise the whole temptation that he can employ, whether by force or by deceit, in order to seduce human beings—either compelling them violently into his party or tricking them fraudulently. If he were permitted to do this throughout so long a period and amid the great weakness of many, he would overthrow many faithful people whom God does not wish to undergo such things and would prevent others from believing. To prevent this, he has been bound.

### 2.

He will be released, however, when the short period arrives. For it is written that he will rage with all the strength of himself and his followers for three years and six months [Note: [Col. 0670] Compare *On the Apocalypse of John*, chapter 11, verse 2.]. Those with whom he must wage war will be such that they cannot be overcome by the force and stratagems of his attack.

If he were never released, his malignant power would be less apparent, and the faithful endurance of the holy city would be less fully proved. Finally, it would be less clearly perceived how greatly the Almighty made use of his great evil—[Note: [Col. 0670] The printed editions have *omnipotens Deus* (“God Almighty”). The word *Deus* is absent from the manuscripts.]—who did not remove him altogether from the temptation of the saints, although he cast him out from their inner persons [Note: [Col. 0670] The Louvain edition reads *interioribus omnibus* (“from all inner [parts]”). Other printed editions and the manuscripts more correctly read *interioribus hominibus* (“from the inner persons”).], where belief in God resides, so that they might advance through his external assault; and who bound him among those who belong to his party, lest, by pouring out and exercising as much wickedness as he could, he should frighten some of the innumerable weak people from the faith of devotion, from whom the Church had to be multiplied and filled—some who would yet believe, others who already believed: frightening these and breaking those.

And he will release him at the end [Note: [Col. 0671] The Vienna and Amiens manuscripts read, “and he would release”; Erasmus and Louvain, “and he will be released”; but the manuscripts read, “and he will release”: namely, the Almighty who bound him.], so that the city of God may behold, with the immense glory of its Redeemer, Helper, and Liberator, how powerful an adversary it has overcome.

What are we in comparison with those saints and faithful people who will exist at that time? For such a great enemy will be released to test them, whereas we struggle against him amid such dangers while he is bound.

Nevertheless, there certainly have been and still are soldiers of Christ so prudent and brave that, even if they were living in this mortality when he is released, they would wisely avoid and patiently endure all his schemes and attacks.

### 3.

This binding of the devil did not occur only from the time when the Church began to spread beyond the Jewish land into one nation after another; it is also occurring now and will continue until the end of the age, when he is to be released.

Even now people are converted from the unbelief in which he possessed them to the faith, and without doubt they will continue to be converted until that final time. The strong man is certainly bound in each person when that person is snatched from him as one of his goods.

Nor is the abyss in which he is confined emptied when those who were alive at the time when he began to be confined die. Others have succeeded and continue to succeed them through birth until this age ends—people who hate Christians, in whose blind and deep hearts he is enclosed daily, as if in an abyss.

There is, however, some question whether, during those final three years and six months, when he is released and will rage with all his strength, anyone will come to the faith who had not previously belonged to it.

For how will the statement stand: “Who enters the house of a strong man to seize his goods unless he first binds the strong man?” (Matthew 12:29), if goods are seized even while he is released?

This statement therefore seems to compel us to believe that, during that brief period, no one will be added to the Christian people, but that the devil will fight against those who are already found to be Christians. Even if some of these are defeated and follow him, they will not belong to the predestined number of God’s children.

For the apostle John himself, who also wrote this Apocalypse, did not say without reason in his epistle concerning certain people: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

But what will happen to little children? It is exceedingly incredible that, at that time, no children already born and not yet baptized will be claimed as Christian children; that none will be born during those very days; or that, if there are any, they will not in some manner be brought by their parents to the bath of regeneration.

If this happens, how will these goods be seized after the devil has been released, when no one enters the strong man’s house to seize his goods unless he first binds him?

Rather, we should believe that at that time there will be neither a lack of people falling away from the Church nor a lack of people joining the Church. But their parents will be so strong on behalf of their children’s baptism, and those who then first come to believe will be so strong, that they will overcome the strong man even though he is not bound—that is, even though he is laying snares with every kind of art and pressing upon them with forces such as he had never previously employed. They will understand his attacks vigilantly and endure them patiently, and thus they will be snatched from him even though he is not bound.

Nor will that evangelical statement therefore be false: “Who enters the house of a strong man to seize his goods unless he first binds the strong man?”

For, according to the truth of that statement, this order has been preserved: first the strong man was bound, and after his goods had been seized, the Church was multiplied far and wide among all nations from the strong and the weak, so that, through the very firm faith produced by the divinely foretold and fulfilled events, it might also seize his goods when he was released.

For just as we must acknowledge that the love of many will grow cold when iniquity abounds (Matthew 24:12), and that, during the unprecedented and immense persecutions and deceptions of the devil after his release, many who are not written in the book of life will yield, so we must also consider that the time will find not only good and faithful people, but that some who are still outside will, with God’s grace assisting them through consideration of the Scriptures—in which both other events and the end itself have been foretold, and whose arrival they already perceive—become more steadfast in believing what they did not previously believe and stronger in overcoming the devil even though he is not bound.

If this is so, then his binding must be said to have preceded this, so that the despoiling of his goods would follow both while he was bound and while he was released. For concerning this matter it was said: “Who will enter the house of a strong man to seize his goods unless he first binds the strong man?”

## CHAPTER IX  
### What the Reign of the Saints with Christ for a Thousand Years Is, and How It Differs from the Eternal Kingdom

### 1.

Meanwhile, while the devil is bound for a thousand years, the saints [Note: [Col. 0672] The printed editions read “saints of God”; the manuscripts omit “of God.”] reign with Christ for those same thousand years, unquestionably to be understood in the same way—that is, as referring to the present time of his first coming.

Apart from that kingdom of which he will speak at the end—“Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matthew 25:34)—unless his saints already reign with him now in some other way, certainly unequal to that future reign, to whom he says, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20), the Church would not even now be called his kingdom or the kingdom of heaven.

For it is precisely in this period that the scribe is instructed in the kingdom of God who brings forth from his treasure things new and old (Matthew 13:52), of whom we spoke above.

And from the Church those reapers will gather the weeds that he allowed to grow together with the wheat until the harvest. Explaining this, he says: “The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matthew 13:39–41).

Are they to gather them from that kingdom in which there are no scandals? They will therefore gather them from this kingdom of his, which is the Church.

Again he says: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19).

He speaks of both within the kingdom of heaven: both the one who does not do the commandments that he teaches—for this is to loosen them, not to keep or perform them—and the one who does them and teaches them. But he calls one least and the other great.

He immediately continues: “For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees”—that is, the righteousness of those who loosen what they teach [Note: [Col. 0673] All the manuscripts have: “that is, unless it exceeds those who loosen what they teach.”]—“you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20).

For elsewhere he says of the scribes and Pharisees: “They say and do not do” (Matthew 23:3). Unless, therefore, your righteousness exceeds theirs—that is, unless you do what you teach rather than loosen it—“you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

The kingdom of heaven must therefore be understood in one way where both kinds are present: both the one who loosens what he teaches and the one who does it—the former least, the latter great [Note: [Col. 0673] The manuscripts read, “the former great.”]. It is understood in another way where only the one who does it enters.

Accordingly, where both kinds are found, there is the Church as it now is; where only the latter kind will be found, there is the Church as it will then be, when no evil person is in it.

Therefore the Church is even now the kingdom of Christ and the kingdom of heaven. Thus his saints reign with him even now, though in a different way from how they will reign then. Yet the weeds do not reign with him, although they grow together with the wheat in the Church.

Those reign with him who do what the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2). Of such people he likewise says that “their citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

Finally, those reign with him who are in his kingdom in such a way that they themselves are also his kingdom. But how are those people the kingdom of Christ who—even if I say nothing else, and although they remain there until, at the end of the age, all scandals are gathered out of his kingdom—seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21)?

### 2.

Concerning this kingdom of warfare, in which the Church is still engaged in battle with the enemy, sometimes resisting hostile vices and sometimes ruling over vices that yield [Note: [Col. 0673] Several manuscripts have *pugnantibus vitiis* (“vices that are fighting”). Immediately afterward, the same manuscripts and all the others have *aliquando cadentibus* (“sometimes when they fall”).], until it reaches that most peaceful kingdom where it will reign without an enemy, this book speaks as follows about the first resurrection, which is now taking place.
