After saying that the devil would be bound for a thousand years and afterward released for a short time, it immediately recapitulates what the Church does, or what takes place within it, during those thousand years:

“And I saw thrones, and those seated upon them, and judgment was given.”

This should not be understood as referring to the final judgment. Rather, the thrones of those presiding, and those very presiding officers, are to be understood—those through whom the Church is governed now.

The judgment given should be understood in no better way than by reference to the statement: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:18).

Hence the Apostle says: “For what have I to do with judging those outside? Is it not those within whom you judge?” (1 Corinthians 5:12).

“And the souls,” he says, “of those who were killed because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God”—we must supply what he is going to say afterward: “they reigned with Jesus for a thousand years” (Revelation 20:4). These are the souls of the martyrs, not yet restored to their bodies.

For the souls of the faithful dead are not separated from the Church, which is even now the kingdom of Christ. Otherwise their memory would not be made at the altar of God in the sharing of Christ’s body; nor would it be of any benefit, amid dangers, to hasten to his baptism so that this life might not end without it; nor would it benefit reconciliation if someone had been separated from that same body through repentance or an evil conscience.

Why are these things done except because the faithful, even after death, are members of Christ?

Although, therefore, they do not yet reign with him in their bodies, their souls already reign with him while these thousand years run their course.

Hence, in this same book, we read elsewhere: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord; from now on,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labors, for their works follow them” (Revelation 14:13).

Thus the Church now reigns with Christ, first in the living and the dead. Moreover, as the Apostle says, “Christ died so that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead” (Romans 14:9).

He mentioned only the souls of the martyrs because the dead reign especially when they have fought for the truth even to death. But, by taking the part for the whole [Note: [Col. 0674] That is, a figure by which the whole is understood from a part.], we understand the other dead who belong to the Church as well, since the Church is the kingdom of Christ.

### 3.

What follows—“and those who did not worship the beast or his image, and did not receive his inscription on their forehead or on their hand”—we must understand as referring both to the living and to the dead.

What this beast is requires more careful investigation, but it is not contrary to sound faith to understand it as the impious city itself, and as the people of unbelievers opposed to the faithful people and the city of God.

Its image, I think, is its simulation, namely, in those people who appear to profess the faith but live unbelievingly. They pretend to be what they are not, and they are called Christians not by a true likeness but by a deceitful image.

For belonging to the same beast are not only the openly hostile enemies [Note: [Col. 0674] The printed editions have *non solum averti inimici* (“not only enemies turned away”). The manuscripts have *non solum aperte inimici* (“not only openly hostile enemies”).] of the name of Christ and of his most glorious city, but also the weeds that will be gathered at the end of the age from his kingdom, which is the Church.

And who are those who do not worship the beast or its image except those who do what the Apostle says: “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14)?

They do not worship it—that is, they do not consent or submit. Nor do they receive its inscription: the mark of crime on the forehead, because of profession, and on the hand, because of action.

Free from these evils, whether they are still living in this mortal flesh or have died, they reign with Christ even now, in a manner suited to the present age, throughout the entire interval signified by the number one thousand years.

### 4.

“The rest of them,” he says, “did not live.” For “the hour is now when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live; but the rest of them will not live” (John 5:25).

What he added—“until the thousand years are ended”—must be understood to mean that during that period they did not live when they ought to have lived, namely, by passing from death into life.

Therefore, when the day comes on which the resurrection of bodies also occurs, they will not come forth from their tombs to life but to judgment—to condemnation, that is, which is called the second death.

Until the thousand years are ended, whoever has not lived—that is, whoever throughout the entire period in which the first resurrection is taking place has not heard the voice of the Son of God and passed from death into life—will certainly pass, in the second resurrection, which is the resurrection of the flesh, into the second death together with that flesh.

For the text continues: “This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in this first resurrection” (Revelation 20:5–6)—that is, who participates in it.

The one who participates in it is not merely the person who rises again from the death that is in sins, but also the one who remains in that renewed life.

“Over these,” it says, “the second death has no power.” It therefore has power over the rest, concerning whom he said above: “The rest of them did not live until the thousand years were ended.”

For throughout that entire interval, which he calls a thousand years, no matter how long any of them lived in the body, they did not rise again from the death in which impiety held them, so as to become participants in the first resurrection by rising again and so that the second death would have no power over them.

## CHAPTER X  
### What Should Be Answered to Those Who Think That the Resurrection Pertains Only to Bodies and Not Also to Souls

There are some who think that resurrection can be spoken of only with reference to bodies, and therefore insist that this first resurrection too will take place in bodies.

“For whatever falls,” they say, “is what rises again. Bodies fall by dying; indeed, corpses are called *cadavera* from *cadere*, ‘to fall’” [Note: [Col. 0675] See Sermon 241, section 2.]. “Therefore,” they say, “there can be no resurrection of souls, but only of bodies.”

But what do they say against the Apostle, who calls it resurrection? For those to whom he says, “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Colossians 3:1), had certainly risen according to the inner person, not according to the outer person.

He expresses the same meaning elsewhere in other words: “Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4).

This is also the meaning of: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14).

But they say that no one can rise unless he falls, and therefore think that resurrection pertains to bodies, not souls, because falling belongs to bodies. Why do they not listen to the words: “Do not withdraw from him, lest you fall” (Ecclesiasticus 2:7); “He stands or falls before his own master” (Romans 14:4); and “Whoever thinks that he stands, let him beware lest he fall” [Note: [Col. 0675] The manuscripts have: “Whoever thinks that he stands, let him beware lest he fall.”] (1 Corinthians 10:12)?

I think that this fall must be guarded against in the soul, not in the body.

If, then, resurrection belongs to those who fall, and souls also fall, it must certainly be acknowledged that souls also rise again.

After saying, “Over these the second death has no power,” he adds: “But they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.”

This is not said only of bishops and presbyters, who are now properly called priests in the Church. Rather, just as we call all Christians priests because of the mystical chrism, so all are priests because they are members of the one Priest.

The Apostle Peter speaks of them: “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9).

Although briefly and in passing, he also indicated that Christ is God by saying, “priests of God and of Christ”—that is, of the Father and the Son. Yet because of the form of a servant, just as Christ became the Son of man, so also he became a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 109:4).

We have spoken of this matter more than once in this work.

[Note: [Col. 0676] Thus the martyrs openly professed that Christ was God, when, being ordered to sacrifice to the gods, they replied that they sacrificed to the one God and to Christ. Thus the blessed Crispina, who suffered under the proconsul Anulinus at the colony of Theveste during the second consulship of Diocletian and the consulship of Maximian Augustus, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, as her acts of martyrdom report, published in the third volume of the *Ancient Analecta*, said: “I have never sacrificed, nor do I sacrifice, except to the one God and our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, who was born and suffered.”

And the martyr Mammarius, whom the acts published in the fourth volume of the *Ancient Analecta* attest to have suffered under the same proconsul Anulinus, in the city of Vaga, during the reign of Maximian and Gallienus, said: “I never sacrifice to demons, but to the one God,” and so forth. A little later he says: “We sacrifice to the Lord Jesus Christ, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. In this God we believe and serve him.”

The pagans themselves attributed this faith in Christ and his worship to the Apostles, as may be seen above, in book 18, chapter 53, and in book 1 of *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, sections 11 and 12. Cyprian too—something that should not be passed over in silence—is called “the priest of Christ and God” by Pontius in his *Life*.]

## CHAPTER XI  
### On Gog and Magog, Whom the Devil, Once Released Near the End of the Age, Will Incite to Persecute the Church of God

“And when the thousand years are ended,” he says, “Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and he will draw them into war; their number is like the sand of the sea.”

He will then deceive them for this purpose: to draw them into that war. For previously also he deceived them in every way he could, through many and various evils.

“He will go out” means that he will burst forth from the hiding places of hatred into open persecution. This will be the final persecution, when the final judgment is imminent, which the holy Church will suffer throughout the whole world—the entire city of Christ from the entire city of the devil, however large each may be upon the earth.

The nations whom he calls Gog and Magog should not be understood as though they were certain barbarians settled in some particular region of the earth—whether the Getae and Massagetae, as some suspect on account of the first letters of these names, or some other foreign peoples separated from Roman law.

For these nations are signified as existing throughout the whole world when it is said: “The nations that are at the four corners of the earth”; and he identifies them as Gog and Magog.

We have learned that the interpretation of these names is: Gog, “roof”; Magog, “from the roof” [Note: [Col. 0676] He found this interpretation in Jerome’s commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 38.]—as though they were the house and the one who proceeds from the house.

The nations, therefore, are those in whom we previously understood the devil to be confined as if in an abyss; and he is, in a certain sense, raising himself up and proceeding from them. Thus they are the roof, and he is from the roof.

If, however, we refer both names to the nations, rather than referring one to them and the other to the devil, then they themselves are the roof because the ancient enemy is now enclosed and, in a certain sense, concealed in them; and they themselves will be “from the roof” when they burst forth from concealment into open hatred.

As for the statement, “They went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city” (Revelation 20:7–8), this does not signify that they came, or will come, to one particular place, as though the camp of the saints and the beloved city were to exist in one location.

The beloved city is nothing other than the Church of Christ, spread throughout the whole world. Accordingly, wherever it then exists—since it will exist among all nations, which is signified by the expression “the breadth of the earth”—there will be the camp of the saints and there will be the city beloved by God.

There it will be surrounded by all its enemies, since they too will be with it among all nations, by the enormity of that persecution. That is, it will be compressed, harassed, and hemmed in by the distress of tribulation, yet it will not abandon its service, which is designated by the term “camp” [Note: [Col. 0677] The Louvain edition has *malitiam* (“wickedness”). The reading is corrected from other printed editions and the manuscripts, which have *militiam* (“service” or “military service”).].

## CHAPTER XII  
### Whether the Punishment of the Impious Concerns the Final Punishment, Since Fire Is Said to Have Descended from Heaven and Consumed Them

As for the statement, “Fire came down from heaven and consumed them” (Revelation 20:9), this should not be understood as the final punishment that will occur when it is said, “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41).

Then they themselves will be thrown into the fire; fire will not come down from heaven upon them.

Here, however, the fire from heaven can properly be understood as the very steadfastness of the saints, by which they will not yield to those who rage against them in order to make them do their will.

For heaven is a firmament; by its steadfastness they will be tormented with most ardent zeal, because they will not be able to draw Christ’s saints over to the party of the Antichrist.

That steadfastness itself will be the fire that consumes them, and this will be from God, because it is by God’s gift that the saints become unconquerable, and from this their enemies are tormented.

For just as it is said in a good sense, “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10), so, conversely, it is said: “Zeal has seized an untaught people, and now fire will consume the adversaries” (Isaiah 26:11, according to the Septuagint)—and this now, of course, apart from the fire of that final judgment.

Or, if he called the plague by which the persecutors of the Church will be struck, when Christ has already come and finds them alive upon the earth, “fire descending from heaven and consuming them”—when he will kill the Antichrist by the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8)—even this will not be the final punishment of the impious. Rather, the final punishment will be what they will suffer after the resurrection of their bodies.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Whether the Time of the Antichrist’s Persecution Should Be Counted among the Thousand Years

[Note: [Col. 0677] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Whether, before the time of the Antichrist’s persecution, the thousand years should be counted.”]

This final persecution, which is to come from Antichrist [Col. 0678] (as we have already said, since it is also set forth earlier in this book [Rev. X and XI], and in the prophet Daniel [Dan. XII]), will last three years and six months. Although this period is short, there is a justified ambiguity as to whether it belongs to the thousand years during which he says that the devil is bound and the saints reign with Christ, or whether this brief interval is added to those same years and lies outside them. For if we say that it belongs to those same years, the reign of the saints with Christ will be found to extend for a longer period, not merely for that length of time, than the devil’s imprisonment. For assuredly the saints will reign with their King even during the persecution itself, overcoming such great evils, when the devil will no longer be bound, so that he can persecute them with all his strength.

How, then, does this Scripture determine both matters by the same thousand years—the binding of the devil, that is, and the reign of the saints—when, by an interval of three years and six months, the devil’s binding ends before the reign of the saints with Christ in these thousand years? But if we say that this brief period of persecution is not included in the thousand years, but is added after they have been completed, so that the statement may properly be understood as follows: after saying, “The priests of God and of Christ will reign with him for a thousand years,” he added, “And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison”; then, in this way, he indicates that both the reign of the saints and the devil’s bondage will cease at the same time. Consequently, the period of that persecution would belong neither to the reign of the saints nor to Satan’s imprisonment—both of which are contained within the thousand years—but would be added afterward and counted outside them. We would then be compelled to admit that the saints will not reign with Christ during that persecution.

But who would dare to say that his members will not reign with him at the time when they will cling to him most closely and most steadfastly, and when, the more fierce the assault of the battle, the greater will be the glory of not yielding [Note: [Col. 0678] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read *non cedenti*, “of the one who does not yield.”], and the denser the crown of martyrdom? Or if, because of the tribulations they will suffer, they are not to be called reigning, it will follow that, during the preceding days within those same thousand years, any of the saints who were suffering likewise did not reign with Christ during the time of their tribulation. And consequently those whose souls the author of this book says he saw, slain because of their testimony to Jesus and because of the word of God, were not reigning with Christ when they were suffering persecution; nor were they themselves the kingdom of Christ, whom Christ possessed in a more excellent manner. That is utterly absurd and must be rejected in every way.

Certainly, however, the victorious souls of the most glorious martyrs, after overcoming and completing every pain and hardship, reigned and reign with Christ after laying aside their mortal bodies, until the thousand years are completed, so that afterward, having received immortal bodies as well, they may reign. Therefore, during those three and a half years, the souls of those slain for his martyrdom—both those who had already departed from their bodies and those who will depart during that final persecution—will reign with him until the mortal age comes to an end and there is a passage to that kingdom where there will be no death.

Accordingly, the years of the saints reigning with Christ will be more numerous than the years of the devil’s bondage and imprisonment, because they will reign with their King, the Son of God, even while the devil is no longer bound, throughout those three and a half years. It remains, therefore, that when we hear, “The priests of God and of Christ will reign with him for a thousand years,” and, “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison,” we must understand either that the thousand years of this reign of the saints are not being said to come to an end, but the thousand years of the devil’s bondage and imprisonment; so that the thousand years—that is, the full periods assigned to each—are completed by the two parties according to different and proper durations, the reign of the saints being longer and the devil’s bondage shorter; or, certainly, because the brief period of three years and six months is so short, it may be thought that it was not intended to be counted, whether because the devil’s bondage appears shorter or the saints’ reign longer. I discussed a similar matter concerning the four hundred years in the sixteenth book of this work (ch. 24), since they were somewhat more [Note: [Col. 0679] Some manuscripts read, “some were more.”], and yet they were called four hundred. Such things are often found in Holy Scripture, if one pays attention.

## CHAPTER XIV — The Damnation of the Devil with His Associates, and, by Recapitulation, the Bodily Resurrection of All the Dead and the Judgment of the Final Retribution

After this mention of the final persecution, he briefly gathers together everything that the devil and the hostile city with its prince will suffer at the final judgment. For he says:

“And the devil who was deceiving them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet are; and they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever” (Rev. XX, 9–10) [Note: [Col. 0679] Thus the manuscripts, following the Greek. The printed editions read, “and the false prophets will be tormented.” Moreover, the conjunction “and” immediately before “they will be tormented” is absent from printed editions of the Vulgate, but is found in ancient Latin Corbie Bibles.].

We have already said above that the beast is rightly understood as the impious city itself. Its false prophet is either Antichrist or that image—that is, that fabrication—of which we spoke there.

After this, recounting by recapitulation the final judgment itself, which will take place at the second resurrection of the dead, the resurrection of the body, he relates how it was revealed to him:

“And I saw,” he says, “a great white throne and the one seated upon it, from whose face heaven and earth fled, and their place was found no more” (ibid., 11).

He does not say, “I saw a great white throne and the one seated upon it, and from his face heaven and earth fled,” because this did not happen at that time—that is, before judgment had been passed upon the living and the dead. Rather, he says that he saw him seated on the throne, from whose face heaven and earth fled—but this was to happen afterward. For after the judgment has been completed, this heaven and this earth will cease to exist when the new heaven and the new earth begin to exist. The world will pass away through a change in its properties, not through its complete destruction. Hence the Apostle also says, “For the form of this world is passing away; and I want you to be without anxiety” (1 Cor. VII, 31–32). The form, therefore, passes away, not the nature.

When John had said that he saw the one seated on the throne, from whose face heaven and earth would afterward flee, he continues:

“And I saw the dead, great and small; and the books were opened; and another book was opened, which is the book of the life of each person [Note: [Col. 0680] The words “of each person” are absent from the Vulgate and from the Greek text of the Apocalypse.]; and the dead were judged from the contents of the books, according to their works” (Rev. XX, 12).

He said that books were opened, and one book; but he did not leave unspecified what kind of book it was: “which,” he says, “is the book of the life of each person.” Therefore, the books that he placed first are to be understood as the holy Scriptures, both the Old and the New, in which it would be shown what God had commanded to be done. But in the book that is the life of each person, it would be shown what each had failed to do or had done.

If this book is imagined in a material way, who could estimate its size or length? Or how much time could be required to read a book in which the whole lives of all people were written? Will there be as many angels as there will be human beings, so that each person will hear his life recited by an angel assigned to him? Therefore, there will not be one book for everyone, but separate books for separate persons. Yet Scripture, wishing this to be understood as one, says, “And another book was opened.”

A certain divine power must therefore be understood, by which it will come about that each person’s works, whether good or evil, are all recalled to memory and perceived with the mind’s gaze in wondrous swiftness, so that knowledge may accuse or excuse conscience; and thus all and each may be judged at once. This divine power, clearly, has received the name “book.” For in it, so to speak, whatever is recalled through its operation is read [Note: [Col. 0680] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have, “whatever is recalled by the one who acts.”].

But in order to show which dead are to be judged—small and great—he says by recapitulation, as though returning to what he had passed over or postponed:

“And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and death and Hades gave up the dead whom they held” (ibid., 13).

This undoubtedly happened before the dead were judged, and yet it was mentioned first. This, then, is what I said: by recapitulation he returned to what he had omitted. Now, however, he has kept the order, and, in order to make that order clear, he has more appropriately repeated in its proper place what he had already said about the judged dead. For after saying, “The sea gave up the dead who were in it, and death and Hades gave up the dead whom they held,” he immediately added what he had stated shortly before: “And each was judged according to his works.” This is what he had said above: “And the dead were judged according to their works.”

## CHAPTER XV — Who Are the Dead Whom the Sea Gave Up for Judgment, and Whom Death and Hades Returned

But who are the dead whom the sea gave up, who were in it? Surely those who die at sea are not in Hades, or their bodies preserved in the sea; nor, more absurdly, did the sea possess good dead people while Hades possessed evil ones. Who could believe this?

Yet some appropriately understand the sea in this passage as signifying this present age. Thus, when he also indicated that those whom Christ will find here established in the body will be judged together with those who are to rise, he called these people dead as well—both the good, to whom it is said, “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3), and the evil, concerning whom it is said, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22).

They may also be called dead because they bear mortal bodies. Hence the Apostle says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. VIII, 10), showing that in a living human being, established in this body, there are both a dead body and a living spirit. Yet he did not say “mortal body,” but “dead body,” although shortly afterward he also calls them “mortal bodies,” as is more customary (ibid., 11).

These, then, are the dead whom the sea gave up, who were in it: it gave up human beings, whoever were in this age, because they had not yet died. “And death and Hades,” he says, “gave up the dead whom they held.” The sea gave them up because they appeared just as they had been found; but death and Hades returned them because they recalled them from the life from which they had already departed.

Perhaps it was not without reason that it was insufficient to say either “death” or “Hades,” but both were mentioned: death on account of the good, who could suffer death alone, but not Hades; and Hades on account of the evil, who also pay penalties among the dead. For if it does not appear absurd to believe that the ancient saints who held faith in the coming Christ were indeed in places very far removed from the torments of the impious, but were nevertheless among the dead until the blood of Christ and his descent to those places rescued them from there, then certainly thereafter the good faithful, having been redeemed by that price once it had been poured out, know nothing of Hades until, having also received their bodies, they receive the good things they have earned.

After saying, “And each was judged according to his works,” he briefly added how they were judged:

“And death and Hades,” he says, “were thrown into the lake of fire.”

By these names he signifies the devil, since he is the author of death and of the punishments of Hades, and the entire fellowship of demons together. This is what he had already said more explicitly above by anticipation: “And the devil who was deceiving them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur.” But what he had added there more obscurely, saying, “where the beast and the false prophet also were,” he states more clearly here:

“And those who were not found written in the book of life were thrown into the lake of fire” (Rev. XX, 14–15).

This book does not recall God, as though he might be deceived through forgetfulness. Rather, it signifies the predestination of those to whom eternal life will be given. For God does not fail to know them and then read about them in this book in order to know them; rather, his very foreknowledge of them, which cannot be deceived, is the book of life in which they are written—that is, known beforehand.

## CHAPTER XVI — The New Heaven and the New Earth

After the judgment has been completed, in which he foretold the judgment of the wicked, it remains for him to speak also about the good. He has already explained what the Lord stated briefly: “These will go away into eternal punishment.” It follows that he should explain what is connected with this there as well: “But the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV, 46).

“And I saw,” he says, “a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth passed away [Note: [Col. 0681] In all the manuscripts, *prima*, “first,” is absent.], and the sea is no more” (Rev. XXI, 1).

This will take place in the order that he had already stated above by anticipation: that he saw the one seated on the throne, from whose face heaven and earth fled. For after those who are not written in the book of life have been judged and cast into eternal fire—what kind of fire this will be, and in what part of the world or of creation it will exist, I believe no human being knows, unless perhaps the divine Spirit has revealed it to someone—then the form of this world will pass away through the conflagration of worldly fires, just as the flood came about through the inundation of worldly waters.

In that conflagration of the world, therefore, as I have said, the properties of corruptible elements that were suited to our corruptible bodies will utterly perish by burning; and the substance itself will acquire properties that correspond, through a wondrous transformation, to immortal bodies, so that the world, renewed for the better, may be suitably adapted to human beings who themselves have been renewed for the better in the flesh.

As for his statement, “And the sea is no more,” whether it will be dried up by that immense heat or itself be transformed for the better, I would not readily say. For we read that there will be a new heaven and a new earth; but I do not recall having read anywhere about a new sea, except that in this same book there is something described as “a glassy sea like crystal” (Rev. IV, 6; XV, 2). But at that point he was not speaking about the end of this age; nor does he seem to have said “sea” literally, but “as a sea.”

Although even now, since prophetic speech likes to mingle transferred expressions with proper words, and thus in a certain way to veil what it says, he may have been speaking of that sea when he said, “And the sea is no more”—the sea of which he had said above, “The sea gave up the dead who were in it.” For then this present age, turbulent and stormy with the life of mortals, which he represented under the name of the sea, will no longer exist.

## CHAPTER XVII — The Glorification of the Church without End after the End [Note: [Col. 0682] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have “after death.”]

“And I saw,” he says, “the great city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a great voice from the throne saying, Behold, the dwelling of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, but neither will there be any pain, because the former things have passed away. And the one seated on the throne said, Behold, I make all things new” (ibid., XXI, 2–5).

This city is said to descend from heaven because it is heavenly grace by which God made it. For this reason he also says to it through Isaiah, “I am the Lord who makes you” [Note: [Col. 0682] This follows the wording of the Septuagint, which in Greek has *ho ktisas se*, “who made you”; the Latin Vulgate has *creavi eum*, “I created him.”] (Isa. XLV, 8).

Indeed, it descended from heaven from the beginning of its existence, from the time when, throughout the course of this age, its citizens have continually increased through the grace of God coming from above by the washing of regeneration in the Holy Spirit sent from heaven [Note: [Col. 0682] Several manuscripts omit *in*, “in.”].

But through the judgment of God, which will be the final judgment through his Son Jesus Christ, such great and such new splendor will appear in it as a gift from God that no trace of its former state will remain—since bodies themselves will pass from their former corruption and mortality into a new incorruption and immortality.

To understand this as referring to the present time, during which it reigns with its King for a thousand years, seems to me excessively shameless, since he says most openly, “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, but neither will there be any pain.”

Who, indeed, could be so absurd and so insane in his obstinate insistence as to dare to affirm that, amid the hardships of this mortality, not merely the holy people but any individual saint who is living, will live, or has lived this life has no tears and pains—when, rather, the holier a person is and the fuller of holy desire, the more abundant is his weeping in prayer?

Is it not the voice of a citizen [Note: [Col. 0683] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have *civitatis*, “of the city,” instead of *civis*, “of a citizen,” less appropriately.] of the Jerusalem above: “My tears have become my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI, 4)? And: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI, 7)? And: “My sighing is not hidden from you” (Ps. XXXVII, 10)? And: “My pain has been renewed” (Ps. XXXVIII, 3)?

Or are they not his children who groan while burdened, desiring not to be stripped but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Cor. V, 4)? Are they not the same people who, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within themselves as they await adoption, the redemption of their body (Rom. VIII, 23)?

Was the Apostle Paul himself not a citizen of the Jerusalem above—or was he not all the more so when, for the sake of his Israelite brothers according to the flesh, he had great sorrow and continual pain in his heart (Rom. IX, 2)?

When, then, will there be no death in this city, except when it is said, “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death? The sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. XV, 55–56) [Note: [Col. 0683] He therefore seems to have read in Paul not *nîkos*, as the Vulgate does, which translates it “victory,” but *neîkos*. Ambrose and Jerome likewise read it thus. Ludovicus Vives.]. This certainly will not exist then, when it is said, “Where is it?” But now, not merely some lowliest citizen [Note: [Col. 0683] Most manuscripts read *infirmus*, “weak,” instead of *infimus*, “lowliest.”] of that city, but John himself cries out in his Epistle, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I, 8).

Many things are said obscurely in this book, whose title is the Apocalypse, so that they may exercise the mind of the reader; and there are few passages in it from whose clarification the rest can be discovered only with difficulty. This is especially so because he repeats the same matters in many ways, making them appear to be different things, when he is pursuing the same subjects in different forms of expression.

But in these words—“God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, but neither will there be any pain”—the statements about the future age and the immortality and eternity of the saints are expressed with such clarity (for only then and only there will these things be absent) that, if we consider these obscure, we ought not to seek or read anything explicit in Holy Scripture.

## CHAPTER XVIII — What the Apostle Peter Proclaimed concerning the Final Judgment of God

Let us now see what the Apostle Peter also wrote about this judgment:

“In the last days,” he says, “scoffers will come, scoffing and proceeding according to their own desires, and saying, Where is the promise of his coming? For from the time when the fathers fell asleep, everything continues in the same way from the beginning of creation. For they deliberately overlook this: that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; and through these the world that then existed, flooded with water, perished. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and of the destruction of ungodly human beings.

“But let this one thing not escape you, beloved: that one day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day. The Lord is not delaying the promise, as some consider delay; but he patiently endures for your sake, not wishing anyone to perish but all to turn to repentance.

“But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. On that day the heavens will pass away with great force; the elements, burning, will be dissolved; and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up. Since all these things are to perish, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct, waiting for and hastening toward the coming of the day of the Lord, because of which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will be melted by the heat of fire? But according to his promises, we await new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells” (2 Pet. III, 3–13).

Here he said nothing about the resurrection of the dead, but he spoke sufficiently about the destruction of this world. In mentioning what happened before the flood, he also seems in a certain way to have warned us how we should believe that this world will perish at the end of the age.

For he said that the world which then existed perished at that time; and he meant not only the earth itself but also the heavens, which we understand to be these atmospheric heavens, whose place and space the waters had then surpassed as they increased. Therefore all, or nearly all, of this windy air—which he calls heaven, or rather heavens, but certainly the lower ones, not those highest heavens where the sun, moon, and stars have been established—had been transformed into a watery substance [Note: [Col. 0684] Compare *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, book 3, §§2–3]. In this way it perished together with the earth, whose former surface had certainly been destroyed by the flood.

“But the heavens and earth that now exist,” he says, “have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and of the destruction of ungodly human beings.” Therefore the heavens and the earth—the world—which was stored up from the same water in place of the world that perished in the flood, is itself reserved for the final fire on the day of judgment and of the destruction of ungodly human beings.

He does not hesitate to say that the destruction of human beings will occur because of a great transformation, even though their nature will remain, albeit in eternal punishments.

Perhaps someone may ask: if this world will burn after the judgment has taken place, before a new heaven and a new earth are established in its place, where will the saints be during the conflagration, since embodied beings must necessarily exist in some bodily place?

We can answer that they will be in the higher regions, which the flame of that burning will not reach, just as the wave of the flood did not reach them. Their bodies will be of such a kind that they may be wherever they wish to be.

But once they have been made immortal and incorruptible, they will not fear the fire of that conflagration either, just as the corruptible and mortal bodies of the three men were able to remain unharmed and alive in the blazing furnace (Dan. III, 24) [Note: [Col. 0685] Our manuscripts read *si*, “if.”].

## CHAPTER XIX — What the Apostle Paul Wrote to the Thessalonians concerning the Revelation of Antichrist, Whose Time Will Be Followed by the Day of the Lord

1. I see that I must pass over many Gospel and apostolic sayings concerning this final divine judgment, lest this volume be extended to excessive length [Note: [Col. 0685] Several manuscripts read *protendatur*, “be prolonged.”]. But in no way may we pass over the Apostle Paul, who, writing to the Thessalonians, says:

“We ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly shaken in mind or terrified, either by spirit or by word or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent. Let no one deceive you in any way. For unless the deserter [Note: [Col. 0685] The Vulgate has *discessio*, “apostasy” or “departure.”] comes first, and the man of sin, the son of destruction, is revealed—the one who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying [Note: [Col. 0685] Several ancient books read *ostendens*, “showing.”] himself as though he were God—do you not remember that when I was still with you I used to tell you these things?

“And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work. Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst; and then the lawless one will be revealed [Note: [Col. 0685] The printed editions have *iniquus ille*, “that lawless one.” *Ille* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.], whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming—him whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power, signs, and lying wonders, and with every deceit of unrighteousness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved.

“And therefore God will send them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie and be judged—all who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness” (2 Thess. II, 1–11).

2. There is no doubt that he spoke these things about Antichrist, and that the day of judgment—for he calls it “the day of the Lord”—will not come unless the one whom he calls the deserter comes first, certainly one who has deserted the Lord God. If this can rightly be said of all the impious, how much more of this particular one?

But in what temple of God he will sit [Note: [Col. 0685] The printed editions have, “so that he may sit as God.” The words “as God” are absent from the manuscripts.], is uncertain: whether in the ruins of the temple built by King Solomon, or in the Church. For the Apostle would not call the temple of an idol or demon the temple of God.

Hence some wish Antichrist to be understood here not as the prince himself but, in a certain way, his entire body—that is, the multitude of human beings belonging to him—together with their prince. They more correctly think that the words should be rendered in Latin, as they are in Greek, not “he may sit in the temple of God,” but “he may sit into the temple of God” [Col. 0686] [Note: [Col. 0686] Greek: ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὡς Θεὸν καθίσαι, “so that he himself may sit into the temple of God as God.”], as though he himself were the temple of God, which is the Church. This is like saying, “He sits into a friend,” that is, as a friend, or anything else customarily expressed in this manner.

As for what he says, “And now you know what restrains him”—that is, what delays him, what causes his postponement, so that he may be revealed in his own time—you know this because he said that they knew it, but he did not wish to state it openly. Therefore, we who do not know what they knew desire, though with difficulty, to arrive at what the Apostle meant, and we cannot—especially because the things he added make this meaning more obscure.

For what does this mean: “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work. Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst; and then the lawless one will be revealed”? I freely confess that I have no idea what he meant. Nevertheless, I will not conceal the opinions of people that I have been able either to hear or to read.

3. Some think that this was said about the Roman Empire. For this reason, they believe that the Apostle Paul did not wish to write it openly, lest he incur the charge of wishing evil upon the Roman Empire, which was expected to be eternal. Thus, by saying, “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work,” he may have intended Nero, whose deeds already seemed like those of Antichrist. Hence some suspect that Nero will rise again and become Antichrist [Note: [Col. 0686] Compare Jerome, *On Daniel* XI, and Sulpicius Severus, *History*, book 2, ch. 29.].

Others do not think that he was killed, but rather that he was removed and made to appear to have been killed; they believe that he is being kept alive in the vigor of the same age at which he was when he was thought to have died, until he is revealed at his proper time and restored to the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0686] See Suetonius, *Nero*, ch. 57, and Tacitus, *Histories*, book 2, ch. 8.].

But I find the great presumption of those who hold these opinions exceedingly strange. Nevertheless, what the Apostle says, “Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst,” is not absurdly believed to have been said about the Roman Empire—as though he had said, “Only let the one who now rules continue to rule, until he is removed from the midst,” that is, until he is taken away.

“And then the lawless one will be revealed”: no one doubts that Antichrist is signified by this.

Others, however, do not think that what he says, “You know what restrains him,” and “the mystery of iniquity is at work,” refers to anything except the evil and false people who are in the Church, until they reach such a number as to provide Antichrist with a large people. They believe that this is the mystery of iniquity because it appears hidden.

They also think that the Apostle exhorts the faithful to persevere steadfastly in the faith they hold when he says, “Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst”—that is, until the mystery of iniquity, which is now hidden, comes out from the midst of the Church.

For they believe that the mystery itself includes what the evangelist John says in his Epistle: “Children, it is the last hour; and as you heard that Antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have arisen; from this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John II, 18–19).

Therefore, just as before the end, in this hour that John calls the last, many heretics went out from the midst of the Church, whom he calls many antichrists, so then all who will belong not to Christ but to that final Antichrist will go out from there, and then he will be revealed.

4. Thus one person conjectures one thing and another person another concerning the Apostle’s obscure words. Yet there is no doubt that he said this: Christ will not come to judge the living and the dead unless his adversary Antichrist first comes to deceive the dead in soul, although the fact that they will be deceived by him already belongs to the hidden judgment of God.

For his coming will be, as has been said, according to the working of Satan, with every power, signs, and lying wonders, and with every deceit of unrighteousness for those who are perishing. Then Satan will be released, and through that Antichrist he will work with all his power, wondrously indeed, but falsely.

There is often a question whether the expressions “signs and wonders of falsehood” are used because he will deceive mortal senses through apparitions, making it appear that he does what he does not do; or because those very signs, even if they are genuine wonders, will lead those who believe to falsehood, since they will not know the power of the devil and will think that such things could have been done only by divine power—especially when he has received a power as great as he never previously possessed [Note: [Col. 0687] Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and the manuscripts read this way. Erasmus and the Louvain editions have “he will receive power.”].

For when fire fell from heaven and in one assault consumed the holy Job’s entire household together with his great flocks, and when a whirlwind rushed upon the house, bringing it down and killing his children (Job I), these were not apparitions. Yet they were works of Satan, to whom God had given this power.

Why, then, these wonders and signs are called signs of falsehood will become clear at that time. But whatever the reason for the expression, those who deserve to be deceived will be deceived by those signs and wonders:

“Because,” he says, “they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved.”

The Apostle did not hesitate to add:

“And therefore God will send them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie” [Note: [Col. 0687] Ambrose, John Chrysostom, Theodoret, others, and Jerome himself, in question 11 of Epistle 151 to Algasia, explain this as referring to the Jews. Coquaeus.].

God will send it because God will permit the devil to do these things, by his own just judgment, although the devil does them according to an unjust and wicked plan.

“So that they may be judged,” he says, “all who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness.”

Therefore, those judged will be deceived, and those deceived will be judged. But the judged will be deceived by those judgments of God that are secretly just and justly secret—judgments by which, from the beginning of the rational creature’s sin, he has never ceased to judge. The deceived, however, will be judged by the final and manifest judgment through Jesus Christ, who will judge most justly, although he was judged most unjustly.

## CHAPTER XX — What the Same Apostle Taught in His First Epistle to the Same People concerning the Resurrection of the Dead

1. But this Apostle said nothing here about the resurrection of the dead. Writing to the same people in his first Epistle, however, he says:

“We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.

“For we say this to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have already fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead in Christ will rise first [Note: [Col. 0688] Our manuscripts read *primi*, “first,” masculine plural.]; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. IV, 12–16).

These apostolic words most clearly show that the resurrection of the dead will take place when the Lord Christ comes, certainly to judge the living and the dead.

2. But it is commonly asked whether those whom Christ will find alive here—those whose person the Apostle was representing in himself and in those who would then be living with him—will never die at all; or whether, at that very moment when they are caught up with the risen in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, they will pass through death into immortality with miraculous speed [Note: [Col. 0688] See Letter 193, to Mercator; *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question 3; and elsewhere.]. For it cannot be said that it is impossible for them, while being carried upward through the air, both to die and to revive within that interval. For what he says, “And so we shall always be with the Lord,” must not be understood as though he had said that we would always remain with the Lord in the air; for he himself certainly will not remain there, since he is passing through it as he comes. We shall go out to meet him as he comes, not remain with him as he stays there. Rather, “we shall be with the Lord” means that we shall possess everlasting bodies [Note: [Col. 0688] Printed editions read, “always possessing.” “Always” is absent from the manuscripts.] in whatever place we are with him. 

The Apostle himself seems to press us toward this interpretation—namely, that even those whom the Lord will find alive here will, within that brief interval, both suffer death and receive immortality—when he says, “In Christ all shall be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 22), while elsewhere, speaking of this very resurrection of the bodies, he says, “What you sow is not made alive unless it dies” (ibid., 36). How, then, will those whom Christ finds alive here be made alive through immortality, even if they do not die, when we see that this was said for that very reason: “What you sow is not made alive unless it dies”? [Note: [Col. 0688] Printed editions have, “unless it first dies.” The word “first” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.]

Or, if we rightly say that only those human bodies are sown which, by dying in whatever manner, return to the earth—as is also expressed in the sentence divinely pronounced against the transgressor, the father of the human race, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19)—then we must admit that those whom Christ will find, at his coming, not yet departed from their bodies are not held by these words of the Apostle or by those from Genesis. For, being caught up into the clouds above, they are certainly not sown, since they neither go into the earth nor return to it—whether they experience no death whatsoever, or die for a little while in the air.

3. But another difficulty again arises from what the same Apostle said when speaking to the Corinthians about the resurrection of the bodies: “We shall all rise,” or, as other manuscripts read, “We shall all sleep” [Note: [Col. 0689] See Letter 205, to Consentius, no. 14, and *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question 3, no. 4.] (I Cor. XV, 51). Since resurrection cannot occur unless death has preceded it, and since in that passage we cannot understand “sleep” except as death, how will all either sleep or rise, if so many whom Christ will find in the body will neither sleep nor rise?

If, therefore, we believe that the saints who will be found alive when Christ comes and who will be caught up to meet him will, in that very rapture, leave their mortal bodies and immediately return to those same bodies made immortal, we shall encounter no difficulty in the Apostle’s words—whether where he says, “What you sow is not made alive unless it dies,” or where he says, “We shall all rise,” or, “We shall all sleep.” For they too will not be made alive through immortality unless they first die, however briefly; and consequently they will not be excluded from the resurrection, which is preceded by sleep [Note: [Col. 0689] Manuscripts have, “which they precede by sleeping.”], although that sleep will be extremely brief, yet not nonexistent.

Why should it seem incredible to us that that multitude of bodies will somehow be sown in the air and there immediately revive immortally and incorruptibly, when we believe what the same Apostle most plainly says [Note: [Col. 0689] Printed editions have, “the Apostle elsewhere most plainly says.” “Elsewhere” is absent from the manuscripts.]: that the resurrection will occur “in the twinkling of an eye” (I Cor. XV, 52), and that the dust of the bodies of the ancient dead will return, with such ease and such immeasurable speed, to limbs destined to live without end?

Nor do we think that those future saints will be exempt from the sentence spoken to humanity, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” if the bodies of those who die do not fall back into the earth, but, just as they die in the very act of being caught up, so also rise again while they are being carried into the air. “To earth you shall go” means: you shall go, once life has been lost, into that which you were before you received life. That is, you shall be lifeless as you were before you were animated.

For God breathed the breath of life into the face of the earth when the human being was made a living soul—as though it were said: “You are animated earth, which you were not; you shall be lifeless earth, as you were.” This is what all the bodies of the dead are even before they decay; and so those bodies too will be, if they die, wherever they die: when they are deprived of life, which they will immediately receive again.

Thus they will go into the earth, because from living human beings they will become earth—just as what becomes ash goes into ash, what becomes old goes into old age, and what becomes a potsherd from clay goes into a potsherd. We speak in this way of hundreds of other things.

But how what we now conjecture as best we can, according to the limits of our reasoning, will actually happen—that will be the time when we shall be able to know. If we wish to be Christians, we must believe that the resurrection of the dead will take place in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0689] Manuscripts have, “that the resurrection will also take place in the flesh.”—Correct. M.] when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead. But our faith concerning this matter is not therefore empty merely because we cannot fully comprehend how it will happen.

Now, however, as we promised above [Col. 0690], we must show, insofar as seems sufficient, what the ancient prophetic books also foretold concerning this final judgment of God. As I think, this will not require so much time to discuss and explain if the reader takes care to make use of what we have already set forth.

## CHAPTER XXI.—What the Prophet Isaiah said concerning the resurrection of the dead and the retribution of judgment

1. The prophet Isaiah says: “The dead shall rise, and those who were in the tombs shall rise; and all who are in the earth shall rejoice. For the dew that is from you is healing for them; but the earth of the impious shall fall” (Isa. XXVI, 19, according to the Septuagint).

All the preceding part refers to the resurrection of the blessed. But what he says, “The earth of the impious shall fall,” is rightly understood as meaning, “The bodies of the impious shall be overtaken by the ruin of condemnation.”

Now, if we wish to examine more carefully and distinctly what was said concerning the resurrection of the good, the statement “The dead shall rise” should be referred to the first resurrection, while what follows, “and those who were in the tombs shall rise,” should be referred to the second. And if we seek also those holy people whom the Lord will find alive here, what he adds will appropriately be assigned to them: “And all who are in the earth shall rejoice; for the dew that is from you is healing for them.” Here we most correctly understand “healing” as immortality. For that is perfect healing which is not restored by nourishment as by daily medicines.

Again, giving hope first to the good and then terrifying the wicked concerning the day of judgment, the same prophet speaks as follows:

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace and like an overflowing stream the glory of the nations. Their children shall be carried upon shoulders and shall be comforted upon knees. As a mother comforts someone, so I will comfort you; and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted. And you shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall sprout like grass” [Note: [Col. 0690] So read our manuscripts; the Benedictine Fathers consistently have here, “like grass,” below. M.] “And the hand of the Lord shall be known to those who worship him, and he shall threaten the stubborn. For behold, the Lord shall come like fire, and his chariots like a storm, to repay vengeance in wrath and destruction in a flame of fire. For in the fire of the Lord all the earth shall be judged, and in his sword all flesh; many shall be wounded by the Lord” (ibid. LXVI, 12–16, according to the Septuagint).

In the promise made to the good, “a river of peace” must certainly be understood as the abundance of that peace beyond which no greater peace can exist. At the end we shall be watered by this peace, of which we spoke at length in the preceding book. He says that this river turns toward those to whom he promises such great blessedness that we understand all things to be satisfied by this river in the region of that happiness which is in heaven.

But because the peace of incorruption and immortality will also flow from there into earthly bodies, he says that this river turns toward them, so that it may, as it were, pour from above over what is below and make human beings equal to the angels.

By Jerusalem, too, let us understand not that Jerusalem which is in bondage with her children, but our free mother, which, according to the Apostle, is eternal in heaven (Gal. IV, 26). There, after the labors of mortal troubles and cares, we shall be comforted, as though carried as her little ones upon her shoulders and knees. For, inexperienced and new as we are, that blessedness unfamiliar to us will receive us with the tenderest assistance.

There we shall see, and our heart shall rejoice. He did not specify what we shall see; but what else except God? Thus the evangelical promise will be fulfilled in us: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). All those things that we do not now see, though we believe them, we conceive according to the measure of human capacity as far less than they are and incomparably less than they truly are.

“And you shall see,” he says, “and your heart shall rejoice.” Here you believe; there you shall see.

2. But because he said, “And your heart shall rejoice,” lest we should think that those good things of Jerusalem pertain only to our spirit, he adds: “And your bones shall sprout like grass.” Here he briefly touched upon the resurrection of the bodies, as though restoring what he had not said. For we shall not see when the resurrection has not yet occurred; we shall see when it has occurred [Note: [Col. 0691] Printed editions have, “they shall sprout, but when they have sprouted.” The manuscripts have, “it shall sprout, but when it has sprouted,” with “resurrection” understood.].

He had already spoken above of the new heaven and the new earth, when, in repeatedly and variously describing what is promised to the saints at the end [Note: [Col. 0691] Several manuscripts have, “he said repeatedly.”], he said:

“There shall be a new heaven and a new earth, and they shall not remember the former things, nor shall they come” [Note: [Col. 0691] In the manuscripts here and below, book 22, chapter 3, “nor shall it come.” The Septuagint has *oud’ epélthē* (“nor shall it come”).] “into their heart; but they shall find joy and exultation in it. Behold, I will make Jerusalem an exultation and my people a joy; and I will exult in Jerusalem and rejoice in my people; and no longer shall the voice of weeping be heard in her” (Isa. LXV, 17–19, according to the Septuagint)—and the other things which some try to refer to those carnal thousand years [Note: [Col. 0691] Only the Lovaniensis edition, with the order of the words changed, has, “which some carnal people refer to those thousand years,” as though Augustine were calling the authors of this interpretation carnal. They followed Papias of Hierapolis (as Eusebius testifies, *Ecclesiastical History* 3.33, and Jerome in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers), Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*; Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 5.32; Tertullian, *On the Hope of the Faithful* and *Against Marcion* 3.24; Lactantius, *Institutes* 7.24 and 26, and others. Jerome teaches in his commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 19, that one should depart from them in this matter only modestly and prudently: “Although,” he says, “the Jews think that a golden and jeweled Jerusalem is to be restored, and again the sacrifices and offerings, the marriages of the saints, and the earthly reign of the Lord Savior, although we do not follow these things, nevertheless we cannot condemn them, because many ecclesiastical men and martyrs have said these things; let each person abound in his own understanding, and let all things be reserved for the Lord’s judgment.”]

For figurative expressions are mingled with literal ones in the prophetic manner, so that sober attention may reach spiritual understanding through a certain useful and salutary labor. Carnal laziness, however, or the sluggishness of an uneducated and untrained mind, satisfied with the surface of the letter, thinks that nothing inward need be sought.

This is enough to say concerning the prophetic words written before this passage. But in the passage from which we digressed, after saying, “And your bones shall sprout like grass,” thereby showing that he was recalling the resurrection of the flesh, but of the good [Note: [Col. 0691] So read the manuscripts. Printed editions have, “but only of the good.”], he added: “And the hand of the Lord shall be known to those who worship him.”

What is this except the hand that distinguishes his worshipers from those who despise him? Concerning these he continues: “And he shall threaten the stubborn,” or, as another translator says, “the unbelieving.”

He will not merely threaten them then; rather, what is now uttered as a threat will then be fulfilled effectively. “For behold,” he says, “the Lord shall come like fire, and his chariots like a storm, to repay vengeance in wrath and destruction in a flame of fire. For in the fire of the Lord all the earth shall be judged, and in his sword all flesh; many shall be wounded by the Lord.”

Whether by fire, storm, or sword, he signifies the punishment of judgment, since he says that the Lord himself will come like fire—certainly to those for whom his coming will be punitive. His chariots—for they are spoken of in the plural—we may appropriately understand as the angelic ministries.

But when he says that all the earth and all flesh will be judged in his fire and by his sword, we should not here understand spiritual people and saints, but earthly and carnal people, of whom it is said, “Those who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. III, 19), and, “To set the mind according to the flesh is death” (Rom. VIII, 6), and whom the Lord altogether calls flesh when he says, “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3).

What is placed here, “Many shall be wounded by the Lord,” signifies that the second death will occur through this wound.

Fire, sword, and wound can indeed also be understood in a good sense. For the Lord said that he wished to cast fire into the world (Luke XII, 49). And tongues divided as if by fire appeared to them when the Holy Spirit came (Acts II, 3). And the same Lord says, “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X, 34). Scripture calls the word of God a two-edged sword (Heb. IV, 12), because of the twofold edge of the two Testaments. And in the Song of Songs the holy Church says that she has been wounded by love, as though pierced by the force of love (Song of Songs II, 5, according to the Septuagint).

But here, when we read or hear that the Lord is to come as an avenger, it is clear how these things are to be understood.

3. After briefly mentioning those who will be consumed by this judgment, signifying sinners and impious people under the figure of foods forbidden in the Old Law—foods from which they did not abstain—he goes back to the beginning and recapitulates the grace of the New Testament, carrying and bringing his discourse to its conclusion, from the first coming of the Savior up to the final judgment, which is now our subject.

For he relates that the Lord says that he is coming to gather all the nations, and that they will come and see his glory (Isa. LXVI, 17–18). For, as the Apostle says, all have sinned and lack the glory of God (Rom. III, 23).

He also says that he will leave signs among them, so that, marveling at them, they may believe in him; and that he will send from them those who have been saved to various nations and to distant islands which have not heard his name or seen his glory; and that they will announce his glory among the nations.

They will bring the brothers of those to whom he was speaking—that is, the brothers in faith of the elect Israelites, under God the Father—from all the nations as a gift to the Lord, upon animals and in vehicles. These animals and vehicles are rightly understood as divine aids through ministries of every kind, whether divine, angelic, or human [Col. 0693], to the holy city Jerusalem, which is now spread throughout the earth in the holy faithful.

For wherever they are divinely aided, there they believe; and wherever they believe, there they come.

The Lord compared them, as though by analogy, to the children of Israel offering their sacrifices to him with psalms in his house—which the Church now does everywhere—and he promised that from them he would take priests and Levites. We see this likewise happening now.

For they are not chosen according to flesh and blood, as the first priests were according to the order of Aaron, but, as was fitting in the New Testament, where Christ is the high priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX, 4), we now see priests and Levites chosen according to whatever merit divine grace has conferred upon each. They must be judged not by this name—which the unworthy often attain—but by that holiness which is not common to the good and the wicked.

4. After he had spoken of this clear and very familiar mercy of God now being bestowed upon the Church, he also promised the ends toward which, after the distinction between good and evil has been made by the final judgment, we shall come. The prophet says—or the prophet himself speaks concerning the Lord:

“For just as the new heaven and the new earth shall remain before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name stand; and there shall be month after month and sabbath after sabbath. All flesh shall come to worship before me in Jerusalem, says the Lord; and they shall go out and see the limbs of the people who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh” (Isa. LXVI, 22–24, according to the Septuagint).

To this the prophet brought his book to its conclusion, just as the age will be brought to its conclusion. Some translators, however, translated not “the limbs of people,” but “the corpses of men” [Note: [Col. 0693] So in the Vulgate.], thereby signifying the evident bodily punishment. Yet a corpse is not ordinarily called anything except lifeless flesh, whereas those bodies will be alive; otherwise they could feel no torments—unless, perhaps, because they will be the bodies of the dead, that is, of those who will fall into the second death, they may also, not improperly, be called corpses.

This is the meaning of the statement which I cited above from the same prophet: “The earth of the impious shall fall.” Who does not see that corpses are so called from falling? [Note: [Col. 0693] Above, at the beginning of chapter 10 of this book.]

That those translators substituted “men” for “people” is obvious. For no one will say that transgressing women will not be present in that punishment. Rather, the two sexes are included under the more prominent term, especially since woman was made from man.

But what most concerns the matter is this: when it is said of the good also, “All flesh shall come,” because this people will consist of every kind of human being—for not all human beings will be there, since more will be in punishments—when, as I began to say, flesh is named both in connection with the good and limbs or corpses in connection with the wicked, it is plainly declared that the judgment by which good and evil will be separated into their respective destinations will take place after the resurrection of the flesh. The faith in that resurrection is fully confirmed by these terms applied to things [Col. 0694].

## CHAPTER XXII.—What the departure of the saints will be like when they go to see the punishments of the wicked

But how will the good go out to see the punishments of the wicked? Will they leave those blessed dwellings by bodily movement and proceed to places of punishment, so that they may observe the torments of the wicked with a bodily presence? Certainly not. Rather, they will go out through knowledge.

For this word signifies that those who will be tormented will be outside. Therefore the Lord also calls those places “the outer darkness” (Matt. XXV, 30). Opposed to this is the entrance of which it is said to the good servant, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid., 21). The wicked should not be thought to enter there so that they may be known; rather, knowledge goes out to them, as it were, through which the good will know them, because they will know what is outside.

Those who are in punishments will not know what is happening within, in the joy of the Lord. But those who are in that joy will know what is happening outside, in the outer darkness. Thus it is said, “They shall go out,” because even those who are outside them will certainly not be hidden from them [Note: [Col. 0694] Several manuscripts have, “those things which will be outside them.”].

If they could know these things, which had not yet happened, through what God was—however little of God there was in their mortal minds—how will the immortal saints then fail to know what has happened, when God will be all in all (I Cor. XV, 28)?

Therefore, in that blessedness of the saints, their seed and their name shall stand: the seed, namely, of which John says, “And his seed remains in him” (I John III, 9); and the name of which it is said through this Isaiah, “I will give them an everlasting name” (Isa. LVI, 5).

And there shall be for them month after month and sabbath after sabbath, as moon after moon and rest after rest. They themselves will be both of these, when they pass from the old and temporal shadows into those new and eternal lights.

In the punishments of the wicked, the unquenchable fire and the living worm have been explained in different ways by different people. Some have referred both to the body, others both to the soul; still others have referred the fire properly to the body and the worm figuratively to the soul, which seems more credible. But there is no time now to dispute this distinction [Note: [Col. 0694] Printed editions have, “this is not the time for this.” “This” is absent from the manuscripts.].

We undertook to fill this volume with the final judgment by which the good and the wicked will be separated. The rewards and punishments themselves must be discussed more carefully elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—What Daniel prophesied concerning the persecution of Antichrist, the judgment of God, and the kingdom of the saints

1. Daniel prophesies concerning this final judgment in such a way that he also foretells the prior coming of Antichrist and carries his narrative forward to the eternal kingdom of the saints.

When, in a prophetic vision, he had seen four beasts signifying four kingdoms, and the fourth overcome by a certain king who is recognized as Antichrist, and after these things the eternal kingdom of the Son of Man, who is understood to be Christ, he says:

“My spirit was horrified—I, Daniel—in my condition” [Note: [Col. 0695] Printed editions have, “in my dullness.” The manuscripts more correctly have, “in my condition”; for the Greek Septuagint has *hexei* (“condition” or “state”).], “and the visions of my head troubled me. And I approached,” he says, “one of those standing there, and I sought the truth from him concerning all these things; and he told me the truth.”

Then, as though explaining to him what he had heard from the one whom he had questioned about all these matters, he says:

“These four great beasts are four kingdoms that shall arise upon the earth, which shall be taken away, and the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom; and they shall possess it forever and unto the age of ages.

“And I was carefully inquiring,” he says, “about the fourth beast, which was different from every beast, exceedingly terrifying, with iron teeth and bronze claws, devouring and crushing and trampling the remainder with its feet; and about its ten horns, which were on its head; and about the other horn that arose and uprooted three of the former ones; and about that horn which had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, whose appearance was greater than the others.

“I saw, and that horn was making war against the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came and gave the kingdom to the saints of the Most High; and the time arrived, and the saints took possession of the kingdom.”

Daniel said that he had asked these things. Then, immediately adding what he had heard, he says:

“And he said”—that is, the one whom he had questioned answered and said—“The fourth beast shall be the fourth kingdom upon the earth, which shall surpass all kingdoms. It shall devour the whole earth, trample it, and crush it.

“And its ten horns are ten kings who shall arise; and after them another shall arise, who shall overcome in evils all those who were before him [Note: [Col. 0695] Printed editions have, “with his evils,” or “in his evils.” “His” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Septuagint.]; and he shall humble three kings; and he shall speak words against the Most High, and wear down the saints of the Most High.

“And he shall presume to change times and law; and they shall be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time.
