“And judgment shall sit, and they shall remove his authority” [Note: [Col. 0695] Printed editions have, “he shall remove.” The manuscripts have, “they shall remove.” The Greek is *metastēsousi* (“they shall remove”).] “to destroy and annihilate it to the end. And the kingdom, power, and greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the saints of the Most High.

“And his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom; and all authorities shall serve and obey him.

“Thus far,” he says, “is the end of the matter. I, Daniel, was greatly troubled by my thoughts, and my appearance was changed within me; and I kept the matter in my heart” (Dan. VII, 15–28).

Some have explained those four kingdoms as the Assyrians, Persians, Macedonians, and Romans. Those who wish to know how appropriately they have done so should read the book of the presbyter Jerome on Daniel, written with sufficient care and learning.

Yet concerning the most savage kingdom of Antichrist against the Church, which must be endured for only a brief period until, at God’s final judgment, the saints receive the eternal kingdom, no one who reads this even half-asleep is permitted to doubt.

For the expression “a time, times, and half a time” is shown to mean one year, two years, and half a year, and therefore three and a half years, also by the number of days given later; sometimes Scripture expresses this by the number of months as well.

The word “times” appears to have been used here indefinitely in Latin, but it was expressed in the dual number, which Latin does not possess. The Greeks have this number, and the Hebrews are said to have it as well. Thus “times” was said as though “two times” had been said.

I confess, however, that I fear we may perhaps be mistaken concerning the ten kings whom Antichrist seems likely to find as though they were ten men, and that he may therefore arrive unexpectedly, with so many kings not existing in the Roman world. For what if this number ten signifies the totality of kings, after whom he will come, just as totality is often signified by a thousand, a hundred, or seven, and by various other numbers which it is not necessary to mention now?

2. In another passage the same Daniel says:

“And there shall be a time of tribulation such as has not existed from the time that a nation came upon the earth until that time. And at that time all your people who are found written in the book shall be saved. And many of those sleeping in the mound of the earth shall rise: some to everlasting life, and others to everlasting reproach and shame. And those who understand shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and many of the righteous like the stars forever” (Dan. XII, 1–3).

This passage is very similar to the evangelical statement, and concerns specifically the resurrection of the bodies of the dead. For those who are said there to be in the tombs are the same as those who are here said to be sleeping in the mound of the earth—or, as others have interpreted it, in the dust of the earth. And just as it is said there, “They shall come forth,” so here it is said, “They shall rise.”

Just as there it says, “Those who have done good things, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment,” so here too: “Some to everlasting life, and others to everlasting reproach and everlasting shame” (John V, 28–29).

It should not be thought that there is a difference because there it says, “All who are in the tombs,” whereas here the prophet does not say “all,” but “many of those sleeping in the mound of the earth.” Scripture sometimes uses “many” in place of “all.” Thus it was said to Abraham, “I have made you the father of many nations,” while elsewhere it says, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XVII, 5; XXII, 18).

Concerning such a resurrection, this same prophet Daniel is told shortly afterward:

“And you, come and rest; for there are still days until the completion of the consummation. And you shall rest and rise in your portion at the end of the days” (Dan. XII, 43).

## CHAPTER XIV.—What is prophesied in the Psalms of David concerning the end of this age and the final judgment of God

1. Many things are said in the Psalms concerning the final judgment, but most of them only in passing and briefly. Yet I will by no means pass over in silence what is stated there most plainly concerning the end of this age:

“In the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment, and you shall change them like a cloak, and they shall be changed. But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 26–28).

Why is Porphyry—who praises the piety of the Hebrews, by which they worship as great, true, and terrifying even to the gods themselves the God whom they worship—accusing Christians of the greatest folly on the basis even of the oracles of his own gods, because we say that this world is destined to perish? [Note: [Col. 0696] See above, book 19, chapter 23.]

Behold, in the writings of the piety of the Hebrews [Col. 0697], it is said to God, whom, as that philosopher admits, even the gods themselves dread: “The heavens are the works of your hands; they shall perish.”

When the heavens perish, will the world not perish, since those same heavens are its higher and more secure part? If this statement displeases Jupiter, who, as that philosopher writes, is blamed in Christian belief by an oracle of supposedly greater authority, why does he not similarly blame as folly the wisdom of the Hebrews, in whose most pious books this statement is found?

Moreover, if in that wisdom [Note: [Col. 0697] Printed editions have, “in the wisdom of the Jews.” “Of the Jews” is absent from the manuscripts.] which pleases Porphyry so greatly that he praises it even by the voices of his gods, it is read that the heavens will perish, why is this deception so exceedingly vain that they condemn among the Christian beliefs, whether among other things or above all else, the belief that the world will perish—a world whose heavens cannot perish unless the world itself perishes?

In the sacred writings which are properly ours, not the Hebrew writings held in common with us—that is, in the evangelical and apostolic books—we read, “The form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 31); we read, “The world is passing away” (I John II, 17); we read, “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. XXII, 35).

But I think that “is passing away,” “is passing,” and “shall pass away” are sometimes milder expressions than “shall perish.”

In the Epistle of the Apostle Peter, where the world that then existed is said to have perished when it was overwhelmed by water (II Pet. III, 6), it is sufficiently clear both what part of the world is signified by the whole, to what extent it is said to have perished, and which heavens are reserved and kept for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly people.

And when he says shortly afterward, “The day of the Lord will come like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with great violence, while the elements, burning, will be dissolved, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up”; and then adds, “Since all these things are perishing, what sort of people ought you to be?” (ibid., 10–11), those heavens may be understood as destined to perish which he said were reserved for fire. The elements that will burn may be understood as those that subsist in this lowest part of the world, stormy and turbulent, in which he said that those heavens were kept, while the higher heavens remain safe and intact, containing the stars in their firmament.

For the statement written elsewhere, that the stars will fall from heaven (Matt. XXIV, 29)—apart from the fact that it can be understood in another and much more probable way—more clearly indicates that those heavens will remain, if the stars are to fall from them; unless the expression is figurative, which is more credible, or unless something is to occur in this lower heaven, something certainly more marvelous than what happens now.

Thus also Virgil writes:

“A star, carrying a torch with much light, ran on, and hid itself in the Idaean forest” (*Aeneid* II, lines 694, 696).

But the passage from the Psalm that I cited seems to leave no heaven unmentioned as destined to perish. For where it says, “The heavens are the works of your hands; they shall perish,” just as none of them is excluded from the work of God, so none is excluded from destruction.

They will not deign, on the basis of the Apostle Peter’s statement—whom they intensely hate—to defend the piety of the Hebrews, which has been approved by the oracles of their gods [Col. 0698], so that at least the whole world may not be thought destined to perish by understanding a part as signified by the whole in the words, “They shall perish,” with only the lowest heavens destined to perish. This is just as in that apostolic Epistle a part is understood by the whole when the world is said to have perished in the flood, although only its lower part, together with its heavens, perished.

But because, as I have said, they will not deign to do this—lest they either approve the meaning of the Apostle Peter or grant to the final conflagration as much power as we say the flood possessed, since they maintain that the entire human race cannot perish through any waters or flames—there remains only for them to say that their gods praised the wisdom of the Hebrews for this reason: they had not read this Psalm.

2. In the forty-ninth Psalm also, what is said is understood of God’s final judgment:

> “God shall come manifestly, our God, and shall not keep silence. Fire shall burn before him, and a mighty tempest round about him. He shall summon heaven above, and the earth, to distinguish his people. Gather to him his righteous ones, who establish his covenant over sacrifices” (Ps. 49:3–5).

We understand this of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom we expect to come from heaven to judge the living and the dead. For he shall come manifestly to judge justly among the just and the unjust—the one who first came hidden, to be judged unjustly by the unjust. He himself, I say, shall come manifestly and shall not keep silence; that is, he shall appear openly in the voice of a judge. Previously, when he came hidden, he remained silent before the judge, when he was led like a sheep to the slaughter and, like a lamb before its shearer, was without a voice, as we read that it was prophesied of him through Isaiah (Isa. 53:7) and see fulfilled in the Gospel (Matt. 26:63).

Concerning the fire and the tempest, when we were treating something similar in Isaiah’s prophecy and explaining how these things should be understood, we have already spoken (ch. 21). But what is said, “He shall summon heaven above”—since the saints and the righteous are rightly called heaven—surely means what the Apostle says: “Together with them we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thess. 4:16). For according to the surface meaning of the letter, how is heaven summoned “above,” as though it could be anywhere but above?

But if what follows, “and the earth, to distinguish his people,” is understood as though only “he shall summon” were supplied—that is, “he shall summon heaven and the earth,” without supplying “above”—the meaning seems, according to sound faith, to be that heaven is understood as those who will judge with him, and earth as those who will be judged. Thus, “He shall summon heaven above” should not here be understood as “He shall snatch them into the air,” but as “He shall raise them to judicial seats.”

The phrase may also be understood in this way: “He shall summon heaven above,” that is, he shall summon the angels in the heavenly and exalted places, with whom he will descend to execute judgment; “he shall also summon the earth,” that is, the human beings on earth who are to be judged.

But if both expressions are to be supplied when it says “and the earth”—that is, “he shall summon” and “above,” so that the sense is, “He shall summon heaven above, and he shall summon the earth above”—I think nothing better can be understood than the human beings [Note: All the manuscripts read “than all human beings.”] who will be caught up to meet Christ in the air, with heaven referring to their souls and earth to their bodies. Moreover, what is it to “distinguish his people” except to separate the good from the evil by judgment, as sheep from goats?

Then the address is turned to the angels: “Gather to him his righteous ones.” Certainly so great a work must be accomplished through angelic ministry. But if we ask which righteous ones the angels will gather to him, the Psalm says: “Those who establish his covenant over sacrifices.”

This is the whole life of the righteous: to establish God’s covenant over sacrifices. Either works of mercy are placed “over sacrifices,” that is, preferred to sacrifices, in accordance with God’s saying, “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6).

[Note: The printed editions read “I desire mercy more than sacrifice.” The manuscripts lack the word “more,” which is also absent from the Septuagint.]

Or, if “over sacrifices” is understood to mean “in sacrifices”—just as something done on earth is said to be done “over the earth,” although it is certainly done on earth—then plainly the works of mercy themselves are sacrifices by which God is pleased,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “by which God is pleased,” rather than “by which God is placated.”]

as I remember having discussed in the tenth book of this work (ch. 6, and elsewhere). In these works the righteous establish God’s covenant, because they perform them on account of the promises contained in his New Covenant.

Therefore, after gathering his righteous ones to himself and placing them at his right hand, Christ will say at the final judgment:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:34–35),

and the other things there presented concerning the good works of the good and their eternal rewards, in the final sentence of the one who judges.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “of those who are to be judged.”]

## CHAPTER XXV — The prophecy of Malachi, by which God’s final judgment is declared, and the purification of certain persons through purifying punishments is mentioned

[Note: The manuscripts read “Malachiel.” At the beginning of the chapter they likewise read “the prophet Malachihel, or Malachi”; some read “or Malachim.” The Vindobonensis, Antwerp, and Erfurt editions read “Malachiel, or Malachias.”]

The prophet Malachias, or Malachi—who was also called the Angel, and whom some believe to have been Ezra the priest, whose other writings have been received into the canon

[Note: The Basel, Antwerp, Erfurt, and manuscript witnesses read “received in the canon.”]

—for Jerome says that this was the opinion of the Hebrews concerning him (Preface to Malachi)—prophesies the final judgment, saying:

> “Behold, he comes, says the Lord Almighty; and who shall endure the day of his coming, or who shall be able to bear it when he appears? For he enters like a refiner’s fire and like the herb of those who wash; and he shall sit refining and cleansing, like gold and silver, and he shall cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver; and they shall be offering sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness. And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall please the Lord, as in former days and as in former years. And I shall draw near to you in judgment, and I shall be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and those who swear falsely in my name; against those who defraud the laborer of his wage

[Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “who defraud the laborers of their wages.” The Basel, Antwerp, and manuscript witnesses read “who defraud the laborer of his wage.” The Greek Septuagint has misthòn misthōtoû, “the wage of the laborer.”]

and oppress widows by force, strike orphans, pervert the judgment of the stranger, and do not fear me, says the Lord Almighty. For I am the Lord your God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:1–6).

From these words it appears more clearly that, in that judgment, certain persons will undergo purifying punishments. For when it is said, “Who shall endure the day of his coming, or who shall be able to bear it when he appears? For he enters like a refiner’s fire and like the herb of those who wash; and he shall sit refining and cleansing, like gold and silver, and he shall cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver,” what else should be understood?

Isaiah says something similar:

> “The Lord shall wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and shall cleanse the blood from their midst by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” (Isa. 4:4).

Unless perhaps we should say that they are cleansed from their filth and, so to speak, refined when the wicked are separated from them by a punitive judgment, so that the segregation and damnation of those others constitutes the purification of these, since thereafter they will live without any further mixture with such people.

But when he says, “He shall cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver, and they shall be offering sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness, and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall please the Lord,” he plainly shows that those who are cleansed will thereafter please the Lord with sacrifices of righteousness, and therefore will themselves be cleansed from the injustice in which they had displeased the Lord. Once cleansed, they themselves will be sacrifices in complete and perfect righteousness. What more acceptable offerings can such people present to God than themselves?

Nevertheless, this question concerning purifying punishments must be postponed to another time so that it may be treated more carefully. By the sons of Levi, Judah, and Jerusalem we must understand the very Church of God, gathered not only from the Hebrews but also from the other nations—not as she is now, when, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8), but as she will then be: like a threshing floor winnowed by the final judgment and thereby purified, including those cleansed by fire for whom such purification is necessary. Thus there will be no one at all who offers a sacrifice for his sins. For all who offer such sacrifices are evidently in sins, for the remission of which they offer; and when they have offered them and the offering has been accepted by God, then those sins are remitted.

## CHAPTER XXVI — The sacrifices which the saints will offer to God and which will please him as in former days and former years

1. Wishing to show that his city would not then remain in its present condition, God said that the sons of Levi would offer sacrifices in righteousness. Therefore they will not offer them in sin, and consequently not for sin.

From what he adds immediately afterward—“And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall please the Lord, as in former days and as in former years”—it can be understood that the Jews vainly promise themselves the former times of their sacrifices according to the law of the Old Testament. For at that time they offered sacrifices not in righteousness but in sins, since they offered them especially and primarily for sins. Indeed, even the priest himself, whom we must surely believe to have been more righteous than the others, according to God’s command regularly offered first for his own sins and then for those of the people (Lev. 16:6; Heb. 7:27).

We must therefore explain how the words “as in former days and as in former years” are to be understood. Perhaps they recall the time when the first human beings were in paradise. Then, pure and uncorrupted by every stain and blemish of sin, they offered themselves to God as the purest sacrifices.

But from the time when they were expelled from there because of their transgression, and human nature was condemned in them—apart from the one Mediator, and from those little ones who have undergone the bath of regeneration—“no one is clean from defilement,” as it is written, “not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

If it is answered that those who offer in faith may also rightly be said to offer sacrifices in righteousness—for “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17)—although such a person deceives himself if he says that he has no sin (1 John 1:8), and therefore cannot say that he lives by faith, will anyone claim that this time of faith should be equated with that final time when those who may offer sacrifices in righteousness will be cleansed by the fire of the final judgment?

[Note: The printed editions read “those who offer”; the manuscripts read “those who may offer.”]

Since, after such purification, the righteous are to be believed to have no sin, that time, insofar as it concerns the absence of sin, is comparable to no other time except that when the first human beings lived in the most innocent happiness in paradise before their transgression. Thus it is rightly understood that this is signified by the words “as in former days and as in former years.”

For after Isaiah promised a new heaven and a new earth, among the other matters that he explains there concerning the blessedness of the saints through allegories and enigmas—whose fitting exposition our concern to avoid excessive length prevented us from giving—he says:

> “According to the days of the tree of life shall be the days of my people” (Isa. 65:22).

Who has encountered the sacred Scriptures and does not know where God planted the tree of life? When those human beings were separated from its fruit, at the time when their iniquity drove them from paradise, a terrifying and fiery guard was placed around that same tree.

2. If someone insists that the days of the tree of life mentioned by the prophet Isaiah are the present days of the Church of Christ, and that Christ himself was prophetically called the tree of life because he is the Wisdom of God, of whom Solomon says, “She is a tree of life to all who embrace her” (Prov. 3:18); and if he also insists that the first human beings did not spend any years in paradise, since they were expelled so quickly that they had no son there, and that therefore the time referred to by “as in former days and as in former years” cannot be understood as that time—I pass over this question, lest I be compelled to examine everything at length in order to have the truth of one of these possibilities made clear.

[Note: The Basel, Antwerp, Erfurt, and many manuscript witnesses read “made clear.”]

For I see another meaning, lest we believe that the prophet promised us, as some great gift, the former days and former years of bodily sacrifices.

Those sacrifices of the Old Law, which were commanded to be offered from various animals, unblemished and entirely without defect,

[Note: The manuscripts read as above. The printed editions instead have “from unblemished animals, without any defect,” and so forth.]

signified holy human beings, such as Christ alone was found to be, entirely without sin. Therefore, after the judgment, when those worthy of such purification have also been cleansed by fire, no sin at all will be found in any of the saints. They will thus offer themselves in righteousness, and such sacrifices will be entirely unblemished and without any defect. They will therefore be as in former days and as in former years, when sacrifices were offered in the shadow of this future reality in the utmost purity.

For this will be the purity then present in the immortal flesh and mind of the saints, which was represented in the bodies of those sacrifices.

3. Then, concerning those who are worthy not of purification but of damnation, he says:

> “And I shall draw near to you in judgment, and I shall be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers,”

and so forth. After listing these condemnable crimes, he adds:

> “For I am the Lord your God, and I do not change,”

as though he were saying: “Although your guilt will have changed you for the worse and my grace for the better, I do not change.”

He says that he will be a witness because in his judgment he has no need of witnesses, and a swift witness either because he will come suddenly and the judgment will be extremely swift through the unexpectedness of his arrival, although it had seemed exceedingly delayed, or because he will convict the consciences themselves without any lengthy speech.

“For,” as it is written, “the interrogation of the wicked will be in their thoughts” (Wis. 1:9). And the Apostle says:

> “Their thoughts accusing or even excusing them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 2:15–16).

Thus the Lord should also be understood as a swift witness because, without delay, he will recall to mind the matters by which he will convict and punish the conscience.

## CHAPTER XXVII — The separation of the good and the evil, by which the distinction of the final judgment is declared

That passage also which, while treating another subject, I quoted from this prophet in the eighteenth book (ch. 35, at the end) pertains to the final judgment. He says:

> “They shall be mine, says the Lord Almighty, on the day when I act for acquisition, and I shall choose them as a man chooses his son who serves him. And you shall turn, and you shall see what difference there is between the just and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.

[Note: The printed editions and most manuscripts read “and I shall turn.” This is corrected from the old Corbie manuscript; the Septuagint likewise reads *kai epistraphēsesthe*, “and you shall turn,” as does the Vulgate.] For behold, the day comes, burning like a furnace, and it shall consume them; and all foreigners and all who commit iniquity shall be straw. The coming day shall set them ablaze, says the Lord Almighty, and no root or branch shall be left among them. But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings; and you shall go out and leap like calves released from their bonds. And you shall trample the wicked, and they shall be ashes beneath your feet, says the Lord Almighty” (Mal. 3:17–18; 4:1–3).

This difference between rewards and punishments, which separates the righteous from the unrighteous, is not perceived under this sun, amid the vanity of the present life. But when it becomes clear under that sun of righteousness, in the manifestation of the life to come, there will certainly be a judgment such as has never existed before.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — The law of Moses to be understood spiritually, lest the carnal sense fall into condemnable murmuring

What the same prophet adds—“Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel” (Mal. 4:4)—appropriately recalls the precepts and judgments after such a great future distinction has been declared between observers and despisers of the law. It does so also so that they may learn to understand the law spiritually and find Christ in it, through whom this very distinction between the good and the evil will be made by the judge.

For the same Lord did not say to the Jews without reason:

> “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

By receiving the law carnally, and failing to recognize that its earthly promises were figures of heavenly realities, they fell into such murmuring that they dared to say:

> “He is vain who serves God. And what more have we gained, because we have kept his commandments and walked as suppliants before the face of the Lord Almighty? And now we call the outsiders blessed, and all who commit iniquity are built up” (Mal. 3:14–15).

[Note: The Louvain edition reads “simple”; all the other printed editions and the manuscripts read “suppliants,” in accordance with the Septuagint, *hiketai*.]

Because of these words of theirs, the prophet was in a sense compelled to foretell the final judgment, when the wicked will not even falsely be blessed but will appear openly most miserable, while the good will suffer no temporal misery at all but will enjoy clear and everlasting blessedness.

For above he had also mentioned certain similar words of theirs:

> “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him” (Mal. 2:17).

To such murmuring against God, I say, they came by receiving the law of Moses carnally. Hence he says in the seventy-second Psalm that his feet were almost moved and his steps nearly poured out—that is, toward a fall—because he was jealous of sinners, observing the peace of sinners. Among other things he said:

> “How has God known, and is there knowledge in the Most High?”

He also said:

> “Have I then justified my heart in vain, and washed my hands among the innocent?”

[Note: The Louvain edition reads “among the innocent,” and shortly afterward “I shall understand at the end.” Augustine, however, commonly reads “in the last things” and “among the innocent”; the manuscripts likewise have these readings.]

But to resolve this extremely difficult question, which arises when the good seem miserable and the wicked happy, he says:

> “This is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand in the last things” (Ps. 72:11, 13, 16–17).

At the final judgment it will not be so. In the manifest misery of the wicked and the manifest happiness of the righteous, an entirely different state of affairs from the present will then appear.

## CHAPTER XXIX — The coming of Elijah before the judgment, through whose preaching, by opening the secrets of the Scriptures, the Jews will be converted to Christ

After he had admonished them to remember the law of Moses—for he foresaw that for a long time still they would not receive it spiritually, as they ought—he immediately added:

> “And behold, I shall send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and illustrious day of the Lord comes. He shall turn the heart of the father to the son and the heart of the human being to his neighbor, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth utterly” (Mal. 4:5–6, according to the Septuagint).

It is widely known in the sayings and hearts of the faithful that through this great and wondrous prophet Elijah, after the law has been expounded spiritually for them at the end of time before the judgment, the Jews will believe in the true Christ—that is, in our Christ.

It is not without reason that he is expected to come before the advent of the Savior who is to judge, since it is also not without reason believed that he is still alive.

[Note: The printed editions read “who”; most manuscripts read “because.”] For he was snatched from human affairs in a fiery chariot, as Holy Scripture most clearly testifies (2 Kings 2:11).

When he comes, therefore, by expounding spiritually the law which the Jews now understand carnally, he will “turn the heart of the father to the son,” that is, the heart of the fathers to the sons. The Septuagint translators used the singular in place of the plural.

The meaning is that the sons too—that is, the Jews—will understand the law in the way their fathers understood it, namely, the prophets, among whom Moses himself was also present. Thus the heart of the fathers will be turned to the sons when the fathers’ understanding is brought to the understanding of the sons, and the heart of the sons to their fathers,

[Note: This reading follows the Vulgate.]

when the sons agree with what the fathers understood. The Septuagint, however, says, “and the heart of the human being to his neighbor.”

For fathers and sons are very close to one another. Nevertheless, in the words of the Septuagint translators, who interpreted prophetically, another and even more excellent meaning may be found: Elijah may be understood as turning the heart of God the Father toward the Son—not by causing the Father to love the Son, but by teaching that the Father loves the Son—so that the Jews may love the one whom they previously hated, the same Christ who is ours.

[Note: The printed editions, differing from the manuscripts, read “Christ” and continue below, after “our Christ,” as follows: “because they do not believe him to be God or the Son of God. To them, therefore,” and so forth.]

For at present, in the case of the Jews, God’s heart is turned away from our Christ, because they think this. Therefore his heart will then be turned toward the Son for them, when, with their hearts converted, they learn the Father’s love for the Son.

As for what follows, “and the heart of the human being to his neighbor”—that is, “Elijah will also turn the heart of the human being toward his neighbor”—what can better be understood than the heart of the human being toward the human Christ? Although our God exists in the form of God, he deigned, by taking the form of a servant, also to become our neighbor.

This, then, is what Elijah will do. “Lest perhaps,” he says, “I come and strike the earth utterly.” For those who set their minds on earthly things are earth, as the carnal Jews have been until now. From this fault came those murmurings against God: “The wicked please him,” and “He is vain who serves God” (Mal. 2:17; 3:14).

## CHAPTER XXX — When God is read as saying in the books of the Old Testament that he will judge, the person of Christ is not shown explicitly; but from certain testimonies, in which the Lord God speaks, it becomes unmistakable that he himself is Christ

1. There are many other testimonies of the divine Scriptures concerning God’s final judgment. If I collected them all, it would be excessively long. Let it therefore suffice that we have proved this event to have been foretold both in the new and in the old sacred writings.

But in the old writings it is not expressed as clearly as in the new that judgment will take place through Christ—that is, that Christ the judge will come from heaven. The reason is that when the Lord God says there that he will come, or when the Lord God is said to be coming, Christ is not consequently understood. For the Lord God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, we must not leave this matter unexamined. First, therefore, it must be shown how Jesus Christ speaks as the Lord God in the prophetic books, and yet Jesus Christ is clearly revealed, so that when he is not revealed in this way, but the Lord God is nevertheless said to be coming for that final judgment, Jesus Christ may still be understood.

There is a passage in the prophet Isaiah that clearly demonstrates what I am saying. For God says through the prophet:

> “Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am the first, and I am forever; and my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established heaven. I shall call them, and they shall stand together, and all shall be gathered and shall hear. Who announced these things to them?

[Note: The Basel, Antwerp, and Erfurt editions follow the Greek Septuagint in reading “Who announced these things to them?” The Louvain edition reads “Who announced these things?” omitting “to them”; several manuscripts have “to him” instead.]

> Loving you, I did your will against Babylon, to remove the seed of the Chaldeans. I spoke, and I called; I brought him, and I made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret. When these things happened, I was there. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:12–16).

Clearly, it is he who was speaking as the Lord God. Yet Jesus Christ would not be understood unless he had added, “And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit.”

He said this according to the form of a servant, using a verb in the past tense for a future event, just as it is read in the same prophet:

> “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. 53:7, according to the Septuagint).

He does not say, “He will be led,” but uses a past-tense verb for what was going to happen. Prophecy frequently speaks in this way.

[Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “the prophet”; the other printed editions and the manuscripts read “prophecy.”]

2. There is another passage in Zechariah that clearly demonstrates the same point: the Almighty sent the Almighty. Who sent whom, except God the Father sending God the Son?

For it is written:

> “Thus says the Lord Almighty: After the glory he sent me against the nations that plundered you, for whoever touches you is like one who touches the apple of his eye. Behold, I shall bring my hand against them, and they shall be plunder for those who served them; and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me” (Zech. 2:8–9).

Behold, the Lord Almighty says that he has been sent by the Lord Almighty. Who would dare understand this speaker as anyone other than Christ, speaking, of course, to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel?

For in the Gospel he says:

> “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

Here he compared them to the apple of God’s eye because of the surpassing affection of his love. The Apostles themselves also belonged to this kind of sheep.

But after the glory of his resurrection—which, before it took place, the Evangelist says had not yet occurred: “Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7:39)—he was also sent to the nations in his Apostles.

[Note: The manuscripts have this wording. The printed editions read: “the Evangelist John says, ‘The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.’”] Thus what is read in the Psalm was fulfilled:

> “You shall rescue me from the contradictions of the people; you shall establish me as head of the nations” (Ps. 17:44).

Those who had plundered the Israelites, and to whom the Israelites had been subjected when they were under the nations, were not in turn plundered in the same way; rather, they themselves became plunder for the Israelites.

For he had promised this to the Apostles, saying:

> “I shall make you fishers of human beings” (Matt. 4:19).

And to one of them he said:

> “From now on you shall catch human beings” (Luke 5:10).

Thus they would become plunder—but for good, like vessels snatched from the strong man who had been bound by one stronger than he (Matt. 12:29).

[Note: The Vindobonensis edition and the manuscripts read “would become”; the Antwerp, Erfurt, and Louvain editions read “will become.”]

3. Again, through the same prophet the Lord says:

> “And it shall be on that day that I shall seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem, and I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and mercy; and they shall look upon me because of the things with which they mocked me, and they shall mourn over him with a mourning like that over a beloved one, and they shall grieve with a grief like that over an only-begotten” (Zech. 12:9–10).

Does it belong to anyone but God to destroy all the nations hostile to the holy city Jerusalem, which come against it—that is, oppose it—or, as others have translated, come upon it, that is, in order to subject it to themselves? Does it belong to anyone but God to pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of that same city the Spirit of grace and mercy?

This certainly belongs to God, and it is said through the prophet in the person of God. Yet this God, performing such great and divine works, shows himself to be Christ by adding and saying:

> “And they shall look upon me because of the things with which they mocked me, and they shall mourn over him with a mourning like that over a beloved one—or ‘a loved one’—and they shall grieve with a grief like that over an only-begotten.”

On that day the Jews—including those who will receive the Spirit of grace and mercy—will repent that they mocked Christ in his passion, when they look upon him coming in his majesty and recognize him as the one whom they previously mocked in his humble condition.

Their ancestors, who were responsible for such great impiety, will also see him when they rise again, but they will rise to be punished, not yet to be corrected.

The ancestors themselves, therefore, are not to be understood in this passage where it says, “I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and mercy; and they shall look upon me because of the things with which they mocked me.” Rather, those are meant who will come from their lineage and believe in Christ at that time through Elijah.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “will come.”]

Just as we say to the Jews, “You killed Christ,” although their ancestors did this, so these people will grieve as though they themselves had done what their ancestors did, since they descend from their lineage.

Although, after receiving the Spirit of grace and mercy, they will be believers and will not be condemned with their impious ancestors, they will nevertheless grieve as though they themselves had done what those ancestors did. They will not grieve, therefore, from guilt for the crime, but from an affectionate devotion.

The Septuagint translators said, “And they shall look upon me because of the things with which they mocked me.” In the Hebrew this has been translated:

> “And they shall look upon me whom they pierced.”

[Note: This is the reading of the Vulgate.]

By this word Christ crucified appears more explicitly. But the mockery which the Septuagint preferred to include was not absent from any part of his entire passion. For they mocked him when he was arrested, bound, condemned, dressed in the disgraceful clothing of dishonor, crowned with thorns, struck on the head with a reed, worshiped with mockery while kneeling,

[Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “worshiped with mockery while bending their knees.” The Basel, Antwerp, and manuscript witnesses read “worshiped with mockery while fixing their knees.”]

when he carried his cross, and when he was already hanging on the wood.

Therefore, by not following one translation alone but joining both together, when we read both “they mocked” and “they pierced,” we recognize more fully the truth of the Lord’s passion.

4. When, therefore, in the prophetic writings God is read as coming to execute the final judgment, even if no further distinction of his person is given, Christ must be understood on account of the judgment itself. For even if the Father judges, he will judge through the coming of the Son of Man.

For he himself, through the manifestation of his presence, judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), who will be manifested as a human being to judge, just as he was judged as a human being.

Who else is meant in the passage where God likewise speaks through Isaiah under the name of Jacob and Israel, from whose seed he received a body? It is written:

> “Jacob is my servant; I shall receive him. Israel is my chosen one; my soul has accepted him. I have given my Spirit upon him; he shall bring judgment to the nations. He shall not cry out, nor cease, nor shall his voice be heard outside. He shall not break the bruised reed, and he shall not extinguish the smoking flax; but in truth he shall bring forth judgment. He shall shine forth and shall not be broken until he establishes judgment on earth; and in his name the nations shall hope” (Isa. 42:1–4, according to the Septuagint).

In the Hebrew, “Jacob” and “Israel” are not read there. Instead, what is read is “my servant.” The Septuagint translators, wishing to indicate how this should be understood—namely, that it was said because of the form of a servant in which the Most High humbled himself to the lowest condition—placed the name of the human being by which he might be signified, since that servant-form was assumed from his lineage.

The Holy Spirit was given to him, which was also shown in the form of a dove, as the Gospel bears witness (Matt. 3:16). He brought judgment to the nations because he foretold what was to come, something that had been hidden from the nations.

In his gentleness he did not cry out, yet he did not cease preaching the truth. But his voice was not heard outside, nor is it heard, since those who have been cut off from his body and are outside it do not obey him.

He did not crush or extinguish his persecutors, the Jews, who are compared to a bruised reed because they had lost their integrity and to smoking flax because they had lost their light. He spared them because he had not yet come to judge them but to be judged by them.

[Note: Jerome discusses all these points admirably in his interpretation of this same passage from Isaiah, *Letter* 151 to Algasius, question 2. — Coquaeus.]

In truth he brought forth judgment by foretelling to them when they would be punished if they persisted in their wickedness. His face shone on the mountain (Matt. 17:1–2), and his fame shone throughout the world. He was not broken or crushed, because neither in himself nor in his Church did he yield to his persecutors so as to cease to exist.

Thus what his enemies said, or say, did not and will not happen:

> “When will he die and his name perish?” (Ps. 40:6).

“Until he establishes judgment on earth.” Behold, what we were seeking, hidden away, has been revealed. This is the final judgment, which he will establish on earth when he himself comes from heaven.

We already see fulfilled what was placed last in this passage:

> “And in his name the nations shall hope.”

Through what cannot be denied, let what is shamelessly denied also be believed. For who would have hoped that the nations would hope in Christ’s name when he was being held, bound, beaten, mocked, and crucified; when even the disciples themselves had lost the hope which they had begun to place in him?

What at that time scarcely one robber hoped for on the cross, now nations spread far and wide hope for. And, lest they die eternally, they are marked with the very cross on which he died.

5. Therefore no one either denies or doubts that through Jesus Christ there will be a final judgment such as is foretold in these sacred writings—unless someone, with I know not what incredible [Note: [Col. 0708] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “incredulous.”] obstinacy or blindness, does not believe the same writings, which have already demonstrated their truth to the whole world. At that judgment, or around the time of that judgment, we have learned that the following events will occur: Elijah the Tishbite, the faith of the Jews, Antichrist who will persecute, Christ who will judge; there will be the resurrection of the dead, the separation of the good from the wicked, the conflagration of the world, and its renewal. We must indeed believe that all these things will come to pass; but the experience of events will then teach more clearly in what ways and in what order they occur than human understanding is now able fully to grasp. Nevertheless, I think they will occur in the order in which I have mentioned them.

6. Two books relevant to this work remain for us, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may complete what was promised: one will concern the punishment of the wicked, the other the happiness of the righteous. In these books, insofar as God grants it, human arguments will chiefly be refuted—arguments by which wretched people seem cleverly to gnaw at the things foretold and promised by God, and scorn the nourishment of salutary faith as false and ridiculous. Those who have wisdom according to God, however, possess this greatest argument concerning all things that seem incredible to human beings but are nevertheless contained in the Holy Scriptures, whose truth has already been established in many ways: namely, the truthful omnipotence of God. They are certain that he could in no way have lied in these matters, and that he can do what is impossible for an unbeliever.

# BOOK TWENTY-ONE

On the due end of the city of the devil—namely, the eternal punishment of the damned—and on the arguments of unbelievers against it.

[Col. 0709]

## CHAPTER ONE

On the order of the discussion: that the perpetual punishment of the damned with the devil must be discussed before the eternal happiness of the saints.

When, through Jesus Christ our Lord, the judge of the living and the dead, the two cities have reached their appointed ends—the one belonging to God, the other to the devil—we must discuss in this book, as carefully as divine assistance enables us, what sort of punishment is to be inflicted upon the devil and all who belong to him. I preferred to follow this order so that afterward I might discuss the happiness of the saints, because both will involve bodies; and it seems more incredible that bodies should endure eternal torments than that they should remain in eternal blessedness without any pain. Accordingly, when I have demonstrated that this punishment ought not to be considered incredible, it will greatly assist me in making it much easier to believe that the immortality of the bodies of the saints will be wholly free from suffering.

Nor is this order contrary to the divine utterances. Sometimes the blessedness of the good is placed first, as in the passage: “Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29). Sometimes it is placed afterward, as in the passage: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin, and they will cast them into the furnace of blazing fire” [Note: [Col. 0709] The manuscripts read “blazing,” feminine, rather than the printed edition’s “blazing,” masculine.]; “there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:41–43); and: “So these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (ibid. 25:46). In the Prophets also, if one examines them, one finds now the one order and now the other, though it would take too long to cite them. But I have explained why I chose this order.

## CHAPTER TWO

Whether bodies can remain forever in the burning of fire.

What, then, can I show by which unbelievers may be convinced that living human bodies can not only never be dissolved by death but can also endure the torments of eternal fires? They do not wish us to refer this to the power of the Almighty; instead, they demand to be persuaded by some example. If we reply that there are certainly corruptible living creatures, since they are mortal, which nevertheless live amid fires—and that a certain kind of worm is found in the springs of hot waters, whose heat no one can touch with impunity, while those creatures not only exist there without any injury to themselves but cannot exist outside them—they either refuse to believe it if we are unable to show it, or, if we can demonstrate the things themselves to their eyes or teach them through reliable witnesses, they will still contend, with the same unbelief, that this is not a sufficient example of the matter under discussion. They will say that these animals do not live forever and that they live in those heats without pain, being nourished rather than tormented by elements suited to their nature—as though it were not more incredible to be nourished by such things than to be tormented by them. For it is remarkable to suffer pain in fires and yet live; but it is more remarkable to live in fires without suffering pain. If the latter is believed, why not the former also?

## CHAPTER THREE

Whether bodily pain must be followed by the destruction of the flesh.

1. “There is no body,” they say, “that can suffer pain without being able to die.” And how do we know this? For who is certain about the bodies of demons—whether they suffer pain in them when they confess that they are afflicted by great torments [Note: [Col. 0710] This is established by Jerome, Against Vigilantius and in the Epitaph of Paula; by John Chrysostom, Homily 66, To the People of Antioch; by Cyprian, Letter 2, To Donatus, Letter 76, To Magnus, and his books To Demetrianus and On the Vanity of Idols. Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 2, chapter 16: “Often, after uttering the greatest howls, the demons proclaim that they are being scourged by heat and are already, already departing.” COQUAEUS.]? If the reply is that there is no solid and visible earthly body of this sort—or, to express it by a single term, that there is no flesh capable of suffering pain but incapable of dying—what else is being said than what human beings have inferred from bodily sensation and experience? For they know no flesh except mortal flesh, and their entire reasoning is this: they suppose that what they have not experienced cannot possibly exist.

For what sort of reasoning is it to make pain evidence of death, when it is rather an indication of life? Even if we ask whether something can live forever, it is nevertheless certain that everything that suffers pain is alive, and that no pain can exist except in a living thing. Therefore, what suffers pain must live; but it is not necessary that pain should kill. Even among these mortal bodies, which will certainly die, not every pain kills; and when some pain is able to kill, this happens because the soul is so joined to the body that it yields to the greatest pains and departs, since the very structure of the limbs and vital organs is so frail that it cannot withstand the force producing great or extreme pain.

Then, however, the soul will be joined to such a body in such a way that, just as the bond is not dissolved by any length of time, so it cannot be broken by any pain. Therefore, even if there is now no flesh capable of enduring the sensation of pain and incapable of dying, there will then be such flesh—flesh unlike anything that exists now—just as there will then be a kind of death unlike anything that exists now. For it will not be no death, but an eternal death, when the soul can neither live without possessing God nor be free from bodily pains by dying. The first death drives the unwilling soul out of the body; the second death keeps the unwilling soul in the body. Both deaths have this in common: the soul suffers from its own body what it does not wish to suffer. [Col. 0711] [Note: [Col. 0711] The Louvain edition adds here “nevertheless.”]

2. These opponents observe that there is now no flesh capable of suffering pain and incapable of dying; but they fail to observe that there is nevertheless something greater than a body that has this property. The soul itself—for through its presence the body lives and is governed—can suffer pain and cannot die. Here, then, a thing has been found that possesses the sensation of pain and yet is immortal.

This, therefore, will also be the case then in the bodies of the damned, which we now know to exist in the souls of all. If we consider the matter more carefully, the pain called bodily pain pertains more to the soul. It is the soul that suffers, not the body, even when the cause of its suffering arises from the body, since it suffers at the place where the body is injured. Thus, just as we speak of sensing bodies and living bodies, although sensation and life come to the body from the soul, so we also speak of suffering bodies, although pain can exist in the body only through the soul.

The soul, therefore, suffers with the body at the place in it where something occurs that causes pain. It also suffers when alone, although it is in a body, whenever some invisible cause makes it sorrowful while the body itself remains unharmed. It suffers even when it is not situated in a body: for certainly that rich man in the underworld suffered when he said, “I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24). A body, however, neither suffers when lifeless nor suffers when animated without the soul.

If, then, pain were rightly taken as an argument for death—so that death could occur because pain could occur—it would pertain more to the soul to die, since suffering pain pertains more to the soul. But when that which can suffer pain more intensely cannot die, what reason does this give us for believing that those bodies, because they will be in pain, will therefore also die? The Platonists did indeed say that souls derive fear, desire, pain, and joy from earthly bodies and mortal limbs [Note: [Col. 0711] Aristotle, in the first book of On the Soul, denies that the soul is angry, joyful, or fearful, any more than it weaves or builds, since it performs these actions through the body in the same way as those. But if we admit this concerning anger and joy, pain too will certainly be excluded from the soul on the same grounds; Aristotle’s interpreters, Alexander of Aphrodisias and Themistius, likewise exclude it from the soul apart from the body. LUD. VIVES.]. Hence Virgil says:

“From this,” he says—that is, from the mortal limbs of the earthly body—“they fear and desire, suffer and rejoice” (Aeneid 6.733).

But in the fourteenth book of this work we convicted them of holding that souls, according to their own teaching, had been purified from every stain of the body and nevertheless possessed a dreadful desire by which they began once again to wish to return to bodies [Note: [Col. 0711] Vindobonensis, the Ambrosian manuscript, and all the manuscripts read “in the twelfth.” This is an error either of the author or of the copyist, for Augustine dealt with this matter against the Platonists in book 14, chapters 3 and 5.]. Wherever desire can exist, pain can certainly exist as well. For frustrated desire—whether because it fails to reach what it was pursuing or because it loses what it had reached—is turned into pain.

Therefore, if the soul, which either alone or chiefly suffers pain, nevertheless possesses a certain immortality appropriate to its condition [Col. 0712] [Note: [Col. 0712] It is not immortal in such a way that it previously lived eternally, nor in such a way that it could not be extinguished by any force; rather, once created by God, it will never perish in such a way as to become nothing, although it can suffer the death we call the second death, which will endure forever as punishment. LUD. VIVES.], those bodies will not be able to die merely because they will suffer pain.

Finally, if bodies cause souls to suffer pain, why can they inflict pain upon them but not death, except because it does not follow that what causes pain also causes death? Why, then, is it incredible that fires should be able to inflict pain upon those bodies without causing death, just as bodies themselves cause souls to suffer pain without thereby compelling them to die? Pain, therefore, is not necessarily evidence of a future death.

## CHAPTER FOUR

On natural examples whose consideration teaches that living bodies can remain amid torments.

1. Therefore, if—as those who have investigated the natures of animals more carefully have written—the salamander lives in fires, and certain famous mountains of Sicily, which have burned with flames for so long, through such an immense duration of time and antiquity, and continue to do so, remaining intact, are sufficiently reliable witnesses that not everything that burns is consumed; and if the soul shows that not everything capable of suffering pain is also capable of dying, what further examples are demanded from us by which we may show that it is not incredible for the bodies of human beings punished with eternal torment both not to lose their souls in the fire and to burn without damage and to suffer without destruction?

For the substance of the flesh will then possess a quality bestowed upon it by the one who has bestowed such remarkable and varied qualities upon so many things that we see that, because they are numerous, we do not marvel at them. For who but God, the creator of all things, gave the flesh of a dead peacock the property of not rotting? When this was reported and seemed incredible, it happened that at Carthage this bird was served to us cooked. We ordered as much flesh as seemed appropriate to be cut from its breast and preserved. After an interval of days long enough for any other cooked meat to rot, it was brought out and served, and it offended none of our sense of smell. It was then put away again, and after more than thirty days it was found unchanged; and after a year it was still the same, except that it had become somewhat drier and more contracted in its flesh.

Who gave straw either such a cooling power that it preserves buried snow, or such a heating power that it ripens unripe fruit?

2. Who could explain all the wonders of fire itself? Everything it burns becomes black, although fire itself is luminous; and it discolors almost everything it surrounds and licks with the most beautiful color, turning a glowing coal into a most hideous black ember. Nor is this determined by any fixed rule, for conversely stones thoroughly baked by blazing fire themselves become white; and although the fire is redder, they grow white. Nevertheless, what is white accords with light just as black accords with darkness.

Thus, when fire burns in wood so that it may bake stones, it produces contrary effects in things that are not contrary. For although stones and wood are different, they are not opposites in the way that white and black are: one of these qualities fire produces in stones and the other in wood—brightening the stones and darkening the wood—although the fire would fail to produce the former effect in the stones if it did not live in the wood.

What of coals? Is it not astonishing that they possess both such great weakness, so that they are broken by the lightest blow and crushed by the slightest pressure, and such great strength, so that they are corrupted by no moisture and overcome by no age? They are even commonly placed beneath the stones of those who establish boundaries, in order to refute any litigant who might arise after however long a time and deny that the fixed boundary stone is a boundary. Who but that fire, the corrupter of things, made it possible for them to remain so long uncorrupted when buried in damp earth, where wood would rot? [Note: [Col. 0713] Samius, son of Rhoecus, was the first to recommend placing coals beneath the foundations of the temple of Diana at Ephesus. See Diogenes Laertius, book 2, §103. LARCHER.]

3. Let us also consider the wonder of lime, apart from what we have already sufficiently discussed: that it becomes white through fire [Note: [Col. 0713] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “becomes incandescent.”], by which other things are made black. It also secretly receives fire from fire and preserves it so hidden within the lump, which is cold to the touch, that it is entirely imperceptible to our senses; yet experience discovers it, and even when it does not appear, we know that it is present, lying dormant. For this reason we call it “living lime,” as though the hidden fire itself were the invisible force of a visible body.

How astonishing, moreover, that when it is extinguished, it is then kindled! To deprive it of its hidden fire, water is poured into it or poured over it; and although it was previously cold, it grows hot from that by which all hot things are cooled. As the fire that lay hidden departs, as though the lump were expiring, it becomes visible; and afterward it is so cold, as though dead, that when water is added it does not burn. What we called living lime, we call extinguished lime.

What could seem capable of being added to this wonder? Yet something is added. For if you apply not water but oil, which is more fuel for fire, it does not grow hot from being drenched or filled with it [Note: [Col. 0713] Compare Pliny, book 33, chapter 30.].

If we were reading or hearing this wonder about some Indian stone and could not test it ourselves, we would certainly either think it a lie or marvel at it greatly. But the daily evidence of things that takes place before our eyes, though no less wondrous in kind, loses its value through constant familiarity. Thus, even from India itself—a distant part of the world—we have ceased to marvel at certain things whose wonders have been brought to us.

4. Many people among us possess a diamond, especially goldsmiths and those who are skilled in precious stones. This stone is said to be overcome by neither iron nor fire [Note: [Col. 0713] A diamond placed in a suitable vessel for melting metals evaporates into smoke. LARCHER.] nor any other force, except by the blood of a he-goat [Note: [Col. 0713] Compare Pliny, book 37, chapter 15.]. But those who possess and know it—do they marvel at it in the same way as those to whom its power is shown for the first time? Those to whom it is not shown perhaps do not even believe it; or, if they believe, they marvel at what they have not experienced. If they happen to test it, they still marvel at what is unfamiliar, but repeated experience gradually removes the stimulus to wonder.

We know the magnet stone to be a marvelous attractor of iron. When I first saw this, I was struck with intense astonishment. I saw an iron ring snatched up and suspended by a stone; then, as though it had passed on its own power to the iron it had seized and made it common to that iron, the same ring was brought near another and suspended it. Just as the first ring clung to the stone, so the second ring clung to the first. A third was added in the same way, and a fourth; and now a chain of rings hung from one another, linked in mutual circles—not entangled within one another but adhering externally.

Who would not be astonished at this power of the stone, which was not merely present in it but passed through so many suspended objects and bound them with invisible bonds?

But what I learned about this stone from my brother and fellow bishop, Severus of Milevis, is much more remarkable. He said that he himself had seen how Bathanarius, formerly Count of Africa, when a bishop was dining with him, brought out this same stone and held it beneath a silver plate, then placed iron above the silver. As he moved the hand holding the stone beneath, the iron above moved likewise; with the silver between and entirely unaffected, the stone below was drawn back and forth by the man, while the iron above was carried along at great speed by the stone.

I have said what I myself saw; I have said what I heard from one whom I believed as though I had seen it myself. Let me also report what I have read about this magnet. When a diamond is placed beside it, it does not attract iron; and if it had already attracted iron, as soon as the diamond approaches it, it immediately releases it [Note: [Col. 0714] Pliny, book 37, chapter 15.].

India sends us these stones. But if we have ceased to marvel at them because we already know them, how much more might those from whom they come cease to marvel, if they have them readily at hand—perhaps just as we do not marvel at lime, which is heated by water in a marvelous way, although water usually extinguishes fire, and does not grow hot from oil, by which fire is usually kindled, simply because these things are readily available to us?

## CHAPTER FIVE

How many things there are whose explanation cannot be known, and yet whose truth is beyond doubt [Note: [Col. 0714] The title of the fifth chapter was corrupted in earlier editions, which read: “How great are the things that cannot rightly be understood.” It is corrected from the manuscripts.].

1. Nevertheless, unbelieving people who, when we proclaim divine miracles—whether past or future—that we cannot display for them to experience, demand an explanation of these things from us, and who, because we cannot provide one—for these things exceed the powers of the human mind—suppose that what we say is false, ought themselves to explain the countless marvelous things that we can either observe or do observe.

If they perceive that this cannot be done by a human being, they must admit that something did not therefore fail to exist, or will not therefore fail to occur, merely because no explanation can be given for it, since there are likewise things for which no explanation can be given.

I will not proceed through the many things committed to writing—not events that have occurred and passed away, but things that remain in particular places, so that anyone who wished and was able to go there could investigate whether they are true. I shall mention only a few.

They report that Agrigentine salt, when brought near fire, flows as though in water; but when brought into water itself, crackles as though in fire [Note: [Col. 0715] Pliny, book 31, chapter 7.].

Among the Garamantes there is said to be a spring so cold by day that it cannot be drunk, and so hot by night that it cannot be touched [Note: [Col. 0715] The same, book 5, chapter 5.].

In Epirus there is another spring in which torches, once kindled as in other springs, are extinguished; but, unlike other springs, once extinguished they are rekindled [Note: [Col. 0715] The same, book 2, chapter 103, from Pomponius Mela, book 2, chapter 3.].

There is said to be a stone of Arcadia called asbestos because, once kindled, it can no longer be extinguished [Note: [Col. 0715] The same, book 37, chapter 10.].

The wood of a certain Egyptian fig tree, unlike other wood, does not float in water but sinks; and, more remarkably, after remaining for some time at the bottom, it rises again to the surface, although once soaked it ought to have been weighed down by the weight of the moisture [Note: [Col. 0715] The same, book 13, chapter 7.].

Apples are said to grow in the land of Sodom and to reach the appearance of ripeness; but when tested by a bite or pressure, they vanish into smoke and ash as their skin disintegrates [Note: [Col. 0715] Josephus, book 4, On the Jewish War, chapter 8; Solinus, chapter 35; Tacitus, Histories, book 5, chapter 7.].

The Persian pyrites stone is said to burn the hand of the person holding it if it is pressed too strongly; for this reason it received its name from fire [Note: [Col. 0715] Pliny, book 36, chapter 19, and book 37, chapter 11.].

In the same Persia there is said to grow a stone called selenite, whose inner whiteness increases and decreases with the moon [Note: [Col. 0715] The same, book 37, chapter 10.].

In Cappadocia, mares are said to conceive from the wind, and their offspring live no longer than three years [Note: [Col. 0715] Solinus, chapter 45. See also Pliny, book 8, chapter 42.].

The island of Tylon [Note: [Col. 0715] In some manuscripts, “Thylen.”] in India is said to be preferred to all other lands because every tree that grows there is never stripped of its covering of leaves [Note: [Col. 0715] Pliny, book 12, chapter 11. Tylos is an island in the Persian Gulf.].

2. Let these unbelievers, who refuse to believe the divine Scriptures, give an account, if they can, of these and countless other marvels recorded not as historical events that have occurred and passed away but as features of enduring places. What else can they be doing except supposing that the Scriptures are not divine because they contain incredible things, such as the matter we are now discussing?

“There is no explanation,” they say, “that allows flesh to burn without being consumed, to suffer pain without dying.” Truly, great reasoners—people who can explain all the things that are admittedly marvelous.

Let them therefore give an account [Note: [Col. 0715] “Give an account” is understood.] of the few things we have mentioned. Without doubt, if they did not know that these things existed and we said that they would occur in the future, they would believe us even less than they now refuse to believe that the things we proclaim will one day occur.

For who among them would believe us if, just as we say that in the future human bodies will be alive, always burning and suffering pain but never dying, we were also to say that in the future age there would be salt that fire would make flow as though in water and that water would make crackle as though in fire? Or that there would be a spring whose water would burn during the coolness of night so that it could not be touched, but during the heat of day would be so cold that it could not be drunk? Or that there would be a stone that would burn the hand of the person who held it by its own heat, or one that, once kindled from any source, could not be extinguished at all? And so with the other things that, leaving aside countless additional examples, I have decided for the moment to mention.

If we said that these things would occur in that future age, and the unbelievers replied, “If you want us to believe them, give an explanation of each,” we would admit that we could not do so, since the weak reasoning of mortals is overcome by these and similar marvelous works of God. Yet we would maintain that it is rational for the Almighty to do things for which the feeble human mind cannot give a rational account, even though we do not know with certainty what he intends in many matters. We would nevertheless hold it absolutely certain that nothing he wills is impossible for him. We would believe him when he foretells these things, since we cannot believe that he is either powerless or deceitful.

What, then, do these critics of faith and exactors of explanations say about things for which no human explanation can be given, yet which exist and seem contrary even to the reasoning of nature? If we said that such things would occur in the future, unbelievers would demand an explanation from us in the same way as they demand one for the things we say will occur.

Accordingly, when human reasoning, both of the heart and of speech, fails before such works of God, just as these things do not fail to exist for that reason, so those other things will not fail to occur for the reason that no human being can give an account of either.

## CHAPTER SIX

That not all miracles are natural, but many are fashioned by human ingenuity and many others contrived by the art of demons.

1. At this point they may perhaps reply: “Certainly neither these things exist nor do we believe them; false things have been said and written about them.” They may add, reasoning as follows: “If such things are to be believed, then you too must believe what has been recorded in the same writings: that there was or is a certain shrine of Venus, and in it a candelabrum with a lamp burning in the open air in such a way that no storm and no rain could extinguish it. Hence, like that stone, this lamp was called λύχνος ἄσβεστος—that is, an unquenchable lamp.”

They may say this in order to force us into a difficult response. If we say that it should not be believed, we weaken the written accounts of miracles; but if we concede that it should be believed, we shall confirm the gods of the pagans.

But, as I already said in book eighteen of this work (chapter 18), we are not obliged to believe everything contained in the histories of the nations. Even historians themselves, as Varro says, disagree with one another extensively, as though deliberately and intentionally. We believe, if we wish, those things that do not conflict with the books that we have no doubt we ought to believe.

Concerning these places of miracles, however, the evidence sufficient for persuading unbelievers about the future is supplied by those things that we too can experience and for which it is not difficult to find reliable witnesses.

As for the shrine of Venus and its unquenchable lamp, we are not merely confined by narrow difficulties; rather, a broad field opens before us. For to this unquenchable lamp we add many miracles, both of human arts and of magical arts—that is, demonic arts practiced through human beings [Note: [Col. 0717] Thus Vindobonensis, the Ambrosian manuscript, and the manuscripts. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “demonic arts.”]—as well as many miracles performed by the demons themselves. If we wished to deny these, we would oppose the truth of the very sacred Scriptures in which we believe.

Either human craftsmanship fashioned something from asbestos stone in that lamp, or it was made by magical art so that people would marvel at it in the temple, or some demon, under the name of Venus, manifested itself with such power that this prodigy both appeared to human beings there and continued for a long time [Note: [Col. 0717] A tomb was opened, remembered by our ancestors, in which a lamp had been burning. An inscription showed that it had been placed there more than fifteen hundred years earlier; and as soon as people began to handle it, it crumbled between their hands and immediately became the finest dust. LUD. VIVES.].

Demons are enticed to inhabit created things—not things they themselves made, but things God created—by various objects of delight suited to their different natures. They are not attracted by foods as animals are, but by signs suited to the pleasure of spirits: through various kinds of stones, herbs, woods, animals, songs, and rites [Note: [Col. 0717] Psellus, On Demons, at the final chapter, says that he learned this very thing from a certain Ephesian who had dealings with demons: namely, that there is no kind of thing by which certain demons cannot be attracted. COQUAEUS.].

But in order to be enticed by human beings, they first deceive them through the most cunning trickery, either by inspiring a hidden poison in their hearts or by appearing in deceptive friendships. They make a few of them their own disciples and teachers of very many others. For no one could learn, unless the demons first taught them, what each demon desires or abhors, by what name it is invited, and by what name it is compelled. From this magical arts and their practitioners arose.

Most of all, they possess the hearts of mortals—a possession in which they take particular pride—when they transform themselves into angels of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).

Thus their deeds are very numerous, and the more we acknowledge them to be marvelous, the more carefully we must avoid them. Yet for the matter we are now discussing, they too are useful to us. If unclean demons can do these things, how much more powerful are the holy angels, and how much more powerful than all of them is God, who made even the angels themselves agents of so many miracles?

2. Therefore, if so many and such great marvels, which they call *mechanēmata* (μηχανήματα), are produced through human arts employing God’s creation, so that those who do not know their origin suppose them to be divine—this is how it happened that in a certain temple, when magnetic stones had been placed in the floor and ceiling in proportion to their size, an iron statue hung in the space between the two stones, by what seemed to be the power of a deity to those who did not know which was above and which below [Note: [Col. 0717–0718] Rufinus reports this in book 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 23, among the deceptions discovered in the temple of Serapis at Alexandria: “There was another kind of deception of the following sort. The nature of the magnet stone is said to possess the power of seizing and drawing iron toward itself. An image of the Sun had been fashioned from iron by an artist’s exceptionally delicate workmanship for this very purpose, so that the stone, whose nature we have said is to draw iron toward itself, had been fixed above in the ceiling.
