When the image had been placed directly beneath it in proper balance, it appeared to the people that the image rose and hung in the air, since the stone naturally drew the iron toward itself.” Prosper also reports the same event, part 3 of On the Predictions, chapter 38. COQUAEUS.];

something similar, as we have already said, could also have been made in that lamp of Venus from asbestos stone by an artisan. If the work of magicians—whom our Scripture calls sorcerers and enchanters—could exalt demons to such a degree that a distinguished poet seemed to be speaking appropriately to human perceptions when he wrote of a woman skilled in such arts:

“She promises by spells to release the minds  
of whomever she wishes, but to impose harsh cares on others;  
to halt the water in rivers and turn the stars backward;  
and to stir the nocturnal spirits—you will see the earth bellow  
beneath her feet and the ash trees descend from the mountains.”  
(Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.487–491.)

How much more powerful is God in doing things that are incredible to unbelievers but easy for his power, since he himself created the power of stones and other things, the ingenuity of human beings who use them in marvelous ways, and angelic natures more powerful than all earthly living creatures—surpassing every marvel by a marvelous power, and using all things with the wisdom of working, commanding, and permitting as wonderfully as he created them?

## CHAPTER SEVEN

That in marvelous things the supreme basis for belief is the omnipotence of the Creator.

1. Why, then, should God be unable both to raise the bodies of the dead and to torment the bodies of the condemned with eternal fire, when he made the world full of innumerable marvels—in heaven, on earth, in the air, and in the waters—since the world itself is without doubt a greater and more excellent marvel than everything with which it is filled? Yet these people with whom, or against whom, we are dealing believe both that there is a God by whom the world was made and that there are gods made by him through whom the world is governed; and they either do not deny, or even openly proclaim, that worldly powers are producers of miracles, whether spontaneous, or commanded through some form of worship and ritual, or even magical.

[Note: [Col. 0718] Erasmus and the manuscripts read *imperatorum* (“of emperors”); the Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Louvain editions read *impetratorum* (“of petitioners,” or “obtained by petition”).]

Accordingly, when we present to them the marvelous power of other things which are neither rational animals nor spirits endowed with reason—such as those few examples we have mentioned—they usually reply: “This is the force of nature; this is how their nature is constituted; these are the natural efficacies proper to them.”

Thus, the entire explanation of why Agrigentine salt makes a flame flow, and water crackle, is that this is its nature. Yet this seems rather to be contrary to nature, since nature gave fire, not water, the power to dissolve salt, while it gave fire, not water, the power to burn it. But, they say, the natural force of this salt is such that it undergoes these opposites.

The same explanation is offered for that Garamantian spring, where one channel is cold by day and hot by night, each force being unpleasant to those who touch it. The same is offered for that other spring which, though cold to those who handle it and extinguishing a lighted torch like other springs, nevertheless, in a different and marvelous way, lights the same torch again once it has been extinguished.

[Col. 0719]

The same is offered for the stone asbestos, which, although it possesses no fire of its own, nevertheless, once it has received fire from elsewhere, burns in such a way that it cannot be extinguished. The same is offered for the other phenomena which I am reluctant to recount again: although an unusual force contrary to nature may seem to be present in them, no other explanation is given except that this is their nature.

This, I admit, is a brief explanation and a sufficient answer. But since God is the author of all natures, why do they refuse to let us give the stronger explanation

[Note: [Col. 0719] The printed editions read “are willing” (*volunt*); most manuscripts read “are unwilling” (*nolunt*), rightly. Augustine complains of unbelievers because they refuse the explanation he calls stronger: namely, that this is the will of almighty God.]

 when they are unwilling to believe something as impossible, and when they ask us to explain it, we answer that it is the will of almighty God? He is called almighty for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills. He was able to create so many things which, unless they were displayed before us or reported by witnesses whose testimony is still accepted today, would certainly be thought impossible—not only things almost unknown among us, but also things I have presented that are widely known.

As for those things which have no witnesses among us except the people whose books about them we have read, and which were written by persons who were not divinely instructed and may perhaps have been deceived as human beings, anyone may reasonably refuse to believe them without blame.

2. For I myself do not wish everything I have presented to be believed rashly, since I do not myself believe these things as though my mind entertained no doubt about them—apart from what I have either experienced myself or what anyone can easily experience. Such are the following: that quicklime boils in water but is cold in oil; that the magnet, by some imperceptible attraction, does not move a straw but draws iron; that peacock flesh does not decay, although Plato’s flesh has decayed; that straw is so cold that it prevents snow from melting, yet so hot that it compels fruit to ripen; and that a shining fire, according to its brightness, makes stones white by cooking them, while, contrary to that same brightness, it darkens many things by burning them.

The same kind of thing occurs when black stains are cast upon shining oil, and black lines are impressed upon white silver. It also occurs with coals: when fire is applied, they are changed into the opposite condition,

[Note: [Col. 0719] The manuscripts read *accendente* (“when fire kindles”); the printed editions read *accedente* (“when fire approaches”).]

 so that from beautiful wood they become foul, from hard material fragile, and from what was capable of decaying they become incapable of decay.

Some of these things I know together with many others; some I know together with everyone. There are many more which I could have inserted into this book, but it would have been tedious to do so. Of the things I have presented that I have not experienced myself but have read about, I have been unable to find any reliable witnesses from whom I could learn whether they were true, apart from that spring where burning torches are extinguished and extinguished ones are lit again, and apart from the fruits of the land of Sodom, outwardly appearing ripe but inwardly filled with smoke.

I did not find the spring itself, though I found people who said they had seen it in Epirus, and others who knew of a similar one in Gaul, not far from the city of Gratianopolis.  
[Note: That is, Grenoble.]

As for the fruits of the trees of Sodom, not only do trustworthy writings testify to them, but so many people claim to have experienced them that I cannot doubt them on this account. I have formed no definite decision about the rest, neither affirming nor denying them. I included them because

[Col. 0720]

 I read of them in the histories of those with whom we are dealing, in order to show the kinds of things—and how many of them—these people believe, without any explanation being supplied, in the writings of their learned authors, while they refuse to believe us when we say that almighty God will do what surpasses their experience and the evidence of their senses, and do not even deign to accept an explanation.

For what better and stronger explanation can be given of such matters than that the Almighty is declared able to do them, and is said to be going to do what is read as having been foretold there—where many other things were foretold that are shown to have occurred? He himself will do these things because he foretold that he would do them: he who promised and brought about the belief, among unbelieving nations, of things that unbelievers considered impossible.

## CHAPTER VIII — That it is not contrary to nature when, in something whose nature is known, it begins to differ from what was known

1. But if they reply that they do not believe what we say about human bodies that will always burn and never die because we know that the nature of human bodies was established quite differently, then the explanation given for those marvelous natures cannot be applied here: one cannot say, “This is the natural force; this is the nature of this thing,” since we know that this is not the nature of human flesh.

We do, however, have an answer from the sacred writings: namely, that human flesh itself was established differently before sin, so that it could never suffer death, but differently after sin, in the condition revealed through the misery of this mortality, so that it cannot retain perpetual life. Thus, at the resurrection of the dead, it will be established differently from the way in which it is known to us.

But since these people do not believe the writings that tell how human beings lived in paradise and how far they were removed from the necessity of death—and if they did believe them, we would not have to argue with them so laboriously about the future punishment of the condemned—we must produce something from the writings of those who were most learned among them, so that it may become clear that anything may come to have a different condition from that which had previously become known through the established character of its nature.

2. In the books of Marcus Varro, entitled *On the Race of the Roman People*, there is the following passage, which I shall reproduce here in the same words in which it is found there:

> “In heaven,” he says, “a marvelous portent appeared. For in the star Venus, the most famous star, which Plautus calls *Vesperugo* (*Amphitryon*, act 1, scene 1, verse 119), while Homer calls it *Hesperus* and describes it as the most beautiful (*Iliad* X, verse 318), Castor writes that such a portent occurred that it changed its color, size, shape, and course—something that happened neither before nor afterward. Adrastus of Cyzicus and Dion of Naples, distinguished mathematicians, said that this occurred under King Ogyges.”

[Note: [Col. 0720] Most manuscripts read *Adrastos Cyzicenos* or *Cyzichenos*.]

[Note: [Col. 0720] The manuscripts have *Ogygo*. Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmus have *Ogygio*. See above, book 18, chapter 8, and the notes there.]

[Note: Compare what the highly learned Fréret wrote about this portent in *Mémoires de l’Académie des Belles-Lettres*, volume 10, pp. 357–376. Larcher.]

[Col. 0721]

Varro, so great an authority, certainly would not have called this a portent unless it seemed to be contrary to nature. We call all portents contrary to nature—but they are not. For how can something be contrary to nature that occurs by God’s will, when the will of so great a Creator is itself the nature of every created thing?

A portent, therefore, occurs not contrary to nature, but contrary to nature as it is known. And who can count the multitude of portents contained in the histories of the nations?

Let us now attend to this one example, insofar as it bears upon the matter under discussion. What has been established by the author of the nature of heaven and earth like the most orderly course of the stars? What has been secured by laws so fixed and certain? Yet when he willed it—he who rules with supreme dominion and power what he created—the star most conspicuous among the others for its size and brilliance changed its color, size, shape, and, what is more marvelous, the order and law of its course.

At that time, surely, he disturbed whatever astronomical canons may already have existed—canons which they regard as having been written with an unerring calculation of the past and future movements of the stars.

[Note: [Col. 0721] Erasmus and most manuscripts read *inenarrabili* (“inexpressible”); an old Corbie manuscript reads *itinerabili* (“trackable” or “calculable”).] By following those canons, they dared to say that what happened to Lucifer had happened neither before nor afterward.

We, however, read in the divine books that the sun itself also stood still when the holy man Jesus Nave [Joshua] asked this of the Lord God, until the battle that had begun was brought to victory (Joshua 10:13). We also read that the sun went backward, so that fifteen additional years of life might be granted to King Hezekiah, this marvel being added as a sign confirming God’s promise (Isaiah 38:8).

Yet when these people believe that such miracles, which were granted in response to the merits of the saints, occurred, they attribute them to magical arts. Hence the words of Virgil which I quoted above:

> To halt the river waters, and turn the stars backward.  
> (*Aeneid* 4.489)

For we read in the sacred writings that a river stood still above and flowed below when the people of God, led by the aforementioned Jesus Nave, were making their way across (Joshua 4:18); and that the same thing happened when the prophet Elijah crossed over, and afterward when his disciple Elisha crossed (2 Kings 2:8, 14). We have just mentioned that the greatest star was turned backward during the reign of Hezekiah. But Varro did not say that what he wrote about Lucifer had been granted in response to any human request.

3. Let unbelievers, then, not create darkness for themselves out of their knowledge of natures, as though something could not happen divinely in a given thing that differs from what they have learned about its nature through their human experience. Even those things in the nature of the world which are known to everyone are no less marvelous. They would be astonishing to all who considered them, if people were accustomed to marvel at marvels except when they are rare.

For who, after reflecting rationally, would not see that, amid the innumerable multitude of human beings and their great similarity of nature, it is highly marvelous that individuals have individual faces? If they were not similar to one another, their species would not be distinguished from the other animals; and again, if they were not dissimilar to one another, individuals would not be distinguished from the other human beings.

[Col. 0722]

Thus, the people whom we acknowledge to be similar, we also find to be dissimilar. Yet the consideration of their dissimilarity is more marvelous, since common nature seems more justly to demand similarity. Nevertheless, because rare things are themselves marvelous, we are much more amazed when we find two people so alike that, in distinguishing them, we are always or frequently mistaken.

4. But although they may not believe that what Varro wrote—despite his being their historian and a highly learned man—really happened, perhaps because the course of that same star did not remain altered for long but returned to its customary path,

[Note: [Col. 0722] The Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and manuscripts read *alius* (“other” or “changed”).]

 and so they are less moved by this example, they have another example which can still be displayed. I think it ought to be sufficient to remind them that, when they observe something

[Note: [Col. 0722] The manuscripts read *commoneantur* (“be reminded”); the printed editions read *commoveantur* (“be moved”).]

 in an institution of nature and have made it thoroughly familiar to themselves, they must not prescribe limits to God on that account, as though he could not turn and change it into something very different from what they know.

The land of Sodom certainly was not as it is now. It formerly lay with an appearance like that of other lands and possessed the same, or even greater, fertility; for in the divine utterances it is compared with the paradise of God (Genesis 13:10). Afterward, when it was struck from heaven—as the history of those people also testifies, and as it is now seen by those who visit the region—it became a horror through its monstrous soot, while its fruits enclose inner ash beneath the deceptive appearance of ripeness.

Behold: it was not such, and now it is such. Behold: by the marvelous transformation of the Creator of natures, its nature has been changed into this most hideous dissimilarity; and what happened after so long a time has continued for so long a time.

5. Therefore, just as it was not impossible for God to establish whatever natures he wished, so it is not impossible for him to change the natures he established into whatever he wishes.

Hence there grows up that multitude of miracles which are called monsters, signs, portents, and prodigies. If I wished to review and recount them, what end would there be to this work?

It is said that *monsters* are so called from “showing” (*monstrare*), because by signifying something they demonstrate it; *signs* (*ostenta*) from “displaying” (*ostendere*); *portents* from “portending” (*portendere*), that is, showing beforehand; and *prodigies* because they speak ahead, that is, they foretell the future.

Let their interpreters see whether they are deceived by these things, or whether, under the influence of spirits concerned to entangle minds deserving of such punishment in the nets of harmful curiosity, they sometimes even foretell the truth; or whether, by saying many things, they occasionally happen upon something true.

For us, however, these things which occur—as it were—contrary to nature, and are said to occur contrary to nature (in the manner in which human beings speak, as the Apostle also did when he said that the wild olive was grafted contrary to nature into the cultivated olive and became a sharer in the richness of the olive tree [Romans 11:17, 24]), and which are called monsters, signs, portents, and prodigies, ought to demonstrate, display, show beforehand, and foretell this: that God will do what he foretold he would do concerning human bodies, with no difficulty hindering him and no law of nature prescribing limits to him.

I think I sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding book how he foretold this, by extracting from the sacred Scriptures, both the Old and the New, not everything that bears upon the matter, but what I judged sufficient for this work.

[Col. 0723]

## CHAPTER IX — Concerning Gehenna and the nature of eternal punishments

1. What God said through his prophet about the eternal punishment of the condemned will therefore happen—absolutely will happen:

> “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished.”  
> (Isaiah 66:24)

To impress this more forcefully, the Lord Jesus too, when he used the limbs that cause a person to stumble as figures for those people whom someone loves as his own limbs—his right hand, as it were—and commanded that these limbs be cut off, said:

[Note: [Col. 0723] The Vindobonensis and the manuscripts read *pro his hominibus* (“as figures for these people”); Erasmus and Louvain read *pro his omnibus* (“as figures for all these things”).]

> “It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and their fire is not extinguished.”

He said the same concerning the foot:

> “It is better for you to enter eternal life lame than, having two feet, to be cast into the Gehenna of unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.”

He spoke no differently concerning the eye:

> “It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.”  
> (Mark 9:42–47)

He was not reluctant to say the same words three times in one place.

[Note: [Col. 0723] The manuscripts read *enim* (“for”) in place of *eum* (“him”).] Who would not be terrified by this repetition and by so vehement a threat of that punishment from the divine mouth?

2. Those who wish both the fire and the worm to refer to punishments of the soul rather than of the body say that those separated from the kingdom of God are also burned by the sorrow of a late and fruitless repentance. They therefore argue that fire could appropriately be used for this burning pain. Hence the Apostle’s words:

> “Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?”  
> (2 Corinthians 11:29)

They think that the same pain should also be understood as the worm.

[Note: [Col. 0723] Supply “pain” (*dolorem*).] For, they say, it is written:

> “As a moth consumes clothing and a worm wood, so sorrow torments the heart of a man.”  
> (Proverbs 25:20)

Those, however, who do not doubt that punishments of both soul and body will exist in that judgment affirm that the body will be burned by fire, while the soul will in some way be gnawed by the worm of sorrow.

Although this is said more plausibly—for it is certainly absurd to suppose that pain will be absent there either from body or from soul—I nevertheless find it easier to say that both refer to the body than that neither does.

[Note: [Col. 0723] The manuscripts read: “I judge it easier that …” (*facilius aestimo ut*).] The pain of the soul is therefore left unstated in those words of divine Scripture because it is understood to follow even if it is not expressed: when the body suffers in this way, the soul too will be tormented by barren repentance.

For we also read in the Old Testament:

> “The vengeance of the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worm.”  
> (Sirach 7:19)

It could have been said more briefly: “The vengeance of the ungodly.” Why, then, was “the flesh of the ungodly” said, unless because both fire and worm will be punishment of the flesh?

Or, if he wished to speak of “vengeance of the flesh” because what will be punished in a human being is what he lived according to the flesh—for this is why he will come into the second death, which the Apostle indicated

[Note: [Col. 0724] The Louvain edition reads “and into the second death”; *and* is absent from the other books.]

 when he said, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die” (Romans 8:13)—let each person choose what pleases him: either to assign the fire to the body and the worm to the soul, understanding the former literally and the latter figuratively, or to assign both literally to the body.

I have already argued sufficiently above that animals can live even in fires—in burning without being consumed, in pain without dying—through the miracle of the omnipotent Creator. Whoever denies that this is possible does not know from whom comes whatever power exists in all natures.

For he is the God who made all the great and small miracles in this world that we have mentioned, and incomparably more that we have not mentioned, and enclosed them within the single world itself, the greatest of all miracles.

Let each person therefore choose whichever of the two alternatives he prefers: whether he thinks that the worm also refers literally to the body, or that the word has been transferred from bodily things to incorporeal things and refers to the soul.

Which of these is true, the matter itself will more readily disclose when the knowledge of the saints is so great that they will not need experience in order to know those punishments, but the wisdom that will then be full and perfect will itself be sufficient for this knowledge also. For now we know in part, until perfection comes (1 Corinthians 13:9).

Let us nevertheless believe in no way that those bodies will be such that they cannot be affected by any pain from the fire.

## CHAPTER X — Whether the fire of Gehenna, if corporeal, can burn evil spirits, that is, incorporeal demons, by its touch

[Note: [Col. 0724] Erasmus and Louvain read *incorporalis noxius* (“harmful incorporeal [fire]”); *noxius* is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.]

1. The question now arises: if the fire will not be incorporeal, like the pain of the soul, but corporeal and harmful by contact, so that bodies can be tortured by it, how will the punishment of evil spirits also exist in it?

The same fire will be assigned as punishment to human beings and demons, since Christ says:

> “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”  
> (Matthew 25:41)

Unless, perhaps, demons also possess bodies of their own, as learned men have thought, made from that thick and moist air whose movement is perceived when the wind blows.

[Note: Origen holds this view in book 2 of *On First Principles*, where he says that God alone is incorporeal; Tertullian likewise says in his book *On the Flesh of Christ* that angels are corporeal, although they do not possess flesh. Basil, in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 16, not only wishes angels to be corporeal but also says that they can appear in their own bodies and have sometimes been seen in them. At the seventh ecumenical council, session 4, various testimonies of Greek authors are cited in the same sense. Coquaeus.]

If this kind of element were incapable of suffering anything from fire, it would not burn when heated in baths. For in order to burn, it is first burned itself, and it does what it suffers.

But if anyone insists that demons possess no bodies, there is no need either to pursue an elaborate investigation of the matter or to contend about it quarrelsomely. Why should we not say that, although in marvelous ways, incorporeal spirits can also be afflicted by the punishment of corporeal fire, if the spirits of human beings—who are certainly themselves incorporeal—can now be enclosed within corporeal limbs and can then be bound indissolubly by the bonds of their bodies?

[Col. 0725]

Thus, if demons have no bodies, the spirits of demons—or rather, the demons as spirits—will cling to corporeal fires and be tormented by them, though incorporeal. This does not mean that the fires to which they cling will be animated by their union with them and become living creatures composed of spirit and body. Rather, as I have said, by clinging to them in marvelous and ineffable ways, they will receive punishment from the fires without giving life to the fires.

For the other way in which spirits cling to bodies and become living creatures is itself wholly marvelous. It cannot be comprehended by human beings—and the human being himself is an example of it.

2. I would indeed say that spirits will burn without any body of their own, just as the rich man burned in hell when he said, “I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24), if I did not see that an appropriate answer could be given: namely, that the flame was of the same kind as the eyes which he raised and with which he saw Lazarus, the tongue into which he desired a little moisture to be introduced, and the finger of Lazarus by which he requested that this be done for him. Yet the souls were there without bodies.

Thus that flame in which he burned was incorporeal, as was the drop that he requested. So too are the visions of sleeping people or of those who see things in ecstasy: they concern incorporeal things, yet possess the likeness of bodies. For even when a human being is present in such visions with the spirit rather than the body, he nevertheless sees himself so much like his own body that he cannot distinguish the difference at all.

But Gehenna, which is also called the lake of fire and sulfur (Revelation 20:9), will be a corporeal fire and will torment the bodies of the condemned—either the bodies of both human beings and demons, solid bodies in the case of human beings and aerial bodies in the case of demons; or only human bodies together with their spirits, while the demons, as spirits without bodies, cling to the corporeal fires and receive punishment without imparting life to them.

There will be one fire for both, just as the Truth said (Matthew 25:41).

## CHAPTER XI — Whether the justice of the matter requires that the duration of punishments not exceed the duration of sins

Some of those against whom we defend the City of God think it unjust that, for sins—however great—committed in a short time, a person should be condemned to eternal punishment, as though any justice of the law ever takes account of such a rule: that a person should be punished for as long a period as the period during which he committed the offense for which he is punished.

Tullius writes that there are eight kinds of punishments in the laws: damages, imprisonment, scourging, retaliation, disgrace, exile, death, and slavery.

[Note: [Col. 0725] The Twelve Tables read: “If he has broken a limb, unless he makes settlement with him, let there be retaliation.” *Talio* meant suffering what one had done: one who put out another’s eye would lose his own; one who cut off another’s nose would forfeit his own. The justice of this law is discussed by Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* 20.1. Ludovicus Vives.]

Which of these is compressed into a brief period according to the speed with which each sin was committed, [Col. 0726]

so that punishment lasts exactly as long as the offense took to be committed, unless perhaps retaliation? Its purpose is that each person should suffer what he has done. Hence the saying of the Law:

> “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth.”  
> (Exodus 21:24)

It can happen that a person loses an eye through the severity of punishment in as short a time as he himself took to deprive another of it through the wickedness of his sin.

Moreover, if it is reasonable to punish with blows the kiss pressed upon another man’s wife, is not the person who did this in a moment beaten for an immeasurable number of hours, and is not the pleasure of a brief moment punished by prolonged pain?

Again, in the case of imprisonment, must someone be judged to deserve confinement only as long as he took to do the thing that earned him imprisonment,

[Note: [Col. 0726] The printed editions read “What of imprisonment? Is he there …?” The manuscripts omit *there* (*ibi*).]

 when it is entirely just for a slave to remain for years in fetters because, in a word or a blow passing very quickly, he either provoked or struck his master?

As for damages, disgrace, exile, and slavery, when these are often imposed without any pardon releasing the condemned, do they not seem, relative to the duration of this life, similar to eternal punishments? They cannot be eternal because the life that is punished by them does not last forever. Yet the sins punished by the longest punishments are committed in the briefest time. No one has ever proposed that the torments of the guilty should end as quickly as the homicide, adultery, sacrilege, or any other crime was committed, since such offenses are measured not by their temporal duration but by the magnitude of their iniquity and impiety.

When someone is condemned to death for a grave crime, do the laws assess his punishment by the brief delay during which he is killed, rather than by the fact that they remove him forever from the society of the living?

What it is, then, to remove people from this mortal city through the punishment of the first death, is to remove them from that immortal city through the punishment of the second death. For just as the laws of this city do not restore to it someone who has been killed, so the laws of that city do not restore to eternal life someone condemned to the second death.

“How, then,” they say, “is what your Christ said true—‘In the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured back to you’ (Luke 6:38)—if a temporal sin is punished by eternal punishment?”

[Note: [Col. 0726] See Letter 102 to Deogratias, question 4, sections 22 and following.]

They do not consider that the measure was spoken not because the temporal duration is equal, but because of the reciprocity of evil: that the one who has done evil should suffer evil.

This saying can, however, be understood more specifically in the matter about which the Lord was speaking when he said it—that is, judgments and condemnations. Therefore, if someone judges and condemns unjustly, and is judged and condemned justly, he receives according to the same measure, although he does not receive the same thing that he gave. He acted through judgment and suffers through judgment, although he did what was unjust by condemnation and suffers what is just by condemnation.

## CHAPTER XII — Concerning the magnitude of the first transgression, on account of which eternal punishment is owed to all who are outside the grace of the Savior

[Col. 0727]

Eternal punishment therefore seems harsh and unjust to human perceptions because, in this weakness of our dying senses, we lack that sense of the highest and purest wisdom by which we could perceive how great a crime was committed in that first transgression.

For the more greatly human beings enjoyed God, the greater was the impiety with which they abandoned God. They became deserving of eternal evil because they destroyed in themselves the good that could have been eternal.

Hence the entire mass of the human race was condemned. The one who first committed this transgression was punished together with the race that had been rooted in him,

[Note: [Col. 0727] Most manuscripts read *primus* (“the first man”) rather than *primitus* (“at first”).]

 so that no one might be liberated from this just and deserved punishment except by mercy and unmerited grace.

Thus the human race is distributed in such a way that, in some, the power of merciful grace is demonstrated, while in others the justice of retribution is demonstrated. For both would not be demonstrated in everyone. If all remained in the punishments of just condemnation, merciful grace in the act of redemption would appear in no one;

[Note: [Col. 0727] The word *redimentis* (“of the redeemer”) is absent from the manuscripts.]

 and again, if all were transferred from darkness into light, the severity of retribution would appear in no one.

[Note: [Col. 0727] Most manuscripts read *veritas* (“truth”) rather than *severitas* (“severity”).]

For this reason, there are many more in the latter group than in the former, so that what was owed to all may thereby be shown. If it were rendered to all, no one could justly criticize the justice of the one who punishes. But because so many are liberated from it, there is reason to give the greatest thanks for the gratuitous gift of the one who liberates.

## CHAPTER XIII — Against the opinion of those who think that punishments are imposed on criminals after death for the purpose of purification

The Platonists, although they do not wish any sins to remain unpunished, nevertheless think that all punishments are imposed for correction—whether inflicted by human or divine laws, whether in this life or after death, if someone is spared here or is punished in such a way that he is not corrected here.

Hence Virgil’s statement. After speaking of earthly and dying bodies, and of the souls who

> Fear and desire these things, grieve and rejoice, and do not look up to the air,  
> Shut in by darkness and a blind prison,

he continues:

> Yet when life has departed with the final light—that is, when this life has left them on the last day—  
> not all evil has departed from wretched souls, nor have all bodily diseases  
> wholly left them; and it is necessary that many things, deeply fixed in them,  
> grow ingrained through marvelous ways.  
> Therefore they are exercised by punishments and pay the penalties  
> of their former evils: some are spread out empty,  
> suspended in the winds; for others, beneath the vast abyss,  
> the infected sin is washed away or burned out by fire.  
> (*Aeneid* 6.733–742)

Those who hold this opinion wish all punishments after death to be purifying punishments, so that, since the elements above the earth are water, air, and fire, what was contracted through earthly contamination may be cleansed by expiatory punishments through one of these elements.

Air is understood in the words “suspended in the winds”; water in “beneath the vast abyss”; and fire is explicitly named when he says, “or burned out by fire.”

We, however, acknowledge that even in this mortal life there are certain purifying punishments—not punishments by which those who suffer them are made neither better nor worse, but punishments that are purifying for those who are corrected by being restrained through them.

[Col. 0728]

All other punishments, whether temporal or eternal, are inflicted according to the way in which each person is dealt with by divine providence: either for past sins, or for sins in which the person being punished is still living, or for the exercise and demonstration of virtues. They are inflicted through human beings and angels, whether good or evil.

For even if someone suffers some evil through another person’s wickedness or error,

[Note: [Col. 0728] The Vindobonensis and manuscripts read *quisque* (“anyone” or “each person”) rather than *quisquam*.]

 the human being who inflicts evil through ignorance or injustice certainly sins; but God does not sin when, by a just though hidden judgment, he permits this to occur.

Some people therefore suffer temporal punishments only in this life, some after death, and some both now and then—but before that most severe and final judgment.

Not all who endure temporal punishments after death come to the eternal punishments that will follow that judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0728] The printed editions read “which will be for these”; *for these* (*his*) is absent from all manuscripts.] For we have already said above that, for some, what is not forgiven in this age is forgiven in the age to come (Matthew 12:32)—that is, they are not punished by the eternal penalty of the age to come.

## CHAPTER XIV — Concerning the temporal punishments of this life, to which the human condition is subject

Very few people suffer no punishments in this life but only after it. Nevertheless, we have both known and heard of some who reached extreme old age without experiencing even the slightest fever and led a peaceful life.

Yet life itself is wholly a punishment for mortals, because it is wholly a time of testing, as the sacred Scriptures proclaim when it is written:

> “Is not human life upon the earth a time of testing?”  
> (Job 7:1, according to the Septuagint)

For ignorance or lack of learning is itself no small punishment. It is rightly judged so deserving of avoidance that children are compelled, through punishments full of pain, to learn every craft and letters. Learning itself—the thing to which they are driven by punishments—is so painful to them that they sometimes prefer to endure the very punishments by which they are compelled to learn rather than to learn.

Who would not shudder, and choose death, if offered the choice between enduring death or returning to infancy? Infancy, moreover, begins this light not with laughter but with weeping, and, without knowing what evils it has entered, somehow prophesies them.

They say that Zoroaster alone laughed when he was born.

[Note: Pliny, *Natural History* 7.15, at the end.]

That monstrous laughter did not portend anything good for him. For he is said to have been the inventor of magical arts, which could not help him even toward the empty happiness of this present life against his enemies. He was defeated in war by Ninus, king of the Assyrians, although he himself was king of the Bactrians.

In every respect, the statement is fulfilled:

> “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all.”  
> (Sirach 40:1)

It must be fulfilled so completely that even infants, though already released through the bath of regeneration from the bond of original sin—the only bond by which they were held—suffer many evils; and some of them even at times endure attacks by evil spirits.

[Col. 0729]

May such suffering never harm them, if they complete this life at that age, even when the suffering itself grows heavier and drives the soul from the body.

[Note: Compare *Enchiridion*, section 17.]

# CHAPTER XV  
## That the whole work of God’s grace, rescuing us from the depth of the ancient evil, pertains to the newness of the age to come

Nevertheless, within the grievous yoke laid upon the children of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all, this remarkable evil is also found [Note: [Col. 0729] Printed editions have *hoc medium miserabile* (“this miserable intermediate condition”). Most manuscripts have *hoc malum mirabile* (“this remarkable evil”): namely, in the case of the very infants regenerated, discussed in the preceding chapter.]—so that we may be sober and understand that this life was made punitive for us because of that exceedingly wicked sin committed in paradise, and that everything accomplished with us through the New Testament pertains only to the new inheritance of the new age. Thus, having now received the pledge, we may in its proper time obtain that of which this pledge is a pledge. For the present, however, let us walk in hope, and, progressing from day to day, put to death by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh (Rom. 8:13).

“For the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19), and “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14)—by grace, however, not by nature. For the only Son of God by nature, moved by mercy toward us, became the Son of Man, so that we, who by nature are children of man, might through him by grace become children of God [Note: [Col. 0729] Only the Louvain edition has: “so that we might become children of God through his grace.”]. Remaining himself unchanged, he took from us the nature in which he would receive us; and, holding fast to his divinity, he became a participant in our weakness. Thus, changed for the better, we lose through participation in his immortality and righteousness what we are as sinful and mortal beings, while what he made good in our nature is preserved, brought to completion by the supreme Good in the goodness of his nature.

For just as through one sinful man we came into this exceedingly grievous evil (Rom. 5:12), so through one man who is also God and who justifies us, we shall come to that good so sublime. Nor should anyone trust that he has passed from this condition to that one until he is there where no temptation will exist, and until he has held fast to the peace which, amid the many and varied battles of this war—“the flesh lusting against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17)—he seeks.

This war would never exist if human nature had remained, through free choice, in the uprightness in which it was made. But now, because it did not happily wish to have peace with God, it unhappily fights against itself; and although this is a pitiable evil [Note: [Col. 0729] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have: “and although this too, since it is a pitiable evil …”], it is nevertheless better than the earlier conditions of this life. For it is better to struggle against vices than to have them rule without any struggle [Note: [Col. 0729] Most manuscripts omit *cum* (“with,” yielding “than [to have them] rule without any struggle”).]. Better, I say, is war with the hope of eternal peace than captivity without any thought of liberation.

Indeed, we desire to be free even from this war, and we are inflamed by the fire of divine love to attain that perfectly ordered peace in which inferior things are subjected to superior with the firmest stability [Col. 0730] [Note: [Col. 0730] The Louvain edition has *infirmiora* (“weaker things”). Other printed editions and most manuscripts have *inferiora* (“inferior things”).]. But if—God forbid—there were no hope of that great good, we ought still to prefer remaining amid the hardship of this struggle to permitting vices to rule over us by refusing to resist them [Note: [Col. 0730] The philosophers also said this, those who held that souls were mortal or merely long-lived. For, setting aside every price, living well is more pleasing than living badly; virtue itself is its greatest reward; and the good, even while they live here, are happier than the wicked, however fortunate. This is what Christ promises his followers: a great reward not only in the future life but also in the present. —LUDOVICUS VIVES.].

# CHAPTER XVI  
## Under what laws of grace all the ages of the regenerate are held

Yet so great is God’s mercy toward the vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory that even the first age of man—that is, infancy, which is subject to the flesh without any resistance—and the second, called childhood, when reason has not yet undertaken this struggle and lies almost entirely beneath every sinful pleasure—for although the child can now speak and therefore appears to have passed beyond infancy, the weakness of the mind in that age is not yet capable of receiving a command—if the sacraments of the Mediator have been received, even if the child should end this life during those years, having been transferred, that is, from the power of darkness into the kingdom of Christ, is not only not destined for eternal punishments but does not suffer any purgatorial torments after death.

Spiritual regeneration alone is sufficient to prevent what bodily generation contracted along with death from harming the person after death [Note: [Col. 0730] He teaches that Baptism benefits infants and children; but he does not explain here how it benefits those who die at that age. See, however, Letter 98, to Boniface. —HARDUINUS.].

When, however, a person reaches the age that can already receive a command and can be subjected to the authority of the law, war against the vices must be undertaken and waged vigorously, lest it lead to damnable sins. If the vices have not yet been strengthened by the habit of victories, they are more easily conquered and give way; but if they have become accustomed to conquering and ruling [Note: [Col. 0730] The manuscripts have *consuerunt*; the same form occurs frequently elsewhere.], they are overcome only with laborious difficulty.

This does not happen truly and sincerely except through a genuine delight in righteousness; and this is found in faith in Christ. For if the commanding law is present but the assisting Spirit is absent, then, through the very prohibition, desire grows and sin prevails, and the guilt of transgression is added. Sometimes the most obvious vices are conquered by hidden vices that are thought to be virtues, in which pride and a destructive elevation of self-satisfaction rule.

Vices, therefore, are to be regarded as conquered when they are conquered through the love of God—a love that God alone gives, and gives only through the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, who became a participant in our mortality in order to make us participants in his divinity.

Very few possess such good fortune that, from the beginning of adolescence, they commit no damnable sins—whether in disgraceful acts, crimes, or the error of some impious wickedness—but through the great generosity of the Spirit suppress whatever might rule them through carnal pleasure [Note: [Col. 0731] Erasmus and some manuscripts have: “whatever in them might be condemned through carnal pleasure.”].

Most, however, after receiving the commandment of the law, having first been defeated by prevailing vices and become transgressors of the law, then flee to the grace that assists them. Through it they become victorious by repenting more bitterly and fighting more vigorously, after the mind has first been subjected to God and then placed above the flesh.

Whoever, therefore, desires to escape everlasting punishments must not merely be baptized but must also be justified in Christ, and thus truly pass from the Devil to Christ. He should not suppose that there will be any purgatorial punishments except before that final and terrifying judgment.

Nevertheless, it must not be denied that even the eternal fire will be lighter for some and heavier for others according to the diversity of their merits, however evil those merits may be—whether the force and heat of the fire varies according to the punishment each deserves, or whether the fire burns equally but is experienced with unequal anguish.

# CHAPTER XVII  
## Concerning those who think that the punishments of no human beings will last forever

I now see that we must deal with our merciful friends and dispute with them peaceably—those who refuse to believe that everlasting punishment will be imposed either upon all the human beings whom the most just Judge will judge worthy of the punishment of Gehenna or upon some of them. Instead, they think that after the limits of a fixed period, longer or shorter according to the measure of each person’s sin, they will be released from it [Note: [Col. 0731] The Louvain edition has *longiores sive breviores* (“longer or shorter,” agreeing with *periods”). Other printed editions and the manuscripts have *longioris sive brevioris* (“of a longer or shorter [period],” referring to *period of time*).].

In this respect Origen was surely more merciful: he believed that even the Devil and his angels, after punishments more severe and longer in duration according to their deserts, would be rescued from those torments and joined to the holy angels [Note: [Col. 0731] That Origen taught this impiously is also attested by Epiphanius, in his letter on Origen’s errors to John of Jerusalem; by Jerome, in Letter 61 to Pammachius, in the *Apology against Rufinus*, and in Letter 75 to Vigilantius; and by Augustine himself, in *On Heresies*, heresy 43. Genebrardus, in his *Collections on the Life and Writings of Origen*, chapter 6, attempts to defend him against this error. For he claims that in *On First Principles*, from which this doctrine is taken, Origen said it more by way of disputing and examining than by way of establishing and defining it. —COQUAEUS.].

But the Church rightly rejected him both for this and for several other reasons, especially his teaching about endlessly alternating blessednesses and miseries, with movements and returns from the former to the latter and from the latter to the former at fixed intervals of the ages [Note: [Col. 0731] Jerome reports that Origen’s errors were condemned by Pope Anastasius, in the *Apology against Rufinus* and Letter 78 to Pammachius; likewise by Theophilus at the Synod of Alexandria. After Augustine’s time they were condemned also by Pope Vigilius and the emperor Justinian. The Fifth Ecumenical Council condemned Origen’s impious and absurd doctrines through many anathemas, which are found in Nicephorus Callistus, book 17, chapters 27–28, and in the acts of that council, session 4, chapter 11. —COQUAEUS.]. Indeed [Note: [Col. 0731] Thus according to Morel, *Critical Elements*, p. 154. In B, *quia* (“because”). —M.], by doing this he lost even the mercy he seemed to possess: he made true miseries for the saints, in which they would suffer punishments, and false blessednesses in which they would not possess the true and secure—that is, certain without fear—joy of everlasting good.

The mercy of these people, however, errs in a very different way through human emotion. They think that the miseries of those condemned by that judgment are temporary, while the happiness of all who are released sooner or later is eternal. If this opinion is good and true because it is merciful, then it will be better and truer in proportion as it is more merciful. Let the fountain of this mercy, then, be extended and deepened even to the condemned angels, at least to those who are to be liberated after many and endlessly prolonged ages [Note: [Col. 0732] Origen also liberated these beings from punishments, just as, as time proceeded, he made devils out of the holy angels. Such were his reversals. —LUD. VIVES.]. Why does it flow as far as the whole human nature, but, when it reaches the angelic nature, immediately dry up? Yet they do not dare to extend their mercy any farther, so as to reach the liberation even of the Devil himself.

But if anyone dares to do so, he surpasses these people and is nevertheless found to err all the more shamefully and perversely against the straightforward words of God, in proportion as he thinks that he feels more mercifully.

# CHAPTER XVIII  
## Concerning those who think that, at the last judgment, no human being will be condemned because of the intercessions of the saints

### 1.

There are also people whom I myself have encountered in our conversations. Although they appear to honor the holy Scriptures, they are reprehensible in their conduct; and, in presenting their case, they attribute to God a much greater mercy toward the human race than do those others.

They say that what has been divinely foretold concerning wicked and unbelieving people is indeed true: that they are worthy of punishment [Note: [Col. 0732] The word *poena* (“punishment”) is absent from the printed editions of Vienna, Amsterdam, and Erasmus, and from all the manuscripts.]. But when the judgment arrives, they say, mercy will prevail. “The merciful God,” they say, “will pardon them through the prayers and intercessions of his saints. If the saints prayed for them when they were enduring them as enemies, how much more will they pray when they see them humble, suppliant, and prostrate?”

They say that we should not believe that the saints will then lose the inward organs of mercy when they have attained the fullest and most perfect holiness—so that those who then prayed for their enemies, when they themselves were not without sin, would not pray for their suppliants when they had begun to have no sin at all. Or will God not then hear so many such children of his, when, in their great holiness, he will find no impediment to their prayer?

They claim that the testimony of the Psalm, and especially of those who allow unbelieving and impious people to be tormented for at least a long time and afterward rescued from all evils, supports their position: “Will God forget to show mercy, or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?” (Ps. 76:10). “His anger,” they say, “is that all who are unworthy of everlasting blessedness are punished by his judgment with everlasting punishment. But if he permits it to be long-lasting, or indeed to exist at all, then, in order for this to happen, he will restrain his mercies in his anger—something which the Psalm says he will not do.”

For it does not say, “Will he restrain his mercies in his anger for a long time?” Rather, it shows that he will not restrain them at all [Note: [Col. 0732] See below, chapter 24, and *Enchiridion*, nos. 29 and 112.].

[Col. 0733]

### 2.

Thus these people want the threat of God’s judgment not to be false, even though he will condemn no one. They reason that this is like God’s threat in which he said that he would overthrow the city of Nineveh (Jonah 3:4), which we cannot call false; yet, they say, what he foretold without any condition did not happen.

For he did not say, “Nineveh will be overthrown if they do not repent and amend their ways.” Rather, without adding this condition, he announced that the overthrow of that city would occur. They think this threat was truthful because God foretold what they truly deserved to suffer, although he himself was not going to inflict it.

“For although he spared the repentant,” they say, “he certainly knew that they would repent; yet he absolutely and definitively foretold that their overthrow would occur. Thus it was true in the logic of severity, because they deserved it; but it was not true in the logic of mercy, which he did not restrain in his anger, so that he spared those who pleaded with him from the punishment he had threatened against the obstinate.”

“If he spared them then,” they say, “when, by sparing them, he was going to grieve his holy Prophet, how much more mercifully will he spare suppliants then, when all his saints will pray that he spare them?”

But what they imagine in their hearts, they think the divine Scriptures concealed for this reason: so that many might correct themselves through fear of prolonged or eternal punishments, and so that there might be people able to pray for those who did not correct themselves. Yet they do not think that the divine utterances concealed this entirely.

“For what else,” they say, “does it mean that it is written, ‘How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you’ (Ps. 31:20), unless we understand that such abundant and hidden sweetness of divine mercy was concealed because of fear?”

They also add that the Apostle said, “For God has shut up all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32), in order to signify that no one will be condemned by him.

Yet even those who hold this view do not extend their opinion to the liberation or non-condemnation of the Devil and his angels. Their human compassion is stirred only concerning human beings; and they are chiefly pleading their own case, promising a false impunity to their depraved conduct through a supposed universal mercy of God toward the human race. Thus they will surpass those who proclaim God’s mercy by promising this impunity even to the prince of demons and his attendants.

# CHAPTER XIX  
## Concerning those who promise impunity for all sins even to heretics because of their participation in Christ’s body

There are others who promise liberation from eternal punishment not even to all human beings, but only to those washed in Christ’s Baptism who become participants in his body, no matter how they may have lived or in whatever heresy or impiety they may have been found. They rely on Jesus’ words:

“This is the bread that came down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:50–52).

Therefore, they say, it is necessary that these people be rescued from eternal death and eventually brought to eternal life.

# CHAPTER XX  
## Concerning those who promise indulgence not to all, but only to those who were reborn among Catholics, even if afterward they plunged into many crimes and errors

There are likewise people who promise this not to everyone who possesses the Baptism of Christ and the sacrament of his body, but only to Catholics, even if they live wickedly. Their reason is that such people have eaten Christ’s body not merely sacramentally but in reality, having been constituted within Christ’s body, of which the Apostle says, “We, though many, are one bread and one body” (1 Cor. 10:17).

Thus, even if afterward they fall into some heresy or even into the idolatry of the Gentiles, merely because they received Christ’s Baptism and ate Christ’s body while in Christ’s body—that is, in the Catholic Church—they will not die eternally but will eventually obtain eternal life. All that impiety, however great it may be, will contribute not to their eternity but to the length and severity of their punishments.

# CHAPTER XXI  
## Concerning those who define that people who remain in the Catholic faith, even if they have lived most wickedly and therefore deserve to be burned, will nevertheless be saved because of the foundation of faith

There are also people who, because it is written, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13), promise this only to those who persevere in the Catholic Church, even if they live wickedly within it. They say that such people will be saved through fire because of the foundation, concerning which the Apostle says:

“No one can lay a foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, each one’s work will become manifest. For the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test the quality of each one’s work. If anyone’s work that he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:11–15).

They therefore say that a Catholic Christian of any kind of life has Christ as his foundation, a foundation possessed by no heresy that has been cut off from the unity of Christ’s body. Therefore, because of this foundation, even if the Catholic Christian has lived badly—like someone who has built with wood, hay, and straw—they think he will be saved through fire, that is, liberated after the punishments of that fire by which the wicked will be punished at the last judgment [Note: [Col. 0734] Compare *Enchiridion*, no. 18, at the beginning.].

# CHAPTER XXII  
## Concerning those who think that the crimes committed amid works of almsgiving will not be summoned for judgment leading to condemnation

I have also discovered some who think that only those will burn in the eternity of that punishment who neglect to give worthy alms for their sins, in accordance with the Apostle James: “Judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13).

“Therefore,” they say, “if someone gives alms, even though he has not changed his conduct for the better but has lived impiously and wickedly amid his very acts of almsgiving, judgment will come upon him with mercy, so that he will either suffer no condemnation or, after some period—short or long—be liberated from that condemnation.”

For this reason they think that the Judge himself of the living and the dead did not wish to mention anything else that he would say, whether to those on his right, to whom he will give eternal life, or to those on his left, whom he will condemn to eternal punishment (Matt. 25:33 ff.), except almsgiving, whether performed or not performed.

They say that the same thing is indicated by the daily petition in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). For whoever forgives through pardon the person who has sinned against him undoubtedly gives alms. The Lord himself commended this matter in these words:

“For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you” (Matt. 6:14–15).

Therefore, they say, the Apostle James’ statement—that judgment will be without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy—also pertains to this kind of almsgiving. The Lord did not say, they argue, “whether great or small,” but, “Your Father will forgive you your sins if you also forgive people.”

Accordingly, they think that even those who have lived ruinously, until they close the final day of this life, have all their sins—whatever their kind and however great—daily forgiven through this prayer, provided they remember to observe this one thing: whenever those who have injured them by any sin ask them for forgiveness, they must forgive them from the heart.

When, by God’s gift, I have answered all these arguments, this book must be brought to a close [Note: [Col. 0735] Compare *Enchiridion*, nos. 19–20.].

# CHAPTER XXIII  
## Against the opinion of those who say that neither the Devil nor wicked human beings will suffer perpetual punishment

First, we must ask and understand why the Church could not tolerate a human argument that promises purification or pardon even to the Devil after the greatest and longest punishments. For so many saints, instructed in the sacred writings both old and new, did not begrudge purification and the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven to angels of every kind and after punishments of every kind and magnitude. Rather, they saw that the divine sentence could not be emptied or weakened—the sentence that the Lord foretold he would pronounce and declare at the judgment:

“Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

In this way he showed that the Devil and his angels would burn in eternal fire. And what is written in the Apocalypse is to the same effect:

“The Devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet also are; and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever” (Rev. 20:9–10).

There the word is “eternal”; here it is “forever and ever.” Scripture ordinarily signifies by these words nothing other than that the time has no end.

Therefore no other, more just, or more evident reason can be found for holding with the truest piety that the Devil and his angels will have no return to righteousness and the life of the saints, except that Scripture—which deceives no one—says that God did not spare them (2 Pet. 2:4), and that they were thus already condemned by him in advance, being thrust into the prisons of the darkness of hell [Note: [Col. 0736] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have *inferni* (“of hell”) instead.], where they were handed over to be kept for punishment at the last judgment, when eternal fire will receive them and they will be tormented forever and ever.

If this is so, how will all or some human beings be removed from the eternity of this punishment after however long a period, without immediately weakening the faith by which it is believed that the punishment of the demons will be everlasting?

For if all or some of those to whom it will be said, “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41), will not always remain there, what reason is there for believing that the Devil and his angels will always remain there? Or will God’s sentence, which will be pronounced against wicked angels and human beings, be true concerning the angels but false concerning human beings?

That is precisely what will happen if what people imagine is given more weight than what God has said. Since this cannot happen, those who desire to escape everlasting punishment should not argue against God but instead, while there is time, obey the divine command.

Furthermore, what sense does it make to regard eternal punishment as lasting only for an extended period of fire [Note: [Col. 0736] Erasmus and Louvain have *non existimare* (“not to regard”). The word *non* is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.], while believing that eternal life is without end, when Christ, in the very same passage and in one and the same sentence, included both:

“So these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

If both are eternal, then surely either both must be understood as lasting for a long time with an end, or both as perpetual without an end. The two expressions correspond equally: on one side, eternal punishment; on the other, eternal life. To say, in this one and the same sense, “Eternal life will be without end, but eternal punishment will have an end,” is exceedingly absurd.

Therefore, since the eternal life of the saints will be without end, the eternal punishment of those to whom it will belong will likewise certainly have no end.

# CHAPTER XXIV  
## Against the opinion of those who think that, at God’s judgment, all the guilty should be spared because of the prayers of the saints

### 1.

This also applies against those who, in pleading their own case against the words of God, attempt to act as though they possess a greater mercy—so that God’s words are true because the people he said would suffer these things deserve to suffer them, not because they will actually suffer them.

“They will be pardoned,” they say, “through the prayers of his saints, who will then pray for their enemies all the more because they will be so much holier; their prayer will be more effective and more worthy of being heard by God, since they will have no sin whatsoever.”

Why, then, with the same perfect holiness, and with prayers so pure and merciful that they can obtain everything, will they not also pray for the angels for whom eternal fire has been prepared, asking God to moderate his sentence and turn it toward something better, making them strangers to that fire?

Or will there perhaps be someone who dares to suppose that this too will happen, asserting that the holy angels, together with the holy human beings who will then be equal to the angels of God, will pray for the angels and human beings destined for condemnation, so that through mercy they may not suffer what, according to truth, they deserve to suffer?

No one of sound faith has said this, and no one will say it. Otherwise there would be no reason why the Church should not even now pray for the Devil and his angels, since God the Teacher commanded it to pray for its enemies.

The reason, therefore, why the Church does not now pray for the wicked angels, whom it knows to be its enemies, is the very same reason why, at that future judgment, it will not pray even for the human beings who will be tormented in eternal fire, although the Church will then possess perfect holiness.

For now it prays for those whom it has as enemies within the human race because this is the time for fruitful repentance. What does it pray for them above all except that God may grant them, as the Apostle says, repentance, so that they may recover their senses from the Devil’s snare, by whom they are held captive according to his will (2 Tim. 2:25–26)?

Finally, if it were so certain concerning some people that the Church even knew who they were—although they were still living in this life, they had nevertheless been predestined to go into eternal fire with the Devil—it would no more pray for them than it prays for the Devil himself.

But because it is not certain about anyone, it prays for all human beings who are its enemies insofar as they remain in this body. Yet it is not heard on behalf of everyone. It is heard only on behalf of those who, although they oppose the Church, have nevertheless been predestined in such a way that the Church’s prayer for them will be heard and they will become children of the Church.

If some people maintain an impenitent heart until death and are not converted from enemies into children, does the Church now pray for them—that is, for the spirits of such dead people? Why not? Because the person who, while in the body, was not transferred into Christ is now counted among the party of the Devil.

### 2.

The reason, then, why prayers will not be offered for human beings who are to be punished in eternal fire is the same reason why prayers are offered neither now nor then for the evil angels. It is likewise the reason why, although prayers are offered for human beings [Note: [Col. 0737] The printed editions add after *pro hominibus* (“for human beings”): *nunc vivis oretur etiam malis* (“prayer is also offered now for the wicked who are alive”). This is a gloss absent from the older books.], prayers are now no longer offered for unbelieving and impious dead people [Note: [Col. 0737] Erasmus’s edition inserts here certain material found in no other book and not sufficiently connected with the preceding and following words. After “for unbelieving and impious dead people,” it reads:

“Now, the prayer of the Church itself, or of certain devout people, is heard for some of the dead, although those who were reborn in Christ had not lived so badly in the body as to be judged unworthy of such mercy, nor so well that they would be found not to need such mercy. It is also established that, before the day of judgment, such people will not be handed over to the punishments of eternal fire after being purified by the temporal punishments their spirits suffer and by receiving their bodies again. But if this is so, what should be said concerning those who are found living in a similar condition on the day of judgment—that is, those whom that day finds alive—when in a certain way they die and rise again in a single moment, and there is no time for the prayers of the saints to be heard on their behalf or for them to be purified before the judgment by temporal punishment? Are we to say that at the time of judgment they may be handed over to eternal fire and never released from it, even though we admit that they lived such a life that, had they died before the judgment, they would have been cleansed by temporal punishment and the prayers of the saints? The prayer of the Church itself, or of certain devout people, is indeed heard, but for those who, having been regenerated in Christ …” etc.].

For the prayer of the Church itself, or of certain devout people, is heard for some of the dead—but for those whose life in the body, although they were regenerated in Christ, was neither so badly conducted that they are judged unworthy of such mercy, nor so well conducted that they are found not to need such mercy.

Likewise, after the resurrection of the dead, there will be some to whom mercy will be granted after the punishments suffered by the spirits of the dead, so that they will not be cast into eternal fire. For it would not truly be said of some that their sin “will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32), unless there were others whose sin, although not forgiven in this age, would nevertheless be forgiven in the age to come.

But when the Judge of the living and the dead has said, “Come, blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” and, conversely, to others, “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels,” and, “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:34, 41, 46), it is an excessive presumption to say that eternal punishment will not await any of those whom God said would go into eternal punishment. Such presumption would lead people either to despair of or to doubt eternal life itself.

### 3.

Therefore no one should understand the Psalm that sings, “Will God forget to show mercy, or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?” (Ps. 76:10), as though God’s sentence concerning good human beings were true but concerning wicked human beings false, or as though it were true concerning good human beings and wicked angels but false concerning wicked human beings.

What the Psalm says pertains to the vessels of mercy and to the children of promise, one of whom was the Prophet himself. After saying, “Will God forget to show mercy, or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?” he immediately added, “And I said, ‘Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High’” (Ps. 76:11).

He clearly explained what he meant by, “Will he restrain his mercies in his anger?” For the anger of God is also this mortal life, in which human beings have become like vanity and their days pass away like a shadow (Ps. 144:4). Yet in this anger God does not forget to show mercy: he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. Thus he does not restrain his mercies in his anger (Matt. 5:45).

This is especially expressed in what the Psalm says: “Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” For in this very wretched life, which is God’s anger, he changes the vessels of mercy for the better, although his anger still remains amid the misery of this corruption, because even in his anger he does not restrain his mercies.

Since the truth of that divine song is fulfilled in this way, it is not necessary to understand it as applying also to that place where those who do not belong to the City of God will be punished with everlasting punishment.

But those who wish to extend this statement even to the torments of the wicked should at least understand it in this way: while God’s anger remains upon them—an anger pronounced as eternal punishment—God does not restrain his mercies in that anger, and he causes them not to be tormented with punishment as harsh as they deserve, but to suffer punishments milder and lighter than their merits warrant. Thus God’s anger will remain, and in that anger he will not restrain his mercies.

I do not, however, affirm this merely because I do not oppose it [Col. 0739].

### 4

But those who think that the words “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire,” and “These shall go away into eternal punishment” (Matt. 25:41, 46), and “They shall be tormented for ages of ages” (Rev. 20:10), and “Their worm shall not die, and the fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24), and other passages of this kind, were spoken more as threats than as truthful statements, are refuted and disproved—not so much by me as by divine Scripture itself, most clearly and completely.

For the Ninevites repented in this life (Jonah 3:7), and their repentance was therefore fruitful, as though they were sowing in that field in which God willed that seed should be sown with tears, to be reaped afterward with joy (Ps. 125:6). Yet who will deny that what the Lord foretold was fulfilled in them, unless he pays too little attention to the manner in which God overturns sinners not only in anger but also in mercy?

Sinners are overturned in two ways: either as the Sodomites were, so that the people themselves are punished for their sins; or as the Ninevites were, so that the sins of the people themselves are destroyed through repentance. Thus what God had foretold came to pass: Nineveh, which was wicked, was overthrown, and what had not existed—namely, a good city—was built. Although its walls and houses remained standing, the city was overthrown in its depraved morals. [Note: Compare *Expositions of the Psalms* 50.11.]

And so, although the Prophet was saddened because what those people feared would happen when he prophesied did not happen (Jonah 4:1–3), nevertheless what God, in his foreknowledge, had foretold came to pass; for the one who foretold it knew how it would be fulfilled for the better.

### 5

But so that these perversely merciful people may know what is meant by the words that were written, “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you,” let them read what follows: “But you have perfected it for those who hope in you” (Ps. 30:20).

What does “You have hidden it from those who fear you; you have perfected it for those who hope in you” mean, except that for those who wish to establish their own righteousness, which is in the Law, through fear of punishments, the righteousness of God is not sweet (Rom. 10:3), because they do not know it? They have not tasted it. For they hope in themselves, not in him; and therefore the abundance of God’s sweetness is hidden from them. They do indeed fear God, but with that servile fear which is not in love, because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Therefore he perfects his sweetness for those who hope in him by inspiring them with his love, so that, when they glory, they may glory in the Lord with chaste fear—not the fear that love casts out, but the fear that “endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 18:10).
