For the righteousness of God is Christ, who, as the Apostle says, “was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption,” so that, as it is written, “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:30–31).

They do not know this righteousness of God, which grace gives without merits, who wish to establish their own righteousness; and therefore they are not subject to the righteousness of God, which is Christ (Rom. 10:3). In this righteousness is the great abundance of God’s sweetness, because of which it is said in the Psalm, “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9).

In this pilgrimage we taste that sweetness, though we do not take it to satisfaction; rather, we hunger and thirst for it, so that afterward we may be filled with it, when “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2), and what is written will be fulfilled: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15). Thus Christ perfects the great abundance of his sweetness for those who hope in him.

But if God hides from those who fear him the sweetness which they imagine to be his—the sweetness by which he will not condemn the wicked, so that, unaware of this and fearing condemnation, they may live rightly and thus become people who pray for those who do not live rightly—how does he perfect it for those who hope in him, since, according to their dream, through this sweetness he will not condemn those who do not hope in him?

Let them therefore seek that sweetness of his which he perfects for those who hope in him, not the sweetness which they suppose he perfects for those who despise and blaspheme him. [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “because,” less well.] It is therefore in vain that a person seeks after this body what he neglected to acquire for himself while in this body. [Note: Vind., Am., and Er. read: “Therefore it is in vain that a person placed in this body presumes to claim for himself knowledge of God’s hidden judgments.”]

### 6

Nor was the apostolic statement, “For God has concluded all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all,” spoken to mean that he will condemn no one. The preceding context makes clear why it was said.

For when the Apostle was speaking to the Gentiles about the Jews who would later believe—writing, of course, to people who already believed—he said: “For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so they also now have not believed through your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy” (Rom. 11:31–32). [Note: The printed editions read “in their unbelief”; *in* is absent from the manuscripts.] Then he added the statement by which these people, in their error, flatter themselves: “For God has concluded all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.”

Whom does he mean by “all,” except those about whom he was speaking, as though he were saying, “both you and them”? God therefore concluded both Gentiles and Jews—those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29)—in unbelief, [Note: Here only the printed editions add “to become”; Augustine normally omits this word when citing Romans 8:29.] so that, humbled by repentance for the bitterness of their unbelief and converted by faith to the sweetness of God’s mercy, they might cry out in the words of the Psalm: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you, but perfected for those who hope—not in themselves, but in you!”

He therefore has mercy on all the vessels of mercy. What does “all” mean? It means those whom he predestined, called, justified, and glorified from among the Gentiles, and those whom he predestined, called, justified, and glorified from among the Jews—not all human beings, but all of these, none of whom he will condemn.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### Whether those who were baptized among heretics and afterward became worse by living wickedly, or those who were reborn among Catholics and then passed over to heresies or schisms, or those who did not depart from the Catholics among whom they were reborn but persisted in criminal living, can hope, by the privilege of the sacraments, for release from eternal punishment

### 1

But now let us also answer those who promise release from the eternal fire not to the devil and his angels, as neither do the others, nor indeed even to all human beings—rather, only to those who have been washed in Christ’s Baptism and made participants in his body and blood, however they may have lived and whatever heresy or impiety they may have embraced. [Note: See the book *On Faith and Works*.]

The Apostle contradicts them when he says: “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, lustfulness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, contentions, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you, that those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19–21).

This apostolic statement would plainly be false if such people, after however long a time, were released and came to possess the kingdom of God. But since it is not false, they will certainly not possess the kingdom of God. And if they will never possess the kingdom of God, they will be held in eternal punishment, since there is no intermediate place where one who has not been established in that kingdom is not subject to punishment.

### 2

Therefore the meaning of what the Lord Jesus said deserves careful inquiry: “This is the bread that came down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live for ever” (John 6:50–52).

Those to whom we are now replying are deprived of this interpretation by the people to whom we must reply next. These latter promise release not to all who possess the sacrament of Baptism and of Christ’s body, but only to Catholics, even if they live wickedly. They say that they have eaten Christ’s body not merely through the sacrament, but in reality, because they are constituted in his body itself. Of that body the Apostle says, “Because there is one bread, we, though many, are one body” (1 Cor. 10:17).

Therefore, they say, whoever is in the unity of his body—that is, in the structure of Christian members, whose sacrament the faithful who communicate are accustomed to receive from the altar—must truly be said to eat Christ’s body and drink Christ’s blood.

Accordingly, heretics and schismatics, separated from the unity of this body, can receive the same sacrament, but it is not beneficial to them; indeed, it is harmful, so that they may be judged more severely rather than released more slowly. For they are not in that bond of peace which is signified by the sacrament.

### 3

But again, those who correctly understand that one must not say that a person eats Christ’s body if he is not in Christ’s body do not rightly promise release from the punishment of the eternal fire to those who fall away from the unity of that body into heresy or even into the superstition of the Gentiles.

First, they should consider how intolerable and how far removed from sound doctrine it is to suppose that the many, almost all, who founded wicked heresies after leaving the Catholic Church and became leaders of heresies had better grounds for salvation than those who had never been Catholics, once they had fallen into the snares of those heresiarchs.

If the fact that they were baptized in the Catholic Church and initially received the sacrament of Christ’s body in the true body of Christ causes those heresiarchs to be released from eternal punishment, then the deserter from the faith—and, having deserted it, the person who became its attacker—would be in a better position than the one who did not desert a faith that he had never held. Surely that is worse.

Second, the Apostle also confronts these people by using the same words and, after enumerating those works of the flesh, proclaiming the same truth: “Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21).

### 4

Nor should those who persist to the end in depraved and damnable conduct be secure merely because they seem to persevere in communion with the Catholic Church, observing what was said: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Through a wicked life they abandon the very righteousness of life, which is Christ, whether by committing fornication, by perpetrating in their own bodies other uncleannesses of vice which the Apostle did not even wish to specify, by dissolving into the shamefulness of lust, or by doing anything else of the kind concerning which he says, “Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

Accordingly, all who do such things will be in eternal punishment, since they cannot be in the kingdom of God. By persevering in these things until the end of this life, they certainly cannot be said to have persevered in Christ to the end; for to persevere in Christ is to persevere in his faith. That faith, as the same Apostle defines it, “works through love” (Gal. 5:6). But love, as he says elsewhere, “does no evil” (1 Cor. 13:4; Rom. 13:10).

Nor, therefore, can these people be said to eat Christ’s body, since they are not to be counted among Christ’s members. To say nothing of other matters, they cannot at the same time be members of Christ and members of a prostitute (1 Cor. 6:15).

Finally, when he says, “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57), he shows what it means to eat Christ’s body and drink his blood not merely sacramentally but in reality. For this means to remain in Christ, so that Christ may remain in him.

He said this as though he were saying: “Let no one who does not remain in me, and in whom I do not remain, claim or think that he eats my body or drinks my blood.” Those who are not his members do not remain in Christ. But those who make themselves members of a prostitute are not members of Christ—unless they cease to be such through repentance and return to this good state through reconciliation.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### What it means to have Christ as one’s foundation, and to whom salvation is promised as though through the burning of fire

### 1

“But,” they say, “Catholic Christians have Christ as their foundation, from whose unity they have not departed, even though upon this foundation they have built a life as wicked as possible, like wood, hay, and straw” (1 Cor. 3:11–12). Therefore, they argue, the right faith through which Christ is the foundation, although with loss because what has been built upon it will be burned up, can nevertheless eventually save them from the perpetuity of that fire. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read “faith is”; *is* is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts.]

The Apostle James gives them a brief answer: “If anyone says that he has faith but does not have works, can faith save him?” (James 2:14).

“And who is the person,” they ask, “of whom the Apostle Paul says, ‘He himself will be saved, yet so as through fire’?” (1 Cor. 3:15).

Let us inquire together who this person is. Yet it is absolutely certain that he cannot be understood in such a way that the statements of the two Apostles are brought into conflict: one saying, “Even if a person has evil works, faith will save him through fire,” and the other saying, “If he has no works, can faith save him?”

### 2

We shall therefore discover who can be saved through fire if we first discover what it means to have Christ as one’s foundation.

To understand this quickly from the analogy itself: nothing in a building is placed before its foundation. Therefore, whoever has Christ in his heart in such a way that he places neither earthly and temporal things, nor even things that are lawful and permitted, before Christ, has Christ as his foundation.

But if he places such things before Christ, then—even if he appears to have faith in Christ—Christ is not his foundation, since such things have been placed before him. How much more, when someone disregards saving commandments and commits forbidden acts, is he shown not to have placed Christ first but to have placed him last: he has subordinated the one who commanded or permitted these things, while choosing to satisfy his own desire through wicked deeds contrary to Christ’s commands or permissions.

If a Christian loves a prostitute and, cleaving to her, becomes one body with her (1 Cor. 6:16), he no longer has Christ as his foundation.

But if someone loves his wife according to Christ (Eph. 5:25), who would doubt that Christ is his foundation? If, however, he loves her according to this age, carnally, in the sickness of desire, “like the Gentiles who do not know God” (1 Thess. 4:5), the Apostle—or rather Christ through the Apostle—even grants this by way of concession.

Such a person, therefore, may also have Christ as his foundation. For if he places no such affection or pleasure before Christ, then, although he builds wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation, Christ is his foundation; and for this reason he will be saved through fire.

Such delights and earthly loves, which are not condemnable when they arise from the marital union, will be burned away by the fire of tribulation. [Note: Many manuscripts read “delights and loves of this world.”] To this fire belong bereavements and all the calamities that take these things away.

Accordingly, for the person who built it, this building will be damaging, because he will not retain what he built upon it and will be tormented by the loss of what he had enjoyed and therefore rejoiced in. Yet he will be saved through this fire because of the merit of his foundation: even if a persecutor had offered him the choice between retaining that affection and retaining Christ, he would not have placed it before Christ.

Observe in the Apostle’s words a person building gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation: [Note: The printed editions read “upon this foundation”; *this* is absent from the manuscripts.] “The unmarried man,” he says, “thinks about the things of God, how he may please God.” Observe another person building wood, hay, and straw: “But the married man,” he says, “thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Cor. 7:32–33).

“Each person’s work will become manifest: for the day will declare it”—that is, the day of tribulation [Note: Vind., Am., and Er. read: “the day of wrath, the day of tribulation.”]—“because,” he says, “it will be revealed in fire.” [Note: The printed editions, contrary to the older books, add “what sort it is”; immediately afterward they read, “the day of the Lord will declare it.” The word “Lord” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.]

“And the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work which he built upon the foundation remains”—for what each person thinks about is what remains, namely, how he may please God—“he will receive a reward,” that is, he will receive what he had thought about. “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss,” because he will not possess what he had loved.

“But he himself will be saved,” because no tribulation moved him from the stability of that foundation, “yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:13–15). For what he did not possess without enticing love, he does not lose without consuming grief.

Here, as far as I can see, we have found a fire that condemns none of them: it enriches one, causes another loss, and tests both.

### 3

But if we wish to understand that fire here as the fire of which the Lord will say to those on the left, “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41), so that those who build wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation may also be thought to be among them, and so that the merit of their foundation may release them after a time from that fire inflicted for their evil merits, what shall we think about those on the right, to whom it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25:34), except that they are those who built gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation?

But if this is how the fire is to be understood—the fire of which it is said, “yet so as through fire”—then both groups must be sent into it: those on the right as well as those on the left. For both must be tested by the fire of which it is said, “The day will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is” (1 Cor. 3:13).

If, therefore, the fire will test both, so that if anyone’s work remains—that is, if what he built is not consumed by fire—he will receive a reward, but if anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, then this is plainly not that eternal fire.

Only those on the left will be sent into that fire in the final and perpetual condemnation; this fire, however, tests those on the right. It tests some of them in such a way that it does not burn up or consume the building it finds them to have constructed upon Christ as their foundation. It tests others differently: what they built upon the foundation is burned, and they suffer loss because of it; nevertheless they are saved because they held Christ, firmly established as their foundation, with surpassing love.

If they will be saved, then surely they will also stand on the right and, with the others, hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you.” They will not stand on the left, where those who will not be saved will be, and therefore will hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire.”

No one will be saved from that fire, because all those people will go into eternal punishment (Matt. 25:46), where “their worm will not die, and the fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24), and where “they will be tormented day and night for ages of ages” (Rev. 20:10).

### 4

After the death of this body, and until we come to that final day which will follow the resurrection of bodies and will be the last day of condemnation and reward, if the spirits of the dead are said to undergo a fire of this kind during that interval—a fire not felt by those who did not have such habits and loves in the life of this body that their wood, hay, and straw might be consumed, but felt by those who carried buildings of this kind with them, whether only there, or both here and there, or here for the purpose of not being there—and if they find there a transient fire of tribulation that burns away secular things, although these are pardonable and do not entail condemnation, I do not object, because perhaps this is true. [Note: Beraldus, in his manuscript, emends the text by removing *saecularia* (“secular things”).]

For even death itself may belong to this tribulation. It was conceived from the perpetration of the first sin, so that each person may experience the period following death according to the nature of his building.

The persecutions by which the martyrs were crowned, and which all Christians undergo, also test both buildings as though by fire. They consume some together with the builders themselves, if they do not find Christ as their foundation; they consume others without the builders, if they find Christ there, because, although with loss, the builders themselves will be saved; but they do not consume still others, because they find things such as endure forever.

[Note: The older books read as printed in the source. The printed editions instead read: “and, according to each person’s building, undergone by each person in his own time. The persecutions of the Church also can be [included], by which the martyrs ...”]

[Note: Vind., Am., and Er. read: “because, although with loss, they will be saved; they themselves will not be consumed, on account of the merit of Christ found as their foundation, who endures forever.”]

At the end of the age there will also be a tribulation in the time of Antichrist such as has never existed before. How many buildings there will then be—some golden, some made of hay—upon the best foundation, which is Christ Jesus! That fire will test both kinds, bringing joy to some and loss to others; yet it will destroy neither of those in whom it finds this stable foundation.

But whoever places before Christ—not a wife, whose bodily union he also uses for carnal pleasure, but even those names of piety that are themselves remote from such pleasures, loving them carnally in the human manner—does not have Christ as his foundation. [Col. 0746] Therefore he will not be saved through fire but will not be saved at all, because he cannot be with the Savior, who speaks most plainly about this matter: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

But whoever loves these relationships carnally without nevertheless placing them before Christ the Lord, and would rather be without them than without Christ, if he is brought into such a moment of temptation, will be saved through fire; for the pain of losing them must burn him to the degree that love for them had held fast to him.

On the other hand, whoever loves father, mother, sons, and daughters according to Christ, so that he may advise them for the purpose of obtaining Christ’s kingdom and cleaving to him, or loves in them the fact that they are members of Christ, let it be far from us to suppose that this love belongs among the wood, hay, and straw destined to be consumed. It will plainly be assigned to a golden, silver, and jeweled building.

How, indeed, can he love them more than Christ, when he loves them precisely for Christ’s sake? [Note: Compare *On the Morals of the Catholic Church* 63 and *On True Religion* 86 and following.]

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Against the persuasion of those who think that the sins in which they persisted while giving alms will not harm them

### 1

It remains to answer those who say that only those will burn in the eternal fire who neglect to give alms worthy of their sins, on account of what the Apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13).

Therefore, they say, whoever has shown mercy—even if he has not corrected his depraved ways, but has lived wickedly and impiously in the very midst of his almsgiving—will face a merciful judgment, so that he will either not be condemned at all or, after some time, will be released from the final condemnation.

They think that Christ will make the distinction between those on the right and those on the left solely on the basis of their giving or neglecting alms, sending some into the kingdom and others into eternal punishment.

To persuade themselves that the sins they never cease committing—whatever their kind or number—can be forgiven through almsgiving, they try to use the prayer taught by the Lord both as an advocate on their behalf and as a witness.

“For just as there is no day,” they say, “on which this prayer is not recited by Christians, so there is no daily sin, whatever its kind, that is not forgiven through it, when we say, ‘Forgive us our debts,’ provided that we take care to do what follows, ‘as we also forgive our debtors’” (Matt. 6:12).

“For the Lord did not say,” they continue, “‘If you forgive people’s sins, your Father will forgive your daily minor sins’; rather, he said, ‘He will forgive you your sins’” (Matt. 6:14). [Note: “Your” is absent from our manuscripts.] Therefore, whatever their kind or number, even if they are committed every day and a person’s life does not turn away from them and change for the better, they presume that these sins can be forgiven through almsgiving, since mercy is not denied. [Note: The better manuscripts read “does not turn away”; the printed editions read “does not turn away,” with the following wording altered to “forgiveness through almsgiving not denied,” etc.]

### 2

It is good, however, that these people at least insist that alms worthy of their sins must be given. For if they said that any sort of alms could obtain mercy for sins—daily sins, great sins, or sins of whatever kind and however long-standing the habit—so that daily forgiveness would follow, they would see that they were saying something absurd and ridiculous.

They would be forced to admit that a very wealthy man could redeem murders, adulteries, and every sort of impious deed by spending ten small coins a day on almsgiving.

If it is utterly absurd and insane to say this, then, if we ask what kind of alms are worthy of sins—those of which that forerunner of Christ also said, “Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:8)—without a doubt those who stab their lives through to death by the commission of daily crimes will not be found giving such alms. [Note: Compare *Against Faustus the Manichaean* 22.29.]

First, because in taking away other people’s property they seize far more than they distribute, and by giving a very small portion of it to the poor they imagine that they are feeding Christ for this purpose: they believe that they have bought—or rather, that they are buying every day—the license to commit their crimes from him, and so they commit such damnable acts without fear.

If, for a single crime, they were to distribute all their possessions to the needy members of Christ, this would be unable to benefit them unless they ceased such deeds and possessed the love that “does not act wrongly” (1 Cor. 13:4).

Therefore, whoever gives alms worthy of his sins should first begin by giving them to himself. [Note: Many manuscripts read “begins.”] For it is unworthy that a person should not do this for himself when he does it for his neighbor, while hearing the Lord say, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39).

Let him also hear: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24). If he does not give this alms to his own soul—that is, if he does not make it pleasing to God—how can he be said to give alms worthy of his sins?

For this reason also it is written: “He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Sir. 14:5).

Almsgiving helps prayers. And certainly we must consider what we read: “Son, have you sinned? Do not do so again, but pray concerning your past sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Sir. 21:1).

Alms must therefore be given so that, when we pray concerning past sins, we may be heard—not so that, while persisting in those sins, we may suppose that through almsgiving we can purchase permission to do evil.

### 3

For this reason the Lord foretold that he would charge those on the right with the alms they had given, and those on the left with the alms they had not given, in order to show by this how much almsgiving can accomplish toward wiping out past sins, but not toward committing perpetual sins with impunity.

Those who do not wish to change their lives for the better and turn away from their accustomed crimes cannot be said to give alms of this kind. For in saying, “When you did not do it for one of the least of mine, you did not do it for me” (Matt. 25:45), he showed that they do not give even when they think they are giving.

If they gave bread to a hungry Christian as to a Christian, they would certainly not deny themselves the bread of righteousness, which is Christ himself. [Note: All manuscripts read “as to a Christian”; the printed editions read “as to Christ.”]

For God considers not to whom something is given, but with what intention it is given.

Therefore, whoever loves Christ in a Christian offers alms to him with the intention with which he approaches Christ, not with the intention of wishing to withdraw from Christ without punishment. For the more a person loves what Christ disapproves, the more he abandons Christ.

What does it profit anyone to be baptized if he is not justified? Did not the one who said, “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), also say, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20)?

Why do many, fearing the former, hasten to be baptized, while, not fearing the latter, not many take care to be justified?

Therefore, just as a person does not say to his brother, “Fool,” when, in saying this, he is not hostile to the brotherhood itself but to the brother’s sin—otherwise he will be guilty of the fire of Gehenna (Matt. 5:22)—so, conversely, whoever gives alms to a Christian does not give to a Christian if he does not love Christ in that Christian.

But he does not love Christ if he refuses to be justified in Christ.

And just as, if someone has been overtaken by this offense and says to his brother, “Fool”—that is, if he insults him unjustly without wishing to remove his sin—it is not enough for him to make alms in order to redeem this offense, unless he also adds the remedy of reconciliation that follows there.

For the passage continues: “Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24). [Note: Most manuscripts read *offeres* (“you will offer”) rather than *offers* (“you offer”).]

Thus it is not enough to give alms of whatever amount for any crime while remaining in the habitual practice of crimes.

### 4

The daily prayer, which the Lord himself taught [Note: [Col. 0748] All manuscripts read “Jesus.”], and which is therefore also called the Lord’s Prayer, does indeed wipe away daily sins when it is said every day: “Forgive us our debts”; and what follows is not merely said but also done: “as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid. 6:12). But it is said because sins are committed—not so that they may be committed because it is said [Note: [Col. 0748] Compare *Enchiridion*, §§19–20.].

For by means of this prayer the Savior wished to show us that, however justly we may live amid the darkness and weakness of this life, we are not without sins for whose forgiveness we ought to pray, and that we ought to forgive those who sin against us, so that we too may be forgiven. The Lord therefore did not say, “If you forgive people’s sins, your Father will also forgive your sins” (ibid. 6:14), so that, trusting in this prayer, we might confidently commit daily crimes—whether through power, by which we would not fear human laws, or through cunning, by which we might deceive people themselves. Rather, he said it so that through this prayer we might learn not to think ourselves without sins, even if we were free from serious offenses. In the same way, God also reminded the priests of the Old Law of this very matter through the sacrifices that he commanded them to offer first for their own sins and then for those of the people (Lev. 16:6; Heb. 7:27).

The very words of so great a Teacher and Lord of ours must also be examined attentively. For he did not say, “If you forgive people’s sins, your Father will also forgive you whatever sins”; rather, he said, “your sins.” He was teaching a daily prayer, and he was speaking to disciples who were, of course, justified. What then is meant by “your sins,” except sins without which even you, who have been justified and sanctified, will not exist? When, therefore, those who seek through this prayer an opportunity to commit crimes every day say that the Lord meant even serious sins—because he did not say, “He will forgive you minor sins,” but “your sins”—we, considering the people to whom he was speaking and hearing the words “your sins,” ought to understand nothing other than minor sins, since such people no longer had serious ones.

Nevertheless, even those serious sins from which one must wholly turn away through a transformation for the better are not forgiven to those who pray unless what is stated there is done: “as we also forgive our debtors.” For if even minor sins, without which the life of the righteous is not possible, are not forgiven in any other way, how much less will those entangled in many and serious crimes—even if they have now ceased committing them—receive any pardon if they have been unwilling to forgive what each person has sinned against them, since the Lord says: “But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you” [Note: [Col. 0749] The printed editions add “their sins”; this is absent from the manuscripts.] (Matt. 6:15).

To this applies also what the apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 2:13). We should also call to mind that servant whose master remitted the ten thousand talents he owed, but afterward ordered him to repay them because he had not shown mercy to his fellow servant, who owed him a hundred denarii (Matt. 18:23 ff.).

Thus, among those who are children of promise and vessels of mercy, what the same apostle says applies, when he immediately adds: “But mercy triumphs over judgment” (Jas. 2:13). [Note: [Col. 0749] The printed editions read, “Mercy exalts judgment.” Another reading found in certain old books agrees with the Greek, *kai katakauchatai eleos kriseos* (“and mercy boasts over judgment”).]

For those righteous people who lived with such holiness that they also receive others into the eternal dwellings—those whom they made friends through the mammon of unrighteousness (Luke 16:9)—were themselves made such by being freed through mercy by the one who justifies the ungodly, reckoning the reward according to grace, not according to debt. The Apostle is among their number, for he says: “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Cor. 7:25).

### 5

As for those who are received by such people into the eternal dwellings, it must be acknowledged that they are not endowed with such character that their own life could suffice to free them without the aid of the saints. Accordingly, in their case mercy triumphs over judgment all the more.

Nevertheless, no one should therefore suppose that some utterly wicked person, whose life has not been changed into something good or at least more tolerable, is received into the eternal dwellings merely because he has served the saints with the mammon of unrighteousness—that is, with money or riches that had been wrongly acquired—or even if they had been acquired honestly, with riches that are not true riches, but which unrighteousness considers riches because it does not know what true riches are, the riches in which those who also receive others into the eternal dwellings abound.

There is therefore a certain kind of life—not so evil that, for those who live it, the generosity of almsgiving is of no benefit toward attaining the kingdom of heaven, since by it even the poverty of the righteous is supported and friends are made who will receive them into the eternal dwellings; yet not so good that it is itself sufficient for attaining such blessedness unless they obtain mercy through the merits of those whom they have made friends. [Note: [Col. 0750] Lov. reads, “those who live it”; other printed editions, with the manuscripts, have the same reading.]

I am accustomed to marvel that this saying of the Lord is also found in Virgil, where he says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that they too may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). A very similar saying is this: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matt. 10:41).

For when that poet was describing the Elysian Fields, where people suppose that the souls of the blessed dwell, he placed there not only those who had been able to reach those abodes through their own merits, but also added:

> And those who, by their deserving, made others mindful of them;  
> (*Aeneid* 6.664)

That is, those who earned merit for others and, by earning merit for them, made them mindful of themselves. [Note: [Col. 0750] All manuscripts read “as though they were saying”; the printed editions have “as though he were saying.”] It is precisely as though they were saying to them what is commonly heard from Christian lips, when a humble person commends himself to one of the saints and says, “Remember me”—and by earning merit makes it possible for this to happen.

But what this condition of life is, and what sins are those that obstruct entry into the kingdom of God in such a way that they nevertheless obtain pardon through the merits of saintly friends, is exceedingly difficult to discover and extremely dangerous to define. For my part, although I have labored over this matter up to the present time, I have not been able to discover them. Perhaps these matters remain hidden so that zeal for progress in avoiding every sin may not grow sluggish. For if people knew what kinds of offenses they were—offenses for which, even while they continued and were not eliminated by progress toward a better life, the intercession of the righteous should be sought and hoped for—human indolence would complacently entangle itself in them. It would not take care to extricate itself from such entanglements through the exertion of any virtue, but would seek only to be freed through the merits of others whom it had made its friends by the generosity of almsgiving from the mammon of unrighteousness. [Note: [Col. 0750] The manuscripts read, “by generosity.”]

Now, however, since the measure of pardonable unrighteousness is unknown, even if it persists, zeal for progress toward better things is applied more vigilantly through persistence in prayer [Note: [Col. 0750] Vind., Am., and several manuscripts read, “by praying and persisting”], and care is not neglected in making the saints friends through the mammon of unrighteousness.

### 6

Yet this deliverance, whether it comes through each person’s own prayers or through the intercession of the saints, has the effect of preventing a person from being cast into the eternal fire; it does not mean that, once cast into it, the person will be drawn out after however long a period of time.

Even those who think that the passage should be understood in this way—“the good soil bears fruit, one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another a hundredfold” (Matt. 13:8)—so that, according to the diversity of their merits, some saints may free thirty people, others sixty, and others a hundred, usually suppose that this will occur on the day of judgment, not after the judgment.

When someone saw people perversely promising themselves impunity on the grounds that, in this way, everyone might seem capable of belonging to those who could be freed, he is said to have replied most elegantly that one should rather live well, so that each person might be found among those who will intercede for the freedom of others. Otherwise, they might be so few that, once each of them had reached his own number—thirty, sixty, or a hundred—many would remain who could no longer be rescued from punishment through their intercession; and among them would be found anyone who, in the most reckless vanity, promised himself the fruit of another.

This answer should suffice for those who do not despise the authority of the sacred Scriptures that we hold in common, but who, by misunderstanding them, think that what they themselves want will happen rather than what those Scriptures say [Note: [Col. 0752] Compare *Letter* 120, §13.].

With this answer given, we bring the book to an end, as we promised.

## BOOK TWENTY-SECOND [Note: [Col. 0751] Written around the beginning of the year 427.]

On the due end of the City of God, that is, on the eternal happiness of the saints. The faith in the resurrection of bodies is established, and what it will be like is explained. Then, after stating what they will do in holy, immortal, and spiritual bodies, the work is brought to an end.

[Col. 0751]

## CHAPTER I—On the Creation of Angels and Human Beings

### 1

As we promised in the preceding book, this final book of the whole work will contain a discussion of the eternal blessedness of the City of God. It received the name of eternity not because of a long duration extending through many ages, though it will at some time come to an end, but because, as it is written in the Gospel, “Of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

Nor will its appearance of perpetuity be such that, as some depart by dying and others succeed them by being born, it seems to preserve an appearance of continuity—as in a tree clothed with perennial foliage, where the same vigor appears to endure while, as leaves slip away and fall, others that are continually born preserve the appearance of shade. Rather, all its citizens will be immortal, and human beings will attain what the holy angels have never lost.

The almighty God, its creator, will accomplish this. For he promised it and cannot lie; and, in order to establish faith in this also, he has already accomplished many things of his own—not only things promised but also things not promised—and things that were promised.

### 2

For he is the one who in the beginning created the world, full of every good among visible and intelligible things. In it he instituted nothing better than spirits, to whom he gave understanding and made them capable and receptive of contemplating him and possessing him; and he bound them together in one society, which we call the holy and heavenly city. In it God himself is their provision by which they are sustained and their blessedness, as though he were their common life and nourishment.

He granted this intellectual nature free choice of such a kind that, if it wished, it could abandon God—its blessedness—with misery immediately following [Note: [Col. 0751] So several ancient books. The printed editions instead read: “if it wished to abandon God, its blessedness, misery would immediately follow.”]. Although he foresaw that certain angels would become deserters of so great a good through the pride by which they wished to be sufficient to themselves for a blessed life, he did not take this power away from them. He judged it more powerful and better to bring good even out of evil than not to allow evil to exist [Note: [Col. 0751] Compare *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 11, §12 ff.].

Those evils would have no existence at all unless the mutable nature, although good and established by the supreme and immutable Good who created all good things, had made them for itself through sinning [Col. 0752]. By that very sin it is proved, as by its testimony, that it was created good. For unless it too were a great good, although not equal to its Creator, its abandonment of God, as of its own light, could not be its evil [Note: [Col. 0752] See *Enchiridion*, §4.].

For just as blindness is a defect of the eye, and this very fact indicates that the eye was created to see the light, and thus by its own defect the eye is shown to be more excellent than the other members as a member capable of light—for otherwise its defect would not consist in lacking light—so the nature that enjoyed God proves by the very defect through which it is miserable, because it does not enjoy God, that it was created supremely good.

God bound the voluntary fall of the angels by the most just punishment of eternal unhappiness. To the others who remained in that supreme good, he gave, as a reward for their remaining, certainty that they would remain forever. He also made the human being upright, with the same free will: an earthly animal, indeed, but worthy of heaven if he adhered to his Creator; and likewise subject to misery if he abandoned him, a misery suited to such a nature.

Although God foresaw that the human being would likewise sin through transgression of God’s law by abandoning God, he did not take away his power of free choice. At the same time, he foresaw what good he himself would bring out of his evil: for from the mortal race, justly and deservedly condemned, he gathers by his grace so great a people that from it he might fill and restore the part of the angels that had fallen. Thus that beloved and heavenly city would not be deprived of the number of its citizens, but perhaps would even rejoice in a fuller number [Note: [Col. 0752] Ibid., §9.].

## CHAPTER II—On the Eternal and Immutable Will of God

### 1

Many things are indeed done by the wicked against God’s will. But he possesses such wisdom and such power that all things that appear contrary to his will tend toward those outcomes or ends which he himself foresaw as good and just [Col. 0753].

Accordingly, when God is said to change his will, so that those toward whom he was gentle become, for example, objects of his anger, it is they rather than he who are changed; and in what they suffer they in some sense find him changed. It is like the sun changing for wounded eyes, becoming in some way harsh from mild and troublesome from pleasing, while in itself it remains the same as it was.

The will of God is also called that which he effects in the hearts of those who obey his commands. Of this the Apostle says, “For it is God who works in you both the willing” (Phil. 2:13). Just as God’s justice is called not only that by which he himself is just but also that which he creates in the human being whom he justifies, so his law is also called that which is rather the law of human beings, but which was given by him [Note: [Col. 0753] Am., Er., and Lov. read “given to human beings.” “To human beings” is absent from Vind. and the manuscripts.].

For clearly they were human beings to whom Jesus said, “In your law it is written” (John 8:17), while elsewhere we read, “The law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. 36:31). According to this will, which God works in human beings, he is also said to will what he himself does not will, but makes his own people will: just as he is said to have known what he caused to be known by those who had not known him.

For when the Apostle says, “But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God” (Gal. 4:9), we must not therefore believe that God then came to know those whom he had foreknown before the foundation of the world (1 Pet. 1:20). Rather, he is said then to have known them because he then brought about their coming to be known. I have already remembered discussing these modes of expression in the preceding books.

According to this will, therefore, by which we say that God wills what he causes others to will, although they do not know what is to come, he wills many things and does not bring them about.

### 2 [II.]

For his saints, inspired by a holy will, wish many things to happen, and they do not happen. Thus they piously and holily pray for certain people, yet he does not do what they pray for, even though he himself has created in them, through his Holy Spirit, this will to pray.

Accordingly, when the saints will and pray according to God that someone may be saved, we can use that mode of expression and say, “God wills it and does not do it,” meaning by “wills” the one who causes them to will it.

According to that other will of his, however, which is eternal together with his foreknowledge, he has already done in heaven and on earth everything whatever he has willed—not only things past or present but also things future (Ps. 113:3 twice).

Before the time comes when he has willed that what he foreknew and ordained before all times should happen, we say, “It will happen when God wills.” But if we do not know not only the time when it will happen but also whether it will happen at all, we say, “It will happen, if God wills”—not because God will then have a new will that he did not previously possess, but because what has been prepared from eternity in his immutable will will then come to pass:

## CHAPTER III—On the Promise of the Saints’ Eternal Blessedness and the Everlasting Punishments of the Wicked

Therefore, to pass over the many other things, just as we now see fulfilled in Christ what he promised to Abraham when he said, “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22:18), so what he promised to that same seed will be fulfilled when he says through the prophet:

“The dead will rise who were in the tombs”; and when he says, “There will be a new heaven and a new earth, and they will not remember the former things, nor will they ascend into their heart; but they will find joy and gladness in it. Behold, I will make Jerusalem a rejoicing and my people a joy; and I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; and the voice of weeping will no longer be heard in it” (Isa. 26:19, according to the Septuagint; 65:17–19, according to the Septuagint). [Note: [Col. 0754] The printed editions read “And behold.” The particle “And” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Septuagint. See above, book 20, chapter 21, §2.]

And through another prophet, what he foretold when he said to that prophet:

“At that time all your people will be saved who are found written in the book. And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth—or, as some have translated it, in the mound—will rise: some to everlasting life, and others to everlasting reproach and confusion” (Dan. 12:1–2).

And elsewhere through the same prophet:

“The saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever and ever” (Dan. 7:18).

And a little later:

“His kingdom,” he says, “is an everlasting kingdom” (ibid. 7:27).

And the other things pertaining to this that I set forth in the twentieth book (chapter 21 ff.), or that I did not set forth but are nevertheless written in those same Scriptures, will come to pass, just as these things have come to pass—things that unbelievers did not think would come. The same God promised both; he foretold that both would come, the God whom the deities of the pagans dread, as Porphyry, the most distinguished of the pagan philosophers, also bears witness.

## CHAPTER IV—Against the Wise Men of the World Who Think That Earthly Bodies Cannot Be Transferred to a Heavenly Dwelling

Yet learned and wise men, opposing the force of so great an authority—which, just as it foretold so long beforehand, has turned every kind of human being toward believing and hoping in this matter—seem to argue cleverly against the resurrection of bodies. They say what Cicero recorded in the third book of *The Republic*.

For when he asserted that Hercules and Romulus had been made gods from human beings, he said:

> “Their bodies,” he says, “were not carried up into heaven; for nature would not permit what was of the earth to remain anywhere but on earth.”

This is the great reasoning of the wise, “whose thoughts the Lord knows, because they are vain” (Ps. 93:11) [Note: [Col. 0754] Compare *On Faith and the Creed*, §13.].

For if we were souls only—that is, spirits without any body—and, dwelling in heaven, did not know earthly animals, and if we were told that we would in the future be joined by some marvelous bond to earthly bodies in order to animate them, would we not argue much more forcefully in refusing to believe it and say that nature does not permit an incorporeal thing to be bound by a bodily bond?

And yet the earth is full of living souls animating these earthly members, joined and interwoven with one another in a marvelous way [Note: [Col. 0754] The printed editions read: “And yet the earth is full of living souls, to which these earthly members are joined in a marvelous way,” and so forth. The authority of the ancient books corrects this; they do not have “to which” or “are,” but all read “joined to one another in a marvelous way.”].

Why, then, if the same God who made this animal wills it, will an earthly body not be able to be raised into a heavenly body, if the soul—superior to every body and therefore also to a heavenly body—could be joined to an earthly body? Or was so tiny a particle of earth able to hold within itself something better than a heavenly body, so that it might have sensation and life, while heaven would disdain to receive that sentient and living thing, or, having received it, would be unable to sustain it, even though it derives sensation and life from something better than every heavenly body?

But this does not happen now because the time has not yet come when the one who created what now seems commonplace through sight willed it to happen—a work far more marvelous than what these people refuse to believe.

Why, then, do we not wonder more intensely that incorporeal souls, which are superior to heavenly bodies, are joined to earthly bodies than that bodies, although earthly, are raised to bodily abodes, even though those abodes are heavenly? It is because we are accustomed to seeing the former and are the former, whereas we are not yet the latter, nor have we ever seen them.

For surely, when sober reason is consulted, it is found to be a more wondrous divine work to attach bodily things in some way to incorporeal things than to join together bodies—although different, since the one kind is heavenly and the other earthly—bodies to bodies [Note: [Col. 0755] Compare *Letter* 137, near the end of §11.].

## CHAPTER V—On the Resurrection of the Flesh, Which Some Do Not Believe Though the World Believes It

But perhaps this was once incredible. Behold, the world has now believed that Christ’s earthly body was taken up into heaven: the resurrection of the flesh and its ascent to the heavenly dwelling places have now been believed by both learned and unlearned, with very few remaining who are astonished, whether learned or unlearned.

If they have believed something credible, let them see how foolish are those who do not believe it. But if something incredible has been believed, then it is itself also incredible that what is incredible has been believed.

These two incredible things, therefore—the eternal resurrection of our body and the fact that the world would believe something so incredible—the same God foretold would both happen before either had happened (Matt. 26:13). We already see one of these two incredible things accomplished: the world believed what was incredible. Why, then, is the remaining one despaired of, so that what the world believed to be incredible may also come to pass, just as what was likewise incredible has already come to pass—namely, that the world would believe something so incredible—since both of these incredible things, one of which we see and the other of which we believe, were foretold in the same Scriptures through which the world believed?

And if the very manner in which the world believed is considered, it is found to be even more incredible. Christ sent to the sea of this age very few people uneducated in the liberal disciplines and altogether, as far as the learning of those people was concerned, uncultivated—not skilled in grammar, not armed with dialectic, not puffed up with rhetoric—fishermen with the nets of faith. In this way he caught fish from every race, so many and so much more remarkable the rarer they were, including philosophers themselves.

If it pleases us—indeed, because it ought to please us—let us add this third incredible thing to the other two. There are now three incredible things, which nevertheless happened.

It is incredible that Christ rose in the flesh and ascended into heaven with the flesh. It is incredible that the world believed something so incredible. It is incredible that obscure, lowly, very few, and uneducated people were able to persuade the world so effectively of something so incredible, and to persuade even the learned within it [Note: [Col. 0756] Some manuscripts, with Vind., Am., and Er., read “weak” instead of “lowly”; and below, where the text has “of the lowly,” they have “of the weak.”].

Of these three incredible things, the first those with whom we are dealing do not wish to believe; the second they are compelled both to see and to acknowledge. If they do not believe the third, they cannot find the origin of the second.

The resurrection of Christ and his ascent into heaven with the flesh in which he rose are now proclaimed and believed throughout the whole world. If this is not credible, how has it already been believed throughout the entire world? If many noble, eminent, and learned people said that they had seen it and took care to spread abroad what they had seen, it is not surprising that the world believed them; but it is obstinate that these people still refuse to believe.

But if, as is true, the world believed a few obscure, insignificant, and uneducated people who said and wrote that they had seen it, why do a few exceptionally obstinate people who remain still refuse to believe the world that now believes? The world believed because, through such contemptible witnesses, the divinity itself persuaded it in a much more marvelous way.

The utterances of those who persuaded people—what they said—were marvelous deeds, not words. For those who had not seen Christ rise in the flesh and ascend into heaven with it believed those who narrated that they had seen it—not merely speaking, but also performing miraculous signs.

They knew that these men had been acquainted with only one language, or at most two, yet suddenly they heard them speaking miraculously in the languages of all nations (Acts 2). They saw a man lame from his mother’s womb, after forty years, made sound at their word in the name of Christ; handkerchiefs taken from their bodies benefiting the sick by healing them; countless people afflicted with various diseases, placed in order along the road by which they were going to pass, regularly receiving health at once when the shadow of those passing over them fell upon them; and many other astonishing things performed through them in the name of Christ [Note: [Col. 0756] So the manuscripts. Vind., Am., and Er. read “these signs were performed”; Lov. reads “they performed signs,” omitting “were”]—and finally, even the dead rising again (ibid. 3–4).

If they admit that these things happened as they are read, behold, we add so many incredible things to those three incredible things. To make people believe the one incredible claim concerning the resurrection of the flesh and the ascension into heaven, we heap up the testimony of so many incredible events, yet we still do not bend unbelievers, hardened by a dreadful resistance, toward belief.

But if they do not believe that these miracles were performed through Christ’s Apostles so that people would believe them as they proclaimed Christ’s resurrection and ascension, then this one great miracle is sufficient for us: that the whole world believed it without any miracles.

## CHAPTER VI—How Rome Made Its Founder Romulus a God by Loving Him, Whereas the Church Loved Christ as God by Believing in Him [Note: [Col. 0757] In the heading of this sixth chapter, the better manuscripts read, “Whereas the Church loved Christ as God by believing in him”; the Benedictine Fathers ordered this reading to be accepted into the text. [The Church loved Christ the Lord by believing in him.]] 

### 1

Let us also recall here what Tullius admires concerning the divinity attributed to Romulus. I shall insert his words as they are written:

> “What is more remarkable,” he says, “in the case of Romulus is that the others who are said to have been made gods from human beings lived in less educated ages, so that there was greater opportunity for invention, since the unlearned were easily driven to believe. But we see that Romulus’ age, less than six hundred years ago, already possessed long-established letters and learning, and that all that ancient error arising from the uncultivated life of human beings had been removed.”

And a little later he speaks of Romulus in a way relevant to this point:

> “From this it can be understood,” he says, “that Homer lived many years before Romulus, so that, by the time of learned people and of an age itself educated, there was scarcely any room for invention. For antiquity accepted fables, sometimes even those crudely fabricated; but this age, now cultivated, especially rejects and mocks whatever cannot happen” (*On the Republic*, book 2, chapter 10, supplemented here from the context). [Note: [Col. 0757] This was not said by Cicero of himself or of his own times—he was writing approximately in the seven-hundredth year after the founding of the City—but of the younger Scipio Africanus and Laelius, whom he introduced as discussing matters in those books *On the Republic* according to what was said above, book 2, chapter 21. Scipio is reported to have flourished from approximately the six-hundredth to the six-hundred-and-twentieth year of the City’s foundation, while Laelius is recorded as having held the consulship in the six-hundred-and-seventh year.]

M. Tullius Cicero, one of the most learned of men and also the most eloquent of all, therefore says that Romulus’ divinity was remarkably believed because the times were already educated and would not accept the falsehood of fables.

But who believed Romulus to be a god except Rome—and Rome while it was small and just beginning? Then it became necessary for later generations to preserve what they had received from their ancestors, so that, as the city grew up with this superstition imbibed, so to speak, with its mother’s milk, and reached so great an empire, it might spread this opinion from its elevated position, as from a higher place, to other nations also over which it ruled.

Those nations did not actually believe Romulus to be a god, but nevertheless called him one, lest they offend the city they served by naming its founder otherwise than Rome did. Rome had believed this not indeed through love of the error itself, but through an error of love.

Christ, however, although he is the founder of the heavenly and eternal city, was not believed by it to be God because he founded it. Rather, it is being founded precisely because it believed him to be God.

Rome, already built and dedicated, worshiped its founder as a god in a temple. But this Jerusalem placed its founder, Christ God, in the foundation of faith so that it might be built and dedicated.

The former, by loving him, believed him to be a god; the latter, by believing him to be God, loved him. Thus, just as there preceded the basis for Rome to love him and, once she loved him, to believe willingly even what was false as a good, so there preceded the basis for the Church to believe, so that with right faith she might love not something false rashly, but what was true.

For, apart from the many and great miracles that persuaded people that Christ was God, there also preceded prophecies of God that were supremely worthy of belief. In him they are not, as they are still believed by the fathers, awaiting fulfillment; they are already shown to have been fulfilled.

Concerning Romulus, because he founded Rome and ruled in it, people hear or read what happened, not what had been prophesied beforehand [Note: [Col. 0758] Some ancient books read “before it happened”; others, “before it would happen.”]. But the written records maintain that he was received among the gods as something believed, not teach it as something accomplished.

No signs of miraculous events demonstrate that this truly happened to him. That she-wolf as nurse—which appears to have been a great portent—what is it, or how great is it, for demonstrating that he was a god? Certainly, even if that wolf was not a prostitute but a beast [Note: [Col. 0758] See above, book 18, chapter 21.], since it was a portent shared by both brothers, his brother nevertheless is not considered a god. [Note: [Col. 0758] The printed editions add “of the two brothers.” Three lines later, at “since it was shared by both,” they read “since the portent was shared by both brothers.”]

Who, then, was prevented from calling Romulus, Hercules, or other such men gods, and preferred to die rather than not call them gods? Or would any nation have worshiped Romulus among its gods unless fear of the Roman name compelled it?

Who, moreover, could count how many people preferred to be killed with every degree of savage cruelty rather than deny that Christ was God?

Therefore, a fear of whatever slight indignation it was thought might arise in the minds of the Romans if they did not do so compelled certain cities subject to Roman authority to worship Romulus as a god.

But from worshiping Christ God, and even from confessing him, fear could not turn back so great a multitude of martyrs throughout the world—not fear of a slight offense in the minds of their persecutors, but of immense and varied punishments [Note: [Col. 0758] The printed editions Vind., Am., and Er., without the support of the ancient manuscripts, read: “no fear or error could turn them back; no flattery removed them, no promise; nor did violent deprivation of their possessions or the severity of every kind of varied punishment.”], including death itself, which is feared more than all the rest.

Nor did the City of Christ, although it was still journeying on earth and nevertheless possessed the ranks of great peoples, fight against its impious persecutors for temporal safety. Rather, so that it might obtain eternal safety, it did not resist.

They were bound, imprisoned, beaten, tortured, burned, torn apart, slaughtered—and they multiplied. For them, to fight for safety meant nothing other than to despise safety for the sake of the Savior.

## Chapter 2

I know that in the third book of Cicero’s *Republic*, unless I am mistaken, it is argued that no war is undertaken by an excellent state except either for the sake of loyalty or for the sake of safety. What he means by “for the sake of safety,” or what safety he intends, he demonstrates elsewhere, saying:

“But from those punishments which even the most foolish perceive—poverty, exile, imprisonment, scourging—they often escape as private individuals by accepting the swift punishment of death. For states, however, death itself is a punishment which seems to rescue individuals from punishment. A state must indeed be so constituted that it is eternal. Thus the destruction of a republic is not natural, as death is natural to a human being, for whom death is not only necessary but very often desirable. But when a state is removed, destroyed, and extinguished, it is, in a certain way—if we compare small things with great ones—as though this whole world should perish and collapse.”

Cicero said this because, with the Platonists, he holds that the world will not perish. It is therefore clear that he wished a state to undertake war for that safety by which the state remains, as he says, eternal, although individual persons die and are born; just as the shade of an olive tree or laurel, and of other trees of this kind, is perpetual through the falling and arising of individual offspring.

For, as he says, death is not the punishment of individual human beings but of the state as a whole, which generally rescues individuals from punishment. Hence it is rightly asked whether the people of Saguntum acted correctly when they preferred their entire state to perish rather than break the loyalty by which they were bound to the Roman republic itself. Their deed is praised by the people of the earthly republic [Note: Vind., Am., Er., and nearly all manuscripts read, “praised by all”; i.e., “by all the citizens of the earthly republic.”] [Note: See above, Book 3, chapter 20.]

But I do not see how they could have obeyed this argument, in which it is said that no war should be undertaken except for loyalty or for safety. It does not say what should be chosen if these two things should come together in a single danger in such a way that one cannot be maintained without the loss of the other. For certainly, if the people of Saguntum chose safety, they had to abandon loyalty; if they were to preserve loyalty, they necessarily had to lose safety, as indeed happened.

The safety of the City of God, however, is such that it can be retained—or rather acquired—together with loyalty and through loyalty; but once loyalty has been lost, no one can attain it. This conviction made so many martyrs, and martyrs of such great and steadfast endurance, as Romulus, when he was believed to be a god, did not have and could not have had even one.

## Chapter 7 — That it was the work of divine power, not of human persuasion, that the world should believe in Christ

It is extremely ridiculous, when we are speaking about Christ, to mention Romulus’s false divinity. Nevertheless, since Romulus lived nearly six hundred years before Cicero [Note: Ludovicus Vives thinks that *ante Ciceronem* should be read *ante Scipionem*, namely, before Scipio Aemilianus, who is introduced as speaking in the books *On the Republic*. The scholars of Louvain, following his conjecture, attempt to emend the passage, but the conjecture is contradicted by the other printed editions and by all the manuscripts.], and since that age is said already to have been cultivated by learning, so that it rejected everything that could not happen [Note: The printed editions read *omne eludens*, “mocking everything.” *Eludens* is absent from the manuscripts.], how much more, six hundred years later, in Cicero’s own time, and especially afterward under Augustus and Tiberius, in unquestionably more learned ages, would the human mind have been unable to endure the resurrection of Christ’s flesh and his ascension into heaven, rejecting them as things that could not happen and mocking them, unless the divinity of truth itself—or the truth of his divinity—and the accompanying signs of miracles had shown that these things could happen and had happened?

Thus, despite so many and such great persecutions that terrified and opposed them, the resurrection and immortality of the flesh—first in Christ and afterward, at the beginning of the new age, to follow in the others—might be believed with complete faith, proclaimed fearlessly, and sown throughout the world to spring up more fruitfully through the blood of the martyrs. The preceding proclamations of the Prophets were being read [Note: Vind., Am., Er., and several manuscripts read “the proclamations of the preceding prophets.”]; signs of mighty deeds converged; and the truth was being commended to a new custom, not contrary to reason, until the world that had persecuted in fury followed in faith [Note: So the ancient books. The printed editions instead read “continued in faith.”].

## Chapter 8 — On the miracles performed so that the world might believe in Christ, and which do not cease to occur even when the world believes

### 1

“Why,” they ask, “are the miracles which you proclaim to have been performed not performed now?”

I could certainly say that they were necessary before the world believed, in order that the world might believe. Whoever still seeks wonders in order to believe is himself a great wonder: he does not believe while the world believes.

But they say this in order that people may not believe that those miracles were performed even then. From where, then, does Christ continue to be proclaimed everywhere as having been taken up into heaven with his flesh? How, in learned times that rejected everything impossible, did the world believe, without any miracles, things that were exceedingly miraculous and incredible? Or will they perhaps say that these things were credible, and therefore were believed? Why, then, do they themselves not believe?

Our concise conclusion is therefore this: either other incredible things, which nevertheless were happening and were being seen, gave credibility to an incredible event [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “to an incredible event” with a different grammatical construction.] that was not seen; or else a matter so credible that it required no miracles to persuade people of it exposed the excessive unbelief of these men.

I have said this to refute the utterly empty-minded. For we cannot deny that many miracles were performed which testified to that one great and saving miracle by which Christ ascended into heaven with the flesh in which he rose again. All these things—both the deeds that were performed and the reasons why they were performed so that they might be believed—have been written down in the same books, which are wholly truthful. These miracles became known so that they might produce faith; through the faith they produced, they become known much more clearly.

They are read aloud before the peoples so that they may be believed; yet they would not be read aloud before the peoples unless they had been believed. For even now miracles are performed in his name, either through his sacraments or through the prayers or memorials of his saints. But they are not illuminated with the same clarity, so that they are not spread abroad with glory as great as that of the former miracles.

The canon of the sacred writings, which had to be defined [Note: The printed editions, differing from the ancient books, read “which had to be publicized.”], causes those earlier miracles to be recited everywhere and to remain fixed in the memory of all peoples. But whenever these later miracles occur, they are scarcely known there by the entire city or by all the inhabitants of whatever place it may be. Often, even there, only very few know of them while the rest are ignorant, especially if the city is large. And when they are reported elsewhere and to others, the authority supporting them is not so great that they are believed without difficulty or hesitation, even though faithful Christians report them to faithful Christians.

### 2

The miracle that happened at Milan, when we were there, when a blind man received his sight, could become known to many because the city is large, the emperor was then present there, and the event occurred before an immense crowd, which had gathered at the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius. Their bodies had lain hidden and were wholly unknown, but they were revealed to Bishop Ambrose in a dream and discovered. There the blind man, once the old darkness had been driven away, saw the daylight [Note: Compare *Confessions* 9.7.16; Sermon 318.1; *Retractions* 1.13.7; and elsewhere.].

### 3

But at Carthage, who knows—apart from a very small number—the healing that occurred to Innocentius, formerly an advocate of the deputy prefecture, when we were present and saw it with our own eyes?

When my brother Alypius and I came from overseas—at that time not yet clergy, but already serving God—he had received us, as he was a most devout man together with his whole household, and we were then staying with him. He was being treated by physicians. They had already cut open the fistulas [Note: The printed editions read, “He was being treated by physicians because of fistulas”; and below, “they had already cut him.” All the manuscripts omit *propter*, “because of”; some have *they had already cut it for him*, while many more have *they had already cut him*.], which he had numerous and complicated in the rear and lower part of his body, and they were treating the remaining parts with the medicines of their art.

He had suffered long and severe pain during that operation. But one cavity among the many had deceived the physicians and remained so hidden that they did not touch it, although they ought to have opened it with a surgical instrument. Finally, when all the other places that had been opened were healed, this one remained alone, and labor was being expended on it in vain.

Suspecting these delays and greatly fearing that he would be cut again—something which another household physician of his had predicted, but whom the others had not allowed to be present even to observe how they performed the operation when he was first cut, and whom he had angrily expelled from the house and only reluctantly received again—he burst out:

“Are you going to cut me again? Am I to submit to the words of the man whom you refused to have present?”

They mocked that physician as unskilled and tried to soothe the man’s fear with kind words and promises. Many more days passed, and nothing that was being done made any progress. Nevertheless, the physicians persisted in their promise that they would close the cavity not with the knife but with medicines.

They also summoned another physician, already advanced in age and highly praised in that art—he was still alive—named Ammonius [Note: The printed editions read, “I mean Ammonius, who….” The manuscripts do not contain *dico*, “I mean.”]. After examining the place, he promised him the same thing as the others, relying on their diligence and expertise. Made confident by this man’s authority, he mocked his household physician, who had predicted that another operation would be necessary, with witty cheerfulness, as though he were already safe.

What more is there to say? So many days afterward passed uselessly that at last, exhausted and confused, they admitted that he could not possibly be healed without the knife. He was terrified and turned pale, overcome by excessive fear. When he had collected himself and was able to speak, he ordered them to leave and not come near him again.

The exhausted man, worn down by tears and constrained by that necessity, could think of nothing else except summoning a certain Alexandrian, who at that time was considered an extraordinary surgeon, so that he might perform what, in his anger, he did not want the others to perform.

But after the Alexandrian came and, as an expert, examined their work in the scars, he acted as a good man and persuaded him to let those who had labored on him so greatly—indeed, so greatly that he himself admired them when he inspected their work—enjoy the completion of their treatment. He added that the man could not be saved unless he were cut, but that it was very contrary to his character to take away the prize of such great labor from men whose most skillful work, industry, and diligence he admired when he saw them in the scars, merely because a small part remained.

The man’s confidence in them was restored, and it was agreed that, with the Alexandrian assisting, they themselves should open with the knife that cavity which, by everyone’s agreement, was now thought incurable by any other means. The procedure was postponed until the following day.

But when they had gone away, such grief arose in that household from the master’s excessive sorrow that it could scarcely be restrained, like the lamentation at a funeral, by us. Holy men visited him daily: Saturninus, then bishop of Uzalis, of blessed memory; the presbyter Gelosus [Note: Most manuscripts read *Gulosus*.]; and deacons of the Church of Carthage. Among them was Aurelius, then a deacon, and now the only one of them still living—he is now a bishop, and must be named with the honor due to him. We have often spoken with him about the wondrous works of God [Note: Most manuscripts read “the wondrous works of God,” with a different grammatical construction.] concerning this event, and we found that he remembered very well what we are recounting.

When they visited him in the evening, as they were accustomed to do, he asked them with pitiable tears to be so kind as to be present in the morning at his funeral rather than at his suffering. For such fear of the previous pains had seized him that he had no doubt he would die in the physicians’ hands.
