They consoled him and urged him to trust in God and to bear his will courageously. Then we entered for prayer. As was customary, we bent our knees and prostrated ourselves on the ground. He threw himself down as though he had been struck and knocked over by some powerful force, and began to pray.

Who could express in words the manner of his prayer, the feeling, the movement of his soul, the flood of tears, the groans and sobs that shook all his limbs and almost cut off his breath? I did not know whether the others were praying or whether their attention had been diverted toward this. I myself could not pray at all. I said only this briefly in my heart:

“Lord, whose prayers do you hear, if you do not hear these?”

For it seemed to me that nothing more could be added except that he should breathe his last while praying.

We arose, received the Bishop’s blessing, and departed, asking them to be present in the morning and urging him to keep a calm spirit. The feared day dawned. The servants of God were present, as they had promised. The physicians entered. Everything required at that hour was prepared. The dreadful instruments were brought out, while everyone stood stunned and anxious.

Those whose authority was greatest raised his failing courage by consoling him. He was placed on the bed with his limbs arranged for the operation; the knots of the bandages were loosened; the place was exposed; the physician examined it and, armed and intent on cutting the cavity, investigated it. He searched it with his eyes and touched it with his fingers; finally, he tested it in every way.

He found a very firm scar.

Then came the joy, praise, and thanksgiving to the merciful and almighty God, poured from every mouth amid tears of gladness. This must not be entrusted to my words; let it rather be contemplated than described.

### 3

At the same Carthage, Innocentia, a most devout woman from one of the leading families of the city, had a cancer in her breast: a disease, as the physicians say, incurable by any medicines [Note: This evidently applies when the cancer has advanced and become fully developed. See Galen, *Therapeutics to Glaucon*, Book 2, chapter 10. Coquaeus.].

Either the affected member is ordinarily cut away and separated from the body, or, so that a person may live somewhat longer, while death will nevertheless come from that cause, all treatment must be abandoned, according to what is reported to have been Hippocrates’ opinion [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed Vind., Am., and Er. editions instead read: “or, so that a person may live somewhat more peacefully, the disease must be alleviated by frequent fomentations, since, if we hope that death will come from it as late as possible, this is the opinion, as it is reported, of Hippocrates.” The Louvain edition reads: “or, so that a person may live somewhat longer, since death will come from it as late as possible, according to the opinion, as it is reported, of Hippocrates.”] (*Aphorisms* 6.38).

She had received this advice from an experienced physician, a close friend of her household, and had turned to God alone in prayer. As Easter approached, she was warned in a dream that, as she stood among the women at the baptistery, whichever baptized woman first came to her should mark the affected spot on her with the sign of Christ [Note: In ancient times, apart from cases of necessity, Easter and Pentecost were established as the seasons for Baptism. This is clear from Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 19: “Easter provides the more solemn day for Baptism, since the Lord’s passion, in which we are baptized, has been accomplished. From then until Pentecost”—that is, as he says in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3, “from Easter to Pentecost”—“there is a very broad period for arranging baptisms: during it the Lord’s resurrection was repeatedly celebrated among the disciples, and the grace of the Holy Spirit was inaugurated.” Coquaeus.]. She did so, and health immediately followed [Note: Vind., Am., and Er. read “with the sign of the cross of Christ.”].

The physician who had told her to use no treatment if she wished to live somewhat longer later examined her and found her completely healthy—the very disease she had previously had he had recognized by such an examination. He earnestly asked her what she had used [Note: The printed editions read “what treatment she had used.” *Treatment* is absent from the manuscripts.], wishing, as can be understood, to learn the medicine by which Hippocrates’ definition had been defeated.

When he heard from her what had happened, he reportedly replied with a voice and expression of contempt, so that she feared he might utter some insulting word against Christ, but with devout courtesy:

“I thought,” he said, “you were going to tell me something important.”

When she was already becoming frightened, he immediately added:

“What great thing did Christ do by healing a cancer, when he raised a man who had been dead four days?” (John 11).

When I heard this, I was extremely indignant that so great a miracle, performed in that city and in the case of a person who was by no means obscure, should remain hidden in this way. I therefore thought that she should be admonished, almost even rebuked.

When she replied that she had not kept silent about it, I asked the women who happened at that time to be close friends and companions of hers whether they had known of it before [Note: The passage begins at the indicated column in the printed editions.]. They answered that they had known absolutely nothing.

“Look,” I said, “how you do not keep silent, so that even these women who are joined to you by such great intimacy do not hear of it.”

Because I had asked her only briefly, I caused her, while they listened and greatly marveled and glorified God, to report the entire event in order, exactly as it had occurred.

### 4

Who knows of a certain physician [Note: Vind., Am., Er., and five manuscripts read *Mendicum*, “a beggar,” rather than *medicum*, “a physician.”] with gout in the same city who, after giving his name for Baptism, was forbidden in a dream by black, curly-haired boys [Note: Vind. and Am. read *curatis*. Louvain and the manuscripts read *cirratis*, that is, “haired” or “with curls”; for Nonius interprets *cirri* as the hair of the head. Martial, Book 9, epigram 30: “Nor the curl-bedecked crowd of the morning teacher.”], whom he understood to be demons, to be baptized that same year, and who, refusing to obey them, went away even while they trampled on his feet, causing him the most acute pain he had ever experienced [Note: Vind., Am., and some manuscripts read “had burned with fever.”]?

He overcame them still more through the bath of regeneration and, as he had vowed, did not delay being washed. In Baptism itself he was freed not only from the pain with which he was being tortured beyond the usual measure but also from his gout. And after living for a long time afterward, his feet never hurt again.

Who knows of this except the very few brothers to whom the event could have become known? We nevertheless know it.

### 5

A man from Curubis, formerly an actor [Note: The printed editions read *from a neighboring place* rather than *from an actor*; they connect this with the preceding words, “to whom the event could have become known from a neighboring place.”], was healed at his Baptism not only of paralysis but also of a disfiguring enlargement of his genitals. Freed from both afflictions, he rose from the font of regeneration as though he had never had any bodily illness.

Who knows of this apart from Curubis and a very few others who were able to hear of it anywhere? When we learned of it, at the command of the holy bishop Aurelius, we also had him come to Carthage, although we had previously heard it from people whose good faith we could not doubt.

### 6

There is among us a man of tribunician rank, Hesperius [Note: The printed editions read “who is among us”; the word *who* is absent from the manuscripts]. In the territory of Fussala he possesses an estate called Zubedi [Note: Er. reads *Cubedi*. Four manuscripts read *Zabedi*. The others have *Zubedi*.].

When he discovered that, through the affliction of his animals and servants, his household was suffering the harmful power of evil spirits, he asked our presbyters—while I was absent—that one of them go there, whose prayers might cause the spirits to withdraw.

One went. He offered there the sacrifice of Christ’s body, praying as fervently as he could that the harassment might cease. Through God’s immediate mercy, it ceased.

Hesperius had received from a friend some holy earth brought from Jerusalem, where Christ was buried and rose again on the third day. He had suspended it in his bedroom so that he himself might not suffer any harm. But once his house had been cleansed of the infestation, he wondered what should be done with the earth, for he did not wish to keep it any longer in his bedroom out of reverence.

It happened by chance that I and my colleague, the bishop Maximinus of the neighboring church of Sinis [Note: Am., Er., and Louvain read *Synicensis*; Vind. reads *Synistensis*; the manuscripts read *Sinitensis*. See Letter 23, with the note in which this word is discussed.], were nearby. He asked us to come, and we came.

After he had told us everything, he also asked that the earth be buried somewhere and that a place of prayer be established there, where Christians could gather to celebrate the things of God. We did not resist; it was done.

There was there a young peasant who was paralyzed. When he heard of this, he asked his parents to carry him without delay to that holy place. After he had been brought there, he prayed, and immediately departed from the place healed and walking on his own feet.

### 7

There is said to be an estate called Victoriana, less than thirty miles from Hippo Regius. There is a memorial there of the Milanese martyrs Protasius and Gervasius.

A young man was brought there who, while washing a horse at midday during the summer in a deep pool of the river, was attacked by a demon. He lay there either close to death or very much like a dead man.

Toward evening, the mistress of the estate entered the place according to custom, together with her female servants and some consecrated women, for the hymns and prayers. They began to sing hymns.

At the sound of their singing, the young man seemed to be struck and shaken. With a terrible roar, he grasped the altar and, unable or unwilling to move it, held on to it as though he had been bound or fastened to it. With great wailing, he begged that mercy be shown him and confessed where, when, and how he had attacked the young man.

Finally, announcing that he would depart, he named each of the young man’s limbs, threatening that as he departed he would cut them off. Amid these words, he left the man.

But the man’s eye had slipped down into his cheek and hung from within by a thin vein, as though from its root. The entire middle part of the eye, which had been dark, had become white.

When those present saw this—the others had also rushed in, summoned by his cries, and all had thrown themselves down in prayer for him—they rejoiced that he was standing in his right mind, but they were again saddened by his eye and said that a physician should be sought.

Then the husband of his sister, who had brought him there, said:

“God is able, through the prayers of the saints, to restore the light, since he has driven away the demon.”

Then, as best he could, he tied the fallen and hanging eye back into its proper place with a cloth [Note: Here *orarium* means a sweat-cloth or linen cloth intended for wiping the mouth. Jerome, *Letter to Nepotian*: “It is altogether disgraceful to boast of a well-filled purse when you do not possess a sweat-cloth and a mouth-cloth.”]. He thought it should not be untied until seven days had passed. When he did so, he found the eye perfectly healthy [Note: A very similar story about John of Choziba is found in Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History* 4.7. Coquaeus.].

Others were also healed there, but it would take too long to speak of them.

### 8

I know of a certain virgin of Hippo who anointed herself with oil into which a presbyter praying for her had let his tears fall. She was immediately healed of a demon.

I also know of a bishop who once prayed for a young man whom he had not seen, and the young man was immediately freed from the demon.

### 9

There was a certain Florentius, an old man from Hippo, one of our people, a devout and poor man. He supported himself by tailoring. He had lost his cloak and had no means to buy another.

At the memorial of the Twenty Martyrs, whose shrine is exceedingly famous among us [Note: Compare Sermon 325, preached on their feast day.], he prayed aloud that he might be clothed.

Some young men who happened to be present heard him. They mocked him and followed him as he departed, taunting him as though he had asked the Martyrs for fifty *folles* with which to buy clothing [Note: *Folles* were coins named from the age in which they were minted. The term denotes a kind of currency, sometimes bronze and sometimes silver. Here *folles* must be understood not as silver coins but as bronze ones, of approximately the same value as the asses and solidi of the French currency, as Sirmondus thinks in his note on Sermon 389, which is numbered 40 among the Sirmondian sermons. Suidas says that a *follis* is an obol, under the Greek words *pholleis* and *kermata*. Folles are also mentioned in Book 3 against Cresconius, section 33, and in Book 1 of Evodius’s *Miracles of Saint Stephen*, chapter 11, in the Appendix to volume 7 of this edition.].

But as he walked silently, he saw a large fish, still flapping, cast up on the shore. With the young men helping and encouraging him, he seized it and sold it for three hundred *folles* to a cook named Catosus [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed Vind. and Am. editions read *Cartosus*; Er. and Louvain read *Carchosus*], a good Christian, for use in the kitchen, explaining what had happened. He intended to buy wool with the money, so that his wife could somehow make him something to wear.

But when the cook cut open the fish, he found a gold ring in its stomach. Soon moved by pity and struck by religious awe, he returned it to the man, saying:

“See how the Twenty Martyrs have clothed you.”

### 10

At Aquae Tibilitanae [Note: The city of Tibilis is mentioned in Letter 112.], when the bishop Praejectus brought the relics of the most glorious martyr Stephen [Note: The printed Vind. and Er. editions and Louvain read *Projectus*. The ancient books read *Praejectus*.], a great crowd gathered and came to meet them as they were carried to his memorial.

There a blind woman prayed that she might be led to the bishop who was carrying the relics [Note: The printed editions read “that she might be led to the bishop carrying the sacred relics.” The words “sacred relics” are absent from the manuscripts.]. She gave him the flowers she was carrying; she received them back, brought them to her eyes, and immediately saw.

While those present stood astonished, she went ahead rejoicing, making her way along the road and no longer requiring a guide.

### 11

Lucillus, bishop of that place, carried the memorial of the aforementioned martyr, which had been established in the fortress of Siniti, near the colony of Hippo, with the people going before and following behind.

A fistula from which he had long suffered, and whose operation he had been awaiting at the hands of his very close physician [Note: The manuscripts read “who was to cut it.” Shortly afterward, Vind., Am., and Er. add “before he was suddenly healed, when he touched the holy relics.” This is absent from Louvain and the manuscripts.], was suddenly healed while he carried that pious burden. From then on, he no longer found it in his body.

### 12

Eucharius is a presbyter from Spain who lives in Calama [Note: Vind., Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *Chalamae*.] [Note: So the ancient books. The printed editions omit *est*, “is,” and instead of “lives” give “living.” See the note above on Book 14, chapter 24, section 2, concerning Calama.]. He had long suffered from the disease of stones. Through the memorial of the aforementioned martyr, which Bishop Possidius brought there [Note: Below, section 20.], he was healed.

Later, when another illness became severe, that same man lay dead in such a state that his thumbs were already being tied. Through the aid of the aforementioned martyr, when a tunic of the presbyter himself had been brought back from the martyr’s memorial and placed over his prostrate body, he was restored to life.

### 13

There was there a man prominent in his rank named Martialis, already advanced in age and very hostile to the Christian religion. He had, however, a faithful daughter and a son-in-law who had been baptized that same year.

When they urged him, as he lay ill, with many and great tears [Note: The printed editions read “with great prayers and tears”; the manuscripts lack the words “prayers and.”] to become a Christian, he utterly refused and drove them away from him in angry agitation.

His son-in-law decided that he should go to the memorial of Saint Stephen and pray there as earnestly as he could that God would give Martialis a good mind, by which he would not delay believing in Christ.

He did this with immense groaning and weeping and with a sincerely burning feeling of devotion. Then, as he departed, he took some of the flowers that happened to be on the altar and, when night had already fallen, placed them at Martialis’s head. Then they went to sleep.

Before dawn, Martialis suddenly cried out that someone should run for the bishop, who happened at that time to be with me at Hippo. When he learned that the bishop was absent, he asked that presbyters come. They came. He said that he believed, to the astonishment and joy of everyone, and he was baptized.

As long as he lived, he constantly had these words on his lips:

“Christ, receive my spirit.”

He did not know that these were the last words of the most blessed Stephen when he was stoned by the Jews (Acts 7:58). They were also Martialis’s last words, for not long afterward he too died [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “Here” rather than “This.”].

### 14

Two men with gout were healed there through the same martyr: one a citizen and one a foreigner. The citizen was healed completely [Note: Vind., Am., and Er. read “three men with gout, two citizens and one foreigner. But the citizens….”].

The foreigner, however, received through a revelation instructions about what he should apply whenever the pain occurred; and whenever he did so, the pain immediately subsided.

### 15

Audurus is the name of an estate where there is a church containing a memorial of the martyr Stephen.

A small boy was playing in the courtyard when oxen that were pulling a wagon bolted out of control. The wheel crushed him, and immediately he lay gasping out his last breath.

His mother seized him and placed him at the same memorial. He not only came back to life but also appeared unharmed.

### 16

A consecrated woman on a neighboring estate called Caspaliana was suffering from an illness, and her condition was considered hopeless. A tunic from the same memorial was brought to her; but before it could be taken back, she died.

Her parents nevertheless covered her corpse with this tunic, and when she received her spirit again, she was restored alive and safe.

### 17

At Hippo, a certain Syrian named Bassus was praying at the memorial of the same martyr for his sick and endangered daughter. He had brought his daughter’s garment with him.

Then suddenly servants ran from the house and announced that she had died. But while he was praying, his friends intercepted them and prevented them from telling him, lest he should mourn publicly.

When he returned home, which already resounded with the wailing of his family, he threw the garment he was carrying over his daughter. Life was restored to her.

### 18

Again, here among us, the son of a certain tax collector named Irenaeus died of an illness. His lifeless body lay there, and the mourners and lamenters were preparing the funeral rites.

One of his friends, amid the words of the others who were offering consolation, suggested that the body should be anointed with oil from the same martyr. This was done, and he came back to life.

### 19

Likewise, here among us, the tribunician Eleusinus [Note: Some manuscripts read *Eleusinius*.] placed his little son, who had been rendered lifeless by illness, upon the memorial of the martyr [Note: Vind., Am., Er., and several manuscripts read “the memorial of the martyrs.”], which stands on his suburban estate.

After offering a prayer there with many tears, he lifted him up alive.

### 20

What am I to do? The promise to complete this work presses upon me, so that I cannot recount here everything I know. Without doubt, many of our people, when they read this, will regret that I have omitted so much which they know together with me.

I now ask them to forgive me and to consider how long a labor it would be to do what the necessity of the work I have undertaken compels me not to do here.

For if I wished to write down only the miracles of healing, leaving other matters aside, that were performed through this martyr—that is, the most glorious Stephen—in the colony of Calama and in our own colony, many books would have to be completed. Yet even then they could not all be collected, but only those concerning which written reports had been given to be read before the peoples.

We wished this to be done because we saw that signs of divine power resembling those of ancient times were also occurring frequently in our own days, and that they ought not to perish from the knowledge of many.

It is not yet two years since this memorial began to exist at Hippo Regius [Note: From this we understand that this book was written toward the end of the year 426, or not much later. The memorial of the martyr Stephen already existed at Hippo when the miracle presently to be related occurred there, namely, the healing of Paul and Palladia. That healing belongs to the year 425, as can be established in the following way.

In his own written report, contained in Augustine’s Sermon 322, Paul testifies that he and his sister Palladia had been divinely warned “by a vision on the day of the January calendars” to go to Hippo, where they would recover their health “within the third month,” that is, within March. Here Paul is said to have recovered on Easter Sunday itself, and his sister on the third day after Easter Sunday.

From the year 415, when the relics of the martyr Stephen were discovered in Palestine, until 427, when the Vandals occupied Africa, Easter fell in March only in the year 425, when Bucherius says that some Latins celebrated the Easter feast on March 22, although, according to the observation of the Dominical Letter, it ought to have occurred on April 19, as we noted in connection with Sermon 322.

Written accounts of the revelation concerning the martyr Stephen and of his miracles, published under the names of Avitus, Lucianus, Severus, and Evodius, are presented in the Appendix to volume 7 of this edition.].

And although many reports concerning the miraculous events were not given to us—and this is completely certain—the reports that had been given had already reached nearly seventy when I wrote this. At Calama, where the memorial itself was established earlier and where reports are given more frequently, they surpass this number by an incomparable multitude [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “by an incredible multitude.”].

### 21

We have also learned that many remarkable things were performed through the same Martyr at Uzalis, which is a town near Utica. There his memorial was established by Bishop Evodius long before it was established among us. The custom of submitting written accounts does not exist there—or rather, did not exist, for perhaps it has now begun. When we were recently there, we urged Petronia, a woman of the highest distinction, who had been miraculously cured there of a grave and prolonged illness, against which all the aid of physicians had failed, to submit a written account, with the approval of the aforementioned bishop of the place, so that it might be read before the people; and she obeyed most readily. [Note: [Col. 0769] See Sermons 318–324, vol. 5, and also the book *On the Miracles of St. Stephen*, in the Appendix to vol. 7 of this work.] [Col. 0769] In it she also included something that I cannot pass over here, although I am compelled to hasten on to matters demanded by this work.

She said that she had been persuaded by a certain Jew to insert a ring into a girdle of hair, [Note: [Col. 0769] Vind., Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *vinculo*, “bond,” instead of *cingulo*, “girdle.”] which she wore bound around her naked body beneath all her clothing. Under the gemstone of the ring was a stone found in the kidneys of an ox. Bound with this as though it were a remedy, she came to the shrine of the holy Martyr. But after setting out from Carthage, when she had remained at her estate near the border of the river Bagrada, she rose to continue her journey and saw the ring lying at her feet. Astonished, she examined the girdle of hair with which it had been fastened. When she found it still held tight by its very strong knots, exactly as before, she suspected that the ring had burst through and sprung away. When the ring itself too was found completely intact, she presumed that, through so great a miracle, she had received in some way a pledge of the salvation to come; and, undoing that bond, [Note: [Col. 0769] Perhaps “girdle.”] she threw it, together with the same ring, into the river.

Those who do not believe this [Note: [Col. 0769] Some manuscripts read *Non credant*, “Let those not believe”; others, *Non credent*, “Those will not believe.”] do not believe either that the Lord Jesus was born through the intact virginity of his mother, or that he entered to the disciples while the doors were shut. But let them investigate this carefully and, if they find it true, let them believe that as well. She is a woman of the highest distinction, nobly born and nobly married, and she lives at Carthage. So great a city and so prominent a person do not allow the matter to remain hidden from those who seek the truth.

The Martyr himself, through whose intercession she was healed, certainly believed in the Son of the Virgin who remained a virgin, and believed in him who entered to the disciples while the doors were shut. Finally—and this is why all these things are being said by us—he believed in him who ascended into heaven with the flesh in which he had risen. For this reason such great things are performed through him, because he laid down his life for this faith.

Even now, therefore, many miracles are performed by the same God, who performs them through whom he wills and in whatever manner he wills, he who also performed the things we read about. But these miracles do not become known in the same way, nor, so that they may not slip from the memory, are they beaten into the mind by frequent reading, like gravel. For even where there is diligence—as has now begun among us—in having the accounts of those who receive benefits read before the people, those who are present hear it only once, while many are absent. Consequently, even those who were present do not retain what they heard after a few days, and scarcely anyone among them can be found who tells someone whom he knows was absent what he heard. [Note: [Col. 0769] Several manuscripts read *excedant*, “go beyond,” instead of *excidant*, “slip from.”]

### 22

One event occurred among us which was no greater than those I have mentioned, but it was such a clear and illustrious miracle that I believe there is no inhabitant of Hippo who either did not see it or learn of it, and no one who could in any way forget it.

Ten siblings—seven males and three females—from Caesarea in Cappadocia, persons of no little distinction among their fellow citizens, were divinely punished by a recent curse from their mother. Their father had died, leaving her without support; she had suffered with the utmost bitterness the injury [Col. 0770] inflicted upon her by them. They were subjected to such a punishment that all of them were horribly shaken by trembling limbs. Unable to endure the eyes of their fellow citizens while appearing so disgracefully, they wandered almost throughout the whole Roman world, each going wherever he or she thought best.

Two of them, a brother and sister named Paul and Palladia, came even to us. Their misery had already made them known in many other places. They arrived about fifteen days before Easter and attended the church daily, and in it the memorial of the most glorious Stephen, praying that God might now be appeased toward them and restore their former health. Both there and wherever they went [Note: [Col. 0770] Vind., Am., Er., with some manuscripts, read *quocumque*, “wherever [to whatever place].”], they drew the gaze of the city upon themselves. Some people who had seen them elsewhere and knew the cause of their trembling pointed this out to others as best they could.

Easter came. On the morning of that very Sunday, when a large crowd was already present and the young man was holding on to the railings of the holy place where the martyr-shrine was located, [Note: [Col. 0770] Several manuscripts read “where the memorial of the Martyr was located.” This is an interpretation and gloss.] he suddenly fell forward and lay there looking like someone asleep. Yet he was not trembling, as he used to do even in sleep. [Note: [Col. 0770] Er. and Lov. read *per somnium*, “in a dream”; corrected from the other books.] Those present were astonished; some were afraid, others grieved. When certain people wanted to lift him up, others prevented them and said that they should rather await the outcome.

And behold, he rose and was no longer trembling, because he had been healed; he stood unharmed, looking at those who were looking at him. Who, then, could restrain himself from praising God? The church was filled on every side with cries of rejoicing and thanksgiving. From there people ran to me, where I was already seated and about to proceed. One after another rushed in, each later arrival announcing as something new what the earlier one had reported. While I rejoiced and gave thanks to God inwardly, he himself also entered with several others, bowed at my knees, and rose to receive my kiss.

We proceeded to the people. The church was full and resounded with cries of joy: “Thanks be to God! Praise be to God!”—no one remaining silent, but all shouting from every side. I greeted the people, and again they cried out with the same words, now with even greater fervor. At last, when silence had been established, the customary readings from the divine Scriptures were performed.

When the time came for my sermon, I said a few words appropriate to the occasion and to the joy of that delightful event. Indeed, I allowed them to contemplate rather than hear a certain eloquence of God in the divine work. The man dined with us and carefully related to us the whole story of his own calamity and that of his mother and sister.

The next day, after delivering the sermon, I promised that his written account would be read to the people on the following day (Sermon 321). When this was done on the third day after Easter Sunday, on the steps of the apse from which I had been speaking above, I had both siblings stand while their account was being read (Sermon 322). The entire people, men and women alike, looked upon one of them standing without any disfiguring movement, while the other trembled in all her limbs. Those who had not seen him saw in his sister what divine mercy [Note: [Col. 0770] Some manuscripts read “what divine mercy had done in him.”] had done for him. [Col. 0771] They saw in her what they should rejoice over in his case and what they should pray for in hers.

While their account was being read, I ordered them to leave the sight of the people. I had begun to discuss the whole matter somewhat more carefully when, as I was speaking, other voices of fresh rejoicing were heard from the Martyr’s memorial. Those who were listening to me turned in that direction and began to rush together. For after she had descended from the steps on which she had stood, she had gone to pray to the holy Martyr. As soon as she touched the railings, she collapsed in the same way, as though into sleep, and rose healed.

When we were therefore asking what had happened and from where this joyful commotion had arisen, they entered the basilica where we were, bringing her there healed from the Martyr’s shrine. [Note: [Col. 0771] Perhaps “from the martyr-shrine.”] Then such a great cry of astonishment arose from both sexes that the continuing sound, mingled with tears, seemed unable to end (see Sermon 323).

She was led to the place where shortly before she had stood trembling. They rejoiced that she had been made like her brother [Note: [Col. 0771] The printed editions add *factam*, “made,” which is absent from the manuscripts.], for whom they had grieved because she remained unlike him. Although their prayers for her had not yet been poured out, they could already see that their prior intention had been so quickly heard. They rejoiced in the praise of God with a sound without words, with such a volume that our ears could scarcely bear it. [Note: [Col. 0771] Vind., Am., and the manuscripts read *voces*, “voices,” instead of *voce*, “with a voice.”]

What was in the hearts of those rejoicing except faith in Christ, for which Stephen’s blood was shed? [Note: [Col. 0771] Most manuscripts read *quo*, “for which,” rather than *qua*, “for which.”]

## CHAPTER IX

### That all miracles performed through the martyrs in the name of Christ bear witness to the faith in which the martyrs believed in Christ

To what faith, unless to this one, do these miracles bear witness—the faith in which Christ is proclaimed to have risen in the flesh and to have ascended into heaven with the flesh? The martyrs themselves were martyrs, that is, witnesses, of this faith. Bearing witness to it, they endured a world utterly hostile and cruel; and they conquered it not by resisting, but by dying.

For this faith died those who can obtain these things from the Lord, on account of whose name they were killed. For this faith their extraordinary endurance came first, so that in these miracles such great power might follow.

For if the resurrection of the flesh for eternity either did not first occur in Christ, or is not going to occur as Christ foretells it, or as it was foretold by the Prophets through whom Christ himself was foretold, why can those who were killed for the faith by which this resurrection is proclaimed accomplish such great things even after death? [Note: [Col. 0771] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “why can the martyrs.”] [Col. 0772]

Whether God himself performs these things directly, in that wondrous manner by which the eternal God brings about temporal events; or whether he performs them through his ministers; and whether the very things he performs through ministers are also performed in some cases through the spirits of the Martyrs, just as through human beings still living in the body; or whether he accomplishes all these things through Angels, whom he commands invisibly, immutably, and incorporeally, so that the things said to be done through the Martyrs are done because they pray and obtain them, not because they themselves perform them; or whether he does some things in one way and other things in another—ways that mortals can in no manner comprehend—all these things nevertheless bear witness to that faith in which the resurrection of the flesh for eternity is proclaimed.

## CHAPTER X

### How much more worthily the martyrs are honored, who obtain many miracles so that the true God may be worshiped, than the demons, who perform certain things so that they themselves may be believed to be gods

At this point they may perhaps say that their gods too have performed certain miracles. Good—if they are now beginning to compare their gods with our dead human beings. Or will they also say that they have gods who were once human beings and died, such as Hercules, Romulus, and many others whom they suppose to have been admitted into the number of the gods?

But the martyrs are not gods for us, because we know that our God and the God of the martyrs is one and the same. Nor are the miracles reported to have been performed in the temples of their gods in any way comparable with the miracles performed through the memorials of our martyrs.

Yet if some things appear similar, then, just as the magicians of Pharaoh were defeated by Moses (Exod. 8), so their gods have been defeated by our martyrs. Those things were performed by demons with the arrogance of impure pride by which they wished to be regarded as gods. But these things are performed by the martyrs—or rather, by God, whether they pray or cooperate—so that that faith may advance by which we believe that they are not our gods, but that we have one God together with them.

Finally, they built temples for such gods of theirs, established altars, instituted priests, and performed sacrifices. We, however, build for our martyrs not temples as for gods, but memorials as for dead human beings whose spirits live with God. Nor do we erect there altars on which we might sacrifice to the martyrs, but to the one God, both of the martyrs and of us. [Note: [Col. 0772] The printed editions add “we offer sacrifice,” but this is absent from the manuscripts.] At that sacrifice, the martyrs are named in their proper place and order, as human beings of God who conquered the world by confessing him; yet they are not invoked by the priest who offers the sacrifice.

For he sacrifices to God, not to them, although he sacrifices at their memorial, because he is God’s priest, not theirs. The sacrifice itself is the body of Christ, which is not offered to them, because they too are that body.

To whom, then, should we rather give credence when they perform miracles? To those who wish to be regarded as gods by those for whom they perform them, or to those who do whatever wondrous things they do so that belief may be placed in God, who is also Christ? To those who wished even their crimes to be their sacred rites, or to those who do not wish even their praises to be their sacred rites, but wish everything for which they are truly praised to contribute to the glory of him in whom they are praised?

For their souls are praised in the Lord (Ps. 33:3). Let us therefore believe them both when they speak the truth and when they perform miracles. By speaking the truth, they suffered, so that they might be able to perform miracles. Among the truths they proclaimed, the principal one is that Christ rose from the dead and was the first to display in his own flesh the immortality of the resurrection, which he promised would come to us either at the beginning of the new age or at the end of this one.

## CHAPTER XI

### Against the Platonists, who argue from the natural weights of the elements that an earthly body cannot be in heaven

[Col. 0773]

#### 1

Against this great gift of God, these reasoners—whose thoughts the Lord knows to be futile (Ps. 93:11)—argue from the weights of the elements. They have learned, evidently from their teacher Plato, that the two greatest and outermost bodies of the world are joined and connected by the two intermediate bodies, namely air and water.

Consequently, they say, since earth is first as one proceeds upward from here, water is second above the earth, air third above the water, and heaven fourth above the air, an earthly body cannot be in heaven. For the individual elements are balanced by their proper forces so that they may maintain their order.

See by what arguments human weakness, possessed by vanity, opposes the omnipotence of God. What, then, do they make of all the earthly bodies in the air, since air is third from the earth? Unless perhaps the one who, through the lightness of feathers and wings, granted birds—earthly bodies—the ability to be carried through the air cannot grant human bodies, once made immortal, the power by which they too may be able to dwell in the highest heaven.

Even earthly animals that cannot fly, among which human beings are included, ought, on their reasoning, to live beneath the earth just as fish, which are aquatic animals, live beneath the water. Why, then, does an earthly animal derive this life not at least from the second element, that is, from water, but from the third? Why, although it belongs to the earth, would it be suffocated immediately if compelled to live in the second element, which is above the earth, and live in the third in order to survive? Is the order of the elements mistaken here, or does it fail not in the nature of things but in the arguments of these men?

I pass over what I said already in the thirteenth book (chapter 18): how many earthly bodies are heavy, such as lead, and yet receive from an artisan a form by which they can float upon water. [Note: [Col. 0773] Compare Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, book 4, chapter 6. COQUAEUS.] And when it comes to the human body, so that it may receive a quality by which it can be carried into heaven and exist in heaven, are we to oppose the omnipotent Artificer?

#### 2

But when they consider and discuss the order of the elements on which they rely, in opposition to what I said above, they find absolutely nothing to say. For, proceeding upward from here, the order is earth first, water second, air third, and heaven fourth, so that above everything is the nature of the soul.

Aristotle even called it the fifth body, [Note: [Col. 0773] Compare above, book 10, chapter 16, section 2.] while Plato called it no body at all. If it were the fifth, it would certainly be above the others; but since it is no body, it surpasses all the more. What, then, is it doing in an earthly body? What is the most subtle of all things doing in this mass? What is the lightest of all things doing in this weight? What is the swiftest of all things doing in this slowness?

Can it be that, by the excellence of so sublime a nature, it cannot be brought about that its body be lifted into heaven, and that, although the nature of bodies can now press souls downward, the souls will someday be unable to lift earthly bodies upward?

#### 3

Now if we come to the miracles that they set against our Martyrs as having been performed by their gods, will they not themselves also be found to work for us and to benefit us altogether?

Among the great miracles of their gods is certainly the remarkable event reported by Varro: when a Vestal virgin was endangered by a false suspicion of sexual misconduct, she filled a sieve with water from the Tiber and carried it to her judges without a drop falling through any part of it.

Who held the weight of the water above the sieve? Who allowed nothing to fall from it onto the ground through all those open holes? They will answer: Some god, or some demon.

If a god, is he greater than the God who made this world? If a demon, is he more powerful than the Angel who serves God, by whom the world was made?

If, then, an inferior god, or an angel, or a demon could suspend the weight of a liquid element in such a way that the nature of water seemed to have been changed, will omnipotent God—who himself created all the elements—be unable to remove the heavy weight from an earthly body, so that a body made alive may dwell in the same element in which the life-giving spirit wills it to dwell? [Col. 0773]

#### 4

Furthermore, when they place air between the fire above and the water below, what are we to make of the fact that we so often find it between water and water, and between water and earth? What do they suppose watery clouds are, between which and the seas the air lies?

By what weight and order of the elements, I ask, does it come about that the most violent and wave-laden torrents, before they run beneath the air upon the earth, hang above the air in the clouds?

Finally, why is air intermediate between the highest reaches of heaven and the bare lands over which the globe extends in every direction, if its place is established between heaven and the waters, just as the waters are established between it and the earth? [Note: [Col. 0774] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “and the lowest parts of the earth.”]

#### 5

Finally, if the order of the elements is arranged so that, according to Plato, the two outermost elements—fire and earth—are joined by the two intermediate elements, air and water, and if fire occupies the highest place [Note: [Col. 0774] The printed editions read *summum*, “the highest”; the manuscripts read *summi*, “of the highest.”] while earth occupies the lowest, as the foundation of the world, and therefore earth cannot be in heaven, why is fire itself on earth?

According to this reasoning, these two elements—earth and fire—ought to be in their proper places, the lowest and the highest, so that just as they do not wish what is lowest to be able to exist in the highest place, neither should what is highest be able to exist in the lowest place.

Therefore, just as they think that no particle of earth either is or ever will be in heaven, we should have seen no particle of fire on earth. Yet fire is found not only on earth but also beneath the earth, so much so that mountain peaks belch it forth. Apart from this, we see fire both existing on earth for human use and being born from the earth, since it arises from wood and stones, which are unquestionably earthly bodies.

“But that fire,” they say, “is calm, pure, harmless, and everlasting; whereas this fire is turbulent, smoky, corruptible, and destructive.” Yet it does not destroy the mountains in which it continually burns, nor the caverns of the earth.

Very well, let this fire be unlike that one, so that it suits earthly dwellings. Why, then, do they refuse to believe that the nature of earthly bodies will someday be made incorruptible and suited to heaven, just as corruptible fire now suits these earthly regions?

They therefore offer nothing from the weights and order of the elements by which they could prescribe to omnipotent God that he must not make our bodies such that they may also dwell in heaven. [Col. 0775]

## CHAPTER XII

### Against the taunts of unbelievers, who ridicule Christians for believing in the resurrection of the flesh

#### 1

They are accustomed to mockingly investigate with great precision the faith by which we believe that the flesh will rise. They ask: “Will miscarried fetuses rise?” And since the Lord says, “Truly I say to you, not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18), they ask whether all will have equal stature and strength, or whether bodily dimensions will differ.

For if bodies will be equal, where will the aborted fetuses obtain the bodily mass they did not possess here, if they too rise? Or if they will not rise because they were not born but expelled, they raise the same question concerning little children: where will they obtain the bodily measure that we now see they lacked when they die at that age?

For we certainly will not say that those will not rise who are capable not only of generation but also of regeneration.

Then they ask what form this equality itself will take. For if all will be as large and as tall as those who were the largest and tallest here, they ask not only about little children but also about many others: where will they obtain what they lacked here, if each person receives what he had here? [Note: [Col. 0775] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “but they ask also about many large persons.”]

But if the Apostle’s statement, “We shall all come to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13), and the other statement, “Those whom he predestined” [Note: [Col. 0775] The printed editions add *fieri*, “to become”; this word is not found in the manuscripts at this passage of the Apostle, as has already been noted several times.] “to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29), is to be understood in such a way that the stature and bodily form of Christ will be the bodily form of all human beings who will be in his kingdom, they say:

“Much must be taken away from the size and height of many bodies. Where, then, will be the statement, ‘Not a hair of your head will perish,’ if so much will perish from the very quantity of the body?”

They can also ask about the hairs themselves, whether whatever falls from the head under the barber’s shears will return. If it will return, who would not shudder at such deformity? The same conclusion seems necessarily to follow concerning fingernails, so that so much of what bodily care has cut away will return. [Note: [Col. 0775] The printed editions read *cura*, “care”; the manuscripts’ *curatura*, “what care will cut away,” is better.]

Where, then, will beauty be? It must certainly be greater in that immortality than it could have been in this corruption.

But if it will not return, then it will perish. How, then, they ask, will the hair of the head not perish?

They argue similarly about thinness and fatness. For if all will be equal, some will not be thin and others fat. Something will therefore be added to some and diminished from others. Consequently, what is received is not what existed and had to be restored; rather, something that was not there must be added in one place, and something that was there must be lost in another.

#### 2

They are also greatly troubled by the very processes of decay and dissolution in dead bodies: one part turns into dust, [Col. 0776] another evaporates into the air; some are consumed by animals, others by fire; some perish in shipwreck or in other waters, so that their flesh is dissolved by putrefaction into liquid. They do not believe that all these elements can be gathered again and restored to flesh.

They also pursue every kind of deformity and defect, whether acquired [Note: [Col. 0776] Vind., Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *accidant*, “happen,” instead of *accedant*, “are added.”] or congenital. With horror and mockery they mention monstrous births and ask what sort of resurrection each deformity will have.

For if we say that nothing of this kind will return to the human body, they presume that they will refute our answer by pointing to the marks of the wounds with which we proclaim that the Lord Christ rose.

But among all these questions, the most difficult is this: into whose flesh will the flesh return when the body of one person is nourished by the flesh of another, compelled by hunger to eat human entrails? It was converted into the flesh of the person who lived on such food and supplied the losses that emaciation had revealed. To which person, then, will it return—to the one whose flesh it previously was, or rather to the one whose flesh it later became? They ask this in order to mock the faith in the resurrection.

Thus they either promise human souls, like Plato, alternating true miseries and false beatitudes; or, after many such revolutions through different bodies, they acknowledge with Porphyry that the soul eventually ends its miseries and never returns to them—not, however, by possessing an immortal body, but by fleeing every body.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Whether miscarried fetuses do not belong to the resurrection if they belong to the number of the dead

To these objections, which, under God’s guidance, seem to me to be raised by the opposing side, I shall respond as God’s mercy assists my efforts.

I do not dare either to affirm or deny that miscarried fetuses which had already lived in the womb and died there will rise. Yet I do not see how the resurrection of the dead could not pertain to them if they are not excluded from the number of the dead.

For either not all the dead will rise, and some human souls will remain eternally without bodies—souls that carried human bodies, even within their mothers’ wombs—or, if all human souls will receive again their resurrected bodies, which they possessed wherever they lived and left behind when they died, I do not see how I can say that those do not belong to the resurrection of the dead who died even in their mothers’ wombs.

But whatever view someone takes concerning these matters, what we say about children already born must also be understood about them, if they will rise. [Note: [Col. 0776] Compare *Enchiridion*, section 23, at the beginning.]

## CHAPTER XIV

### Whether infants will rise in the bodily condition they would have possessed through the advance of age

What, then, shall we say about infants except that they will not rise in the smallness of body in which they died, but that what would have come to them more slowly through time they will receive through that marvelous and exceedingly swift work of God? [Col. 0777]

In the Lord’s statement, “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18), it is said that what existed will not be lacking; it is not denied that what was lacking will be added.

But the infant who died lacked the complete size of his body. Even a fully developed infant, of course, lacks the perfection of bodily stature; once that has been added, he will be unable to become taller.

All people possess this measure of perfection in such a way that they are conceived and born with it, but they possess it in its principle, not in its mass. In the same way, all the limbs are already present in the seed, even though after birth certain things are still lacking, such as teeth and whatever else is of that kind.

Within the bodily material implanted according to the principle of each person, what does not yet exist—or rather, what is hidden but will come or, better, appear with the passage of time—already seems, so to speak, to have been woven (*liciatum*). [Note: [Col. 0777] Vind., Am., and Er. read *innatum*, “inborn.” The expression is taken from the language of weavers, as though that form were already woven in the child like a fabric, though not yet unfolded. LUDOVICUS VIVES.] According to this principle, the infant is already short or tall, as the person will be who is destined to become short or tall.

Accordingly, in the resurrection of the body we need not fear the loss of anything belonging to the body. For even if all were to be equal, so that all reached gigantic stature, lest those who had been the largest possess anything less in height that would perish contrary to Christ’s statement that not even a hair of the head will perish, how could anything be lacking to the Creator, who created everything from nothing, from which he might add what the marvelous Artificer knew ought to be added? [Note: [Col. 0777] Lov. reads “so that not even those,” but *quidem* is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XV

### Whether the bodies of all the dead will rise according to the measure of the Lord’s body

Christ certainly rose in the bodily measure in which he died. [Note: [Col. 0777] Vind., Am., and Er. read *nefas*, “it is impious,” corrected from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.] Nor is it right to say that, when the time of the resurrection of all comes, such bodily magnitude will be added to him as he did not possess when he appeared to the disciples in the form in which they knew him, so that he might be made equal to the tallest.

But if we say that larger bodies are to be reduced to the measure of the Lord’s body, a great deal will perish from the bodies of many, even though he promised that not a hair would perish.

It remains, therefore, that each person receive his own measure: either the measure he possessed in youth, even if he died an old man, or the measure he would have possessed had he died earlier.

As for the statement made by the Apostle concerning “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13), let us understand it as referring to something else—namely, that as the perfection of all the members is added to that Head in the Christian peoples, the measure of his maturity is completed.

Or, if this is understood as referring to the resurrection of bodies, let us take it to mean that the bodies of the dead will rise neither beyond nor below the form of youth, but in the age [Note: [Col. 0777] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “in that age.”] and strength to which we know Christ attained here. [Col. 0778]

For the most learned men have determined that youth in this present age extends to about thirty years; when that period has been completed, a person begins to decline into the deterioration of more advanced and old age. And therefore the Apostle did not say, “into the measure of the body,” or “into the measure of stature,” but “into the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.” [Note: [Col. 0777] The older books read *juvenalem*, “youthful,” and below, in chapter 16, *juvenali*, “youthful”; they do so consistently.]

## CHAPTER XVI

### What is to be understood by the conformity of the saints to the image of the Son of God

The statement that they were predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God (Rom. 8:29) can also be understood according to the inner person. Thus he says to us elsewhere: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Rom. 12:2). Therefore, where we are transformed so that we are not conformed to this age, there we are conformed to the Son of God.

It can also be understood in this way: just as he became conformed to us in mortality, so we will be conformed to him in immortality. This certainly also pertains to the resurrection of the bodies.

But if we are being instructed by these words as well about the form in which bodies will rise, then, just like that measure, this conformity too must be understood not as a matter of size but of age.

All will therefore rise as large in body as they either were or would have been in the age of youth. Yet it will make no difference even if the form of the body is that of an infant or an old person, since no weakness of mind or of the body itself will remain.

Accordingly, even if someone insists that each person will rise in the bodily form in which he died, there is no need to engage him in a laborious dispute.

## CHAPTER XVII

### Whether the bodies of women will be raised and remain in their own sex
Some, because it is said, “until we all attain [Note: [Col. 0778] Here the Lovaniensis edition alone adds, “to the unity of faith.”] to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13), and “conformed to the image of the Son of God,” do not believe that women will rise again in the female sex, but say that all will be in the male sex [Note: [Col. 0778] Jerome states, in his Letter to Pammachius, that Origen was in this error. Guido the Carmelite attributes the same error to the Armenians and lists it twentieth among their errors. COQUAEUS.]. For God made only the man from clay, and the woman from the man.

But those seem to me to have the sounder view who do not doubt that both sexes will rise again. For there will be no sexual desire there, which is the cause of shame. Before they sinned, they were naked and were not ashamed, the man and the woman. Therefore the defects will be removed from those bodies, while nature will be preserved. The female sex is not a defect, but nature—which then will indeed be free both from intercourse and from childbirth. There will nevertheless be female members, not adapted to their former use but to a new beauty, by which the desire of the one who looks will not be aroused—for there will be no such desire—but the wisdom and mercy of God will be praised: he both made what did not exist and freed what he made from corruption.

For, just as at the beginning of the human race the woman was made from a rib taken from the side of the sleeping man, Christ and the Church had to be prophetically represented already then by such an act. For that sleep of the man (Genesis 2:21) was the death of Christ [Note: [Col. 0778] Compare Book 2 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, no. 37.], whose side, as he hung lifeless on the cross, was pierced by a spear, and from it blood and water flowed (John 19:34). We know these to be sacraments by which the Church is built. For Scripture also used this word where it does not say “formed” or “fashioned,” but “built it into a woman” (Genesis 2:22). Hence the Apostle also speaks of the building up of the body of Christ (Ephesians 4:12), which is the Church.

The woman, then, is God’s creature, just as the man is; but that she was made from the man commends unity, while the manner in which she was made, as has been said, prefigured Christ and the Church. Therefore he who instituted both sexes will restore both.

Finally, Jesus himself, when questioned by the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, about whose wife the woman would be who had belonged to each of seven brothers, each of whom had wished to raise up offspring for his deceased brother, as the Law had commanded, said: “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matthew 22:29). And when there was an opportunity for him to say, “The one about whom you ask me will be a man also, not a woman,” he did not say this. Rather, he said: “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (ibid. 30).

They are like the angels, certainly, in immortality and blessedness, not in flesh—as they are not like them in resurrection, since the angels had no need of resurrection, because they could not die. The Lord therefore denied that marriages would exist in the resurrection, not that women would exist. And he denied it precisely where the question was framed in such a way that, if he had known the female sex would not exist there, he could have settled the matter more easily by denying it. Indeed, he confirmed that it would exist by saying, “They will not marry,” which concerns women, “nor will they take wives,” which concerns men. Therefore there will be those who here are accustomed either to marry or to take wives, but there they will not do this.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### On the perfect man, that is, Christ, and his body, that is, the Church, which is his fullness

Accordingly, when the Apostle says that we will all attain to a perfect man, we must consider the whole context of the passage, which runs as follows:

“He who descended,” he says, “is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ; so that we may no longer be children, tossed and carried about by every wind of doctrine, in the deception of men, in craftiness [Note: [Col. 0779] So the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, have *in astutiam* (“into craftiness”).] for the machination of error. But, practicing the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ; from whom the whole body, joined and compacted through every contact of its support, according to the working in the measure of each individual part, makes the body grow for the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:10–16).

Behold the perfect man: head and body, consisting of all the members that will be completed in their proper time. Yet members are added to this same body every day, as the Church is built up, to which it is said, “You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Corinthians 12:27). And elsewhere: “For the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Colossians 1:24). Again, elsewhere: “We, though many, are one bread, one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

The passage just cited also speaks of the building up of this body: “For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.” Then, in what follows—and this is the subject now under discussion—“until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,” and so forth, it shows that the same measure is to be understood in relation to the body when it says: “Let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ; from whom the whole body, joined and compacted through every contact of its support, according to the working in the measure of each individual part.”

Just as there is therefore a measure of each individual part, so also there is a measure of the whole body, which consists of all its parts: namely, the measure of fullness, of which it was said, “to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” He also mentioned this fullness in the passage where he says of Christ: “And he gave him as head over all things to the Church” [Note: [Col. 0780] The printed editions have “over the whole Church.” But the better manuscripts have “over all things to the Church.” So also the old Corbie Bibles, in accordance with the Greek, so that *ecclesiae* is dative, not genitive. This is also Jerome’s reading in his Commentaries on the Apostle.], “which is his body, the fullness of him who is fulfilled all in all” [Note: [Col. 0780] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *adimplet* (“fills”).] (Ephesians 1:22–23).

But if this were to be referred to the form of the resurrection, in which each person will exist, what would prevent us, when a man is named, from understanding a woman as well, taking “man” as standing for “human being”? Thus, in the statement, “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Psalm 111:1), women who fear the Lord are certainly included.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### That in the resurrection there will be none of the bodily defects that in this life are contrary to human beauty; while natural substance remains, both quality and quantity will converge in a single beauty

1. What should I now say about hair and fingernails? Once it is understood that nothing of the body will perish, in such a way that nothing deformed will remain in the body, it is understood at the same time that whatever excessive matter would have produced deformity will be added to the mass itself, not to those places in which the form of the limbs would be disfigured.

Suppose, for example, that a vessel were made from clay and then reduced again to the same clay, so that the whole vessel would once more be made from the whole mass. It would not be necessary for the portion of clay that had formed the handle to return to the handle, or for the portion that had formed the base to form the base again; provided that the whole returned into the whole—that is, that all the clay returned into the entire vessel, with no part of it lost.

Therefore, if hair that has been cut many times and nails that have been trimmed were to return in a deformed manner to their former places, they will not return there. Yet they will not perish for anyone who rises again, because they will be changed into the same flesh, wherever they occupy a place in the body, with the proper proportion of the parts preserved through the mutability of matter.

Although what the Lord says, “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18), can much more appropriately be understood as referring not to the length but to the number of hairs. Hence elsewhere he says, “All the hairs of your head are numbered” [Note: [Col. 0781] The word “all” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Vindobonensis and Ambrosian editions.] (Luke 12:7).

I do not say this because I think that anything that naturally belonged to any body will perish [Note: [Col. 0781] All the manuscripts have *cuique* (“to each”), rather than *cuiquam* (“to anyone”).], but because what was born deformed—certainly for no other reason than that this too might show how penal is the condition of mortal human beings—will return in such a way that, while the integrity of the substance is preserved, the deformity will disappear.

If a human craftsman can melt down a statue that he had made deformed for some reason and restore it to great beauty, so that none of its substance is lost and only the deformity disappears; and if whatever stood indecently in its former shape and did not correspond to the symmetry of the parts can be scattered and mixed throughout the whole, rather than being cut away and separated from the entire mass from which he made it, so that it neither produces ugliness nor diminishes the quantity—what must we think of the omnipotent Craftsman?

Could he not remove and destroy every deformity of human bodies, not only the ordinary but also the rare and monstrous, which belong to this miserable life but are foreign to the future blessedness of the saints, in such a way that whatever of them constitutes bodily substance, although natural, yet indecorous, may be taken away without any diminution of that substance?

2. Accordingly, the thin and the fat need not fear that they will remain there as they are now—such as, if they could, they would not wish to be here either. For all bodily beauty consists in the proportion of the parts together with a certain pleasantness of color.

Where there is no proportion among the parts, something is offensive either because it is misshapen, or because it is too little, or because it is too much. Therefore there will be no deformity produced by disproportion among the parts: what is misshapen will be corrected; what is less than it ought to be will be supplied from the place known to the Creator; and what is more than it ought to be will be removed, while the integrity of the substance is preserved.

How great will be the pleasantness of color when “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43)? The radiance in Christ’s body after his resurrection should be believed to have been hidden from the eyes of the disciples rather than absent. For the weak human eye could not have endured it, since he had to be seen by his own people in such a way that he could be recognized.

For this reason also he showed, to those who touched him, the scars of his wounds; and he took food and drink, not from need of nourishment, but by that power by which he could also do this.

When something is not seen, although it is present, while other things that are present along with it are seen—as we say that the radiance was present but unseen by those who saw other things—the Greek term is ἀορασία (*aorasia*, “invisibility”). Since our translators were unable to express this in Latin, they translated it in the Book of Genesis as “blindness.”

The Sodomites suffered this when they were seeking the door of the righteous man but could not find it (Genesis 19:11). If this had been a blindness by which nothing at all could be seen, they would have sought not the door through which they might enter, but guides by whom they could be led away from it [Note: [Col. 0782] Compare *Questions on Genesis*, question 43.].

3. [XX.] In some way we are so moved by love for the blessed martyrs that we wish in that kingdom to see on their bodies the scars of the wounds they endured for Christ’s name; and perhaps we will see them. For they will not be deformities in them, but marks of honor, and a certain beauty of virtue will shine forth, though in the body, yet not the beauty of the body.

Nevertheless, if some limbs were cut off and removed from martyrs, they will not be without those limbs in the resurrection of the dead, to whom it was said, “Not a hair of your head will perish.” But if it will be fitting in that new age for the signs of glorious wounds to be visible in that immortal flesh, then where the limbs were struck or cut so that they might be severed, scars will appear—but with those same limbs restored, not lost.

Although, therefore, all the defects that have occurred to the body will then be absent, they should not for that reason be regarded or called defects when they are signs of virtue.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That in the resurrection of the dead the nature of bodies dispersed in whatever manner must be recalled to wholeness from every place

1. Far be it from us to think that the omnipotence of the Creator cannot recall and restore to life everything that beasts or fire have consumed, that has collapsed into dust or ashes, dissolved into moisture, or exhaled into the air.

Far be it from us to think that any recess or hidden place of nature can receive something withdrawn from our senses in such a way that it either escapes the Creator’s knowledge or eludes his power. Cicero, certainly, wishing to define God as he was able, a great authority among them, says: “He is a certain mind, released and free, separated from every mortal mixture, perceiving and moving all things, and endowed with everlasting motion itself” (*Tusculan Disputations* 1.27).

He found this in the teachings of the great philosophers. Therefore, to speak according to them, how can anything be hidden from one who perceives all things, or irretrievably escape one who moves all things?

2. Hence that question must also be resolved which seems more difficult than the others: when the flesh of a dead person becomes the flesh of another living person, to which of them will it be restored in the resurrection?

If someone, overcome by hunger and compelled by it, were to eat human corpses—a calamity that both ancient history attests to have occurred more than once and the unhappy experiences of our own times have demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0782] He perhaps indicates that dreadful famine which afflicted the Romans while they were being besieged by Alaric in the year 409, concerning which see Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* 9.8, and Jerome, Letter 16, to the virgin Principia: “The fury of the starving broke out into unspeakable foods, and they tore one another’s limbs apart, while a mother spared not her nursing infant and received back into her womb the one whom shortly before she had brought forth.” COQUAEUS.]—would anyone reasonably assert that it had all passed through the lower passages, with none of it changed and converted into his flesh, when the wasting away that was present and is no longer present sufficiently indicates what deficiencies were supplied by that food?

I have already set forth some points that will also help to untie this knot. Whatever flesh hunger consumed was certainly exhaled into the air; hence, as we said, omnipotent God can recall what escaped. That flesh, therefore, will be returned to the person in whom human flesh first began to exist. From the other person it must be regarded as having been taken as a loan, and it must be returned to the one from whom it was taken, like a debt.

But the flesh of the one whom hunger had emptied will be restored to him by the one who can also recall what has been exhaled. Even if it had perished in every possible way, and none of its matter had remained in any hidden recesses of nature, the Omnipotent could restore it from wherever he wished.

Yet in view of the saying of Truth, “Not a hair of your head will perish,” it is absurd to think that, although a human hair cannot perish, such great quantities of flesh consumed and destroyed by hunger could have perished.

3. After all these matters have been considered and treated according to the measure of our ability, the following conclusion is reached: in the resurrection of the flesh, the bodies will have eternally the dimensions that the principle of youth, whether approaching completion or already complete, implanted in each body; and the fitting beauty of all the limbs will be preserved in their proportions.

If, for the preservation of this beauty, something is removed from an excessive size established in some particular part and distributed throughout the whole, so that it neither perishes nor disrupts the proportion of the parts anywhere, it is not absurd to believe that something may thereby also be added to the body’s stature. For it is distributed among all the parts so that they may preserve their beauty—something that, if it were abnormally concentrated in one part, would certainly be unbecoming.

Or if it is maintained that each person will rise again in the bodily stature in which he died, there is no need to resist this contentiously. Let only every deformity, every weakness, every slowness, every corruption, and anything else unbefitting that kingdom be absent. In that kingdom the children of the resurrection and of the promise will be equal to the angels of God—not in body, not in age, perhaps, but certainly in blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On the newness of the spiritual body, into which the flesh of the saints will be changed

Therefore whatever has perished from living bodies or, after death, from corpses will be restored. Together with what remained in the graves, it will rise again, changed from the oldness of the animal body into the newness of a spiritual body and clothed with incorruption and immortality.

Even if, through some grave accident or the savagery of enemies, it were wholly crushed into dust and dispersed as far as possible into the air or waters, so that it was nowhere allowed to exist in its entirety, it could in no way be withdrawn from the omnipotence of the Creator; not even a hair of the head in it will perish.

The spiritual flesh, therefore, will be subject to the spirit, yet it will remain flesh, not spirit—just as the spirit itself, while still carnal, was subject to the flesh, yet remained spirit, not flesh.

We have an example of this in the deformity of our punishment. Those to whom the Apostle said, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (1 Corinthians 3:1), were not carnal according to the flesh, but certainly according to the spirit [Col. 0784]. And in this life a person is called spiritual, although he is still carnal in body and sees another law in his members warring against the law of his mind (Romans 7:23).

But he will also be spiritual in body when that same flesh rises again in such a way that what is written may be fulfilled: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise” (1 Corinthians 15:42).

What the grace of the spiritual body will be, and how great it will be, has not yet come within our experience; therefore I fear that every statement made about it may be rash. Nevertheless, since the joy of our hope must not be silent for the praise of God, and since the fervor of holy love has said, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Psalm 25:8), let us, with his help, infer as best we can from the gifts that he grants in this most sorrowful life to the good and the wicked how great that gift will be—although we have not yet experienced it and therefore cannot speak of it worthily.

I pass over the time when he made the human being upright. I pass over the life of the two spouses, happy in the fruitfulness of paradise, because it was so brief that it did not even reach the awareness of those being born [Note: [Col. 0784] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *quando* (“when”).].
