In this life that we know and in which we still are, whose temptations—or rather, which is itself entirely a temptation—we never cease to endure as long as we remain in it, no matter how far we progress: who can explain what signs of God’s goodness there are toward the human race?

## CHAPTER XXII  
### On the miseries and evils to which the human race is justly subject because of the first transgression, and from which no one is freed except through the grace of Christ

1. As for our first origin, the whole offspring of mortals was condemned. This very life—if it ought to be called life—testifies to it, being full of so many and such great evils.

What else does that dreadful depth of ignorance indicate, from which all error arises, which receives all the children of Adam into a kind of dark womb, so that a human being cannot be freed from it without toil, pain, and fear?

What of love itself for so many empty and harmful things, and the biting cares, disturbances, sorrows, fears, insane joys, disagreements, quarrels, wars, ambushes, anger, enmities, deceit, flattery, fraud, theft, robbery, treachery, pride, ambition, envy, murders, parricides, cruelty, savagery, wickedness, lust, wantonness, shamelessness, sexual impurity, fornications, adulteries, incest, and the countless violations and uncleannesses against nature involving both sexes—which it is shameful even to mention—sacrileges, heresies, blasphemies, perjuries, oppression of the innocent, slanders, frauds, transgressions, false testimonies, unjust judgments, violence, banditry, and whatever other such evils do not come to mind but nevertheless do not depart from human life?

These are human evils, indeed, but they come from that root of error and perverse love with which every child of Adam is born. For who does not know with how much ignorance of truth a human being enters this life—an ignorance already manifest in infants—and with how abundant a supply of empty desire, which begins to appear in children? If one were left to live as he wished and to do whatever he wished, he would reach either all or many of the crimes and disgraces I have mentioned and those I have been unable to mention.

2. Yet divine governance does not entirely abandon the condemned, and God does not contain his mercies in his anger (Psalm 76:10). Within the very faculties of the human race, prohibition and instruction keep watch against these darknesses with which we are born, and resistance is set against these impulses [Note: [Col. 0785] Some manuscripts have *apponuntur* (“are placed against”).], though prohibition and instruction themselves are full of labors and pains.

What are the manifold fears employed to restrain the vanities of children? What of tutors, teachers, rods, reins, whips, and that discipline of which Holy Scripture says that the sides of a beloved son must be beaten, lest he grow unrestrained and, once hardened, can scarcely—or perhaps cannot—be subdued (Ecclesiasticus 30:12)?

What is accomplished through all these punishments except that ignorance is defeated and perverse desire restrained [Note: [Col. 0785] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *refrenetur* (“reined in”) instead of *infrenetur* (“restrained”)]—the very evils with which we enter this age?

What is the reason that we remember with effort but forget without effort; learn with effort but remain ignorant without effort; are diligent with effort but sluggish without effort? Does it not appear from this how prone and inclined our corrupted nature is, as though by its own weight, and how much assistance it needs to be freed from this condition?

Indolence, sluggishness, laziness, and negligence are certainly vices by which labor is avoided, although labor itself—even useful labor—is a punishment.

3. But apart from the punishments of childhood, without which children cannot learn what their elders—who scarcely desire anything useful—wish them to learn, who could enumerate in any speech, or comprehend in any thought, how many and how great punishments afflict the human race, not because of the malice and wickedness of the unjust, but because of the shared condition and misery of all?

How great are the fear and calamity arising from bereavements and mourning, from losses and condemnations, from the deceptions and lies of human beings, from false suspicions, from every violent crime and the offenses of others? For from them there often arise plunder, captivity, chains, prisons, exile, tortures, the cutting off of limbs, the deprivation of the senses, and the oppression of the body for the obscene gratification of the oppressor’s lust, along with many other horrors.

What of the countless external accidents feared for the body—heat and cold, storms, rains, floods, lightning, thunder, hail, earthquakes and chasms in the earth, the crushing of collapsing structures, injuries [Note: [Col. 0785] The manuscripts have *ab offensionibus* (“injuries”), plural.] and fear, or even the malice, of beasts of burden; the many poisons of plants, waters, airs, and animals; the bites of wild creatures, merely troublesome or even deadly; the madness that comes from a rabid dog, so that even a beast gentle and friendly to its master is sometimes feared more fiercely and bitterly than lions and dragons, and makes the person whom it happens to touch so mad through infectious disease that he is feared by parents, spouse, and children more than any beast?

What evils do sailors suffer? What do those traveling overland? Who walks anywhere without being subject to unforeseen accidents?

A certain man returning home from the marketplace, sound in his feet, fell, broke his foot, and from that wound ended his life. What seems safer than sitting? The priest Eli fell from the chair on which he was sitting and died (1 Samuel 4:18).

Farmers—or rather, all human beings—how many and how great accidents do they fear from heaven and earth, or from destructive animals, concerning the fruits of the fields? Yet they are usually secure once the grain has finally been gathered and stored. But in some cases, as we know, an unexpected river carried away an excellent harvest of grain from the granaries while people fled.

Who trusts in his own innocence against the thousand-shaped attacks of demons? Indeed, so that no one might trust in this, they sometimes afflict even baptized infants, who are certainly the most innocent of all, in such a way that, with God permitting it, the mournful misery of this life and the happiness of the other life to be desired are shown most clearly in them.

And now, concerning the body itself, there are so many evils of diseases that even the books of physicians do not contain them all. In many of these diseases, and almost all of them, the very aids and medicines are also tortures, so that human beings are rescued from the death of punishment by a punitive remedy.

Did not an enormous thirst drive people to drink even human urine, or even their own? Did not hunger drive them to such a point that they could not abstain from human flesh, consuming not only dead people whom they found, but people whom they had killed for this purpose, and, with unbelievable cruelty produced by raging hunger, even their own children and mothers?

Finally, sleep itself, which properly bears the name of rest: who could explain in words how restless it often is because of the sights of dreams, and how it disturbs the miserable soul and the senses with such great terrors—even though they concern false things—which it presents and in a certain way impresses so vividly that we cannot distinguish them from real things?

Through the falsehood of such visions, people who are awake are also driven about more miserably in certain diseases and from poisons [Note: [Col. 0786] The Lovaniensis edition alone has “more remarkably troubled in diseases and by poisons.”]. And although people who are healthy are sometimes deceived by malignant demons through visions of many kinds of falsehood, even if the demons cannot use these things to lead them over to their side, they nevertheless mock their senses by the mere desire to persuade them in some way of the falsehood.

4. From this life, so miserable that it resembles a kind of underworld, no one frees us except the grace of Christ the Savior, our God and Lord. For this is what the name Jesus itself means: “Savior.” Above all, he saves us so that after this life we do not enter one that is still more miserable and eternal—not life, but death.

For although in this life there are great consolations of healing through holy persons and saints, these benefits are not always granted even to those who ask, lest people seek religion for this reason, when religion should be sought rather for the sake of another life in which there will be no evils at all. In these evils grace helps the better sort of people for this purpose: that they may endure them with a heart proportionately more faithful and stronger.

For this purpose, learned people of this age say that philosophy also is useful. Tullius says that the gods gave true philosophy to a few [Note: [Col. 0787] I do not sufficiently remember where Cicero says this verbatim. A similar statement appears in Book 5 of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, chapter 21: “Plato spoke excellently: Blessed is the one who, even in old age, has been granted the ability to attain wisdom and true opinions.” LUD. VIVES.].

He says: “No greater gift was given to human beings by these gods, nor could any greater gift have been given.” Thus even those against whom we are arguing have, in some way, been compelled to confess divine grace in possessing not just any philosophy but true philosophy.

Moreover, if true philosophy was divinely given to only a few as the one remedy against the miseries of this life, this too makes it sufficiently clear that the human race has been condemned to pay the penalties of its miseries.

And just as they confess that this is no greater divine gift, so we must believe that it is given by no god except the one than whom even those who worship many gods say that there is no greater.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On those matters which, beyond the evils common to the good and the wicked, especially belong to the labor of the righteous

Besides these evils of the present life, which are common to the good and the wicked, the righteous also have certain labors of their own. In them they fight against vices and are involved in the temptations and dangers of such battles.

For sometimes more violently, sometimes more weakly, the flesh does not cease to desire against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do the things we wish (Galatians 5:17). We do not consume every evil desire, but, insofar as we can with divine help, we subject it by refusing to consent to it. We keep continual watch, lest a plausible appearance of truth deceive us; lest a cunning word mislead us; lest the darkness of some error overshadow us; lest what is good be believed evil, or what is evil be believed good; lest fear turn us back from what must be done; lest desire rush us toward what must not be done; lest the sun go down upon our anger (Ephesians 4:26); lest enmity provoke us to repay evil with evil; lest excessive or improper sorrow swallow us up; lest an ungrateful mind produce sluggishness in the doing of good; lest a good conscience be wearied by slanderous rumors; lest a rash suspicion about another deceive us; lest another’s false report about us break us; lest sin reign in our mortal body so that we obey its desires; lest we present our members as weapons of iniquity to sin (Romans 6:12–13); lest the eye follow desire; lest the desire for vengeance prevail; lest either sight or thought linger over what gives wrongful pleasure; lest an offensive or indecent word be heard willingly; lest we do what is forbidden even when we desire it; and lest, in this war so full of labors and dangers, victory be either expected from our own strength or attributed to our own strength once achieved.

Rather, it must be attributed to the grace of him of whom the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57). And elsewhere he says: “In all these things we conquer overwhelmingly through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

Yet however great the virtue with which we fight against vices, or even overcome and subdue them, we must know that, as long as we are in this body, we cannot lack occasion to say to God, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

But in that kingdom, where we will always be with immortal bodies, there will be neither battles nor debts. Neither would ever have existed if our nature had remained as it was created, upright. Therefore this struggle of ours, in which we are endangered and from which we desire to be freed by the final victory, belongs to the evils of this life—a life that we prove condemned by the testimony of so many and such great evils [Note: [Col. 0788] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *probavimus* (“we have proved”).].

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the good things with which the Creator has filled even this life, though it is subject to condemnation

1. We must now consider with what and how many good things the goodness of the Creator, who governs all that he has created, has filled this very misery of the human race, in which the justice of the one who punishes is praised.

First, that blessing which he had pronounced before sin—“Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28)—he did not wish to suppress after sin. Fruitfulness remained as a gift in the condemned stock. Nor could the marvelous power of seeds, or rather the still more marvelous power by which seeds themselves are produced, implanted in human bodies and in a certain manner woven into them, be removed by the defect of sin, through which the necessity of death was also imposed upon us.

Thus both run together in this stream and torrent, as it were, of the human race: the evil drawn from the parent, and the good bestowed by the Creator.

In the original evil there are two things: sin and punishment. In the original good there are two others: propagation and formation. But as far as our present purpose is concerned, we have already said enough about the evils, one of which comes from our audacity—that is, sin—and the other from God’s judgment—that is, punishment.

Now I have begun to speak of the good things of God that he has bestowed, and continues to bestow even now, upon that nature which has itself been corrupted and condemned. For by condemning it he did not remove everything he had given it—otherwise it would not exist at all. Nor did he remove it from his power, although he subjected it punitively to the devil, since he did not even alienate the devil himself from his dominion. For it is he who supremely is who causes even the nature of the devil to subsist, and who causes everything that exists in any manner to exist.

2. Of those two goods, then, which we said flow, as it were, from a certain fountain of His goodness even into nature corrupted by sin and condemned to punishment, He bestowed propagation at the very first works of the world by His blessing, from which works He rested on the seventh day. Formation, however, belongs to that work of His by which He continues to work even now (John 6:17). For if He withdraws His effective power from things, they will neither be able to advance and complete the periods of time through their appointed movements, nor remain at all in the condition in which they were created. Thus God created the human being so as to add to him a certain fertility by which he might propagate other human beings, generating in them also the very capacity for propagation, though not the necessity of it. From certain human beings, however, God willed to remove this capacity, and they became sterile; yet He did not remove from the human race the blessing of generation once given to the first two married couples.[^c0078-1]

This propagation, then, although it was not taken away by sin, is nevertheless not itself such as it would have been if no one had sinned. For ever since the human being, who had been placed in honor, after he sinned was compared to the beasts (Psalm 48:13), he generates in the same manner. Yet a certain spark, as it were, of reason, in which he was made in the image of God, has not been utterly extinguished in him.

If formation were not added to this propagation, propagation itself would not proceed into the forms and patterns proper to its kind. For if human beings had not had intercourse, and God nevertheless wished to fill the earth with human beings, just as He created one without the union of male and female, so He could have created them all. But those who have intercourse cannot become parents unless He, the Creator, causes them to generate. Therefore, just as the Apostle says concerning spiritual instruction, by which a human being is formed for piety and righteousness, “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7), so here too it may be said: “Neither the one who has intercourse nor the one who sows is anything, but God who forms.”[^c0078-2] Nor is the mother who carries the conception and nourishes the offspring anything, but God who gives the growth.

For by that operation through which He continues to work even now, He causes the seeds to unfold their proper numbers and to unroll from certain hidden and invisible coverings into the visible forms of the beauty that we behold. Joining and connecting incorporeal and corporeal nature—the former placed above, the latter subject below—in wondrous ways, He makes an animate being. His work is so great and marvelous that it produces amazement in a thoughtful observer and elicits praise of the Creator not only in the human being, which is a rational animal and therefore superior and more excellent than all earthly living creatures, but also in any tiny little creature.

[^c0078-1]: [Column 0789] Some manuscripts of good authority read *benedictione generali*, “by a general blessing,” instead of *benedictionem generandi*, “the blessing of generation.” [Column 0788] Lov., *si jam*, “if now.” *Jam* is absent from the other printed editions and manuscripts.

[^c0078-2]: [Column 0789] The Louvain edition alone has *informat*, “informs,” instead of *format*, “forms.” Some manuscripts read *ipsa*, “she,” instead of *ipse*, “he.”

3. He therefore gave the human soul its mind, in which reason and understanding lie dormant, as it were, in the infant, almost as though they did not exist, but are to be awakened and brought forth with the advance of age, so that the mind may become capable of knowledge and instruction, and receptive of truth and love of the good. Through this capacity it may absorb wisdom and be endowed with the virtues[^c0078-3a] by which it may prudently, bravely, temperately, and justly struggle against errors and the other inborn vices, and overcome them through desire for no other thing than that supreme and immutable good.

Even if it does not do this, who can adequately express or conceive how great a good is the very capacity for such goods, divinely established in a rational nature, and how marvelous is the work of the Almighty? For, apart from the arts of living well and attaining immortal happiness—which are called virtues and are bestowed upon the children of promise and of the kingdom solely by the grace of God that is in Christ—have not human ingenuity discovered and practiced so many and such great arts, some necessary and others pleasurable,[^c0078-3] that they testify how great a good there is in nature in this outstanding power of mind and reason,[^c0078-3b] even in the matters that it desires though they are superfluous, indeed dangerous and destructive, since it was able either to discover, learn, or practice them?

What marvelous and astonishing skill human beings have attained in the construction of clothing and buildings; how far they have advanced in agriculture and navigation; what they have devised and accomplished in the manufacture of every kind of vessel, and even in the variety of statues and paintings; what marvelous things for spectators to see and incredible things for listeners to hear they have contrived[^c0078-3c] and displayed in theaters; what and how many devices they have found for capturing, killing, and taming irrational animals; against human beings themselves, how many kinds of poisons, weapons, and engines they have devised, and for preserving and restoring mortal health, how many medicines and aids they have discovered; for the pleasure of the throat, how many seasonings and provocations of appetite they have found;[^c0078-3d] for indicating and persuading thoughts, what a multitude and variety of signs, among which words and letters hold the principal place; for delighting the mind, what ornaments of expression and abundance of different poetic forms; for soothing the ears, how many musical instruments and what varieties of song they have devised; how great an expertise in dimensions and numbers, and with what shrewdness they have grasped the paths and arrangements of the stars; with how much knowledge of worldly things they have filled themselves—who could express it, especially if we wished not to heap everything together, but to linger over each individual matter?

Finally, in defending errors and falsehoods, who could adequately assess how brilliantly the minds of philosophers and heretics have shone? For we are speaking now of the nature of the human mind, by which this mortal life is adorned, not of faith and the path of truth, by which immortal life is acquired.

Since the creator of so great a nature is certainly the true and supreme God, who Himself administers all that He has made and possesses supreme power and supreme justice, it would never have fallen into these miseries, nor—apart from those alone who will be delivered—would it have been destined to pass from them into eternal [punishments], unless an exceedingly great sin had first occurred in the first human being, from whom the others arose.[^c0078-4]

[^c0078-3]: [Column 0789] Some manuscripts read *voluntariae*, “voluntary,” instead of *voluptariae*, “pleasurable.” This is also the reading of manuscripts 2051 and 253 M.

[^c0078-3b]: [Column 0790] The Louvain edition alone reads *quantum bonorum habeat in natura*, “how great a wealth of goods it possesses in nature,” instead of *quantum bonum habeat in natura*, “how great a good it possesses in nature.”

[^c0078-3c]: [Column 0790] Some manuscripts read *exspectantibus*, “waiting,” instead of *spectantibus*, “watching.”

4. Now, even in the body itself, although mortality is something we share with the beasts and although the body is found to be weaker than that of many of them, how great the goodness of God and the providence of so great a Creator become apparent! Are not the locations of the senses and the other members arranged in it, and the very appearance, form, and stature of the whole body so proportioned, that it reveals itself to have been made for the service of the rational soul? For human beings were not created, as we see animals devoid of reason created, with their faces turned down toward the earth; rather, the upright form of the body directed toward heaven admonishes them to set their minds on the things above.[^c0078-5]

Moreover, does not the marvelous mobility assigned to the tongue and the hands—apt and well suited for speaking and writing, and for completing the works of the many arts and occupations—clearly show what sort of soul the body was joined to serve? Indeed, even when the necessities of activity are set aside, the harmonious proportion of all the parts and their beautiful correspondence through mutual symmetry are such that one cannot tell whether, in its construction, greater consideration was given to usefulness or to beauty. Certainly, we see nothing created in the body for the sake of usefulness that does not also possess a place of beauty.

This would be more evident to us if we knew the numerical proportions of the measurements by which all its parts are joined and fitted together. Human skill might perhaps deliberately trace these proportions[^c0078-5a] in the parts that project outward; but no one can discover those that are hidden and removed from our sight, such as the immense complexity of the veins, nerves, and internal organs, the secrets of the vital parts. For although the diligence of physicians—some of them cruel, those whom they call anatomists—has cut open the bodies of the dead, or even of the dying while they were in the hands of those dissecting and examining them, and has searched out everything concealed in human flesh with considerable inhumanity, in order to learn what had to be treated, how, and in what places, nevertheless no one has been able to discover—or has dared to seek—the numerical proportions of which I speak, by which the fitting together called in Greek *harmonía* (ἁρμονία), as of a certain instrument, is established throughout the body externally and internally.

If these proportions could have been known, the beauty of reason in the inner organs, which display no visible beauty, would delight us so greatly that it would be preferred by the judgment of the mind itself, which uses the eyes, to every visible form that pleases the eyes.

There are, however, certain parts so placed in the body that they possess beauty alone and not utility: for example, the male breast has nipples, and the face has a beard. That these are not a protection but a masculine adornment is indicated by the smooth faces of women, who, being weaker, would certainly be safer if protected in this way. If, then, among the parts that are visible—and no one doubts this—there is no member so adapted to some function that it is not also beautiful, while there are some whose sole quality is beauty and which have no function, I think it can easily be understood that, in the construction of the body, dignity was placed before necessity.

Necessity will pass away, and the time will come when we shall enjoy one another’s beauty alone, without any lust. This should be referred above all to the praise of the Creator, to whom it is said in the Psalm, “You have clothed Yourself with confession and beauty” (Psalm 103:1).

[^c0078-5a]: [Column 0791] The printed editions read *investigare*, “investigate”; the manuscripts more aptly read *vestigare*, “trace.”

[^c0078-5]: Compare Book 1 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, no. 28. [Column 0790.]

5. Now, what language can encompass the remaining beauty and usefulness of creation, which divine generosity has granted human beings to behold and enjoy, although they have been cast and condemned into these labors and miseries? Consider the manifold and varied beauty of heaven, earth, and sea; the great abundance and marvelous appearance of light itself; the sun, moon, and stars; the shaded groves; the colors and fragrances of flowers; the diversity and multitude of chattering and brightly colored birds; the many-shaped appearance of so many and such great living creatures, among which those are more astonishing that are smallest in bulk—for we are more amazed by the works of ants and bees than by the immense bodies of whales.[^c0078-6]

Consider also the great spectacle of the sea itself, when it clothes itself in different colors as though in garments: sometimes green, and that in many ways; sometimes purple; sometimes blue. How pleasantly it is viewed even whenever it is disturbed and becomes more pleasing for that reason, because it soothes the observer without tossing and shaking the traveler! What of the abundance of food everywhere against hunger? What of the diversity of flavors against satiety, spread abroad by the riches of nature,[^c0078-7] not sought through the art and labor of cooks? How many aids there are in so many things for preserving and recovering health![^c0078-8] How pleasing is the alternation of day and night! How gentle the tempering of the breezes! In shrubs and cattle, what an abundance of material for making clothing!

Who could mention everything? Yet if I wished to loosen and unfold these things, which I have compressed as though into a single mound, like bundles wrapped together, how much time would I need to spend on each one, since each contains so much?

And all these things are consolations for the miserable and condemned, not rewards for the blessed. What, then, must those other things be, if these are so many, so excellent, and so great? What will He give to those whom He predestined to life, who gave these things even to those whom He predestined to death? What goods will He cause them to receive in that blessed life, for whose sake, in this miserable [life],[^c0078-9] He willed His only-begotten Son to endure such great evils even unto death?

Hence the Apostle, speaking of those predestined to that kingdom, says: “He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how will He not also with Him freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).[^c0078-10]

When this promise is fulfilled, what shall we be? What shall we be like? What goods shall we receive in that kingdom, since we have already received such a pledge when Christ died for us? What will the human spirit be like when it has no defect at all—nothing beneath which it lies, nothing to which it yields, nothing against which it must even commendably struggle—but is perfected in the most peaceful virtue? How great, how beautiful, how certain will be the knowledge of all things there, without any error or labor, where the wisdom of God will be drunk from its own fountain, with supreme happiness and without any difficulty?

What will the body be like, entirely subject to the spirit and sufficiently vivified by it, needing no nourishment of any kind? For it will not be animal but spiritual, possessing indeed the substance of flesh, but without any carnal corruption.

[^c0078-7]: [Column 0792] So the manuscripts. The editions have: “against satiety, nature, diffused divinely.”

[^c0078-8]: The manuscripts have “and receiving again” instead of “and recovering.”

[^c0078-9]: The editions have *in hac miseria*, “in this misery.” The manuscripts have *in hac misera*, “in this miserable”; supply “life.”

# CHAPTER XXV  
## On the obstinacy of certain people who attack the resurrection of the flesh, which, as has been said, the whole world believes

But as for the goods of the soul, which the most blessed will enjoy after this life, noble philosophers do not disagree with us; they contend about the resurrection of the flesh and deny it as much as they can. Yet those who believe have left those who deny exceedingly few, and the learned and unlearned, the wise of the world and the foolish, have turned with faithful hearts to Christ, who demonstrated in His own resurrection what seems absurd to these people.

The world believed what God foretold; and He also foretold that the world would believe this matter. For He was not compelled to announce it so long beforehand by the magical arts of Peter, to the praise of those who would believe.[^c0078-11] He is that God whom, as I have already said several times—and I am not reluctant to mention it again,[^c0078-12]—the very divinities recoil from, although Porphyry confessed Him and wished to prove this through the oracles of his gods; he praised Him so highly that he called Him both God the Father and King.

Let it be far from us to understand what He foretold in the manner desired by those who, together with the world, did not believe what He foretold the world would believe. Why should it not rather be understood in the manner in which the world was foretold so long beforehand as believing it, rather than as the very few chatter who refused to believe, together with the world, what it was foretold that the world would believe?

If they say that these things must be believed in another way lest, by saying that what was written is empty, they do injury to that God to whom they bear such great testimony, they do Him an injury that is just as great, or greater, if they say that the things must be understood otherwise than as the world believed them—the world whom He Himself praised, promised, and brought to completion as believing them.

For which is it: can He not make the flesh rise again and live forever, or should we therefore not believe that He will do it because it is evil and unworthy of God?[^c0078-13] But we have already said much about His omnipotence, by which He does so many and such great things that are unbelievable. If they wish to find something that the Omnipotent cannot do, they certainly have it: I say that He cannot lie.

Let us therefore believe what He can do, without believing what He cannot do. Thus, not believing that He can lie, let them believe that He will do what He promised He would do; and let them believe in the manner in which the world believed—the world whose belief He foretold, whose belief He praised, whose belief He promised, and whose belief He has already shown.

Where do they demonstrate that this is evil? There will be no corruption there, which is an evil of the body. We have already discussed the order of the elements and have said enough about the other conjectures of human beings. How great the future ease of movement will be in an incorruptible body, in light of the condition of present good health—which in no way can be compared with immortality—we showed sufficiently, as I think, in Book Thirteen. Let those who have either not read the earlier parts of this work or wish to recall what they read consult them.[^c0078-14]

# CHAPTER XXVI  
## How Porphyry’s definition—that every body must be fled by blessed souls—is overturned by Plato himself, who says that the supreme God promised the gods that they would never be stripped of their bodies

[Column 0794]

“But Porphyry says,” they reply, “that every body must be fled if the soul is to be blessed.” Therefore, they say, it is of no benefit that we have declared the future body incorruptible, if the soul will not be blessed unless it has fled every body.

But in the book mentioned earlier I have already discussed this matter as much as was necessary (chapters 16 and 17). Here, however, I shall recall only one point from it. Let Plato, the teacher of all these people, correct his books and say that his gods, in order to be blessed, will flee their bodies—that is, they will die—although he said that they were enclosed in heavenly bodies. Yet God, by whom they were made, promised them immortality—that is, eternal continuance in those same bodies—so that they might be secure, not because their nature possessed this, but because His purpose prevailed.

Here he also overturns what they say: that because resurrection is impossible, the resurrection of the flesh must not be believed. For, according to that same philosopher, when the uncreated God promised immortality to the gods made by Him—something impossible—He most plainly said that He would do what is impossible.

For Plato reports Him as speaking in this way: “Since you have come into being,” He says, “you cannot be immortal and indissoluble. Nevertheless, you shall not be dissolved, nor shall any fate of death destroy you, nor shall they be stronger than my counsel, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those bonds by which you have been bound.”[^c0078-15]

If those who hear these words are not only absurd but deaf, they certainly do not doubt that, according to Plato, what is impossible was promised to the gods made by the God who made them. For when He says, “You cannot be immortal, but by my will you will be immortal,” what else does He say than: “You will be what cannot happen, because I shall bring it about”?

He, therefore, will resurrect the flesh incorruptible, immortal, and spiritual who, according to Plato, promised that He would do what is impossible. Why do they continue to proclaim impossible what God promised, what the world believed, and what the world itself was promised would believe? We proclaim that God, who according to Plato also does impossible things, will do this.

Therefore, in order that souls may be blessed, the whole body is not to be fled; rather, an incorruptible body is to be received. And in what body will they rejoice more appropriately than in the body in which they groaned while it was corruptible? For then they will not possess that dreadful desire which Virgil, drawing on Plato, attributed to them when he said:

> Again they might begin to wish to return into bodies.  
> (*Aeneid* 6.751)

Thus, I say, they will not have the desire to return to bodies when they will have with them the bodies into which they desire to return; and they will possess them in such a way that they will never cease to have them, never lay them aside through death for even the briefest period of time.

[^c0078-15]: Compare above, Book 13, chapter 16. [Column 0794.]

# CHAPTER XXVII  
## On the contrary definitions of Plato and Porphyry, in which, if each yielded to the other, neither would depart from the truth

[Column 0795]

Plato and Porphyry each said certain things which, if they could have shared them with one another, might perhaps have made them Christians.

Plato said that souls cannot exist forever without bodies. For this reason he said that even the souls of the wise, after however long a period, would nevertheless return to bodies. Porphyry, however, said that the most purified soul, when it has returned to the Father, will never return to the evils of this world.

Accordingly, if Porphyry had granted Plato what he saw to be true—that even the most purified souls of the just and wise will return to human bodies—and if Plato had in turn granted Porphyry what he saw to be true—that holy souls will never return to the miseries of a corruptible body—then, if both of them and each individually had said both things rather than each saying only one, I think they would have seen that it followed that souls would return to bodies and would receive such bodies as would enable them to live blessedly and immortally.

For according to Plato, even holy souls will return to human bodies; according to Porphyry, holy souls will not return to the evils of this world. Let Porphyry therefore say with Plato, “They will return to bodies”; let Plato say with Porphyry, “They will not return to evils”; and they will agree that souls return to bodies in which they suffer no evil.

These, then, will be none other than those bodies which God promises to make, so that blessed souls may live forever with their eternal flesh.[^c0078-16] For, as I think, both of them would now readily grant us this: that those who confessed that the souls of the saints would return to immortal bodies would allow them to return to the bodies in which they endured the evils of this age and in which they worshiped God piously and faithfully so that they might be free from those evils.

[^c0078-16]: So Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Louvain has *victuras*, “that they will live,” instead of *facturus*, “will make.”

# CHAPTER XXVIII  
## What Plato, Labeo, and even Varro could have contributed to the true belief in the resurrection if their opinions had converged in one judgment

Some of our people, because they love Plato for a certain splendid manner of speaking[^c0078-17] and for some things that he perceived truthfully, say that he also held something resembling our view concerning the resurrection of the dead.[^c0078-18] Cicero touches upon this in his books *On the Republic* in such a way that he seems to affirm that Plato intended to present it as play rather than to assert that it was true. For he introduces a man who came back to life and reported certain things that agreed with Platonic discussions.[^c0078-19]

Labeo also says that two men died on the same day and met one another at a certain crossroads; then they were ordered to return to their bodies and agreed between themselves that they would live as friends, and so it happened until they later died.[^c0078-20]

But these authors narrated a resurrection of the body such as occurred in the case of those whom we know to have risen: they were restored to life, but not in such a way that they would not die again.

Marcus Varro, however, records something even more remarkable in the books he wrote *On the Race of the Roman People*. I think his own words should be set down. “Certain astrologers,” he says, “have written that there is a rebirth of human beings which the Greeks call *palingenesía* (παλιγγενεσία). They have written that this is completed in a period of four hundred and forty years, so that the same body and the same soul which were once joined in a human being may return again to union.”

This Varro—or those astrologers, whoever they were, for he did not disclose the names of those whose opinion he mentioned—said something which, although false—for when souls have once returned to the same bodies they bore, they will never afterward leave them—nevertheless demolishes and destroys many of the arguments of that impossibility which these people chatter against us.

For those who think or thought this did not consider it impossible that corpses dispersed into air, dust, ashes, liquids, or the bodies of animals that feed upon them, or even into the bodies of human beings, should return again to what they had been.

Therefore, Plato and Porphyry—or rather, whoever loves them and is still alive—if they agree with us that holy souls will return to bodies, as Plato says, but will not return to any evils, as Porphyry says, so that what Christian faith proclaims follows from this, namely, that they will receive such bodies as will enable them to live happily forever without any evil, let them also accept this from Varro: that they will return to the same bodies in which they formerly were. Among them, then, the entire question concerning the eternal resurrection of the flesh will be resolved.

[^c0078-17]: [Column 0795] “Plato is the swan soothing human beings from the bosom of Socrates, his disciple,” Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 46. COQUAEUS.

[^c0078-18]: [Column 0795] See Eusebius, Book 11 of *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 33, in our *Evangelical Demonstrations*, volume 1 M.

[^c0078-19]: [Column 0795] Plato writes at the end of Book 10 of *The Republic* that Er the Pamphylian, who fell in battle, was restored to life on the tenth day after his death. “Although Cicero’s tale,” Macrobius says in Book 1 of the *Dream of Scipio*, “was mocked by the unlearned as though he himself, truly conscious of it, lamented it, he nevertheless avoided the example of foolish criticism: he preferred to relate that Er was awakened to tell his story rather than that he came back to life.”

[^c0078-20]: [Column 0796] See Pliny, Book 7, chapter 53.

# CHAPTER XXIX  
## On the quality of the vision by which the saints will see God in the age to come

### 1

Now let us see, insofar as the Lord deigns to help us, what the saints will do in immortal and spiritual bodies, when their flesh will no longer be alive in a carnal manner but already in a spiritual manner.

What that activity—or rather, what that rest and leisure—will be like, if I wish to speak truthfully, I do not know. For I have never seen it through the bodily senses. If I say that I have seen it with the mind, that is, with the understanding, what is our understanding, or how great is it, compared with that excellence?

For there is the peace of God which, as the Apostle says, surpasses every understanding (Philippians 4:7)—our own, or perhaps even that of the holy angels? Certainly not God’s.[^c0078-21a] If, then, the saints are to live in the peace of God, they will surely live in that peace which surpasses every understanding.

That it surpasses ours is beyond doubt. But if it also surpasses that of the angels, so that the one who said “every understanding” seems not to have excluded them, we must understand the saying in this sense: the peace of God, by which God Himself is at peace, is known as God knows it, and we cannot know it in that way, nor can any angel. It therefore surpasses every understanding, unquestionably except His own.

Yet because we also, according to our measure,[^c0078-21b] have become participants in His peace and will possess the highest peace within ourselves, among ourselves, and with Him, insofar as our highest capacity permits, the holy angels know it according to their measure, while human beings now know it far below them, however greatly they may excel in the progress of the mind.

We must consider what sort of man it was who said, “We know in part, and we prophesy in part, until the perfect comes” (1 Corinthians 13:9–10); and, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (ibid. 12).

The holy angels already see in this way. They are also called our angels because, having been rescued from the power of darkness and transferred to the kingdom of Christ after receiving the pledge of the Spirit, we have begun to belong to those angels with whom the city of God itself, common to us, will be holy and most sweet; concerning that city we have already written so many books.

Thus they are our angels who are God’s angels, just as Christ is God’s Christ and is our Christ. They are God’s because they did not abandon God; they are ours because they have begun to have us as fellow citizens.

The Lord Jesus said: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10).

As they see, therefore, so shall we see; but we do not yet see in that way. For this reason the Apostle says what I mentioned shortly before: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.”

This vision is therefore reserved for us as the reward of faith. The Apostle John also speaks of it: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

The face of God is to be understood as His manifestation, not as some bodily member such as those we possess in the body and call by that name.[^c0078-21]

[^c0078-21a]: [Column 0796] Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and Louvain add *omnium*, “of all,” which is absent from the manuscripts and Vindobonensis.

[^c0078-21b]: [Column 0797] The Louvain edition alone reads *modulo*, “little measure,” instead of *modo*, “measure.”

[^c0078-21]: Compare Letter 147. [Column 0797.]

### 2

Therefore, when I am asked what the saints will do in that spiritual body, I do not say what I already see; I say what I believe, in accordance with what I read in the Psalm: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115:10).

I say, then, that they will see God in that very body. But whether they will see Him through the body, as through the body we now see the sun, moon, stars, sea, earth, and the things upon it, is no small question.

For it is difficult to say that the saints will then have bodies of such a kind that they will be unable to close and open their eyes whenever they wish. It is more difficult still to say that whoever closes his eyes there will not see God.

For if the prophet Elisha, while absent in body, saw his servant Gehazi receiving the gifts given him by Naaman the Syrian—whom the prophet mentioned had cleansed from the disfigurement of leprosy—which the wicked servant had secretly thought he could do without his master seeing him (2 Kings 5:8–27), how much more will the saints in that spiritual body see everything—not only if they close their eyes, but even from places where they are absent in body?

Then that perfection will come of which the Apostle speaks: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished.”

Then, to show by some comparison, insofar as he could, how far this life is from the life that is to come—not merely the lives of ordinary people, but even of those who possess outstanding holiness here—he says: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:11–12).

If, then, in this life, where even the prophecy of remarkable human beings must be compared to that future life as a child is compared with a young man, Elisha nevertheless saw his servant receiving gifts where Elisha himself was not, when the perfect has come and the corruptible body no longer weighs down the soul, but the incorruptible body impedes nothing, will those saints need bodily eyes to see what Elisha, while absent, did not need in order to see his servant?

According to the translators of the Septuagint, the Prophet’s words to Gehazi are these: “Was not my heart with you when the man turned from his chariot to meet you, and you accepted the money?” (2 Kings 5:26), and so forth.[^c0078-22]

But as the presbyter Jerome translated it from the Hebrew, the words are: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?” He said that the Prophet had seen this with his heart, aided, certainly, in a wondrous manner by divine power, as no one doubts.

But how much more abundantly will all possess that gift then, when God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28)?

Nevertheless, those bodily eyes will also have their own function and will be in their proper place, and the spirit will use them through the spiritual body. For that Prophet, because he did not need them in order to see someone absent, did not therefore fail to use them for seeing what was present—things that he could also see through the spirit even if he closed them, just as he saw what was absent when he himself was not there.

Far be it from us, therefore, to say that the saints in that life will not see God with their eyes closed, whom they will always see through the spirit.

[^c0078-22]: [Column 0798] The manuscripts read: “Was not my heart with you when the man turned …” Vindobonensis, Ambrosianus, and Erasmus have: “Was not my heart with you when the man turned back …” Louvain has: “Was not my heart with you, and I knew that he had turned …”

### 3

But whether they will also see through the bodily eyes, when they have them open, is the question. For if, in the spiritual body, they will have only the same capacity that these eyes themselves now possess, then those spiritual eyes likewise will plainly be unable to see God. Their power, therefore, will be of an entirely different kind if through them that incorporeal nature is to be seen which is not confined to a place but is wholly everywhere. For when we say that God is both in heaven and on earth—for he himself says through the Prophet, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24)—we do not mean that he has one part in heaven and another on earth: he is wholly in heaven and wholly on earth, not at different times but in both simultaneously, something no corporeal nature can do.

The power of their eyes, then, will be extraordinarily greater—not so that they see more sharply than certain creatures are reputed to see, such as serpents or eagles (for however sharp their sight, those animals can see nothing other than bodies), but so that they can see even incorporeal things. Perhaps this great power of seeing was granted for a time, even in this mortal body, to the eyes of the holy man Job, when he says to God, “I had heard you by the hearing of the ear” [Note: [Col. 0799] Thus in the manuscripts; but in the printed editions, *I had heard you* (*obaudiebam*).], “but now my eye sees you; therefore I have despised myself, and melted away, and considered myself earth and ashes” (Job 42:5–6, according to the Septuagint). Yet there is nothing here to prevent our understanding “the eye of the heart,” of which the Apostle says: “Having the eyes of your heart enlightened” (Ephesians 1:18).

No Christian who faithfully accepts what that divine Teacher said doubts that God will be seen by them when he is seen: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). But whether he will also be seen there by bodily eyes is the question we are considering.

### 4

For what is written, “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6), can without any difficulty be understood as though it had been said, “And every human being shall see Christ, God’s salvation.” He was certainly seen in the body, and in the body he will be seen when he judges the living and the dead. That he himself is God’s salvation is also made clear by many other testimonies of Scripture; but the words of that venerable old man Simeon declare it more plainly. When he had taken the infant Christ into his hands, he said:

> “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

That which the aforementioned Job says—“And in my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:26, as found in the copies translated from the Hebrew)—certainly prophesied the resurrection of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0799] Thus Jerome, *Letter 61 to Pammachius*, quoting this passage from Job: “What,” he says, “is clearer than this prophecy? No one after Christ speaks so openly of the resurrection as this man before Christ.” COQUAEUS.]. Yet he did not say, “Through my flesh.” If he had said that, Christ God could be understood, since he will be seen through the flesh, in the flesh. But now it can also be understood in this way: “In my flesh I shall see God,” as though he had said, “I shall be in my flesh when I see God.” [Note: [Col. 0799] In Vind., Am., and Er. the following is added here: “my Savior.”]

Nor does what the Apostle says, “Face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), compel us to believe that we shall see God through this bodily face, where bodily eyes are located, although we shall see him unceasingly in spirit. For unless there were also a face belonging to the inner person, the same Apostle would not say: “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as though by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18) [Note: [Col. 0799] The printed editions have, “as though toward the Spirit of the Lord.” This has been corrected from the manuscripts.].

Nor do we understand otherwise what is sung in the Psalm: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm 33:6). For one draws near to God by faith, and faith is certainly of the heart, not of the body. But since we do not know how many approaches the spiritual body will possess—for we are speaking about something beyond our experience—whenever no authoritative passage of divine Scripture presents or supplies an interpretation that cannot be understood otherwise [Note: [Col. 0800] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions of Am., Er., and Lov. have *nequeant* (“cannot”); and below, where the manuscripts have *non occurrit* (“does not present itself”), they read *succurrit auctoritas* (“authority supplies [it]”).], it is necessary that what is written in the Book of Wisdom should happen to us: “The thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our plans are uncertain” (Wisdom 9:14).

### 5

That philosophical reasoning by which they argue that intelligible things are perceived by the mind’s vision, and sensible things—that is, corporeal things—by bodily sense, so that the mind cannot perceive intelligible things through the body, nor bodily things by itself (*per se ipsam*) [Note: [Col. 0800] Thus Vind., Am., and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read *per se ipsa*.], would certainly establish that God could in no way be seen through the bodily eyes, even of the spiritual body, if that reasoning could be made absolutely certain for us. But both sound reason and prophetic authority mock this argument.

Who is so turned away from the truth that he would dare to say that God does not know these corporeal things? Does he therefore have a body through whose eyes he can learn them? Further, what we said shortly before about the prophet Elisha sufficiently indicates that corporeal things can be seen in spirit, not through the body. For when that servant received the gifts, the act was certainly performed corporeally; nevertheless, the Prophet saw it not through the body but through the spirit.

Therefore, since it is established that bodies are seen by the spirit, what if the power of the spiritual body will be so great that the spirit itself will be seen through the body? For God is spirit. Moreover, each person knows his own life—the life by which he now lives in the body and gives vitality to these earthly members, making them living—by an inner sense, not through bodily eyes; yet he sees the lives of others, although they are invisible, through the body. For how do we distinguish living bodies from nonliving ones unless we see both bodies and the lives within them, which we cannot see except through the body? We do not see lives without bodies with bodily eyes.

### 6

For this reason it is possible, and highly credible, that we shall then see the worldly bodies of the new heaven and the new earth in such a way that, through the bodies we shall bear, and wherever we direct our eyes, we shall see God, who is everywhere present and governs all corporeal things, with the clearest transparency. This will not be as now, when “the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20), are seen “through a mirror in an enigma, and in part” (1 Corinthians 13:12), when faith—which makes us believe—has greater force in us than the appearance of corporeal things that we perceive through bodily eyes.

Rather, just as, when we look at human beings among whom we live, moving and displaying the motions of life, we do not believe that they live but see it, although we cannot see their life without their bodies and yet clearly perceive it in them through their bodies, without any ambiguity, so, wherever we carry the spiritual lights of our bodies, we shall behold the incorporeal God who governs all things, even through bodies.

Either God will therefore be seen through those eyes in such a way that, in their supreme excellence, they will possess something resembling the mind, by which an incorporeal nature may also be perceived—a claim that would be difficult or impossible to demonstrate by any examples or testimonies of divine Scripture—or, which is easier to understand, God will be so known and visible to us that he will be seen in spirit by each of us within each of us; he will be seen by one person in another; he will be seen in himself; he will be seen in the new heaven and the new earth, and in every creature that shall then exist; and he will be seen through bodies in every body wherever the vision of the spiritual body’s eyes is directed.

Our thoughts, too, will be open to one another. Then what the Apostle said will be fulfilled. After saying, “Judge nothing before the time,” he immediately added: “Until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of the heart; and then each person shall have praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5) [Note: [Col. 0801] Thus in the manuscripts; the printed editions have, “will reveal” (*manifestet*).].

## CHAPTER XXX — On the Eternal Happiness of the City of God and the Perpetual Sabbath

### 1

How great will that happiness be, where there will be no evil and no good will remain hidden, and where we shall devote ourselves to praising God, who will be all in all! For I do not know what else will be done there, where there will be neither idleness to cease from nor want to endure.

I am also reminded of the holy Song, where I read—or hear—“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; throughout the ages of ages they shall praise you” (Psalm 83:5). All the members and inward parts of the incorruptible body, which we now see distributed among various necessary functions, will then advance in the praises of God, since necessity itself will no longer exist, but complete, certain, secure, everlasting happiness will exist.

All those bodily harmonious proportions of which I have already spoken, which are now hidden, will then be hidden no longer; they will be arranged throughout the entire body, inwardly and outwardly. Together with the other great and wondrous things that will be seen there, they will kindle rational minds to praise so great an Artificer through the delight of rational beauty [Note: [Col. 0801] In the Lov. edition alone, “rational” (*rationalis*).].

I do not dare rashly to define what movements such bodies will have there, because I cannot conceive them. Yet both movement and rest, whatever form they take, will be fitting, just as their appearance itself will be fitting, since there will be nothing unfitting there. Certainly, wherever the spirit wishes, the body will immediately be present; nor will the spirit wish for anything that could be unfitting either to the spirit or to the body.

There will be true glory, where no one will be praised through anyone’s error or flattery. True honor will be given to no one unworthy and denied to no one worthy; nor will any unworthy person strive after it, since no one will be permitted to exist there except the worthy. There will be true peace, where no one will suffer anything adverse, either from himself or from another.

The reward of virtue will be the one who gave virtue and who promised to give himself to it—the one beside whom nothing better or greater can exist. For what else did he say through the Prophet, “I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (Leviticus 26:12), than: “I shall be what satisfies them; I shall be whatever human beings rightly desire—life, salvation, nourishment, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good”?

Thus also what the Apostle says is rightly understood: “That God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). He himself will be the end of our desires: he will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without exhaustion. This gift, this affection, this activity will certainly be common to all, just as eternal life itself is common.

### 2

But who is capable of imagining, let alone expressing, what degrees of honor and glory will exist according to the merits of the rewards? Yet that there will be such degrees cannot be doubted.

That blessed city will also regard as a great good within itself the fact that no inferior will envy any superior, just as the other Angels do not now envy the Archangels. Each person will be no more desirous of being what he has not received than he will be unwilling to remain bound to the one who has received it by the most peaceful bond of concord. The eye does not wish to be a finger, even though the peaceful structure of the whole flesh contains both members.

Thus one person will have a gift less than another, in such a way that he will also possess this gift: not to desire more.

### 3

Nor will they lack free will because they will be unable to take pleasure in sins. Rather, their freedom will be greater, liberated from the pleasure of sinning into an unchanging pleasure in not sinning [Note: [Col. 0802] Codex 258 has *indeclinabile*, “unchanging.” M.].

The first free will, which was given to human beings when they were first created upright, could refrain from sinning but could also sin. The final free will, however, will be more powerful precisely because it will be unable to sin. Yet this too will be a gift of God, not a capacity belonging to nature by itself.

For it is one thing to be God and another to be a partaker of God. By nature God cannot sin; the partaker of God receives from him the inability to sin. The ordered stages of the divine gift were therefore these: first, free will by which a person could refrain from sinning; finally, free will by which a person could not sin. The former was for acquiring merit, the latter for receiving the reward.

But because this nature sinned when it was able to sin, it is liberated by a more abundant grace and brought to that freedom in which it cannot sin [Note: [Col. 0802] Compare *Enchiridion*, no. 28.]. For just as the first immortality—the ability not to die—was lost by Adam through sin, so the final immortality will be the inability to die. Likewise, the first free will was the ability not to sin; the final free will will be the inability to sin.

The will toward piety and equity will therefore be as incapable of being lost as the will toward happiness. For by sinning we did not retain either piety or happiness; yet we did not lose the will toward happiness even when we lost happiness itself. Surely God himself is not to be denied free will because he cannot sin.

Therefore, in that city there will be one free and inseparable will in all and in each individual, liberated from every evil and filled with every good, enjoying without failure the delight of eternal joys, forgetful of sins and forgetful of punishments—but not for that reason forgetful of its liberation, so that it would not be grateful to its Liberator [Note: [Col. 0802] Lov. has “so that it would not be ungrateful.” The word “not” should be deleted, as it is rightly omitted in the printed editions of Vind., Am., and Er.; alternatively, instead of “ungrateful,” one should read “grateful,” as in the better manuscripts.].

### 4

As far as rational knowledge is concerned, therefore, they will remember even their former evils; but as far as the sensation of experience is concerned, they will be entirely forgetful.

An extremely skilled physician knows almost all bodily diseases in the way they are known through medical art; but in the way they are felt in the body, he knows many of them not at all, because he has not suffered them himself. Thus there are two kinds of knowledge of evils: one by which they do not escape the power of the mind; the other by which they cling to the senses of one who has experienced them. For all vices are known one way through the teaching of wisdom and another through the wretched life of folly.

There are likewise two kinds of forgetfulness of evils. The educated and learned person forgets them in one way; the person who has experienced and suffered them, in another: the former if he neglects his knowledge, the latter if he is freed from misery.

According to the forgetfulness I placed second, the saints will not remember their former evils, for they will be free from all of them, so that those evils will be utterly erased from their senses. Nevertheless, the power of knowledge—which will be great in them—will not leave them ignorant not only of their own past but also of the eternal misery of the condemned.

Otherwise, if they will not know that they themselves were once miserable, how will they sing the mercies of the Lord forever, as the Psalm says (Psalm 88:2)? Nothing will be more pleasing to that city than this song in praise of the grace of Christ, by whose blood we have been set free.

There the words will be fulfilled: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11). This will truly be the greatest Sabbath, one without evening, which the Lord commended in the first works of the world, where we read:

> “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works which he had made; and God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works which God began to make” (Genesis 2:2–3).

For we ourselves shall be the seventh day when we are filled and refreshed by his blessing and sanctification [Note: [Col. 0803] In most manuscripts, “perfected.”]. There, being at rest, we shall see that he is God—the very thing we wished to be when we fell away from him, hearing from the deceiver, “You shall be as gods” (Genesis 3:5), and withdrawing from the true God, by whose making we would have been gods through participation, not through abandonment.

For what have we accomplished without him except that, in his anger, we have wasted away (Psalm 89:9)? Restored by him and perfected by greater grace, we shall rest forever, seeing that he is God, with whom we shall be filled when he himself is all in all.

Even our good works, when they are understood to belong more truly to him than to us, will then be credited to us for attaining this Sabbath. For if we attribute them to ourselves, they will be servile works; yet Scripture says of the Sabbath, “You shall do no servile work on it” (Deuteronomy 5:14) [Note: [Col. 0804] The words “on it” are absent from the older books.].

For this reason it is also said through the prophet Ezekiel: “I gave them my Sabbaths as a sign between me and them, so that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them” (Ezekiel 20:12). We shall know this perfectly then, when we rest perfectly and see perfectly that he is God.

### 5

The number of the ages, as of days, will make this Sabbath rest still more evident if it is reckoned according to those divisions of time that appear to be expressed in Scripture, since it is found to be the seventh.

Thus the first age, like the first day, extends from Adam to the Flood; the second from then to Abraham—not in equal lengths of time but in the number of generations, for each is found to contain ten generations. From that point, as the evangelist Matthew determines, three ages follow up to Christ’s coming, each comprised of fourteen generations: one from Abraham to David, another from David to the transmigration to Babylon, and the third from the transmigration to Christ’s bodily birth.

Thus there are five ages in all. The sixth is now proceeding and is not to be measured by any number of generations, because it was said, “It is not for you to know the times which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7).

After this, as on the seventh day, God will rest, causing the seventh day—which we shall be—to rest in God himself [Note: [Col. 0804] Er. and Lov. have “in God himself” (*in se ipso Deus*). The other printed editions and the manuscripts more correctly have “in God himself” (*in se ipso Deo*).].

It would now be too long to discuss these individual ages carefully. This seventh age, however, will be our Sabbath, whose end will not be evening, but the Lord’s Day, as an eternal eighth day, sanctified by Christ’s resurrection and prefiguring the eternal rest not only of the spirit but also of the body.

There we shall rest and see; we shall see and love; we shall love and praise. Behold what will be at the end without end. For what other end is ours than to reach the kingdom whose end there is none?

### 6

With the Lord’s help, I seem to have discharged the obligation imposed by this immense work. Let those for whom it is too little or too much forgive me; but let those for whom it is sufficient give thanks not to me but to God, joining their thanks with mine. Amen.

# APPENDIX TO VOLUME SEVEN OF THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

Several writings are presented concerning the discovery, translation, and miracles of the martyr Stephen, namely:

- Avitus’s letter to Palchonius, concerning the relics of Saint Stephen and concerning the letter of Lucian, translated by Avitus from Greek into Latin.
- Lucian’s letter to the whole Church and to the Christians of the entire world, concerning the revelation of the body of the martyr Stephen.
- Anastasius’s letter to Landuleus, concerning the account of the translation of the martyr Stephen.
- An account of another discovery and translation of Saint Stephen to the city of Byzantium, which Anastasius rendered into Latin.
- Severus’s letter to the whole Church, concerning the miracles performed on the island of Minorca through the relics of Saint Stephen.
- Two books to Evodius concerning the miracles of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr.

[Col. 0805]

[Col. 0805]

# AVITUS’S LETTER TO PALCHONIUS, CONCERNING THE RELICS OF SAINT STEPHEN AND THE LETTER OF LUCIAN, TRANSLATED BY AVITUS HIMSELF FROM GREEK INTO LATIN

[Note: [Col. 0805] Concerning this letter, Gennadius says the following in his *On Illustrious Men*: “Avitus, a presbyter, a Spaniard by birth, translated into Latin before the account of the presbyter Lucian; and, adding his own letter, gave it to the Westerners through the presbyter Orosius.”]

(C, S)

To the most blessed and beloved Pope Palchonius, ever in the Lord, and to the entire clergy and people of the Church of Braga, Avitus the presbyter sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

I wish and beseech you to remember me, just as I, insofar as I am able, do not cease to remember you, sharing in your tribulations with my own grief and shedding unceasing tears in the holy places for the separation of your homeland [Note: [Col. 0805] In several older manuscripts, “your” is absent; in its place the Ulimmerius codex and Baronius under the year 415 have “our.”]. May the Lord either restore freedom to you, whom he wished to admonish, or grant gentleness to those whom he permitted to prevail.

Indeed, most blessed brothers—for I speak with our Lord Jesus Christ as my witness—I often wished to come to you, so that I might either endure evils with you or enjoy good things with you. But my desire was obstructed, since the enemy had now spread throughout all Spain. For I feared that, abandoning the holy places and perhaps failing to reach you, I might be intercepted somewhere and pay the penalty for irrational daring.

But because the merciful God, prompted by my wish and your merit [Note: [Col. 0805] Thus in Baronius. Lov. has “to provoke.” An old codex of the Abbey of Saint Gall has “to provide.”], deigned to grant the grace of his indulgence, first by arranging that my most beloved son and fellow presbyter, Orosius, should be sent from the African bishops to these regions—his affection and consolation restored the presence of all of you to me [Note: [Col. 0806] Gennadius says of Orosius in *On Illustrious Men*: “This is the Orosius who, sent by Augustine to Jerome to learn about the nature of the soul, brought back to the West, as the first to do so, the relics of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, which had recently been discovered.” See Augustine’s Letter 166, no. 2.]—and then by arranging that, on the very days when he himself was preparing to return with extraordinary longing, blessed and truly holy Stephen, the first martyr, the crown of our glory in Christ Jesus, should deign to reveal and manifest himself through signs and miracles that followed most clearly.

I considered it more fitting to send him, received through the providential opportunity afforded by God, the arranger of such great events [Note: [Col. 0806] An old codex of Saint Gall has, “having received the occasion provided by the arranging God.”], ahead to Your Charity, so that he might be present as an advocate and patron, deigning to assist the petitions of those who obey him—he who, while suffering, also deigned to pray for his enemies.

Therefore, most blessed and beloved brothers, continually remembering you and seeing the fitting providence of the arranging God, I was eager to obtain from the presbyter to whom the revelation had been made some portion of the body that had been discovered. I did not delay sending it to you, having requested it hastily and received it secretly.

For this reason I have sent you, through my holy son and fellow presbyter Orosius, relics from the body of blessed Stephen, the first martyr: namely, dust from the flesh and sinews, and—what ought to be believed with greater faith and certainty—solid bones, clearly marked by their holiness and richer than new spices or perfumes.

So that there could be no doubt, I have also sent you, appended to my writings, the letter and written account of the holy presbyter to whom these things were revealed. At my request and insistence that he set out the truth more fully, he dictated it first in the Greek language [Col. 0808], but it was afterward translated into Latin by me.

I implore you, holy and blessed brothers, to receive it as faithfully as the events themselves were truthfully accomplished. For I am certain that, just as the blessed Martyr himself deigned to announce and reveal himself for the salvation of the world in peril, so, with the help and presence of so great a patron, if you cherish such a pledge with worthy devotion, you will henceforth live safe and at peace.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit be with you, beloved in the Lord. Amen.

[Col. 0807]

## LUCIAN’S LETTER TO THE WHOLE CHURCH

### Notice Concerning the Following Letter

Augustine appears to indicate Lucian’s letter to the whole Church and to the Christians of the entire world in *Tractate 120 on John*, when he says in section 4:

> It is to be understood that Nicodemus came to Jesus not only then, but then for the first time; afterward he continued coming, so that by listening he might become a disciple. This is now made known to almost all peoples in the revelation of the body of the most blessed Stephen.

He confirms a large part of the account of the revelation given here in *Sermon 318*, section 1, speaking of Stephen as follows:

> His body remained hidden from that time until these days; but recently it appeared, as the bodies of holy martyrs are accustomed to appear, through God’s revelation, when it pleased the Creator. It was truly revealed to the man who showed the things that had been found. For the place was indicated by preceding signs; and just as it had been revealed, so it was found. Many received relics from it, because God willed it, and they came here.

Likewise, in *Sermon 319*, section 6:

> His body remained hidden for so long; it came forth when God willed, enlightened the lands, and performed so many miracles. Though dead, he makes the living dead, because he himself is not dead.

Gennadius, who lived near those times, likewise mentions the same letter in his own words in *On Illustrious Men*:

> Lucian, a presbyter and holy man, to whom God revealed, during the reigns of the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, the place of the tomb and relics of the body of the holy Stephen, the first martyr, wrote the account of the revelation in Greek to the people of all the Churches.

It is unnecessary to add as witnesses those who copied Gennadius’s very words, such as Marcellinus in his *Chronicle*, Bede in *The Six Ages of the World*, and various later writers.

There is some disagreement concerning the date between Marcellinus and Bede: Bede assigns the revelation to the seventh year of Honorius’s reign, whereas Marcellinus assigns it to the tenth year of Honorius’s consulship. Lucian, in the form first published by John Ulimmerius and afterward by the Louvain editors and others, supports Marcellinus, since he records the same consuls. It is surprising that Bede did not notice them, since he read this very Lucian in the Ulimmerian version and transcribed several passages from it into chapter 8 of his *Book of Retractations on Acts*.

Certainly this consular notice is absent from another copy of Lucian found in several old manuscripts. That other copy, preserved in the Floriacensis codex, also lacks, at the end of section 9, these words:

> “From these relics, therefore, I sent [some] to Your Beatitude”—words not suited to one writing to the representatives of all the Churches.
