Perhaps Lucian said this in a style directed toward those at whose request, and on whose behalf, he composed the account—at the request of Avitus, who had also given him a portion of the relics to be sent to them, as is clear from Avitus’s letter.

Here we present both versions of Lucian’s account: the Ulimmerian version—so it may be called, since it was formerly published through the care of Ulimmerius—reviewed against several manuscripts, and another version recently copied from a Floriacensis book approximately five hundred years old, which is also found in several other manuscripts.

This latter version was certainly not unknown to the ancients. For Chrysippus, the presbyter of Jerusalem, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, codex 171, and Ado in his *Martyrology* follow it throughout and copy from it many passages lacking in the Ulimmerian version.

Photius adds that Gamaliel instructed Lucian not thereafter to allow those relics to be damaged through negligence by sun and rain; but this statement is now found in no copy.

# LUCIAN’S LETTER TO THE WHOLE CHURCH, CONCERNING THE REVELATION OF THE BODY OF STEPHEN, THE FIRST MARTYR, AND OF OTHERS

[Note: [Col. 0807] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0807]

## From the Editions of Ulimmerius and Louvain, Reviewed Against Several Manuscripts

Lucian, in need of God’s mercy and the least of all human beings, presbyter of the Church of God that is in the village of Caphargamala in the territory of Jerusalem, sends greetings in the Lord to the holy Church and to all the saints who are in Christ Jesus throughout the world.

### 1

The vision [Note: [Col. 0807] The word “vision” (*Visio*) is absent from the manuscripts.] that appeared three times to my lowliness from God, concerning the revelation of the relics of the blessed and glorious protomartyr Stephen, Christ’s first deacon, and of Nicodemus, who is mentioned in the Gospel, and of Gamaliel, who is named in the Acts of the Apostles, I considered it necessary to disclose to Your Devotion in Christ. I was entreated—indeed, rather commanded—to do so by the holy and God-fearing father Avitus the presbyter, so that, like a son obeying his father, I might diligently and fully set forth the whole truth in all simplicity, just as I had learned it, to one inquiring with faith brought to fullness.

### 2

On the day of Preparation—that is, Friday, the third day before the Nones of December—during the tenth consulship of Honorius and the sixth of Theodosius, the Augusti [Note: [Col. 0809] December 3 of the year 415], as night came on, I was sleeping in my chamber, in the holy place of the baptistery, where it was my custom to sleep and to guard the ecclesiastical objects entrusted to my care.

At the third hour of the night, which is the first watch, I became as if in ecstasy, half-awake, and saw an old man, tall and priestly in appearance—that is, worthy of a priest—gray-haired and wearing a long beard. He was clothed in a white pallium in which were set golden gems bearing within them the sign of the holy cross, and he held a golden staff in his hand.

He came and stood at my right side, struck me with the golden staff, and called me three times by my name, saying: “Lucian, Lucian, Lucian.” Then he said to me in Greek:

> “Go to the city called Aelia, which is Jerusalem, and say to the holy John, who is its bishop: ‘How long shall we remain shut in, while you do not open for us? And especially because in the time of your priesthood we ought to be revealed. Open quickly for us the monument where our relics have been placed in neglect, so that through us God, and his Christ, and the Holy Spirit may open the door of his mercy in this world. For this age is in peril because of the many falls or sins [Note: [Col. 0809] That is, falls or sins.] that occur in it every day. And I am concerned not so much for myself as for those holy and greatly honored ones who have been placed with me.’”

### 3

I answered him, saying: “Who are you, lord, and who are those with you?”

He answered me: “I am Gamaliel, who brought up Paul the Apostle of Christ and taught the Law in Jerusalem. And the one who lies with me on the eastern side of the monument is my lord [Note: [Col. 0809] The printed editions here and in certain other places read *dominus* (“lord”); the manuscripts read *domnus*.] Stephen, who was stoned by the Jews and the chief priests in Jerusalem for the faith of Christ, outside the gate to the north that leads toward Cedar.

“There he lay cast out day and night, so that he would not be given burial, according to the command of the wicked rulers, in order that his body might be consumed by wild beasts. But by God’s will not one of them touched him—not a wild beast, not a bird, not a dog.

“I, Gamaliel, taking pity on Christ’s servant and hastening to obtain a reward and a share with the holy man in faith, sent during the night as many religious and believing people in Christ Jesus as I knew, living in Jerusalem among the Jews. I encouraged them, supplied them with the necessities of life, and persuaded them to go secretly and carry his body in my vehicle to my village, that is, to Caphargamala—which means ‘Village of Gamaliel’—twenty miles from the city.

“There I had mourning made for him for forty days [Note: [Col. 0809] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions have seventy days. Bede has forty-five days.], and I ordered him to be placed in my monument, in the eastern compartment. I also ordered that whatever was necessary for his mourning should be supplied from my own resources [Note: [Col. 0809] Bede, *Book of Retractations on Acts*, chapter 8.].

“Lord Nicodemus himself was also placed in another compartment. He came to the Savior Jesus at night and was evangelized by him, hearing: ‘Unless a person is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven’ (John 3:5). After leaving, he was baptized by Christ’s disciples.

“When the Jews learned of this, they removed him from his position of authority, anathematized him, and exiled him from the city. Since I regarded him as having suffered persecution for Christ, I took him to my estate, fed and clothed him until the end of his life, and buried him honorably beside Lord Stephen.

“Likewise, my most beloved son Abibas [Note: [Col. 0811] Older books read *Adbibas*, or *Abbibas*.], who received Christ’s Baptism with me from his disciples, died before me at the age of twenty and was buried in a third, higher compartment. I myself was afterward placed there when I died.

“My wife, whose name was Ethna, and my firstborn, Selemias, because they refused to be worshipers of the faith of Christ, were buried in another village belonging to their mother, namely Capharsemelia.”

Then I, the humble presbyter Lucian, asked: “And where shall we seek you?”

He said to me: “In the middle of the *proastion*”—that is, the area near the village estate—“which is called Delagabri, that is, ‘Men of God.’”

4. And I awoke, and prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, if this vision is from you and is not a deception, grant that it may appear to me again, a second and a third time, whenever and however you will.” So I began to fast and to subsist on dry food [Note: [Col. 0811] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “to take.”] until the following Good Friday. And again Lord Gamaliel appeared to me in the same likeness and form, as in the first vision, saying: “Why have you neglected to go and tell Saint Bishop John?” And I answered: “I was afraid, lord, to report this to him immediately after the first vision, lest I should appear to be a deceiver. But I prayed that, if you had been sent to me by the Lord, you would appear to me a second and a third time.” Gamaliel then said to me: “Obey me, obey me, obey me.” And again he said to me: “Since you have asked about the relics of each one—how and where they have been placed—apply your understanding and observe carefully what is shown to you.” And I said: “Yes, lord.” Immediately he brought four baskets, three of gold and one of silver. Three of them were full of roses: two contained white roses, and the third red ones, the color of blood; the fourth basket, the silver one, was full of sweet-smelling saffron. And he placed them before me. And I said to him: “What are these, lord?” And he said to me: “They are our relics. The one that has red roses is Lord Stephen, who is placed on the right, toward the east, from the entrance of the tomb. The second basket is Lord Nicodemus, placed opposite the door. The one silver basket is Abibas, my son, ‘from the womb of testimony,’ that is, renewed in the Law; he departed from his mother’s womb undefiled and therefore appeared in the likeness of the purest silver. Do you not see that the saffron in it is of the sweetest fragrance? And he is joined to my basket in the elevated place, where the two of us are placed like twins.” And when he had said this, he vanished again from my eyes.

5. And when I had awoken, I gave thanks to almighty God and devoted myself to my customary fasts until the third revelation. In the third week, therefore, on the same day and at the same hour, the man mentioned above came, threatening and raging, and said to me: “Why have you delayed until now, and refused to go and tell Bishop John what has been said and shown to you? What excuse will you have before God, or what forgiveness for this contempt will you hope for on the day of judgment? Do you not see how great the drought and tribulation are throughout the whole world? And you act negligently! Do you not consider that there are many men better than you, holy men in the desert, whom, passing them over, we wished to make known through you? For this reason we wished you to be a priest here, having come from another place, so that we might be revealed through you. Rise, then, go, and tell him to open for us and make a place of prayer, so that through our intercession the Lord may have mercy on his people.”

And when I trembled at his words, I said: “I have not been negligent, my lord, but was awaiting your third coming. Now, without waiting for tomorrow, I shall go and tell him everything you have commanded me.” And while he stood angrily before me, I seemed, as though in another rapture of mind, to have reached Jerusalem and to be standing in the presence [Col. 0813] of Bishop John, recounting the entire vision to him. And I seemed to hear him say: “If these things are as you say, dearest one, and the Lord has revealed them to you in our times, I ought to take from that estate the great ox, the chief plow-animal, which is fit both for cart and plow, and release the estate to you with everything else.”

To him I said: “What use is an estate to me, my lord, if I do not have that ox by which the estate may be managed and plowed?” And the bishop said to me: “So it has pleased us, dearest one, since our city is supplied with vehicles, and we are short by one ox for that great cart; the one you are said to be hiding on your estate. For it is proper that it should be in the famous city rather than on a small estate. Are the two remaining smaller oxen not sufficient for cultivating the land of your vehicle?”

6. And when I had heard this in ecstasy—that is, in a rapture of mind—I immediately awoke, blessed the Lord, and went to the city to Saint Bishop John. And when I had told him everything I had seen, I kept silent about the vision of the ox, awaiting what I would hear from him. For I understood that Saint Stephen himself was the great ox, and that the carts of which he spoke were the holy Churches, and that Sion, the first Church, was itself the greater cart. And because I knew that the holy bishop would ask me for the relics of blessed Stephen, I therefore did not wish to tell the bishop about the vision of the ox.

When Bishop John heard these things, he wept for joy and said: “Blessed is the Lord God, the Son of the living God. If you heard these things as you say, dearest one, and God revealed them to you, I ought to transfer from there blessed Stephen, the first martyr and archdeacon of Christ, who first waged the Lord’s battles against the Jews, and, while placed on earth, saw the Lord standing in heaven in his majesty, and appeared like an angel in the assembly of men.”

And all these things happened just as I saw them, and everything proved harmonious with it. The holy bishop then said to me: “Go, dig in the heap that is in the field itself; and if you find anything, report it to me.” And I said to him: “I walked through the field and saw a heap of small stones in the middle, where I supposed they were.” And the pope said to me: “I have already told you: Go, dig; and if you find anything, sit there and guard the place, and send me word through a deacon to come to the site.” And so he dismissed me. When I had come to the village, I sent heralds so that all the inhabitants of the village would rise at dawn and dig in the heap.

7. That same night Lord Gamaliel himself appeared to a certain monk named Migetius [Note: [Col. 0813] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “Nugetius.”], an innocent and simple man, in the same likeness in which he had appeared to me, and said to him: “Go, tell the presbyter Lucianus: You are laboring in vain in that heap. We are not there now, but we were placed there when they mourned us according to the custom of the ancients; for this reason the heap was made as a testimony of lamentation. But seek us in another place, which lies to the north [Note: [Col. 0813] The printed editions read “which is Boran.” The reading is corrected according to the ancient codices.], and at a place called in the Syriac language Debatalia, which is interpreted in Greek as ἀνδρῶν ἀγαθῶν (andrōn agathōn), “of good men,” which we may render “of strong men.”

At dawn, rising for the hymns, I found that monk preaching to all the brothers. After the hymns had been recited, I began to say: “Let us go to that heap and dig in it.” Then some said to me: “First hear what the monk Migetius says.” And when the monk Migetius had been summoned, I asked him what he had seen. He told me all the signs of Lord Gamaliel that I had seen, and how he had seen the field lying toward the south, and in it a monument, as though neglected and ruined. There he had seen three golden beds spread out, one higher than the others, on which two men were lying, one old and one young; on each of the other two beds there was one man.

And the one who was in the higher bed answered and said: “Go, tell the presbyter Lucianus that we were the lords of this place. If you wish to find the great and just one, he is placed on the eastern side.”

Hearing this from the monk, I glorified the Lord, because another witness to the revelation had been found.

8. We therefore went to the heap and, digging, found nothing. We then turned to that monument where the monk had seen the vision that night, and, digging, found three coffins, just as they had appeared to me in the form of the baskets. We found, buried there, a stone inscribed in very large letters with “Keayea Celiel,” which is interpreted as “Servant of God,” and “Apaan Dardan,” which is interpreted as “Nicodemus and Gamaliel” [Note: [Col. 0815] In the manuscripts it reads as follows: “bearing Celiel, which is interpreted ‘Stephen of God’; and Nardam, which is interpreted ‘Nicodemus.’”]. Pope John interpreted this, as I myself heard from the holy bishop.

I immediately reported it to the bishop while he was in Lydda, which is Diospolis, presiding over a synod [Note: [Col. 0815] The manuscripts read “at the synod.”]. He took with him two other bishops, Eleutherius [Note: [Col. 0815] More correctly, in another copy from the Floriacensis codex, Eustonius or Euthonius, who is also named among the bishops of the Diospolitan synod by Augustine in Book One against Julian, no. 19.] of Sebaste and Eleutherius of Jericho, and they came to the site.

When they had uncovered the coffin of Lord Stephen, an earthquake immediately occurred, and such sweetness and fragrance of odor came forth from it as no human being remembered either having heard or experienced, so that we thought we had been placed amid the delights of paradise. A multitude of people were with us, among whom were very many sick with various ailments. At that very hour, seventy-three persons were immediately healed by the sweetness of its fragrance. Demons were driven out of some; in others the fountain of blood was stopped; some were freed from scrofula and boils; others were healed of fistula; others of tertian and quartan fevers; fever left some, and jaundice others; some were cured of headache, and some of hemicrania; others were freed from hidden pain in the viscera. The people experienced many other cures, which it would be lengthy to enumerate.

And after kissing the holy relics, they closed them again. Then, with psalms and hymns, they carried the relics of the most blessed Stephen to the holy Church of Sion, where he had been ordained archdeacon. They left us small joints from the Saint’s limbs—or rather, very great relics: the earth with the dust where all his flesh had been consumed; they carried away the rest [Note: [Col. 0815] In the manuscripts, after “or rather, very great relics,” it reads: “they carried away the rest together with the dust where all his flesh had been consumed.”].

9. From these relics, therefore, I have sent these to Your Beatitude. When you have received them, pray for my lowliness, that I may be found worthy in the sight of the Lord, supported by the merits of the most blessed martyr Stephen and by your prayers. His relics were translated on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [December 26]. At that time there was continuous and unending drought; but at that very hour a great rain descended, and the earth was abundantly drenched. And everyone there glorified the Lord because of his holy Stephen and because of his heavenly treasure of mercy and compassion, which Jesus Christ our Lord deigned to open for the endangered world; he lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## FROM THE FLORIACENSIS CODEX AND OTHER MANUSCRIPTS

[Col. 0808]

LUCIANUS, in need of mercy and the least of all men, presbyter of the Church of God which is in the village of Caphargamala in the territory of Jerusalem, sends greetings in the Lord to the holy Church and to all the saints who are in Christ Jesus throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0808] In the Germanensis codex, approximately four hundred years old, the inscription reads as follows: “To the holy and venerable Bishop Himesius, the most humble and lowest of all, Lucianus the presbyter from the village of Caphargamala [Col. 0810] in the territory of Jerusalem, perpetual salvation in Christ Jesus.” And it begins: “The revelation that was shown to me I have deemed worthy to disclose to Your Holiness.” Another Germanensis manuscript, apparently written six hundred years ago, agrees with the Floriacensis book, which we follow here. Lucianus himself perhaps altered the inscription of the letter when he sent Stephen’s relics to Himesius.].

1. I have deemed it worthy to disclose to Your Holiness the revelation of Saint Stephen, which was shown to me through the grace of our Lord and Savior—not out of any boastfulness, but for the strengthening of those who hear it.

2. For the third time it was shown to me while I was resting in the basilica of the baptistery, on the dawning of Friday, around the third hour of the night, while I was still nearly awake. As though carried into a rapture of mind, I saw an old man in years, tall in stature, handsome in face, with a flowing beard, clothed in white and wrapped in a cloak, at whose upper edge there were what appeared to be golden crosses woven into it (and he held a golden staff in his hand). His feet were shod in boots gilded on the surface. He walked before me in silence.

When I saw this, I hesitated inwardly and said: “Who, do you suppose, is he? Is he from God, or from the opposing side?” For I had not forgotten the Apostle’s saying: “For even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). As I watched him walking, I began to think in my heart and say: “If this man is from God, he will call me by my name a third time; but if he calls me only once, I will not answer him.”

Without any hesitation, ceasing his pacing, he came to me and, striking me with the staff he held in his hand, called me by name three times, saying: “Lucianus, Lucianus, Lucianus.” I answered him: “Who are you, lord?” He said to me: “Rise, go, and tell John, bishop of Jerusalem: How long shall we remain shut up? How long will you not open for us, especially since we are to be revealed in your times? Open for us quickly, so that through our prayer God may open to the human race the door of his mercy. For the time is pressing when this world will perish because of the multitude of its iniquities, which people commit daily.”

After this he said: “I am not concerned only for my own sake, but also for those who are with me. For they deserve to be heaped with the greatest honors on earth, since the place in which we lie is very despised.”

3. When I had heard this, I said to him: “Tell me, lord, who are you, and who are those with you?” And he said to me: “I am Gamaliel, who nourished Paul, who afterward became an apostle. The one who lies with me is Lord Stephen, who was stoned by the Jews at Jerusalem. Day and night he lay outside the city (in exapeleo), cast out onto the road by which travelers go toward Cedar, at the command of the impious priests, so that he might be devoured by beasts and birds [Note: [Col. 0810] The Germanensis codex reads: “He lay in the exapoli in the city. From there he was dragged out onto the road by which travelers go toward Cedar, at the command of the impious priests, so that he might be devoured by beasts and birds.”].

Yet neither the beasts nor the birds dared touch him. But I, Gamaliel, knowing the man’s holiness, faith, and devotion, and believing that I would share with him in the resurrection, sent to religious and faithful men, commanding them and saying: ‘Fear no one; obey my instructions, collect the body of Saint Stephen, and carry it to my estate, which I have called Caphargamala after my name. Lay him in my new tomb, and perform the customary solemn rites for forty days, at the estate itself, which lies at the twenty-second milestone. Whatever is spent on the solemn rites, I shall have supplied from my own resources.’

The other one who lies with him is Nicodemus, my nephew, who used to come to the Savior by night so that he might recognize the words of truth and be reborn through water and the Holy Spirit. When he heard this from the Lord, he was baptized by the holy apostles Peter and John. Because of this baptism, the chief priests became enraged against Nicodemus and planned to kill him; but out of respect for me and for our kinship [Note: [Col. 0810] In the Germanensis manuscript: “and rights.”] they did not do so. Nevertheless, after inflicting many blows on him, they left him half dead, anathematized him, and expelled him from the city, plundering all his property.

I had this man also collected and brought to my estate, instructing my steward to provide whatever he needed. After living a little longer, he fell asleep in the Lord. I had him buried at the feet of blessed Stephen, as a confessor for the Name.

The third one who lies with me is Abibas, my son, who believed together with me in Christ’s commandments and together with me received baptism from the holy Apostles. He was about twenty years old, possessed great knowledge of the Law, chaste in body, and had known no stain of woman; he was always occupied in the temple of God with Paul, my disciple. He had gone beforehand to God undefiled [Note: [Col. 0812] Photius, in the Bibliotheca, codex 171, second section, and Ado in his Martyrology, who also reports what follows.].

Near him [Note: [Col. 0812] Thus the Floriacensis codex. The Germanensis reads: “and together with me received baptism from the aforementioned Apostles. For, being about twenty years old, possessing the fullest knowledge of the Law, a virgin in mind and body, and knowing no sin involving a woman, but always occupied in the temple of God with my disciple Paul, who afterward became an apostle and went beforehand to God. Near him,” etc.] are placed those of whom I have spoken above, and with them I too lie. But my wife Ethna [Note: [Col. 0812] The Germanensis codex reads “Athea.” Another, older Germanensis manuscript reads “Emna.”] and my firstborn son Selemias, who did not wish to believe in Christ, withdrew from us and were buried in their maternal estate, which is called Capharselemia, because they were considered unworthy of our fellowship.

So that you may believe, when you begin to dig you will find my wife’s and my son’s place empty.” And just as he said, so we found it. And when I, most wretched, asked, saying: “Where shall we find you, lord?” he said to me: “You will find us in my estate, which is now called in the Syriac language Delangabria [Note: [Col. 0812] The same Germanensis codex reads “Delagabria.”], or Debathalia, which is interpreted as ‘the estate of the men of God,’ or ‘of warriors’ [Note: [Col. 0812] Ado in his Martyrology reads “of blessed men.”].”

And when he had foretold all these things, he vanished from my eyes.

4. After this vision I rose, prostrated myself in prayer, implored the Lord’s mercy, and said: “Lord Jesus, if this revelation or vision is according to your will, grant that it may be manifested to me a second and a third time, so that, trusting confidently, I may announce the revelation of your Saints.” From that day I began to fast, abstaining from everything, and taking no food except bread and salt, and drinking water, as we customarily do during the days of holy Lent.

On the following Friday Saint Gamaliel came again in the same clothing in which he had appeared before, at the same hour of the night, while I was not yet deeply asleep. And he said to me: “Why have you delayed, dearest brother, and not gone and reported to Bishop John? Do you not see how great the drought is upon the earth and the tribulation throughout the whole world? And you act negligently! Rise, then, go, and tell him to open for us and make a place of prayer, so that through our intercession the Lord may have mercy on his people.”

I said to him: “I have not acted evasively, my lord; but I prayed to the Lord and said: ‘Lord Jesus, if this revelation is from you, let it appear to me a second and a third time.’ And now, lord, behold, you have come a second time and made me glad; but if you come a third time, you will gladden me more completely.”

When he heard this, he signaled with his hand, saying: “I forgive, I forgive, I forgive.” And when he had said this, he said to me: “Listen, presbyter.” I answered him: “Speak, lord, for I am listening.” And he said to me: “Because you hesitated in your mind, saying: ‘If I find the place, do you suppose I shall find them all placed in one location? And if that happens, how shall I distinguish the relics of each one?’ These were the thoughts you were entertaining within yourself.”

I could not deny it to him and said: “It is true, lord; that is what I was turning over in my mind. You know everything, and nothing is hidden from you.” And he said to me: “We are not, as you suppose, placed in one location; each of us has his own place. Pay attention, therefore, to what I tell you, and apply your mind.”

And looking up, I saw him stretching out his hands toward heaven and praying. Immediately he set down there four baskets, three of gold and one of silver, full of roses. One of them was full of saffron. One of the three baskets had very red roses, like blood, and he placed it on my right. The other two were full of white roses, like lilies, though they were roses. [Col. 0814] The fourth basket contained saffron, whose fragrance was exceedingly sweet.

He placed them before me and said to me: “Do you see these baskets?” And I said to him: “Yes, lord.” And he said to me: “These are our coffins in which we lie, and these roses are our relics. Just as you see this basket, placed on your right, containing the most beautiful roses, so, when you begin to open the place, you will find the entrance to the tomb; and when you enter, you will find a coffin on the right. It is Saint Stephen’s. And do not doubt, for he alone among us deserved to be crowned with martyrdom. Therefore he is placed on the eastern side.

The coffin placed toward the north, that is, the north wind, is that of Saint Nicodemus the neophyte [Note: [Col. 0814] The Germanensis manuscript reads “my nephew.”]. The other coffin, which is somewhat higher, is mine and my son’s, because we too were neophytes.”

And I said to him: “I ask you, my lord, why is one basket silver?” And he said to me: “Because my chaste and undefiled son departed from the world, he therefore appeared in the likeness of the purest silver” [Note: [Col. 0814] The Germanensis codex reads “virgin and undefiled.”]. “Do you not see that the saffron in it is of the sweetest fragrance?” And when he had said this, he vanished again from my eyes.

5. And when I had awoken, I gave thanks to almighty God and devoted myself to the fasts I had established until the third revelation. In the third week, therefore, on the same day and at the same hour, the man mentioned above came, threatening and raging, and said to me: “Why have you delayed until now, and refused to go and tell Bishop John what has been said and shown to you? What excuse will you have before God, or what forgiveness for this contempt will you hope for on the day of judgment? And do you not consider that there are many men better than you—holy men in the desert—whom, passing over them, we wished to make known through you? For this reason we wished you, having come from another basilica, to be a priest here [Note: [Col. 0814] The same Germanensis codex, agreeing more closely with the Ulimmerian copy, reads: “For this reason we wished you to be a presbyter here, having come from elsewhere, so that we might be revealed through you.”], so that we might be revealed through you.”

And when I trembled at his words, I said: “I have not been negligent, my lord, but was awaiting your third coming. Now, without waiting for tomorrow, I shall go [Note: [Col. 0814] The same codex reads “I shall go without delay.”] and tell him everything you have commanded me.”

And while he stood angrily before me, I seemed as though I had entered another rapture of mind and had arrived in Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0814] In the same Germanensis codex: “to have reached Jerusalem.”], and as though I were standing in the presence of Bishop John, recounting the entire vision to him. And I seemed to hear him say: “If these things are as you say, dearest one, and the Lord has revealed this to you in our times, I ought to take from that estate the great ox, the chief plow-animal, which is suited to cart and plow, and release the estate to you with everything else.”

To him I said: “What use is an estate to me, my lord, if I do not have an ox by which the estate may be managed and fed?” And the bishop said to me: “So it has pleased us, dearest one, since our city is supplied with vehicles, and we are short by one ox for that great cart—the one you are said to be hiding on your estate. For it is proper that it should be in the famous city rather than in a small estate. Are the two remaining oxen, and one calf, and the equipment of the great ox not sufficient for cultivating the land of your vehicle?”

6. And when I had heard this in ecstasy—that is, in a rapture of mind—I immediately awoke, blessed God, and went to the city to Saint Bishop John. And when I had recounted to him everything I had seen, I kept silent about the vision of the ox, awaiting what I would hear from him. For I understood that Saint Stephen himself was the great ox, and that the carts of which he spoke were the holy Churches, and that Sion, the first Church, was itself the greater cart. And because I knew that the holy bishop would ask me for the relics of Saint Stephen, I therefore did not wish to tell the bishop about the vision of the ox.

When Bishop John heard this, he wept for joy and said: “Blessed is the Lord God, the Son of the living God. If you heard these things as you say, dearest one, and God revealed them to you, I ought to transfer from there blessed Stephen, the first martyr and archdeacon of Christ, who first waged the Lord’s battles among the Jews, and, while placed on earth, saw the Lord standing in heaven in his majesty, and appeared like an angel in the assembly of men.” [Col. 0816]

When Saint John had said this, he dismissed me. And when I had come to the village, I sent a herald to all the inhabitants of the village, that they should rise at dawn and dig in the heap.

7. That same night Lord Gamaliel himself appeared to a certain monk named Migetius, an innocent and simple man, in the same likeness in which he had appeared to me, and said to him: “Go and tell the presbyter Lucianus: You are laboring in vain in that heap. We are not there now, but we were placed there when they mourned us according to the custom of the ancients; for this reason the heap was made as a testimony of lamentation. But seek us elsewhere, in a place called in the Syriac language Debathalia, which in Greek is interpreted Andragathon, which we may render ‘of good men.’”

At dawn I arose and found that monk preaching to all the brothers. After the hymns had been sung, I began to say: “Let us go to that heap and dig in it.” Then some said to me: “First hear what the monk Migetius says.” When the monk Migetius had been summoned, I asked him what had happened. He told me all the signs of Gamaliel that he had seen [Note: [Col. 0816] The Germanensis manuscript reads “that I had seen.”], and how he had seen the field lying toward the south, and a monument in it, as though neglected and ruined. There he saw three golden beds spread out, one higher than the others, on which two men were lying, one old and one young; on each of the other two beds there was one man.

And the one who was in the higher bed answered and said: “Go and tell the presbyter Lucianus that we are the lords of this place. If you wish to find the great and just one, he is placed to the east of us.”

Hearing this from the monk, I glorified the Lord, because another witness to the revelation had also been found. And all these things happened just as I saw them [Note: [Col. 0816] The same Germanensis manuscript reads “as I saw it”;] and everything proved harmonious with it.

8. Immediately, therefore, I reported to the blessed bishop. But he sent for his fellow bishops. When they had assembled, they came to the site. They ordered it to be dug, and after a very large portion of earth had been removed, we found a stone on which were engraved the words “Celeliel, Nasoon, Gamaliel, Abbibabel” [Note: [Col. 0816] The same Germanensis manuscript reads: “Cheliel, Nasuam, Gamaliel, Abbiba.”]—Hebrew words, but written in Greek letters.

The interpretation of the names is as follows: Celeliel is called Stephen; Nasoon is Nicodemus; Abbibabel signifies the son of Gamaliel. When we had reached the bottom, we found the place of Saint Stephen on the eastern side, just as I had heard. Immediately an earthquake occurred, and such sweetness and fragrance of odor came forth from it as no human being remembered having experienced, so that we thought we had been placed amid the delights of paradise.

A multitude of people were with us, among whom were very many sick with various ailments. At that very hour, seventy-three persons were immediately healed by the sweetness of its fragrance. Demons were driven out of some; in others the fountain of blood was stopped; some were freed from scrofula and boils; others were healed of a more hidden sickness; others of tertian and quartan fevers. [Col. 0815] Fever left some, and jaundice others; some were cured of headache and hemicrania. The people experienced many other cures, which it would be lengthy to enumerate.

At that time the bishops John of Jerusalem, Eustonius, bishop of the city of Sebaste, and Eleutherius of Jericho were present with all their clergy. And so, with psalms [Note: [Col. 0816] The Germanensis codex reads: “John of Jerusalem, Hestonius of the city of Sebaste, and Eleutherius of Jericho: all these came with their clergy, and so, with psalms,” etc.] and hymns, they carried the relics of the most blessed Stephen to the holy Church of Sion, where he had been ordained archdeacon. They left us small joints from the Saint’s limbs—or rather, very great relics, together with the dust where all his flesh had been consumed [Note: [Col. 0816] The same Germanensis codex, just as it differs from the Floriacensis codex in the heading of the Letter addressed to Bishop Himesius, also differs in its conclusion and reads as follows: “where all his flesh had flowed away. From these holy relics, therefore, I have sent some to Your Beatitude. When you have received them, pray for my lowliness, that I may be found worthy in the sight of the Lord Jesus Christ, aided by the merits of blessed Stephen, the first martyr. And remember our humility, and love me as though I were present, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.” It does not add that Stephen’s relics were found on the third day before the Nones of August.].

[Col. 0817]

9. Therefore I beg you, pray for my lowliness, that I may be found worthy in the sight of the Lord, aided by the merits of the most blessed martyr Stephen and by your prayers; Christ Jesus our Lord reigning, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. The relics of the most blessed Stephen were found on the third day before the Nones of August [August 3].

## ON THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT STEPHEN

[Col. 0817]

## NOTICE ON THE LETTER OF ANASTASIUS AND ON THE FOLLOWING WORK

From an old Floriacensis book there comes this letter of Anastasius, in which he indicates that, through his own labor, he translated the following work from Greek into Latin. By what author the work was composed in Greek and fabricated is not known. Nevertheless, many Greeks lend it credibility, and they generally place the discovery of Stephen the martyr, which it recounts, and his subsequent translation to the city of Constantinople, several years after the revelation made to Lucianus.

Indeed, this translation is said to have taken place “when the body of Saint Stephen was hidden at Jerusalem in holy Sion”—that is, when it had been transferred there by John of Jerusalem after Lucianus’s revelation, according to Lucianus’s own Letter. Nevertheless, Nicephorus, in Book 14, chapter 9, reports that Stephen’s relics were first carried to Constantinople under Constantine, and then adds that a certain portion of his relics, perhaps concealed and left behind in Palestine, was later discovered by Lucianus through divine revelation.

Moreover, the falsity of the following work is exposed by many details that conflict with the history of the times. Stephen’s coffin is said to have been “placed in the oratory built by Alexander, in the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the tenth time”; yet Constantine the emperor is recorded in the Fasti as consul only eight times. Cyril, who is here named bishop of Jerusalem, did not assume the episcopate under Constantine but under Constantius, certainly many years after the death of the bishop Eusebius. Nevertheless, Eusebius is imagined as sitting at Constantinople and receiving Stephen’s body.

[Col. 0817]

## LETTER OF ANASTASIUS TO LANDULEUS, ON THE ACCOUNT OF THE TRANSLATION OF THE FIRST MARTYR STEPHEN, WHICH HE TRANSLATED FROM GREEK INTO LATIN (S)

To the distinguished and God-worthy Landuleus, bishop of Capua, Anastasius, humble librarian of the Apostolic [Note: [Col. 0817] Supply: “of the See.”], sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Since the holy Church over which Your Venerability is rightly recognized to preside is celebrated and distinguished by the relics and memory of blessed Stephen, and since Your Holiness therefore burns with great devotion toward him, I considered it appropriate, while residing near the city of Mantua on a mission of the Apostolic See to the Augusti, to translate into the Roman language the account of the translation of his sacred body, written in Greek and unexpectedly brought to me, which I had previously nowhere found in Latin, and to dedicate it to your pious devotion. Thus I would both remove from myself the reproach of idleness and ensure that the Latin language was not deprived of knowledge of such great miracles.

It also happened that I was earnestly requested to do this by the inhabitants of the aforementioned city, because a church of this martyr, constructed with honorable excellence, exists there.

2. Receive, therefore, this little work, and, learning the miracles performed after his passing by the first martyr and deacon of Christ the Lord—miracles that perhaps until now you have not known—render worthy praises to their author. Celebrate solemnly the anniversary day in commemoration of this wonderful translation, remembering me as well.

But since at that time, while I was staying there, I also translated the discourse on virginity concerning Anna and Simeon—or rather, the discourse on the three professions which Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, had delivered—I have taken care to send this also, together with the aforesaid little work, to Your Holiness. For I have judged that there is scarcely anything more beneficial spiritually than to offer spiritual things.

May Your Beatitude remain well forever, mindful of me, as God’s dwelling-places obtain this through their prayers.

[Col. 0817]

## ACCOUNT OF THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT STEPHEN FROM JERUSALEM TO THE CITY OF BYZANTIUM (S)*
1. It happened that, while the body of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, was kept at Jerusalem in holy Sion, in the days of John, bishop of Jerusalem, a certain senator named Alexander conceived the plan of building a chapel of Saint Stephen. When this had been completed, he earnestly begged John the bishop to place the body of Saint Stephen the martyr in that same chapel. The bishop then placed the coffin there and fastened an inscription to its exterior with nails, in the month of December, on the fourteenth day, in the fifth indiction [Note: [Col. 0819] Thus the Floriacensis manuscript. But the codex of John Ulimmer, who first published this writing, and other editions thereafter, read “in the second indiction.” And below: “Therefore after two years.”], in the tenth consulship of our lord the emperor Constantine Augustus. Five years later, Alexander the senator fell ill and made his will to the holy Church, to the poor, and to his wife Juliana. He adjured John the bishop by our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “After my death, let a Persian coffin be made, and place me beside the tomb of the first martyr Saint Stephen, for I also built his house from my own resources.” Having said this, he fell asleep in peace. The next day the bishop came with a multitude of people, took him up, and placed him beside Saint Stephen the first martyr.

2. After eight years, his wife Juliana, reflecting and judging it to be a good thing, wished to take her husband’s body and carry it to Byzantium, to her own estate. Having made this decision, she went to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, and said to him: “I wish to carry my husband’s body to Byzantium, to my own possession.” He said to her: “I cannot do this and disturb the people.” Then Juliana, weeping, went away to her house, wrote a letter, and sent it to her father, who was residing in Byzantium [Note: [Col. 0819] Thus the Floriacensis codex. The editions, however, read “to the presbyter.”], writing as follows:

> “Your own daughter Juliana sends greetings in the Lord to my father. I offer you fitting honors, and I ask you to grant that I may be received by you. For I send not words filled with flattering expressions, nor a message announced by a heavenly mystery, nor a plea composed in rhetorical language; rather, I direct prayers to my father and lord, since, as a widow, I suffer violence from powerful men in the matter of marriage. Hasten, therefore, so that a Sacra may be issued and sent by the great emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0819] At this point the Floriacensis manuscript reads “Constantius”; but shortly afterward it reads “Constantine.”] to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, so that I too may come and bring my husband’s body to my own possession.”

He, having received a Sacra from the great emperor Constantine, sent it to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem.

3. The bishop therefore read the Sacra, and being unable to oppose it, brought the woman before him and said: “How can we do this, since I do not know which coffin is that of Saint Stephen the first martyr and which is that of your husband? Go, then, prepare what is necessary for the journey, and inform me.” After preparing what was suitable for the journey, she went to the bishop in the church. As evening grew late, they descended farther into the chapel where the relic of the Saint lay. When they opened the place, they found two coffins.

The bishop said to the woman: “I do not know which coffin is that of Saint Stephen the first martyr and which is your husband’s.”

The woman replied: “I know which is my husband’s coffin, since I made it.”

When the bishop heard this, he ordered her to take the one she recognized. She immediately rushed forward and embraced the relic of Saint Stephen, thinking that it was her husband’s body. Taking it, she placed it in a litter. Then, bidding farewell to the bishop, she proceeded joyfully on her way.

Throughout the whole night a hymn was sung along the road, and the scent of richly fragrant ointment wafted through the air. Unclean spirits cried out, saying: “Woe to us, for the first martyr Stephen is passing by, scourging us with dreadful fire.” The woman sat in her carriage, while boys walked in front of the litter and were afraid, saying: “What is happening to us, since the spirits are crying out about Saint Stephen? Could this be his body, and we not know it? For a multitude of angels are singing a hymn before the litter. But what shall we do, our lady? Perhaps this is not your husband’s body, but that of Saint Stephen the first martyr.”

When she heard this, she remained silent, weeping. She commanded the boys to tell no one what had appeared to them on the journey [Col. 0820]. “But if anyone asks,” she said, “in the city or in the countryside, whose litter this is, say: ‘It belongs to the husband of our lady, and she is going to Byzantium.’”

That same night we passed through three stations. During the day we rested, and in the evening we traveled; but in the deep night the spirits cried out, saying: “He who scourges us is passing by. We cannot endure the power of the holy body, for it is fire, and it consumes us in the air. We cannot withstand the power of Saint Stephen the first martyr.” Many healings and miracles took place on the road.

4. We came to maritime Ascalon and found a ship sailing to Byzantium. After summoning the shipmaster, the woman gave him fifty gold pieces, saying: “I have a secret to tell you, and do not oppose me. I have a coffin to transport to Byzantium. See that you carry it safely, and you will receive your reward from almighty God.”

He said to her: “I do not wish to oppose my lady, because the first martyr Stephen, who is great, is with you; in him are my life and my hope, for today my eyes have seen the most glorious things. Come, therefore, my lady, and board the ship. We shall sail with the power of God and of the holy body.”

When everyone had boarded the ship, it was released from the shore by a favorable wind. When they reached the middle of the sea, a storm suddenly arose, so that the waves rose above the ship’s rigging. As the sea surged violently, everyone, seized with fear, rose and worshiped the holy body. While they mourned and wept, great calm suddenly arose upon the sea, and Saint Stephen the first martyr appeared to them, saying: “I am he; do not be afraid.” When he had said this, the wind ceased, and a great calm came to pass (Matthew 8:26).

When morning came, we reached the narrows of Chalantis, because of the prince Augustus [Note: [Col. 0820] Thus the ancient codex. The editions read: “When morning came, we reached the narrow places of Chalantis, because of the prince of Augustus.”]. Suddenly an earthquake occurred in that place, so that the foundations of the earth were shaken until the ship of Saint Stephen the first martyr had passed through; then the shaking earth became still.

The demons cried out against the prince, saying: “Most impious prince, why did you not burn the ship that passed through there, but allowed it to pass against us? That ship itself caused the earthquake.”

When the prince heard this, he sent five dromons to seize and burn the ship. When the dromons reached the ship, an angel came out of it, struck the dromons, and sank them. Great joy arose in the ship, because God was with them.

After sailing for three days and an equal number of nights, we came to Chalcedon, and the ship was left in the harbor. When we had spent five days there, all who had demons came near the sea, tormented and crying out: “The servant of God has come, who was stoned by the wicked Jews.” By the grace of Saint Stephen the spirits cried out: “Woe to us, for he burns us fiercely! Where shall we flee from his terrible threats?”

They came out violently, driven away from the people as though from fire. All who had sick persons carried them outside the sea, and all were healed by the power of Saint Stephen the first martyr.

From there we moved on and came to Sosas. Almost the whole city, hearing of it, ran out to meet us: the Christians rejoicing, but the pagans grieving. From there we departed again, because of the crowd gathered around us, and came to the city of Staurium [Note: [Col. 0820] The editions read “Taurum.” The manuscripts, however, read “Staurium.”].

5. When Eusebius, bishop of Constantinople, learned of the body of Saint Stephen the first martyr and that the whole Christian multitude had been stirred to see the power of the holy body, he hastened to the emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0820] Here again the ancient codex reads “Constantius.” But Eusebius, mentioned above, was bishop of Constantinople during the reign not of Constantius but of Constantine.] and informed him about Saint Stephen’s body.

The emperor inquired how the body had come from Jerusalem and who had brought it. They brought the woman before him, saying: “Lord Emperor, this is the woman who brought the body of the first martyr.”

The emperor said to her: “How did you bring Saint Stephen’s body? Tell me the truth.”

She replied: “Lord Emperor, my husband himself built the chapel of Saint Stephen at Jerusalem, and he himself, together with Bishop John, reinterred Saint Stephen. Some years later my husband died, having deposited his will with Bishop John and saying: ‘After my end, place me near the first martyr Stephen.’ And so it was done.”

The emperor said: “How, then, did you bring it here?”

She replied: “Lord Emperor, suffering violence from powerful men as a widow, and unwilling to be joined to another husband, I informed my father that I wished to come here and bring my husband’s body to my own possession. When my father heard this [Note: [Col. 0821] The same codex reads: “When my lord heard this,” and so forth.], he received a Sacra from your imperial authority and sent it to me and to the bishop, so that I might take my husband’s body. I therefore went down at night with Bishop Cyril, intending to take my husband’s body, and I took Saint Stephen’s instead.”

She also gave the Sacra to the emperor. When the emperor read it, he recognized his own handwriting.

Then the woman answered the emperor: “Lord Emperor, you have power over my body; but over my soul is God, who performs miracles in heaven and on earth. If you do not believe this, lord, send a Hebrew to the ship, where the Saint’s coffin lies and where an inscription is also affixed, written in Hebrew letters. When you read them, you will know the certainty of the matter.”

The emperor summoned a Hebrew and adjured him by his own law, saying: “Go and see what is written.”

The Hebrew went with two guards, and, after reading it, said: “This is a great spectacle.”

The guards said: “What spectacle is it? Tell us.”

The Hebrew replied: “It is Saint Stephen the first martyr, and in him are my life and my hope [Note: [Col. 0821] The ancient codex does not contain the words “and in him are my life and my hope”], for today my eyes have seen the most glorious things” [Col. 0822].

The guards then came and announced to the emperor that it was Saint Stephen the first martyr. He rejoiced greatly, summoned Bishop Eusebius, and said to him: “Go to the ship with a multitude of people, and I shall send a wagon. Bring the coffin to me in the palace.”

6. The bishop went, and all the people ran with candles. The bishop descended into the ship, took the coffin, placed it on a wagon, and hurried to the palace. The mules proceeded, dragged along forcibly by angels. When they came to the place called Constantinianus, they stopped and could not go farther.

They therefore beat the animals. One of them, speaking with a human voice through angelic power before the whole people, said: “Why are you striking our faces? He must be reinterred here in this place. Do not labor at all; otherwise you will have to see signs and wonders.”

The bishop, trembling and unable to endure the torment, reported to the emperor: “I cannot bring the Saint’s body.”

When the emperor heard this, he was saddened and sent twelve other animals to pull the wagon. They too stopped in the same way because of the angels’ power and were unable to move the wagon.

Then the bishop [Note: [Col. 0822] In the Floriacensis codex: “the people.”] cried out, saying: “You alone are God almighty, who alone performs wonders (Psalm 71:18) over your holy first martyr Stephen, who suffered martyrdom for your name. Grant us, therefore, grace and mercy through the prayers and intercessions of the first martyr.”

Then the bishop took the coffin from the wagon and placed it there, building its chapel over the course of five months; in it he deposited the coffin with every precaution.

Healings and miracles were performed upon the sick in those days, to the glory of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, to whom belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0821]

## LETTER OF SEVERUS TO THE WHOLE CHURCH, CONCERNING THE MIRACLES PERFORMED FOR THE CONVERSION OF THE JEWS ON THE ISLAND OF MINORCA IN THE PRESENCE OF THE RELICS OF SAINT STEPHEN [Note: [Col. 0821] It is cited below, in Book One of the Miracles of Saint Stephen, chapter 1.] (C, S)

To the most holy and blessed lords, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the entire brotherhood of the whole world: Severus, a bishop in need of God’s mercy and the least of all, eternal salvation in Christ our Redeemer.

1. Since the archangel Raphael urges us that it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God (Tobit 12:20), it is certainly dangerous to be silent about or conceal the works of Christ. Yet, in recounting them, grace is greater if they are reported in common and simple speech. For the most beautiful loveliness of a miracle is in a way concealed if it is surrounded and disguised by excessively elaborate language. Therefore I too undertake to relate the great things Christ has accomplished among us, not in a polished but in a truthful manner.

2. The island of Minorca is one of the Balearic Islands, whose name is widely known among all peoples and even in the writings of secular authors. Situated approximately midway between Caesarean Mauretania and Spain, it is enclosed within very narrow boundaries: it is thirty miles long and three thousand paces wide. I have mentioned this so that it may be understood that the Lord chooses the despised things of the world not only among human beings but also among places (1 Corinthians 1:27).

On this island, then, which in smallness, aridity, and harshness is the most insignificant of all lands, two small towns, founded opposite one another and bearing names given by the Carthaginians, face each other: Jammona looks toward the west, and Magona toward the east. In these towns the burden of priestly office was recently placed upon me, the least of all mortals.

Jammona, however, still retains an ancient gift from God: Jews are entirely unable to live there. For tradition relates that many who rashly attempted it were overtaken by illness, driven away, extinguished by sudden death, or even struck down by lightning. So celebrated is the report of this matter that it has instilled fear even in the Jews themselves, lest they venture to attempt it again.

Nor do we regard this as unworthy of belief, since we also observe that wolves, foxes, and all harmful animals are absent, while there is a great abundance of beasts suitable for food. What is even more astonishing is that there are very many snakes and scorpions, but they have completely lost the power to cause harm.

Since, therefore, no Jew—who is rightly compared with wolves and foxes in savagery and wickedness—dared even to approach Jammona under the right of hospitality, Magona alone, like a place teeming with snakes and scorpions, as the report had it, was constantly infested with them, so that the Church of Christ was bitten by them every day. But that ancient carnal benefit has recently been renewed for us spiritually, so that this “generation of vipers” (Luke 3:7), which raged with poisonous bites, was suddenly compelled by divine power [Col. 0823] to cast off that deadly venom of unbelief.

3. For almost at the very time when I, although unworthy, acquired the title of so great a priesthood, a certain presbyter [Note: [Col. 0823] Orosius.] of distinguished holiness came from Jerusalem and stayed for some time at Magona. When he was unable to cross over to Spain, as he desired [Note: [Col. 0823] Spain was under siege by the Goths at this time. Baronius, under the year 418.], he decided to return again to Africa. Having determined to carry with him to Spain the relics of blessed Stephen, which had recently been discovered, he placed them, undoubtedly inspired by the Martyr, in the church of the aforesaid town.

Once this had been done, that fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth and which he greatly desires to see burning (Luke 12:49) was immediately kindled by his love. At once our lukewarmness grew warm, and our heart became, as it is written, “burning on the way” (Luke 24:32). Then zeal was already burning in faith, and was lifted up by hope of saving the multitude.

Finally, the duties of greeting were immediately interrupted; not only was the habit of familiarity broken off, but even the harmful appearance of long-standing affection was changed into temporary hatred, for the sake of the love of eternal salvation. In every street battles over the Law were waged against the Jews; in every house battles of faith were fought.

4. The Jewish people relied chiefly upon the authority and influence of a certain Theodorus, who was prominent not only among the Jews but also among the Christians of that town, both in wealth and in worldly honor. Among the Jews he was a teacher of the Law and, to use their own expression, “father of fathers.” In the city he had been released from all curial duties and had already become its defender; even then he possessed the patronage of the municipality.

The Christians, humble both in heart and in strength but superior in the power of truth, pleaded for the patronage and protection of Stephen. At length, when both armies had appointed a day for battle, they withdrew after a truce had been granted. The Jews were eagerly awaiting the return from the island of Majorca of Theodorus, upon whose strength the entire synagogue depended and who had perhaps gone there to inspect a property.

As soon as a delegation was sent to him, he returned. By his authority he terrified many, but he did not extinguish the fire of the conflict; he merely lulled it. For immediately it burst into flame with greater violence, and the neighboring town too was seized by the fire of faith. And so that Solomon’s saying might be fulfilled, “A brother helping a brother will be exalted like a strong and lofty city” (Proverbs 18:19), many servants of Christ, refusing to shrink from the labor of the journey, resolved to devote all the strength of their minds to this battle.

5. While the battle was still pending, the Memorandum appended to this letter demonstrates what weapons we had prepared. We did not wish to publish it for the instruction of certain people—for we ourselves are entirely in need of such instruction, and hope for it still more from Your Blessedness—but so that it might be recognized that, according to the measure of our ability, we had taken up the contest with no small concern.

Christ, however, whose kingdom is not in speech but in power, completed everything by his own strength while we had not uttered even a word, and granted his army, without any exertion in battle, a victory which no one had dared either to desire or to hope for.

The Jews therefore encouraged themselves with examples from the time of the Maccabees and longed even for death in defense of their ancestral laws. They began not only to review their books but also to bring stones, stakes, javelins, and every kind of weapon to the synagogue, so that, if circumstances demanded it, they might repel the Christian line, fortified by the power of the Holy Spirit, with bodily force as well.

6. While these preparations were being made and both sides were eagerly arranging the coming war, the two armies were shaken by indescribable and perfectly clear dreams. If I were to make no mention at all of them, I would seem to have concealed no small part of the divine glory.

For this reason Luke inserted into his sacred history the dream of the holy apostle Paul, saying that a Macedonian man appeared in a night vision and asked him to help him; and that, warned by this vision, the Apostle turned the course of his journey, which had been directed elsewhere, toward Macedonia (Acts 16:9–10).

How much greater, then, is the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to reveal to insignificant and unworthy servants what Scripture did not conceal when it was shown even to the blessed Apostle? For the sake of brevity, therefore, lest I perhaps cause Your Blessedness weariness, I shall insert only two dreams.

7. Among us there was a certain devout and most religious woman named Theodora, who, by the virginity of her body, the religious purpose of her life, and the meaning of her name, deserved to bear a type of the Church. In a night vision she saw a certain most noble widow send letters to me—who exercise the priesthood not according to merit but through the abundance of the divine gift—by means of which she humbly offered me all her fields for sowing [Note: [Col. 0824] Perhaps “inscribed,” or “addressed.”] [Note: [Col. 0824] Alternatively, “had sent beforehand.”].

In a similar dream he also deigned to gird and urge me, the least of sinners, to sow. For another most noble widow, who clearly represented the synagogue, begged me to receive her uncultivated fields and, when the season for sowing pressed upon us, to cultivate them diligently.

And who is this other most noble widow except the one who, by impiously killing Christ, cruelly widowed herself? The dream of both women is one and the same. It is clear that we saw it about thirty days before it was fulfilled and, although we did not know its interpretation, nevertheless reported it to the brothers.

8. Among the Jews also, by a marvelous order of divine providence, the name Theodorus and the association with my office came together in one man. Theodorus, who was high priest of that faithless people, disclosed the dream he had seen not only to the Jews but also to a certain prominent mother of a household, a leading woman of the city, and to many other Christians, long before the time when it was fulfilled.

He said: “As I was going to the synagogue, twelve men extended their hands toward me and said: ‘Where are you going? A lion is there.’

“When I began to tremble upon hearing the name of the lion, I nevertheless found a place from which I could look in while preparing to flee, and I saw monks singing psalms there with extraordinary sweetness. Immediately a greater terror was added to me; and unless I had entered the house of a certain man named Ruben and from there rushed headlong to my kinswoman, I would never have escaped the deadly terror. She took me, lifeless as I was, into her bosom, and rescued me alike from danger and fear.”

His dream is exceedingly clear and needs no interpretation. For who is the lion except “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (Revelation 5:5)? And who is that kinswoman except she of whom it is written, “One is my kinswoman” (Song of Songs 6:8)?

Only this seemed obscure: that the Jew, terrified by the lion, entered the house of Ruben. But this was later explained to us most clearly by the very lion who had frightened him, so that he might save him. We shall explain this in its proper place. For now I shall continue the account of what had begun.

9. From the city of Jammona a multitude of Christ’s servants gathered to set out; they were thought to be staying in the town itself. They completed the labor of that most difficult journey with such eagerness that they traversed thirty thousand paces more gladly than if they had been invited to some most pleasant suburb for a banquet.

We therefore reached Magona. I immediately sent clerics to announce my arrival to the Jews and requested that they deign to come to the holy church. They sent us an unexpected reply, instructing that they ought not to enter the church that day—lest, I suppose, they be polluted—for it was the Sabbath, whose festival they had corrupted by their actions.

Again I requested [Col. 0825] that, if they preferred, they await me at the synagogue, since entry into the church seemed to them an act of pollution. I certainly did not wish them to be compelled by us on the day of the Sabbath festival to perform servile work. Rather, there would be an honorable dispute concerning the Law, and quarrels should not be stirred up or stories introduced. Or, if they were not craftily avoiding the contest and were offering a straightforward excuse, they should show the commandment by which conversation on that day was forbidden.

When they obstinately answered all this with every kind of opposition, at last, compelled by fear of that lion, they gathered at the house where I was staying as a guest.

There I said: “I ask you, brothers, why have you gathered heaps of stones and every kind of weapon as though against robbers, especially in a city subject to Roman laws? We wish to win you over; you desire to destroy us. As I see it, it is not right for us to suffer through such a varied dispute with one another. You, as I see, thirst for our blood; we thirst for your salvation.”

At this they were somewhat frightened and denied that it had happened. Although our people affirmed that it was so, they resisted even with an oath.

Then, wishing to cut through the knot of the dispute that had begun, I said: “Where the matter can be proved by the eyes, what need is there of an oath? Let us therefore go to the synagogue, and whether your assertion rests upon falsehood or truth will be established by your own testimony.”

10. We therefore began to proceed to the synagogue, singing a hymn to Christ through the streets in the joy of the multitude. The psalm, which even the Jewish people sang out with great delight, was this: “Their memory has perished with a crash, but the Lord endures forever” (Psalm 9:7–8).

Before we reached the synagogue, however, certain Jewish women—by God’s providence, I believe—presuming upon their boldness, so that the gentleness of our people might be provoked, began to hurl enormous stones at us from an elevated place. Marvelous to say, although the stones descended upon the densely packed multitude like hail, they harmed none of us, not only by a blow but not even by a touch.

At this the terrifying lion withdrew a little of his gentleness from his lambs. For, although we protested, everyone took up stones, and, setting aside the shepherd’s admonition, zeal for Christ rather than anger suggested to all the same counsel: that the wolves should be attacked with horns. No one can doubt, however, that this happened by the will of him who alone is the good shepherd.

Finally, lest he seem to have given his flock a bloody victory, none of the Jews even pretended—out of envy, perhaps, as is customary—that he had been touched.

Yet, because we must avoid falsehood in every way, one man was found among all the Christians who wished to be like Achan, who under Joshua son of Nun coveted spoils from what had been devoted to destruction (Joshua 7). For, while the servant of a certain Christian alone desired to seize something from the synagogue, he stumbled against a stone of offense.

One of our men threw a stone, as if against a Jew. It struck the servant’s head and reminded him to remember his head—that is, Christ. Although the wound was dangerous, it compelled him to confess his desire for plunder, and it frightened everyone by this immediate punishment, lest they fall in the same way.

After the Jews had yielded and we had taken possession of the synagogue, no one took anything from it; indeed, no one even thought of plundering it. Fire consumed all its furnishings, except the books and the silver; it consumed the wall itself as well. We removed the holy books so that they would not suffer injury at the hands of the Jews; but we returned the silver to them, so that they might not complain either of our plunder or of their own loss.

After the synagogue had been demolished while all the Jews looked on in amazement, we went with hymns to the church. Giving thanks to the author of our victory, we poured out prayers and asked that the Lord conquer the true caverns of unbelief and that the infidelity of their darkened hearts be exposed by the light.

11. A certain Jew named Ruben was chosen by the Lord to be appointed the firstborn of all. For, bringing joy to the hearts of many by a most holy cry, he begged to be released from the bonds of Jewish superstition. Immediately made a Jacob of the firstfruits, he received the sign of salvation; thereafter he clung to our side and counsels and joined us in rebuking the obstinate hardness of all the others.

Three days had passed, if I am not mistaken, since our people had persevered in prayer and the Jews in unbelief. After this Theodorus came, surrounded by the procession of his people, to the place where apparently only the walls of the synagogue remained—walls that were later overthrown when the Jews believed. A multitude of Christians also gathered there.

There Theodorus spoke boldly about the Law, ridiculing and twisting everything that was brought against him. When the Christian people saw that he could not be overcome by human words, they implored help from heaven.

All together, therefore, they cried out with the greatest thunder of united voices: “Theodore, believe in Christ!”

Through the marvelous mercy of the most indulgent Lord, little was being asked, yet greater things had been granted—or rather, there is nothing astonishing in a miracle performed by the Almighty. For he changed the power of this cry in the ears of the Jews, just as he once caused the four lepers of the king of Syria, who had besieged Samaria, to take possession of the enemy camp; and just as through Gideon he confused the ranks of the Midianites and gave his three hundred men a great victory without labor, causing the enemy multitude to be overthrown by the terror of mutual wounds.

So now this voice was received by the Jews standing around in a very different way from that in which it was uttered by our people. For they all thought that the words were: “Theodore has believed.”

Thus, supposing that the leader of their unbelief had been converted to the faith of Christ, they were all terrified and trembled where there was no cause for fear. Their women, running up with their hair disheveled and with savage howling, repeatedly accused Theodorus by name, saying: “O Theodore, what have you done?”

Some of the men fled to remote woods and clefts [Note: [Col. 0826] Perhaps: “some fled to remote woods and clefts in the mountains.” Below, no. 12: “they had fled to the woods or caves”; and no. 13: “they gathered at one cave, or rather rock.” M.]; others ran through the narrow lanes of the town itself, seeking a place where they might hide.

12. Theodorus himself, struck with amazement, saw the divine sentence being fulfilled among his people: “The wicked flee when no one pursues” (Proverbs 28:1). Yet it was not no one who pursued them. That terrifying lion was pursuing them—the lion who, from the site of the synagogue, had uttered a roar through the monks, as had been revealed to Theodorus, and by that roar had made the resisting enemies tremble.

Theodorus therefore stood in precisely the place where, long before, the terror of the lion had been instilled in him through a dream. As he searched for the cause of such great trembling and heard only the name of our lion, he saw no savagery there, as had been reported; he saw only monks singing psalms. Abandoned by the whole multitude of his people and preparing to slip away, he too sought a path for his feet.

When the most holy Ruben saw him seized by dreadful fear and deprived not only of the color of his face but even of the use of his voice, he quickly approached. Addressing him gently while he trembled, he urged him toward the faith of Christ. Offering him, as support against fear, the example of his own belief, he seemed in a way to fulfill the image of the house to which Theodorus had fled in terror of the lion.

But, so that we may faithfully recount everything and so that you, who seek not verbal ornament but truth, may listen more willingly, I shall insert Ruben’s own words and omit nothing from the simplicity of his speech. He said:

“Why are you afraid, Lord Theodore? If you truly wish to be secure, honored, and wealthy, believe in Christ, just as I too have believed. At present you are standing and I am sitting with the bishops. If you believe, you too will sit, and I shall stand before you.”

Theodorus received these words deeply into his mind and said to us: “I shall do what you wish. Keep this promise, he said; but allow me first to address my people, so that I may receive a greater reward for my conversion even from the rest.”

His pledge was received by everyone with inestimable admiration [Col. 0827]. Some rushed upon him affectionately and caressed his face and neck; others embraced him gently with their arms; still others longed to join their right hands and converse with him.

Theodorus therefore proceeded happily to his own courtyard, though not entirely free from anxiety. For although, by his promise, we were already entering the house of Ruben, he was still trembling when he went in, since he had not yet come to his kinswoman, who, after three days, received him in her motherly bosom and freed him from every turmoil of fear.

We went as usual to the church with hymns. Blessed is the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who gave water to our head and a fountain of tears to our eyes, so that we might weep for the wounded of our people.

When the rites had been completed and we had left the church, we saw that a very large multitude of Jews had gathered to meet us. They all unanimously begged to receive the mark of Christ from me, although I was an unworthy shepherd.

We therefore returned to the church and, giving thanks to the Lord with our whole heart, immediately impressed the sign of salvation upon their foreheads.

What miracles were accomplished through the power of Christ among those who had fled to the woods or caves—which tongue could tell? Especially since each one of them has his own personal history of conversion.

Just as it is impossible for us to tell everything, so it would be ungrateful to pass over everything. Therefore, aided by your prayers, I shall unfold one miracle of Christ, which we learned from men of proven faith and integrity.

### 13

Two leading Jews, Meletius, the brother of Theodore, and Innocentius, who had recently escaped the devastation of Spain and had come to this island with his servants—as they themselves now also confirm, even with the solemn interposition of oaths—gathered at a certain cave, or rather rocky shelter, joining themselves to two Jews of humble origin who had chosen these men as leaders of their common flight.

After they had sat there for a little while, trembling and panting, they sent the two younger men, who were vigorous and bold, back to the town to investigate, and were left there alone. Then Meletius first said:

“What is this, brother? Why can I not tear from my heart a blasphemous utterance, as our religion teaches? Ever since the Christian people proclaimed that my brother had been converted, nothing else is suggested to my heart except this phrase, wholly unknown to me until this day: ‘Christ, in your name.’ The more earnestly I strive to drive it from my soul, the more violently and tenaciously it clings to me.”

To this Innocentius replied: “This utterance, which—as everyone of sound judgment can attest—your heart neither previously conceived nor ever expressed, has not been inserted so violently into your mind here without reason, especially as you say. I think it is from God. Nevertheless, I beg you, exert yourself and, turning away from these fancies, drive out the intrusion of this troublesome thought.”

Then Meletius began to make such a din and resound with confused cries that Innocentius could see him wrestling with his own mind, not merely from the movements of his face but also from the evidence of his whole body. When he realized that this achieved not even the slightest result, he added still more: he spoke certain profane and shameful words, now drawing up his nostrils and sucking in the air while producing indecent noises, now bursting into foul laughter. But this madness could not extinguish Christ’s name from his mind, because the fire of healing had already penetrated all his marrow.

“What then, brother Innocentius,” he said, “do these words achieve when turned to the contrary? I cannot extort the removal of Christ’s name from myself either by buffoonery of language or by blasphemies made up of obscene sounds themselves. For I feel that something else is being returned to me: it does not cease, with unremitting shouting, to thrust the name of Christ into the ears of my heart, which I strive in vain to block.”

To these words of Meletius, Innocentius replied:

“The Christian people [Col. 0828] testified, in these very ears, that my brother Theodore—older than I in teaching, honor, and age—had been converted to the faith of Christ.
