Can it be that you too, constrained by the example of your own brother, might abandon the Jewish religion? Why, then, do we waste more time in this terrible solitude? How long will we be able to endure the hardship of lacking food? Why should we waste away from hunger, dry up from thirst, and stiffen from cold? And finally, why should we be held—as we already are—by the dreadful silence of this solitude? Are we fleeing the chains of robbers, or the swords of barbarians? Does so merciful a people, whom we have seen weeping for us, desire our blood? Let us remember, I beg you, whom any one of our people has ever injured by violence, or at least wronged. Let us return to our innocent enemies, whom we have harmed in nothing; and let what pleases God be done.”

To this Meletius answered:

“I think you have forgotten, brother Innocentius—you whom I know to be learned not only in Latin but also in Greek letters, and continually meditating on the Law—what the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel: ‘The soul that sins, it shall die’ (Ezek. 18:20). If you have read this, why do you think that I can be drawn to the faith of Christ by the example of my brother Theodore? He has his own soul, and likewise his own sin; and that sin will not harm me if I do not abandon the Lord God.

“But I call to witness the one who led our fathers out of the land of Egypt: if the violence of winter did not prevent me, I would seize any vessel and migrate alone to any land whatsoever. Neither love of property nor affection for those dear to me would hold me back; I could easily give them up, provided only that I were not compelled to deny the God of my fathers.

“As for your decision that we should return to the city by this useless plan, I am astonished that you, the most prudent of men, do not foresee in your mind what you think will happen to us if Theodore, the pillar of our synagogue in whom we placed all our confidence, has been compelled to apostatize. It is therefore wiser for us to go to my estate and no longer expose ourselves to the eyes of the Christians. There we can hide for the time being, until at a suitable moment we emigrate to foreign lands.

“For hatred of our religion has grown so greatly among everyone on this island that anyone who has not left his homeland cannot preserve the faith of his fathers. Why, then, should we not voluntarily undertake the exile to which, as circumstances show, the hatred of our fellow citizens will consign us even against our will?”

With this counsel confirming the judgment of both men, they undertook the labor of the journey they had planned. But as they entered a very narrow path, the darkness of their thoughts obscuring the light of their eyes, they lost the very track they were unknowingly following and remained in deserted and impassable places.

When they were torn by thorns and brambles and had disfigured their bodies with long wounds, they first reached such anxiety, and then such despair and fear, that they were compelled to confess that they were suffering these things by the just judgment of God because of their unbelief. Accordingly, they invoked the name of Christ, which they had previously driven away when it thrust itself before them of its own accord. Their legs now lacerated, they seized the path that led them back to the town against their will and contrary to their purpose.

But when they had reached the city unwillingly and in fear, they made careful inquiries and heard that Theodore was still a Jew and had suffered none of the violence from the Christian people that they had imagined. Astonished and unable to believe what had happened to them, they directed their steps to Theodore’s house. There, when he had received them almost at the end of the midday meal, he immediately asked the reason why they had withdrawn from him and from the city; and he learned the whole sequence of events, more with laughter than with astonishment.

### 14

After three days, when Theodore was preparing to address his people and summon them to the faith of Christ, he also encountered a spontaneous uprising of the Jews who offered themselves for confession. For scarcely any of them failed to declare publicly that they had experienced the power of Christ.

At their first assembly, a certain young man, Theodore’s cousin, named Galilaeus—so that, as has been said, the fitting mystery contained in the names might carry the story of what had happened through to its conclusion—[Col. 0829] began to cry out with intense indignation:

“I call you all to witness that I cannot remain in possession of the Jews’ property. For I have Christians as partners in it, and, if I wish to persist in Judaism, I may perhaps have to be killed by their hatred. I shall therefore take precautions for my life and now go to the church, so that I may escape the death being prepared for me.”

As Galilaeus said this while preparing to flee for a time, as though he had thereby given the reasons for his conversion, and without then thinking at all about the death of the future age, he was unknowingly speaking the truth.

A respectable man, Caecilianus, happened to be passing by. He was prominent not only among the Jews but also throughout the city, so prominent indeed that he has now been elected defender of the city. He declared that Galilaeus was speaking truthfully and testified that he had a similar reason and feared similar things.

By these words he gave the young man mentioned above such confidence that, in the sight of everyone, he ran at full speed to assist our Galilaeus in winning the prize of faith, and sought to be baptized by our humility, so that thereafter he might be designated by its name.

Caecilianus, however, being the father of the Jews, took counsel with Florinus, his brother, likewise a father and elder of the Jews. Then, as we learned, he addressed the synagogue in these words:

“Since I am first in the honor of the synagogue after Theodore, I do not, like the young Galilaeus, address and call all of you to witness as though in fear. Rather, I exhort and admonish you, declaring that, if possible, we should all together hasten to the faith of the Church, abandoning the error of this crooked path.

“But if such power does not draw you to Christ, then certainly my brother Florinus and I—just as we cannot use force to impose so great a salvation upon you if you refuse it—will nevertheless abandon, together with our entire household, the mockery of this religion, which we cannot establish, and join the number and faith of the Christians. They would certainly never have convicted not only you, brother Theodore, who seem more learned than the rest, but also all of you by the countless testimonies of Scripture, unless they were following the truth, which cannot be defeated.”

We learned that Caecilianus addressed his people with this understanding, and with ineffable rejoicing we received many Jews who, on that same day, joined him in the faith of Christ.

### 15

The prodigies that then occurred from heaven I cannot adequately express, but I dare not remain silent about them. At about the seventh hour we solemnly began to celebrate the Lord’s Mass. For while we were either exhorting the Jews who were coming to the faith of Christ or recording them—for we wrote down their names—the greater part of the day had passed, while the people, filled with the banquet of such great joy, had forgotten bodily food.

The entire people was waiting with us for Mass in the church, situated somewhat apart from the city, where the recently deposited relics of the holy martyr Stephen rested. Two monks, whom the Lord had chosen beforehand as witnesses of his miracles, were lying in the grass in the field extending before the church doors.

A respected man named Julius, coming toward the church with another man from the city, had just begun to pass by them when one of the monks responded. On seeing the miraculous sign, Julius was disturbed and uttered a confused cry. Then, turning toward them and extending his hand, he indicated what he was seeing, although he could not explain it in words.

There was a sphere of the whitest light, equal in height to a man’s stature, resembling the vessels commonly called *orcae*. It was of such brilliance and radiance that, as it seemed, the sun itself appeared to be falling upon the brother who noticed it first, as we learned from his own report.

As these men saw it, the sphere descended in a slow fall as though across the basilica in which all the people had gathered with us. Yet they thought it so near that the same brother, overcome with astonishment, rushed forward, believing that it had fallen behind the basilica. But the other brother held him back and stopped his movement. He maintained that it had indeed seemed so to him as well, but that it was farther away—not as one certain of the matter, but as one forming an estimate.

At that time some Jewish women [Col. 0830], among them the wife of that Meletius mentioned above, looked out from the upper room and affirmed that they too had seen the same thing, as though it had fallen above the basilica.

But whether what appeared was an angel or Stephen himself remains uncertain.

At approximately the fourth hour of the same day—that is, shortly before this sign appeared—very small hail fell, not everywhere in abundance. The inhabitants of that island call it *albigistinum* in their native language. When it began to give off the fragrance of honey, many who had been struck by it along the road tasted it and found it sweeter than honey.

Accordingly, many learned men, seeing that the children of Israel had that same day come out of Egypt—from their faithlessness [Note: Perhaps *perfidiosa*, “treacherous” or “faithless.”] and from slavery—compared what had happened with the signs that we read about in Exodus. They believed that manna was being renewed for this people, who, gazing upon God with believing hearts, had deserved even the true name of Israel (Exod. 16).

They also thought that the pillar of fire that preceded the fathers in the wilderness (ibid. 13:22) had been shown in order to provide guidance to their children as well, who had come forth from the true Egypt and from the iron furnace, as it is written (Deut. 4:20), leading them toward life.

And indeed, as the reading from Exodus attests, the likeness of the signs is in no way incongruous. For what we believed to be snow was comparable to small coriander seed and carried the taste of honey; and what appeared clearly had the appearance of a pillar of fire.

We know that both signs were also revealed to the brothers who were staying at Jammona. Many who were given the understanding to seek and the discernment to recognize it tested the rain of honey; and that pillar of the whitest light presented itself to the eyes of many whom the Lord judged worthy.

From this it may be understood that the Jews throughout the whole world are to be visited by the light of faith. For such a splendor of heavenly grace shone upon us who are settled on this island and in this little world, so to speak, that the sight of the signs reached even to the farthest boundaries of your land.

### 16

On the following day, the intense expectation of everyone urged Theodore to fulfill his pledge. He thought that the wishes of all should be delayed for what seemed to be justifiable reasons, saying that he first wished to bring here his wife, whom he had left on the island of Majorca. He feared that, if she learned that her husband had been converted without her consent, she might—as often happens—be obstinate in unbelief and, driven from her senses by her mother’s persuasion and counsels, withdraw from her husband’s marriage on grounds of religion.

When Theodore had disclosed this to the Christians, the converted Jews resisted with the utmost agitation. The delay was therefore cut short, and Theodore himself hurried to the bosom of his close relative, as he had seen in his dream. After him, as though an obstacle had been removed, the entire synagogue flocked to the church.

It is remarkable to relate: the teachers of that ancient Law believed without any dispute of words and without any contest over Scripture. Merely asked whether they wished to receive the faith of Christ, they declared that they wished to believe in Christ and become Christians.

One man, as they say, was one hundred and two years old, both in age and in his unbelief. Without exchanging three words, this decrepit man, invigorated by hope of future life, eagerly expressed his wish that at the end of his days he might return through the faith of Christ to spiritual infancy. He presented his limbs, already decayed by old age, to us so that he might be reborn as quickly as possible through Baptism.

### 17

There were certain Jews who had arrived there in passing and were watching for a favorable opportunity of time and winds. When the opportunity for sailing was granted, they preferred to believe.

Only three women, therefore—all of them very noble among the Jews—did Christ allow to remain for a while in the stubbornness of their unbelief, so that the glory of his power might be enlarged.

Artemisia, daughter of Lectorius, who recently governed this province and is now said to be a count, was moved by the conversion of her husband Meletius. [Col. 0831] She left her husband’s house with one close friend, a nurse, and a few maidservants and, forgetting feminine weakness, escaped to a certain cave. Although it was in a vineyard, it was situated in a somewhat more remote place.

In it there was a small, new winepress, and a newly constructed vat seemed in some way to represent the believing people. For we both believe and see that these people have received the must of the New Testament not as old wineskins but as new vats.

The matron remained in this place for two days, implacable in her anger against her husband. As soon as the third day dawned, she ordered the maidservants to draw water. When she sensed that it conveyed the sweetness of honey in smell and taste, she began at first to grow angry with the servant and indignantly asked why she had put honey into the same pitcher.

Then, wishing to expose her as though she were denying it, she went to the vat. Drawing a little from it with hollowed hands, she found that the water she had used for two days had been changed into the sweetness of the most delicious honey.

She called all the women who were present and asked them to taste it, lest perhaps the deceptive taste merely counterfeit sweetness in her own mouth. All who tasted it were affected with wondrous delight: they judged it not water coated with the flavor of honey but pure honey, with only the appearance of water.

Struck with astonishment, they prepared to return to the city. As they proceeded, they also tasted the dew that lay on many of the grasses and found it similar.

The matron mentioned above went to the city, reported these things to her husband, and through him made them known to everyone. Immediately she consented, without resistance, to the faith of Christ.

But on the very day when Meletius’s wife was compelled by honey to cast away the bitterness of unbelief—that same day, I say, on which the daughter of Israel, placed as though in the wilderness, perceived that the ancient pool of Marah had been sweetened by the insertion of the wood of the cross (Exod. 15)—the whole church was so wonderfully and truly filled with a heavenly fragrance that almost the entire brotherhood sensed the presence of the Holy Spirit. We had already sensed it several times before, but only a very few of us had done so.

Everyone found it remarkable that during those same days, although the weather remained almost continuously clear, frequent showers descended, and the rain preceded the Jews who were gradually coming to the faith of Christ. Observing this, we would commonly say among ourselves, almost jokingly:

“Look, it is already raining. Know that whichever Jews are going to come to the faith of Christ are approaching.”

Remarkably, while we were still often saying such things, the door of faith was being knocked upon by some of the Jews. Nor was this without reason, as it is written: “The Lord will set apart a willing rain for his inheritance” (Ps. 67:10).

From above were the women who refused to run toward the fragrance of Christ’s ointments.

### 18

The matron of that Innocentius whom we mentioned above, a venerable widow with her child, as rumor has it, immediately upon seeing that Innocentius, her sister’s husband, had been converted, boarded a ship. We not only permitted but even advised her to do so, because they could not be moved to the faith of Christ either by words or by miracles.

Innocentius’s wife, however, for nearly four days received the word of salvation that we presented with hardened ears. Since she rejected every remedy and was oppressed by the incurable illness of unbelief, and since she could be moved neither by the threats, prayers, nor tears of her husband Innocentius, the entire multitude of the brotherhood gathered, at Innocentius’s request, at the house where she lived. They were deeply grieved that one woman was resisting the fullness of such great joy, for she was already plainly regarded as their sister.

After we had long achieved nothing by pouring empty words into deaf ears [Col. 0832], we fled to the familiar aid of prayer and turned toward heavenly mercy the prayers that human impiety rejected. Thus, almost until the third hour, the army labored in battles of hymns and prayers against Amalek, the enemy of Jesus our leader (Exod. 17).

Then, when—as must be confessed—we were almost giving up in despair and preparing to withdraw, we gathered our strength again, ordered everyone to pray, and lay prostrate for a long time in tears. When, at the conclusion of the prayer, the people cried out “Amen,” she added that she wished to believe and become a Christian.

We therefore rejoiced and returned to our dwellings, since she too had been rescued from the snares of the devil.

### 19

On the following day, finally the eighth day after we had come to Jammona, we decided to return, carrying away the finest and most glorious joys of victory.

But when we had prepared for the journey and were leaving the city, the Lord added to his people, as though for provisions along the way, the one joy that seemed still to be lacking.

That widow, a relative of Innocentius, had been brought back from the sea. Suddenly she threw herself at my knees and tearfully begged for the assistance of our faith.

I said to her: “Why, woman, did you wish to abandon your brothers with such fickleness of spirit?”

She replied: “The prophet Jonah also wished to flee from the presence of the Lord, and yet he fulfilled the will of God, although unwillingly (Jonah 1). Receive, then, not only me but also these orphans, and nourish them for Christ.”

As she cried this out pitifully, she pressed her two little daughters upon me amid her tears.

Who did not weep for joy? Whom did the magnitude of that happiness not force to shed tears? I truly received the sheep whom we had thought to be the only one of the whole number to have gone astray, and with her twin offspring I brought her back to Christ’s sheepfolds.

### 20

During these eight days in which these events took place, before the beginning of Lent, we celebrated the festival of Easter. It is established that five hundred and forty souls were added to the Church.

I do not think it empty or superfluous, although I shall omit many things because of their immeasurable abundance, to mention at the end that no one from the immense multitude of the people of Jammona—who had come from thirty thousand paces away so many days earlier—placed before this work either the care of his household, the provision of his livelihood, or the affection of his desires.

What is still more remarkable and more worthy of rejoicing is that we see the very land of the Jewish people, long unproductive, now, after the thorns of unbelief have been cut away and the seed of the Word received, producing abundant fruit of righteousness. Thus, in hope, we rejoice over so many new fields: from the place where we uprooted the conspicuous forest of unbelief, the most fertile works of faith are sprouting.

For first they overturned the very foundations of the synagogue; then, for the construction of a new basilica, they not only contribute expenses but also carry stones on their shoulders.

### 21

Let Your Beatitude know that these things were undertaken by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ on the fourth day before the Nones of February and completed by him over eight days, after the eleventh consulship of the lord Honorius and the second victory of Constantius.

Therefore, if you graciously admit the words of one unworthy and sinful, embrace the zeal of Christ against the Jews—but for God’s sake and for their perpetual salvation. Perhaps the time foretold by the Apostle has now arrived, so that, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel may be saved (Rom. 11:25). And perhaps the Lord wished this spark from the farthest edge of the earth to be kindled so that the whole world might blaze with the fire of charity.

---

[Col. 0831]

## TWO BOOKS ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT STEPHEN THE PROTOMARTYR (C)

### ADMONITION TO THE FOLLOWING BOOKS

The two books *On the Miracles of Saint Stephen the Martyr* are by an uncertain author. Neither did they bear the name of Bishop Evodius of Uzala, to whom they were dedicated by the scholars of Louvain, in the previously published codex of Joannes Ulimmerius, nor in the old book of Fleury.

The author testifies in the prologue that they were composed at Evodius’s command, and he himself also indicates that he is a different person from Bishop Evodius in the sixth and thirteenth chapters of the first book and at the end of the second book.

Accordingly, in the summary prefixed to the first book by the writer, where these miracles are said to have been made known to the faithful at Evodius’s direction in the Church of Uzala, Evodius is signified not as the author and writer of the work but as the one who urged and approved it and ordered it to be written and read.

We do not know whether Augustine had this work before his eyes when, intending to narrate in Sermon 323.3 the miracle described here at the end of the first book, he said:

“At Uzala, where my brother Evodius is bishop, ask what great miracles take place there, and you will find them. Apart from the others, I will point out to you one that happened there, so that you may see how great is the presence of majesty there.”

## BOOK ONE

The account of the divine works displayed through the venerable merit of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, and made known to the faithful at Evodius’s direction in the Church of Uzala, whose bishopric that most worthy priest administered; with Aurelius Augustine at that time established at Hippo as dispenser of the Lord’s sowing.

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0833]

Because the holy angel Raphael deigns to exhort us not so much to keep the works of God hidden as rather to make them public for God’s glory, admonishing us and saying, “It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God” (Tob. 12:7)—because, just as failing to believe what has been learned is unbelief, so refusing to proclaim what has been learned for the edification of others is envy—I have therefore carefully taken pains, most blessed Pope Evodius, to obey the commands of Your Paternity, relying not so much on my own strength as assisted by the grace of God and your holy prayers.

My purpose is not to suppress, through malicious silence, the things that Christ has worked among us through our patron Stephen, his first martyr, and still deigns to work, thereby depriving others of them; rather, I wish to recount them with pious devotion, so that the glory of the Friend of God may be announced to the ears of the brethren.

I do not claim to enhance them by any power of talent or language; instead, I desire faithfully to explain the truth of the events themselves, insofar as God grants it. Thus our account should not so much dare to seek the pomp of words as strive to avoid the embellishment of lies. Wherever the matter requires it, we ought not to be ashamed simply to set down even the words of the people themselves, just as they were spoken by them.

For good and religious people prefer whatever is said truthfully, even in faulty language, to falsehood expressed in polished and ornate speech.

No one, however, should think that we have wished to narrate these things as though we might thereby confer some glory upon the blessed Martyr. We can neither diminish him by remaining silent nor contribute anything to him by speaking. The miracles of his virtues themselves need no proclamation by a human tongue; they have already raised their trumpet and resound everywhere.

We wish only, with humility, to demonstrate our devotion for the edification of the brethren and in order to receive the reward of obedience. We also fear what we have read was terribly said by the Lord himself: “If you are silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19:40).

I ask all of you who will piously and religiously wish to hear or read these things to deign always to remember in your holy prayers this least and last of sinners, who wrote this in the name of the Lord. And if anything is expressed by us in rustic language, do not be offended; but rejoice simply because it is spoken truthfully.

### CHAPTER ONE  
#### On the servant of God’s vial of blood shown in a dream

At a time when there could not yet have been even a rumor [Col. 0834] that the relics of the holy Stephen, first among the confessors of Christ in martyrdom, were going to come to us unworthy servants of the Lord—for we neither had the thought nor could even suspect that this might happen—the same glorious man began, from an earlier time, to reveal himself to certain holy souls among us.

On one occasion and in one place, certain servants of God were discussing the aforesaid relics. They possessed them, though we did not know it, having received them from the regions of the East. A woman who was also present at the conversation, a sacred servant of God, heard this and, as commonly happens, did not readily believe it. She began silently to say to herself:

“Who knows whether these really are the relics of martyrs?”

Immediately, however, on the following night, a certain vial appeared to her in a dream. It contained within it a sprinkling of blood and something resembling ears of grain or bones. A certain priest held it in his hand and, with her present, spoke to her brother, who was a monk:

“Do you wish to know how the relics of martyrs are proved?”

Having said this, he put the vial into his mouth, and immediately a flame of fire [Note: [Col. 0834] Thus the Fleury manuscript. The printed editions, however, read: “and immediately a flame of blood.”] began to pour forth through his ears and eyes.

Receive with gracious attention how the reality itself was revealed. Just as the servant of God saw the vial with her eyes in the revelation of a dream, so afterward the priest of God received it in his own hands when the matter itself was made manifest. What she had previously held as a certain doubt within herself, the reality itself now revealed in some people.

What else did it signify when the fire, through the vial, seized his ears and eyes, except that the proclamation of the holy relics, reaching the mouths of the monks, set the one body of the Church ablaze through hearing and sight with the fire of God’s glory, so that all might rightly say, “As we have heard, so we have seen” (Ps. 47:9)?

Nor was it meaningless that the priest who appeared applied the vial, which emitted fire, to the monk’s mouth. He was the one who had recently returned from the East and, placing in the mouths of God’s servants the word concerning the holy relics that he had seen there, brought the vial near, as it were, and kindled them with the holy fire.

But I would already like to proceed to the more evident and manifest miracles of our patron Stephen, were it not that I thought it relevant to present one further vision to Your Holiness. I ask you to deign to hear it patiently and, as I think, not without benefit.

### CHAPTER TWO  
#### Where Saint Stephen appeared to a virgin

Another sacred virgin dreamed that she was traveling to the place of the ancient martyrs [Col. 0835] situated in the suburb of the city, who are called Felix and Gennadius. She was not traveling by the road usually taken as a shortcut from the city, but by one somewhat indirect and winding.

Along this road she saw countless joyful and singing crowds approaching, carrying candles and lights with great ceremony and escorting a small white-clad figure, while repeatedly crying out to him:

“Confessor of Christ! Confessor of Christ!”

When they had brought him to the church and raised him above the pulpit, she saw that the same little figure suddenly extended his hands and, with his mouth close to the people, said:

“Behold, you have a martyr.”

It is marvelous to relate how completely the truth of this vision too was fulfilled. Nor was it without reason that long ago it was foretold by the divine voice through the prophet:

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. And upon my servants and my maidservants I will pour out my Spirit, and I will give signs in heaven above and on earth below” (Joel 2:28–30).

It is also reported that a star appeared at the place of the aforesaid martyrs, seen by those who were then in the field.

If it pleases you, let us begin to show the fruit of the second vision. Approximately forty days after these things had been revealed, we received the relics at the place of our aforementioned martyrs, to which she had seen herself traveling. After the rites of the faithful had been celebrated there, we began to return to the city, singing and praising God amid the choirs of an immense multitude.

The holy relics were carried along the very road that had been shown to the girl, in a vehicle in which the holy bishop was seated, just as that little white-clad figure had appeared to her.

In respect of the portion of his body, that little figure is understood to be the confessor of Christ. Do you doubt that the little figure is a martyr? Is he not little because of his innocence as an infant, and small because of his humility?

Finally, the hymn sung by the mouth of the whole people—“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117:26)—when it was repeated again and again, what else is it understood to have signified except what was said while she listened: “Confessor of Christ! Confessor of Christ”?

Moreover, just as it had been shown to the girl, the people shone with candles and lights. We also entered the same church that she had seen in her vision.

Only one final element of the entire vision remains: the girl had seen the confessor raised onto the pulpit and had heard him extend his hands and say to the people, “Behold, you have a martyr.”

Deign to accept for a time how this too was fulfilled through divine providence. On the very day when the relics of blessed Stephen entered the church, at the very beginning of the canonical readings, a letter from a certain holy bishop named Severus of the island of Minorca was brought to us. It was read from the pulpit into the ears of the Church with immense applause. It contained the mighty works of the glorious Stephen, which he had accomplished on that island through the presence of his relics for the salvation of all the Jews who believed there.

Thus, through the reading of such deeds of his, as though by the extension of his hands, while the faithful cried out and rejoiced, he himself seemed to say, “Behold, you have a martyr.”

Let these things be said so that, in some manner, we may commend to the brethren how the relics of Saint Stephen seem to have reached us, however insignificant and sinful we human beings may be, not casually or recklessly but through divine favor.

### CHAPTER THREE  
#### On the blind woman who touched the cloth with the relics and recovered her sight
Now, therefore, as we promised, let us turn to more familiar miracles. When, on the evening of that same day, the relics had been placed in the apse upon a veiled chair, a certain woman named Hilara, blind, known to the townspeople as a maker of bread, was stirred by faith in the Martyr’s great glory and, wavering in no doubt of unbelief—for “whoever hesitates,” says the apostle James, “will be like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind” [Col. 0836] [James 1:6]. Thus strengthened in faith, confirmed in hope of receiving light, and inflamed by love of divine grace, she asked a religious woman to give her her hand and lead her to the place where the relics were, a place which she herself could not physically approach because the eyes of her flesh impeded her, but to which she had already arrived in spirit through the shining eyes of her heart. When she had been brought there with the help of another’s hand, she grasped with wandering hand the pall laid over the relics and immediately applied it to both her eyes. From that point she departed, not yet illumined in body, but already irradiated by the light of faith. For, praying now with her mouth and now in her heart, she invoked the name of the glorious Martyr and did not keep silence about Christ the Lord either.

After she had been led back to her house, she continued to fight by unremitting prayer, even within the walls of her own home, to dispel the darkness of blindness, as though against the enemy Amalek with Jesus’ help [Note: [Col. 0836] The printed editions have “with Jesus assisting”; “assisting” is absent from the Floriacensis manuscript.] (Exodus 17). A short part of the night had passed when, behold, the woman, having gone out across the threshold of her doorway, gradually began to recover her light, so that she could see the walls opposite her and distinguish the paving stones of the street by sight.

Immediately she called her son and began to address him in these words: “My son, surely these are the walls of the house of the infant bailiff?” [Note: [Col. 0836] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “bailiff” (vilici).—The edition designated GG adds here: “This seems to be a proper name in this passage, unless one prefers to take the preceding word, infantis, in the sense of someone to whom the office of bailiff had been assigned. If the latter interpretation is preferred, infantis would mean ‘of a boy.’ For Baronius observes (as reported by Du Cange in his Glossary of Medieval Latin), under the year 303, no. 36, that among Africans especially all boys were called infantes, on the authority of Victor of Utica, On the Vandal Persecution, book 3, p. 43, where he writes that very young readers were handed over to exile. It should also be considered that these words are spoken by an old woman, who might have called even a more grown boy by that name.” M.]

“Look—there are also the paving stones of the street.”

Her son said to her, “Why are you lying?” He thought that she was saying this as a test, not because she could see.

Again raising her eyes toward heaven, she said, “Look, I can see, and the moon is still half above the theater.”

Her son said to her, “Why did you pretend not to see?”—as though his mother had never previously been blind, but rather had pretended to be blind [Note: [Col. 0836] Here after finxisset, “had pretended,” and in several other places, we supply lacunae with the help of the Floriacensis manuscript.].

Nor is it surprising that the merely natural man did not yet perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), being ignorant that it had long ago been foretold: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isaiah 35:5). But she was giving thanks to Christ’s Friend, not for a simulated former blindness, as her son thought, but because she knew, as the truth showed, that she had received a new light. For not in vain had she sung to God: “You will light my lamp, Lord; my God, you will enlighten my darkness” (Psalm 17:32); and, “You, wondrously enlightening from the everlasting hills” (Psalm 75:5). Thus she had been heard and enlightened from the everlasting hills.

The next morning she went alone to the church, with no one accompanying her, but led by her own light. She did not conceal the praises of God and of God’s Friend; she recounted to the faithful, who rejoiced and marveled, what had wondrously taken place in her. This, then, is the first miracle known among us at the arrival of the holy relics.

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the man who fell and broke his foot and was restored, and on many who were cured of various illnesses

At about the same time, a barber of the city named Concordius had broken his foot in a fall. Lying in bed for a long time, he was tormented by various pains. On one side the thought of his poverty, on the other concern for his little children, wore him down in the sorrow of his great misfortune. Behold, one night, while he was sleeping—but not He who guards Israel sleeping or slumbering (Psalm 120:4), He who made the small and the great and cares equally for all (Wisdom 6:8)—he dreamed that he had been led up a certain steep and narrow ascent of a mountain [Col. 0837], from which he had no possibility of returning and no way of escape.

What else was being shown by this except that he should know and understand that, in the straits of his afflictions, he ought to seek help not from human beings but from God alone? For he said that a woman of venerable appearance had appeared to him and, seeing him so afflicted and filled with the bitterness of pain, had offered him the appearance of a fig, so that through the sweetness it signified he might perceive the pleasantness of spiritual grace. Receiving from this a confidence that his prayers would be answered, he persisted in prayer and asked her for health.

But she, who undoubtedly bore the type of the Church, said, “Now approach Saint Stephen, and he will make you well.”

Faith in the statement was followed by its fulfillment. For when she departed, and he lamented that he was being left behind her, saying, “Are you leaving me and taking yourself away?”—behold, he saw her, just as she had promised him, approaching Saint Stephen, pleading for him and saying these words: “I ask you by your holiness: heal him; have mercy on him [Note: [Col. 0837] The Leuven edition omits “have mercy on him.” M.]; have mercy on his children; free this innocent man from affliction.”

Then he saw the one who was being entreated enter toward him and the room where he lay, clothed in a white garment and handsome in appearance. As soon as he recognized him—as a sick man recognizes a physician, a needy man one who is abundant in resources, a suppliant his patron—he tearfully entreated him in these words: “Dear Friend of Christ, heal me; free me from affliction; have mercy on me; have mercy on my children.”

The petitioner had scarcely finished speaking when the one who heard his prayer was already answering him, saying, “Rise; you have been healed.”

At once, as though he had heard the command of the one speaking while his body slept but his spirit was awake, he sprang from his bed and began to walk with firm steps before his bed. Thus he fulfilled that prophetic word: “Then the lame man shall leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6).

Afterward he rose in the morning and hastened to fulfill his vows to the Martyr at the place where those same relics had been received. Because of the length of the journey, he thought that he still needed to lean on a staff. But after he had prayed there for a long time, he lit candles, abandoned his staff, and from then on returned carrying his little son on his shoulders. He came into the church and proclaimed the glory of God and of God’s Friend by bearing witness to his healing.

After the relics had been placed in the church with immense public celebration, as though a healing station had been established there—whence we sang, “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Psalm 47:10)—it would be long and almost impossible for us either to retain in memory or arrange in speech or commit to writing all the crowds that began to flock there from every direction from that day onward, all the benefits that were bestowed and continue daily to be bestowed, all the miracles displayed, all the blind who were given sight, the paralytics who were healed, the many cured of various diseases and afflictions, and also the dead who were raised. Each miracle, as is known, has a particular history of its own.

Nevertheless, among all these things—which we can neither explain fully nor ought entirely to pass over—we choose the fewer and better-known examples, so that we may neither flood the ears of those who might grow weary nor defraud the diligence of those who are eager to learn.

## CHAPTER V  
### On the woman who invoked Saint Stephen for her husband and was heard

A woman from the place of Memplon [Note: [Col. 0837] So the Floriacensis manuscript. The printed editions read, “A certain woman from the place of Embloniturna,” and so forth. See below, book 2, chapter 4, no. 2.] had a husband who had long been away. She was neither certain of his death nor secure about his life. Nearly three years had passed, during which she had been tormented by conflicting reports about her husband and had been placed in an uncertain and doubtful condition concerning her own life. Her womanly mind, hanging upon uncertainty, fluctuated, and she did not know in which direction, distressed, to throw herself: on one side marriage was urged upon her, poverty was placed before her, anxiety was inflicted upon her, and the frailty of the flesh lay in wait; on the other side chastity, her husband, reputation, and religion were set before her eyes.

At last, amid the turmoil of thoughts that opposed one another within her, certain people—surely not without divine providence—urged and encouraged her to seek the protection of the most powerful advocate, Stephen. She hurried as a suppliant to his Memorial and there prostrated herself with tears. While she was praying, she was deemed worthy to hear: “Your husband has arrived.”

She quickly returned home and found her husband safe. Thus her chastity was preserved, and it became known, through God’s wondrous grace, how great was God’s Friend’s care for a soul in danger.

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the man whom a collapsed house had buried and who was found alive when his wife prayed to Saint Stephen

At about the same time, in our city, a certain house collapsed in a ruin and buried a man named Dativus. His body was subsequently dug out and carried to a nearby house, where it was mourned with the rites of burial. His wife, struck by such grief for her husband, went to the Memorial of glorious Stephen to prostrate herself there with tears for her husband’s life.

While she had been knocking for some time at the ears of God’s Friend, persevering in prayer, behold, suddenly, in the sight of the mourners standing around the funeral and invoking the name of the revered Martyr, her husband began to open his eyes and move his body in the place where he lay. Everyone present saw and marveled. Then, after some time had passed on that same day, he returned to the living and sat up. He said to the owner of the house:

“Blessed are you, brother, because today an angel of God entered your house.”

He began to recount what had been revealed to his soul. He said that he had been surrounded by a multitude of the dead, some of whom he recognized and others he did not. Then a certain young man entered, shining in a white garment and bearing the appearance of a deacon. By the authority of his compassion he commanded the dead, saying, “Withdraw.” Immediately those crowds of the dead disappeared.

Then he approached Dativus and said to him, “Return what you received.”

Since he did not understand, the young man repeated, “Return what you received.” A third time he was similarly commanded to return it, and he replied, “Do you order me to return the Creed?”

When the young man said, “Return it,” he recited the Creed in order and added, “If you command it, I will also return the Lord’s Prayer.” When the young man assented, he recited it.

Then the young man marked the heart of the one lying there with the saving sign and said to him, “Rise now, healed.”

He rose and, as he had been told, was made well.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Where Saint Stephen prevented the bishop from daring to transfer his relics

At the same time, our venerable bishop had arranged to place part of the relics of that same saint in the church at Promontorium. The day on which this was to be done had also been fixed.

Behold, about three days before that day, one of two priests of our Church, the older of the two, named Zumurus [Note: [Col. 0838] The Floriacensis codex reads Zurius.], was warned—as he later reported—that he should go to the bishop in the morning and tell him not to carry out what he had planned to do with part of the relics.

When the priest treated this negligently and did not report it to the bishop, he was rebuked a second time, severely, and was struck in the face with a slap.

The other priest, named Donatus, reported that in the very place of the Memorial he had seen our bishop standing opposite him, carrying in his hands and around his neck the sacred objects, white as snow, in a pall. Immediately he addressed him firmly:

“Put down here what you are carrying.”

When another priest standing on the bishop’s left said to him, “And who else will carry it?” he replied, “What is that to you? Let what the bishop is carrying be put back here in its proper place.”

As it had been revealed, so it was fulfilled three days later. For, when a vehicle was already being prepared on the preceding day so that the bishop might depart with part of the relics, news of this matter suddenly spread throughout the city, and an immense crowd gathered at the church. Tumult and a great outcry began [Col. 0839]; zeal for the faith and love of God’s Friend inflamed everyone.

The bishop was surrounded by pressing crowds; he was begged and detained, and was not released until he had also given an oath that he would remove none of the relics from the city. Only then did that storm of the people, aroused by zeal for the faith, subside, and the relics were gathered together in one place. In the same Memorial where part of the relics had first been placed, the other part was likewise restored.

In a dream, the priest Donatus seemed, as has been said, to compel the bishop who was carrying the sacred objects—that is, carrying a portion of the holy relics—to put back in its proper place what he was carrying away. I believe this happened so that no opportunity for division might be given, especially because this was being done in a Church that had first been usurped through the division of the Donatists and was later restored to Catholic unity, where it remains to this day. Hence it also received its name, so that it deserved to be called the Restored Church.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### On the blind man who touched the little reliquary and received his sight

On the very day on which these things were taking place, that portion of the relics was brought out from the monastery dwelling and carried to the church by the hands of the priest, amid immense public rejoicing and the sweet melodies of singing choirs. Behold, a certain blind man seized the silver reliquary in which the aforesaid portion of the relics was kept and began, with the strongest faith, to do violence to the kingdom of heaven. And because “those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11:12), he immediately received his sight. Thus Christ added no small joy to his whole Church.

## CHAPTER IX  
### On two prisoners freed through glorious Stephen

Likewise, when certain men were being held under strict confinement in public custody, bound in chains, one of them, pierced by the torment and pain of punishment, invoked holy Stephen, dear to Christ, for help.

Behold, amid the tears and cries of the one who lamented, the chains suddenly fell from his hands. After this, when he went of his own accord to the officer in charge of the prison and confessed the occurrence of so great a miracle, the guard did not dare to put the fetters on him again. Instead, becoming—as a result of this—more cautious and vigilant, he bound another prisoner who was likewise chained more tightly and firmly, as though anything could be unbreakable before divine power, ignorant that “the word of God is not bound” (2 Timothy 2:9).

But when that man, compelled by a similar harshness of chains, supplicated the same author of so great a miracle with words and tears like those of his companion, he too was deemed worthy to be heard. His chains were likewise loosened, and he proclaimed and recounted the works of God.

## CHAPTER X  
### On the prisoner who was released and healed through the merits of Saint Stephen

When the wounds caused by the chains of another prisoner swelled in the heat and steam of the public baths and inflicted the gravest pain upon him, faith came to his aid, so that he implored God’s Friend for help.

When he had gone out toward the bathing pool, his chains too suddenly fell off. All who saw it began to magnify Christ and his first confessor, Stephen.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Where a paralytic was deemed worthy of healing

Restitutus, a blacksmith of the Zaritans in the territory of Hippo [Note: [Col. 0839] In the earlier printed editions, Zaritorum is absent; in its place perhaps Piarrythorum would be better. Here it is restored as written in the Floriacensis codex, in which afterward, instead of Restitutus, “Resti” is found.], had been bedridden for a very long time. He could neither walk with his feet nor articulate words with his tongue.

At last, when news of blessed Stephen reached him, he gestured as best he could to urge his parents to carry him to the Memorial of the glorious Martyr [Col. 0840]. This was done. There, during the winter, he lay praying for a long time upon the mosaic pavement in such severe cold—a practice ordinarily contrary to illnesses of this kind. About the twentieth day, he reported that a young man of youthful appearance, handsome in garment and dignified in bearing, had appeared to him at night in a dream. He had been summoned by this man and ordered to go on his own feet to the place of the Memorial. From that time, his gait and his tongue gradually began to return to their proper functions.

When four months had passed, because he had not yet recovered full health, he began to think of returning home. He said that he had then been warned and told that he should not wish to hurry, but ought to wait another four months, after which he would return home on his own feet [Note: [Col. 0840] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “when four months had been completed,” from which point, and so forth.].

This was fulfilled exactly as it had been promised, on the day and at the time announced. For, as both our own conscience bears witness and he himself confessed to the glory of God, he returned home on his own feet and began to pronounce words more distinctly with his own mouth.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Where a man was freed from paralysis of the tongue and feet

A certain man from the city of Utica was afflicted with paralysis of his feet and tongue and was confined to bed. His mother hurried with the firmest faith to the Memorial of Saint Stephen. After entrusting her son’s case to the best advocate, she took away from there some dust for sanctification and, returning home, applied it to her son as he lay there.

Immediately he felt the benefit of healing, rose from his bed, and began not only to walk on his own feet but also to travel twelve thousand paces on foot to the Memorial of the blessed Martyr. In his heart he gave thanks for the health he had received in his feet, while still pouring out prayers that his own tongue might be released.

Accordingly, since he had no prayer-cloth, he removed a sleeve from his tunic and, thrusting his hand through the little window [Note: [Col. 0840] The same manuscript reads “through the window.”] of the Memorial, sent it into the inner places where the holy relics were. Then he drew back his right hand and brought it to his mouth. By touching his tongue, he gradually loosened the knots that prevented speech through the grace of faith.

By doing this repeatedly, as though taking healing food from a heavenly storeroom, he applied it to his diseased member. Thus he refreshed his parched tongue and, aided by God’s grace, recovered the ability to speak. In both respects, therefore, that prophecy was fulfilled, which had once been spoken: “The tongue of the mute shall be clear” (Isaiah 35:6) [Note: [Col. 0840] So the Floriacensis manuscript. The printed editions read “the tongue of the mute shall be full.”].

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Where a blind man from Pisita received the light of his eyes

A certain blind man from the city of Pisita, named Donatianus, came to the healing station of the most powerful physician, Stephen. There, knocking with the devotion of faith, on the eighth day—like the sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the third day after his Passion but, in the reckoning of the days after the Sabbath, on the eighth day—on that day, as I have said, he received the light of his eyes through faith, at the time when the whole world received the light of its minds [Note: [Col. 0840] So the Floriacensis manuscript. The printed editions instead read “when the light of the nations.”] through the Lord’s Resurrection.

Desiring to fulfill his vows to the holy Martyr, he offered a silver candle as an expression of his devotion—and rightly did he offer a candle, since he had received light. He was summoned by the venerable bishop and asked to tell him what had been done for him and why he was offering that gift. With the whole Church standing by, he confessed even with his mouth that, while the spiritual chief physician was healing him, he had been restored illumined in both heart and body.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Where Saint Stephen appeared to a man who had heard that his son had been killed by robbers

[Col. 0841]

A butcher of our city named Rusticanus [Note: [Col. 0841] The Floriacensis manuscript reads Rusticianus.] had sent his son, together with another servant of his, to buy pigs nearly two hundred thousand paces away, supplying them with the required money. Several days had passed, and they had not yet returned, when a certain friend began to reproach and criticize him for having wished to send his son and his servant to such a distant region. He said that he had heard that they had already been killed by robbers.

On hearing this, the man, as though struck by grievous mourning, returned home weeping and lamenting. He spent the whole day feeding upon tears instead of food. Meanwhile, when night found him oppressed by the darkness of sorrow, behold, in a dream he saw a handsome young man appear to him, bearing the face and appearance of a certain honored and leading citizen named Uzalensis [Note: [Col. 0841] So the Floriacensis manuscript. The printed editions read Honorius.]. The young man said to him with a cheerful face:

“Why are you crying?”

He replied, to use his own simple words [Note: [Col. 0841] The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “He replied in supplicating words.”]:

“My lord, I am crying because I have heard that my servant and my son have been killed.”

The young man consoled him and said, “They have not been killed.”

“Who, then, are you?” he asked.

The other replied, “My lord Uzalensis.”

“Good,” said the man himself [Note: [Col. 0841] The Leuven edition reads “the other said.”], “you have said that you are Uzalensis; but you are not the one you think. For I am Stephen.”

“Since you are sad about your son and your servant, know that they are already on their way back here. You gave them twenty-five solidi; in addition, they borrowed nearly twenty thousand folles, and they are bringing with them forty-four pigs, all choice. They will arrive on the day of the Roman city, at the first hour.”

Everything that had been revealed in the dream was afterward fulfilled in reality. The men returned unharmed, the stated number of pigs was brought back, the same amount of borrowed money was found, and the day and hour of their arrival followed exactly as foretold, without the slightest error.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the little boy who died a catechumen and was restored alive to his mother through the merits of Saint Stephen

[Col. 0842]

1. A certain woman’s little son had died as a catechumen. She carried him in her arms amid immense wailing and pitiable cries and laid him before the very Memorial of glorious Stephen. She handed over the dead child so that she might receive him back alive.

As she knocked at the ears of God’s Friend with the faith of devotion, struck by the double grief of bereavement—because she had lost her son in the present life and could not have him safe in the future, since he lacked the grace of Baptism—behold, amid the pain and cries of the wretched mother, who had long been lamenting and shrieking, the child suddenly received back his spirit, life was granted him, and a voice was given to the living child.

Immediately a priest was summoned, Baptism was administered to the child, and the sacraments were completed. Thus, after his soul had been freed from the deadly chain of sins, he was at once stripped of the bond of mortal flesh and released with the greatest speed into the spiritual embraces of God.

In this way consolation no small was granted to the mother, who was allowed to rejoice in the restoration of her son [Note: [Col. 0842] So the Floriacensis manuscript. The printed editions read, “she was allowed to rejoice in her redeemed son.”], and true salvation was granted to the child. He certainly received life for a short time so that he would not die eternally; he was permitted to die in time so that he might enjoy everlasting life [Note: [Col. 0842] Augustine reports this miracle in Sermon 323, no. 3, and in Sermon 324.].

2. From the many and almost countless miracles, we have meanwhile selected these few, lest we perhaps become a burden to our present hearers, who have come from afar for the Martyr’s festival. Otherwise, if we wished to remember and recount everything, as was said above, we would produce an excessively long book.

For we believe that the most widely known and most glorious miracles themselves are sufficient for their own proclamation. They do not need the ability of a human tongue, since they prevail through the manifest truth of divine power.

Nevertheless, we have wished to offer some portion of our devotion for the edification of the brethren in the name of Christ, so that we may receive through your prayers the reward of filial obedience and, with the favor of divine mercy, obtain the blessing of glorious Stephen, the first witness of Christ:

through Christ our Lord, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK TWO [Note: [Col. 0841] Absent from the Floriacensis manuscript.]

[Col. 0841]

## CHAPTER I  
### Address concerning the addition of a second book to the preceding one

Your Holiness, most holy fathers and brethren, remembers well with me that, when the miracles of the Lord Stephen, Christ’s first martyr, had been faithfully recorded and confirmed by public testimony and, before this time, were publicly read to you who were present at the gathering of our Uzalensian Church [Note: [Col. 0841] Compare above, On the City of God, book 22, chapter 8, no. 21.] [Note: [Col. 0841] “When” is superfluous.]—this too was presented to your Love as a gift of complete rejoicing, with the Friend of God himself, as we believe, arranging it: that after the reading of the divine works and deeds, a clear demonstration and personal testimony might also be given of the very people in whom those miracles had occurred, insofar as any of them could still be found in the present. In this way they would not merely bear witness to the truth through our writings, but would also impress the certainty of truth upon your eyes and your sight.

Thus it happened that, while the very works of God were first announced to your ears through reading, they were also presented to your eyes with the evidence of eyewitness faith [Note: [Col. 0841] The Ulimmerius codex reads “with kissed faith.”], so that in you what is written in the Psalm might be fulfilled: “As we have heard, so also have we seen” (Psalm 47:9).

There was indeed a great spectacle of heavenly glory in so extraordinary an event. Whenever the reader had announced any story—for example, first the story of a certain blind woman who had afterward been given sight [Note: [Col. 0842] Above, book 1, chapter 3]—as soon as the reading had ended, this same person would be sought out among the people, found, and brought forward into the midst of the entire Church. While everyone marveled and rejoiced with her, she could be seen walking alone, without any companion or guide, as she had previously been accustomed to do. She herself would then climb the steps of the apse and stand there, visible to all from a distance, proclaiming in herself the testimony of divine grace through the illumination of her own eyes, as though by a silent preaching of faithful witnesses.

Likewise, when the reading had proceeded to the story of a paralytic who had been healed and was previously known to many [Note: [Col. 0842] Above, book 1, chapter 2], the same man who had been cured of such an illness was immediately brought forward from the crowd. He was seen walking on his own feet, to the great joy of the whole Church, confirming the proclamations of divine praise through tangible evidence: the sound and healed limbs of his body.

While these things were taking place, and while at the same time the events themselves wondrously corresponded in harmonious unity to each of the written accounts [Col. 0843], one would surely have thought that the past was not being narrated so much as the present being displayed. For what was spoken in the reading was immediately seen in the present deed itself, so that by another and greater miracle the miracles themselves were made more wondrous.

Who was so hard and iron-hearted that he did not burst into tears? Who did not melt into devotion and humility? Who could ever speak of this with praise worthy of it?

A cry of rejoicing arose as the reading was heard; then an even greater exultation was aroused by the sight of the vision. Thus, through hearing and sight, the flame of divine love penetrated every human heart at that time.

I could not pass over these things in silence, both to renew the memory of those who had been present at that time and not to deprive those who were unaware of them of knowledge. Moreover, since many religious people immediately received and wrote down the very things that had been read, each with its conclusion [Note: [Col. 0843] Perhaps one should read “conceived.” M.], for this reason, with the Lord’s help, we have taken from this point the beginning, as it were, of a second little book, in order to narrate what followed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, I shall recount for you the wondrous deeds of our common patron Stephen—deeds that had taken place and a memorable history well known to many—for the praise and glory of God.

## CHAPTER II  
### On Megetia, who had been struck by paralysis, had wasted away in the hands of physicians, and, running to Saint Stephen, was cured of a double illness

1. There was in the city of Carthage a woman noble by birth and nobler in the faith of Christ, named Megetia, wealthy in worldly possessions and richer in God. Her mother was a Christian named Vitula, but her husband, father-in-law, and father were pagans.

When she was four months pregnant, because of something—I do not know what—that first caused her nausea and retching, and as she repeatedly suffered violent contractions of the stomach, distension of the mouth, and an urge to vomit, she was brought into the perverse and destructive condition of paralysis. Her mouth fell open so completely that, with the very joints of her teeth and arteries displaced from their proper positions, she could not close it at all. Nor could she make the normal and undisturbed movements of her palate and tongue either to emit anything from her mouth or to receive anything into it.

There remained in this pious and modest woman a deformed and repulsive appearance, and the mark of the defect was fixed upon the part of her body where it could by no means be concealed. It was her face, of which someone had said, “The forehead displays the human being, and it cannot be covered without disgrace.”

When the functions of other limbs are impeded by some defect, a certain ingenuity can withdraw them from shame. But when the face itself has been disfigured by some ugliness, whatever covering is applied out of modesty only increases that very shame. What, then, could the noble matron do, concealing her disfigured mouth with a veil, when the ordinary fellowship and courtesy of life compelled her, whenever other noble women came to visit her, either to give them a kiss or to converse with them? I say nothing of food and drink, which she could scarcely chew or swallow with difficulty.

For a long time the skill and ingenuity of the physicians who labored much around her were useless. They could not merely provide her with no healing; the condition continued to grow worse. And no wonder: in her, the God who is the creator and redeemer of all nature had not yet restored what is formed only by his power, by whose judgment the whole human body is both constrained by discipline and relaxed through healing.

Overcome, therefore, by such grief and pain, and helped by no relief from any remedies or medicines, the delicate body and spirit of the girl had by now wasted away for nearly six months. For this reason, she was also retaining within the enclosure of her womb the dead thing she carried, already deprived of vital spirit.

Thus, while her very life had previously recoiled under the single defect of paralysis, another, more serious and dangerous condition was added, leaving her not even the possibility of continuing to live. For if the girl had so failed under the strain of a defective mouth, how could she live with the collapse of dead matter within her womb?

The seventh month had begun. Her diseased face was not freed from its deformity, nor was her womb freed from its dead burden.

Her father Pontius, her father-in-law Avitianus, and her husband Adventius, still bound by the errors of paganism, fruitlessly and vainly exhausted themselves in attempting whatever they could for the life of the dying Megetia—not only through the skill of physicians but also through the arts of demons and the inventions of superstitious vanities.

But, wretched error, what did you think you could contribute to human salvation, when you have always tried to take it away? The voice of truth refutes you in the most sacred Psalms, testifying generally and briefly from whom all salvation of soul and body truly comes, saying: “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 3:9).

For to God alone this is rightly sung: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord” (Psalm 35:7). The one who deigned to create has plainly also deigned to heal.

2. Therefore, while those persons mentioned above were for a long time laboring uselessly in such matters, sleeping—not in body, but in heart—behold, that divine Teacher who neither sleeps nor slumbers, who guards Israel (Ps. 120:4), that God, I say, whose concern is for everyone (Wis. 6:8), kindled religious Vitula, Megetia’s mother, with faithful warmth and inspired her to hasten to the assistance of his friend, the Lord Stephen.

When the blessed woman had set out from the city of Carthage for Uzal, to the place of the sacred relics, the most merciful and compassionate Lord received her, heard her, helped her, made her mistress of her daughter’s recovery, and allowed her to triumph as victor over the defeated adversary, the devil. It cannot be said with what lamenting words that devout woman assailed the Friend of God, or with what compassion, prostrate before the threshold of the glorious Martyr, she expressed the outpourings of her heart’s grief, bursting forth in these words:

“Lord Stephen, friend of Christ, help a wretched mother who flees to you for the safety of her daughter, whose life is in danger. Here I beg you with my lamentations; there, I implore you, let your servant feel you present as her physician. You yourself know the causes from which Megetia suffers and the peril in which her life stands. For behold, how long she has lain here, wretched throughout her body, undone by paralysis and wasted in her viscera. Moreover, it is imminent that, when the seventh month is complete, she will enter the eighth. Everyone despairs of Megetia’s recovery; but I, who have fled to Christ and to you, his Friend, believe that such grief over my daughter will not be laid upon my head. I ask and beg that, when I return from here, from your shrine, and hasten to set out for your servant, my soul may be revived by some good news about my daughter.”

After she had seemed to herself, through many such words and others like them, to have furnished the holy Stephen with a suitable advocate before Christ the Judge, the mother, heavy with childbearing grief, hastened back to visit her daughter, her one and only, greatest concern. Yet she also carried with her from the Memorial of the blessed Martyr sanctified oil and a cloth or handkerchief, a testimony of her prayers [Note: [Col. 0844] Ulimm. reads *grationum*.] and of the sweat of her labors for the recovery of her suffering daughter.

Behold, then, on the road, when she had withdrawn to avoid the heat—for it was summer, when the fiery sun scorched the earth—a messenger suddenly arrived and handed her a letter sent from Carthage by her husband, just as she had requested in her prayers. In it the daughter’s liberation, soon to come, was announced. For it was said that, on the following day, the daughter would enter her eighth month, yet was somewhat stronger, that the signs of her delivery were already beginning, and that the mother should be of good courage concerning her daughter. All this was announced to the devout mother Vitula not by human speech but by a divine oracle.

Thus relieved by these first indications of the fulfillment of her prayers, the mother flew swiftly onward. When she reached Carthage and found her daughter lying at the very crisis of her life, she immediately anointed the girl’s limbs with the sacred oil and gave her the handkerchief to clasp against her breast. Once this had been done, the revived Megetia, relieved of the burden of her womb by childbirth, entered the eighth month’s terrifying threshold for pregnant women [Note: [Col. 0845] Perhaps *limina* (“thresholds”) rather than *lumina* (“lights”).], and from the very realm of death was restored once more to the vital air. Thus, when one deadly cause had been dispelled, another remained at once to be treated by the heavenly chief physician.

To accomplish this immediately, faithful mother Vitula wished to bring her liberated daughter back with her to the spring of the life-giving fountain from which she had brought and healthfully administered the heavenly drink to her sick child. But Megetia’s strength had not yet returned; after the labor of her dangerous delivery, it utterly prevented her from undertaking the additional exertion of the journey.

3. Meanwhile, the girl’s husband, father-in-law, and father—still unmoved to praise God and his true Martyr, the first, for the deliverance of the womb from such misery—again began, in order to treat the remaining illness, namely the deformity of her defective mouth, to consult those human remedies and errors and to waste long stretches of time uselessly. For a whole year and nearly several additional months had now passed in this way.

At last faithful mother Vitula summoned to her a certain chief physician of the city of Carthage, named Felix, exceptionally trustworthy and a friend of her household, and bound him by an adjuration concerning the health of her only child, saying:

“By the life of your only daughter, can Megetia be cured of this paralysis, or not?”

He replied: “I tell you faithfully that your daughter cannot be cured at all of this condition, since you have compelled me to answer you so. The very jointing, as of a cart, where certain restraints of the mouth and jaws are held, has been displaced from its proper places.”

Mother Vitula, grounded in the steadfastness of her faith, immediately replied:

“I do not believe in my Christ that my daughter will be left in this great affliction of paralysis.”

But he, greatly admiring the woman’s firmness of faith, said: “It is possible for the almighty God in whom you believe to do this; for your hope must come from nowhere among us.”

When devout Vitula heard this, she dismissed the chief physician, took her Megetia with her, and went to her husband and to her daughter’s husband. Inflamed with pious grief, she began to speak:

“Until now we have pitifully yielded to you; nor have we women been able to resist men. For a long time we have endured your wishes, from which no fruit of recovery for our daughter, no result whatever, has come. Behold, for a year and the additional months that have elapsed, my daughter’s body has merely been wearied among the hands of physicians, and, as you see, she has not been cured at all by accomplishing anything. I beg you: allow us, at last, to do what is expedient for us also. Let us too go to our physician. I believe in him, because he who did not allow Megetia to die with her dead offspring will himself also cause her to walk among human beings with a healthy countenance.””

After she had lamented these and similar complaints, just and true, those men could in no way resist such a woman clothed in manly courage. They preferred to yield voluntarily rather than depart defeated by any other judge.

4. Thus they bent to Mother Vitula’s resolve: Megetia’s husband and father—the husband still a pagan, but the father, a man of senatorial rank named Pontius, already made a Christian catechumen. It is fitting that, since we have begun to proclaim his faith in Christ, we should now also begin to mention his name with due honor. Since the occasion seems to require it, we shall not hesitate to explain how he was initiated under the Christian name.

When devout Vitula had gone to the Friend of God, while Megetia had not yet been delivered from the danger of childbirth, she had also prayed concerning the faith of this venerable husband of hers [Col. 0846], that he might be imbued with Christian faith and name. This was indeed revealed to her that very night in the following vision.

She seemed to see, near the Memorial of the blessed Martyr, two luminous candlestands, both blazing with fire. Her husband Pontius was also present and appeared beside her. She seemed to hear these words addressed to her: “Vitula, our candlestick shines more brightly; therefore I want you to know that I have now placed the *jugulos* [‘necks’].”

After seeing and hearing this, devout Vitula awoke from sleep. When morning came [Note: [Col. 0846] Perhaps *facto* (“when it had come”) rather than *facta*.] and she had completed her prayer, she began to recount to certain maidservants of God what she had seen in her sleep. She herself first interpreted her dream and replied, addressing the virgins standing around her:

“Let your Holiness know that Pontius will soon believe in Christ, as I trust in my Christ. For this is what he signified to me in the dream when he said: ‘I want you to know, Vitula, that I have now placed the *jugulos* [“necks”]’—surely under no yoke except that of Christ.””

Thus, as I have said, the honorable Pontius became first a Christian catechumen in the following year, on the same days when the blessed Stephen had been entreated by devout Vitula for the eternal salvation of her husband.

5. But, as I had begun to say, when their husbands had consented, mother Vitula and her Megetia set out together from Carthage, reached the Memorial of the blessed Martyr together, and then prostrated themselves before his sacred threshold. Weeping and wailing day and night, filthy with ashes and sackcloth, these noble women, not ashamed before human beings in order to be pleasing to God, embraced what they had heard said in the Psalms:

“My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. 41:4).

For even in regard to our Christian religion itself, pious and noble women did not lack reproaches from unbelievers. Thus, before the Lord, in plaintive voices and bitter words, as it is written, they remembered and poured out their souls over themselves. The enemies of our faith were saying: “Where is your God?”

Therefore mother Vitula cried into the ears of the Friend of God:

“Lord Stephen, behold, I have brought your Megetia to you, whom you yourself liberated from death. You have not made us come into the joy of the enemy, nor handed us over to those who trouble us—those who revile and despair of Christ our Lord and of you, his great Friend. I beg you, do it: make them again ashamed by the complete and perfect recovery of your Megetia, just as you have already made them ashamed by the most dangerous travail of her womb. You who have granted greater things will not wholly fail in lesser ones. Fulfill, for your own sake, what I promised her pagan husband about you. Let the mother who has placed her hope in you and fled to you not be put to shame because of her daughter. Surely, in order that the eye of the heart of those who do not yet believe and who insult us may be healed, let the girl’s mouth be cured; and in order that the health of their souls may be gained, let health be granted to the girl’s limbs.”

6. After such tearful words, spoken in this sense, had been lamented, the seventh day had passed when, behold, in the dead of night Megetia was visited in sleep. She saw before her a distinguished-looking man wearing the dress of a deacon. She began to ask him, as though he were a spiritual physician, to inspect her mouth and, if he deigned, to cure it.

But as soon as he had inspected her mouth, he looked upon her with a cheerful and serene expression and said [Note: [Col. 0846] Perhaps *intuitus* (“having looked”) rather than *ait* (“he said”).]:

“Indeed, your mouth is still not straight; but look upward and see what is flying above your head.”

Immediately, raising her eyes above herself, she saw a most hideous serpent flying over her by the beating of its wings and wandering here and there in twisting coils.

But when Megetia was terrified by the horrible and monstrous sight, the distinguished man strengthened her with his exhortation, saying to her:

“Unless you first kill that serpent, you cannot be healed. But do not be afraid: engage it with courage, and you will certainly overcome it.”
