When she heard this, Megetia, strengthened by the power of faith and armed with the protection of so great a helper, seized at the proper moment what seemed to be a rod offered to her and fought against that most hideous and most twisted dragon. Although she was long engaged and exhausted by the adversary’s prolonged resistance, at last, when she struck it on the head, she immediately overthrew it.

Awakening in trembling joy, she sprang up from her bed and awoke. As she considered what the meaning of her dream might portend, but could not clearly understand it, she thereafter prayed and asked that she be visited and confirmed [Note: [Col. 0847] According to Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, pp. 359–360, one should read: “thereafter she prayed that she might be visited and confirmed.”]. Then she gave herself over to rest.

Behold, once again she saw that handsome young man, splendid in his appearance, shining in a snow-white garment. As she lay there, she saw him extend what seemed to be a hand toward her and heard him command and say at the same time:

“Rise; thus you are healed.”

But Megetia, as she had been accustomed to do previously with a human physician, inclined her head toward him and offered him her mouth as though it were to be treated. But he, correcting the action of one who did not understand, replied:

“Why are you doing this? Your eyes must first be cured.”

She answered:

“My lord, I have healthy eyes, but I beg you to cure my mouth.”

And he said:

“I have already told you: your eyes must first be cured.”

Then, as a heavenly chief physician inspecting the secrets of her heart in spirit, he applied what was like a medicinal eye-salve to her skin, spread it over her eyes, and departed [Note: [Col. 0847] The passage is corrupt.].

When morning came, devout Megetia was recounting this dream to her dearest and holiest women. In the very course of narrating it, she was suddenly pierced in heart and reminded of a certain sin. She did not delay confessing her sin, but, as it is written, she acknowledged her transgression and did not conceal her iniquity (Ps. 31:5).

Behold, then, which eyes had first to be cured—not those of the body, but those of the heart. The glorious Stephen, as a spiritual physician, had declared this to her when he said: “Your eyes must first be cured.” For what was hidden as diseased in her mind had to be healed, so that what was seen to be deformed in her body might finally be healed.

Hence that most hideous serpent which flew above her head—because it occupied the ruling mind of the rational soul—had to be crushed and conquered. For when the guilt of each sin is humbly acknowledged, the serpent’s head is shattered through repentance, and the eye of the heart is cleansed through confession.

On the twelfth day after she had come with her mother to the Friend of God, while she was praying at the place of the sacred Memorial and knocking with the piety of faith—not only through the feeling of her heart but also through the movement of her body—she herself pushed open the little doors of the Memorial, forced her way into the kingdom of God, thrust her head inside, and fixed it above the bed of the holy relics. With her tears she washed and watered everything there.

But behold, he who is merciful from above, who draws near to the contrite in heart (Ps. 146), caused Megetia, the servant of God, to feel that her mouth was being corrected and caressed by a visible and tangible hand.

After she had risen from prayer, surrounded by choirs of holy virgins who were singing praises to God there for her and with her, she tremblingly and joyfully announced this to them. What and how great the joy then was in every heart, and what an impulse to weep before God it aroused, can scarcely be expressed.

7. But before we come to the most desired conclusion of the event, where we shall demonstrate the full and perfect recovery of devout Megetia, through the care and help of the Friend of God in the name of Christ, we must not pass over something else that wonderfully occurred in the midst of these events.

When mother and daughter had remained for nearly forty days in prayer around the place of the holy Martyr, letters suddenly arrived, sent to them from Carthage, reporting that the girl’s father, the honorable Pontius, was said to be physically ill. They set out from the city of Uzal to visit him.

When, however, midway through the journey, they wished to use baths to refresh their bodies because of the heat, a certain household woman, known to Megetia through an unbeliever and sent to meet her [Note: [Col. 0847] Perhaps: “sent to meet Megetia by design.”], appeared there—not so much to greet her as to investigate her.

Since she eagerly wished to see the blessed Megetia’s bare mouth and face, she entered with her into the lodging [Note: [Col. 0848] Perhaps one should read *in hospitium* (“into the lodging”) rather than *in obsequium*.]. When she had gazed as long as she wished at the face of the servant of God, she saw that Megetia’s mouth was entirely intact and healthy.

The household woman was astonished and amazed, having found something other than what she had hoped for. She immediately turned to a certain holy virgin standing nearby and addressed her by name:

“Little Helpidiana, Lady Megetia is completely well!”

For God’s grace was so vigorous in Megetia that, although the fuller care of her remained in some respect deferred in the body, the perfect appearance of health was nevertheless set before the eyes of the unbelievers to confound them.

Understanding the great mystery of God, that servant of God replied to the woman:

“Unbelievers, believe now at least!”

8. Again, at Carthage, one day when the blessed Megetia was conversing with her pagan husband, she appeared before him in conversation with her mouth and face intact. Moved by this sight, her husband began to rejoice and say:

“Lady Megetia, I see that you are completely well.”

But she concealed for the moment, by pretending not to notice, what divine power had displayed in her and continued the course of their conversation. He likewise could not remain silent about what he saw, and, as before, kept saying to her:

“You are entirely well, thanks be to God.”

Then, filled with joy, she finally smiled and said to her husband:

“Will you now at least believe in Christ?”

And he replied:

“What do you want me to do for my father? For I too wish to become a Christian.”

9. But, to come now to the conclusion we promised, the most holy day of Easter was approaching. Behold, the blessed Megetia was asked by a certain friend and noblewoman named Rustica to go with her to Mappalia to fulfill her vow to the blessed martyr Cyprian and to take part in the solemnity.

Megetia excused herself, saying that she could not do this, since she knew what God’s power was displaying in her to the eyes of unbelievers and what the grace of heavenly salvation was reserving for its full completion [Note: [Col. 0848] Perhaps “for complete salvation.”]. Yet, unwilling to grieve her friend, she did not refuse outright; rather, she clearly promised that she would do on that day whatever God wished.

When her friend had departed, Megetia did not cease to persist in prayer day and night. Every day she first took a small morsel dipped in sanctified oil; then she ate the other foods.

One night she was visited in a dream. She thought she was standing beside the Memorial of the blessed Stephen, and there she saw that handsome young man, bathed in white light and mounted upon a splendid horse. Many lamps were shining, and a most magnificent procession preceded him. He said to her in a clear voice:

“This light belongs to you, Megetia; receive it.”

After this vision she awoke filled with joy. As soon as she felt herself well, she placed her hands upon her mouth and face to examine them. Almost unable, in her overwhelming joy, to believe herself, she called out loudly and awakened her maidservants, who were resting around her bed, summoning them to come quickly and inspect and contemplate her.

When they saw that God’s gift had been fulfilled in their mistress and that everyone’s vow had been completed, they all cried out together in joy and broke into praise of God.

The day appointed by her friend also arrived. Various people came to devout Megetia so that, as she had promised, she might graciously go to the designated place without abandoning her dear companions.

But Megetia, the servant of God, still with her mouth covered by a veil as she habitually kept it, came out from her inner chamber to her friends. After allowing them for some time to remain sad on her account, she suddenly removed the veil from her face, displayed her countenance, and said:

“Behold, see what God has deigned to accomplish in me; rejoice with me and give thanks to the Lord himself on my behalf.”

When they had all seen her, they began, rejoicing and blessing the Lord, to kiss her and embrace her. Then they all went together with her to the church and fulfilled their vows to the Lord.

After the holy Easter of the Lord had been celebrated, devout Vitula also came to the city of Uzal [Col. 0849] together with her Megetia and other devout women. In the sight of all our Church, which rejoiced and shared in their joy, she cheerfully rendered, fervently presented, and fruitfully fulfilled her vows to Christ the Lord and to Christ’s Friend concerning her daughter’s complete and perfect recovery.

## CHAPTER III

A certain Donatus, who had a wine storehouse, found nearly two hundred vessels of spoiled wine. At his command, his servant brought a bottle filled from all the vessels; Donatus ran to Saint Stephen, placed it there, and prayed. On returning with the bottle, he poured some of it into all the vessels, and the wine was restored.

A certain Donatus is said to have been the father of a most respectable son named Rusticus, a cashier of the prefects, well known to everyone. On his suburban estate, in a place known by the name of [text uncertain], he was accustomed each year to store and preserve wines of good quality.

Meanwhile, as is the custom of landowners, who at times prefer to announce for sale whatever fruits have been stored in the earth when prices rise through the greedier competition of buyers seeking the profits they desire, the aforesaid owner of the estate decided to enter his wine storehouse for the first time with one of his men, a highly skilled wine-taster, and to inspect each vessel and approve the wines.

As soon as the taster applied the wine drawn from a vessel to the judgment of his lips, the man’s face immediately grew pale in astonishment. For, besides the fact that the wine’s utterly horrible color presented to the eyes a sight that invited aversion, its most miserable flavor inflicted on the lips a taste of grief.

When it was thought that this evil existed in only one vessel, the loss was not considered so troubling a damage to the head of the household [Note: [Col. 0849] Perhaps *damno* (“loss”); in B, the margin reads “the passage is corrupt,” M.]. But when they began to go around to each vessel and it was found, after examining them all—nearly two hundred in number—that they had similarly deteriorated and perished, who could fail to understand what the owner’s state of mind was there, or what mourning afflicted the keeper of the storehouse?

For it was not, in truth, a small or contemptible loss or damage that had occurred. Nearly two hundred vessels, as I have said, which were thought to be completely full of very sweet wine, were instead found filled not even with vinegar, but with the filth of some utterly corrupted and sediment-laden liquid.

What could the owner of such a ruined property do, having suffered the destruction of his vintage not still on the vines but, what is more grievous, in the very storehouse? What, I say, could he do? What could he do with wine so spoiled that it could no longer even be named?

Perhaps he might sell it for some worthless price. But what buyer so foolish would approach such a foolish transaction? Or at least might he pour it out and throw it away? But who would be so forgetful of his labors as readily to expose the produce of an entire year, whatever its quality, to be trampled by human beings and beasts?

At last, the soul wavering amid such griefs, breathed upon by a breeze of divine inspiration, was led by grace under full sail into the surest harbor and safest anchorage. For, as the owner revolved many thoughts within himself, this better decision settled in his mind: he must flee to the holy Friend of God, Stephen, Christ’s first martyr.

Accordingly, he ordered the taster of his wine to fill one small flask from each of his vessels, carry it at dawn to the Blessed Memorial to be blessed, and immediately bring it back sanctified. Then he was to pour a little from it over all the vessels and depart.

O Lord, Lord, whose concern is for humanity, who kindly do everything for the sake of humanity, who once healed bitter and barren waters through your saints by throwing in wood and casting a vessel of salt into them (Exod. 15:25; 2 Kings 2:21), and who yourself, Lord, changed water into wine (John 2:1–11)—now also, through your holy friend Stephen, you restored the ruined wines to their former state, changing bitterness into sweetness, blackness into whiteness, and sorrow into rejoicing!

The faithful servant therefore promptly carried out his master’s orders: [Col. 0850] he drew the flask as he had been commanded, went, placed it there, brought it back, poured a very small amount into each vessel, and departed.

The next day, remembering his faith and his instructions, the head of the household rose early, met the servant responsible for the task, and took him along as his companion to the storehouse. All the vessels were inspected again in order; wine was drawn, brilliance was seen in its color, its taste was approved on the palate, sorrow was changed into joy, and it was discovered how great and how powerful faith in Christ and in his most glorious Friend is. Everyone who heard and marveled acknowledged it.

Finally, those excellent wines were distributed to buyers at a price worthy of them. Behold how divine providence serves human needs! And what, in the end, is offered or repaid to God for such great benefits of his?

## CHAPTER IV

Where a magnificent dragon appeared from heaven. At its sight the entire populace fled to Stephen’s threshold; while they were praying, it gradually disappeared among the folds of the clouds and was no longer seen.

1. One day a market was being held in our city, and although it was already midday, the serene face of the sky suddenly changed into a dark and gloomy turbulence of the air.

Behold, a fiery dragon of immense size was seen above, hanging down from the clouds over the city. This should not seem so unusual or unprecedented, not only because of common knowledge but also because of the authority of Holy Scripture, which speaks of dragons in this way:

“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm-wind, which perform his word” (Ps. 148:7–8).

For “abyss” means not only the immeasurable depth of waters below, but also, above, the vastness of this dark air that we look upon, which seems to grow dense from the moisture of sea and land. Through its movement, shifting breezes are stirred, clouds are driven about like fleeces of wool, and fiery lightning is sent forth.

So that these things would not be believed to happen by chance and accident, as foolishly wise people suppose, Holy Scripture made careful provision. After saying, “Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-wind,” it immediately added, concerning the Creator and Ruler of the universe himself, “which perform his word.”

Accordingly, while the dragon hung from this providential ordering of God, as I have said, and blazed amid the clouds as though proceeding and flashing forth from the upper abyss, the movement of the air carried and drove it here and there for some time. It appeared to those present, trembling and astonished, that it was about to fall upon the middle of the city.

The crowd began to flee from the public gathering, scattering wherever fear drove them, each as best he could. The entire marketplace was finally thrown into confusion and dissolved. Abandoning every earthly business, people feared only for their lives. For who would then seek monetary profit while lamenting the peril of his soul? Or who would think about bodily sustenance while fearing the final destruction of his life? Who, moreover, would desire clothing while losing his mind from fear of death?

A great multitude also rushed to the embrace of Mother Church and immediately flew to the mercy of God the Father. People of every age and of both sexes lay prostrate before the sacred Memorial of the Friend of God.

At last, when amid the tears of all a fitting prayer had been poured forth to Christ, Stephen’s Lord, and the mercy of God assented, that horrifying dragon gradually began to withdraw from human sight and hide itself among the barriers of the clouds, then to be dispersed and driven away in the direction the winds were blowing, as the serene face of the sky returned.

Thus, when their spirits had been restored and they had been led from such great sorrow into joy, abundant thanks were rendered to God and to his Friend, with immense tears shed in an outpouring of unexpected rejoicing.

2. To this another thing, even more marvelous than the miracle itself, must be added, lest human frailty, ignorant in all things and not sufficiently instructed by this clearer and more evident lesson concerning divine judgments and benefits, should fail to show the gratitude that was fitting.

Behold, on the following day, through the administration of divine providence, a certain merchant who had never been known in our region came of his own accord to our subdeacon, named Sennodus, at a place called Memblotutan [Note: [Col. 0851] Perhaps *Memblonitanus*, as above, Book 1, chapter 5.]. He called him over and asked him who he was and where he came from.

When the subdeacon had identified himself as belonging to the Church of Uzal, that unknown man immediately replied—if indeed he was merely a man; for it must be believed that he was both angel and man. For it is neither unheard-of nor unexperienced, whether in the Christian religion or in human knowledge, that holy angels have often appeared to human beings in earthly dress and visible form.

He therefore gave the aforesaid subdeacon a veil painted in various colors. On it there was the following picture: on the right side of the veil, Saint Stephen himself appeared standing, carrying upon his own shoulders a glorious cross. With the point of the cross he seemed to be striking the city gate; from it the most hideous dragon was seen fleeing and emerging, as the Friend of God approached. Yet the harmful serpent was not even safe in its flight: it was shown crushed and pressed beneath the triumphant foot of Christ’s Martyr.

When the subdeacon had brought and hung this painted veil before the Memorial of so great a patron, every age and sex began to look upon it and marvel, as at a great spectacle—namely, by whose agency and through whose deliverance the dragon had been destroyed and the enemy conquered.

The testimony of the following day commended in everyone’s heart the truth of what had happened on the preceding day. For what they were observing more intently on the veil was now held more credibly in reality. The picture corresponded with grace, and the benefit of salvation divinely accomplished the day before was recalled as clearly as it was afterward recognized in the image on the veil.

Finally, from the correspondence between the preceding and following days, from the truth of events and the image of certain representations, such astonishment, love, admiration, and rejoicing were kindled in many that everyone said and affirmed nothing else but this:

“Truly, God has delivered this city through his Friend and driven away from us a great plague.”

And in truth there was a kind of address from God to humanity in the veil, silently signifying and in a certain manner saying:

“O wretched mortals, understand from the depiction on this veil what conflagration of the dragon you escaped yesterday and what advocacy and assistance was accepted on your behalf; and rejoice. Compare within yourselves the temptation that preceded and the deliverance that followed. Then, no longer doubtful but certain, give thanks to your God through my Friend.

“Behold, you see the dragon driven and expelled from your city; behold, you see my first Martyr crushing its head; behold, the trophy of the Cross by which you conquered the enemy.”

Thus, when our city had first been delivered from so great a danger and afterward instructed and enlightened by such a fitting depiction on the veil, every devout soul was gladdened in the glory of God by this double miracle.

## CHAPTER V

On the liberation of the treasurer of the public funds of Carthage.

1. In the miracles of our common patron, the lord Stephen, mentioned above, we remember that we arranged the wonders of healings, visions in dreams, and their effects according to the modesty of our ability. Now, however, with the Lord’s help, we desire to relate the bodily appearances and manifestations, in human guise, of the Friend of God himself—openly displayed, though with his identity concealed—to people who were awake and watching, in the forum, in the courts, in broad daylight, and in assemblies of the people and of dignitaries of the various orders.

The treasurer of the public funds of the city of Carthage, a man named Florentius, had incurred the displeasure of the judicial authorities to the point of risking his life. This is something that commonly happens to officials in such fiscal functions: they often provoke the movements of the authorities under whom they live and whose jurisdiction they serve. Accordingly, on the order of the proconsul—I do not know from where it came—he was hastily commanded to be seized and immediately brought before him.

When the officer had fulfilled this assignment without any delay [Note: The Benedictine Fathers note in the margin here: “Perhaps *parebat* or *petebat* should be read.”], and had presented the seized treasurer to the proconsul, who was seated in the public secretariat, an immense pallor immediately began to spread through the hearts of those who were present and watching. Out of human compassion they grieved for the man and feared for his danger.

Meanwhile, as soon as the enraged official saw the man whom he had been furiously seeking, he rose with a terrible voice and, by a threatening interrogation, threw the treasurer into confusion. But the terrified man’s mind, driven away by fear, could find nothing to say.

And behold, that divine Teacher, looking down from heaven upon the children of men, mingling gentleness with severity, turning threats into kindness, loving while chastising, consoling while loving, a judge in punishments and a father in caresses, faithful everywhere and cruel nowhere—God the Lord himself therefore sent his angel to deliver that man, of whom it is said: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33:8).

For while that treasurer, uncertain and doubtful of his life, stood amid such great fear before the terrifying authority among the torturers, he suddenly felt himself struck from behind. Immediately, lowering his neck slightly and furtively turning his eyes backward, he saw what seemed to be one of the executioners standing near him and suggesting what he should do, telling him whom he ought to ask and saying by way of admonition: “Invoke Saint Stephen.”

When Florentius saw and heard this, he was restored to his own mind and understanding. His spirit, revived after fear had driven it into flight, was strengthened, and he did not cease to pray inwardly to and invoke the glorious Stephen. Then, raising his face slightly toward the judge who was interrogating him, he fixed his eyes upon the judge’s assessor.

When he saw him shining and gleaming with a new face and a new expression, and perceived that he was not the man he knew so well but another, unknown and wondrous counselor of the judge, it was as though the assessor’s familiar face, formerly disfigured in every respect by age, withered and marked by old age, had been replaced by the youthful beauty and radiant brightness of the man who appeared to him.

At this sight Florentius was deeply and profoundly moved. No longer doubtful but steadfast and certain, he believed that the glorious Stephen was present there, that he was directing his attention from a hidden seat, and that he was either sitting as judge in his case or standing beside the judge.

Moreover, so that Florentius might receive fuller and more perfect confidence from this vision and appearance of the Friend of God, he saw the same advocate of his cause and most merciful counselor in his trial actually nodding to him with his hand, signaling with his right hand that he should fear absolutely nothing, smiling at him with a cheerful face, and promising him the fullest hope of salvation.

What more need be said? Little by little the judge’s furious impulses and swelling anger began to be brought down to complete tranquility and gentleness. Thus Florentius no longer feared the judge but recognized him as a father; he did not dread the one whose ax he feared for his head, but hoped for the favor by which his own safety would be secured.

O Lord, Lord, who commandest that thy true praises be sung in the sacred psalms dedicated to thee—not arrogantly, but mercifully; not for thy own vaunting, but for our protection—when it is said: “Thou rulest the power of the sea, but thou stillest the movement of its waves” (Psalm 88:10)!

The authority of the Gospel likewise agrees with this, where, when the turbulent waves and winds were calmed at the command of thy Christ, the astonished disciples said: “Who is this, that he commands the winds and the sea, and they obey him?” (Luke 8:25).

And most true is what Sacred Scripture says elsewhere in its discourse concerning thee: “The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord, like flowing water; he turns it wherever he wills” (Proverbs 21:1).

For, Lord, by the proconsular authority—first enraged and afterward calmed toward the treasurer—you displayed in our own times what you had previously shown in the ancient authority of Scripture through the royal power that first raged and then became gentle toward the holy woman Esther, and what you gave to posterity to read and know in remembrance (Esther 15).

Accordingly, the proconsul ordered the treasurer Florentius, no longer as his official but as a son, with the executioners removed, to come closer to him and to his embrace without any fear. He began to admonish him familiarly with paternal affection; then, granting him pardon and sparing his life, he allowed him to leave the secretariat as a free man.

When this had happened, those who were standing by and trembling with pious concern for the man’s danger—once the treasurer had departed acquitted and unharmed—were filled with joy mingled with astonishment. At one moment they stood bewildered, at another they rejoiced, and at another they said to one another in wonder and inquiry:

“Whence came this sudden change and reversal of circumstances, which stripped the proconsular authority of all its severity and brought it to such humanity and gentleness that it recalled a man from the very threshold of death to life?”

2. Florentius, however, although the danger had passed, returned home still somewhat wounded in spirit by his former fear. At that time he did not tell any of his household what had happened, what he had seen, or what he had escaped [Note: Elsewhere, “who escaped.”].

But that same night, in a dream, he saw the man whom he had seen in the secretariat, dressed in youthful form. From the threshold he heard him address him by name: “What is it, Florentius? Do you recognize me? I am the one who appeared to you in the secretariat and delivered you from death.”

When Florentius recognized him and understood that he was Stephen, [Col. 0854] he wished to worship him; but Stephen placed his hand beneath his chin and lifted him up.

When Florentius awoke, he rose early, desiring to give thanks to God and to fulfill his vows to his Friend. Alone, he set out for the city of Uzalis. But since the roads were unknown to him, the inexperienced traveler prayed silently within himself and implored the guidance of that same glorious Martyr of Christ.

While he was offering this prayer, behold, a presbyter of our Church named Firmus, coming upon Florentius from elsewhere, joined him in the silence of his prayer. When Florentius saw him, he asked where he was traveling.

The presbyter replied that he was going to the city of Uzalis, and he also disclosed that he was a presbyter. Then Florentius, his spirit gladdened, began greatly to rejoice. He could not conceal all his happiness; rather, from the very beginning of what had happened, he related in order to the aforementioned presbyter, now joined to him as his companion on the journey, what divine mercy had accomplished for him through his glorious Friend.

When the journey was completed, Florentius arrived at the city together with the presbyter. He entered the blessed Martyr’s shrine with humble devotion and, prostrate upon the pavement, gave thanks to the almighty Lord Jesus Christ and to his most blessed Friend.

He also entered the monasteries and related all these things to the venerable bishop and to the choir of the servants of God who gathered around him. He likewise stirred us and kindled us most fervently to the praises of God and of the martyr Stephen’s crown, together with him, through abundant thanksgiving.

These are only a few of the many things that our pen was able to investigate, and we have commended them to devout hearts for reading with eagerness rather than weariness.

**BOOK FIVE.**—At the beginning he removes belief in fate, lest there ultimately be people who wish to attribute to fate the strength and growth of the Roman empire, which he showed in the preceding book could not be attributed to false gods. From there, turning to the question of God’s foreknowledge, he proves that human free choice is not removed by it. He then speaks about the ancient morals of the Romans and about the merit of those morals—or, rather, about the judgment of God—by which it happened that the true God himself, whom they did not worship, helped them enlarge their empire. Finally, he teaches what should be regarded as the true happiness of Christian emperors. Ibid.

**BOOK SIX.**—Thus far he has argued against those who think that the gods should be worshiped for the sake of this temporal life; now, however, he turns against those who believe that worship should be offered to them for the sake of eternal life. Augustine is going to refute them in the five following books, and here first shows how contemptible an opinion of the gods Varro himself, the most highly regarded writer on pagan theology, held. According to Varro, he presents three kinds of theology—mythical, natural, and civil—and immediately demonstrates, concerning the mythical and the civil, that these kinds contribute nothing to the happiness of the life to come. 173–174

**BOOK EIGHT.**—He comes to the third kind of theology, which is called natural, and undertakes, with the Platonists—who are easily the leaders among the other philosophers and come closer to the truth of the Christian faith—to examine the question concerning the gods belonging to it: namely, whether worshiping these gods is useful for attaining the blessed life that is to come after death. First he refutes Apuleius and all others who wish worship to be offered to demons as messengers and interpreters between gods and human beings. He shows that the demons themselves, being subject to vices, and having introduced and clearly shown themselves to favor and delight in those things that upright and prudent people reject and condemn—that is, the sacrilegious inventions of poets, theatrical mockeries, and the magic arts’ spells and crimes—cannot in any way reconcile human beings to the good gods. 223–224

Having rejected this distinction, he proves that the office of mediator for human beings’ blessedness belongs not to any demon whatsoever but to Christ alone. 255–256

# BOOK ELEVEN

The second part of the work begins here: it concerns the origin, progress, and appointed ends of the two cities, the earthly and the heavenly. In this first book Augustine demonstrates how the beginnings of these cities preceded one another in the separation of the good and evil angels; on this occasion he treats of the creation of the world, which is described in the sacred writings at the beginning of the Book of Genesis. 315–316

# BOOK TWELVE

Augustine first investigates the angels: whence some have a good will and others an evil one, and what was the cause of the blessedness of the good angels and the misery of the evil angels. Afterwards he treats of the creation of humanity and teaches that the human being was created not from eternity but in time, and by no author other than God. 347–348

# BOOK FIFTEEN

After treating in the four immediately preceding books of the origin of the two cities, the earthly and the heavenly, Augustine adds an equal number of books on their progress. He approaches this subject in such a way as to discuss the principal points of sacred history that pertain to it—first, in this fifteenth book, the events recorded in Genesis from Cain and Abel to the Flood. In this book the ends of the two cities—the earthly and the heavenly—are discussed. The opinions of the philosophers concerning the ends of good and evil are reviewed: those who vainly attempted to establish blessedness for themselves in this life. An account of the divine works that were displayed through the venerable merit of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, and also committed to the knowledge of the faithful by Evodius in the Church of Uzalis, whose episcopate was administered by that most worthy priest; Augustine at that time being established at Hippo as the administrator of the Lord’s station.
